in this paper we introduce a new approach for approximately counting in bounded degree systems with higher - order constraints. our main result is an algorithm to approximately count the number of solutions to a cnf formula @xmath0 with at least @xmath1 variables per clause and degree at most @xmath2 when @xmath1 is logarithmic in @xmath2. this closes an exponential gap between the known upper and lower bounds. moreover our algorithm extends straightforwardly to approximate sampling, which shows that under lovsz local lemma - like conditions it is not only possible to find a satisfying assignment, it is also possible to generate one approximately uniformly at random from the set of all satisfying assignments. our approach is a significant departure from earlier techniques in approximate counting, and is based on a framework to bootstrap an oracle for computing marginal probabilities on individual variables. finally, we give an application of our results to show that it is algorithmically possible to sample from the posterior distribution in an interesting class of graphical models.

we present high angular resolution, near - infrared imaging and spectroscopy of a low - mass companion to the lithium - depleted, double - line spectroscopic binary hbc 425 (st 34) obtained using the near infrared spectrograph (nirspec) and the keck ii adaptive optics system. positioned @xmath0 southeast of the primary pair, the companion, hbc 425c, is @xmath12.4 magnitudes fainter at 2.2 @xmath2 m. moderate - resolution (@xmath3) @xmath4 and @xmath5band spectroscopy reveal hbc 425c to have an m5.5 (@xmath60.5) spectral type. comparisons with pre - main sequence evolutionary models imply a mass of @xmath10.09 m@xmath7 and ages of 810 myr, assuming the nominal distance of taurus - auriga (@xmath1140 pc), or @xmath125 myr if placed at @xmath190 pc. we also present high dispersion, optical spectra of hbc 425 and hbc 425c obtained using the high resolution echelle spectrometer (hires) on keck i. we detect strong @xmath86708 absorption in the spectrum of hbc 425c. using curves of growth for the @xmath86708 doublet, we estimate its abundance level to lie between log @xmath9(li)=1.9 and 3.1 dex. the spectrum of hbc 425 exhibits h & k, @xmath105876, 6678, and strong balmer line emission, consistent with accretion. we place more restrictive upper limits on the surface abundance of lithium and find that hbc 425 retains less than @xmath10.1% of its primordial abundance. the presence of lithium in the photosphere of hbc 425c does not resolve the discrepancy between isochronal and lithium depletion ages for the primary pair. however, if lithium were depleted relative to interstellar abundance levels, even minimally, considerable support would be gained for the more advanced age of this hierarchical triple system.

we consider principal component analysis (pca) in decomposable gaussian graphical models. we exploit the prior information in these models in order to distribute its computation. for this purpose, we reformulate the problem in the sparse inverse covariance (concentration) domain and solve the global eigenvalue problem using a sequence of local eigenvalue problems in each of the cliques of the decomposable graph. we demonstrate the application of our methodology in the context of decentralized anomaly detection in the abilene backbone network. based on the topology of the network, we propose an approximate statistical graphical model and distribute the computation of pca.

predicting the popularity of content is important for both the host and users of social media sites. the challenge of this problem comes from the inequality of the popularity of content. existing methods for popularity prediction are mainly based on the quality of content, the interface of social media site to highlight contents, and the collective behavior of users. however, little attention is paid to the structural characteristics of the networks spanned by early adopters, i.e., the users who view or forward the content in the early stage of content dissemination. in this paper, taking the sina weibo as a case, we empirically study whether structural characteristics can provide clues for the popularity of short messages. we find that the popularity of content is well reflected by the structural diversity of the early adopters. experimental results demonstrate that the prediction accuracy is significantly improved by incorporating the factor of structural diversity into existing methods. = 10000 = 10000

a mathematical model for behavioral changes by pair interactions (i.e. due to direct contact) of individuals is developed. three kinds of pair interactions can be distinguished: imitative processes, avoidance processes, and compromising processes. representative solutions of the model for two different interacting subpopulations are illustrated by computational results. the equations of game theory are shown to result for a special case of imitative processes. moreover, a stochastic version of game theory is formulated. it allows the derivation of equations for the most probable or the expected distribution of behavioral strategies and of (co)variance equations. the knowledge of the (co)variances is necessary for the calculation of the reliability of game theoretical descriptions. the use and application of the introduced equations is illustrated by concrete examples. especially, computational results for the selforganization of social conventions by competition of two equivalent strategies are presented.

features that are indeed present in the observations. depending on the relative values of the rise and decay times of the intrinsic light curve, the spectral / temporal behavior, as seen by an observer, will produce the hard - to - soft evolution and the so called tracking pulses. in our model the observed spectrum is a superposition of many intrinsic spectra arriving from different parts of the fireball shell with varying spectral shifts. therefore, it will be broader than the emitted spectrum and its spectral parameters could have complex relations with the intrinsic ones. furthermore, we show that the softening of the low - energy power - law index, that has been observed in some pulses, can be explained by geometric effects and does not need to be an intrinsic behavior.

we compare the statistical properties of galaxies found in two different models of hierarchical galaxy formation: the semi - analytic model of cole et al. and the smoothed particle hydrodynamics (sph) simulations of pearce et al. these two techniques model gas processes very differently: by approximate, analytic methods in the case of the semi - the reliability of the approximations commonly adopted in the calculation of static optical (hyper)polarizabilities is tested against exact results obtained for an interesting toy - model. the model accounts for the principal features of typical nonlinear organic materials with mobile electrons strongly coupled to molecular vibrations. the approximations introduced in sum over states and finite field schemes are analyzed in detail. both the born - oppenheimer and the clamped nucleus approximations turn out to be safe for molecules, whereas for donor - acceptor charge transfer complexes deviations from adiabaticity are expected. in the regime of low vibrational frequency, static susceptibilities are strongly dominated by the successive derivatives of the potential energy and large vibrational contributions to hyperpolarizabilities are found. in this regime anharmonic corrections to hyperpolarizabilities are very large, and the harmonic approximation, exact for the linear polarizability, turns out totally inadequate for nonlinear responses. with increasing phonon frequency the role of vibrations smoothly decreases, until, in the antiadiabatic (infinite vibrational frequency) regime, vibrations do not contribute anymore to static susceptibilities, and the purely electronic responses are regained.

we consider a model of nomadic agents exploring and competing for time - varying location - specific resources, arising in crowdsourced transportation services, online communities, and in traditional location - based economic activity. this model comprises a group of agents, and a set of locations each endowed with a dynamic stochastic resource process. each agent derives a periodic reward determined by the overall resource level at her location, and the number of other agents there. each agent is strategic and free to move between locations, and at each time decides whether to stay at the same node or switch to another one. we study the equilibrium behavior of the agents as a function of dynamics of the stochastic resource process and the nature of the externality each agent imposes on others at the same location. in the asymptotic limit with the number of agents and locations increasing proportionally, we show that an equilibrium exists and has a threshold structure, where each agent decides to switch to a different location based only on their current location s resource level and the number of other agents at that location. this result provides insight into how system structure affects the agents collective ability to explore their domain to find and effectively utilize resource - rich areas. it also allows assessing the impact of changing the reward structure through penalties or subsidies.

swarming peer - to - peer systems play an increasingly instrumental role in internet content distribution. it is therefore important to better understand how these systems behave in practice. recent research efforts have looked at various protocol parameters and have measured how they affect system performance and robustness. however, the importance of the strategy based on which peers establish connections has been largely overlooked. this work utilizes extensive simulations to examine the default overlay construction strategy in bittorrent systems. based on the results, we identify a critical parameter, the maximum allowable number of outgoing connections at each peer, and evaluate its impact on the robustness of the generated overlay. we find that there is no single optimal value for this parameter using the default strategy. we then propose an alternative strategy that allows certain new peer connection requests to replace existing connections. further experiments with the new strategy demonstrate that it outperforms the default one for all considered metrics by creating an overlay more robust to churn. additionally, our proposed strategy exhibits optimal behavior for a well - defined value of the maximum number of outgoing connections, thereby removing the need to set this parameter in an ad - hoc manner. bittorrent, overlay construction, preemption, robustness, outgoing connections

observations of stars in the the solar vicinity show a clear tendency for old stars to have larger velocity dispersions. this relation is called the age - velocity dispersion relation (avr) and it is believed to provide insight into the heating history of the milky way galaxy. here, in order to investigate the origin of the avr, we performed smoothed particle hydrodynamic simulations of the self - gravitating multiphase gas disks in the static disk - halo potentials. star formation from cold and dense gas is taken into account, and we analyze the evolution of these star particles. we find that exponents of simulated avr and the ratio of the radial to vertical velocity dispersion are close to the observed values. we also find that the simulated avr is not a simple consequence of dynamical heating. the evolution tracks of stars with different epochs evolve gradually in the age - velocity dispersion plane as a result of: (1) the decrease in velocity dispersion in star forming regions, and (2) the decrease in the number of cold / dense / gas as scattering sources. these results suggest that the avr involves not only the heating history of a stellar disk, but also the historical evolution of the ism in a galaxy.

an investigation on stochastic deflection of high - energy negatively charged particles in a bent crystal was carried out. on the basis of analytical calculation and numerical simulation it was shown that it exists a maximum angle at which most of the beam is deflected. the existence of a maximum, which is taken in the correspondence of the _ optimal radius of curvature _, is a novelty with respect to the case of positively charged particles, for which the deflection angle can be freely increased by increasing the crystal length. this difference has to be ascribed to the stronger contribution of incoherent scattering affecting the dynamics of negative particles that move closer to atomic nuclei and electrons. we therefore identified the ideal parameters for the exploitation of axial confinement for negatively charged particle beam manipulation in future high - energy accelerators, e.g., ilc or muon colliders.

interacting dark matter. relativistic streaming between outgoing baryons and ingoing dark matter leads to mass inflation near the inner horizon. when enough dark matter has been accreted that the center of mass frame near the inner horizon is ingoing, then mass inflation ceases and the fluid collapses to a central singularity. a null singularity does not form on the cauchy horizon. although the simultaneous presence of ingoing and outgoing fluids near the inner horizon is essential to mass inflation, reducing one or other of the ingoing dark matter or outgoing baryonic streams to a trace relative to the other stream makes mass inflation more extreme, not the other way round as one might naively have expected. consequently, if the dark matter has a finite cross - section for being absorbed into the baryonic fluid, then the reduction of the amount of ingoing dark matter merely makes inflation more extreme, the interior mass exponentiating more rapidly and to a larger value before mass inflation ceases. however, if the dark matter absorption cross - section is effectively infinite at high collision energy, so that the ingoing dark matter stream disappears completely, then the outgoing baryonic fluid can drop through the cauchy horizon. in all cases, as the baryons and the dark matter voyage to their diverse fates inside the black hole, they only ever see a finite amount of time pass by in the outside universe. thus the solutions do not depend on what happens in the infinite past or future. we discuss in some detail the physical mechanism that drives mass inflation. although the gravitational force is inward, inward means opposite direction for ingoing and outgoing fluids near the inner horizon. mass inflation is driven by a feedback loop in which the general relativistic contribution to the gravitational force sourced by the radial pressure accelerates the ingoing and outgoing fluids through each other, which increases the radial pressure, which increases the gravitational force. = 3000

nanogranular metal composites, consisting of immiscible metallic and insulating phases deposited on a substrate, are characterized by two distinct electronic transport regimes depending on the relative amount of the metallic phase. at sufficiently large metallic loadings, granular metals behave as percolating systems with a well - defined critical concentration above which macroscopic clusters of physically connected conductive particles span the entire sample. below the critical loading, granular metal films are in the dielectric regime, where current can flow throughout the composite only via hopping or tunneling processes between isolated nanosized particles or clusters. in this case transport is intrinsically non - percolative in the sense that no critical concentration can be identified for the onset of transport. it is shown here that, although being very different in nature, these two regimes can be described by treating percolation and hopping on equal footing. by considering general features of the microstructure and of the electrical connectedness, the concentration dependence of the dc conductivity of several nanogranular metal films is reproduced to high accuracy within an effective medium approach. in particular, fits to published experimental data enable us to extract the values of microscopic parameters that govern the percolation and tunneling regimes, explaining thus the transport properties observed in nanogranular metal films.

dynamical patterns in complex networks of coupled oscillators are both of theoretical and practical interest, yet to fully reveal and understand the interplay between pattern emergence and network structure remains to be an outstanding problem. a fundamental issue is the effect of network structure on the stability of the patterns. we address this issue by using the setting where random links are systematically added to a regular lattice and focusing on the dynamical evolution of spiral wave patterns. as the network structure deviates more from the regular topology (so that it becomes increasingly more complex), the original stable spiral wave pattern can disappear and a different type of pattern can emerge. our main findings are the following. (1) short - distance links added to a small region containing the spiral tip can have a more significant effect on the wave pattern than long - distance connections. (2) as more random links are introduced into the network, distinct pattern transitions can occur, which include the transition of spiral wave to global synchronization, to a chimera - like state, and then to a pinned spiral wave. (3) around the transitions the network dynamics is highly sensitive to small variations in the network structure in the sense that the addition of even a single link can change the pattern from one type to another. these findings provide insights into the pattern dynamics in complex networks, a problem that is relevant to many physical, chemical, and biological systems.

the successful construction and operation of highly sensitive gravitational - wave detectors is an achievement to be proud of, but the detection of actual signals is still around the corner. even so, null results from recent searches have told us some interesting things about the objects that live in our universe, so it can be argued that the era of gravitational - wave astronomy has already begun. in this article I review several of these results and discuss what we have learned from them. I then look into the not - so - distant future and predict some ways in which the detection of gravitational - wave signals will shape our knowledge of astrophysics and transform the field.

the internet of things (iot) is experiencing fast adoption in the society, from industrial to home applications. the number of deployed sensors and connected devices to the internet is changing our perspective and the way we understand the world. the development and generation of iot applications is just starting and they will modify our physical and virtual lives, from how we control remotely appliances at home to how we deal with insurance companies in order to start insurance schemes via smart cards. this massive deployment of iot devices represents a tremendous economic impact and at the same time offers multiple opportunities. however, the potential of iot is underexploited and day by day this gap between devices and useful applications is getting bigger. additionally, the physical and cyber worlds are largely disconnected, requiring a lot of manual efforts to integrate, find, and use information in a meaningful way. to build a connection between the physical and the virtual, we need a knowledge framework that allow bilateral understandings, devices producing data, information systems managing the data and applications transforming information into meaningful knowledge. the first column in this series in the previous issue of this magazine titled "internet of things to smart iot through semantic, cognitive, and perceptual computing," reviews iot growth and potential that have energized research and technology development, centered on aspects of artificial intelligence to build future intelligent system. this column steps back and demonstrates the benefits of using semantic web technologies to get meaningful knowledge from sensor data to design smart systems.

as language data and associated technologies proliferate and as the language resources community rapidly expands, it has become difficult to locate and reuse existing resources. are there any lexical resources for such - and - such a language? what tool can work with transcripts in this particular format? what is a good format to use for linguistic data of this type? questions like these dominate many mailing lists, since web search engines are an unreliable way to find language resources. this paper describes a new digital infrastructure for language resource discovery, based on the open archives initiative, and called olac the open language archives community. the olac metadata set and the associated controlled vocabularies facilitate consistent description and focussed searching. we report progress on the metadata set and controlled vocabularies, describing current issues and soliciting input from the language resources community.

we review some recent developments in the statistical mechanics of isolated quantum systems. we provide a brief introduction to quantum thermalization, paying particular attention to the ` eigenstate thermalization hypothesis' (eth), and the resulting ` single - eigenstate statistical mechanics'. we then focus on a class of systems which fail to quantum thermalize and whose eigenstates violate the eth: these are the many - body anderson localized systems; their long - time properties are not captured by the conventional ensembles of quantum statistical mechanics. these systems can locally remember forever information about their local initial conditions, and are thus of interest for possibilities of storing quantum information. we discuss key features of many - body localization (mbl), and review a phenomenology of the mbl phase. single - eigenstate statistical mechanics within the mbl phase reveals dynamically - stable ordered phases, and phase transitions among them, that are invisible to equilibrium statistical mechanics and can occur at high energy and low spatial dimensionality where equilibrium ordering is forbidden. key words: closed systems, entanglement, eigenstate, non - equilibrium, glass.

using methods from algebraic graph theory and convex optimization, we study the relationship between local structural features of a network and spectral properties of its laplacian matrix. in particular, we derive expressions for the so - called spectral moments of the laplacian matrix of a network in terms of a collection of local structural measurements. furthermore, we propose a series of semidefinite programs to compute bounds on the spectral radius and the spectral gap of the laplacian matrix from a truncated sequence of laplacian spectral moments. our analysis shows that the laplacian spectral moments and spectral radius are strongly constrained by local structural features of the network. on the other hand, we illustrate how local structural features are usually not enough to estimate the laplacian spectral gap.

plasma originates from mass lost by the planet s rings and moons. it is tightly coupled to the magnetic field and its motion can be ascribed to the large scale interchange of flux tubes. heavily loaded tubes drift outward and are replaced by lightly loaded ones which drift inward. _ this process of rotationally driven convection is responsible for breaking the axisymmetry of saturn s external magnetic field. _ the convection pattern rotates rigidly with the angular velocity of the plasma at its source. its rotation provides the clock that controls the periods of both the skr bursts and the nonaxisymmetric magnetic perturbations. we distinguish two types of currents. those that flow in the azimuthal direction in both the ionosphere and the plasma disk provide a radial force that enables latitudinal direction in the ionosphere and the radial direction in the plasma disk. these act to transfer angular momentum from the planet s spin to the outflowing plasma. they slow down the rotation rate of the ionosphere below that of the underlying atmosphere and are the reason the clock referred to above runs slow. moreover, these currents are the source of nonaxisymmetric magnetic simulations are used to examine the microscopic origins of strain hardening in polymer glasses. while stress - strain curves for a wide range of temperature can be fit to the functional form predicted by entropic network models, many other results are fundamentally inconsistent with the physical picture underlying these models. stresses are too large to be entropic and have the wrong trend with temperature. the most dramatic hardening at large strains reflects increases in energy as chains are pulled taut between entanglements rather than a change in entropy. a weak entropic stress is only observed in shape recovery of deformed samples when heated above the glass transition. while short chains do not form an entangled network, they exhibit partial shape recovery, orientation, and strain hardening. stresses for all chain lengths collapse when plotted against a microscopic measure of chain stretching rather than the macroscopic stretch. the thermal contribution to the stress is directly proportional to the rate of plasticity as measured by breaking and reforming of interchain bonds. these observations suggest that the correct microscopic theory of strain hardening should be based on glassy state physics rather than rubber elasticity.

large scale motion of cytoplasm called cytoplasmic streaming occurs in some large eukaryotic cells to stir the cell s constituents. in _ drosophila _ oocytes, microtubules have been observed to undergo undulating motion, curving to form travelling waves during cytoplasmic streaming. here we show that this wave - like motion can be understood physically as due to the hydrodynamic drag of streaming impellers attached to kinesin motors moving toward the plus - ends of microtubules whose minus ends are anchored to the cell cortex. the tangential forces applied to such microtubules by kinesin give rise to bending and leads to chiral symmetry breaking causing the microtubules to propagate long travelling waves. the waves are reminiscent of those seen in flagellar motion but of a much longer time scale and by a different physical mechanism. we show how kinesin movement can produce a bulk flow of cytoplasm surrounding a microtubule with the range of flow greatly enhanced by the effect of hydrodynamic coupling between impellers. that is, a relatively small number of motors can move a large amount of fluid. the chaotic nature of the fluid motion of cytoplasm caused by kinesin movement along constantly changing microtubule trajectories is important as it greatly enhances the efficiency of mixing. existing data on _ in vitro _ microtubule gliding assays also show this chiral instability in two dimensions and an analysis of this gives quantitative estimates for the forces exerted by motors and the drag coefficient.

quantum measurement theory has fallen under the resticting influence of the attempt to explain the fundamental axioms of quantum theory in terms of the theory itself. this has not only led to confusion but has also restricted our attention to a limited class of measurements. this paper outlines some of the novel types of measurements which fall outside the usual textbook description. # 1#2 figure # 1 _ # 2 _ the problem of quantum measurement has been with us since the foundations of the the theory were laid in the mid 1920 s. it has generated much discussion, with little resolution of the questions raised. I will argue in this talk that this situation has arisen in part because of the confusion brought about by giving two very different concepts the same name, with the expected result that the valid questions related to the two concepts become entangled. it furthermore has led to a restriction on the types of measurements considered within the theory. in this talk I am not going to propose any radical or even very new interpretations of the theory of quantum mechanics. I am rather going to engage in an ancient philosophical past time, name to propose that we use distinct terms for distinct concepts. I am then going to review some of the novel insights which have been obtained recently (especially by the group around aharonov) regarding some novel types of measurement.

bilayer lipid membranes (blms) are an essential component of all biological systems, forming a functional barrier for cells and organelles from the surrounding environment. the lipid molecules that form membranes contain both permanent and induced dipoles, and an electric field can induce the formation of pores when the transverse field is sufficiently strong (electroporation). here, a phenomenological free energy is constructed to model the response of a blm to a transverse static electric field. the model contains a continuum description of the membrane dipoles and a coupling between the headgroup dipoles and the membrane tilt. the membrane is found to become unstable through buckling modes, which are weakly coupled to thickness fluctuations in the membrane. the thickness fluctuations, along with the increase in interfacial area produced by membrane buckling, increase the probability of localised membrane breakdown, which may lead to pore formation. the instability is found to depend strongly on the strength of the coupling between the dipolar headgroups and the membrane tilt as well as the degree of dipolar ordering in the membrane.

sampled: We present the results of a large-scale molecular line survey of the Galactic Center's Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), focusing on NH3 inversion transitions observed with the Tsukuba 32-meter radio telescope. Our survey covered 2655 on-source positions across the main region of the CMZ, with simultaneous observations of multiple NH3 transitions enabling precise determination of line intensity ratios with minimal systematic uncertainties. The three lowest NH3 transitions were successfully detected at signal-to-noise ratios exceeding 3σ at 2323 positions (93% of all observed locations), with individual transitions showing varying detection rates of 54%, 43%, and 51% for progressively higher energy levels. Analysis of Boltzmann plots reveals a two-component temperature structure consisting of cold molecular gas at approximately 15-20 K and warm gas at 30-40 K. The measured line intensity ratios averaged 0.71, 0.45, 0.65, and 0.17 for the respective transition pairs, displaying significant spatial variations across the surveyed region. These ratio variations indicate diverse rotational temperatures throughout the CMZ, which we interpret as resulting from different mixing fractions of the cold and warm gas components. Our comprehensive dataset provides crucial constraints on the physical conditions and temperature structure of molecular gas in the Galactic Center environment.

Measurements of the Milky Way's circular rotation speed at the solar radius have yielded conflicting results, with traditional emission-based methods estimating 220 km/s while recent VLBI parallax and proper motion data from the Bessel and VERA surveys suggest a higher value of approximately 240 km/s. When this curvature is properly accounted for, the systematic bias in velocity estimates from emission data that assumed a flat rotation curve is revealed and corrected. Our analysis reconciles the discrepancy between the two measurement techniques and supports the higher rotation speed of ~240 km/s at the solar radius.

We develop the Coulomb-gas formalism for minimal models on the half-plane by deriving screening prescriptions through perturbative expansion of Liouville theory with imaginary coupling and Neumann boundary conditions on the bosonic field. These insertions enable systematic construction of correlation functions for arbitrary boundary conditions. The formalism provides an explicit realization of boundary conformal field theory in the Coulomb-gas picture, with applications to critical statistical systems such as the Ising model on domains with boundaries.

The density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method has proven highly successful for calculating ground state properties of one-dimensional strongly correlated quantum systems with remarkable accuracy. However, extending DMRG to compute dynamical properties presents significant challenges. We present and compare two complementary approaches for calculating dynamical correlation functions within the DMRG framework. The first method optimizes the DMRG basis to represent Lanczos vectors, which are subsequently used to evaluate spectral functions. This Lanczos vector approach offers computational efficiency and straightforward implementation, though accuracy deteriorates at higher frequencies. The second method involves optimizing the basis for correction vectors at specific target frequencies, enabling highly accurate calculations of dynamical correlations at these chosen frequencies. By computing correction vectors at multiple frequencies and interpolating between them, complete spectral functions can be reconstructed with controlled accuracy. For systems with open boundary conditions, we demonstrate techniques for constructing momentum-resolved operators using appropriately designed filter functions, thereby enabling the calculation of momentum-dependent dynamical properties despite the absence of translational symmetry.

We present results from a comprehensive spectroscopic and photometric investigation of NSVS06507557, a low-mass eclipsing binary system with V=13.4 mag and an orbital period of 0.515 days. The system is located at a distance of 111±9 pc. Comparison with theoretical models shows interesting evolutionary characteristics. While the primary component's radius is consistent with zero-age main-sequence (ZAMS) predictions, the secondary component appears to be substantially inflated, exhibiting a radius approximately 35% larger than expected for a ZAMS star of equivalent mass. This radius inflation is commonly observed in young, active low-mass stars. Several indicators point to the pre-main-sequence nature of this system. Our spectroscopic and photometric results demonstrate good agreement with theoretical predictions for pre-main-sequence stars at this evolutionary stage, making NSVS06507557 a valuable benchmark for testing stellar evolution models in the low-mass regime.

The proliferation of big data offers unprecedented opportunities for understanding and predicting social and economic phenomena, yet the heterogeneous nature of information—varying in importance, relevance, and surprise value—poses significant challenges for predictive analytics. We demonstrate that aggregating web user behavior can effectively address this limitation in forecasting financial market dynamics. Analyzing 100 highly capitalized US stocks during 2012-2013, we find that sentiment analysis of news articles alone, or user browsing activity in isolation, yields negligible predictive power for price movements. However, constructing a weighted news signal that combines sentiment analysis with user engagement—specifically, computing click-weighted average sentiment of news articles—substantially improves forecasting accuracy. Our Granger causality analysis reveals that this composite signal predicts hourly price returns for approximately 50% of analyzed companies at both intra-day and daily frequencies. This enhancement stems from a "wisdom-of-the-crowd" mechanism, wherein collective user behavior effectively filters and prioritizes information by implicitly identifying relevant and surprising news content. Users' clicking patterns serve as a distributed curation system that assigns appropriate weights to news items based on their actual market significance rather than algorithmic sentiment scores alone. Our findings suggest that integrating behavioral data with content analysis can substantially improve prediction in complex systems where information quality varies dramatically, offering a practical framework for enhanced financial forecasting and broader applications in computational social science.

Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of this three-eigenfrequency regime to next-generation detectors, specifically the Einstein Telescope, showing potential for significant sensitivity improvements in the critical detection band for astrophysical sources.

We present comprehensive first-principles calculations of the residual resistivity ρ0 in Fe1−xCrx binary alloys that successfully reproduce and explain the experimentally observed anomalous concentration dependence deviating from Nordheim's rule. Through systematic ab initio calculations, we demonstrate that this unusual plateau feature originates from the spin-dependent electronic structure of these alloys near the Fermi energy. Our analysis of the Bloch spectral function reveals that minority spin electrons dominate the electrical conductivity in iron-rich Fe-Cr alloys, and crucially, their contribution remains essentially constant with increasing Cr concentration in the plateau region. This insensitivity of the minority spin channel to compositional changes explains the observed resistivity behavior. We further investigate the role of local atomic arrangements using the nonlocal coherent-potential approximation (nl-CPA), finding that short-range ordering and clustering effects have minimal impact on the resistivity anomaly, confirming that the phenomenon is primarily driven by the underlying electronic structure rather than local chemical order. Based on our physical understanding, we predict that iron-rich Fe1−xVx alloys should exhibit similar resistivity behavior, a prediction we verify through explicit calculations. Both Fe-Cr and Fe-V systems belong to the same branch of the Slater-Pauling curve, and we establish a fundamental connection between the resistivity plateau and the linear variation of average magnetic moment characteristic of these materials. The minority spin electronic states responsible for the constant conductivity contribution are the same states that determine the magnetic moment variation. We therefore postulate that this anomalous resistivity behavior represents a general characteristic of alloy systems on this Slater-Pauling branch, providing a unified understanding of both transport and magnetic properties in these technologically important materials.

We study random walks in uniformly elliptic, i.i.d. random environments (RWRE) under perturbation and derive the speed derivative with respect to perturbation parameters. These results provide a generalized Einstein relation for RWRE, connecting the speed response to environmental perturbations. The proof employs a modified Lebowitz-Rost argument combined with a novel regeneration structure specifically designed for perturbed balanced environments. This framework allows us to rigorously analyze the derivative of the speed functional, extending classical results to the random environment setting and providing new tools for studying transport properties in disordered media.

We investigate the expansion dynamics of bosonic Mott insulators in optical lattices following the sudden removal of a confining potential using the Gutzwiller mean-field approximation. Two distinct experimental configurations are analyzed. First, we examine one-dimensional expansion, demonstrating the formation of two well-defined momentum condensates—a phenomenon with potential applications for atom laser generation in optical lattices. Second, we analyze three-dimensional expansion, where mean-field theory predicts the emergence of a single condensate whose bosonic constituents occupy multiple nonzero momentum modes. For both scenarios, we provide analytical insights by exploiting the exact dispersion relation in the hard-core boson limit. Our results reveal the rich momentum-space structure arising from the interplay between lattice geometry, interaction effects, and expansion dynamics, offering theoretical guidance for experimental realizations of controlled matter-wave sources and the study of quantum transport in periodic potentials.

We present a novel temperature correction procedure for Monte Carlo radiative transfer calculations in dusty astrophysical environments. Traditional methods for determining equilibrium dust temperatures require iterative calculations that can be computationally expensive and suffer from convergence problems, particularly when using Λ-iteration schemes. Our approach exploits the fundamental property of Monte Carlo simulations that individual photon packets are tracked throughout their propagation history. The method operates by monitoring where photon energy is deposited when packets are absorbed within the computational grid. Upon absorption, a packet heats its host cell, and to maintain radiative equilibrium, the packet is immediately re-emitted. The key innovation is that the re-emission frequency is strategically selected to correct the temperature of the cell's emission spectrum toward its equilibrium value. The re-emitted packet continues propagating—undergoing further scattering, absorption, and re-emission events—until it ultimately escapes the system. As the simulation progresses, the dust temperature distribution naturally evolves toward equilibrium, and the emergent spectral energy distribution (SED) simultaneously relaxes to its steady-state form without requiring iteration between separate radiative transfer and temperature calculation steps. This eliminates the computational overhead typically associated with iterative temperature corrections. The computational cost is essentially equivalent to that of a pure scattering calculation with predetermined temperatures. Our method offers several significant advantages: (1) exact energy conservation, as all injected photons eventually escape; (2) long-range energy transport, since packets are never destroyed but continuously scattered until escape; (3) elimination of convergence difficulties inherent to Λ-iteration methods; and (4) simultaneous calculation of equilibrium temperatures and emergent SEDs. We validate the procedure against established benchmark problems and demonstrate its application to two-dimensional axisymmetric dust distributions, confirming its accuracy and computational efficiency for realistic astrophysical geometries.

We investigate the evolution of higher-order nonclassicality and entanglement criteria in atmospheric channels characterized by fluctuating losses. By deriving input-output relations for moment matrices, we analyze how such channels affect quantum correlation measures. This work extends our previous analysis of Gaussian entanglement [Phys. Rev. A **94**, 010302(R) (2016)] by examining both second-order and higher-order scenarios, enabling comprehensive characterization of nonclassicality and entanglement in non-Gaussian multimode radiation fields subject to fluctuating attenuation. Through detailed analysis of various criteria and quantum states, we uncover unexpected phenomena, including the dependence of squeezing transfer on coherent displacement amplitudes. Significantly, we demonstrate that certain non-Gaussian entangled states exhibit superior robustness against atmospheric losses compared to their Gaussian counterparts. We further propose an experimental detection scheme for measuring the relevant moments after atmospheric propagation. These findings provide valuable insights for developing and optimizing non-Gaussian quantum light sources in free-space quantum communication applications, where atmospheric turbulence and losses present fundamental challenges to preserving quantum correlations over extended distances.

We introduce the linear dependence graph associated with a finite dimensional vector space over a finite field, where vertices represent vectors and edges connect linearly dependent pairs. We investigate fundamental graph-theoretic properties including connectedness, completeness, planarity, clique number, and chromatic number. A key result establishes that two vector spaces are isomorphic if and only if their corresponding linear dependence graphs are isomorphic, providing a graph-theoretic characterization of vector space isomorphism. We determine the adjacency spectrum, Laplacian spectrum, and distance spectrum of these graphs, revealing connections between algebraic properties of vector spaces and spectral properties of their associated graphs. This work bridges linear algebra and graph theory, offering new perspectives on vector space structure through combinatorial methods and demonstrating how spectral graph theory can illuminate properties of finite dimensional vector spaces over finite fields.

We examine the predictions for both spin-dependent and spin-independent direct detection rates in a variety of new particle physics models with dark matter candidates. These include the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) with both neutralino and sneutrino dark matter, extensions of the MSSM with an additional singlet, models with universal extra dimensions (UED), and little Higgs models with T-parity. We demonstrate that a determination of both spin-independent and spin-dependent scattering amplitudes on protons and neutrons can in principle discriminate between different dark matter candidates, though some ambiguities remain. We emphasize the critical importance of performing measurements with different spin-dependent sensitive detector materials and the necessity for significant improvements in detector sensitivities to achieve this discrimination. Scenarios where the exchange of new colored particles contributes significantly to elastic scattering cross sections are often the most difficult to identify unambiguously. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) should provide crucial indications as to whether such scenarios are relevant for direct detection experiments. Our analysis highlights the complementarity between direct detection and collider searches in identifying the nature of dark matter.

Humans naturally perceive relationships between objects based on visual appearance, categorizing them as either alternatives (e.g., two pairs of jeans) or complements (e.g., jeans and a matching shirt). These perceptions influence everyday decisions, from purchasing clothing to social interactions. This work presents a computational model to capture human understanding of visual object relationships based on appearance. Rather than relying on detailed manual annotations, we leverage large-scale data and develop a scalable approach to uncover implicit visual relationships. We formulate this as a network inference problem on graphs of related images, introducing a comprehensive dataset for training and evaluation. Our framework learns to distinguish between complementary and alternative relationships among visual items without explicit supervision. The resulting system can predict which clothing items and accessories coordinate well together, enabling applications in fashion recommendation, visual compatibility assessment, and understanding human aesthetic preferences. By modeling these relationships at scale, we demonstrate that visual compatibility patterns can be automatically discovered from data, providing insights into how humans perceive visual harmony and make aesthetic judgments based on object appearance.

We present high spatial resolution ultraviolet and optical spectroscopy of nuclear structures in four "warm" ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs), obtained using the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) aboard the Hubble Space Telescope. Our observations reveal the presence of active galactic nuclei (AGN) in at least three, and likely all four targets, each hosted within compact, optically luminous "knots." In three cases, these knots were previously identified as potential AGN nuclei through multiband optical imaging studies. Additionally, three galaxies harbor vigorous starburst activity in one or more knots, indicating that these optically luminous structures represent the primary sites of both dust-enshrouded starburst and AGN activity responsible for powering the infrared emission characteristic of ULIRGs. The four AGN exhibit remarkably diverse spectroscopic properties. Two are classical narrow-line AGN, one displays both broad and narrow emission lines with evidence for multiple lines of sight sampling regions from the narrow-line region through to the broad-line region, and one is plausibly identified as an FeLoBAL (iron low-ionization broad absorption line) AGN. The probable detection of an FeLoBAL AGN—a class extremely rare among the general quasar population—lends support to evolutionary models suggesting that LoBAL AGN may represent youthful systems heavily obscured by gas and dust, rather than simply representing orientation effects. The three starbursts for which detailed age constraints are obtainable show relatively uniform properties. All three are young systems: two have ages of approximately 5 Myr, while the third has an age of ~20 Myr. This age distribution suggests that ULIRGs experience multiple episodes of intense star formation during their evolution. None of the starbursts exhibit evidence for initial mass functions with slopes steeper than approximately 3.3. Metallicity measurements indicate that all knots have abundances of at least 1.5 times solar. Notably, one starburst knot displays properties consistent with it representing the forming core of an elliptical galaxy, supporting merger-driven evolutionary scenarios. Our results demonstrate that detailed spatially-resolved studies of ULIRG knots provide crucial insights into the most extreme starburst and AGN phenomena in both the local and high-redshift universe.

We investigate the dynamics of tilted accretion discs around spinning black holes subject to Lense-Thirring precession in the context of active galactic nuclei and X-ray binaries. Through detailed analysis, we demonstrate that differential precession induced by frame-dragging causes initially continuous tilted discs to fragment into multiple distinct orbital planes with only weak connections between them. This "disc breaking" phenomenon is particularly significant when the initial misalignment exceeds @xmath0, which occurs in approximately @xmath1% of randomly oriented accretion events. In such configurations, the differential precession of disc fragments naturally produces regions of partially counter-rotating gas flows. The interaction between these counter-rotating streams leads to efficient angular momentum cancellation, driving rapid infall as material attempts to re-circularize at progressively smaller radii. When disc breaking occurs near the black hole, it facilitates direct dynamical accretion, while breaking at larger radii channels gas to scales where conventional accretion mechanisms can proceed efficiently. Even for smaller misalignment angles, disc breaking may manifest through observable signatures such as quasi-periodic oscillations. These effects are suppressed only when the black hole spin is negligibly small or nearly perfectly aligned with the disc. Our results generalize to any differentially precessing accretion disc, including external discs surrounding misaligned binary black holes.

We establish Lagrangian structures for a class of three-dimensionally consistent quad-equation systems on Z3, focusing on cases where constituent equations exhibit mixed degeneracy patterns in their biquadratic forms. We prove that these systems admit variational formulations and demonstrate flip-invariance of the corresponding action functionals, extending the Lagrangian formalism beyond previously studied symmetric cases. Our results provide a variational framework for analyzing the novel asymmetric integrable systems recently discovered, confirming their fundamental geometric and algebraic properties within discrete integrable systems theory.

We present a comprehensive mode coupling theory (MCT) framework for studying the relaxation dynamics and glass transition in systems of interacting self-propelled particles. Our approach incorporates both self-propulsion forces, modeled as Ornstein-Uhlenbeck colored noise with characteristic persistence time, and thermal fluctuations, providing a unified description of active matter dynamics in the dense regime. Importantly, in the limit @xmath11, the critical temperature recovers the expected value for passive Brownian systems, demonstrating proper limiting behavior. The framework naturally reduces to conventional MCT for passive systems and provides a versatile platform for extensions to more complex scenarios, including active-passive mixtures and systems with anisotropic interactions, opening new avenues for understanding nonequilibrium glassy phenomena in active matter.

We investigate the third-order nonlinear optical properties of a one-dimensional Mott insulator using an extended Hubbard-Holstein model that incorporates electron-phonon coupling. Employing the dynamical density-matrix renormalization group method, we calculate the third harmonic generation (THG) spectrum and analyze the interplay between electronic correlations and lattice degrees of freedom. Our results demonstrate that electron-phonon interactions enhance THG intensity when the on-site Coulomb repulsion is comparable to the bandwidth; however, this enhancement remains modest for realistic parameters representative of prototypical Mott insulators such as Sr2CuO3. To elucidate the mechanism of phonon-assisted processes, we complement our analysis by computing the linear optical susceptibility in the doped Hubbard-Holstein model, revealing distinct spectral features compared to the half-filled case. These findings provide insights into the role of electron-phonon interactions in the nonlinear optical properties of strongly correlated systems and suggest THG spectroscopy as a sensitive probe of spin dynamics in Mott insulators.

We present a Floquet-based theoretical framework for analyzing time-periodic quantum Langevin equations in steady state. Our approach demonstrates that two-time correlation functions of system operators admit a Fourier series expansion, and we establish a generalized Wiener-Khinchin theorem connecting the Fourier transform of the zeroth component to observable spectra. The method is applied to bichromatically driven cavity optomechanical systems, which have recently enabled the preparation of quantum-squeezed mechanical states. This framework offers an intuitive and systematic procedure for computing power spectral densities of periodically driven quantum systems described by Langevin equations, with the flexibility to work in arbitrary rotating reference frames. Our results facilitate the analysis of complex time-dependent quantum noise in periodically modulated open quantum systems.

This paper addresses the important challenge of solving linearly constrained separable convex programs with multiple blocks of variables, a problem structure that arises frequently in machine learning and related fields. While the classical Alternating Direction Method (ADM) and its Linearized variant (LADM) are well-established for two-block problems, their direct extension to multi-block cases is non-trivial and lacks theoretical guarantees. We propose LADMPSAP (Linearized ADM with Parallel Splitting and Adaptive Penalty), a novel algorithmic framework specifically designed for efficiently solving multi-block separable convex programs. Our method incorporates parallel splitting strategies and adaptive penalty parameter selection, enabling practical scalability to problems with arbitrary numbers of variable blocks. Our theoretical contributions are substantial and improve upon existing ADM-based methods. Under the assumption of bounded subgradients for component objective functions, we establish stronger convergence guarantees, notably: (1) allowing the penalty parameter to be unbounded, removing restrictive upper bound requirements, and (2) deriving both sufficient and necessary conditions for global convergence, providing a complete characterization of convergence behavior. Furthermore, we introduce a simple yet effective optimality measure and prove convergence rates in an ergodic sense, quantifying the algorithm's performance. For problems involving additional convex set constraints, we develop a practical variant with refined parameter estimation strategies to accelerate convergence. We also extend LADMPSAP to handle more complex objective functions through selective linearization techniques. LADMPSAP is particularly well-suited for sparse representation and low-rank recovery applications, as its subproblems admit closed-form solutions while preserving the sparsity and low-rank structure throughout iterations. The algorithm's inherent parallelizability makes it ideal for distributed computing environments. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate LADMPSAP's superior performance in both computational speed and numerical accuracy compared to existing methods, validating its practical utility for large-scale optimization problems.

We investigate the phase transition phenomena in random constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) by analyzing the geometric structure of their solution spaces. For problems like random k-SAT and random graph coloring, a significant gap exists between the constraint density threshold where solutions provably exist and the density at which polynomial-time algorithms successfully find solutions. We prove that well before the satisfiability threshold, the solution space undergoes a fundamental structural transformation: solutions fragment into an exponential number of well-separated clusters. Within each cluster, the solution space exhibits rigidity—most variables become frozen, taking only a single value across all solutions in that cluster. This clustering phenomenon provides a rigorous explanation for why local search algorithms and other polynomial-time heuristics fail at densities significantly below the satisfiability threshold: such algorithms cannot efficiently navigate between distant clusters or escape local optima imposed by frozen variables. Our results provide the first rigorous validation of a key assumption underlying survey propagation, a physics-inspired algorithm that has demonstrated remarkable empirical performance on random CSPs. This work bridges statistical physics intuition and rigorous computer science theory, offering new insights into computational complexity and algorithm design for random constraint satisfaction problems.

The Haumea collisional family represents a unique opportunity to study the outcome of a catastrophic impact in the trans-Neptunian region. Through detailed numerical simulations of the family's long-term dynamical evolution, we investigate the temporal constraints on the collision event and quantify the preservation of family members over billion-year timescales. Our integrations demonstrate that the family's current dynamical configuration is inconsistent with formation within the last 100 Myr, and we establish with 95% confidence that the collision occurred at least 1 Gyr ago. We model the orbital evolution of family members with various initial velocity dispersions and find that gravitational perturbations from Neptune remove approximately 25-35% of bodies initially ejected with velocities between 100-300 m/s over 3.5 Gyr. These dynamical losses are primarily driven by resonance capture and subsequent chaotic diffusion. The survival fraction depends sensitively on the initial ejection velocity, with slower ejecta experiencing higher retention rates due to tighter clustering around Haumea's orbit. We apply these loss rates to evaluate two competing formation mechanisms: (1) a graze-and-merge collision between comparably sized, differentiated Kuiper Belt Objects, and (2) the catastrophic disruption of a large satellite of Haumea. For the graze-and-merge scenario, current observations have identified 30-40% of the predicted family mass at low relative velocities (<150 m/s), suggesting 1-2 Haumea masses remain undetected at higher velocities. The satellite disruption model predicts that identified members represent 60-70% of the expected family mass. While both scenarios are statistically consistent with observations when accounting for survey incompleteness (at 2σ level), both predict a larger population of high-velocity members (>200 m/s) than currently observed, suggesting either model refinement or improved observational surveys are needed to discriminate between formation mechanisms.

Under this interpretation, we can constrain the potential locations and masses of unseen planetary companions. These predictions can be tested through future multi-wavelength observations combining near-infrared imaging with thermal emission and potentially direct planet detection techniques. This component cannot be explained within our framework, which accurately accounts for GDR splitting arising from nuclear deformation and Coriolis effects. The presence of this unexplained peak near the half-maximum of experimental cross sections leads to systematic overestimation of extracted GDR widths and deformations derived from these widths. Consequently, empirical formulae that reproduce these widths may obscure important physical information contained in the cross-section data. We suggest that fully microscopic GDR calculations and careful reexamination of experimental data are necessary to elucidate the nature of the 17 MeV component. Additionally, we analyze @xmath1-softness in the free energy surfaces of @xmath0Gd and discuss its influence on GDR properties, providing insights into the interplay between shape fluctuations and collective excitations in hot rotating nuclei.

We investigate the computational complexity of geometric variants of the 3-dimensional (axial) assignment problem and the 3-dimensional matching problem. In these special cases, the elements are represented as points in a Cartesian space, and the cost coefficients correspond to the perimeters of triangles formed by triples of points, measured according to various norms. For the minimization version, we establish NP-hardness for every norm, even when restricted to 2-dimensional Cartesian spaces. This demonstrates the inherent difficulty of minimizing triangle perimeters regardless of the metric used. In contrast, the maximization version exhibits a complexity dichotomy. When the dimension of the Cartesian space is fixed and the norm possesses a polyhedral unit ball, the problem becomes polynomially solvable. Remarkably, we observe significant enhancement of elastic coupling at current densities orders of magnitude below the critical current density. The results have important implications for understanding vortex matter phases and the optimization of flux pinning in high-temperature superconductors for practical applications.

We compare our findings with CERES Pb+Au measurements at equivalent beam energy and PHENIX Au+Au results from top RHIC energies, providing insights into the energy dependence of parton-medium interactions. These azimuthal correlation patterns serve as important probes for understanding the properties of hot, dense matter created in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

We investigate a system of interacting Brownian particles subject to short-range repulsive potentials and systematically derive a continuum description via nonlinear diffusion equations in the dilute limit. The accuracy of our approach is assessed through numerical simulations comparing three closure schemes: our asymptotic method, mean-field approximation, and Kirkwood superposition approximation, validated against Monte Carlo simulations of the full stochastic particle system. Our analysis reveals that the matched asymptotic approach excels for highly repulsive short-range potentials, while mean-field approximations perform better for long-range interactions. The Kirkwood superposition approximation proves accurate across all interaction ranges but requires significantly greater computational resources. These findings provide guidance for selecting appropriate coarse-graining strategies based on the characteristic length scale of particle interactions in diffusive systems.

Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) observations at cosmological distances reveal an accelerating universe dominated by a dark energy component with negative pressure. The nature of this dark energy remains enigmatic, with various theoretical models predicting different equations of state. If dark energy arises from a scalar field, its equation of state parameter w evolves with time according to the field's potential. We examine the fundamental degeneracies inherent in luminosity distance measurements and their implications for constraining dark energy properties. Through detailed analysis of realistic high-statistics SNe Ia surveys, we quantify the expected precision achievable in determining the equation of state parameter and its potential time evolution. Our results demonstrate both the power and limitations of SNe Ia as cosmological probes, highlighting the statistical requirements necessary to discriminate between competing dark energy models and establish the physical origin of cosmic acceleration.

We establish fundamental connections between private quantum channels and operator algebraic structures, specifically conditional expectations and trace vectors. Private quantum channels generalize the classical one-time pad to quantum information theory. We provide a novel geometric characterization of single-qubit private quantum channels using trace vectors, demonstrating that these operator-theoretic tools naturally capture privacy properties. For quantum channels that are conditional expectations, we prove that trace vectors completely determine the associated private states. Our results reveal that operator algebra theory provides a unified framework for understanding quantum privacy, connecting decades-old mathematical structures to modern quantum information concepts. Several illustrative examples demonstrate the practical utility of this characterization for analyzing private quantum communication protocols.

We investigate the construction of split supersymmetry (split-SUSY) within the framework of grand unified theories (GUTs), motivated by the successful gauge coupling unification that underlies the split-SUSY scenario. Our analysis reveals that implementing split-SUSY mass spectra in GUT models presents significant challenges and theoretical constraints. When R-symmetry breaking sources are introduced in the GUT sector, the heavy GUT particles effectively act as messengers in a gauge mediation framework, potentially generating substantial contributions to gaugino masses that must be carefully controlled. Through detailed analysis of the consistency conditions required for viable split-SUSY GUT models, we derive an upper bound on soft scalar masses of approximately 10^10 GeV. This bound emerges from the requirement that the hierarchy between scalar and gaugino masses remains stable under radiative corrections involving GUT-scale physics. We also explore the possibility of constructing R-symmetric GUT models as an alternative approach to avoiding problematic contributions from GUT messengers. Our results demonstrate that while split-SUSY provides an attractive phenomenological framework with gauge coupling unification, its embedding into GUT theories requires careful consideration of the interplay between SUSY breaking, GUT physics, and the resulting mass spectrum.

We discuss the calculation of collective excitations in atomic clusters using the time-dependent local density approximation (TDLDA). A particularly efficient implementation for large clusters employs a coordinate space mesh combined with algorithms for operators and evolution equations originally developed for nuclear time-dependent Hartree-Fock theory. This approach proves remarkably successful in describing strong excitations in alkali metal clusters and carbon-based systems. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through calculations of the benzene molecule's optical spectrum, which exhibits two prominent features that are accurately reproduced. The systematic behavior of linear carbon chains is also well captured by the TDLDA formalism and can be understood through relatively simple physical arguments. The method's efficiency and accuracy make it a valuable tool for investigating collective electronic excitations in medium to large-scale atomic cluster systems.

The *Fermi* satellite has revealed additional spectral components in the GeV energy range for several gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), exhibiting power-law characteristics that potentially extend into the X-ray band. While limited photon statistics complicate the determination of whether these GeV photons originate from internal or external shocks, we present numerical simulations based on internal dissipation scenarios to explain these extra components. Our leptonic model successfully reproduces the observed GeV excess through synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) emission and accounts for low-energy excess via late-time synchrotron radiation from remnant electrons. Hadronic models alternatively explain the keV-GeV power-law components through synchrotron and SSC emissions from secondary electron-positron pairs, though these typically require proton energies substantially exceeding gamma-ray energies. Notably, the flat keV-GeV spectrum observed in GRB 090902b is well-reproduced with comparable proton and gamma-ray energies. We critically evaluate the advantages and limitations of both leptonic and hadronic frameworks. To address challenges inherent in internal dissipation models, we propose incorporating continuous particle acceleration mechanisms analogous to second-order Fermi acceleration. This modification may provide a more comprehensive explanation for the complex multi-wavelength emission observed in *Fermi*-era GRBs.

Using fragmentation functions for charged pions, charged kaons, and (anti)protons recently extracted from experimental data of electron-positron annihilation at the Z-boson resonance and at centre-of-mass energy 29 GeV, we perform a global study of inclusive charged-hadron production in proton-proton, electron-proton, and electron-positron collisions at next-to-leading order in the parton model of quantum chromodynamics. Comparisons of our results with proton-proton data from CERN SppS and the Fermilab Tevatron, electron-proton data from DESY HERA, and electron-positron data from CERN LEP2 allow us to test the universality of the fragmentation functions predicted by the factorization theorem. Furthermore, we perform comparisons with electron-positron annihilation data from LEP2 to test the scaling violations predicted by the Altarelli-Parisi evolution equations. Our analysis demonstrates the consistency of the fragmentation function framework across different collision types and validates perturbative QCD predictions at next-to-leading order.

We present evidence for a quasi-biennial (~2 year) periodicity in solar acoustic oscillation frequencies, distinct from the well-established 11-year solar cycle. Using helioseismic data, we analyze temporal variations in p-mode frequencies, which serve as sensitive probes of conditions in the solar interior. Our analysis reveals a persistent ~2 year signal that appears independent of, yet modulated by, the dominant 11-year magnetic activity cycle. The existence of this quasi-biennial oscillation suggests the presence of additional physical mechanisms operating in the solar interior beyond those responsible for the primary solar cycle. These findings demonstrate that solar variability operates on multiple timescales simultaneously, with implications for understanding the complex dynamics of solar magnetism and internal structure.

We demonstrate that arbitrary Gaussian pure states can be deterministically generated in dissipative open systems through quasilocal interactions and local coupling to the environment. Quasilocality—restricting interactions to a few subsystems—is essential for practical implementation of engineered dissipation. Our protocol employs an auxiliary system that couples locally to the environment and interfaces with the target system via two-body Hamiltonians, driving the system toward the desired pure state. We establish that even a single-mode auxiliary system suffices to deterministically generate arbitrary approximate Gaussian cluster states when combined with an appropriate switching scheme. The method exploits the stabilizing effects of dissipation while maintaining experimental feasibility through limited connectivity requirements. We analyze the robustness of dissipation-induced pure Gaussian states against realistic imperfections, specifically examining how decoherence and parameter errors affect state fidelity through concrete examples. This work provides a scalable framework for continuous-variable quantum state preparation relevant to quantum information processing and quantum simulation with systems such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, and optomechanical devices.

We report ROSAT High Resolution Imager (HRI) observations of the transient X-ray source conducted on March 31, 1996. The improved X-ray position confirms identification with a previously discovered variable radio source. Analysis of the dust scattering halo yields an extinction value of @xmath0, constraining the source distance to d @xmath1 68.5 kpc. This distance estimate indicates that radiates at or near the Eddington limit for a 1 M⊙ compact object. The presence of the dust scattering halo requires an extended period of X-ray activity preceding the ROSAT observation. Combined with the non-detection by GRANAT during earlier Galactic center observations, we suggest that the X-ray activation of occurred during November/December 1995. These findings provide important constraints on the nature and temporal evolution of this transient X-ray source.

We present a comprehensive analysis of $\Upsilon$-meson two-point sum rules incorporating next-to-leading order corrections within the non-relativistic QCD (NRQCD) framework. Analytical expressions for the perturbative spectral density and gluon condensate contributions are derived, including resummed Coulomb corrections. These sum rules are employed to extract the $b$-quark mass from QCD vacuum correlation functions. Using the obtained results, we perform numerical estimates of various definitions of the $b$-quark mass, along with the decay constants and masses of the lowest-lying $\Upsilon$-meson resonances. The inclusion of next-to-leading order corrections and Coulomb resummation significantly improves the theoretical precision and reliability of the extracted hadronic parameters, providing stringent constraints on heavy quark phenomenology.

We present measurements of double parton scattering in @xmath0 jet events using data collected by the D0 experiment. The double parton scattering fraction (@xmath1) and the effective cross section @xmath2, a fundamental parameter characterizing the transverse spatial distribution of partons within the nucleon, are determined in three intervals of the second-highest transverse momentum jet (@xmath4) spanning @xmath5 GeV. Additionally, we measure differential cross sections as a function of the azimuthal angle between the transverse momentum of the leading jet system and that of the additional jet(s) in @xmath7 and @xmath0 final states. These angular correlations provide sensitive probes of multiple parton interaction dynamics. The experimental results are compared with theoretical predictions from various multiple parton interaction models implemented in the PYTHIA and SHERPA Monte Carlo event generators, testing our understanding of the multi-parton structure of hadron collisions.

We investigate exotic nuclear configurations including bubble and toroidal structures using semiclassical extended Thomas-Fermi calculations with the Skyrme SkM@xmath0 interaction. Variational equations for neutron and proton density distributions are solved self-consistently in spherical geometry for bubble nuclei and cylindrical coordinates for toroidal systems. We explore potential bubble configurations relevant to astrophysical environments and examine the stability of toroidal nuclei under quadrupole deformations. Our calculations reveal that heavy toroidal nuclei exhibit a global energy minimum, suggesting these exotic structures may represent stable nuclear configurations under specific conditions.

We investigate an extended bosonic t-J model in an optical lattice using both the Gutzwiller variational method and quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations. The model describes two-component hard-core bosons with nearest-neighbor pseudo-spin interactions and both inter- and intra-species dipole-dipole interactions (DDI), focusing specifically on the case where the two components possess anti-parallel polarized dipoles. Our calculations reveal a rich global phase diagram featuring multiple ordered phases. Both theoretical approaches consistently demonstrate the emergence of stripe solid ordering alongside the conventional checkerboard solid phase as a consequence of the DDI. Through detailed QMC simulations, we identify two distinct supersolid (SS) phases—checkerboard SS and stripe SS—characterized by coexisting crystalline and superfluid orders. Additionally, we uncover evidence of an exotic intermediate phase existing between the stripe solid and checkerboard SS regions. We apply our findings to analyze the t-J-like model recently realized experimentally by de Paz et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. **111**, 185305 (2013)], providing theoretical insights into experimentally accessible parameter regimes. Our results establish the crucial role of dipolar interactions in stabilizing complex quantum phases in ultracold bosonic systems.

We analyze a spatially extended Lotka-Volterra system of two competing species subject to two correlated noise sources: (i) an external multiplicative time-correlated noise representing environmental fluctuations, and (ii) a dichotomous stochastic process with periodic jump rate modeling the interaction parameter between species. Using a mean field approach and Gaussian approximation, we derive moment equations for species densities and investigate the effects of temporal correlations in the external noise on ecosystem dynamics. Our analysis reveals that first-order moments (mean densities) are independent of the multiplicative noise characteristics, while second-order moments exhibit strong sensitivity to both the intensity and correlation time of the multiplicative noise. This demonstrates that environmental noise significantly affects population fluctuations and spatial correlations, even when mean densities remain unaffected. We validate our theoretical predictions through comparison with numerical simulations using a coupled map lattice model, finding good agreement between the analytical and computational approaches. These results provide insights into the role of correlated environmental fluctuations in spatially distributed competitive ecosystems.

We propose a novel mechanism addressing two fundamental cosmological problems: cosmic acceleration and the coincidence problem.
