The framework's connection to quasi-modular forms is explicitly demonstrated through the local @xmath0 geometry and its mirror. We extend our construction to several compact Calabi-Yau geometries with one-dimensional moduli spaces, illustrating the broad applicability of this approach to string compactifications.

We present a novel inverse method for reconstructing the phonon relaxation time distribution in materials from thermal spectroscopy measurements. Unlike conventional approaches, our method circumvents the effective thermal conductivity approximation by directly solving an optimization problem that minimizes discrepancies between experimental relaxation traces and solutions of the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE). The relaxation time distribution, including polarization dependencies, is determined through this minimization procedure, which can employ either analytical or numerical BTE solutions depending on the problem complexity. We validate the approach using synthetic thermal grating relaxation data generated via Monte Carlo simulations. The reconstruction demonstrates excellent agreement with the known relaxation times used in the synthetic data generation, maintaining accuracy and stability even when experimental uncertainty and measurement noise are introduced. This method provides a rigorous framework for extracting fundamental phonon transport properties from thermal spectroscopy experiments without relying on simplified thermal conductivity models, enabling more accurate characterization of nanoscale heat transport in advanced materials.

We present a comprehensive digital control system for quantum optics experiments that offers significant improvements over traditional analog approaches. The freely available software package enables automatic, sequential re-locking of multiple optical components with enhanced scalability, reduced cost, and improved flexibility. Key features include integrated white-noise network analysis tools for lock optimization and real-time system monitoring from a centralized interface. We demonstrate the system's long-term stability through extensive testing and showcase its practical advantages through application to optical Schrödinger cat state characterization experiments. The digital architecture facilitates systematic optimization of individual feedback loops while maintaining coordinated control across the entire experimental setup. This open-source platform provides the quantum optics community with a robust, adaptable solution for managing increasingly complex multi-component optical systems, with particular benefits for experiments requiring precise, stable optical configurations over extended periods.

We present refined optical orbital ephemeris for the low-mass X-ray binary 4U 1735–44 based on observations spanning 1984–2007. Our analysis combines new optical photometry obtained during 1997–2007 with previously published observations from 1984–1993. The linear fit to the times of maximum optical light yields the ephemeris HJD = 2445904.0494(90) + [n × 0.19383222(29)] with χ2 = 1.1 for 16 degrees of freedom and a phase-zero scatter of σ = 0.061 days. This refined ephemeris resolves a previous discrepancy between optical and spectroscopic determinations of the orbital phase, bringing the optical maximum to spectral phase 0.47 ± 0.05, consistent with the companion star's radial velocity curve that defines the system's true dynamical phase zero. These results support the standard geometric model for low-mass X-ray binaries, in which optical maximum occurs near inferior conjunction of the companion star due to X-ray heating of its inner hemisphere. Our multi-epoch dataset provides additional evidence supporting the canonical LMXB model. We find a positive correlation between mean optical flux and simultaneous RXTE All-Sky Monitor X-ray flux, with the relative increases indicating that the intrinsic (non-X-ray-heated) optical contribution from the companion star comprises approximately 20 percent of the total optical emission. The amplitude of optical modulation shows no significant dependence on X-ray flux level. Analysis of ASM light curves folded on the refined ephemeris reveals no evidence for orbital modulation, eclipses, or dipping behavior in any energy band, consistent with the system's low orbital inclination.

We develop and analyze Lie group integrators for numerical simulation of nonlinear stochastic differential equations (SDEs) whose solutions evolve on smooth finite-dimensional manifolds. The theoretical framework exploits Lie group actions that generate transport along the manifold: the stochastic flow on the manifold is pulled back to the Lie group through the group action, and subsequently to the corresponding Lie algebra via the exponential map. Approximations to the stochastic flow are constructed using closed operations in the Lie algebra, then pushed forward through the exponential map to the Lie group and finally to the manifold. This coordinate-free approach guarantees that numerical approximations remain on the manifold throughout the integration process. We introduce stochastic Munthe-Kaas methods, extending classical deterministic Lie group integrators to the stochastic setting, particularly suitable for SDEs with non-commutative vector fields. Additionally, we present stochastic Lie group integration schemes based on Castell-Gaines methods, which employ underlying ordinary differential equation integrators to approximate flows generated by truncated stochastic exponential Lie series. When Munthe-Kaas methods serve as the underlying integrator, these become genuine stochastic Lie group schemes. Our theoretical analysis establishes that certain Castell-Gaines methods achieve uniformly superior accuracy compared to corresponding stochastic Taylor schemes. The efficacy of our methods is demonstrated through numerical simulations of rigid body dynamics, specifically a satellite and an autonomous underwater vehicle, both subjected to two independent multiplicative stochastic noise processes. These examples illustrate the practical advantages of structure-preserving integration for stochastic systems evolving on manifolds. **Keywords:** stochastic Lie group integrators, stochastic differential equations on manifolds **MSC:** 60H10, 60H35, 93E20

We present comprehensive spectroscopic data for 485 faint emission-line objects (magnitude @xmath0) selected using the ultraviolet-excess (UVX) criterion across 24.6 deg@xmath1 in the South Galactic Pole region. We successfully classified 429 Type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGNs), with 373 objects falling within the redshift range @xmath2. Complete spectra, positions, magnitudes, and colors are provided for all targets. This sample has enabled measurement of distinct clustering evolution patterns in quasi-stellar objects compared to galaxies, as detailed in La Franca et al. (1998). The survey region overlaps with both the ESO Imaging Survey (EIS) and the 2dF QSO Redshift Survey, facilitating multi-wavelength studies of AGN populations.

This article presents a comprehensive summary of a splinter session held at the Cool Stars XV conference in St. Andrews, Scotland, featuring three review talks and four contributed presentations focused on protoplanetary disk research. The session brought together international experts to discuss state-of-the-art approaches for understanding the structure, composition, and evolutionary processes of the gaseous component in protoplanetary disks surrounding low-mass stars. The presentations encompassed a broad range of methodological approaches, from multi-wavelength observational spectroscopy spanning ultraviolet, infrared, and millimeter wavelengths, to sophisticated chemical modeling and hydrodynamical simulations. The session specifically concentrated on disks around low-mass stellar objects, including classical T Tauri stars, transitional disks representing intermediate evolutionary stages, and more evolved debris disk systems. Key themes emerged throughout the discussion, with particular emphasis placed on the detection and characterization of water and organic molecules within these disk environments—species crucial for understanding prebiotic chemistry and habitability. Speakers examined the intricate connections between disk properties and planet formation processes, addressing how disk evolution influences and is influenced by planetary system architecture. Significant attention was devoted to the formation mechanisms and observational signatures of holes, gaps, and cavities in the inner disk regions, features potentially carved by forming planets or driven by photoevaporation and other clearing mechanisms. The interdisciplinary nature of the session, combining observational constraints with theoretical modeling, provided valuable insights into disk dissipation timescales, chemical enrichment processes, and the environmental conditions under which planetary systems emerge. This summary captures the current understanding and outstanding questions in protoplanetary disk research as represented by leading researchers from major international institutions across the United Kingdom, United States, Germany, and the Netherlands.

We examine the non-stationary dynamics of a coupled qubit-transmission line resonator system subjected to external driving fields and environmental decoherence. By analytically solving the equation of motion for the non-stationary resonator field, we establish the fundamental requirements for implementing single-shot, non-destructive dispersive measurements of phase qubit states. Our analysis demonstrates that reliable qubit readout necessitates effective isolation from electromagnetic noise, achievable through a configuration where the system interacts with external fields exclusively via a resonator weakly coupled to the qubit. We derive a comprehensive set of inequalities governing the resonator-qubit detuning, coupling strength, resonator decay rate, and measurement duration, while simultaneously satisfying the condition for multi-photon output flux. A key finding reveals an inherent trade-off: reducing measurement time demands increased resonator leakage, which consequently degrades the quality factor and diminishes the frequency resolution between resonator eigenstates corresponding to different qubit states. We verify the self-consistency of these constraints using two distinct sets of experimental parameters from recent implementations. These results provide quantitative guidelines for optimizing experimental architectures, system parameters, and measurement protocols in circuit quantum electrodynamics, facilitating improved qubit readout fidelity while minimizing back-action and measurement-induced decoherence.

We investigate whether the equilibrium time-averaged state of a self-organizing system with many internal degrees of freedom, 2D-Daisyworld, can be described by optimizing a single quantity. Unlike physical systems where a principle of maximum entropy production (MEP) has been observed, Daisyworld follows evolutionary dynamics rather than Hamiltonian dynamics. We find that this is sufficient to invalidate the MEP principle, finding instead a different organizing principle: the system self-organizes to a state which maximizes the amount of life. This result suggests that biological systems operating under evolutionary constraints may exhibit fundamentally different optimization principles than purely physical systems, with implications for understanding planetary-scale self-regulation and the Gaia hypothesis.

We investigate defects arising in adiabatic quantum control when the controlled system is entangled with its environment. The methodology is demonstrated using the atomic STIRAP (Stimulated Raman Adiabatic Passage) protocol, where the controlled atom is entangled with an auxiliary atom. Our results quantify the robustness of the STIRAP process under such entanglement conditions, revealing how environmental coupling degrades adiabatic transfer fidelity. This geometric approach provides both qualitative insight into decoherence mechanisms and quantitative measures of control protocol resilience in open quantum systems, with potential applications to quantum information processing and quantum state engineering.

Consequently, quantum TST (QTST) has traditionally been understood as any quantum rate theory that reproduces classical TST in the appropriate limit, with widespread agreement that no unique QTST preserving all classical TST properties can exist. Recently, Hele and Althorpe (HA) challenged this consensus, proposing that a true QTST can be defined as the exact @xmath0 limit of a specific quantum flux-side time correlation function, which they claimed to be equivalent to ring polymer molecular dynamics (RPMD) TST. This work critically examines the theoretical foundations and implications of their proposal. We identify several concerns with the HA formulation. First, we demonstrate that their starting time correlation function lacks proper grounding in linear response theory, which constitutes the essential first step in relating a @xmath1 limit to experimentally measurable rates. Second, our theoretical analysis reveals problematic assumptions in a crucial step of their proof, which appears not to rely on exact quantum mechanical identities. When this step is corrected, the true @xmath1 limit of HA's QTST diverges from the RPMD-TST rate expression, instead yielding the well-established path integral quantum transition state theory rate expression for the special case of a centroid dividing surface. Building on these findings, we formulate an alternative quantum rate expression by starting from rigorous linear response theory and employing a recently developed formalism for real-time dynamics of imaginary-time path integrals. This approach provides a more theoretically sound foundation for quantum rate calculations. Significantly, we demonstrate that the @xmath2 limit of our new rate expression vanishes in the exact quantum limit, which has important implications for understanding quantum tunneling and other quantum effects in chemical reaction dynamics. Chimera states, characterized by the counterintuitive coexistence of spatially separated coherent and incoherent oscillator populations, have attracted considerable attention across diverse dynamical systems. While previous investigations have predominantly focused on simple coupling functions such as sinusoidal or diffusive interactions, we explore chimera dynamics in networks of nonlocally coupled phase oscillators with biharmonic interaction terms. Our analysis reveals novel chimera patterns with distinctive properties: oscillators within individual coherent clusters can bifurcate into two subgroups exhibiting phase differences of approximately π/2, while oscillators in neighboring coherent domains may display phase differences approaching π. We systematically examine how the coupling ranges associated with the first and second harmonic components differentially influence chimera formation and stability, drawing insights from the synchronization behavior of globally coupled oscillator networks. These findings demonstrate that enriching the coupling architecture through biharmonic interactions generates qualitatively new chimera phenomenology, thereby opening promising avenues for understanding complex spatiotemporal patterns in natural and engineered systems.

We present a detailed spectroscopic analysis of the globular cluster RZ2109 in NGC 4472, which harbors the first definitively identified black hole within a globular cluster environment. These extreme line ratios significantly exceed predictions from standard photoionization models assuming solar abundance gas by factors of several. The outflow properties and emission line kinematics support an accretion-powered wind model where processed material from the white dwarf donor dominates the emission spectrum. Additionally, we constrain the age and metallicity of the host globular cluster RZ2109, providing context for understanding the formation and evolution of this remarkable system.

We investigate the morphological properties of galaxy clusters as powerful probes of the concordance ΛCDM cosmological model by examining the relationship between dark matter halo shapes and observable cluster properties. Our work presents a simple analytical framework for predicting X-ray observations of galaxy clusters, modeling them as isothermal systems in hydrostatic equilibrium with dark matter haloes approximated as homeoidal ellipsoids—triaxial structures with uniform axial ratios throughout their volume. To validate our analytical approach, we perform detailed comparisons with high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations of galaxy clusters. These tests demonstrate that our simplified prescription successfully reproduces cluster X-ray ellipticities observed in simulations, particularly when focusing on cluster regions less affected by recent merger activity. This finding establishes the reliability of our model for the relatively relaxed cluster populations typically studied in observational surveys. Applying our model to the halo shape distribution predicted by ΛCDM cosmology, we derive expectations for observable cluster morphologies. For clusters in the mass range @xmath3, we predict a mean X-ray ellipticity of @xmath1 with scatter @xmath2. Importantly, we demonstrate that incorporating the mass-dependence of halo shapes is crucial when comparing theoretical predictions to observational samples dominated by very massive systems, as halo triaxiality exhibits systematic trends with mass. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of four independent observational cluster samples, accounting for various systematic effects in the measurements. Our ΛCDM predictions show statistical compatibility with all samples examined. Notably, we find excellent agreement with two recent *ROSAT* X-ray surveys without invoking radiative cooling processes, suggesting that the morphological signatures of clusters primarily reflect the underlying dark matter distribution rather than baryonic physics. We extend our analysis to Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect predictions, finding more limited success. The reduced performance for SZ observables reflects physical limitations of the homeoidal ellipsoid approximation: dark matter haloes exhibit radially-varying triaxiality and misalignment of isodensity shells at different radii. These geometric complexities imprint observable signatures on the intracluster gas distribution that appear detectable in current data, indicating that while homeoidal models capture first-order morphological properties, they cannot fully characterize the three-dimensional structure of dark matter haloes across all observational diagnostics.

Agent-based stochastic models have emerged as crucial tools for understanding evolutionary dynamics in finite populations, extending beyond traditional infinite population assumptions. While ultimate fixation probabilities have been extensively studied, the transient pre-fixation behavior remains less understood despite its fundamental importance. Here we investigate the transient dynamics of the well-mixed Moran process by constructing a landscape function that serves as a unifying theoretical framework. This landscape integrates three previously disconnected perspectives: the stable equilibria of deterministic replicator dynamics, long-time fixation probabilities, and continuous diffusion approximations valid for large populations. Our analysis reveals several critical features of transient evolutionary dynamics. First, we identify multiple time scales emerging from intra-attractoral relaxation and inter-attractoral transitions in the landscape. Second, we demonstrate discontinuous transitions in stochastically stationary processes, analogous to Maxwell constructions in equilibrium statistical mechanics. Third, we highlight fundamental challenges facing diffusion approximations when applied to discrete stochastic processes. Importantly, we show that rare events—occurring with exponentially small probabilities yet corresponding to uphill movements and barrier crossings between landscape wells—play a disproportionate role in evolutionary dynamics. These rare events, enabled by strong nonlinear dynamics rather than noise alone, are essential for explaining the emergent complexity observed in biological systems. Our landscape approach thus provides new insights into the rich, multiscale temporal structure of evolutionary processes in finite populations.

Our results combine combinatorial graph theory with commutative algebra to establish necessary and sufficient conditions for this important class of toric ideals.

Knowledge bases provide applications with the benefit of easily accessible, systematic relational knowledge but often suffer in practice from their incompleteness and lack of knowledge of new entities and relations. Much work has focused on building or extending them by finding patterns in large unannotated text corpora. In contrast, here we mainly aim to complete a knowledge base by predicting additional true relationships between entities, based on generalizations that can be discerned in the given knowledge base. We introduce a Neural Tensor Network (NTN) model which predicts new relationship entries that can be added to the database. This model can be improved by initializing entity representations with word vectors learned in an unsupervised fashion from text, and when doing this, existing relations can even be queried for entities that were not present in the database. Our model generalizes and outperforms existing models for this problem, and can classify unseen relationships in WordNet with an accuracy of 75.8%.

We investigate the potential contamination of radio galaxy host measurements by active galactic nucleus (AGN) emission using mid-infrared imaging observations. Taylor et al. claimed that nuclear contributions artificially brighten the low-redshift @xmath0@xmath1 relation by approximately 0.5 magnitudes, which would significantly impact studies of radio galaxy evolution and their use as cosmological probes. We present 15@xmath2 m imaging data for a nearly-complete sample of low-redshift radio galaxies, enabling precise identification and characterization of unresolved nuclear components that would be difficult to detect at optical wavelengths. Nuclear sources are detected in five targets, exhibiting broad-band colors consistent with dust-reddened quasar spectra. For all five detections, the ratio of intrinsic near-infrared luminosity to narrow emission line luminosity matches typical quasar values, supporting their AGN origin. Our analysis reveals a correlation between inferred nuclear extinction and radio core-to-lobe ratio, providing new constraints on obscuring torus geometry. While we confirm that AGN emission does affect the @xmath0@xmath1 relation, the magnitude of this effect (@xmath3mag) is substantially smaller than Taylor et al.'s estimate. Assuming radio galaxy nuclei possess intrinsic near-infrared spectra similar to quasars, our multi-wavelength imaging constrains any possible brightening of the relation to less than 0.3 magnitudes. These results indicate that while AGN contamination exists, it does not severely compromise the utility of radio galaxies for cosmological studies, and the @xmath0@xmath1 relation remains a viable tool for investigating galaxy evolution across cosmic time.

We present an analysis of near-infrared CO fundamental emission from 35 young stellar objects, including T Tauri stars, Herbig Ae/Be stars, and transitional disks, to investigate the physical structure of molecular gas in the inner disk regions. Using CO line profile modeling, we determine inner radii of CO emission and find a strong correlation with total system luminosity (stellar plus accretion) for optically thick disks, consistent with emission originating near the dust sublimation radius. Transitional disks follow the same luminosity trend but exhibit systematically larger inner radii, indicating the presence of inner gas cavities. Through rotation diagram analysis of classical T Tauri disks, we derive emitting areas corresponding to narrow rings (~0.15 AU width) at the CO inner radius, while transitional disks show smaller emitting areas. We measure systematically lower rotational temperatures for both transitional disks and Herbig Ae/Be systems compared to T Tauri disks. Significantly, the derived rotational temperatures are comparable to or slightly below the expected blackbody temperatures of dust grains at the CO inner radius, contrary to theoretical predictions of significant gas-dust thermal decoupling in the inner disk. These results provide important observational constraints on inner disk structure and gas-dust coupling in protoplanetary disks.

We present a comprehensive three-dimensional analysis of motion camouflage, a biological stealth strategy employed by certain insects during pursuit. The model utilizes Frenet frames and relatively parallel adapted frames to describe pursuer and evader trajectories, with natural curvatures serving as control parameters. A high-gain feedback control law is developed and analyzed for achieving motion camouflage in three dimensions. We examine the biological feasibility of implementing such feedback mechanisms and establish connections to missile guidance systems. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. This work extends previous two-dimensional motion camouflage results to the more realistic and complex three-dimensional setting.

We construct asymptotically free renormalization group trajectories for the generic nonabelian Higgs model in four-dimensional spacetime. These ultraviolet-complete trajectories emerge through a generalization of renormalization/boundary conditions in defining the theory's correlation functions. While accessible via controlled weak-coupling analysis, these trajectories originate from threshold phenomena invisible to conventional perturbative analyses restricted to the deep Euclidean region. We identify a candidate three-parameter family of renormalization group trajectories connecting the asymptotically free ultraviolet regime to a low-energy Higgs phase. Low-energy properties are estimated with application to the Standard Model Higgs sector in mind. Notably, we discover a two-parameter subclass of asymptotically free Coleman-Weinberg-type trajectories that naturally avoid the hierarchy problem. This framework provides a consistent ultraviolet completion for spontaneous symmetry breaking while maintaining perturbative control, offering new perspectives on the triviality problem and naturalness in scalar field theories with gauge interactions.

The effect of solar irradiation on plasmonic silver nanocrystals has been investigated using transmission electron microscopy and size distribution analysis for solar cell light harvesting applications. Initially spherical nanocrystals on carbon film with log-normal size distributions were exposed to solar irradiation, resulting in particle growth with one nanocrystal reaching 638 nm diameter after four hours. Larger particles exhibited shape deformation from spherical morphology. The average nanocrystal diameter evolution follows Ostwald ripening model predictions when accounting for sample area fractions. However, the size distribution maintains an approximately log-normal character rather than converging to steady-state distributions predicted by Ostwald ripening theory. This discrepancy suggests the system remains in a transient state during the experimental timeframe. These findings have important implications for understanding the stability and morphological evolution of plasmonic nanostructures in solar energy harvesting devices, where long-term exposure to solar irradiation is inevitable and particle size distributions critically influence optical performance.

We introduce an extension of a variationally optimized perturbation method by combining it with renormalization group properties in a straightforward perturbative form. This leads to a very transparent and efficient procedure, with clear improvement of non-perturbative results compared to previous similar variational approaches. We illustrate this by deriving optimized results for the mass gap of the @xmath0 Gross-Neveu model, comparing them with exactly known results for arbitrary @xmath1. At large @xmath1, the exact result is reproduced already at the very first order of the modified perturbation using this procedure. For arbitrary values of @xmath1, using only the original perturbative information known at two-loop order, we obtain controllable accuracy at the percent level or better for any @xmath1 value, as compared with the exactly known result for the mass gap from the thermodynamical Bethe ansatz. The procedure is very general and can be extended straightforwardly to any renormalizable Lagrangian model, being systematically improvable provided that knowledge of enough perturbative orders of the relevant quantities is available.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between continuum luminosity and emission-line strength in NGC 5548, a prototypical Seyfert 1 galaxy. Utilizing 13 years of ground-based optical monitoring observations, we investigate the response of the Hβ emission line to continuum variations. Our analysis confirms the non-linear relationship between continuum and Hβ fluxes previously reported by Gilbert and Peterson (2003). Crucially, we demonstrate that this non-linearity exhibits temporal variability: the slope of the flux-flux relationship systematically decreases with increasing continuum luminosity. These findings provide strong observational support for photoionization models that predict luminosity-dependent emission-line responses in active galactic nuclei. The year-to-year variations in line responsivity suggest that the broad-line region structure and ionization state evolve on timescales comparable to the monitoring baseline. Our results have important implications for reverberation mapping studies and understanding the physical conditions in AGN broad-line regions.

The Standard Model of particle physics has been remarkably successful in describing fundamental interactions, though certain anomalies persist, particularly regarding @xmath0 measurements and subtle tensions in electroweak precision data. While the Higgs mechanism is essential for generating particle masses, theoretical alternatives continue to be explored. Fundamental questions regarding flavor physics, grand unification, and quantum gravity necessitate extensions beyond the Standard Model. Additionally, astrophysical and cosmological observations—particularly the existence of dark matter and the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe—provide compelling evidence for new physics. Supersymmetry emerges as an especially attractive framework for TeV-scale physics, naturally addressing several of these outstanding issues. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) represents our best opportunity to uncover the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking, with excellent prospects for dark matter discovery and potential insights into unification and quantum gravity. Complementary approaches through precision low-energy experiments, astrophysical observations, and cosmological studies will play crucial roles in the comprehensive search for physics beyond the Standard Model, offering multiple pathways to discover new fundamental physics.

Network centrality measures quantify node importance across diverse applications, yet their reliability under imperfect network data remains poorly understood. We investigate the robustness of three widely-used centrality metrics—degree centrality, betweenness centrality, and dynamical importance—against link uncertainties using two stochastic models capturing false-positive and false-negative link errors. Through extensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate how measurement inaccuracies systematically affect centrality rankings and node identification. We develop an analytical framework that predicts centrality degradation as a function of error rates, achieving excellent agreement with simulation results. Our findings reveal differential sensitivities among metrics, with betweenness centrality showing particular vulnerability to missing links. This work provides quantitative guidelines for assessing centrality measure reliability in real-world networks where link errors are inevitable, informing robust network analysis strategies.

We study elementary cellular automata with memory, where conventional cellular automaton rules are applied to cells that retain information about their past states over a specified temporal interval. Focusing on Rule 30, a canonical example of chaotic behavior in cellular automata, we implement a majority memory function that records the most frequent state of each cell during the memory interval. We demonstrate that this memory mechanism fundamentally transforms the quasi-chaotic dynamics characteristic of classical Rule 30 into structured domains containing traveling localized patterns (gliders) with predictable trajectories and interactions. Through systematic analysis, we characterize the morphological complexity of these memory-enriched systems and develop a comprehensive classification of glider dynamics. Our formal framework employs multiple analytical tools including de Bruijn diagrams for state transition analysis, descriptions of soliton-like collision reactions, and quasi-chemical notations for particle interactions. This work reveals how memory can serve as a control mechanism to regulate emergent complexity in chaotic discrete dynamical systems, transforming unpredictable behavior into organized, information-carrying structures suitable for computation.

We investigate quantum correlations in two-qubit systems through the lens of one-way quantum deficit, a measure connecting quantum thermodynamics with information theory. We develop a novel analytical method to evaluate one-way deficit for a specific class of two-qubit states, focusing on @xmath0 states characterized by five parameters. By examining the dynamics under decoherence channels, we demonstrate that one-way deficit exhibits greater robustness compared to entanglement when subjected to environmental noise. This enhanced resilience suggests that quantum deficit captures correlations beyond entanglement, providing deeper insights into quantum non-locality and the thermodynamic aspects of quantum information processing. Our results have implications for understanding work extraction protocols in open quantum systems and highlight the fundamental role of quantum correlations in noisy environments, establishing one-way deficit as a more stable resource than entanglement for certain quantum information tasks.

We present comprehensive Keck adaptive optics imaging observations of the HD 130948BC L4+L4 binary system, supplemented by archival Hubble Space Telescope and Gemini-North data spanning approximately 70% of the binary's orbital period. Through precise astrometric analysis of the relative orbit, we determine a total dynamical mass of 0.109±0.002 M☉ (114±2 M_Jup). The near-unity flux ratio between the components confirms that both objects are unambiguously substellar across any plausible mass ratio. An independent age constraint is provided by the primary star HD 130948A (spectral type G2V, [M/H] = 0.0). Multiple age indicators, including stellar activity, chromospheric emission, and kinematic properties, suggest an age comparable to the Hyades cluster (~625 Myr). The most precise age estimate derives from gyrochronology analysis of the primary's rotation period. Consequently, HD 130948BC represents a unique benchmark system among field L and T dwarfs, possessing well-determined masses, luminosities, and age. Our analysis reveals significant discrepancies between observations and current substellar theoretical models: (1) Both components appear overluminous by a factor of approximately 2-3 compared to evolutionary model predictions. Reconciling this luminosity discrepancy would require the system to be substantially younger than the gyrochronology age indicates. (2) Effective temperatures derived from evolutionary models for HD 130948B and C are inconsistent with temperatures determined through spectral synthesis for objects of similar spectral type. These inconsistencies persist regardless of the adopted system age, indicating systematic errors in either evolutionary models, atmospheric models, or both. The masses of HD 130948B and C lie near the theoretical lithium-burning mass limit (~0.06 M☉), making differential lithium depletion measurements between the components a uniquely discriminating test of model physics. The potential systematic underestimation of luminosities by evolutionary models carries wide-ranging implications for brown dwarf astrophysics, making refined age determination for this system critically important for future investigations.

We investigate natural cluster structures in rings of regular functions on simple complex Lie groups and their compatibility with Poisson-Lie structures. Our main conjecture proposes a correspondence between Belavin-Drinfeld classes of Poisson-Lie structures on $\mathbb{G}$ and cluster structures in $\mathcal{C}[\mathbb{G}]$. Previous work established this correspondence for the standard Poisson-Lie structure on arbitrary $\mathbb{G}$ and for all Belavin-Drinfeld classes in $SL_n$ with $n \leq 4$. This paper proves the conjecture for the Cremmer-Gervais Poisson-Lie structure on $SL_n$, which differs maximally from the standard structure. This result significantly extends our understanding of the interplay between cluster algebras and Poisson geometry in the context of simple Lie groups, providing strong evidence for the validity of the general conjecture.

We present a comprehensive spectroscopic and photometric study of 41 RR Lyrae stars and one probable high-amplitude δ Scuti star in the *Kepler* field. Our analysis includes spectroscopic iron-to-hydrogen ratios [Fe/H], radial velocities, atmospheric parameters, and photometric characterization based on up to 970 days of high-precision Q0-Q11 *Kepler* long- and short-cadence observations. The sample comprises 37 fundamental-mode pulsators (RRab stars), of which 16 exhibit the Blazhko effect, and four first-overtone multiperiodic pulsators (RRc stars). Spectroscopic metallicities for 34 stars range from [Fe/H] = -2.54 dex (NR Lyr) to -0.02 dex (V784 Cyg), spanning more than two orders of magnitude in iron abundance. For 19 non-Blazhko stars previously studied photometrically by Nemec et al. (2011), our spectroscopic abundances show excellent agreement with their photometric metallicity estimates. We confirm four metal-rich RR Lyrae stars identified by Nemec et al. (KIC 6100702, V2470 Cyg, V782 Cyg, and V784 Cyg) and identify four additional metal-rich objects (V839 Cyg, KIC 5520878, KIC 8832417, and KIC 3868420). A significant metallicity dichotomy emerges: five non-Blazhko RRab stars are more metal-rich than [Fe/H] > -0.9 dex, while all 16 Blazhko stars are more metal-poor than this threshold, suggesting a potential metallicity dependence for the Blazhko phenomenon. We derive new period-amplitude-metallicity relationships utilizing the unprecedented precision and time baseline of *Kepler* photometry. With the exception of some Blazhko variables, spectroscopic and photometric [Fe/H] determinations show good agreement, validating photometric metallicity calibrations. Several stars with unique characteristics are identified, including V838 Cyg, a Blazhko variable exhibiting the smallest known amplitude and frequency modulations, providing crucial constraints for understanding the Blazhko mechanism. These results demonstrate the power of combining space-based photometry with ground-based spectroscopy for characterizing RR Lyrae populations.

The Nikolaevskiy equation, a model for pattern formation with continuous translational and Galilean symmetries, displays spatiotemporal chaos characterized by strong scale separation between short-wavelength patterns and long-wavelength modulations. Through extensive numerical simulations, we investigate the statistical properties of the chaotic attractor and uncover anomalous scaling behavior in the long-wave modes. The amplitude and correlation time of these modes exhibit scaling exponents that deviate from predictions of the leading-order multiple-scale theory developed by Matthews and Cox. We demonstrate that incorporating systematic higher-order corrections to the asymptotic theory successfully captures the observed anomalous scaling, resolving the discrepancy between analytical predictions and numerical observations.

This paper presents a comprehensive collection of formulae for computing the strong coupling constant and quark masses across different energy scales and numbers of active flavours. All equations incorporate state-of-the-art QCD corrections up to three-loop order, with some calculations extending to four-loop precision. The authors provide a Mathematica package containing practical procedures for implementing these calculations. This work serves as a valuable computational tool for precision QCD phenomenology and theoretical predictions in particle physics. PACS numbers: 12.38.Aw, 12.38.-t, 14.65.-q

This paper provides a comprehensive survey of recent advances in quantum linear systems theory, presenting key developments within a unified theoretical framework. Quantum linear systems represent a fundamental class of quantum mechanical systems whose dynamics are governed by linear quantum stochastic differential equations (QSDEs). These systems are ubiquitous in quantum optics and related fields, encompassing diverse physical implementations including interconnected optical cavities, beam-splitters, phase-shifters, optical parametric amplifiers, squeezers, and cavity quantum electrodynamic systems. As quantum technologies mature, the feedback control of quantum linear systems has emerged as a frontier challenge in control theory, with far-reaching implications across multiple domains. Applications include quantum computing architectures, quantum error correction protocols, quantum communication networks, gravitational wave detection, precision metrology, atom laser systems, and superconducting quantum circuits. The unique characteristics of quantum systems—particularly the fragility of quantum coherence and the constraints imposed by quantum measurement—necessitate fundamentally new control paradigms. A particularly promising approach involves coherent quantum feedback control, where the controller itself is implemented as a quantum linear system. This strategy offers several critical advantages: preservation of quantum information, high-speed operation, and potential for efficient physical implementation. The paper examines recent breakthroughs in H-infinity optimal controller synthesis for linear quantum systems within the coherent control framework, addressing both performance optimization and robustness considerations. A central challenge in both modeling and controller synthesis is the physical realizability problem: determining whether a given set of QSDEs corresponds to a physically implementable quantum system that satisfies fundamental quantum mechanical principles. This paper reviews recent theoretical advances connecting physical realizability to established concepts in linear systems theory, particularly the theory of lossless bounded real systems and dual J-J unitary systems. These connections provide powerful mathematical tools for characterizing admissible quantum linear systems and designing physically realizable quantum controllers. By synthesizing these developments, this survey establishes a coherent mathematical foundation for quantum linear systems theory and highlights promising directions for future research in quantum feedback control.

We investigate the stability of non-homogeneous stationary states for the one-dimensional Vlasov equation with an attractive cosine potential. Focusing on stationary states that are monotone decreasing functions of the energy, we establish that all such states within a Sobolev space @xmath0 (@xmath1) neighborhood of a reference stationary state are nonlinearly stable. This result demonstrates a striking difference from the homogeneous case, where stability analysis requires control over more than one derivative to exclude unstable stationary states in the vicinity of a given equilibrium. Our findings reveal that the non-homogeneous structure provides additional stability mechanisms that reduce the regularity requirements for orbital stability. The proof exploits the specific properties of energy-decreasing distribution functions and the geometric constraints imposed by the cosine potential, yielding improved stability estimates compared to classical results for homogeneous systems.

We propose a functional distance $d_H$ based on the Hausdorff metric between function hypographs for the space $\mathcal{F}$ of non-negative real upper semicontinuous functions defined on a compact interval. This work demonstrates that the metric space $(\mathcal{F}, d_H)$ is particularly well-suited for statistical analysis of functional data characterized by highly irregular graphs and narrow, sharp peaks—features commonly observed in spectrograms from magnetic resonance imaging and mass spectrometry applications. From a theoretical perspective, we establish that $(\mathcal{F}, d_H)$ forms a complete, separable, locally compact metric space. A key result shows that $d_H$-convergence of a function sequence implies convergence of the corresponding maximum values, providing crucial stability properties for statistical inference. We explore the probabilistic and statistical ramifications of these findings, with particular emphasis on establishing consistency of $k$-nearest neighbor ($k$-nn) classifiers for supervised classification problems involving functional data in $\mathcal{F}$ under the $d_H$ metric. On the applied side, we present results from simulation studies evaluating the performance of our methodology. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical utility of our approach through two real-world supervised classification problems involving mass spectrometry data, confirming the effectiveness of the Hausdorff-based distance for spectrum-type functional data analysis.

We present deep near-infrared Hubble Space Telescope (HST) observations of the low-metallicity blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxy VII Zw 403, obtained using the Near-Infrared Camera and Multi-Object Spectrometer (NICMOS). Single-star photometry was performed using the F110W and F160W filters (HST equivalents of ground-based J and H bands), achieving limiting magnitudes of approximately 25.5 and 24.5 magnitudes, respectively. The photometry demonstrates high precision (0.1 mag) with greater than 90% completeness down to magnitude 23, representing a significant improvement over previous ground-based near-infrared studies. The resulting color-magnitude diagram contains approximately 1000 resolved point sources. We provide a preliminary transformation of the near-infrared photometry to the ground-based system and investigate the tip-of-the-red-giant-branch (TRGB) distance determination method in the J and H bands. By combining our empirical results with globular cluster data and stellar evolution models, we establish a TRGB absolute magnitude calibration of M_J = -5.5 ± 0.1 for the metallicity range -2.3 ≤ [Fe/H] ≤ -1.5. Analysis of the stellar content employs evolutionary tracks and a classification scheme utilizing optical and near-infrared colors. We identify asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars and discuss the blue Hertzsprung gap population. For red stars, we utilize M_bol as an indicator of stellar mass after carefully evaluating bolometric corrections at low metallicity. By calculating the fractional contribution of individual stellar populations to the integrated light, we determine that young red supergiants combined with young and intermediate-age AGB stars contribute approximately 50% of the integrated light in I, J, and H bands, while old red giant branch stars contribute less than 15%. Young main-sequence stars and blue supergiants account for the remaining flux and dominate in the V band. These results illuminate the complex stellar populations underlying BCD galaxies and explain the difficulty in characterizing their nature from integrated photometry alone, as the integrated colors are dominated by young stellar populations that can mask the underlying older stellar component.

We present _Hubble Space Telescope_ Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 ultraviolet (UV; 2200 Å) and optical _V_-band imaging observations of 20 low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs), predominantly spectroscopically classified as low-ionization nuclear emission-line regions (LINERs). The primary objective is to identify potential photoionizing continuum sources that could power the observed emission-line spectra. Of the 20 galaxies observed, six (30%) exhibit detectable UV emission. The morphology of these UV sources varies significantly: two galaxies (NGC 3642 and NGC 4203) harbor compact, unresolved nuclear UV point sources suggestive of concentrated emission from active nuclei or nuclear star clusters, while four galaxies (NGC 4569, NGC 5005, NGC 6500, and NGC 7743) display spatially extended UV emission consistent with more distributed star formation or scattered nuclear radiation. Combining our observations with previous studies by Maoz (1995), we perform statistical analysis to identify factors governing UV detectability. We find that UV detection probability correlates strongly with low internal dust reddening and low galaxy inclination angles, indicating that dust obscuration represents the primary factor determining observational success. Additionally, objects displaying large emission-line equivalent widths and broad-line components show enhanced UV detection rates. These results suggest that most LINERs likely contain intrinsic nuclear UV sources that remain hidden by dust. For the compact UV sources in NGC 3642 and NGC 4203, assuming power-law spectral energy distributions with slope α = -1 extending into the extreme ultraviolet, we calculate that the extrapolated ionizing photon luminosities are sufficient to photoionize the observed narrow-line regions, supporting an active galactic nucleus interpretation. The _V_-band images reveal prominent dust lanes in many sample galaxies, providing direct evidence for the obscuring material. These findings have important implications for understanding the nature and prevalence of nuclear activity in nearby galaxies.

We present a comprehensive framework for projecting the four-dimensional two-body Bethe-Salpeter equation onto the three-dimensional light-front hypersurface using the quasi-potential approach. This technique establishes a crucial connection between the projection methodology and the effective dynamics governing the valence component of the light-front wave function. The formalism enables systematic construction of the Fock expansion for both the light-front effective interaction and the electromagnetic current operator, with the latter satisfying the appropriate Ward-Takahashi identity. We emphasize the fundamental role of Fock-space content in operators defined on the light-front hypersurface, demonstrating how multi-particle contributions emerge naturally within this framework. Special attention is devoted to the electromagnetic current's gauge invariance and its consistency with the underlying dynamical structure. The methodology is extended to accommodate three-particle systems, providing a foundation for studying more complex bound states. This approach offers significant advantages for relativistic few-body calculations while maintaining proper covariance and current conservation properties essential for accurate predictions of hadronic structure and electromagnetic form factors.

We investigate the Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi metric coupled with an inhomogeneous viscous fluid representing an interactive mixture of radiation and matter in the pre-decoupling era. Employing the framework of extended irreversible thermodynamics (EIT), we analyze the transport properties of this cosmological mixture. Our analysis using the complete EIT transport equation demonstrates that the relaxation time associated with shear viscosity significantly exceeds the Thomson collision time between photons and electrons by several orders of magnitude. This result has important implications for understanding the decoupling process. We compare our findings with predictions from truncated transport equations commonly used in cosmological models and show that such simplified approaches fail to adequately capture the physics of matter-radiation decoupling, highlighting the necessity of the full EIT formalism for accurate description of this crucial epoch in cosmic evolution.

We present analytical expressions for the one- and two-body terms in the cluster expansion of charge form factors and densities of s-p and s-d shell nuclei with N=Z. These expressions depend on the harmonic oscillator parameter b and the correlation parameter β derived from the Jastrow correlation function. Using these analytical formulas, we perform a systematic investigation of short-range correlation effects on nuclear form factors and charge densities, examining the mass dependence of both parameters. The parameters b and β are determined by fitting to experimental charge form factors. The inclusion of correlations successfully reproduces experimental data at high momentum transfers (q≥2 fm−1), a regime where mean-field descriptions typically fail. Our analysis reveals that while β remains approximately constant for doubly closed-shell nuclei (4He, 16O, and 40Ca), it exhibits significantly larger values (indicating weaker correlations) for open-shell nuclei. This systematic variation demonstrates a pronounced shell effect in closed-shell systems, where short-range correlations are more important. These results provide quantitative insight into the role of nucleon-nucleon correlations across different nuclear structures. **PACS numbers:** 21.10.Ft, 25.30.Bf, 21.45.+v, 21.60.Cs

We investigate the electropion production reaction $ep \to e'\pi^+ nn$ in parallel kinematics using a comprehensive dynamical model. The study employs a unitary $\pi NN$ framework to systematically examine nuclear medium effects, including final-state nucleon-nucleon interactions, pion rescattering from the spectator nucleon, and intermediate $\Delta$ and $N^*$ resonance contributions. While these $\pi NN$ mechanisms individually produce relatively small modifications, we find they generate significant contributions to the cross sections through quantum mechanical interference with the dominant one-body impulse term. For longitudinal cross sections, interference between the pion pole term and other production mechanisms proves particularly substantial. These results demonstrate that interference effects are crucial for proper interpretation of experimental data. Any extraction of potential medium modifications to the pion electromagnetic form factor or the $\pi NN$ vertex from deuteron electropion production measurements must account for these interference patterns. Neglecting these effects could lead to incorrect conclusions about in-medium modifications of hadronic properties.

The diffuse galactic γ-ray emission observed by EGRET aboard the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory exhibits a significant excess above 1 GeV compared to conventional model predictions, particularly pronounced in the inner galaxy region. This study examines two potential mechanisms to explain this spectral hardening: (1) the contribution from unresolved galactic cosmic ray (GCR) sources distributed throughout the galaxy, and (2) non-uniform transport of cosmic rays across the galactic disk. Both scenarios naturally produce a harder γ-ray spectrum than would be expected from the locally measured GCR spectrum near the solar system. Our analysis demonstrates that the unresolved source contribution constitutes a necessary and substantial component of the diffuse γ-ray background. Additionally, we propose that spatially variable cosmic ray transport represents a plausible supplementary mechanism contributing to the observed spectral characteristics, though alternative explanations remain viable.

We establish a necessary and sufficient condition characterizing when the natural boundary of a Hilbert geometry forms a corona. We prove that every Hilbert geometry possesses uniform contractibility and exhibits bounded coarse geometry properties. These structural results enable us to demonstrate that the coarse Novikov conjecture is valid for Hilbert geometries satisfying a mild geometric condition. Additionally, we determine that the asymptotic dimension of any two-dimensional Hilbert geometry equals precisely two. Our methods combine techniques from metric geometry with coarse geometric analysis, providing new insights into the large-scale geometric structure of Hilbert geometries and their boundaries, with implications for index theory and geometric group theory.

We investigate the stability and mass spectrum of cosmological perturbations in Kaluza-Klein compactifications featuring four-dimensional inflationary geometry. This framework combines higher-dimensional models with early- or late-time cosmological dynamics. Our comprehensive analysis encompasses all perturbation sectors: scalar, vector, and tensor modes. While scalar perturbations have been previously examined, we present novel results for the vector and tensor sectors. A key finding is that potential instabilities in these compactifications are confined exclusively to the scalar sector. Both vector and tensor perturbations exhibit non-negative mass-squared eigenvalues, indicating stability in these channels. We incorporate form fields with non-trivial background flux in the extra dimensions as matter sources, which generate both scalar and vector perturbations in the effective four-dimensional theory. As a concrete example, we perform detailed perturbation analysis in Freund-Rubin compactifications. Although this serves as a toy model, we anticipate that our qualitative conclusions extend to similar configurations with extra dimensions and form field backgrounds. Our analysis reveals two distinct instability channels within the scalar perturbation sector that must be addressed in any cosmological model incorporating extra dimensions and form fields. Significantly, one instability channel directly originates from perturbations of the form field itself. These findings have important implications for the viability and stabilization requirements of higher-dimensional cosmological models with inflationary phases.

We examine a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) network proposed for solving optimization problems from the perspective of neural network theory. The system consists of interconnected two-component BECs that map onto Ising model Hamiltonians. We demonstrate that this bosonic system is mathematically equivalent to a stochastic continuous Hopfield network, with the crucial advantage of enhanced cooling rates due to bosonic stimulated scattering processes. This equivalence reveals the BEC network as a physical implementation of simulated annealing with an intrinsic speedup factor proportional to the boson number @xmath0. We analyze the network's capabilities for standard neural network applications, including associative memory, learning algorithms, and pattern recognition tasks. Our analysis shows that pattern recognition processes can achieve acceleration by a factor of @xmath0 compared to classical implementations, while maintaining the convergence properties of traditional Hopfield networks. This work establishes a rigorous connection between quantum many-body physics and computational neuroscience, suggesting new pathways for quantum-enhanced machine learning architectures based on ultracold atomic systems.

We investigate the feedback stabilization problem for a non-relativistic charged particle confined in a one-dimensional infinite square potential well under the influence of a spatially uniform, time-dependent electric field control. The quantum system is modeled by a bilinear Schrödinger equation on a bounded domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions, where the state is represented by a complex probability amplitude. Using Lyapunov-based techniques, we construct explicit feedback control laws that achieve almost global approximate stabilization of the system's eigenstates. Our approach addresses the fundamental challenges inherent in quantum control, including the bilinear nature of the control operator and the preservation of the norm constraint. The results contribute to the theoretical foundations of quantum control systems and demonstrate the feasibility of stabilizing quantum states through measurement-based feedback strategies.

We present compelling observational evidence for remarkably high gas fractions and spatially extended molecular gas reservoirs in normal, near-infrared selected BzK galaxies at redshift z≈1.5. Our findings are based on comprehensive multi-configuration CO[2-1] observations conducted using the IRAM Plateau de Bure Interferometer. All six star-forming galaxies in our sample were detected with high statistical significance, providing robust constraints on their molecular gas properties. High spatial resolution observations successfully resolve the CO emission in four targets, revealing molecular gas reservoirs with characteristic sizes of 6-11 kpc. The resolved kinematics suggest the presence of ordered rotational motion, indicative of relatively settled disk structures. The UV morphologies of these galaxies are consistent with clumpy, gravitationally unstable disks, with UV-traced sizes comparable to those measured in CO emission, suggesting spatial coincidence between star formation and gas reservoirs. Remarkably, these galaxies exhibit uniformly low star formation efficiencies throughout the sample, similar to those observed in local spiral galaxies. This translates to extended gas depletion timescales of approximately 1 Gyr—substantially longer than the rapid depletion times characteristic of high-redshift submillimeter galaxies and quasars. The CO luminosities correlate tightly with observed star formation rates and stellar masses, with predictions accurate to within 0.15 dex, implying fundamental scaling relations between gas content and galaxy properties. We employ novel dynamical models specifically designed for clumpy disk galaxies to derive dynamical masses. These models successfully reproduce the distinctive spectral line profiles observed in the CO emission. After careful accounting for stellar and dark matter contributions, we derive molecular gas masses of 0.4-1.2×1011 M☉. The implied CO-to-H2 conversion factor (α_CO ≈ 3.6 M☉(K km s−1 pc2)−1) is consistent with Galactic values but approximately four times higher than the conversion factor typically assumed for local ultraluminous infrared galaxies and commonly applied to high-redshift systems. Most strikingly, the molecular gas mass in these galaxies equals or exceeds the stellar mass, with gas accounting for an impressive 50-65% of baryons within the galaxies' half-light radii. We are thus observing genuinely gas-dominated systems at z≈1.5, a result that naturally explains the elevated specific star formation rates characteristically observed in massive z>1 galaxies. These BzK galaxies can be conceptualized as scaled-up analogs of local disk galaxies, hosting low-efficiency star formation within extended, low-excitation molecular gas disks. This population appears markedly distinct from both local ULIRGs and high-redshift submillimeter galaxies and quasars, which typically exhibit higher gas excitation states and more spatially compact molecular reservoirs.

Diffusive shock acceleration (DSA) at relativistic shocks represents a fundamental mechanism for particle acceleration in high-energy astrophysical environments, particularly in extragalactic jets associated with active galactic nuclei and gamma-ray bursts. These objects are considered prime candidates for the production of ultra-high energy cosmic rays, making understanding of the acceleration physics crucial for modern astrophysics. This paper presents comprehensive Monte Carlo simulations of DSA in test-particle, relativistic, oblique magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) shocks, examining key predictions relevant to cosmic ray ion and electron production. The simulations explore acceleration efficiency across diverse scattering scenarios, including both large-angle and small-angle scattering regimes, and investigate various shock obliquities, extending into superluminal configurations where the de Hoffman-Teller frame ceases to exist. The simulation results reveal that distribution function power-law indices exhibit strong sensitivity to two critical parameters: the mean magnetic field orientation relative to the shock normal and the characteristics of MHD turbulence propagating along field lines in the shock environment. These indices show excellent agreement with predictions from alternative theoretical approaches, validating the simulation methodology. A particularly intriguing finding concerns the generation of flat particle spectra, which the simulations attribute to shock drift acceleration mechanisms. This result has important implications for interpreting observations of high-energy astrophysical sources. The theoretical predictions presented here have direct observational consequences for gamma-ray burst and blazar studies. Recent observations from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope are already providing meaningful constraints on fundamental environmental parameters characterizing relativistic shocks, including particle scattering frequencies and magnetic field turbulence levels. These observational constraints, when combined with the theoretical framework developed here, enable more robust physical interpretations of these extreme cosmic accelerators. The convergence of advanced simulation techniques and high-quality gamma-ray observations promises to significantly advance our understanding of particle acceleration in relativistic shock environments and the origin of the highest energy cosmic rays observed in nature.

We present a novel mechanism for generating a large running of the spectral index within the slow-roll inflationary paradigm. In standard slow-roll inflation, the running is proportional to @xmath0, making it extremely small and currently undetectable. Our mechanism employs a curvaton field characterized by both a large mass term and a time-dependent normalization coefficient. Such configurations naturally arise in models where an angular field component evolves in the presence of a dynamically changing radial direction. Through a single fine-tuning between the mass parameter and the rate of temporal variation in the normalization, the curvaton can be rendered effectively light at cosmological scales relevant to CMB observations, yielding a spectral tilt consistent with current data. However, this effective lightness is transient; the field becomes heavy at scales probed later, producing a substantially enhanced and potentially observable running of the spectral index. This work demonstrates that massive fields need not decouple from inflationary dynamics and opens new avenues for constructing viable inflationary models with distinctive observational signatures in the primordial power spectrum.

We introduce a Wigner function formalism for quantum mechanics on graphs, enabling investigation of the semiclassical limit. The classical dynamics derived from this framework is compared with quantum evolution via the propagator method. For extended open graphs exhibiting classically diffusive dynamics, we demonstrate how transport properties manifest in the quantum regime through scattering resonances and temporal evolution, establishing a clear connection between classical diffusion and quantum mechanical behavior on graph structures.

We present a new COMPASS measurement of the gluon polarization Δg/g in the nucleon using high transverse momentum hadron pairs from deep inelastic muon-nucleon scattering. The analysis covers the photon virtuality range Q2 = 1 (GeV/c2)2, significantly reducing the statistical uncertainty of Δg/g by a factor of three to 0.10 compared to previous measurements. The analysis employs an improved neural network-based weighted method and incorporates updated extraction formulas that properly account for leading order and QCD Compton process contributions previously neglected in earlier analyses.

Local diffusion coefficients in disordered systems, including spin glasses and living cells, exhibit significant spatial heterogeneity and temporal variability. These characteristics lead to irreproducible single-particle-tracking measurements, a phenomenon conceptualized as weak ergodicity breaking in stochastic processes. We present a rigorous theoretical framework for the annealed transit time model, describing heterogeneous diffusion in cellular environments under both equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions. Through analytical solutions, we characterize the mean square displacement (MSD) and the relative standard deviation of time-averaged MSD for various scenarios. Our analysis reveals that while time-averaged MSD exhibits linear growth with time, the underlying diffusion coefficients possess intrinsic randomness in non-equilibrium systems. This randomness fundamentally distinguishes non-equilibrium behavior from equilibrium dynamics. The results demonstrate how environmental disorder generates distributional effects in transport coefficients, providing theoretical insights into the statistical properties of diffusion in complex, time-dependent media. These findings establish a foundation for understanding ergodicity breaking and the emergence of irreproducibility in measurements of transport phenomena in disordered systems, with implications for interpreting experimental single-particle-tracking data in heterogeneous biological and physical environments.

We present a comprehensive analysis of community structures in two distinct social networks constructed from musical artist relationships: a similarity network based on editorial assessments of musical resemblance, and a collaboration network derived from joint performances. Our investigation reveals fundamental organizational patterns that illuminate the mechanisms driving network growth and structure formation in the music domain. In the similarity network, we observe a pronounced correlation between identified artist clusters and established musical genres, suggesting that stylistic and aesthetic properties constitute primary organizing principles. The detected communities align closely with genre boundaries, indicating that musical similarity serves as a robust basis for network segmentation and reflects the underlying taxonomic structure of musical categorization. The collaboration network exhibits a more complex dual-community structure. We identify two distinct types of communities operating at different scales: (1) relatively compact, localized structures corresponding to music bands and geographically-constrained collaborative groups, and (2) substantially larger communities organized around extensive collaborative clusters involving numerous participants, with temporal coherence linked to the historical periods during which artists were active. This hierarchical organization suggests that collaboration patterns are governed by both practical constraints (band membership, geographic proximity) and broader historical-cultural factors (musical movements, technological eras). Through network centrality analysis, we successfully identify leading artists within their respective communities and characterize their functional roles by examining topological properties including degree centrality, betweenness, and clustering coefficients. This node-level analysis reveals the structural importance of specific artists in maintaining community cohesion and facilitating inter-community connections. Our findings demonstrate that community detection methods effectively capture meaningful social and musical structures in artist networks. The strong correspondence between detected communities and musical genres validates the sociological reality of genre classifications while revealing how collaborative and similarity relationships reinforce these categorical boundaries. Furthermore, the analysis provides insights into network evolution mechanisms, showing how musical and social forces jointly shape the topology of artist interaction networks. These results have implications for music recommendation systems, historical musicology, and understanding cultural network formation more broadly.

The COSLAB effort has primarily concentrated on topological defect formation during phase transitions, but cosmological phase transitions present another significant observable: magnetic field generation. Phase transitions associated with baryogenesis—the preferential production of matter over antimatter—are theoretically predicted to generate helical (left-handed) magnetic fields. Laboratory studies of analogous processes offer crucial insights into helical magnetic field production mechanisms. The detection of such fields in the universe would provide invaluable constraints for both particle physics models and cosmological scenarios. This represents a complementary approach to studying early universe physics, linking laboratory experiments with astrophysical observations. Understanding the connection between phase transitions, matter-antimatter asymmetry, and magnetic field helicity could illuminate fundamental questions about the universe's evolution and the origin of cosmic magnetic fields observed today.

We investigate the quantum phase stability of a Bose-Fermi mixture confined in a quasi-one-dimensional optical lattice geometry, where bosons and fermions experience effective dimensional separation. The bosons, being heavier, are tightly confined to individual one-dimensional tubes, while lighter fermions retain mobility in the transverse directions, enabling inter-tube tunneling. Taking the @xmath0Yb-@xmath1Li system as our experimental reference, we map out the complete equilibrium phase diagram using exact Bethe ansatz solutions for the one-dimensional bosonic component. Our analysis reveals fundamental constraints on the phase structure imposed by the exact treatment of quantum correlations. For both attractive and repulsive Bose-Fermi interactions, transitions from the pure fermionic phase to any mixed phase with finite boson density are necessarily first-order, precluding continuous quantum phase transitions and leading to macroscopic phase separation in density space. In contrast, the transition from the pure bosonic phase to the mixed regime exhibits order-parameter dependence: it becomes second-order when fermions possess inter-tube hopping capability, but reverts to first-order under strict one-dimensional confinement of both species. These results provide critical insights for interpreting current experiments on @xmath0Yb-@xmath1Li mixtures and suggest design principles for engineering mixed-dimensional Fermi-Fermi systems with tunable mass imbalance in optical lattices.

We report *Spitzer Space Telescope* IRAC 3.6, 4.5, 5.8 and 8 μm and MIPS 24 and 70 μm observations of the 32 Orionis stellar group, a recently identified nearby young association located toward northern Orion. At a distance of approximately 93 pc, this proximity enables sensitive detection of circumstellar dust around member stars. With an estimated age of ~20 Myr, the 32 Ori group represents a critical evolutionary phase roughly corresponding to the epoch of terrestrial planet formation in our solar system, making it an ideal laboratory for studying debris disk evolution and planet formation processes. We present a comprehensive analysis of infrared excess emission attributable to circumstellar dust among confirmed group members, combining available optical photometry (Hipparcos, Tycho), near-infrared data (2MASS), and our *Spitzer* infrared observations. Our survey of 14 group members reveals that 4 objects exhibit statistically significant 24 μm excess emission exceeding 4σ above predicted photospheric levels (~20% excess): HD 35656 (A0Vn), HD 36338 (F4.5), RXJ0520.5+0616 (K3), and HD 35499 (F4). Notably, these objects show excess only at 24 μm, lacking shorter-wavelength infrared excesses. Additionally, two sources display 70 μm excess: HD 35656 and RXJ0520.0+0612, though the latter does not show corresponding 24 μm excess. The derived 24 μm disk fraction of 29±4% for the 32 Ori group is consistent with other associations of comparable age. Significantly, 32 Ori ranks as the young stellar group with the second-highest incidence of 24 μm excesses among groups without accreting T Tauri stars, trailing only the β Pictoris moving group. We model the observed infrared excesses using circumstellar dust disk models, constraining key parameters including dust mass, temperature, characteristic grain distance, and emitting area. Our analysis indicates that steady-state collisional evolution models can reasonably explain the observed dust masses for all excess sources.

We present a novel implementation of linear covariant gauges on the lattice utilizing a minimizing functional analogous to a spin-glass Hamiltonian with random external fields. This approach successfully addresses key challenges in previous implementations, particularly circumventing the no-go theorem established by Giusti (Nucl. Phys. B 498, 331, 1997). We perform numerical tests in four-dimensional SU(2) gauge theory to validate our method. Additionally, we provide preliminary measurements of the transverse gluon propagator for various values of the gauge parameter α, demonstrating the practical viability of our gauge-fixing procedure. Our results suggest this method offers a robust framework for studying gauge-dependent quantities in lattice gauge theory.

The direct detection of gravitational waves (GWs) from stellar-mass black hole binary coalescences by LIGO has confirmed compact binary coalescences (CBCs) as the most promising sources for ground-based interferometric detectors. However, the detection sensitivity of these instruments is significantly compromised by non-Gaussian and non-stationary noise transients, commonly referred to as "glitches." Understanding and mitigating the impact of these instrumental artifacts is crucial for improving CBC detection confidence and reducing false alarm rates. In this study, we investigate two important classes of transient noise artifacts that frequently contaminate detector data and mimic CBC signals: (1) sine-Gaussian glitches, parametrized by a central frequency @xmath0 and quality factor @xmath1, and (2) chirping sine-Gaussian glitches, which additionally incorporate a chirp parameter. We systematically analyze how template banks designed for CBC inspiral searches respond to these glitch families through matched-filtering analysis.
