These sections naturally map to @xmath5 integral lattice points within a @xmath1-dimensional simplex, providing a geometric interpretation of quantum states. We further develop this connection by employing local mirror symmetry techniques to relate @xmath0 quantum systems to configurations of type II D-branes at singularities of local Calabi-Yau manifolds. Detailed analysis of specific examples reveals rich geometric structures: the @xmath6 system corresponds to the mirror of an ALE space with @xmath8 singularity, while @xmath7 relates to a generalized conifold geometry. This framework opens new avenues for applying sophisticated tools from algebraic geometry and string theory to quantum information processing, potentially yielding insights into entanglement structures and quantum computational complexity through geometric invariants.

We present efficient theoretical tools for describing optical pumping of atoms by light propagating at arbitrary angles relative to an external magnetic field under intermediate buffer-gas pressure conditions. The pressure regime examined is sufficiently low to permit velocity-selective optical pumping (VSOP) while being high enough to induce significant collisional relaxation of both atomic velocities and spin states. These conditions are directly relevant to sodium atoms at approximately 100 km altitude, which serve as laser guidestars in adaptive optics systems for ground-based telescopes to compensate for atmospheric turbulence-induced aberrations. Our theoretical framework employs spin and velocity relaxation modes to characterize atomic distributions in both spin space (encompassing populations and coherences) and velocity space. We utilize cusp kernels to model velocity-changing collisions and represent optical pumping operators as sums of poles in the complex velocity plane. Simulations using these methods demonstrate excellent agreement with published experimental data and preliminary measurements from our laboratory, validating the approach for practical applications in atmospheric physics and astronomical imaging.

We investigate the propagation of gravitational perturbations in plane wave spacetimes, addressing whether these backgrounds exhibit tail-free evolution analogous to electromagnetic waves in such geometries. While Huygens' principle generically fails in curved spacetimes due to backscattering effects that produce tails lingering behind wavefronts, plane wave geometries represent exceptional cases where electromagnetic fields propagate sharply along null geodesics without tails. We construct the retarded Green function for metric perturbations in the Lorenz gauge and analyze the resulting evolution of generic initial data. Our analysis reveals a nuanced picture: first-order perturbations to all locally-constructed curvature scalars satisfy Huygens' principle and propagate without tails. However, gravitational tails do exist at the metric level, though with a remarkable constraint—they can only transform one plane wave spacetime into another plane wave spacetime locally. This result has important physical implications: a weak, localized beam of gravitational radiation traversing an arbitrarily strong plane wave background leaves behind only a mild perturbation to the background waveform, preserving its essential plane wave character. Crucially, the planar symmetry cannot be disrupted by any linear tail effect. These findings illuminate the unique propagation properties of gravitational waves in symmetric backgrounds and demonstrate that curvature-based observables maintain sharp propagation even when the metric itself develops tail contributions.

We present a novel approach for estimating the initial Lorentz factor of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) that does not rely on delayed early afterglow emission analysis. Our method exploits the temporal overlap between prompt emission and afterglow onset, allowing us to measure the Lorentz factor at the end of the prompt emission phase using established GRB jet dynamics relations. By incorporating the efficiency of converting explosion energy to radiation, we establish a connection between this measured Lorentz factor and the initial bulk Lorentz factor of the relativistic outflow. This framework enables the calculation of the corresponding rest-frame spectral peak energy. We apply this methodology to a sample of GRBs with known redshifts and well-constrained afterglow break times. Our statistical analysis reveals that the initial Lorentz factor distribution peaks at approximately @xmath0, with the majority of sources exhibiting values within the range @xmath1. The corresponding rest-frame peak energy distribution shows a maximum at @xmath2, predominantly occupying the interval @xmath3. These results provide important constraints on GRB jet physics and the energy conversion mechanisms operating in these extreme cosmic explosions. The tight distributions suggest a degree of uniformity in the initial conditions of GRB jets, while the spread reflects intrinsic variations in progenitor properties and environmental conditions. This approach offers a complementary technique to existing methods for characterizing the fundamental physical parameters of GRB outflows.

We present comprehensive third-order relativistic many-body perturbation theory calculations of Breit interaction corrections to fundamental properties of atomic @xmath0Cs. Our analysis encompasses corrections to ground and excited state energies, hyperfine-structure constants, off-diagonal hyperfine @xmath1 amplitudes, and electric-dipole matrix elements. We find that Breit corrections arising from electron correlations are of comparable magnitude to those at the Dirac-Hartree-Fock level, demonstrating the importance of treating the Breit interaction beyond the mean-field approximation. The impact of Breit corrections on the parity-nonconserving @xmath1 amplitude is evaluated, yielding a weak charge for @xmath0Cs consistent with Standard Model predictions within theoretical uncertainties. Additionally, we estimate the neutron skin correction to the parity-nonconserving amplitude at -0.2% with approximately 30% uncertainty, informed by recent antiprotonic atom measurements. This work extends our previous letter [Phys. Rev. Lett. (2000)] by providing detailed theoretical formalism, comprehensive numerical data, and refined analysis of parity violation measurements in atomic cesium.

We establish a fundamental connection between entanglement and quantum fluctuations in the context of quantum phase transitions. We demonstrate that the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, one of the most elementary measures of quantum fluctuations, serves as a powerful probe for detecting critical behavior in light-matter systems. Specifically, we investigate superradiant quantum phase transitions in the Dicke model, where an ensemble of two-level systems couples to a single-mode bosonic field. Through exact analytical calculations, we reveal a striking scaling behavior: the product of position and momentum uncertainties @xmath1 exhibits a divergence proportional to @xmath2 at the quantum critical point, where @xmath0 represents the number of two-level systems. This divergence directly reflects the entanglement structure between light and matter subsystems. We extend our analysis to the double quadrature Dicke model, where both quadratures of the electromagnetic field interact with independent sets of two-level systems, confirming the universality of our findings. Importantly, we establish a general scaling relation between entanglement entropy and Heisenberg uncertainty in critical regions, providing a conceptually simple yet physically profound diagnostic tool for quantum criticality. Our theoretical predictions are experimentally accessible in platforms such as ultracold atoms in optical cavities and circuit quantum electrodynamics systems, offering new pathways to probe and characterize quantum phase transitions through fundamental quantum mechanical principles.

Glycine (NH2CH2COOH), the simplest amino acid, represents a crucial target for understanding prebiotic chemistry in astrophysical environments. While previous searches have focused primarily on hot molecular cores without conclusive detections, we investigate the detectability of glycine in the cold pre-stellar core L1544, a low-mass star-forming region that may serve as a better analog for early Solar System chemistry. Recent observations of water vapor toward L1544 indicate that approximately 0.5% of grain mantle material has been desorbed into the gas phase, presumably through non-thermal processes such as photodesorption. We perform one-dimensional spherically symmetric radiative transfer modeling to predict glycine emission from L1544, assuming that glycine is co-desorbed with water and adopting a solid-phase abundance of glycine relative to water of 10−3. Our calculations demonstrate that several glycine rotational transitions in the 67-80 GHz frequency range exhibit peak brightness temperatures exceeding 10 mK under these conditions. This represents the first theoretical demonstration that glycine could reach detectable levels in cold pre-stellar cores, despite their low temperatures and densities compared to hot cores. The physical conditions in L1544—characterized by cold temperatures, relatively high densities, and ongoing grain mantle desorption—provide a favorable environment for preserving and detecting complex organic molecules. Our results suggest that cold pre-stellar cores like L1544 offer promising targets for glycine searches using current and near-future submillimeter instrumentation, particularly the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) Band 2 receivers. Successful detection would provide critical insights into the formation pathways of prebiotic molecules in environments analogous to the early Solar System and their potential role in the chemical inventory delivered to nascent planetary systems.

Chiral Perturbation Theory (ChPT) has proven remarkably successful in describing low-energy hadronic properties within the non-perturbative regime of quantum chromodynamics. ChPT predictions, subject to intensive experimental scrutiny, provide stringent tests of fundamental hadron properties, including electromagnetic polarizabilities. Despite this theoretical framework, significant discrepancies persist among existing pion polarizability measurements from various experiments (MARK II, VENUS, ALEPH, TPC/2γ, CELLO, Belle, Crystal Ball). Meson polarizabilities can be accessed through Compton scattering via the Primakoff reaction, offering a direct experimental probe. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of ChPT predictions for SU(3) meson electromagnetic polarizabilities and establishes their connection to Primakoff cross sections at kinematics relevant to planned Jefferson Lab experiments. By clarifying the theoretical framework underlying these measurements, we aim to resolve existing experimental tensions and guide future precision measurements of meson polarizabilities.

We develop a comprehensive framework for sensitivity analysis of linear programs (LPs) under uncertainty, where both objective coefficients and right-hand side parameters may be simultaneously perturbed within a compact, convex uncertainty set. This framework generalizes and unifies various existing approaches in LP sensitivity analysis while establishing connections to robust optimization and two-stage adaptive optimization methodologies. We focus on characterizing the minimum (best-case) optimal value @xmath0 and maximum (worst-case) optimal value @xmath1 over the uncertainty set. We analyze fundamental properties including finiteness, attainability, and computational complexity of these quantities. Our main theoretical contribution demonstrates that @xmath0 and @xmath1 can be reformulated as optimal values of two distinct but related copositive optimization problems. However, since these copositive programs are generally intractable, we develop tight conic programming relaxations—specifically, semidefinite programming approximations—that yield computable lower bounds for @xmath0 and upper bounds for @xmath1. We introduce methods for evaluating the approximation quality of these bounds and provide extensive computational validation on benchmark instances from the literature. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed bounds are remarkably strong in practice, consistently matching or exceeding the quality of existing results for special cases previously studied in the literature. The framework thus provides both theoretical insights and practical tools for comprehensive LP sensitivity analysis under uncertainty.

We systematically compare the accuracy of various equation-of-state (EOS) formulations by analyzing both theoretical total energy calculations and experimental pressure-volume measurements for H2O, Ne, Pt, and Ta. These materials span the complete compression range relevant to minerals and volatiles in Earth's interior. Our analysis demonstrates that the Vinet equation provides the most accurate representation across this range. We examine the physical origins underlying the different behaviors exhibited by various EOS formulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that residual analysis from EOS fits can serve as a sensitive tool for detecting subtle phase transitions. Applying this methodology, we identify a previously unrecognized change in the electronic structure of Ta at high pressures and suggest evidence for a possible new transition in H2O, illustrating the diagnostic power of systematic EOS comparison.

We investigate quasiparticle interference (QPI) induced by impurities in parent compounds of iron-pnictide superconductors using a phenomenological two-orbital four-band model combined with the t-matrix formalism. Our analysis reveals that QPI patterns exhibit strong sensitivity to the magnitude of magnetic ordering, which varies across different compound families. In the weak magnetic order regime, the local density of states (LDOS) oscillations display two-dimensional characteristics, consistent with standing wave patterns observed in BaFe2As2 systems. Conversely, for strong magnetic ordering, the spatial modulation of the LDOS is dominated by one-dimensional stripe structures, reproducing the nematic features observed in FeSe parent compounds. Both regimes preserve C4 rotational symmetry, while in-gap bound states emerge exclusively in the strong magnetic order case. We present corresponding QPI signatures in momentum space and demonstrate that the LDOS modulation patterns at finite energies arise from the interplay between the underlying electronic band structure and Fermi surface topology. Our results provide a unified framework for understanding the diverse experimental observations of impurity-induced phenomena in iron-based superconductors and highlight the crucial role of magnetic ordering strength in determining QPI characteristics.

We present results of an X-ray search for bona-fide and candidate brown dwarfs in the ρ Ophiuchi cloud cores using the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Our observations targeted two fields near the cloud center using the ACIS-I array, covering approximately 17' × 17' with ~100 ks exposure time. From a sample of 18 bona-fide and candidate brown dwarfs previously identified through infrared spectroscopy, we detected X-ray emission from 7 sources above the 99.9% confidence level, yielding a detection rate of approximately 40% for infrared-selected brown dwarfs in this region. For the four brightest X-ray sources, we performed spectral analysis and successfully fitted the data with a thin-thermal plasma model, yielding temperatures of 1-2.5 keV. We also observed significant temporal variability, including rapid flare events from two brown dwarfs, indicating dynamic coronal activity. For fainter or non-detected sources, we estimated X-ray luminosities or upper limits by assuming a 2 keV temperature and applying the empirical relationship between count rate and flux. The X-ray luminosities of detected sources range from 0.3-90 × 1028 erg s−1, with X-ray-to-bolometric luminosity ratios (Lx/Lbol) spanning 10−4 to 10−3. These values are remarkably similar to those observed in low-mass pre-main-sequence stars and dMe stars, suggesting a common physical mechanism. Our findings strongly support the hypothesis that X-ray emission from brown dwarfs originates from magnetic activity at their surfaces, analogous to the coronal heating processes observed in low-mass stars. This work demonstrates that brown dwarfs maintain sufficiently strong magnetic fields to generate significant coronal activity despite their substellar masses and cooler effective temperatures.

We present a general construction that associates abstract polytopes with Cayley graphs of symmetric groups. For any connected graph @xmath0 with @xmath1 vertices and @xmath2 edges, we construct a corresponding Cayley graph @xmath3 of the symmetric group @xmath4. This Cayley graph serves as the @xmath6-skeleton of a vertex-transitive simple polytope of rank @xmath2, which we call the *graphicahedron* @xmath5. This construction generalizes the classical permutahedron, which emerges as the special case when @xmath0 is a path graph. We investigate the symmetry properties of graphicahedra and provide detailed structural analysis for small graphs. The construction establishes new connections between graph theory, group theory, and polytope theory, offering a systematic framework for generating families of symmetric polytopes from combinatorial data.

We consider estimation procedures which are recursive in the sense that each successive estimator is obtained from the previous one by a simple adjustment. We propose a wide class of recursive estimation procedures for the general statistical model based on estimating equations and stochastic approximation methods. The recursive estimators are constructed using a step-by-step updating scheme that incorporates new observations sequentially. We establish conditions for strong consistency and asymptotic normality of these estimators under general regularity conditions. The results extend classical stochastic approximation theory to statistical estimation problems and provide a unified framework for analyzing recursive procedures in various models, including regression and time series contexts.

We investigate the statistical properties of a stochastic system described by a Langevin equation whose deterministic dynamics undergoes a saddle-node bifurcation. Near the bifurcation point, we demonstrate that relaxation trajectories exhibit critical behaviors in the weak-noise limit, despite the discontinuous jump in the deterministic solution's final state. Using a systematic singular perturbation approach, we develop a framework for analyzing the path probability measure that reveals the underlying mechanism: the critical phenomena originate from the neutral stability of the saddle point, which leads to divergent exit times. This theoretical formulation quantitatively captures the scaling properties and probability distributions observed in numerical simulations, providing a complete characterization of noise-induced criticality in systems near saddle-node bifurcations.

we present a reanalysis of four spitzer / irac observations at 3.6 and 4.5 μm of the primary transit of the warm neptune gj436b, employing advanced blind source separation techniques. these observations are crucial for characterizing the atmospheric composition of gj436b, a benchmark exoplanet in the transition regime between hot jupiters and smaller planets. previous analyses of these datasets reported significant inter - epoch variations in transit parameters, attributed to stellar variability, which raised concerns about reliably extracting an atmospheric signal. additionally, these earlier studies yielded discrepant results, motivating this independent reanalysis. our methodology employs independent component analysis (ica) applied to pixel - level light curves — time series extracted from individual detector pixels — within each photometric observation. this approach, previously validated on 3.6 μm transit observations of the hot jupiter hd189733b, operates under the sole assumption that instrumental and astrophysical signals are statistically independent. this assumption - minimizing framework provides enhanced objectivity relative to parametric detrending methods that rely on instrument - specific systematics models. the gj436b datasets analyzed here present greater challenges due to the planet's smaller size and the host star's lower luminosity compared to previous test cases. our findings substantially revise earlier conclusions: (1) we find no evidence for inter - epoch variations in orbital or stellar parameters; (2) we achieve photometric stability at approximately 10 ppm in the infrared; (3) transit depth measurements at both wavelengths agree within 1σ uncertainty. furthermore, we (4) detect a potential transit duration variation of approximately 80 seconds at 2σ significance — previously unreported in the literature — and (5) confirm the absence of transit timing variations exceeding 30 seconds. these results demonstrate improved consistency and precision, enabling more reliable atmospheric interpretation and highlighting the effectiveness of model - independent detrending approaches for challenging spitzer observations.

We introduce the **arithmetic site**, a novel algebraic geometric framework that establishes a profound connection between algebraic geometry and the non-commutative geometric approach to the Riemann hypothesis. Our central result demonstrates that a specific non-commutative space—the quotient of the adèle class space of Q by the maximal compact subgroup of the idèle class group—can be naturally identified with the set of geometric points of the arithmetic site over the tropical real numbers semifield. This quotient space was previously shown to encode the correct counting function needed to realize the complete Riemann zeta function as a Hasse-Weil zeta function. The arithmetic site exhibits several remarkable features. Its underlying topological space is given by the topos of functors from the multiplicative semigroup N* to the category of sets, revealing an intrinsic relationship between number theory and topos theory. The structure sheaf consists of characteristic one semirings, with global sections forming the semifield of tropical integers. A key dynamical aspect is that the natural action of R*+ on the adèle class space corresponds precisely to the action of Frobenius automorphisms on geometric points. Despite its countable combinatorial nature, the arithmetic site supports a continuous one-parameter semigroup of Frobenius correspondences, realized as sub-varieties of its square—itself a semi-ringed topos whose structure involves Newton polygons. We conclude by elucidating the deep relationship between the arithmetic site and the absolute point in non-commutative geometry, suggesting fundamental connections between these geometric frameworks and the distribution of prime numbers.

The _Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement_ (GUM) advocates using an effective number of degrees of freedom for calculating measurement uncertainty intervals. However, the GUM does not prescribe methods for calculating this quantity when (i) the measurand is vector-valued or (ii) errors in input quantity estimates are statistically dependent. While previous work has addressed vector-valued measurands with independent errors (_Metrologia_ **39** (2002) 361-369) and scalar measurands with dependent errors (_Metrologia_ **44** (2007) 340-349) separately, many practical measurement problems exhibit both features simultaneously. This paper extends these earlier analyses to develop a comprehensive method for determining effective degrees of freedom when the measurand is multidimensional _and_ input quantity errors are correlated. The resulting procedure provides an explicit, general framework that naturally reduces to simpler forms when appropriate constraints apply. The methodology is demonstrated through an example from radio-frequency metrology, where measured quantities are complex-valued and naturally represented as two-element vectors. This work fills an important gap in uncertainty analysis methodology, providing metrologists with practical tools for rigorous uncertainty evaluation in multivariate measurement scenarios involving correlated input quantities.

Polar ring galaxies represent unique laboratories for studying gas dynamics and mass distribution in galaxies with orthogonal rotating components. Contrary to conventional understanding that restricts stable polar structures primarily to early-type (E/S0) galaxies with depleted gas reservoirs, observations reveal their presence across diverse morphological types, including late-type and gas-rich dwarf galaxies. Three-dimensional spectroscopic techniques enable independent kinematic analysis of gaseous material in both the host disk and polar structures. The synergy between optical emission-line (H II region) and radio (H I 21-cm) observations provides the most comprehensive characterization of gas kinematics and underlying gravitational potential. This review synthesizes recent observational findings from combined optical-radio studies, emphasizing the kinematic properties of polar structures across different galaxy types and examining the direct dynamical interactions between gas components rotating in perpendicular planes, which offer crucial insights into galaxy evolution and dark matter distribution.

In cognitive radio networks (CRNs), efficient spectrum utilization is achieved by allowing secondary users (SUs) to opportunistically access licensed channels without interfering with primary users. A critical challenge in such networks is the rendezvous problem, where two SUs must establish communication by selecting a common available channel simultaneously in a distributed manner, without prior coordination or knowledge of each other's channel availability patterns. This paper addresses the blind rendezvous problem for two SUs operating under both spatial and temporal channel variation. Unlike existing approaches that primarily assume static channel conditions, we explicitly incorporate temporal dynamics of channel availability into our analysis. For synchronous systems in stable environments with static channel availability, we derive a time-adaptive rendezvous strategy that achieves optimal expected time-to-rendezvous (TTR). We then extend our framework to dynamic environments that more accurately model real-world CRNs where channel availability varies over time due to primary user activity. For dynamic settings, we first establish optimal strategies for two special cases and subsequently prove that our proposed strategy maintains asymptotic optimality in general dynamic scenarios. The time-adaptive nature of our approach allows SUs to adjust their channel selection strategies based on observed patterns, significantly improving rendezvous efficiency. Extensive simulation results validate our theoretical analysis and demonstrate superior performance compared to existing methods. We systematically investigate the impact of key system parameters on TTR, including the number of available channels, channel availability probabilities, the degree of environmental dynamics, and the presence of malicious intruders. Our findings provide practical insights for designing efficient rendezvous protocols in realistic CRN deployments.

Neutron scattering measurements are presented investigating magnetic correlations in the spin ice compound dysprosium titanate (Dy2Ti2O7) using an isotopically enriched sample to reduce neutron absorption. At zero field, no magnetic ordering was observed down to 50 mK, with diffuse scattering consistent with the expected disordered ground state of dipolar spin ice. Application of a magnetic field along the [111] direction (2 T) induced long-range magnetic order. In contrast, a field applied along the [110] direction produced an unusual coexistence of long-range ferromagnetic and short-range antiferromagnetic correlations, attributed to field-induced pinning of only half the magnetic moments. Magnetization hysteresis loops in both field orientations exhibited distinctive steps and plateaus, reflecting the complex magnetic response of this geometrically frustrated system. These results demonstrate the highly anisotropic behavior and field-tunable magnetic states characteristic of spin ice materials.

The utilisation of semiconductor materials as detectors and devices operating in high radiation environments, at future particle colliders, in space applications, or in medicine and industry, necessitates obtaining radiation harder materials. A systematic theoretical study has been performed investigating the interaction of charged hadrons with semiconductor materials and the mechanisms of defect creation by irradiation. The mechanisms of primary interaction of hadrons with nuclei of the semiconductor lattice have been explicitly modelled, and the Lindhard theory of partition between ionisation and atomic displacements has been considered. The behaviour of silicon, diamond, and some A@xmath0B@xmath1 compounds (GaAs, GaP, InP, InAs, InSb) has been investigated. The nuclear energy loss and the concentration of primary defects induced in the material bulk by unit hadron fluence have been calculated. The peculiarities of proton and pion interactions, as well as the specific properties of the semiconductor materials, have been identified. Results demonstrate material-dependent responses to hadron irradiation, with implications for radiation hardness in various applications. The theoretical framework provides quantitative predictions for defect formation rates and enables comparison of radiation tolerance across different semiconductor materials. *PACS*: 61.80.Az; 61.82.-d

The integral relations formalism, previously introduced for treating 1+2 reactions below breakup threshold, is extended to collision energies above the target breakup threshold. This generalized framework is applied using the adiabatic expansion method to describe 1+2 reactions. The approach is validated using neutron-deuteron breakup, where benchmark calculations exist for comparison. Applications include the @xmath1-wave collision between @xmath2He atoms and @xmath2He@xmath3 dimers above breakup threshold. The methodology incorporates soft-core two-body potentials combined with short-range three-body forces. Results for three-body recombination and collision dissociation rates are presented and compared with previous theoretical calculations, demonstrating the formalism's capability to handle complex few-body scattering processes above breakup threshold.

The random vortex world-surface model is extended to the gauge groups @xmath0 and @xmath1. Compared to the @xmath2 and @xmath3 models studied previously, which reproduce the infrared properties of the corresponding Yang-Mills theories on the basis of a simple vortex world-surface curvature action, new dynamical characteristics become important. In the @xmath0 case, an explicit dependence of the vortex effective action on the configuration of the abelian magnetic monopoles residing on the vortices emerges. In the @xmath1 case, a new "stickiness" contribution to the vortex action serves to drive the deconfinement phase transition towards the correct first-order behavior. These extensions demonstrate that the vortex world-surface model successfully captures essential non-perturbative features of non-abelian gauge theories beyond the simplest cases, incorporating monopole dynamics and proper phase transition characteristics for higher-rank gauge groups.

We report polar Kerr effect measurements in ultrathin films of Cr-doped Bi2Se3 (Bi2−xCrxSe3), a magnetically doped topological insulator. Spectroscopic measurements of the complex Kerr angle across photon energies of 0.7-6.5 eV reveal a distinctive resonant feature: a peak in the real component and zero crossing in the imaginary component of the Kerr signal. This resonance, located approximately 1.6 eV above the Fermi level, is attributed to spin-orbit coupling effects at an avoided band crossing. The resonant enhancement enables sensitive detection of magnetic properties in films as thin as 3-6 quintuple layers. Temperature and magnetic field-dependent measurements demonstrate a sharp magnetic transition at 6 K for 6 quintuple layer films, with magnetization vanishing below this thickness. These results agree with theoretical predictions regarding the thickness-dependent nature of magnetic exchange interactions in topological insulators, where the proximity to surfaces critically influences impurity spin coupling and long-range magnetic order.

We present new high-frequency radio continuum observations of the galaxy cluster hosting 3C129, obtained with the Sardinia Radio Telescope (SRT) in the 6000–7200 MHz frequency range. These observations represent the first systematic study of large-angular-scale emission from radio sources in this cluster at C-band frequencies. Using the recently commissioned ROACH2-based backend, we acquired full-Stokes image cubes covering a 1°×1° field centered on the radio galaxy 3C129, achieving an angular resolution of 2.9 arcminutes. We developed and applied advanced data reduction techniques, including modeling and deconvolution of the telescope beam pattern and correction for off-axis instrumental polarization using measured polarization beam patterns. Our total intensity imaging reveals 14 radio sources in the field, including the tailed radio galaxy 3C129 and the cluster-center source 3C129.1. Combining our high-frequency data with archival lower-frequency observations, we traced the synchrotron spectral variations along 3C129's radio tail. Under the assumption of equipartition magnetic field strength, we derived a radiative age of approximately @xmath3 Myr for the source. The tail's projected linear extent of 488 kpc, combined with the age estimate, implies supersonic motion of the host galaxy through the intracluster medium with a Mach number of @xmath4, consistent with ram-pressure stripping as the dominant mechanism shaping the radio morphology. Polarimetric analysis reveals significant linearly polarized emission from both 3C129 and 3C129.1. Notably, 3C129 exhibits exceptionally high fractional polarization levels reaching 70% in the faintest tail regions, where the magnetic field alignment is nearly parallel to the tail direction. This high polarization degree suggests ordered magnetic field structures preserved in the aged plasma and provides constraints on the magnetic field configuration in the tail. These results demonstrate the capability of the SRT for sensitive polarimetric studies of extended radio sources at high frequencies.

We present lattice QCD calculations of the static quark potential with two flavors of dynamical quarks using three different lattice spacings (a≈0.22, 0.16, and 0.11 fm). The simulations employ an RG-improved gauge action and tadpole-improved Sheikholeslami-Wohlert clover quark action on various lattice volumes at sea quark masses yielding mπ/mρ≈0.7-0.8. We analyze the scaling behavior of the Sommer scale r0 and examine dynamical quark effects on the potential, comparing results across different lattice spacings to assess continuum limit behavior.

The Kramers-Kronig relations provide fundamental constraints on linear response functions through causality, establishing exact equalities between real and imaginary parts. In contrast, Bode's 1937 relation between magnitude and phase of transfer functions yields an inequality rather than equality. This article elucidates this distinction through accessible examples, demonstrating that while Kramers-Kronig relations emerge from general causality requirements, Bode's relation incorporates additional constraints from minimum-phase systems. The inequality nature fundamentally arises from information delays inherent in combined physical-measurement systems. We show that excess phase shifts beyond Bode's minimum create the inequality gap, reflecting non-minimum-phase behavior from time delays, right-half-plane zeros, or measurement apparatus dynamics. These pedagogical insights clarify subtle distinctions between causality-based constraints in linear response theory.

We analyze the optimal release angle in shot put through progressively sophisticated models. The simplest textbook model, assuming horizontal ground-level release, predicts an optimal angle of 45°, contradicting measurements of elite athletes that consistently show release angles around 37°. By incorporating the athlete's release height above ground, our theoretical prediction decreases to approximately 42° for typical top-athlete parameters. However, when we account for empirical correlations between initial velocity, release angle, and release height—reflecting biomechanical constraints—our model predicts optimal angles around 37°, in excellent agreement with observed data. This demonstrates that biomechanical coupling between kinematic parameters is essential for understanding optimal throwing techniques in shot put.

A novel quantum communication protocol is presented that enables secure direct communication between two parties using entangled qubit pairs, eliminating the requirement for pre-shared secret keys. The protocol operates deterministically, ensuring that all transmitted qubits carry meaningful message information without necessitating qubit disposal. Security analysis demonstrates robust protection against both active and passive eavesdropping attacks, with a minimum detection rate of 25% for active intrusions. The protocol achieves optimal quantum efficiency of 1 bit per transmitted qubit, representing a significant advancement in quantum communication. This deterministic approach offers practical advantages over probabilistic quantum key distribution methods by maximizing information transfer while maintaining secure direct communication channels through quantum entanglement properties.

The ATLAS trigger system employs a three-level architecture designed to reduce the initial 40 MHz bunch-crossing rate to a manageable 200 Hz output rate suitable for offline processing and storage. At the LHC's nominal luminosity of @xmath0 @xmath1s@xmath2, the trigger must evaluate events every 25 ns, with approximately 23 simultaneous interactions per bunch crossing. This demanding environment requires sophisticated selection algorithms across all trigger levels to achieve the necessary event rejection while preserving physics signals of interest. The LHC startup in summer 2008 will begin at reduced luminosity (@xmath3 @xmath1s@xmath2) with fewer bunches than nominal operations, followed by a gradual ramp-up period. This evolution necessitates flexible trigger configurations that can adapt to varying beam conditions while maintaining physics sensitivity and satisfying detector operational constraints. This paper describes the preparation and implementation strategy for the ATLAS trigger menu during the initial data-taking period. We present our approach for deploying trigger selections from first collisions through the transition to nominal luminosity conditions. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate expected trigger rates, rejection factors, and physics performance across different operational scenarios, ensuring robust event selection throughout the commissioning phase and beyond.

Rapidly oscillating Ap (roAp) stars represent a crucial laboratory for investigating stellar atmospheric structure under conditions where atomic diffusion processes dominate chemical stratification. These pulsating chemically peculiar stars bridge our understanding of stellar evolution and magnetism with asteroseismology. We present results from a systematic spectroscopic survey targeting nine luminous Ap stars occupying a previously unpopulated region of the roAp instability strip in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. These targets were specifically selected based on their position in the colour-magnitude diagram as evolved main-sequence Ap stars theoretically capable of supporting rapid oscillations. Using the high-resolution UV-Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES) at the Very Large Telescope, we conducted the first dedicated spectroscopic search for rapid pulsations in this evolutionary phase. Our time-series observations achieved sensitivities sufficient to detect radial velocity variations with amplitudes @xmath0 and measurement precisions of @xmath1 in combined neodymium and praseodymium spectral lines—rare-earth elements that typically show enhanced pulsational amplitudes in roAp stars. Cross-correlation analyses corroborate our findings. Despite achieving excellent sensitivity, all nine targets yielded null detections. Magnetic field measurements were obtained for four stars, including three newly identified magnetic Ap stars, with at least six of the nine targets confirmed as magnetic. Significantly, four stars possess magnetic field strengths below @xmath2 kG. Current theoretical models suggest such field strengths may be insufficient to suppress convection in the envelope regions near magnetic poles in more evolved Ap stars—a process considered essential for the κ-mechanism operating in the hydrogen ionization zone to efficiently drive high-overtone pulsations. Our results suggest that more evolved roAp stars may require substantially stronger magnetic fields (>5 kG) to exhibit observable pulsations, though three targets with fields exceeding this threshold also showed no oscillations, indicating additional complexity in the pulsation excitation mechanism at later evolutionary stages.

Fair resource allocation has emerged as a fundamental challenge across diverse application domains, yet distributed algorithmic solutions for general α-fair allocations have remained elusive. This paper addresses weighted α-fair packing problems, a broad class encompassing utility maximization under linear constraints. We consider two formulations: maximizing weighted geometric and harmonic means for α > 1, and maximizing weighted products for α = 1, subject to constraints Ax ≤ b where A and b are non-negative matrices and vectors, and x represents allocation variables with positive weights. We develop the first distributed algorithm for general α-fair packing that achieves poly-logarithmic convergence time in problem size—specifically, O(poly(log n, log m, 1/ε)) iterations to reach an (1+ε)-approximate solution, where n and m denote problem dimensions. Our algorithm operates under a standard distributed computation model, employing simple local update rules without requiring global coordination or state maintenance. The algorithm is stateless, supporting asynchronous updates, self-stabilization, and incremental adjustments, making it particularly suitable for dynamic networked environments. Beyond algorithmic contributions, we provide comprehensive structural characterizations of α-fair allocations across the fairness spectrum. Our analysis reveals how allocation properties transition as α varies, with particular attention to limiting cases: α → 0 (proportional fairness), α → 1 (weighted Nash bargaining), and α → ∞ (max-min fairness). These theoretical insights illuminate fundamental trade-offs between efficiency and fairness, enhancing our understanding of resource allocation mechanisms. Our results bridge a significant gap between centralized optimization theory and practical distributed implementation, with implications for network resource management, cloud computing, and multi-agent systems requiring fairness guarantees.

We investigate an anyon model constructed on a toric honeycomb lattice, demonstrating that its ground states and low-lying excitations are equivalent to those of Kitaev's toric code model, with excitations obeying mutual semionic statistics. This framework provides enhanced geometric symmetry for understanding anyonic toric codes. Through Jordan-Wigner transformation, we establish a direct correspondence between this toric honeycomb model and a system of boundary-coupled Ising chains arranged on a square lattice. We prove the equivalence of these two models in their low-energy sectors, thereby showing how anyonic excitations can be realized within conventional fermionic systems. This mapping offers insights into implementing topological quantum systems using more accessible condensed matter platforms and illustrates the deep connections between topological and conventional quantum phases.

We investigate nonmagnetic impurity effects in MgB@xmath0 employing quasiclassical equations of superconductivity within a weak-coupling two-band model framework. Model parameters are determined to optimize agreement with experimental observations of MgB@xmath0. We calculate the quasiparticle density of states and specific heat across various interband impurity scattering strengths. Our results demonstrate that the density of states exhibits a gradual transition from a characteristic two-gap structure to a conventional single-gap structure with increasing interband scattering. Notably, we find that the excitation threshold displays non-monotonic behavior as a function of interband scattering strength. The calculated specific heat shows excellent quantitative agreement with experimental measurements on irradiated samples, validating our theoretical approach and providing insights into disorder effects in multiband superconductors.

Memristors represent promising candidates for neuromorphic computing, having successfully modeled spike-timing dependent plasticity and Hodgkin-Huxley neuronal dynamics. Their characteristic DC response—a current spike—suggests potential for direct neuron-memristor interfacing. We investigate this possibility by connecting spiking memristor networks to live neuronal cells. Our results demonstrate significant bidirectional interaction: upon connection to aqueous biological media, memristor spike morphology is fundamentally altered, with traditional voltage spikes suppressed. Current decay rates shift consistently with memristor state changes, while voltage-current relationships become increasingly linear. Most significantly, memristor spiking frequency increases in response to neuronal activity, indicating genuine communication between biological and electronic components. These findings establish that neurons can directly modulate memristor behavior without computational intermediation, opening pathways for hybrid biological-electronic systems. The observed changes in memristor dynamics—spike suppression, modified decay kinetics, and activity-dependent frequency modulation—collectively demonstrate functional coupling between living neural tissue and memristive devices, advancing prospects for bio-integrated neuromorphic architectures and neuroprosthetic applications.

We report high-frequency electron spin resonance (ESR) measurements on the quasi-one-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet KCuGaF6 with exchange constant J ≈ 103 K in pulsed high magnetic fields. When an external magnetic field is applied, a staggered field is induced perpendicular to the applied field due to the staggered g-tensor and Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya (DM) interaction with alternating D-vector. This system is therefore described by the quantum sine-Gordon model. We observed numerous resonance modes including soliton resonance, breather excitations, interbreather transitions, and two-breather excitations. The resonance conditions are excellently described by quantum sine-Gordon field theory with one adjustable parameter α. Complementary magnetic susceptibility measurements were performed with varying field orientations to investigate the relationship between the Curie term arising from the DM interaction and the proportionality coefficient α, providing crucial insights into the field-induced staggered field mechanism and validating the sine-Gordon theoretical framework.

We introduce a scheme for generating entanglement between two quantum dots using a plasmonic waveguide composed of metal nanoparticle arrays. The approach exploits dipole-induced interference effects combined with detection-based postselection to create robust entangled states. Notably, our scheme demonstrates resilience to plasmonic losses, enabling operation over extended nanoparticle array distances while maintaining high fidelity even in the presence of practical imperfections such as quantum dot energy level detuning. This represents a departure from previously proposed dissipative driven schemes for plasmonic entanglement generation. Our results challenge the conventional perspective that optical loss fundamentally limits quantum plasmonic applications. Instead, we demonstrate that appropriately designed protocols can generate robust entanglement despite inherent dissipation in metallic nanostructures. This loss-tolerant entanglement generation scheme provides a versatile and practical building block for quantum state engineering and control at the nanoscale, opening new avenues for quantum information processing in plasmonic architectures.

We investigate log-periodic corrections to scaling in the moments of energy dissipation rates in high Reynolds number (@xmath0) three-dimensional turbulence experiments. Building upon Zhou and Sornette's earlier work [Physica D 165, 94-125, 2002], we employ two complementary analytical approaches. First, we develop a canonical averaging variant utilizing a pairwise correlation-based rephasing scheme across different samples, corroborating previous findings. Second, we implement a local spectral method followed by ensemble averaging of multiple local spectra. This approach provides compelling evidence for log-periodic undulations, revealing over 20 harmonics of a fundamental logarithmic frequency @xmath1, associated with a preferred scaling ratio @xmath2. Our results strengthen the statistical significance of log-periodic corrections in fully developed turbulence, suggesting an underlying discrete scale invariance in the cascade process. These findings have important implications for understanding intermittency and multifractal properties in turbulent flows.

We propose a dephasing model inspired by Büttiker's fictitious probe approach, wherein infinite probes are uniformly distributed throughout the conductor. The dephasing rate is incorporated as an adjustable parameter for conductance calculations. Applying this framework to a one-dimensional delta function scatterer, we perform numerical simulations and demonstrate how dephasing mechanisms influence the computed conductance, revealing the interplay between quantum coherence loss and transport properties in mesoscopic systems.

We present a local routing algorithm that guarantees delivery in all connected graphs embedded on known surfaces of arbitrary genus @xmath0. This algorithm, which we call GFR (Genus Face Routing), represents a fundamental advance in understanding routing on non-planar surfaces and serves as a natural generalization of face routing (FR), the classical algorithm for planar graphs. The algorithm requires @xmath1 memory and completes in @xmath2 time, where @xmath3 denotes the graph size. A key requirement is access to a homology basis for the embedding surface. Our previous work demonstrated that standard face routing fails to guarantee delivery on positive genus surfaces, primarily due to the existence of homologically non-trivial closed walks that can trap the right-hand rule traversal. The central technical contribution of this paper is proving that such problematic walks do not impede GFR, leveraging an important mathematical property of homology bases established in Lemma [lem: connectfacebdr]. This work has significant implications for both practical applications and theoretical understanding. Face routing forms the foundation of most routing algorithms in modern two-dimensional ad hoc networks, where additional local techniques handle edge-crossings to enable FR application. Similarly, GFR should be viewed as a base algorithm suitable for adaptation to sensor networks deployed on surfaces in three-dimensional environments. Currently, no known efficient local routing algorithms with logarithmic memory exist for 3D ad hoc networks. From a theoretical perspective, our results suggest that the efficiency advantages of face routing stem from the codimension-one nature of graph embeddings in surfaces rather than planarity per se. This insight opens new directions for routing algorithm design in higher-dimensional and topologically complex environments.

We present an experimental and theoretical investigation of a toy geyser system that reproduces periodic eruptions observed in natural geysers. The apparatus consists of a water pool positioned above a heated reservoir, connected by a narrow tube. When heated, the system exhibits regular eruptions of hot water and steam, mimicking natural geyser behavior. We systematically measure eruption frequencies as functions of heating power and system height, finding strong dependencies on both parameters. A thermodynamic model is developed that successfully predicts inter-eruption intervals by considering heat transfer, pressure buildup, and vapor bubble dynamics in the confined geometry. We identify critical geometric and thermodynamic conditions necessary for geyser-like behavior, including minimum tube length and heating thresholds. The study is extended to a configuration with two reservoirs connected to a single tube, revealing complex coupling dynamics where eruptions in one reservoir can trigger eruptions in the other. This coupled system exhibits rich temporal behavior analogous to interacting natural geysers. Statistical analysis of the eruption patterns reveals correlations between reservoirs and non-trivial waiting time distributions. We develop a theoretical framework incorporating thermal and hydraulic coupling to explain the observed collective behavior, providing insights into both toy model dynamics and natural geyser systems.

We investigate the finite-size corrections to the equilibrium magnetization of an Ising model on random graphs with @xmath0 nodes and @xmath1 edges, where @xmath2. Through appropriate rescaling of the coupling constant, we ensure the free energy remains extensive. The system exhibits a mean-field type phase transition at the critical temperature of the fully connected Curie-Weiss model for all considered values of @xmath3. We analyze finite-size corrections using two complementary theoretical frameworks: a replica-based finite @xmath0 expansion and a cavity method approach. Our theoretical predictions are validated through extensive numerical simulations. The comparison reveals that the cavity-based analysis provides superior agreement with numerical results compared to the replica approach. These findings elucidate the role of graph connectivity in determining finite-size scaling behavior and demonstrate the effectiveness of different theoretical techniques for analyzing critical phenomena on random networks. Our results have implications for understanding phase transitions in systems with heterogeneous interaction structures. **Keywords:** Ising model, random graphs, finite-size effects, replica method, cavity method **PACS numbers:** 05.70.Fh, 64.60.aq, 64.60.an, 75.10.Hk

Mergers of neutron stars (NS+NS) or neutron stars with stellar mass black holes (NS+BH) eject a small fraction of matter at sub-relativistic velocities. Upon rapid decompression from nuclear density, this matter condenses into neutron-rich radioactive nuclei. The subsequent radioactive decay provides a sustained heat source for the expanding envelope, powering a brief optical transient with peak luminosity comparable to supernovae and emission predominantly in the UV-optical range. We present a simplified analytical model of this phenomenon, providing formulae to estimate transient parameters as functions of the uncertain physical properties of mergers. These events may be detectable in high-redshift supernova surveys as rapid transients, often appearing far from identifiable host galaxies due to neutron star kicks. We suggest that the enigmatic optical transients reported by Schmidt et al. (1998), which typically lack visible host galaxies, may be associated with such neutron star merger events, representing a new class of electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational wave sources.

We present K-band (2.1 μm) near-infrared observations of four nearby flocculent spiral galaxies that reveal previously undetected low-level spiral structure. These observations demonstrate that kiloparsec-scale organized spiral patterns are more common in flocculent systems than optical studies have indicated. Most notably, NGC 5055, the archetypal flocculent spiral, exhibits regular two-arm spiral structure extending to a radius of 4 kpc in the near-infrared, with a modest arm-interarm surface brightness contrast of 1.3. While the spiral features in all four galaxies are significantly weaker than those observed in grand design spirals, their presence is notable. These galaxies are unbarred and lack large, nearby companions, making them inconsistent with tidal interaction scenarios. The results support modal theory predictions that spiral density waves can be intrinsic disk phenomena rather than requiring external forcing. We discuss both intrinsic density wave mechanisms and alternative scenarios involving weak non-axisymmetric perturbations. These findings underscore the critical importance of near-infrared imaging in revealing large-scale dynamical processes and density wave phenomena that remain obscured at optical wavelengths by dust extinction and young stellar populations.

We investigate collective neutrino flavor transformations in the dense-neutrino region above a supernova core (@xmath0 km), where neutrino-neutrino refraction dominates. These interactions produce characteristic "spectral splits"—sharp divisions at energy @xmath1 that separate the neutrino spectrum into regions of nearly pure but distinct flavors. We demonstrate that when ordinary MSW resonances are absent in the dense-neutrino region, the split energy @xmath1 is uniquely determined by flavor-lepton number conservation. The physical mechanism generating spectral splits involves an adiabatic transition as neutrinos propagate from high to low neutrino-density regions. We analytically solve the equations of motion in the adiabatic approximation and derive explicit expressions characterizing this phenomenon for a generic configuration, providing physical insight into this collective flavor conversion process.

We investigate the nonlinear amplitude modulation of dust-acoustic waves in unmagnetized, weakly-coupled, fully ionized plasmas with electrons, positive ions, and charged dust particles. A nonlinear Schrödinger-type equation is derived to analyze oblique perturbations relative to the carrier wave direction. The stability analysis reveals that waves may become unstable depending on the angle θ between modulation and propagation directions. We obtain explicit expressions for instability growth rates and thresholds in terms of system dispersion relations. The angular dependence significantly affects the modulational instability characteristics, with stability domains varying between parallel and oblique propagation geometries. Our results demonstrate that the obliqueness parameter plays a crucial role in determining wave packet stability and the formation of localized structures. The conditions for existence of envelope solitons and other localized excitations are established, providing insights into nonlinear dust-acoustic wave dynamics in multi-component plasma systems.

We investigate chaotic dynamics in the planar 3-centre problem on small negative energy level sets. While previous work has established the existence of chaotic motions under the assumption that one centre is positioned far from the other two using Poincaré-Melnikov theory, we adopt a different approach by removing any positional constraints on the third centre. Instead, we treat the system as a perturbation of the 2-centre problem by assuming the third centre has very small intensity. For a dense subset of possible positions of the perturbing centre in the plane, we prove the existence of uniformly hyperbolic invariant sets containing both periodic and chaotic almost collision orbits. Our proof employs a general result due to Bolotin and MacKay, which requires the construction of appropriately defined chains of collision arcs. We accomplish this construction by utilizing the classical regularisation of the 2-centre problem and exploiting periodic orbits of the regularised system that pass through the third centre. This work extends previous results on chaotic dynamics in multi-centre problems by demonstrating that chaotic behavior persists under different perturbation schemes, specifically when the perturbation arises from intensity rather than distance.

We report measurements of hadron-hadron and direct photon-hadron correlations using the PHENIX experiment in d+Au and Au+Au collisions at @xmath3 GeV. Comparing jet characteristics between these collision systems enables investigation of medium-induced modifications to jet production. Hadron-hadron correlations reveal differences in jet widths and yields, providing insight into jet-medium interactions. For the first time, we measure direct photon-hadron correlations in both collision systems. Near-side associated yields are consistent with zero in d+Au and Au+Au collisions. Away-side jet yields show evidence of suppression for photon-triggered hadrons in Au+Au collisions, consistent with theoretical expectations for energy loss in the hot, dense medium created in heavy-ion collisions.

To address systematic verification under uncertain information within possibility theory, we investigate possibilistic computation tree logic (poctl), extending previous work on model checking of linear-time properties with possibility measures. This paper makes three key contributions to the theoretical foundations and practical applications of poctl. First, we analyze the expressiveness of poctl, demonstrating that unlike its probabilistic counterpart, poctl—particularly qualitative poctl—exhibits greater expressive power than standard ctl. We provide detailed equivalent expressions for basic ctl formulae using qualitative poctl formulae and present poctl formulae that cannot be expressed in ctl, including qualitative properties of repeated reachability and persistence. Second, we adapt the classical ctl model-checking algorithm to develop a comprehensive method for solving the poctl model-checking problem, with detailed analysis of its computational time complexity. Third, we illustrate the practical applicability of our approach through a concrete example demonstrating the poctl model-checking method. Our results establish poctl as a powerful framework for reasoning about systems with uncertain information modeled by possibility measures, bridging theoretical expressiveness with algorithmic feasibility. **Keywords:** computation tree logic; possibilistic Kripke structure; possibility measure; qualitative property; quantitative property.

We apply the complex-shift method to the Kuzmin-Toomre family of axisymmetric disc potentials to generate a comprehensive family of non-axisymmetric flat matter distributions. These distributions are subsequently superposed to construct non-axisymmetric flat ring configurations. Additionally, we derive triaxial potential-density pairs from these non-axisymmetric flat systems through appropriate coordinate transformations. The utility of the imaginary components of complex-shifted potential-density pairs is examined, demonstrating their physical relevance. These analytical solutions provide valuable tools for modeling non-axisymmetric galactic structures and studying their dynamical properties, extending classical disc theory to more realistic geometries relevant for understanding galactic kinematics and dynamics.

We investigate quantum loop effects of exotic heavy leptons on vector boson pair production in electron-positron annihilation. Closed analytic expressions for vector-boson self-couplings and differential cross sections are derived within two new-physics scenarios: (i) a fourth-generation Majorana-neutrino model and (ii) an E6-inspired model with sequential mirror isodoublets. These models are constrained by requiring their contributions to oblique electroweak parameters to be consistent with recent global fits to precision data. We systematically analyze the loop-induced deviations in the LEP2 cross section for W-boson pair production predicted by these constrained models. Our results demonstrate how heavy lepton multiplets can generate observable modifications to gauge boson self-interactions while remaining compatible with electroweak precision tests. The framework provides testable predictions for distinguishing between different heavy lepton scenarios through precise measurements of vector boson production processes at collider experiments.

This work investigates transport coefficients in non-equilibrium hot metals using the kappa distribution framework. We examine how the kappa parameter's temperature dependence characterizes non-equilibrium states, contrasting this approach with classical distribution functions. The generalized electrical conductivity is derived from the evolving kappa distribution, revealing deviations from equilibrium predictions at elevated temperatures. We revisit the correlation between material-dependent coefficients extracted from thermionic emission data and melting points, expanding the analysis to encompass additional thermionic emitter metals. Utilizing the Wiedemann-Franz law as a guiding principle, we formulate a novel generalized thermal conductivity expression consistent with the kappa distribution formalism. Applications to various metals demonstrate the framework's capability to describe transport phenomena in non-equilibrium conditions, providing improved agreement with experimental observations compared to traditional equilibrium-based models.

The Tunka-133 extensive air shower (EAS) Cherenkov array represents a significant advancement in cosmic ray detection, featuring approximately 1 km2 geometric acceptance area in the Tunka Valley, located 50 km from Lake Baikal. This facility enables comprehensive investigation of cosmic ray energy spectrum and mass composition across the energy range 1015 - 1018 eV using a unified methodological approach. The detector array comprises 19 clusters, each containing 7 optical detectors equipped with 20 cm photomultiplier tubes (PMTs). Operational since November 2008 with 12 clusters, full array commissioning was completed in September 2009. This paper presents the array architecture, data acquisition system, preliminary experimental results, and future development plans, including implementation of radio antenna networks and muon detector arrays for enhanced cosmic ray characterization capabilities.

This paper analyzes a three-species Lotka-Volterra model consisting of two prey and one predator species. We establish sufficient conditions on model parameters ensuring the existence of an invariant set and permanence of all species populations. Additionally, we derive conditions under which the predator population inevitably declines toward extinction. The dynamical behavior of the system is characterized through stability analysis, where we employ Lyapunov function techniques to prove global asymptotic stability of equilibrium solutions. Our results provide complete characterization of the long-term dynamics, distinguishing between coexistence scenarios and predator extinction, thereby contributing to understanding of predator-prey interactions in multi-species ecosystems.

We investigate continuous dynamics for a class of Petri nets where routing decisions at non-free choice places are governed by priority rules. The dynamics is formulated using policies that identify bottleneck places in the system. We establish a characterization of stationary solutions and prove their equivalence to the stationary solutions of the corresponding discrete dynamics. This result demonstrates fundamental consistency between discrete and continuous representations of this Petri net class. Through numerical experiments on an emergency call center case study, we demonstrate that pathological behaviors observed in discrete models—specifically oscillations around limits that differ from the stationary limit—are eliminated in the continuous Petri net framework. These findings suggest that continuous approximations provide not only computational advantages but also improved stability properties for analyzing systems with priority-based routing mechanisms.

We present a comprehensive theoretical investigation of the electronic structures and phonon spectra of the recently discovered isostructural superconductors LaNiBN (T_c = 4.1 K) and LaPtBN (T_c = 6.7 K) using first-principles calculations. Our analysis reveals substantially three-dimensional electronic structures, indicating metallic character in both the transition metal boride (NiB/PtB) layers and the intervening LaN layers. This three-dimensionality suggests that both structural components participate actively in the superconducting state. Through detailed ab initio phonon calculations, we demonstrate that nearly all phonon modes contribute to the electron-phonon coupling (EPC) mechanism, confirming the involvement of both layers in mediating superconductivity. For LaNiBN, we calculate an EPC strength λ = 0.52 and a logarithmically averaged characteristic phonon frequency ω_log = 376 K, yielding a theoretical T_c = 3.9 K in excellent agreement with experiment. In LaPtBN, the heavier Pt mass reduces the characteristic phonon frequencies by approximately 70% compared to the Ni modes in LaNiBN, resulting in a modestly enhanced λ = 0.56 and a 20% reduction in ω_log, producing an estimated T_c = 5.4 K, consistent with experimental observations. Importantly, our calculations reveal no signatures of magnetic instability in either compound, strongly suggesting conventional phonon-mediated superconductivity rather than unconventional pairing mechanisms. Furthermore, we identify a compelling systematic trend: T_c increases monotonically with boron height in the transition metal boride layers across both borocarbide and boronitride superconductor families, suggesting a potential avenue for T_c enhancement through structural optimization.

We investigate ultracold collisions of ground-state heteronuclear alkali dimers undergoing four-center chemical reactions of the type 2AB → A2 + B2 at sub-microkelvin temperatures. Through ab initio calculations of van der Waals coefficients and quantum scattering theory, we analyze how reaction dynamics depend on molecular species, temperature, external electric fields, and optical lattice confinement. Using a quantum threshold model, we systematically characterize reaction rate dependencies across parameter space. For fermionic species, we find LiNa exhibits minimal reactivity while LiCs shows maximal reactivity. Among bosonic dimers (LiNa, LiK, LiRb, LiCs, and KRb), LiK demonstrates the highest reactivity in zero field. Remarkably, all bosonic species converge to a universal reaction rate under sufficiently strong electric fields, suggesting field-induced suppression of species-dependent effects. Our results provide crucial insights for controlling ultracold chemistry through external parameters, with implications for quantum simulation and precision measurements using ultracold polar molecules in optical lattices.

We investigate the domain size dependence of piezoelectric properties in ferroelectric materials using a continuum Ginzburg-Landau model incorporating long-range elastic and electrostatic interactions. Microstructures with controlled domain sizes are generated by quenching from the paraelectric phase with biased initial conditions. Three distinct two-dimensional microstructures featuring different @xmath0 domain sizes are simulated. Electric fields are applied along both polar and non-polar directions, and the resulting piezoelectric response is computed as a function of domain size for each configuration. Our simulations demonstrate that piezoelectric coefficients increase with decreasing domain size, in agreement with recent experimental observations by Wada and Tsurumi (Brit. Ceram. Trans. **103**, 93, 2004) on domain-engineered @xmath1 single crystals. These results provide theoretical support for domain engineering strategies to enhance piezoelectric performance in ferroelectric materials.

We report high-precision gravity measurements using a LaCoste-Romberg D gravimeter during a total solar eclipse to investigate gravitational field effects. An observed anomaly (@xmath0) during the eclipse suggests possible gravitational shielding properties. The measurements aimed to detect variations in Earth's gravitational field potentially caused by the eclipse configuration. Our results indicate deviations from expected values, warranting further investigation into gravitational phenomena during solar eclipses and their implications for gravitational theory. PACS: 04.80.c, 95.10.g, 91.10, 04.80.n

We investigate the $A$-discriminant of toric varieties, reducing its computation to irreducible configurations and analyzing its behavior under variable specialization to zero. We characterize dual defect toric varieties using their Gale duals and provide a complete classification of dual defect toric varieties in codimension at most four. Our results contribute to understanding sparse discriminants and the geometric properties of dual defect varieties in the toric setting.

We investigate the tight packing of nematic polymers confined within a hard spherical cavity using a theoretical framework that combines continuum Frank elastic free energy with density-dependent contributions. Our model explicitly accounts for chain connectivity, distinguishing polymer nematics from simple liquid crystals. The free energy formulation captures the isotropic-to-nematic orientational ordering transition characteristic of polymer solutions. Through numerical solution of the coupled Euler-Lagrange equations for both director and density fields, subject to appropriate spherical boundary conditions, we map the spatial distribution of molecular orientation and polymer concentration. The physical configuration is critically determined by two key parameters: the spatial locations of the polymer chain termini within the confining sphere. By systematically varying these end-point positions and the sphere radius, we demonstrate that the system exhibits a rich variety of equilibrium configurations with distinct topological defect structures. This geometric frustration, arising from the competition between bulk nematic ordering, surface anchoring, and chain connectivity constraints, produces complex director field patterns and defect geometries unique to confined polymer nematics.

We have investigated the magnetoresistance properties of RuO2-based resistors (Scientific Instruments RO-600) in the temperature range 0.05-0.3 K under magnetic fields up to 8 T. The magnetoresistance exhibits a characteristic crossover behavior: initially negative around 0.5 T, transitioning to positive at higher fields. The negative magnetoresistance component shows strong temperature dependence, increasing dramatically at lower temperatures, while the positive component displays weaker temperature sensitivity. Zero-field resistance measurements below 50 mK reveal behavior consistent with variable-range-hopping (VRH) conduction mechanisms down to 15 mK. These findings demonstrate the reliability of RuO2-based resistors as practical thermometers for ultralow temperature applications, with validated performance extending to at least 15 mK, making them valuable tools for cryogenic temperature sensing in scientific instrumentation.

We investigate the induction of time-reversal and parity-violating electric dipole moments (EDMs) in quantum systems by radial magnetic fields.
