This exact solution enables a systematic expansion in @xmath2, bridging toward the extensively studied polymer case (@xmath3). We report results to order @xmath4, maintaining complete resummation over all orders in @xmath0. This work represents initial progress toward comprehensively solving the self-avoiding manifold problem, with potential implications for polymer physics. The approach demonstrates how exact solutions in limiting cases can provide pathways to understanding more complex physical systems.

We investigate the rectified transport of underdamped active noninteracting particles in asymmetric periodic potentials. While overdamped active particles exhibit unidirectional ratchet motion along the easy direction of substrate asymmetry, incorporating inertial effects reveals a richer phenomenology. We demonstrate that inertial contributions enable multiple reversals of the ratchet current, allowing particle transport against the substrate's natural asymmetry direction. The average velocity exhibits non-monotonic behavior as functions of both the friction coefficient and self-propulsion force, undergoing several directional reversals. This inertia-induced phenomenon provides a novel mechanism for particle separation: by appropriately tuning system parameters, active particles with distinct self-propulsion strengths can be directed along different trajectories. Our findings establish underdamped dynamics as a crucial control parameter for manipulating active matter transport and offer practical strategies for sorting and separating active particles based on their intrinsic motility properties.

We study the behavior of quadruple points in generic regular homotopies of immersions of closed orientable surfaces into three-dimensional space. Building upon previous work establishing that the number mod 2 of quadruple points is a regular homotopy invariant, we investigate how this invariant transforms under the action of diffeomorphisms of the surface. For a generic immersion @xmath5 and a diffeomorphism @xmath6 such that @xmath2 and @xmath7 are regularly homotopic, we establish an explicit formula relating @xmath4 to the induced map @xmath9 on the first homology group @xmath11, the genus @xmath12 of the surface, and the orientation character @xmath13 of the diffeomorphism. This result provides a complete characterization of the quadruple point invariant under the mapping class group action, connecting topological properties of surface diffeomorphisms with the geometry of immersions.

Simulations are performed at three pion masses: @xmath2, @xmath3, and @xmath4. Using chiral perturbation theory to extrapolate from the lattice quark masses to the physical point, we obtain a scattering length of @xmath6, showing good agreement with experimental results. This fully-dynamical lattice QCD study demonstrates the successful application of finite-volume techniques to two-hadron scattering and validates theoretical predictions for low-energy pion-kaon interactions.

We analyze brane inflation models in light of the WMAP five-year data release, examining their consistency with updated cosmological constraints. While the five-year results maintain the preference for a red-tilted primordial power spectrum at two standard deviations—consistent qualitatively with three-year data—the spectral index shows a quantitatively higher value. This shift has significant implications for brane inflation scenarios. Our analysis reveals that the KKLMMT (Kachru-Kallosh-Linde-Maldacena-McAllister-Trivedi) model remains viable at the one standard deviation level when confronted with these new constraints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the stringent fine-tuning requirements on the parameter @xmath0, previously problematic for the model's naturalness, are substantially relaxed when considering the two standard deviation confidence region, improving the model's theoretical appeal and reducing the severity of fine-tuning concerns.

We investigate the ultraviolet contributions to the quark determinant in lattice QCD through effective Wilson loop models. Complete Dirac spectra are computed for extensive ensembles of SU(3) gauge configurations at β = 6.0 on 64, 84, and 104 lattices, enabling the first systematic analysis of volume dependence in the effective loop action. We establish connections to the hopping parameter expansion in the heavy quark regime and perform comparative studies of computational methods for extracting the quark determinant. Specifically, we evaluate the relative efficiency and accuracy of Lanczos diagonalization versus stochastic estimator techniques across configuration ensembles. Our results demonstrate that while both approaches yield consistent determinations of the quark determinant, they exhibit distinct advantages depending on the physical regime and lattice volume. The volume scaling behavior of the effective action coefficients provides insights into the ultraviolet structure of the fermionic determinant and validates truncated loop representations for practical simulations.

Background:** Accurate estimation of disease severity during influenza outbreaks is essential for guiding public health interventions and resource allocation. Direct measurement of case-fatality ratios (CFR), intensive care unit (ICU) admission rates, and hospitalization rates is challenging due to incomplete surveillance, ascertainment biases, and fragmented data sources. **Methods:** We developed and applied Bayesian evidence synthesis methods to coherently integrate multiple surveillance data streams and estimate age-specific case-severity risks across three waves of the 2009 A/H1N1 influenza pandemic in England. The complex probabilistic framework accounts for under-ascertainment, reporting delays, and biases inherent in surveillance systems. We extended previous analyses of the first two pandemic waves (2009) to include the third wave during the 2010/2011 season, adapting the model to accommodate evolving surveillance infrastructure. Two analytical approaches were compared: (a) a two-stage sequential analysis using posterior distributions from waves 1-2 as prior information for wave 3, and (b) a unified one-stage model simultaneously analyzing all three waves. **Results:** Both approaches yielded consistent findings. First, case-severity risks exhibited a characteristic U-shaped age distribution, with elevated risks in young children and older adults across all waves. Second, infection attack rates showed distinct age-specific temporal patterns: school-age children experienced the highest attack rates during waves 1-2, while adults over 25 years demonstrated increasing attack rates from wave 2 to wave 3. Third, overall case-severity appeared to increase across successive waves when averaged across age groups. **Conclusions:** Bayesian evidence synthesis provides a rigorous framework for estimating epidemiological parameters from imperfect surveillance data. The observed increase in aggregate severity across waves may partially reflect shifts in the age distribution of infected individuals rather than changes in intrinsic pathogen virulence. These findings demonstrate the importance of age-stratified severity assessments and highlight how temporal changes in population susceptibility patterns can influence apparent disease severity during multi-wave pandemics.

We investigate optimal dynamics in infinite population evolution models with general symmetric fitness landscapes. The identification of optimal evolutionary trajectories is complicated by sharp transitions resembling shock waves in evolution dynamics, occurring even with smooth fitness landscapes such as the commonly used quadratic fitness function. We derive exact analytical solutions for discontinuous dynamics in the large genome length limit. For fixed fitness landscapes, we determine optimal mutation rates that maximize evolutionary efficiency. Our results demonstrate that single-peak fitness landscapes yield the fastest dynamics for transferring the vast majority of the population from initial to final sequence neighborhoods. These findings provide fundamental insights into evolutionary optimization and the relationship between fitness landscape topology and population dynamics in sequence space.

We present a comprehensive multiwavelength analysis of the reddening properties and star formation history of 19 starburst galaxies using spectroscopic data spanning 0.12–2.2 μm and new near-infrared (J, H, K band) photometry of their central starburst regions. Our investigation reveals a wavelength-dependent differential reddening effect between stellar continuum and ionized gas emission. While infrared-derived reddening values for stellar continuum and ionized gas show good agreement, a significant divergence emerges at shorter wavelengths. Specifically, in the ultraviolet regime, the mean optical depth of dust obscuring stellar populations is only ~60% of that affecting nebular gas emission. This differential reddening cannot be explained by uniform dust screen models and suggests that UV-bright stellar populations and ionized gas occupy distinct spatial distributions. We propose a foreground clumpy dust geometry with different covering factors for gas and stars to reconcile these observations. This configuration allows UV photons from young stars to partially escape through dust-free sightlines while ionizing radiation remains more heavily attenuated. By combining reddening-corrected UV, optical, and infrared data from all sample galaxies, we construct a "template starburst spectrum" that serves as a diagnostic tool for investigating star formation history. Spectral synthesis modeling of this template indicates ongoing star formation at approximately constant rates over the past 1–2 × 107 years, consistent with supernova rate estimates derived from [FeII] emission line luminosities in the infrared. The stellar population analysis reveals complexity beyond simple continuous star formation. At least two, and likely more, intermediate-age populations (ages ~2 × 108 years) contribute significantly to optical and near-infrared emission. Conversely, populations older than 1–2 × 109 years make negligible contributions to the integrated spectrum. This age distribution points toward episodic star formation over the past 109 years, with historical star formation rates comparable to or exceeding current values. Our synthetic stellar population models employ a Salpeter initial mass function (IMF) with slope α = 2.35 over the mass range 0.1–100 M☉. These models successfully reproduce multiple observational constraints, including the spectral energy distribution of the template spectrum, hydrogen recombination line equivalent widths, and mass-to-light ratios. Importantly, our data show no evidence requiring either high-mass truncation or low-mass deficiency in the IMF of starburst galaxies, supporting the universality of the Salpeter IMF across different star-forming environments. These results have important implications for interpreting integrated light from unresolved starburst systems and understanding the physical conditions driving intense star formation activity.

The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve is a fundamental tool for evaluating the classification accuracy of continuous diagnostic tests. While the partial area under the ROC curve (pAUC) serves as a widely accepted summary measure offering generality and probabilistic interpretability, its extension to time-to-event data presents unique challenges in biomarker evaluation for disease detection over time. This paper proposes novel nonparametric estimators for time-dependent pAUC that feature closed-form expressions and computational efficiency without relying on trapezoidal approximation rules. We establish the asymptotic properties of these estimators as gaussian processes and derive explicit variance-covariance function estimates, facilitating the construction of valid confidence intervals for statistical inference. The finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology is comprehensively evaluated through extensive simulation studies, demonstrating robust behavior across various scenarios. We illustrate the practical utility of our approach by analyzing CD4 cell counts as predictors of survival time in the AIDS Clinical Trials Group (ACTG) 175 study. Furthermore, we extend the framework to enable comparative inference between time-dependent pAUCs across patient subgroups, specifically contrasting patients with and without prior antiretroviral therapy. The proposed methods provide researchers with accessible and statistically rigorous tools for evaluating time-dependent biomarker performance in clinical applications.

Astronomy has historically driven civilization's advancement through both conceptual frameworks and practical applications derived from celestial observations. In modern times, space sciences have served as the foundational engine for space technology development, fundamentally shaping contemporary society. However, current trends demonstrate a declining emphasis on science within space programs, prioritizing commercial and applications-driven approaches over fundamental research. This shift threatens societal autonomy in space-related matters that increasingly affect daily life on Earth. Reversing this trend is essential to ensure that modern societies maintain independent capabilities and decision-making authority in space sciences and technologies, preserving the scientific foundation necessary for continued innovation and self-determination in an era where space-based systems are integral to global communication, navigation, and resource management.

We investigate the origin of large-scale cosmic ray anisotropy observed at TeV energies through a modified Compton-Getting effect in magnetized flows from aged supernova remnants. Our model identifies an optimal energy scale for anisotropy detection and relies on two fundamental assumptions: cosmic ray propagation governed by Kolmogorov turbulence and particle transport dominated by stellar winds from progenitor stars. The framework predicts characteristic energy-dependent behavior: reduced anisotropy amplitude at lower energies resulting from incomplete velocity field sampling, and suppression at higher energies due to enhanced diffusive smearing. This interpretation provides a self-consistent explanation for the observed @xmath0 TeV anisotropy and offers testable predictions for multi-energy observations of cosmic ray arrival directions.

We propose a novel approach to image segmentation based on the eigenvalue problem of an anisotropic diffusion operator, where the diffusion matrix is constructed adaptively from features of the input image. The eigenfunctions of this operator and the projection of the input image onto selected eigenspaces effectively capture essential structural information and salient features present in the image. A particularly advantageous property of our model is that, for a broad class of input images, the leading eigenfunctions exhibit piecewise constant behavior, making them naturally suited for image segmentation, edge detection, and related vision tasks. We establish theoretical connections between our continuous eigenvalue formulation and the algebraic eigenvalue problems arising in discrete spectral clustering methods commonly employed in image analysis. This relationship provides deeper theoretical insight into spectral segmentation algorithms and facilitates the development of more efficient numerical implementations with rigorous mathematical foundations. Unlike energy-minimization approaches such as geodesic active contours, our method requires no initial guess or manual initialization, enhancing its robustness and ease of use. Furthermore, the multi-scale characteristics emerge naturally from the anisotropic diffusion operator itself, eliminating the need for solving eigenvalue problems across multiple resolution levels. For numerical implementation, we develop a finite element scheme incorporating an adaptive mesh refinement strategy specifically designed for anisotropic structures. Our computational experiments demonstrate that this adaptive approach yields significantly more accurate eigenfunctions compared to uniform mesh discretizations. Through extensive numerical examples, we examine several interesting theoretical and practical features of the proposed model, including its behavior on various image types, computational efficiency, and potential applications in computer vision and image processing tasks.

We investigate the magnetic properties of isolated mesoscopic metallic grains, demonstrating that electron-electron interactions can be effectively described by a simple interaction Hamiltonian containing only three coupling constants: charging energy, exchange interaction, and superconducting pairing. This universal description requires large Thouless conductance, ensuring negligible sample-to-sample fluctuations in coupling constants. Nevertheless, thermodynamic properties remain sample-specific due to mesoscopic fluctuations in the single-particle spectrum. For grains composed of materials near the ferromagnetic instability threshold, we find dramatically enhanced mesoscopic magnetization fluctuations. The system exhibits multi-stability, where the free energy landscape as a function of magnetization develops numerous local minima. We develop a statistical theory for characterizing these minima and establish universal scaling properties governing their distribution. These scaling laws describe how the density and depth of metastable states depend on system parameters and grain size. Our numerical simulations confirm the predicted scaling behavior and reveal the complex energy landscape characteristic of mesoscopic Stoner instability. This work provides a framework for understanding magnetic bistability and sample-specific magnetic properties in nanoscale ferromagnetic systems, with implications for magnetic memory applications and quantum dot magnetism.

We investigate the non-perturbative properties of N=1 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory through numerical lattice simulations, focusing on the spectrum of bound states and the emergence of supersymmetry in the continuum limit. Using improved lattice techniques at fine lattice spacing, we compute the masses of key particles including the gluino-glue state, mesonic states, and scalar glueballs with unprecedented statistical precision and enhanced control over systematic effects such as finite volume artifacts and lattice discretization errors. Our results represent a significant advancement over previous lattice studies in terms of both statistical accuracy and systematic uncertainty control. Within the combined statistical and systematic error bars of our calculations, we observe that the masses of fermionic and bosonic bound states are compatible with forming degenerate supermultiplets, as required by unbroken supersymmetry. This mass degeneracy provides strong evidence that supersymmetry is preserved in the continuum limit without spontaneous breaking, contradicting earlier lattice investigations that suggested possible supersymmetry breaking. These findings have important implications for understanding the non-perturbative dynamics of supersymmetric gauge theories and their potential role in physics beyond the Standard Model.

We investigate the Klein-Gordon (KG) equation through a five-dimensional space-time framework, demonstrating that this approach provides new insights into relativistic quantum mechanics. We explicitly show that the KG equation in flat space-time admits a consistent probabilistic interpretation with positively defined probability density, addressing long-standing concerns about negative probabilities. However, we find that this probabilistic interpretation lacks covariance under Lorentz transformations. In the non-relativistic limit, our formalism naturally reduces to the standard Schrödinger equation, ensuring consistency with non-relativistic quantum mechanics. The 5D perspective reveals alternative interpretations of the KG equation and their corresponding non-relativistic limits. As a concrete application, we apply our framework to analyze hydrogenic spectra and calculate the canonical partition function of the hydrogen atom. This five-dimensional approach offers a unified perspective bridging relativistic and non-relativistic quantum theory while clarifying foundational issues in the interpretation of the Klein-Gordon equation.

This paper presents a comprehensive review of the Very Large Array (VLA) 74 MHz system, developed through a collaboration between the Naval Research Laboratory and the National Radio Astronomy Observatory and commissioned in 1998. Operating at 73.8 MHz, this low-frequency capability represents a significant advance in radio astronomy, offering unprecedented sensitivity (approximately @xmath0) combined with angular resolutions ranging from 25" on standard VLA baselines to 12" when extended to include the Pie Town antenna of the Very Long Baseline Array. The primary technical challenge at these frequencies stems from ionospheric phase fluctuations, which fundamentally influence observing strategies and data calibration approaches. We describe two distinct calibration methodologies developed to address varying ionospheric conditions. The first, an **angle-invariant calibration strategy**, applies when observing restricted fields of view or during periods of exceptionally quiescent ionospheric conditions—specifically when the ionospheric isoplanatic patch size exceeds the field of view. This approach employs a single phase correction per antenna, typically derived through self-calibration, analogous to techniques used at higher radio frequencies. The second, a **field-based calibration strategy**, becomes necessary for wider fields of view or more typical ionospheric conditions when the isoplanatic patch size is smaller than the observed field. This innovative approach models the ionosphere above the array using Zernike polynomials, allowing phase corrections to vary spatially across the field of view. We present observational results demonstrating both calibration strategies. Images of moderately strong 3C catalog sources exemplify routine angle-invariant calibration and illustrate typical data quality. Flux density measurements of sources with well-established low-frequency spectra confirm that the VLA 74 MHz flux scale is stable to within a few percent, with absolute flux densities referenced to the Baars et al. value for Cygnus A reliable to at least 5%. Additionally, we present a wide-field image constructed using field-based calibration, demonstrating the detection of hundreds of weaker sources in fields without dominant bright objects. Beyond calibration, we address other practical considerations unique to low-frequency observations, including radio frequency interference excision techniques and wide-field imaging methodologies that differ substantially from higher-frequency practice. The hardware implementation, system performance characteristics, and operational procedures are thoroughly documented. This work provides both a practical guide for observers using the VLA 74 MHz system and a valuable reference for the design and operation of emerging low-frequency radio telescopes worldwide. The lessons learned from this system—particularly regarding ionospheric calibration strategies and wide-field imaging—offer important insights for next-generation instruments operating in this challenging but scientifically rich frequency regime.

We develop a coordinate space quasi-particle random phase approximation (QRPA) formalism, extending the RPA model of Shlomo and Bertsch to open-shell nuclei by incorporating pairing correlations and continuum coupling. Applying this framework to @xmath0Sn, we demonstrate that pairing correlations substantially affect low-lying excitation modes, while their influence on giant resonances remains minimal. Our analysis reveals that the impact of pairing correlations on low-lying collective modes exhibits parity dependence. This coordinate space approach provides an effective tool for studying nuclear excitations in open-shell systems where both pairing and continuum effects play crucial roles in determining the collective properties of nuclei.

We report the discovery of broad Wolf-Rayet (WR) emission features in the Multiple Mirror Telescope (MMT) spectrum of the northwest component of I Zw 18, the most metal-poor blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxy known. Two characteristic broad WR bumps are detected at wavelengths λ≈4650 Å and λ≈5800 Å, indicating the presence of both nitrogen-sequence (WN) and carbon-sequence (WC) Wolf-Rayet stars. From the luminosities of the broad He II λ4686 and C IV λ5808 emission lines, we derive total numbers of 17±4 WN stars and 5±2 WC stars. The derived WR-to-O star number ratio of N(WR)/N(O)≈0.02 is in satisfactory agreement with predictions from massive stellar evolution models incorporating enhanced mass-loss rates. While the WC stars can contribute to the observed nebular He II λ4686 emission, the measured line intensity exceeds model predictions by a factor of several, suggesting that additional sources of hard ionizing radiation (λ<228 Å) are required to explain the observed emission.

We present security proofs for a quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol based on encoding in finite high-dimensional Hilbert spaces. This protocol extends Bennett and Brassard's original two-basis, two-state encoding to a multi-basis, multi-state framework. We analyze the mutual information between legitimate parties and an eavesdropper, along with the error rate, as functions of the Hilbert space dimension. Our analysis considers both optimal incoherent and coherent eavesdropping attacks. We derive upper bounds on the tolerable error rate for the legitimate parties to ensure unconditional security against these eavesdropping strategies. The security thresholds are computed as functions of the dimensionality of the encoding space. Additionally, we incorporate realistic noise models accounting for detector imperfections. Our results demonstrate that high-dimensional encoding can provide enhanced security margins and improved noise tolerance compared to conventional two-dimensional protocols, offering practical advantages for implementing secure quantum communication systems.

We investigate quantum tunneling through an oscillating delta-function barrier by exploiting the system's time periodicity. The time-dependent Schrödinger equation is transformed into an infinite matrix equation, which we solve analytically using Toeplitz matrix techniques to reduce it to a tractable @xmath0 matrix form. Analysis of the frequency-dependent transmission amplitudes reveals a novel characteristic time scale governing the tunneling dynamics, distinct from the Büttiker-Landauer traversal time. We present a detailed comparison and establish the relationship between these two fundamental time scales, providing new insights into time-dependent quantum tunneling phenomena.

We demonstrate a proof-of-principle implementation of hybrid quantum-classical simulation for strongly correlated fermion systems in the thermodynamic limit. Using a two-site dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework, we map the Hubbard model onto a self-consistent quantum impurity problem. This approach yields a minimal representation requiring only four qubits to encode the impurity degrees of freedom, supplemented by a single ancilla qubit for measurement operations. The self-consistency loop characteristic of DMFT is handled classically, while the quantum processor solves the impurity problem—a task intractable for classical computers in more complex scenarios. We present a detailed protocol for implementing this hybrid algorithm using superconducting qubit architectures, demonstrating that meaningful simulations of correlated electron systems are achievable with current and near-term quantum hardware. This work establishes a practical pathway toward quantum advantage in condensed matter physics using noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

We investigate the full counting statistics (FCS) of charge transport in interferometers for chiral Majorana fermions, focusing on systems with two incoming and two outgoing Dirac fermion channels. For non-interacting systems, the FCS is determined by the scattering matrix relating outgoing to incoming Dirac fermions. We derive explicit expressions for higher-order current correlations in a modified Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer configuration. Analysis of the cumulant-generating function reveals a remarkable factorization property: unit-charge transfer processes decompose into two independent half-charge transfer processes, equivalently described as two independent electron-hole conversion processes. Through combined analytical calculations and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that this factorization holds universally for arbitrary scattering matrices, establishing it as a fundamental property independent of specific interferometer geometries. This result provides new insights into fractional charge transport in Majorana-based quantum devices.

We investigate the hadronic matrix elements of local four-quark operators relevant for neutrinoless double beta decay processes in nuclei and hyperons within the MIT bag model framework. These operators induce charge changes of two units (@xmath0) and violate lepton number conservation. Using a low energy effective Lagrangian, we calculate the matrix elements without relying on the standard factorization approximation commonly employed for four-quark operators. As a concrete application, we compute the decay amplitude and transition rate for the process @xmath1, which violates lepton number by @xmath2. We present a detailed comparison between results obtained using the full calculation and those derived from the factorization approach, highlighting the differences and assessing the validity of the approximation. This study provides insights into the hadronic aspects of lepton number violating processes in baryon systems.

We analyze the left-right vector-axialvector correlator using spectral functions from hadronic τ decays measured by ALEPH. By computing low-order spectral moments with appropriately chosen weight functions that suppress duality violations, we extract fundamental QCD chiral symmetry breaking parameters. We estimate systematic uncertainties from quark-hadron duality violations using resonance parametrizations constrained by short-distance operator product expansion requirements. Our pinched-weight analysis yields precise determinations of the effective chiral low-energy constants L10 and C87, which characterize the chiral symmetry breaking pattern, along with dimension-six and dimension-eight condensate contributions in the operator product expansion. The method demonstrates excellent control over non-perturbative effects and provides stringent tests of chiral perturbation theory predictions against experimental data from τ hadronic decays.

We investigate coexisting fluctuations toward multiple ordered states in strongly correlated electronic systems using a non-linear sigma model framework. Motivated by observations in underdoped cuprate superconductors showing simultaneous short-range charge order and superconducting fluctuations, we develop a theoretical description accommodating @xmath0 competing orders. We calculate the transverse thermoelectric transport coefficient in the analytically tractable large-@xmath0 limit, quantifying the contribution of order parameter fluctuations to the Nernst signal. Our findings remain applicable at high temperatures for finite @xmath0 and demonstrate consistency with prior Gaussian superconducting fluctuation models. This work provides a unified framework for understanding how competing orders manifest in thermoelectric transport, offering insights into the complex phase diagrams of cuprate superconductors and other strongly correlated materials exhibiting multiple proximate ordered phases.

Zero forcing is a combinatorial game played on graphs where vertices are colored black with the objective of minimizing "unforced" moves needed to color all vertices. The resulting zero forcing number provides an upper bound for the maximum nullity of matrices associated with the graph. We introduce a novel variation of the zero forcing game designed to bound the maximum nullity of graph-associated matrices having exactly @xmath0 negative eigenvalues. This variant constrains the possible number of positive eigenvalues for such graphs, enabling the construction of lower bounds for a graph's inertia set. Our approach extends classical zero forcing techniques to incorporate spectral information about eigenvalue signs, providing a new tool for studying the relationship between graph structure and matrix properties. This work bridges combinatorial graph theory and linear algebra, offering insights into the inertia characteristics of graph-associated matrices through game-theoretic methods.

We investigate quintessence models with potentials characterized by conditions @xmath0 and @xmath1, focusing on scenarios with nonzero initial field velocity. We develop an analytical approximation describing the temporal evolution of the equation of state parameter @xmath2 for the quintessence field. Our analysis reveals a distinctive two-phase evolutionary pattern: an initial "rapid freezing" epoch where @xmath2 decreases temporally, followed by a "slow thawing" phase during which @xmath2 increases. This behavior demonstrates early-time similarity to constant-@xmath3 models, with significant late-time deviations. The analytical framework successfully reproduces numerical solutions with excellent precision, providing insights into the dynamical evolution of quintessence dark energy. These findings have important implications for distinguishing between different dark energy models through observational constraints on the equation of state evolution.

Nonthermal radiation from astrophysical systems containing relativistic jets and shocks, including gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), active galactic nuclei (AGNs), and microquasars, typically displays characteristic power-law emission spectra. Recent particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations of relativistic electron-ion and electron-positron jets propagating into stationary media demonstrate that particle acceleration occurs primarily in the downstream jet region. In collisionless relativistic shocks, acceleration of particles (electrons, positrons, and ions) results from plasma waves and associated instabilities, particularly the Weibel (filamentation) instability generated in the shock region. These simulations reveal that the Weibel instability generates and amplifies highly non-uniform, small-scale magnetic field structures. Such turbulent fields cause transverse deflection of electrons in the post-shock region, producing "jitter" radiation with properties fundamentally different from standard synchrotron radiation, which assumes uniform magnetic fields. We propose that jitter radiation may provide crucial insights into the complex temporal evolution and spectral features observed in gamma-ray bursts, relativistic jets, and supernova remnants, offering an alternative interpretation to conventional synchrotron models.

This paper presents a characterization of compact subsets of the fuzzy number space equipped with the level convergence topology. Based on this characterization, we establish that compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness in the fuzzy number space under the level convergence topology. Diamond and Kloeden previously provided a characterization of compact sets in fuzzy number spaces equipped with the supremum metric, while Fang and Xue offered a characterization for one-dimensional fuzzy number spaces with the supremum metric, the latter being a special case of the former. However, we identify a fundamental conflict between our characterization and those presented by these authors. Through a counterexample, we demonstrate that the characterizations given by Diamond-Kloeden and Fang-Xue are incorrect. Our results provide a corrected understanding of compactness in fuzzy number spaces and clarify the relationship between different topological structures on these spaces, particularly concerning the level convergence topology and supremum metric. **Keywords:** fuzzy numbers; supremum metric; level convergence; compactness; sequential compactness

We investigate the stationary state solutions of a bond-diluted kinetic Ising model subjected to a time-dependent oscillating magnetic field on a honeycomb lattice using effective-field theory (EFT). The system's temporal evolution is described through a master equation formalism. Our analysis focuses on how bond dilution, along with the external field's frequency @xmath1 and amplitude @xmath2, influences dynamic phase diagrams. We demonstrate that the system undergoes first-order phase transitions characterized by a dynamic tricritical point (DTCP) in low-temperature, high-amplitude regimes, contrasting with previous findings for undiluted systems. Bond dilution introduces several novel phenomena, including reentrant behavior, and systematically suppresses first-order transitions and the DTCP. These effects reflect the competing influences of thermal fluctuations, disorder-induced frustration, and time-dependent driving forces. Additionally, we examine how the bond percolation threshold varies with the oscillating field's amplitude and frequency, revealing intricate interplay between structural disorder and dynamic ordering. Our results provide insights into the role of quenched disorder in driven magnetic systems and contribute to understanding non-equilibrium phase transitions in diluted lattice models with applications to disordered magnetic materials and related systems.

We present results from the second phase of the Super-Kamiokande solar neutrino measurement and compare them with first-phase observations. The solar neutrino flux spectrum, temporal variations, and oscillation parameters demonstrate statistical consistency across both phases, with no evidence of spectral distortion. Combined data from phases I and II span the complete solar cycle 23, revealing no correlation between neutrino flux and solar activity. The measured @xmath0B total flux is determined to be @xmath1, while the day-night asymmetry yields @xmath2. Our analysis reveals no systematic differences between the two experimental phases, strengthening confidence in the detector's long-term stability and the robustness of solar neutrino measurements. These results provide important constraints on neutrino oscillation parameters and confirm the MSW effect predictions for solar neutrinos traversing Earth.

We investigate non-LTE (NLTE) effects for magnesium and calcium in the atmospheres of late-type giant and supergiant stars. The aim of this paper is to provide a comprehensive grid of NLTE/LTE equivalent width ratios for Mg and Ca lines covering a wide range of stellar parameters: effective temperatures @xmath1 K, surface gravities @xmath2 dex, and metallicities [Fe/H] @xmath3 ∈ [-4.0, 0.5] dex. We employ realistic model atoms incorporating state-of-the-art atomic physics and fine structure effects. Our analysis focuses on Mg and Ca lines in the optical and near-infrared spectral regions, with particular emphasis on lines within the _Gaia_ Radial Velocity Spectrograph (RVS) wavelength domain [8470, 8740] Å. The computed NLTE corrections are presented both as tabulated functions of stellar parameters in electronic format and as polynomial fits specifically for the _Gaia_/RVS lines. These corrections are essential for accurate abundance determinations and will facilitate the interpretation of large-scale spectroscopic surveys of evolved stars in the Galaxy.

We present a generalization of Landauer-Büttiker theory for networks of interacting metallic carbon nanotubes. Beginning with symmetric starlike junctions, we extend our approach to asymmetric systems. The symmetric case admits closed-form solutions, while asymmetric configurations require combined perturbative and non-perturbative methods. For @xmath0 repulsively interacting nanotubes, the symmetric system's only stable fixed point represents an isolated node. We provide detailed results for both symmetric and asymmetric systems at @xmath1, corresponding to carbon nanotube Y junctions. This framework enables systematic analysis of interaction effects in nanotube network geometries, revealing the role of symmetry in determining transport properties.

This letter presents an optimal discriminant function framework for modulation classification utilizing sampled distribution distance metrics. The proposed low-complexity approach classifies candidate signal constellations by measuring distribution distances at strategically selected testpoints along the cumulative distribution function. Employing Bayesian decision criteria, the method asymptotically achieves minimum classification error for a given testpoint set. Performance is further enhanced through testpoint location optimization. Simulation results demonstrate substantial improvements over existing distribution-based classification techniques, offering superior accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency in distinguishing various modulation schemes.

This paper addresses boundary stabilization of a cascade ODE-heat system with state delay under actuator saturation constraints. A state feedback controller is designed using the backstepping method to achieve system stabilization. The domain of attraction is characterized through Lyapunov-based analysis, providing explicit bounds on initial conditions guaranteeing stability. Exponential stability of the delayed cascaded system is rigorously established using Halanay's inequality, which handles the time-delay effects. The saturation nonlinearity is incorporated into the controller design to ensure practical implementability. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, validating theoretical results and illustrating convergence properties within the estimated domain of attraction for various initial conditions and delay parameters.

Quantum link models provide an alternative non-perturbative formulation of abelian and non-abelian lattice gauge theories. They are ideally suited for quantum simulation, for example, using ultracold atoms in an optical lattice. This holds the promise to address currently unsolvable problems, such as the real-time and high-density dynamics of strongly interacting matter, first in toy-model gauge theories, and ultimately in QCD. Unlike traditional lattice gauge theory with continuous gauge fields, quantum link models employ discrete quantum degrees of freedom on links, making them naturally compatible with quantum computing architectures. This approach circumvents the sign problem that plagues Monte Carlo simulations at finite density and enables direct investigation of real-time dynamics.

We investigate the nonlinear dynamics of series arrays of Josephson junctions in the large-@xmath0 limit, where @xmath0 represents the number of junctions in the array. The system under consideration consists of identical, overdamped Josephson junctions driven by a constant bias current and globally coupled through a common load impedance. Previous numerical simulations of such arrays have revealed surprisingly simple dynamical behavior, suggesting the existence of hidden symmetries or other underlying mathematical structures that constrain the system's evolution. These intriguing observations were subsequently explained through the discovery of @xmath1 constants of motion, which confine the system's trajectories in phase space to low-dimensional invariant manifolds. In this work, we demonstrate that the effective dimensionality of the system can be reduced even further by focusing on a special family of states recently identified by Ott and Antonsen in their studies of large populations of coupled oscillators. In geometric terms, the Ott-Antonsen ansatz corresponds to an invariant submanifold whose dimension is one less than that of the manifolds found in earlier investigations. This additional reduction yields significant analytical tractability while capturing the essential dynamics of the system. We derive the governing equations for the flow on this reduced submanifold and provide detailed analysis for two physically important special cases: arrays with purely resistive loading and arrays with resistive-inductive-capacitive (RLC) loading. For both cases, we obtain analytical or semi-analytical results that characterize the stability, bifurcations, and long-time behavior of the coupled junction arrays. Our results successfully recover previous findings that were based on linearization arguments and perturbative analyses, while in some instances providing improvements and extensions. Specifically, we obtain exact results in parameter regimes where earlier approximations were necessary, and we identify new dynamical features that were not accessible through previous methods. The mathematical framework developed here provides new insights into the collective behavior of Josephson junction arrays and demonstrates the power of the Ott-Antonsen reduction technique in systems with global coupling. From a practical perspective, understanding these simplified dynamics is crucial for optimizing the performance of Josephson junction arrays in applications such as voltage standards, oscillators, and detectors. More broadly, our work contributes to the general understanding of how complexity can emerge from, or be suppressed by, the collective dynamics of many coupled nonlinear oscillators, with potential applications extending beyond superconducting devices to other coupled oscillator systems in physics, biology, and engineering.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the electromagnetic self-energy and self-force acting on a scalar point-like charged test particle at rest in the spacetime of a global monopole with general spherically symmetric internal structure. The investigation is carried out by constructing the three-dimensional Green function appropriate for this physical configuration. Our results demonstrate that for observation points exterior to the monopole's core, the scalar self-energy decomposes into two distinct contributions: the first arises from the non-trivial topological structure of the global monopole treated as a point defect, while the second represents a correction term attributable to its finite internal structure. For interior points, the self-energy maintains a similar decomposition, though the primary contribution now depends explicitly on the internal spacetime geometry. To illustrate our general formalism, we examine two specific models for the monopole's interior region: the "flower-pot" and "ballpoint-pen" configurations. For both scenarios, we derive exact analytical expressions for the self-energies and self-forces in both the exterior and interior regions of the global monopole. These results provide insight into how the internal structure of topological defects affects quantum field theoretical quantities and may have implications for particle physics phenomenology in curved spacetimes containing such defects. Accretion disks around black holes are fundamental systems for understanding matter inflow and energy release in extreme gravitational environments. Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence drives the angular momentum transport that enables accretion. Recent global general relativistic MHD simulations have provided unprecedented quantitative insights into this process, revealing several previously unrecognized phenomena. These include unexpectedly strong magnetic stresses operating in the marginally stable and plunging regions immediately surrounding the black hole event horizon, and the spontaneous formation of electromagnetically-dominated conical relativistic jets emerging directly from the accretion flow without requiring large-scale magnetic fields. The energy release mechanisms associated with both enhanced near-horizon stresses and jet formation can substantially exceed classical predictions derived from purely hydrodynamic models, with important implications for observed high-energy emission from accreting black holes across the mass spectrum.

We present a kinematic analysis of 75 star-forming galaxies at z~2 in the COSMOS legacy field using near-infrared spectroscopy from Keck/MOSFIRE as part of the ZFIRE survey. Our Ks-band selected sample from the ZFOURGE survey spans stellar masses of log(M*/M☉)~9-11, including 28 galaxies in a known overdensity at z=2.095. We measure Hα emission-line integrated velocity dispersions ranging from 50-230 km s−1, consistent with previous studies of z~2 field galaxies. Using these measurements, we estimate virial, stellar, and gas masses and examine correlations between these properties for both cluster and field populations. Our analysis indicates that baryons dominate the mass budget within the central effective radius. Importantly, we find no statistically significant kinematic differences between cluster and field star-forming galaxies at z~2. This suggests that environmental effects on galaxy kinematics are not yet prominent at this epoch, and that the distinct kinematic properties observed in lower-redshift cluster galaxies develop at later times. These results provide important constraints on the timescales of environmental processing in galaxy clusters.

October 2004 marks the 400th anniversary of the sighting of SN 1604, now marked by the presence of an expanding nebulosity known as Kepler's supernova remnant. Of the small number of remnants of historical supernovae, Kepler's remnant remains the most enigmatic. The supernova type, and hence the type of star that exploded, is still a matter of debate, and even the distance to the remnant is uncertain by more than a factor of two. As new and improved multiwavelength observations become available, and as the time baseline of observations gets longer, Kepler's supernova remnant is slowly revealing its secrets. This review examines recent and current observations of Kepler's supernova remnant across the electromagnetic spectrum, from radio to X-ray wavelengths, and discusses what these observations indicate about the nature of this intriguing object. Progress in understanding the progenitor system, explosion mechanism, and interaction with the surrounding interstellar medium is evaluated, highlighting remaining questions and future observational prospects.

We present comprehensive data reduction algorithms developed for the Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS) instrument, drawing upon extensive preflight testing, modeling, and refinement through initial flight observations. The Ge:Ga bulk photoconductor arrays exhibit various systematic artifacts requiring careful correction for accurate photometric calibration, while the Si:As array, though more stable, also demonstrates specific instrumental effects necessitating removal. Our data reduction pipeline comprises three sequential stages: (1) conversion of non-destructive readout ramps into flux slopes while correcting artifacts with time constants comparable to individual exposure durations; (2) calibration of slope measurements addressing longer-timescale artifacts; and (3) iterative refinement exploiting observational redundancy inherent in MIPS scanning modes to enhance artifact removal. For each processing stage, we provide detailed descriptions of the underlying physics informed by laboratory characterization experiments and theoretical frameworks, accompanied by the mathematical formulations implemented in the calibration algorithms. We demonstrate the efficacy of these approaches through comparison of preflight predictions with actual on-orbit performance. These reduction techniques are broadly applicable to similar infrared detector systems and provide valuable insights into the systematic behaviors characteristic of space-based photoconductor arrays. The algorithms successfully mitigate instrumental signatures, enabling precise photometric measurements essential for MIPS science objectives.

We investigate correlation-driven orbital Mott transitions in two-dimensional pyrochlore lattices through a model Hamiltonian incorporating Hund's coupling between itinerant and localized electrons alongside Coulomb interactions. To map the complete phase diagram, we implement static auxiliary field Monte Carlo simulations that explicitly preserve spatial correlations, enabling systematic exploration of finite-temperature behavior. Our results elucidate the interplay between electronic correlations and orbital degrees of freedom in geometrically frustrated lattices, revealing distinct orbital ordering transitions driven by interaction strength and temperature variations in this frustrated magnetic system.

We demonstrate deterministic coupling between single semiconductor nanowire quantum dots with visible emission and plasmonic gold nanoantennas. Specifically, we observe enhanced nanowire absorption cross-sections and accelerated quantum dot spontaneous emission rates, with enhancement factors reaching twofold in optimally coupled antenna-quantum dot configurations. These results establish a reliable fabrication methodology for integrating semiconductor nanostructures with plasmonic elements, advancing prospects for quantum nanophotonic devices operating in the visible spectrum.

We investigate the influence of a primordial background magnetic field, consistent with current observational bounds, on the linear evolution of cosmological density perturbations at sub-Hubble scales. These findings offer important insights into the magnetic field structure and evolution in GRB jets, with implications for interpreting current and future polarimetric observations of these energetic cosmic phenomena.

We establish fundamental connections between cyclic presentations of groups and cyclic branched coverings of @xmath0-knots. We establish a sufficient condition for finite-time wave breaking in strong solutions to the Camassa-Holm equation, based on the decay rate of initial data at infinity. The threshold between blow-up and persistence is precisely characterized by the soliton decay rate. Fundamental principles in quantum optics dictate that deterministic linear amplification of quantum states inevitably introduces noise, degrading pure states into mixed states. Recent advances have demonstrated that probabilistic, non-deterministic amplifiers can circumvent this limitation, enabling noiseless amplification. We present a novel noiseless amplification scheme that exploits the intrinsic stochastic fluctuations of the quantum field itself as the energy source for amplification, eliminating the need for external energy injection. This approach fundamentally differs from conventional amplification schemes. We analyze the trade-off between amplification gain and success probability, characterizing the statistical properties of output states for both successful and unsuccessful amplification attempts. Through optimization of beam splitter reflectivities, we determine the maximum achievable success rates and establish the operational parameter space. Our analysis reveals the relationship between this fluctuation-driven amplification mechanism and previously proposed noiseless amplification protocols, providing insights into the fundamental limits and practical implementations of probabilistic quantum amplification. This work advances our understanding of energy redistribution in quantum optical systems and offers new perspectives for quantum information processing applications.

We investigate the emergence of symmetry restoration in highly excited hadronic states through semiclassical analysis. We investigate the physical mechanisms governing the low-redshift Lyα forest using hydrodynamic simulations of four cold dark matter cosmological models. While our primary conclusions are robust across different cosmologies, they critically depend on our modeling of a declining UV ionizing background that tracks the decreasing quasar population at low redshift. Our analysis reveals that cosmic expansion drives rapid evolution in the line number density dn/dz (counting absorbers above a specified equivalent width threshold) at z > 1.5. However, at lower redshifts, the fading UV background counterbalances expansion effects, resulting in remarkably slow evolution of dn/dz. The gravitational infall of gas from low-density regions into collapsed structures produces a modest but measurable impact on dn/dz evolution, particularly for high equivalent width systems. At all redshifts, we find a systematic relationship between line strength and physical origin: weak absorbers predominantly trace moderate density fluctuations in the diffuse, unshocked intergalactic medium (IGM), while stronger systems arise in shocked or radiatively cooled gas at higher overdensities. However, cosmic expansion causes the neutral hydrogen column density of structures at fixed overdensity to decline with time. Consequently, absorbers at z ~ 0 are dynamically analogous to systems with 10-50 times higher column densities at z ~ 3. The mildly overdense IGM fluctuations responsible for most forest opacity at z ~ 3 produce only optically thin lines at z ~ 0, whereas marginally saturated lines (NHI ~ 10^14 cm^-2) at low redshift typically originate in gas overdense by factors of ~5-10. We observe no sharp boundary between absorption arising in "galaxy halos" versus large-scale structures; rather, galaxies preferentially inhabit dense IGM regions that produce strong Lyα lines. This continuous distribution naturally explains key observational characteristics of the low-redshift forest: (1) the pronounced transition in dn/dz evolution near z ~ 1, (2) stronger evolutionary trends for higher equivalent width absorbers, (3) an extended correlation between Lyα equivalent width and galaxy impact parameter reaching ~1 h^-1 Mpc, and (4) the association of strong lines with galaxy environments while weak lines trace more diffuse cosmic structure. Our simulations thus provide a coherent physical framework unifying the distinctive observed properties of low-redshift Lyα absorption systems.

This paper investigates the fundamental memory-transmission-rate tradeoff in caching systems using a novel computer-aided approach that departs from conventional analytical methods in information theory. We leverage linear programming (LP) characterizations of the entropy space as our foundation, but extend significantly beyond traditional information inequality proofs. Our methodology begins by identifying and formalizing the inherent symmetry structure in caching problems, which allows us to establish the existence of optimal symmetric solutions. Through symmetry reduction techniques, we develop tractable linear programs that identify the boundary of the memory-transmission-rate tradeoff region for several fundamental cases, yielding tight outer bounds. These computational results serve as the basis for formulating general hypotheses about the optimal tradeoff region, which we subsequently prove analytically. This approach yields a complete characterization of the optimal tradeoff for two-user systems and partial characterizations for two-file systems. A key contribution is our reverse-engineering methodology: by carefully analyzing the joint entropy structure revealed by outer bounds in specific cases, we derive novel code constructions that generalize to a broader class of achievable schemes. This demonstrates how computational insights can guide practical coding strategies. Furthermore, we develop techniques for computing strong outer bounds through strategic relaxation of the LP formulation. This approach provides two significant benefits: (1) it enables us to deduce generic characteristics of converse proofs, revealing common structural elements across different problem instances, and (2) it makes computation tractable for larger problem instances that would otherwise be computationally infeasible. Our work demonstrates the power of combining computational and analytical techniques in information theory, establishing a framework for computer-aided analysis that can accelerate progress on fundamental problems in network information theory and coded caching.

We investigate statistical properties of random walks on experimental crumpled wire configurations rigidly jammed in two dimensions. The observed diffusion exhibits anomalous behavior with an exponent closely matching that of two-dimensional percolation threshold. We compare our system with other physically relevant systems and discuss experimental implications. The crumpled wire provides a novel experimental realization for studying anomalous transport in disordered media with intricate geometrical and topological properties.

First-order Fermi acceleration at astrophysical shocks represents a fundamental mechanism for generating non-thermal particle populations in various cosmic environments. While the test-particle approximation provides a simplified framework where accelerated particles negligibly influence the shock structure, realistic scenarios often require consideration of particle backreaction on the fluid dynamics. This backreaction introduces the non-linear regime of shock acceleration, characterized by significant modifications to both shock structure and particle spectra. We present a semi-analytical methodology for treating non-linear effects in diffusive shock acceleration, examining how energetic particle pressure affects the compression ratio, precursor formation, and spectral steepening. Our approach is validated through systematic comparisons with previous theoretical treatments and state-of-the-art numerical simulations, demonstrating improved consistency in predicting maximum particle energies and acceleration efficiencies in strongly modified shocks relevant to supernova remnants and other high-energy astrophysical sources.

We present a comprehensive diagnostic framework for investigating gamma-ray emission lines from radioactive isotopes, specifically 26Al and 60Fe, in galactic stellar clusters and associations through multi-wavelength analysis. For coeval stellar populations, we trace the temporal evolution of 26Al and 60Fe production, calculating the equivalent 26Al yield per ionizing O7V star and other observable quantities. Our analysis reveals four distinct phases in the 1.809 MeV 26Al emission line: (1) a stellar wind-dominated phase lasting approximately 0-3 Myr, (2) a SN Ib-dominated phase from 3-7 Myr, (3) a SN II-dominated phase extending from 7-37 Myr, and (4) an exponential decay phase beyond 37 Myr. The equivalent 26Al yield emerges as an exceptionally sensitive age indicator, enabling differentiation between Wolf-Rayet and supernova nucleosynthesis contributions within stellar associations. Additionally, the 26Al/60Fe emissivity ratio serves as an independent age constraint that quantifies the relative importance of explosive nucleosynthesis. Applying our models to solar metallicity populations at steady state, we determine the fractional contributions to 26Al production: approximately 30% from pre-WR phase stars, 30% from WR stars, 25% from SN Ib events, and 15% from SN II explosions. For 60Fe, we find that 20% originates from SN Ib while 80% comes from SN II. Normalizing to the Galaxy's total ionizing flux, we predict production rates of 1.5 M⊙ Myr−1 for 26Al and 0.8 M⊙ Myr−1 for 60Fe, corresponding to present-day interstellar medium masses of 1.5 M⊙ and 1.7 M⊙, respectively. To facilitate rigorous quantitative analysis of observational data, we develop a Bayesian statistical framework that properly accounts for initial mass function stochasticity and observational uncertainties. We implement Monte Carlo techniques to generate probability distributions for all relevant observables, providing a robust methodology for comparing theoretical predictions with measurements. We demonstrate this approach through application to a hypothetical massive stellar association, establishing the foundation for detailed analyses. Forthcoming companion papers will present applications to observed regions including Cygnus and Vela, demonstrating the diagnostic power of this integrated multi-wavelength approach.

We investigate time-independent, radially symmetric BPS soliton solutions in a @xmath0 model coupled to an Abelian gauge field with standard Maxwell dynamics. This bound is saturated by solutions satisfying a specific set of coupled first-order BPS differential equations. Using appropriate boundary conditions, we obtain numerical solutions corresponding to regular, finite-energy configurations. The main characteristics of these solitonic structures are discussed in detail. Notably, we examine different solution branches corresponding to distinct choices of an auxiliary function @xmath1 that parameterizes the model. Despite the apparent differences between these branches, we demonstrate that all resulting scenarios exhibit identical phenomenology and are physically equivalent. Two-dimensional angular correlations from 200 GeV Au+Au collisions reveal a same-side (SS) peak at azimuth $\Delta\phi \approx 0$ that exhibits characteristics consistent with jet formation in peripheral collisions. As collision centrality increases, this SS peak undergoes systematic modifications: it becomes elongated along pseudorapidity $\Delta\eta$ and shows altered transverse momentum $p_t$ structure. This elongated feature, termed the "soft ridge," has been interpreted as evidence for collective flow phenomena, including triangular and higher harmonic flows potentially connected to initial-state geometry. This work establishes the connection between so-called "higher harmonic flows" and SS 2D peak properties. A comprehensive analysis of the SS peak across all centralities supports a consistent jet-based interpretation, challenging flow-based explanations and providing an alternative framework for understanding these correlation structures in heavy-ion collisions.

We investigate vector soliton emission from two-component elongated Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) through temporal manipulation of inter- and intra-species scattering lengths via Feshbach resonance tuning. Our study reveals phenomena unique to multi-component systems without single-species analogues. We demonstrate vector soliton out-coupling through interspecies interaction tuning, show how one species' evolution can be controlled by modulating the dynamics of the other, and present implementations of supersolitons. The analysis employs numerical simulations of the one-dimensional coupled Gross-Pitaevskii equations, complemented by analytical arguments providing qualitative physical insight. These results establish novel control mechanisms for matter-wave engineering in binary condensates, exploiting the rich interplay between components through time-dependent scattering length manipulation. Our findings open new avenues for coherent atom optics and nonlinear wave management in multi-component quantum gases.

We present a comprehensive study of super giant molecular complexes (SGMCs) in the merging galaxy system NGC 4038/39 (the Antennae) using previously published CO emission observations to investigate the formation mechanisms of young massive star clusters. Alternative scenarios suggest the Antennae may be experiencing a relatively brief burst of intense cluster formation; otherwise, the eventual merger remnant would possess a globular cluster specific frequency far exceeding values observed in elliptical galaxies. Finally, we evaluate two theoretical models for massive cluster formation. Our observational constraints favor the scenario wherein young massive clusters form from dense cores embedded within the observed SGMCs, providing new insights into cluster formation physics in merger-driven environments and its implications for understanding globular cluster systems in early-type galaxies.

There have been numerous prior attempts to theoretically justify the effectiveness of inverse document frequency (IDF). Approaches based on Robertson and Spärck Jones's probabilistic model rely on strong or complex assumptions. We demonstrate that a more intuitively plausible assumption suffices for this justification. Moreover, our new assumption, while conceptually simple, provides an elegant solution to an estimation problem previously considered intractable by Robertson and Walker (1997). This work contributes to information retrieval theory by offering a cleaner theoretical foundation for IDF, one of the most fundamental and widely-used term weighting schemes. Our approach maintains mathematical rigor while achieving greater conceptual clarity, thereby strengthening our understanding of why IDF works effectively in practice.

We review and extend with nonrelativistic nuclear mean field calculations a previous study of the impact of the nuclear symmetry energy on the structure and composition of the outer crust of nonaccreting neutron stars. We develop a simple analytical "toy model" that identifies the most relevant physical quantities determining crustal properties: the nuclear symmetry energy and the electron gas pressure. While the electron gas contribution is well-established, the nuclear symmetry energy—particularly its density dependence—remains poorly constrained. We systematically investigate how different parametrizations of the symmetry energy affect the crustal composition using several nonrelativistic mean field models calibrated to reproduce terrestrial nuclear data. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between the stiffness of the symmetry energy and the neutron richness of crustal nuclei. Models featuring stiffer symmetry energies, which predict thicker neutron skins in heavy nuclei and exhibit lower symmetry energy values at subsaturation densities, produce significantly more neutron-rich (exotic) isotopes in the stellar crust compared to models with softer symmetry energies. These results demonstrate the crucial role of the symmetry energy in determining neutron star crust properties and highlight the importance of constraining this fundamental nuclear physics quantity through both laboratory experiments and astrophysical observations.

We investigate a simple model with hard local constraints that exhibits multiple time scales in the complete absence of disorder, contrary to typical disordered systems. The model's dynamics emerge from local collective rearrangements spanning various length scales, where the characteristic behavior is governed not by microscopic scales but by a length scale @xmath0 that increases as energy decreases. Spatially, we observe a hierarchical organization of fast and slow dynamical regions: slow regions are geometrically isolated from faster degrees of freedom, which remain confined within fast pockets below their respective percolation thresholds. This spatial segregation suggests a novel mechanism for dynamical slowing. We propose a tentative connection to structural glass physics, wherein the dramatic slowdown of relaxation dynamics results from the increasing size of mobile elementary excitations rather than from growing static correlation lengths or domain sizes, offering an alternative perspective on glass formation mechanisms.

We investigate anomalous tunneling spectroscopy in mechanically exfoliated superconducting 2H-TaS2 flakes, revealing unexpected zero-bias conductance peaks. Through theoretical modeling, we propose that these features arise from unconventional pairing symmetry in atomically thin samples. Our minimal model describes a single unit cell layer with a simplified two-dimensional Fermi surface, where Coulomb repulsion induces sign-changing Cooper pair wavefunctions. The superconducting gap exhibits nodal character in the central Γ pocket, contrasting with conventional s-wave pairing. Non-perturbative tip-sample coupling generates weak scattering at the nodal Fermi surface, producing Andreev bound states responsible for the observed zero-bias peaks. These results suggest dimensional confinement fundamentally alters the pairing mechanism in 2H-TaS2, driving a crossover from conventional s-wave superconductivity in bulk crystals to sign-changing pairing in few-atom-thick samples. Our findings demonstrate how quantum confinement can qualitatively modify electronic correlations and superconducting properties in transition metal dichalcogenides.

We present a comprehensive analysis of systematic uncertainties affecting the W-boson mass and width measurements arising from imperfect knowledge of electroweak radiative corrections. The intrinsic theoretical uncertainties in the YFSWW-based 4-fermion generator employed by the DELPHI collaboration are evaluated following the recommendations of the original authors. Our assessment utilizes the complete DELPHI simulation, reconstruction, and analysis chain to propagate these uncertainties through the experimental procedure. Additionally, we perform a comparative study with RACOONWW, an alternative 4-fermion calculation implementing doubly-resonant photonic corrections at O(α). The results demonstrate that systematic uncertainties on the W-boson mass measurement remain below 10 MeV across all decay channels considered in the analysis, indicating excellent control of electroweak radiative effects in precision measurements at LEP-II energies.

We present a second-order accurate method for incorporating arbitrary force density distributions into the lattice Boltzmann formulation of hydrodynamics. The method handles both momentum-conserving internal forces and non-momentum-conserving external forces, including singular force densities such as point forces. Validation against analytical solutions demonstrates excellent agreement across multiple test cases. The approach is applied to develop a minimal model for dilute sedimenting particle suspensions, offering significant computational efficiency advantages over conventional methods.
