These constructions are optimal in the number of disjoint paths achieved, and we demonstrate flexibility in the choice of underlying combinatorial structures (bipartite graphs and transversal designs) to which the @xmath0-step method can be applied. Critically, we maintain explicit control over path lengths, which directly impacts network latency. **One-to-many communication:** We extend our analysis to broadcast-type scenarios, proving the existence of pairwise link-disjoint paths from all servers adjacent to a source switch to arbitrary identically-sized collections of target servers distributed throughout the network. Unlike the one-to-one case, target servers need not be co-located at a single switch, reflecting realistic communication patterns in distributed applications. Long-term ("superorbital") periods or modulations have been detected in a wide variety of both low and high-mass X-ray binaries at X-ray and optical wavelengths. A variety of mechanisms have been proposed to account for the variability properties, such as precessing and/or warped accretion discs, amongst others. The All Sky Monitor on board the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer provides the most extensive (~15 years) and sensitive X-ray archive for studying such behaviour. It is also clear that such variations can be intermittent and/or a function of X-ray spectral state. Consequently, we use a time-dependent dynamic power spectrum method to examine how these modulations vary with time in 25 X-ray binaries for which superorbital periodicities have been previously reported. Our aim is to characterize these periodicities in a completely systematic way. We find that some systems (such as Her X-1 and LMC X-4) exhibit remarkably stable superorbital periods, while others show a range of properties, from even longer variability time-scales to quite chaotic behaviour. We discuss the implications of these results for the physical mechanisms responsible for superorbital modulations in X-ray binary systems.

This paper presents refined results on interpolation properties of planar spiral curves, extending previous work. The main contribution establishes boundary regions within which spiral and piecewise spiral splines can be constructed to match prescribed interpolation data. The width of these admissible regions provides a quantitative measure of the fairness and interpolability of given point sets. We demonstrate that this measure characterizes the geometric quality of data configurations and their suitability for smooth interpolation. Applications to tolerance control in manufacturing, particularly for curvilinear profile verification and quality assessment, are discussed and illustrated.

We propose a scheme for on-demand generation of polarization-entangled N-photon states using trapped atoms in optical cavities. This cavity-QED-based approach overcomes probabilistic limitations of spontaneous parametric down-conversion sources, enabling deterministic generation of multiphoton entangled states. Such controllable sources are crucial for scalable linear optics quantum computing, secure quantum cryptography, and precision tests of quantum nonlocality with increasing particle numbers.

The results provide a numerical check of theorems about the Hilbert space structure describing the confined phase of four-dimensional compact U(1) lattice gauge theories. Our findings demonstrate the utility of this modified order parameter in efficiently probing the particle spectrum and validating theoretical predictions about confinement in compact gauge theories.

We examine two recently proposed models of charge ordering (CO) in nominally quarter-filled, quasi-one-dimensional organic charge transfer solids. These models are distinguished by their characteristic site charge density patterns: "1010" (alternating charges) and "1100" (charge pairing). Using the Peierls-extended Hubbard model, we incorporate both electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions to investigate the competition between these CO states. First, we demonstrate that Hartree-Fock mean field theory yields qualitatively and quantitatively incorrect predictions for the critical nearest-neighbor Coulomb repulsion required to stabilize the "1010" ordered state, when compared with exact many-body calculations for the purely electronic Hamiltonian. Second, we establish that spin-Peierls order can emerge in both CO patterns and construct a comprehensive phase diagram incorporating on-site and inter-site electron-phonon coupling. Third, we analyze the expected temperature dependence of CO and metal-insulator transitions for both ordering patterns. Finally, we compare our theoretical predictions with experimental observations, demonstrating that the "1100" CO state is clearly realized in 1:2 anionic charge transfer salts and (TMTSF)2X materials. However, results for (TMTTF)2X compounds with narrower bandwidths remain ambiguous, suggesting that the nearest-neighbor Coulomb interaction in these materials lies near the critical value separating the two CO regimes. Our findings provide a framework for understanding CO patterns across different families of quasi-one-dimensional organic conductors.

Finding satisfying assignments for variables involved in constraint satisfaction problems can be formulated as a bounded model generation problem: searching for bounded models of a theory in some logical framework. The current state-of-the-art approach for bounded model generation in rich knowledge representation languages (such as FO(·) and ASP) and constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) modeling languages (such as MiniZinc) is the ground-and-solve paradigm. This approach reduces the theory to a ground or propositional form and then applies a search algorithm to the resulting theory. However, a critical bottleneck in this method is the exponential blow-up in theory size caused by the grounding phase, which can render problems intractable. Lazy grounding—deferring the grounding of theory components until necessary during search—offers a promising solution to this bottleneck. We present a comprehensive theoretical framework and practical implementation for lazy grounding in the context of the FO(·) knowledge representation language. Our approach avoids grounding all parts of a theory by deriving justifications for selected components. Given a partial assignment for the grounded portion of the theory and valid justifications for formulas in the non-grounded portion, these justifications provide a constructive recipe for extending the partial assignment to a complete satisfying assignment. During search, when a justification becomes invalid, we derive a new one; if this fails, we strategically split the formula into a part requiring grounding and a part that can be justified. Experimental results demonstrate that this lazy grounding approach significantly improves performance and showcases both the power and generality of our framework across diverse problem domains.

We analyze collisional decoherence of atoms or molecules prepared in coherent superpositions of nondegenerate internal states at ultralow temperatures within an ultracold buffer gas. Our treatment is valid for arbitrary bath-to-tracer particle mass ratios. Both elastic and inelastic collisions contribute to decoherence processes. Special attention is given to the mass-ratio dependence in the regime of light bath particles and heavy tracer species. These analytical expressions provide accurate decoherence rate estimates essential for low-temperature applications. Our results suggest a novel experimental method: determining scattering lengths of atoms and molecules in different internal states through measurements of decoherence-induced damping of coherent oscillations. This approach offers a new spectroscopic tool for characterizing ultracold collision dynamics and extracting interaction potentials from observed decoherence timescales.

This paper presents a workshop designed for grade eleven high school students conducted during a university open day, introducing the abstract mathematical concept of metric spaces. The pedagogical approach employed a two-stage methodology: participants initially explored fundamental properties of distance through concrete, real-life examples to develop intuitive understanding. Following this preparatory phase, the formal definition of metric spaces was systematically introduced. Students then engaged with the abstract concepts through collaborative problem-oriented exercise sessions in small groups, allowing for active learning and peer discussion. This workshop demonstrates an effective bridge between intuitive geometric understanding and formal mathematical abstraction, making advanced mathematical concepts accessible to pre-university students while maintaining mathematical rigor and fostering collaborative problem-solving skills.

We report the discovery of a variable, compact steep spectrum radio source located ~65 arcsec (~4 kpc) from the center of the starburst galaxy NGC 3310, detected during an ongoing radio supernova monitoring program. At the distance of NGC 3310, the source exhibits a 5 GHz luminosity of approximately 10^26 W Hz^-1. The combination of its high luminosity, variability characteristics, compact structure (~17 mas), and spatial association with HII regions strongly suggests this is a previously uncatalogued Type II radio supernova. Analysis of archival data reveals an associated X-ray source with luminosity consistent with known radio supernovae. These multi-wavelength observations provide compelling evidence for ongoing massive star formation and supernova activity in NGC 3310's starburst environment, contributing to our understanding of supernova rates in starburst galaxies.

Motivated by the foundational work of McClure and Dyer (Class. Quantum Grav. **23**, 1971 (2006)), we present a comprehensive analysis of solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell equations that describe charged black holes embedded in cosmological backgrounds. Our investigation begins with a detailed examination of electromagnetic sources for a sufficiently general metric ansatz, systematically deriving the electromagnetic four-current and conserved electric charge for each configuration. We revisit the charged McVittie solution, performing a thorough study of its causal structure. Our analysis demonstrates that this solution can represent a charged black hole in an expanding universe, with the notable feature that the black hole horizon forms only at infinite late times. We extend our investigation to charged versions of metrics originally proposed by Vaidya (VD) and Sultana-Dyer (SD), revealing that the charged Sultana-Dyer metric necessarily requires a global electric current in addition to a central spherically symmetric electric charge. To facilitate comparison with the charged McVittie metric, we construct new generalized charged solutions of both VD and SD types, wherein the original mass and charge parameters are promoted to specific functions of cosmological time. Our analysis reveals distinct evolutionary behaviors: in the generalized charged Vaidya metric, the black hole horizon never forms, while in the generalized Sultana-Dyer case, both Cauchy and black hole horizons develop asymptotically at infinite late times. We also introduce and analyze a charged version of the Thakurta metric, representing a novel solution to the Einstein-Maxwell equations. Similar to the charged Sultana-Dyer case, the electromagnetic field in this spacetime is sourced by both a central electric charge and an additional global electric current. A study of the global causal structure confirms that this spacetime can indeed represent a charged black hole in a cosmological background. A common feature of all solutions examined is the presence of initial singularities, analogous to those found in the original McVittie metric. Our work provides new insights into the interplay between electromagnetic fields, black hole horizons, and cosmological expansion, offering a systematic framework for understanding charged black holes in dynamical spacetimes.

We present a refined phase-connected post-glitch timing ephemeris for the Geminga pulsar that successfully fits all available post-glitch data from EGRET and subsequent observations. Phase-resolved spectroscopic analysis of two X-ray observations obtained in 2002 and 2004 is performed to investigate the pulsar's emission properties. We critically examine a previously reported detection of a small hot spot on the neutron star surface. Our analysis demonstrates that this claimed feature was likely an artifact resulting from overly restrictive modeling assumptions, specifically the constraint of a constant spectral index for the non-thermal emission component. When we permit the spectral index to vary with rotational phase, we observe systematic phase-dependent variations in this parameter. Importantly, these more flexible spectral models adequately describe the observations without requiring an additional hot blackbody component, thereby challenging the existence of the previously claimed hot spot feature.

We present a model explaining bipolar resistive switching in transition metal oxides through electric field-enhanced oxygen vacancy migration at the nanoscale. Our numerical analysis reveals that intense electric fields concentrate at highly resistive dielectric-electrode interfaces, producing spatially inhomogeneous oxygen vacancy distributions that drive the resistive switching phenomenon. The model successfully captures the underlying physical mechanisms governing the non-volatile resistance changes characteristic of these materials. We validate our theoretical framework against experimental resistance hysteresis measurements, demonstrating qualitative agreement with non-trivial switching behaviors. This combined theoretical-experimental approach provides fundamental insights into the interfacial processes controlling resistive switching in oxide-based memory devices.

Whole genome sequencing (WGS) has rapidly transitioned from an ambitious research endeavor to an accessible technology with transformative potential for personalized medicine and disease understanding. While WGS promises revolutionary healthcare applications through improved diagnosis, treatment selection, and disease prevention, it simultaneously introduces significant privacy and ethical concerns. Human genomic data uniquely identifies individuals and reveals sensitive information about disease susceptibility, ancestry, and familial relationships, creating unprecedented privacy risks. This article examines the tension between genomic innovation and privacy protection by reviewing recent technological advances in WGS and analyzing the resulting privacy implications. We identify critical research challenges including secure data storage and sharing, protection against re-identification attacks, informed consent in the genomic era, and balancing scientific progress with individual privacy rights, highlighting the urgent need for comprehensive privacy-preserving frameworks.

We present a comprehensive theoretical investigation of electron-positron pair creation in collisions between a laser beam and a nonlaser photon using the S-matrix formalism. The laser field is modeled as a finite pulse, extending our previously developed framework for Compton scattering. We examine the nonperturbative regime where the laser intensity is sufficiently high that perturbative approaches become inadequate. Our calculations focus on energy-angular distributions of the created particles under various field configurations. A key finding is that energy spectra computed using the finite pulse model show excellent agreement with those obtained via the modulated plane wave approximation when the laser pulse duration is sufficiently long. However, significant deviations emerge for short pulses, highlighting the importance of proper pulse modeling. We demonstrate that pair production rates exhibit strong polarization dependence in the nonperturbative regime, with linear polarization yielding maximal production rates. Consequently, we conduct detailed analysis of how the relative orientation of linear polarizations between the laser pulse and nonlaser photon affects pair creation efficiency. Furthermore, we explore carrier-envelope phase effects on angular distributions of created particles, revealing the potential for phase control in pair production processes. Our results provide important insights for experimental design and interpretation in strong-field quantum electrodynamics, particularly for next-generation high-intensity laser facilities approaching the nonperturbative regime.
