We develop simple analytical approximations to characterize the magnetic fields generated by the lattice structure and determine key trap parameters. Experimental demonstration shows successful loading of ultracold atoms into at least 30 lattice sites positioned approximately 10 μm above the film surface. This work represents a significant advancement toward implementing quantum information processing protocols using neutral atoms confined in magnetic lattice potentials, offering scalability and precise control for future quantum applications.

We perform numerical simulations of the lattice-animal problem at the upper critical dimension @xmath0 on hypercubic lattices to investigate logarithmic corrections to scaling. Our stochastic sampling method employs the pruned-enriched Rosenbluth method (PERM), adapted from linear polymer studies, achieving high statistics for animals with up to 8000 sites. We estimate partition sums (total number of distinct animals) and radii of gyration. Our results confirm the Parisi-Sourlas prediction for leading critical exponents and compare logarithmic-correction exponents against two competing theoretical predictions from literature. The data discriminate between these predictions. Additionally, we propose and verify a novel Parisi-Sourlas-type scaling relation specifically applicable to logarithmic-correction exponents, providing new theoretical insight into critical phenomena at the upper critical dimension for branched polymers.

We construct numerous exact solutions to the nonlinear mean-field Gross-Pitaevskii equations describing multicomponent Bose-Einstein condensates confined in one-, two-, and three-dimensional optical lattices. Both stationary and nonstationary solutions are presented in closed analytical form. Notable examples include a vortex-antivortex array configuration on square optical lattices and oscillatory modes where multiple components periodically transfer between adjacent potential wells. For condensates on simple cubic lattices, we obtain diverse solutions, including a particularly interesting configuration where one component remains stationary while the other exhibits flow through a complex three-dimensional network of intersecting vortex lines. Through direct numerical integration of the time-dependent Gross-Pitaevskii equations, we demonstrate that several physically significant solutions maintain dynamical stability over extended parameter ranges, confirming their potential experimental relevance and observability in ultracold atomic systems.

We reexamine the classical problem of tippe top dynamics, specifically analyzing the spinning and inversion behavior of an eccentric sphere model on a horizontal table. Our analysis employs a modified Coulomb friction law that depends continuously on the slip velocity @xmath0 at the contact point and vanishes at @xmath1, providing a more physically realistic treatment than traditional discontinuous models. A central focus of our investigation is the relevance of the gyroscopic balance condition (GBC) to the tippe top inversion phenomenon. This condition, originally discovered by Moffatt and Shimomura in their study of rapidly spinning hard-boiled eggs, plays a crucial but different role in tippe top dynamics. We introduce a diagnostic variable @xmath2 where @xmath3 indicates satisfaction of the GBC, and track its evolution throughout the motion. Our key finding is that unlike the spinning egg case, the tippe top does not initially satisfy the GBC. However, numerical simulations reveal that tippe tops destined to invert do approximately satisfy the GBC shortly after the motion begins. This observation proves fundamental to understanding the inversion mechanism. Through analysis combining the GBC with geometric constraints, we establish a complete classification of tippe tops into three distinct groups based on their inversion behavior: Group I tippe tops never invert regardless of initial spin; Group II exhibits complete inversion when spun sufficiently rapidly; and Group III inverts only to a maximum inclination angle @xmath4 where @xmath5 holds. We identify three steady states for the spinning motion and develop a new stability criterion to analyze these states as functions of the initial spin velocity @xmath6. This analysis yields a critical initial spin value @xmath7 necessary for Group II tippe tops to achieve complete inversion. Our results provide a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding this fascinating dynamical system, resolving longstanding questions about the conditions governing tippe top inversion.

We present a comprehensive tight-binding approach for computing Zeeman splittings in semiconductor nanostructures. The methodology operates within the electron-hole framework and naturally extends to exciton calculations through incorporation of Coulomb interactions. This technique effectively captures quantum confinement effects and g-factor anisotropy arising from nanostructure geometry. We demonstrate the method's capabilities through numerical calculations on CdSe and CdTe nanostructures, illustrating how structural morphology influences the magnetic response. The framework provides a versatile tool for investigating magnetooptical properties in confined semiconductor systems with arbitrary shapes.

We present spectral results from a coordinated, multi-satellite, broad-band campaign on the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy Ton S180 conducted at the end of 1999. We construct the spectral energy distribution (SED) by combining simultaneous Chandra, ASCA, and EUVE observations with contemporaneous FUSE, HST, and ground-based optical and infrared data. The assembled SED reveals that the bulk of the radiative output emerges in the 10–100 eV regime, indicating that the primary energy source dominates in the extreme ultraviolet and soft X-ray bands. The ultraviolet continuum shows no evidence for a spectral turnover, and the strong soft X-ray emission together with the overall SED shape imply that thermal emission from the accretion disk peaks between approximately 15 and 100 eV. High-resolution FUSE spectra exhibit ultraviolet absorption due to O VI, whereas the Chandra spectrum shows no detectable X-ray absorption, jointly demonstrating the presence of a low column density, highly ionized absorber along our line of sight. The highly ionized state of the circumnuclear gas is most likely maintained by the high luminosity and steep ionizing continuum of the active nucleus. Given the intense ionizing flux in Ton S180, clouds within a few tens of light-days of the central source may be over-ionized and thus inefficient at producing strong emission lines. We therefore infer that the narrow widths of the permitted emission lines arise because the dominant line-emitting region is located at larger radii where the gravitationally induced velocities are lower. These results provide a self-consistent picture linking the EUV-peaked disk emission, steep soft X-ray spectrum, and the ionization state and geometry of the circumnuclear medium in this prototypical narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy.

We develop a Horn-Schunck-type variational optical flow model for image sequences on non-Euclidean, time-varying domains. A time-dependent Riemannian metric encodes the geometry and deformation of the evolving surface and underpins an intrinsic spatio-temporal regularizer coupled with the optical flow constraint. The functional naturally generalizes static-domain models by Weickert and Schnorr (2001) and Lefvre and Baillet (2008). We establish existence of minimizers and well-posedness of the estimation problem, and derive the Euler-Lagrange equations together with necessary and sufficient optimality conditions. A geometry-preserving discretization and efficient solver are presented. Experiments on synthetic data and real sequences on deforming surfaces demonstrate accurate motion recovery, improved temporal coherence, and robustness to noise relative to Euclidean and static-manifold baselines. We also discuss practical parameter selection and quantify the influence of surface curvature on flow smoothness and stability properties. The framework provides a principled tool for motion estimation on evolving surfaces and opens avenues for applications in biomedical imaging and computer vision.

We study neutrino mass matrix phenomenology within the inverse seesaw framework, imposing a scaling ansatz alongside texture zeros. A systematic scan shows that, to retain compatibility with current oscillation data, at most four texture zeros can be assigned across the Dirac and singlet Majorana sectors. The resulting effective neutrino mass matrices are organized into four generic categories. When the scaling ansatz is softly broken to accommodate realistic mixing, one category is excluded because it yields an unacceptable reactor angle. In all viable cases the mass ordering is inverted. A distinctive prediction of every surviving category is an almost vanishing leptonic CP violation, with J_CP strongly suppressed by the smallness of the relevant mixing parameter(s), notably the reactor angle. Consequently, any future observation of sizable CP violation would disfavour these texture–scaling constructions within inverse seesaw.

I present a new census of the members of the Chamaeleon I star-forming region based on comprehensive spectroscopic and ancillary analysis. Optical spectroscopy has been obtained for 179 objects previously identified as possible cluster members that lacked either accurate spectral classifications or clear evidence of membership and are optically visible. Combining these spectra with all available constraints from the literature—including gravity-sensitive features, lithium absorption, Hα emission, photometry, infrared excesses, X-ray detections, and kinematics—I reassess the spectral types and membership status for a total of 288 candidate members that have appeared in published studies. The resulting census contains 158 confirmed members, 8 of which have spectral types later than M6 and are therefore likely to be brown dwarfs. I find that a significant fraction of objects reported as members in recent surveys are actually field interlopers. In contrast, 7 of 9 candidates discovered by a previous study are confirmed as members, including the coolest known member of Chamaeleon I with a spectral type of M8. For confirmed members, I estimate extinctions, effective temperatures, and bolometric luminosities and use these to construct a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram for the cluster. Comparison to pre-main-sequence evolutionary models indicates a median age of a few million years, making Chamaeleon I similar in age to IC 348 and slightly older than Taurus. Because the known members were identified through disparate selection methods across multiple studies, the present sample is not suitable for deriving a robust initial mass function. A reliable measurement of the IMF for Chamaeleon I will require an unbiased, magnitude-limited survey with uniform selection and follow-up. This revised membership census provides a foundation for future studies of the cluster’s stellar and substellar populations, star formation history, and environmental influences on early stellar evolution.

Within the standard paradigm of structure formation, massive present-day elliptical galaxies are often hypothesized to originate from major mergers of spiral progenitors. We investigate this pathway through a suite of hydrodynamical simulations that span a range of mass ratios, gas fractions, orbital parameters, and feedback prescriptions. We quantify the dynamical and morphological relaxation of the remnants using photometric (Sersic index, isophotal shape) and kinematic (v/sigma, misalignment) diagnostics, defining the relaxation time as the epoch when these metrics stabilize and tidal debris becomes dynamically inconsequential. We then confront the resulting timescales with expectations from hierarchical assembly by coupling Press-Schechter merger trees to our simulation-based relaxation criteria. For mergers of near-equal mass spirals, photometric relaxation typically occurs within about 1-2 Gyr of first pericenter, whereas kinematic equilibration and the decay of low-surface-brightness debris persist for up to about 3-5 Gyr, with significant dependence on gas content and orbit. When mapped onto cosmological histories, a non-negligible fraction of halos hosting present-day ellipticals would require relaxation times shorter than allowed by the simulations. This tension implies that a subset of ellipticals likely formed through channels other than major spiral-spiral mergers.

We investigate the spin-dependent electron–phonon scatterings of the @xmath0 and @xmath1 valleys and the band structure near the conduction-band minima in germanium. To capture the spin and symmetry, we construct a @xmath2 @xmath3 Hamiltonian in the vicinity of the @xmath0 point that reproduces the dispersions and symmetries of the lowest three conduction bands and the highest two valence bands. This Hamiltonian enables a transparent analysis of spin-related properties of conduction electrons, including spin admixture that governs spin relaxation. Building on this framework, we derive the phonon-induced electron scatterings of the @xmath0 and @xmath1 valleys, encompassing intra-@xmath1/@xmath0 valley, inter@xmath1-@xmath0 valley, and inter@xmath0-@xmath0 valley processes. We determine the selection rules and provide complete scattering matrices for all channels. In particular, the scattering matrices for the intra-@xmath1 valley scattering, the inter@xmath1-@xmath0 valley scattering, and the decomposition of the intra-@xmath1 valley scattering into optical-phonon and separated transverse-acoustic and longitudinal-acoustic contributions are reported for the first time. Coefficients are obtained from pseudo-potential calculations that verify the selection rules and wave-vector dependences. This furnishes a compact parametrization for predictive transport modeling in germanium devices. We further analyze the Elliott–Yafet mechanisms in these electron–phonon scatterings using the @xmath4@xmath5@xmath6 eigenstates at the @xmath0 and @xmath1 valleys, clarifying the roles of spin mixing and spin-dependent couplings. These results provide essential inputs for modeling optical spin orientation and hot-electron relaxation in germanium, and establish a symmetry-grounded description of spin-dependent transport and dynamics.

We investigate the scaling of the weak gravitational lensing signal with stellar mass around a carefully selected sample of relatively isolated galaxies. This lens selection minimizes environmental and satellite contributions, simplifying the physical interpretation of the measured shear. Our analysis combines deep imaging and shape measurements from the Red-Sequence Cluster Survey with spectro-photometric data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, enabling robust stellar mass estimates and lens–source geometry. By stacking lenses in stellar-mass bins, we measure the amplitude of the galaxy–galaxy lensing signal and find that its dependence on stellar mass is well described by a power law with best-fit slope @xmath0. This empirical relation is inconsistent with the prediction from Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND), which expects slope @xmath1; instead we obtain @xmath2 with 99.7% confidence. As a complementary test, we derive the MOND mass-to-light ratio as a function of luminosity and show that the most luminous galaxies require additional mass beyond stars and gas (@xmath3). We further rule out an extended halo of baryonic gas or active neutrinos as viable reconciliations within MOND. Although our analysis centers on a specific alternative gravity framework, the results provide a stringent, model-independent benchmark for any modification to gravity that aims to explain galaxy-scale lensing without dark matter.

Determinants of linear maps encode fundamental invariants of vector-space morphisms. Modern theory extends this notion in two directions: determinants of linear complexes (nilpotent chains of maps) and resultants of non-linear mappings. We present an elementary, self-contained introduction to both generalizations and clarify their deep relation: the resultant of a polynomial map equals the determinant of the associated Koszul complex. The paper develops unified definitions, constructive algorithms, and transparent proofs, illustrated by low-dimensional examples and explicit computations. We discuss algebraic and homological properties, normalization choices, and functorial behavior, and indicate prospective applications to theoretical physics, including constraints, anomalies, and effective actions. The exposition aims to make these tools accessible for future use across mathematics and physics.

Detailed radio and X-ray observations of massive OB and WR binaries over the past decades have revealed thermal and non-thermal components dominated by wind–wind shocks, yet most modeling has relied on hydrodynamics with ad hoc magnetic prescriptions. We present the first fully magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of colliding stellar winds in massive binaries that self-consistently evolve the magnetic field, the shocked plasma, and radiation diagnostics. Our models span a parameter space in wind momenta, mass-loss rates, terminal velocities, orbital separation, and eccentricity, enabling synthetic observables for free–free and synchrotron emission. We compute frequency-dependent free–free spectra and images and quantify their dependence on stellar and orbital properties, including phase-dependent absorption and cooling regimes. From the MHD fields we derive particle acceleration efficiencies and synchrotron emissivity, and integrate along lines of sight to obtain radio maps and light curves; inverse Compton scattering implications for the X-ray band are also assessed. We find that magnetic amplification at the shocks, driven by compression, shear, and turbulence, produces field strengths exceeding those inferred from assuming proportionality between B and the plasma density. As a result, the synchrotron contribution to the total radio flux is larger than previously estimated, and can dominate at centimeter wavelengths for microphysical parameters, even in systems with free–free opacity. The combined thermal–non-thermal emission is strongly modulated with orbital phase, with enhanced brightness and spectral flattening near periastron in eccentric systems. Our work removes key uncertainties in magnetic field geometry and normalization, provides testable predictions for multi-frequency monitoring, and establishes MHD wind–wind interaction as essential for interpreting radio and X-ray emission from massive binaries.

We introduce a driven two-species particle model on an open chain with bulk non-conserving dynamics and species-exchange symmetry. The model displays spontaneous symmetry breaking and localized shocks, arising from the interplay of boundary reservoirs and bulk creation/annihilation processes. Using a mean-field approximation, we compute steady-state density profiles, currents, and phase boundaries in several regions of parameter space, and compare these predictions with Monte Carlo simulations, finding agreement and identifying regimes where correlations matter. In the limit of vanishing particle-number fluctuations, we obtain an exact solution that determines shock locations and observables. We propose a unifying physical picture that explains the emergence and stability of the phases and the transitions between them.

We study a minimal Hubbard-type system across interaction strengths U, analyzing the density response to a strong, nonperturbative excitation using nonequilibrium Green’s functions within the generalized Kadanoff-Baym ansatz (GKBA) and the Second Born (2B) approximation. The computed spectra exhibit pronounced correlation-induced structures and reveal an involved double-excitation process. Benchmarking against exact Green’s-function results, we uncover an anomalous U dependence of the double-excitation energy in 2B+GKBA, deviating from the exact trend. This behavior mirrors earlier observations for quantum wells [Balzer et al., EPL 98, 67002 (2012)], highlighting limitations of 2B+GKBA in the nonlinear regime. Our findings delineate the regimes of validity and motivate higher-level self-energies for accurate nonlinear response.

Mode changing and nulling in pulsars are typically treated as independent phenomena, yet PSR B1822–09 exhibits a striking coupling between them. Using phase-resolved single-pulse analysis, we show that a precursor feature just ahead of the main pulse (MP) undergoes episodic nulls during which an interpulse (IP) becomes detectable at a rotation phase separated by roughly 180 degrees from the precursor. The rapid, reversible exchange of emission power between these components implies an information transfer on timescales of a few rotations that is difficult to reconcile with distinct, spatially separated emission sites. We propose that both the precursor/MP and IP originate in the same emission region, with the coherent radio emission intermittently reversing its propagation direction: outward when the precursor is active, inward when the IP appears. This bidirectional beaming naturally accounts for the lack of weak off-pulse radiation and for the apparent instantaneous coupling between components, while the reversals inherently produce nulls. The model demands that pulsar radio mechanisms allow emission into two opposite directions and that radio waves can traverse inner magnetospheric regions with strong magnetic fields. PSR B1822–09 thus offers compelling evidence for inward radio emission and places new constraints on magnetospheric geometry, propagation, and coherence in pulsar radio physics.

We report the low-temperature magnetic properties of the pyrochlore pr@xmath0hf@xmath0o@xmath1. Polycrystalline and single-crystal samples were investigated by time-of-flight neutron spectroscopy and macroscopic measurements, respectively. Crystal-field analysis reveals that pr@xmath2 hosts a non-Kramers doublet ground state with pronounced Ising-like anisotropy. Below 0.5 K, ferromagnetic correlations emerge, indicating entry into a spin-ice-like regime consistent with metamagnetic behavior observed near @xmath3 T. In this low-temperature state, the neutron spectra develop a discrete inelastic excitation, evidencing spin dynamics likely driven by cooperative quantum fluctuations. Our results establish pr@xmath0hf@xmath0o@xmath1 as a candidate quantum spin ice in which anisotropic crystal-field effects, emergent ferromagnetism, and field-tuned metamagnetism intertwine to produce unconventional low-energy excitations.

We study an arbitrary linear first-order elliptic differential operator with smooth coefficients acting between sections of complex vector bundles over a compact smooth manifold with smooth boundary. In a collar neighborhood of the boundary we exhibit analytic and topological features of the operator and analyze several product decompositions that isolate its tangential part. Using sectorial projections of the tangential operator, we construct families of invertible doubles via suitable local boundary conditions and develop Poisson-type solution operators with distinct mapping properties. A canonical Calderón projection is obtained by an intrinsic procedure that avoids auxiliary choices and is stable under perturbations. Applications include a generalization of the cobordism theorem and criteria ensuring continuous dependence of the Calderón projection and of well-posed selfadjoint Fredholm extensions on the underlying geometric and analytic data. Implications are noted.

We revisit Wald’s argument showing that extremal Kerr–Newman black holes cannot be converted into naked singularities by plunging test particles. Using a refined capture analysis that enforces energy, charge, and angular-momentum constraints at the horizon, we extend to near-extremal geometries and identify regimes where horizon destruction is permitted within the test-particle approximation. For black holes with a small departure from extremality, we derive analytic inequalities delineating a window in particle energy, angular momentum, and charge such that the post-capture parameters violate the Kerr–Newman bound, producing a naked singularity. To reduce the impact of radiative and self-force backreaction, we determine optimal particle choices, giving minimal angular momentum and charge that still overspin or overcharge, and quantify their scaling with the deviation from extremality and background fields. We outline an astrophysical pathway in radio galaxies: charged clumps or jets aligned with rapidly rotating candidates can be tuned to the optimal window, potentially driving horizon loss. We discuss consistency, observational signatures, and implications for cosmic censorship.

Decades after the inception of density functional theory, the exact energy functional in terms of the electron density remains elusive. We propose a phase-space density functional theory (PSDFT) grounded in Wigner distributions and establish Hohenberg–Kohn–Levy-type theorems in phase space. We address the N-representability problem for reduced Wigner functions and analyze key properties of the universal functional, including convexity, lower semicontinuity, scaling, and coordinate and gauge invariances, alongside exact constraints. A comprehensive natural Wigner orbital (NWO) theory is developed, yielding orbital equations, idempotency conditions, occupation bounds, and representability criteria. Guided by these structures, we construct exchange–correlation functionals on phase space, propose constrained approximations, and connect to semiclassical limits. A new proof of the overbinding property of the Muller functional is provided within this framework, elucidating the origin of delocalization errors. We show how the Thomas-Fermi model emerges as the exact mean-field limit, thereby finding a rigorous home in PSDFT. Illustrative calculations for atoms and model systems demonstrate systematic improvements. The framework unifies density, current, and momentum information, enabling tighter bounds for correlation energies and improved treatment of strong correlation and external magnetic fields.

We investigate how substrate material and film thickness control the Peierls transition temperature (T_P) in tetrathiafulvalene–tetracyanoquinodimethane (TTF–TCNQ) thin films grown by physical vapor deposition. By varying substrates and thicknesses, and combining structural (AFM, XRD) and transport measurements, we show that substrate choice and growth conditions strongly impact film morphology, inducing roughness, grain boundaries, and strain. Thin films exhibit reduced T_P relative to single crystals. We attribute the suppression of T_P to defect-mediated scattering and altered charge-density-wave coherence arising during growth. These findings clarify morphology–transition correlations and guide optimization of charge-transfer conductors.

We revisit astrophysical limits on theories with an ultra-light gravitino, extending previous studies to broader model spaces and to scenarios with R-parity violation. We compute gravitino production and emission in supernova cores and related environments, incorporating the dependence on scalar moduli masses that mediate the relevant interactions. A global parameter scan is analyzed with both frequentist profiling and Bayesian marginalization; the two approaches yield consistent bounds, though the Bayesian posteriors exhibit mild volume effects. We find that, in a model-independent treatment, only a narrow window of gravitino masses is excluded by SN cooling. Assuming specific scalar mass spectra leads to substantially stronger, but model-dependent, exclusions.

We propose a discrete spacetime classical field theory framework that unifies covariant and initial-data descriptions via a transfer matrix, mirroring lattice field theory and spin foam compositions. Solutions on elementary spacetime cells are computed and consistently amalgamated when boundary data satisfy simple gluing conditions that coincide with the composition rules of cellular amplitudes/propagators in spin foam models. The formalism is derived from a discrete variational principle and carries a multisymplectic structure that induces local conservation laws and well-posed evolution across cells. We discuss effective, scale-dependent models within this setting, and develop tools for coarse graining, including cellular renormalization, and criteria for continuum limits. Examples illustrate the approach and clarify its relation to lattice constructions.

We demonstrate that non-perturbative effects are logarithmically enhanced in transverse-momentum-dependent observables, including electroweak boson transverse momentum spectra in hadronic collisions and jet broadening in e+e- annihilation. The enhancement originates from the collinear anomaly, characteristic of transverse measurements, which generates a logarithmic dependence on the hard scale in the product of soft and collinear matrix elements. Using an operator product expansion, we establish a systematic, model-independent framework to quantify robustly non-perturbative corrections for this class of observables. For jet broadening, we relate the leading power correction to the well-known non-perturbative shift of the thrust distribution, enabling consistent parameterization. Our results refine resummed predictions, constrain universality patterns of non-perturbative effects, and suggest phenomenologically relevant tests across processes and energy scales.

We investigate the non-equilibrium dynamics of electrons in metals and cold plasmas to extract microscopic parameters of Coulomb and electron-phonon interactions. To overcome the complexity of collision integrals, we recast the time-dependent Boltzmann equation into an equivalent partial differential Schrödinger-like equation in imaginary time, defined in a one-dimensional coordinate space reciprocal to energy. This transformation yields closed-form analytical solutions for electron-electron and electron-phonon relaxation, including eigenmode spectra and exact temporal evolution of energy distributions. From these solutions, we derive exact relaxation rates and compare them with quasi-equilibrium (time-dependent temperature) predictions across temperature regimes. We find systematic deviations from quasi-equilibrium at low temperatures, while convergence emerges at high temperatures. The framework enables transparent identification of dominant scattering channels and direct extraction of coupling strengths, offering benchmarks for pump–probe experiments and guiding the interpretation of ultrafast relaxation in metals.

We report shell-model calculations for odd-odd nuclei in the lower fp shell using a new isospin-nonconserving microscopic effective interaction. The interaction is derived from the high-precision charge-dependent Bonn nucleon–nucleon potential by the folded-diagram renormalization method. Calculated level schemes, band structures, and electromagnetic observables show excellent agreement with available data up to band terminations, including a successful reproduction of the relative ordering and spacing of the T=0 and T=1 bands. Comparable results are obtained with an alternative interaction constructed from the Idaho-A chiral potential, demonstrating the robustness of our conclusions. The calculations account for the presence of high-spin isomeric states associated with configurations in the f7/2 subshell. As case studies, we discuss in detail the spectroscopy and isospin structure of 50V and 54Mn, and provide predictions for unobserved or uncertain levels and transition rates. For 54Mn, where experimental information remains incomplete, our results offer guidance for future measurements.

Open quantum systems are commonly modeled as embedded in a single environment, the continuum of scattering states, yet many realistic devices couple to more than one continuum, as in cavities with distinct input and output channels. We develop a generic description of a system coupled to two channels and benchmark it against the one-channel case. Employing an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and the associated S-matrix, we trace the evolution of complex eigenvalues and biorthogonal eigenstates as the couplings are varied, with emphasis on parameter regions governed by exceptional (singular) points. In these regimes, the environment mixes the system’s states and renders the dynamics intrinsically nonlinear. For one-channel scattering, the nonlinear processes reorganize widths and phases so as to restore a conventional resonance structure in the cross section, obviating their explicit treatment in most practical calculations. For two-channel transport, by contrast, the same processes produce qualitatively new effects: a pronounced enhancement of conductance through an open cavity, accompanied by eigenstate reorientation and reduced phase rigidity, yet not attributable to the formation of a superradiant state. The enhancement derives from the structure of the eigenstates of the non-Hermitian operator and appears robust across microscopic implementations. We outline experimentally accessible signatures in conductance lineshapes and parameter sweeps, providing a direct test of non-Hermitian quantum physics in mesoscopic platforms. Our comparative analysis establishes the universal role of exceptional points in shaping open-system dynamics.

We consider the heating of biological tissue by injecting gold nanoparticles (GNPs) and exposing the system to radio-frequency (RF) electromagnetic fields, a strategy proposed for localized hyperthermia in cancer treatment. While several studies have reported substantial local heating around small conductors, other recent publications challenge whether metal nanoparticles can be appreciably heated at RF. This work provides a classical electromagnetic analysis of the mechanisms available to homogeneous conducting nanospheres suspended in a lossy medium representative of tissue. Starting from exact vector spherical wave solutions and associated energy balance relations for lossy materials, we formulate a near-field optimization in which the power absorbed inside the nanoparticles is maximized subject to constraints on total power deposition and current distribution in the surrounding medium, including limitations imposed by skin effect. Under these assumptions, we show that capacitive coupling—i.e., using strong electric fields to induce electric dipoles in the particles—cannot yield significant nanoparticle-specific heating unless the GNP volume fraction is unrealistically high for biomedical applications, or unless additional mechanisms not captured by homogeneous sphere models are present. Examples of such mechanisms include ligand coatings that enable electrophoretic motion and associated dispersive resonances. By contrast, a quasi-magnetostatic treatment indicates that inductive coupling, via eddy currents driven by RF magnetic fields, can in principle produce enhanced local absorption, provided the incident magnetic field amplitude is sufficiently large. However, when the exterior medium is modeled as saline water to approximate tissue conductivities, the optimization reveals that bulk skin effect dominates the near field at commonly regulated RF frequencies, severely limiting the magnetic field penetration and thus the achievable eddy-current heating within GNPs. Under realistic constraints, the simple inductive-heating paradigm is therefore predicted to be ineffective for homogeneous metallic nanoparticles in tissue at RF. These results reconcile conflicting reports by delineating the limits of classical dipole mechanisms in lossy environments and by quantifying the role of skin effect in RF near-field coupling. Future research should investigate plausible dispersion and charge-transport mechanisms in coated GNPs, including electrophoretic resonances, as potential avenues for achieving significant, selective RF absorption. The analysis clarifies limits under regulatory RF bands, highlighting key dependencies on tissue conductivity, particle size, and field delivery, and provides guidance for designing alternative nanoparticle-based hyperthermia strategies.

Extracting performance from contemporary multicore processors demands detailed insight into microarchitecture and the increasingly intricate thread and cache topology. We present LIKWID, a lightweight set of command-line utilities that (1) probe thread and cache topology, (2) enforce thread–core affinity, (3) measure hardware performance counter metrics, and (4) toggle hardware prefetchers. An accompanying API exposes counter functionality to user code, and we delineate conceptual and practical differences to the widely used PAPI interface. We demonstrate LIKWID’s capabilities on two case studies: the OpenMP STREAM Triad benchmark, where explicit thread pinning improves bandwidth scalability by reducing thread migration and contention, and a stencil kernel optimized to exploit shared caches on multicore chips, where affinity control and counter-based analysis reveal bottlenecks and guide tuning, including prefetcher settings. These results underscore LIKWID as a practical, low-overhead toolbox for understanding node topology, enforcing affinity, and driving quantitative, architecture-aware performance engineering.

We present a spectroscopic study of the magnetic, chemically peculiar A star HR 710 (HD 15144 = ADS 1849A = AB Cet), which is in a nearly circular binary with a period of about 3 days—unusually short for Ap stars. The system emits moderately hard X-rays that are best explained by a white dwarf secondary (ADS 1849AB). High-resolution UVES spectra obtained at a single epoch reveal exceptionally strong Sr II features; the Sr II resonance lines display a pronounced core-nib morphology closely analogous to the stronger Ca II K line. Standard, homogeneous atmospheric models constrained by effective temperature, surface gravity, and global abundances provide only loose fits. Multiple diagnostics (strong-line profiles, anomalous excitation/ionization equilibria) point to substantial departures from traditional assumptions, including indications of lower electron and gas pressures than expected from the star’s parallax and brightness. The behavior of weak lines—profile shapes and small wavelength shifts—argues for abundance patches on the stellar surface rather than contamination by a secondary spectrum. We interpret the spectrum in the context of vertical abundance stratification coupled with horizontal inhomogeneities. Because our conclusions are based on one-epoch data, additional high signal-to-noise, high-resolution spectroscopy spanning rotational and orbital phases is essential to refine the atmospheric structure, map abundance distributions, and test the white dwarf companion scenario.

We investigate dynamical heterogeneities in the collective relaxation of concentrated microgel suspensions, a prototypical soft colloid system whose effective packing fraction can be tuned continuously by temperature via particle deswelling. Combining photon correlation imaging to map spatiotemporal fluctuations with oscillatory shear rheology to probe mechanical response, we chart how the range of spatial correlations in the dynamics evolves across fluid, glassy, and squeezed regimes. As the packing fraction increases toward the fluid–solid transition, where the low-frequency behavior shifts from viscous to elastic, the correlation length associated with dynamical activity grows markedly, indicating increasingly cooperative motion. At and just beyond this transition, correlations become system-spanning, saturating at the size of the observable field of view, consistent with a critically enhanced collective relaxation. Upon further densification, a second transition emerges: the dynamics partition into extended zones of markedly different activity separated by relatively sharp boundaries, and the correlation range decreases, revealing a striking non-monotonic dependence of spatial correlations on volume fraction. This phenomenology mirrors that reported at the jamming/rigidity transition in athermal granular systems and signals the onset of stress-driven dynamics. We identify this regime as a squeezed state in which particles develop enduring contacts and direct, imbalanced stresses govern rearrangements. Concomitantly, the frequency dependence of the storage and loss moduli evolves from largely decoupled, thermally dominated behavior to a more tightly coupled response, reflecting increased dissipation from frictional and contact-mediated processes. Our results establish a unified picture in which thermal glassiness and athermal jamming are connected by a crossover from thermally activated to stress-controlled dynamics. To our knowledge, these measurements provide the first direct observation of a qualitative change in dynamical heterogeneity accompanying the transition from purely thermal to contact-driven relaxation in soft colloidal microgels.

We show that single-particle resonances in quantum wires are Fano-type, yielding channel-dependent scattering phase behavior: certain transverse modes exhibit sharp phase drops while others remain smooth. Using multichannel scattering theory and a Friedel-sum-rule analysis, we quantify how channel-resolved phase shifts encode the integrated charge localized near a scatterer. We derive criteria—based on symmetry, mode coupling, and Fano parameter q—that determine which channels are maximally informative. Numerical simulations for realistic geometries identify a small subset of modes that optimizes sensitivity, guiding experimental measurements.

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) bispectrum is a key probe of the non-Gaussianity of primordial perturbations. Weak gravitational lensing by the intervening large-scale structure remaps primary anisotropies, smoothing features in the angular power spectrum; we show it likewise smooths and suppresses the primary bispectrum generated at last scattering. Using the standard lensing remapping in harmonic space, we compute the lensed bispectrum for the local model and quantify the scale-dependent suppression across the acoustic regime. Lensing reduces the amplitude by an amount that grows with multipole, yielding an overall decrease at multipoles between 100 and 2000. We propagate this effect through optimal estimators and Fisher forecasts to assess biases in measurements of primordial non-Gaussianity. Because current estimators for @xmath0 neglect lensing of the primary bispectrum, they return biased-low values. For WMAP-like data analyzed to @xmath1, the bias is about 6% for the local shape. For a high-resolution experiment such as Planck, the bias reaches roughly 30% unless the lensing modification is included. Lensing also degrades sensitivity: the minimum detectable @xmath0 for the local type increases from about 5 to 7 for Planck, and for a cosmic variance limited experiment from less than 3 to @xmath2 5. We provide lensed bispectrum templates and a practical prescription to incorporate lensing into estimators, thereby removing bias and recovering near-optimal sensitivity. Our results demonstrate that weak lensing is an essential component of precision bispectrum analyses and must be accounted for to derive robust constraints on primordial non-Gaussianity.

We present sub-arcsecond mid-infrared observations with the Gran Telescopio Canarias/CanariCam, comprising 8.7 μm imaging and 7.5–13 μm slit spectroscopy, for six nearby systems that host an active galactic nucleus (AGN) and show nuclear star formation (Mrk 1066, Mrk 1073, NGC 2273, Arp 299, NGC 6240, and IRAS 17208−0014). Our primary aim is to test whether the carriers of the 11.3 μm polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) feature survive in the immediate vicinity of AGN. We detect the 11.3 μm PAH feature in the nuclear regions of all targets and trace extended PAH emission over scales of a few hundred parsecs. Radial profiles of the PAH equivalent width (EW) reveal pronounced minima at the nuclei, with EWs increasing steadily with radius to reach values characteristic of star-forming regions at distances of a few hundred parsecs. We interpret the depressed nuclear EWs as the result of dilution by a strong AGN-heated continuum rather than destruction of the PAH carriers. Spectral decompositions and comparisons with ancillary star formation indicators support this view, showing that the absolute 11.3 μm PAH flux persists while the underlying continuum rises toward the nucleus. These results imply that the PAH molecules responsible for the 11.3 μm feature can survive in nuclear environments as close as approximately 10 pc from the AGN for Seyfert-like luminosities. We propose that shielding by dusty tori, compact nuclear gas disks, and/or circumnuclear interstellar material provides sufficient column density to protect PAH molecules from the AGN radiation field. Our findings reinforce the utility of the 11.3 μm PAH feature as a tracer of star formation in composite AGN–starburst nuclei when high spatial resolution is available to mitigate continuum dilution.

Using the density functional theory of fermion condensation, we develop a unified framework for non‐Fermi‐liquid behavior in strongly correlated Fermi systems, with treatments of both lattices and homogeneous matter. We derive self‐consistent equations for the quasiparticle effective mass M* near the fermion‐condensation quantum phase transition and show that its strong dependence on temperature, carrier density, and magnetic field produces the observed departures from Landau Fermi‐liquid phenomenology. Low‐temperature thermodynamic and transport responses remain governed by quasiparticles, but with variable M* that yields universal scaling. Quantitative predictions for the specific heat, magnetization, energy scales, longitudinal magnetoresistance, and magnetic entropy are presented and compared with recent measurements on the heavy‐fermion metal @xmath0, revealing agreement and a description of the LFL–NFL crossover.

Magnetic phase transitions in ferromagnetic crystals are known to induce anomalous temperature dependence in electron and spin resistivity, often attributed to spin-dependent scattering between itinerant electrons and lattice spins. Here we investigate this behavior in ferromagnetic films using extensive Monte Carlo simulations to compute the resistivity of a spin current as a function of temperature, from the low-temperature ordered phase to the high-temperature paramagnetic phase. We systematically analyze the roles of film thickness, surface exchange interactions, and different impurity types on the evolution of spin resistivity across the critical region. The simulations reveal a pronounced resistivity peak near the Curie temperature, which we trace to the formation of magnetic domains and enhanced critical spin fluctuations that increase spin-dependent scattering. Thinner films and modified surface interactions modulate the peak’s amplitude and width, while impurity type and concentration governingly tune the baseline and critical enhancement of resistivity. Building on these results, we construct a transport theory based on the Boltzmann equation in the relaxation-time approximation, with temperature-dependent scattering rates extracted from the simulations. The theoretical predictions quantitatively reproduce the Monte Carlo trends and are in good agreement with available experimental observations. Implications for tailoring spin transport in ferromagnetic nanostructures are discussed.

We investigate the combined influence of nontrivial topology induced by a straight cosmic string and planar boundaries on fermionic vacuum polarization. The system consists of a massive Dirac field in the conical spacetime with arbitrary planar angle deficit, bounded by two parallel plates perpendicular to the string axis and imposing the MIT bag boundary condition. Employing a mode-summation technique supplemented by an Abel–Plana type summation formula, we obtain exact representations for the fermionic condensate and the vacuum expectation value of the energy–momentum tensor in the region between the plates. The vacuum observables are decomposed into boundary-free (pure cosmic string) and boundary-induced contributions, allowing a clear separation of topological and boundary effects for general deficit angles. We show that the boundary-induced parts of both the fermionic condensate and the energy–momentum tensor vanish on the string. The condensate is positive in the vicinity of the string and becomes negative at large radial distances, while the vacuum energy density is negative everywhere. The radial stress equals the energy density. In the massless limit, the boundary-induced contribution to the energy–momentum tensor is nonzero only between the plates and is independent of the coordinate along the string axis. For both massive and massless fields, the topological contributions between the plates exhibit exponential decay at large radial distances from the string, in contrast to the power-law decay characteristic of the boundary-free conical geometry for a massless field. The vacuum pressure on the plates is spatially inhomogeneous, vanishing at the string’s location, and the resulting Casimir forces are attractive. Our results, presented in closed integral forms, elucidate the interplay between conical topology and boundary conditions, and characterize the dependence of vacuum polarization on the fermion mass, plate separation, and angle deficit, with consistent asymptotic behaviors and conservation properties. PACS numbers: 03.70.+k, 98.80.Cq, 11.27.+d.

We present a comprehensive review of neutrino phenomenology in the minimal seesaw model (MSM), an economical extension of the Standard Model with two heavy right-handed Majorana neutrinos. With current oscillation data, the MSM predicts a rank-2 light-neutrino mass matrix, implying one massless neutrino and fixing the mass ordering and absolute mass scale up to small uncertainties. We quantify the resulting ranges for the effective electron-neutrino mass in tritium beta decay and the effective Majorana mass governing neutrinoless double-beta decay. Five equivalent schemes to parameterize the neutrino Yukawa matrix are outlined, enabling transparent mapping between low-energy observables and high-scale model inputs. Incorporating texture zeros in the Dirac mass matrix, we analyze lepton flavor mixing, CP phases, and the viability of baryogenesis via leptogenesis. An analytic upper bound on the CP-violating asymmetry in the decay of the lighter right-handed neutrino is derived, and renormalization-group evolution of mixing parameters is evaluated, emphasizing correlations between low-energy CP violation and high-energy asymmetries. We show that resonant leptogenesis at the TeV scale can naturally reproduce the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry. In a supersymmetric MSM, we discuss lepton-flavor-violating rare decays such as mu -> e gamma, identify parameter regions consistent with current bounds, and highlight experimental prospects and collider searches.

We analyze synchronizability of delay-coupled networks of identical units in the regime of large coupling delays. Using the master stability function (MSF), we prove a universal structure: the MSF becomes rotationally symmetric about the origin in the complex plane and grows monotonically with radius. This universality decouples dynamical details from topology, yielding a simple classification of networks solely in terms of the spectrum of the coupling matrix. We provide derivations of the asymptotic MSF, delineate stability boundaries via eigenvalue radii, and show how directedness and weights affect spectral radii. The classification is illustrated for topologies including rings, lattices, and scale-free networks.

Cocomparability graphs are those whose complements admit a transitive orientation, while interval graphs arise as intersection graphs of intervals on the real line. Motivated by recent results showing that algorithms designed for interval graphs often extend, with minor modifications, to cocomparability graphs, we investigate structural relationships that explain this algorithmic proximity. Our main contribution is a new characterization of cocomparability graphs via a lattice structure on the set of their maximal cliques. This lattice-based perspective unifies and clarifies several known properties and, in particular, yields a structural proof that in any cocomparability graph G, every maximal interval subgraph of G is also a maximal chordal subgraph of G. Although the maximal-clique lattice can be exponential in size, it provides a principled framework for designing and analyzing algorithms on cocomparability graphs that preserve cocomparability orderings. Leveraging this framework, we introduce Local Maximal Neighborhood Search (LocalMNS), a new graph search that preserves the relevant ordering structure. We show that LocalMNS yields a linear-time algorithm to compute a maximal interval subgraph of a cocomparability graph, improving upon the best known bounds. Using related ideas, we further present a linear-time algorithm to compute all simplicial vertices in cocomparability graphs, again advancing the state of the art. These results strengthen the algorithmic bridge between interval and cocomparability graphs and illustrate the power of lattice-theoretic viewpoints—specifically maximal antichain and maximal clique lattices—in guiding efficient graph algorithms on comparability-related classes. Keywords: cocomparability graphs, interval graphs, chordal graphs, posets, maximal antichain lattices, maximal clique lattices, graph searches, LocalMNS, simplicial vertices, transitive orientations.

Dust-producing Wolf–Rayet stars, though rare, exhibit exceptionally high dust formation rates and strong infrared excesses, particularly in WC8–WC9 subtypes. A subset of WC9d stars display spiral “pinwheel” nebulae, an indirect signature of colliding-wind binaries with a companion. For many WC9d systems, however, current single-aperture angular resolution is insufficient to determine whether similar structures are present. We report the possible detection of a pinwheel-like nebula surrounding WR 118 and discuss the evidence and uncertainties. We further assess the capability of modern infrared interferometry to image such nebulae, emphasizing the resolving power required to trace the dust spiral, measure orbital parameters, and quantify dust production. Interferometric surveys of WC9d stars promise tests of binarity and the physics of dust formation in extreme stellar winds.

During its nine-year mission, the Energetic Gamma Ray Experiment Telescope (EGRET) on the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory detected gamma-ray emission from more than 67 blazars. We searched the EGRET archive and selected all blazars with multiple observations and sufficient brightness to permit spectral fits with single power-law models. The sample comprises 26 sources: 18 flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), 6 low-frequency-peaked BL Lacs (LBLs), and 2 high-frequency-peaked BL Lacs (HBLs). Using skymaps regenerated to reflect time-dependent instrument performance, we derived photon indices and fluxes for individual viewing periods and examined spectral variability, flux-index correlations, and flare evolution. Our key findings are: (1) no universal relation between spectral index and flux across the sample; (2) several blazars show no significant spectral variability; (3) a subset exhibits spectral hardening with increasing flux; and (4) five blazars display a flux-hardness anticorrelation at low flux. The best observed sources (3C 279, 3C 273, PKS 0528+134, PKS 1622-297, PKS 0208-512) show no consistent long-term spectral trend with flux, but occupy both hard and soft states. In three FSRQs with well-sampled flares lasting about 3-4 weeks, we find previously unreported spectral hysteresis on weekly timescales, with counterclockwise loops in the flux-index plane despite different flux profiles. Interpreted within inverse-Compton scenarios for the EGRET band, including external Compton and synchrotron self-Compton, the loops imply a lag of spectral hardening relative to the flux rise—consistent with gradual particle acceleration or evolving Compton dominance during flare onset—followed by cooling-driven softening. These results highlight the diversity of gamma-ray spectral variability among blazars and constrain the timescales and radiative processes governing GeV emission. The recalibrated EGRET dataset provides a benchmark for comparative studies of blazar variability across missions.

We consider, for a graph G on n vertices, the Cayley graph on the symmetric group S_n generated by the transpositions (i j) corresponding to edges ij of G. For complete multipartite G, we derive a closed expression for the Laplacian spectrum of this Cayley graph using irreducible characters evaluated at transpositions and Littlewood–Richardson coefficients describing induction from Young subgroups. In particular, we identify the spectral gap and show it matches the Fiedler value of G. Consequently, Aldous’s spectral gap conjecture—equality of gaps for the simple random walk on G and the interchange process—holds for all complete multipartite graphs. Our approach unifies and extends prior cases (complete, bipartite) and suggests representation-theoretic tools for broader families.

Ion–water clusters offer a microscopic window on hydration, and it is often argued that extending such studies to larger cluster sizes can yield single-ion absolute hydration free energies that are inaccessible to classical thermodynamic methods. We reexamine this claim using recent computations and molecular theories of ion hydration, focusing on H+, Li+, Na+, and HO− and, by extension, neutral ion pairs. By combining modern statistical mechanical frameworks with high-level computational estimates of excess chemical potentials, we evaluate hydration free energies across cluster sizes and compare them with bulk thermodynamic benchmarks. The hydration free energies of neutral pairs computed here are in good agreement with experimental measurements, underscoring the robustness of pairwise thermodynamic quantities. In contrast, the calculated single-ion absolute hydration free energies and excess chemical potentials systematically deviate from values recently tabulated from ion–water cluster data. We demonstrate that these single-ion quantities are not disentangled from the potential of the phase in cluster-based analyses, even in the limit of large clusters, so that extrapolations inherently retain contributions extraneous to the local ionic environment. Consequently, naive calculations on ion–water clusters should agree with experimental cluster studies precisely because both include the phase potential, but they do not yield absolute single-ion hydration free energies as defined in bulk. These results clarify the interpretation of cluster data and highlight neutral ion pairs as the appropriate objects for rigorous thermodynamic comparison.

We report the discovery of a molecular cavity in the Norma near arm in the direction of Westerlund 1 (Wd1), but not associated with that cluster. The cavity exhibits a mean radial velocity of @xmath0 kms@xmath1, differing by up to @xmath240 kms@xmath1 from the mean radial velocity of Wd1 stars, and is bounded by a fragmented molecular shell of diameter ~100 pc and mass ~10@xmath3 m@xmath4. The shell is expanding at 6–@xmath5 kms@xmath1, implying a total kinetic energy of order @xmath6 erg. Within the cavity, the atomic H I surface density reaches a minimum. Remarkably, the morphology of the recently reported very high energy (VHE) @xmath7-ray emission by the H.E.S.S. Collaboration coincides with the cavity: the @xmath7-ray brightness traces the inner wall of the molecular shell rather than the dense gas surrounding the massive stars of Wd1. We argue that a likely source powering both the cavity and the VHE emission is the pulsar PSR J1648−4611, whose wind and past supernova activity could have driven the expansion and accelerated particles to TeV energies. We discuss the implications for particle transport and feedback in the Norma arm.

We present a one-dimensional, spherically symmetric, comoving numerical code for cosmic-ray (CR) shock acceleration that self-consistently evolves the particle distribution, gas dynamics, and their nonlinear coupling at expanding supernova remnant (SNR) shocks. To resolve the extremely wide dynamic range of CR diffusion length scales inherent to diffusive shock acceleration, the method combines subzone shock tracking with adaptive mesh refinement, ensuring the shock discontinuity remains within a single grid zone throughout the calculation. This design substantially relaxes spatial resolution requirements relative to typical fixed-grid Eulerian schemes and improves numerical convergence by yielding more accurate estimates of the compression rate experienced by CRs traversing the subshock, avoiding artifacts associated with subshock drift across the mesh. Using a Bohm-like diffusion model and a thermal leakage injection prescription, we compute CR acceleration and the associated nonlinear feedback during the Sedov–Taylor phase of SNR evolution. The simulations demonstrate strong shock modification, a pronounced CR precursor, enhanced total compression ratios, and spectrally concave CR distributions, closely mirroring behavior observed in plane-parallel shocks. The injected particle fraction is of order 10^-3, and up to 60% of the initial explosion energy is transferred to the CR component, consistent with previous nonlinear spherical CR shock results by Berezhko and collaborators. These findings validate the accuracy and efficiency of the comoving, shock-tracking approach for spherical shocks and establish a robust framework for future studies of time-dependent CR acceleration, shock modification, and multi-scale transport in SNRs and other astrophysical outflows.

This work reviews the present understanding of lepton energy spectra in inclusive semileptonic decays of beauty hadrons, and assesses their use as analyzers of b-quark polarization at the Z0 peak. Starting from the parton-level decay b -> q l nu with V-A couplings, we summarize the polarization dependence of the double differential distributions in lepton energy and angle, and trace how these correlations map into laboratory-frame energy spectra at LEP. Perturbative QCD corrections at O(alpha_s) and finite charm-mass effects are presented, together with scheme and scale dependencies. Nonperturbative contributions are discussed within the heavy-quark expansion, including 1/mb^2 terms governed by mu_pi^2 and mu_G^2, as well as models of Fermi motion and shape functions relevant near the endpoint. We review hadronization and polarization transfer to weakly decaying beauty hadrons, contrasting mesons, where spin depolarization is substantial, with baryons, where sizable polarization may survive. The impact of species fractions, fragmentation, and weak decays on the observable spectra is quantified. Both charged-lepton and neutrino spectra are considered; the latter, reconstructed from missing energy, offers complementary analyzing power and systematics. We outline experimental strategies to isolate primary b -> l decays from cascade backgrounds, and propose polarization-sensitive observables based on energy moments and forward-backward energy asymmetries that reduce dependence on |Vcb| and mb. Comparisons with Monte Carlo implementations are provided. We conclude that inclusive lepton spectra at the Z0 can yield competitive measurements of b polarization and tests of electroweak couplings, with theoretical uncertainties dominated by nonperturbative effects but controllable at the few-percent level.

We present statistical properties of diffuse Lyα halos (LAHs) around high-@xmath1 star-forming galaxies using large Subaru samples of Lyα emitters (LAEs) at @xmath2. In contrast, we do not detect a clear correlation between @xmath3 and UV magnitudes in the rank statistics. The cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm predicts cuspy inner density profiles in dark matter halos, yet observations of some low-mass galaxies indicate that cored halos better reproduce their internal kinematics. Clumps launched on wider orbits with semi-major axis @xmath4 pc can avoid prompt dissolution; however, dynamical friction causes their orbits to decay toward the center, ultimately erasing the substructure. In contrast, within cored halos the clumps remain coherent for a Hubble time, even when as extended as @xmath5 pc, consistent with the observed longevity of cold substructures in Sextans. We further explore the modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) framework and find that extended clumps with radius @xmath5 pc can also survive for a Hubble time; however, reproducing the observed kinematics requires an unrealistically high stellar mass-to-light ratio of @xmath6. Our results favor a cored dark matter halo in Sextans and demonstrate that the persistence of kinematically cold substructures provides a sensitive probe of the inner halo profile in low-mass systems.

We investigate @xmath0 photoproduction via @xmath1 scattering within a coupled-channel chiral unitary framework grounded in the Weinberg–Tomozawa meson–baryon interaction. Despite reasonable parameter stability, the present model scarcely reproduces the recent @xmath3-photoproduction measurements by the LEPS Collaboration at SPring-8. We investigate the threshold dimension t(G), the minimum number of threshold spanning subgraphs whose union covers the edges of G. A threshold graph admits a nonnegative vertex weight function w and a threshold T such that uv is an edge iff w(u)+w(v) ≥ T. We focus on permutation graphs, i.e., intersection graphs of line segments connecting two parallel lines. We prove that for every permutation graph G, t(G) ≤ α(G), where α(G) is the maximum size of an independent set in G, and we exhibit infinite families showing this bound is tight. As a direct corollary, using α(G) ≥ n/χ(G), we derive t(G) ≤ n/χ(G) for permutation graphs on n vertices, and we again provide tight examples. Our proofs exploit the geometric segment representation to construct explicit threshold covers and to certify optimality via matching independent-set certificates. These results refine the understanding of decomposition parameters on permutation graphs and link threshold dimension to classical invariants such as independence number and chromatic number.

We present the third installment in a series devoted to identifying high-redshift quasars using five-color (ugriz; @xmath0) imaging from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) obtained along the celestial equator during the commissioning phase. In this paper, we report spectroscopic observations of 14 newly discovered bright high-redshift quasars (@xmath1, @xmath2) in the SDSS Fall equatorial stripe, together with SDSS photometry for two previously known high-redshift quasars in the same region. Combining these with the discoveries detailed in Fan et al. (1999) and Schneider et al. (2000b), we construct a uniform, color-selected, flux-limited sample of 39 quasars spanning @xmath3 to @xmath4 over a total effective area of 182 deg@xmath5. From this sample, we measure ensemble spectral properties in the rest-frame ultraviolet for quasars at @xmath6. The average continuum power-law slope is @xmath7 (defined for f_ν ∝ ν^α) with a standard deviation of 0.34, consistent with expectations for luminous quasars at these redshifts. The mean rest-frame equivalent width of the Ly@xmath8 + N V emission complex is 69 Å, with a standard deviation of 18 Å, indicating modest dispersion in line strengths across the population. To quantify selection biases, we determine the completeness of our multicolor selection using synthetic quasar colors that incorporate distributions of intrinsic continuum slopes, emission line strengths, line and continuum absorption by intervening material, and realistic SDSS photometric uncertainties. The average completeness of the resulting selection function is approximately 75% across the targeted redshift and magnitude ranges. The derived selection function will be used to correct for incompleteness in this color-selected sample, enabling a robust determination of the high-redshift quasar luminosity function in a forthcoming paper. In an appendix, we present observations of an additional 18 faint quasars (@xmath9, @xmath10) discovered within the portion of the equatorial stripe that was imaged twice, demonstrating the efficacy of repeat imaging in recovering fainter candidates. Several quasars in our sample display noteworthy characteristics, including a radio-loud quasar at @xmath11 and a narrow-line quasar with FWHM = 1500 km s@xmath12 at @xmath13, offering valuable laboratories for studying quasar emission physics and evolution at early cosmic times.

We compute the one‐loop effective potential of a five‐dimensional SU(2) gauge theory at finite temperature @xmath0 and radius @xmath1. For the first time, the calculation treats background fields with two constant components: @xmath2 along the compact extra dimension of radius @xmath3 and @xmath4 along the compact Euclidean time of radius @xmath5. The potential exhibits two discrete symmetries, @xmath6 and @xmath7, whose realization governs the phase structure. Revisiting the qualitative arguments behind the phase diagram in Ref. @xcite, we derive the phase boundaries, identify symmetry‐breaking patterns, and assess the stability of the minima. To test our analysis, we perform lattice simulations of a simple phenomenological model with two scalar fields coupled through the computed potential, finding good agreement and refining the location of transition lines and critical points.

This paper extends the bounded real lemma to stochastic linear discrete-time invariant systems subject to random disturbances with imprecisely known probability distributions. Statistical uncertainty is modeled in entropy-theoretic terms via the mean anisotropy functional, and disturbance attenuation is quantified by the anisotropic norm, a stochastic counterpart of the H-infinity norm. We derive a state-space sufficient condition guaranteeing that the anisotropic norm of the system is bounded by a prescribed threshold. The resulting strict anisotropic norm bounded real lemma comprises an inequality on the determinant of a positive definite matrix coupled with a linear matrix inequality. We show that a mild reformulation of these conditions enables efficient evaluation of the anisotropic norm through convex optimization, leveraging standard semidefinite programming tools. The analysis clarifies the relation between entropy-based uncertainty descriptions and robust performance metrics, and it yields computationally tractable tests and synthesis procedures for systems operating under statistical ambiguity. Examples illustrate the conservatism and scalability of the proposed criteria.

We investigate double-barrier interfaces separating asymptotically subsonic and supersonic Bose-Einstein condensate flows, hosting at least one sonic black-hole horizon. Using Bogoliubov-de Gennes scattering theory and non-equilibrium boundary conditions, we analyze phonon transmission through the coherent double barrier and the resulting analog Hawking radiation emitted upstream. The multiple scattering strongly modulates the transmission coefficient, making it highly frequency-dependent and producing resonant tunneling in a set of narrow bands. Consequently, the radiation spectrum is markedly nonthermal, exhibiting sharp peaks. By tracing the poles of the scattering matrix in the complex frequency plane, we show that the dominant peaks correspond to decaying resonances, with only rare features linked to dynamical instabilities. Finite-temperature calculations demonstrate that, for experimentally realistic parameters, peak intensities can be governed by spontaneous emission (amplified zero-point fluctuations) rather than by stimulated processes. Our results establish double-barrier sonic structures as tunable resonant emitters of nonthermal analog Hawking radiation.

We investigate whether the discrete long-range ordered states of Er2Ti2O7 can be selected energetically at the mean-field level, as an alternative to selection by thermal fluctuations (order-by-disorder). Starting from a nearest-neighbour exchange model on the pyrochlore lattice, we find that exchange alone is insufficient to lift the classical degeneracy. Incorporating anisotropies arising from excited single-ion crystal-field states of Er3+, together with symmetry-allowed anisotropic exchange couplings, stabilizes the required k=0 order within the Gamma5 manifold and reproduces the observed domain selection. The single-ion anisotropy is weak, implying a small selection energy; consequently, thermal or quantum fluctuations are expected to play an essential role. Calculated magnetic Bragg peak intensities versus field agree with recent experiments, supporting this mixed energetic-fluctuational scenario overall.

We present a method to quantify the distribution of electron-density fluctuations along pulsar sightlines and to estimate pulsar distances using a simple two-component scattering model. Building on Gwinn et al. (1993), the approach combines scintillation observables, proper-motion constraints, and independent measurements of angular and temporal broadening to solve for two key parameters: the fractional distance to a discrete scattering screen and its relative scattering strength. When the location of a discrete scatterer, such as an H II region, is known, the model yields robust pulsar distances and disentangles the contributions of extended interstellar turbulence and localized structures. As a case study, we analyze PSR B0736–40 and demonstrate that a minimal characterization of the Gum Nebula—guided by data from the Vela pulsar—provides sufficient leverage to constrain the screen properties and, in combination with pulse-broadening measurements, to infer the pulsar’s distance. The method improves distance and velocity estimates and offers a framework for mapping scattering structures in the interstellar medium.

Protein function emerges from structure and is mediated by dynamics, where local fluctuations cooperatively amplify motions in specific regions and seed biologically relevant pathways. We examine how such dynamically activated regions offer energetically comparable conformational substates that can be selectively trapped by binding partners. To quantify this mechanism, we compute residue‐resolved dynamics for monomeric and dimerized HIV protease, and for insulin‐like growth factor II receptor (IGF2R) domain 11 in its free state and within the IGF2R:IGF2 complex. We employ the coarse‐grained Langevin Equation for Protein Dynamics (LE4PD), which accurately predicts functionally relevant motions from structural ensembles. LE4PD is driven by both simulation‐derived models and experimental NMR conformers, enabling minimal computational overhead. Results reveal cooperative fluctuation networks, binding‐competent basins, and dynamic shifts upon dimerization or complexation, establishing LE4PD as an efficient framework linking protein structure, dynamics, and function.

Classical fractional-order derivatives, unlike integer-order derivatives, generally map non-constant periodic functions to non-periodic signals, which precludes non-constant periodic solutions in time-invariant fractional systems unless the lower terminal is set to minus infinity—an impractical requirement. This limitation narrows the applicability of fractional modeling for real-world periodic phenomena. We address this gap by introducing a modified Grünwald–Letnikov fractional derivative that fixes a finite memory length while allowing the lower terminal to vary in time, maintaining a sliding window of past information. We prove that under this definition the derivative of a periodic function preserves its period, thereby enabling periodic responses in autonomous fractional systems. The proposed operator retains linearity and causality, offers a controllable trade-off between memory and fidelity, and converges to classical formulations as the memory length increases. Analytical results and numerical illustrations (including sinusoidal inputs) demonstrate periodicity preservation and practical implementability. The framework broadens the scope of fractional modeling and control in oscillatory and harmonic regimes encountered in signal processing, vibration analysis, and power systems.

We present the design, fabrication, and performance of a full‐wafer CCD comprising 10,580 × 10,560 pixels over a 95 × 95 mm active area, with 9 μm square pixels and 16 outputs. Developed and tested at Semiconductor Technology Associates and fabricated at DALSA in 2006, the device was funded by the Office of Naval Research SBIR program at the request of the U.S. Naval Observatory for next‐generation astrometric sky surveys. Using Leach electronics, low‐noise readout of the 111 million pixels requires 16 s at 0.9 MHz. Alternative STA electronics support 20 MHz readout. We summarize key performance, including quantum efficiency, charge transfer efficiency, dark current, and uniformity, as well as device operability. Design upgrades are discussed, such as anti‐blooming drains, increased output channels to reduce frame time, and p‐channel implementations to enhance radiation tolerance in space applications.

We present a general framework to assess linear stability of generic spherically symmetric thin-shell wormholes. Using Darmois–Israel junction conditions, we derive the master equation governing radial perturbations around static throats. We prove, in full generality, that linear stability is equivalent to suitable properties of the exotic matter on the throat, encoded in an equation-of-state parameter and its derivative. As an application, we study the thin-shell Ellis wormhole for both vanishing momentum flux and non-zero external fluxes, computing the stability domains in parameter space. We show that external fluxes modify the effective potential and can enlarge the stable region. Our results provide model-independent criteria for designing dynamically stable thin-shell wormholes.

In the 1+1-dimensional large-N Gross–Neveu model, we generalize the recently obtained closed-form solution for two-baryon scattering within the time-dependent Dirac–Hartree–Fock approach to processes with arbitrary numbers and complexity of scatterers. Building on a joint ansatz for the scalar mean field and Dirac spinors, we construct analytical multi-baryon solutions whose dynamical parameters are fixed entirely by one- and two-baryon input. The resulting multi-body scattering states exhibit pairwise factorization of time delays and phase information at the level of composite multi-fermion baryons. Numerical checks up to eight baryons, including analogues of proton–nucleus and nucleus–nucleus collisions, confirm self-consistency of the mean field and the predicted trajectories, while a rigorous proof remains open. The framework accommodates arbitrary velocities and internal baryon structures and yields closed expressions for the evolving mean field, bound spinors, and continuum states.
