These findings support an emergent factorized S-matrix for composite objects in this toy model, extending soliton-like integrability to baryonic degrees of freedom.

We investigate the origin of the prolate (long-axis) rotation observed in the dwarf spheroidal Andromeda II, a satellite of M31, using N-body simulations. We propose that And II formed from the merger of two disky dwarf galaxies of comparable mass but different disk scale lengths. The progenitors approach on a radial orbit with angular momenta inclined by 90 degrees. The remnant is a stable, triaxial stellar system that exhibits rotation only about its longest axis. This prolate rotation emerges from the symmetry of the initial configuration and the conservation of angular-momentum components along the merger direction. Stars from the two progenitors retain distinct surface-density profiles while sharing very similar kinematics, reproducing the observed structural and velocity properties of And II. We contrast this with a tidal-stirring scenario in which a single disky dwarf is transformed by a host. Although residual intrinsic rotation arises in this case, it is predominantly around the shortest axis and does not match And II’s velocity field. The prolate state persists over many dynamical times and is robust to moderate variations in mass ratio and orbit, whereas tidal stirring yields only transient or fine-tuned long-axis rotation. Our results favor a merger-driven origin for And II and indicate that dwarf–dwarf interactions can shape the kinematics of low-mass galaxies in the Local Group.

We analyze the security of two-state quantum key distribution over lossy, noisy channels under individual attacks, assuming Alice and Bob employ two nonorthogonal single-photon polarization states. To enable tractable estimation of an eavesdropper’s information, we introduce a modified B92 protocol that uses inconclusive measurement outcomes and a symmetrization step by Bob on the received states. Within this framework, Alice and Bob infer Eve’s information gain from a small set of experimentally accessible parameters that capture device imperfections and channel disturbances. We derive upper bounds on Eve’s information and identify counter-intuitive regimes in which her maximum information decreases as the disturbance increases. For small noise rates, Eve can obtain perfect information when the angle between Alice’s signal states is small or large, while perfect information is unattainable for intermediate angles. We further quantify the secret key gain, defined as the net growth of secret key per emitted pulse, incorporating losses, detector inefficiency, and error rates. Combining these results, we delineate the parameter region in which the modified B92 protocol achieves security against individual attacks on realistic channels, and provide guidelines for state-angle choice to maximize secure key throughput under typical operating conditions.

This work presents the first quantitative analysis of the mechanical reliability of all-solid-state batteries, focusing on fracture of the solid electrolyte (SE) driven by intercalation-induced expansion of active particles within dense microstructures. We develop and implement a fully coupled electro–chemo–mechanical framework with nonlinear kinematics to resolve microstructural details, capture stress localization, and predict damage evolution via a cohesive zone formulation. Three-dimensional, microstructure-resolved simulations quantify how electrode expansion, SE elastic stiffness, and SE fracture energy jointly control crack initiation and propagation. Parametric studies reveal a safe operating window in which fracture is avoided when particle expansion remains below about 7.5% and the SE fracture energy exceeds a critical threshold. Counter to prevailing assumptions, compliant electrolytes with Young’s modulus on the order of several gigapascals exhibit greater susceptibility to microcracking than stiffer oxides, owing to enhanced localization under finite strains captured by our model. The results establish that sulfide SEs are not inherently superior to oxide SEs for bulk-type cells from a mechanical standpoint. We further demonstrate that mechanical degradation directly limits power density: cracks in solid Li-ion conductors act as transport barriers that elevate overpotentials and accelerate rate-performance decay. The framework provides quantitative design guidelines linking materials properties, microstructure, and operating conditions to reliability, enabling informed selection of SE chemistry and modern architecture for durable, high-rate all-solid-state batteries.

We present a deep Very Large Array (VLA) image of the optically powerful quasar E1821+643 at 18 cm that reveals low-surface-brightness radio emission extending over more than 280 kpc, far beyond the confines of the host galaxy. The morphology is elongated and shows a systematic decline in surface brightness with increasing distance from the bright core, a hallmark of Fanaroff–Riley type I (FR I) radio sources. Despite this conventional FR I structure, the quasar’s radio luminosity at 5 GHz places it within the class commonly labeled “radio-quiet,” while its 151 MHz luminosity lies near the canonical transition separating FR I and FR II sources. E1821+643 thus provides the first clear example of an optically powerful quasar exhibiting a standard FR I radio morphology. We assess why such systems have likely been missed in previous surveys. At low frequencies, current sensitivities and plausible spectral indices for radio-quiet quasars make detection of diffuse, extended emission challenging. Moreover, targeted follow-up of optically selected quasars has typically relied on short VLA exposures, biasing against the recovery of faint, large-scale structures and leading to severe underestimates of true extents. These selection effects have implications for the claimed radio bimodality of quasars, suggesting that a continuum of radio properties may be more appropriate once low-surface-brightness structures are properly accounted for. On arcsecond scales, the inner jet of E1821+643, together with the large-scale morphology, indicates a precessing jet axis, reminiscent of Galactic microquasar systems such as SS 433. We explore a scenario in which precession arises from a binary supermassive black hole whose components have not yet coalesced. If precession is common among radio-quiet, highly accreting quasars, it may help suppress the observed radio luminosity by distributing jet power over a wide solid angle. Establishing the prevalence of precession and diffuse FR I structures in such quasars will require deeper, more sensitive radio imaging across broad frequency ranges.

We investigate the Drinfeld center Z(C) of an autonomous (rigid) monoidal category C under the assumption that certain coends exist in C. We show that the canonical forgetful functor U: Z(C) → C is monadic, and we reconstruct Z(C) from its associated endo-monad T on C. The monad T naturally acquires the structure of a quasitriangular Hopf monad, and the center Z(C) is braided equivalent to the category Z_T of T-modules, thereby encoding half-braidings through the quasitriangular structure of T. More generally, given a Hopf monad H on C, we construct its centralizer K on C via universal coends and exhibit a canonical distributive law λ: KH ⇒ HK. Beck’s theory yields two key consequences. First, the λ-twisted composite D = K ∘_λ H is a quasitriangular Hopf monad on C, called the double of H, and Z(C) identifies, as braided categories, with the category of D-modules. As an illustration, for a Hopf algebra A in a braided autonomous category, we define its double D(A) so that the center of the category of A-modules is braided equivalent to the category of D(A)-modules, generalizing the classical Drinfeld double. Second, the distributive law λ lifts K to a Hopf monad on the Eilenberg–Moore category of H-modules, and we identify its coend explicitly. In particular, for suitable C, we obtain a concrete description of the Hopf algebra structure on the coend of Z(C) purely in terms of the structural morphisms of C (duals, evaluation/coevaluation, and tensor constraints). These results have applications in quantum topology: when C is a spherical fusion category, Z(C) is modular, and our explicit doubles and coends furnish canonical algebraic data for three-manifold invariants and topological field theories.

We present first results from multifrequency VLBA observations of the quasar 3C 273 obtained in 2003 at 5.0, 8.4, 15.3, 22.2, 43.2, and 86.2 GHz. Using a new model-fitting based approach, we constructed spectra for 16 emission features along the parsec-scale jet by registering components across frequencies and constraining their sizes. From the measured spectra and angular sizes we derived the magnetic field strength and the energy density of relativistic electrons in different jet regions using synchrotron self-absorption diagnostics, without invoking equipartition. We find a magnetic field of order 1 G in the VLBI core, where the magnetic energy density dominates that of the electrons, implying a magnetically dominated launching region. Downstream, the inferred energy densities become roughly consistent with equipartition. We detect a transverse gradient in magnetic field strength across the jet at ≈1.5 mas from the core, coincident with a transverse velocity structure: the slower, northern superluminal component B2 exhibits a magnetic field two orders of magnitude lower than the faster, southern components B3 and B4. These results provide spatially resolved constraints on magnetic field stratification and particle energetics in 3C 273, informing models of jet acceleration and collimation.

We present two-dimensional special-relativistic hydrodynamic simulations of the dynamics of gamma-ray burst (GRB) jets and their afterglow emission in both uniform and stratified external media, performed with the Mezcal code. The jet is initialized as a conical wedge of half-opening angle θ0 whose radial structure is taken from the self-similar Blandford–McKee solution. We explore ambient density profiles of the form ρ ∝ r^−k over 0 ≤ k ≤ 2, thereby encompassing the commonly assumed uniform interstellar medium (k = 0) and wind-like environments expected around long-duration GRB progenitors (k ≈ 2). For each configuration we compute the resulting broadband afterglow emission for a range of observer viewing angles relative to the jet axis. The jet dynamics in stratified media broadly resemble those in a uniform medium, with lateral expansion becoming significant once the bulk Lorentz factor Γ drops below θ0^−1. Beyond this point the jet half-opening angle increases approximately logarithmically with time or radius. However, the detailed evolution depends on k: for steeper profiles (larger k) the lateral expansion is relatively faster at early times (when Γθ0 ≳ 1) and slower at late times, with the subsequent Newtonian phase and approach toward spherical symmetry occurring over progressively longer timescales as k increases. Contrary to common analytic expectations for wind-like environments, our simulations exhibit a reasonably sharp jet break in the afterglow light curve even for k ≈ 2. The morphology of this break is influenced more strongly by the observer viewing angle than by the external density slope: larger viewing angles (θobs ≲ θ0 but closer to θ0) yield smoother, later jet breaks, while increasing k tends to produce more gradual breaks at fixed θobs. The counter-jet becomes visible as it transitions to sub-relativistic speeds. For k = 0 this produces a pronounced bump-like feature in late-time radio light curves. For steeper density profiles, the more gradual deceleration leads instead to a mild late-time flattening that may be difficult to detect given realistic sensitivities and cadences. We assess implications for late-time radio calorimetry, which often assumes quasi-spherical dynamics near the non-relativistic transition. For k = 0, this approach systematically overestimates the true kinetic energy by up to a factor of a few. For k > 0 the bias is smaller in magnitude and can be of either sign, depending on viewing geometry and microphysical parameters. Our results provide a unified, simulation-based framework for interpreting GRB afterglows across a range of circumburst environments and observer orientations.

Bulk flows in the universe imprint the cosmic microwave background via the kinematic Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (kSZ) effect. We present a detailed study of its statistical properties with an emphasis on galaxy clusters. We derive, analytically, the correlation function and the angular power spectrum of projected peculiar velocities, incorporating the spatial clustering of the cluster population. Using a line-of-sight formalism, we compute the all-sky kSZ power spectrum and show that, at large angular scales (low multipoles), the local bulk flow produces a visible excess above the Poisson-like fluctuations that dominate at smaller scales, while the coupling between density and velocity perturbations yields a subdominant contribution. We evaluate the prospects for detection and cosmological exploitation with forthcoming high-resolution CMB surveys, focusing on the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and the South Pole Telescope (SPT). We propose two complementary analysis strategies: a “deep and narrow” method tailored to ACT-like surveys that leverages velocity correlation statistics within small fields, and a “wide and shallow” method optimized for SPT-like surveys that extracts the kSZ signal from the angular power spectrum and cross-correlations over large areas. Forecasts indicate that both approaches can achieve constraints on the dark energy equation-of-state parameter w at the level of 5–10%, probing complementary redshift ranges and offering sensitivity to time evolution. These constraints arise from the strong response of the peculiar velocity field to the onset of late-time cosmic acceleration. Our determination of w does not rely on knowledge of cluster masses; it uses cluster redshifts and minimal assumptions about cluster physics. We discuss mitigation of contaminants and provide guidance for survey design to maximize kSZ sensitivity to bulk flows and dark energy.

We relate intermittent fluctuations of velocity gradients in turbulence to a continuum of local dissipation scales, generalizing the notion of a single mean dissipation length. Using direct numerical simulations of forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence, we determine the statistical distribution of these local scales as a function of Reynolds number with unprecedented spectral resolution, exceeding standard practice by at least a factor of eight. The core of the distribution agrees closely with theoretical predictions, while increasing Reynolds number generates progressively finer local dissipation scales. This trend coincides with a less steep decay of the energy spectrum at large wavenumbers in the dissipation range. Notably, the energy spectrum at the highest accessible Taylor microscale Reynolds number shows no bottleneck. These findings refine turbulence phenomenology and constrain advanced predictive intermittency-aware modeling and subgrid closures.

Many problems in planetary dynamics require reliable estimates of the collision probability between bodies on nearly Keplerian orbits. Classical linearized treatments near orbit-intersection points have provided useful formulas, but they exclude or become ill-behaved for tangential encounters. We develop a simpler and motivated derivation that covers both non-tangential collisions and tangential cases. Our expressions are symmetric in the orbital parameters and radii of the two bodies. As in linearized approaches, we approximate the relative motion near intersection or minimum-separation points and assume a uniform distribution of impact parameters within the collision radius. We show that the standard linearization exhibits a spurious singularity as the geometry approaches tangency. To remove this pathology, we introduce a parabolic approximation of the relative trajectory in the tangential limit, yielding finite, continuous collision probabilities and rates across all encounter geometries. The resulting closed-form formulas recover the classical results away from tangency, clarify the role of geometry and relative velocity, and are simple to implement for population studies. Applications include small-body collision statistics, debris and ring particle interactions, and other settings where near-tangential orbital encounters are common.

We investigate an anisotropic holographic superconductor within Einstein–Maxwell–Dilaton theory coupled to a charged scalar field. By introducing tunable spatial anisotropy, we numerically construct condensed phases and extract thermodynamic and transport observables. We find that the superconducting critical temperature monotonically decreases with increasing anisotropy. The superconducting energy gap grows relative to Tc, yielding Eg/Tc larger than in the isotropic limit. Moreover, anisotropy induces a pseudogap in the conductivity and spectral response above Tc. These results highlight anisotropy-driven modifications of strongly coupled superconductivity.

We define a (pseudo) radiative pumprate for OH 1612 MHz masers and apply it to a sample of 44 OH/IR sources, independent of the pumping mechanism. Using IRAS color indices to trace evolutionary status, we compare the derived pumprates among stellar, post-AGB, and interstellar masers. Stellar OH masers exhibit nearly constant pumprates with small dispersion, in agreement with expectations for radiatively pumped 1612 MHz emission from circumstellar envelopes around AGB stars. In contrast, interstellar OH masers display low pumprates that vary by more than two orders of magnitude. We argue that this broad spread reflects differing numbers of quiescent absorbing OH cloudlets along the line of sight, diversity of maser pumping pathways, competitive gain between mainline and 1612 MHz transitions, and anisotropy in maser beaming. Post-AGB sources occupy an intermediate locus in the pumprate–color plane, with pumprates that likely decline with increasing IRAS C color, consistent with evolving dust temperatures and envelope geometries. The proposed pumprate metric thus provides a simple, accessible diagnostic that links maser physics to source evolution from AGB through post-AGB phases and into interstellar environments.

We present time-resolved optical spectroscopy of the soft X-ray transient XTE J2123058 during outburst, covering 3700–6700 Å across two orbital cycles. The spectrum is dominated by He II λ4686 and the Bowen blend C III/N III λ4640, with weaker He II and C IV lines also present. The Balmer lines exhibit complex profiles, likely contaminated by He II emission. The orbital light curves of He II λ4686 and the Bowen blend differ, implying distinct emission sites within the system. He II λ4686 profiles show multiple S-wave components, and Doppler tomography places the emission away from the companion star at velocities too low for Keplerian disk material, suggesting an origin in overflowing or splashing accretion-stream material. The continuum is well described by a steep blue power law consistent with the Rayleigh–Jeans tail of a hot blackbody. Orbital modulations show no wavelength dependence, as expected if both the accretion disk and the companion are sufficiently hot that their spectral energy distributions peak in the ultraviolet. The hot continuum and the presence of high-excitation lines indicate strong X-ray heating of the system during outburst. These results support a geometry in which stream overflow contributes significantly to the optical emission and highlight the diagnostic power of time-resolved spectroscopy and Doppler tomography for mapping emission regions in soft X-ray transients.

This paper presents the concept and optimized design for a large wide-field telescope and camera with optical throughput exceeding 200 m2 deg2, achieving 260 m2 deg2 in our baseline. An 8.4 m primary and a 3-degree field of view feed a 2.3 gigapixel focal plane built from modular imagers using 10 micrometer pixels. In a dedicated all-sky monitoring mode, the system reaches 24th magnitude in a single 10-second exposure, enabling discovery of faint moving or bursting optical transients, from near-Earth asteroids to energetic events at the edge of the optical universe. With a monthly cadence, up to 14,000 deg2 of sky will be surveyed with many 10-second exposures; over time, 30,000 deg2 will be covered deeply in multiple bandpasses. This represents a paradigm shift from survey follow-up to survey direct science, delivering real-time alert streams, time-tagged photometry, precise astrometry, and morphology for billions of sources. The data system will generate and curate a ~15 petabyte imaging archive and photometric catalog designed for rapid access and community use. The high throughput and cadence open unexplored regions of parameter space in motion, variability, and low surface brightness structure, enabling investigations in Galactic structure, Solar System inventory, time-domain astrophysics, gravitational lensing, and cosmology. Together these capabilities will transform discovery space and deliver constraints on fundamental physics and the observable sky.

Graphene sheets encapsulated between hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) slabs exhibit exceptionally low extrinsic disorder, enabling highly tunable, low-loss plasmonics across a broad spectral range. We develop a microscopic theory of collective electron-density oscillations in an hBN/graphene/hBN heterostructure with semi-infinite hBN cladding, accounting for the anisotropic dielectric response of hBN and the nonlocal electrodynamics of graphene. Graphene plasmons hybridize with hBN’s infrared-active optical phonons to form hybrid plasmon–phonon (HPP) modes that feature strong field confinement and frequency tunability from the terahertz to the mid-infrared. We quantify intrinsic losses arising from two key scattering channels in these stacks: graphene’s acoustic phonons (via deformation-potential coupling) and hBN optical phonons (via polar Fröhlich coupling). Using linear-response theory and perturbative scattering rates consistent with the full HPP dispersion, we find that at room temperature damping is dominated by graphene’s acoustic phonons over most of the accessible spectrum, while hBN optical phonons contribute prominently near the Reststrahlen bands. The resulting inverse damping ratios (quality factors) are predicted to be on the order of 20–60, with weak dependence on carrier density and a pronounced dependence on illumination frequency, decreasing near phonon resonances. Crucially, we demonstrate that plasmon lifetimes are not simply tied to dc mobility and can even be anti-correlated, reflecting the distinct phase space and frequency dependence of dynamic conductivity. Our results provide design rules for optimizing HPP propagation by spectral positioning and thermal management in hBN/graphene/hBN platforms.

We present new millimeter interferometric observations of the CO rotational transition in Titan’s atmosphere. Radiative transfer modeling of resolved spectra indicates a vertically uniform CO mixing ratio of 52 ppm, with uncertainties of 6 ppm between 40–200 km and 12 ppm between 200–300 km. The uniform profile is favored over gradient models. These results confirm CO’s long photochemical lifetime and suggest efficient global mixing, with little evidence for active sources or sinks. Our measurements refine prior constraints and provide benchmarks for circulation and chemistry models.

We present results from 1.5D diffusion simulations of magnetic field evolution in the Kippenhahn-Schlueter prominence model that explicitly include the ambipolar (Cowling) resistivity terms. The early-time dynamics are controlled by the ratio of horizontal to vertical magnetic field strengths: when this ratio is large, the embedded current sheet thins; when it is small, the sheet thickens; and in a marginal regime a new characteristic current-sheet length scale emerges. At later times, after exceeding the Cowling resistivity timescale, the sheet thickness grows as a power law in time, with an exponent independent of the initial field-strength ratio. This transition to a universal thickening regime highlights the dominant role of ambipolar diffusion in partially ionized prominence plasmas. A direct consequence is a substantial acceleration of the tearing mode: the tearing instability timescale is reduced by more than an order of magnitude when the horizontal-to-vertical field ratio is 0.2 or less. Over the course of a prominence’s lifetime, Cowling resistivity therefore can markedly remodel the magnetic structure, in some cases enabling the onset of reconnection via tearing.

Partitioning strongly influences the effectiveness of preconditioning in parallel iterative solutions of large linear systems, yet standard graph-based strategies typically ignore matrix coefficient information. We propose a spectral partitioning algorithm tailored to symmetric positive definite (SPD) systems that explicitly incorporates coefficients to enhance additive Schwarz preconditioning. The method derives partitions from a coefficient-aware spectral relaxation that targets reduction of the Cauchy–Bunyakovski–Schwarz (CBS) constant across subdomain interfaces, thereby strengthening the preconditioner while maintaining balance and sparsity. Concretely, we formulate a generalized eigenvalue problem linked to a weighted graph representation of the SPD matrix and use its dominant eigenvectors to guide cuts that minimize coefficient-weighted couplings. The approach is scalable and integrates seamlessly with domain decomposition frameworks and parallel matrix–vector operations. Numerical experiments on benchmark SPD problems, including highly heterogeneous and anisotropic diffusion discretizations, demonstrate notable improvements in robustness: reduced iteration counts, lower effective condition numbers, and diminished sensitivity to coefficient contrast, with modest preprocessing overhead. These results indicate that coefficient-informed spectral partitioning offers a practical path to more reliable parallel solvers. Keywords: graph partitioning, iterative linear system solution, preconditioning, Cauchy–Bunyakowski–Schwarz constant, symmetric positive definite, spectral partitioning. MSC: 15A06, 65F08, 65F10, 65N22.

We present a gated silicon single-photon detector based on a commercially available avalanche photodiode. It achieves a photon detection efficiency of 45@xmath05% at 808 nm, with 2@xmath110@xmath2 dark count per ns at −30 V excess bias and −30@xmath3c. We compare gated and free-running operation and show significant advantages in two representative scenarios: detecting a single photon hidden in faint continuous light and detecting one after a strong pulse. We also characterize the “charge persistence” effect, whereby the detector clicks some time after illumination, exploring its dependence on temperature and incident light intensity. Our implementation is simple and compatible with existing setups.

We derive exact analytical solutions of the steady resistive MHD equations describing reconnective annihilation in curvilinear geometry. The current density varies in both radial and azimuthal directions, generalizing earlier radially dependent models. The solutions furnish self-consistent magnetic, velocity, and pressure fields, enabling estimates of reconnection and energy-release rates. Potential applications to coronal loop geometries and solar flare triggering are discussed, with parameter dependencies and observational implications highlighted.

We revisit a claim that the effective capacity of service processes can be computed via a CLT approximation. We show analytically that this approach is invalid because it interchanges limits: it replaces the large-deviations limit of the log-moment generating function with the limit of the cumulative process, yielding erroneous estimates. Using a correlated on–off service model, we derive the correct effective capacity from the MGF, quantify discrepancy with the CLT method, and delineate regimes where the approximation misestimates QoS exponents.

Protein synthesis in cells is executed by ribosomes, molecular motors that convert chemical free energy into directed motion along messenger RNA (mRNA) while catalyzing polypeptide elongation. Individual ribosomes advance through an alternating sequence of translocation steps and stochastic pauses. Using a quantitative kinetic model that resolves the full mechanochemical cycle of a single ribosome, we derive an exact analytical expression for the distribution of dwell times at successive codons on the mRNA track. The inverse mean dwell time obeys a Michaelis–Menten–like dependence on substrate concentration and agrees with the general expression for the average velocity of molecular motors with unbranched mechano-chemical cycles. By incorporating an external load into the cycle kinetics, we obtain a closed-form force–velocity relation for the ribosome. Extending the single-motor framework to many-body dynamics, we account for steric exclusion among ribosomes translating the same mRNA and map the ensuing nonequilibrium phases. We compute the full phase diagram in a three-dimensional space spanned by experimentally tunable parameters, including initiation and termination rates, nucleotide fuel concentration, and opposing force. Our results yield testable predictions for dwell time statistics, velocity under load, and traffic-induced current–density relations. We propose experimental validations using single-molecule assays with optical or magnetic tweezers, controlled variation of GTP-tRNA concentrations, and ribosome profiling to locate phase boundaries along transcripts. Parameter inference strategies are also discussed.

We introduce a statistically principled method to reconstruct the density matrix @xmath0 of a system of @xmath1-qubits and to estimate its rank @xmath2 from quantum state tomography data collected over @xmath3 repeated measurements. The procedure minimizes the empirical risk of a linear estimator @xmath4, obtained via the moment method, under a rank-penalization that ranges from 1 to @xmath5. This yields, in a single optimization, a rank selector and the associated density matrix estimate. We derive nonasymptotic performance guarantees: an upper bound on the Frobenius-norm error of the penalized estimator of order @xmath6, and consistency of the rank estimator. The methodology is computationally efficient, scalable to multi-qubit systems, and robust to experimental imperfections. We illustrate its practical merits on representative example states and on real experimental data sets.

Since 2010, the LHC has operated with the world’s highest stored beam energy, reaching 140 MJ at 4 TeV—nearly 50 times other accelerators—making machine protection the principal constraint throughout the cycle. We review how protection requirements shape commissioning, ramp, squeeze, collision, and turnaround, and how low-intensity pilot beams—the only relatively safe beams—are used to validate optics, collimation, interlocks, beam loss monitors, and abort systems before intensity increases. The paper analyzes credible failure modes, loss scenarios, and protection margins, and details operational procedures, permits, and surveillance that balance availability with risk. Lessons from incidents and tests inform thresholds, hierarchy, and automation to ensure safe, efficient routine operation during physics runs.

We develop a gravitational theory arising from spontaneous Lorentz-symmetry breaking. Starting with a rank-2 massless tensor endowed with a linear kinetic term and a nondifferentiated potential, we show that, about a stable vacuum, the Nambu–Goldstone modes reproduce the graviton of linearized general relativity. We then implement a gravitational bootstrap based on consistent self-coupling to the total energy–momentum tensor. Requiring the bootstrap to close for the potential constrains its admissible structure sharply; nonetheless, we identify families of potentials supporting stable vacua. The non-Goldstone excitations are massive and decouple at low energies, leaving an effective theory equivalent to general relativity in a fixed gauge. We discuss stability conditions, constraint structure, the emergence of diffeomorphism invariance in the infrared limit, and phenomenology, together with observational and theoretical implications.

We investigate the full counting statistics of heat transfer across general nonlinear phononic junctions. Using the two-time observation protocol combined with a nonequilibrium field-theoretical/algebraic framework, we derive practical, time-dependent formulae for the cumulant generating function (CGF) that treat transient and steady-state regimes on equal footing. The formalism yields all heat cumulants and makes fluctuation symmetries transparent. As an application, we analyze a single-site junction with a quartic on-site pinning potential. We obtain an explicit first-order anharmonic correction to the CGF and associated cumulants, and we verify the Gallavotti–Cohen fluctuation symmetry in the steady state. To address strong nonlinearities, we introduce a self-consistent numerical scheme that remains accurate beyond perturbative limits. Computations reveal pronounced anharmonic modifications to current, noise, and higher-order cumulants. The methodology is general and provides a versatile tool for nonlinear phononic heat transport.

We construct an effective lowest-band Bose–Hubbard description that explicitly incorporates interaction-induced on-site correlations. Starting from the exact few-body problem on a single lattice site, we define ladder operators that create and annihilate locally correlated many-body states rather than single-particle Wannier orbitals. This correlated-operator formulation yields a systematic single-band reduction and naturally generates an extended Bose–Hubbard Hamiltonian containing not only effective multibody on-site interactions but also multibody-induced single-particle tunneling, pair tunneling, and higher-order nearest-neighbor interaction processes. We provide an equivalent representation in terms of occupation-dependent hopping amplitudes and interaction parameters, establishing a practical route for modeling experiments. Using realistic optical-lattice parameters, we estimate the size of these corrections and show that they can be strongly enhanced near Feshbach resonances while remaining within current experimental resolution. The resulting modifications of the superfluid–Mott-insulator phase boundary and of low-energy excitation spectra are quantified. By analyzing the local energy reduction mechanism, we demonstrate that it cannot be captured by a mere spatial broadening of single-particle Wannier functions, highlighting the essential role of genuine correlations in the on-site many-body wave function. Our framework provides controlled microscopic input for extended lattice models of ultracold bosons and identifies observable signatures of multibody-induced tunneling and interactions. Implications for quantum simulation are discussed.

We reanalyzed phase-shift data of @xmath0 and @xmath1 scatterings and obtained robust evidence for the light scalar mesons @xmath2 and @xmath3, long sought yet elusive. Together with the established resonances @xmath4 and @xmath5, these states can be consistently classified as members of a single scalar @xmath6-nonet emerging in the @xmath7 linear @xmath6-model. The extracted mass of the iso-singlet flavor-octet member, and the masses of @xmath3 and @xmath4, satisfy the Gell–Mann–Okubo mass formula within uncertainties, supporting the nonet assignment. A repulsive background phase shift @xmath8, crucial for revealing the @xmath9-existence in our phase analyses, is quantitatively accounted for in the linear @xmath6 framework. There, @xmath8 arises from a compensating @xmath10-interaction mandated by chiral symmetry, providing a dynamical origin for the observed background. Our results unify the phenomenology of light scalar mesons and clarify the role of chiral dynamics in low-energy @xmath0 and @xmath1 scattering, and constrain key effective couplings.

We consider @xmath0 pure or random quantum Ising chains of @xmath1 spins coupled either via a single star junction at their origins or via two star junctions at their two ends, forming a watermelon geometry. The finite-size energy gap is analyzed by a sequential self-dual real-space renormalization procedure that can be explicitly solved in terms of Kesten variables built from the initial couplings and the initial transverse fields. In the pure case at criticality, the gap is found to decay as a power law @xmath2 with a dynamical exponent @xmath3 for the single star junction (the case @xmath4 corresponds to @xmath5 for a single chain with free boundary conditions) and @xmath6 for the watermelon geometry (the case @xmath4 corresponds to @xmath5 for a single chain with periodic boundary conditions). In the random case at criticality, the gap follows the infinite-disorder fixed-point scaling @xmath7 with the same activated exponent @xmath8 as the single chain corresponding to @xmath4. The amplitude @xmath9 is an @xmath10 random positive variable whose distribution depends on the number @xmath11 of chains and on the junction geometry (star or watermelon). Our framework provides explicit, geometry-dependent scaling laws and distributions for the gap, illuminating how connectivity and boundary conditions control dynamical critical behavior in both clean and disordered quantum Ising networks.

We present a deep, wide-field CCD survey of the Fornax Cluster and its surrounding environment designed to identify low-luminosity, low–surface-brightness galaxies that are expected to be strongly dark-matter dominated. Using a large-format camera and image processing, we detect a substantial population of such systems and statistically associate them with Fornax. The resulting dwarf sample implies a steep faint-end slope of the galaxy luminosity function, reaching to low luminosities, and signals a diffuse component previously underrepresented in cluster censuses. Despite their individual faintness, the integrated light of these galaxies is comparable to that of the bright members, while their spatial distribution is significantly more extended, with a scale about four times larger than that of the luminous galaxies. These findings satisfy two key predictions of hierarchical structure formation in cold dark matter halos: a steep low-mass (luminosity) function and a more extended mass distribution relative to light traced by bright systems. We also report a concentration of low–surface-brightness galaxies in the vicinity of the nearby galaxy NGC 1291, suggesting localized environmental drivers of dwarf formation and survival.

Motivated by a recent MIT experiment, we study collisions of two spin-polarized atomic Fermi gas clouds near a Feshbach resonance. Despite underlying attractive interactions, in the strongly interacting regime the dilute clouds exhibit a bounce. Using a hydrodynamic framework that quantitatively reproduces the observed dynamics, we attribute this counterintuitive behavior to the formation of a novel metastable many-body state with effectively repulsive interactions. Our analysis provides compelling evidence for repulsive hydrodynamics emerging from attractive microscopic forces.

We reformulate adiabatic elimination as the leading term of a singular perturbation expansion and develop systematic corrections using the invariant manifold formalism for dynamical systems. This construction connects to established quantum perturbative schemes and yields effective Hamiltonians beyond standard adiabatic approximations. We prove convergence under strong energy scale separation and address hermiticity, providing criteria and explicit constructions for hermitian improved effective generators across quantum systems.

We investigate the decay modes of heavy quark–antiquark bound states generated by an attractive Higgs-boson exchange potential. Assuming small mixing between a hypothetical fourth generation and lighter quarks, weak decays are suppressed and annihilation of the bound state dominates. Within a nonrelativistic potential framework, we compute binding energies and partial widths for S-wave states. For the vector state, the leading annihilation channels are Higgs plus photon and Higgs plus Z, yielding distinctive, monochromatic electroweak signatures. For the pseudoscalar state, the strong two-gluon decay mode overwhelms electroweak channels. The bound states are predicted to be very narrow: away from the near-threshold region, the ratio of the total width to the binding energy remains below one percent, becoming larger only extremely close to the critical mass where binding weakens. These conclusions extend to any heavy fermion–antifermion bound state, including heavy leptons and heavy neutrinos, provided their masses support Higgs-mediated binding.

We propose a unified multivariate Variance–Gamma framework that extends and consolidates several constructions used in option pricing. Complementing the Grigelionis (2007) class, our overarching model is obtained by subordinating a multivariate Brownian motion to a subordinator from Thorin’s class of generalized gamma convolutions. This yields a rich family of Lévy processes whose dependence is encoded via the Thorin measure and that subsumes the multivariate models of Pérez-Abreu and Stelzer (2014), Semeraro (2008), and Guillaume (2013) as special cases. We derive explicit canonical measures, Lévy triplets, and characteristic functions, enabling efficient pricing via PIDEs and tree-based methodologies. A key structural result establishes invariance under Esscher transforms, ensuring stability under changes of measure and facilitating risk-neutral valuation and calibration. Numerical illustrations for best-of and worst-of both European and American options on two assets demonstrate accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. The framework supports superposition, captures realistic tail behavior and dependence, and is readily implementable.

We study general non-equatorial photon motion in Kerr–de Sitter black hole and naked singularity spacetimes. The dynamics is parametrized by an impact parameter @xmath0 tied to axial symmetry and an impact parameter @xmath1 tied to the hidden symmetry (Carter constant). We construct effective potentials for the latitudinal and radial motion and examine their structure using a Chinese boxes technique to delineate admissible regions in terms of @xmath0 and @xmath1 for given spacetime parameters @xmath2 (spin and cosmological constant). Two classes of trajectories are identified: orbital paths crossing the equatorial plane (@xmath3) and vortical paths confined above or below it (@xmath4). We derive bounds on @xmath0 and @xmath1 and show that for @xmath1 < 0 the latitudinal reality conditions impose stronger constraints on @xmath0 than those from radial motion, thereby excluding vortical motion at constant radius. We analyze latitudinal turning points, radial barriers, and transitions between black hole and naked singularity regimes. A classification of spacetimes is proposed based on the qualitative behavior of the effective potentials. Implications for photon capture and lensing in Λ>0 backgrounds follow.

We present an extension of the Dirac–Frenkel time‐dependent variational approach with Davydov ansätze to finite‐temperature quantum dynamics, targeting energy and charge transfer in molecular aggregates and light‐harvesting complexes via the paradigmatic spin–boson model. Thermal effects are incorporated through Monte Carlo importance sampling over initial bath configurations, enabling unbiased averaging of real‐time trajectories generated by optimized Davydov trial states. Benchmarking against the numerically exact iterative quasi‐adiabatic propagator path integral (QUAPI) shows excellent agreement for population dynamics at high temperatures across common spectral densities. At low temperatures, the single Davydov ansatz exhibits noticeable deviations from QUAPI, reflecting insufficient variational flexibility to capture strong system–bath correlations. Increasing the multiplicity of Davydov trial states systematically improves accuracy, recovering QUAPI benchmarks over broader regimes and mitigating low‐temperature discrepancies while retaining favorable computational scaling. We analyze convergence with respect to the number of Davydov states and Monte Carlo samples, and delineate temperature and coupling ranges where the approach is reliable. The proposed finite‐temperature Davydov framework thus offers a sophisticated yet efficient tool for simulating dissipative quantum dynamics over wide spectral profiles, providing a practical alternative to exact path‐integral methods at moderate cost and enabling realistic modeling of transport in complex condensed‐phase environments.

We present a perturbative NRQCD study of the inclusive decay of spin–triplet bottomonium states into charm hadrons. At leading order, we include both color–singlet and color–octet ^3S1 annihilation mechanisms and compute the corresponding decay rates and the momentum distribution of the charm quark. The infrared divergences arising in the color–singlet channel are absorbed into the short-distance factor multiplying the probability density at the origin for a ^3S1 pair in a color–octet state, ensuring consistent factorization. This nonperturbative parameter is determined phenomenologically from the measured fraction of decays that produce charm hadrons. Using its universality, we then predict partial widths to light hadrons for all four states in the P-wave bottomonium multiplet, with controlled theoretical uncertainties quantified.

We compute the cosmic Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) rate, defined as the number of SNe Ia per unit time and unit comoving volume, with the dual aim of predicting the frequency of explosions at very high redshift and assessing whether current observations permit discrimination among proposed delay-time distribution (DTD) models. Assuming SNe Ia arise from thermonuclear explosions of carbon–oxygen white dwarfs in binary systems, we consider both the single-degenerate and double-degenerate progenitor scenarios. We embed these progenitor channels within two competing frameworks for galaxy formation and cosmic star formation history: a monolithic collapse scenario characterized by star formation rising with redshift, and a hierarchical clustering scenario with a declining star formation rate at high redshift. The SN Ia rate is calculated using an analytical formalism that relates the rate following an instantaneous burst of star formation to the time delay between progenitor birth and explosion, and more generally by convolving assumed DTDs with parameterized star formation histories. We further compute the SN Ia rate in typical elliptical galaxies with different initial luminous masses (representative of low-, intermediate-, and high-mass spheroids) and quantify the integrated iron mass produced by SNe Ia in each case. Our results confirm that, with present SN Ia counts and rate measurements, it remains challenging to uniquely select a preferred DTD. This difficulty arises because the cosmic star formation rate and its redshift dependence exert a dominant influence on the inferred cosmic SN Ia rate, often masking the subtler signatures of different delay-time distributions. In the context of galaxy formation, the monolithic scenario predicts an increasing trend of the SN Ia rate toward high redshift, primarily driven by the early, intense star formation in massive spheroids. In contrast, a hierarchical scenario tied to a declining cosmic star formation rate yields a pronounced drop in the predicted SN Ia rate at high redshift. For elliptical galaxies, we find that the epoch of maximum SN Ia activity depends sensitively on initial mass, with the most massive ellipticals exhibiting an earlier peak (around 0.3 Gyr after the onset of star formation), consistent with downsizing whereby star formation is both earlier and more rapid in larger systems. The present-day SN Ia rate per unit stellar mass is higher in bluer, less massive ellipticals than in redder, more massive ones, reflecting differences in stellar population ages and residual star formation histories. Finally, the integrated iron production from SNe Ia in our elliptical galaxy models scales with initial mass and star formation timescale, with implications for the chemical enrichment of galaxies and the intracluster medium. Keywords: stars—binaries; supernovae—Type Ia; galaxies—evolution; delay-time distribution; cosmic star formation history; chemical enrichment.

Evidence for very-high-energy emission from GRB 970417a previously reported with Milagrito is revisited using scaler data that recorded photomultiplier count rates. Combining shower-trigger and scaler observations, we derive constraints on the TeV fluence and spectral shape. The joint analysis requires photon energies exceeding 650 GeV if the signal is astrophysical. We discuss implications for prompt GRB emission mechanisms, intergalactic absorption, and source energetics, and note prospects for tests with current and future VHE instruments. Subject headings: gamma-ray bursts, observations.

Accretion flows onto weakly magnetized neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries are governed by both strong-field general relativity and dynamically significant magnetic stresses. Even when the stellar magnetic field is too weak to establish a well-defined magnetosphere, the inner disk can still experience substantial magnetic torques that reshape its structure and dynamics. We construct magnetic slim disk models tailored to neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries that self-consistently incorporate general relativistic gravity and a phenomenological description of magnetic field–disk coupling. Our framework allows for both closed field line configurations that connect the star and disk, and open configurations that enable angular momentum extraction via magnetically driven stresses. Within this model, we show that magnetic stresses can appreciably shift the sonic transition of the inflow relative to the pure general relativistic expectation, even for surface magnetic fields as low as ~10^7–10^8 G. In the limit of small disk viscosity and gas pressure, we derive an analytical expression for the sonic radius that isolates its dependence on the stellar surface field strength and mass accretion rate through a single control parameter: the ratio of magnetic stress to accretion ram pressure, modulated by the azimuthal pitch of the field threading the disk (i.e., the toroidal-to-poloidal field ratio). As this magnetization parameter increases, the sonic radius grows and smoothly approaches the classical Alfvén radius where a true magnetosphere forms; as the parameter decreases, the sonic radius asymptotes to the general relativistic value expected near the innermost stable circular orbit for slowly rotating neutron stars. This continuity suggests that the traditional distinction between a “magnetospheric radius” and a “disk sonic radius” may be artificial; in practice there exists a single generalized sonic radius determined jointly by relativistic gravity and magnetic stresses. We apply these results to interpret kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillations in the X-ray fluxes of low-mass X-ray binaries, under the hypothesis that the dominant QPOs reflect the orbital frequency at the disk’s inner edge. The predicted correlations between QPO frequency and mass accretion rate provide diagnostics of magnetic coupling and enable stringent constraints on the stellar surface field. Requiring kHz orbital frequencies at the sonic radius yields an upper limit B_* ≲ few × 10^8–10^9 G, with the precise bound set by the field topology and pitch angle. Current observational trends favor complex, possibly multipolar magnetic geometries in these systems.

We continue the nonmodal linear stability program initiated in Phys. Rev. Lett. 112 (2014) 191101 by analyzing odd (axial) linear perturbations of the Einstein–Maxwell system about a Reissner–Nordström (A)dS black hole. We prove that all gauge-invariant information carried by the metric and electromagnetic perturbations is captured by two spacetime scalar fields constructed from first-order variations of the Weyl tensor and the Maxwell field and their Hodge duals. The full linearized Einstein–Maxwell system is shown to be equivalent to a coupled system of wave equations for these scalars on the fixed background. For nonnegative cosmological constant, we establish pointwise boundedness throughout the outer static region by deriving energy and Morawetz estimates for the coupled system. In contrast, in the interior we show that both scalars generically diverge as the Cauchy horizon is approached from the inner dynamical region, lending support to strong cosmic censorship. In the asymptotically anti-de Sitter case, the dynamics depends on boundary conditions at the conformal timelike boundary; in particular, a class of Robin boundary conditions gives rise to instabilities.

Recent claims suggest that Type Ia supernova observations might be explained within general relativity using only cold dark matter, without invoking dark energy, by adopting “Swiss cheese” cosmologies in which a homogeneous Friedmann–Robertson–Walker (FRW) background is modified by mass-compensating spherical inhomogeneities described by the Lemaître–Tolman–Bondi (LTB) metric. If these inhomogeneities consist of underdense cores surrounded by overdense shells, they can alter the luminosity distance–redshift relation and potentially mimic accelerated expansion. We critically assess this proposal by analyzing light propagation through such structures in the weak-field regime, identifying the effect as standard gravitational lensing. Underdenser regions focus light less than a homogeneous background, leading to demagnification of supernova fluxes and an apparent brightening–distance tension that can resemble acceleration. However, we show that the large apparent acceleration reported in some constructions arises from insufficient randomization of void placements and lines of sight, which induces coherent defocusing and anomalously large cumulative demagnification. Using ensembles of mass-compensating LTB voids embedded in FRW, with void positions, orientations, and sightlines properly randomized, we compute magnification distributions and associated shifts in distance moduli. Flux conservation and the statistical symmetry of randomized configurations limit the mean demagnification to small values, with residual effects comparable to standard weak lensing scatter and far below what is required to fit the supernova Hubble diagram without dark energy. Our results demonstrate that, once selection biases and line-of-sight coherence are controlled, Swiss cheese inhomogeneities cannot reproduce the observed acceleration, and that previous large effects are artifacts of inadequate randomization rather than evidence against dark energy.

Asteroid belts have been hypothesized to influence both the emergence and the evolution of complex life by mediating volatile delivery, impact rates, and dynamical environments on terrestrial planets. We investigate the conditions under which compact asteroid belts form by computing the location of the snow line with numerical models of protoplanetary discs, incorporating realistic opacity, irradiation, and accretion histories. We propose that asteroid belts preferentially assemble near the snow line, where the jump in solid surface density facilitates rapid growth of giant planet cores exterior to the line while inhibiting full planet formation just interior to their orbits, leaving behind a reservoir of planetesimals. We compare this prediction to observations of warm dust in exo-solar systems, commonly attributed to collisional cascades within asteroid belts, and show that the inferred dust temperatures and radial locations broadly coincide with theoretical snow line positions. We further analyze the impact of giant planet migration, which likely disrupts or disperses nascent belts if planets traverse the snow line region. A survey of currently known giant exoplanets indicates that only a small fraction reside exterior to their host stars’ estimated snow lines. Although this pattern may be shaped by strong observational selection effects, it is consistent with the expectation that compact, long-lived asteroid belts are uncommon. If such belts play a favorable role in fostering complex life, then their relative rarity could imply that complex life is not expected to be prevalent in many observed systems. Future measurements of warm dust populations and direct detections of cold giant planets will critically test these predictions.

We propose a new hadronization mechanism, jet–fluid string (JFS) formation and decay, to comprehensively describe observables in intermediate to high-@xmath0 regions of heavy-ion collisions. In the JFS model, hard partons produced in jets lose energy while traversing the quark–gluon plasma (QGP) fluid, evolved with fully three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations. Upon escaping the fluid, a jet parton picks up a partner parton from the medium to form a color-singlet string, which subsequently decays into hadrons. The JFS framework reproduces spectra and azimuthal anisotropies and predicts high-@xmath1 @xmath2 values approximately twice those of the independent fragmentation model, consistent with current observations.

We investigate warm inflation driven by vector fields in a locally rotationally symmetric Bianchi type I universe. Within the slow-roll regime, we formulate the background field equations and derive the perturbation sector, obtaining scalar and tensor power spectra and their spectral indices in terms of the directional Hubble parameter. Two expansion histories are examined—intermediate and logamediate inflation—while the dissipation coefficient is treated both as a scalar-field–dependent function and as a constant. For each case, we present closed-form expressions for the slow-roll parameters, e-folds, spectra, and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, and analyze their dependence on anisotropy and dissipation. Confronting our results with WMAP7 and Planck constraints shows that the anisotropic warm inflation model accommodates the observed scalar tilt and bounds on the tensor amplitude. The graphical behavior of the observables illustrates viable parameter regions and supports the consistency of warm vector-field inflation in anisotropic backgrounds.

We present a Green’s-function-based solver for the modified Bessel equation designed as a core component for Poisson problems in cylindrical geometries. The method discretizes the radial coordinate with a discrete Hankel transform and represents the Green’s function with modified Bessel functions of the first and second kind. To ensure numerical stability for large azimuthal orders and highly refined angular grids, we implement scaled evaluations of the Bessel functions that mitigate exponential growth and near-origin singular behavior. The solver is validated on monotonic and oscillatory inputs, with careful assessment of interpolation and aliasing errors. Across all tests, the error consistently attains machine precision, while computational cost scales linearly with the number of radial nodes. These properties make the approach robust and efficient for high-resolution cylindrical Poisson solves, enabling accurate treatment of challenging parameter regimes and large-order modes.

We investigate the incremental computation of minimal unsatisfiable cores (MUCs) for quantified Boolean formulas (QBFs). We extend the incremental QBF solver DepQBF with a novel clause-group API that enables adding and removing sets of clauses across solving invocations, while internally managing selector variables and assumptions. The API hides these mechanisms from users, simplifying tool integration and reducing engineering overhead. We describe the design and implementation of clause groups, their interaction with dependency-aware QBF reasoning, and optimizations for core extraction. We present the first experimental study of MUC computation for QBFs with DepQBF, evaluating benchmark suites from verification and synthesis. Results show competitive performance, modest overhead for incrementality, improved scalability on iterative workflows, and practical usefulness for QBF-based applications in industrial practice.

Understanding the conditions that produce high-energy particles and gamma-ray emission in relativistic jets remains a central challenge. We combine high-resolution millimeter Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) imaging with broadband variability from Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) to probe the emission mechanisms at the base of the blazar jet S5 0716+714. Cross-correlation of gamma-ray light curves with mm-VLBI core flux and parsec-scale kinematics reveals a significant association between gamma-ray activity, core brightening, and changes in jet orientation. The strongest flares coincide with superluminal components and position-angle swings, implying the dominant high-energy site is co-spatial with, or just downstream of, the mm-VLBI core. These findings support scenarios in which shocks and magnetic reconnection in a magnetized inner jet modulate particle acceleration and radiative efficiency. Timing analysis indicates short lags, consistent with very compact emission zones. We summarize current constraints on the origin, location, and processes of blazar high-energy radiation from these multiwavelength observations.

Cryptanalysis seeks to recover the meaning of encrypted data without access to secret information, traditionally leveraging techniques such as differential cryptanalysis, advanced statistical methods, brute-force search, and algebraic reductions to systems of equations. We present a boolean-function-centered algebraic framework for block cipher analysis that models the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) entirely as a set of boolean functions and computes their algebraic normal forms (ANFs) via Möbius transforms. Our approach departs from prior reductions to quadratic systems by exploiting structural properties of boolean functions, enabling a specific representation that preserves sparsity, highlights symmetry, and separates linear diffusion from nonlinear substitution. We derive explicit ANFs for AES round transformations—including SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey—and reorganize the resulting equations into layered constraints that facilitate combinatorial reasoning (e.g., parity relations, low-degree interactions, and variable partitioning across state bytes and key material). The proposed representation is readily implementable, compatible with XOR-aware SAT and CSP solvers, and supports hybrid strategies that combine algebraic elimination with combinatorial pruning. Preliminary analyses on reduced-round instances indicate smaller, more structured equation sets relative to naive quadratic encodings and improved solver amenability, without altering the security assumptions of full-round AES. By harnessing Möbius-based ANF computation and a tailored constraint layout, this work provides a new class of equation systems for cipher analysis, opening avenues for systematic exploration of boolean-function properties in modern block ciphers and informing the design of solver-friendly cryptanalytic models. Keywords: block cipher, boolean function, cryptanalysis, AES

Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) underpin modern cosmology as standardizable candles, yet their reliability hinges on disentangling intrinsic evolution and extinction with redshift and host-galaxy environment. This review synthesizes observational evidence for evolution and dust effects as a function of redshift and host morphology. High-redshift (z up to about 1) SNe Ia display systematically bluer colors than local counterparts, a trend that disfavors simple dust extinction as the sole cause of their diminished apparent brightness and points to intrinsic evolution in their spectral energy distributions. Host-dependent correlations support progenitor-driven evolution: SNe Ia in elliptical galaxies (older stellar populations) tend to be dimmer with reduced dispersion, while those in spiral galaxies (younger populations) are brighter with greater scatter. These trends are consistent with changes in progenitor age and metallicity, with carbon abundance emerging as a key parameter: lower carbon content is associated with lower peak luminosity and tighter peak-brightness scatter, characteristic of present-day elliptical hosts. Selection effects compound these patterns. Malmquist bias and surface-brightness selection favor discovery of less obscured events, and high-z SNe Ia are more frequently found at larger galactocentric radii, where dust columns are lower and host contamination is reduced, contributing to the lower inferred extinction at high redshift. The observed high-z samples also exhibit smaller Hubble-diagram scatter and a paucity of slow-declining, intrinsically bright events, indicating sample evolution with redshift. This absence has been interpreted as an age effect linked to younger progenitors at early cosmic times, with consequences for the distribution of light-curve shapes. Together, these factors can bias distance estimates and cosmological inferences if unmodeled, potentially mimicking or counteracting cosmological signals. Robust use of SNe Ia as distance indicators therefore requires explicit accounting for host morphology, progenitor age and metallicity evolution, dust properties, and survey selection functions across redshift. Keywords: Type Ia supernovae, cosmology, dust extinction, progenitor evolution, metallicity, carbon abundance, host morphology, Malmquist bias, redshift dependence, star formation.

We compute Shannon and Onicescu information measures for fermionic nuclei and bosonic atoms in traps, modeling short-range correlations of variable strength via one- and two-body density and momentum distributions. Distinguishability between correlated and uncorrelated states is quantified using Kullback–Leibler relative entropy and Jensen–Shannon divergence. We find monotonic increases in Shannon entropies and decreases in Onicescu information with stronger correlations, reflecting delocalization and high-momentum tails. KL and JS divergences grow with correlation strength, providing sensitive measures of distance and the detectability of correlations in position and momentum space. Identical qualitative information-theoretic behaviors emerge in fermionic and bosonic systems, indicating universality across quantum statistics. The framework enables parameterized exploration of correlation strength with consistent trends across observables, establishing information measures and relative entropies as diagnostic tools for many-body correlations in nuclear and ultracold platforms.

We present a deep, wide-field imaging survey of the old open cluster M67 covering the entire @xmath0 diameter to a depth of @xmath1, using the UHcam mosaic imager on the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope. From these data we construct a color–magnitude diagram (CMD) traced from stars on the giant branch at @xmath2 down through the main sequence to at least @xmath3. At the faint end, the CMD reaches stars of masses below @xmath4. A modest white dwarf (WD) cooling sequence is detected, commencing slightly fainter than @xmath5 and, after correction for background galaxy and stellar field contamination, terminating near @xmath6. The observed WDs follow closely a theoretical cooling locus for @xmath7 pure carbon–core DA WDs with hydrogen-rich atmospheres. Using these tracks, we infer a cooling time to @xmath8 = 14.6 of @xmath9 Gyr, which we take as the WD cooling age of M67. A fit of isochrones to the cluster CMD indicates a main-sequence turnoff age of @xmath10 Gyr. The agreement between the WD cooling age and the turnoff age suggests that ages derived from WD cooling are as reliable as those from other techniques. Artificial-star tests confirm our completeness limits. The WDs presently contribute about 9% of the total cluster mass, but the number seen appears somewhat low compared with the number of giants, possibly reflecting dynamical evolution or incompleteness at the faint end.

Microblogging platforms such as Twitter have become vital channels for sharing time-critical updates during crises, yet the volume, noise, and redundancy of posts hinder rapid sensemaking by humanitarian responders. We present a novel framework that automatically produces concise, abstractive situational summaries from crisis tweets and identifies salient sub-topics with short, informative per-topic summaries. The framework operates in two stages. First, an integer-linear programming optimization selects a compact set of tweets that maximizes relevance and coverage while minimizing redundancy, yielding a diverse backbone that captures the evolving crisis landscape. Second, a word-graph and concept–event-based abstractive module fuses lexical variants, aligns event triggers with their participants, and resolves referential ambiguity to generate coherent summaries that foreground who, what, where, and when. To surface finer-grained situational facets, we perform topic induction over the selected tweets to detect sub-topics such as missing and found people, urgent needs, infrastructure damage, and service disruptions; each topic is then summarized abstractively to support rapid triage and targeted action. We evaluate on multiple real-world disaster datasets with both automatic metrics (e.g., ROUGE, redundancy/diversity measures, and classification F1 for situational filtering) and human judgments of informativeness, coherence, and actionability. Results show high accuracies across tasks and consistent gains over competitive extractive and lead baselines, with substantially reduced redundancy and improved coverage of critical situational facts. Ablation studies highlight the complementary benefits of ILP-based selection and concept–event abstraction, and runtime analyses indicate suitability for near real-time deployment. Our contributions advance information extraction, summarization, and web/social media search for crisis informatics, delivering actionable situational awareness to humanitarian organizations through compact, topic-aware, abstractive summaries.

Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and supermassive black holes (SMBHs) populate galactic nuclei across a broad range of bulge masses, coexisting in intermediate systems while tending to exclude each other at the smallest and largest scales. We propose a dynamical pathway that transforms dense NSCs into SMBHs via runaway tidal captures once the cluster surpasses critical thresholds in central density and velocity dispersion. The principal bottleneck, common to collisional runaways, is achieving the first e-fold increase in black hole mass. We show that a stellar-mass black hole can cross this bottleneck by repeatedly tidally capturing stars and consuming them through episodic mass transfer at pericenter, driving rapid early growth. As the black hole approaches a characteristic mass @xmath0, the tidal capture channel weakens, but tidal disruption events persist and can continue to build the seed to larger masses. The runaway slows to sub-exponential growth once the seed depletes the NSC core, regulating the subsequent evolution. Although the bulk of the cosmic SMBH mass density is produced by episodic gaseous accretion in very massive galaxies (as implied by the Soltan–Paczynski argument), our framework suggests that the smallest SMBHs likely originate from strong tidal encounters within NSCs. Seeds grown for a duration @xmath1 entirely through this channel obey simple power-law relations with their host galaxy’s velocity dispersion, @xmath2; in the simplest regime the scaling is @xmath3, with exponents and prefactors modestly altered by the efficiency of loss-cone refilling. Using loss-cone dynamics and cluster evolution models, we delineate the parameter space for runaway onset and predict current tidal disruption event rates that are consistent with observations. This mechanism naturally accounts for the observed coexistence and exclusion patterns of NSCs and SMBHs and yields testable predictions linking NSC structure, velocity dispersion, and low-mass SMBH demographics.

Low-loss dielectric crystals hosting defects from paramagnetic or rare-earth impurity ions underpin emerging quantum hybrid systems spanning optical and microwave domains. We investigate single-crystal yttrium aluminium perovskite (YAlO3, YAP) using the whispering gallery mode technique. Multiple resonant microwave modes were tracked from room temperature down to 20 mK, enabling precise determination of the microwave permittivity tensor. The tensor is found to be biaxial and its temperature dependence is quantified with estimated uncertainties below 0.26%. Complementary electron spin resonance spectroscopy at 20 mK reveals previously unreported transitions with zero-field splittings of 16.72 and 9.92 GHz. Spin–photon coupling strengths of 4.2 and 8.4 MHz are observed at residual impurity concentrations, exceeding the photon cavity linewidth of 116 kHz while remaining comparable to the linewidths of the identified spin transitions. These results establish YAP as a well-characterized, low-loss platform for coherent microwave photon–spin interactions, and inform materials selection and device design for quantum hybrid applications.

We construct equations of state (EoS) for dense matter with large strangeness content, including hyperonic matter, Bose–Einstein condensates of antikaons, and deconfined strange quark matter. First-order phase transitions from hadronic matter to antikaon-condensed and quark phases are modeled, with the hadronic sector described within a relativistic field theoretical framework. The resulting EoS are applied to equilibrium sequences of uniformly rotating compact stars, enabling a systematic study of mass–radius relations, moment of inertia, and stability. We examine the influence of rotation on the emergence and robustness of a third family branch for antikaon-only EoS. Furthermore, we analyze the back-bending phenomenon triggered by a first-order transition from antikaon-condensed to quark matter in rotating sequences.

We theoretically demonstrate that Majorana fermions associated with Majorana flat bands emerge as zero-energy modes on the [110] edge of single-layer and multilayer nodal superconductors with d-wave pairing and Rashba spin–orbit coupling. Using Bogoliubov–de Gennes modeling and symmetry/topological analysis, we identify the conditions under which edge Majorana modes appear and persist. When global inversion symmetry is broken and an in-plane magnetic field parallel to the [110] edge is applied, the coexistence of Majorana modes with conventional fermionic Andreev bound states produces a characteristic triple-peak structure in tunneling conductance: a robust zero-bias peak from Majoranas flanked by field-split side peaks. Simulated Blonder–Tinkham–Klapwijk spectra, including interlayer coupling, show robustness to moderate disorder, establishing tunneling spectroscopy as a probe of Majorana physics in d-wave superconductors.

This article reviews how the Milky Way’s formation and evolution can be reconstructed from the spatial distribution, kinematics, ages, and chemical abundances of long-lived stars. We outline methods to derive component-specific star formation histories, chemical enrichment pathways, and constraints on the stellar initial mass function. We assess the Galaxy’s accretion and merger timeline—identifying what merged and when—through chemo-dynamical diagnostics, and benchmark these in state-of-the-art simulations. Advancing surveys and analysis frameworks are transforming models, ushering in a data-rich era.

We revisit the origin of antibiotic-tolerant persister cells and propose cellular senescence as a mechanistic basis for persistence, in contrast to stochastic phenotype switching. We develop an age-structured population model in which physiological age modulates growth, metabolic activity, and susceptibility to antimicrobial agents. The model couples cell division, aging, and drug-mediated killing with batch and chemostat environments, yielding analytical expressions and numerical simulations for population dynamics and killing curves. Without invoking heritable mutations or reversible switching, senescence alone generates biphasic kill kinetics and a small, resilient subpopulation. The predicted persister fraction increases with culture age in batch growth and decreases with dilution rate in continuous culture, reproducing classical observations. The framework explains why rapidly growing, young cohorts are preferentially eliminated, leaving older, slow-growing cells transiently tolerant; upon resumption of growth, newly born cohorts restore drug susceptibility. Parameter exploration identifies regimes where senescence dominates persistence and delineates experimental signatures distinguishing senescence from stochastic switching, including age-dependent kill slopes and recovery delays. Our results integrate physiological aging into persistence theory, unify disparate empirical trends, and suggest interventions that modulate age structure—via growth phase control, nutrient pulsing, or dilution—to minimize persister prevalence and improve antimicrobial efficacy in practice.

We propose cooperative ring exchange as a mechanism for quantum melting of vortex lattices in rapidly rotating Bose–Einstein condensates. Adapting the Kivelson et al. (Phys. Rev. Lett. 56, 873, 1986) framework to a Wigner crystal of vortices in the pseudomagnetic field of a superfluid background, we evaluate multi-vortex tunneling via path integrals. The ring-exchange amplitude follows a perimeter law with a renormalized fugacity; balancing it against lattice elasticity yields a melting criterion governed by a parameter set by rotation, healing length, and interaction strength. When this parameter exceeds unity, exchange loops destabilize crystalline order. We outline experimental signatures, such as Bragg-peak suppression and shear softening, and emphasize BECs as pristine platforms to probe quantum melting.

We present Spitzer IRS mid-IR spectroscopy of the prototype WN star EZ CMa (HD 50896, WN4b). The spectra reveal numerous He II wind lines alongside fine-structure lines [Ne III] 15.5 μm and [O IV] 25.9 μm. We perform a non-LTE spectroscopic analysis including line blanketing and clumping and compare to the mid-IR diagnostics. Using these combined constraints, we derive elemental abundances by number of Ne/He = (1.2–1.8) × 10^-4 and O/He = (4.2–4.8) × 10^-5, the first such determinations for an early WN star. We further obtain large nitrogen enhancements with N/C ≈ 34 and N/O ≈ 50, in excellent agreement with predictions for rotating massive stars nearing the end of core hydrogen burning. These results validate evolutionary models and demonstrate the diagnostic power of mid-IR spectroscopy for WN winds.
