A companion paper presents a fast algorithm for estimating orbital actions in axisymmetric potentials, enabling efficient, likelihood-based fitting of parametrised stellar distribution functions to large kinematic data sets from the solar neighbourhood. Here we test the predictive power of such action-based models and assess how strongly global Galactic structure can be constrained by data confined to the solar cylinder. We adopt a flexible Milky Way potential comprising a gas disc, thin and thick stellar discs, a central bulge, and a dark halo, and we model the stellar phase-space distribution with a two-component disc distribution function. We first fit the thin-disc component to the Geneva–Copenhagen Survey velocity distribution at the solar radius. The resulting model reproduces the observed vertical density profile of the disc at the solar radius in good agreement with independent constraints. Incorporating a thick-disc component, we extend the fit to match the classical star-count measurements of Gilmore and Reid at large heights above the plane. Without further adjustment, the combined model predicts the vertical profile of the velocity dispersion measured by the RAVE survey and the distributions of velocity components at several heights from SDSS, providing stringent out-of-sample validation. The success of these predictions, which rely on data not used in the fitting, indicates that the adopted potential—close to a maximum-disc configuration—approximates the true Galactic potential. By contrast, substituting another plausible potential yields systematically overestimated kinematic diagnostics, such as vertical dispersions, underscoring the sensitivity of the fits to the mass model. The models imply that the thick disc is more strongly supported by vertical than radial random motions, in contrast to the thin disc, a prediction that will be directly testable with forthcoming data. Allowing parameters to vary without external constraints tends to produce unphysical radial trends (e.g., in scale height), revealing degeneracies that cannot be broken with solar-cylinder data alone. This highlights the need for kinematic and density measurements that extend well beyond the solar neighbourhood. Finally, we discuss how these self-consistent, action-based models can aid the interpretation of integral-field spectroscopy of external disc galaxies by linking observed kinematics to underlying mass distributions and anisotropy. Keywords: galaxies: kinematics and dynamics; the Galaxy: disc; solar neighbourhood.

We investigate the flavor asymmetry of polarized antiquark distributions in the nucleon within the meson cloud framework, incorporating both direct vector meson contributions and interference between pseudoscalar and vector mesons. Using bag-model wave functions, we construct the polarized valence quark distribution of the rho meson and the corresponding interference distributions, and embed them in a convolution formalism to obtain the nucleon’s polarized sea. We find that pseudoscalar–vector interference yields a modest but systematic enhancement of the polarized flavor asymmetry at intermediate Bjorken x, while leaving the small- and large-x behavior largely unchanged. The predicted asymmetry remains small in magnitude but non-vanishing across a broad range of reasonable cutoff and coupling choices. We also evaluate the Pauli blocking contribution from the nucleon’s valence structure and discuss its interplay with meson cloud effects, noting partial compensation at low x and reinforcement at intermediate x. The combined results provide a consistent, testable pattern for polarized sea flavor asymmetry, relevant to forthcoming polarized Drell–Yan and electroweak production measurements.

Motivated by ultrafast time‐domain measurements of atomic ionization, we investigate the transient dynamics and characteristic times that accompany the tunneling decay of a localized quantum state. Using time‐dependent solutions of the Schrödinger equation and monitoring density and current at the barrier edge and in the far field, we show that tunneling initiates immediately, yet a finite time is required for outgoing flux to develop. This short‐time behavior depends sensitively on the initial state. For tightly localized preparations, where early evolution is dominated by over‐the‐barrier components, the timescale governing flux propagation across the barrier is close to the Büttiker–Landauer traversal time. Following this transient, a quasistationary, slowly decaying regime emerges, enabling diffraction in time at longer times and distances. To define an operational tunneling time at the barrier boundary, we back‐extrapolate the motion of the escaped wave packet; the resulting time significantly exceeds local flux and density buildup times, clarifying delays directly relevant to attosecond tunneling measurements.

Path-pairable graphs are those in which every pairing of vertices can be connected by edge-disjoint paths. Previously, all known families had diameter at most 3. Quadrupole amplitudes in the N-to-Delta transition are a key probe of nucleon deformation. Bars are key drivers of secular evolution in disk galaxies, redistributing angular momentum, funneling gas, and shaping bulge and disk growth. We present a study of the bar fraction in a mass-complete sample of disk galaxies in the COSMOS field over a broad redshift interval using high-resolution HST imaging and multiwavelength photometry. Bars were identified with quantitative isophotal analyses and visual inspection, and host galaxies were characterized by stellar mass, disk morphology, and specific star formation rate (SSFR). We find that the fraction of barred disks depends strongly on stellar mass, disk type, and SSFR. At intermediate mass, the bar fraction in morphologically early-type disks is higher at all redshifts by a factor of about two relative to late-type disks. At higher mass, this trend reverses: early-type disks have a significantly lower bar fraction than late-type disks across the same redshift range. When galaxies are segregated by SSFR, low-SSFR systems exhibit bar fractions that closely track the early-type population, whereas high-SSFR systems mirror the late-type population, indicating a close correspondence between morphology and SSFR in disk galaxies at these epochs. The total bar fraction in intermediate-mass disks increases by roughly a factor of two over the redshift interval probed, while the bar fraction in the most massive disks remains approximately constant. These results suggest that, by earlier times in the universe, spectral and morphological transformations in the most massive disk galaxies had largely converged to the familiar Hubble sequence observed locally, whereas intermediate-mass disks continued to evolve to later epochs. Our findings underscore the necessity of mass-limited samples to robustly quantify the evolution of barred galaxies and reveal that the buildup of barred populations is largely insensitive to large-scale environmental density within the scales accessible to photometric redshift-based measures.

Understanding cosmic reionization is a key goal of observational cosmology, and high-redshift quasar spectra provide backlighting to measure absorption by intervening neutral hydrogen. We present a deep Keck/DEIMOS spectrum of the z=6.4 quasar CFHQSJ2329−0301. This source is 2.5 magnitudes fainter than the well-studied z=6.4 quasar SDSS J1148+5251, yielding a smaller Strömgren sphere and reduced proximity effect, enabling a probe of intergalactic H I absorption at the highest redshifts. We measure transmitted flux in the Lyα, Lyβ, and Lyγ forests, finding that the average transmission over a ≈200 comoving Mpc path length is consistent with zero. This implies a stringent lower limit on the effective optical depth, indicating saturated absorption and a largely neutral intergalactic medium near z≈6.4. Our results are consistent with strong evolution of optical depth with redshift, supporting a rapid increase toward the end of reionization. These observations extend hydrogen absorption constraints to unprecedented redshift and highlight faint quasars as powerful laboratories for the early universe, black hole growth, and galaxies at high redshift.

Precise measurements of cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization offer a unique window into inflationary physics through the search for primordial gravitational waves encoded in B-mode patterns. We quantify the principal limiting factors in optimizing space-based, balloon-borne, and ground-based CMB polarization experiments using current detector technology. Employing end-to-end sensitivity forecasts that incorporate instrument noise, sky coverage, lensing B-modes and delensing, polarized Galactic foregrounds, and residuals from component separation, we find that foreground contamination and subtraction residuals ultimately dominate the error budget in attempts to detect a primordial tensor signal. For full-sky space-based experiments, these foregrounds hinder the detection of tensor-to-scalar ratios of @xmath0 on large angular scales, while for ground-based experiments the same limitations impede the efficacy of delensing techniques needed to isolate the inflationary signal from lensing-induced B-modes. Considering a suite of currently planned or proposed ground-based and balloon-borne designs, we show that a value of @xmath1 can be measured at the @xmath2–@xmath3 level. A small space-based CMB polarization mission with full-sky coverage and present-day detector performance can detect @xmath4 at the @xmath5–@xmath3 level, but will require markedly improved knowledge of polarized foregrounds to achieve robust significance. We advocate as wide a frequency coverage as possible to enable percent-level foreground subtraction, which is necessary to reach sensitivity to such small primordial tensor amplitudes. We further assess theoretical implications: to produce a clearly detectable (@xmath63–@xmath3) tensor component in a realistic CMB experiment, inflation must either involve large-field variations, @xmath7, or multi-field/hybrid dynamics. Hybrid models can be distinguished from large-field models by their characteristically blue scalar spectral index. Therefore, a joint observation of a tensor/scalar ratio and @xmath8 with experiments of the type considered here may indicate that inflation is driven by physics in which the inflaton cannot be described as a fundamental field. Keywords: cosmology: cosmic microwave background; cosmology: theory; cosmology: early universe

Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) exhibit rich valley-dependent electronic and magneto-optical phenomena that demand accurate few-band descriptions near the @xmath1-valleys. Using TB parameterizations from the literature, we derive material-specific sets for MoS@xmath3, WS@xmath3, MoSe@xmath3, and WSe@xmath3, and construct the corresponding six-band @xmath0 Hamiltonians. From these, we compute effective masses, Landau level spectra, and the effective exciton @xmath4-factor @xmath5 across different TMDCs. We find that previously reported TB parameterizations yield small absolute values of @xmath5 that are inconsistent with experimentally measured @xmath6. To address this discrepancy, we develop two additional @xmath0 parameter sets by building new TB models via simultaneous fitting to ab initio dispersions obtained within density functional theory (DFT) and the @xmath7 approach, together with targeted values of @xmath5. We show that modest adjustments to TB couplings, which minimally affect the dispersion of higher conduction and deep valence bands, can nevertheless produce a substantial increase in @xmath8, thereby yielding @xmath5 values close to experiment. This pronounced sensitivity of @xmath5 to specific TB parameters underscores the importance of valley-resolved magnetic response in constraining low-energy models, and it provides a practical pathway for improving DFT and TB descriptions of TMDCs relevant to valley Zeeman physics, magneto-excitons, and quantum magnetotransport.

Since the discovery of gamma-ray burst (GRB) afterglows three years ago, afterglow emission has become central to GRB research. With distance scales established through redshift measurements, late-time emission now offers powerful diagnostics of GRB origins and their connection to host-galaxy environments in the early universe. This review synthesizes X-ray observations of GRB afterglows and assesses their implications for progenitor models, jet geometry, and energetics. Time-resolved spectroscopy and light-curve analyses provide constraints on beaming via achromatic breaks, enabling estimates of the true energy release. Detection of transient iron features in several events links GRBs to massive progenitors embedded in star-forming regions, and supports scenarios with dense circumburst media. Joint modeling of spectral indices and temporal decay slopes favors fireball interpretations and indicates that, on average, the expansion is not strongly collimated, implying moderately wide jet opening angles. Absorption measurements further probe gas and dust in the host, illuminating both local environments and line-of-sight conditions. Together, X-ray afterglow studies are reshaping our understanding of GRBs as endpoints of stellar evolution.

Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) are compact stellar systems found in galactic nuclei, often coexisting with a central massive black hole (MBH). We investigate NSC formation and evolution driven by the inspiral of multiple star clusters that host intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs). Using N-body simulations, we follow the dynamics of the IMBHs and stars as the clusters decay and merge. We find that the IMBHs sink to the NSC core through dynamical friction and mass segregation, forming a bound subsystem. Although IMBHs strongly scatter one another and the surrounding stars, none is ejected from the NSC. The IMBHs are excited to high orbital eccentricities, and their spatial distribution develops a steep power-law cusp. The stellar component likewise develops a cusp, replacing the central core seen in simulations without IMBHs, but with a shallower slope than the IMBH cusp. The presence of IMBHs accelerates the NSC’s two-body relaxation, acting as massive perturbers that efficiently refill the loss cone. As a result, TDE rates are strongly enhanced for the MBH and IMBHs, to levels incompatible with observations. Therefore, empirical tidal disruption rates can provide cumulative constraints on the prevalence and masses of IMBHs in NSCs, informing models of nuclear cluster assembly and the coevolution of MBHs and their stellar environments.

We consider a Brownian particle in a translating harmonic trap subject to viscous friction and external asymmetric Poissonian shot noise (PSN). This non-Gaussian noise decouples fluctuations from dissipation and establishes a paradigmatic nonequilibrium steady state. We analyze the statistics of the mechanical work required to maintain the steady translation, treating two cases: (i) pure PSN and (ii) PSN supplemented by thermal white Gaussian noise. Using exact calculations, we derive the large-deviation form of the work distribution for finite observation times and identify how trap relaxation, driving, shot-noise rate, and amplitude scales control its shape. The resulting distributions exhibit pronounced asymmetries and nonanalytic features inherited from PSN. We demonstrate a systematic violation of the conventional steady-state fluctuation theorem: in a parameter regime, rare negative work fluctuations are more probable than corresponding positive ones, although the mean work remains strictly positive. Our results quantify how external non-Gaussian forcing reshapes energetic fluctuations and provide testable predictions for driven colloids and nanomechanical systems.

Classical barium stars are long-period binaries composed of a late-type giant enriched in carbon and slow neutron-capture (s-process) elements and an evolved white dwarf companion that is optically faint or invisible. The youngest examples are surrounded by planetary nebulae (PNe) ejected shortly after the mass-transfer episode when the white dwarf progenitor was on the asymptotic giant branch (AGB), offering rare laboratories in which the chemistry of both the polluted star and the ejected nebula can be measured and directly linked to AGB nucleosynthesis. We present evidence that Hen 2-39 (PN G283.8−04.2) harbors such a system, making it one of only a handful of known PNe with a barium-star central binary. High-resolution optical spectroscopy of the central cool giant reveals marked enhancements in carbon and barium, with carbon elevated relative to iron and [Ba/Fe] characteristic of barium stars. The spectrum is best matched by a cool carbon-rich giant with an early R-type carbon-star classification (C-R3), but the strong barium enrichment and indications of binarity argue that the star is more appropriately interpreted as a barium star rather than a true member of the peculiar early R-type class. The polluted giant in Hen 2-39 closely resembles that in WeBo 1 (PN G135.6+01.0), including evidence for chromospheric activity and low-amplitude photometric variability. The variability indicates rapid rotation for a giant, with a period of order a few days, plausibly induced by angular momentum accreted from the AGB wind. Photoionized nebular spectroscopy shows a high degree of ionization, implying the presence of a hot pre–white dwarf companion that escapes direct detection at optical wavelengths; ultraviolet observations will be required for unambiguous confirmation. Narrowband imaging reveals an apparent ring-like morphology consistent with an equatorial density enhancement arising from binary interaction, as seen in other PNe surrounding barium stars such as WeBo 1 and A 70. Nebular abundance determinations classify Hen 2-39 as a non–Type I PN, with no evidence for the strong nitrogen enrichment characteristic of higher-mass progenitors. This aligns with the emerging trend that non–Type I PNe are more likely to exhibit signatures of s-process enrichment. Comparison with AGB nucleosynthesis models indicates that the observed photospheric abundance pattern of the cool giant is reproduced by a model with an initial AGB mass around 1.8 solar masses and a relatively large 13C pocket. Matching the observed carbon and barium enhancements requires highly efficient, largely conservative mass transfer—consistent with wind Roche-lobe overflow—from the AGB star to the companion. Hen 2-39 thus expands the small sample of PNe with barium-star central binaries and provides a valuable benchmark for testing AGB nucleosynthesis and binary mass-transfer physics.

We present comprehensive grids of stellar models and associated adiabatic oscillation frequencies developed for the CoRoT Seismology Working Group during the mission’s scientific preparation. Models were computed with the CESAM stellar evolution code, and mode frequencies were derived using the ADIPLS oscillation program. The grids span masses from a wide range, metallicities, and evolutionary phases representative of CoRoT primary targets, including main-sequence to subgiant stages. We describe input physics, calibration procedures, and quality checks, and assess sensitivities to key parameters. These resources support target selection, seismic diagnostics, pipeline testing, and inversion studies. All models and frequency sets are publicly accessible via the ESTA web site for download.

Duality-covariant formulations such as heterotic double field theory and exceptional field theory provide manifest T- and U-duality symmetries for the low-energy limits of heterotic string, type II string, and M-theory compactifications. We generalize these frameworks to encompass non-geometric backgrounds by introducing dual fields canonically associated with non-geometric fluxes. We present complementary parameterizations of the generalized metric: a conventional frame in terms of the spacetime metric, B-field, and gauge fields, and a dual frame involving bivector- and higher dual potentials that naturally encode Q- and R-type fluxes and their heterotic counterparts. Under simplifying assumptions on the coordinate dependence that are compatible with the section condition, we construct a duality-covariant effective action for non-geometric fluxes. We show its reduction to standard supergravity and heterotic supergravity in geometric regimes and establish the equivalence of the two parameterizations via field redefinitions and integrations by parts. Using the action, we obtain explicit non-geometric backgrounds sourced by exotic branes and determine their duality monodromy matrices around nontrivial cycles. The generalized charges extracted from these monodromies match precisely those computed from integrals of the corresponding non-geometric fluxes, providing a stringent consistency check. We analyze the modified gauge symmetries, Bianchi identities, and equations of motion in the dual frame and clarify the role of section constraints. Our results extend duality-covariant field theories to truly non-geometric regimes, offering a unified description of exotic branes and flux compactifications. We conclude with prospects for relaxing the simplifying assumptions, incorporating the full heterotic gauge sector and alpha-prime corrections, and addressing global patching with duality transition functions.

We detect a fast outflow of neutral and ionized gas in the radio galaxy 3C 293, with velocities up to 1000 km s−1 emerging from its central kiloparsec. Optical spectroscopy maps the ionized component and locates the bulk of the outflow at a bright radio hot spot in the inner jet, about 1 kpc east of the nucleus. In the same region the radio jet is distorted and large reservoirs of cold gas are present, indicating a strong jet–ISM interaction capable of accelerating multiphase material. The kinematics and location of the broad H I component mirror those of the ionized gas, implying that—even at high energies—a substantial fraction of the outflowing gas remains, or rapidly recombines to become, neutral. These results support jet-driven feedback that is powerful yet inefficient at fully ionizing the swept-up ISM. We also report H I emission from three nearby companions of 3C 293, revealing a gas-rich environment that may influence its evolution and its future activity.

We investigate the nonequilibrium dynamics of trapped two-component Bose gases initiated by a composition quench: starting from the ground state of a single-component condensate, half the atoms are instantaneously transferred to a second hyperfine state. Small differences between intra- and intercomponent interactions generate rich post-quench behavior. Combining a stability analysis tailored to inhomogeneous traps with large-scale simulations of the coupled Gross–Pitaevskii equations, we chart a dynamical phase diagram versus trap strength and interaction ratio. We identify regimes of stable miscible oscillations, breathing and spin–density modes, demixing and domain formation, and full phase separation, and determine their onset thresholds via trapped Bogoliubov analysis. Our framework explains observed patterns across parameters and provides experimentally testable predictions.

We present high angular resolution Plateau de Bure Interferometer images (0.33 arcsec beam) of the HC3N J=27→26 transition from several vibrationally excited levels (v7=1 and v6=1) toward the Cepheus A HW2 region. These data reveal two dominant heating sources within the cluster: one centered on the disk that collimates the HW2 radio jet (the HW2 disk), and a second associated with a compact hot core located 0.3 arcsec northeast of HW2 (the HC). This is the first spatially resolved detection of vibrationally excited HC3N emission arising from a circumstellar disk. The kinematics of the vibrational emission across the HW2 disk follow a Keplerian rotation law, demonstrating a centrally dominated gravitational potential. From the excitation analysis of HC3N along the HW2 disk and within the HC, we derive temperature profiles that show both sources are centrally heated and exhibit clear temperature gradients. The inner, hotter regions reach 350 ± 30 K in the HW2 disk and 270 ± 20 K in the HC, while the outer, cooler regions decline to 250 ± 30 K and 220 ± 15 K, respectively. The inferred luminosities of the heating sources are approximately 2.2 × 10^4 L⊙ for the HW2 disk and about 3 × 10^3 L⊙ for the HC. The most massive protostar in the HW2 region is identified as the driving source of the HW2 radio jet. We discuss the implications for clustered massive star formation and propose that the proximity of the HC to HW2 indicates a likely binary system of B-type protostars, naturally accounting for the observed precession of the HW2 radio jet.

We investigate the effect of hydrostatic pressure on magnetostriction in the ab plane and along the c axis of a (La,Pr)1.2Sr1.8Mn2O7 bilayered manganite single crystal across the field-induced ferromagnetic metallic (FMM) transition. For comparison, pressure dependences of isothermal magnetization curves were measured at corresponding temperatures. Pressure markedly lowers the critical field required for the FMM transition and enhances the remanent magnetostriction. An anomalous pressure effect on the remanent lattice relaxation is observed, closely paralleling the pressure dependence of remanent magnetization along the c axis. These behaviors indicate that pressure strengthens the double-exchange interaction and stabilizes the FMM state, likely via reduced lattice distortions and enhanced bandwidth. The anisotropic responses reveal strong spin–lattice coupling and provide a route to tune phase competition in layered manganites.

Social influence fundamentally entails one person eliciting a response in another, yet most measurements in social media rely on platform-specific cues (retweets, hashtags, mentions) or brittle behavioral models. Such approaches overlook the diverse, poorly understood modes and motivations of online expression. We introduce content transfer, an information-theoretic, model-free measure that directly quantifies the directional effect of one user’s content on another’s, with a predictive interpretation: how much knowing A’s content reduces uncertainty about B’s subsequent content. Estimation combines recent advances in non-parametric entropy and mutual information estimation with modern content representations, including bag-of-words, topic models, and neural embeddings, enabling flexible application across modalities. Using longitudinal Twitter data from thousands of users, we show that content transfer detects non-trivial, predictive relationships that persist after controlling for temporal proximity, global trends, and exogenous events, and that frequently occur between users not linked in follower or mention graphs. Compared to baselines based on network ties and interaction counts, content transfer provides stronger and more interpretable signals of directional influence and improves next-post content prediction. These results indicate that large volumes of previously under-utilized social media content can be brought into rigorous statistical causal analysis, opening avenues for influence mapping, intervention evaluation, and theory-building in computational social science.

We investigate synchronization transitions in the Kuramoto model with bimodal natural frequency distributions. Prior work associated proximity to the unimodal–bimodal boundary with hysteretic, first-order-like transitions, attributing them to shallow central dips. Using a parametrized family of bimodal distributions, we disentangle dip width and depth and show that vanishing dip width, without decreasing depth, need not yield hysteresis. Combining self-consistent order-parameter analysis, Ott–Antonsen reduction, and linear stability, we derive precise conditions for multistability and continuous versus discontinuous onset. Our results clarify how distribution shape controls critical coupling and eliminate misleading heuristics near the unimodal–bimodal border.

Quantum steering enables one party to influence, and thereby communicate with, a remote party even when the sender is untrusted, offering both practical advantages for quantum information and a clear conceptual boundary between quantum and classical resources. In both modalities, the ratio between measured witnesses and classical bounds increases with @xmath0, evidencing enhanced steerability and a growing quantum–classical separation in higher dimensions. The protocol relies only on local projective measurements and minimal trust assumptions, providing a practical certification tool. We analyze the effective potential of the conformal factor within the effective average action formulation of Quantum Einstein Gravity. Exploiting renormalization group properties alone, without truncations or ad hoc approximations, we show that the existence of a non-Gaussian ultraviolet fixed point ensuring asymptotic safety imposes a distinctive, universal behavior of the potential near vanishing conformal factor. The resulting near-origin structure reflects scale invariance at the fixed point and constrains infrared deformations. We discuss phenomenological consequences and argue that this signature should be accessible to numerical simulations of quantum gravity. Our findings offer a diagnostic for asymptotic safety beyond truncations.

We revisit the standard synchrotron afterglow model for gamma-ray burst blast waves expanding relativistically into an external medium, incorporating magnetic-field amplification and prompt acceleration of electrons into a power-law energy distribution behind the shock. Including both adiabatic losses and radiative cooling via synchrotron and inverse-Compton processes, we derive a complete set of spectra composed of smoothly connected power-law segments. By integrating the emissivity over the full shocked fluid described by the Blandford–McKee self-similar solution, rather than adopting a thin-shell approximation, we obtain more accurate expressions for the characteristic break frequencies and the flux normalization, and quantify the intrinsic smoothness of the spectral transitions. We identify five distinct spectral regimes defined by the ordering of the self-absorption, injection, and cooling breaks, and we present analytic formulae for each regime and for the associated temporal evolution. The improved treatment yields light-curve morphologies and break shapes during frequency crossings that differ from simpler prescriptions by up to a factor of a few in both normalization and transition width, and reveals regimes previously neglected. Our results refine broadband afterglow fitting, constrain microphysical parameters and ambient density profiles more robustly, and provide practical tools for interpreting multiwavelength observations, including cases where inverse-Compton cooling is significant. Jet-break implications noted.

We develop a six–degrees-of-freedom rotational model for Titan that treats the moon as a three-layer body composed of a rigid inner core, a global subsurface ocean, and a floating outer ice shell. The ice shell is allowed to exhibit partially compensated lateral thickness variations chosen to simultaneously match the observed degree-two gravity and shape coefficients. The rotational dynamics include the gravitational torque from Saturn, gravitational coupling between the core and the shell, and pressure coupling at the fluid–solid interfaces. By exploring a broad interior parameter space, we identify a range between @xmath0 and @xmath1 of our model Titans whose obliquity, arising from a resonance with the @xmath2-year periodic annual forcing, is consistent with the observed value. Successful models favor shells with mean thicknesses of @xmath3 to @xmath4 km overlying an ocean of @xmath5250 km thickness. Time-domain simulations of the obliquity evolution indicate that the Cassini obliquity determination reflects an instantaneous measurement rather than a long-term mean. We predict a secular and periodic variation of the obliquity, with an amplitude of roughly 7 arcmin over the duration of the Cassini mission. Future measurements of the time derivative of Titan’s obliquity would place stronger constraints on the ocean thickness, shell compensation state, and interior coupling parameters, refining Titan interior models.

We investigate the discovery and discrimination potential of a future high-energy @xmath0 collider for @xmath1 bosons arising in a @xmath2 gauge extension of the Standard Model. We define @xmath1 model-lines and perform fits to extract couplings and set mass reaches. For order-one couplings, discovery reach extends to several TeV, with the attainable scale dependent on energy and channel selection. At 200 GeV, the collider is unlikely to reveal models not already accessible in late-stage LHC datasets, but it can refine coupling determinations and distinguish competing scenarios. At 300 GeV, previously inaccessible parameter space opens, while 500 GeV enables robust discovery and coupling profiling. The proposed program provides complementary coverage to hadron colliders and sharpens tests of @xmath2 dynamics via multi-channel analyses.

We investigate state conversion in bipartite entanglement under local operations and classical communication (LOCC) and its stochastic variant (SLOCC), focusing on catalysis. We introduce self-catalysis, where an additional copy of the source state enables a conversion otherwise impossible or less likely, and present explicit examples. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for self-catalysis in terms of majorization and probabilistic convertibility, establishing criteria for both LOCC and SLOCC. Using numerical sampling over random Schmidt spectra, we estimate the prevalence of self-catalytic conversions and analyze its dependence on dimension. We show that employing multiple copies as catalysts increases conversion probabilities but never renders the process deterministic. Finally, we conjecture that, under LOCC, the probability of self-catalysis is not monotonically increasing with dimension, whereas under SLOCC it exhibits monotonic growth.

This paper develops a Lie-group framework for crystals with a uniform distribution of defects and derives the discrete structures naturally associated to them as discrete subgroups of the ambient group. For a class of three-dimensional solvable Lie groups arising in continuum models of defective crystals, we compute the geometric symmetries of these discrete sets by analyzing changes of generators that preserve the subgroup. Since only three distinct Lie-group types model uniformly defective crystals, our calculations provide a complete classification of the symmetry groups of the corresponding discrete subgroups. We show that the symmetries induced by automorphisms of the discrete subgroup extend uniquely to automorphisms of the ambient Lie group, and we interpret these extensions as restrictions of elastic deformations of the continuous defective crystal. Symmetries that do not admit such extensions are accordingly classified as inelastic. The classification clarifies the correspondence between discrete and continuum descriptions, establishes algebraic criteria for symmetry preservation, and identifies conditions for extendability and rigidity, thereby advancing the structural understanding and mechanical interpretation of uniformly defective crystalline media.

We propose a generic, computational model of ecosystems featuring a hierarchical food-web architecture in which trophic interactions coevolve with population dynamics. Using long-duration simulations, we allow the ecosystem to evolve continuously over geological time scales, enabling tracking of extinction cascades and speciation events. In the model, speciation produces both horizontal diversification within trophic levels and vertical biodiversity through the emergence of new levels, capturing the transition from simple to more complex forms of life. Starting from a single trophic level, the system self-organizes to five to six trophic levels after sufficiently long evolution, a result robust across parameters. High-frequency sampling permits analysis of micro-evolutionary processes, including the birth, ageing, and death of individual organisms, and their feedback on macro-evolutionary patterns. We examine the statistical properties of species lifetimes, turnover, and food-web structure, and mechanisms that couple ecological dynamics to evolutionary innovation.

We calculate the joint probability distribution of the Wigner–Smith time-delay matrix and the scattering matrix for quantum scattering from a chaotic cavity with ideal point contacts. Exploiting energy-dependent scattering matrices, we prove Wigner’s conjecture on the unitary invariance of the associated distribution functional. Within random-matrix theory, we show that the distribution of the inverse proper delay times (the inverses of the eigenvalues of the time-delay matrix) belongs to the Laguerre ensemble. Using the method of orthogonal polynomials, we compute the exact eigenvalue density and its scaling limits. The general framework yields quantitative predictions for mesoscopic observables, including the thermopower, magnetoconductance, and capacitance of a quantum dot.

Phase transitions in the dense interiors of neutron stars can create sharp interfaces that carry conformal boundary degrees of freedom, as in phases exhibiting quantum Hall–like order, superconductivity, or superfluidity. We investigate a spherically symmetric neutron star with an inner core undergoing such a transition and analyze the dynamical implications of conformal matter localized on the phase boundary. Assuming mechanical equilibrium of the bulk phases, we solve the Israel junction conditions with a traceless surface stress-energy tensor to determine whether a static phase boundary is compatible with the boundary’s conformal dynamics. We find that the inclusion of conformal boundary degrees of freedom can frustrate staticity: even when pressures are balanced, the interface may have a net tendency to migrate, allowing one phase to engulf the other without compressing or decompressing the core. From the junction conditions we derive stability criteria and delineate the region in parameter space that admits a static, radially stable interface. The relevant control parameters are not only the density discontinuity across the boundary but also the difference in the radial slopes of the density profiles on the two sides. For realistic neutron-star equations of state and plausible core phases, these parameters lie within a phenomenologically reasonable range that can support stable interfaces. In regimes where the interface tends to move, we discuss an astrophysical consequence: small, sudden shifts of the phase boundary can induce abrupt changes in the star’s moment of inertia, providing a potential microscopic origin for microglitches or similar timing irregularities. Our results furnish testable constraints on interior phase structure and boundary dynamics in neutron stars. Keywords: junction conditions, neutron stars, conformal boundary degrees of freedom PACS: 04.40.Dg, 04.20.Jb, 26.60.+c, 11.25.HF Preprint: CECS-PHY-07/20

We study a discrete two-dimensional nonlinear lattice admitting discrete breather solutions. Employing spectral analysis of thermalized dynamics, we characterize equilibrium excitations and identify signatures of localized modes. A cooling protocol is introduced to quantify breather populations at thermal equilibrium and extract distribution statistics. Our findings confirm a finite energy threshold for breather formation and demonstrate that the cooling-based methodology offers a robust computational tool for measuring and analyzing breather distributions in nonlinear lattices.

Epitaxial thin films of the theoretically predicted half metal co@xmath0cr@xmath1fe@xmath2al were grown by dc magnetron sputtering on various substrates and buffer layers. Structural characterization by x‐ray diffraction and reflection high‐energy electron diffraction revealed B2 ordering of the heusler phase with minor disorder on co lattice sites. Magnetic tunnel junctions comprising a co@xmath0cr@xmath1fe@xmath2al electrode, an alo@xmath3 barrier, and a co counter electrode were fabricated and measured. Using the Jullière model, a spin polarization of 54% for co@xmath0cr@xmath1fe@xmath2al at T = 4 K was deduced. We investigated the dependence of tunneling magnetoresistance on the annealing temperature of the heusler electrodes. The trends are discussed in terms of morphology and surface order, supported by in situ tunneling microscopy and rheed analyses, and their impact on spin‐dependent transport.

We report a study of the low-excitation magnetic response of granular high-temperature superconductor La2-xSrxCuO4 at low temperatures. Using ultra-low-field magnetometry and ac susceptibility, we separate the intergrain Josephson contribution from intragrain magnetization. Intergrain currents are found to be fully irreversible, providing shielding against weak fields while not generating Meissner magnetization. The response exhibits hysteresis, slow relaxation, and freezing into a glassy state even in zero external field, consistent with frustration produced by d-wave pairing and pi-junctions in random Josephson networks. The macroscopic diamagnetic response to minute field variations is strongly irreversible yet qualitatively distinct from any known critical-state behavior: minor loop shapes, scaling, and history dependence cannot be described by Bean-type models or simple creep. We introduce a phenomenological "fractal" model of irreversibility, in which a hierarchical, scale-free distribution of weak-link clusters governs current flow, reproducing the observed glassiness, memory, and anomalous loop dynamics. These results elucidate the interplay of pairing symmetry and granularity in cuprates and provide a framework for low-field transport in disordered superconductors.

We report the discovery of a new ultra-faint stellar cluster, Muñoz 1, in the constellation Ursa Minor, identified as a compact overdensity in deep, wide-field stellar photometry from the MegaCam imager at the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope (CFHT). Color–magnitude diagrams reveal an old, metal-poor population consistent with a Milky Way halo globular cluster. A maximum-likelihood analysis of the spatial distribution yields a half-light radius of @xmath2, corresponding to @xmath3 pc, and an ellipticity consistent with zero, indicating a round, dynamically relaxed system. From isochrone fitting we infer a heliocentric distance of @xmath0 kpc; the object lies at a projected separation of @xmath1 from the center of the Ursa Minor dSph galaxy. Keck/DEIMOS spectroscopy of candidate members provides a heliocentric radial velocity of @xmath7 km s@xmath8. The three-dimensional separation of @xmath9 kpc and a velocity offset of 110 km s@xmath8 relative to Ursa Minor suggest that Muñoz 1 is not physically associated with the dSph, despite the very close angular alignment. We estimate an absolute magnitude of @xmath4, corresponding to a luminosity of @xmath5 L@xmath6, placing Muñoz 1 securely in the regime of ultra-faint clusters. Its photometric and structural properties argue against a dwarf galaxy classification. Along with Segue 3, Muñoz 1 is among the faintest stellar clusters known, extending the low-luminosity frontier of Milky Way globular clusters.

Stochastic gradient algorithms are increasingly studied for online, computationally efficient learning with large-scale, high-dimensional data. We develop a general asymptotic theory in separable Hilbert spaces. First, we establish a central limit theorem for classical stochastic gradient estimators and for their Polyak–Ruppert averaged versions, identifying the limiting Gaussian distribution under mild regularity assumptions. Because asymptotic normality is practically useful only with reliable variance quantification, we propose a fully recursive estimator of the asymptotic covariance for the averaged estimator. We prove its almost sure convergence with an explicit rate, together with its convergence rate in quadratic mean, ensuring online consistency and precision. The theory is illustrated in robust statistics through stochastic estimation of geometric quantiles and the geometric median, highlighting stability to outliers and scalability to high dimensions in practical, large-scale applications worldwide.

We investigate low angular momentum accretion onto stellar-mass black holes formed in the collapse of massive stellar cores, focusing on quasi-spherical inflow in the hypercritical regime where neutrinos dominate the cooling. Revisiting the commonly adopted criterion for the onset of a luminous state, we show that a transition to highly radiative accretion occurs when the specific angular momentum of the infalling gas is only marginally above the threshold for disk formation, rather than requiring substantially higher rotation. In this regime, a compact “dwarf” disk forms, in which gas spirals rapidly into the black hole primarily due to general relativistic effects and strong gravitational curvature, without relying on horizontal viscous stresses to transport angular momentum. As the rotation rate increases beyond this marginal threshold, the flow develops large, hot equatorial bubbles near the event horizon, and these structures supply the bulk of the neutrino luminosity. We find that the highest neutrino luminosities, the most energetic neutrino spectra, and the largest neutrino–antineutrino annihilation energy deposition rates are obtained for angular momenta just above the disk formation threshold. Within the range of specific angular momentum explored here, and for hypercritical accretion rates where neutrino cooling remains efficient, low angular momentum cores are therefore more conducive to producing strong neutrino-driven explosions following core collapse. This mechanism can assist in powering energetic supernovae and may enhance central engine activity in gamma-ray bursts by maximizing energy deposition in the polar regions. Our results highlight the pivotal role of general relativistic dynamics in marginally rotating flows and revise the conditions under which nascent black holes become luminous neutrino sources during core collapse.

SN 1996cr in the Circinus galaxy at 3.7 Mpc is notable for its late-time X-ray brightening: undetected at ~1000 days yet after ~10 years reaching a 0.5-8 keV luminosity of a few x 10^39 erg/s. We present modeling and analysis of deep Chandra HETG observations. Employing a hydrodynamic ejecta-circumstellar interaction model, we reproduce the X-ray light curves and spectra. The model indicates a massive progenitor (about 20-30 solar masses) that evolved from a red supergiant to a brief Wolf-Rayet phase, producing a low-density bubble bounded by a dense wind-blown shell at a radius of order 0.3 pc, within which the explosion occurred. The delayed rise in X-rays arises as the forward shock encounters and transits the dense shell, enhancing emission measure and ionization. We further exploit velocity-resolved line profiles in the deep 2009 epoch, fitting prominent Si and Fe lines with axisymmetric emission models. The best-fit symmetry axis is inclined by about 55 degrees to our line of sight, and the highest-ionization Fe XXVI emission is confined to high latitudes, whereas lower-ionization species trace broader equatorial zones. The most parsimonious explanation is an anisotropic CSM with enhanced polar densities coupled to a symmetric ejecta explosion. This geometry naturally accounts for the observed line shapes and the evolution of ionization and luminosity, and it constrains the progenitor’s mass-loss history. We discuss scenarios in which a slow, dense red-supergiant wind is reshaped by subsequent fast Wolf-Rayet winds or binary interaction, yielding polar CSM overdensities. Our results demonstrate that high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy, combined with physically motivated hydrodynamic modeling, can recover 3D CSM/ejecta geometries in young core-collapse supernovae. With future higher-throughput observatories, similar diagnostics may be extended to other supernovae and to gamma-ray burst remnants, enabling robust constraints on progenitors and circumstellar environments.

We investigate the long-term time evolution of the power spectrum of density fluctuations in an expanding one-dimensional universe, focusing on stages that follow the first appearance of caustics (shell crossings). For scale-free initial conditions, with an initial power spectrum proportional to k raised to a spectral index n, we demonstrate that the subsequent evolution of the power spectrum is self-similar: all times can be mapped onto one another by rescaling with a single evolving nonlinear scale. In this regime, the spectrum exhibits three distinct behaviors that correlate with the underlying dynamical state of the matter distribution. We identify a linear regime at the largest scales where growth remains perturbative, a single-caustic regime at intermediate scales where isolated fold singularities dominate, and a multi-caustic regime at the smallest scales where repeated crossings and complex phase-space structures appear. Each regime is characterized by a well-defined effective slope of the power spectrum; the small-scale slopes depend systematically on the initial index n through the statistics of caustic formation and the ensuing hierarchical clustering. We then extend the analysis to initial power-law spectra with a finite cutoff scale. In this case, exact self-similarity is not maintained after caustic formation because the cutoff introduces an additional invariant scale. The spectrum below the cutoff separates into a virialized regime, where collapsed structures imprint a slope set by the distribution and spacing of singular points, and a smallest single-caustic regime, where the imprint of the most recent individual caustics controls the spectral shape. We determine the corresponding indices and show how they vary with the initial conditions and with time. Finally, we outline general properties of the power spectrum’s shape for arbitrary initial conditions, emphasizing how caustic statistics and the emergence of a dominant nonlinear scale govern the transitions between regimes. These results clarify the mechanisms that set spectral slopes in one-dimensional cosmological dynamics and provide a foundation for analogous scaling arguments in higher dimensions.

We analyze the stellar populations of host galaxies for a sample of 53 X-ray–selected, optically dull active galactic nuclei (AGN) at 0.34 < z < 1.07 using ultra-deep (m < 26.5, 3σ) optical medium-band photometry from the Survey for High-z Absorption Red and Dead Sources (SHARDS). The SHARDS filter set (R ≈ 50) provides sufficient spectral resolution to consistently measure the strength of the 4000 Å break, a robust age indicator for stellar populations, while the optical dullness of the AGN minimizes nuclear contamination and enables reliable host characterization. We confirm that moderate-luminosity AGN (L_X ≈ 10^42–10^44 erg s^-1) predominantly reside in massive galaxies (typically M* ≈ 10^10–10^11 M⊙), and that the observed fraction of galaxies hosting an AGN increases strongly with stellar mass. To isolate intrinsic differences in stellar populations, we construct extensive random control samples of inactive galaxies matched in stellar mass and redshift, thereby removing the primary dependences of the AGN fraction. Comparing stellar age diagnostics, we find no significant differences in the distributions of rest-frame U − V colors between AGN hosts and mass- and redshift-matched inactive galaxies, consistent with previous studies. In contrast, AGN hosts exhibit significantly shallower 4000 Å breaks, indicating younger stellar populations. Employing a model-independent estimate of dust extinction, we derive extinction-corrected U − V colors and light-weighted average stellar ages. After accounting for extinction, AGN hosts show systematically younger stellar populations and higher dust attenuation than inactive counterparts of the same mass and redshift. Specifically, we find a highly significant excess of AGN hosts with D(4000) ≤ 1.4 and light-weighted ages of 300–500 Myr, alongside a deficit of AGN in intrinsically red (older) galaxies. These results suggest that, at fixed mass and epoch, moderate-luminosity AGN preferentially occur in galaxies experiencing recent star formation and enhanced dust, likely reflecting phases of rapid growth and obscuration. We argue that previous failures to detect these trends stem from the age–extinction degeneracy, which can mask genuine differences when relying solely on observed colors. Our findings underscore the power of medium-band spectroscopy-like photometry to disentangle stellar age and dust effects and to clarify the link between AGN activity and host galaxy evolution.

We report the discovery of a nearby late-type L dwarf identified by cross-matching the WISE preliminary data release with 2MASS. The source, WISEP J180026.60+013453.1 (W1800+0134), exhibits a proper motion of 0.42 arcsec yr^-1 and normal near-infrared colors, with spectroscopy indicating an L7.5 spectral type. Photometric distance estimates place it at @xmath1 pc, which would make it the sixth closest known L dwarf, though a trigonometric parallax is required to confirm its distance. The object was previously overlooked because of its location near the Galactic plane (@xmath2). Given its brightness and proximity, W1800+0134 constitutes a valuable benchmark for investigating cloud-related phenomena, atmospheric structure, variability, and weather in cool substellar atmospheres, and merits detailed follow-up observations in multiple wavelength regimes.

We present a systematic study of HCN J=1–0 hyperfine emission toward 24 young stellar objects (YSOs) of Classes 0 and I to probe envelope kinematics and excitation conditions in the earliest stages of star formation. The three hyperfine components are well separated in most sources and display rich spectral morphologies, including pronounced asymmetries, double-peaked profiles, and broad wings. We quantify how line shapes and apparent velocity shifts vary among the hyperfine components as a function of their relative optical depths, and compare these kinematic diagnostics with those derived from CS J=2–1, H^13CO+ J=2–1, and HCO+ J=4–3 and 3–2 reported by Mardones et al. (1997) and Gregersen et al. (1997). The different molecular tracers do not consistently exhibit the same sense of asymmetry, underscoring species- and transition-dependent radiative transfer effects and excitation regimes. Nevertheless, the velocity shifts correlate more strongly between HCN and CS than between HCN and H^13CO+, indicating that these two high-density tracers are similarly sensitive to infall and outflow motions in protostellar envelopes. Notably, the most opaque HCN hyperfine component (F=2–1) shows velocity shifts comparable to CS despite our larger beam size, suggesting that HCN F=2–1 is an especially effective probe of internal dynamics. In many sources we find systematic changes in velocity shift across the hyperfine triplet, with a monotonic decrease (i.e., increased blue shift) from F=0–1 to F=2–1 occurring more frequently, consistent with increasing optical depth enhancing blue-skewed profiles produced by inward motions. To interpret these signatures, we model L483 with a detailed radiative transfer framework that includes hyperfine overlap. The observed profiles indicate convincing infall on parsec scales but are incompatible with the standard inside-out collapse model (Shu 1977). Improved fits require an augmented envelope density and moderate infall velocities, together with a diffuse, static, turbulent, and geometrically thick outer layer that contributes scattering and alters emergent hyperfine ratios. Across the sample, the distribution of HCN hyperfine intensity ratios departs from local thermodynamic equilibrium and resembles anomalies previously documented in cold dark clouds and translucent cores. While such behavior can arise from radiative transfer in static or systematically moving cores, several sources point to the presence of scattering envelopes. Finally, HCN is detected much more selectively in Class 0/I objects than in starless cores or Class II sources, implying that protostellar envelopes achieve high densities and elevated HCN abundances over a relatively narrow evolutionary window, making HCN a powerful diagnostic of early-stage infall and envelope structure.

We present two coordinated ground-based observing campaigns to establish a grid of approximately 200 spectrophotometric standard stars (SPSS) for the absolute flux calibration of Gaia. The program targets an internal @xmath01% precision and ties the flux scale to Vega within @xmath03%. We describe the selection criteria and provide a vetted list of candidates spanning a range of spectral types, magnitudes, and sky positions while minimizing crowding and known variability. The survey strategy combines low- to medium-resolution spectroscopy with calibrated imaging, and uniform data reduction and analysis pipelines designed to control systematics and ensure homogeneity. All candidates are monitored for photometric constancy on short and long timescales, aiming for stability within @xmath15 mmag (approximately); cross-checks against literature and CALSPEC are performed. We discuss notable rejections and difficult cases arising from misidentifications, discordant literature data, visual companions, or detected variability. In particular, we report that CALSPEC standard 1740346 is a @xmath2 Scuti variable discovered during a 12 h monitoring campaign. The resulting SPSS grid will anchor Gaia spectrophotometric calibration.

The Hohenberg–Kohn theorem establishes an invertible one-to-one mapping between the ground-state density of an interacting many-body system and its Hamiltonian, with the standard caveat that Hamiltonians differing only by an additive constant are physically equivalent. The Runge–Gross extension to the time-dependent case similarly asserts a unique correspondence between the time-dependent density and the Hamiltonian, with Hamiltonians related by an additive, purely time-dependent function considered indistinguishable at the level of the density. In this work, we revisit these uniqueness claims and identify a class of counterexamples in which Hamiltonians that differ by an intrinsic constant or intrinsic time-dependent function represent genuinely different physical systems while nonetheless producing identical densities. By intrinsic we mean parameters that encode physical information not removable by a gauge choice or trivial energy shift, such as boundary-condition phases, superselection-sector labels, or topological couplings. We construct explicit families of degenerate Hamiltonians parameterized by such intrinsic constants or functions and show that their ground-state densities, and in the time-dependent setting their densities for all times within a well-defined interval, coincide. The intrinsic parameter alters physical features beyond the density—e.g., current distributions, response kernels, excitation spectra, or phase-dependent observables—yet leaves the density invariant. This demonstrates that while the proofs of Hohenberg–Kohn and Runge–Gross are formally independent of whether the constant or time function is additive or intrinsic, their applicability is restricted: the density cannot distinguish between different physical systems within an intrinsically degenerate family. The corollary is that degenerate Hamiltonians representing distinct physical systems, but differing only by an intrinsic constant or intrinsic time-dependent function, cannot be discriminated on the basis of the Hohenberg–Kohn or Runge–Gross theorems. We discuss criteria for identifying intrinsic versus extrinsic parameters, provide solvable model constructions, and analyze implications for density functional theory and time-dependent density functional theory. Our results indicate that the uniqueness mapping must be augmented by additional variables—such as currents, phases, or sector indices—to restore distinguishability and ensure well-posed functional constructions in the presence of intrinsic degeneracies.

We show that the fundamental quadratic form governing classical string propagation in D-dimensional constant curvature backgrounds obeys one of three integrable scalar equations: the sinh-Gordon, cosh-Gordon, or Liouville equation. In both de Sitter and anti–de Sitter spacetimes, including the D-dimensional black hole AdS background, all three sectors are indispensable to capture generic string dynamics. By exploiting the structural properties and associated potentials of these equations, we extract universal features of worldsheet evolution, stability, and phase structure independent of explicit solutions. This completes and generalizes previous analyses that were limited to the sinh-Gordon sector in de Sitter space. Furthermore, we construct explicit families of multi-string configurations in each sector, expressed in terms of elliptic functions, and present their behavior across dS and AdS geometries. The framework extends straightforwardly to constant curvature spacetimes of arbitrary dimension by replacing the sinh-Gordon, cosh-Gordon, and Liouville equations with their higher-dimensional generalizations. These results provide a unified, integrable description of classical string motion in curved backgrounds and open avenues for analyzing scattering, bound states, and nonperturbative phenomena in cosmological and black hole spacetimes.

We investigate the phenomenology of a QCD pomeron modeled as the exchange of a pair of non-perturbative gluons with finite vacuum correlation length, and confront it with chiral symmetry breaking derived from Schwinger–Dyson equations for the quark propagator using the same gluon dynamics. Employing infrared-finite correlators and effective gluon mass scales that reproduce diffractive cross sections, we find that the parameters and momentum dependence required by the pomeron yield Schwinger–Dyson solutions that underproduce dynamical mass generation and condensates. Conversely, gluon kernels that trigger realistic chiral symmetry breaking spoil observed diffractive phenomenology. We trace incompatibility to assumptions about factorization of two-gluon exchange, gauge and truncation dependence of the gluon–quark vertex, and neglect of confinement-induced correlations. Implications for unified non-perturbative QCD modeling are discussed, and future phenomenological and lattice tests to resolve the tension are proposed.

We investigate the anisotropic three-dimensional nearest-neighbor Ising model with competing interactions under a uniform longitudinal magnetic field. Ferromagnetic couplings act along one lattice direction, while antiferromagnetic couplings act along the transverse directions on a simple-cubic lattice. Using an effective-field theory with four-spin clusters (EFT-4) and large-scale Monte Carlo simulations, we compute phase diagrams in the field–temperature plane for a representative anisotropy of the simple-cubic lattice and examine the two-dimensional square-lattice limit. For the square lattice, both approaches yield solely continuous (second-order) transition lines for all fields. In three dimensions, we find a low-temperature first-order transition line that evolves into a second-order line at higher temperatures, the two meeting at a tricritical point. EFT-4 additionally predicts a low-temperature reentrant behavior absent in our Monte Carlo results, indicating a known tendency of cluster effective-field methods to overestimate ordering in the presence of competing interactions. Overall, Monte Carlo corroborates the topology of the phase diagram while refining the order of transitions and excluding reentrance.

We investigated common student difficulties with rotational and rolling motion in introductory physics and an intermediate mechanics course. We compared calculus-based and algebra-based introductory cohorts with physics juniors who had formal instruction in rotational dynamics. Methods included demonstration-based interviews with six juniors and ten introductory students, administered free-response and multiple-choice items to large introductory classes, and think-aloud interviews with six introductory students during test design. Across populations, students exhibited similar conceptual difficulties, indicating that higher mathematical sophistication did not yield deeper understanding. Recurring issues included conflating linear and angular quantities, misunderstanding torque, moment of inertia, the role and direction of static friction in rolling without slipping, and confusion between tangential and centripetal acceleration, and energy partitioning. Some difficulties arose from preexisting misconceptions about linear motion, while others were specific to rotational and rolling phenomena. Results suggest the need for targeted instruction that explicitly bridges linear and rotational concepts, uses structured demonstrations and diagnostic assessments.

We revisit the Lawrence–Krammer–Bigelow representation of the braid group by realizing it as the monodromy representation on the twisted homology of the fiber in a fiber bundle whose base and total space are complements of braid arrangements, and whose fiber is the complement of a discriminantal arrangement. Motivated by this viewpoint, we develop a general construction producing nontrivial fiber bundles over the complement of an arbitrary arrangement @xmath0, with fibers given by products of discriminantal arrangements. This construction yields a canonical homomorphism @xmath1 from the arrangement group @xmath2 to a product of groups @xmath3 associated to a specified collection @xmath4 of rank-two flats. Generalizing an argument of T. Stanford, we describe the kernel of @xmath1 in terms of iterated commutators, under a natural compatibility condition on chosen generators of the factors of @xmath3. This commutator description provides a practical test for the injectivity of @xmath5, which we apply to show that @xmath1 is injective for several well-studied decomposable arrangements. When @xmath0 is central, the homomorphism @xmath1 induces a natural map @xmath6 from the projectivized group @xmath7 into a product @xmath8 whose factors are free groups. We prove that @xmath6 is injective if and only if @xmath1 is. In the injective case, @xmath9 is isomorphic to a finitely presented, combinatorially determined subdirect product of free groups. As consequences, @xmath9 is residually free, residually torsionfree nilpotent, a-T-menable, and linear. Furthermore, we show that the image of @xmath6 is a normal subgroup with free abelian quotient, and we compute the rank of this quotient from the incidence graph of @xmath4 with @xmath0. When @xmath1 is injective, we deduce that @xmath9 is of type @xmath10 but not of type @xmath11. We study optimal trade execution when the mid-price follows a displaced diffusion, a flexible class interpolating between arithmetic and geometric Brownian dynamics via a shift parameter and permitting a prescribed lower bound (positive or negative) for the mid-price. Within an adapted strategy class and a price impact model with convex execution costs, we derive optimal liquidation policies under three risk criteria: Value-at-Risk, Expected Shortfall, and a new squared-asset expectation (SAE) objective closely related to a cost-variance measure. Using dynamic programming and calculus of variations, we obtain characterizations of optimal controls via Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations and first-order conditions, provide closed-form solutions in tractable regimes, and compute efficient numerical solutions otherwise. We analyze how the shift parameter, market impact intensity, and risk aversion affect execution speed and residual risk, and we establish limiting connections that recover classical ABM- and GBM-based execution policies as special cases of the displaced diffusion setting. Comparative statics reveal that while optimal schedules across risk criteria remain qualitatively similar, quantitative differences become material for high risk aversion and assets with low market impact, where VaR and ES favor faster front-loaded execution than SAE. Numerical experiments illustrate these effects across a range of market conditions, highlighting the trade-offs between expected cost and tail-risk control, and the role of the displaced diffusion’s support in mitigating price-floor or price-cap risks. The results provide a unified framework for tail-sensitive optimal execution under realistic mid-price dynamics and broaden the toolkit of implementable, risk-aware strategies. Keywords: optimal trade execution; displaced diffusion; algorithmic trading; HJB; calculus of variations; risk measures; VaR; Expected Shortfall; squared-asset expectation; market impact.

We evaluate differential distributions for exclusive production of the scalar @xmath0 meson, a glueball candidate, in proton–proton reactions at @xmath1 (FAIR@GSI) and @xmath2 (J-PARC@Tokai). We present, for the first time, a unified calculation of three mechanisms: QCD diffractive exchange, pion–pion meson-exchange current (MEC), and a double-diffractive process mediated by an intermediate pionic loop. The diffractive component is modeled both with two-gluon impact-factor techniques and within the Khoze–Martin–Ryskin framework developed for diffractive Higgs production, using several unintegrated gluon distribution functions to assess model dependence. Near the production threshold the reliably computed pion–pion fusion dominates, while the gluonic diffractive contribution, for which only an upper limit can presently be established, may become significant only at higher energies. For PANDA kinematics we predict sizable cross sections from the pion–pion channel and a negligible gluonic yield. We provide rapidity, transverse-momentum, momentum-transfer, and azimuthal distributions, quantify uncertainties, and discuss sensitivity to the choice of UGDFs. Production of @xmath0 close to threshold offers a means to constrain the @xmath3 form factor at larger pion virtualities. A detailed assessment of the two-pion continuum background is given, together with experimental strategies to isolate the @xmath0 signal at FAIR and J-PARC, and to validate the proposed mechanisms.

We present predictions for the @xmath0 transition amplitudes between the nucleon (@xmath1) and nucleon excitations (@xmath2) in the third resonance region. First, we determine the amplitudes for the second radial excitation of the nucleon, interpreted as the @xmath3 state, within the covariant spectator quark model, constraining radial wave functions by elastic and low-lying transition data. Next, we combine covariant spectator quark model inputs with the single quark transition model to obtain @xmath0 amplitudes when @xmath2 belongs to the @xmath4-multiplet @xmath5. The calculated @xmath6 and @xmath7 helicity amplitudes serve as inputs to derive the longitudinal and transverse amplitudes @xmath8 and @xmath9 for the transitions @xmath10, @xmath11, @xmath12, and @xmath13. We compare our estimates with available electroproduction measurements and Particle Data Group averages, discussing consistency and tensions across kinematics. To facilitate confrontation with forthcoming high-@xmath14 data, we provide simple analytic parametrizations for all amplitudes, constructed to reproduce the expected falloff at large @xmath14 and the correct threshold behavior. Our results supply a unified, dynamical baseline for interpreting resonance electroexcitation in the third region and offer quantitative guidance for planned measurements at upgraded facilities.

This paper generalizes absorbing-layer approaches for free-surface wave damping in Navier–Stokes-based flow simulations by formulating momentum sinks whose coefficients are rigorously linked to wave parameters. Using two-dimensional wave propagation and decay tests, we demonstrate that reliable damping requires coefficient magnitudes and spatial distributions scaled to the incident wave period, celerity, and steepness. A scaling law is derived that ensures similarity of damping performance between model and full scale, enabling consistent attenuation and minimized reflection across scales. The influence of damping-layer thickness, wave steepness, mesh fineness, and coefficient selection is systematically quantified, and an efficient procedure to estimate an optimal damping setup from readily available wave data is proposed. Three-dimensional ship resistance computations using the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method verify that the scaling laws transfer to practical applications: appropriately scaled coefficients improve convergence, reduce spurious reflections, and stabilize resistance predictions in both model and full scale. The study culminates in practical recommendations for robust damping of regular and irregular free-surface waves, including guidance on layer placement, thickness-to-wavelength ratios, grid resolution, and coefficient tuning. The results indicate that adjusting damping coefficients for each simulation is essential to ensure accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency. Keywords: damping of free surface waves, absorbing layer, Volume of Fluid (VOF) method, damping coefficient, scaling law.

Uncertainties in the dense-matter equation of state (EOS) preclude unique neutron-star (NS) models, yet remarkably robust EOS-independent relations have been identified among macroscopic observables. In particular, the frequency of the fundamental fluid f-mode, the mass, and the moment of inertia obey nearly universal relations, and the I–Love–Q trio links the dimensionless moment of inertia, tidal Love number, and quadrupole moment with minimal EOS dependence. We investigate the persistence of these universal relations in Eddington-inspired Born–Infeld (EiBI) gravity, a metric theory that departs from general relativity (GR) mainly at supranuclear densities through nonlinear matter–gravity coupling. Employing the apparent-EOS formulation of EiBI gravity developed by Delsate and Steinhoff, we construct slowly rotating and tidally perturbed NS models and compute moments of inertia, tidal deformabilities, quadrupole moments, and f-mode frequencies across a representative set of microphysical EOSs and for coupling constants consistent with current astrophysical bounds. We find that the I–Love–Q relations and the f-mode–mass–inertia relations in EiBI gravity are essentially indistinguishable from their GR counterparts: best-fit coefficients agree within uncertainties, and residuals remain at the percent level or below across the entire parameter space studied. The modest theory-induced structural changes largely cancel in the dimensionless combinations entering the universal relations. Our results imply that the practical use of universal relations for inferring NS properties and EOS constraints is robust to EiBI modifications of gravity within viable couplings, but conversely that these relations alone cannot discriminate EiBI gravity from GR.

We report the discovery of a hot DQ white dwarf that is a likely member of the 150 Myr open cluster Messier 35 (NGC 2168), designated NGC 2168:LAWDS 28. Radio relics detected in the outskirts of galaxy clusters are thought to trace radio-emitting relativistic electrons accelerated at cosmological shocks. Using cosmological hydrodynamic simulations of large-scale structure formation and a diffusive shock acceleration model for cosmic-ray electron production, we construct synthetic radio and X-ray maps of simulated clusters projected onto the sky plane. From these maps, we extract shock properties and relic observables, including the shock Mach number, radio spectral index, and luminosity, and compare them with published measurements. We find that a substantial fraction of shocks identified in both radio and X-ray bands involve multiple shock surfaces stacked along the line of sight, and the apparent morphology of shock distributions depends strongly on projection direction. Among multiple shocks in a given line of sight, radio emission preferentially highlights stronger shocks with flatter radio spectra, whereas X-ray emission more readily selects weaker shocks that carry larger kinetic energy flux. Consequently, Mach numbers and shock locations inferred from radio versus X-ray data can diverge for the same region. The distributions of spectral index and radio power of synthetic relics are broadly consistent with observations but show notable differences: simulated relics tend to reside farther from cluster centers and exhibit flatter spectra compared to observed samples, which include more relics closer to the core and with steeper indices. We suggest that these discrepancies could be reconciled if very weak shocks with low Mach numbers accelerate electrons more efficiently than assumed in the adopted diffusive shock acceleration model. Our results emphasize the importance of projection effects, multi-shock superposition, and microphysical uncertainties in interpreting relic properties, and motivate refined electron injection prescriptions and joint radio–X-ray analyses to robustly constrain shock acceleration in the intracluster medium.

We present a comprehensive comparison between time-dependent radiative-transfer and non-LTE nebular models and late-time observations of core-collapse supernovae, focusing primarily on SN 1987A.
