We further argue that the @xmath5 reported by CDF can be interpreted as @xmath6 or as @xmath4; precise measurements of its total width, spin, and key decay modes are required to distinguish these options. Our results provide partial widths, branching fractions, and radiative rates to guide forthcoming experimental studies and future searches.

We analyze high-cadence, high-resolution observations of a C3.2 solar flare by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly on the Solar Dynamics Observatory on 2010 August 1. This long-duration event exhibits soft X-ray and extreme-ultraviolet emission persisting for more than four hours. Post-flare arcade evolution indicates sustained magnetic reconnection and sequential loop formation for over two hours. AIA 1600 Å images resolve footpoint responses, revealing rapid brightenings with rise times of a few minutes followed by decays extending beyond 30 minutes. We use rise-phase UV light curves to construct empirical, loop-specific heating functions and to model coronal plasma evolution in the corresponding loops. Summing modeled loop radiation, we compare the total coronal output with contemporaneous GOES soft X-ray and AIA EUV fluxes. The agreement in timing and magnitude supports a scenario of prolonged, reconnection-driven energization of newly formed loops throughout the flare. This approach enables observational inference of heating functions for many flare loops and offers constraints on coronal heating and reconnection models. By linking footpoint UV emission to energy deposition, this data-driven method reconstructs the chronology of loop energization and is readily extendable to other long-duration flares.

This work investigates nuclear anapole moments of cesium, thallium, lead, and bismuth within the single-particle approximation. Analytical expressions are derived for a harmonic-oscillator mean field without spin–orbit coupling, illuminating parameter dependences and selection rules. We then perform numerical calculations using a Woods–Saxon potential that incorporates realistic spin–orbit interaction and surface diffuseness. The two approaches yield consistent anapole moments, demonstrating a remarkable stability with respect to the choice of mean-field potential and to reasonable variations of single-particle parameters. The results support the reliability of single-particle estimates for heavy nuclei of current experimental interest and provide benchmarks for interpreting atomic parity-nonconservation measurements and constraining hadronic parity-violating couplings in nuclei.

Fractal basin boundaries provide a robust diagnostic of chaos. We extend this approach to general relativity, where traditional measures such as Lyapunov exponents are difficult to define in an observer-independent manner. We analyze geodesic motion of test particles in two- and three-black-hole spacetimes, addressing conceptual and numerical obstacles to characterizing relativistic chaos. By computing basins of attraction for capture by each hole and for escape, we find intricate, self-similar structures with fractal boundaries, demonstrating chaotic dynamics. We also implement coordinate-invariant procedures to estimate Lyapunov exponents numerically, and identify trajectories with positive exponents. These results provide observer-independent evidence of chaos in multi-black-hole configurations within general relativity.

We present time-resolved photometry and optical spectroscopy of the interacting binary WX Cen (WR 48c) that confirm the orbital period previously reported by DS95 and refine its value to @xmath1 d. This morphology closely resembles that observed in V Sge, V617 Sgr, and other compact binary supersoft sources (CBSS), suggesting similar accretion-driven variability and system geometry. The optical spectrum is dominated by high-excitation emission, including Balmer, He II, C IV, N V, O V, and O VI lines. An analysis of the He II Pickering series decrement demonstrates the presence of a significant hydrogen component in the emitting gas. Between the 1991 and 2000/2002 epochs, He II 4686 weakened markedly, indicating substantial changes in the ionizing flux and the accretion state. We present a model-independent cosmographic reconstruction of f(R) gravity. Using a Taylor expansion of f(R) around the present curvature, we map f(R) and its low-order derivatives to the cosmographic parameters H0, q0, j0, and s0. We perform a Monte Carlo analysis on contemporary distance and expansion-rate data, obtaining bounds that do not assume any specific f(R) form and are applicable across a wide class of models. Under the assumptions of analyticity and the cosmological principle, this strategy constrains the dynamics and reconstructs the functional form of f(R) in a data-driven manner. Our main result is model-independent constraints on f(R) and its derivatives, compatible with theory and current observations. We infer a phenomenological expression for f(R) consistent with the cosmographic bounds and only mildly deviating from a constant term, suggesting a near-LambdaCDM behavior and a gently evolving dark-energy equation of state. These findings quantify allowable deviations from LambdaCDM and provide a robust, assumption-light framework to test modified gravity with future surveys and to guide theoretical developments.

We test the “pulse start conjecture,” that prompt gamma-ray burst (GRB) pulses begin simultaneously at all observed energies. Using four-channel, 64 ms BATSE data and a parametric pulse-fitting model, we measure energy-resolved pulse start times across a large sample of bursts. For the long GRB class, start times are statistically consistent across channels within measurement uncertainties, providing broad support for the conjecture. Apparent discrepancies are concentrated in intervals with low signal-to-noise, unresolved or hidden substructure, and significant pulse overlap, conditions that bias start-time estimation. Typical timing uncertainties are small compared with pulse durations for long GRBs, are even smaller for a substantial fraction of pulses, and are larger for short GRBs owing to their brevity and higher contrast. Combined with the well-established hard-to-soft spectral decline within pulses, these results imply that energy is injected at the onset of each pulse and that subsequent spectral and intensity evolution primarily track radiative losses from this initial injection.

We numerically investigate how optical absorption reshapes transmission channels in random media by studying a two-dimensional disordered waveguide. By computing the eigenchannels of the transmission and reflection matrices while tuning the absorption, we identify distinct transport regimes. In the weak-absorption regime, where the sample length is shorter than the diffusive absorption length, the maximal-transmission channel remains diffusive and coincides with the minimal-reflection channel. Its spectral bandwidth is set by the width of the underlying quasimodes. When absorption becomes strong, light transport through the maximal-transmission channel undergoes a sharp transition to ballistic-like propagation. The channel’s bandwidth increases with absorption, with the scaling dependent on the specific disorder realization. In this regime the minimal-reflection channel decouples from the maximal-transmission channel and is governed by absorption rather than diffusion. Counterintuitively, we find that in some samples the minimum reflection eigenvalue grows with increasing absorption. These results reveal that strong absorption can convert open channels in random media from diffusive to ballistic-like transport and qualitatively alter reflection behavior, with implications for controlling energy delivery, imaging through turbid systems, and the design of absorptive photonic structures.

We demonstrate a genuine route for the creation of a high-dimensional (d>3) chaotic attractor, bypassing any intermediate low-dimensional chaotic stage. The attractor emerges in a heteroclinic global bifurcation that produces an infinite family of unstable invariant tori. The mechanism is elucidated in a system of three coupled Lorenz oscillators, where continuation, numerical integration, and Lyapunov-spectrum computations reveal the onset of high-dimensional chaos and a Kaplan–Yorke dimension. We analyze the organizing heteroclinic network and its manifolds, establishing parameter dependence. This route serves as a prototype for high-dimensional chaotic behavior, analogous to the Lorenz model for low-dimensional chaos.

The origin of chromospheric Moreton waves and coronal EIT waves during solar eruptions remains debated. We investigate this problem with resistive magnetohydrodynamic simulations of a magnetic configuration containing a current-carrying flux rope that represents a filament. After a catastrophic loss of equilibrium, the flux rope undergoes rapid acceleration and expansion, driving a complex disturbance field comprised of velocity vortices in its wake and both fast- and slow-mode shocks ahead of it. The vortices form on either flank of the rope and propagate roughly horizontally away from their source region, while the shocks expand laterally around the rope’s flanks. In our simulations, the forward fast-mode shock can refract and reach the lower boundary representing the chromosphere, where its impact produces two reflected disturbances that propagate back into the corona. By contrast, the slow-mode shock and the vortical perturbations dissipate in the low corona and do not reach the lower boundary. The boundary interaction of the fast shock generates a rapid chromospheric disturbance consistent with a Moreton wave observed in Hα, whereas the coronal disturbance associated with the slow shock and the vortices manifests as a broader, slower EIT wave whose speed is approximately 40% of the Moreton wave speed. These results naturally explain the co-existence and differing kinematics of Moreton and EIT waves and their spatially distinct propagation paths. The simulations further clarify the observed association of type II radio bursts with fast-mode shocks, and the linkage of EIT waves to CME lateral expansion and flare-driven coronal restructuring. The framework provides a unified, dynamically consistent mechanism for wave generation during eruptive events and predicts diagnostic relationships among shock signatures, EUV fronts, and chromospheric wave observations.

Cloud computing promises cost reductions and productivity gains, yet adoption is hampered by the loss of user control over devices processing personal data. To address this skepticism, the SensorCloud project investigates techniques for trustworthy integration of sensors and actuators deployed in private environments with cloud applications. This paper offers an interdisciplinary overview of core social and technical research challenges and outlines design principles for cloud-based systems embedded in everyday life. We synthesize perspectives from software engineering, security and privacy, human–computer interaction, and social science to identify barriers and propose remedies across three domains: ease of development (modular reference architectures, declarative programming models, and interoperable APIs), security and privacy (end-to-end encryption, differential access controls, data minimization, and accountability mechanisms), and social dimensions (transparency, consent, explainability, and participatory design). We present prototype patterns and case studies in domestic scenarios, and distill evaluation criteria for trust, usability, and performance. When these challenges are systematically addressed, sensor-enabled cloud services become more attractive and acceptable to users who currently distrust cloud technologies.

We investigate the general massive two-loop self-mass diagram with four denominators and study the master integral via the differential equation it satisfies in the external invariant @xmath0. Exploiting this equation, we derive analytically the expansion of the master integral around @xmath1, including the coefficients up to a sufficiently high order to serve as precise starting data. We then assemble a coupled system comprising this equation and those of the master integrals of the general massive two-loop sunrise topology, and solve it numerically across the complex @xmath0 plane using adaptive Runge–Kutta integration. Particular attention is devoted to the behavior near physical thresholds and pseudo-thresholds: we develop a dedicated procedure to approach and cross branch points, control the choice of integration contours, and match to local asymptotic forms, thereby ensuring accuracy and stability. The method delivers high-precision values for the master integral in all kinematic regions, provides reliable error estimates, and can be straightforwardly extended to related multi-scale two-loop self-energy integrals. Consistency is checked against known limits and independent evaluations.

We present a theoretical study of the surface phase behavior of a two-dimensional hard-rod fluid confined between parallel hard lines. As a first step, we analyze the semi-infinite geometry where an isotropic fluid contacts a single hard line and find complete wetting by the columnar phase at the wall–isotropic interface, characterized by a diverging columnar film thickness as coexistence is approached. Extending to slit pore confinement, we show that capillary columnar ordering occurs via a first-order phase transition, with confinement shifting the transition relative to the bulk. At higher chemical potentials, the confined fluid exhibits a cascade of discrete layering transitions, which persist even for extremely narrow slits approaching the one-dimensional limit, underscoring the robustness of entropic packing-induced stratification under severe confinement. The theoretical framework is a density-functional theory based on the fundamental-measure functional, applied to hard rectangles within the restricted-orientation (Zwanzig) approximation, enabling accurate treatment of excluded-volume correlations and interfacial ordering. We discuss how these predictions can be tested in quasi-two-dimensional granular media composed of rod-like particles, where external vertical agitation and steric interactions allow exploration of dense stationary states that maximize configurational entropy. Our results suggest that the wetting, capillary ordering, and layering phenomena identified here should be observable in driven granular monolayers, providing a bridge between equilibrium hard-body fluids and non-equilibrium granular systems.

We present Submillimeter Array imaging of the central @xmath0 kpc of NGC 253 at 60 pc resolution in the J=2–1 transitions of CO, 13CO, C18O, and the 1.3 mm continuum. The molecular gas and dust are mainly in a 500 pc radius circumnuclear disk; its inner region hosts warm (T~40 K), high area-filling factor gas. We discover two prominent molecular shells/cavities within the disk, each ~100 pc in diameter, exhibiting large line widths of 80–100 km s^-1 and kinematic signatures consistent with ~50 km s^-1 expansion. Simple expanding-bubble models imply ages of ~0.5 Myr, kinetic energies of order @xmath1 J (~10^53 erg), and mean mechanical luminosities of @xmath2 W (~10^33–10^34 W) per shell, qualifying them as superbubbles. The required power can be supplied by a compact super star cluster of mass ~@xmath3 Msun, suggesting that such clusters are key building blocks of the nuclear starburst. Alternatively, a single hypernova could account for the energetics, and the inferred superbubble formation rate is comparable to plausible hypernova rates in the starburst. The circumnuclear molecular disk is therefore highly perturbed on ≲100 pc scales by clustered feedback and explosive events, in addition to the well-known global superwind. Our results provide direct evidence that feedback from young massive clusters and extreme stellar explosions shapes the molecular ISM on parsec-to-hundred parsec scales in NGC 253, with implications for star formation regulation and the driving of galactic winds in starbursts. These data set strong constraints on feedback timescales and efficiencies.

We build on a recently constructed renormalizable two-loop field theory for the quasi-static depinning of elastic manifolds in quenched disorder and explore further properties of the framework. We develop a systematic method to compute higher-order correlation functions of the displacement field and uncover drastic simplifications that lead to streamlined diagrammatic rules. As an application, we analyze the universal scaled width distribution. An expansion in @xmath0 shows that, to lowest orders, the scaled distribution coincides with that of a Gaussian theory with propagator @xmath1, where @xmath2 denotes the roughness exponent. We quantify the small deviations from the Gaussian result and express them through higher correlation functions, computed here under various boundary conditions. Beyond the width distribution, we define and evaluate additional universal quantities and perform a general stability analysis of the fixed point. This yields a correction-to-scaling exponent @xmath3, rather than @xmath4 as assumed in parts of the simulation literature, with implications for data collapse and finite-size scaling. We further provide a detailed treatment of the upper critical dimension, demonstrating that interface roughness grows as a power of a logarithm, rather than a pure power law. Our results supply simplified computational rules and refined predictions amenable to numerical and experimental tests.

We introduce a system of renewal equations on a graph to model the exploitation of a biological resource. Within this framework we formulate an optimal control problem acting on fluxes along edges and recruitment at nodes. We prove the existence of optimal controls and show that the target cost functional is a polynomial in the control variables. In several relevant configurations we refine this characterization, identifying the degrees and coefficients induced by the dynamics. Consequently, in some settings all optimal solutions are necessarily bang–bang, while in others the computational burden of optimization can be markedly reduced. The analysis connects conservation laws, renewal processes, and resource management, and suggests tractable design principles.

We develop a general asymptotic framework for the spectral stability of multi-parameter solitons in Hamiltonian systems. The analysis reduces stability to evaluating a hierarchy of determinants constructed from derivatives of the system’s invariants with respect to soliton parameters; the well-known Jacobian determinant appears as the first element of this series. Higher-order terms yield the first analytical criterion for oscillatory (Hamiltonian–Hopf) instability and predict a novel stationary instability regime. Successive asymptotic corrections provide eigenvalues with, in principle, arbitrary accuracy and expose the organizing role of codimension-2 bifurcations. The approach is model-independent and implementable across Hamiltonian PDEs, including nonlinear optics, fluid, and plasma contexts, thereby unifying and extending existing stability criteria.

We present an analysis of the shape, size, and spatial orientation of galaxy superclusters, modeled as triaxial ellipsoids derived from the distribution of their member clusters. Using a uniform catalog, we estimate semi-axes from inertia tensors and quantify flattening and triaxiality across richness classes. We find that superclusters are predominantly flattened, triaxial systems; no object in our sample is consistent with spherical geometry. Sizes correlate with richness: the median semi-major axis is 42 units for rich superclusters and 31 for poor systems, while the median semi-minor axis is 12 and 5, respectively. Orientation analyses show no preferred alignment. The axes of the fitted ellipsoids are distributed nearly randomly with respect to the line of sight, features of the large-scale structure, and the principal axes of neighboring superclusters. These results constrain models of structure formation and the anisotropic growth of the cosmic web.

We study the relative isoperimetric inequality inside open convex cones, which asserts that, for fixed volume, spherical sectors (intersections of the cone with balls centered at the vertex) minimize the perimeter relative to the cone. Observing that this principle follows from the anisotropic isoperimetric inequality, we adapt a variant of Gromov’s proof to obtain a sharp quantitative stability estimate. Specifically, we show that a natural Fraenkel-type asymmetry from spherical sectors is bounded by a constant times the square root of the relative isoperimetric deficit, with optimal exponent and constants depending only on the dimension and the aperture of the cone. Our argument overcomes the lack of translation invariance via a new cone-localized symmetrization.

We investigate curvature corrections to static, axisymmetric Dirac–Nambu–Goto membranes embedded in a spherically symmetric black hole spacetime in an arbitrary number of dimensions. In the effective brane action, the next-to-leading-order terms are quadratic in the brane thickness @xmath0, and we therefore develop a linear perturbation scheme in the small parameter @xmath1 around the thin-brane solutions. Our treatment is fully general: the perturbations are not confined to the Rindler zone and do not rely on near-critical approximations of the unperturbed system. An unexpected asymmetry emerges between subcritical (non–horizon-crossing) and supercritical (horizon-crossing) configurations. Specifically, for configurations in which the brane does not intersect the black hole horizon, the linearized perturbation equations fail to admit regular solutions near the axis when the number of the brane’s spacetime dimensions equals @xmath2, indicating a breakdown of the perturbative approach in this sector. This obstruction is absent for horizon-crossing solutions, which remain regular under the same curvature corrections. Consequently, for subcritical-type solutions near the axis with @xmath2, a different, non-perturbative methodology is required. Nevertheless, for @xmath3 and @xmath4—corresponding to a 1-dimensional string and a 2-dimensional sheet, respectively—the perturbative framework is well-posed, enabling a controlled analysis of topology-changing phase transitions. Using energy considerations for quasi-static evolutions from the equatorial configuration, we illustrate the phase transition in the case of a @xmath5 brane and find that small thickness perturbations do not alter the order of the transition: it remains first order, as in the vanishing-thickness limit. Our results delineate the validity of curvature-corrected effective actions for brane–black hole systems, identify the special role of low-dimensional branes, and point to the necessity of non-perturbative approaches in higher-dimensional cases.

We study electron dynamics in diverse media under magnetic fields using relativistic wave equations. For a nonmoving medium and a constant homogeneous magnetic field, we demonstrate quantization of electron energies and characterize bound-state spectra. We analyze eigenvectors and eigenvalues for a broad class of effective Hamiltonians, establishing conditions for self-adjointness and completeness. Exact solutions are obtained and applied to electron motion in rotating neutron-star environments, incorporating matter-induced potentials and magnetic-field effects. The resulting spectra and wavefunctions elucidate transport and stability regimes, offering quantitative tools for magnetospheres and dense-matter astrophysics. Keywords: relativistic wave equations, exact solutions, bound states.

Measurements of the Hubble constant H0 to distant galaxy clusters using the Sunyaev–Zeldovich (SZ) effect tend to be systematically low relative to values obtained by other methods. A common assumption in SZ/X-ray analyses is a spherical, isothermal β-model for the intracluster medium (ICM), despite the fact that cluster formation, mergers, and ongoing accretion render real systems neither spherical nor isothermal. We present a statistical assessment of temperature-induced bias in H0 determinations using a sample of 27 numerically simulated X-ray clusters drawn from a ΛCDM cosmology at z = 0.5. The simulations employ adaptive mesh refinement to self-consistently capture cluster assembly and gas dynamics under adiabatic conditions, achieving high spatial resolution (15.6 h−1 kpc) in the cores that dominate X-ray and SZ signals. For each cluster, we compute the angular diameter distance along three orthogonal lines of sight by fitting synthetic X-ray images and Compton-y maps to the standard spherical, isothermal β-model. We characterize the bias through the dimensionless ratio f = H0,SZ / H0,sim, finding a broad, skewed distribution with mean 0.89, median 0.83, and standard deviation 0.32. Declining radial temperature profiles systematically depress H0 estimates by approximately 10–20% when the ICM is forced to be isothermal in the analysis. The declining temperature trend in our adiabatic simulations is consistent with results that include radiative cooling and supernova feedback reported elsewhere, underscoring its physical robustness. Motivated by this, we introduce and apply a non-isothermal β-model that explicitly incorporates measured temperature gradients. For a refined subset of clusters with well-constrained temperature profiles, this model reduces the bias, improving f by about 9% toward the true value. We further examine the roles of morphology and gas clumping. Triaxiality, merger-induced substructure, and line-of-sight inhomogeneities add substantial scatter to f, contributing an uncertainty of roughly 30%. Our results demonstrate that the spherical, isothermal assumption is a principal source of the low H0 values inferred from SZ/X-ray methods, and that accounting for realistic temperature profiles and ICM substructure is essential for precision cosmology with galaxy clusters. Improved modeling and targeted selection of relaxed systems can mitigate both bias and scatter, enabling SZ-based measurements of H0 that are consistent with independent determinations.

We report the discovery of several energetic, highly dispersed radio bursts at 34 MHz with the Gauribidanur radio telescope. The bursts exhibit two canonical signatures of propagation through the ionized interstellar medium: frequency-dependent dispersive delays across the observing band and Faraday rotation of the plane of linear polarization. The measured dispersion measures span 1.4–3.6 pc cm^-3 and vary on minute-long timescales. By grouping bursts with consistent dispersion measure and polarization properties, and by considering the sky location and observing geometry, we identify the source as the radio-quiet gamma-ray pulsar Geminga. These detections provide direct evidence for occasional, sporadic radio emission from Geminga at very low radio frequencies. The rarity of the events, together with rapid DM variability that may originate in the intervening medium or within the pulsar magnetosphere, offers a natural explanation for previous nondetections in sensitive searches. We describe the observations and the burst search pipeline, present a detailed characterization of the burst temporal, spectral, and polarization properties, and outline multiple lines of evidence supporting the association with Geminga. We briefly discuss possible emission mechanisms and propagation effects that could produce bright, low-frequency bursts from an otherwise radio-quiet pulsar, and optimized strategies for future low-frequency pulsar searches.

We develop a nonrelativistic formalism for mechanical systems with internal degrees of freedom in a scalar potential Phi that depends on relative coordinates, time, speed, and accelerations. Within this framework we derive the general equations of motion and identify a generalized energy that becomes an integral of motion when Phi satisfies a definite differential constraint linking its explicit temporal and kinematic dependence. For a free mass point endowed with internal structure, we solve the dynamics in the center-of-inertia frame moving uniformly and obtain families of exact trajectories of the center of mass: helices and more intricate bounded paths winding around the inertial direction. This trembling motion (zitterbewegung) arises purely from classical coupling between translational and internal dynamics, showing a classical origin of zitterbewegung in the nonrelativistic regime. We further write down a general equation of motion for the spin vector with a transparent classical interpretation, establishing its precession under effective fields from the potential and inertial couplings. Applying the theory to the electron suggests a revised conception of electric charge, with the sign determined by the spin polarization, offering a unified classical picture of spin-charge correlation. Analytical conditions for stability and frequency are presented. PACS: 14.60.Cd, 45.20.D, 45.50.J. Keywords: classical mechanics, internal degrees of freedom, equations of motion, energy conservation, electron.

We extend the homogeneous model for the synchrotron emission from plerions to obtain more realistic surface brightness distributions across frequency. Abandoning uniform particle density, we assume particles are injected only near the pulsar and subsequently advected by MHD flow in a magnetic field with spatially uniform, time-variable intensity. Solving for the resulting transport and synchrotron losses, the model reproduces the integrated spectrum and radio surface brightness profile of the Crab Nebula, including the observed radial decline. At higher frequencies (mm–optical–X-ray), however, the predicted emitting region is too compact compared with observations, indicating that cross-field particle diffusion is required in addition to advection. We discuss diffusion needed and implications for turbulence, magnetic topology, and energy-dependent transport in plerions.

Many complex networks exhibit a percolation transition yielding a macroscopic component with universal features independent of microscopic rules and geometry. In contrast, we show the transition to full connectivity is dominated by boundary details. Decomposing bulk, surface, edge, and corner contributions, we identify an alternative universality governed by boundary codimension. Our framework distinguishes connectivity in domains with identical bulk behavior, predicts thresholds across dimensions, and is validated by simulations. The results enable strategies to promote or suppress full connectivity in diverse geometries.

Baryons, as composite bound states of quarks and gluons, exhibit a rich spectrum of excitations, prominently in the 1–2 GeV mass region for light-flavoured systems. Their properties can be probed with electromagnetic and strong interactions using beams of electrons, photons, and pions. Despite decades of effort, the fundamental degrees of freedom governing the excitation spectrum remain incompletely resolved, and the search for predicted yet unobserved resonances continues worldwide. Recent photo- and electroproduction measurements, enabled by polarization observables and high-statistics data, reveal evidence for new states and provide refined insights into the structure of established nucleon resonances. In parallel, global multi-channel amplitude analyses have re-evaluated legacy data, challenging earlier claims and reshaping the baryon spectrum. Breakthrough results have also emerged in the heavy-baryon sector: e+e− B factories and the Tevatron mapped numerous charm baryons, while first LHC results, especially from LHCb, demonstrate rapid progress on bottom-baryon spectroscopy, quantum numbers, and decay dynamics. We review these experimental advances and survey theoretical approaches, including lattice QCD, quark-model and diquark descriptions, unitary coupled-channel dynamics, Dyson–Schwinger and effective field theory frameworks, and ideas involving hybrids and dynamically generated states. We emphasize synergy between precise amplitudes and ab initio calculations, and outline future opportunities with upgraded facilities, new observables, and data-driven fits.

We investigate how substitutional disorder affects transport in heavy‐fermion systems by extending dynamical mean‐field theory for the periodic Anderson model to a coherent‐potential approximation for disordered, strongly correlated electrons. Using a binary alloy with arbitrary concentration x and two distinct local environments, we treat disorder both on the f-electron sites and on the ligand (conduction) sites. We compute spectral functions, self‐energies, resistivity as a function of temperature, and thermoelectric power. Disorder broadens the Kondo resonance, renormalizes hybridization, and produces coherence, yielding the characteristic concentration dependence and order of magnitude of transport in metallic heavy‐fermions and Kondo insulators. We find temperature‐ and concentration‐driven sign changes of the Seebeck coefficient arising from the competition between particle‐hole asymmetry and Kondo coherence. The framework captures the crossover from a heavy Fermi liquid to an incoherent scattering regime and gap filling in Kondo insulators.

We investigate a cosmological model in which a complex scalar field drives both primordial inflation and current cosmic acceleration. Decomposing the field into amplitude and phase, we identify the modulus as the inflaton and the phase as a quintessence field. Using dynamical-systems methods and numerical integrations, we uncover heteroclinic trajectories connecting an early-time unstable critical point to a late-time de Sitter attractor. The resulting evolution exhibits two distinct accelerated epochs without fine-tuned initial conditions. We discuss stability and parameter ranges, highlighting this framework as a unified and natural account of cosmic acceleration.

We analyze the Eckhaus instability of plane waves in the one-dimensional Complex Ginzburg–Landau Equation (CGLE) and describe the nonlinear dynamics that arise in the Eckhaus-unstable regime. Near the Eckhaus boundary, quasi-periodic coherent structures—modulated amplitude waves (MAWs)—emerge and organize the dynamics; their existence is delimited by saddle-node bifurcations. MAWs are characterized by an average phase gradient q and a spatial period L of the amplitude modulation. Using numerical bifurcation and continuation methods complemented by direct simulations and spectral (Floquet) stability analysis, we chart the existence and stability of MAWs across (q, L). We find that MAWs are stable for sufficiently large q and intermediate L, while for other parameter ranges they exhibit instabilities leading to splitting and to attractive interactions between successive amplitude extrema, which promote coarsening and collisions. Defects (phase singularities) form from perturbed plane waves when parameters lie above the saddle-node threshold of the corresponding MAWs, thereby providing a coherent-structure mechanism for defect nucleation. The breakdown of wound-up phase chaos—phase-chaotic states with nonzero average phase gradient—is thus directly related to these saddle-node bifurcations. We establish bounds for this breakdown: a lower bound given by the necessary presence of MAW saddle nodes and an upper bound given by the absence of MAW splitting instability; within these bounds wound-up phase chaos persists. These results unify coherent-structure and defect-based descriptions in the CGLE, clarify modulation scale selection, and quantify transitions from phase chaos to defect chaos in one dimension. Keywords: Complex Ginzburg–Landau equation; coherent structures; modulated amplitude waves; phase chaos. PACS: 05.45.Jn, 03.40.Kf, 05.45.-a.

We investigate cosmological implications of a classical nonlocal extension of gravity in which gravitational interactions retain memory of past events. In the Newtonian regime, this nonlocality reproduces the phenomenology of dark matter in galaxies and clusters. We extend the framework to an expanding cosmological background and derive a nonlocal cosmological Poisson equation with a time-dependent memory kernel. The nonlocal analog of the Zel’dovich approximation is formulated, yielding integro-differential evolution equations for the displacement field and density contrast. Linear analysis shows scale- and time-dependent enhancement of perturbation growth that can emulate cold dark matter, enabling structure formation without particle dark matter for admissible kernels consistent with galactic dynamics. Nonlinear consequences, including modified collapse thresholds and growth rates, are examined. We discuss observational signatures and constraints, and outline implications for fσ8, weak lensing, and future N-body simulations.

We investigate Raman-type laser excitation of a trapped atom as a platform to realize quantum analogs of nonlinear optical phenomena, including Kerr-like nonlinearities, parametric amplification, and multimode mixing. Interference between the atomic motional wave function and driving fields generates giant effective nonlinearities that restructure the motional phase space into zones with distinctly different dynamical behavior. This partitioning enables nonlinearly modified coherent displacements of the motional state, producing pronounced amplitude squeezing and interference fringes. We present a theoretical framework, identify regimes for strong effects, and discuss observable signatures and experimental pathways for engineering tailored quantum states.

We revisit the self-healing of optical beams and show that, contrary to prevailing views, any realistic beam exhibits partial self-reconstruction after obstruction; the Arago spot is a ubiquitous manifestation. By unifying scalar diffraction theory and modal decomposition, we derive a general, closed-form expression for the minimum reconstruction distance that applies to arbitrary beams, including Gaussian, Bessel, and vortex fields. The formula reveals the roles of angular spectrum, obstruction geometry, and coherence in governing recovery. We introduce a witness function that quantifies self-reconstruction capacity, calibrate it against simulations and experiments with controlled masks, and benchmark across beam classes. Our results reconcile disparate observations and provide practical guidelines for robust beam propagation in complex environments.

Recent advances in time‐resolved single‐electron detection enable precise measurements of full counting statistics in Coulomb‐blockaded nanostructures, demanding accurate theoretical tools. We develop a general framework for calculating zero‐frequency current cumulants of arbitrary order for transport through strongly interacting nanostructures. Our approach is based on a recursive evaluation of the cumulant generating function within generalized master equations augmented by counting fields, and it applies to systems with many internal states as well as to non‐Markovian dynamics. The method is stable and scalable, allowing efficient access to high‐order cumulants. We illustrate its versatility with three cases: bunching transport through a two‐level quantum dot, nano‐electromechanical transport subject to dynamical Franck–Condon blockade, and coherently coupled quantum dots embedded in a dissipative environment. In all cases the framework captures interaction‐induced super‐Poissonian statistics and characteristic patterns of high‐order cumulants, and it clarifies subtleties arising from non‐Markovian memory. Our results provide diagnostic signatures for mechanisms behind rare‐event fluctuations and offer a platform for comparison with full counting statistics measured in counting experiments.

We present a novel thermodynamic integration (TI) scheme to compute the crystal–liquid interfacial free energy, @xmath0, from molecular dynamics simulations. The method employs extremely short-ranged, impenetrable Gaussian flat walls to confine liquid and crystal phases, thereby eliminating hysteresis arising from translational drift of the crystal–liquid interface in previous TI approaches. We apply the scheme to the Lennard–Jones system and determine @xmath0 for the (100), (110), and (111) crystal orientations at three temperatures under coexistence conditions. For the (100) interface at temperature @xmath1 (reduced units), finite-size scaling within capillary wave theory is used to extrapolate @xmath0 to the thermodynamic limit, demonstrating that interfacial fluctuations are preserved and not suppressed by the walls or integration pathway. The TI protocol is numerically stable, reversible, and yields orientation-dependent interfacial free energies consistent with available benchmarks. Our results establish a robust, transferable framework for accurate interfacial free-energy calculations in molecular systems across diverse conditions.

We report the first secure detections of deuterium-bearing molecules beyond the Milky Way. Sensitive millimeter-wave spectroscopy toward three star-forming regions in the Large Magellanic Cloud (N113, N44BC, N159HW) reveals DCO+ emission, and DCN is detected toward N113. From line analyses we derive HCO+/DCO+ abundance ratios of 19 ± 3, 24 ± 4, and 67 ± 18 for N113, N44BC, and N159HW, respectively, and an HCN/DCN ratio of 23 ± 5 in N113. Comparison with gas-phase fractionation models indicates kinetic temperatures of about 20 K and an elemental D/H ratio of order a few 10^-5, comparable to values in Galactic molecular clouds. If the cloud temperatures are closer to 30 K, the observed fractionation would require elemental D/H values up to an order of magnitude larger. Because the deuterium abundance in the LMC provides a firm lower limit to the primordial D/H ratio, our measurements imply that the cosmic baryon density is insufficient to close the Universe, reinforcing the need for nonbaryonic dark matter.

We investigate the dependence of giant-arc production on cosmology using numerical simulations of galaxy clusters in standard CDM (SCDM; @xmath0, @xmath1), @xmath2CDM with reduced small-scale power, open CDM (OCDM; @xmath3, @xmath1), and spatially flat, low-density CDM (@xmath4CDM; @xmath3, @xmath5). All models are normalized to the local abundance of rich clusters. We perform ray-tracing through simulated cluster mass distributions to compute lensing cross-sections and optical depths for arcs with length-to-width ratio ≥ @xmath6. We find pronounced cosmology dependence: OCDM yields the largest optical depth; @xmath4CDM is lower by about one order of magnitude, and S/@xmath2CDM lower by about two orders. These differences arise from earlier cluster formation and higher concentrations in OCDM and from the nonlinearity of strong lensing with central surface mass density. The predicted arc redshift distribution peaks at intermediate source redshifts and is consistently higher in OCDM. Comparing to observed giant-arc abundances, only OCDM reproduces the data, whereas @xmath4CDM and S/@xmath2CDM underpredict arcs by orders of magnitude. The results are robust to variations in source redshift distribution and cluster orientation assumptions. Arc statistics thus provide sensitive constraints on cosmology and cluster assembly.

We present a comprehensive comparison between single parton scattering (SPS) and double parton scattering (DPS) mechanisms in the production of @xmath0 and in @xmath1 meson correlations. The SPS contribution is calculated in the collinear factorization framework using exact tree-level matrix elements for the @xmath2 and @xmath3 subprocesses. We find that the gluon–gluon channel dominates, yielding a cross section roughly 50 times larger than the quark–antiquark annihilation contribution. The new exact results are confronted with earlier predictions obtained with an approximate high-energy matrix element for @xmath2. The exact treatment leads to an enhancement primarily at small invariant masses and for small rapidity separations between two @xmath4 quarks (or two @xmath5 antiquarks), while differences diminish in other kinematic regions. We analyze rapidity correlations of two @xmath4 (or two @xmath5) for both SPS and DPS, highlighting their distinct topologies. Finally, we compare our predictions for @xmath1–@xmath1 observables with recent LHCb measurements, including single-meson invariant mass spectra, meson–meson rapidity separation, and dimeson invariant mass distributions. While the predicted shapes are in good agreement with the data, a deficit in overall strength remains. Our results reinforce the conclusion that DPS provides the dominant contribution to events with double charm production in the studied kinematics.

We develop mean-field kinetic equations for a lattice-gas model of a binary alloy with vacancies (ABV) in which diffusion proceeds via a vacancy mechanism. The framework is applied to phase separation in finite portions of an unstable mixture embedded in a stable vapor. Owing to the enhanced mobility of surface atoms, the most unstable modes of spinodal decomposition are localized at the vapor–mixture boundary. Numerical simulations reveal checkerboard-like ordering at the surface and surface-directed spinodal waves. A linear stability analysis yields growth rates for bulk and surface modes and delineates the parameter regimes controlling interfacial instabilities. From these results, we deduce explicit relations between interaction strengths, mobilities, and the emergent structure and length scale of surface patterns. The thickness of the interfacial patterns is shown to be set by concentration fluctuations in the initial state, linking early-time noise to late-stage morphology.

We present a new numerical code that derives spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for arbitrary three-dimensional stellar and gaseous configurations in dusty starburst galaxies. The method couples N-body/hydrodynamic simulations with a ray-tracing radiative transfer scheme that self-consistently treats extinction, scattering, and thermal re-emission by dust, enabling simultaneous dynamical and photometric evolution. Applied to major merger simulations, the code reproduces the emergence of ultra-luminous infrared galaxies as strong internal dust extinction suppresses UV/optical light and reradiates energy into the far-infrared, yielding L_IR >= 10^12 L_sun and SED features consistent with observations. We explore how geometry, star formation rate, and gas fraction regulate the IR peak and attenuation curves across redshift. Strengths include flexible geometry, physical coupling to dynamics, and time-resolved SEDs; limitations involve resolution dependence, dust composition/opacity assumptions, computational expense, and omission of AGN in the current release.

Simultaneous observations of air showers with more than two imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes overconstrain shower geometry, enabling robust reconstruction when image quality is optimally combined. We discuss and implement algorithms that weight image parameters by their estimated uncertainties, testing them on Mkn 501 data taken with the HEGRA IACT system. The methods yield event-by-event estimates of reconstruction accuracy, permitting selection of higher-quality subsamples for precision measurements. We compare performance across algorithms, assess stability against systematics, and demonstrate improved angular reconstruction and consistency with simulations, enhancing sensitivity and reducing biases in gamma-ray analyses.

We experimentally demonstrate acoustic coupling between two air bubbles immersed in water. The pair is driven by a controlled acoustic field, and the resulting pressure response is measured. Observations confirm the two theoretically predicted eigenmodes, symmetric and antisymmetric, and their resonance frequencies vary with bubble separation. Measured frequencies agree with coupled-oscillator theory within experimental uncertainty, providing a robust benchmark for bubble interactions and guiding acoustofluidic applications.

We present exact analytical results for a one-dimensional hard-sphere fluid confined between two attractive boundaries and in osmotic equilibrium with a bulk reservoir. Using the grand-canonical partition function of an extended Tonks gas, we derive closed-form expressions for the free energy and the effective, particle-mediated interaction potential between the boundaries. The potential displays two distinct minima: a contact minimum arising from depletion and a second minimum at separations near one particle diameter generated by a single adsorbed particle that bridges the boundaries. For sufficiently large boundary binding energies, the bridging minimum becomes the global minimum, yielding strong adhesion. The corresponding effective adhesion energy exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on reservoir concentration and is maximal at intermediate particle concentrations, reflecting the competition between depletion, binding, and steric crowding. We further analyze a two-dimensional lattice of independent one-dimensional columns as a discrete approximation to a three-dimensional confined gas, showing that the qualitative features persist. Our exact results provide transparent design rules for tuning surface adhesion via particle size, binding affinity, and concentration, with implications for colloidal stabilization, nanoparticle-mediated cohesion, and membrane adhesion.

We demonstrate the correspondence between quantum-mechanical and quantum field-theoretical descriptions of Mössbauer neutrino oscillations. In the field-theoretical approach, we compute the combined rate for neutrino emission, propagation, and detection by treating the neutrino as an internal line of a tree-level Feynman diagram. Homogeneous line broadening from fluctuating electromagnetic fields in the source and detector crystals is incorporated explicitly, and we show that the resulting expression coincides with the formula previously derived for inhomogeneous broadening. We then develop a quantum-mechanical description in which the neutrino state is modeled as a superposition of Lorentz-shaped wave packets with suitably chosen central energies and widths. Within this framework, the oscillation phase, coherence damping, and resonance enhancement terms of the field-theoretical result are reproduced, establishing the equivalence of the two descriptions. However, the emission rate and detection cross section, including localization effects and Lamb–Mössbauer factors, are not predicted intrinsically by quantum mechanics and must be inserted phenomenologically. Our analysis delineates the domain of validity of each approach and informs the interpretation and design of Mössbauer neutrino experiments.

We investigate the Shannon and Rényi entropies of the ground-state wavefunction in pure and random quantum Ising chains using the self-dual Fernandez–Pacheco real-space renormalization. Focusing on the leading extensive term, we characterize its critical behavior at the quantum phase transition. In the pure chain, the derivative of the entropy density with respect to the control parameter exhibits a logarithmic divergence, signaling a conventional critical singularity. In the random chain, the derivative displays a cusp, reflecting infinite-randomness physics. The cusp singularity is corroborated independently via the strong-disorder renormalization group. Our results clarify universal features of wavefunction statistics and inform entropy-based probes of quantum criticality.

Nitrogen–vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are widely regarded as promising, indefinitely stable single-photon sources, yet NVs hosted in nanodiamonds exhibit a large spread in fluorescence decay rates that is commonly attributed to strong nanophotonic mode-density variations at near-unity quantum efficiency. Here we experimentally quantify the brightness, radiative decay rate, nonradiative decay rate, and quantum efficiency of individual NV centers in diamond nanocrystals and test this prevailing interpretation. For NV centers in 25 nm nanocrystals, we modulate the local density of optical states (LDOS) at a dielectric interface by varying the refractive index of surrounding liquids. Despite substantial LDOS changes, the measured decay rates are essentially insensitive, indicating that LDOS does not govern the observed rate dispersion. These measurements instead imply widely distributed, intrinsically low quantum efficiencies, spanning approximately 0%–20% in 25 nm nanocrystals. In contrast, for single NV centers in larger 100 nm nanocrystals, we reversibly tune the LDOS by nanomechanically approaching a metallic mirror and observe clear, systematic decay-rate modulation. Using this scanning mirror method as an absolute calibration of LDOS, we extract quantum efficiencies for individual NVs and find a broad distribution across nominally identical nanocrystals, ranging from about 10% to 90%. Our results challenge the assumption of near-unity quantum efficiency for NVs in nanodiamonds and identify nonradiative pathways as a dominant source of variability. These findings have direct implications for integrating NV centers into hybrid photonic structures and cavity quantum electrodynamics experiments, highlighting the need for pre-selection and detailed screening of individual nanocrystals to ensure predictable performance.

We study ordered equilibrium structures of patchy colloids with four surface patches arranged tetrahedrally. Using global optimization grounded in evolutionary algorithms, we generate a comprehensive set of candidate lattices and retain both the globally optimal structures and selected local minima on the enthalpy landscape. We then apply constant-pressure, constant-temperature Monte Carlo simulations to assess thermodynamic properties along representative isobars and isotherms, determine ranges of mechanical and thermodynamic stability, and map structural transitions. The analysis quantifies the competing roles of lattice energy, vibrational entropy, and packing efficiency, revealing regime-dependent stabilization: energetically favored open networks at low temperature, entropy-assisted arrangements at intermediate conditions, and dense packings under elevated pressure. Our results provide a quantitative framework linking patch geometry to equilibrium crystal structures and furnish benchmarks for designing tetrahedrally functionalized colloids, relevant for experimental realization efforts.

We present a two-epoch X-ray morphological and spectroscopic study of the high-velocity pulsar B2224+65 and its apparent jet-like features, in the context of the ram-pressure confined pulsar wind nebula known as the Guitar Nebula. The dominant X-ray structure, which exhibits a substantial directional offset from the nebular axis, shows clear temporal evolution: it is broader in apparent width and displays evidence for spectral hardening in the second epoch relative to the first, significant at the 95 percent confidence level. Measuring the sharp leading edge of this feature, we find a proper motion consistent with that of the pulsar, approximately 180 mas yr−1, supporting a physical association. Combining the two epochs also reveals a counter-feature aligned with the main structure, though markedly fainter and shorter. We investigate spatially resolved spectral behavior along both the major and minor axes of the principal feature. While indications of spectral gradients are present, they are only marginally detected in the available data; notably, there is weak evidence for softening counter to the direction of proper motion. We discuss interpretive frameworks in which diffuse energetic particles are guided by an organized ambient magnetic field, as well as a ballistic jet scenario emanating from the pulsar. The former may struggle to reproduce the observed inter-epoch spectral changes and the gradient along the major axis, whereas the latter faces challenges in explaining the remarkable linearity and stability of the feature. Given the low counting statistics across both epochs, definitive discrimination between these scenarios is currently not possible. We outline observational tests and higher-sensitivity, multi-epoch X-ray and radio measurements that could resolve the nature of these enigmatic features.

We analyze the variability in accretion-related emission lines for 40 classical T Tauri stars to probe the extent of accretion variations in young stellar objects. Our analysis is based on multi-epoch, high-resolution spectra of stars in Taurus–Auriga and Chamaeleon I, with typically four epochs per target spanning hours to months. As proxies for the accretion rate, we use the Hα 10% width and the Ca II 8662 Å line flux. While these two indicators are correlated, their variability amplitudes are not. When converted to accretion rates, the Ca II fluxes imply typical changes of 0.35 dex, with 32% of objects exceeding 0.5 dex, whereas the Hα 10% widths suggest larger changes of 0.65 dex, with 66% exceeding 0.5 dex. We infer that line fluxes provide a more robust quantitative measure of accretion variability than the Hα width, and that intrinsic accretion-rate changes do not exceed 0.5 dex on timescales of days to months. The variability amplitude saturates after a few days, indicating that stellar rotation and the visibility of accretion structures are the dominant drivers. We observe a decline of inferred accretion rates toward later spectral types, consistent with the positive correlation between stellar mass and accretion rate. The distribution shows a clear gap between accretors and non-accretors, pointing to a rapid shutdown of accretion. Finally, the four orders of magnitude scatter in the accretion rate versus stellar mass relation is explained by object-to-object differences rather than intrinsic variability within individual sources.

We investigate the feasibility of detecting extrasolar planets in the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) via pixel-lensing observations. Using a Monte Carlo approach, we draw physical parameters of binary lens systems composed of a host star and a planetary companion, and compute the corresponding pixel-lensing light curves, explicitly incorporating finite-source effects. The latter are crucial in the M31 regime because microlensed sources are predominantly giant stars, whose extended disks smooth and broaden planetary perturbations. Planetary signals are identified by selecting light curves that exhibit statistically significant deviations from the standard Paczyński shape expected for single-lens events. We find that the characteristic duration of planetary anomalies increases with source size, reaching timescales of order 3–4 days for the largest giants. This implies that a modest observational cadence—on the order of a few exposures per day, subject to the required photometric precision—can be sufficient to reveal planetary companions. While the mean planet mass in the subset of selected events is comparatively high, we show that even lower-mass planets can imprint detectable signatures in data obtained with large telescopes, particularly when finite-source smoothing does not completely erase caustic features. Nonetheless, the overall probability of detecting planetary anomalies in pixel-lensing light curves remains low, at most a few percent among events that are themselves detectable, indicating that sizeable samples and sustained monitoring campaigns are necessary to secure robust detections of exoplanets in M31. Finally, our analysis supports the interpretation that the anomaly observed in the candidate event PA-99-N2 toward M31 is consistent with the presence of a planetary (or low-mass) companion orbiting the lens star, reinforcing the potential of pixel lensing for extragalactic exoplanet studies.

We introduce a method that randomly rearranges the @xmath0 and @xmath1 components of produced particles on the circumference of an ellipse with half major and minor axes @xmath2 and @xmath3. Heavy quarkonium provides a sensitive probe of strong‐interaction dynamics in QCD. We investigate the thermodynamic properties of an S=1 tetrameric Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain with an alternating AF–AF–AF–F coupling pattern using the transfer-matrix renormalization group method in conjunction with a Jordan–Wigner fermion mapping. Notably, in the Luttinger liquid phase the magnetization shows a low-temperature crossover behavior that falls within the same universality class as that observed in the S=1 Haldane chain. Within the plateau regime, thermodynamic quantities exhibit marked changes at a characteristic field, which we attribute to the crossing of two distinct excitation spectra. The fermionic description reveals four branches associated with fermion and hole excitations, providing a unified microscopic origin for the observed thermodynamic features. Our results elucidate how alternating couplings and spectral structure shape finite-temperature properties, offering concrete predictions for future experimental and numerical studies of quasi-one-dimensional quantum magnets.

We previously proposed a non-Newtonian, phenomenological interaction between exotic dark matter and baryons—the gravitational suppression (GraS) scheme—that accurately reproduces the inner kinematics of gas-rich, low-surface-brightness galaxies. We derive GraS predictions for stellar motions in dwarf spheroidal galaxies and for vertical kinematics in the solar neighborhood, and confront them with quality data under realistic dark-matter density profiles. Relative to Newtonian dynamics with the same halos, GraS predicts measurable departures in line-of-sight dispersion profiles and vertical forces. We discuss observational diagnostics and future tests capable of discriminating GraS from Newtonian gravity.

Since Cho and Kim (2005) established that the competition graph of a doubly partial order is an interval graph, it is natural to ask whether analogous interval properties persist for other competition-based structures. We then give a complete characterization of those doubly partial orders whose competition hypergraphs are interval, via a finite family of forbidden subhypergraphs and an equivalent structural condition on the underlying order. Middleboxes are special network devices that provide security and performance functions but introduce routing challenges in Software-Defined Networking (SDN). Resource constraints in switches (TCAM/memory) and middleboxes (processing capacity), together with traversal constraints requiring flows to visit specific services in order, complicate traffic engineering. Our algorithm constructs resource- and traversal-aware MPTPTs that aggregate flows toward required service endpoints, minimizing per-switch rule footprint while respecting middlebox processing limits. We prove that the approach guarantees optimal throughput under given constraints and characterize its low computational complexity. Simulations on diverse network topologies demonstrate substantial reductions in routing rules and stable throughput, even under dynamic demand and failures. The lightweight control makes it suitable for real-time operation. Keywords: Software-Defined Networking, middlebox, multipoint-to-point tree, traffic engineering, routing.

NGC 1672 is a nearby barred spiral galaxy exhibiting vigorous circumnuclear star formation and has been proposed to host a Seyfert 2 nucleus. We present new X-ray observations that place quantitative constraints on both the starburst and putative active galactic nucleus components. Two high-resolution imaging exposures obtained in 1992 and 1997 are used to assess long-term variability of known X-ray sources and to search for new emission sites. We detect large-amplitude variability from X-3, an off-nuclear source located near the end of the galactic bar, with a peak observed 0.2–2.0 keV luminosity indicative of a luminous compact object. The variability pattern and luminosity suggest X-3 is most likely a luminous X-ray binary or a young supernova remnant. In contrast, we do not detect significant variability from the nuclear source X-1 or from the bright off-nuclear source X-2 over the same baseline. Our imaging analysis also reveals two previously unreported off-nuclear sources, one spatially associated with a bright optical region along a spiral arm, and diffuse X-ray emission on kiloparsec scales distributed across a substantial fraction of the disk, consistent with hot gas linked to widespread star formation. To probe the hard X-ray properties, we analyze complementary data obtained in 1995. While X-1 is the dominant soft X-ray source in NGC 1672, the majority of the 2–10 keV and 5–10 keV flux is spatially coincident with X-3, which exhibits an apparent 0.2–8 keV luminosity characteristic of powerful off-nuclear sources. Joint spectral fitting with a nonthermal power-law component plus a Raymond–Smith thermal plasma yields an acceptable description of the full-band spectra, supporting a composite origin involving both compact and diffuse emission. We find no evidence for a luminous, heavily absorbed nuclear X-ray source. If NGC 1672 harbors a Seyfert 2 nucleus, it must be obscured by Compton-thick material with a column density high enough to suppress direct continuum emission below 10 keV, implying only scattered or reflected components would be detectable in the observed band. These results demonstrate that the galaxy’s X-ray output is dominated by starburst-related processes, with any active nucleus either intrinsically weak or buried behind extreme obscuration.

Bolometers are among the most promising detectors for rare event searches, such as neutrinoless double beta decay (0νββ) and dark matter interactions, owing to their excellent energy resolution, high detection efficiency, and the broad availability of absorber materials. A central challenge for these experiments is event-by-event particle identification to suppress backgrounds, which has traditionally required a double read-out of heat and scintillation light or heat and ionization. While effective, this approach increases complexity and integration effort for large cryogenic arrays like CUORE and EURECA. We investigate an alternative route: recognizing the interacting particle through the shape of the thermal pulse in scintillating macro-bolometers. Detailed pulse-shape analyses in purely thermal detectors have not yielded useful discrimination, but we show that scintillating bolometers with absorber masses of 10–500 g exhibit clear, systematic differences between electron/gamma and alpha-induced events. As a case study, we report results from a CaMoO4 crystal operated as a bolometer, where distinct variations in rise time and decay components enable robust separation of alpha interactions from beta/gamma events, the dominant background for 0νββ searches. We present an interpretation based on energy partition between the phonon and scintillation channels and the material-dependent scintillation kinetics, which modulate the timing of phonon production and thus the thermal pulse morphology. This single-channel pulse-shape discrimination reduces the need for auxiliary light or ionization sensors, offering a pathway to simplify detector assembly while preserving background rejection capabilities. The approach has broad relevance to next-generation bolometric arrays targeting ultra-low background conditions in rare event physics. PACS numbers: 23.40.B, 95.35.+d, 07.57.K, 29.40.M, 66.70.-f

We further construct pseudo-Anosov diffeomorphisms on these surfaces whose contracting foliations have zero SAF invariant, illustrating the phenomenon in the hyperbolic mapping class context. An appendix establishes containment criteria for trigonometric fields arising from polygonal angles.

We trace these differences to strong directionally induced correlations and mass conservation constraints inherent in the model, which reshape cluster geometry and correlation lengths. We present a quantum electrodynamical analysis of emission from a radiating source embedded in a photonic lattice, treating the lattice and surrounding free space as a coupled system. Both the emitter and the electromagnetic field are quantized, and modal coupling at the lattice–vacuum interface is included. Calculated spectra reveal departures from the blackbody distribution: intracavity emission is suppressed at spectral gaps and enhanced near resonant passbands, reflecting the lattice density of states. Under rapid population relaxation, where populations in the lattice and an equivalent blackbody share the same equilibrium statistics, spectral enhancement does not translate into external intensities exceeding the blackbody at a given frequency. In contrast, for slow relaxation, nonequilibrium populations develop within the lattice, allowing output intensities to surpass blackbody levels, even for identically pumped structures, highlighting kinetics as a design lever.

We address two long-standing bottlenecks in solution growth of intermetallic single crystals: (i) locating a melt composition that exposes the primary solidification surface of the desired phase in the often unknown equilibrium alloy phase diagram, and (ii) selecting crucible materials that withstand corrosive high-temperature melts. By comparing realistic thermodynamic simulations with experimentally measured differential thermal analysis (DTA) curves, we extract actionable guidance without requiring full phase-diagram determination. We show that complex DTA signatures can be interpreted to choose starting compositions and to design heat-treatment schedules (including cooling rates and isothermal holds) that promote selective nucleation and growth of the target phase. The same DTA data reveal melt-container reactions, enabling rapid screening and identification of compatible crucible materials. We validate the approach on three systems, Tb-Al, Pr-Ni-Si, and Y-Mn-Al, obtaining single-crystalline samples reproducibly. The methodology improves efficiency, reduces trial-and-error, and increases crystal size and phase purity. These results illustrate DTA-guided solution growth as a versatile route for rare-earth intermetallics and related compounds, offering a practical framework to navigate complex multicomponent solidification landscapes. The protocol is general and readily transferable to new alloy families globally.

We present simultaneous observations of H2O maser emission (22 GHz) and 1.3 cm radio continuum acquired with the Australia Telescope Compact Array toward two sources catalogued as planetary nebula (PN) candidates, IRAS 16333-4807 and IRAS 12405-6219, for which single-dish H2O masers have been previously reported. Our aim was to unambiguously confirm the spatial association of the masers with the putative ionized nebulae. We detect and map H2O maser components in both fields. In IRAS 16333-4807, the maser emission is spatially coincident, within the astrometric uncertainties, with the compact radio continuum source that traces the ionized gas, demonstrating that the masers originate in the circumstellar environment of a young PN. Together with its clearly bipolar morphology, these properties confirm IRAS 16333-4807 as the fifth known H2O maser–emitting PN and reinforce the emerging picture that water masers can persist into a short-lived phase at the onset of ionization in bipolar PNe, likely associated with collimated outflows and nebular shaping. In contrast, in IRAS 12405-6219 the H2O maser spots are not associated with the continuum peak; combined with the radio and infrared characteristics, this indicates that the object is a compact H II region rather than a PN. These results highlight the diagnostic power of high-resolution maser–continuum imaging to discriminate between very young PNe and compact H II regions.

Accurate estimation of land surface temperature (LST) from spaceborne thermal infrared observations is critical for climate, hydrological, and ecological applications.
