Quantum graphity is a background-independent model in which macroscopic locality, spatial geometry, and matter emerge from dynamics on graphs with @xmath0 vertices. States are encoded as dynamical adjacency configurations, and the Hamiltonian favors different connectivity regimes across energy scales. At high energy, the graph is highly connected and the physics is invariant under the full symmetric group acting on vertices, reflecting permutation symmetry. We present evidence for a low-energy phase in which permutation symmetry is spontaneously broken and the graph becomes ordered, low-dimensional, and local. A free-energy analysis of the dominant interaction terms shows that this phase is thermodynamically stable against local perturbations. In the ground state, string-net condensation à la Levin and Wen yields an emergent @xmath1 gauge theory living on the effective lattice. We reformulate the model in graph-theoretic language, identify appropriate order parameters, and compare its dynamics to common graph processes, including random rewiring, edge percolation, and annealing, to clarify its phase structure and universality.

Street gangs increasingly use Twitter to intimidate rivals, broadcast outrageous images and statements, and publicize recent illegal activities. These posts may offer timely signals for law enforcement to identify ongoing crimes and anticipate future ones, but exploiting them requires reliably locating gang member profiles amid a population exceeding 320 million users. This paper addresses the challenge of automatically finding gang members on Twitter. We outline a principled pipeline to curate one of the largest sets of verifiable gang-affiliated profiles to date, combining multi-source validation and careful annotation. A comparative review of these profiles reveals consistent differences in linguistic style, hashtags, visual content, external YouTube links, and emoji usage relative to the broader Twitter population. We operationalize these insights into multimodal features and train a suite of supervised classifiers under severe class imbalance, using stratified cross-validation and calibration to control false alarms. Our models achieve promising F1 performance with a low false positive rate, demonstrating utility for prioritization. We discuss robustness, ethical safeguards, and limitations, and release guidance to support reproducible social media analysis of gang activity.

Time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) is commonly implemented with the adiabatic local-density approximation (ALDA) for the dynamical exchange-correlation (xc) potential. We analyze an exact, nonadiabatic extension of the ground-state LDA to time-dependent situations, which endows the xc potential with memory and renders the many-electron dynamics intrinsically dissipative. To elucidate the physical origin and limits of this behavior, we investigate two interacting electrons confined to a finite two-dimensional quantum strip. TDDFT simulations within ALDA and with the nonadiabatic, memory-dependent functional are benchmarked against numerically exact solutions of the two-electron time-dependent Schrodinger equation. We demonstrate explicitly how apparent dissipation in the one-body description emerges from multiple particle-hole excitations in the exact dynamics. While the nonadiabatic extension systematically fails for finite systems, it becomes asymptotically exact in the thermodynamic limit, thereby clarifying when memory-dependent local approximations can capture many-body relaxation.

We investigate the dynamical behavior of two-gene regulatory modules with two or three connections by comparing continuous dynamics of mRNA and protein concentrations to a Boolean model of gene activity. Using a generalized analytical framework, we unify multiple continuous formulations and regulatory functions to derive conditions for stable oscillations. Oscillatory regimes depend on relative time scales of transcription, translation, and degradation, the degree of cooperativity in regulation, and the signs and topology of interactions. We show that Boolean oscillations do not necessarily imply continuous oscillations, and vice versa, and provide criteria and simulations. These results guide design and interpretation of gene circuits.

We present Jordan-Brans-Dicke and general scalar-tensor gravity in extra dimensions and analyze non-topological boson configurations (Q-stars) in asymptotically flat and anti-de Sitter spacetimes. Solving the coupled scalar, matter, and metric equations in D = 4-7 dimensions with appropriate boundary conditions, we obtain families of stable stars and quantify their dependence on the scalar-tensor coupling and background curvature. Relative to general relativity, equilibrium parameters (mass, radius, particle number, and binding energy) shift by a few percent, with trends controlled by dimensionality and the AdS scale. Implications for compact-object phenomenology and constraints on scalar-tensor theories are discussed in detail.

We present a detailed analysis of GRB 041006, detected by HETE-2 at 12:18:08 UT on 06 October 2004, which exhibits a pronounced soft X-ray precursor preceding the main prompt emission and a soft X-ray tail persisting after the primary peak. The multi-band light curves reveal strong energy-dependent morphology: at higher energies, the emission is structured into several sharp peaks, whereas at lower energies a single, broader bump dominates. This behavior suggests a composite origin comprising multiple physical components with distinct energetics and variability timescales. To investigate this structure, we performed time-resolved spectroscopy and successfully decomposed the emission into several components. These components fall into two classes. The first class displays an exponential decay in flux with a characteristic timescale shorter than about 30 seconds, and its spectrum is well described by a broken power-law function. This behavior is consistent with the internal-shock paradigm commonly invoked for prompt GRB emission, and it accounts for the rapidly variable, multi-peaked high-energy light curve. The second class maintains an almost steady flux on timescales longer than about 60 seconds, exhibits very soft emission, and varies more slowly. Its spectrum can be fitted either by a broken power law or by a blackbody, indicating a quasi-thermal origin. We interpret this soft component as arising from a relatively wide, lower-velocity jet or from the fireball photosphere. Assuming a thermal interpretation for the soft component, the inferred initial radiation radius is comparable to that of a blue supergiant, and the implied expansion velocity in the source frame is on the order of kilometers per second, consistent with an extended stellar envelope. Our results highlight the multi-component nature of GRB 041006, demonstrate that distinct emission mechanisms dominate different energy bands and phases, and support scenarios in which internal shocks produce the prompt, hard variability while a broader jet sheath or photospheric emission contributes the soft precursor and tail.

We present spectroscopic and imaging follow-up of candidate cataclysmic variables (CVs) identified by the Catalina Real Time Survey (CRTS), which has discovered over 500 CV candidates, the majority previously unknown. We obtained spectra for 36 of the brighter objects; nearly all exhibit features characteristic of CVs in quiescence (minimum light), including Balmer emission and, in several cases, weak signatures of late-type secondaries. One target is instead consistent with a flare star, and another shows a CV-like spectrum while residing at the center of a compact nebulosity, suggesting an intriguing local environment. Orbital periods were measured for eight systems, primarily through time-resolved spectroscopy, and distances were estimated for two based on the spectral properties of their secondary stars. We also secured direct imaging for an overlapping sample of 37 objects, providing calibrated magnitudes and colors that further support their classification and help constrain system parameters. Most newly measured periods lie shortward of the 2–3 hour period gap, reinforcing the prevalence of short-period dwarf novae in transient-selected samples. Cross-identifications with external catalogs, including the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, indicate that a substantial population of CVs remains uncatalogued. By contrasting the CRTS sample with previously known CVs that CRTS did not recover, we find that CRTS preferentially selects systems with large outburst amplitudes, and hence shorter orbital periods—a bias we attribute to the survey cadence. These results highlight both the discovery power and selection effects of time-domain surveys for mapping the Galactic CV population.

We introduce the concept of stationary metastable states (SMS) and a systematic prescription to study them using a restricted partition function formalism. The key step is to define a continuous entropy function even for finite systems, a common but often implicit practice, in order to permit differentiation and establish thermodynamic consistency. Within this framework, the SMS free energy is shown to exist and remain stable down to absolute zero. We formalize a “reality condition” stating that the entropy of any set of coupled degrees of freedom must be nonnegative; the entropy crisis, while not jeopardizing stability, is precisely identified as a violation of this condition. Using general thermodynamic arguments, we rigorously uncover a universal mechanism underlying the entropy crisis in SMS. The free energy of any SMS must coincide with the equilibrium crystal free energy at two distinct temperatures. Stability then requires that the SMS free energy possess a maximum at an intermediate but strictly positive temperature, at which the energy attains a specific value. The continuation of the SMS branch below a critical temperature leads to negative entropy, signaling the crisis; the physically admissible description must therefore replace this unphysical branch by an ideal glass with constant energy and vanishing entropy. The temperature at which this replacement occurs is identified as the Kauzmann temperature. The ideal glass energy is higher than the crystal energy at absolute zero, consistent with the empirical observation that the extrapolated energy of real glasses at zero temperature exceeds that of their crystalline counterparts. We validate these general predictions through two exact calculations, one of which goes beyond mean-field theory. These results demonstrate that the notion of SMS is both nonvacuous and not an artifact of mean-field analysis, and they reveal that certain widely held expectations cannot be substantiated. Our formalism provides a coherent thermodynamic foundation for metastable states and the ideal glass, clarifying the origin of the entropy crisis and its resolution.

We investigate the hypothesis that the tension between predicted and observed WW and ZZ production cross sections at the LHC arises from an overlooked contribution of the double Drell-Yan process (DDYP), i.e., two concurrent quark-antiquark annihilations in a single proton-proton collision. Using a previously proposed, simple DDYP model, with no free parameters beyond standard inputs, we evaluate its impact on dilepton and four-lepton final states. When added to the conventional single-parton calculations, the DDYP component yields a satisfactory, parameter-free description of the dilepton invariant-mass spectrum in jet-vetoed WW->l nu l nu events and of the four-lepton mass spectrum in ZZ->4l events, removing the need to invoke a Higgs-boson contribution to reproduce data. We delineate an experimental program to validate or falsify this scenario, based on: jet-bin systematics; flavor, charge, rapidity-gap and azimuthal correlations between the two lepton pairs; vector-boson pT and polarization observables; scaling with center-of-mass energy and luminosity; comparisons between pp and pA collisions; and dedicated extractions of the quark-induced double-parton effective cross section. These measurements would constrain potential spin, flavor, and longitudinal-momentum correlations in double parton distributions and definitively quantify the DDYP contribution to diboson production.

We derive the random-phase approximation (RPA) for spin excitations in general multi-band Hubbard models, starting from a collinear ferromagnetic Hartree–Fock ground state. We benchmark the RPA spectra against a recently proposed variational many-body approach to spin waves in itinerant ferromagnets. For one- and two-band realizations, the two methods yield qualitatively different spin-wave dispersions and damping, including contrasting Goldstone behavior and magnon–Stoner mixing. We trace the discrepancies to Hartree–Fock’s inadequate treatment of local moments and short-range correlations inherent in correlated-electron systems. Our analysis clarifies the regimes of validity of RPA and highlights the necessity of beyond–mean-field descriptions for itinerant ferromagnetism.

We study splittable network routing games in which a finite set of agents each controls a prescribed amount of flow and may divide it among multiple paths. Prior work compares the social cost at Nash equilibria with the optimal social cost. We depart from this benchmark by introducing a selfish Stackelberg leader who allocates and commits her flow first, after which followers best respond. We formalize the additional social cost induced by leadership relative to simultaneous-play Nash, and show that even on simple networks a leader can improve her own cost while increasing social cost. Focusing on the two-player case, we characterize structural properties of Stackelberg outcomes and derive worst-case performance guarantees. We prove upper and lower bounds on the extra cost incurred by leadership, providing tight bounds up to constant factors, and illuminate when and how leadership harms efficiency.

Chains of magnetic adatoms deposited on the surface of an ordinary s-wave superconductor can host one-dimensional topological superconductivity with unpaired Majorana fermions localized at their ends. In minimal 1D effective descriptions, the adatom moments form a spiral whose pitch self-adjusts so that, whenever feasible, the electronic band lies in the topological regime. We investigate the microscopic origin of this self-organization using a more realistic setup: a two-dimensional superconducting surface coupled to a one-dimensional adatom chain. Treating both the superconducting order parameter and the adatom magnetization self-consistently, we find that the spiral continues to select a pitch that maximizes the topological gap and stabilizes Majorana end states. The resulting phase diagram retains the self-organized topological region, though it occupies a somewhat smaller portion than in the 1D model due to surface dimensionality and local suppression of pairing near the chain. We further explore the impact of imperfections, including positional disorder and variations in exchange coupling, and show that, once established, the topological phase is robust against moderate disorder, preserving localized Majorana modes and a finite excitation gap overall.

We investigate strong gravitational lensing by a Schwarzschild black hole in the strong-deflection regime and characterize, in addition to the familiar primary and secondary images, an infinite sequence of images on both sides of the optic axis that we term relativistic images. These arise from photons experiencing large deflection angles after skirting the photon sphere at @xmath0, with closest approach @xmath1 constrained by @xmath1 > @xmath2. Using the strong-deflection limit and an appropriate lens equation, we derive analytic expressions for the angular positions, magnifications, and time delays of these images, and we map the sky such that sources across the universe are projected into the immediate vicinity of the black hole. For the Galactic supermassive black hole, the relativistic images lie at ≈@xmath3 microarcseconds from the optic axis. They are mutually unresolved with foreseeable instrumentation but remain separable from the primary and secondary images. Their magnifications are extremely small unless the observer, lens, and source are nearly perfectly aligned, rendering near-term detection improbable. Nevertheless, any future observation would constitute a definitive strong-field test of general relativity and would set an upper bound, @xmath4, on the compactness of the lens, thereby reinforcing the black hole interpretation. We discuss requirements and prospects with next-generation long-baseline interferometry.

We propose a coherent spin-filtering scheme for particles with arbitrary spin quantum number, implemented by a one-dimensional periodic chain of magnetic atoms acting as a quantum device. Within a tight-binding framework, we develop an analytical mapping that establishes a precise equivalence between the spin-resolved dynamics in a magnetic chain and transport on a multi-strand ladder network. This mapping is pivotal for engineering tunable spin-dependent band gaps via the judicious choice of the magnetic substrate. Exploiting this correspondence, we derive an exact correlation between the magnitude of the incoming particle’s spin and the magnetic moment of the substrate atoms required to open spectral gaps separating spin-resolved subbands. Spin-polarized transport is calculated using a transfer-matrix formalism for half-integer spins and higher-spin states, demonstrating that the chain can be configured to admit transmission for selected spin projections within specific Fermi-energy windows while suppressing all others across the remaining spectrum. The resulting spin filtering is broadband, reconfigurable through substrate parameters, and does not rely on fine-tuned disorder or spin-orbit coupling. We further assess robustness against deviations from the ideal magnetic pattern by introducing a spin-spiral substrate. Remarkably, the spiral not only preserves spin-selective filtering over sizable energy intervals but also induces controllable spin flipping, governed by the interplay between the device length and the spiral period. These findings suggest a versatile route to implement spin filters, analyzers, and spin-flip elements in a unified, minimal platform. The proposed scheme is amenable to realization with ultracold quantum gases in optical lattices with engineered magnetic textures, and may also inspire solid-state implementations in atomically patterned magnetic chains. Our results provide analytic design rules for scalable, high-fidelity spin control across a broad range of spin magnitudes.

We present a critical review of the exact renormalization group equations (ERGE) in the context of scalar field theories. After surveying the main formulations—Polchinski-type and effective average action (Wetterich) equations—we emphasize the derivative expansion as a practical nonperturbative approximation, with particular focus on its leading order (local potential approximation), which serves as a textbook illustration of Wilson’s renormalization group. We discuss conceptual issues (universality, scheme dependence, regulator choice) and technical aspects (convergence, truncation errors), and compile benchmark results for fixed points and critical exponents in d dimensions. The review is intentionally introductory, confined to scalar fields, yet it concludes with a curated guide to extensions and applications to more complex systems. PACS: 05.10.Cc, 05.70.Jk, 11.10.Gh, 11.10.Hi.

We present the stellar kinematics of a representative sample of elliptical and lenticular galaxies observed with our custom-built SAURON integral-field spectrograph on the William Herschel Telescope. The data were acquired and processed homogeneously using a dedicated reduction and analysis pipeline, producing datacubes that were spatially binned to a constant minimum signal-to-noise ratio. Stellar kinematics were extracted with an optimized penalized pixel-fitting routine that fits spectra in pixel space using optimal templates and mitigates contamination from nebular emission. From these fits we derived two-dimensional maps of the mean stellar velocity V, velocity dispersion sigma, and the Gauss–Hermite moments h3 and h4 of the line-of-sight velocity distribution, typically extending to approximately one effective radius. The kinematic maps reveal a variety of structures, including kinematic twists, kinematically decoupled components, central stellar disks, and other features. These results provide stringent constraints on the intrinsic shapes, angular momentum content, and assembly histories of early-type galaxies, and illustrate the power of integral-field spectroscopy for disentangling their dynamical complexity. An interpretation of the diverse kinematic morphologies and their implications for formation and evolution scenarios will be presented in subsequent papers of this series.

We compute the light‐scattering spectrum of a Maxwell fluid in a nonequilibrium steady state sustained by an external temperature gradient. Heat conduction is modeled by Fourier’s law, and fluctuations are treated within fluctuating hydrodynamics. We derive the dynamic structure factor and analyze the modification of Rayleigh and Brillouin components due to finite stress relaxation. The non‐Newtonian character introduces gradient‐dependent couplings and relaxation‐controlled line broadening and shifts. In the Newtonian limit our results reduce to classical predictions. Experimental signatures and parameter regimes are discussed.

Black holes (BHs) in asymptotically anti–de Sitter (AdS) spacetimes have been extensively studied via frequency-domain analyses and nonlinear evolutions, yet time-domain studies of linear perturbations remain limited. We bridge this gap by evolving linearized scalar wavepackets on rotating AdS black hole backgrounds. Using high-order finite-difference schemes with reflective AdS boundary conditions, we track waveform, energy fluxes, and mode content over long times. For small AdS BHs we observe an early-to-intermediate regime indistinguishable from asymptotically flat BHs, including standard ringdown followed by power-law tails. At late times, repeated reflections between the timelike boundary and the horizon lead to thermalization and the emergence of discrete AdS normal modes. For rapidly spinning BHs, wavepackets localized near the ergoregion exhibit exponential amplification, indicating a superradiant instability consistent with frequency-domain predictions. Our results establish the time-domain phenomenology of linear perturbations in Kerr–AdS, clarify the crossover between flat and AdS behavior, and provide benchmarks for future nonlinear studies.

In particular, in the context of knots in @xmath6 and in the @xmath7, @xmath8 case, the splicing operad (denoted @xmath9) encodes a homotopy-theoretic version of Larry Siebenmann’s splicing construction @xcite. This framework yields new structural decompositions of spaces of long knots and their operadic symmetries. The space of long knots in @xmath10, denoted @xmath11, was shown in @xcite to be a free algebra over the @xmath12-cubes operad, freely generated by the subspace @xmath13 of prime long knots under connect-sum. One of our main results strengthens and refines this statement: @xmath11 is free as an algebra over the splicing operad @xmath9, with free generating subspace strictly smaller than @xmath13, namely the subspace @xmath14 of torus and hyperbolic knots. Thus operadic freeness persists for a richer operad that simultaneously organizes cabling and satellite operations and the splicing of knot complements. We further establish a structural decomposition of @xmath9 as a free product of two operads. The first free summand is a semi-direct product @xmath15 operad that is not equivalent to the framed discs operad, reflecting additional geometric structure inherent in splicing. The second free summand is a free @xmath16-operad on @xmath16-spaces that encode cabling and hyperbolic satellite operations. We determine the @xmath16-homotopy types of these generating spaces by placing hyperbolic links in @xmath6 in adapted maximal symmetry positions and analyzing the resulting symmetry groups and cusp actions. Collectively, these results provide, in principle, an explicit operadic description of the homotopy type of the space of knots in @xmath6. Apart from the remaining task of determining symmetry groups and their cusp actions for classes of hyperbolic links, this yields a closed-form description of the homotopy type and a unifying operadic framework for classical and hyperbolic knot operations.

This article introduces, for the first time, a set of spatio-temporal standardised statistical databases that renders the systems of cities in seven of the world’s largest countries or regions—China, India, Brazil, Europe, the former Soviet Union (FSU), the United States, and South Africa—empirically comparable. We first articulate the concept of a generic evolutionary urban unit (“city”), deriving a theoretically grounded definition that can be operationalised across heterogeneous national statistical systems. We document the adaptations needed to reconcile disparate administrative delineations, census practices, and spatial granularities, and provide rules for harmonising temporal updates so that urban entities are consistently traced over five decades. The databases provide harmonised city definitions, regular population series since 1960, and georeferenced boundaries for cross-national analyses. Second, we compare, at the macro scale, the hierarchical structure and growth processes of these urban systems using Zipf’s rank-size regularity and Gibrat’s law of proportionate growth. In line with an evolutionary theory of urban systems, we find striking commonalities in size distributions and growth dynamics across BRICS countries as well as Europe and the United States, despite their location at different stages of the urban transition. Structural peculiarities—such as primacy effects, regional concentration, and policy-induced discontinuities—are interpretable within the same framework and reflect distinctive institutional histories and infrastructural investments. Third, at the micro scale, we map and classify the individual demographic trajectories of approximately 10,000 cities over the last fifty years. A cluster analysis reveals a limited set of recurrent evolutionary paths—stable, accelerating, decelerating, resurgent, and stagnating growth—whose geographic patterns vary systematically. The Chinese case exhibits a specific spatial repartition linked to coastal opening, inland industrial policies, and administrative reclassification, underscoring the interaction between national development strategies and urban evolution. Beyond substantive findings, the study addresses a pervasive methodological gap: urban theories and models are too seldom tested on properly defined and standardised datasets. Many contradictory results in urban studies stem from inconsistent city delineations and non-comparable statistics. By grounding data construction in a common theoretical definition of the city and by harmonising spatial and temporal dimensions, we establish a replicable empirical baseline. We conclude that macro-level regularities, distilled as stylised facts, provide robust constraints and targets for simulation models of urban systems. Concurrently, the micro-level trajectories we identify are internally consistent and sufficiently informative to underpin plausible scenario-building and future population projections. Together, these contributions advance comparative urban science by linking theory, data, and modelling across diverse contexts and stages of urbanisation.

We study the deformation of a long cosmic string by the spacetime geometry of a nearby rotating black hole. Using the Nambu–Goto description and analytic estimates complemented by numerical integrations of string worldsheet dynamics in Kerr backgrounds, we characterize the twisting and stretching of string segments that penetrate the ergosphere. We determine the conditions under which the deformed segment can self-intersect, thereby chopping off a closed loop. Loop formation via this mechanism is found to be rare, confined to a narrow region of collision phase space controlled by the string velocity, impact parameter, and the black hole spin. Outside this region the string is generically deflected or captured, with no topology change. We quantify the dependence of self-intersection thresholds on spin and kinematics and outline consequences for cosmic string network evolution, and provide estimates of event rates in astrophysical environments.

In this work, we investigate radiative leptonic decays of @xmath0 and @xmath1 mesons within the Standard Model and the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (Type II). Using a systematic factorization framework, we compute decay amplitudes and rates including contributions up to order @xmath2. The required meson wave functions are taken from a relativistic potential model, enabling consistent treatment of bound-state effects. We present numerical predictions for branching fractions and spectral distributions, and analyze the sensitivity of the decay mode @xmath3 to charged-Higgs exchange. Employing current constraints on the free parameters of the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model from previous studies, we find that the charged-Higgs contribution to @xmath3 can be sizable, reaching as large as about @xmath4. We discuss implications for ongoing and future flavor experiments and precision tests.

We present X-ray, radio, and infrared observations of the 68 ms pulsar PSR J1420−6048 and its surrounding nebula, a possible counterpart to the gamma-ray source GeV J1417−6100/3EG J1420−6038. ASCA reveals a hard-spectrum X-ray nebula, AX J1420.1−6049, within which pulsed X-ray emission at the radio period is marginally detected. At radio wavelengths, PSR J1420−6048 is strongly linearly and circularly polarized, and the polarization sweep is measured, constraining the viewing geometry. High-resolution ATCA imaging of the Kookaburra’s upper wing (G313.6+0.3) shows filamentary structure surrounding the pulsar and nebula. Comparison with infrared images indicates that the radio emission is partly non-thermal, consistent with synchrotron radiation from a pulsar wind nebula. These results support an association with the unidentified GeV source.

We present a comprehensive spatial and dynamical investigation of the poorly populated stellar system ESO65SC03 to clarify its nature and evolutionary state. Radial density profiling yields a small core radius and a cluster radius of approximately 5.4 arcmin, but the surface number density profile exhibits no clear enhancement relative to adjacent field regions, indicating weak or absent central concentration. To mitigate field contamination, we apply a statistical cleaning procedure to construct colour–magnitude diagrams (CMDs) over an optimized isochrone grid, from which we derive a consistent distance modulus and a reddening E(B−V) ≈ 0.45 mag. The system’s mean proper motion in right ascension and declination is found to be essentially indistinguishable from that of the surrounding field, underscoring the difficulty of kinematic membership discrimination in such sparse aggregates. The mass function inferred for the brighter members is notably steep, exceeding expectations for a bound open cluster and suggesting significant dynamical evolution. Taken together—weak spatial overdensity, field-like proper motions, and an anomalously high bright-end mass function—these diagnostics constrain ESO65SC03 to be either an asterism or a dissolving open cluster remnant (POCR). We favor the POCR interpretation, in which the system is in an advanced stage of dynamical erosion, having preferentially lost main-sequence stars through internal relaxation and external tidal effects. Our analysis of the CMD, two-colour diagram, and dynamical properties provides a coherent framework for ESO65SC03 as a transient remnant, and highlights the necessity of deeper photometry and high-precision astrometry to unambiguously assess membership and mass segregation in sparse stellar systems.

We investigate structural and static properties of finite two-dimensional assemblies of repelling charged particles laterally confined by a parabolic potential, the classical analog of quantum dots. Using Monte Carlo sampling with Newton-based energy minimization, we systematically obtain the energies and configurations of the ground state and all metastable states for particle numbers spanning few to several tens. To characterize transitions, we locate saddle points connecting minima and trace downhill paths to map the network of basins and barriers, yielding geometric descriptors of the energy landscape. The ground state exhibits concentric shell arrangements whose radii and occupancies follow simple scaling with particle number and confinement strength. Barrier heights display broad distributions that control reconfiguration pathways and thermal activation rates. We further assess sensitivity to the form of interparticle interactions and the confinement, demonstrating changes under screened Coulomb forces and anharmonic traps, including shell rearrangements and altered stability hierarchies. These results provide benchmarks for charged clusters and classical dots. PACS: 45.05.+x, 61.46.+w, 73.22.-f.

In this paper, we study the min-cost flow problem in planar networks. We introduce two transformations: one leveraging geometric duality of planar graphs and another based on linear programming duality. The resulting instance is a min-cost flow problem in a related planar network whose balance constraints are induced by the original costs, while its arc costs are determined by the original capacities. This dual-dual correspondence enables new structural insights and algorithmic simplifications. Using the transformation, we derive an @xmath0 time algorithm for min-cost flow in an @xmath1-vertex outerplanar network, improving practical efficiency and clarifying complexity. Our approach suggests broader applications to specialized planar flow models.

Hydrodynamic studies of core-collapse supernovae indicate that neutrino-heated ejecta emerging from a nascent neutron star accelerate to supersonic velocities and are subsequently impacted by a reverse shock from the earlier supernova ejecta, forming a wind termination shock. We investigate how this termination shock reshapes neutrino-driven winds and its role in the @xmath0-process. Supersonic outflows are modeled using a semi-analytic neutrino-driven wind framework, and the subsonic, post-shock evolution is obtained by applying the Rankine–Hugoniot jump conditions. Nucleosynthesis calculations along these trajectories are performed to assess consequences for the @xmath0-process. Two robust shock-induced effects emerge. First, the termination shock produces a sudden slowdown in the temperature decline, prolonging elevated temperatures through @xmath0-process freezeout and thereby redirecting the nucleosynthetic path. Second, termination-shock heating induces an entropy increase of up to several @xmath1. We explore a range of proto–neutron star masses, neutrino luminosities, electron fractions, and expansion timescales to map how shock radius, temperature history, and entropy respond to wind conditions. We find that the temperature slowdown is the decisive factor shaping the @xmath0-process abundance patterns: only termination-shocked winds with comparatively small shock radii (≲ @xmath2 km) reproduce the bulk of the solar @xmath0-process abundances (@xmath3). In contrast, the heaviest portion of the solar @xmath0-process curve (@xmath4) can be obtained in both shocked and unshocked winds. The entropy jump, on the other hand, has negligible impact on yields because substantial entropy amplification occurs only when the shock forms at large radii (≳ @xmath5 km), by which time the @xmath0-process has already ceased. These results underscore the importance of the dynamical coupling between neutrino-driven winds and the surrounding supernova ejecta, and they suggest that the range of progenitor masses capable of producing small-radius termination shocks may be constrained by the requirement to match the solar @xmath0-process distribution.

Counter-rotating gas can be supplied to galactic discs either by the deposition of a counter-rotating cloud onto the surface of an existing co-rotating disc or by the inward migration of counter-rotating material to the disc’s outer edge. At the interface, opposing angular momenta cancel, producing gas with near-zero net angular momentum that tends to free-fall toward the center. We present high-resolution axisymmetric hydrodynamic simulations of viscous, counter-rotating discs that explore two generic configurations: vertically separated counter-rotating layers and radially separated components with an inner co-rotating disc and an outer counter-rotating disc. Viscosity is modeled as isotropic with the full viscous stress tensor retained. In the vertically separated case, a pronounced shear layer forms at the interface. Efficient mixing within this layer cancels angular momentum and drives a centrally directed, near-ballistic inflow originating near the middle of the shear layer. Relative to a conventional, single-sense disc with the same viscosity, the mass accretion rate is substantially enhanced. The shear-layer thickness and the degree of accretion enhancement depend sensitively on the viscosity and on the mass fraction carried by the counter-rotating component, with larger viscosity and higher counter-rotating mass fractions yielding broader layers and stronger inflow. In the radially separated case, the mutual torques between the inner and outer discs generate a gap whose width and depth evolve quasi-periodically as mixing proceeds. This cyclical opening and closing of the gap produces episodic accretion bursts, with time-averaged accretion rates exceeding those of a single-sense disc at the same viscosity. Our results demonstrate that counter-rotating accretion provides an efficient channel for rapid angular-momentum cancellation and central fueling. The predicted shear layers, gap variability, and elevated inflow rates offer diagnostics for interpreting kinematically decoupled gas in spiral galaxies, the fueling of galactic nuclei, and transient accretion episodes during galaxy assembly and evolution.

We derive expectation values of functions of time-integrated two-level telegraph noise and evaluate them under simple control pulses. Both the Gaussian limit and exact non-Gaussian telegraph noise are analyzed. Applying the framework to a superconducting qubit, we obtain closed-form error probabilities and design rules, illustrating practical performance estimation and pulse optimization against discrete switching noise effects.

Motivated by problems in molecular biology, we revisit Bayesian directional statistics for circular data modeled by the von Mises distribution. A long-standing bottleneck has been efficient sampling from the posterior distribution of the concentration parameter. We present a novel algorithm that delivers accurate inference with dramatic gains in computational efficiency. The method provides valid draws under broad priors, scales robustly across sample sizes, and integrates seamlessly into hierarchical models. Extensive simulations and case studies demonstrate superior mixing, reduced autocorrelation, and speedups over common alternatives.

We investigate the possibility of generating thermal waves in a two‐dimensional electron gas (2DEG) within the framework of quantum heat transport. We formulate a 2D quantum hyperbolic heat transfer equation that incorporates finite thermal relaxation time and nonlocal quantum effects, and solve it numerically for material and confinement parameters. The solutions exhibit propagating, damped thermal waves in 2DEGs, with dispersion and attenuation governed by relaxation and boundary conditions. As an illustrative case, we model thermal wave patterns in quantum corrals, highlighting signatures accessible to scanning probe thermometry and implications for nanoscale heat management.

We reexamine the purported equivalence between 2+1 dimensional Einstein gravity and Chern–Simons theory. Using an explicit counterexample, we show that the gauge-equivalence classes of physical states in Chern–Simons theory are not in one-to-one correspondence with those in Einstein gravity, even though the field equations are locally related. The mismatch originates from global issues and from allowing singular or degenerate metrics within the first-order formulation. Such configurations, natural in the Chern–Simons phase space of flat connections, produce gauge-inequivalent sectors that do not represent admissible spacetime geometries, or merge distinct geometries into the same Chern–Simons class. We analyze the impact on the reduced phase space, holonomy data, and observables, and discuss boundary conditions under which a correspondence can be recovered, with implications for quantization.

We present a spectroscopic analysis of the late O-type star VFTS102 in 30 Doradus obtained within a multi-epoch survey. Extreme line broadening in He I and He II features yields a projected rotational velocity v sin I exceeding 500 km s−1 and likely approaching 600 km s−1, identifying VFTS102 as the most rapidly rotating massive star known. Its radial velocity is offset by approximately 40 km s−1 from the 30 Doradus mean, consistent with runaway kinematics. The star lies about 12 pc from the X-ray pulsar PSR J0537–6910, aligned with the tail of the pulsar’s diffuse X-ray emission. We propose a shared binary origin, in which VFTS102 was spun up by mass transfer from the pulsar’s progenitor and received a supernova kick that produced its velocity offset. These results inform scenarios of chemically homogeneous evolution and potential links to long-duration gamma-ray burst progenitors.

We study local models of étale-local structure of @xmath0-adic integral models of Shimura varieties and their characterization by explicit moduli problems. Building on the group-theoretic construction of flat parahoric local models for tamely ramified groups by Pappas–Zhu, and on earlier work of Rapoport–Zink, Pappas, and Pappas–Rapoport for ramified, quasi-split @xmath1, we propose a refined moduli problem formulated in linear-algebraic terms on lattice chains. Our refinement augments the usual Kottwitz and determinant conditions by an additional compatibility condition tailored to the ramified setting. We prove that, in a certain special maximal parahoric case with signature @xmath2, this refinement is both necessary and sufficient: the resulting moduli functor is representable by a projective scheme over the @xmath0-adic base and canonically identifies with the Pappas–Zhu local model. As consequences, we obtain flatness and the expected generic fiber, and we analyze the special fiber via affine Schubert stratifications, yielding geometric properties and applications to integral models of Shimura varieties.

Compact symmetric objects (CSOs) are key laboratories for probing the earliest stages of radio galaxy evolution. Their sub-kiloparsec morphology and kinematic ages of order thousands of years, together with the high incidence of absorption toward the central parsecs, indicate dense circumnuclear environments. Using the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), we obtain continuum images and spectral-line observations at milliarcsecond resolution to map the velocity field of absorbing gas, tracing a torus feeding the central engine. These measurements constrain accretion, orientation, and jet–interstellar medium interactions in young sources. From the VLBA Calibrator Survey we identify nine new CSOs, increasing the known population by nearly fifty percent. The expanded sample enables improved statistics, targeted absorption studies, and tests of youth and evolution in radio galaxies.

Renewable energy sources, especially wind energy, are poised to assume a much larger role in supplying electricity to industrial and domestic consumers. This transition is well advanced in several European countries and accelerating in the United States and economies such as Brazil, India, and China. Realizing full benefits requires overcoming technological, environmental, and political challenges associated with integrating variable, partially predictable generation into existing systems. This article argues that mathematicians and statisticians can make substantial contributions at the interface of meteorology and operational decision-making by developing and evaluating forecasts tailored to specific planning, trading, and control problems. After a concise overview of the physical basics of wind energy conversion, we motivate modeling wind power generation as a stochastic process, emphasizing the need to accommodate uncertainty across multiple scales. We then describe representative operational decision problems faced by market participants and system operators, and underline why forecasts should be issued within a probabilistic framework across multiple forecast horizons, even when users ultimately receive single-valued predictions. Existing approaches to wind power forecasting are reviewed, with attention to point forecasts, predictive marginal densities, and space–time trajectory forecasts that preserve temporal and spatial dependencies. Finally, we discuss upcoming challenges, including improving calibration and sharpness of ensembles, characterizing extremes and ramps, achieving coherent multivariate forecasts, integrating new data sources and high-resolution numerical weather prediction, verifying forecasts with appropriate metrics, and quantifying forecast value for diverse users. These advances are crucial to support robust, cost-effective, sustainable power system operations.

We construct a canonical chain-level morphism from Bloch’s higher Chow complexes to Deligne–Beilinson homology for smooth complex quasi-projective varieties. Our approach uses complexes of currents and differential forms with logarithmic singularities along normal crossings compactifications, providing an explicit cycle-to-current assignment. For projective varieties we derive an integral formula that simultaneously generalizes Griffiths’ Abel–Jacobi map for codimension-p cycles and the regulator maps of Borel, Beilinson, and Goncharov for higher cycles, recovering known constructions in low degrees and extending them to all n. Examples and comparison results illustrate agreement with classical regulators and yield computable expressions for higher Chow classes. Dedicated to the memory of Fabio Bardelli.

This paper investigates existence of solutions and approximate controllability for a class of fractional nonlocal delay semilinear differential systems in Hilbert spaces. Employing semigroup theory, tools from fractional calculus, and Schauder’s fixed point theorem, we establish existence results under multi-delay control actions and a fractional nonlocal initial condition. We derive a set of sufficient conditions ensuring approximate controllability of the associated fractional nonlocal multi-delay control system. The analysis accommodates linear operators and nonlinear perturbations satisfying compactness and continuity assumptions. An illustrative example demonstrates the applicability of the theoretical results. Keywords: approximate controllability, fractional multi-delay, nonlocal condition, semigroups.

We present an overview of the Gaia mission, set for launch in late 2011, which will survey at least one billion stars and obtain parallaxes and spectra down to V=17. Among these targets, several million hot and emission-line stars will be observed in the Milky Way and Local Group, including the Magellanic Clouds. We describe codes and methods under development to automatically derive astrophysical parameters and perform spectral classification for these populations. Our approach combines machine learning, template fitting, and line profile diagnostics to estimate Teff, log g, metallicity, v sin i, and emission characteristics, validated on ground-based data.

This study presents analytic calculations and computational experiments on adaptive predictors—agents that learn to model, control, and forecast—operating in an evolving chaotic environment and co-adapting to one another. We construct a simple, calculable iterated-map testbed and endow agents with bounded memory and model complexity, updating parameters to minimize prediction error and maximize control efficacy. For a single agent exposed to chaotic dynamics, parameter sweeps and stability analyses reveal an interior optimum: both memory and model complexity have nonmonotonic effects on performance, with optimal values that are small when the map changes rapidly. Counterintuitively, predictive power increases when we impose additional chaos or exogenous random noise on the map, which regularizes overfitting and amplifies informative fluctuations. Introducing a second adaptive predictor transforms the task: each agent attempts to model and influence both the environment and its opponent. The resulting co-adaptation exhibits distinct regimes, ranging from fully chaotic competition to metastable emergent behavior characterized by leader–follower alternation and intermittent synchronization. Across regimes, we observe a robust correlation between optimal adaptation, minimal sufficient complexity, and the onset of structured emergent dynamics. These findings provide preliminary support for the hypothesis of optimal co-adaptation near the edge of chaos and suggest design principles for multi-agent predictive control in nonstationary real-world settings.

We present milliarcsecond Very Long Baseline Interferometry observations of 22 GHz H2O maser and radio continuum emission from the nucleus of the nearby active galaxy NGC 3079 (distance ≈16 Mpc), resolving sub-parsec structures. The maser emission arises in compact clumps distributed over parsec scales along an axis approximately aligned with the major axis of the galactic disk. The line-of-sight velocities of the clumps are consistent with their location within the inner parsec of a rotating molecular disk bound by a central mass, and the sense of rotation matches that of the edge-on, kiloparsec-scale molecular disk seen in CO. However, the velocity field exhibits substantial departures from purely circular rotation, revealing a significant non-rotational component that may reflect supersonic turbulence and/or dynamical perturbations within the disk. This geometry and kinematics differ markedly from those of the archetypal megamaser galaxy NGC 4258, where masers delineate an extremely thin, nearly Keplerian disk around a more massive central object. At 22 GHz, the radio continuum is dominated by a compact source displaced by about 0.5 pc to the west of the brightest maser feature. No bright maser emission is co-spatial with any detected compact continuum source, implying that the high apparent luminosity of the maser is not produced by beamed amplification of a high–brightness temperature background core. Complementary imaging at 5 and 8 GHz reveals two compact continuum components with a projected separation of approximately 1.5 pc; both exhibit inverted spectra between 5 and 8 GHz and steep spectra between 8 and 22 GHz. These spectral and structural properties indicate that NGC 3079 may be a nearby, low-luminosity example of a compact symmetric gigahertz-peaked spectrum radio source. We further detect a third continuum component aligned with the other two, strongly suggesting the presence of a parsec-scale nuclear jet. Faint maser emission occurs near this axis, potentially tracing a second maser population associated with jet–ISM interactions rather than the rotating disk. Together, the maser and continuum data reveal a complex nuclear environment in NGC 3079, where a turbulent molecular disk coexists with a young or frustrated jet. These results underscore the diversity of megamaser-host nuclei and demonstrate the diagnostic power of combined VLBI maser and continuum imaging for probing sub-parsec structures and dynamics in active galaxies.

Observations of isolated radio pulsars reveal long-term spin-down evolutions and significant, quasi-periodic modulations in their braking rates that are incompatible with a standard, constant-torque magnetic dipole model. The origin, magnitude, and variability of the torque remain debated, impeding a unified understanding of neutron-star magneto-thermal evolution. We apply a recently developed phenomenological framework for pulsar timing noise to high-precision timing data of a sample of young, isolated neutron stars. By incorporating Hall effects in the crustal magnetic field evolution, our model naturally produces time-varying external torques that reproduce the observed secular spin-down changes and the quasi-periodic timing modulations. The agreement across sources indicates that crustal Hall drift, rather than core field evolution, dominates the long-term braking behavior of these pulsars. This interpretation links timing noise, braking index variability, and magneto-thermal processes within a single physical picture. Constraining the crustal magnetic evolution through timing data improves physical modeling of pulsar spin-down, reduces stochastic timing noise, and enhances sensitivity of gravitational-wave searches that rely on pulsars, including pulsar timing arrays and continuous-wave analyses. Our results highlight timing noise as a diagnostic of neutron-star interiors and a lever for precision gravitational astrophysics.

We present further optical and near-infrared imaging of a sample of radio sources in the North Ecliptic Cap, yielding several new host-galaxy identifications and improved astrometry. We report on a second epoch of Chandra X-ray imaging spectroscopy of the spatially resolved old nova remnant GK Persei. An ACIS-S3 observation totaling 97.4 ks was conducted in November 2013, 13.8 years after the first Chandra visit in 2000. Relative to the earlier epoch, the X-ray emitting nebula appears significantly fainter and more patchy. The decline is most pronounced in the lower-surface-brightness regions, with a mean flux decrease of approximately 30–40% in the 0.5–1.2 keV band. Proper-motion measurements indicate a typical expansion of the brightest portion of the remnant of about 1 arcsecond, corresponding to an angular expansion rate on the order of 0.1 arcseconds per year. Soft X-ray spectra extracted from both epochs are well described by a non-equilibrium ionization collisional plasma model subject to interstellar absorption. While the spectral fits do not uniquely constrain the physical driver of the flux evolution, the inferred plasma temperature has not changed appreciably since 2000, arguing against significant radiative cooling as the dominant cause of fading. Instead, the brightness decline is largely attributable to geometric expansion, implying that the shock has recently advanced into a lower-density ambient medium. This interpretation is qualitatively consistent with the known inhomogeneous circumstellar environment documented in early optical photographs acquired shortly after the 1901 nova outburst. The more rapid fading of the fainter regions relative to the brighter knots supports a picture in which local density variations control both emissivity and expansion rate. Future monitoring will test this scenario.

We investigate the spectrum of Andreev bound states (ABSs) in a prototypical four-terminal superconducting structure comprising four chaotic cavities connected by quantum point contacts (QPCs) both to the superconducting terminals and to each other, forming a ring-shaped device we call the 4T-ring. Realizations are feasible in high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas–superconductor hybrids and graphene-based proximitized structures. Focusing on the short-junction limit with large QPC conductances, the device hosts many ABSs constituting a quasi-continuous spectrum whose energies are tunable by the superconducting phase differences across the terminals. We reveal phase-controlled opening and closing of spectral gaps, encompassing the conventional proximity minigap around zero energy and a distinct class of “smile” gaps that segment the quasi-continuous spectrum into separated bands. A central result is a pronounced crossover in the global spectral organization governed by the ratio of the inner to outer QPC conductances. In the closed limit (large ratio), the levels exhibit generic disordered-spectrum features: Wigner-Dyson-like level repulsion and parametric “Brownian motion” as the phases are varied. In the open limit (small ratio), the spectrum restructures into narrow, quasi-degenerate bunches separated by wide smile gaps. These bunches are dominated by ABSs formed by Andreev reflection between pairs of adjacent terminals, leading to nearly regular phase dispersion within each bunch. We analyze in detail the crossings between bunches and identify two distinct types: crossings with regular, predictable phase dependence and crossings where Brownian motion induces apparently irregular phase dispersion and mixing. To explain these observations, we develop a perturbation theory in the open-limit regime. At the microscopic level, we use a scattering approach incorporating random, mode-preserving transmission in the chaotic cavities; at the phenomenological level, we construct a description in terms of positively defined random matrices that captures the stability of bunching and the statistics of level splittings at crossings. The theory yields quantitative predictions for the scaling of gap widths, bunch degeneracies, and level-velocity distributions with the conductance ratio and number of modes, and it clarifies the conditions under which irregular crossings emerge. The unusual spectral properties trace back to subtle topological mechanisms. A semiclassical topology, linked to the winding of the semiclassical Green’s function in phase space, underlies the closing of proximity gaps. A second topology, rooted in the discrete mode count of the QPCs, enforces the formation of robust smile gaps and constrains inter-bunch hybridization. A third topology associated with Weyl points in the multi-phase parameter space is identified but lies beyond the scope of the present study. Our results provide design rules and testable signatures for multi-terminal superconducting devices, enabling phase-engineered control of ABS spectra in scalable mesoscopic platforms.

We investigate proton emission from nuclei via the nuclear photoeffect in the simultaneous presence of a gamma-ray photon and an intense laser wave. An S-matrix description of the process is developed by adapting nonperturbative techniques from laser–atom interactions, using laser-dressed continuum states. As a case study, we analyze photo-proton ejection from halo nuclei. The laser field induces pronounced sideband structures in the photo-proton energy spectra, arising from multi-photon absorption and emission. We explore their sensitivity to laser intensity, frequency, and polarization, the gamma-ray energy, and the relative field orientation, and discuss observable signatures and experimental feasibility.

We develop a unified, dimension-agnostic framework for the algebraic classification of the Weyl and Ricci tensors in Lorentzian spacetimes, based on alignment theory and the boost-weight decomposition, and refined through an operator-centric perspective. Treating curvature tensors as linear operators (the Weyl operator acting on bivectors and the Ricci operator acting on vectors), we exploit the relationship between a tensor’s algebraic type and the restricted eigenvector and eigenvalue structure of its associated operator. This viewpoint yields necessary conditions for particular algebraic types by constraining eigenvalue multiplicities, Jordan structure, and eigenspace alignment properties. Central to our analysis is the study of the discriminants of the characteristic polynomial of the curvature operators. We derive a set of discriminants whose vanishing and sign structure completely determine, up to degeneracies, the eigenvalue configuration of the operator, including multiplicities and the onset of non-diagonalizable blocks. Since the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial are expressible in terms of scalar polynomial curvature invariants (SPCIs), we formulate all discriminant conditions as syzygies among SPCIs. These syzygies provide invariant, coordinate-independent tests that are practical to evaluate and that supply necessary conditions for higher-dimensional Weyl and Ricci tensors to be of special algebraic type. We focus in particular on type II and type D, presenting general necessary conditions in arbitrary dimensions for the corresponding curvature operators. For these cases, we characterize the required eigenvalue degeneracies, constrained boost-weight content, and alignment properties, and then translate these into explicit discriminant-based syzygies among SPCIs. In five dimensions, we determine concrete sets of scalar polynomial invariants whose vanishing relations serve as necessary conditions for the Weyl and Ricci tensors to be of type II or type D. We illustrate the method through several examples, emphasizing computational tractability and robustness to coordinate choices. As a detailed case study, we analyze the five-dimensional rotating black ring, showing how the curvature-operator discriminants and associated syzygies diagnose its eigenvalue structure and refine its algebraic classification within the alignment scheme. Our results provide an algorithmic pipeline: compute SPCIs, evaluate discriminant syzygies, infer the eigenvalue structure (including degeneracies), and thereby establish necessary conditions for specific algebraic types. This approach furnishes a systematic, invariant toolkit for probing the algebraic structure of curvature in higher-dimensional Lorentzian geometry, with direct implications for exact solutions and classification problems in higher-dimensional gravity.

Understanding the formation and evolution of Magellanic-type dwarf irregular galaxies requires constraints on their three-dimensional structure and dynamical state. We present new measurements of the stellar velocity dispersion in NGC 1569, a nearby post-starburst dwarf irregular galaxy, and combine these with the maximum rotational velocity to assess the kinematic “temperature” of the stellar disk. The vertical stellar velocity dispersion, coupled with the observed maximum rotation, yields a ratio Vmax/σz = 2.4 ± 0.7, indicating that the stars reside in a geometrically thick, dynamically hot disk rather than a thin, rotation-dominated configuration. To place the stellar dynamics in context, we analyze ionized gas kinematics along the morphological major axis. The gas shows clear signatures of outflow originating from the central starburst region and evidence for an expanding shell in the vicinity of the supermassive star cluster SSC A. The stellar velocity dispersion increases locally near SSC A, consistent with dynamical heating associated with the expanding shell, and the stellar line-of-sight velocities closely track the gas motions, reinforcing the coupling between stars and the ionized interstellar medium in the inner disk. High-resolution imaging and spectroscopy reveal a distinct cloud impacting the eastern edge of NGC 1569 and an ultra-dense cloud extending to its west. We interpret the latter as the remnant of a dense bridge that once threaded the current central starburst zone. The impacting cloud likely acted as the catalyst for the recent starburst, compressing the dense gas and driving rapid star formation over a short timescale of less than about 1 Gyr. To quantify the mass distribution, we perform a careful spectral energy distribution analysis using infrared, optical, and ultraviolet photometry to construct a state-of-the-art stellar mass model. This modeling shows that stars dominate the gravitational potential within the inner 1 kpc. The dynamical mass inferred from the rotation curve suggests a relative paucity of dark matter in the inner disk, while comparison with the expected virial mass from halo abundance matching indicates consistency between the dark matter profile and the observed mass distribution at a radius of 2.2 kpc. Together, these results portray NGC 1569 as a kinematically hot, thick-disk system whose recent starburst and structural evolution were likely triggered by external gas accretion, with baryons dominating the inner potential and a more conventional dark matter halo at larger radii.

In the currently accepted model for gamma‐ray bursts (GRBs), the violent formation of a rapidly rotating, solar‐mass black hole is expected to produce gravitational waves (GWs). Detecting GWs from GRBs would provide a critical test of this model, while even stringent non‐detections (upper limits) can constrain progenitor energetics and geometry. Realizing such constraints requires coordinated observations with gamma‐ray and GW detectors. We analyze how the quality of upper limits on GW strain associated with GRBs depends on the relative orientation between the GRB instrument and the GW detector network. Using the Swift Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) and the LIGO interferometers as a case study, we combine BAT’s sky exposure and localization capabilities with the LIGO antenna patterns to quantify sensitivity to GRB‐triggered GW searches. We derive a science‐based figure of merit that maps each potential Swift pointing to the expected improvement in GW upper limits, accounting for detector duty cycles and sky visibility. This metric identifies pointing strategies that preferentially sample sky regions of high network response, thereby maximizing the probability of constraining GW emission from GRBs. We discuss implications for future joint GRB–GW campaigns.

We investigate the position vector of rectifying slant helices in Euclidean three-space. We derive general expressions linking curvature and torsion under the rectifying condition and the slant helix constraint. From these relations, we formulate a second-order linear differential equation for the position vector and solve it explicitly. The solutions yield a family of rectifying slant helices whose trajectories lie on circular cones, providing a geometric characterization and parametric representations. Examples illustrate the theory and highlight properties of these curves.

We present new Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array observations of the molecular clump G0.253+0.016 at 3 mm, mapping dust continuum and multiple molecular transitions at ~0.07 pc resolution. The data reveal a complex network of structures, ranging from compact condensations to extended filaments, with features seen both in emission and in absorption against bright backgrounds. The dust column density morphology is most faithfully traced by lines with higher upper-level energies and critical densities, consistent with a clump whose interior is denser than its envelope. Statistical analyses indicate that turbulence plays a dominant role in shaping the observed gas structure. In particular, the spatial power spectrum of the optically thin dust continuum exhibits a clear break at a scale of ~0.1 pc, which we interpret as the transition where self-gravity begins to overcome thermal (and possibly turbulent) pressure and to organize the flow. These results suggest that G0.253+0.016 is on the verge of forming a high-mass, Arches-like cluster through the assembly of hierarchical, filamentary substructures produced by a turbulent medium. Whereas the stellar distributions in Arches-like clusters are compact, centrally condensed, smooth, the present-day gas in G0.253+0.016 is extended, lacks a central high-mass concentration, and exhibits pronounced hierarchical complexity. If this clump forms a massive cluster and its stars inherit the initial hierarchical gas arrangement, the nascent system must rapidly evolve into a centrally concentrated configuration through dynamical processes such as subcluster merging and violent relaxation. Our findings provide constraints on the initial conditions and scale-dependent physics governing massive cluster formation in the Galactic Center environment.

We revisit the role of negative index of refraction within transformation optics and its connection to transformations that reverse the orientation of the underlying manifold. In particular, we compare the conventional Pendry–Veselago lens, which achieves subwavelength resolution via amplification of evanescent modes in a negative-index slab, with transformation-designed lenses and the recent Leonhardt–Philbin concept that eschews negative index and evanescent amplification. Our analysis shows that a negative index is not an intrinsic requirement of transformation optics; it arises from a specific resolution of the sign ambiguity when mapping fields under orientation-changing transformations. Moreover, the transformation-designed lens does not amplify evanescent waves. The evanescent spectrum observed at the image point is generated by a duplicated source produced by the multi-valued mapping, leading to identical propagating fields at distinct points but preventing genuine near-field transfer. Consequently, these devices deliver perfect imaging in the far field by construction, while failing to reconstruct the near field. By clarifying the roles of orientation, sign choice, and multi-valued mappings, we identify conditions for realizing transformation-optical lenses without invoking negative index. These insights refine the foundation of perfect imaging and guide the design of practical metamaterial lenses.

We use the Nahm transform to construct and analyze doubly periodic SU(2) instantons of unit topological charge exhibiting radial symmetry. By studying the Nahm data and its zero modes, we identify two special points on the dual torus at which the zero-mode singularities are softened. These points mark the locations of the instanton’s core constituents and provide a natural, gauge-invariant definition of constituent structure. On a square torus the constituent picture appears in the action density, which displays two localized peaks aligned with the special points. As the torus is deformed to rectangular shapes with large aspect ratios, the cores approach and merge, and the configuration acquires monopole-like characteristics, interpolating to periodic monopole behavior. For particular parameter values, the torus admits a cutting along symmetry lines that yields two copies of a twisted charge-1/2 instanton, clarifying how fractional topological charge emerges in the presence of twists. We illustrate these phenomena with numerical plots of the action density on two-dimensional slices passing through the constituent centers and compare with analytic expectations from the Nahm construction. Our results unify the constituent and monopole pictures. These results connect with caloron constituent models and clarify twisted boundary conditions on tori.

We report design principles and benchmarking results for a new open-source GBRV library of ultrasoft pseudopotentials tailored for high-throughput density-functional theory. The potentials are constructed to be soft, transferable, and efficient across diverse oxidation, coordination, and magnetic states. Accuracy is assessed by systematic comparison to all-electron calculations and cross-benchmarking against two widely used pseudopotential sets. Metrics include structural parameters, relative energies, and formation enthalpies for representative elemental, oxide, and intermetallic phases. The GBRV library achieves reliable agreement with all-electron references at modest plane-wave cutoffs, enabling robust screening workflows. Our results clarify strengths and limitations of modern pseudopotentials in varied chemical environments and provide practical guidelines for high-throughput materials design.

We investigate the electron-doped cuprate Pr2-xCexCuO4 (PCCO) in the pseudogap regime using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and a generalized dynamical mean-field framework with k-dependent self-energy (LDA+DMFT+Sigma_k). The inferred scattering wave vector and energy scales are consistent with short-range AFM correlations. These results establish that the pseudogap in nearly optimally doped PCCO arises from the interplay of strong electronic correlations and finite-range AFM fluctuations, and demonstrate the utility of the LDA+DMFT+Sigma_k approach for electron-doped cuprates.

We present a multiwavelength study of IRAS 03256+3055 in the NGC 1333 star-forming region, combining optical narrowband imaging, near-infrared broad- and narrowband imaging, K-band spectroscopy, and imaging polarimetry with submillimeter continuum maps. The submillimeter data reveal extended, complex emission with multiple clumps within a fragmented molecular core. One clump coincides with the driving source of a bipolar, S-shaped jet traced by Hα, [S II], and H2 emission lines, establishing an unambiguous link between the jet and the submillimeter structure. Detailed images in Hα, [S II], and the I, J, H, and K bands, together with a K-band spectrum and polarimetric measurements, show that the near-infrared morphology is a composite of shocked line emission from the jet and scattered light from an embedded source with a steeply rising continuum. The strong polarization and reflection nebulosity indicate that the continuum is dominated by scattered light from cavities carved by the outflow. The jet’s morphology and measured proper motions are consistent with a precessing outflow, which we interpret in the context of a binary system with a misaligned, precessing disk. We conclude that the molecular core associated with IRAS 03256+3055 comprises several clumps, only one of which exhibits clear evidence of recent star formation detectable at optical and near-infrared wavelengths. We also report a second, newly identified near-infrared source coincident with a compact submillimeter continuum peak near IRAS 03256+3055; its properties suggest it may be physically unrelated to the cluster of molecular clumps. These results highlight the importance of coordinated submillimeter and near-infrared observations in disentangling complex environments and in identifying the driving sources of protostellar outflows.
