These results establish benchmarks for electroproduction studies of hypernuclei and motivate refined models. Keywords: hypernuclei, electroproduction reactions. PACS: 21.80.+a, 25.30.Rw, 21.60.Cs.

Dynamic bandwidth allocation (DBA) mechanisms are central to improving bandwidth utilization, minimizing channel idle times, and reducing packet delays in passive optical networks (PONs). Most prior DBA evaluations implicitly assume that the REPORT message, which conveys bandwidth demands from optical network units (ONUs) to the optical line terminal (OLT), is scheduled at the end of an ONU’s upstream transmission, following payload data. This article provides a detailed investigation of report message scheduling (RMS), contrasting placement at the beginning (before payload) versus the end of the upstream burst, and quantifies the impact on PON performance. We present an analytical characterization of the reduction in upstream channel idle time achieved with beginning-of-burst reporting relative to end-of-burst reporting, capturing the dependencies on polling cycle timing and propagation delays. Extensive simulation experiments for both Ethernet PON (EPON) and Gigabit PON (GPON) standards validate the analysis. For DBAs employing offline sizing and scheduling of ONU grants at the end of a polling cycle, which batch-process requests from all ONUs, beginning-of-burst reporting yields substantial reductions in mean packet delay at high loads by enabling earlier request visibility and tighter idle-time control. In contrast, for high-performing DBAs with online grant sizing and scheduling—immediately processing individual ONU requests—or schemes that interleave groups of ONUs, the average packet delays are essentially unaffected by RMS, as prompt per-request decisions or interleaving inherently suppress idle gaps. The results offer clear design guidance: RMS is a critical lever for cycle-based DBAs, while online and interleaved DBAs are robust to RMS placement. Implications for long-reach PONs and multi-thread polling are discussed. Keywords: dynamic bandwidth allocation (DBA), report message scheduling (RMS), EPON, GPON, long-reach PON (LRPON), multi-thread polling (MTP), passive optical networks (PON), packet delay, idle time.

We study the dynamics and radiative outcome of a relativistic fireball propagating into a modest amount of material that remains just outside the progenitor star. Even a small fraction of the expected baryonic mass is sufficient to efficiently decelerate the fireball, dissipating most of its kinetic energy at radii comparable to the stellar surface where the scattering optical depth is still large. The dissipated energy is temporarily trapped and couples to the shocked medium, accelerating it back to relativistic speeds. This “reborn” outflow resembles the birth of a second fireball at R ≈ @xmath0 cm, not far from the transparency radius, and launches with bulk Lorentz factor Γ ≈ @xmath1. In the observer frame, the regenerated fireball appears collimated within an angle ≈ @xmath2. If the central engine operates intermittently, the funnel can partially refill and the process can recur, naturally producing multiple pulses and rapid variability. We discuss how this mechanism enhances prompt radiative efficiency, favors photospheric and Comptonized spectra, and mitigates shortcomings of conventional internal shocks, including low efficiency and spectral–variability tensions. We outline observational diagnostics and parameter constraints, and implications for jet structure and early afterglow.

We present a statistical analysis of the timing relationships among hard X-ray (HXR), soft X-ray (SXR), and Hα emissions for a sample of 503 solar flares observed simultaneously. To quantify energy release and transport processes, we measured start times, peak times, and end times in each wavelength and compared interband offsets, with particular emphasis on the onset of thermal preheating and the linkage between nonthermal and thermal phases. Thermal preheating, identified as an SXR rise preceding the impulsive HXR/Hα phase, is found in more than 90% of events; on average, the SXR emission begins about 3 minutes before both HXR and Hα. The duration of this preheating shows no significant correlation with flare importance and does not differ between impulsive and gradual flare classes. In at least half of the flares, the end of the nonthermal HXR emission coincides closely with the maximum of the thermal SXR and Hα emission, supporting the beam-driven chromospheric evaporation model in which accelerated electrons deposit energy that drives upflows and thermal plasma buildup. Conversely, in approximately 25% of the events, thermal emission continues to increase beyond the cessation of HXR, indicating prolonged evaporation and sustained heating after the end of electron acceleration. These cases point to an additional energy transport mechanism—most plausibly thermal conduction—contributing significantly to the late-phase energy input. Our results provide quantitative constraints for flare models and highlight the ubiquity of preheating and the frequent interplay of beam-driven evaporation and conductive heating.

In order to clarify the thermodynamic stability of Mg‐based long‐period stacking ordered (LPSO) structures, we systematically investigate energetic preferences across multiple stacking sequences and compositions in randomly mixed Mg–Y–Zn alloys using the special quasirandom structure (SQS) approach. Formation free energies computed for SQS configurations reveal a strong tendency toward phase separation into Mg‐rich and Y–Zn‐rich domains, consistent with prior theoretical predictions. Calculated bulk moduli for diverse compositions, stackings, and atomic arrangements cluster around 35 GPa and show negligible dependence on Mg concentration, indicating that phonon contributions are unlikely to govern LPSO phase stability. Notably, introducing stacking faults into hexagonal close‐packed (hcp) stacking yields a negative energy gain, establishing a direct energetic link between stacking fault creation and the emergence of long‐period stacking order. These results provide a unified thermodynamic picture of LPSO formation in Mg–Y–Zn systems and offer guidance for alloy design targeting fault‐mediated stabilization mechanisms.

We present a refined calculation of the quark-loop contribution to hadronic light-by-light scattering, emphasizing the impact of transverse components of the quark–photon vertex. Using momentum-dependent dressing functions to model nonperturbative dynamics, we quantify how transverse structures modify the quark-loop amplitude and its contribution to the muon’s anomalous magnetic moment. We compare and contrast our results with those obtained in extended Nambu–Jona-Lasinio (NJL) models, highlighting both qualitative and quantitative differences arising from vertex dressings and momentum dependence. While transverse components generically suppress the quark-loop contribution to g−2, we find that commonly used simplified quark–photon interactions overestimate this suppression. Our analysis clarifies the role of vertex transversality and dressing functions, and provides improved constraints for phenomenological modeling. Implications for g−2 estimates are discussed.

This paper investigates clock offset estimation in a two-way timing message exchange regime when timestamp likelihoods follow Gaussian, exponential, or log-normal distributions. We first present a parameterized maximum likelihood estimator formulated as a convex optimization problem, delivering efficient and globally optimal solutions that avoid the graphical maximization techniques prevalent in earlier approaches. To accommodate oscillator imperfections that induce time-varying offsets, we introduce a Bayesian framework based on a factor graph representation of the posterior over offset trajectories. By applying max-product message passing on this graph, we derive closed-form message updates and an explicit estimator, enabling scalable inference with clear analytical structure. Complementing these estimators, we develop several lower bounds on estimator variance for arbitrary exponential-family likelihood functions. These bounds serve dual roles: benchmarking the proposed estimators and contributing generally applicable insights to both classical and Bayesian parameter estimation theory. Extensive simulations spanning diverse network conditions and delay statistics compare the classical ML and the Bayesian estimators against the derived bounds. The results demonstrate that the proposed methods approach the fundamental performance limits across the considered likelihood models, while offering computational tractability and robustness to timing noise and model variations. The overall framework provides a unified and rigorous treatment of clock offset estimation that is well suited to clock synchronization tasks in resource-constrained wireless sensor networks. Keywords: clock synchronization, factor graphs, message passing, estimation bounds, wireless sensor networks.

We study the Langevin dynamics of the spherical Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) spin glass and compute the asymptotic distance between two real replicas evolving under identical thermal noise from distinct initial conditions. Despite the model’s simplicity, its nonequilibrium dynamics is nontrivial and exhibits aging. We derive analytic expressions for the two-replica overlap and distance, and identify a family of initial states that are arbitrarily close at t=0 yet yield a maximal asymptotic separation. The asymptotic distance undergoes a dynamical transition at a temperature coinciding with the static spin-glass transition. Our results clarify noise-induced decorrelation, link dynamical and static criticality, and provide benchmarks for replica-based dynamics.

We investigate the density and photoexcitation sensitivity of X-ray spectra from Fe L-shell ions using the Livermore X-ray Spectral Synthesizer (LXSS), a suite of IDL codes that constructs spectral models of highly charged ions based primarily on HULLAC atomic data. The models are applicable to collisionally ionized laboratory and astrophysical plasmas with electron temperatures around 0.24 keV (≈3 MK) and a broad range of electron densities. We identify robust density diagnostics for Fe L-shell ions, with particular emphasis on the Fe XVII 17.10/17.05 Å and Fe XXII 11.92/11.77 Å line ratios. These ratios are driven by the population kinetics of metastable and excited levels and exhibit complementary sensitivity to electron density and to radiative pumping from external ultraviolet/soft X-ray radiation fields. We construct model grids that quantify the competing effects of collisional excitation, de-excitation, and photoexcitation, enabling discrimination between high-density conditions and strong radiation fields. Applying these diagnostics to the Chandra High Energy Transmission Grating spectrum of the intermediate polar EX Hya, we find that the strengths of Fe L-shell lines are consistent with high electron densities characteristic of accretion column plasmas. The observed Fe XVII 17.10/17.05 Å ratio implies densities well above typical coronal values, while the Fe XXII 11.92/11.77 Å ratio provides an independent constraint that confirms the high-density interpretation and limits the impact of photoexcitation on the derived parameters. Together, the diagnostics yield mutually consistent density estimates and demonstrate the utility of LXSS/HULLAC-based modeling for tightly constraining plasma conditions in high-energy astrophysical environments. We discuss implications for accretion physics and outline applications to other X-ray bright sources and laboratory plasmas.

This paper studies the regularized Tyler’s scatter estimator (TSE) for elliptical distributions, a robust covariance estimator that has gained prominence in high-dimensional “small n, large p” regimes. While several shrinkage variants of TSE have been proposed and shown empirically effective, their existence, uniqueness, and algorithmic convergence have not been fully characterized. We establish a general sufficient condition for the existence of a broad family of shrinkage TSEs, quantitatively demonstrating that regularization lowers the sample size required for consistent estimation and ensures convergence of associated fixed-point algorithms. For two specific shrinkage TSEs, we further prove necessity of the condition and uniqueness of the solution, and we show that these two estimators are equivalent. Building on a majorization–minimization (MM) framework, we derive practical iterative algorithms with provable convergence to the unique solution under the stated conditions. Extensive simulations corroborate the theory across a range of dimension-to-sample ratios and contamination levels, and a real-data example illustrates the advantages of the proposed estimators in robust high-dimensional covariance estimation. Implications for design of robust estimators are discussed.

We investigate how augmenting the Top‐BESS effective Lagrangian with a neutral scalar resonance of mass @xmath0 impacts the consistency of the model with low‐energy observables and the allowed ranges of its free parameters. Top‐BESS is a BESS‐like framework in which a @xmath1 vector resonance triplet couples directly only to the third quark generation, capturing a potential special role of the top quark in electroweak symmetry breaking. We construct the scalar-extended low‐energy effective theory by integrating out heavy states and matching to electroweak precision and flavor observables. Using global fits to Z‐pole data, the W mass, oblique parameters, and selected flavor transitions, we evaluate goodness‐of‐fit and derive credible intervals for the couplings, mixing angles, and resonance masses. The scalar resonance yields a systematic improvement in fit quality, as quantified by likelihood ratios and information criteria, relative to the minimal Top‐BESS case. The preferred parameter region features suppressed direct couplings to light fermions, enhanced interactions with the third generation, and modest vector–scalar mixing. Best‐fit values favor a higher degree of compositeness for the top than for the bottom quark, while remaining compatible with precision constraints.

We study geodetic lines on a surface obtained by a small deformation of the standard two-dimensional sphere. To capture the organization of geodesic coils and almost closed geodesics, we construct an auxiliary Hamiltonian system whose loops are well approximated by great circles of the sphere. The phase portrait of this system is encoded by a separatrix graph: vertices represent almost closed geodesics, while edges correspond to geodetic coils that connect them. We show that the topological type of this graph depends on the parameters governing the deformation, and we delineate the associated bifurcations. Using the method of averaging for nearly integrable dynamics, combined with computer modeling of the auxiliary flow, we obtain a detailed visualization of geodesics on the deformed sphere and map the parameter domains supporting coils and near-periodic geodesics.

We present an exact, single-step Eriksen transformation of the @xmath0, @xmath1, and @xmath2 states of the relativistic hydrogen-like atom by expanding each transformed function (TF) as a linear combination of eigenstates of the Dirac Hamiltonian with a Coulomb potential. The TFs are constructed numerically as four-component spinors in which the two lower components vanish within numerical accuracy, demonstrating the correct decoupling of positive- and negative-energy sectors. The TFs preserve the spatial and spin-angular symmetries of their respective initial states. For all nuclear charges @xmath3, the contribution of the initial bound state to the TF exceeds 86% of the total probability density, establishing that the Eriksen transformation maintains a dominant bound-state character after projection. The next largest contribution arises from negative-energy continuum states with energies close to @xmath4, where @xmath5 denotes the binding energy of the initial state, while the cumulative contribution of all remaining states is below @xmath6 of the total probability density. The near-vanishing of the other spinor components further corroborates both the validity of the Eriksen transformation and the accuracy of the numerical implementation. In the nonrelativistic limit, the TFs of the @xmath0 and @xmath1 states are close to the hydrogenic @xmath7 and @xmath8 states, respectively, whereas the TF of the @xmath2 state differs qualitatively from @xmath8. Functions obtained via a linearized Eriksen transformation, equivalent to the second-order Foldy–Wouthuysen transformation, are compared with the exact Eriksen TFs and show very good agreement across the tested @xmath3 domain.

We compute the complete one-loop corrections to the Wilson coefficient of the kinetic operator in the operator product expansion for the differential semileptonic B→X_clν decay rate. Using analytic matching and renormalization in the heavy-quark expansion, we quantify the impact on experimentally relevant spectral moments with a moderate cut on the charged-lepton energy. The one-loop terms modify the kinetic-operator contributions to lepton-energy and hadronic-mass moments by about ten percent, amounting to small shifts in most observables, but producing sizable effects for moments that vanish at leading order. We provide compact formulas suitable for global fits and study scheme and scale dependence, showing perturbative stability. Combined with the existing two-loop calculation of the leading-power rate and the one-loop corrections to the chromo-magnetic operator, our results enable a high-precision determination of |V_cb| and of the b- and c-quark masses from inclusive data. Numerical illustrations and uncertainty estimates are presented, highlighting reduced theoretical errors in semileptonic B-decay phenomenology and improved global constraints.

We study exclusive @xmath0 and @xmath1 reactions at high energies within the tensor pomeron model. Using an effective field-theoretic formulation, we construct amplitudes with explicit spin structures. For the @xmath0 process, we consider both diffractive and photoproduction mechanisms and include the non-resonant @xmath2 continuum together with resonances @xmath3, @xmath4, @xmath5, and @xmath6. We discuss how two pomerons couple to the tensor meson @xmath5 and quantify interference between resonances and the dipion continuum. The relative contributions of @xmath6, @xmath7, and the continuum are shown to depend strongly on cuts on proton transverse momenta. For exclusive central @xmath8 production we incorporate channels proceeding via intermediate @xmath9 and @xmath10 states, including soft survival factors. Theoretical results are compared to available experimental data and used to predict outcomes for planned or ongoing measurements (e.g., STAR, ATLAS–ALFA) at RHIC and the LHC. We present differential distributions and polarization observables that can discriminate production mechanisms and constrain tensor-pomeron couplings.

We analyze conformations of a short closed DNA segment modeled as a cylindrically symmetric elastic rod subject to a fixed linking-number constraint. Using variational mechanics and integrable reductions of the Kirchhoff equations, we derive analytic expressions for families of spatial configurations that continuously interpolate from the planar circular state to a figure-eight state marking the onset of interwinding. The framework also generates knotted loops within the same constraint class. We evaluate stability via second-variation criteria, identify parameter regimes for buckling and bifurcation, and quantify fluctuation corrections to the free energy using normal-mode analysis. The approach suggests constructive pathways to other biologically relevant configurations and offers insight into how torsional stress and thermal noise shape closed-DNA morphologies.

We study directional dependence in high-redshift supernova data using a statistic previously introduced in the literature. Such dependence may reflect departures from the cosmological principle or direction-dependent systematics. We apply the method to the Gold supernova samples and the Union2 catalogue. Across three data sets we find a weak but consistent directional signal. Error distributions in the 2007 Gold compilation are compatible with Gaussianity, whereas the other two data sets exhibit non-Gaussian features. These results quantify potential anisotropies and systematics impacting distance moduli, inform constraints on cosmological parameters, and motivate improved treatment of survey inhomogeneities in large-scale structure and supernova cosmology.

We present an off-lattice statistical thermodynamic model for a single polymer chain in a mixed solvent, formulated within self-consistent field theory that incorporates polymer conformational entropy, renormalization of local solvent composition near the backbone, universal excluded-volume repulsion, and van der Waals attractions. To resolve the coupling between chain conformation and solvent mixing, the system volume is partitioned into two subdomains: an inner domain occupied by the polymer (including its solvation shell) and the bulk solution. Enforcing equilibrium of chemical potentials and pressure between these subvolumes yields a solvation free energy expressed in terms of the chain’s radius of gyration and the co-solvent mole fraction within the inner domain. Minimization of this free energy with respect to both arguments produces a unified description of co-nonsolvency, the reentrant coil–globule–coil transition observed upon varying co-solvent composition. This yields phase diagrams in temperature–composition space with critical thresholds and coexistence boundaries. The theory predicts two qualitatively distinct regimes. At sufficiently high temperatures, the reentrant transition is continuous, with variations of the radius of gyration and the inner-domain composition. Below a threshold temperature, the coil–globule transition becomes first order, characterized by discontinuous jumps in chain size and local co-solvent fraction, manifesting as abrupt changes in composition space. Analysis of the decomposed free-energy contributions reveals that polymer collapse is driven by a concurrent, sharp increase in both enthalpic and entropic terms, demonstrating that co-nonsolvency originates from enthalpy–entropy compensation rather than a purely energetic or entropic mechanism. From first principles, our framework rationalizes earlier molecular dynamics observations of enthalpic–entropic interplay and reproduces the qualitative temperature dependence of the solution heat-capacity change upon polymer solvation. In particular, predicted heat-capacity signatures align with differential scanning calorimetry measurements for poly(N‐isopropylacrylamide) in aqueous methanol. The model provides transparent physical insight, bridges simulation and experiment, and offers a tractable basis for predicting mixed-solvent effects on single-chain thermoresponsive behavior across temperatures and compositions.

Pairings are bilinear maps, and by the universal property of the tensor product every pairing factors as a group homomorphism out of a tensor product. Building on this observation, we develop an elliptic-curve-free framework for pairings on arbitrary abelian groups and modules. We make the tensorial viewpoint explicit by computing tensor products of finite abelian groups and by identifying structural criteria for the existence and quality of pairings. Central to our approach is the canonical bilinear map A × B → A ⊗ B; we show that the feasibility of constructing non-degenerate (left-, right-, or perfect) pairings hinges on the non-degeneracy of this universal map. In particular, for any finite abelian group G and any finite abelian group H, we establish general existence results for pairings G × H → T with natural targets such as the character group Hom(H, Q/Z) or groups of roots of unity, obtained via group duality. We propose new constructions that exploit duality, annihilators, and quotient structures, yielding practical recipes to engineer non-degenerate pairings beyond elliptic curves. Our results unify and extend pairing theory across abelian groups, clarify when perfect pairings exist, and provide explicit computational tools for finite cases. Mathematics Subject Classification (2010): 15A69, 11E39.

We review dynamical symmetry breaking driven by strong gauge dynamics with a large fermion mass anomalous dimension, providing a unified introduction to tightly bound composite Higgs frameworks such as walking technicolor, strong extended technicolor, and the top-quark condensate. Emphasis is placed on how near-conformal (“walking”) behavior and nontrivial short-distance dynamics in gauged Nambu–Jona-Lasinio (gauged NJL) models—gauge theories supplemented by four-fermion interactions—generate an enhanced anomalous dimension that reshapes operator scaling, amplifies condensates, and naturally addresses flavor hierarchies and flavor-changing constraints. We highlight the critical phenomenon of the gauged NJL system, characterized by a Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless–type transition, which yields a simple and robust rationale for the exceptionally large top-quark mass relative to other fermions within top-condensation scenarios. We further discuss the recent observation that, unlike the purely four-fermion NJL theory, the four-fermion sector becomes renormalizable and nontrivial in the presence of gauge interactions, admitting a continuum limit associated with ultraviolet fixed structures. Applying the requirement of renormalizability and nontriviality to top condensation embedded in a grand unified framework with walking gauge couplings, we show that electroweak symmetry breaking can emerge dynamically with predictive power, naturally pointing to top and Higgs masses of order 180 GeV. The analysis synthesizes Schwinger–Dyson dynamics, renormalization-group flows, and phenomenological constraints, and outlines implications for precision electroweak observables, compositeness scales, and collider tests. We conclude with prospects for lattice studies and ultraviolet completions of near-conformal dynamics.

We investigate the gravitational collapse of rotating thin shells in three-dimensional Einstein gravity with and without a cosmological constant. The interior and exterior spacetimes are taken to be stationary and asymptotically of constant curvature (anti–de Sitter, de Sitter, or flat). Employing the Darmois–Israel junction conditions in a co-rotating frame, we derive exact equations of motion that reduce the problem to an effective radial dynamics governed by the ADM masses, total angular momentum, cosmological constant, and the shell’s equation of state. The co-rotating formulation eliminates discontinuities in the shift vector, yields a conserved angular momentum parameter, and enables a transparent characterization of collapse trajectories across a broad parameter space. For arbitrary angular momentum, we find a rich spectrum of end states. Depending on initial radius and velocity, and on the relative interior/exterior parameters, collapsing shells can form a BTZ black hole (for negative cosmological constant), a three-dimensional Kerr–de Sitter spacetime (for positive cosmological constant), or a horizonless geometry corresponding to spinning point masses (including conical defects). For pressureless dust shells, nonzero angular momentum generically generates a centrifugal barrier near the origin that prevents the formation of curvature singularities, leading to bounce behaviors or delayed collapse into a horizon when permitted by the parameters. In contrast, when the shell pressure is nonvanishing, we show that broad classes of polytropic-type equations of state—including perfect fluids and generalized Chaplygin gases—can overcome the angular momentum barrier. Under generic initial conditions, these shells can collapse to naked singularities in asymptotically AdS, dS, and flat backgrounds. We delineate the phase structure and thresholds for horizon formation versus censorship violation as functions of mass, spin, and equation-of-state parameters. We conclude that in three dimensions angular momentum does not, in general, protect cosmic censorship: while it shields dust shells, pressureful rotating shells can still produce naked singularities. PACS: 04.20.Dw, 04.40.-b, 04.60.Kz, 04.70.Bw.

We introduce a nonparametric transformation framework based on Mallows distance to quantify and test location and variance differences between two samples. The method decomposes inter-group disparity into optimal shift-and-scale components, requires no parametric assumptions, and is supported by a convexity theory that ensures uniqueness, stability, and efficient computation. We further show how analogous procedures arise under alternative discrepancy measures, including the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, yielding flexible tools for heterogeneous distributions. Asymptotic properties and inference (estimation, hypothesis tests, confidence intervals) are established, and simulations benchmark performance against classical metrics (mean, median, sample standard deviation). Applications to real datasets demonstrate robustness, interpretability, and improved sensitivity to distributional changes. Keywords: Mallows distance; shift-and-scale; Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance.

We analyze the duration of the unbiased Avoider–Enforcer game played on the edge set of the complete graph with @xmath0 vertices, under three natural targets for Avoider: keeping his claimed-edge graph outerplanar, diamond-free, and @xmath1-degenerate. While each game is an Enforcer win, our focus is the largest number of moves Avoider can make before inevitably losing. Using extremal graph theory, we obtain general upper bounds for the allowable length, and we complement them with explicit strategies that achieve lower bounds within an additive constant of optimal. Specifically, we design a strategy that allows Avoider to maintain outerplanarity for at least @xmath2 moves, only @xmath3 short of the maximum possible. For the diamond-free game, noting that a diamond-free graph on @xmath0 vertices has at most @xmath4 edges, we prove that Avoider can safely play for at least @xmath5 moves. Finally, when @xmath1 is small compared to @xmath0, we show that Avoider can keep his graph @xmath1-degenerate for as many as @xmath6 moves, where @xmath6 equals the maximum edge count of a @xmath1-degenerate graph. Our constructions yield asymptotically tight duration bounds across these settings and illuminate how structural constraints can be preserved against optimal opposition in unbiased positional games, under standard play assumptions.

We present 350 μm dust continuum maps of fifty-one dense cores associated with water masers, selected for their very high luminosities, @xmath0, indicative of ongoing or imminent massive star formation. For each source we provide contour maps, radial intensity profiles, and calibrated photometry. The submillimeter dust emission peak is, on average, nearly coincident with the water maser position, reinforcing the close spatial association between masing activity and dense, warm envelope material. For a subset of 31 sources, we modeled spectral energy distributions and normalized radial profiles using a one-dimensional dust radiative transfer code, assuming a power-law density distribution in the envelope, @xmath1. The best-fit density power-law exponent, @xmath2, spans 0.75–2.5 with @xmath3, consistent with the mean value reported by Beuther et al. (2002) for a large sample of massive star-forming regions. The mean @xmath2 is comparable to that inferred in regions forming only low-mass stars, yet @xmath4 is more than two orders of magnitude larger for these massive cores, highlighting fundamentally different energetic and mass throughput regimes. The mean @xmath2 disfavors a logatropic sphere (with @xmath2 = 1), although other collapse or turbulence-regulated star formation models cannot be excluded. We compare mass estimates derived from the radiative transfer fits, standard submillimeter flux–based methods, and temperature-dependent conversions, and report mean gas and dust masses within the half-power radius defined by the dust emission, @xmath5 = 2.0 @xmath6 0.6, and within the radius at which the total density exceeds @xmath7, @xmath8. We evaluate evolutionary diagnostics commonly used for low-mass protostars, such as @xmath9, and find they may retain utility in the massive regime, with appropriate caveats. Finally, adopting a methodology parallel to extragalactic studies, we compute the luminosity-to-dust-mass ratio, @xmath10 /, for these cores; the resulting values are comparable to those measured in high-redshift starburst galaxies. These results support centrally condensed, luminous envelopes around water-maser cores and provide quantitative constraints for models of massive star formation and for bridging Galactic and extragalactic star-forming environments.

We present new results on the HESS J1731−347/SNR G353.6−0.7 system from XMM-Newton and Suzaku X-ray observations, complemented by Delinha CO observations. We discover extended, hard X-ray emission that is spatially coincident with both the bright, extended TeV source HESS J1731−347 and the radio shell of the supernova remnant. Spatially resolved X-ray spectra extracted from multiple regions across the shell are generally well described by an absorbed power-law model with a photon index Γ ≈ 2, characteristic of non-thermal emission from shock-accelerated particles. A bright, compact X-ray source, XMMU J173203−344518, is detected near the geometric center of the remnant. We find no evidence for a radio counterpart or for extended X-ray morphology associated with this source, disfavoring an interpretation as a pulsar wind nebula. Its X-ray spectrum is well fit by an absorbed blackbody with temperature kT ≈ 0.5 keV plus a steep power-law tail, reminiscent of the spectral properties of magnetars. CO observations toward the inner part of the HESS source reveal a bright molecular cloud component at a local standard of rest velocity of approximately −20 km s−1. Kinematic considerations place this cloud at a distance of about 3.2 kpc, consistent with the estimated distance to the SNR. The morphological correspondence between the molecular material and the high-energy emission, together with the likely association between the X-ray and γ-ray components, suggests that the extended TeV emission originates from the interaction of the SNR shock with adjacent CO clouds rather than from a pulsar wind nebula powered by the central X-ray source. These results identify HESS J1731−347 as a shell-type accelerator and highlight the crucial role of the surrounding molecular environment in shaping its broadband high-energy phenomenology.

Massive binary black holes (BBHs) formed in galactic mergers are widely expected to stall once their separation shrinks to parsec–sub-parsec scales, where stellar dynamical friction becomes inefficient—the so-called final parsec problem. We propose and analyze a natural gas-driven pathway that enables such BBHs to coalesce within a Hubble time via coupled evolution with a “triple-disk” configuration: an accretion disk around each black hole and a circumbinary disk that feeds them. In this framework, the circumbinary disk removes the BBH’s orbital angular momentum through binary–disk resonant torques, while mass transfer from the circumbinary disk to the individual accretion disks adds angular momentum back to the binary orbit by delivering gas with nonzero specific angular momentum. We derive a critical mass-transfer rate at which these opposing effects exactly balance. Below this critical rate, the net torque leads to a monotonic decay of the semi-major axis and a secular growth of orbital eccentricity; above it, the semi-major axis expands and eccentricity damps. The characteristic evolutionary timescale is set by the product of the circumbinary disk’s viscous timescale and the ratio of the BBH total mass to the circumbinary disk mass, encapsulating the efficiency of angular momentum extraction relative to the available gas reservoir. Evaluating the parameter space relevant to massive galactic nuclei, we find that the minimum critical mass-transfer rate required to stall or reverse inspiral generally exceeds the Eddington accretion rate for black hole masses in the ~10^6–10^9 solar mass range when the desired evolutionary timescale is shorter than a Hubble time. Consequently, in typical gas-limited environments the actual mass-transfer rate is expected to remain sub-critical, ensuring continued angular momentum removal, shrinking separations, and eccentricity excitation until gravitational-wave emission dominates. This mechanism therefore robustly drives most massive BBHs across the final parsec barrier, leading to prompt coalescence on cosmological timescales. Our results predict that BBHs entering gravitational-wave bands may retain significant eccentricities, with implications for detection strategies by space-based interferometers and pulsar timing arrays. The proposed triple-disk coupling offers a unified, physically motivated solution to the final parsec problem and provides testable electromagnetic signatures, including periodic accretion variability and characteristic line profiles arising from circumbinary streams and mini-disks in gas-rich galactic nuclei.

We present an analysis of bolometric luminosities and ultraviolet (UV) extinction properties for more than 200 spectroscopically identified, optically selected star-forming galaxies in the GOODS-North field, leveraging very deep Spitzer MIPS 24 μm observations. The rest-UV-selected sample is complemented by photometrically identified near-IR-selected BzK and DRG galaxies and submillimeter sources at similar redshifts in the same field, providing a representative census of relatively massive galaxies at high redshift. We focus on the redshift interval z ≈ 1.5–2.6, for which the observed 24 μm band probes the rest-frame mid-IR around 8 μm and directly traces the strength of prominent PAH emission features. For objects with precise spectroscopic redshifts, the rest-frame 8 μm luminosities are particularly well constrained, enabling robust inferences of total infrared (IR) luminosity and star-formation rate (SFR). Using stacked X-ray observations and a subset of galaxies with Hα measurements to validate our calibrations, we demonstrate that the rest-frame 8 μm luminosity provides a reliable estimator of the bolometric IR luminosity (integrated over 8–1000 μm) for the majority of star-forming galaxies at z ~ 2, and thus a robust proxy for SFR in this regime. Across the optical/near-IR-selected samples, we find total IR luminosities spanning approximately 10^10–10^12 L⊙, with a mean of order 10^11 L⊙. The luminous infrared galaxy (LIRG) population at z ~ 2 largely overlaps with galaxies selected via their optical/near-IR colors, indicating that the bulk of vigorous star formation at these epochs is hosted by typical UV/optically selected systems rather than being confined to rare, extreme submillimeter sources. Objects with LIRG to ultraluminous IR galaxy (ULIRG) luminosities are found across the full range of stellar masses in our samples, from ~10^9.5 to ~10^11.5 M⊙, underscoring that intense star-forming episodes are not restricted to the most massive systems. We use the MIPS 24 μm data to independently assess dust extinction at high redshift and show that, as in the local universe, obscuration correlates strongly with bolometric luminosity. Within our sample, the IR-to-UV luminosity ratio (a measure of obscuration) spans more than two orders of magnitude. However, the average obscuration at fixed bolometric luminosity (or SFR) is lower at z ~ 2 than at z ~ 0 by a factor of ≈2–3, implying that similar levels of attenuation occur at correspondingly higher luminosities at early times. Estimates of total IR luminosity and obscuration derived from the UV spectral slope (β) generally agree well with those inferred from the mid-IR for systems with L_IR ≲ 10^12 L⊙. For ULIRGs (L_IR ≳ 10^12 L⊙), UV-based methods commonly underpredict the bolometric output by factors of ~3–5, consistent with heavy dust obscuration hiding substantial star formation. Finally, using the specific SFR (SFR per unit stellar mass) as a proxy for cold gas fraction, we find a broad range of evolutionary states among z ~ 2 galaxies, from systems just commencing significant star formation to those that have already assembled most of their stellar mass and are transitioning to passive evolution. These results highlight the utility of mid-IR observations for quantifying star formation and dust in the high-redshift universe and reveal an evolving relationship between luminosity, obscuration, and galaxy growth.

We present a first-principles numerical investigation of the real-time dynamics of electromagnetically interacting, chirally imbalanced lattice Dirac fermions within the classical-statistical field theory framework. The fermionic sector is evolved exactly using the Wilson–Dirac Hamiltonian, while the U(1) gauge field is described by a non-compact action and coupled self-consistently to the vacuum expectation value of the fermionic electric current. This setup enables us to resolve the interplay between anomaly-induced transport, screening, and backreaction far from equilibrium. We find that the dynamical backreaction of the fermions on the electromagnetic field generically prevents the system from building up a sustained chirality imbalance. During chirality pumping by parallel electric and magnetic fields, the electric field becomes efficiently screened by on-shell fermion production, arresting the accumulation of axial charge. For evolutions initiated with a finite chirality imbalance, axial charge is dynamically transferred into electromagnetic helicity. Simulations on large lattices reveal that this decay is often accompanied by an inverse cascade that moves energy from short- to long-wavelength electromagnetic modes, producing long-lived helical magnetic fields. Strikingly, in a subset of runs we observe a robust inverse cascade without a concomitant decay of axial charge, indicating that the relation between helicity generation and axial charge dissipation is more subtle than suggested by the simplest anomalous Maxwell equations. Our results demonstrate the importance of self-consistent fermion backreaction in real-time anomaly dynamics and provide quantitative benchmarks for effective descriptions of chiral plasmas and magnetohydrodynamic evolution in extreme conditions.

Cygnus OB2 is one of the nearest and largest associations of massive stars and lies at the heart of the Cygnus X complex of star-forming regions. Its distance has remained uncertain because kinematic distances along this sightline are degenerate and extinction is heavy and patchy. To refine the three-dimensional geometry of key Cygnus X constituents, we obtained distances to four eclipsing, double-lined OB-type spectroscopic binaries—MT91 372, MT91 696, CPR2002 A36, and Schulte 3—that are probable Cyg OB2 members. By jointly modeling radial-velocity and multiband light curves with atmosphere-based surface brightness relations, we derive individual distances that are consistent and adopt a weighted mean of 1.33 ± 0.06 kpc. This distance agrees with recent spectrophotometric estimates and with VLBI parallax measurements of protostellar masers in adjacent molecular clouds, linking ongoing star formation in those clouds to Cyg OB2. We also identify Schulte 3C (O9.5 V), the 4′′ visual companion to the 4.75-day binary Schulte 3, as a previously unrecognized association member. Our results sharpen the distance scale of Cygnus X and anchor extinction mapping and massive-star feedback studies.

We analyze @xmath0 ks of Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer observations of the neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary and atoll source 636 acquired over nearly three years (April 1996–February 1999). The color–color diagram (CD) and hardness–intensity diagram (HID) reveal significant secular displacements of the atoll track, reminiscent of behavior seen in some Z sources. These secular shifts are most pronounced in the HID, where intensity offsets up to @xmath1 are observed. We show that the intensity shifts in the HID account for the “parallel tracks” seen in the kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillation (kHz QPO) frequency versus intensity relation: the kHz QPO frequency correlates with intensity within individual intervals, but long-term intensity offsets produce parallel, displaced correlations. In the frequency versus color plane the tracks partially overlap, yet systematic long-term shifts remain detectable. We further examine broad-band power spectra as a function of source position @xmath2 along the CD track. Across the full range of @xmath2, the timing properties are characteristic of the lower and upper banana states of atoll sources, exhibiting very low-frequency noise (VLFN), band-limited noise (BLN), and occasionally one or two kHz QPOs. In several intervals the VLFN is not well described by a single power law due to excess power between 20 and 30 mHz; this excess is well modeled by an additional Lorentzian component. The characteristic frequency of the BLN shows a trend to decrease with increasing @xmath2 at high @xmath2 values, indicating longer characteristic timescales toward softer, higher-intensity states. These results connect long-term secular motion to apparent parallel-track phenomena and refine the phenomenology of VLFN and BLN across the banana states, offering constraints on the evolution of the accretion flow and boundary layer in atoll sources.

We investigate superconductivity of quasi-one-dimensional electrons under a magnetic field, modeled as one-dimensional electrons without orbital frustration. Nearest-chain attractive interactions are assumed, yielding nodal lines in the zero-field gap. The applied field modifies the effective pairing through its dependence on field strength and transverse momentum. Within this framework we derive the field-dependent pairing kernel and compute transition temperatures for spin-singlet and spin-triplet channels. We find that increasing magnetic field enhances the effective interchain coupling anisotropically, producing an oscillatory dependence of the triplet transition temperature associated with quantized transverse momenta, while the singlet transition temperature grows monotonically with field. The results delineate regimes where singlet pairing dominates and suggest experimental signatures in organic conductors and other quasi-one-dimensional materials under strong fields.

We analyze neuronal spike trains from behaving monkeys’ visual cortex using a spatio-temporal adaptive penalized spline model. We present, to our knowledge, the first three-dimensional locally adaptive smoothing framework extending P-splines to jointly model space, time, and stimulus dynamics, enabling reconstruction of visual receptive fields, preserving sharp features. Estimation employs the Separation of Overlapping Penalties (SOP) algorithm, delivering numerical stability and speed-ups for large bases. Applications to experimental datasets show improved fit, predictive accuracy, and uncertainty quantification versus nonadaptive or smoothed alternatives, revealing anisotropic response patterns. The methodology facilitates mapping of neural dynamics in natural behavior.

We analyze the response function of an Unruh–DeWitt detector undergoing time-dependent acceleration along a one-dimensional trajectory in Minkowski spacetime. To extract the underlying physics and provide estimators of excitation, we develop an adiabatic expansion of the response, ordered by time derivatives of the acceleration (jerk, snap, and higher). This systematic framework yields the instantaneous click rate for general trajectories and clarifies departures from uniform acceleration. At leading order, the spectrum is Planckian with an effective temperature proportional to the detector’s instantaneous acceleration, reproducing the Unruh result locally. Successive orders introduce controlled corrections in powers of the derivatives, with well-behaved, computable spectral coefficients that encode non-adiabatic effects and modify the high- and low-frequency tails. We illustrate the method on a trajectory that is initially inertial and attains a fixed acceleration over a finite switching time, demonstrating convergence, the transient build-up of thermality, and quantitative criteria for adiabaticity.

Coronal loops, the basic building blocks of active regions, are primary sites for diagnosing coronal heating. Despite advances in observations and theory, their fundamental thermal structure and heating distribution remain poorly constrained. We report unprecedented observations of accelerating slow magnetoacoustic waves propagating along a coronal loop, exhibiting differential phase speeds in two extreme-ultraviolet temperature channels. The measured speed disparity reveals a multi-stranded, multi-thermal loop, and, when combined with nonlinear force-free magnetic field extrapolations to obtain the field-aligned path length, enables determination of the temperature variation along the loop in both channels. We resolve, for the first time, two individual thermal components of a multi-thermal loop and retrieve positive temperature gradients with height in each component. These gradients imply quasi-uniform heating along the loop, rather than concentrated footpoint heating, and provide stringent constraints for coronal heating models. Our results showcase coronal seismology as a tool to disentangle multi-thermal structuring in active-region loops.

We investigate photon diffusion in a two-dimensional random packing of monodisperse disks as a model for granular media and wet foams. Applying the formula to glass beads immersed in air or water, we obtain transport-mean-free paths that are approximately half of reported experimental values, indicating the role of dimensionality and microstructural heterogeneity beyond idealized assumptions. For air bubbles dispersed in water, the predicted @xmath3 varies linearly with @xmath4, where @xmath5 denotes the liquid volume fraction in the model wet foam, providing a mechanistic basis for the empirical law of Vera et al. (Applied Optics 40, 4210, 2001). These results clarify scaling relations in turbid media and support the development of more realistic optical transport models.

We develop a relativistic light-front formulation of nuclear dynamics and apply it to infinite nuclear matter by incorporating two-nucleon correlations within a Brueckner framework. Starting from a hadronic meson–baryon Lagrangian consistent with chiral symmetry, we derive a light-front one-boson-exchange nucleon–nucleon potential (OBEP) and solve the associated scattering equation to benchmark against NN data. The resulting description of phase shifts and deuteron observables is comparable in quality to relativistic OBEP models, validating the light-front construction. Within the same formalism we obtain the Hartree–Fock and Brueckner–Hartree–Fock equations appropriate for infinite matter. Using the light-front OBEP in these equations, we reproduce nuclear matter saturation properties in a reasonable manner and predict a compressibility of 180 MeV, noticeably smaller than values typical of alternative relativistic approaches that tend to overestimate incompressibility. Because the derivation begins from a meson–baryon Lagrangian, we demonstrate that replacing explicit meson degrees of freedom by a nucleon–nucleon interaction is a controlled approximation. The light-front framework provides a systematic expansion that enables organized evaluation of corrections beyond the OBEP. A key advantage is the simplicity of the light-front vacuum, which streamlines the derivations and avoids spurious vacuum contributions. We also compute the mesonic Fock-space components of the nuclear wave function and determine the plus-momentum distributions of nucleons and mesons in matter. The analysis reveals a modest enhancement of the pion content, corresponding to approximately 0.05 excess pions per nucleon. These results establish light-front Brueckner theory as a practical and internally consistent relativistic approach to correlated nuclear matter and offer a basis for future extensions to finite nuclei and dynamical observables.

We derive a cavity-modified master equation for a coherently driven V-type three-level atom coupled to a single-mode cavity in the bad-cavity limit. When the cavity is resonant with an atomic dressed-state transition, the atom–cavity interaction is enhanced, enabling steady-state population inversion in both the bare and dressed bases. Within the dressed-state framework, we express the populations in terms of cavity-modified transition rates and identify regimes of cavity-assisted pumping and interference-controlled decay. We calculate the atomic fluorescence and weak-probe absorption spectra, showing that their profiles can be tuned by the cavity frequency: Autler–Townes-like splittings shift with detuning, while selective peak suppression and line narrowing arise near dressed-state resonance under suitable drive and decay asymmetries. These results enable inversion and spectral engineering via dissipative cavity control.

IP anycast routes packets to the topologically nearest server according to BGP proximity. Historically, UDP-based, single request–response services such as DNS resolvers and multicast rendezvous points have been first adopters, while a prevailing belief in the Internet measurements community holds that stateful services cannot safely run atop anycast due to path instabilities. In this paper we provide a first look at the nature and dynamics of anycast-enabled Content Delivery Networks (A-CDNs), shedding light on their deployment and operational characteristics. Our methodology combines active and passive measurements. Building on prior work, we use active probes to detect anycast usage among servers hosting popular websites and to geolocate A-CDN caches. We then characterize traffic to A-CDNs in the wild using a month-long dataset collected passively from a large European ISP. We analyze service mix, protocol usage, client reach, and route stability. Our results show that major A-CDNs, including Cloudflare and EdgeCast, routinely serve popular web content over TCP, challenging assumptions about anycast’s suitability for stateful services. A-CDN servers are contacted by users on a daily basis across diverse regions, indicating mainstream adoption. Contrary to the instability hypothesis, BGP routes to A-CDN servers exhibit high stability over time, with few changes observed at the ISP vantage point. These findings suggest that carefully engineered anycast deployments can support stateful, latency-sensitive web workloads and highlight the need to revisit measurement methodologies and operational guidelines for anycast-based content delivery.

We adapt an anelastic spectral code to simulate a stratified, turbulent convective layer with imposed external shear representative of tidal forcing. We derive the governing anelastic equations for compressible, low-Mach-number hydrodynamics, describe the pseudo-spectral spatial discretization and semi-implicit time-integration scheme, and present verification tests of accuracy, stability, and energy conservation. Using controlled shear perturbations, we compute the turbulent response and apply a perturbative framework to estimate the effective eddy viscosity as a function of forcing frequency. The resulting scaling exhibits a transition between low- and high-frequency regimes, with magnitudes consistent with estimates. Comparison with an independent, realistic simulation of the upper solar convective zone shows general agreement in amplitude and frequency dependence, supporting the use of anelastic spectral methods for modeling turbulent dissipation of shear in stratified convection.

This paper revisits algebraic subspace clustering (ASC), a simple approach based on polynomial fitting and differentiation, which succeeds on noiseless data drawn from unions of subspaces but breaks down when subspace dimensions are unequal and noise perturbs algebraic estimators. We introduce a new ASC algorithm that accommodates noisy observations from subspaces of arbitrary dimensions. The method constructs, for each point, a decreasing sequence of subspaces containing the true subspace through that point, and defines an affinity between points by aggregating their distances to each subspace in the sequence. This distance-based affinity attenuates noise, avoids explicit dimension estimation, and yields sharper within-subspace connectivity and cross-subspace separation than existing algebraic, sparse, or low-rank affinities. We provide theoretical guarantees on affinity separation and robustness to noise. We demonstrate consistent gains in clustering accuracy on the Hopkins 155 motion segmentation benchmark, outperforming sparse and low-rank subspace clustering baselines while remaining computationally simple.

We investigate the surface intermetallic cept@xmath0/pt(111) by x-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) together with its linear (XLD) and circular (XMCD) magnetic dichroisms to quantify the key local interactions and energy scales that govern its low-temperature behavior. The combined spectroscopies provide element- and symmetry-selective access to the Ce 4f configuration, enabling us to determine the crystal-field level scheme, effective paramagnetic moments, their Kondo screening, and the evolution of mutual interactions. By exploiting the tunability of the Ce valence via thickness-dependent epitaxial strain at the cept@xmath0/pt(111) interface, we systematically vary the 4f–conduction-electron hybridization strength and assess its impact on these energy scales. Pronounced Kondo screening is observed for all investigated cept@xmath0 thicknesses and is strongest where hybridization is maximal. For specimen temperatures @xmath2 K, the magnetic response is consistent with an impurity Kondo scale of order @xmath1 K. At lower temperatures, however, this single-impurity description breaks down. A detailed XMCD study at a representative thickness reveals a distinct anomaly in the susceptibility at @xmath3 K, which we tentatively attribute to the onset of lattice coherence in the emergent heavy-fermion state. Upon further cooling, we observe paramagnetic saturation characterized by a small Ce @xmath4 saturation magnetization. Interpreted within an itinerant @xmath4-electron framework, this saturation arises from a field-induced Lifshitz transition involving an ultraheavy band with a correspondingly low degeneracy temperature of @xmath5 K. Our results establish XLD/XMCD as powerful, largely underutilized probes of Kondo screening, crystal-field anisotropy, and coherence in correlated 4f systems, and they demonstrate strain- and valence-control as effective routes to tuning hybridization in surface intermetallics.

We present 350 @xmath0 m photometry for all 17 galaxy candidates in the Lockman Hole identified in a 1.1 mm Bolocam survey, enabling direct constraints on their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) near the thermal peak. Nine Bolocam candidates are detected at 350 @xmath0 m, and two additional galaxies are serendipitously detected at 350 @xmath0 m, bringing the number of serendipitous 350 @xmath0 m detections in the literature to three. Five galaxies have published spectroscopic redshifts, allowing tests of photometric redshift techniques and derivation of dust temperature ranges. Because 350 @xmath0 m lies near the SED peak for @xmath2 thermally emitting galaxies, we can measure luminosities without extrapolating from longer-wavelength detections at @xmath3 850 @xmath0 m. The derived infrared luminosities are characteristically in the range @xmath4 l@xmath5, with dust temperatures between 40 K and 70 K, depending on the adopted spectral index and the wavelength at which optical depth reaches unity. We investigate the structure of the N*(1440) Roper resonance within a dynamical coupled-channel meson-exchange model of pion–nucleon scattering. The effective coupling to multi-hadron states is implemented through the σN, πΔ, and ρN channels, with interactions within and between channels derived from an effective chiral Lagrangian supplemented by established vertices for the Δ(1232) isobar, the ρ meson, and the scalar–isoscalar ππ correlation (σ). The scattering equations are solved with full channel coupling, unitarity, and analyticity constraints, allowing a consistent description of elastic and inelastic pion–nucleon observables. We find that the Roper resonance emerges dynamically from meson–baryon interactions without the need for a genuine three-quark bare state. The resulting amplitudes reproduce the P11 phase shifts and inelasticities and elucidate the role of correlated two-pion exchange and πΔ thresholds in shaping the Roper pole. Implications for hadronic structure and resonance generation in QCD are discussed. Model uncertainties and fits are detailed.

We investigate how entanglement in bipartite quantum systems shapes wave–particle duality in the neutral-kaon sector. Building on the quantitative “triality” relation of Jakob and Bergou for two qubits, we model free-space propagation of the K0 meson while incorporating its weak decay products as a second party. Using the KS–KL basis and an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, we derive time-dependent expressions for (i) the distinguishability between decay-product states correlated with the two propagation modes, (ii) the visibility of strangeness (path) interference, and (iii) the entanglement between the kaon and its decay environment as quantified by the reduced von Neumann entropy. We prove a new triality inequality that links these three quantities, generalizing the complementarity between strangeness oscillations and lifetime information previously discussed for kaons. The relation clarifies how lifetime tagging functions as a which-path measurement coupled by entanglement, and how entanglement modulates the trade-off between interference and path knowledge. In the ideal limit the inequality is saturated; realistic effects such as small CP violation and decoherence produce controlled departures without invalidating the bound. We further outline experimental scenarios in which the time-resolved oscillations K0–K0bar render the role of entanglement in quantum complementarity directly observable.

We investigate the influence of galaxy interactions on massive star formation using a representative, distance-limited sample of almost 1500 of the nearest galaxies, all within @xmath0 mpc. We define the massive star formation rate (SFR) from far-infrared emission, and the specific star formation rate (SSFR) as SFR normalized by stellar mass, and examine their distributions as functions of morphological type and stellar mass. Control populations are created for each galaxy by matching non-interacting systems in type, mass, distance, and environment; relative enhancements are computed as SFR/SFR_med and SSFR/SSFR_med of the matched controls. We find statistically significant increases in both SFR and SSFR with increasing interaction strength, with median enhancements rising from weakly interacting systems to mergers, where mergers reach a factor of 1.9. Despite this population-level trend, many individual interacting galaxies exhibit little or no enhancement, underscoring the stochastic nature of star formation triggering and the role of internal structure, gas fraction, and orbital geometry. The most extreme enhancements define a robust, interaction-driven starburst subset. The trend is consistent across morphological classes and across stellar mass bins. Our sample includes a large fraction of low-mass and dwarf/irregular galaxies, enabling assessment across the full local mass spectrum. We assess selection effects and derive stellar masses from photometry. The measured, moderate enhancement factors place empirical constraints on merger-driven star formation recipes and should inform interpretations of elevated SFRs in more distant samples, where selection biases and incomplete interaction diagnostics can exaggerate inferred starburst amplitudes.

We study the robustness of nonlinear filters for continuous-time, finite-state Markov chains observed in additive white noise under simultaneous model misspecification. As the misspecified model—comprising the prior, transition rates, and observation function—converges to the true data-generating mechanism, we prove that the misspecified filter approaches the optimal filter uniformly on the infinite time axis. The key estimate controls the filtering error via an exponential bound for the derivative of the nonlinear filter with respect to its initial condition. Under a mixing condition on the signal, this yields uniform convergence in probability and in L1. Misspecification of the initial distribution and of the transition generator is handled by elementary coupling and stability arguments; misspecification of the observation function requires Skorokhod integration and anticipative stochastic calculus. Our results provide quantitative, global-in-time robustness guarantees and clarify which structural assumptions are essential for stability.

In this paper we develop a coherent framework for the Schlesinger system, centered around the tau-function, local factorization of solutions to Fuchsian systems, and holomorphic deformations of their coefficients. We introduce the notion of an isoprincipal deformation: a holomorphic deformation of a Fuchsian system with possibly resonant matrix residues that preserves the principal (Levelt) factors at each singularity. We prove that every isoprincipal deformation yields a solution of the Schlesinger system and is, in particular, isomonodromic. Conversely, we show that in the non-resonant case isomonodromic deformations are automatically isoprincipal, establishing an equivalence between the two notions; in the resonant case we exhibit obstructions and additional gauge freedoms that prevent such an equivalence in general. Our approach is based on a detailed local factorization of fundamental solutions near regular singular points and on a careful analysis of the holomorphic dependence of these factors on deformation parameters. Within this framework we revisit the construction and basic properties of the Jimbo–Miwa–Ueno tau-function, describing its analytic and divisor structure in terms of the pole–zero data of rational matrix functions naturally associated with the system. We also fix a concise notation for the complex plane and sphere, matrix spaces, commutators, identity matrices, and classes of rational matrix-valued functions together with their pole and zero sets, which we use systematically throughout. The techniques developed here—combining local factorization, parameterized Riemann–Hilbert methods, and realization theory for rational matrix functions—prepare the ground for a sequel, where we present an explicit class of rational solutions to the Schlesinger system. These solutions are constructed via state-space realizations and are characterized by transparent algebraic conditions on residues and pole configurations.

We investigate Einstein–aether gravity obtained by modifying the Einstein–Hilbert action through a dynamical unit timelike vector field (the aether). In a spatially flat Friedmann–Robertson–Walker background, we derive the modified Friedmann equations and identify the effective energy density and pressure associated with the aether sector. Under suitable constraints on the free coupling function, these effective quantities can mimic dark energy, with one parameter taken proportional to the Hubble rate or its square. Assuming two power-law scale-factor evolutions (Type I and Type II), we reconstruct the unknown coupling function from holographic dark energy (HDE) and new agegraphic dark energy (NADE), as well as from their entropy-corrected extensions, ECHDE and ECNADE. The corresponding Einstein–aether dark-energy equation-of-state parameter is obtained in each case. For HDE and NADE, the Type I scale factor yields a quintessence-like regime (w > −1), while the Type II scale factor generates a phantom regime (w < −1). In contrast, the entropy-corrected models permit a transition between quintessence and phantom phases for both scale-factor types, enabling phantom crossing. A perturbative analysis indicates that the reconstructed models are classically unstable, as signaled by a negative squared sound speed, and we discuss the implications for their cosmological viability.

Coherent feedback provides a nonmeasurement-based, back-action-free approach to controlling quantum systems. We focus on squeezing enhancement, a nonclassical effect in quantum optics, and report the first experimental demonstration of coherent feedback in this context. Our setup incorporates realistic time delays and optical losses within the loop, and performance agrees well with theory that models these imperfections. The results quantify squeezing improvement, delineate stability and bandwidth constraints, and clarify both the benefits and limitations of coherent feedback for practical quantum control in realistic settings.

We develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework for joint estimation of graphical models across multiple individuals, targeting conditional independence networks that share structure yet exhibit subject-specific differences. The formulation is general and accommodates a variety of model classes, including time-varying and interventional settings. Motivated by biological time-course studies with perturbations, we introduce a computationally efficient deterministic algorithm that achieves exact inference under our hierarchy by exploiting modular likelihoods and conjugate priors. Simulation studies demonstrate that borrowing strength across individuals substantially improves recovery of each subject’s network, enhances detection of between-individual differences, and yields calibrated uncertainty quantification. We further propose scalable approximations based on structured variational objectives and message passing, which preserve accuracy while reducing runtime by orders of magnitude. The methodology provides a principled tool for integrative analysis of multivariate systems and enables reproducible, interpretable network inference in high-dimensional time-series with interventions.

We present a minimal dynamical model for randomly branched, isotropic polymers and analyze it within renormalized field theory. In the swollen phase, our formulation offers an alternative derivation of dimensional-reduction results, clarifying their origin from the dynamics of the model. At the collapse (θ) transition, we uncover a hidden Becchi–Rouet–Stora (BRST) supersymmetry that enforces the dominance of tree configurations, thereby constraining the universal behavior. Exploiting this structure, we correct long-standing one-loop estimates of the critical exponents and extend the calculation to two-loop order. For a second collapse transition, the renormalization-group flow exhibits a runaway, lending support to a fluctuation-induced first-order scenario. The dynamical setting further enables, for the first time, a direct computation of the fractal dimension of the shortest path (chemical distance) on randomly branched polymers in the swollen phase and at collapse, together with related fractal dimensions. Our results provide a unified field-theoretic framework for branched-polymer universality and sharpen quantitative predictions for experiments and simulations, and large-scale numerical benchmarks.

Both cavity QED and photonic qubits are promising candidates for quantum information processing. We combine them by using a single photon to traverse spatially separated, low-Q cavities and entangle embedded atomic qubits via cavity input–output scattering. We derive a general input–output relation for a single atom in a lossy cavity, valid over detunings, couplings, and decay rates, without assuming the strong-coupling regime. Building on this, we design quantum information protocols based on polarization-dependent Faraday rotation, enabling remote entanglement, state transfer, and gate operations with single photons. Our schemes are robust to realistic loss and dephasing, require moderate cooperativity, and are feasible with available technology, without high-Q strong coupling.

X-ray computed tomography (CT) is widely used for medical and dental imaging, yet standard filtered backprojection requires complete projection data; when data are limited or truncated, the inverse problem becomes ill-posed and severe artifacts arise. We study two-dimensional CT reconstruction from horizontally truncated projections with the goal of recovering the entire image, rather than only a region of interest. We introduce a variational framework that couples tight-frame regularization with simultaneous sinogram extrapolation. The image is promoted to be piecewise smooth via analysis sparsity in a data-driven wavelet frame, while the extrapolated sinogram is constrained to be consistent with the forward projection of the evolving image and the measured rays. The resulting nonconvex, nonsmooth optimization is efficiently addressed by a Bregmanized operator splitting algorithm that alternates updates of the image, frame coefficients, and sinogram, with adaptive frame learning tailored to anatomical structures. Numerical experiments on simulated and real CT datasets with severe horizontal truncation demonstrate markedly reduced truncation artifacts, improved recovery of global structures outside the region of interest, higher PSNR and SSIM, and enhanced robustness to noise and model mismatch, outperforming existing sparsity-model-based approaches employing fixed transforms. These findings indicate that joint tight-frame regularization and sinogram extrapolation is a promising strategy for limited tomography.

Using Type Ia supernova data, we determine the three parameters of a power-law expanding universe model with a time-dependent power @xcite. By inputting @xmath0 and @xmath1, we reconstruct the @xmath2 evolution curve, finding that parameter choices @xmath3 and @xmath4 provide an excellent fit to the supernova data. The model yields a transition redshift @xmath5 from deceleration to acceleration. The effective dark energy inferred in this framework exhibits phantom behavior (w<-1), yet the universe avoids a big rip singularity because the total energy density decreases toward a finite minimum. Assuming the parameterized model remains valid in the future, we predict a monotonic decline in cosmic energy density approaching its minimum.

We investigate nucleation in the Ising model on complex networks and quantify how degree heterogeneity shapes the nucleation rate. Combining Monte Carlo simulations with forward flux sampling, we map nucleation kinetics across ensembles with tunable degree distributions and external fields. For weak fields, the nucleation rate decreases monotonically as heterogeneity increases, indicating that hubs suppress critical droplet formation. Under relatively strong fields, however, the rate exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on heterogeneity, attaining a maximum at an intermediate level, revealing competing facilitation and inhibition. To rationalize these trends, we develop a heterogeneous mean-field framework that estimates the free-energy barrier of nucleation across degree classes. The theoretical predictions reproduce the qualitative patterns observed in simulations. Our results demonstrate that degree heterogeneity exerts regime-dependent control on phase transition dynamics in networked Ising systems.

We investigate suppression of unphysical reflections in grid-based simulations of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for strong-field dynamics using exterior complex scaling (ECS) as an absorbing boundary condition. We show that ECS can be implemented consistently in both length and velocity gauges when the electron–field coupling is transformed with suitable restrictions, ensuring gauge consistency and numerical stability. Systematic tests on model atoms driven by intense few-cycle pulses demonstrate that ECS yields markedly lower reflection errors than standard masking (window) functions over wide parameter ranges and for long propagation times. We further show that ECS prevents spurious recollisions that contaminate high-harmonic generation spectra, enabling cleaner plateaus and cutoffs. Practical guidelines for ECS contours and matching regions are provided for routine use.

We compare the observable properties of stellar populations with the structural and dynamical characteristics of dark halos across galaxies, groups, clusters, and voids. Using kinematics, weak lensing, X-ray/SZ measurements of hot gas, and cosmological simulations, we assess how baryons populate and respond to the dominant non-baryonic component. Modern data indicate an overall matter density of @xmath0, with about @xmath1 % in non-baryonic dark matter and about @xmath2 % in baryons, primarily as hot intra-cluster and intragroup gas, with the remainder in the stellar populations of galaxies. All bright galaxies reside within extended dark matter halos of characteristic outer radii ~@xmath3 kpc, composed mostly of non-baryonic matter with a minor hot-gas component. We quantify environment-dependent trends in mass-to-light ratios, baryon fractions, and the stellar-to-halo mass relation, and show that dark matter governs the dynamical evolution of galaxies in groups and clusters, while dark energy (cosmological constant) dominates the global expansion. Stellar populations encode baryonic physics shaped by halo assembly, feedback, and environment.

We derive an explicit formula for the mean spectral measure of a random Jacobi matrix obtained as the infinite-size limit of Gaussian beta ensemble tridiagonal matrices under a fixed-parameter scaling. The mean measure is characterized by its Stieltjes transform, admits a closed-form density, and its moments satisfy a self-convolutive recurrence, enabling efficient computation and asymptotic analysis. Our approach links orthogonal polynomial techniques with random matrix limits and operator theory, yielding precise structural and asymptotic information.

Non-analyticity of QCD with a @xmath0 term at @xmath1 may signal spontaneous breaking of parity and time reversal. We probe this by studying the large-volume limit of the topological susceptibility @xmath2 in pure @xmath3 gauge theory on the lattice. Using simulations across volumes, we analyze scaling of the charge distribution and its cumulants, testing analyticity in @xmath0 and the possibility of a nonvanishing order parameter at @xmath1. We derive an upper bound on the symmetry-breaking order parameter @xmath4 from the volume dependence of @xmath2 and the tunneling rate among topological sectors. As a byproduct, we determine @xmath5 at @xmath6 (@xmath7 fermi).
