The quoted uncertainties are the statistical error from ensembles, the one propagated from the input @xmath8 used for scale setting, and an estimate of systematic effects (finite volume, discretization, topology sampling). Our results support analyticity in @xmath0 at @xmath1 in pure @xmath3 and disfavor P and T breaking in the infinite-volume limit.

We present a systematic first-principles investigation of the recently discovered superconducting Ba_xK_1−xFe2As2 (x = 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00). Prior calculations overestimated the Fe magnetic moment in BaFe2As2; by introducing a negative on-site energy parameter, we obtain a moment of 0.83 μB per Fe, in excellent agreement with experiment (0.87 μB). Potassium substitution increases the density of states at the Fermi level and modulates magnetic instability: it is strengthened at low K content and progressively suppressed with higher doping. We analyze competing magnetic configurations, Fermi-surface evolution, and site-selective K energetics, identifying preferred substitution patterns and their impact on electronic structure, magnetism, and superconducting propensity.

We investigate the photo-stability of pristine and super-hydrogenated pyrene cations by gas-phase action spectroscopy. Optical absorption spectra and photo-induced dissociation mass spectra were recorded for mass-selected ions, and fragment yields were measured as a function of pulsed laser intensity to determine the number of photons—and thus the energy—required to break the carbon backbone. Pristine pyrene (C16H10+) fragments after absorption of three photons of energy just below 3 eV each, hexahydropyrene (C16H16+) after two such photons, and hexadecahydropyrene (C16H26+) after only a single photon. These thresholds align with reported dissociation energies for the corresponding ions. The data show that added hydrogen increases heat capacity but simultaneously weakens the polycyclic carbon framework, so that hydrogenation lowers the multiphoton threshold for backbone cleavage rather than stabilizing it. In photodissociation regions, super-hydrogenated PAHs have been proposed as catalysts for H2 formation; our results imply that carbon backbone fragmentation represents a significant competing channel under UV irradiation, at least for small hydrogenated PAHs like pyrene. The quantitative photon-number thresholds reported here provide constraints for astrochemical models of PAH lifetimes and reactivity and motivate systematic studies across PAH sizes and hydrogenation degrees under interstellar radiation fields.

We report a measurement of the ratio of electron and muon partial widths of the @xmath0 meson using direct @xmath0 -> l+ l- decays recorded with the KEDR detector at the VEPP-4M e+e- collider. The obtained ratio, @xmath1, agrees with lepton universality within uncertainties. Improved event selection, luminosity calibration, and radiative-correction treatment enable future determinations of the @xmath0 leptonic width with ≈1% precision. Results test the Standard Model.

Accurate neutron capture tagging reduces random coincidences in antineutrino detectors and enables capture‐gated spectrometry. We evaluate a composite detector of plastic scintillator with cerium‐doped lithium gadolinium borate crystal shards, millimeter‐scale and comprising a mass fraction. Laboratory tests with thermal neutrons characterize optical transport, timing, and capture signatures. Optical attenuation and scattering are marginal, limiting energy resolution and uniformity, yet capture identification is robust. Distinct delayed, quenched pulses from Li and Gd captures, confirmed by pulse‐shape and timing, provide efficient thermal neutron detection. These results support background suppression and capture‐gated neutron spectrometry, motivating optimization of shard size and loading.

Dynamical generation refers to the emergence of multiple hadronic resonances from a single seed state through hadronic loop effects resummed at the level of s-wave propagators. We investigate this mechanism by analyzing propagator poles in two scalar-resonance settings and assess next-to-leading-order (NLO) corrections to decay amplitudes. First, within a minimal quantum field theory where a scalar seed field S couples to two pions, Dyson-resummed pion loops generate, in addition to the original resonance pole, a second pole on the first Riemann sheet below the two-pion threshold, corresponding to a stable bound state. Second, using the extended linear sigma model (eLSM) as input, we numerically study the pole structure of the isovector scalar a0(1450). In this more realistic framework, no extra pole appears beyond the seed resonance; in particular, an a0(980)-like state does not arise dynamically from a0(1450). Finally, we quantify NLO corrections to the S → ππ decay amplitude and find them to be small despite sizeable effective couplings, indicating that loop hierarchies remain controlled and that leading-order treatments are typically adequate. These results clarify when loop-induced pole doubling can occur and delineate its model dependence.

We present a recursive graphical method for constructing QED Feynman diagrams with their correct multiplicities. The approach begins from the vacuum energy, treated as a functional of the free electron and photon propagators and the interaction, and exploits a functional differential equation it obeys. By successive functional differentiation with respect to the propagators and the interaction, we generate all n‐point functions directly from the vacuum sector. The procedure avoids external sources used in conventional formalisms, yielding an algorithmic derivation of complete diagram sets with verified symmetry factors. Extensions and implementations are discussed.

Building on our general theoretical framework [JETP 112, 246 (2011)], we compute the spatial distribution of atomic excitation in a dense, cold cloud illuminated by weak monochromatic light. The model includes resonant dipole–dipole coupling and the vector character of the electromagnetic field, enabling resolution of excited-state Zeeman sublevel populations across the sample. By varying atomic density and excitation frequency, we map how scattering and cooperative shifts redistribute excitation and modify sublevel occupations. We find that near the cloud boundaries symmetry breaking and anisotropic local fields induce orientation and alignment of the excited-state angular momentum, whereas the interior remains isotropic. Despite entering regimes where the Ioffe–Regel criterion for strong localization is fulfilled, the vectorial treatment shows no signatures of Anderson localization: excitation profiles are extended and lack confinement. In contrast, a scalar approximation to the dipole–dipole interaction yields strong localization under comparable conditions, underscoring the role of vector and near-field couplings.

We investigate potential Lorentz symmetry violations in gravity within the Standard-Model Extension (SME), focusing on nonminimal operators that modify short-range interactions. Using recently analyzed short-range gravity data from two independent experimental groups operating at micrometer distances, we search for SME-induced deviations from Newtonian gravity, including anisotropic and distance-dependent corrections. A comprehensive likelihood analysis reveals no evidence of Lorentz violation, yielding null results across all tested channels. The absence of a signal translates into stringent, model-independent bounds on nonminimal SME coefficients, improving existing limits by up to orders of magnitude and constraining the accessible parameter space for gravitational Lorentz violation.

The Gottesman–Knill theorem shows that stabilizer circuits—quantum circuits built solely from CNOT, Hadamard, and phase gates—can be efficiently simulated on a classical computer. This paper strengthens that theorem along four complementary axes. First, we present a faster simulation algorithm that dispenses with Gaussian elimination, reducing practical runtime while incurring only a modest linear increase in the number of bits required to represent the stabilizer state. We implement this method in a freely available software package, CHP (CNOT–Hadamard–Phase), which easily scales to thousands of qubits and enables large-scale benchmarking. Second, we establish that classical simulation of stabilizer circuits is complete for the complexity class Parity-L (⊕L), implying that such circuits are unlikely to be universal even for classical computation. Third, we give efficient procedures for computing inner products between arbitrary stabilizer states, placing any n-qubit stabilizer circuit into a canonical normal form using at most O(n^2) gates, and performing related tasks that facilitate analysis and optimization. Fourth, we extend our simulator to mixed-state inputs, circuits with a bounded number of non-stabilizer gates, and circuits acting on general tensor-product initial states that include only a limited number of measurements. Together, these results refine the algorithmic, complexity-theoretic, and practical understanding of stabilizer computation in quantum information.

We investigate the boundary action of self-similar groups generated by bounded automata on the space X^ω of infinite words over a finite alphabet X. For each boundary point w we consider the associated Schreier graph of the orbit, and determine its number of ends. Our approach uses sofic subshifts encoding the asymptotic behavior of the automaton along w, which allows a complete computation of the end number for every Schreier graph. With respect to the Bernoulli measure on X^ω, we show that almost all Schreier graphs have one or two ends, and we give a precise characterization of bounded automata for which the two-end case occurs almost surely. We further relate these asymptotic types to the topology of the limit and tile spaces of the group, identifying when (local) cut points are present.

Physical equivalence between distinct systems enables transfer of insight and highlights universal dynamical laws. We establish a rigorous mapping showing that a spin–transfer–torque-driven magnetic nanopillar is dynamically equivalent to a rotating magnetic plate, thereby recasting the nanopillar as a macroscopic parametric resonator subject to time-modulated energy injection. This equivalence yields a comprehensive phase diagram and predictive criteria for emergent magnetic states, including solitons, stationary textures, oscillatory localized modes, and other nonlinear behaviors. Analytical considerations and large-scale micromagnetic simulations corroborate the predictions, quantify stability boundaries, and reveal parameter regimes for controllable state selection and dynamical transitions, robust.

We investigated the 46Ti compound nucleus formed in the fusion–evaporation reaction 27Al + 19F at a beam energy of 144 MeV. Light charged particles were measured in coincidence with evaporation residues using the ICARE multidetector array at the VIVITRON tandem facility (IReS, Strasbourg). Energy spectra and angular distributions were analyzed with CACARIZO, a Monte Carlo implementation of the statistical-model code CASCADE. Calculated spectral shapes for evaporated α particles were compared with the data. While global features are reproduced by the statistical model, a detailed comparison indicates the need for spin-dependent level densities and enhanced deformability parameters, providing evidence for large deformations of the compound nucleus at high excitation energy and angular momentum.

We present a survey of neutral atomic carbon [C I] emission in high-redshift (z ≳ 2) submillimeter galaxies (SMGs) and quasar host galaxies (QSOs). Sensitive observations of the [C I](1–0) and [C I](2–1) lines were obtained with the IRAM Plateau de Bure Interferometer and the IRAM 30 m telescope. A total of 16 [C I] transitions were targeted across 10 sources, yielding 10 line detections and thereby doubling the number of [C I] detections in such systems reported to date. We augment our sample with previously published data, adding five additional detected sources to the analysis. Our principal result is that the [C I] properties of high-redshift systems do not differ markedly from those in the local universe, including the Milky Way. The line luminosity ratios show little variation across the sample, with L_[CI](2–1)/L_[CI](1–0) = 0.55 ± 0.15 and L_[CI]/L_CO(3–2) = 0.32 ± 0.13. The [C I] lines are not a significant contributor to the cooling budget of the molecular gas, indicating that their emission traces rather than dominates the thermal regulation of the cold ISM. From the [C I] line ratio, we derive a mean carbon excitation temperature of 29.1 ± 6.3 K, broadly consistent with dust temperatures inferred for high-redshift star-forming systems, but lower than typical gas temperatures found in local starbursts. The inferred carbon abundance, X(C)/X(H2) ≈ 8.4 × 10^-5, is comparable to values measured in the Milky Way and nearby galaxies. These results imply that the high-z galaxies studied here are already significantly enriched in carbon on galactic scales, despite substantial lookback times, with the average redshift of our sample corresponding to a cosmic age of about 2 Gyr.

During a Swift/XRT program aimed at securing arcsecond localizations for a sample of presumed Galactic X-ray binaries, we identified one target that is not a binary but the counterpart to a long, X-ray-rich gamma-ray burst originally detected by the BeppoSAX Wide Field Cameras (2–28 keV) and Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor (40–700 keV). Reanalysis of the BeppoSAX prompt emission, combined with precise Swift/XRT positioning, disentangles the transient from nearby persistent sources and establishes its GRB nature. The prompt light curve is extended and structured, with multiple pulses and a T90 of roughly a few minutes. Time-resolved spectroscopy is well fit by a Band function with a low peak energy in the tens of keV and a high X-ray-to-gamma-ray fluence ratio, securely placing the event in the X-ray-rich class. Swift/XRT detected the X-ray afterglow within minutes and followed it to very late times, revealing the canonical steep–plateau–normal decay sequence and an achromatic break at late times consistent with a collimated jet. The afterglow exhibits modest intrinsic absorption exceeding the Galactic column. Optical counterparts are faint and red, consistent with dust extinction and/or a moderately high redshift; we identify a faint host-galaxy candidate at the XRT position. Deep late-time observations in X-rays and optical bands show no persistent emission typical of an accreting binary, and radio upper limits constrain the circumburst density to be low. The inferred energetics and spectral parameters are consistent with established correlations for X-ray-rich bursts, supporting a continuum with classical long GRBs and compliance with standard afterglow closure relations in a homogeneous medium. This case highlights the power of Swift/XRT arcsecond localizations to resolve longstanding classification ambiguities in crowded Galactic fields, updates the BeppoSAX–Swift sample with a well-characterized long, X-ray-rich burst, and underscores the need for systematic re-examination of transient catalogs where GRB afterglows may masquerade as Galactic binaries.

We present an extension of CMB interferometric sensitivity formalism to the three-dimensional 21 cm EoR power spectrum, explicitly incorporating line-of-sight modes and instrumental chromaticity. Our framework replaces earlier approximate estimates and yields accurate sensitivity forecasts that include thermal noise, sample variance, and array configuration effects. We derive analytic scaling relations with integration time, bandwidth, collecting area, element size, and baseline distribution, mapping uv coverage to k_perp and channelization to k_parallel. The results show that compact antenna distributions maximize sensitivity to large-scale EoR modes, while smaller elements increase independent baselines at fixed area. We quantify the trade-offs between antenna size, stationization, and correlator capacity, emphasizing the N_ant^2 cost of full correlation and the need for spectral resolution. These relations provide concrete guidance for designing EoR observatories and operations.

This article presents an analytical description of three-dimensional nonlinear wave interactions within a broad class of quasilinear first-order systems. We focus on systems whose hydrodynamic reductions are homogeneous semi-Hamiltonian, i.e., diagonalizable and endowed with infinitely many conservation laws, and employ the generalized hodograph method to resolve multiwave dynamics. We establish that the interaction of n waves proceeds as a superposition of simple waves outside a finite collision region, while inducing computable phase and amplitude distortions. Explicit formulas quantify the post-collision deformation and provide diagnostic criteria for integrability and stability and robustness.

Observations of the X-ray luminosity–temperature (Lx–T) relation for the diffuse intracluster medium indicate departures from self-similar scaling, implicating nongravitational heating in galaxy-cluster formation. We investigate quasar feedback as a plausible heating source and quantify its imprint on the microwave sky via the thermal Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (tSZ) effect. Using a simple one-dimensional Sedov–Taylor blast-wave model to describe energy outflows into the intergalactic medium, we compute the resulting Compton-y distortions and their angular power spectrum. For reasonable feedback energetics and redshift distributions, the temperature fluctuation amplitude on arcminute scales is of order one microkelvin, with power peaking at multipoles l ~ thousands. This level of signal lies near the noise floor of surveys such as the Atacama Cosmology Telescope and the South Pole Telescope, but should be detectable with Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array integrations or through stacking analyses of many quasar-centered microwave images. We discuss parameter dependences and implications for structure formation.

We present a systematic experimental investigation of the origin of the broadened and lowered Verwey transition in magnetite (Fe3O4) thin films compared to bulk crystals. Using x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, x-ray diffraction, and temperature-dependent resistivity measurements on films grown on different substrates and with varying thickness, we disentangle the roles of oxygen stoichiometry and substrate-induced microstructure. We find that the transition is drastically influenced not only by achieving full stoichiometry, but particularly by the domain landscape set by epitaxial growth. For fully stoichiometric films, the transition temperature, the resistivity jump, and the conductivity gap all depend on the average domain size, which increases monotonically with thickness. Moreover, the breadth of the transition scales with the width of the domain-size distribution, while the hysteresis width is strongly enhanced by antiphase boundaries. Films grown on MgO (001) exhibit the highest and sharpest transitions; a 200 nm film reaches a Verwey temperature of 122 K, close to the bulk value. In contrast, films grown on substrates with large lattice mismatch display very broad transitions. Despite the broadening, all films show clear hysteresis, demonstrating that the transition remains first order. These results establish microstructural control, alongside stoichiometry, as the key lever to recover bulk-like Verwey physics in Fe3O4 films.

We present preliminary observational results on tidal synchronization in detached, solar-type binary stars in the open clusters M35 (∼150 Myr) and M34 (∼250 Myr). These clusters host rich populations of close late-type binaries at ages that critically test models of synchronization during the early main-sequence. We combine stellar rotation periods derived from precision time-series photometry with binary orbital periods and eccentricities measured from multi-epoch spectroscopy to compute the primary’s angular rotation velocity and the orbital angular velocity at periastron. Comparing these quantities yields the synchronization state of individual systems through the ratio of spin to orbital angular velocity. The initial results reveal a range of behaviors: near-synchronous rotation in short-period binaries, supersynchronous rotation in eccentric systems approaching pseudo-synchronization, and clear departures from synchronization at longer periods. Trends with period, eccentricity, and cluster age broadly align with theoretical expectations, motivating expanded samples and continued monitoring.

We present the first circular polarization measurements of circumstellar H2O masers around a sample of late-type stars. Using interferometric observations and both LTE and non-LTE polarization analyses, we derive magnetic field strengths in the H2O maser zones ranging from a few hundred milligauss up to a few gauss. The inferred radial profile is consistent with a solar-type dependence, with B decreasing as r^-2 from the star. No linear polarization is detected down to <1%. These results provide constraints on magnetic fields in evolved-star envelopes and their role in maser excitation and wind dynamics.

The warm–hot intergalactic medium (WHIM), at temperatures of order @xmath0 K, is believed to harbor 30–50% of the baryons in the local Universe. Yet all current X-ray detections of the WHIM at redshifts @xmath1 remain of low statistical significance (@xmath2) and/or are controversial. We aim to establish the practical detection limits of current X-ray observatories and to define quantitative requirements for next-generation X-ray telescopes to study the WHIM through resonance absorption lines. We analyze all available grating observations of the bright blazar Mrk 421, deriving spectra with signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) of @xmath3 and 190 per 50 m spectral bin from Chandra and XMM-Newton observations, respectively. Despite these being among the highest S/N X-ray absorption spectra ever obtained with current facilities, we cannot confirm the two WHIM systems reported by Nicastro et al. (2005). Bootstrap simulations, which include realistic continuum uncertainties and instrumental systematics, indicate that spectra with such high S/N still can not constrain WHIM absorbers with column densities @xmath4 (corresponding to equivalent widths of 2.5 m for a Doppler velocity of @xmath5) at the @xmath6 significance level. The simulations further show that measuring the @xmath8 absorption at @xmath9 confidence from a background QSO with flux @xmath10 mCrab (1 Crab = @xmath11 at 0.5–2 keV) would require integration times of @xmath7 Ms with Chandra and 140 Ms with XMM-Newton. To achieve comparable constraints in practical exposures, future X-ray spectrographs must deliver spectral resolution of @xmath12 and effective area of @xmath13, enabling detections in @xmath14 Ms per sightline. A survey of 15 QSOs with fluxes of @xmath16 mCrab, along which clear intergalactic absorbers have been identified, would then require a total exposure of @xmath15 Ms. These results delineate the limitations of current missions and provide concrete performance benchmarks for future facilities to complete the low-redshift baryon census via the WHIM.

Dust extinction remains a dominant, poorly tractable systematic in astronomy, especially for Type Ia supernova cosmology. Past studies often used the equivalent width of interstellar absorption in low-resolution spectra as a surrogate for extinction, based on tentative correlations. Using 443 low-resolution spectra of 172 Type Ia supernovae with independently determined extinction and measured equivalent widths of interstellar features (e.g., Na I D), we find only a weak correlation, with large scatter that renders the proxy unusable for individual objects. We trace the scatter to line saturation and blending, ISM components, dust-to-gas ratios, circumstellar contributions, and resolution/SNR effects. Reliable extinction estimates require multi-wavelength photometry or high-resolution spectroscopy.

We present a deep, wide-field @xmath0- and @xmath1-band imaging survey with Suprime-Cam on the Subaru Telescope targeting fields along the south–east minor axis of the Andromeda (M31) spheroid. Our photometry reaches the red clump, enabling robust star–galaxy separation, completeness characterization, and contamination subtraction. From a large, reliable red giant branch sample, we derive photometric metallicity distributions as a function of projected radius and a surface-brightness profile spanning out to @xmath266 kpc from M31’s center. The metallicity distributions exhibit a relatively high mean and a broad spread ([Fe/H]@xmath3), with no significant metallicity gradient across the surveyed range. The surface-brightness profile at @xmath4 kpc is markedly flatter than previously reported from narrower or shallower datasets. These findings suggest that this sector of the halo may include as-yet unidentified, metal-rich substructure superimposed on the underlying spheroid. Our results place new constraints on the structure and assembly history of M31’s outer spheroid and its stellar populations.

This article reviews the theory of the linear optical response of quantum-well excitons and planar microcavity polaritons in light of existing experiments. For quantum wells, we show that structural disorder predominantly perturbs the exciton center-of-mass motion, which can be described by an effective two-dimensional Schrödinger equation with realistic disorder potentials. For microcavity polaritons, we develop a unified framework that incorporates quantum-well interface roughness and fluctuations of cavity thickness, enabling a unified treatment of excitonic and photonic disorder. Numerical simulations demonstrate that polaritons are chiefly sensitive to photon-sector disorder, corroborating prior indications that exciton disorder plays a secondary role. From the computed spectra and spatial profiles, we estimate polariton localization lengths of a few micrometers, with a systematic dependence on disorder amplitude, in quantitative accord with recent measurements.

We demonstrate in situ fluorescence detection of @xmath0Li atoms in a one-dimensional optical lattice with single-atom precision. Although illuminated lithium atoms tend to boil out, a sufficiently deep lattice combined with optical molasses beams, without extra cooling, retains atoms while generating enough photons for reliable readout. For a potential well depth of 2.4 mK at an antinode, a single atom remains trapped for 30 s while scattering probe photons at a rate of @xmath1 s@xmath2. We introduce a simple model that captures the dependence of atom lifetime on well depth, consistent with measurements. As the number of trapped atoms is reduced, the integrated fluorescence shows clear stepwise changes, unambiguously signaling single-atom detection. Even with a photon-collection efficiency of only 1.3% due to a small numerical aperture, the presence or absence of an atom is determined within 300 ms with an error below @xmath3. This approach enables robust, site-resolved detection in lithium lattices without high-NA imaging.

In this work, we examine the dark energy problem as a consequence of the self-gravitating nature of vacuum fluctuations, suggesting that its resolution belongs to quantum gravity and can be approached within string theory. We focus on a recent string-inspired framework in which nonlinear dynamics of short-distance perturbation modes generate late-time acceleration without fine-tuning of parameters. The model predicts a time-dependent equation of state w(z), providing a distinctive observational signature relative to cosmological constant or simple quintessence scenarios. We outline theoretical consistency conditions, discuss stability and causality of the effective fluid, and derive phenomenological predictions for expansion history and growth of structure. We show how precision cosmology—supernovae, BAO, CMB, and weak lensing—can constrain w(z), potentially yielding indirect evidence for string-theoretic physics in upcoming surveys.

We report the emergence of two C IV narrow absorption systems in the spectrum of the quasar SDSS J095254.10+021932.8, located at @xmath0 and @xmath1 and exhibiting velocity offsets of @xmath2 and @xmath3 with respect to the quasar systemic frame. These features, imprinted on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) III spectrum obtained on 2011 March 25, are absent in the earlier SDSS-I/II spectrum from 2000 December 30, corresponding to a rest-frame interval of 1186.4 days. Detailed spectral decomposition shows that the continuum and broad emission-line fluxes, as well as proxies for the mass accretion rate, remain stable between epochs, while the C IV doublet ratios indicate obviously partial coverage of the background emission sources. The stability of the ionizing continuum and emission-line properties argues against ionization-state changes as the driver of the observed variability, and the abrupt appearance of both systems is unlikely to reflect a newly launched outflow in a previously quiescent sightline. Instead, the data favor a scenario in which multiple, compact streams of outflowing gas move transversely across the quasar sightline, intermittently occulting the continuum and broad-line regions. Partial coverage constrains the absorbers to sub-parsec to parsec scales relative to the emission regions and supports a clumpy outflow geometry. This case provides a clear example of absorption-line variability dominated by transverse motions, offering new constraints on the structure, kinematics, and covering properties of quasar outflows. Continued spectroscopic monitoring will refine the crossing speeds and sizes of the absorbing clumps.

We investigate the relationship between the regularized multi‐propagator framework (“Reg PT”) and standard perturbation theory (SPT) for modeling the nonlinear evolution of cosmological dark matter fluctuations. Reg PT has been widely used as an interpolation between the large‐scale solution obtained via SPT and the small‐scale limit derived from the multi‐point propagator method. We provide an alternative explanation grounded entirely in the SPT formalism and demonstrate that Reg PT does not introduce additional effective information about nonlinear matter evolution beyond that already contained in SPT. Analytically, we show that the Reg PT construction corresponds to a particular rearrangement and partial resummation of SPT contributions, without improving the underlying dynamics. Numerically, by comparing predictions to high‐resolution N‐body simulations over a broad range of redshifts and wavenumbers, we find that SPT at two‐loop order reproduces the nonlinear matter power spectrum more accurately than Reg PT, especially in the high‐k regime. This indicates that two‐loop SPT remains among the most reliable perturbative predictions available today. Nonetheless, the practical use of SPT has been limited by divergences that arise at small scales. To address this, we propose a modified SPT scheme that regularizes the UV behavior of loop integrals while preserving the correct large‐scale limit and the accuracy of two‐loop contributions. Our approach eliminates the spurious divergence without resorting to ad hoc interpolation, yielding stable, precise predictions for the nonlinear power spectrum.

We study fusion frames that decompose signals into weighted linear subspace components. For positive integers k, we introduce k‐fusion frames, a refinement of fusion frames capturing higher‐order subspace interactions. Tight k‐fusion frames are linked to Grassmannian designs and cubature formulas, analyzed via harmonic analysis on Grassmann spaces. We define the k‐fusion frame potential, establish lower and upper bounds, and characterize its minimizers. Connections to equiangular configurations and the simplex bound are developed, yielding existence criteria, structural constraints, and construction principles for tight k‐fusion frames.

We analyze velocity profiles of X-ray emission lines resolved by the Chandra High Energy Transmission Grating Spectrometer at four epochs spanning the approach to periastron and near apastron in the η Carinae binary. Far from periastron, lines are symmetric and centered near the systemic velocity. Closer to periastron, profiles broaden, shift to the blue by a few hundred km s−1, and develop pronounced asymmetry. Abrupt X-ray flares are accompanied by very high-velocity emission reaching ~2,000 km s−1. While quiescent emission and small centroid shifts can be explained by continuous colliding winds and the orbital motion of the secondary, these transient high-velocity components cannot. We therefore interpret the flaring emission as a fast, collimated outflow of ionized gas launched near periastron, plausibly from the wind–collision zone or an accretion flow onto the secondary. This model accounts for the blue-shifted asymmetry, timing, and velocity extremes, and yields constraints on outflow geometry, density, and energetics, with implications for episodic mass loss in η Car.

We investigate the merging and splitting of quasi‐two‐dimensional Bose–Einstein condensates with strong dipolar interactions. Using a combination of variational theory and time‐dependent Gross–Pitaevskii simulations, complemented by measurements on tilted dysprosium condensates, we compare dynamics along axes parallel and perpendicular to the in‐plane projection of the dipoles. When the dipoles have a finite in‐plane component, the evolution is markedly anisotropic: one direction exhibits faster coalescence or fragmentation, enhanced density ripples at the roton wavelength, and earlier instabilities. We trace this behavior to the directional character of the roton‐like minimum in the Bogoliubov spectrum. Tilting the dipoles to be normal to the plane restores isotropy, despite roton softening. The anisotropy scales with tilt angle and dipolar strength, enabling controlled pattern formation and interferometry.

We enumerate triangulations of a convex n-gon whose every side is subdivided by r boundary points, yielding exact counts for the resulting n(r+1) boundary-vertex configurations. We derive closed formulas expressed via Catalan convolutions and ballot-type numbers, together with univariate and bivariate generating functions that encode n and r. Using analytic combinatorics (Lagrange inversion and singularity analysis), we obtain precise asymptotics in several regimes: (i) n→∞ with r fixed, exhibiting universal n^{-3/2} behavior and an r-dependent exponential growth rate; (ii) r→∞ with n fixed; and (iii) joint scalings r≈ρn with an explicit entropy function. We connect these results to the open problem of minimizing triangulation counts over planar point sets in general position, providing perturbation-based constructions, structural insights, and refined universal lower bounds.

We present results from a next-to-leading order (NLO) event generator for purely gluonic contributions to three-jet production at hadron colliders, representing the first step toward full NLO three-jet predictions. We implement several commonly used jet algorithms and assess their numerical stability. We find pathological behavior in the iterative cone algorithm, which renders it unsuitable for fixed-order calculations beyond leading order, whereas sequential recombination algorithms exhibit stable performance. We quantify the impact of NLO corrections on jet rates and kinematic distributions and demonstrate improved renormalization and factorization scale dependence relative to leading order. These findings inform algorithm choice for precision QCD studies and provide a validated foundation for extending to channels with quarks and full NLO three-jet production.

We investigate phase structures of boson–fermion mixed condensates in ultracold atomic gases when boson–fermion composite fermions (quasi‐bound BF states) can form under equilibrium. Using an algebraic treatment of the number and chemical‐potential constraints, we construct phase diagrams versus temperature and interaction strength, highlighting low‐T competitions between BF degenerate states and Bose–Einstein condensates (BEC). We derive a criterion for BEC realization in the presence of BF formation and quantify shifts in temperature and density. Our results delineate regimes of coexistence, exclusion, and crossover relevant to quantum atomic gases.

We present the most extensive molecular multiline study to date of the low-metallicity interstellar medium in the Small Magellanic Cloud, targeting the star-forming region LIRS36. Emission from CO, CS, SO, HCN, and HNC is securely detected, while NO and, most notably, CN remain undetected. Rare isotopologues are observed and tentatively confirmed in several transitions, enabling constraints on isotopic ratios and excitation conditions. From the CO analyses we derive an H2–to–CO integrated intensity conversion factor that is slightly elevated relative to the local Galactic disk value, yet on sub-cloud scales (less than about 10 pc) the inferred conversion approaches disk-like values. This scale-dependent behavior supports a predominantly molecular nature of the neutral gas within dense cores despite the globally reduced heavy-element content. Beam-averaged CO column densities and line ratios indicate warm (temperatures above roughly 10 K) molecular gas subject to a strong ionizing radiation field. The detection of CS in the J = 2–1, 3–2, and 5–4 transitions requires high densities consistent with a compact core (n ≳ 10^5 cm−3). The 13CO/12CO line intensity ratio points to a relative underabundance of 13C-bearing CO compared to Galactic clouds, in line with expectations for a chemically young, metal-poor environment. Intensity ratios involving HCN and HNC are close to unity, further supporting warm, moderately excited conditions and enhanced ionization. Fractional abundances of CO and CS are lower by about an order of magnitude than typical values in Galactic disk molecular clouds. Nitrogen-bearing species are even more strongly suppressed: HCN, HNC, and likely CN exhibit fractional abundances reduced by roughly two orders of magnitude. In contrast to star-forming regions in the Large Magellanic Cloud, the CN N = 1–0 line is substantially weaker than the corresponding ground rotational transitions of HCN, HNC, and CS, yielding CN/CS abundance ratios well below unity. Chemical modeling suggests that the SMC’s small metallicity amplifies CN destruction pathways while leaving CS comparatively unaffected, and that the high core densities further favor CN removal. These results highlight the profound impact of metallicity and density on molecular inventories and isotopic chemistry in dwarf-galaxy star-forming environments.

We review recent advances in black hole accretion disk theory that underscore the pivotal role of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) stresses in transporting angular momentum. The near-universality of accretion-related winds and jets points to large-scale MHD torques that effect vertical angular momentum transport, thereby enhancing the global removal of angular momentum and enabling appreciable accretion rates. When vertical transport is significant, the disk’s radial structure at small radii is systematically altered, changing local dissipation and the emergent emission spectrum relative to standard, purely radial-viscous models. We present a simple framework in which energetic, magnetically driven outflows extract angular momentum and power from the disk, reducing inner-disk radiative efficiency and redistributing emission. The resulting spectra exhibit diminished inner-disk contribution and modified continuum shapes. Comparing these predictions to quasar spectral energy distributions, we find improved consistency and infer that mass accretion rates derived under standard disk assumptions are likely severely underestimated. These results have implications for black hole growth histories, radiative efficiencies, and feedback in active galactic nuclei.

We report an experimental study of the yellow exciton series in Cu2O in magnetic fields up to 32 T. Strong fields optically activate direct and phonon-assisted paraexciton luminescence via mixing with the quadrupole-allowed orthoexciton state. Analysis of phonon-assisted emission provides quantitative information on the statistical occupation and energy distribution of paraexcitons. Time-resolved spectroscopy grants direct access to the temporal evolution of thermodynamic variables of the paraexciton gas, including temperature and chemical potential, under non-equilibrium and relaxation conditions. Remarkably, the paraexciton lifetime remains largely unchanged by magnetic-field activation, preserving long-lived populations. These findings establish a pathway to probe quasi-equilibrium paraexciton ensembles and open avenues toward Bose-Einstein condensation of excitons in bulk semiconductors.

We present a relativistic three-body equation on the light-front to analyze the stability of isolated triplets and medium-induced correlations at finite temperature and density. Employing a zero-range interaction, we uncover the relativistic analog of the Thomas collapse and explore conditions under which the nucleon can emerge as a Borromean system. Within a systematic Dyson-equation framework, in-medium propagators and self-energies yield the three-body Mott transition and the critical temperature for the onset of color superconductivity. Our results quantify relativistic medium effects and constrain few-body dynamics relevant to dense QCD matter.

We investigate the fundamental limits of quantum reading, a communication protocol that retrieves information from digital memories using quantum probes. Building on quantum information theory, we formalize a memory model and define the quantum reading capacity as the maximum rate of reliable readout per memory use. We establish coding theorems and converse bounds, identify operational regimes where quantum probes surpass classical strategies, and quantify gains in fidelity, data density, and energy efficiency. A central result is the super-additivity of the quantum reading capacity, demonstrating that joint strategies across multiple memory cells can exceed rates achievable by separable uses. We further derive conditions under which entangled ancillas improve performance, and construct probe-ancilla ensembles that achieve these gains. Case studies for optical memories illustrate rates and resource trade-offs. Our results unify and extend the theory of quantum-enhanced readout, guiding the design of quantum readers.

We study two continuous prenormal forms for local analytic diffeomorphisms of @xmath0: the trimmed form and the Poincaré–Dulac normal form. We begin with a self-contained introduction to Jean Écalle’s mould formalism, presenting definitions, operations, and structural properties. We establish a dictionary between moulds and the classical Lie-algebraic formalism via noncommutative formal power series, clarifying correspondences between derivations, substitutions, and prenormalization procedures. Building on this framework, we provide proofs and details for results announced by Écalle and Bruno Vallet concerning the trimmed form of diffeomorphisms. We then develop a mould-theoretic approach to the Poincaré–Dulac normalization, emphasizing algorithmic construction and resonance handling. Finally, we discuss the universal character of moulds in normalization problems and the ensuing canonical structures.

We investigate whether the two nearly circular concentric infrared shells of the LBV star candidate nebula G79.29+0.46 are interacting with the infrared dark cloud (IRDC) G79.3+0.3 located at the southwestern border of the inner shell. We conducted Jansky Very Large Array observations of NH3 (1,1) and (2,2) and c-C3H2, and combined them with archival Effelsberg single-dish data to recover extended emission. The NH3 emission reveals a dominant clump, G79A, elongated parallel to the IRDC, plus two fainter, smaller northern cores that spatially coincide with the inner infrared shell. We analyzed NH3 spectra at each detected position to derive linewidths, rotational temperature, column density, and abundance maps. The results show: (i) NH3 (1,1) linewidths of ~0.5 km s−1 in the northern cores, slightly larger than in adjacent regions; (ii) an enhancement of NH3 abundance by nearly one order of magnitude toward the northwestern side of G79A; (iii) a localized hot slab at the interface between the inner infrared shell and the NH3 peak of G79A; and (iv) chemical differentiation along the western and southern edges of G79A, with c-C3H2 tracing more external layers than NH3, consistent with photodissociation region (PDR) stratification. The kinematics, temperature structure, and chemical gradients of G79A indicate a combination of shock-driven and UV radiation-driven chemistry plausibly induced by feedback from the LBV star. These findings support an interaction between the shells and the IRDC and argue against a physical association of the IRDC with the star-forming region DR15. Instead, the IRDC appears to lie farther away, near G79.29+0.46, at a distance of approximately 1.4 kpc. Our results highlight how massive stellar feedback shapes the dense gas and chemistry in the vicinity of evolved massive stars.

We study Fourier restriction to quadratic surfaces in finite field vector spaces. In two dimensions, we obtain sharp estimates by analyzing sums of two points on quadratic curves, yielding optimal L^p→L^2 bounds. In higher dimensions, we prove decay for the Fourier transform of characteristic functions of quadratic surfaces, recovering the Tomas–Stein exponent. Using incidence theorems for points and quadratic varieties, we derive extension estimates under size constraints for subsets of quadratic surfaces. The arguments hinge on bounds for Gauss and Kloosterman sums and related exponential sums, capturing oscillation and cancellation. Our results advance finite field restriction and extension theory for nondegenerate quadratic forms and connect harmonic analysis with additive combinatorics.

We investigate two-surface wave decay (TSWD) as an absorption channel in ultrashort, intense laser–solid interactions. Extending fluid theory to warm plasmas with consistent boundary conditions, we derive modified dispersion and growth rates, quantify temperature-dependent thresholds, and recover the cold-plasma limit. Test-particle simulations in the TSWD fields reveal localized enhancement of electron acceleration near the surface, producing a modulation of the injected current density. This modulation can seed current filamentation instabilities. The results clarify TSWD-driven absorption and fast-electron generation, and delineate parameter scalings with temperature and density gradients.

We present comprehensive calculations of edge-mode velocities in quantum Hall droplets with realistic Coulomb interactions and confinement across filling fractions. Using exact diagonalization and modeling of gate potentials, we extract charged and neutral edge velocities and show that the charge-mode velocity scales approximately with the valence Landau-level filling and the Coulomb energy of the active level. At filling nu=5/2, the disparity between the fast bosonic charge mode and the slow fermionic neutral mode yields strong thermal smearing of non-Abelian quasiparticle interference. We quantify the coherence temperature and its dependence on confining potential strength, showing that softer confinement suppresses coherence, whereas stronger confinement can enhance the non-Abelian state and improve interferometric visibility.

We investigate dissipative chaos and phase-space symmetries in a parametrically driven nonlinear Kerr resonator (PDNR) excited by a train of Gaussian pulses that induces degenerate down-conversion. Combining semiclassical dynamical analysis with quantum phase-space techniques, we map the transition from regular to chaotic operation and the concomitant changes in nonclassical statistics. In the chaotic regime, Poincaré sections exhibit a strange attractor with robust two-fold symmetry, and contour plots of the resonator mode Wigner functions display the same symmetry in phase space. We demonstrate a strong breakdown of quantum-to-classical correspondence: parameter regions showing classical chaos yield quantum steady states that retain two-fold symmetric structures and nonclassical features not captured semiclassically. By evaluating the second-order correlation function, we show that the high photon correlations responsible for squeezing in the regular regime markedly diminish upon entering chaos. Consequently, photon-number correlation measurements provide a sensitive probe of the onset of chaos and reveal symmetry properties of the PDNR.

The advent of the Semantic Web has motivated tools and techniques for presenting and organizing knowledge. Concept hierarchies are integral to domain ontologies, and have gained significant attention for structuring unstructured text. We propose a novel unsupervised approach to identify relevant concepts from plain text and learn subsumption-based hierarchies. Our method first models topics with probabilistic topic models to discover latent semantic structure; then applies lightweight linguistic processing (POS tagging, noun phrase chunking, lexico-syntactic patterns, distributional cues) to extract semantically rich concept candidates; and finally establishes "is-a" relations via subsumption tests based on contextual distributions, topic-conditioned co-occurrence, head–modifier analysis, and Hearst-like patterns; assembling a coherent, acyclic hierarchy with pruning and consistency checks. The design is domain-agnostic, requiring no annotated or domain-specific training corpus. Experiments on large, real-world corpora (BBC News and Reuters) demonstrate superior performance over strong baselines for concept extraction and taxonomy construction, improving precision, recall, and F1 while producing deeper, more coherent hierarchies. Ablations show that guiding relation induction by topic modeling significantly increases concept salience and reduces spurious links. The method scales linearly with corpus size and maintains robustness across heterogeneous domains, enabling rapid ontology bootstrapping for Semantic Web applications, knowledge management, and text mining. Case studies illustrate interpretability and alignment with expert ontologies. The approach supports incremental updates and accommodates evolving corpora. Keywords: probabilistic topic models; concept extraction; subsumption hierarchy learning; natural language processing; semantic web; text mining.

We investigate the radio source regions of the type II burst on 2013 May 22 using direction-finding (DF) analysis of Wind/WAVES and STEREO/WAVES (S/WAVES) observations at decameter–hectometric (DH) wavelengths. The event exhibited an enhancement in the type II emission temporally coincident with the interaction of two coronal mass ejections (CMEs) launched in close succession along neighboring trajectories. Triangulation of the S/WAVES source directions places the ecliptic projections of the regions near the line connecting the Sun and the STEREO-A spacecraft. Combined WAVES and S/WAVES DF solutions reveal shifts in source latitude, indicating that the dominant site of type II generation migrated during the CME–CME interaction. At frequencies near 1 MHz, the Wind/WAVES source directions coincide with the leading edge of the primary CME identified in LASCO/C3 coronagraph images. This spatial correspondence, across instruments and wavelengths, supports the interpretation that the CME–CME interaction region acted as the driver of the type II enhancement. A comparison of radio source locations with white-light morphology further shows that, at lower DH frequencies, interplanetary scattering substantially alters radio wave propagation, producing displacements of the radio sources. Our results highlight how DF triangulation, combined with multi-viewpoint coronagraphy, can diagnose the evolving geometry of CME-driven shocks and their radio emission sites.

We present a new “multicomponent and variable velocity” (MVV) galactic outflow prescription for cosmological smoothed particle hydrodynamic (SPH) simulations that captures the multiphase origin of winds and ties their mass loading to galaxy stellar mass. In MVV, wind material is launched from distinct interstellar medium phases and its velocity scales with galaxy properties, yielding mass-loading factors that increase toward lower stellar masses. Implemented in SPH runs, the MVV model produces: (i) minimal thermal impact on the intergalactic medium (IGM), with mean IGM temperatures comparable to no-wind simulations; (ii) suppressed cosmic star formation rates (SFRs) relative to no-wind, but higher than constant-velocity wind models; (iii) IGM metal enrichment consistent with observations, including a match to the evolution of CIV; and (iv) a flattened low-mass end of the stellar mass function compared to previous SPH results, alleviating the excess of low-mass galaxies. These outcomes emerge because enhanced mass loading in dwarfs expels metals efficiently without overheating the IGM, while variable wind speeds allow more massive galaxies to retain gas and sustain star formation. The MVV framework reconciles metal enrichment and SFR regulation in a motivated feedback model, improving agreement with high-redshift observables. Our results demonstrate that incorporating multiphase wind launching and mass-dependent loading in SPH simulations yields realistic galaxy evolution and IGM properties, outperforming constant-velocity prescriptions, and helps resolve discrepancies in the low-mass galaxy population.

We analyze atomic population trapping in the Jaynes–Cummings model from the dressed-state perspective. For arbitrary pure initial atom–field states, we derive a general condition for partial or total trapping, expressed as a bound on the variation of the atomic inversion over time. We show that, whenever initial atomic coherence or atom–field coherence is present, the ensuing population dynamics is not determined by the field’s bare photon-number distribution, but by a weighted dressedness distribution that characterizes the joint state in the dressed basis. This distribution provides a compact and physically transparent description of the mechanism of trapping and its sensitivity to initial correlations. Moreover, individual revivals of the atomic inversion can be captured analytically, to good accuracy, directly in terms of the weighted dressedness distribution, even in regimes of pronounced trapping and for large photon numbers. These results follow from a generalization of the Poisson summation formula approach to revival analysis developed originally by Fleischhauer and Schleich [Phys. Rev. A 47, 4258 (1993)].

The high‐performance computing community increasingly augments homogeneous CPU clusters with GPUs, yet the SPMD paradigm often leads to underutilized accelerators when CPU/GPU resources are asymmetrically provisioned. We address this mismatch by introducing a GPU resource virtualization approach that decouples physical GPU ownership from individual processes and enables microprocessors to efficiently share devices. Our design exposes a virtual GPU abstraction that multiplexes kernels and memory across applications, while preserving SPMD programmability. We develop execution models that characterize throughput and interference under shared execution, guiding scheduling and partitioning policies for compute- and memory-bound workloads. We implement a lightweight virtualization infrastructure that consolidates contexts, orchestrates concurrent kernel execution via streams, and manages memory residency and data movement to minimize contention. Transparent to existing CUDA/OpenCL applications, the system requires no source modifications. Experiments with microbenchmarks and HPC applications demonstrate considerable performance gains and improved utilization on asymmetrical nodes, while incurring low overhead from the virtualization layer. Our results show that GPU virtualization enables efficient resource sharing, balance between CPUs and GPUs, and higher efficiency under SPMD.

We propose a dynamical model in which a network’s topology coevolves with load and failure, driving the system to self-organized criticality and elucidating the emergence of fractal and small-world architectures. The model couples stochastic growth with decay through cascading overload failures, capturing the intrinsic instability of large functional networks. Using extensive simulations and scaling analysis, we show robust SOC signatures: power-law distributions of avalanche sizes, cluster sizes, and inter-avalanche waiting times, with cutoffs controlled by system size. As the network evolves, critical cascades induce a percolation transition that spontaneously yields fractal networks characterized by long-range correlations and scale-invariant geometry. Away from criticality, rapid reconnection and redundancy generate small-world structures with short path lengths and high clustering. We further demonstrate a dynamic crossover from fractal to small-world organization as the system departs from the critical regime. Our results provide a minimal mechanism linking growth, failure, and topology in complex networks.

Sunspot regions frequently organize into long-lived complexes that span several solar rotations and constitute a major component of solar magnetic activity. While extreme ultraviolet images reveal coronal magnetic connectivity between closely spaced active regions, the existence of common subsurface roots or nests has remained uncertain. We investigate the subsurface structure and dynamics of the complex NOAA 10987–10989 observed during the SOHO/MDI Dynamics Run in March–April 2008, an interval of the Whole Heliospheric Interval campaign. The three regions emerged within a narrow latitudinal band, suggestive of a shared toroidal flux system. Using MDI full-disk Dopplergrams, we measure travel-time perturbations of acoustic waves over a range of skip distances and turning depths with time-distance helioseismology, and invert these measurements to obtain three-dimensional maps of sound-speed perturbations and vector flows beneath the complex. The subsurface flow maps reveal persistent shearing motions associated with the decay phase of the active regions, pointing to a role in driving the observed flaring and coronal mass ejection activity during WHI. The seismic sound-speed inversions, together with the distribution of deep-focus travel-time anomalies, indicate diverging subsurface roots consistent with omega-loop magnetic structures. However, within the probed depth range of approximately 0–48 Mm, we find no definitive evidence for direct subsurface connectivity among NOAA 10987, 10988, and 10989. These results suggest that coronal magnetic connections can exist without subsurface linkage, and that the emergence of closely spaced regions may arise from large-scale toroidal structuring without a single coherent root. We discuss the implications for models of flux emergence and active-region evolution, and the constraints helioseismology places on subsurface magnetic topology in complex activity nests.

We determine the phase diagram of the two-dimensional generalized fully frustrated XY model on the square lattice using large-scale Monte Carlo simulations. Tracking the staggered magnetization (chirality), the helicity modulus, and the fourth-order helicity modulus, we identify a crossing between the Ising-like chirality transition and the Kosterlitz-Thouless (KT) transition, as well as a stable phase with finite helicity modulus and unbroken chirality symmetry. At the crossing, the behavior is consistent with a conventional critical point: the helicity modulus exhibits no universal jump and follows finite-size scaling with system size L characterized by a critical exponent nu. Beyond the crossing, the KT transition line remains continuous but eventually turns first order, as indicated by discontinuities and anomalies captured by the energy-like observables and the fourth-order helicity modulus.

Accurate short- and long-horizon wind speed forecasts are critical for renewable energy integration and asset management. We propose a new nonparametric forecasting framework based on indexed semi-Markov chains that explicitly captures the dwelling-time distributions and state-transition dynamics of wind regimes. The index process aggregates past information to reproduce the empirical statistical behavior of wind speed across multiple sampling intervals. Using observational datasets, we generate one-step-ahead forecasts at different time scales and extend predictions over very long horizons while preserving forecast skill. Model performance is assessed via root mean square error between observations and predictions and benchmarked against a persistence model. Results show consistent RMSE reductions and improved reliability, demonstrating that indexed semi-Markov models provide a flexible, data-driven alternative for operational wind speed forecasting.

We review and expand on a Bayesian model selection technique for detecting gravitational waves from neutron-star ring-downs associated with pulsar glitches. The algorithm operates on power spectral densities computed from overlapping time segments, which can spuriously yield multiple detections for a single signal. We introduce an extension that exploits posterior information on the signal’s frequency content to cluster temporally adjacent events, merging consistent candidates into a single detection while aggregating cross-segment evidence. In simulations with injected ring-downs and in representative interferometer data, the method reduces duplicate triggers, lowers false-alarm rates, and increases sensitivity by coherently combining support from neighboring segments. We present performance metrics, robustness to nonstationary noise, and implementation details, demonstrating a practical pathway to reliable ring-down searches in current datasets.

This paper addresses linear parameter-varying (LPV) systems whose scheduling parameters are only piecewise differentiable, a class for which rigorous analysis tools have been lacking. We propose a hybrid-systems-based framework that reformulates the LPV model as an equivalent hybrid system via suitable state augmentation, thereby encoding both the plant dynamics and the structural properties of the parameter trajectories, including continuous evolution and discrete jumps. Leveraging a stability result for hybrid systems, we derive two stability conditions that naturally generalize and unify the classical quadratic stability and robust stability criteria within a single coherent framework. The resulting conditions are infinite-dimensional due to their dependence on trajectory features; to render them tractable, we develop sum-of-squares–based relaxations that yield finite-dimensional semidefinite programs. A practical computational procedure is provided. The approach is illustrated on two benchmark examples from the literature, demonstrating reduced conservatism compared to existing methods and effectiveness in handling nondifferentiable parameter segments, thereby filling an important gap in LPV system analysis.

We study a chain of @xmath0 coupled harmonic oscillators coupled to heat baths at temperatures @xmath1 and @xmath2 at sites @xmath3 and @xmath0, subject to non-momentum-conserving bulk stochasticity ensuring Fourier conductivity. We derive the hydrodynamic equations governing macroscopic energy and displacement profiles under diffusive scaling, establish boundary conditions, and identify transport coefficients. We characterize stationary and dynamical fluctuations via Gaussian limits and obtain large-deviation principles with explicit rate functionals. Two representative models are analyzed, revealing universality and model-dependent corrections in nonequilibrium steady states.

We present numerical results on particle dispersion in weakly nonlinear Rayleigh–Bénard convection at Prandtl number near unity, where bi-stability between straight rolls and weak turbulence as spiral defect chaos prevails. Using Lagrangian pair statistics, we show that hallmarks of mass transport from fully developed turbulence also emerge in these states, even in the weakly turbulent regime. At short times, pair separations display Richardson-like scaling from coherent advection with molecular diffusion. We explain this behavior with a quantitative model capturing the interplay of deterministic roll-driven advection and stochastic diffusion. At long times, dispersion crosses over to diffusion-like spreading that becomes insensitive to individual particle noise and depends on large-scale flow organization. The effective spreading rate increases with the degree of spatio-temporal chaos, linking transport efficiency to pattern disorder. These results identify convection systems without strong turbulence as fertile ground for universal dispersion phenomenology and provide a framework for predicting transport in weakly chaotic flows.

We propose a topological approach that establishes a direct connection between thermodynamics and topology in the microcanonical ensemble. Focusing on interacting classical spin systems in the thermodynamic limit, we show that key equilibrium properties, including the occurrence of phase transitions, can be captured using topology arguments alone. The method relies on Morse theory, taking the potential energy as the Morse function and exploiting its critical points to track topology changes in energy submanifolds. Our central result is that the Euler characteristic encodes the essential features needed to reconstruct several magnetic thermodynamic quantities of the models studied, notably the magnetization, correlation function, susceptibility, and critical temperature. These quantities obey the laws of thermodynamics, with the proviso that van der Waals loop states are recognized as mean-field artifacts. We further analyze the relationship between an Euler entropy, defined as the logarithm of the modulus of the Euler characteristic per site, and the Boltzmann microcanonical entropy, clarifying conditions under which both descriptions agree and identifying regimes where they diverge due to topological irregularities. In particular, we find that loss of regularity in the Morse function is associated with unstable and metastable thermodynamic solutions in the mean-field case, providing a geometric criterion for their onset. The reliability of the approach is tested in two exactly solvable spin systems subject to a magnetic field: the infinite-range (mean-field) XY model and a short-range XY model. In both cases we verify the topological hypothesis, namely that phase transitions in the microcanonical ensemble are accompanied by topology changes of the relevant energy submanifolds, and we show that the Euler characteristic suffices to describe the observed thermodynamic behavior. Our results support topology-based characterizations of classical spin systems and motivate further studies to assess the scope and limits of this proposal across broader classes of models and interactions. Keywords: topology, thermodynamics, phase transitions, Euler integral.

We present multicolor (@xmath0) light curves of the eclipsing classical nova V Per and report twelve new eclipse timings for the system. Combined with published timings, these measurements yield a revised ephemeris for the times of mid-eclipse, given by @xmath1. The eclipse profiles are analyzed with a parameter-fitting model that resolves four luminosity components: a white dwarf primary, a main-sequence secondary, a flared accretion disk with a rim, and a bright spot at the intersection of the mass-transfer stream and the disk periphery. Model parameters include the temperatures of the white dwarf (@xmath2) and secondary (@xmath3), the radius (@xmath4) and temperature (@xmath5) of the disk periphery, the inner disk radius (@xmath6), the power-law exponent of the disk temperature profile (@xmath7), the disk thickness (@xmath8), and a bright spot temperature enhancement factor (@xmath9). A matrix of model solutions is computed over an extensive range of physically plausible parameter values, and the solution space is explored to determine optimum parameter values and associated errors. In configurations that treat the accretion disk as a flat structure without a rim, acceptable fits require a nearly flat radial temperature profile. Introducing a truncated inner disk (@xmath10) steepens the inferred temperature gradient, yet steady-state profiles characterized by @xmath11 are recovered only in models that incorporate a significant disk rim. Sensitivity analyses within the solution matrix indicate that @xmath7 and @xmath8 are tightly coupled to the adopted rim geometry, while the eclipse depths across @xmath0 constrain @xmath2 and @xmath3. The bright spot enhancement @xmath9 is necessary to reproduce phase-dependent asymmetries and color changes near eclipse. Comparison of the observed brightness and color at mid-eclipse with the photometric properties of the best-fitting model suggests that V Per lies at a distance of @xmath12 kpc. These results refine the system’s ephemeris and support a disk with measurable vertical structure in V Per.

We report a systematic study of baryon enhancement at intermediate transverse momentum in relativistic heavy-ion collisions at RHIC. We analyze identified hadron spectra in Au+Au and Cu+Cu at sqrt(s_NN)=200 GeV and Au+Au at 62.4 GeV. We observe a large enhancement of (anti)protons relative to pions at 2–5 GeV/c in central Au+Au, persisting across energies with magnitude dependent on system size and centrality. Nuclear modification factors reveal weaker suppression for baryons than mesons, especially at intermediate pT. Comparisons suggest recombination/coalescence and collective flow contribute; the effect decreases in smaller systems and peripheral events, constraining hadronization dynamics models.

We analyze radiative mass generation for four-dimensional adjoint scalars arising from Kaluza–Klein compactifications of higher-dimensional Yang–Mills theories. These scalars originate from the internal components of the gauge field and are massless at tree level, yet are known to acquire masses through quantum effects. Working within an effective field theory framework, we compute the one-loop mass corrections using the background field method combined with Schwinger proper-time regularization, ensuring a manifestly gauge-invariant treatment of the effective action. Particular care is devoted to the organization of the Kaluza–Klein sums and to the separation of ultraviolet-sensitive contributions from genuine infrared data tied to the compactification. We show that, after appropriate matching, the resulting mass corrections are finite, depend only on the compactification radius and group-theory factors, and are insensitive to details of the short-distance completion. To clarify the universality of these results, we revisit the same problem in two distinct ultraviolet completions of Yang–Mills theory: perturbative string theory and lattice gauge theory. In the string setting, we compute the relevant amplitudes for gauge fields localized on D-branes compactified on a large circle or torus, and demonstrate that in the regime where the compactification radius is much larger than the string length, the induced scalar mass reproduces the effective field theory result and is independent of the string scale. The structure of the string computation further suggests that this UV-independence persists beyond one loop by virtue of gauge invariance and modular properties. In the lattice completion, we formulate the higher-dimensional gauge theory on an anisotropic lattice and evaluate the one-loop scalar mass in the limit where the compactification radius greatly exceeds the lattice spacing. We again find agreement with the effective field theory prediction and no residual dependence on the lattice cutoff. Moreover, for super Yang–Mills theories obtained by dimensional reduction, the lattice analysis indicates a strong suppression of the adjoint scalar masses despite the explicit breaking of supersymmetry by the regulator, due to the interplay between higher-dimensional gauge invariance and near boson–fermion degeneracy. These results support the universality of the mass corrections for any local, gauge-invariant UV completion.

Although Sr3Ru2O7 has not been reported to exhibit superconductivity, ac susceptibility on regions cut from Sr3Ru2O7–Sr2RuO4 eutectic crystals revealed multiple superconducting transitions. Based on complementary experiments, we propose that thin Sr2RuO4 slabs comprising a few RuO2 layers are embedded as stacking faults within the Sr3Ru2O7 host, and that the distribution of slab thicknesses produces multiple transition temperatures. To test this scenario, we measured the resistivity along the ab plane (ρab) of a Sr3Ru2O7-region sample cut from the eutectic crystal, and along the c axis (ρc) of the same specimen. Resistance drops associated with superconductivity were observed only in ρab, while ρc showed no corresponding features, indicating strongly anisotropic superconducting paths confined to quasi-two-dimensional inclusions. These transport results, together with the ac susceptibility, support the embedded Sr2RuO4 thin-slab scenario. Furthermore, resistivity measurements on a single crystal of pure, high-quality Sr3Ru2O7 revealed no superconductivity down to 15 mK, demonstrating that the superconducting signals in eutectic specimens arise from intergrowths rather than intrinsic behavior of Sr3Ru2O7.

We analyze spontaneous emission in an effective atomic two-level system driven by an intense, coherent, low-frequency field whose frequency is below the natural linewidth. The strong auxiliary field opens multiphoton excitation and de-excitation channels that compete with vacuum-induced decay. The resulting interference among multiple transition pathways modifies the radiative dynamics and can significantly and markedly inhibit emission. From microscopic considerations we derive an effective Hamiltonian retaining processes up to third order. We incorporate both the coupling to the vacuum modes and the coherent drive, yielding a master-equation description. Numerical wavefunction and density-matrix simulations are carried out for parameters relevant to rubidium, including realistic decay rates and drive intensities. The calculations predict substantial suppression of spontaneous decay over a wide range of detunings and field strengths, with optimal inhibition occurring when the drive frequency lies well below the natural linewidth. Practical implications for lifetime engineering, decoherence control, and potential experimental implementations are outlined.

Using the Parkes–Tidbinbilla Interferometer (PTI), the first precise measurements of the Vela pulsar’s proper motion established its projected birth site. Building on this 275 km, 1.6 GHz baseline with 140 mas resolution, we extend the analysis to the third dimension via annual parallax, yielding a direct distance and three-dimensional space velocity. Combining astrometry with pulsar polarization geometry, we determine the offset between the spin axis and the proper-motion vector and use this misalignment to constrain the duration and nature of the natal kick imparted by the supernova explosion. These results provide a self-consistent kinematic model for Vela and stringent limits on post-supernova acceleration timescales.

We investigate parametric level statistics of discretized excitation spectra within a moving vortex core in layered superconductors with impurities. Using numerical simulations, we evaluate the universal conductivity over rescaled vortex velocities @xmath0, spanning the clean to dirty limits. In the large-@xmath0 regime, the spectra exhibit level correlations and conductance fluctuations consistent with random matrix theory, confirming its prediction quantitatively. At low velocities, we observe @xmath1, revealing a distinct super-clean behavior governed by Landau–Zener transitions at avoided crossings. This mechanism accounts for energy dissipation and nonuniversal scaling of conductivity. Our results establish the crossover between RMT universality and super-clean dynamics in layered systems.

We present a combined search for the Standard Model Higgs boson using data from the CDF and DØ experiments in proton–antiproton collisions at the Fermilab Tevatron with a center-of-mass energy of 1.96 TeV. The combination includes 1.0–1.9 fb−1 from CDF and 0.9–1.7 fb−1 from DØ across multiple channels, with systematic uncertainties treated coherently. We set 95% confidence level upper limits of 6.2 (1.4) times the Standard Model cross section for Higgs masses of 115 (160) GeV/c^2; the corresponding median expected limits are 4.3 (1.9). These preliminary results substantially extend the sensitivity beyond the individual experiments’ limits.

Using the long, homogeneous magnetogram record from the Michelson Doppler Imager aboard the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory spanning Solar Cycle 23, we investigate the cyclic behavior of small-scale magnetic elements across the quiet Sun and active regions. More than 13 million network elements were automatically identified and characterized in terms of number, individual flux, and total flux, and their variability was compared to the sunspot cycle using monthly and running-average diagnostics. We find that quiet regions dominated the Sun’s surface magnetic flux for approximately 8 of the 12.25 years of Cycle 23. Over the cycle, the monthly average magnetic flux of quiet regions exceeded that of active regions by 12% on average. The ratio of quiet-region flux to the total solar flux provides a robust descriptor of cycle phase: its six-month running mean remained above 90% for 28 consecutive months, from July 2007 to October 2009, effectively capturing the prolonged minimum between Cycles 23 and 24. Examining the flux dependence of network-element variability reveals three regimes across the element flux spectrum: no correlation, anti-correlation, and positive correlation with sunspot number for, respectively, the smallest, intermediate, and largest elements. The anti-correlated elements in an intermediate flux range constitute 77.2% of all elements by number and contribute 37.4% of the quiet-Sun flux. These findings demonstrate that the quiet Sun not only carries a substantial share of the photospheric magnetic budget through most of the cycle, but also that flux-dependent small-scale populations respond differently to the global dynamo, offering a natural explanation for anti-phased variations of small-scale magnetic activity over the solar cycle.

We study the distribution of pseudo‐Anosov elements in the Cayley graph of the mapping class group of a closed surface, with respect to arbitrary generating sets. For balls of large radius centered at the identity, we analyze the proportion of vertices that represent pseudo‐Anosov mapping classes.
