We introduce a unified class of probabilistic models grounded in an operator algebra for stochastic processes and represented by stochastic parameterized grammars. A grammar’s syntax is mapped to semantics in a ring of operators, making grammatical composition correspond to operator addition and multiplication; these operators generate the time evolution of the associated stochastic dynamics. This framework subsumes and connects data clustering models, probabilistic logic programs, ordinary and stochastic differential equations, graph grammars, and stochastic chemical reaction kinetics. By importing methods from operator algebra and quantum field theory, we derive compact representations, composition laws, and inference procedures for interacting systems. We illustrate the approach with examples across multiple domains, showing modularity and practical solution schemes. This formulation bridges disparate formalisms and suggests algorithmic and theoretical tools.

We report the detection of X-ray emission from the unusual Galactic radio source known as the “Tornado,” using observations obtained with the Chandra X-ray Observatory. The data reveal up to three distinct X-ray emitting regions associated with the source: a relatively bright, spatially extended component coincident with and interior to the brightest radio emission at the Tornado’s “head,” and two fainter, diffuse regions that may be associated with structures along the “tail.” No X-ray point sources coincident with the Tornado are detected down to a stringent luminosity limit in the 0.5–10 keV band, assuming a distance of 12 kpc, which constrains the presence of compact accretors or luminous pulsars in the system. Spectral analysis of the brightest X-ray region indicates a heavily absorbed thermal plasma, with column densities consistent with a large intervening gas and dust path length and a temperature in the keV range. An absorbed power-law model provides an alternative description of the spectrum but requires an unusually steep photon index, disfavoring a purely nonthermal origin for the head emission. Taken together, the morphology and spectral properties tentatively point to an interpretation of the Tornado as a supernova remnant (SNR). Within this framework, the head appears to be a limb-brightened radio shell hosting centrally filled, thermal X-rays, and shows evidence for interaction with a molecular cloud, suggesting shock heating and mixing that are characteristic of “mixed-morphology” (thermal composite) SNRs. The Tornado’s extended tail remains puzzling in this picture. We consider the possibility that its morphology arises from SNR expansion into an elongated progenitor wind bubble, which could imprint a highly asymmetric density structure on the ambient medium. Alternative scenarios, including powering by outflows from an X-ray binary or a relativistic pulsar wind, cannot be definitively excluded by the present data. Further deep, multiwavelength observations will be essential to discriminate between these possibilities.

We investigate the mobility of nonlinear localized modes in a generalized discrete complex Ginzburg–Landau lattice modeling a one-dimensional waveguide array embedded in an active Kerr medium with intrinsic, saturable gain and damping. Combining numerical continuation in a co-moving frame, direct time-domain simulations, and Floquet stability analysis, we demonstrate the existence of exponentially localized, traveling discrete dissipative breather–solitons that arise as stable attractors without any external drive or symmetry-breaking perturbation. Mobility is enabled by a self-organized balance between gain and damping that dynamically overcomes the Peierls–Nabarro barrier of the corresponding conservative system via time-periodic oscillations of the soliton’s power (norm) and energy (Hamiltonian). The resulting moving states exhibit asymmetric exponential tails, with distinct decay rates in forward and backward directions. Parameter scans reveal bistability between fast, weakly oscillating modes and slower modes with large oscillation amplitudes. The soliton velocity and its internal oscillation period are typically locked by lattice commensurability, and systematic parameter variations produce period-doubling cascades leading to chaotically walking states. Incorporating an inter-site Kerr nonlinearity reduces the conservative Peierls–Nabarro barrier, substantially enlarging the mobility domain and yielding a richer dynamical scenario that includes Hopf bifurcations to incommensurate drift and phase-locking intervals. The moving breathers remain robust under weak structural disorder, indicating structural stability of the attractors. These results establish an intrinsic, autonomous mechanism for sustained soliton transport in active photonic lattices and delineate regimes and bifurcation pathways relevant for experiments on waveguide arrays with saturable gain and loss, with implications for controllable energy transport and reconfigurable light routing in nonlinear dissipative lattices.

Truemper configurations—theta, wheel, prism, and pyramid—are fundamental in decomposition theorems for hereditary graph classes. We establish two structure theorems: (i) a decomposition for graphs excluding thetas, wheels, and prisms as induced subgraphs; and (ii) a decomposition for graphs excluding thetas, wheels, and pyramids as induced subgraphs. These characterizations yield polynomial-time recognition algorithms for both classes, and provide insights into their structural properties. Our results clarify Truemper-free graph structure and improve recognition in hereditary classes. AMS Classification: 05C75.

We investigate entanglement generation in a double-@xmath0 atomic system interacting with a two-mode field. Using standard laser theory, we derive coupled dynamical equations for the field and obtain transient solutions. Entanglement criteria are evaluated to identify feasible regimes and thresholds for entanglement existence. Analysis reveals that, for appropriate detunings, pump strengths, and decay rates, the two-mode field becomes entangled while simultaneously experiencing amplification.

Computing the finite-temperature density matrix without explicit diagonalization is central to large-scale electronic-structure calculations. Building on a previous polynomial-expansion-plus-iterative-inversion approach, we present substantive algorithmic advances that markedly improve efficiency and robustness. We reformulate the original complex-valued framework into a purely real scheme that preserves Hermiticity and positivity while simplifying implementation and reducing memory traffic. A Chebyshev polynomial expansion provides near-optimal uniform approximation to the Fermi–Dirac occupation, and a tailored iterative inversion for shifted systems is combined with fast summation techniques to accelerate series evaluation. These innovations reduce the dependence on the Hamiltonian spectral width from linear to approximately its cubic root, yielding substantial savings at low temperatures or when high energy resolution is required. For sparse matrices, the overall complexity is effectively linear in system size, and the method parallelizes naturally. Benchmarks on insulating and metallic test cases and ab initio molecular dynamics demonstrate accuracy comparable to diagonalization and rational FOE methods at a fraction of the cost. We discuss error control, parameter selection, and applicability to Kohn–Sham DFT and tight-binding Hamiltonians.

We investigate quantum Kagome-ice hardcore bosons, the XY limit of the quantum spin-ice Hamiltonian. Using a large-S expansion, we estimate zero-temperature thermodynamic quantities, including energy, condensate fraction, and dynamical structure factors. Our semi-classical analysis captures the low-energy excitations and correlators, and shows quantitative consistency with finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo simulations, establishing a reliable framework for benchmarking and interpreting Kagome-ice bosonic phases.

Diabetes imposes substantial global burdens, yet much of its morbidity is preventable through tight glycemic control. However, reliance on finger-stick calibration and sensor insertion limits adherence to continuous glucose monitoring. We report a noninvasive optical approach based on the vibrational overtone circular dichroism (VOCD) of glucose. Using polarization‐modulated near‐infrared spectroscopy, we measure the differential absorption of left- and right‐circularly polarized light at overtone bands where glucose exhibits chiroptical responses. Experiments in aqueous solutions, human serum, and tissue‐mimicking phantoms demonstrate concentration‐dependent VOCD signals across the physiologic range with specificity against water and common metabolites. Monte Carlo modeling and benchtop measurements establish penetration depths and signal‐to‐noise under realistic scattering. Prototype instrumentation with lock‐in detection yields readouts resilient to motion and temperature drift. These results support VOCD as a viable pathway to noninvasive glucose monitoring with potential to improve compliance and reduce costs.

We investigate magnetotransport in a thin graphite wire on SiO2, demonstrating strong electric-field control with back and side gates. Conductance exhibits reproducible mesoscopic fluctuations versus gate voltage, magnetic field, and temperature. Analysis of weak localization yields a phase-coherence length exceeding the wire width across carrier densities, rendering transport effectively one-dimensional. The coherence length increases linearly with conductivity over the explored range, indicating disorder-limited diffusion with dephasing dominated by electron–electron interactions. At 1.7 K, quantitative fits support e–e interaction–driven decoherence, while universal conductance fluctuations and gate-tunable magnetoresistance corroborate phase-coherent transport. Results constrain scattering mechanisms in graphite nanowires.

The precise measurement of the neutrino mixing angle θ13 has opened a gateway for next-generation reactor experiments to address the neutrino mass hierarchy and the leptonic CP-violating phase. Future reactor programs will emphasize mass hierarchy determination and precision measurements of oscillation parameters by exploiting the fine interference structure in the disappearance of reactor electron antineutrinos arising from two separated oscillation modes. Both relative and absolute spectral measurement strategies are being developed to maximize sensitivity while controlling reactor and detector systematics. The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) proposes a 20 kton liquid scintillator detector at a baseline of about 53 km from reactors with a total thermal power near 36 GW, targeting an energy resolution of order a few percent per square root of energy. Accounting for core spatial distribution and detector response uncertainties, JUNO is projected to achieve a few-sigma sensitivity to the mass hierarchy and to measure three mixing parameters with better than 1% precision. Multiple detector configurations are under study, with key technical challenges including the development of high-efficiency photomultiplier tubes and ultra-transparent liquid scintillator, alongside robust calibration systems. Funding has been approved by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and a similar Korean initiative, RENO-50, is planned. Both experiments anticipated commencing data taking around 2020, aiming for definitive hierarchy resolution and high-precision oscillation physics.

We present a unified treatment of electric and thermal transport in disordered Weyl ferromagnets using the Keldysh formalism in curved spacetime. We compute the anomalous thermal Hall conductivity from a Kubo response and heat magnetization, without assuming the Wiedemann–Franz law. Nonmagnetic impurity scattering is incorporated via a self-consistent T-matrix approximation, capturing both extrinsic Fermi-surface and intrinsic Fermi-sea contributions. We show that, in the low-temperature limit, the Wiedemann–Franz relation holds separately for these two channels. Our gauge-invariant framework clarifies the roles of disorder broadening and Berry curvature and lays a foundation for a unified finite-temperature theory of the anomalous Hall effect that consistently treats disorder and interactions, offering implications for magnetic Weyl semimetals.

We investigate a hybrid seesaw framework in which type I generates tri-bimaximal (TBM) mixing while type II provides the perturbation required to accommodate a non-zero reactor angle @xmath1 and a non-trivial leptonic Dirac phase @xmath0. Starting from TBM at leading order, we derive the most general type II neutrino mass matrix consistent with current oscillation data and identify the phase structures capable of inducing observable CP violation. We analyze two regimes: (i) a sub-leading type II contribution and (ii) a type II term comparable to type I. In both cases we establish analytic and numerical correlations among the type II parameters, @xmath0, and the lightest neutrino mass, for normal and inverted orderings. We further impose the requirement of successful leptogenesis, with washout, to delineate the allowed regions. The combined constraints yield ranges for @xmath0 and the lightest mass, a lower bound on the type II strength, and characteristic textures of the type II mass matrix that can be probed by upcoming oscillation and neutrinoless double beta decay experiments.

This paper introduces SAMTLA (Search and Mining Tools with Linguistic Analysis), a digital humanities system co-designed with historians and linguists to support corpus-scale inquiry across heterogeneous textual collections. SAMTLA enables quantification and exploration through approximate phrase search, document comparison, and integrated text mining workflows. Its retrieval engine departs from conventional word-based approaches by employing a character-level n-gram statistical language model, delivering language-agnostic, robust query processing that accommodates orthographic variation, transliteration, and historical spelling. To support efficient, scalable access, SAMTLA indexes content using a space-optimized character-based suffix tree coupled with a relational store of document content and rich metadata. The platform provides visualizations and tools for pattern discovery, comparative analysis, and community trend monitoring. We detail the system architecture, user interface design, probabilistic models and algorithms, and data storage schemas underpinning SAMTLA, and report case studies spanning historical newspapers, religious texts, and archival manuscripts. A crowdsourced evaluation of ranking performance demonstrates competitive effectiveness against baselines while highlighting the benefits of character-level modeling in multilingual and diachronic contexts. We conclude with broader implications for global digital humanities practice and future development and adoption.

We investigate how departures from unitary leptonic mixing influence the measurement of the Dirac CP phase in three-neutrino oscillations and the capability of long-baseline experiments to discover CP violation. Allowing for non-unitary mixing introduces additional CP-violating phases that can be degenerate with the standard phase, potentially biasing or weakening sensitivities. Using a general non-unitary parametrization, we derive oscillation probabilities for the baselines and energies of NOvA, T2K, and DUNE, and perform sensitivity studies including matter effects and realistic systematics. We present CP violation discovery reach for each experiment and for their joint combination, marginalizing over non-unitary parameters. While non-unitarity induces degeneracies that degrade individual sensitivities, combining data from the three experiments mitigates these effects and improves the CP violation sensitivity.

We study noninteracting bosons in a harmonic trap subjected to an adiabatic change of trap curvature and analyze fluctuations of the work performed. Starting from a grand-canonical equilibrium state specified by temperature and chemical potential, we derive the full work probability distribution via the adiabatic mapping of occupations and level rescaling. We identify reservoir conditions under which the exponentiated work average (EWA) diverges when the trap widens, even though the protocol is adiabatic. The divergence originates from an exponential work tail tied to large occupation fluctuations enabled by bosonic statistics and to the absence of a normalizable equilibrium reference state for the final Hamiltonian at the same chemical potential. At low temperatures the work distribution is highly asymmetric, with a steep fall-off on one side and an exponential tail on the other; at high temperatures it becomes more symmetric and approaches a Gaussian. These features diagnose the convergence or divergence of the EWA and clarify its connection to the existence of the hypothetical equilibrium state underlying the thermodynamic potential changes in the Crooks relation and the Jarzynski equality.

We present deep, multi-epoch radio imaging of the starburst galaxy M83 with the Very Large Array, spanning 15 years and incorporating previously unpublished observations from 1990 and 1998. Calibration, imaging, and astrometric registration yield a catalog of 55 compact sources whose flux densities and spectral indices are tracked across epochs. The sample includes four of the six known historical supernovae and 10 objects with Chandra counterparts. All X-ray–associated sources exhibit non-thermal radio spectra; most are consistent with supernova remnants based on their spectral indices, variability behavior, and multiwavelength properties. Cross-matching with optical and X-ray surveys identifies three sources as optical/X-ray supernova remnants. Nearly half of the detected radio sources coincide with cataloged H II regions embedded in the spiral arms, indicating ongoing star formation and a mixed population of thermal and non-thermal emitters. In the nuclear region, we detect complexity and variability at 20 cm, and confirm that the brightest radio peak is offset from the optical center. A fainter radio peak aligns with the optical/infrared nucleus. The distribution of radio emission is consistent with previous dynamical evidence for a “dark” nuclear mass, potentially associated with compact radio peaks. These results provide a time-resolved view of energetic feedback and nuclear dynamics in M83.

We present a first systematic investigation of halo stellar populations in spiral galaxies using Hubble Space Telescope imaging that resolves individual red-giant branch (RGB) stars. Our sample comprises eight nearby spirals observed along their minor axes at projected radii of 2–13 kpc. Color–magnitude diagrams of resolved RGB stars allow us to assess metallicity distributions and mean abundances from the RGB color locus. We find that more luminous host galaxies exhibit broader RGB color distributions and redder mean colors, indicating both higher average metallicities and larger heavy-element abundance spreads with increasing galaxy luminosity. A clear correlation emerges between the mean metallicity of the stellar halo and the parent galaxy luminosity. Notably, the Milky Way’s halo lies nearly 1 dex below this luminosity–metallicity relation, identifying it as an outlier and implying that massive spirals with metal-poor halos are atypical. The observed luminosity–halo abundance trend matches the scaling expected for stellar systems embedded in dominant halos, consistent with scenarios in which the bulk of halo stars formed in situ within the gravitational potential of their host galaxies. These results provide new empirical constraints on the chemical enrichment and assembly of spiral halos and establish a benchmark for models of halo formation across a range of galaxy masses.

Dual-record systems (DRS), equivalent to two-occasion capture–recapture, are widely used to estimate sizes of homogeneous human populations. The popular Chandrasekar–Deming model allows time variation in capture probabilities but ignores behavioral change after first capture. We study the joint time-and-behavior response model (M_tb) and tackle its intrinsic identifiability problem. We propose two approximate Bayesian strategies that yield practical estimates via simple Gibbs sampling. The first exploits prior knowledge on the direction and strength of the behavioral response (trap-happy or trap-shy) when such information exists. The second is designed for settings with unknown or ambiguous behavioral effects, imposing mild stochastic constraints to stabilize inference without strong assumptions. We examine their properties, provide guidance on method selection, and assess performance through extensive simulations covering population size, capture intensity, and response magnitude. Results show improved bias, mean squared error, and coverage relative to available alternatives. A real DRS application illustrates the approaches and their robustness. The proposed methods mitigate nonidentifiability and deliver stable approximate Bayes estimates for human population studies. Keywords: approximate Bayesian computing; behavioral response effect; homogeneous human population; identifiability; model M_tb.

We investigate the spin photogalvanic effect in two-dimensional electron systems with structure inversion asymmetry by solving the semiconductor optical Bloch equations. Accounting for Rashba spin–orbit coupling and spin-split conduction bands, we show that normal-incidence, linearly polarized light injects a pure spin current without net charge flow, whereas obliquely incident, circularly polarized light generates a spin-dependent photocurrent. We derive an explicit relation connecting the circularly induced photocurrent to the linearly induced pure spin current, enabling quantitative extraction of spin-current amplitude from experimentally accessible measurements. The framework clarifies polarization dependence and incidence-angle effects and provides guidelines for optical spin-current sources in semiconductor heterostructures. Our results offer a practical route to generate and calibrate spin currents optically, facilitating quantitative studies of spin transport and spin–orbit phenomena in low-dimensional systems.

Our position inside the Galaxy requires all-sky surveys to reveal its large-scale properties. Unlike standard relative measurements that reference a source to its local surroundings, all-sky surveys must recover emission on all angular scales above the instrumental resolution, including isotropic components. At frequencies up to a few GHz, Galactic synchrotron emission dominates; extensive total-intensity surveys exist to 1.4 GHz, and full-sky linear polarization at 1.4 GHz has only recently become available. At higher frequencies, WMAP provides all-sky total intensity and polarization maps from 23 GHz upward, complementing ground-based data. Galactic plane surveys achieve finer angular resolution with single dishes or synthesis arrays, but filtering of large angular scales complicates interpretation. Polarized diffuse emission exhibits structures unrelated to total intensity, arising from Faraday rotation and depolarization in the magneto-ionic interstellar medium. Robust physical inference from these polarization features critically depends on setting the absolute zero level of Stokes U and Q. Absolute calibration of Stokes I, U, and Q is therefore indispensable. We discuss zero-level calibration requirements, quantify offsets' impact on rotation measures and field reconstruction, and propose combining absolutely calibrated all-sky maps with high-resolution plane surveys for faithful, multi-scale views of Galactic magnetism. This framework enables consistent modeling of the interstellar medium and reliable foreground characterization for cosmological studies.

Strong galaxy–galaxy gravitational lenses, in which a background galaxy is closely aligned with a massive foreground galaxy, enable precise measurements of the total mass distribution and the dark matter density profile in the lens, independent of dynamical assumptions. However, only a handful of such systems with confirmed source redshifts and sufficient optical brightness are currently available for high-resolution imaging with the HST Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS). Motivated by the success of identifying lenses via anomalous background emission lines superimposed on the spectra of massive early-type galaxies, we conducted a systematic search for such features within the luminous red galaxy (LRG) subsample of the SDSS DR3 spectroscopic database. Our methodology parallels recent successful approaches, while deliberately extending sensitivity to higher-redshift lensed sources by allowing for single, narrow emission lines at wavelengths consistent with [O II] λλ3726, 3729 and associated transitions. We report follow-up imaging and spectroscopy for two candidates, both confirmed as gravitational lenses through the detection of multiple images in [O II]. In J145957.1−005522.8, the lens comprises two LRGs at intermediate redshift; the anomalous [O II] line is corroborated by detection of Hβ from the source, securing its redshift and confirming the lensing configuration. In J230946.3−003912.9, a single LRG lenses a background source whose redshift is established by partially resolving the [O II] doublet. These systems enlarge the small sample of galaxy–galaxy lenses suitable for ACS, and their image separations and line fluxes indicate Einstein radii on kiloparsec scales. With high-resolution imaging and lens modeling, they will yield robust constraints on the inner mass profile, dark matter fraction, and mass-to-light ratio in massive early-type galaxies. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of emission-line selection in LRG spectra and open a path to building a statistically meaningful sample for testing ΛCDM predictions on galaxy scales.

We investigate how the X-ray luminosity of young, isolated pulsars powered by the ejection of relativistic particles depends on magnetospheric electric field intensity, spin-down power, magnetic field, rotation period, and other neutron-star parameters. Using measurements, we analyze the empirical L_X–dot E and L_X–characteristic age relations, and assess how magnetic field strength and evolutionary effects (cooling, field decay, braking index evolution, geometry) shape these dependences. We find that L_X scales sublinearly with spin-down power, steepening for the youngest objects, and declines with increasing characteristic age. Only pulsars with X-ray luminosities greater than about 10^34 erg s^-1 host detectable pulsar wind nebulae. Pulsars detected in gamma rays exhibit low X-ray luminosities. Keywords: pulsar, SNR, X-ray.

We investigate the construction of large photonic cluster states for universal quantum computation using probabilistic fusion of small primitives under storage-induced decoherence. First, we analyze assemblies built exclusively from dephased two-qubit clusters, assuming all fusion attempts succeed and no further dephasing during construction, to isolate how phase noise in the primitives maps onto imperfections of larger clusters. We derive fidelity and entanglement scaling laws that quantify error propagation across fusions and identify regimes where primitive dephasing produces local versus correlated phase errors on the assembled cluster. We then consider a more realistic scenario in which decoherence occurs prior to every attempted fusion and fusion operations can fail. Using fidelity as the accuracy metric, we optimize strategies to build a five-qubit cluster, comparing direct versus staged assembly, recycling of remnants after failed fusions, and parallel versus serial scheduling. The optimal protocol balances storage time against fusion depth, favoring parallel assembly and recycling under a dephasing threshold. Finally, we discuss photon loss, its interplay with dephasing, and its impact on fusion success and cluster integrity, highlighting the benefits of heralding, loss-aware routing, and adaptive retry policies. Our results provide practical design guidelines for photonic cluster construction.

We study enumerative questions for meromorphic functions on compact Riemann surfaces with fixed critical values and prescribed multiplicities at critical points and values. For the Riemann sphere and polynomial maps, we provide an elementary computation of the exact count. In general, as the multiplicities of critical points grow, we prove an asymptotic formula: the number of such functions is governed by the volume of a moduli space of graphs obtained by gluing circles. We characterize this volume combinatorially and represent it explicitly as a matrix integral, providing a geometric–combinatorial framework.

Understanding out-of-equilibrium dynamics in interacting quantum spin systems is central to quantum information processing, statistical mechanics, and nanotechnologies, yet requires efficient large-scale computational simulations. We address this challenge using the Trotter–Suzuki (TS) decomposition to approximate real-time evolution and present a GPU-based implementation of a TS scheme previously restricted to single-core CPUs. By exploiting massive parallelism, locality of two-spin gates, and coalesced memory access, our approach accelerates the simulation of many-body spin dynamics while retaining the controllable Trotter error. Benchmarks on prototypical models (e.g., transverse-field Ising and XXZ chains) demonstrate substantial speedups over CPU execution. The GPU implementation reduces execution time considerably and enables simulations of up to 27 spins, with limits set by device memory. Validation via energy conservation, state fidelity, and norm preservation confirms robust accuracy. This framework expands accessible regimes in nonequilibrium quantum dynamics and facilitates rapid exploration of parameter spaces.

The relationship between logarithmic space (L) and nondeterministic logarithmic space (NL) remains one of the central open problems in computational complexity. The switching network model provides a combinatorial framework for studying the directed connectivity problem that captures monotone and non-monotone analogues of these classes. In earlier work, by restricting attention to inputs consisting of a single directed path together with isolated vertices, we established tight quasi-polynomial lower and upper bounds for monotone switching networks: any monotone network that solves directed connectivity on n vertices must have size at least n^{Ω(log n)}, and this bound is achievable. Extending such lower bounds to general switching networks for directed connectivity would imply a separation between L and NL, but pursuing this direction requires stronger monotone lower bounds. To advance this program, we examine a different family of inputs that we initially believed to be hard for monotone switching networks. Contrary to expectation, we show that these inputs admit a polynomial-size monotone switching network via a construction that exploits structural symmetries and reachability constraints in a nonstandard way. While “monotone knowledge” appears insufficient to capture the full power needed, the construction demonstrates that monotone switching networks can circumvent intuitive bottlenecks through a “weird” but efficient wiring. We then focus on certain-knowledge switching networks, a natural and intuitive subclass of monotone switching networks tailored to directed connectivity. For the same family of inputs, we prove that no polynomial-size certain-knowledge switching network can exist, establishing superpolynomial lower bounds. Together, these results give a strict separation: monotone switching networks for directed connectivity are strictly more powerful than certain-knowledge switching networks. Our findings refine the landscape of lower-bound techniques for directed connectivity, indicating that approaches successful for certain-knowledge networks cannot, by themselves, yield the stronger monotone lower bounds needed to attack general switching networks. This suggests that any path toward resolving L versus NL via the switching network model will require fundamentally new insights beyond the certain-knowledge paradigm.

We study Toral's Parrondo games with @xmath0 players and one-dimensional spatial dependence as modified by Xie et al. Using computer graphics, we sketch Parrondo and anti-Parrondo regions for @xmath1, delineating parameter regimes producing paradox and reversal. Motivated by Li et al., who reduced the state space from @xmath2 to @xmath3 via equivalence classes, we analyze lumpability under dihedral symmetry. We show that their reduced Markov chains are not lumpable for the Xie et al. dynamics and thus inconsistent with the model. Our results clarify symmetry reductions valid in cooperative Parrondo games. Key words: Markov chain, equivalence class, lumpability, dihedral group, Parrondo's paradox, cooperative Parrondo games.

We investigate a rapidly oscillating scalar field as quintessence within a nonminimal kinetic coupling framework. Upon time averaging, the field behaves as a perfect fluid with a variable equation-of-state parameter expressible as a function of the Hubble rate, enabling a closed evolution via the continuity equation. We show that the field mimics dark energy at the present epoch and dynamically evolves toward dark-matter-like behavior in the future, naturally inducing a transition from the current acceleration to a decelerated phase without invoking explicit interactions. We further analyze an interacting extension between dark sectors that alleviates the coincidence problem and delineate the viable parameter space. A dynamical-systems and stability analysis identifies stable attractor solutions associated with dark-energy–dominated and matter-like regimes, and establishes conditions for background and perturbative stability across cosmic evolution.

This review surveys computational approaches for Casimir forces and fluctuation-induced interactions between bodies of arbitrary shapes and materials, drawing explicit parallels to established techniques in classical electromagnetism. We organize methods by (i) problem formulation (scattering, stress-tensor, stochastic fields), (ii) basis choice (modal, voxel, boundary), and (iii) solution strategy (analytical, FEM/FDTD, BEM, integral-equation). We discuss material dispersion, temperature, and nontrivial geometries, and highlight modifications required to adapt mature classical tools to quantum fluctuations. Benchmark comparisons, accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, and best practices are presented, providing a unified framework to select and implement reliable Casimir computations.

Motivated by the triple coincidence problem, we propose and analyze a cosmological scenario with three interacting fluids—pressureless matter, radiation, and dark energy—coupled through interaction terms that mediate energy exchange. Within a flat FRW background, we derive the dynamical equations, obtain scaling solutions, and identify parameter regions that alleviate the coincidence by locking the density ratios near unity at late times. Using effective equation-of-state diagnostics, we determine the criteria under which the combined dark sector crosses the phantom divide, and classify the stability of such trajectories. Observational constraints and viability conditions are discussed.

This paper explores conceptual issues arising from speed-up and slowdown phenomena in small Turing machines, and presents an experimental test intended to spur empirical approaches to computational irreducibility. The test attempts to outrun the computation of a large corpus of machines—exhaustively covering all 3- and 4-state, 2-symbol Turing machines—by predicting their evolving integer sequences with a specialized function-finder program. By systematically comparing prediction trajectories with ground-truth executions, we quantify success and failure regimes, identify robustness and fragility to short training windows, and expose thresholds where prediction collapses despite determinism. The experiment motivates a finer analysis of rates of convergence for decision procedures, illuminates practical limits on decidability for naturally occurring sets derived from machine behaviors, and connects these limits to the halting problem and the problem of induction. We argue that this methodology offers a novel bridge between algorithmic epistemology and computational experiments, demonstrating philosophical questions about predictability and knowledge can be operationalized within simulations. Keywords: computational irreducibility; unpredictability; problem of induction; algorithmic epistemology; halting problem. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 68Q01, 68Q17, 68Q15.

We calculate hydrodynamic timescales for a spherical ultra-relativistic ejecta shell decelerated by the interstellar medium (ISM) and relate them to the temporal structure of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). We show that the burst duration traces the deceleration timescale, short-timescale variability arises from ISM density inhomogeneities, and faint precursors are produced by internal shocks within the shell. Using reasonable, non–fine-tuned astrophysical parameters, these associations reproduce observed durations and variability amplitudes. Furthermore, the distinct behavior of Newtonian versus relativistic reverse shocks naturally yields a bimodal distribution of GRB durations. Our framework offers unified, testable connections between shell dynamics and GRB temporal phenomenology.

We present HARES, a High-Performance Fortran adaptive-grid real-space electronic-structure implementation of density-functional theory for both infinite periodic and finite systems. The code combines high-order finite-difference discretizations, adaptive curvilinear grids, and multigrid Poisson solvers with domain decomposition and communication-avoiding strategies to attain high efficiency on parallel architectures. We analyze the scaling of the principal kernels—Hamiltonian application, orthonormalization/diagonalization, charge-density updates, and Poisson solves—and compare them with plane-wave methods, highlighting favorable memory footprints, reduced FFT-related communication, and superior performance for heterogeneous length scales and large unit cells. Implementation details of the HPF parallelization and load balancing are described. Applications to elemental crystalline solids, molecules, and complex crystalline materials, including blue bronze and zeolites, illustrate accuracy commensurate with plane waves and substantial improvements in parallel efficiency and wall-time, demonstrating the broad applicability of HARES.

We use first-principles density functional theory to investigate epitaxial spin-filter tunnel junctions based on the ferromagnetic semiconductor europium monoxide (EuO), focusing on Cu(100)/EuO(100)/Cu(100) structures. Spin-resolved transmission coefficients and current–voltage characteristics are computed as a function of EuO thickness and Cu–EuO interface spacing, and interpreted with the EuO density of states and the complex band structure. We further analyze how interface geometries affect level alignment and tunneling. Our results show that the interface spacing sensitively controls the band alignment via charge transfer between EuO and Cu, shifting the Fermi level relative to the Eu 5d conduction and Eu 4f valence bands. For epitaxial EuO on Cu, the junction acts as a near-perfect spin filter, with spin polarization approaching 100%, sustained over a wide bias range. Both Eu 5d and Eu 4f states contribute to transport depending on the alignment, and symmetry filtering is observed: Delta1 states dominate the transmission through EuO(100), producing an effective transport gap larger than the fundamental EuO band gap. The decay of evanescent states and the thickness dependence of conductance follow the predictions of the complex band structure. These findings highlight the crucial role of interface control in maximizing spin-filter performance and provide guidelines for spin-polarized tunnel devices.

This paper addresses consensus tracking in multi‐agent systems with an active leader under variable interconnection topology. The leader’s state evolves dynamically and may be unmeasurable. We design for each autonomous agent a neighbor‐based local controller coupled with a neighbor‐based state‐estimation rule to reconstruct the leader state and achieve tracking using only relative information. Under standard connectivity assumptions on the switching graph, we prove that all agents asymptotically follow the leader when its acceleration input is known. When the leader input is unknown, the proposed estimator yields bounded tracking with provable error bounds and convergence of the estimation error. Lyapunov analysis establishes stability. Keywords: multi‐agent systems; consensus; state estimation; active leader.

We present a comprehensive spectroscopic investigation of the electronic states correlated to the 4s+5s atomic asymptote in KRb. Using Fourier-transform spectroscopy, we recorded extensive rovibrational data constraining an accurate potential energy curve up to internuclear distances of 14.8. The ground-state dataset of C. Amiot et al. (J. Chem. Phys. 112, 7068 (2000)) is augmented with newly observed levels near the asymptote. A global coupled-channels fitting procedure yields complete molecular potentials for both electronic states. Together with line frequencies, published positions of Feshbach resonances in 40K–87Rb mixtures (F. Ferlaino et al., Phys. Rev. A 74, 039903 (2006)) are incorporated to constrain near-threshold scattering. The resulting potentials reproduce observed cold-collision features and enable reliable predictions of scattering lengths and Feshbach resonances for other isotopic combinations. The potentials furnish interaction models for KRb relevant to ultracold molecule formation and quantum control. These benchmarks support precision modeling of mixed-alkali systems and guide experiments on resonance control and sympathetic cooling.

Desorption characteristics of molecules on interstellar dust grains govern the exchange between icy mantles and the gas phase. We present laboratory measurements of the desorption of CO, O2, and CO2 from three astrophysically relevant substrates: non‐porous water ice, crystalline water ice, and silicate surfaces, at both sub‐monolayer and multilayer coverages. Experimental desorption profiles were modeled with the Polanyi–Wigner formalism, yielding a parameterization that reproduces monolayer and multilayer regimes for each molecule–surface combination. The results reveal substrate-specific binding energies and kinetics in the monolayer regime, with zero‐order kinetics dominating multilayer desorption. The combined model enables extrapolation to low heating rates and long timescales, predicting release sequences under interstellar conditions. We discuss the implications for icy mantles, CO, O2, and CO2 desorption, and the treatment of the solid–gas interface in astrochemical simulations. The framework offers parameter sets suitable for incorporation into astrochemical models.

A 0535+262 is a transient Be/X-ray binary that remained in a prolonged quiescent phase from 1994 to 2005. We report on an INTEGRAL observation in October 2003 that yielded a significant detection of the source in hard X-rays. The source was detected for approximately 6000 seconds in the 18–100 keV band at a luminosity of about 3.8 × 10^34 erg s^-1, consistent with the high end of the range expected for quiescent emission from Be/X-ray binaries. Timing analysis reveals coherent pulsations with a period P = 103.7 ± 0.1 s, demonstrating that the system was outside the centrifugal inhibition (propeller) regime and accretion onto the magnetic poles was ongoing. Examination of the pulse history since the onset of quiescence in 1994 shows a steady spin-down, indicating the persistent presence of an accretion disk that supplies a net negative torque to the pulsar even in the absence of major outbursts. The hard X-ray detection and variability confirm that the system remains active and highly variable during quiescence, without recent Type I or Type II X-ray outbursts. These results provide direct evidence for low-level, disk-mediated accretion and torque in quiescent Be/X-ray binaries and underscore the value of hard X-ray monitoring in characterizing their long-term evolution.

We demonstrate that Jaynes–Cummings dynamics can emerge in mesoscopic atomic ensembles driven by a classical electromagnetic field within the Rydberg blockade regime. Owing to the atom-number dependence of collective Rabi frequencies, the time evolution of the average number of Rydberg excitations exhibits collapses and revivals characteristic of the Jaynes–Cummings model. For randomly loaded optical dipole traps, the distribution of interacting atom numbers induces dephasing and subsequent rephasing, yielding predictable revival structures. Using a combination of master-equation simulations and Monte Carlo sampling over atom-number distributions, we quantify how finite interaction strengths (imperfect blockade) and finite laser linewidth reduce the visibility of revivals, and identify conditions under which they remain robust. Our results establish collapses and revivals of collective Rabi oscillations as a practical, non-destructive signature of Rydberg blockade, enabling verification without direct measurement of the exact number of Rydberg excitations and providing guidelines for experimental implementation.

Reports of resonant enhanced transmission and collimation through subwavelength slits in metal films prompt a fundamental question: can an ultrashort light pulse be simultaneously enhanced and localized in space and time by a nanoscale aperture? We analyze the spatial distribution of the energy flux of a femtosecond wave packet diffracted by a nanometer-wide slit using a conventional rigorous approach based on the Neerhoff–Mur solution of Maxwell’s equations, reconstructing the time-domain field from its spectral components. The calculations show orders-of-magnitude enhancement of the transmitted peak energy flux accompanied by simultaneous confinement in the near-field diffraction zone, with lateral localization on nanometer scales and temporal localization on femtosecond scales. Temporal broadening and spatial spreading remain minimal within the near field. These results indicate that subwavelength slits can act as ultrafast nanofocusing elements, enabling applications in nanophotonics, including near-field microscopy, nanoscale spectroscopy, nanolithography, and on-chip optical interconnects.

We investigate the use of the Hurst exponent, dynamically computed over a moving time window, to evaluate firm-level stability and instability. We introduce a generalized Hurst exponent (GHE) estimator that assigns larger weights to recent observations, mitigating the influence of distant, large fluctuations and better capturing evolving market conditions. Applying the method to equity price time series around the 2007–2010 credit crisis, we find that financial firms subsequently bailed out exhibit a clear, monotonic increase in the weighted GHE in the months preceding the crisis unfolding, consistent with a transition toward stronger persistence and reduced mean reversion. In contrast, firms in more resilient sectors display opposite dynamics, with declining or low GHE values. We further analyze the scaling properties of the tails of log-returns and compare their tail-scaling exponents with GHE-based scaling, documenting significant discrepancies indicative of true multi-scaling in the underlying price processes. Robustness checks across window sizes, weighting schemes, and sampling frequencies confirm the stability of the results. Our findings suggest that dynamic scaling measures provide informative, forward-looking signals of fragility and can complement conventional risk metrics for real-time monitoring of firm stability. Keywords: generalized Hurst exponent, multi-scaling analysis, econophysics.

We investigate the superconducting gap structure of Ba1−xKxFe2As2 single crystals by controlled introduction of point-like defects via 2.5 MeV electron irradiation at doses up to 5.2 x 10^19 electrons/cm^2. Compositions studied include x = 0.19 (Tc = 14 K), x = 0.26 (Tc = 32 K), and x = 0.34 (Tc = 39 K). Electrical resistivity and London penetration depth were measured before and after irradiation, and the low-temperature behavior of Delta lambda(T) was analyzed using a power-law Delta lambda(T) = A(T/Tc)^n. For all x, irradiation increased residual resistivity and suppressed Tc, consistent with pair breaking by non-magnetic scattering in a sign-changing s-wave state. Near optimal doping, x = 0.26 and 0.34, despite noticeable Tc suppression, the power-law exponent n remained high (n ~ 3 to 4), indicating robust, nearly isotropic full gaps with weak low-energy quasiparticle excitation. In underdoped x = 0.19, which exhibits coexistence of superconductivity with long-range magnetic order, Tc was suppressed more rapidly and n decreased toward the dirty-limit value n ~ 2, signaling enhanced gap anisotropy or deep minima. Irradiation also reduced the structural/magnetic transition temperature Tsm from 103 K to 98 K, consistent with the itinerant character of the magnetism and its sensitivity to point-like disorder. These results demonstrate that underdoped Ba1−xKxFe2As2 compositions, particularly in the coexistence regime, are most susceptible to non-magnetic impurity scattering. The contrasting robustness of optimally doped samples implies a smaller interband-to-intraband pairing ratio and more isotropic gaps near optimal doping, while moving away from optimal doping enhances interband coupling and gap anisotropy. Our study provides a controlled-disorder probe of multiband pairing and gap structure in iron-based superconductors. These insights inform disorder-engineering strategies and theoretical modeling.

We present time-resolved spectroscopy and circular spectropolarimetry of the SW Sex star RXJ1643.7+3402. We detect significant, coherent circular polarisation exhibiting a clear modulation at a period of @xmath0 min, and contemporaneous emission-line flaring that occurs predominantly at twice the polarimetric period. The phase-coherent polarimetric signal and the harmonic flaring behaviour provide strong evidence for a magnetic white dwarf driving magnetically channelled accretion in this system. Interpreting the observed periodicities within a magnetic accretion framework for SW Sex stars, we suggest that in RXJ1643.7+3402 the circular polarisation varies at @xmath1, while the emission lines flare at @xmath2, in contrast to the behaviour previously reported for LS Pegasi, the first SW Sex star with modulated circular polarisation. Nevertheless, an alternative @xmath3/@xmath4 assignment cannot be ruled out with the present data. Together with LS Peg and V795 Her, RXJ1643.7+3402 thus becomes the third SW Sex system known to display modulated circular polarisation, strengthening the case that a substantial fraction of SW Sex stars are magnetic, intermediate-polar-like cataclysmic variables.

We perform a non-perturbative analysis of the strong interaction between gapless nodal fermions and the nematic order parameter in two-dimensional d-wave superconductors. We show that critical nematic fluctuations can dynamically generate a nodal gap when the fermion flavor N is below a threshold Nc. The emergent gap drives an additional s-wave Cooper pairing instability, producing a fully gapped s-wave superconducting dome near the nematic quantum critical point. The dynamical gap has several consequences: saturation of fermion velocity renormalization, weak confinement of nodal quasiparticles, and suppression of low-energy thermodynamic and transport responses. Our results clarify the fate of nodal physics near nematic criticality and suggest experimental signatures.

We use the five-year data from WMAP to place stringent, internally consistent limits on departures from the minimal, six-parameter ΛCDM model and to constrain key aspects of early- and late-time cosmology. Combining WMAP with Type Ia supernova (SN) distance measurements and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data from galaxy surveys, we find no convincing evidence for deviations from the minimal model. We present a non-relativistic quantum mechanical theory in which the universe is a continuum of mutually interfering worlds. We develop a two-mode logical framework treating time and world as independent dimensions of existence, analogous to the temporal continuum, allowing well-formed propositions about objects across multiple worlds. The ontology comprises a continuous substance of worlds, each with definite particle configurations guided by a universal wavefunction; interference between worlds replaces stochastic collapse. Postulates specify: (i) the state consists of a wavefunction ψ on configuration space together with a measure over the world continuum whose density equals |ψ|^2; (ii) deterministic evolution per Schrödinger dynamics and guidance equations coupling worlds; (iii) measurement is interaction yielding effective decoherence across the world continuum without splitting. We show that standard quantum predictions follow, and that the Born rule emerges as subjective probability due to ignorance of which world index obtains; probabilities assigned by the world-measure reproduce Born statistics. Apparent collapse arises as Bayesian conditioning on the observer’s world after measurement and coarse-graining under decoherence; yet global dynamics remains deterministic. The theory shares with Bohmian mechanics a clear ontology of trajectories and with Everettian interpretations the multiplicity of worlds, but differs by positing a continuum without branching or creation of worlds. The calculus enables precise treatment of cross-world propositions and counterfactuals. We discuss implications for the measurement problem and nonlocality, routes to extending the framework to open systems and relativistic fields. The result is a unified, axiomatic interpretation explaining subjective probabilities, their quantitative Born value, and effective collapse while preserving determinism.

The proposed correction of @xmath1 mag/dex is applied to Magellanic Cloud distances derived from a Galactic VI@xmath0 Wesenheit calibration anchored to ten nearby classical Cepheids with HST parallaxes. The resulting @xmath2-corrected distances for the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) and @xmath3 are found to be in significant disagreement with the mean of @xmath4 published estimates compiled in NED-D, as well as with distances inferred from a universal Wesenheit template built from eleven @xmath5 Scuti, SX Phe, RR Lyrae, and Type II Cepheid variables with HST/Hipparcos parallaxes. In contrast, adopting a null metallicity correction (i.e., @xmath6 mag/dex) brings the Magellanic Cloud distances into mutual agreement and consolidates them with independent benchmarks. Together with existing lines of evidence, these results support the conclusion that variations in chemical composition among Cepheids constitute a comparatively negligible source of uncertainty in W@xmath7-based extragalactic distances and determinations of @xmath8. We outline a new approach to expand the set of Galactic Cepheid calibrators and enable further tests of the VI@xmath0 Wesenheit function’s relative insensitivity to abundance. For select sightlines, this relation can be leveraged to determine absolute Wesenheit magnitudes for younger Cepheids associated with those clusters, while mitigating extinction and crowding biases. The expanded calibrator sample will permit a more rigorous quantification of any residual metallicity effects across a broader parameter space, reinforcing the robustness of the Cepheid-based distance scale.

We review universal and nonuniversal critical exponents in three-dimensional Ising systems with weak quenched disorder. Experimental measurements, Monte Carlo simulations, and analytical approaches are surveyed, with special emphasis on field-theoretical renormalization group methods. We compare minimal subtraction and massive schemes, discuss resummation techniques, and analyze the divergent perturbative series that underlie exponent estimates. The interplay between disorder strength, crossover behavior, and scaling corrections is clarified, providing a coherent picture of consensus and open issues.

The min-sum (MS) algorithm is arguably the second most fundamental message-passing decoder, owing to its optimality on tree graphs with respect to block error probability and its close conceptual connection to linear programming (LP) decoding. Despite this importance, its fundamental properties have not been investigated as thoroughly as those of the sum-product (belief propagation, BP) algorithm. This paper addresses two central questions about MS decoding. First, we characterize the stability condition of MS under density evolution on memoryless channels. We prove that, for standard binary-input symmetric channels, the MS stability threshold is governed by essentially the same spectral-radius condition as in BP decoding, thereby aligning the onset of reliable iterative convergence for the two algorithms despite their distinct message-update rules. Second, we conduct degree-distribution optimization for irregular LDPC ensembles under MS on the AWGN channel. In contrast to BP, where optimized ensembles approach the Shannon limit, the best MS-optimized ensembles we find exhibit thresholds significantly bounded away from capacity: the gap to capacity is @xmath0 dB for a rate @xmath1 code and @xmath2 dB for a rate @xmath3 code, with the gap decreasing monotonically as the rate increases. We further explore a modified MS rule in which check-node outputs are scaled by a constant @xmath4. Using the same optimization framework, we observe that for @xmath5 the scaled-MS variant achieves uniformly better thresholds than unscaled MS, yet the gaps remain sizable, ranging from 0.75 dB to 0.2 dB for design rates between 0.3 and 0.9. These findings delineate inherent performance limitations of MS relative to BP on AWGN channels and quantify the extent to which simple scaling can mitigate them. We conclude by identifying several open problems, including tighter converse bounds on MS thresholds, principled design of nonuniform or state-dependent scalings, and a deeper characterization of the MS–LP decoding relationship.
