The scaling is further supported by independent determinations of @xmath4 from samples with X-ray and gravitational-lensing mass estimates, with all measurements agreeing within the quoted uncertainties as @xmath7 across @xmath6 Mpc. The resulting constraints are consistent with the expectations of open CDM (OCDM; @xmath8) and flat ΛCDM (@xmath9) models, whereas the standard CDM scenario shows a distinct, incompatible behavior. Taken together, these results favor cosmological models with a low matter density and demonstrate that scale-invariant cluster abundance provides a robust, multi-probe test of CDM cosmogonies.

We present high-angular-resolution imaging of the newly identified T dwarf SDSS J153417.05+161546.1, resolved into a 0.11 arcsec binary using the Keck II sodium laser guide star adaptive optics system. The system’s integrated-light near-infrared spectrum indicates an overall spectral type of T3.5±0.5. Near-infrared photometry and colors of the resolved components yield estimated spectral types of T1.5±0.5 and T5.5±0.5, consistent with modeling the integrated spectrum as a blend of two substellar atmospheres. The measured near-infrared flux ratios are unique among known brown dwarf binaries: the component that is fainter in the H and K bands is brighter in the J band. This inversion provides a direct, differential manifestation of the J-band brightening within a single, coeval system. Because both components share a common distance, age, and metallicity and exhibit very similar surface gravities, the observed J-band brightening must be intrinsic to ultracool photospheres. The phenomenon is therefore best explained by atmospheric processes—such as condensate cloud disruption and/or rapid increases in cloud sedimentation—rather than by ensemble effects driven by a wide range of masses, ages, or metallicities among field T dwarfs. We further propose that the large amplitude of the J-band brightening reported for early- to mid-T dwarfs may be inflated by a high incidence of unresolved binaries, whose blended light enhances apparent brightening. Accounting for binarity would imply a more modest intrinsic amplitude and suggests that truly single objects in these spectral subclasses are relatively rare, consistent with the narrow effective temperature range inferred for the L/T transition. SDSS J1534+1615AB thus serves as a new benchmark for testing atmospheric and cloud models across the L/T transition. Future resolved spectroscopy, precise parallax measurements, and orbital monitoring will refine component properties and yield dynamical masses, enabling stringent tests of substellar evolution and the physical origin of the J-band brightening.

We investigate the gravitational capture of galactic dark matter by the Solar System through three-body interactions between the Sun, a planet, and a passing particle. We derive an analytical estimate of the capture cross-section and its scaling with particle velocity, planetary mass, and orbital parameters. From these results we infer upper and lower bounds on the total mass of dark matter that can be retained within the Solar System over its lifetime. We discuss spatial distributions and density estimates, noting model dependence. In the most optimistic scenarios, the local dark matter density could be enhanced by three orders of magnitude relative to the Galactic value, yet still lies about two orders of magnitude below observational limits.

We investigate heavy-flavor transport in the quark–gluon plasma (QGP) possibly formed in p–Pb collisions at the CERN LHC using a (3+1)-dimensional viscous hydrodynamics description of the medium coupled to an improved Langevin framework for heavy-quark dynamics. The transport model includes both collisional scattering and medium-induced gluon radiation, and hadronization is implemented via a hybrid fragmentation–recombination scheme constrained by vacuum baselines. We quantify the in-medium modification of charm propagation and its imprint on D-meson observables. The QGP evolution enhances the D-meson @xmath0 at low transverse momentum due to coalescence and radial flow, while inducing a suppression at intermediate momenta driven by energy loss. We further compute the D-meson elliptic flow and assess its sensitivity to the spatial–temporal extent of the medium. Using a diffusion coefficient calibrated to reproduce central @xmath1 data at the LHC, we predict a significantly smaller D-meson @xmath2 than that of light hadrons in p–Pb, indicating incomplete thermal coupling of heavy quarks to the medium. This behavior reflects the reduced size and lifetime of the QGP in small systems compared to A+A collisions and provides discriminating constraints on heavy-quark transport coefficients.

We present three-dimensional adiabatic hydrodynamic simulations of planar shocks interacting with dense, elongated clouds (filaments) in an interstellar medium context. We systematically vary filament length, orientation with respect to the incident shock, shock Mach number, and cloud–ambient density contrast, and compare the resulting flow evolution to equivalent simulations of spherical clouds. The morphology of the interaction depends sensitively on filament geometry and shock parameters: for long, oblique filaments the post-shock flow develops three parallel rolls that separate with time, and periodic vortex shedding occurs from the filament ends. Filaments initially oriented sideways-on to the shock are accelerated more rapidly than spherical clouds and exhibit faster early-time mass loss owing to their larger surface-area-to-volume ratio. At later times, however, their mass-loss rate declines relative to spheres because the filament experiences a reduced velocity difference with the post-shock flow. Acceleration and mixing timescales vary by up to a factor of two with filament orientation, and oblique filaments can acquire transverse velocities approaching 10% of the shock speed. We compare these behaviors to laboratory and numerical studies of flow past rigid cylinders, noting similarities and differences arising from cloud compressibility and ablation. These results have implications for cloud survival, turbulence generation, and momentum transfer in shocked, multiphase interstellar environments, including supernova remnants.

HD 109648 is a rare triple-lined spectroscopic triple among late-type systems, distinguished by an exceptionally short outer orbital period of 120.5 days and a small outer-to-inner period ratio of 22:1. Such extreme architecture predicts secular three-body interactions that can drive measurable variations in orbital elements on decadal timescales. We have monitored the system’s radial velocities with the CfA Digital Speedometers over eight years, obtaining homogeneous, high-cadence velocity sets for all three components. Global orbital solutions that allow for time-variable elements reveal clear, statistically significant modulation in the longitudes of periastron of both the inner and outer binaries, and in the radial-velocity amplitudes of the three stars. These variations are consistent with apsidal motion and nodal precession arising from mutual gravitational perturbations within the hierarchical triple. In contrast, we find no definitive evidence for modulation of the inner binary eccentricity over the observing baseline, limiting the amplitude of any Kozai-Lidov–type cycles and implying a mutual inclination below the threshold for large eccentricity excitation. By combining the observational constraints with targeted N-body integrations, we delineate the range of mutual inclinations and nodal orientations consistent with the measured secular trends. HD 109648 thus serves as a benchmark for testing secular dynamics in compact late-type triples and demonstrates that decade-scale monitoring can directly resolve three-body interactions in hierarchical stellar systems. Keywords: celestial mechanics, stellar dynamics, binaries: spectroscopic, stars: individual: HD 109648.

Direct measurements of Cepheid radii are essential for unraveling their physical structure and constraining pulsation properties. We present numerical experiments designed to test the accuracy of radii inferred with the classical Baade–Wesselink (BW) method and the revised CORS approach, and to assess the consistency of the underlying physical assumptions. Both techniques are applied to synthetic light, color, and radial-velocity curves generated by full-amplitude, nonlinear, convective pulsation models at solar composition. By analyzing radii recovered from different photometric passbands, we find systematic biases: determinations based on optical bands tend to underestimate the “theoretical” radii, whereas those relying on near-infrared bands tend to overestimate them. In contrast, when the revised CORS method adopts a surface-brightness calibration built from a bidimensional fit to stellar atmosphere models that explicitly accounts for the cycle-dependent variations in effective temperature, surface gravity, and bolometric correction, the recovered radii agree very well with the model radii across periods and amplitudes. A modest mismatch detected for a bump Cepheid indicates that phases affected by the secondary bump should be excluded from BW and CORS analyses, because the quasi-static approximation—implicit in both methods—breaks down during these dynamical phases. Our results clarify the conditions under which radius determinations are unbiased, inform optimal passband choices and calibrations, and strengthen the reliability of Cepheid-based constraints on pulsation physics and the extragalactic distance scale. These findings guide robust radius and distance estimates.

We study the time delay between relativistic images produced by black hole gravitational lensing in the strong field limit for spherically symmetric lenses. Using the strong deflection framework, we derive analytic expressions for the inter-image delay and show that the delay between the first two images is proportional to the minimum impact angle. The ratio of these quantities provides a robust and precise distance estimator for the black hole. Furthermore, combining the measured image separation with their luminosity ratio allows us to extract the black hole mass. Applying our formulae to the Galactic Center, we predict delays of only a few minutes, whereas for supermassive black holes in the Local Group with masses of order 10^9 solar masses the delay reaches several days, enabling accurate measurements with high-cadence monitoring.

Automated facial expression recognition (FER) remains challenging, particularly under domain shifts and in-the-wild conditions where traditional approaches lack generalizability. Most existing methods rely on engineered features such as HOG, LBPH, and Gabor, with classifier hyperparameters tuned for peak performance on a single dataset or closely related collections, yielding limited gains when applied to novel data. We propose a deep neural network architecture designed to improve cross-dataset robustness in FER. The network comprises two convolutional layers, each followed by max pooling, and four stacked Inception layers, forming a single-component model that ingests registered facial images and classifies them into the six basic emotions or neutral. We evaluate our approach comprehensively on seven publicly available benchmarks: MultiPIE, MMI, CK+, DISFA, FERA, SFEW, and FER2013, encompassing lab-controlled, spontaneous, and in-the-wild settings. Across these datasets, our model achieves accuracy comparable to or better than state-of-the-art methods and consistently outperforms conventional convolutional neural networks, both in recognition accuracy and training time. Cross-database experiments demonstrate improved generalization to unseen identities and imaging conditions without task-specific fine-tuning. These results indicate that a compact, multi-scale deep architecture can provide an effective and efficient solution for FER across diverse environments, advancing practical deployment in real-world applications. We further report ablations confirming the contribution of Inception modules to multi-scale feature learning and robustness.

We present new mid-infrared (N-band) images of a sample of eight nearby Seyfert galaxies obtained at high spatial resolution, enabling us to isolate nuclear emission from circumnuclear structure. In all targets we detect a central, unresolved source, in several cases identified for the first time at these wavelengths. Notably, we detect mid-infrared emission from the active nucleus of NGC 4945, which had previously remained undetected at any wavelength other than hard X-rays. We also detect circumnuclear extended emission in the Circinus galaxy aligned with its major axis, and find marginal evidence for extended circumnuclear emission in NGC 3281. The angular resolution of our data allows us to separate the flux of the nuclear point source from any surrounding starburst component where present. To place these results in context, we complement our Seyfert sample with literature data for non-active starburst galaxies, and relate the nuclear N-band fluxes to published hard X-ray fluxes. We find tight and well-separated correlations between nuclear N-band and hard X-ray fluxes for both Seyfert and starburst nuclei, spanning over three orders of magnitude in luminosity. This separation provides a powerful, extinction-resilient diagnostic of nuclear activity. Applying this mid-infrared–X-ray diagram as a classification tool, we find strong evidence against NGC 1808 currently harbouring an active Seyfert nucleus, while the position of NGC 4945 confirms its nature as a Seyfert 2 galaxy. Our results demonstrate that high-resolution mid-infrared imaging, combined with hard X-ray measurements, offers a robust means to identify and characterize active galactic nuclei and to effectively disentangle them from circumnuclear star formation in nearby galaxies.

We present an analysis of archival ROSAT observations for three recently identified, nearby (@xmath0 pc), young (@xmath1 Myr) stellar associations: the TW Hydrae Association (TWA), the Tucana–Horologium Association (Tuc–Hor), and the beta Pictoris Moving Group (beta Pic). Using ROSAT Position Sensitive Proportional Counter data, we compile X-ray count rates and hardness ratios (HR1, HR2) for confirmed F–M type members to characterize their coronal emission properties. The distributions of HR1 and HR2 for all three associations, whose membership is dominated by low-mass, weak-lined T Tauri stars, are tightly clustered and remarkably similar, indicating broadly comparable X-ray spectral properties across these coeval, nearby groups. By contrast, TW Hya itself—the only bona fide classical T Tauri star among these associations—exhibits a distinctly anomalous HR1, highlighting the impact of accretion and/or circumstellar material on its X-ray spectrum. We compare the hardness ratio distributions of these nearby associations with those of pre-main-sequence T Tauri stars, the Hyades cluster, and field main-sequence dwarfs. The comparison reveals a clear age-dependent softening of X-ray spectra from T Tauri ages to the Hyades and on to the older field population. Moreover, F and G stars exhibit a more rapid evolution in spectral hardness than K and M stars, suggesting mass- or structure-dependent coronal evolution. The physical origin of this trend remains ambiguous: it may reflect intrinsic changes in coronal temperature distributions and emission measures, decreasing circumstellar absorbing columns with age (e.g., dispersal of residual disks), and/or the waning influence of star–disk interactions on high-energy emission. These results demonstrate that ROSAT hardness ratios provide an efficient diagnostic for identifying nearby, young associations and for assessing the X-ray emission properties of their members. Archival X-ray spectral data thus offer a powerful, uniform basis for probing the evolution of stellar coronae across time and mass.

This paper investigates the structure of optimal policies for discounted, periodic-review, single-commodity inventory control problems with total costs and fixed ordering costs over both finite and infinite planning horizons. While classical results provide conditions under which (s,S) policies are optimal—separately for finite- and infinite-horizon formulations—these conditions need not hold in many practical settings. We develop a unified characterization that remains valid beyond those assumptions by introducing a scalar parameter that, together with the discount factor and the horizon length, determines the optimal policy’s form. For the infinite-horizon problem, we show that the optimal policy exhibits a dichotomy: depending on the parameter and the discount factor, the optimal policy is either an (s,S) policy or a policy that never orders. For the finite-horizon problem, three regimes arise: (i) a pure (s,S) policy throughout the horizon, (ii) an (s,S) policy in early stages followed by a no-order region in later stages, or (iii) a policy that never orders at any stage. We delineate the boundaries between these regimes and provide structural conditions that partition the parameter–discount–horizon space accordingly. The paper further establishes continuity of optimal value functions and identifies alternative optimal actions at specific boundary states, clarifying indifference regions and ensuring robustness of the structural results. These findings unify and extend existing theory, offering actionable guidance for policy design when fixed ordering costs and discounting interact in ways that violate standard assumptions. Keywords: inventory control; finite horizon; infinite horizon; optimal policy; (s,S) policy.

Broken-symmetry electronic states (charge, spin, and orbital orders) are implicated in high-temperature superconductivity. In particular, nematicity confined within a single unit cell has only recently been formulated theoretically but is now established in iron-pnictides and doped cuprates. Here we show that a recently discovered titanium oxypnictide superconductor and its nonsuperconducting parent host a symmetry-breaking nematic ground state. Using transport anisotropy, elastoresistance, and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, complemented by spectroscopy, we uncover a tetragonal-to-orthorhombic distortion that onsets well above the superconducting transition, without superlattice formation or magnetic order. The absence of translation-symmetry breaking and magnetism, together with an electronic anisotropy, is naturally explained by an intra-unit-cell nematic charge order with a d-wave form factor. The key structural features of these materials (Ti2O square nets and pnictogen coordination) are intermediate between cuprates and iron pnictides, positioning titanium oxypnictides as a bridge between the two families. Our results point to the ubiquity of intra-unit-cell nematicity and establish titanium oxypnictides as a platform to unravel its origin and its relationship to superconductivity.

Radiometric tracking of the Pioneer 10 and 11 spacecraft at heliocentric distances of roughly 20–70 astronomical units revealed a persistent, small, blue-shifted Doppler frequency drift that limited precise orbit reconstruction. Interpreted as a nearly constant, sunward-directed acceleration of order 8 × 10^−10 m s^−2 for each vehicle, this signature became known as the Pioneer anomaly. We report on a renewed investigation enabled by a substantially expanded Doppler data set, recovered flight telemetry, original project documentation, and newly developed analysis tools. These resources allow reconstruction of the spacecrafts’ thermal, electrical, and attitude histories and support the development of a high-fidelity thermal model that quantifies anisotropic heat radiation from on-board sources—principally the radioisotope thermoelectric generators, electronics, and thermal control elements—and the resulting recoil force. By embedding telemetry-driven thermal recoil estimates within precise orbit determination and reprocessing the enlarged tracking data, we evaluate the contributions of on-board systematics relative to external forces and media calibrations, and we assess the temporal evolution of the signal in light of power decline and plutonium decay. Preliminary results indicate that anisotropic thermal radiation can account for a substantial fraction, and possibly the majority, of the observed acceleration, with a decay rate and directionality consistent with the spacecraft geometry and thermal history. The refined force budget improves orbit reconstructions and reduces Doppler residuals, thereby constraining any remaining unmodeled dynamics. We further apply these techniques to the New Horizons mission, projecting that anisotropic thermal radiation will impart a small, decaying acceleration on the order of a few 10^−10 m s^−2, and we discuss calibration strategies to mitigate its impact on navigation and science. The methodology and lessons learned from the Pioneer analysis are broadly applicable to deep-space missions, informing spacecraft design, telemetry requirements, and navigation strategies for precision tests of gravitation and the interplanetary medium.

We present new results from our spectral analyses of very hot central stars of planetary nebulae obtained since the IAU Symposium on Planetary Nebulae held in Canberra in 2001. Our study exploits ultraviolet and far-ultraviolet spectroscopy with the Hubble Space Telescope and the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer, complemented by ground-based observations at the Very Large Telescope and other facilities. The wavelength coverage and high signal-to-noise enable secure line identifications and robust abundance constraints across ionization stages. Using non-LTE, line-blanketed model atmospheres, we determine effective temperatures, surface gravities, and photospheric CNO abundances for hydrogen-rich central stars, constraining their positions in the post-AGB evolutionary plane and the imprint of prior nucleosynthesis. For hydrogen-deficient central stars of spectral type PG1159, we identify and analyze previously unrecognized neon and fluorine lines in the UV and far-UV. These lines are detected for the first time in any astrophysical object. Our abundance determinations reveal marked neon and fluorine enhancements, providing direct evidence that PG1159 photospheres expose intershell material from helium burning. The compositions strongly support a late helium-shell flash that mixes intershell matter outward, extinguishes residual hydrogen, and exposes it in the post-AGB phase. Together, these results refine fundamental parameters for hot central stars and tighten constraints on mixing, mass loss, and nucleosynthesis along the AGB and post-AGB evolutionary pathways. They also demonstrate the diagnostic power of UV and far-UV spectroscopy, combined with optical data, for disentangling the structural and chemical evolution of these stars and their planetary nebula progenitors.

We present the first results of an ongoing project to study morphological, kinematical, dynamical, and chemical properties of satellite galaxies around external giant spirals. Satellites were drawn from the Zaritsky et al. (1997) catalog; here we analyze deep imaging and photometric structural parameters for a subsample of 60. The satellites display wide-ranging morphologies and surface-brightness profiles, with roughly two-thirds classified as spirals or irregulars and one-third as early types. Measured scale lengths, concentrations, and asymmetries reveal environmental diversity, and several systems exhibit signatures of interaction between satellite pairs. We discuss these cases and outline spectroscopic and kinematic follow-up.

We present a rotationally invariant, unbiased estimator of the angular trispectrum of a scalar random field on the sphere and detail its geometric structure through Wigner couplings and selection rules. We analyze its sampling distribution, variance, and covariance under isotropy, and address masking, beam, and inhomogeneous noise with linear-term and Monte Carlo debiasing. An efficient implementation in HEALPix is described and validated on simulations. Applied to the 4-year COBE-DMR maps, the estimator detects a statistically significant non-Gaussian excess traceable to a known instrumental systematic. Excluding data acquired during affected periods renders all trispectrum amplitudes consistent with Gaussian predictions, underscoring the power of harmonic-space methods for quantifying non-Gaussianity.

Stars host diverse magnetic morphologies, including small-scale spot fields, global large-scale fields, and internal toroidal components. Internal toroidal fields likely arise ubiquitously from differential rotation, whereas small-scale fields correlate with envelope convection across low- and high-mass regimes. In contrast, stable large-scale fields in ∼10% of intermediate-mass and massive stars may reflect dynamical binary interactions, mergers, imprinting fossil magnetism. We synthesize these ideas across evolutionary pathways, linking stellar magnetism to magnetic white dwarfs and neutron stars via flux conservation and amplification. We assess consequences for angular-momentum transport, mass loss, and explosion physics, highlighting roles in core-collapse supernovae (e.g., magnetorotational mechanisms) and thermonuclear supernovae through ignition and detonation conditions.

Single-sample face recognition is among the most challenging settings in face analysis due to the lack of intra-class variability and illumination exemplars. We present a novel SRC-based approach that reduces the gallery to one image per class while remaining robust to misalignment and pixel corruption. To compensate for missing illumination information typically provided by multiple gallery images, we introduce sparse illumination learning and transfer (SILT). This design decouples identity from nuisance factors, allowing identity to be represented by the single gallery sample while nuisances are captured sparsely. SILT learns an illumination dictionary by sparsely fitting examples from auxiliary subjects and enforces sparse activation when representing the query image. Coupled with alignment, the method recovers and transfers illumination and pose parameters to recognition, yielding consistent representations. The algorithm integrates illumination normalization, fine-grained alignment, and SRC-based decision making in a unified pipeline without hand-labeled initialization. Experiments on benchmark datasets show single-sample alignment accuracy comparable to deformable SRC using multiple gallery images per class. In recognition, our approach outperforms SRC and extended SRC baselines, even when they are assisted by manual alignment. The method maintains high accuracy under occlusion, pixel corruption, and moderate pose variation, and scales with the number of classes due to its sparse structure. Results indicate that transferable illumination learned from auxiliary data and sparsity at both stages are key to closing the performance gap in the single-sample regime, enabling practical low-shot recognition with minimal galleries.

We use first-principles calculations to demonstrate that the magnetic properties of a two-dimensional antiferromagnetic transition-metal surface are modified at the atomic scale by adsorption of small organic molecules. Specifically, we investigate benzene (C6H6), cyclooctatetraene (C8H8), and a small transition-metal–benzene complex (BzV) adsorbed on a single atomic layer of Mn deposited on the W(110) surface, which exhibits an almost antiferromagnetic alignment of magnetic moments in adjacent Mn rows. Owing to spin-dependent hybridization between the molecular π orbitals and the Mn d states, adsorption produces a significant reduction of the local magnetic moments in the Mn monolayer. Concomitantly, the spin polarization at the organic–antiferromagnetic interface is strongly modulated on the atomic scale: depending on the local registry and molecular geometry, it can be enhanced or inverted relative to the clean surface. To resolve these effects, we simulate spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy (SP-STM) contrasts, revealing a spatially varying spin-resolved vacuum charge density above the adsorbed molecules, with different regions sustaining opposite signs of spin polarization. For the pristine Mn/W(110) surface, states with s and p symmetry dominate the vacuum charge density near the Fermi energy. After adsorption, however, Mn d states—normally suppressed in the vacuum by symmetry—become relevant due to their interaction with molecular orbitals and the resultant symmetry breaking, thereby controlling the local SP-STM contrast. Projected densities of states and real-space spin-density maps corroborate the π–d hybridization mechanism underlying the moment reduction and polarization inversion. We further model small deviations from perfect antiferromagnetic order associated with the spin-spiral ground state of Mn/W(110), showing that slight canting of Mn moments subtly modifies the SP-STM contrast without altering the qualitative conclusions. Our results establish organic adsorption as a viable pathway to engineer and read out spin polarization at antiferromagnetic surfaces with submolecular resolution, with implications for molecule-based spintronics and magnetic sensing at the nanoscale.

We investigate reduced-order modeling strategies for optimal control of the convective FitzHugh–Nagumo (FHN) system, a prototypical excitable media model comprising a semilinear activator and a linear inhibitor, relevant to blood coagulation dynamics in moving media. Three Galerkin-projected approaches are compared: Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), POD combined with Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (POD–DEIM), and POD combined with Dynamic Mode Decomposition (POD–DMD). While POD and POD–DEIM reduce computational complexity, the nonlinear activator dynamics render their reduced optimal control problems non-convex, necessitating iterative nonlinear solvers. In contrast, DMD is employed as an equation-free, data-driven approximation of the nonlinear term; integrating DMD into the POD Galerkin framework yields a linear reduced activator system, thereby transforming the optimal control problem into a convex program. The full-order reference is a discontinuous Galerkin finite element discretization for convection-dominated wave-type solutions with terminal tracking controls. We benchmark the reduced models against this reference in terms of state/control accuracy and CPU time, across varying convection strengths and terminal control weights. Numerical experiments demonstrate that POD achieves the highest fidelity to the full-order solution but incurs greater computational cost due to nonlinear reduced dynamics. POD–DEIM offers a balanced compromise, reducing online complexity while maintaining good accuracy. POD–DMD delivers the fastest runtimes and a convex optimization landscape, at the expense of moderate accuracy loss in strongly nonlinear regimes. These results clarify trade-offs and provide guidance for selecting ROMs in time-critical control of excitable media. Keywords: FitzHugh–Nagumo equation; optimal control; discontinuous Galerkin; proper orthogonal decomposition; discrete empirical interpolation; dynamic mode decomposition.

Magain et al. (2005) reported that the host galaxy of the quasar HE0450-2958 appears substantially under-luminous relative to the mass they inferred for its central black hole, and suggested that the quasar’s black hole may have been ejected from a nearby ultra-luminous infrared galaxy (ULIRG) during a merger. We use kinematical information from optical spectra of the quasar and the companion ULIRG to test this hypothesis. By comparing systemic redshifts, line widths, and the dynamics implied by the observed emission-line gas, we find that the kick velocity required to expel the black hole from the companion galaxy would need to be extremely large, exceeding plausible dynamical limits and incompatible with the presence of narrow emission-line gas at the same redshift as the quasar nucleus. This rules out the ejection scenario. Furthermore, the quasar exhibits spectral characteristics of a narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy, including relatively narrow permitted lines and strong Fe II emission, indicative of high accretion rates onto a comparatively low-mass black hole. Using these diagnostics, we derive a black hole mass approximately an order of magnitude smaller than the value adopted by Magain et al. With this revised mass, the expected host galaxy luminosity is consistent with the upper limits previously reported, removing the need for an anomalously under-luminous host.

We study type II Hermite–Padé approximants to a vector of Cauchy transforms of smooth complex measures supported on the real line when the supports form two symmetrically overlapping intervals. This setting interpolates between the well-understood Angelesco (disjoint supports) and Nikishin (coincident supports with a structural relation) systems. Assuming that the ratio of the measures admits a holomorphic extension to a region whose size reflects the degree of overlap, we develop a Riemann–Hilbert framework for the associated multiple orthogonal polynomials (the common denominator) and perform a Deift–Zhou steepest descent analysis. This yields Szegő-type formulae for the strong and ratio asymptotics of the denominators and numerators, including precise boundary behavior across the cuts and local parametrices at the endpoints. We provide a sharp description of convergence and divergence regions in the complex plane. Divergence domains, characteristic of Angelesco systems, persist for sufficiently small holomorphic extension or larger effective separation, but shrink and ultimately disappear as the holomorphic domain enlarges toward the Nikishin regime. Conversely, we identify overinterpolation zones, a hallmark of Nikishin systems, arising from analytic cancellation driven by the holomorphic ratio; these zones expand with the overlap. The resulting phase diagram, parameterized by the overlap and the extension domain, quantifies rates of convergence in capacity and the zero distribution of the common denominator via an explicit vector equilibrium and g-function construction. Our results unify and extend the asymptotic theory for Angelesco and Nikishin systems, reveal new mixed regimes in the overlapping case, and clarify the mechanisms behind divergence and overinterpolation in simultaneous rational approximation.

Digital records of social interactions offer temporal resolution for studying how interaction patterns shape collective dynamics. Human activity is typically bursty, with short bursts of intensive contacts alternating with long inactive intervals, which can either speed up or hinder spreading. We introduce a history-dependent contagion model in which a susceptible individual requires repeated interactions with infecteds within a short time window to become infected, capturing reinforcement effects. Using numerical simulations on empirical temporal networks of face-to-face proximity and calls, and comparing with time-shuffled controls, we quantify outbreak size, growth, and thresholds. We find that burstiness concentrates exposures, lowers thresholds, and accelerates spread in our model. These results highlight the critical role of temporal correlations and memory in contagion dynamics and intervention design.

Traveling-wave theory offers a tractable description of evolution in asexual populations by coupling deterministic dynamics of the bulk genotype distribution with a stochastic treatment of the highest-fitness class. Building on this semi-deterministic framework, we derive expressions for the rate of accumulation of deleterious mutations under Muller’s ratchet and for the speed of adaptation under positive selection. We introduce improved methods for modeling the stochastic edge in both settings and obtain analytic correction terms that compensate for biases introduced by approximating discrete fitness classes with a continuum. For Muller’s ratchet, the resulting traveling-wave predictions for the mutation accumulation rate agree with stochastic simulations across ranges of mutation rates, selection strengths, and population sizes. For adaptive evolution, the theory yields speeds of adaptation over wide parameter regimes, including regimes with clonal interference, and predicts that the adaptation rate increases logarithmically with population size until populations become large. Our analysis clarifies how mutation supply and selection shape the wave’s leading edge, provides formulae for empirical inference, and establishes traveling-wave theory as a unified tool for quantifying both fitness loss and gain in asexual populations.

We present a measurement of the galaxy power spectrum from the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey, which has now obtained in excess of @xmath0 galaxy redshifts. Using a direct FFT-based estimator, we compute the @xmath1-space power spectrum and demonstrate that, within the @xmath1-space region @xmath2, its shape closely traces that of the linear matter perturbations convolved with the survey window. We derive the survey window function, quantify its mode-coupling kernel, and assess its impact on the recovered spectrum. By convolving model linear spectra with this window and fitting to the data, we obtain constraints on the matter content of the Universe. Assuming scale-invariant primordial fluctuations, we find that models exhibiting baryon acoustic oscillations are mildly preferred over featureless spectra. From a likelihood analysis, we determine 68% confidence limits on the shape parameter @xmath3 and on the baryon fraction @xmath4. These results demonstrate that the 2dFGRS power spectrum provides a precise probe of cosmological parameters on quasi-linear scales.

We present a determination of the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio (D/H) from a near-ultraviolet spectrum of the quasar QSO 2206−199 obtained with a long series of Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph exposures on the Hubble Space Telescope. Along this sight line we identify a damped Lyman-alpha (DLA) absorber whose kinematic structure is unusually simple, enabling a clean separation of neutral hydrogen and deuterium absorption features. The neutral hydrogen column density is tightly constrained from the damping wings, and detailed profile fitting of the DI and HI lines yields a D/H measurement whose uncertainty is dominated by the limited signal-to-noise ratio of the spectrum rather than by modeling systematics. The absorber is among the most metal-poor DLAs known, with very low heavy-element abundances, implying negligible astration of deuterium; accordingly, the inferred D/H closely traces the primordial abundance produced in Big Bang nucleosynthesis. We place this result in the context of all six published high-redshift quasar absorber D/H determinations. A systematic trend emerges: the three DLAs with the most reliable neutral hydrogen column densities yield consistently lower D/H values than the three Lyman limit systems. Taking the weighted mean of the DLA measurements, we derive a primordial D/H that implies a cosmic baryon density in excellent agreement with that inferred from analyses of the cosmic microwave background angular power spectrum, while remaining compatible with present-day interstellar D/H measurements and models of Galactic chemical evolution. These findings highlight DLAs as promising laboratories for precision D/H studies, but additional observations are essential. Future high signal-to-noise detections of deuterium in DLAs with simple velocity fields will test whether the apparent DLA–LLS difference reflects genuine methodological advantages or is a statistical fluctuation, and will further refine cosmological constraints from primordial light-element abundances.

Autonomous robotic agents rely on logical inference to ensure safe and permitted behavior, yet doing so requires verifying the mutual consistency of rules, perception-based beliefs, planned actions, and their consequences. This paper investigates model checking as a mechanism for such verification. We model a robot’s rule set as a Boolean Evolution System with synchronous semantics and translate it into a labelled transition system. Within this framework, we characterize stability and consistency as temporal properties expressible in Computation Tree Logic and Linear Temporal Logic. Building on these formulations, we present two algorithms that perform real-time checks for consistency and stability, respectively. An implementation of the algorithms enables on-board analysis of rule–belief–action coherence, providing a computational tool for efficient runtime assurance. The approach offers a scalable path to verifying autonomous behavior and lays a foundation for integrating formal verification into the decision loops of robotic agents.

We present a statistical analysis of a sample of 477 solar-type binaries within 67 pc with projected separations larger than 50 au. A new method infers orbital eccentricities using the speed and direction of relative motion measured along short astrometric arcs or derived from known visual orbits. The joint distribution of these kinematic quantities is compared to numerical simulations, and the observed distribution is inverted with their aid to recover the underlying eccentricity distribution. We find that wide binaries have an average eccentricity of 0.59±0.02 and that their eccentricity distribution can be modelled as @xmath1. Systems that contain inner subsystems (i.e., triple or higher-order multiples) show significantly smaller eccentricities, with an average @xmath2 and a peak at @xmath3. We demonstrate that the catalog of visual orbits is strongly biased against large eccentricities. There is marginal evidence for eccentricity increasing with separation (or orbital period). Comparison with spectroscopic binaries corroborates the reality of the controversial period–eccentricity relation: the average eccentricity rises with period, being 0.39 for periods from @xmath4 to @xmath5 days and 0.59 for the wide binaries studied here (@xmath6 to @xmath7 days).

We investigate the real-time evolution of local occupation numbers in the two-dimensional Hubbard model on a square lattice using a non-equilibrium generalization of cluster perturbation theory (CPT). The lattice is tiled into small plaquettes whose interacting contour-ordered Green’s functions are computed exactly, while inter-plaquette hopping is incorporated through a multiple-scattering construction and a component decomposition on the Keldysh–Matsubara contour. We focus on “classical” product initial states built from 2×2 plaquette states and analyze how inter-plaquette coupling controls the ensuing dynamics. Two fully polarized excitations on a plaquette are examined: a staggered spin Néel state and a charge-density-wave (CDW) state. A central result is the identification of a dynamical symmetry of the time-evolution operator and relevant observables, generated by an anti-unitary transformation combining time reversal, an asymmetric particle–hole mapping, and a staggered sign operation. For global quenches in which all plaquettes are excited identically, this symmetry links the initial Néel and CDW configurations and enforces constraints on the short-time dynamics. In particular, the CDW exhibits inhibited relaxation on the fast charge timescale set by t, whereas spin degrees of freedom evolve on the slower superexchange timescale J ~ 4t^2/U. By contrast, for local quenches where only a single plaquette is excited, coupling to the surrounding environment breaks the symmetry relation. The CDW then relaxes rapidly via charge transport and dephasing, while the Néel state displays a markedly slower decay and longer memory, consistent with the separation of energy and time scales. We quantify these behaviors through the time dependence of local densities, staggered magnetization, and plaquette-resolved correlators, and discuss the implications for quench experiments in ultracold atoms and for pump–probe studies of correlated materials.

Multi-Higgs-doublet theories lacking natural flavor conservation generically introduce new CP-violating phases and anomalous charged-Higgs Yukawa structures. We analyze CP violation induced by the charged Higgs in a two-Higgs-doublet model that treats the top quark nonuniversally. Using a general Yukawa parameterization subject to current flavor and collider bounds, we compute charged-Higgs contributions to meson mixing and penguin amplitudes. We show that the effective Standard Model phase extracted from the B system can span a wide range, and the time-dependent CP asymmetry in the gold-plated mode B -> J/psi K_S may differ markedly, even flipping sign, relative to the SM expectation. Kaon observables and rare decays exhibit correlated shifts distinguishing this framework from NFC 2HDMs. We also identify a novel mechanism, dominated by top-charged-Higgs two-loop (Barr-Zee) graphs, that can yield a neutron electric dipole moment near the current limit. We delineate viable parameter space and highlight tests in B/K physics and upcoming EDM searches.

We investigate the imaginary part of the Lorentzian gravitational action for bounded regions, extending and clarifying the analysis of arXiv:1301.7041. By juxtaposing the Lorentzian calculation with a Euclidean one, we explain why the general formula for this imaginary contribution reproduces the standard expression for black hole entropy. Within Lovelock gravity, we identify the topological origin of the imaginary term and relate it to boundary and corner structures. We then evaluate the imaginary part for several representative geometries: cylindrical slabs covering the exterior of stationary black holes, maximal diamonds in highly symmetric spacetimes, and local near-horizon patches. In the slab setup, the entropy contributes to the imaginary part while conserved charges govern the real part. In the diamond and near-horizon cases, the imaginary part coincides exactly with the corresponding entropy.

In this letter, we propose a unified, time-ordered emission model in which the merger of two supermassive black holes acts as an engine powering consecutive signals: a burst of low-frequency gravitational waves, production of high-energy neutrinos, acceleration of ultra–high-energy cosmic rays, and a delayed, luminous radio afterglow. The sequence is triggered by the spin-flip of the dominant black hole and a gravitational-wave burst, followed by final coalescence, rapid reconfiguration of the magnetosphere, and the launch of a newly aligned relativistic jet. Particle acceleration in the nascent jet and its interaction with the circumnuclear medium naturally produce a peak in radio flux density and spectral hardening at radio frequencies. To test this framework, we cross-correlate the Parkes radio catalogue and the second Planck catalogue of compact sources with the arrival directions of track-type neutrino events detected by IceCube. Two flat-spectrum radio sources emerge as plausible associations. We highlight the blazar PKS 0723-008 as a compelling case, showing indications of a historical spin-flip, consistent high-energy neutrino emission, and a five-fold increase in radio flux density over the past decade. We outline observational diagnostics and multi-messenger predictions that can falsify or confirm this merger-driven scenario.

We develop an all-orders resummation of a gauge-invariant class of lattice QCD diagrams that dominate discretization artifacts, including tadpoles and link self-energies. The procedure yields an improved perturbative expansion with reduced scheme and scale dependence, and is compatible with Symanzik improvement and common gauge/fermion actions. Applied to renormalization factors, the static potential, and plaquette observables, the resummed predictions agree well with nonperturbative Monte Carlo and step-scaling benchmarks. Implications for lattice renormalization are discussed.

We present a modification to conventional X-ray fluorescence (XRF) that employs electrons as an alternative excitation source for the study of pigments, and we compare its performance to traditional X-ray excitation. To this end, we built a laser-driven source capable of generating both X-rays and electrons, enabling seamless switching between modalities. Owing to their substantial penetration depth, X-rays yield fluorescence signals that integrate responses from multiple layers, complicating stratigraphic interpretation. In contrast, low-energy electrons are confined to the uppermost layers, providing surface-sensitive compositional information. Comparative measurements on layered pigment specimens demonstrate that combining electron-induced XRF with conventional XRF yields complementary depth sensitivity, enhancing non-destructive discrimination of overpaints, varnishes, and substrate contributions, and offering improved insight into artwork structure and conservation state.

We present a unified survey of the principal dielectric relaxation models—Kohlrausch–Williams–Watts, Cole–Cole, Cole–Davidson, Havriliak–Negami (including its modified form), and excess wing—linking their frequency-domain formulations to explicit time-domain relaxation and response functions. Through Laplace-transform analysis, we express these kernels in terms of generalized and three-parameter (Prabhakar) Mittag–Leffler functions, and establish rigorous conditions under which they are completely monotone. Using Bernstein’s theorem and spectral (measure) representations, we provide necessary and sufficient parameter constraints that ensure causality, passivity, and thermodynamic consistency. A fractional-calculus framework is developed that characterizes each model via Caputo, Prabhakar, and distributed-order fractional differential operators, thereby clarifying their interrelations and limiting transitions. We derive short- and long-time asymptotics, discuss numerical inversion and stable evaluation strategies, and interpret the excess wing as an additive power-law tail compatible with complete monotonicity. The results yield a cohesive hierarchy of relaxation models, furnish inversion formulas for time-domain kernels, and offer practical guidelines for parameter estimation, data fitting, and simulation in complex dielectric systems.

In the classical two-user Gaussian interference channel, the sum degrees of freedom (DoF) is limited to one and can be attained by orthogonal time sharing. Moreover, conventional relaying architectures that incur at least a one-symbol processing delay relative to the direct source-destination paths do not increase this DoF. Motivated by recent advances on instantaneous (without-delay) relaying for point-to-point links, we investigate the impact of instantaneous relays on the two-user interference channel. We show that when a relay performs memoryless instantaneous forwarding, an achievable sum DoF of @xmath0 is obtained for almost all channel realizations. The proposed transmission strategy is inspired by aligned interference neutralization: through carefully chosen linear mappings at the relay and appropriate precoding at the sources, the interfering components are aligned so that the relayed signal neutralizes interference at each destination while preserving the desired signal. Notably, the DoF gain is realized without block memory or symbol buffering at the relay. We formalize the model, specify the required channel state information, and analyze the achievable scheme under generic real/complex coefficients. We discuss finite-SNR gains. The results demonstrate that instantaneous relaying can boost capacity and DoF in interference-limited networks, highlighting the fundamental distinction between conventional delayed relays and truly instantaneous, memoryless relaying mechanisms.

We present a two-part investigation into the nature and location of the microlensing lenses detected toward the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). First, motivated by the persistent ambiguity surrounding the interpretation of LMC microlensing events, we compute the microlensing optical depth and expected event rates for all relevant intervening populations using an updated, self-consistent description of the LMC disk-bar geometry and internal kinematics. The modeled lens populations include LMC self-lensing by low-mass stars in the disk and bar, the Milky Way thin/thick disks and stellar halo (spheroid), and compact dark objects in the Galactic and LMC halos. We confront the predicted optical depths, spatial distributions across the LMC, and time-scale distributions with the ensemble of reported events. Within uncertainties and small-number statistics, we find that several (about 3-4) of the reported LMC events can be explained by self-lensing from low-mass LMC stars, but the entirety of the sample is unlikely to arise from self-lensing alone. An origin in which lenses are drawn from multiple populations—low-mass stars in the LMC, thick disk and spheroid stars in the Milky Way, and a non-negligible contribution from genuine massive compact halo objects (MACHOs) in the halos of the Milky Way and possibly the LMC—is consistent with the data. We also summarize recent microlensing searches toward M31 using the pixel-lensing method; current statistics remain insufficient to provide definitive constraints on the MACHO content of M31. In the second part, we report a preliminary synthesis of the final results from the EROS-2 program. Monitoring 33 million LMC and SMC stars over 6.7 years, EROS-2 sets stringent, wide-ranging upper limits on the fraction of the standard Galactic halo composed of MACHOs across 10^-4 to 100 solar masses. The limits exclude MACHOs as a major constituent of the halo over most of this mass range, with halo fractions constrained to less than about 20% for masses approximately 2×10^-4-10 solar masses and less than about 5% for approximately 10^-3-0.1 solar masses. This program delivers the most sensitive data set for MACHO searches in the Galactic halo, substantially narrowing the viable parameter space for compact dark matter candidates.

We present an energetic analysis and comparison of nonlinear simulations of drift-wave turbulence in the Large Plasma Device (LAPD), benchmarked to measurements in the experiment. The simulations employ a common reduced plasma model but differ in axial boundary conditions: periodic, zero-value, zero-derivative, and a sheath boundary that admits a conducting wall mode. Linear stability varies across scenarios because the boundary conditions select distinct axial structures for the drift-wave instability; in the sheath case, the conducting wall mode is as unstable as the drift waves. Despite these linear differences, the fully developed turbulence is similar in all cases. Energy budgets show that a robust nonlinear instability dominates the saturation dynamics, preferentially driving axisymmetric (m=0) potential energy. They three-wave couple to m=1 components, access the adiabatic response, and transfer energy to kinetic fluctuations. The turbulence self-organizes to sustain this pathway, which disrupts linear eigenmode structures and renders linear instabilities ineffective in the saturated state. Comparisons with LAPD measurements show consistent spectra, transport, and spatial patterns, supporting the conclusion that nonlinear energy transfer, rather than linear growth, governs the turbulent regime across boundary conditions. These results clarify boundary-condition effects and underscore a universal saturation mechanism.

Scalable quantum state tomography for large particle numbers demands not only an appropriate measurement protocol but also an efficient reconstruction of the density operator from finite data. Since reconstruction typically entails solving non-linear, high-dimensional optimization problems, it constitutes the principal bottleneck for current approaches. We present an efficient state reconstruction scheme for permutationally invariant (PI) quantum state tomography that is compatible with commonly used estimators, including maximum likelihood and least squares. The key is a representation of PI states derived from spin-coupling theory that compresses the problem into blocks acting on the symmetric subspace, dramatically reducing dimensionality. Combined with convex optimization, this yields reliable convergence, improved numerical stability, and quantifiable control over constraints such as positivity and normalization. We analyze computational complexity and demonstrate that the method achieves substantial speed-ups over standard routines while preserving accuracy and robustness to statistical noise. Prototype implementations reconstruct PI states of up to 20 qubits within minutes on a standard desktop computer using realistic, finite data sets. These results enable practical, scalable tomography in contemporary experiments and open pathways to larger systems.

We investigate exciton energy levels and fine-structure splitting (FSS) in laterally coupled quantum dot molecules using a microscopic model that includes electron and hole tunneling, direct Coulomb interaction, and both intra- and interdot exchange. Configuration-interaction calculations reveal that the two lowest exciton manifolds acquire FSS from competing exchange channels whose magnitudes are highly sensitive to the structural symmetry and tunnel coupling between dots. As the interdot separation decreases, enhanced tunneling amplifies the ground-state FSS while suppressing the FSS of excited states, reflecting a redistribution of exchange and correlation. We quantify the dependence of FSS on Coulomb correlation and identify regimes where correlation mitigates exchange-induced splittings. Our results provide design guidelines for controlling excitonic fine structure in quantum dot molecules for quantum photonics applications.

We present mid-infrared and submillimeter observations of Centaurus A (Cen A, NGC 5128), the nearest radio-loud active galactic nucleus (AGN) host. High-resolution maps of thermal dust emission from the inner few kiloparsecs reveal a striking bisymmetric morphology, with a characteristic diameter of about 5 kpc centered on the nucleus. The geometry and brightness distribution closely resemble those of a barred spiral: a prominent bar embedded in dusty spiral arms, with the bar lying in a plane inclined by approximately 18 degrees to the line of sight. The dust-defined structure is offset from, and more coherent than, the patchy optical obscuration, underscoring the importance of long-wavelength tracers for penetrating the complex inner regions of Cen A. The combined mid-infrared and submillimeter continuum maps, which trace warm and cold dust components, respectively, constrain the distribution of column density and support a close association with molecular gas, reinforcing the barred spiral interpretation. We interpret the feature as a quasi-stable barred spiral formed from tidally captured, gas-rich debris accreted within the last ~10^8 years into the core of the giant elliptical. The total size and interstellar gas mass of the central barred spiral are comparable to those of the Local Group spiral Messier 33. The morphology and implied dynamics support a scenario in which the bar efficiently channels gas inward, potentially sustaining nuclear activity. These observations motivate a broader reconsideration of dusty hosts of giant radio galaxies as symbiotic systems—barred spirals embedded within ellipticals—where secular bar-driven inflow regulates AGN fueling.

Computer simulations have transformed the study of general relativity’s strong-field regime, enabling predictions and revealing phenomena. This review surveys the present status of numerical relativity, emphasizing formulations (BSSN, generalized harmonic), gauge and constraint control, finite differences, spectral discretizations, adaptive mesh refinement, and relativistic (magneto)hydrodynamics. Applications span binary black hole and neutron star mergers, gravitational-wave modeling, tests of cosmic censorship and black-hole stability, and dynamical spacetimes with matter. I discuss verification and uncertainty, multiphysics coupling, and computational challenges. Open problems include extreme mass ratios and spins, long-timescale accuracy, microphysical realism, turbulent magnetized flows, and quantum-gravity-motivated scenarios; future prospects are outlined.

As the resolution of cosmological N-body simulations continues to increase, the accurate detection of subhaloes has become critical for studies of structure formation, for building reliable merger trees, and for seeding semi-analytic galaxy formation models. We assess the performance of two widely used halo-finding strategies for subhalo identification: a configuration-space overdensity method and an adaptive mesh refinement approach. Using a controlled suite of stable mock dark matter haloes with Navarro–Frenk–White profiles, we embed a single subhalo at varying radii within a more massive host and attempt recovery with SUBFIND (a friends-of-friends based overdensity finder) and AHF (an adaptive mesh-based finder). We find that the subhalo mass recovered by SUBFIND exhibits a pronounced dependence on the subhalo’s radial location within the host, and that neither finder can reliably identify and characterize the subhalo when it lies very near the host’s centre. This radial dependence arises from the subhalo definition as an overdensity: the elevated background density of the host biases truncation radii and hence inferred masses. In contrast, defining subhalo size via the peak of the circular velocity profile yields a markedly more stable estimate across radii, though the associated maximum circular velocity is a poor tracer of tidal stripping and is sensitive to numerical resolution. These results underscore the need for caution when interpreting subhalo properties in dense environments and highlight systematic differences that impact downstream applications such as merger tree construction. We conclude that future halo finders aiming to recover all bound subhalo particles robustly will need to incorporate searches in phase space, leveraging both positional and velocity information to disentangle substructure from the host background.

We present a diffusion–reaction model for bacterial colony growth that embeds cooperative motility under stress as density- and nutrient-dependent nonlinear diffusion. The motility response includes hysteresis, yielding distinct spreading regimes. Numerical simulations, varying only agar concentration and initial nutrient levels, reproduce the morphological spectrum observed in Bacillus subtilis OG-01, including compact, branched, and concentric patterns. The model delineates a diagram linking environmental constraints to colony architecture, and explains pattern transitions via feedback between nutrient depletion and stress-induced motility.

Exponential surface brightness profiles are ubiquitous in stellar discs, and the neutral hydrogen layers that extend beyond them often follow nearly exponential distributions. Both stars and gas commonly exhibit pronounced lopsided (m=1) asymmetries in the outer regions, yet their dynamical consequences have not been systematically assessed. Building on Lindblad’s idea of kinematic density waves, we show that the outskirts of exponential discs are intrinsically favorable for sustaining global lopsided modes with low pattern speeds and long coherence times. We construct a linear perturbation framework for a two-component (stellar and gaseous) disc and compute the associated angular momentum transport, including both gravitational torques and advective contributions, for cases with and without an embedding dark matter halo. In a pure disc, the free precession frequency of the lopsided mode exhibits a transition from retrograde to prograde with radius, reversing the sign of the angular momentum flux and producing an unphysical inward transport in the outer disc. The inclusion of a dark matter halo removes this reversal by modifying the precession profile and stabilizing the mode, thereby enforcing a net outward angular momentum flow provided the lopsidedness is leading in nature. This outward transport complements the well-established spiral-driven torques in the inner disc, enabling a coherent, galaxy-wide pathway for gas inflow from the circumgalactic medium, plausibly along cosmic filaments, while simultaneously promoting secular disc evolution. We discuss observational signatures—radially increasing lopsided amplitudes, slow pattern speeds, and correlations with halo dominance—and outline tests with resolved HI and stellar kinematics. These results identify outer-disc lopsidedness as a viable driver of angular momentum redistribution and long-term growth in spiral galaxies. Keywords: galaxies—structure; galaxies—kinematics and dynamics; galaxies—spiral; galaxies—evolution; galaxies—halos.

We develop Hartle’s slow-rotation formalism in the presence of a cosmological constant Λ and derive the generalized Hartle–Thorne vacuum solution, the Hartle–Thorne–(anti)–de Sitter metric. We show that, for arbitrary Λ, the exterior solution is always asymptotically (anti)–de Sitter and reduces to the standard Hartle–Thorne geometry in the Λ→0 limit. The structure of the rotational corrections (mass, angular momentum, and quadrupole moments) and the gauge is analyzed to second order in the angular velocity. We then place Wahlquist’s rotating perfect-fluid interior into Hartle’s framework and study its junction to the exterior across a timelike surface. Using the second-order matching conditions, we demonstrate that Wahlquist can be consistently matched to a Hartle–Thorne–(anti)–de Sitter exterior, overcoming the known obstruction in asymptotically flat spacetimes. This establishes Wahlquist as a viable model of an isolated rotating body embedded in a cosmological background, accurate to order O(Ω^2).

We investigate the cosmological implications of the simple scalar–torsion (@xmath0) mode within Poincaré gauge theory of gravity. For the non-constant (affine) curvature case, we show that the early-time evolution of the torsion density @xmath1 exhibits a radiation-like asymptotic behavior @xmath2, where @xmath3 denotes the scale factor. We further identify a stable fixed point for the torsion pressure (@xmath4) and the density ratio @xmath5 in the high-redshift regime @xmath6, contrasting previous results. To resolve the solutions, we employ a Laurent expansion and derive controlled asymptotics. Numerical computations corroborate the analytic predictions. Our findings refine early-universe torsion phenomenology and inform viable PGT cosmologies and observations.

We analyze plasmon oscillations of metallic triaxial ellipsoid nanoparticles within the quasistatic approximation. We present a general method to obtain analytical expressions for the electrostatic potential and resonance frequencies for arbitrary multipolarity. Closed-form solutions are derived for the first 24 modes, revealing dependencies on aspect ratios and material parameters. Higher-order modes are computed numerically and compared with analytical trends. The results provide spectra and field distributions for designing ellipsoidal nanoplasmonic resonators.

We investigate the two‐Higgs‐doublet model (2HDM) admitting two electroweak‐breaking, CP‐conserving minima, where the phenomenologically correct vacuum could be metastable—a “panic vacuum.” Focusing on the softly broken Peccei–Quinn 2HDM, we derive analytic, necessary and sufficient inequalities on the scalar‐potential parameters that forbid panic vacua. The bounds are expressed in terms of physical masses, mixing angles, and quartic couplings, enabling direct confrontation with data. We further show that present LHC measurements of the 125 GeV Higgs boson and associated Higgs couplings confine the model to the safe region: the observed vacuum is necessarily the global minimum, independent of assumptions about tunneling rates or cosmological history.

We present a comprehensive overview of the physical mechanisms that generate coronal polarization across radio, infrared, visible, and ultraviolet regimes. We review diagnostic techniques that exploit polarized emission and scattering to infer coronal magnetic fields, electron densities, temperatures, and velocities, and assess uncertainties. We highlight strategies—advanced inversion methods, multi-wavelength observations, and next-generation polarimeters—needed to improve thermodynamic constraints and magnetic mapping of the solar corona in future campaigns.

We study supervised PageRank models that incorporate relevance and behavioral features beyond the classical PageRank paradigm. To address the extremely high-dimensional latent parameterization, we develop a random gradient-free optimization framework for training model parameters. We establish a non-asymptotic convergence theorem and derive complexity bounds that quantify the number of arithmetic operations required to attain a prescribed objective accuracy. Furthermore, we identify optimal algorithmic hyperparameters that minimize the computational cost for a given accuracy target. We instantiate the approach for web page ranking via a parametric graph model of user behavior, where edge weights depend on query– and page-specific features, and learn parameters from supervision. Empirical evaluations on query–URL datasets demonstrate that the proposed, tuned gradient-free method consistently improves ranking quality over an untuned baseline, while matching theoretical efficiency predictions. Our results provide both principled guarantees and practical gains for learning high-dimensional supervised PageRank models in real-world web settings.

We compute quark-to-quarkonium fragmentation functions for an S-wave spin-triplet heavy Q Q̄ pair within NRQCD factorization, including both color-singlet and color-octet channels. The analysis treats cases where the fragmenting light or heavy quark flavor differs from that of the heavy constituent, as well as the same-flavor scenario, and provides polarized and unpolarized results. For the polarization-summed 3S1 Q Q̄ states, our expressions reproduce established results. For longitudinally polarized 3S1 states, our new derivation confirms previous calculations in the same-flavor case and identifies and corrects a sign and normalization error in the different-flavor case. These fragmentation functions furnish ingredients for precision quarkonium production and polarization predictions at high energies, and refine theoretical inputs used in global analyses and event generators and phenomenology.

We investigate quantum enhancement of optical pulse timing accuracy in the Heisenberg picture. Using Heisenberg equations of motion for pulse position and momentum operators, we quantify the roles of optical loss, group-velocity dispersion, and Kerr nonlinearity in realistic fibers. The formalism treats loss-induced decoherence via Langevin noise and beam-splitter models, and captures Gordon–Haus jitter from amplified spontaneous emission and dispersion. We apply the framework to adiabatic soliton control proposed to beat the timing standard quantum limit, analyzing regimes identified by Tsang [97, 023902 (2006)]. Theory and numerics show that appreciable enhancement over the standard limit is attainable with current technology, albeit with increased jitter dominated by the Gordon–Haus effect. We map operating windows where quantum advantage survives transmission loss, and delineate design rules for dispersion, nonlinearity, and loss that preserve quantum-enhanced timing information over practical distances.

We investigate the evolution of cosmological domain-wall networks produced during an anisotropic epoch in the very early universe. When walls are generated within an inflationary era, their comoving configuration rapidly freezes, preserving the anisotropic morphology even as inflation drives the background spacetime toward isotropy. The network remains anisotropic until late times when the characteristic major-axis size of wall segments falls below the Hubble radius, at which point causal dynamics accelerates the approach to isotropy. Consequently, imprints of the primordial anisotropic phase can survive to the present if the major-axis scale is of order the current Hubble radius, or if walls re-entered the horizon only very recently. Depending on the wall mass scale, earlier horizon re-entry can occur while the subsequent evolution remains friction-dominated due to plasma interactions, further delaying isotropization and enhancing the preservation of anisotropic signatures. We describe the expected morphological and statistical manifestations—direction-dependent curvature radii, anisotropic correlation functions, and biased stress-energy anisotropies—and discuss observational consequences for cosmological perturbations and defect searches. These behaviors arise generically in topological-defect scenarios, implying that domain-wall networks can act as fossil records of pre-inflationary anisotropy under broad conditions, and motivate targeted, late-time observational probes.

We develop universal polynomials for characteristic classes associated to the @xmath0-classification of map-germs @xmath1→@xmath2. These Thom-polynomial type formulas systematically extend classical enumerative results for projective surfaces in @xmath3- and @xmath4-spaces. Accurate read alignment in high-throughput sequencing is fundamentally constrained by the abundance of non-unique sequences in the genome. While longer reads are generally expected to improve unique mappability, a quantitative assessment of how read length influences mappability across a broad range has been lacking. Here, we systematically analyze the human reference genome’s k-mer landscape for k spanning 20 to 1000 base pairs. For each k, we compute the full k-mer frequency spectrum and use the proportion of non-singleton k-mers (those occurring more than once) as a proxy for the mappability of reads of length k. The fraction of non-singleton k-mers declines with increasing k but does so slowly and is well described by piecewise power-law relationships, with distinct scaling exponents in different k ranges. The more rapid decay at smaller k indicates diminishing returns in mappability gains as read lengths extend beyond approximately 200 base pairs. Across k, k-mer frequency distributions exhibit heavy tails consistent with power-law-like behavior, and rank–frequency curves display a characteristic concave Zipf profile. The most frequent 1000-mers cluster into approximately 172-kilobase regions, including four extended stretches on chromosomes 1 and X that overlap genes of biomedical relevance. Notably, even read lengths of 1000 base pairs would be insufficient to uniquely resolve these particular regions. These results provide a quantitative framework for anticipating mapping ambiguity as a function of read length and underscore that increasing read length alone cannot fully overcome repetitive sequence constraints, motivating complementary strategies such as long-range linkage, assembly-based approaches, and graph-based reference representations.

Electromagnetic metamaterials composed of subwavelength structures can manipulate radiation via tailored anisotropy. We design metamaterial wave plates that exhibit a positive refractive index along one axis and a negative index along the orthogonal axis, yielding strong birefringence and enabling subwavelength thickness. To overcome the narrow usable bandwidth of previous realizations, we implement the Pancharatnam method by cascading rotated anisotropic layers and optimize the stack using a combination of finite element simulations and transmission-line models. Fabricated prototypes are characterized and compared with the models. Measurements demonstrate broadband phase retardation, low insertion loss, and high polarization conversion efficiency, with agreement to predictions. These results enable broadband polarization control.

We address the Global Attractor Conjecture for complex-balanced mass-action systems, equivalently for toric dynamical systems on the positive orthant. The conjecture asserts that, within each positive stoichiometric compatibility class (positive linear invariant subspace), trajectories converge to a unique positive equilibrium. Building on the foundational work of Horn and Jackson, we introduce toric differential inclusions, a class of set-valued dynamics associated with the polyhedral geometry of reaction networks. We show that every positive trajectory of a toric differential inclusion is confined to an invariant region bounded away from the origin and the boundary, establishing persistence and precluding extinction. Using an embedding of complex-balanced mass-action systems into toric differential inclusions and an entropy-like Lyapunov function, we deduce global convergence to the complex-balanced equilibrium in each class, thus proving the Global Attractor Conjecture. As corollaries, all detailed-balanced systems and all weakly reversible deficiency-zero networks possess the global attractor property. Our results reveal structural stability and simple asymptotic behavior for a large family of nonlinear polynomial systems on the positive orthant.

We report new X-ray observations of a pulsar in a highly eccentric, 3.4-year orbit around a Be star, whose circumstellar disc is intersected twice per orbit just before and just after periastron. In this system the unpulsed radio, X-ray, and gamma-ray emission is widely attributed to the collision of the relativistic pulsar wind with the Be-star wind and disc. Our 2004 monitoring campaign followed the source as the pulsar approached the disc and is combined here with earlier, previously unpublished X-ray data and contemporaneous TeV measurements. The resulting detailed X-ray light curve reveals two sharp enhancements per orbit that are well described by the pulsar traversing a Gaussian-profile disc of finite half-opening angle projected onto the orbital plane. The intersection of the disc mid-plane with the orbital plane is inclined with respect to the orbit’s major axis, setting the phases of the two crossings and naturally explaining the observed asymmetry around periastron. Comparing the X-ray light curve with the TeV light curve, we find that the increase of TeV flux some 10–100 days after periastron is unambiguously tied to disc passage. Spectrally, the X-ray photon index hardens at disc entrance, from a steeper pre-crossing value to a significantly harder slope, before returning to a softer index as the pulsar exits the disc. Such behavior is difficult to reconcile with a model in which X-rays are synchrotron emission from the shocked pulsar wind alone. We argue instead that the hardening reflects the emergence of inverse-Compton or relativistic bremsstrahlung emission from 10–100 MeV electrons that also produce the radio synchrotron component, enabled by the enhanced photon and matter densities in the disc. These findings establish the disc geometry and crossings as the primary drivers of high-energy variability in this binary and provide new constraints on particle acceleration and cooling in colliding-wind pulsar systems.
