Our model couples black hole mass distributions derived from the Press–Schechter theory of structure formation to a physics-based quasar emission model that incorporates time-dependent accretion-disk phenomena, including fueling, growth, and feedback. The resulting QLF reproduces the normalization, slope, and break luminosity at redshifts higher than @xmath4 2.0, providing a reasonable match. We attribute the remaining disagreement at lower redshift to mergers and post-merger evolution that modulate fueling and obscuration. Anchoring the merger-free high-redshift regime allows us to estimate the merger rate at lower redshift, and we argue that this rate should depend on redshift like @xmath5. This work explores the information loss problem through non-perturbative effects, emphasizing the role of instantons. We analyze diverse thin-shell instantons and tunneling channels that can mediate transitions to trivial geometries lacking singularities and event horizons. These mechanisms suggest unitary resolutions in semiclassical gravity. We also identify subtle, model-dependent behaviors in asymptotically de Sitter settings, highlighting open questions and directions for further investigation regarding boundary conditions and global structure.

Full-duplex (FD) operation promises significant spectral efficiency gains but is hindered by loop interference (LI) and increased multiuser interference in dense deployments. We develop a tractable stochastic geometry framework for large-scale FD cellular networks where base stations and users employ directional antennas. Building on experimental evidence, we model passive LI suppression as a deterministic function of the angular separation between transmit and receive antennas and incorporate it with residual self-interference and network interference. For sectorized antenna patterns, we derive closed-form expressions for outage probability, rate, and mean interference, and validate them via Monte Carlo simulations. Our analysis quantifies the joint benefits of antenna directionality and passive suppression, revealing regimes where FD outperforms half-duplex under realistic hardware constraints. We identify optimal antenna beamwidths and separation angles that balance LI mitigation and inter-cell interference, and provide design guidelines for FD deployment in directional cellular networks. Results indicate substantial throughput gains with modest additional complexity. Overall.

We investigate the critical temperature of Bose–Einstein condensation of @xmath0 mesons in neutron star matter using finite‐temperature relativistic field theoretical models in which nucleon–nucleon and (anti)kaon–nucleon interactions are mediated by meson exchange. Implementing charge neutrality and beta equilibrium, we compute condensate thermodynamics and examine its melting for several antikaon optical potential depths. The results show that the critical temperature of the antikaon condensate increases with baryon number density, reflecting the strengthening of attractive kaon–nucleon correlations at high density. Conversely, the critical temperature is reduced as the antikaon optical potential becomes less attractive. We further construct the comprehensive phase diagram of neutron star matter with an @xmath0 condensate.

We investigate trigonometric invariants associated with lattice angles in lattice geometry and develop a theory of lattice trigonometric functions. We introduce a notion of the sum of lattice angles and prove an existence criterion for lattice triangles: three angles occur as the angles of a lattice triangle if and only if a relation between lattice tangents holds. This furnishes a lattice analogue of the Euclidean condition that three angles form a triangle when their sum is @xmath0. We obtain a necessary and sufficient condition for an ordered @xmath1-tuple of angles to be realized as the angles of a convex lattice polygon. Applications to complex projective toric varieties are discussed, and open problems are presented.

We present recent next-to-leading order results relevant for LHC phenomenology obtained with the GOLEM method. After reviewing the status of this Feynman diagrammatic approach for multi-leg one-loop calculations, we discuss three applications: a loop-induced process and the virtual corrections to representative five- and six-point reactions. The GOLEM tensor-integral reduction and scalar basis yield numerically stable amplitude representations well suited to efficient phase-space integration across the full kinematic range. In this context we propose a practical reweighting of leading-order, unweighted event samples by local K-factors to incorporate virtual effects with minimal overhead. We validate our approach against independent tools and outline phenomenological implications for key LHC observables and experimental comparisons.

Many multi-dimensional consistent discrete systems admit soliton solutions on nonzero backgrounds, complicating the analysis of their integrable properties. This letter addresses that difficulty for the lattice potential Korteweg–de Vries (lpKdV) equation by deriving an infinite hierarchy of conserved quantities via the inverse scattering transform. The construction relies on two key ingredients: the independence of the scattering data with respect to discrete space and time, and the analytic properties of Jost solutions of the associated discrete Schrödinger spectral problem. The resulting conserved densities differ from previously reported forms and, crucially, are asymptotically vanishing as either lattice index tends to infinity, making them well adapted to nonzero-background solutions. To obtain these results, we reconstruct a discrete Riccati equation using a conformal map that sends the upper complex plane into the unit disc, thereby providing a natural domain for analytic continuation. A convergent series solution to the Riccati equation is then built from the analytic and asymptotic behavior of the Jost functions. The framework refines conservation-law derivations for discrete integrable systems and offers a pathway to treating other multidimensionally consistent models with nonzero backgrounds. Keywords: conserved quantities, analytic properties, inverse scattering transform, conformal map, lattice potential KdV equation.

We improve estimates of stellar mass and mass‐weighted average age of Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) host galaxies by combining ultraviolet and near‐infrared photometry with optical data in spectral energy distribution fitting. Using 206 SNe Ia drawn from the three‐year supernova survey (median redshift @xmath0) and host‐galaxy photometry, we present statistically significant evidence, at the @xmath1 confidence level, for a correlation between Hubble‐diagram residuals and the mass‐weighted average age of the hosts. Older galaxies host SNe Ia brighter than average after standard light‐curve corrections. We also confirm, at the @xmath2 level, the trend that more massive galaxies host brighter SNe Ia after light‐curve correction. Including UV and near‐IR data reduces age–dust–metallicity degeneracies, yielding tighter host parameters and reduced dispersion in Hubble residuals. These results motivate incorporating host‐galaxy age and mass into SN Ia standardization to mitigate cosmological biases.

We consider stationary face-to-face tessellations of Euclidean space and introduce consistent percolation models by coloring faces black. Our main focus is cell percolation, where each cell is independently declared black with probability p. We study geometric properties of the union of black faces and, under natural integrability conditions, derive explicit formulas for asymptotic mean values of intrinsic volumes expressed via Palm expectations associated with face processes. In the second part, we analyze the asymptotic covariance structure of intrinsic volumes of the black union observed in expanding polytope windows, assuming existence of suitable asymptotic covariances for the underlying face processes. These assumptions are verified in the important case of the Poisson–Voronoi tessellation, yielding concrete mean and covariance expressions. For normal tessellations, particularly in two dimensions, our formulas simplify substantially, providing tractable expressions for area, perimeter, and Euler characteristic functionals. Our results unify and extend percolation-based integral-geometric limit theory for tessellations and offer tools for statistical inference on geometrically structured random media. Key words: tessellation; percolation; Poisson–Voronoi tessellation; Archimedean lattice; Euler characteristic; intrinsic volumes; asymptotic mean; asymptotic covariance.

We present a spatial and dynamical analysis of the E4 galaxy NGC 3923 using archival ROSAT PSPC and HRI observations to probe the shape of the X-ray emitting gas and the radial mass distribution. The X-ray isophotes are markedly elongated and, within the uncertainties, their position angles are aligned with the optical isophotes, indicating that the hot gas traces the same large-scale structure as the stellar light. Applying the geometric test for dark matter, which does not rely on knowledge of the gas temperature profile, we find that the observed PSPC isophote ellipticities exceed those expected if mass strictly follows light under both oblate and prolate symmetries. This result, detected at marginal significance, argues for a non-stellar dark matter component and a gravitational potential flatter than the stellar distribution alone would produce. Detailed hydrostatic models assuming an isothermal atmosphere further imply gravitating-mass ellipticities that exceed the intensity-weighted ellipticity of the B-band optical light, strengthening the case for a flattened dark halo. Under the assumption—supported by the PSPC spectrum—that the gas is approximately isothermal and that the central surface brightness is not substantially altered by multi-phase cooling flows, magnetic fields, or discrete sources, we favor mass density profiles that are shallower than steeper alternatives. These potential systematics are unlikely to be significant in NGC 3923, and the inferred range of halo flattening is robust against such effects. Finally, our spatial analysis constrains the contribution of discrete, hard-spectrum sources to the ROSAT emission to be well below that implied by the hard component measured with ASCA, suggesting that the ASCA excess is not dominated by sources detectable in the ROSAT band. This study provides stringent, temperature-independent constraints on the shape and radial structure of NGC 3923’s dark halo.

We interpret the 750–760 GeV diphoton resonance as one or more spin-0 components of singlet superfields arising from the three 27-dimensional representations of E6 in F-theory grand unified models, which also contain three copies of color-triplet vector-like fermions and inert Higgs doublets that couple to the singlets. For definiteness, we adopt without modification a previously proposed explicit construction that includes such states alongside bulk exotics, yielding consistent gauge coupling unification. In this framework, the diphoton signal is produced via gluon fusion through loops of vector-like quarks and decays into photons via loops of charged vector-like fermions and inert doublets. We present benchmark couplings consistent with perturbativity and unification that reproduce the observed cross section, allowing for one or multiple nearly degenerate singlet scalars. A smoking-gun prediction is the existence of additional scalar resonances with similar properties, possibly close in mass to 750–760 GeV, together with three families of vector-like fermions, leading to correlated signatures in dijet, diphoton, and multilepton channels. We discuss constraints from current LHC searches and anticipate rates for associated Z gamma and ZZ decays. Prospects for near-future verification are outlined.

We investigate hysteresis in a two-dimensional, spin-1/2, nearest-neighbor kinetic Ising ferromagnet driven by a sinusoidal magnetic field, combining large-scale Monte Carlo simulations with complementary analytical theory. Attention is confined to small lattices and weak field amplitudes at temperatures below the critical temperature, where magnetization reversal proceeds via the random nucleation of a single droplet aligned with the instantaneous field. In this single-droplet regime, we develop a quantitative description of stochastic hysteresis based on time-dependent nucleation theory coupled to the framework of variable-rate Markov processes. Without adjustable parameters, the theory yields accurate predictions for the distributions of switching times, hysteresis-loop areas, and magnetization trajectories observed in simulations, highlighting the essential role of finite-size fluctuations and rare-event kinetics. The stochastic response we uncover differs qualitatively from mean-field expectations and from behaviors seen in larger, spatially extended systems where multi-droplet nucleation and domain coarsening dominate. We characterize the frequency dependence of the probability density for the loop area and show that its mean exhibits a slow crossover to a logarithmic decay with decreasing frequency and amplitude in the asymptotic low-frequency limit. Both the average loop area and the residence-time distributions reveal pronounced signatures of stochastic resonance, reflecting the synchronization between the periodic drive and the nucleation-controlled switching dynamics. Furthermore, we establish a direct link between residence-time statistics and the power spectral densities of the magnetization time series, enabling spectral diagnostics of stochastic hysteresis. These results inform the interpretation of recent experiments on switching in ferromagnetic and ferroelectric nanoparticles and ultrathin films, and they advance the general understanding of periodically driven arrays of coupled bistable units subject to noise, where finite-size effects and single-nucleation events crucially shape dynamical hysteresis.

Frustrated intercomponent Josephson couplings in multicomponent superconductors can produce complex phase structures, including time‐reversal symmetry breaking. We develop a systematic classification of frustrated N‐component superconductors based on the graph‐theoretical operation of Seidel switching, which partitions the large set of phase‐locking and phase‐antilocking patterns into a small number of physically equivalent classes. This mapping organizes the parameter space and clarifies when distinct coupling sign configurations yield identical ground‐state and excitation properties. Focusing on the four‐component case, we numerically compute ground states, normal modes, and characteristic length scales within a Ginzburg–Landau framework. Linearization around the minima yields the mass spectrum of collective phase modes (including Leggett‐type modes) and multiple coherence lengths. We identify explicit conditions under which new accidental continuous ground‐state degeneracies emerge, generating additional soft modes beyond global gauge symmetry. The results encompass and generalize the known time‐reversal symmetry breaking in three‐component systems, and are directly relevant to multiband superconductors, Josephson‐coupled multilayers, and Josephson‐junction arrays. We discuss phase diagrams, criteria for locked, antilocked, and mixed states, robustness to amplitude anisotropies, and experimental signatures such as multiple healing lengths and soft collective excitations.

We review recent measurements of high-frequency dynamic magnetic susceptibility in high-Tc superconductors La2−xSrxCuO4 and YBa2Cu3O6+x, performed with the HET and MARI chopper spectrometers at the ISIS spallation source. Data are placed on an absolute intensity scale, enabling systematic cross-material trends and quantitative comparison with spin dynamics theories. In the insulating antiferromagnetic parent compounds we observe a renormalization of spin-wave spectral intensity relative to linear spin-wave expectations. With hole doping, the magnetic response exhibits significant broadening in wave vector and redistribution of spectral weight over frequency, consistent with damping and emergent incommensurability. These results constrain models of cuprate magnetism and superconductivity.

We investigate convergence properties in homogeneous shearing-box simulations of magneto-rotationally driven turbulence without imposed mean magnetic flux. By nondimensionalizing the equations with the diffusive scale, the computational domain size becomes the sole control parameter, framing convergence as the asymptotic behavior as box size increases. Using a high-order, low-dissipation numerical scheme, we conduct suites of simulations spanning large dynamic ranges in domain size and weak background flux. We find that statistical steady states, including spectra, stress ratios, and intermittency measures, become asymptotically independent of box size, demonstrating numerical convergence in the zero-flux limit. Moreover, cases with weak mean flux connect smoothly to the zero-flux regime as the flux tends to zero, indicating a continuous transition overall. The observed saturation and transport are consistent with a subcritical small-scale dynamo sustaining turbulence in the absence of net flux. Consequently, the angular momentum transport scales with the diffusive flux, implying modest efficiencies and limited astrophysical relevance for net-flux-free MRI turbulence.

We introduce a simple, mesh-free Monte Carlo algorithm for the initial-boundary value problem of the heat equation, the random walk on heat balls (RWHB). It generalizes the walk-on-spheres method for Laplace’s equation by replacing spherical exits with parabolic heat balls derived from a new mean value formula for caloric functions. The walk samples exit times and locations so as to respect initial data and Dirichlet boundary conditions, yielding unbiased estimators of the solution. Using submartingale techniques and Riesz potential bounds, we establish almost-sure termination, consistency, and convergence, with dimension-robust complexity. Numerical experiments on smooth and irregular domains demonstrate high accuracy and efficiency compared with classical time-stepping schemes; the implementation is straightforward and highly parallel. This framework extends to variable coefficients and source terms.

We revisit the 2011 XENON100 constraints on dark matter–nucleon interactions, which excluded candidates with masses down to 6 GeV for cross sections larger than @xmath0, and address the debated dependence of the exclusion limit on the scintillation efficiency @xmath1 at low nuclear recoil energies. The XENON100 analysis profiled @xmath1 as a nuisance parameter with a Gaussian likelihood whose mean followed the best-fit @xmath1, smoothly extrapolated to zero below 3 keVnr. While robust, that approach does not explore more extreme extrapolations nor anticipate how limits would shift if future data supported a flat @xmath1 below 3 keVnr. We perform a maximum likelihood ratio analysis, following the XENON100 methodology, but do not treat @xmath1 as a nuisance prior; instead, @xmath1 is obtained directly from fits to the data. We then define frequentist confidence intervals for the spin-independent cross section by marginalising over @xmath1, yielding data-driven exclusion bands that transparently encode @xmath1 uncertainties. We quantify the impact on light dark matter, finding that admissible @xmath1 extrapolations below 3 keVnr can modify the 90% confidence level limit at mχ ≈ 6–10 GeV by order unity: flat @xmath1 strengthens the limit relative to the profiled Gaussian treatment, whereas extrapolations to vanishing @xmath1 weaken it, with variations up to about a factor of two at 6 GeV. For mχ ≳ 10 GeV, the dependence becomes negligible. Our framework clarifies the residual systematic room relevant for models near the published limit @xmath0 and enables anticipating shifts from future low-energy @xmath1 measurements.

We investigate the universal low-energy physics of two particle species confined to two dimensions and interacting via isotropic short-range potentials, with the interspecies interaction fine-tuned to a p-wave resonance. Employing a systematically constructed low-energy effective field theory analyzed by the renormalization group, we reveal the emergence of the super Efimov effect in the corresponding three-body problem composed of two particles of one species and a single particle of the other. Specifically, we demonstrate an infinite tower of three-body bound states with orbital angular momentum one whose binding energies obey a doubly exponential scaling law. This phenomenon occurs when the heavy-to-light mass ratio exceeds critical values: 4.03404 for identical bosons and 2.41421 for identical fermions. As the mass ratio increases beyond these thresholds, the super Efimov spectrum becomes progressively denser, thereby improving the feasibility of experimental detection in ultracold atomic mixtures with tunable p-wave resonances. The doubly exponential scaling and associated universal structure are independent of microscopic short-range details. Finally, we show that the Born–Oppenheimer approximation fails to reproduce the universal asymptotic scaling characteristic of the super Efimov effect, underscoring the necessity of the full renormalization-group analysis.

We analyze the temperature dependence of the order parameter of the Schwinger model within the Euclidean functional integral framework. The theory is solved on a finite torus, and the spatial extent is sent to infinity at the end, yielding a consistent finite-temperature limit. We derive induced effective actions, identify and treat fermionic zero modes, and compute two-point Green functions and Wilson loop correlators. These ingredients allow an exact evaluation of the chiral condensate for arbitrary temperature. In particular, for temperatures large compared to the induced photon mass, the condensate exhibits the asymptotic behavior @xmath0. Our construction clarifies topology and boundary conditions in two-dimensional QED, yields nonperturbative condensate and correlators, and establishes a consistent Euclidean path-integral treatment of finite-temperature field theory. Published as Helvetica Physica Acta 65 (1992) 652–678.

We investigate the survival probability that no particle of a lattice gas with constant density, modeled by the symmetric simple exclusion process, reaches a spherical absorber of radius R up to a long but finite time T. Using macroscopic fluctuation theory, we compute the probability P(T) of non-hitting and reconstruct the conditioned density history that realizes this rare event. The results depend on the spatial dimension d and on a rescaled control parameter combining R, T, and the diffusivity D. For small values of this parameter and sufficiently high dimension, P(T) is governed by a stationary MFT solution. In contrast, for large rescaled times, and for any value in one dimension, the optimal trajectories are non-stationary; the scaling of P(T) with system parameters changes accordingly. We further show that the non-stationary regime is sensitive to the preparation of the gas, with distinct asymptotics for deterministic (quenched) versus random (annealed) initial conditions. These features persist for dilute gases of non-interacting random walkers. We validate asymptotic scalings numerically. Finally, we extend the formalism to diffusive lattice gases with interactions and discuss universality and model-dependent corrections.

We study the Kuramoto model with a phase frustration parameter on graphs and introduce the notion of an @xmath0-Kuramoto partition, capturing oscillator synchrony via induced graph partitions. We prove that every equitable partition is an @xmath1-Kuramoto partition, yet the converse fails in general. Furthermore, we derive an exact characterization of @xmath0-Kuramoto bipartitions, clarifying interplay between network symmetry, frustration, and collective dynamics.

We investigate the evolution of static dielectric constants and polarization with doping by synthesizing established experimental results and developing a theory for the doping-dependent screened Coulomb potential. The justification for these trends arises from the influence of ionization energy (@xmath0) on static dielectric functions within ionization-energy-based Fermi–Dirac statistics (IFDS). In limits, the bare Coulomb potential is recovered when @xmath1, while the Thomas–Fermi screened potential emerges for finite carrier density when @xmath2. These phenomenological models unify dielectric, polarization, and screening behaviors across doped systems and provide predictions for materials design.

We investigate the numerical efficiency of schemes for solving the Liouville–von Neumann equation within multilevel Redfield theory. We benchmark two implementations of Runge–Kutta against time-propagation methods tailored for large linear systems: short iterative Arnoldi, Chebyshev, and Newtonian propagators, and assess a symplectic integrator. Using a two-center electron transfer model, we compare accuracy, stability, computational cost, and scalability under time-independent and time-dependent potentials. For time-independent Hamiltonians, the Newtonian propagator consistently offers superior efficiency and accuracy at larger timesteps. For time-dependent driving, explicit Runge–Kutta implementations achieve the best balance of accuracy and cost with robust step-size control. Arnoldi and Chebyshev show favorable stability but higher setup overhead, while the symplectic integrator preserves structure yet underperforms in dissipative Redfield dynamics. Recommendations and parameter guidelines are provided.

We study threshold widths of symmetric properties formed as products of failure sets from reliability theory. We give general composition bounds for the product’s threshold location and width in terms of its factors. The results delineate asymptotic regimes between 0 and 1, specify when sharp thresholds persist under products, and quantify width amplification or attenuation. Examples from network reliability and monotone Boolean functions demonstrate the applicability and yield constructions.

Modern e-commerce and internet platforms generate vast quantities of ratings and comparisons that are inherently incomplete and imbalanced, challenging the construction of reliable global rankings. We propose a principled statistical framework for deriving global rankings from such cardinal data (scores and ratings), while offering insights applicable to ordinal data as well. Starting from raw observations, we transform ranking information into pairwise comparisons encoded as edge flows on a graph whose vertices represent items and edges capture observed preference or rating differences. Central to our approach is the graph Helmholtzian, the graph-theoretic analogue of the vector Laplacian, analyzed through combinatorial Hodge theory. This perspective provides a transparent decomposition of edge flows into orthogonal components that separate signal from inconsistency. We show that any pairwise ranking edge flow decomposes into a gradient flow, which yields the least-squares optimal global ranking, and a divergence-free flow that quantifies violations of global consistency. A large divergence-free component indicates that the dataset resists a meaningful global ranking. Moreover, the divergence-free flow further splits orthogonally into a curl flow, capturing locally cyclic inconsistencies, and a harmonic flow, capturing inconsistencies that are globally cyclic but locally acyclic. This multiscale diagnosis distinguishes whether conflicts in the data arise from local cycles (e.g., small groups of items with rock–paper–scissors preferences) or from global topological effects (e.g., rank ambiguities induced by the comparison graph’s holes). Algorithmically, the discrete Hodge decomposition reduces to linear least-squares regression and convex optimization, bypassing the NP-hardness of classical ordinal methods such as Kemeny optimization. We also study L1 projections of edge flows to enhance robustness and sparsity. Specifically, the L1 projection onto divergence-free flows admits a dual formulation as correlation maximization over bounded divergence-free flows, while the L1-approximate sparse cyclic ranking admits a dual as correlation maximization over bounded curl-free flows. These dual views connect our framework to established ranking strategies, clarify the role of regularization, and enable scalable computation on large graphs. We delineate conceptual and practical links to ordinal techniques, including Kemeny optimization and Borda count, and demonstrate how Hodge-theoretic diagnostics guide the choice between global ranking and local aggregation. Together, these contributions furnish a unified, interpretable, and computationally efficient toolkit for ranking under missingness, imbalance, and inconsistency, with broad applicability to modern data ecosystems.

Orthorhombic single crystals of TbMn@xmath0Fe@xmath0O@xmath1 were investigated via temperature- and field-dependent magnetization measurements along the principal axes @xmath2, @xmath3, and @xmath4. The data reveal strong magnetic anisotropy and multiple correlated transitions. A broad feature at @xmath5 = 286 K signifies the paramagnetic-to-@xmath6 ordering of the transition-metal sublattice. On further cooling, a sharp transition at @xmath7 = 28 K is most pronounced along the @xmath4 axis, appearing as a distinct jump in magnetization indicative of a spin reorientation into the @xmath8 configuration. Below @xmath9, negative magnetization emerges along @xmath4, consistent with domain-wall pinning and compensation effects. Isothermal field scans uncover a weak ferromagnetic component along @xmath4 below 28 K, while hysteresis loops measured along @xmath3 exhibit field-induced step-like transitions, reflecting anisotropic spin rearrangements and metastable states. No evidence of Tb-sublattice long-range order is observed down to 2 K, highlighting the dominant role of the Mn/Fe moments. These findings position TbMn@xmath0Fe@xmath0O@xmath1 as a promising platform for probing magneto-dielectric coupling across spin-reorientation and magnetization-reversal regimes.

We investigate the @xmath0 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the kagom lattice using a Green’s function approach based on a controlled decoupling of the equations of motion. This framework yields thermodynamic quantities and spin–spin correlation functions that consistently identify a two-dimensional quantum spin-liquid state without magnetic long-range order. Real-space correlations decay exponentially with distance down to low temperatures, indicating short-range entanglement-dominated physics. The entropy analysis reveals a finite missing entropy at @xmath1 equal to @xmath2. Within the present scheme, the specific heat displays a single-peak structure across temperature and follows a @xmath3 dependence at low temperatures, in accord with a disordered quantum ground state.

We present the discovery of a brown dwarf companion to the debris-disk host star HR 2562 using the Gemini Planet Imager (GPI). High-contrast imaging and integral-field spectroscopy reveal a point source at a projected separation of 20.3 ± 0.3 au from the star. Leveraging GPI’s high astrometric precision, we confirm common proper motion between HR 2562 and the companion over a one-month baseline at greater than 5σ significance, establishing it as a bound object and ruling out a background contaminant. Low-resolution spectra in the J, H, and K bands show morphology characteristic of L/T transition objects. By comparison to spectral standards and spectral indices, we assign a spectral type of L7 ± 3 to HR 2562 b and derive a bolometric luminosity of log(L/Lsun) = −4.62 ± 0.12. Adopting an estimated system age of 300–900 Myr and using evolutionary models, we infer a mass of 30 ± 15 Jupiter masses, placing the companion firmly in the brown dwarf regime. Several spectroscopic and photometric features, including a red continuum and weakened alkali lines, are consistent with a relatively young age. The companion’s position angle is consistent with an orbit co-planar with the debris disk recently resolved with Herschel, and its projected location appears interior to the disk’s inner cavity. The companion’s presence within the dust-depleted region suggests it may contribute to clearing or shaping the inner disk through gravitational perturbations. While the current uncertainty in the cavity’s extent precludes strong dynamical mass limits, future high-spatial-resolution observations of the disk will enable tighter constraints on the companion’s mass and orbit. HR 2562 b is the first brown dwarf–mass object identified within the inner hole of a debris disk, offering a unique laboratory to test substellar formation pathways above the deuterium-burning limit and disk–companion interactions in circumstellar environments.

We analyze new 13CO data from the BU–FCRAO Galactic Ring Survey to quantify the morphology and kinematics of molecular clouds. Using a catalog of over 500 clouds, we measure aspect ratios, position angles relative to the Galactic plane, and velocity gradients. Clouds are preferentially elongated parallel to the plane, while their spin axes inferred from velocity gradients show no preferred orientation. The absence of coherent rotation supporting elongation implies that internal velocity fields are anisotropic. Because supersonic linewidths require continuous energy input, any viable driving mechanism must both maintain the dispersion and produce systemic elongation. Localized stellar feedback, such as winds and supernovae, lacks the directional coherence to align clouds with the plane and is therefore disfavored as the dominant driver. The observed morphology and kinematics favor large-scale processes, including differential Galactic rotation, shear, and spiral-arm streaming, as primary sources of ongoing turbulent energy in molecular clouds.

We investigate the macroscopic manifestation of the chiral anomaly for massless spin-1/2 fermions in heavy-ion collisions, focusing on the chiral magnetic effect (CME) during the pre-thermal stage. Using the recently developed chiral kinetic theory, we construct a phenomenological framework to model out-of-equilibrium CME currents in the presence of a rapidly decaying, event-dependent magnetic field. The kinetic description incorporates Berry-curvature–induced velocity corrections, anomalous phase-space measure, and axial-charge dynamics to compute the time-resolved generation of vector currents and the resulting charge separation. We quantify the magnitude and temporal profile of the CME signal, its sensitivity to initial axial imbalance, collision geometry, relaxation rates, and magnetic-field lifetime, and we provide estimates for the charge dipole carried into the hydrodynamic stage. The pre-equilibrium CME imprint is then mapped onto hydrodynamic initial conditions to assess how subsequent expansion, viscosity, and electromagnetic backreaction modify the observable correlations. Our study indicates that a sizable fraction of the eventual charge separation can be created before local equilibration, and that its survival depends critically on early-time transport and field dynamics. We discuss implications for CME searches via charge-dependent azimuthal correlations, strategies to disentangle backgrounds, and constraints for future measurements at RHIC and the LHC.

We report a search for tribaryon states at KEK-PS using the 4He(K-,p) reaction to populate states with strangeness −1, charge 0, and isospin 1. An inclusive missing-mass spectrum was measured with high resolution, covering 3000–3200 MeV/c^2. No significant narrow structure was observed throughout the mass region. Studies of backgrounds and systematic effects were performed, and no evidence for previously suggested signals was found. Upper limits on the formation branching ratio were established at the 95% confidence level for hypothetical narrow states with assumed widths of 0, 20, and 40 MeV/c^2. These results place stringent constraints on models of deeply bound kaonic nuclear systems and tribaryon resonances. PACS: 13.75.Jz, 25.80.Nv.

This short review surveys selected topics in Heavy Quark Effective Theory (HQET) relevant to exclusive heavy-hadron decays. We summarize heavy-quark symmetries, scaling laws, matching and renormalization, and 1/m_Q power corrections. Applications include parameterizations of form factors through the Isgur–Wise function, constraints from sum rules, and strategies to extract CKM elements |V_cb| and |V_ub| from B→D(*)lν and B→π(ρ)lν. We comment on factorization, soft-collinear dynamics, and lattice inputs, and discuss current uncertainties and prospects for precision phenomenology at fixed-target experiments and future experimental measurements.

We study kinetic freeze-out of a massive nucleon gas across a finite layer with time-like normal, incorporating in-medium nucleon mass shifts. Within a hydrodynamic–kinetic framework, we quantify how mass modification alters the evolution of thermodynamic fields. Relative to calculations with the vacuum mass, we find substantial changes in temperature, flow velocity, energy density, and particle density after freeze-out. The resulting particle distribution functions exhibit distortions, underscoring the importance of in-medium effects for interpreting freeze-out observables in hadronic matter.

Using the parametrization, we derive generalized bounds that also exploit the CP asymmetry in the latter decay, and we investigate their sensitivity to possible rescattering and EWP effects. We point out that existing experimental data on @xmath5 allow a complete inclusion of rescattering processes in these bounds, effectively constraining the relevant hadronic parameters. In addition, we provide an improved theoretical treatment of EWP amplitudes based on isospin relations and short-distance Wilson coefficients, which reduces associated uncertainties. Numerically, we argue that rescattering effects may enhance the combined @xmath5 branching ratio by a factor of @xmath6 to the @xmath7 level, and that such effects may be responsible for the currently small central value of the ratio of the combined @xmath4 and @xmath3 branching ratios reported by the CLEO collaboration. If confirmed, this observation would exclude values of @xmath2 within a large region around @xmath8. We discuss the implications for strategies to constrain and determine @xmath2 from @xmath9 decays, emphasizing observables and combinations that minimize hadronic uncertainties while retaining sensitivity to weak phases. Our results provide a transparent, model-independent tool for precision studies of @xmath9 decays.

We analyze the time series of total solar irradiance (TSI) from satellite observations spanning 1978 to the present, constructed from the ACRIM and PMOD composites. Using multi-taper and Lomb–Scargle spectral methods, wavelet transforms, cross-spectral coherence, and superposed-epoch alignment to planetary ephemerides, we assess whether planetary-induced forcing signatures are embedded in TSI variability while controlling for instrumental artifacts and internal solar cycles. Long-term trends, including the 11-year sunspot cycle, are removed to isolate annual and sub-annual components. Results reveal a clear signature of the 1.09-year Earth–Jupiter conjunction cycle, especially during Solar Cycle 23 maximum, suggesting a slight irradiance anisotropy with the Jupiter-facing side of the Sun marginally brighter. The effect emerges when Earth crosses the Sun–Jupiter conjunction line every 1.09 years. Additional spectral peaks are coherent with established planetary harmonics: the Mercury–Venus spring-tidal cycle (0.20 year); the Mercury orbital cycle (0.24 year); the Venus–Jupiter spring-tidal cycle (0.32 year); the Venus–Mercury synodic cycle (0.40 year); the Venus–Jupiter synodic cycle (0.65 year); and the Venus–Earth spring-tidal cycle (0.80 year). We also detect a strong 0.5-year semiannual cycle plausibly associated with Earth’s twice-yearly crossings of the solar equatorial plane, implying a latitudinal luminosity asymmetry. The amplitudes of these components are enhanced near sunspot maxima, consistent with nonlinear modulation. We conjecture that both gravitational tidal forcing, emphasizing spring cycles, and electromagnetic interactions linked to solar barycentric wobble, emphasizing synodic cycles, act with internal nonlinear feedbacks to modulate TSI. Robustness is supported by three complementary tests: (1) significance against red-noise and AR(1) nulls via Monte Carlo and phase-shuffled surrogate spectra; (2) replication across the independent ACRIM and PMOD composites; and (3) superposed-epoch and wavelet-coherence analyses phase-locked to planetary ephemerides, persisting under alternative detrending and insensitive to aliasing from Earth-orbital sampling. These findings support a measurable planetary-induced forcing and modulation of solar activity at annual and sub-annual scales, particularly during active phases, and motivate further work on physical coupling pathways and solar–terrestrial implications.

Accurate interpretation of near-infrared color–magnitude diagrams requires isochrones and extinction treatments that are consistent with the real transmission of commonly used filters. We compute theoretical isochrones using the Padova stellar evolutionary models of Girardi et al. for five filter pairs near the J and K atmospheric windows: J–K, J–Ks, J–K′, HST/NICMOS F110W–F205W, and F110W–F222M. Synthetic photometry is performed with the full filter transmission functions, and we provide magnitude transformations among several K-band filters as functions of color. We also present reddened isochrones incorporating extinctions up to AK = 6 mag. We show that reddened isochrones differ systematically among filter pairs, behaving as if each pair obeys a distinct extinction law, and that reddening vectors for the NICMOS pairs are markedly nonlinear in color–magnitude space. These effects lead to biases in extinction estimates derived from NICMOS photometry that can reach 1.3 mag if simple linear or delta-function filter assumptions are adopted. By fitting the synthetic results, we find that the near-infrared extinction between J and K implied by the observations of Rieke et al. is better described by a power law with exponent 1.66 rather than the commonly used 1.59 obtained under idealized filter assumptions. Our isochrones, transformations, and extinction prescriptions enable more robust analysis of heavily reddened stellar populations observed with both HST and ground-based instruments.

We introduce a generic theoretical framework for pore/bulk mixture equilibrium that enables modulation of the composition of confined fluids without altering the bulk state. The approach exploits two robust mechanisms—the intrinsic sensitivity of pore adsorption to bulk thermodynamic conditions and the action of an external electric field—and combines them to achieve precise in situ control. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate two operation modes: a continuous, analog tuning of composition and a discontinuous, switch-like transition. Strikingly, in the vicinity of the bulk demixing instability, a modest field induces a population inversion within the pore, reversing the majority species relative to the bulk. The requirements for practical implementation are most readily satisfied in colloidal systems, yet the underlying mechanisms render the strategy transferable to selected molecular fluids.

This paper addresses the confusion and inefficiency arising from the plethora of existing data models. We propose the Concept-Oriented Model (COM), a unified approach that treats data as functions and uses functional semantics as the basis for formalization. COM rethinks the question “what is data?” by articulating a small set of core notions that capture identities, values, and relationships in a natural manner. The model integrates and reconciles relational, hierarchical, graph, object, and multidimensional perspectives within a coherent framework. We present COM principles, formal constructs, and algebra; show how schemas, constraints, queries, and analytics are expressed uniformly; and discuss implications for design simplicity and expressiveness. Examples demonstrate reduced complexity and consistent data management.

We present 1.2 mm continuum observations of dust emission in a gravitationally lensed Lyman break galaxy. The detected flux is unexpectedly low, implying substantially weaker far-infrared output than predicted from its rest-UV reddening when scaled from local starburst calibrations. We examine multiple, independent estimates of the source’s dust content—using UV slope, energy balance, and lensing-corrected luminosities—and find that the most plausible explanation for the mismatch is uncertainty in the intrinsic UV spectral slope. Alternative scenarios invoking elevated dust temperatures or strong differential magnification offer poorer fits to the data. Our results highlight a systematic risk in inferring cosmic star formation histories from rest-UV indicators alone, and motivate joint UV-mm constraints for high-redshift galaxies.

We analyze velocity–jump process models of persistent search for a single target in bounded domains. The searcher travels along ballistic trajectories at constant speed and is absorbed upon collision with the target boundary; upon reaching the confining boundary, it selects a new direction uniformly at random and continues. For circular domains with circular targets, we develop a Markov chain approximation of successive boundary-to-boundary flights to estimate the mean first passage time (MFPT). The approximation yields formulas and asymptotic scalings that agree closely with Monte Carlo simulations. Both analysis and numerics show that the MFPT decreases as the target is positioned closer to the domain boundary. Allowing a small probability of in-domain turning (direction switching) further reduces the MFPT, with a weak, approximately linear dependence on the turning probability for small rates. We extend the exit-time framework to partitioned domains comprising multiple disjoint subdomains with a single target located in one subdomain. Given an average inter-domain transition time tau, we identify an optimal switching rate r* that minimizes the MFPT and scales inversely with tau. We assess approximation accuracy across parameters and outline implications for biological search.

We present SoftKiller, an event-level, particle-based method for pileup mitigation that removes the softest particles up to a dynamically determined transverse-momentum threshold on an event-by-event basis. Unlike jet-by-jet corrections, SoftKiller exploits global event information to suppress diffuse contamination while preserving hard radiation. In Monte Carlo studies spanning a broad range of pileup conditions, it achieves substantially improved jet transverse-momentum and mass resolution, with reduced residual biases, relative to commonly used jet-based and jet-area techniques. The procedure is simple, parameter-light, and numerically stable, and delivers nearly two orders of magnitude speed gains over area-based methods, enabling robust, scalable performance for high-luminosity hadron-collider environments. CERN-PH-TH/2014-116, July 2014.

We investigate the impact of a minimum measurable length on inflation within Jacobson’s thermodynamic formulation of gravity, where spacetime dynamics emerge from horizon thermodynamics. Incorporating a fundamental length modifies the horizon entropy and, consequently, the Friedmann equations. Using the Hamilton–Jacobi framework, we derive inflationary dynamics directly from a modified Hubble flow, obtain slow‐roll parameters, and compute the scalar power spectrum, spectral index, running, and tensor‐to‐scalar ratio. The minimum length introduces scale-dependent corrections that can suppress tensors and mildly shift the tilt, yielding viable inflation without fine-tuning. We explore representative potentials and reconstruct classes consistent with the modified dynamics. Confronting predictions with current CMB and large-scale structure constraints, our parameter space includes regions compatible with Planck and BICEP/Keck bounds. The results highlight testable signatures of quantum-gravity-induced minimal length in early-universe cosmology and future surveys.

We present observations of the Lynx arc, a gravitationally lensed galaxy at redshift z = 3.357 discovered during spectroscopic follow-up of the galaxy cluster RX J0848+4456 from the ROSAT Deep Cluster Survey. The arc exhibits a very red continuum color and strong, narrow emission lines. HST WFPC2 imaging and Keck optical and near-infrared spectroscopy show that the source is magnified by a complex cluster potential, enabling study of its physical conditions. The line spectrum, the presence of absorption components in Lyman-alpha, and the rest-frame ultraviolet continuum are consistent with a compact H II region model powered by a population of hot O stars. Best-fit photoionization models require an extremely hot ionizing continuum, a high ionization parameter, and very low nebular metallicity. The narrowness of the lines implies a low mass-to-light ratio for the ionizing stars, indicative of an extremely metal-poor stellar cluster. An apparent silicon overabundance suggests enrichment by past pair-instability supernovae, pointing to progenitors of high mass. The Lynx arc thus offers a rare, magnified window on massive star formation and chemical evolution in the early universe.

Spontaneous breaking of continuous symmetries generates low-energy Nambu–Goldstone modes (NGMs) with either linear (type-I) or quadratic (type-II) dispersion. We present a general framework, grounded in the standard Gross–Pitaevskii–Bogoliubov theory, that not only counts NGMs but also determines the leading dispersion coefficients directly from microscopic data. Our approach exploits zero-mode solutions of the Bogoliubov–de Gennes equation produced by spontaneous symmetry breaking and a set of generalized orthogonality relations that naturally emerge from Bogoliubov transformations in an indefinite inner product space; we refer to these relations as @xmath0-orthogonality. In contrast to previous treatments, the framework applies without modification when additional zero modes lacking a symmetry origin (quasi-NGMs) are present and when spacetime symmetries are spontaneously broken in backgrounds containing topological solitons or vortices. We derive classification criteria that distinguish type-I and type-II NGMs in terms of the @xmath0-orthogonality structure of zero modes, and we obtain closed expressions for the linear velocities and quadratic coefficients in the dispersion relations as overlap integrals of zero-mode wavefunctions with the Gross–Pitaevskii ground state. The method handles degeneracies and linearly independent zero-mode multiplets systematically, providing robustness in realistic settings with competing orders or defects. As a by-product, we compile a concise and self-contained summary of the mathematics of bosonic Bogoliubov equations and transformations, clarifying the roles of indefinite metrics, generalized eigenvectors, and canonical structures, thereby offering a common foundation for analyzing Bogoliubov quasiparticles. We illustrate the general results with spinor Bose–Einstein condensates, analyzing spin-1, spin-2, and spin-3 phases in uniform and defected configurations. For spin-3 condensates, we predict a type-I to type-II transition and a pronounced enhancement of the type-II dispersion coefficient induced by a linearly independent pair of zero modes. Numerical Bogoliubov spectra corroborate these predictions and elucidate how extra zero modes near solitons and vortices reshape low-energy dynamics.

We discuss implications for progenitor systems and the possibility of incomplete disruption with a bound remnant in the host galaxy UGC 12182.

We report the first detection of >100 MeV gamma rays associated with a behind-the-limb solar flare, providing a new probe of high-energy flare emission and particle acceleration. On 2013 October 11 an M1.5-class flare occurred 9.9 degrees behind the east solar limb as viewed by STEREO-B. RHESSI observed hard X-ray emission above the limb, consistent with a loop-top source, with the footpoints occulted. Unexpectedly, the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) detected >100 MeV gamma rays for about 30 minutes, with photon energies up to 3 GeV. The LAT emission centroid is statistically consistent with the RHESSI hard X-ray source, although the localization uncertainty does not require a common origin. Time-integrated gamma-ray spectra are well fit either by bremsstrahlung from relativistic electrons following a hard power law with a high-energy exponential cutoff, or by neutral pion decay from accelerated protons and ions characterized by an isotropic pitch-angle distribution and a power-law momentum spectrum with index ≈3.8. Radiative-transfer calculations demonstrate that the optical depth for >100 MeV photons from a source located behind the limb is too large for the gamma rays to originate at the flare site. A high-corona trapping scenario could in principle reduce attenuation, but would demand atypically low densities and long confinement times inconsistent with the observed timing and energetics. We therefore favor a model in which particles accelerated at the associated coronal mass ejection shock access magnetic footpoints on the visible solar hemisphere, where they interact in the lower atmosphere to produce the observed gamma rays. This event establishes a new diagnostic of shock-accelerated particles and magnetic connectivity in solar eruptive events.

We theoretically investigate the formation and propagation of two-component probe light in a Raman-active medium driven by four pump fields. Using a coupled-mode framework, we show that only a specific coherent superposition of the probe components couples to the matter and acquires a superluminal group velocity, while the orthogonal superposition remains uncoupled. Individual probes lack a well-defined group velocity inside the medium. Calculations based on susceptibility and dispersion predict envelope advancement of the coupled component relative to vacuum propagation, clarifying conditions for superluminal response.

We examine the crescent singularity forming in a developable cone (d‐cone) created by pushing a thin elastic sheet into a circular container, in a setting akin to Cerda et al. (Nature 401, 46, 1999). Using numerical simulations and scaling analysis, we show that stretching is confined to a small core near the pushing tip, while bending dominates the outer region. In the outer domain we identify two distinct stress contributions that decay differently with distance from the tip, reflecting geometric compatibility and force transmission, respectively. We estimate the d‐cone’s elastic energies and derive conditions under which the core size exhibits a well‐defined scaling. Measurements of the pushing force and direct geometric probes yield consistent numerical evidence that the core size scales as R_c ∼ h^{1/3} R^{2/3}, where h is the sheet thickness and R the container radius, in agreement with the proposal of Cerda et al. We further argue that this scaling should not represent the true asymptotic behavior for vanishing h/R. Additional predicted properties are verified numerically and support our analysis.

Deterministic numerical weather prediction models generate ensembles by running with perturbed initial conditions, but such ensembles are often under-dispersive and uncalibrated. We apply Bayesian model averaging (BMA) to calibrate wind speed forecasts from the operational Limited Area Model Ensemble Prediction System of the Hungarian Meteorological Service. We develop two BMA formulations: a gamma mixture with bias-corrected member means and variance linked to forecast magnitude, and a truncated normal mixture with member-specific weights. Parameters are estimated using rolling training windows. Verification shows BMA improves reliability and sharpness: probability integral transform histograms approach uniformity, continuous ranked probability scores and mean absolute errors decrease, prediction interval coverage improves, and high-wind events are better represented. Learned weights reflect member skill, enabling adaptive combination. BMA is an effective, efficient post-processing tool providing calibrated probabilistic wind forecasts for decision support.

We investigate whether the defining property of black holes—the presence of an event horizon—manifests in the variability of soft X-ray transients (SXTs). Comparing SXTs with dynamical evidence for accreting black holes to analogous systems harboring neutron stars, we quantify luminosity changes between outburst and quiescence using archival X-ray data. Black hole SXTs exhibit markedly larger dynamic ranges, with quiescent luminosities suppressed by orders of magnitude relative to neutron-star SXTs. This contrast matches accretion models in which energy advected across a horizon is not radiated, whereas neutron stars re-emit accretion energy from a solid surface. We assess systematic uncertainties (distances, absorption, inclination) and consider alternative mechanisms. The observed dichotomy provides empirical support for event horizons in astrophysical black holes and constrains accretion physics in compact binaries.

We investigate the dynamical feasibility of habitable Earth-mass planets and moons in the Kepler-16 circumbinary system, which hosts a Saturn-mass planet (Kepler-16b), by mapping orbital stability across the standard and extended habitable zones (HZs). Using long-term direct N-body integrations that include the binary, Kepler-16b, and massless test and Earth-mass bodies, we delineate regions of stability, secular forcing, and Hill safety. We find that Earth-mass satellites in S-type, satellite-like orbits bound to Kepler-16b can remain stable within the standard HZ, enabling the possibility of habitable exomoons. In contrast, Earth-mass planets in circumbinary P-type orbits cannot persist within the standard HZ. However, P-type Earth-mass planets are permitted exterior to Kepler-16b within the extended HZ if substantial atmospheric back-warming enhances climate retention. The viable ranges for inferior and superior P-type HZ orbits are 0.657–0.71 AU and 0.95–1.02 AU, respectively. We briefly assess detectability: exomoons may be revealed via transit timing and duration variations of Kepler-16b, while circumbinary Earth-mass planets could be probed by transits and eclipse timing. These results refine targets and strategies for habitable-world searches in circumbinary systems.

We investigate inter-Landau-level transitions of Bloch electrons in doped graphene driven by an arbitrary time-dependent magnetic field within the long-wavelength approximation. Additionally, we compute current probabilities for the @xmath3 and @xmath4 Landau levels, revealing oscillatory behavior governed by a modified cyclotron frequency. The results elucidate tunable suppression and enhancement of transitions, informing magneto-spectroscopy and coherent control in graphene.

We present a Fisher-matrix forecast for constraints on key Epoch of Reionization (EoR) model parameters—the minimum virial temperature, ionizing efficiency, and mean free path of ionizing photons—using thermal-noise levels appropriate to current low-frequency arrays, MWA and LOFAR. Assuming perfect foreground removal, we compare parameter sensitivities derived from the 21 cm power spectrum to those obtained from the 21 cm bispectrum, with the latter computed from semi-numerical realizations with 21cmFAST. We construct the joint covariance of the two statistics, account for survey geometry and observing time, and marginalize over cross-correlations. Across plausible reionization scenarios, the bispectrum delivers tighter constraints than the power spectrum because it is more responsive to non-Gaussian ionization topology. Furthermore, combining the bispectrum with the power spectrum substantially reduces parameter degeneracies, yielding markedly improved multi-parameter constraints. Our results underscore the promise of higher-order 21 cm statistics for EoR inference with existing facilities and motivate bispectrum-aware analysis pipelines.

We analyze sunspot area decay using the Debrecen Photoheliographic Data to quantify statistical departures from the parabolic mean decay law established in the first paper of this series. Focusing on the logarithmic deviation of the instantaneous area decay rate from the mean law, we find that this deviation follows a Gaussian probability distribution with a correlation time of about 3 days, indicating short-term memory in the decay dynamics. As a direct consequence of the Gaussian behavior of the logarithmic deviation, both the instantaneous decay rate and its time-averaged counterpart exhibit approximately lognormal distributions, in agreement with earlier findings. To investigate environmental influences, we combine the sunspot decay analysis with Kitt Peak magnetograms and measure the same-polarity plage magnetic flux within an annulus surrounding each spot. We uncover a significant physical anticorrelation between the logarithmic deviation and the surrounding same-polarity plage flux. Interpreted within a generalized turbulent erosion framework—extended to flux tubes embedded in a preexisting homogeneous plage field—this anticorrelation implies that the decay rate depends inversely on the amplitude of the plage field. The relationship is close to logarithmic, indicating that the plage field acts as multiplicative noise in the erosion process. If the surrounding plage field strengths are themselves Gaussian distributed, the multiplicative coupling naturally yields the observed lognormal distribution of sunspot decay rates. These results highlight the pivotal role of the local magnetic environment in modulating sunspot decay, identifying surrounding plage fields as a major contributor to the large, lognormally distributed random deviations from the mean parabolic law. The measured correlation time, the form of the probability distributions, and the magnetically mediated anticorrelation furnish quantitative constraints for physics-based models of sunspot erosion and for predictive schemes of active-region evolution.

We investigate the edge-state theory of symmetric double-layer quantum Hall systems with interlayer electron tunneling. We show that the interacting edge reduces to the direct sum of a free chiral mode and a single chiral Bose field with a self-interaction of sine-Gordon type. Using perturbative renormalization group methods, we demonstrate that the flow of this chiral sine-Gordon theory is distinct from that of the standard non-chiral sine-Gordon model, in contradiction with a claim by Renn. In particular, at the marginal point @xmath1, the interacting theory is equivalent to two Majorana fermions with different, dynamically generated velocities, yielding velocity anisotropy. For the experimentally observed bilayer 331 state at filling factor @xmath2, this mapping predicts trifurcation of electrons injected at the edge into three chiral components. Our results supply scaling dimensions and tunneling exponents, clarify the role of chirality in sine-Gordon flows, and suggest transport and interferometry signatures that can distinguish the chiral regime from its non-chiral counterpart, and guide future edge experiments.

In this letter, we investigate magnetic transport in AA-stacked bilayer honeycomb chiral magnets with either ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic interlayer coupling. Using a topological magnon framework, we show that chirality induces band gaps, supports chirally protected edge modes, and yields finite magnon Hall and magnon spin Nernst responses. For ferromagnetically coupled layers, the thermal Hall and spin Nernst conductivities retain their sign over broad ranges of magnetic field and temperature, mirroring single-layer honeycomb ferromagnetic insulators. In contrast, antiferromagnetically coupled layers exhibit a sign reversal of these conductivities upon magnetic-field inversion, reflecting opposite Berry curvature contributions from the two layers. We outline experimentally accessible honeycomb bilayer quantum materials and measurement protocols to observe these effects. Supplementary data are available online at http://stacks.iop.org/jphyscm/28/47lt02/mmedia for direct experimental comparison.

Fast magnetic reconnection is widely invoked to explain explosive energy release in solar flares, yet the onset and development of instabilities within reconnecting current sheets remain uncertain because most theoretical treatments adopt simplified magnetic and velocity profiles that do not satisfy the full magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations. We revisit the stability of reconnecting current sheets using the exact global steady, incompressible reconnection solutions of Craig and Henton, which self-consistently couple magnetic fields and plasma flows. Employing numerical simulations, we analyze outflow-dominated and inflow-dominated solution branches and assess their susceptibility to Kelvin–Helmholtz (KH) and tearing modes. We find that current sheets produced by strong shearing outflows are KH unstable, developing vortical structures that disrupt the sheet and enhance mixing. In contrast, sheets formed by rapid, weakly sheared inflow exhibit classical tearing instability, generating magnetic islands and facilitating plasmoid-mediated reconnection. While linear stability theory provides qualitative guidance, the magnetic and velocity geometry inherent to the Craig–Henton solutions modifies growth rates and, in some parameter regimes, stabilizes the sheet against KH or tearing. The sensitivity of instability onset and amplification to the global reconnection geometry offers a route to resolving the flare trigger problem, by linking observable magnetic configurations to the timing and explosiveness of energy release.

Ordered chains, such as amino-acid sequences, underlie cellular function and motivate models in which the relevant degrees of freedom are permutations of a fixed list. We introduce and analyze a statistical physics framework whose configuration space is the symmetric group and whose energy penalizes deviations from a designated reference ordering. Unlike conventional lattice or spin models with factorizable product state spaces, this non-factorizable space yields thermodynamic behavior that is qualitatively distinct even for non-interacting Hamiltonians and markedly richer with interactions. Using distance-based energies and a mean-field treatment, we derive the partition function, free energy, and order parameters characterizing alignment with the reference sequence. The resulting phase diagram exhibits five regimes separated by two transition temperatures and organized by a triple point and a quadruple point, reflecting competing tendencies toward ordered alignment, partially ordered ranked phases, and disordered permutation ensembles. We quantify fluctuations and susceptibilities and identify finite-size scaling with factorial entropy. Finally, we outline extensions to energies on cosets and combinatorial state spaces, and connections to inference and glassy dynamics in statistical mechanics.

We study birack modules as modules over the algebra associated to a finite birack X. Building on earlier work where birack module structures enhanced the birack counting invariant, we introduce birack modules over Laurent polynomial rings to define an Alexander polynomial–style signature for each X-labeled diagram. The multiset of these polynomials over all labelings gives an enhancement of the birack counting invariant. We prove invariance under Reidemeister moves and properties such as normalization and behavior under disjoint union. Explicit computations for both knots and links demonstrate that the new invariant strictly strengthens the unenhanced count and is not determined by the generalized Alexander polynomial.

Despite the imminent advent of exascale systems, only a fraction of HPC applications fully exploit petascale platforms. We argue that preparing applications for exascale must begin prior to hardware availability. We analyze fundamental challenges—massive concurrency, deep memory hierarchies, resilience, energy efficiency, programmability, and performance portability—and recommend solutions spanning formal modeling, static analysis and optimization, runtime monitoring and adaptation, and autonomic computing. We present a conceptual framework that integrates these techniques to guide the systematic porting and co-design of applications and runtimes for exascale. The framework defines interfaces, metrics, and workflows for analysis-driven optimization across the software stack. We also outline concrete steps and tool support for incremental adoption and validation on today’s systems.

We present the results of a pilot study for the Extended MACS Survey (eMACS), a comprehensive search for distant, X-ray luminous galaxy clusters at @xmath0. To extend the probed luminosity regime to poorer systems, we also lower the redshift threshold to @xmath3. These findings highlight the necessity of high-resolution X-ray follow-up to establish robust cluster luminosities and to secure a clean, well-understood sample for eMACS. If borne out by full-sky execution, eMACS is expected to deliver a sample of over 100 extremely massive clusters at @xmath5—representing a dramatic increase over the presently known two dozen systems from X-ray, optical, and Sunyaev–Zel’dovich surveys combined. Such a collection would be invaluable for discovering and characterizing the most powerful gravitational lenses in the universe and for conducting both detailed and statistical studies of the physical properties, assembly histories, and intracluster medium of the most massive galaxy clusters out to @xmath6. This pilot demonstrates the feasibility of eMACS, clarifies the trade-offs inherent in RASS-based selection without stringent X-ray cuts, and underscores the critical role of high-resolution X-ray imaging in mitigating point-source contamination and securing reliable cluster samples. We compare the electronic structures of ground states in cuprates, conventional 3-dimensional superconductors, doped semiconductors, and low-dimensional systems to identify ingredients that favor superconductivity.
