While a high DOS at @xmath2 underpins standard estimates of @xmath3, we show that superconductivity can persist with a low DOS provided the FS is sufficiently simple, which enhances phase stiffness and reduces competing scattering channels. In underdoped cuprates, coupling to long-wavelength collective modes naturally promotes superconducting fluctuations; however, the short coherence length impedes the establishment of long-range order. Across material classes, thermal disorder emerges as a robust limiting factor for achieving large @xmath4, largely independent of carrier concentration. Our results delineate microscopic routes—via FS simplification, controlled coupling to bosonic modes, and minimized disorder—by which disparate materials can attain and stabilize superconductivity.

We study the paramagnetic Anderson–Hubbard model with statistical dynamical mean-field theory (statDMFT), which treats disorder and strong electronic correlations on equal footing. For each disorder realization we construct an approximate nonlocal Green’s function using an atomic-limit self-energy and perform configuration averaging. The approach is implemented on two-dimensional lattices with up to 1000 sites in the strong-disorder regime. From real-space Green’s functions we compute the inverse participation ratio and analyze scaling at quarter- and half-filling. We uncover a nonmonotonic dependence of the localization length on interaction strength, reflecting competing tendencies of interaction-assisted delocalization and correlation-driven localization. In the strong-disorder limit we find no evidence of an interaction-induced insulator–metal transition; instead, the disorder potential remains unscreened near the Mott transition. Moreover, near half-filling, strong correlations suppress the Altshuler–Aronov anomaly in the single-particle density of states. These results demonstrate the utility of statDMFT for disordered correlated systems and clarify the fate of localization under strong correlations.

We present a comprehensive survey of agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms, emphasizing efficient implementations available in R and other software ecosystems. We examine hierarchical self-organizing maps and probabilistic mixture-model formulations, and review grid-based clustering with a focus on hierarchical density-based methods. Finally, we detail a recently developed, linear-time hierarchical algorithm that unifies grid-based perspectives, discuss its theoretical properties, practical performance, and applicability, and outline challenges and directions for research.

This paper investigates whether Romania could experience a credit crunch as a consequence of the United States subprime financial crisis by situating recent events within a broader, global trend of accelerating private indebtedness. We present comparable data on debt accumulation for Australia and the United States, alongside tentative indicators for Romania, to assess the extent to which private debt has systematically outpaced income growth and to evaluate the macroeconomic risks posed by a reversal of this trend. As this study goes to press, the Dow Jones Industrial Average has entered a correction, and U.S. house prices have fallen more than eight percent from their peak, declining at over one percent per month—an historically unprecedented rate. While professional opinions vary regarding the duration and severity of the subprime crisis, the minimal expectation is a recession defined by two or more consecutive quarters of negative growth. We argue that more severe outcomes are plausible once the subprime episode is understood as part of a multi-decade expansion of private credit relative to GDP. Drawing on research by the Reserve Bank of Australia (Battellino 2007), we document that in 15 major OECD countries over 1977–2007, private debt (household plus business) rose faster than nominal GDP, with the United States toward the lower end of the international scale. The private debt-to-GDP ratio more than doubled in the U.S., compared with an elevenfold increase in the Netherlands and a doubling in Germany; Australia’s experience is near the median, with a threefold rise in the past 30 years and a sixfold increase since the mid-1960s. Japan appears as a special case. These patterns indicate that the U.S. debt build-up is not anomalous but emblematic of a wider, unsustainable leverage cycle. To analyze the dynamics of a credit crunch, we develop a model of a pure credit economy with endogenous money creation, in which bank lending generates deposits and aggregate demand is sensitive to net changes in private credit. The model formalizes how shifts in lending standards and borrower repayment behavior can transition the system from expanding credit to net deleveraging, reducing the flow of new money and precipitating a decline in output, asset prices, and employment. We identify threshold conditions under which repayment propensities, falling collateral values, and tighter bank practices jointly produce a self-reinforcing contraction. Applying these insights to Romania, we use tentative data on private credit growth and external funding structures to pose the question of vulnerability to a sudden tightening of credit conditions transmitted from global markets. We conclude that when the decades-long rise in private indebtedness reverses, economies will shift from debt-driven expansion to credit-constrained contraction, with implications that may exceed a mild recession. Policy responses must acknowledge endogenous money, the centrality of private leverage, and the risks of abrupt deleveraging.

Estimating supermassive black hole (SMBH) masses in active galactic nuclei (AGN) commonly assumes that the broad-line region (BLR) is virialized. This assumption is problematic if the BLR comprises both a Keplerian accretion disk and an accelerating wind, because wind dynamics must eventually be dominated by outward forces that overcome gravity. We investigate the validity of the virial assumption by analyzing hydrodynamic simulations of four representative disk-wind models: an isothermal wind, a thermal wind from an X-ray heated disk, and two line-driven winds, one including and one excluding X-ray heating and cooling. For each model we compute volume-integrated internal, kinetic, and gravitational energies that enter the scalar virial theorem and assess whether gravity governs the flow. The isothermal and thermally driven winds are non-virialized, with kinetic and internal energies exceeding the gravitational binding at modest radii. In contrast, both line-driven winds remain virialized out to relatively large distances, owing to their slow radial acceleration, dominance of rotational over radial velocities, and dense wind bases that preserve strong gravitational binding. For the virialized line-driven winds, the projected virial factor exhibits a systematic dependence on inclination, consistent with expectations for flattened, rotationally supported flows, implying a predictable orientation bias in SMBH mass estimates. Finally, by comparing angular momentum prescriptions, we show that outflows launched from Keplerian disks become unvirialized more gradually when they conserve specific angular momentum—as in the models studied here—than when they conserve angular velocity, as in magneto-centrifugal winds. These results provide a physical framework for when BLR virial methods are reliable, highlight the importance of wind driving mechanisms and orientation in interpreting reverberation-based SMBH masses, and motivate incorporating wind dynamics into BLR models to reduce systematic uncertainties.

We develop a first-principles formalism to evaluate conduction eigenchannels of atomic-sized contacts by combining the multiple-scattering Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker Green’s function method with Kubo linear-response theory. We prove that the eigenvectors of the transmission matrix obtained within this framework are identical to the Landauer-Büttiker eigenchannels, thereby providing a rigorous bridge between Green’s-function and scattering approaches. The method is applied to ballistic electron transport through Cu, Pd, Ni, and Co single-atom contacts. We compute channel-resolved transmissions and classify the eigenchannels by the irreducible representations of the contact symmetry as well as by their orbital character via projections onto the contact atom. The analysis reveals material-specific channel composition and degeneracies, elucidating the roles of s and d orbitals in setting conductance and enabling transparent interpretation of experiments on metallic nanocontacts.

We present a suite of 12 extremely high–resolution adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) cosmological hydrodynamic simulations of Population III star formation in a @xmath0CDM universe. By systematically varying the simulation box size and the realized large-scale structure, we quantify environmental and methodological effects on the formation of primordial protostellar cores. Our methodology includes non-equilibrium primordial chemistry and cooling, and excludes a photodissociating ultraviolet background to isolate intrinsic trends. The results are qualitatively consistent with earlier studies by Abel, Bryan, & Norman (2002), Bromm, Coppi, & Larson (2002), and Yoshida et al. (2006). We find that the dark matter halos hosting the first stars exhibit spin parameters comparable to galaxy-mass halos that form at @xmath1, in agreement with previous simulations of high-redshift halos. In the redshift range studied (@xmath2), the threshold halo mass for the formation of a Population III protostar shows little systematic evolution but displays substantial scatter (@xmath3 m@xmath4 m@xmath5), driven by diverse halo assembly histories: halos that assemble more slowly develop cooling cores at lower mass than rapidly assembling halos, consistent with (2003). In contrast, we observe pronounced evolution in protostellar accretion rates with redshift. Objects forming later exhibit higher maximum accretion rates, with typical values of @xmath6 m@xmath7/yr at @xmath8 compared to @xmath9 m@xmath7/yr at @xmath10. This trend arises from the redshift dependence of halo virial properties (mass, temperature, and density) and the kinetics of molecular hydrogen formation and cooling at low densities. These findings imply that the mass distribution of Population III stars, as inferred from their accretion histories, may be broader than previously assumed and may evolve with redshift. Finally, our collapsing protostellar cloud cores do not fragment, consistent with prior results, indicating that Population III stars forming in halos of mass @xmath11 m@xmath7 do so in isolation. Our study underscores the importance of sampling diverse cosmic environments when predicting the properties of the first stars.

We report joint measurements of extensive air showers with the Andyrchy EAS array and the Baksan Underground Scintillation Telescope (BUST) to investigate the primary cosmic-ray spectrum and composition around the knee. The electromagnetic component is recorded by Andyrchy, while high-energy muons (Eμ ≥ 230 GeV) are detected by BUST located directly beneath, enabling simultaneous observations of both components. We present shower size and muon multiplicity distributions, their correlations, and comparisons with Monte Carlo simulations using hadronic interaction models. The data demonstrate spectral steepening near the knee and indicate a progressive mass shift toward heavier nuclei, constraining interaction models.

We demonstrate, within the operator product expansion and renormalization group frameworks, that in asymptotically free theories the temperature‐ and chemical‐potential dependence of the zeroth moment of spectral functions is completely fixed by the one‐loop structure. Logarithmic corrections are essential to the derivation and render the result exact, independent of higher‐loop and nonperturbative details. This universality constrains admissible spectral shapes at finite T and μ, yielding sharp predictions for their evolution and implying striking, model‐independent effects near phase transitions. The constraints must be satisfied by phenomenological parameterizations commonly used in lattice‐QCD analyses and in QCD sum rules at finite temperature and baryon density. We illustrate the exact sum rule explicitly in the Gross–Neveu model, confirming the general arguments and clarifying the role of scale dependence and operator mixing.

In this work we solve the Dyson–Schwinger equation for the quark self-energy in the rainbow truncation employing an infrared-vanishing gluon propagator characterized by an IR mass scale @xmath0. The framework yields a @xmath0-dependent critical coupling α_c signaling the onset of dynamical chiral symmetry breaking (DCSB). For realistic QCD couplings we find a decoupling between the strength and characteristic scale of DCSB and the IR scale when @xmath0 is small, whereas for sufficiently large @xmath0 the system remains chirally symmetric and no dynamical mass is generated. The resulting quark propagator exhibits a pole at timelike momenta over a wide range of @xmath0, indicating the absence of quark confinement for those parameters. Analyticity analysis shows the propagator is analytic throughout the complex momentum plane except along the timelike axis, validating a naive Wick rotation. Implications for truncation artifacts and the interplay between infrared modeling and chiral dynamics are briefly discussed.

Reported uncertainties are frequently asymmetric, yet their treatment remains inconsistent. We identify two distinct sources of asymmetry in analyses and examine how to combine asymmetric errors. We demonstrate that the commonly used prescription lacks justification and can yield incorrect results. For asymmetric systematic uncertainties, we present a consistent methodology with detailed examples. For asymmetric statistical uncertainties, we outline a general framework. Implications for inference and reporting are discussed.

We revisit Maxwell’s demon in a regime deliberately freed from the usual “work” constraint and place it at a phase boundary at the melting point. We develop a trajectory-resolved analytic framework grounded in Newton’s third law, pairing every forward microprocess with its reverse counterpart to quantify entropy production. The momentum exchanges impose reciprocity relations that bound the component of energy fluxes, yielding a nonnegative entropy functional across all length and time scales. At ultrashort times (collision–phonon timescales), demon-induced sorting is nullified by recoil, latent-heat exchange, impulsive scattering, and reorganization of local chemical environments, which reestablish detailed balance. The analysis exposes why even a “supernatural” demon cannot sustain entropy-reducing trajectories in real chemical systems. Consequently, the second law remains inviolable in perpetuity. Our results provide testable predictions for entropy flux measurements and trajectory correlations. PACS: 05.70.Jk; 34.20.Cf.

Recent analyses have argued that cosmological models allowing a sizable CDM isocurvature contribution remain consistent with CMB anisotropies and the galaxy power spectrum if the primordial entropy spectrum is very blue (@xmath0). However, such spectra generate excessive small-scale matter fluctuations (typically below @xmath1). We revisit this by combining recent CMB and large-scale structure data with high-resolution, high signal-to-noise Lyman-@xmath2 forest flux power spectra. Using a Bayesian framework for mixed adiabatic–isocurvature initial conditions with arbitrary correlation and independent tilts, and calibrations of the IGM, we marginalize over astrophysical and nuisance parameters. Properly incorporating the Lyman-@xmath2 constraints largely eliminates the region with very blue entropy modes. The isocurvature fraction @xmath3, defined at the pivot scale @xmath4 Mpc@xmath5, is bounded above by @xmath6, while @xmath7 (95% confidence). For curvaton scenarios with maximal correlation and a common tilt, we obtain @xmath8 (95% c.l.). In double-inflation models with two gravitationally coupled massive inflatons, the mass ratio must satisfy @xmath9 (95% c.l.). These results favor nearly adiabatic initial conditions and restrict non-adiabatic inflationary parameter space.

We report the discovery of two new variable stars in the metal-poor globular cluster NGC 288 from time-series CCD photometry. Light-curve morphology, amplitudes, and periods identify both variables as SX Phoenicis pulsators oscillating in the fundamental radial mode with periods of order hours. We also refine period determinations for six previously known variables in the cluster. Because SX Phe stars follow well-defined period–luminosity relations and outnumber the cluster’s RR Lyrae, they provide an efficient, consistent distance indicator. From our sample we derive period–luminosity relations for the fundamental and first-overtone modes and use them to estimate the distance to NGC 288. Independent, multi-chromatic isochrone fitting to our UBV color–magnitude diagrams, based on the Dartmouth Stellar Evolution Database, yields [Fe/H] = −1.3 ± 0.1, reddening E(B−V) = 0.02 ± 0.01, and a distance modulus (m−M)0 = 14.72 ± 0.01, in agreement with the SX Phe calibration. The new variables are consistent with the cluster’s blue-straggler population, supporting their identification as Population II pulsators. Our results strengthen the utility of SX Phe stars for precision distance and age constraints in metal-poor systems and add to the census of short-period variables in NGC 288.

Turbulence is central to the structure and evolution of molecular clouds and star-forming regions, yet robust statistical tools for diagnosing turbulent flows remain limited. One-point probability distribution functions (PDFs) of dynamical variables have been proposed as tractable measures, but their interpretation demands controlled numerical benchmarks. We present smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations of supersonic turbulence representative of molecular cloud conditions, exploring both driven and decaying regimes, with and without self-gravity. To quantify the role of sampling variance and projection effects, we further analyze ensembles of random Gaussian velocity fields. Flow properties are characterized via PDFs of gas density, line-of-sight velocity centroids, and line-centroid increments, complemented by measurements of the dispersion and kurtosis of increment PDFs and by maps of the spatial distribution of velocity increments at small separations. Comparisons across models show that including self-gravity yields markedly better agreement with observed PDFs in molecular clouds, particularly for density contrasts and centroid statistics. For small spatial lags, increment PDFs approach exponential forms across all considered velocity fields, consistent with intermittency and the prevalence of shocks and coherent structures. Nevertheless, all configurations produce non-Gaussian signatures, with differences that are gradual rather than decisive. Moreover, the analyzed PDFs exhibit strong dependence on projection, underscoring the sensitivity of line-of-sight observables to viewing geometry. These findings imply that one-point PDFs alone provide limited discriminatory power for distinguishing among physical processes such as driving mechanisms, decay, or the presence of self-gravity. While useful for constraining intermittency and amplitude of fluctuations, adequate characterization of interstellar turbulence requires complementary diagnostics, including multi-point statistics, velocity–density correlations, and spatially resolved analyses. Our results highlight the necessity of incorporating self-gravity in simulation–observation comparisons and caution against over-reliance on one-point PDFs for inferring the physics of molecular cloud turbulence. Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal.

We investigate orbital diamagnetism in weakly doped bilayer graphene under spatially smooth magnetic textures. Using linear-response theory at zero temperature, we derive an analytic expression for the nonlocal orbital susceptibility χ(q, εF) at finite wave number q and Fermi energy εF. The resulting screening factor depends on q, leading to richer magnetic-field screening than in monolayer graphene. From χ(q, εF) we compute the induced magnetization and circulating currents in nonuniform fields, revealing qualitative differences from monolayer graphene and a conventional two-dimensional electron gas. Despite these distinctions, bilayer graphene repels magnetic objects via a diamagnetic force that can be interpreted as arising from a reduced-amplitude mirror image, with the reduction set by characteristic length scales of the object–bilayer geometry and the field’s spatial variation. We identify crossover regimes where the response of bilayer graphene interpolates between monolayer-like and 2DEG-like behavior as doping and wave number are varied. These results provide physical insight into nonlocal magnetic screening in bilayer graphene, with implications for magnetic sensing, imaging, and device design.

We present an exact, simple spacetime describing wormhole formation obtained by regularly gluing Minkowski space to the Roberts solution across null hypersurfaces. The Roberts parameters are chosen so that the supporting massless scalar field has a negative kinetic term, enabling the requisite energy-condition violation. A curvature singularity arises at the formation event but disappears instantaneously. Using radial causal geodesics, we show this transient singularity is weak in both Tipler and Królak senses. The construction offers an analytic framework for dynamical wormhole genesis.

We investigate the collider phenomenology of an inert triplet scalar dark matter candidate at the LHC. Allowing Higgs-portal interactions, we analyze the decay of the Higgs boson into dark matter pairs and confront the model with current limits on the invisible Higgs branching ratio and the Higgs signal strength @xmath0, constraining the parameter space. We further assess bounds from measurements @xmath1 and mono-Higgs production. The dark matter annihilation cross sections into @xmath2 and @xmath3 are calculated analytically and compared to Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data, which impose constraints in the low-mass regime. We find these indirect limits can exceed those from LUX direct detection for dark matter. Combining collider, indirect, and direct probes, we delineate viable regions and highlight discovery prospects at the HL-LHC.

We present an identity obeyed by the kinematic numerators of tree-level diagrams in massless gauge theories, which is the kinematic counterpart of the Jacobi identity satisfied by color factors. Enforcing this correspondence yields nontrivial relations among color-ordered partial amplitudes and streamlines their representation, including compact bases and improved recursion. We explore applications to multiloop constructions via the unitarity method, demonstrating how the identity organizes cuts and correlates distinct contributions to a two-loop four-point QCD amplitude. Extending the framework to gravity, we reorganize gravity tree amplitudes diagram by diagram, exposing structural parallels with the Kawai–Lewellen–Tye relations and deriving novel amplitude relations of a similar type. These results sharpen the gauge–gravity correspondence at the amplitude level and provide building blocks well-suited for higher-loop analyses, with anticipated benefits for probing the ultraviolet behavior of perturbative quantum gravity theories.

Undulator tapering in free-electron lasers (FELs) offers a route to boost radiation power beyond initial saturation, contingent on optimal taper profiles. We present an empirical, multidimensional optimization of variable-gap undulator modules at the X-ray FEL FLASH2, exploring coupled parameters such as gap, phase, and post-saturation section lengths under operational constraints. The optimized profiles yield substantial power and efficiency gains, while preserving spectral quality and stability. Measurements are systematically compared to start-to-end numerical simulations, revealing generally strong agreement, identifying sensitivities to electron-beam properties, and guiding robust taper strategies for high-efficiency FEL operation.

We study three fundamental representation problems for unit interval (UIG) and unit circular-arc (UCA) graphs: unrestricted, bounded, and minimal. In the unrestricted setting, a proper circular-arc (PCA) model is given and the task is to decide whether an equivalent UCA model exists and, if so, to construct it. We present a linear-time algorithm that, in addition to producing an equivalent UCA model when one exists, outputs a succinct negative certificate when none does. The algorithm is amenable to a logspace implementation, highlighting strong space efficiency alongside optimal time complexity. In the bounded version, the PCA model is accompanied by lower and upper bounds on the starting points of arcs in the sought UCA model. For this constraint-aware problem, we design an algorithm that uses linear space and runs in quadratic time. In the minimal version, the circumference of the circle and the common arc length in the target UCA model must be simultaneously minimized. We prove that every UCA graph admits such a minimal model and provide a polynomial-time algorithm to compute it. We further address minimal representations of UIGs, showing that a previously claimed linear-time method fails to yield minimal models on certain inputs. We repair this method and obtain a correct algorithm that operates in linear space and quadratic time. As an application, we leverage our minimal representation algorithms to determine the minimum powers of paths and cycles that contain a given UIG and UCA model, respectively, thereby linking geometric representations to structural containment in graph powers.

We present a search for very-long-term variability (weeks to years) in X-ray binaries (XRBs) in the giant elliptical galaxy M87 using archival Chandra imaging. We constructed multi-epoch light curves for the eight brightest XRB candidates and quantified their variability amplitudes and timescales. Several sources attain peak luminosities exceeding the ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX) threshold of ~1×10^39 erg s^−1, and one object exhibits pronounced flux depressions consistent with dips or eclipses. To assess sensitivity to periodic modulations, we performed a period-recoverability analysis, adopting modulation amplitudes comparable to the Galactic microquasar SS 433. Under the current sampling, detectable periodicities are confined to a narrow range with periods shorter than ~120 days; longer or lower-amplitude modulations are strongly suppressed by the window function and cadence. These results underscore both the prevalence of substantial long-term variability among bright M87 XRBs and the limitations imposed by sparse archival coverage. We conclude that a dedicated monitoring campaign, with an optimized cadence and duration, is essential to robustly detect and characterize long-term periodic and quasi-periodic modulations analogous to those observed in Galactic sources.

We investigate beta-decay properties of proton-rich even-even and odd-A krypton isotopes within a deformed, self-consistent Hartree-Fock framework using density-dependent Skyrme interactions and BCS pairing. Residual spin-isospin correlations are incorporated consistently in particle-hole and particle-particle channels and treated with the quasiparticle random-phase approximation. We highlight methodological differences between even-even and odd-A systems, including blocking and deformation-induced effects on quasiparticle spectra. Calculated Gamow-Teller strength distributions, summed strengths, and half-lives are compared with available data, assessing uncertainties associated with deformation, pairing, and force parameterization. We analyze the sensitivity of observables to prolate-oblate configurations and shape coexistence and identify deformation-dependent signatures in the parent nuclei. The results provide constraints on nuclear shapes near the proton drip line and guide future measurements of GT strengths and beta-decay half-lives. Astrophysical rp-process implications are noted.

Aniline, a prototypical aromatic amine, has rarely been examined under strong magnetic fields. We investigate its electronic response using density functional theory in both independent-particle and interacting-particle frameworks for fields up to tens of tesla. Field-dependent charge-density distributions, energy dispersions, dipole moments, and forces are computed and analyzed across the phenyl ring and amino group. The magnetic field drives redistribution of electron density, enhances ring-current character, and induces anisotropic localization that depends on molecular orientation relative to the field. Energy dispersions exhibit strong fluctuations with field strength, reflecting orbital reordering and interaction-enhanced avoided crossings. Dipole moments show nonlinear magneto-response and anisotropy, while calculated forces indicate moderate magnetostrictive tendencies without destabilizing the geometry. Comparison of independent and interacting treatments reveals amplified field effects when electron–electron interactions are included. These results establish aniline as a sensitive magneto-electronic system and provide benchmarks for magnetochemistry and magnetic-field control of organic molecular properties.

We investigate a two-dimensional electron system in a quantizing magnetic field driven from equilibrium by microwave radiation, where strong magneto-oscillations of the dissipative conductivity arise. Within an electrostatic framework, we demonstrate that under irradiation the dissipative conductivity can become negative while the diffusion coefficient remains positive, reflecting a breakdown of the equilibrium Einstein relation. Solving the coupled linear transport and Poisson equations for a finite sample, we show that carrier diffusion can stabilize uniform steady states even when conductivity is negative. The stabilization criterion is set by the nonequilibrium screening length, which diverges at the conductivity sign change; for samples shorter than its absolute value, the uniform negative-conductivity state is stable and produces a measurable negative resistance. We further analyze the impact of a finite work-function mismatch between contacts, obtaining self-consistent profiles of electrostatic potential and electron density. In the diffusion-stabilized regime, the sample segregates into two regions with opposite electric-field directions, a precursor of the spontaneous domain structure anticipated for microwave-induced zero-resistance states. Our results identify finite-size and boundary-condition controls of negative-conductivity transport and provide experimental signatures in the non-equilibrium magnetotransport of irradiated 2D electron gases.

We consider lossy source coding with side information under a privacy constraint that the reconstruction sequence at a decoder must be kept partially secret from another terminal (eavesdropper, sender, or helper). We study how a reconstruction-privacy requirement at a designated terminal reshapes the rate–distortion tradeoff and characterize the achievable rate–distortion–equivocation region. Allowing the decoder to employ random mappings, we derive general inner and outer bounds for settings in which side information is available non-causally or causally at the decoder. For the special per-symbol reconstruction architecture—where each reconstruction symbol depends only on the source description and the contemporaneous side-information symbol—we provide the complete rate–distortion–equivocation region. Our analysis reveals new fundamental tradeoffs induced by reconstruction privacy and demonstrates the utility of stochastic decoding in enlarging the achievable region. A binary example quantifies the gains and illustrates how privacy constraints can necessitate higher rates or tolerating increased distortion to achieve prescribed equivocation levels, highlighting design guidelines for privacy-aware source coding systems in real deployments.

We introduce a new method for constructing point-line configurations by consecutively inscribing copies of a fixed underlying configuration. The iterative procedure yields a broad class of partial linear spaces. We provide a uniform characterization of this class and of a previously studied class based on coverings by families of closed substructures. The characterizations are formulated via duality, correlations, and the Shult axiom, and lead to representation and construction theorems. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the inscribed iterations to preserve incidence, connectivity, and rank, and we analyze when duality extends to correlations across layers. Examples and counterexamples illustrate the scope and limitations; facts, lemmas, and propositions culminate in corollaries describing extremal cases and canonical decompositions. Applications include new configurations with controlled automorphism groups and embeddings in polar spaces.

We present a spectroscopic analysis of SK41 (AB4, WN5h), the only confirmed single Wolf–Rayet (WR) star in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), using ultraviolet (IUE), optical (AAT), and near-infrared (NTT) observations. Contrary to expectations for low-metallicity environments, SK41 exhibits stellar properties typical of Galactic and Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) WN stars, with a stellar temperature of approximately 42 kK, log(L/Lsun) = 5.7, a terminal wind speed of 1300 km s−1, a mass-loss rate of 3 × 10−5 Msun yr−1 (assuming wind clumping via a volume filling factor), and a hydrogen-to-helium ratio of about 2 by number. Notably, its luminosity is about 50% below the minimum predicted by single-star evolutionary models at SMC metallicity. We further show that emission-line luminosities in SMC WR stars are not systematically reduced relative to their Galactic and LMC counterparts: from samples of 43 late-type and 59 early-type WN stars, we find log L(He II 4686) = 36.0 and 35.8 erg s−1, respectively, and from 25 early-type WC stars, log L(C IV 5801–12) = 36.5 erg s−1. This calibration provides a practical tool for estimating WR populations in young starburst galaxies. Synthetic WN models computed with identical stellar parameters but varying metal abundances, interpreted within the Smith et al. classification scheme, predict earlier spectral subtypes at lower metallicity (e.g., WN3–4 at 0.04 Zsun versus WN6 at Zsun), offering a natural explanation for the prevalence of earlier WN types in metal-poor systems. Overall, SK41 challenges current evolutionary predictions while supporting a strong metallicity dependence in WN spectral classification.

We investigate the process of galaxy formation as it can be observed in the only known galaxies currently in the act of assembly, the so‐called tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs), by tracing their molecular gas via CO emission. Molecular gas is a key element in the galaxy formation process, providing the physical link between a cloud of gas and a bona fide galaxy. Using a sample of nine TDGs, we detect CO in eight objects, yielding an overall detection rate of 80% and demonstrating that molecular gas is abundant in TDGs, with inferred molecular gas masses reaching up to a few 10^8 solar masses, assuming standard conversion factors. The CO emission coincides both spatially and kinematically with the HI emission, indicating that the molecular phase forms in situ from atomic hydrogen where the HI column density is high, consistent with a threshold for HI-to-H2 conversion in compressed tidal debris. A possible trend of more evolved TDGs harboring greater molecular gas masses is observed, in accord with the progressive transformation of HI into H2 and the buildup of the dense phase that precedes star formation. Although uncertainties remain large for individual objects due to unknown geometry and inclination, dynamical masses estimated from CO line widths do not exceed the sum of the visible components (HI + H2 + stars). Thus, TDGs appear to require no dark matter, in contrast to classical dwarf galaxies, reflecting their origin in tidal material stripped from parent disks. We provide evidence that TDGs are self‐gravitating entities, implying that we are witnessing the ensemble of processes in galaxy formation: concentration of large amounts of gas into bound structures, condensation of atomic gas into molecular clouds, and subsequent star formation from the dense molecular component. TDGs therefore offer a unique, observable laboratory for the early phases of galaxy assembly.

We investigate outcome-related competitive learning in populations choosing between two strategies, extending the interfacial model of Mehta and Luck (Phys. Rev. E 60:5218–5230, 1999) to incorporate agents’ own outcomes alongside neighbors’ relative success and local conformity. Individuals update by balancing a tendency to align with the local majority and a preference for the type with higher perceived payoff, augmented by self-performance feedback. Focusing on the treatment of bulk sites, we formulate three distinct update rules that modulate the influence of self-outcome versus neighborhood outcomes. Using numerical exploration and coarse-grained analysis, we construct phase diagrams at coexistence and compare them with those of the original interfacial model. The extensions produce systematic departures, including shifts of coexistence boundaries, the emergence and stabilization of mixed phases, altered interfacial roughening, and regime-dependent transitions (continuous versus discontinuous) and metastability. We further delineate limits connecting these variants to the cooperative model of Mehta and Luck, showing how self-outcome weighting interpolates between competitive and cooperative dynamics. The results highlight how micro-level outcome feedback reshapes macroscopic ordering and learning efficiency.

We study Nflation, in which a collection of uncoupled massive scalar fields collectively drives inflation. By analyzing the slow-roll conditions in the multifield phase space, we show that when the number of fields exceeds the square of the ratio of the Planck scale to the average field mass, the slow-roll inflationary region disappears. This bound implies that successful Nflation relevant to our observable universe requires a number of fields limited by this ratio. Our result aligns with recent black hole physics arguments and clarifies theoretical constraints on multifield inflation model building and phenomenology.

We study the uniqueness of quantum states compatible with prescribed measurement results for a specified set of observables, and we distinguish two notions of uniqueness for a given pure state. In case (1), uniqueness among pure states, no other pure state reproduces the same measurement outcomes. In case (2), uniqueness among all states, no other state—pure or mixed—reproduces the same outcomes. For case (1), it is known that in a @xmath0-dimensional Hilbert space there exists a set of @xmath1 observables that uniquely determines any pure state. Our main result shows that for case (2) a set of only @xmath2 observables suffices to uniquely determine any pure state. This establishes a strict gap between the resources required for uniqueness among pure states and uniqueness among all states, and we present explicit examples illustrating this separation. We further investigate the unique determination of a pure state by reduced density matrices (RDMs), viewing it as a special instance of determination by observables. We improve the best known bound on local dimensions under which almost all pure states are uniquely determined by their RDMs in case (2), thereby strengthening generic-identifiability guarantees for multipartite systems. Beyond bounds, we identify structural conditions under which case (1) implies case (2). Using the convexity of the numerical range, we prove that when only two observables are measured, uniqueness among pure states automatically implies uniqueness among all states. More generally, if there exists a compact symmetry group of the state space whose fixed-point set coincides with the span of the measured observables, then case (1) implies case (2). We analyze the possible dimensions of such spans and show that our framework and results extend naturally to low-rank quantum states, with implications for efficient quantum tomography, phase retrieval, and the geometry of state reconstruction.

We present a simulation method to study electrolyte solutions confined in dielectric slab geometries using a modified three-dimensional Ewald summation. The algorithm is fast, simple to implement, and efficiently resums the infinite series of electrostatic image charges inherent to dielectric discontinuities. In the weak-coupling regime, we develop a complementary mean-field theory that quantitatively predicts ionic distributions between dielectric, charged plates. Comparison shows excellent agreement between theory and simulations, validating both approaches robustly. We further report detailed ionic density profiles in the strong electrostatic coupling limit, highlighting correlation-driven layering. Finally, we investigate the confinement of charge-asymmetric electrolytes between neutral surfaces, elucidating entropic and dielectric effects on partitioning.

We present a comprehensive search for persistent and pulsed gamma-ray emission from 20 magnetars using six years of Fermi Large Area Telescope observations. No source is detected at the positions of any magnetar. We therefore derive the most stringent flux upper limits to date in the 0.1–10 GeV band. Pulsation searches for the four magnetars with reliable timing ephemerides over the observation span yield no periodic signals. In parallel, we analyze the gamma-ray morphology and spectra of seven supernova remnants associated with or adjacent to these magnetars, separating remnant emission from background. Our results impose tight constraints on magnetar high-energy emission mechanisms and particle acceleration.

We investigate whether galaxy clusters, like early-type galaxies, obey scaling relations—Fundamental Plane (FP), luminosity–radius (L–R), and luminosity–velocity dispersion (L–σ)—and explore their physical origin. Using N-body simulations of massive dark-matter halos in a ΛCDM cosmology, we measure halo structural and dynamical properties and derive scaling relations for their dark hosts. The simulated halos define FP-, L–R-, and L–σ-like relations at the level of dark matter, but their slopes are not identical to those observed for clusters. Among the mechanisms capable, in principle, of reconciling the simulated and observed relations—structural non-homology, projection systematics, and variations in stellar content—we find that a luminosity-dependent mass-to-light ratio, M/L(L), is the sufficient solution. The required trend aligns with observational inferences for clusters. Extending the analysis to galactic scales uncovers a tension between cosmological predictions for halo scaling, the observed increase of M/L with luminosity in ellipticals, and the slope of their L–σ relation, which differs from the cluster analogue. This suggests that the scaling laws of elliptical galaxies are not set by dissipationless collapse alone, but are the combined outcome of early cosmological assembly plus dissipative merging that reshapes stellar structure and kinematics. Finally, we discuss the expected redshift evolution of cluster scaling relations, predicting changes in slope and normalization driven by halo concentration and dynamical state, with increasing scatter at higher redshift, offering testable targets for forthcoming surveys.

Combining higher-order abstract syntax (HOAS) with inductive and coinductive reasoning in general-purpose proof assistants has long been challenging. We present the theory and practice of Within, a Coq-based framework that addresses these difficulties by providing a definitional layer in which object languages are specified with HOAS while reasoning proceeds with standard (co)induction and tactics. At its core, Within uses a de Bruijn representation of lambda terms to implement a conservative encoding of binding and substitution. This definitional approach preserves consistency within classical type theory and exposes to users a clean HOAS interface for specifying object logics. Our methodology adopts a multi-level reasoning style, akin to systems such as Twelf and Abella. A dedicated specification logic serves as a middle layer: object-language inference rules are expressed as judgments of this logic, and reasoning about derivability is conducted explicitly within Coq. By shifting hypothetical judgments into the specification logic and proving properties about provability, we support (co)inductive arguments even in the presence of non-stratifiable dependencies that arise in elegant HOAS specifications. We demonstrate the approach on two case studies. First, we give a formal, machine-checked proof of type soundness (subject reduction) for a fragment of a pure functional language, using a minimal intuitionistic specification logic. Second, we establish an analogous soundness result for a continuation-machine presentation of the operational semantics of the same language, this time employing an ordered linear logic as the specification layer. The second case illustrates how features of ordered linear logic yield succinct encodings of a more intricate object logic. These results show that Within accommodates multiple specification logics, scales to richer semantic presentations, and enables modular, tactic-driven proofs about HOAS-encoded systems without sacrificing definitional transparency or foundational guarantees and proof reuse across developments.

We present a measurement of the contributions to the cosmic infrared background (CIB) from known galaxies and their faint, physically associated companions at submillimeter wavelengths. Using the publicly available UltraVISTA catalog of near-infrared selected galaxies together with Herschel HerMES maps at 250, 350, and 500 microns, we develop a stacking framework that intentionally smooths the images prior to stacking. This approach exploits the fact that uncatalogued, correlated sources within the beam can bias stacked flux densities, particularly when image resolution is limited. By progressively smoothing the maps with Gaussian kernels of increasing full width at half maximum and summing the resulting stacked intensities, we capture the cumulative emission from cataloged galaxies and the clustered, faint sources that accompany them. We find that the cumulative CIB rises with increased smoothing scale at all three wavelengths, approaching a substantial fraction of the fiducial, absolute CIB levels. The fractional contributions we infer are consistent across bands, and the dominant uncertainties in these fractions arise from the uncertainties in the absolute CIB measurements themselves rather than the stacking procedure. To interpret these results, we introduce a simple model that combines parametric descriptions of stacked flux densities with empirical stellar mass functions. This model indicates that emission from galaxies with stellar masses above approximately 10^9 solar masses can account for most of the measured total intensities, arguing against a significant role for extended, diffuse components such as intrahalo dust. We conclude by outlining prospects for forthcoming surveys and instruments to refine absolute CIB determinations and to reveal any residual, correlated emission on arcminute scales, thereby closing the remaining gap in the CIB energy budget.

We investigate the dual picture of quantum geometry encoded by spin network states and, from this perspective, introduce and analyze a new geometric operator in loop quantum gravity: the length operator. While the area and volume operators have long provided striking evidence for Planck-scale discreteness, a robust definition of length has remained technically challenging. Building on the combinatorial and algebraic structure of spin networks, we construct a background-independent operator associated with the classical length of a curve embedded in the spatial manifold, expressed in terms of fluxes of the densitized triad and parallel transports along the underlying graph. We show that the length operator is well defined on the kinematical Hilbert space of loop quantum gravity and that its spectrum is discrete, with eigenvalues determined by the spin labels and intertwiners that characterize the spin network. The operator is diagonalized not by the standard spin network basis alone, but by appropriate superpositions of spin network states adapted to the curve, reflecting the nontrivial intertwining of edge and node data required to capture one-dimensional geometric information. We present explicit families of eigenstates and eigenvalues for simple graphs and curves intersecting links and nodes, exhibiting the emergence of a minimal nonzero quantum of length and the characteristic Planck-scale gaps. The semiclassical behavior is tested using states peaked on classical configurations, where expectation values reproduce the classical length to leading order and quantum fluctuations diminish with increasing spins, indicating the correct classical limit. We discuss the conceptual and technical difficulties that must be overcome—such as regulator independence, gauge and diffeomorphism invariance, and cylindrical consistency—and detail the strategy that achieves a graph-preserving, background-independent construction. The relation with previous proposals is clarified, highlighting differences in regularization and operator ordering with earlier attempts and explaining why the present construction yields a discrete spectrum and improved semiclassical properties. Finally, we outline an extension to composite and piecewise analytic curves and comment on commutation properties with area and volume operators. These results further substantiate the picture of quantum geometry in loop quantum gravity and strengthen the case for Planck-scale discreteness across all fundamental geometric observables. Keywords: quantum geometry; spin network states; Planck-scale discreteness PACS: 04.60.Pp; 04.60.Nc

We study scattering by a general system of @xmath0 @xmath1-wave point scatterers and show that there are always @xmath0 eigenmodes (eigenchannels).
