The resulting eigenmode expansion yields compact expressions for the total scattering amplitude and cross section, and provides insight into the positions and widths of resonances, their superradiant or subradiant character, and unsymmetric Fano lineshapes for sharp proximity resonances arising from interference with a broad high-energy tail. Off-resonant eigenmodes for identical proximate scatterers are shown to approximate angular momentum eigenstates.

We present a systematic classification of 4330 X-ray sources drawn from the 2XMMi-DR3 catalog. Sources were selected to be point-like, to have multiple XMM-Newton observations, and to include at least one detection with signal-to-noise ratio greater than 20. For approximately one third of the sample, we obtained reliable source-type identifications from the literature and archival databases, comprising 611 stars, 753 active galactic nuclei (AGN), and 138 compact object systems that include white dwarfs, neutron stars, and stellar-mass black holes. We investigated their X-ray spectral, variability, and multiwavelength properties to establish diagnostic criteria for classification. Nearly 99% of stars can be separated from other source classes through their low X-ray-to-infrared flux ratios and frequent X-ray flaring behavior. AGN exhibit remarkably homogeneous X-ray spectra, characterized by power-law photon indices centered at 1.91 ± 0.31, and modest long-term variability, with 0.2-4.5 keV flux variation factors having a median of 1.48 and 98.5% remaining below 10. In contrast, about 70% of compact object systems display either very soft or very hard X-ray spectra, high amplitude variability, and/or large X-ray-to-infrared flux ratios, distinguishing them effectively from AGN. Using these empirically calibrated diagnostics, we devised a classification scheme to assign source types to the remaining unclassified objects, identifying 644 candidate stars, 1376 candidate AGN, and 202 candidate compact object systems, with estimated false identification probabilities of roughly 1%, 3%, and 18%, respectively. We further report 320 sources associated with nearby galaxies and 151 sources located in the Galactic plane, populations we expect to be dominated by compact object systems or background AGN. Finally, we identify 100 candidate ultraluminous X-ray sources, which exhibit substantially lower long-term variability than other accreting compact objects. These results provide a robust framework for classifying X-ray sources in wide-field surveys and deliver a curated set of candidates for follow-up studies of stellar coronal emitters, accreting compact objects, and AGN.

We investigate CP-violating asymmetry in decay of neutral Higgs boson (scalar or pseudoscalar) into t tbar due to complex stop mixing in MSSM. Using effective couplings and one-loop corrections, we compute helicity-dependent amplitudes and derive CP asymmetry between CP-conjugate polarized final states. The asymmetry arises from absorptive parts near the t tbar threshold and from interference of scalar and pseudoscalar components induced by stop mixing phases. We map parameter dependence on Higgs mass, tan beta, stop masses, and the stop mixing angle and phase, subject to EDM and flavor constraints. Numerical scans show potentially large asymmetries, reaching O(10%) in viable regions. We discuss collider observables based on top polarization distributions and prospects for measuring Higgs-sector CP violation at the LHC and future e+e- colliders.

We investigate the @xmath0Sn(@xmath1,@xmath2)@xmath3Cd reaction at 392 MeV within the distorted-wave impulse approximation (DWIA). Calculations show the process is highly peripheral, driven by strong absorption of @xmath4 by the residual nucleus @xmath3Cd, making @xmath4 clustering on the nuclear surface accessible. We assess the validity of the factorization approximation and find that, although the kinematics of @xmath4 in the nuclear interior is strongly modified by distortion of @xmath3Cd, these effects do not influence measured cross sections due to dominant absorption in that region. Angular distributions and momentum-transfer trends corroborate peripherality, supporting DWIA and factorization for extracting surface clustering information at intermediate energies. Implications for medium-mass nuclei are noted.

Consensus in multi-agent systems is classically guaranteed when the communication digraph contains a spanning arborescence. We study the discrete DeGroot consensus problem when this structural condition is violated and the standard iterations may not converge to agreement. We characterize the set X0 of initial opinion vectors that nevertheless ensure consensus for a given influence matrix, providing an explicit description in terms of invariant subspaces associated with the stochastic dynamics. Building on this characterization, we propose a two-step coordination method: (1) orthogonally project the initial opinion vector onto X0, thereby minimally modifying the initial state while enforcing consensus admissibility; and (2) perform the usual DeGroot iterations with the original influence matrix. We analyze convergence, stability, and sensitivity of the method, and show that, for any non-periodic (aperiodic) stochastic influence matrix, the effective update matrix induced by the orthogonal projection can be interpreted as a regularized power limit of the original iteration operator. This viewpoint clarifies limit behavior, yields computable consensus values, and offers a principled remedy when the communication graph lacks an arborescence.

We present exact, analytic solutions to the Klein–Gordon equation for a charged scalar in the extremal Reissner–Nordström–AdS background. Exploiting these solutions at zero frequency but arbitrary momentum, mass, and charge, we derive closed-form expressions for the holographic Green's function of the dual strongly coupled operator near a quantum critical point. The analytic control allows us to classify two distinct mechanisms of instability encoded in the Green's function: (i) a zero-mode instability that produces a hybridized critical point, and (ii) an instability of the infrared geometry that triggers a bifurcating critical point. We show that these mechanisms can coexist, resulting in a mixed critical point with distinctive scaling. Absent an additional tuning parameter, only the IR-driven instability occurs at zero momentum, while at finite superfluid velocity the scalar may undergo either type of instability depending on parameters. We further demonstrate that a zero mode can be generated by adjusting a double-trace deformation in the boundary theory. The exact solutions enable analytical phase diagrams across charge, mass, momentum, and double-trace couplings, elucidating the interplay between UV hybridization and IR Breitenlohner–Freedman bound violations in holographic quantum criticality.

We investigate stability regimes and nonlinear dynamics of matter-wave bright solitons in a harmonically confined Bose–Einstein condensate with transverse attraction and longitudinal expulsive curvature. Motivated by the observation of bright solitons from attractive condensates (Khaykovich et al., Science 296, 1290, 2002), we analyze the three-dimensional Gross–Pitaevskii equation using a time-dependent variational approach corroborated by numerical simulations. We map critical branches for collapse driven by transverse self-focusing and for explosion induced by the axial expulsive potential, delineating experimentally relevant parameter windows. We quantify particle loss from a soliton following sudden quenches of the trap frequencies and of the s-wave scattering length, and identify diabatic criteria for adiabaticity breakdown. We show that higher-order (breather-like) solitons can be generated with present techniques by an abrupt fourfold increase of the scattering length. Finally, we demonstrate a quantum evaporation mechanism: nonlinear tunneling of atoms through the effective axial barrier depletes the soliton and precipitates its ultimate explosion.

We investigate Hawking radiation in a Higgs–Yukawa system and demonstrate the dynamical formation of a spherical domain wall surrounding a black hole. The wall arises generically when the Hawking temperature is comparable to or exceeds the characteristic energy scale of the field theory, producing symmetry restoration near the horizon and a broken phase far from it. The resulting phase boundary is localized at a finite radius where the effective temperature profile crosses the critical temperature, yielding a quasi-static, spherically symmetric domain wall. We present realistic applications at the electroweak and grand unification scales, showing that electroweak and GUT domain walls can form around sufficiently hot black holes. We further analyze a spontaneous charging-up mechanism: in the presence of C and CP violation localized on the wall, asymmetric reflection and transmission of Hawking-emitted particles induce net charge transport into the black hole. This process allows the black hole to accumulate a substantial global or gauge charge; in particular, with an electroweak wall, a large hypercharge can be acquired. We discuss the conditions for wall formation, the timescales and magnitudes of induced charge, and implications for the evolution of small or primordial black holes embedded in high-temperature particle-physics environments.

Recent work (Pop, Solar Physics 276:351, 2012) showed that daily changes in sunspot number, conditioned on days with nonzero change, follow a Laplace (double-exponential) distribution. We investigate the physical origin of this phenomenology and demonstrate that it arises primarily from intrinsic sunspot formation, evolution, and decay processes, rather than from the apparent changes caused by active regions rotating onto and off the visible solar disc. Building on this insight, we present a simple stochastic procedure to simulate daily sunspot numbers over an entire solar cycle. The method combines the Laplace-distributed day-to-day increments with a smoothly varying model for the cycle-dependent mean sunspot number. We apply the procedure to three recent solar cycles and show that the simulated series reproduce the observed distribution of daily changes and key statistical properties. Our results link the empirical law to underlying solar magnetic activity and provide a practical tool for cycle-scale sunspot number modeling.

We investigate Hopf bifurcations in fast–slow ordinary differential equations and their association with the rapid emergence of large-amplitude periodic orbits, known as canard explosions. A central task is locating the maximal canard that triggers the explosion. Krupa and Szmolyan derived a first‐order asymptotic formula for its parameter location in a canard‐point normal form for one fast and one slow variable. We provide a direct computation of the coefficient in this expansion using the first Lyapunov coefficient at the Hopf bifurcation, circumventing the need for a specialized normal form. The resulting formula applies under standard nondegeneracy conditions and ties canard theory to quantities available in widely used bifurcation software. Numerical examples illustrate accuracy and efficiency, matching normal‐form predictions and enabling routine detection of canard explosions in models from neuroscience, chemical kinetics, and ecology applications.

We study the extremal number @xmath4 of edges among graphs on @xmath1 vertices with exactly one Steiner tree connecting any @xmath5 vertices and @xmath6. Building on Bollobás’s work on maximal local connectivity at most @xmath2 and on results of Li et al. for at most two internally disjoint Steiner trees for triples, we resolve the corresponding extremal problem for the one-Steiner-tree regime. We prove exact formulas for @xmath4 for @xmath7, respectively, and give a complete characterization of all extremal graphs attaining equality. Our approach combines refined counting with structural analysis of minimal separators and Steiner tree blocks, yielding tight upper bounds and matching constructions. The characterizations reveal stability phenomena and show that extremal graphs are uniquely determined up to augmentations from Turán-type templates. These results highlight qualitative differences from classical connectivity and suggest further directions in generalized local connectivity.

We present a spectroscopic survey of candidate satellite galaxies around the nearby spiral NGC 4258, combining new observations from the Apache Point Observatory 3.5 m telescope with archival Sloan Digital Sky Survey spectra. Our campaign provides new redshifts for 15 galaxies. Among 47 objects with spectroscopic information, we identify 8 as probable satellites, 8 as possible satellites, and 17 as unlikely to be associated; due to insufficient velocity and distance constraints, we refrain from assigning membership to an additional 14 candidates. Using the confirmed and candidate satellites to constrain a Navarro–Frenk–White halo model, radial integration yields a total mass of approximately 1.8 × 10^12 solar masses within 200 kpc. The satellites’ projected angular distribution is consistent with isotropy and shows no significant alignment with the host disk. Notably, many of the probable satellites exhibit blue colors and morphologies consistent with star-forming irregulars in SDSS imaging, in contrast to the relative paucity of blue satellites observed in the Milky Way and M31 systems at comparable galactocentric distances.

We introduce an integrable two-component model for quasiparticle condensates with spatio-temporal, binary interaction strengths. For the coupled Gross–Pitaevskii (GP) equation, we derive the associated Lax pair and employ a gauge transformation to construct matter-wave bright solitons. The resulting solutions reveal stabilization mechanisms and controllable pattern formation, showing that time- and space-dependent interactions enable tailoring condensate densities, geometries, and dynamical properties. Our framework establishes a route to designer quasiparticle condensates with robust, tunable nonlinear excitations and offers testable predictions for multi-component cold-atom platforms.

We employ the electromagnetic solver (EMS) to investigate wave propagation and mode formation in a periodic plasma structure operating in the whistler frequency range. Focusing on the radially localized helicon (RLH) mode, we compute the spectral gap produced by axial periodicity and benchmark the gap frequency and width against analytical theory, finding close agreement. By introducing a controlled defect that breaks strict periodicity, we identify a discrete, axially localized eigenmode residing inside the spectral gap. The eigenmode exhibits an axial wavelength approximately twice the lattice period, consistent with Bragg resonance. Parameter scans elucidate the robustness of the gap and defect mode with respect to periodicity strength and plasma profiles. These results suggest a pathway for selective wave localization and control, and indicate that energetic electrons could excite the gap eigenmode, analogous to toroidal Alfvén eigenmode excitation by fast ions in tokamaks.

Classical models of autonomous, homogeneous, mobile point robots often assume see-through agents and complete visibility, a simplification at odds with realistic sensing where robots can obstruct each other’s line of sight. We study a more realistic distributed setting with obstructed visibility, where a robot’s perception may be occluded by other robots, vision is the sole means of sensing and implicit communication, robots operate asynchronously, and there is no agreement on chirality or a global coordinate system. Under these constraints, many existing algorithms that require full knowledge of all positions become inapplicable unless robots are in general position (no three collinear). We present a distributed motion algorithm that, from any arbitrary initial configuration, drives the robots to a general position in finite time. Each robot independently uses only its current visual snapshot to select a collision-free displacement that breaks existing collinearities without introducing new ones, ensuring progress despite asynchrony and partial information. We prove correctness, show that the process terminates, and guarantee collision-free motion throughout. Achieving general position restores complete mutual visibility for point robots under obstructed visibility, enabling subsequent tasks that rely on full awareness. The algorithm thus serves as a robust preprocessing module for pattern formation, rendezvous, coordination, and other visibility-dependent distributed robotic missions.

We report RXTE PCA and HEXTE observations of A3667 obtained between Dec 2001 and July 2002. We analyze @xmath0 ks of RXTE exposure together with archival ASCA/GIS spectra to search for a hard, nonthermal component in addition to the thermal intracluster emission. Joint spectral fits yield only marginal evidence for a secondary power-law, and we derive a 90% confidence upper limit on nonthermal emission in the 15-35 keV band of @xmath1 erg-@xmath2 s@xmath3. Combining this limit with the measured radio flux and spectral index of the dominant extended radio region, we infer a lower limit of @xmath4 G on the mean, volume-averaged intracluster magnetic field in A3667. These results constrain models of relativistic particle populations and magnetic field amplification and dynamical evolution.

High-precision X-ray timing has long been expected to enable measurements of orbital eccentricity and the angle of periastron in bright, persistent high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs), opening the possibility of detecting apsidal motion and inferring the apsidal motion constant of the mass-losing companion. Such measurements directly test stellar structure models for the evolved donors in these systems. We present a timing analysis of archival Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) observations of two canonical HMXBs, Cen X-3 and SMC X-1, aimed at constraining their very small eccentricities and angles of periastron. We apply standard barycentric and binary demodulation to pulse arrival times and assess the impact of instrumental precision versus astrophysical systematics. We find that the dominant limitation to parameter accuracy is not RXTE’s intrinsic time resolution but subtle, orbit-dependent changes in the X-ray pulse profiles. These shape variations introduce correlated timing residuals that degrade sensitivity to the small Roemer delays encoding eccentricity and periastron orientation. Consequently, the attainable precision on the orbital elements, particularly eccentricity and the angle of periastron, is significantly reduced for Cen X-3 and in lower-flux epochs of SMC X-1. However, for SMC X-1 during a high-flux state in 2000, increased signal-to-noise and pulse stability permit a robust determination of a small but non-zero eccentricity and a constraint on the angle of periastron. Our results quantify systematic floors in pulse timing analyses of HMXBs and outline observational regimes under which apsidal motion becomes detectable. Future campaigns combining high throughput, stable pulse templates, and long baselines will be essential to measure apsidal advance and to derive meaningful apsidal motion constants for testing massive-star interior models.

We consider galaxies in typical groups with total mass of order 10^13 solar masses and estimate the corresponding intergalactic medium densities and relative galaxy–IGM velocities. Using an idealized rotating gaseous disk embedded in a fixed galactic potential, we explore the dynamical response to sustained interaction with the IGM. The outer disk is systematically distorted into a characteristic warp morphology comparable to that observed in many nearby systems. The warp is established rapidly, within two rotation periods, and it is long-lived, surviving for at least ten. A second robust outcome is the emergence of a one-arm retrograde spiral wave that propagates through the disk, providing a kinematic signature of the interaction. The amplitude, radial extent, and orientation of the warp and spiral depend on the galaxy’s motion through the group medium, linking morphology to environment. We propose that the ubiquity and geometry of warps can be exploited to reconstruct IGM density profiles and infer individual member orbits within groups, providing a practical probe of group-scale dynamical conditions and their role in galaxy evolution.

We demonstrate a microscopic Ioffe–Pritchard trap realized with a straight, current-carrying wire and auxiliary magnetic fields, and use the spatial distribution of laser-cooled rubidium atoms as a probe of stray magnetic fields. From the equilibrium density we reconstruct a weak field component parallel to the wire, which scales linearly with the transport current and exhibits an approximately sinusoidal modulation along the wire with period @xmath1 m. The radial decay of this component is quantitatively described by the Bessel function @xmath2, consistent with the far field generated by a transversely oscillating current inside the conductor. Our results benchmark atom-based magnetometry of wire microtraps and inform designs mitigating magnetic corrugations.

Pressure-induced superconductivity has been reported in undoped BaFe2As2 at 2–6 GPa, motivating a detailed examination of its structural and electronic responses to compression. Using a full-potential linear augmented plane-wave method within density-functional theory, we investigate the effects of pressure on crystal structure, magnetic order, and electronic states. Our calculations confirm that the experimentally observed striped antiferromagnetic ground state remains energetically stable up to 13 GPa. The antiferromagnetic lattice parameters under pressure show good agreement with available experimental data, whereas calculations constrained to the nonmagnetic state systematically underestimate the Fe–As bond length and the c-axis lattice constant. Analysis of the pressure dependence indicates that the compressibility in the antiferromagnetic phase is nearly isotropic up to about 6.4 GPa, and the FeAs4 tetrahedra exhibit minimal distortion over this range. Notably, we identify a transition in Fermi surface topology in the striped antiferromagnetic state when the unit-cell volume is compressed by more than approximately 8 percent, corresponding to pressures near 6 GPa and to a pronounced change in the c/a ratio. These first-principles results elucidate the interplay between magnetism, lattice degrees of freedom, and electronic structure in FeAs-based materials. They provide a microscopic framework relevant to understanding how pressure tunes antiferromagnetism and may promote superconductivity in BaFe2As2 and related compounds.

We perform test-particle simulations in a two-dimensional, differentially rotating stellar disk subject to a steady, two-armed spiral density wave to quantify the impact of spiral structure on the local velocity field. From the simulated phase-space samples, we construct heliocentric velocity fields and apply a Levenberg–Marquardt least-squares procedure to decompose them into Fourier components up to fourth order. This yields simulated measurements of the Oort constants A, B, C, and K, along with higher-order Fourier coefficients. We derive empirical relations linking these coefficients to key Galactic parameters, including the spiral pattern speed and the phase angle of the solar neighborhood relative to the spiral arms. Our results demonstrate that systematic biases introduced by spiral structure are likely to affect Oort-constant determinations: for moderate spiral amplitudes, errors of order 5 km s−1 kpc−1 arise in A and B. We explore how the coefficients vary with stellar velocity dispersion, pattern speed, and sample depth, finding that all three factors modulate the inferred kinematic parameters. For samples with an average heliocentric distance of 0.8 kpc, we find: (i) if the Sun lies near corotation, C is expected to vanish across phase angles; (ii) for dynamically hot disks, spiral-induced biases in all Oort constants disappear at, and just inward of, the corotation radius; (iii) approaching the 4:1 Lindblad resonances, the fourth-order Fourier term grows and exhibits enhanced azimuthal variability; and (iv) across all simulations, the fourth-order coefficient is larger on average for lower stellar velocity dispersions, in tension with recent observational reports. These results underscore the need to account for non-axisymmetric structure when interpreting local kinematic measurements and provide guidance for mitigating spiral-induced systematics in future surveys.

We construct a model for the pion twist-3 wave function @xmath0 by matching its moments to QCD sum rules. The resulting distribution amplitude exhibits improved end-point behavior relative to the asymptotic form, stabilizing hard calculations. Using this model within the modified pQCD framework with Sudakov resummation, we evaluate the twist-3 contributions to the pion electromagnetic form factor, including both the usual helicity components (@xmath1) and the higher-helicity components (@xmath2). We find that the net twist-3 contribution decreases rapidly with increasing momentum transfer and becomes subleading to the twist-2 contribution for @xmath3. Moreover, the inclusion of higher-helicity components in the twist-3 sector yields an additional suppression of the form factor. We assess model dependence by comparing four representative twist-3 wave-function/DA models and quantify the spread. When power corrections from higher orders in @xmath4, higher helicities, and higher-twist distribution amplitudes are consistently included, the hard scattering contribution is expected to account for existing data in the kinematic region where pQCD applies. Our analysis clarifies the role of twist-3 dynamics and helicity structure in the pion form factor and provides a phenomenologically viable input for precision studies. PACS: 13.40.Gp, 12.38.Bx, 11.55.Hx.

We study η photo- and electroproduction on the nucleon within an isobar model (eta-MAID) comprising Born terms, t-channel vector-meson exchange, and s-channel nucleon resonances. The model is constrained by recent data: differential and total cross sections, beam and target asymmetries for photoproduction, and electroproduction observables. We confirm the S-wave dominance driven by the S11(1535) resonance and show that inclusion of the second S11 state, S11(1650), is essential for a reliable extraction of S11(1535) parameters. Beam-asymmetry data, sensitive to small interference effects, enable determination of tiny ηN decay branching ratios of higher-mass resonances despite S-wave dominance. The resulting parameter set yields a consistent description across photon and electron kinematics. Good agreement with the measured observables is obtained. The eta-MAID model is implemented within the MAID framework. Keywords: eta meson, photoproduction, electroproduction, isobar model, nucleon resonances. PACS: 13.60.Le, 14.20.Gk, 25.20.Lj, 25.30.Rw.

We report the fabrication and characterization of a high-Q Josephson-junction resonator with in situ tunable resonance. By applying a dc magnetic flux to a superconducting loop embedding the junction, the resonance frequency is tuned by more than 10% without degrading coherence. Weak coupling to the environment yields an internal quality factor approximately 7000 when the mean intracavity photon number is below unity. At elevated drive powers, the intrinsic nonlinearity of the junction produces a Duffing-type response with two stable oscillation states. This device enables sensitive assessment of junction losses and noise in the single-photon regime, and provides a robust platform for high-fidelity, microwave bifurcation-based qubit readout at higher photon numbers.

Weak gravitational lensing provides a powerful, model-independent way to estimate cluster masses, but these measurements are contaminated by projected large-scale structure (LSS) uncorrelated with the cluster. We quantify the resulting projection noise and its impact on mass determinations by combining analytical calculations with mock observations that include realistic source redshift distributions and shear covariance. We explore the dependence on cluster mass, redshift, survey depth, and aperture size. For deep observations of massive clusters with velocity dispersions near 1000 km/s at intermediate redshifts, where background sources lie predominantly at higher redshift than the lens, we find the additional uncertainty from distant LSS is relatively small. When the shear signal is measured out to radii of order 1 Mpc, the typical fractional mass error contributed by uncorrelated LSS is only a few percent, often subdominant to shape noise and measurement systematics. In contrast, nearby systems such as the Coma cluster suffer substantially larger projection noise: background structures limit the maximum achievable signal-to-noise of the mass estimate to around five, even for deep data. The LSS-induced variance increases with aperture size, complicating attempts to constrain mass profiles and concentrations at large radii. Because this projection noise is statistical and uncorrelated among clusters, averaging over ensembles reduces its impact approximately as the square root of the sample size.

In distributed source coding, channel codes are often repurposed as source codes. We propose Distributed Arithmetic Coding (DAC), a new paradigm that generalizes arithmetic coding to the distributed setting by introducing ambiguity at the encoder and resolving it via sequential decoding aided by side information at the decoder. We develop a distributed binary arithmetic coder for the Slepian–Wolf problem and a joint decoder that exploits correlation models and side information to perform path pruning and error detection. The scheme supports both asymmetric operation, where one source is decoded using the other as side information, and symmetric operation, where both encoders inject ambiguity, at any combination of rates inside the Slepian–Wolf region. DAC naturally accommodates arbitrary, possibly context-based, source models in the encoder, mirroring classical arithmetic coding, and is particularly effective at short to moderate block lengths. We present complexity analyses and extensive simulations on correlated binary sources and quantized video residuals. Across a range of correlation structures and block sizes, DAC attains compression performance competitive with state-of-the-art turbo and LDPC Slepian–Wolf coders, often outperforming them at small blocks while maintaining low decoding complexity and performance under model mismatch. We also discuss extensions to Wyner–Ziv coding and source–channel scenarios.

Non-Markovian quantum state diffusion (NMQSD) provides an exact trajectory-based description of the reduced dynamics of systems linearly coupled to a bosonic bath, yet its use has been limited by the variational–differential evolution equation with functional derivatives. We show that this equation can be cast into an equivalent closed integrodifferential form with memory kernels, enabling efficient numerical simulation. We give a clear derivation of the modified equations, introduce auxiliary kernel variables to eliminate functional derivatives, and present a practical algorithm based on quadrature of bath correlations. Benchmarks recover the Markovian limit. We then apply the method to intermittent fluorescence of @xmath0mg@xmath1, resolving quantum-jump dynamics across all accessible timescales, including picoseconds. The computed probability density of signal versus signal strength exhibits the two characteristic peaks of bright and dark manifolds, with an area ratio of 16 in quantitative agreement with experiment. We further show that the distribution’s shape is sensitive to bath memory, yet admits a common analytic form in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. These results make NMQSD a practical tool for quantitative studies of non-Markovian open quantum optical systems.

We discuss an idea to realize a spontaneous current in a superfluid Fermi gas. When a polarized Fermi superfluid (N_up ≠ N_down, where N_sigma is the number of atoms in hyperfine state sigma) is loaded into a ring-shaped trap with a weak potential barrier, some of the excess atoms (N_ex) localize around the barrier. As shown previously [T. Kashimura, S. Tsuchiya, and Y. Ohashi, Phys. Rev. A 82, 033617 (2010)], this polarized barrier works as a π-junction in the sense that the superfluid order parameter changes sign across it. Because of this, the phase of the order parameter outside the junction is twisted by π along the ring, which naturally leads to a circulating supercurrent. While the ordinary supercurrent state can appear as a metastable solution, the spontaneous current state is more stable than the case with no current. Using Bogoliubov–de Gennes calculations, we determine parameter regimes where the π-induced current is favored and show its robustness to temperature. Our results indicate that localized excess atoms provide a handle to manipulate the order parameter and engineer dissipationless currents in Fermi gases without rotation.

We investigate the impact of bond dilution on the critical temperatures, phase diagrams, and magnetization of the quantum Heisenberg model in both isotropic and anisotropic cases. For the isotropic model, we map Tc as a function of bond concentration and determine bond percolation thresholds for several two- and three-dimensional lattices, revealing dependencies on lattice topology and coordination. To quantify anisotropy effects, we perform a detailed study on the honeycomb lattice, comparing phase boundaries and magnetization profiles with the isotropic limit. Bond dilution suppresses ordering, shifts phase boundaries, and yields behavior, including second-order reentrant transitions in the temperature–bond concentration plane. The results delineate lattice-specific trends of diluted quantum magnets.

The minimum free-energy path (MFEP) represents the most probable route of nucleation on a multidimensional free-energy surface. We present a phase-field framework to deduce the MFEP of homogeneous nucleation using a square-gradient free-energy functional with a quartic local free-energy density. Starting from a single nucleus embedded in a metastable environment, we perform time integration of the phase-field equation via the numerically efficient cell-dynamics method. By simultaneously tracking the nucleus size and the system free energy during the evolution, we reconstruct the free-energy barrier as a function of nucleus size across subcritical and supercritical regimes along the MFEP. This procedure identifies the critical nucleus and quantifies the barrier height without imposing ad hoc reaction coordinates, providing a self-consistent path dictated by the underlying dynamics. The approach offers a practical route to map nucleation landscapes from continuum models, clarifying the relation between kinetic evolution and thermodynamic driving forces and enabling systematic analysis of nucleation pathways and barriers.

We present high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy of two pre-main-sequence stars: a classical T Tauri star in the TW Hydrae association observed with XMM-Newton, and a weak-lined T Tauri star in the Beta Pictoris moving group observed with Chandra HETGS. Using line diagnostics and global fits, we reconstruct emission measure distributions and determine coronal abundances, searching for first-ionization potential related trends. Densities are constrained from He-like triplet f/i ratios (e.g., O VII, Ne IX, Mg XI), and we compare these properties with previously studied PMS benchmarks. We also assess temporal variability during the observations. Both targets exhibit multi-thermal, magnetically heated coronae characterized by high activity and abundance patterns consistent with inverse-FIP behavior. However, one star departs from this picture, showing unusually cool dominant temperatures and elevated densities indicative of an additional accretion-driven component. The classical T Tauri star also shows a high Ne/Fe ratio consistent with values reported for other accreting PMS systems. These results reinforce that magnetically confined coronae are the primary source of X-rays in cTTS and wTTS, while accretion shocks can contribute in specific objects, shaping the thermal structure and coronal composition.

We study random domino tilings of the Aztec diamond with anisotropic weights assigned to horizontal and vertical dominos and their representation as a determinantal particle system. We establish an explicit relation between the correlation kernel of this process and the inverse Kasteleyn matrix, yielding a closed-form inversion that generalizes Helfgott’s result to the weighted setting. Leveraging this formula, we analyze edge asymptotics for southern dominos near the frozen boundary. At the northern boundary, we prove that the southern domino process converges, under appropriate scaling, to a thinned Airy point process. At the southern boundary, the process of holes in the southern domino configuration converges to a novel multiple point process we term the thickened Airy point process, with parameters determined by the anisotropy of weights. In the unfrozen (liquid) region, we show convergence to the limiting Gibbs measure and identify local statistics via a translation-invariant determinantal kernel. Our approach unifies kernel-Kasteleyn connections and provides precise edge scaling limits and a weighted arctic curve description.

We investigate the prospects for the emergence and persistence of life in planetary systems orbiting sub-giant and red giant stars by quantifying the temporal evolution of the circumstellar habitable zone (HZ) as stars leave the main sequence. As stellar luminosity increases during post–main-sequence evolution, both the mean distance to the HZ and its radial width grow, causing the HZ to migrate outward and sweep across a wider range of orbital distances until the star approaches the tip of the asymptotic giant branch. We place these stellar timescales in the context of terrestrial constraints: although the exact epoch of life’s origin on Earth remains uncertain, isotopic evidence indicates that life existed at least as early as @xmath0 years after Earth formed. If the origin and early evolution of life can occur over intervals spanning @xmath1 to @xmath2 years, then planets in the HZs of evolved stars could plausibly host biospheres. Using a 1 m@xmath3 stellar model in the first stages of post–main-sequence evolution, we estimate that the HZ passes any given distance for durations of several 10@xmath4 years near 2 au and around 10@xmath5 years near 9 au. Under these circumstances, planetary orbits in the range 2–9 au around sub-giant and red giant stars can experience HZ conditions for timescales potentially sufficient for prebiotic chemistry, biogenesis, and early biological evolution. Following the star’s first ascent along the red giant branch and the occurrence of the helium flash, an additional quiescent phase of helium core burning provides a further stable interval during which the HZ resides between approximately 7 and 22 au for about @xmath2 years. These findings imply that, in the far distant future, regions of our own Solar System currently beyond the classical HZ could transiently become clement for surface or subsurface life. We also assess observational implications for forthcoming space missions aimed at detecting signs of life on extrasolar planets. In addition to their main-sequence targets, concepts such as the Terrestrial Planet Finder (TPF) and Darwin should consider sub-giant and red giant hosts, where larger planet–star separations improve angular resolution and reduce inner working angle constraints. A preliminary interferometric analysis indicates that pathfinder missions, including ECLIPSE and the Fourier–Kelvin Stellar Interferometer (FKSI), possess sufficient angular resolution and sensitivity to search for habitable-zone planets around some of the closest evolved stars. Together, these results argue for expanding target lists to include evolved stellar systems, both to test hypotheses about life’s temporal windows and to leverage favorable observing geometries created by outward-moving habitable zones.

We analyze gravitational radiation from binary systems within the adiabatic approximation of general relativity, modeling the motion of a small astrophysical object as a chained sequence of bounded geodesics in the exterior region of a Kerr black hole. We present a comprehensive study of the entire class of bound orbits, including spherical (constant radius) and eccentric trajectories, and elucidate their dependence on energy, axial angular momentum, and the Carter constant. Using analytical methods, we determine the global geometrical locus of all such orbits in the multidimensional space of physical parameters of Kerr spacetime, thereby mapping stability regions, separatrices, and allowable transitions. This locus furnishes a practical criterion for whether distinct orbits can be connected through continuous variation of their physical parameters during adiabatic evolution, and clarifies how orbital classes bifurcate near critical surfaces such as the innermost stable spherical orbit. We further quantify the influence of the black hole’s angular momentum on orbital structure and connectability across prograde and retrograde families, with implications for waveform modeling and parameter inference. PACS numbers: 0420q, 0430d, 0470b.

We investigate space–time correlation and response functions in nonequilibrium growth processes governed by linear stochastic Langevin equations. Exploiting the space- and time-dependent symmetries of the noiseless dynamics, we derive closed forms for the universal scaling functions of two-time quantities, including autocorrelations and linear responses. These symmetry-based predictions coincide with the exact expressions obtained by solving the stochastic equations of motion, demonstrating that the universal aging and dynamic scaling behavior is fixed by the underlying deterministic invariances. To illustrate scope, we analyze two atomistic deposition models, the Family model and the Restricted Family model. Analytical evidence shows that both belong to a single universality class in 1+1 and 2+1 dimensions, contrary to earlier reports that suggested distinct classes in 2+1 dimensions. Our results provide a unifying framework for universal two-time scaling in linear growth.

We present height-resolved Doppler observations at the solar limb in the @xmath0 spectral line, obtained with the Big Coronagraph of the Abastumani Astrophysical Observatory, covering 3800–8700 km above the photosphere. The wavelength measured at observed heights is ~3500 km. Numerical modeling of kink-wave propagation from the photosphere to these heights yields a photospheric wavelength of ~1000 km, consistent with excitation by granular motions. The inferred wave periods lie in the 35–70 s range. These results provide evidence for kink-wave activity in spicules and suggest a granular driver, with implications for the transport of energy and momentum in the chromosphere and corona.

We quantify envelope chemical enrichment driven by these mechanisms and show that the surfaces become carbon- and nitrogen-rich. The net yields, however, depend sensitively on the IMF and on the fraction of primordial baryons converted into stars. We discuss implications for early-universe abundance patterns and constraints from metal-poor stellar observations.

We introduce a global optimization framework that simultaneously optimizes atomic identities and geometry to maximize cohesive stability in finite clusters. We apply this approach to binary Lennard-Jones clusters, with equal interaction strengths but controlled size mismatch, to map how the most stable structure depends on cluster size and atomic size ratio for N up to 100 atoms and 0–30% size difference. We reveal extensive regions dominated by polytetrahedral motifs, including polyicosahedral packings and networks containing disclination lines. In contrast to one-component Lennard-Jones clusters, where such motifs are penalized by geometric frustration and elastic strain, size disparity in the binary system preferentially accommodates local tetrahedral order and reduces strain energy. The most stable configurations frequently adopt core-shell architectures, with larger atoms segregating to the surface and smaller atoms occupying the interior, thereby optimizing surface curvature and packing. Our results provide a comprehensive stability landscape for binary Lennard-Jones clusters and demonstrate that targeted size mismatch is a powerful design parameter for stabilizing otherwise strained structures, offering guidelines for the controllable synthesis of heterogeneous nanoclusters.

We investigate the equilibrium statistical properties of DNA denaturation bubbles within the Peyrard–Bishop–Dauxois (PBD) framework. By evaluating bubble size distributions, formation free energies, and average displacement profiles for homogeneous sequences, we show that nonlinear base-stacking interactions are crucial for stabilizing and shaping bubbles. In their absence, scaled displacement profiles collapse onto a nearly universal form across bubble sizes and temperatures. With nonlinear stacking, large and small bubbles exhibit distinct scaled shapes, reflecting cooperative effects along the strand. Small bubbles (<10 bp) incur substantially higher formation free energies per base pair than larger bubbles, implying a strong nucleation barrier. As the critical temperature is approached, the incremental free energy for further bubble growth tends to zero, signaling incipient macroscopic denaturation.

We develop a group-theoretical framework to describe the dynamics of lossless two-level atoms traversing a standing-wave laser field, where photon recoil intrinsically couples internal and external degrees of freedom. The internal quantum dynamics is parameterized by SU(2) group variables, enabling an explicit construction of the evolution operator after reducing the problem to a single ordinary differential equation for one group parameter. The center-of-mass motion in the standing wave is treated classically via Hamilton’s equations and is nonlinearly coupled to the SU(2) equations through the position-dependent light–matter interaction. Analysis of the resulting coupled system reveals parameter regimes in which the dynamics becomes chaotic, depending on detuning, field strength, recoil frequency, and initial conditions. In these regimes the atom exhibits simultaneous chaotic center-of-mass motion and irregular internal evolution. The onset and character of chaos are controlled by the oscillations of the group parameter that quantifies the mean atom–field interaction energy; its temporal behavior governs energy exchange and triggers resonance-like instabilities. We identify conditions for “chaotic walking,” where atoms alternately localize and drift across nodes and antinodes of the standing wave. The predicted effects are accessible with cold atoms and optical lattice configurations.

We study the strong Lefschetz property (SLP) for Artinian quotients of standard graded polynomial rings. We first show that every Artinian quotient has the SLP when the base field has characteristic zero or is infinite of characteristic larger than the regularity of the quotient. For monomial ideals we improve this characteristic bound and classify precisely the cases in which the general and monomial bounds are sharp. Furthermore, we prove that the Artinian quotient of a monomial ideal has the SLP in every characteristic if and only if the ideal is lexsegment. As a consequence, we exhibit a new explicit family of non-monomial complete intersections that always enjoy the SLP.

We present a technique to improve the momentum resolution of low-momentum charged particles in few-layer silicon tracking detectors by exploiting energy-loss information. Instead of relying solely on curvature-based track fits, particle momenta are inferred from the measured Landau-distributed dE/dx and the Bethe–Bloch relation in the low-momentum region, with corrections for path length, incidence angle, and sensor thickness. A likelihood-based combination of per-layer dE/dx yields a robust estimator of the most probable momentum, mitigating multiple-scattering limitations dominant in sparse trackers. Using simulations and STAR- and ALICE-like geometries, we demonstrate a factor-of-two improvement over standard fitting methods for transverse momenta in the soft regime. This enhancement benefits heavy-ion measurements of soft spectra and flow using stand-alone few-plane silicon trackers. PACS: 29.40.Gx, 29.30.-h, 12.38.Mh.

We present a theoretical analysis of an entangling gate between two trapped Ca+ ions based on dipolar interactions of ionic Rydberg states. In conventional Rydberg excitation, inhomogeneous electric fields induce strong coupling between electronic and vibrational degrees of freedom, generating harmful mechanical forces. We show that microwave-dressed Rydberg manifolds can suppress these forces by engineering state-dependent polarizabilities that cancel motional couplings, while simultaneously enabling long-range dipolar interactions. Using these dressed states, we design a controlled adiabatic phase gate that operates independently of collective vibrational modes. We derive gate conditions, adiabatic protocols, and fidelity limits, and assess robustness against decoherence, electric-field noise, and micromotion. Numerical simulations indicate fast, high-fidelity operation within realistic parameters. Our results chart a route to scalable trapped-ion processors with Rydberg-mediated gates decoupled from motion.

Compact groups (CGs) of galaxies offer exceptional laboratories for probing dense environments where interactions, tidally induced activity, and mergers are frequent. We present first results from a new catalogue of CGs constructed from the Las Campanas Redshift Survey (LCRS), providing a uniform, spectroscopically confirmed sample. Using the equivalent width of [O II] λ3727 as a proxy for recent star formation, we compare CG members to galaxies in loose groups and the field, controlling for morphology. We find strong evidence for depressed star formation in CGs: the distribution of [O II] equivalent widths is shifted to lower values, and the fraction of emission-line galaxies is reduced. Interaction-triggered starbursts appear rare. While part of this trend reflects the high early-type fraction in CGs, a significant residual suppression remains. Late-type CG members exhibit star formation rates roughly one-half to one-third of those in field spirals. These results suggest that gas-stripping and starvation processes operate efficiently in compact-group environments.

RNA duplex stability depends strongly on ionic conditions, yet inside cells RNAs encounter complex mixtures of monovalent and multivalent ions. Here we mechanically unfold and refold a 20 bp RNA hairpin with optical tweezers to probe thermodynamics and kinetics across monovalent and mixed monovalent/Mg2+ conditions. From rupture force distributions we apply Kramers theory to reconstruct the free-energy landscape under tension and extract non-specific ionic corrections to the hairpin formation free energy over a broad salt range. We quantify how the position of the transition state relative to the folded basin shifts with force and ionic strength, revealing salt-dependent changes in effective barrier width. Our measurements validate the tightly bound ion model for RNA duplex stabilization and yield the persistence length of single-stranded RNA under varied ionic environments. Finally, we test the heuristic that divalent cations at a given concentration confer stability comparable to ~100-fold higher monovalent concentrations for small constructs, delineating its regime of validity and deviations. These results provide experimentally grounded corrections and parameters for RNA secondary-structure prediction beyond 1 M Na+, and establish a general framework for integrating mixed-ion effects into RNA folding thermodynamics and kinetics. This advances quantitative modeling in cellular contexts.

We revisit the longstanding problem of chromodyons—solitonic objects carrying both magnetic charge and non-Abelian electric (“color”) charge—in spontaneously broken gauge theories. Previous attempts failed due to topological obstructions preventing a global definition of the unbroken color subgroup. We consider a setting where such obstructions are absent, an SO(5) gauge theory broken to SU(2)×U(1). We first construct a static monopole solution with purely magnetic charge. By exciting a global gauge zero mode around this monopole, we engineer a chromodyonic configuration that approximately satisfies the full nonlinear field equations. We then perform real-time numerical simulations of its evolution to test for relaxation to a stationary chromodyon. Instead, we observe sustained emission of non-Abelian electric radiation: the chromo-electric charge monotonically decreases as the configuration sheds energy and color into the gauge fields. The dynamics show no tendency toward stabilization, indicating eventual complete loss of color charge. Our results provide strong, quantitative evidence against the existence of stable chromodyons in this obstruction-free framework more generally.

We present a hybrid computational framework for modeling planetary formation from an initial ensemble of planetesimals. Full simulations of terrestrial planet formation with the hybrid code reproduce key outcomes of previously published studies, including mass distributions and orbital architectures. These results show the method reliably captures planetesimal-to-planet evolution.

We present a written version of four lectures delivered at the NATO Advanced Study Institute on QCD Perspectives on Hot and Dense Matter (Cargèse, August 2001), offering a contemporaneous snapshot of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) program and early results from the BRAHMS, PHENIX, PHOBOS, and STAR experiments in Run I (√sNN = 130 GeV, 2000). We discuss high-transverse-momentum hadron production and its suppression relative to binary-collision scaling as possible evidence for partonic energy loss in a dense medium, as well as identified-particle spectra, baryon-to-meson systematics, and strangeness production. Two-pion interferometry results and source imaging are presented alongside their tensions with hydrodynamic expectations. We highlight experimental methodologies—centrality determination, Glauber modeling, acceptance and efficiency corrections, and the challenges posed by incomplete p+p baselines—and outline key systematic uncertainties. Many results were preliminary at the time, with critical measurements anticipated from Run II, and we underscore the rapid evolution of the field and the essential interplay between experimental data and theoretical interpretation.

We present emission-line optical spectrophotometry for 55 H II regions across the barred spiral galaxy NGC 1365. The abundance distribution is compared with that of another barred spiral, NGC 3359, and with two well-sampled normal spirals, NGC 2997 and M101, reinforcing the view that bars can drive radial mixing and flatten outer metallicity profiles. This article presents an overview of the SP Theory of Intelligence, a framework that seeks to simplify and integrate concepts across artificial intelligence, computing, and human perception and cognition, with information compression as a unifying theme. The theory is conceived as a brain-like system that receives new information and stores some or all of it in compressed form as old information, and is realized as a computer model, the SP Machine. Central are the matching and unification of patterns and the construct of multiple alignment, which, via heuristic search, assembles structures that are good in terms of compression. For each alignment, the model computes probabilities for associated inferences, enabling probabilistic reasoning. Unsupervised learning derives new structures from partial matches and explores sets of structures that yield superior compression. Consistent with the DONSVIC principle—Discovery of Natural Structures Via Information Compression—learned organizations typically correspond to natural categories and relations judged meaningful. Representations are compact and human-interpretable, promoting transparency, error tolerance, and effective generalization across tasks. We discuss implications for scalable learning, the integration of symbolic and probabilistic processing, and links to neural mechanisms. The SP theory offers interpretations and mechanisms across computing, mathematics and logic, knowledge representation, natural language processing, pattern recognition, several kinds of reasoning, information storage and retrieval, planning and problem solving, information compression, neuroscience, and human perception and cognition. Illustrative examples include parsing and production of language with discontinuous dependencies in syntax; pattern recognition at multiple levels of abstraction integrated with part–whole relations; nonmonotonic reasoning and reasoning with default values; reasoning in Bayesian networks, including explaining away; causal diagnosis; and solving a geometric analogy. By foregrounding information compression as the basis for representation, learning, and inference, the SP framework unifies diverse capabilities within a transparent architecture, offering theoretical coherence and practical efficiency. Keywords: information compression, artificial intelligence, multiple alignment, computing, representation of knowledge, natural language processing, pattern recognition, information retrieval, probabilistic reasoning, planning, problem solving, unsupervised learning.

In the present work, we investigate coupled disordered quantum wells within a random matrix theory framework. The wells, modeled as short repulsive binary alloys embedded by ordered barriers, exhibit well-defined quantized levels from spatial confinement. Finite disordered superlattices display both diffusive-like and localized minibands, enabling systematic study of spectral statistics. We analyze the evolution of the nearest-level-spacing distribution inside each miniband, revealing three distinct mechanisms that suppress level repulsion and drive crossovers between Wigner-Dyson, semi-Poisson, and Poisson regimes. Numerical simulations show a pronounced motional narrowing effect arising from ensemble averaging and constrained coupling, consistent with random matrix predictions. PACS: 71.23.An, 73.20.Jc, 74.40.+K, 73.20.Dx.

These findings support the robustness of @xmath4 as a deconfinement proxy and clarify its correspondence to @xmath1 across the phase diagram.

After a prolonged low-activity phase, the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy PKS 1502+036 exhibited a pronounced gamma-ray flare detected by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) in late 2015. On 2015 December 20, the source reached a daily peak flux in the 0.1–300 GeV band of (93 ± 19) × 10^-8 photons cm^-2 s^-1, and achieved (237 ± 71) × 10^-8 photons cm^-2 s^-1 on 3-hour timescales, corresponding to an isotropic gamma-ray luminosity of (7.3 ± 2.1) × 10^48 erg s^-1. Despite the substantial flux amplification, the flare was not accompanied by significant spectral changes in the gamma-ray band. We present a comprehensive multi-wavelength study of PKS 1502+036 spanning 2008 August to 2016 March, combining observations from Fermi-LAT, Swift, XMM-Newton, the Catalina Real-Time Transient Survey (CRTS), and the Owens Valley Radio Observatory (OVRO) 40 m telescope. An enhancement in optical, ultraviolet, and X-ray emission was recorded by Swift on 2015 December 22, indicating contemporaneous activity at lower energies following the gamma-ray flare. The OVRO 15 GHz light curve reached the highest flux density ever observed from this source on 2016 January 12, revealing a delay of about three weeks between the gamma-ray and 15 GHz peaks. This lag, together with the absence of strong gamma-ray spectral evolution, suggests that the gamma-ray emitting region lies beyond the broad-line region, where external photon fields from circumnuclear dust can dominate inverse-Compton scattering. We modeled the spectral energy distribution (SED) in an average state and during the flare, adopting an external Compton scenario with seed photons supplied by a dust torus. Both SEDs can be reproduced by adjusting the electron energy distribution parameters and the magnetic field, without invoking changes in the location of the dissipation region. The fit to the thermal disc emission in the average state constrains the central black hole mass to be less than 10^9 solar masses. Overall, the SED shape, high-energy emission mechanisms, and gamma-ray properties of PKS 1502+036 are akin to those of flat-spectrum radio quasars, reinforcing the blazar-like nature of its relativistic jet in a narrow-line Seyfert 1 host.

We present a synthesis of X-ray observations of galaxy clusters that demonstrates a decisive role for non-gravitational processes in shaping the distribution of the diffuse, X-ray–emitting intracluster medium (ICM). The imprint of these processes is encapsulated in an entropy minimum (often termed an entropy floor) that cannot be produced by gravitational collapse alone. Preheating scenarios, which posit that cosmic baryons acquired this entropy prior to structure formation, are challenged by constraints from Ly-alpha forest clouds: their thermal history indicates only modest excess heating at high redshift, largely excluding a pervasive entropy plateau in low-density baryons. An alternative “internal heating” framework confines energy injection to virialized halos, naturally avoiding tension with the Ly-alpha forest. However, energetics pose a stringent requirement: achieving the observed entropy minimum typically demands more than 1 keV per particle. Supernova feedback, even accounting for plausible efficiencies and metal yields, falls short by at least a factor of a few, signaling an energy deficit that likely necessitates additional sources, most prominently active galactic nuclei (AGN). We outline key observational and theoretical priorities to resolve this “energy crisis”: calibrating entropy profiles across mass and redshift, quantifying AGN duty cycles and coupling efficiencies, reconciling metal enrichment histories, and modeling multiphase ICM thermodynamics. Determining when and where the excess entropy is generated, and by which mechanisms, will constrain feedback efficiencies, baryon cycling, and the co-evolution of galaxies and their hot atmospheres.

We develop a unified theory for charge and spin currents through an interacting quantum dot connected to canted ferromagnetic leads with noncollinear magnetizations. Our framework treats arbitrary local interactions and captures both equilibrium and nonequilibrium transport driven by voltage or temperature biases and by time-dependent magnetic dynamics. We derive identities that explicitly separate equilibrium and bias- or dynamics-induced contributions, each expressed solely via the dot’s full retarded Green’s function, providing a nonperturbative description. Applying the formalism to a single-level dot with large on-site Coulomb repulsion, we compute the total spin current near the Kondo regime. We find an enhancement of its magnitude compared with the noninteracting case, with angular and bias dependences arising from the interplay of Kondo correlations and noncollinear exchange.

We investigate kaon semileptonic decay form factors within the nonlocal chiral quark model derived from the instanton vacuum, explicitly incorporating flavor SU(3) symmetry breaking. The calculations are performed without adjustable parameters. We compute vector and scalar form factors, analyze their momentum dependence, and verify consistency with both the Callan–Treiman low-energy theorem and the Ademollo–Gatto theorem. SU(3) breaking effects are shown to be essential for reproducing the measured form factors and ensuring the correct normalization at zero momentum transfer. The resulting slopes and curvatures agree well with experimental determinations and are compatible with other theoretical approaches, supporting the robustness of the instanton-based nonlocal chiral framework.

We investigate pairing states at the (001) interface of the spin-triplet superconductor Sr2RuO4 using microscopic, self-consistent multi-band calculations. An interface-induced Rashba spin–orbit interaction drives strong parity mixing between spin-singlet and spin-triplet components and generates substantial interband pair correlations across the spin–orbit–split bands. Remarkably, these interband correlations remain robust despite sizable spin–orbit splitting, a consequence of frustration between the Rashba coupling, which fixes the spin–momentum texture, and the pairing interactions, which favor a triplet d-vector orientation. The resulting interface superconducting state restores time-reversal symmetry, in sharp contrast to the bulk, widely discussed as a chiral p-wave superconductor with broken time-reversal symmetry. We show that the parity-mixed, interband-paired state can be fully gapped and supports the key ingredients of a time-reversal-invariant topological superconductor, including a nontrivial Z2 topology and helical Majorana edge excitations. Our results identify Sr2RuO4 interfaces as a promising platform for engineering and probing topological superconductivity, and they suggest concrete spectroscopic signatures accessible in tunneling and transport measurements.

This review surveys the empirical and theoretical foundations of the “six degrees of separation” phenomenon in human social networks. We synthesize results from classic chain-letter experiments, large-scale communication datasets, and contemporary network models, including small-world and scale-free frameworks. We discuss path-length distributions, clustering, navigability, and the role of heterogeneity, weak ties, and hubs. Methodological challenges—sampling, missing data, and dynamic networks—are highlighted alongside robust inference techniques. We conclude with open questions and implications for information diffusion, resilience, and algorithmic routing in socio-technical systems.

We present a nonempirical, Laplacian-level meta-generalized gradient approximation (meta-GGA) for the positive Kohn–Sham kinetic energy density of ground-state electrons. The functional depends only on the local density, its gradient, and its Laplacian, and is constructed to recover the fourth-order gradient expansion in the slowly varying limit while reducing to the von Weizsäcker form in the rapidly varying, one-orbital limit. It rigorously obeys the lower bound, and enforces key exact constraints, including uniform-gas and one-electron limits, and correct asymptotic scaling. Across a broad set of systems and model densities—atoms, spherical jellium clusters, jellium surfaces, the Airy gas, Hooke’s atom, a one-electron Gaussian, a quasi-two-dimensional electron gas, and a nonuniformly scaled hydrogen atom—the new meta-GGA markedly improves upon the gradient expansion description of the kinetic energy density. Upon spatial integration, it yields an orbital-free kinetic energy functional that is comparable in accuracy to the fourth-order gradient expansion for many real densities, with noticeable gains for molecular atomization energies, and is substantially more accurate for rapidly varying densities. Using the same construction ideas, we develop a Laplacian-level meta-GGA for exchange and correlation by employing our approximate kinetic energy density within the Tao–Perdew–Staroverov–Scuseria (TPSS) framework. The resulting Laplacian-level TPSS recovers nearly identical enhancement factors and exchange–correlation energies to full TPSS, indicating that the kinetic energy density and the density Laplacian carry equivalent information beyond the density and its gradient. These results motivate practical Laplacian-level functionals for orbital-free and Kohn–Sham density functional theory.

Maxwell’s equations, in their standard covariant form, are widely regarded as universally valid. We demonstrate, however, two cosmological paradoxes that challenge this presumption. First, in a homogeneous and isotropic universe endowed with a uniformly distributed net charge, symmetry requires the electromagnetic field tensor to vanish everywhere, making Maxwell’s equations incompatible with such a global charge distribution. Second, in a closed universe with nonzero net charge, integral constraints derived from Maxwell’s equations fail irrespective of the spacetime symmetry or specific charge configuration. These paradoxes imply that Maxwell’s equations must be modified to remain applicable at the scale of the universe. We analyze two broad classes of modifications. The first is of Proca type, adding a photon mass term that can naturally arise from spontaneous symmetry breaking and the Higgs mechanism in quantum field theory, where photons acquire mass by eating Goldstone bosons. While this resolves the paradoxes when the symmetry is broken, restoration of the symmetry drives the mass to zero and reinstates the conflicts, making this option unsatisfactory for cosmological robustness. The second, and in our view more compelling, class introduces curvature-coupled terms in which the electromagnetic potential vector is coupled to the spacetime curvature tensor. This framework does not introduce new dimensional parameters and reduces to Maxwell’s equations in flat or Ricci-flat spacetimes. We show that such terms can emerge from an ambiguity in extending the flat-spacetime equations to curved spacetime via the minimal substitution rule, reflecting the noncommutativity of covariant derivatives and the presence of curvature. We investigate theoretical and observational consequences of the curvature-coupled field equations and find that for reasonable parameter ranges they evade existing laboratory, solar-system, and astrophysical constraints. Nonetheless, the modified dynamics can become significant and testable in environments with high mass density or where radiation gravity influences dynamics, such as neutron star interiors and the early universe. Our results suggest a pathway to reconcile electromagnetic theory with global cosmological properties while preserving agreement with established phenomenology. Keywords: classical general relativity; Maxwell’s equations; classical fields in curved spacetime; photon mass; curvature coupling; cosmology.

We study the simple random walk on the unique infinite cluster of supercritical bond percolation in Z^d, d >= 2. For almost every percolation configuration, we establish a quenched invariance principle: the rescaled walk converges in distribution to a nondegenerate, isotropic Brownian motion. The proof constructs a harmonic deformation of the cluster under which the walk becomes a square-integrable martingale, enabling functional central limit theorems. The deformation is quantified by a corrector whose sublinear growth is obtained via ergodic arguments. These estimates yield tightness and identify the limiting covariance, proving diffusivity and isotropy.

We report results of a search for sub-kilometer Kuiper Belt Objects (KBOs) using the method of serendipitous stellar occultations. High-speed photometric time series were obtained with the 1.8 m telescope at the Dominion Astrophysical Observatory (Victoria, British Columbia) at 40 Hz. The survey comprised 5.0 star-hours on target stars in the ecliptic open cluster M35 and 2.1 star-hours on control stars in the off-ecliptic open cluster M34. To quantify detection efficiency and the limiting detectable size, we injected artificial occultation events into both simulated time series with 1/f, scintillation-like power spectra and into the real data, and processed them with the same pipeline. No viable candidate occultation events were found. From this null result we derive a 95% confidence upper limit on the cumulative surface density of KBOs of @xmath2 deg@xmath3 for objects brighter than m@xmath4 = 35.3, corresponding to diameters larger than @xmath5860 m assuming a geometric albedo of 0.04 and a heliocentric distance of 40 au. We further assess previously reported trans-Neptunian occultations in the literature and find them unlikely to be genuine. Combining our constraints with those from all existing surveys yields an overall 95% confidence upper limit of @xmath6 deg@xmath3 for KBOs brighter than m@xmath4 = 35 (diameters larger than @xmath51 km for the same albedo and distance assumptions). These limits strengthen evidence for a paucity of sub-km KBOs and provide quantitative benchmarks for the design of future high-cadence occultation surveys.

We present Monte Carlo simulations of a Heisenberg spin glass defined on a hypercubic cell of linear size 2 in d dimensions (2^d spins), where each spin interacts with its d nearest neighbors. As d increases, this sparse geometry approaches the completely connected mean-field limit. Using disorder averaging and parallel-tempering equilibration, we analyze the Binder parameter for d=3 and d=4 and find clear crossings that signal a spin-glass phase at low temperatures. In the high-temperature regime, the inverse spin-glass susceptibility exhibits a linear dependence on temperature, consistent with the Curie–Weiss behavior of mean-field theory. Fits to the high-temperature data yield estimates of the critical temperature that agree with the Bethe–Peierls approximation for a Heisenberg spin glass with coordination number d. Our results quantify finite-size effects and establish the hypercubic cell as a useful testbed for mean-field to finite-dimensional crossover.

We present the Extended Chandra Deep Field–South (E-CDFS), a wide, deep Chandra survey composed of four ACIS-I pointings totaling ≈228 ks that covers ~1100 square arcminutes (≈0.3 deg^2) centered on the original CDF-S. This is the largest survey conducted at this depth; in the hard 2.0–8.0 keV band, only one XMM-Newton survey reaches a lower flux limit. Source detection uses conservative and lower significance thresholds, yielding two complementary catalogs. In total we detect 651 unique X-ray sources: 587 in the main catalog and 64 in a supplementary catalog. Of these, 561 are detected in the full 0.5–8.0 keV band, 529 in the soft 0.5–2.0 keV band, and 335 in the hard 2.0–8.0 keV band. Near the aim point, the soft- and hard-band limiting fluxes reach levels characteristic of the CDF-S environs. Simulations quantify the catalog completeness as a function of flux and assess flux uncertainties arising from limited spectral information. We present differential and cumulative number counts that agree well with previous deep X-ray surveys and with predictions from active galactic nucleus (AGN) population synthesis models that reproduce the X-ray background. Spectral hardness ratios indicate that fainter sources have systematically harder spectra, supporting the interpretation that obscured AGN dominate at faint fluxes. The E-CDFS thus provides a crucial bridge between ultradeep pencil-beam surveys and shallower, wider fields, enabling robust studies of the AGN population and the buildup of the cosmic X-ray background.

We analytically and numerically investigate diffusion of chiral active Brownian particles in three dimensions. Using the Fokker–Planck equation for the joint probability over position and swimming direction, we derive an infinite hierarchy of differential–recurrence relations for multipole coefficients in a spherical-harmonic expansion. From this hierarchy we obtain expressions for the marginal position density, its mean-squared displacement (MSD), and its kurtosis. Analytical predictions are validated by Langevin simulations of self-propelled particles subject to constant self-rotation (chirality), translational, and rotational noise. Chirality qualitatively modifies finite-time spreading: the kurtosis of the marginal density oscillates between the Gaussian value and that of a spherical-shell distribution, reflecting accumulation of probability on helical trajectories. These oscillations are damped by rotational noise, with amplitude set by the rotation-to-diffusion ratio. We quantify crossover times and damping rates controlled by propulsion speed and chirality. Despite non-Gaussian transients, the MSD grows linearly in time at long times, allowing definition of an effective diffusion coefficient that depends on propulsion speed, chirality, and rotational diffusivity. For ensembles where each particle rotates around a uniformly distributed random axis, we reveal anomalous, yet Brownian, diffusion: the position distribution remains non-Gaussian over extended intervals while the MSD is strictly linear in time. This behavior arises from quenched orientational disorder rather than long-time memory and is captured by the multipole hierarchy without ad hoc closures. Our study provides a unified framework for chiral active transport in three dimensions and delineates parameter regimes where non-Gaussian normal diffusion occurs.

We synthesize and critically assess a diverse body of evidence favoring dark matter in the form of particles with mass near 10 GeV. We examine gamma-ray observations of the Galactic Center, the synchrotron emission from the Milky Way’s non-thermal radio filaments, and the diffuse microwave/radio excess commonly referred to as the WMAP haze, alongside low-energy signals and annual modulations reported by the DAMA/LIBRA, CoGeNT, and CRESST-II direct detection experiments. We show that these datasets can be simultaneously accommodated by a relatively light weakly interacting particle with an annihilation cross section on the order of 10^-26 cm^3 s^-1, as predicted for a simple thermal relic, and a Galactic halo distribution consistent with that found in numerical simulations. In this framework, annihilation products naturally account for both the spectral shape and angular morphology of the Galactic Center gamma rays, and for the magnitude and spatial correlation of the observed synchrotron components. In contrast, proposed astrophysical explanations—such as unresolved source populations or atypical cosmic-ray injections—struggle to reproduce the combined spectral, angular, and multiwavelength constraints. The phase and amplitude of the annual modulation reported by DAMA/LIBRA, and independently supported by CoGeNT, are inconsistent with known or hypothesized modulating backgrounds but align with expectations for dark matter scattering in the local halo. This scenario remains consistent with existing indirect searches and collider bounds, as well as constraints from CDMS. Tension with xenon-based detectors can be mitigated if the response of liquid xenon to very low-energy nuclear recoils is modestly suppressed relative to previous calibrations, or if the dark matter exhibits isospin-violating couplings that reduce sensitivity in xenon targets.
