We present quantitative morphological and structural measurements for galaxies detected in HST/WFPC2 survey fields, derived with a maximum-likelihood framework for two-dimensional bulge–disk decomposition optimized for faint, under-sampled images. The method fits parametric disk and bulge components convolved with spatially varying PSFs and a realistic noise model, yielding robust estimates of total magnitude, color, effective half-light radius, axis ratios, bulge-to-total flux fraction, bulge-to-disk half-light radius ratio, and surface brightness. Extensive simulations and internal cross-band fits demonstrate unbiased recovery and uncertainties to the one-hour limiting depths in F814W (I), F606W (V), and F450W (B). We describe the fitting procedure, parameter priors, selection functions, and completeness, and we delineate the ranges over which each structural parameter can be reliably measured. We present the observed distributions of the above quantities for galaxies across random pure-parallel and comparable archival primary WFPC2 fields from the Medium Deep Survey. Calibrated catalogs and images are publicly available via a searchable web interface to the database.

We present a statistical comparison between 21 cm rotation measures (RM) and optically thin atomic hydrogen column densities (N_HI) along lines of sight to nearly 2000 unresolved extragalactic radio sources within the Galactic plane of the northern sky. For each source, N_HI is derived from 1-arcminute H I spectral-line data by integrating the brightness temperature to the Galactic edge in the immediate vicinity of the source, assuming optical thinness. The corresponding RM is taken from polarized continuum measurements of each source. RMs are grouped into N_HI bins 4 × 10^20 atoms cm^-2 wide, revealing a strong, monotonic relationship between the number of hydrogen atoms in a unit column through the plane and the mean RM along the same path. The correlation is linear over approximately one order of magnitude in column density, spanning 0.8–14 × 10^21 atoms cm^-2, with a constant slope RM/N_HI = 23.2 ± 2.3 rad m^-2 per 10^21 atoms cm^-2 and a positive intercept of 45.0 ± 13.8 rad m^-2 at zero H I column. Using this slope and adopting an ionization fraction of 8% characteristic of the warm neutral medium (WNM), we infer a mean volume-averaged line-of-sight magnetic field of 1.0 ± 0.1 μG in the second Galactic quadrant, directed away from the Sun. This field strength agrees remarkably well with an independent estimate of 1.2 μG obtained by combining the same RM dataset with a Galactic dispersion measure model. The concordance implies that electrons in the partially ionized WNM are primarily responsible for pulsar dispersion measures, and therefore the partially ionized WNM constitutes the dominant magneto-ionic component of the interstellar medium in these directions.

We study inevitability properties in branching temporal logics, expressed with the syntax @xmath0, where @xmath1 is an arbitrary (timed) CTL formula. Interpreted as "good things will happen," these properties parallel liveness in linear temporal logics. For dense-time models, we analyze inevitability via greatest fixpoint computation and present model-checking algorithms that handle the presence and absence of non-Zeno computations. To accelerate verification, we introduce an early-decision technique that detects stabilization of greatest fixpoints before full convergence. Our algorithms are parameterized by @xmath2, a measure of time progress that modulates iteration granularity and influences the treatment of Zeno behaviors. We implement these methods over timed automata and conduct experiments on performance. Specifically, we evaluate the impact of different @xmath2 values and the enforcement of non-Zeno requirements on the cost of greatest fixpoint evaluation. We further assess safe abstraction techniques tailored to inevitability checking, quantifying their effect on efficiency and precision. The results clarify trade-offs among parameterization, non-Zeno enforcement, and abstraction: appropriate @xmath2 choices can reduce iteration counts; non-Zeno constraints prevent spurious inevitability; and safe abstractions yield speedups with conservatism. Our analysis provides practical guidance for tuning verification workflows for TCTL inevitability properties in real-time systems.

We present new medium-resolution spectroscopy together with optical and near-infrared photometric monitoring of the AGB carbon star V381 Lac. Our multi-epoch observations reveal rapid, deep spectral changes and extreme variability across the optical and near-infrared bands. Most notably, the Na I D lines transition from strong absorption to clear emission, and the [N II] 6548–6584 doublet progressively strengthens in tandem with pronounced photometric fading. The star’s locus in 2MASS and WISE color–color diagrams lies in regions characteristic of objects undergoing dust formation in their circumstellar envelopes, reinforcing the interpretation of episodic mass loss and dust production. The emerging framework is that of a cool AGB carbon star experiencing bursts of high mass ejection and severe occultation of the stellar photosphere, reminiscent of the behavior observed in R Coronae Borealis variables. We model the spectral energy distribution with AGB evolutionary tracks that include dust in the circumstellar environment. The comparison indicates that V381 Lac is the descendant of a star with an initial mass of about 2 solar masses, currently in the terminal AGB phases and converted into a carbon star through repeated third dredge-up episodes. The star is moderately obscured by dust, dominated by amorphous carbon and silicon carbide, with submicron grain sizes. The correlated spectroscopic and photometric evolution supports a scenario in which episodic dust formation along the line of sight drives the fading events, while circumstellar gas gives rise to the observed Na I D emission and growing [N II] lines. V381 Lac thus provides a valuable case study of dust-driven variability and mass-loss processes in late-type carbon-rich AGB stars.

We present preliminary results of an analysis of sub-populations within the Near-Earth Asteroids (NEAs), including Atens, Apollos, Amors, and potentially hazardous asteroids (PHAs), using data from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) and the NEOWISE automated Moving Object Processing System. To extrapolate the detected sample to the underlying population, we quantified survey biases as functions of diameter, albedo, and orbital elements via forward modeling. The resulting detection efficiency surfaces enable debiased estimates of size-frequency and albedo distributions for each subgroup. We place constraints on the number of PHAs larger than 100 m and find that there are @xmath0 such objects. As expected from thermal-infrared selection, WISE reveals distinct albedo distributions, with Atens exhibiting higher median albedos than Amors, while Apollos show intermediate properties. The cumulative size distributions of the subgroups vary modestly between 100 m and 1 km, with slopes consistent with collisional evolution moderated by dynamical delivery. We compare debiased orbital element distributions with dynamical source models and find agreement, with residuals suggesting refinement in ν6 and 3:1 resonance contributions. These results demonstrate the power of WISE to constrain NEA substructure and the PHA inventory.

We investigate the linear stability of a long cylindrical domain in a phase‐separating binary fluid subject to external shear. Using the coupled Cahn–Hilliard and Stokes equations, we derive dispersion relations for long‐wavelength perturbations, allowing arbitrary viscosity contrast between phases. The shear flow suppresses, and can stabilize, the hydrodynamic Rayleigh instability and the thermodynamic varicose instability by coupling axisymmetric modes to nonaxisymmetric perturbations and enhancing mixing. Stability boundaries and eigenvalue scalings are obtained, revealing regimes of shear‐induced robustness consistent with observations of a “string phase” in demixing fluids. Our results clarify the interplay of composition dynamics, viscosity contrast, and shear in controlling cylindrical morphology.

We map the phase structure of SU(2) lattice gauge theory with dynamical fermions in the three-dimensional space spanned by temperature, bare quark mass, and quark chemical potential. Using ensembles at finite temperature and density, we analyze the number density, the static interquark potential, temporal and spatial Polyakov loops, and chiral and diquark susceptibilities. The density exhibits qualitative regime changes as functions of temperature and chemical potential, approaching the scaling expected of a gas of free, massless quarks only in a limited domain. At the thermodynamic onset, the static potential flattens at large separations, signaling enhanced screening and a transition toward deconfinement. Temporal and spatial Polyakov loops respond differently, with the latter remaining nearly insensitive to the chemical potential. Susceptibilities indicate a rotation of the chiral condensate into a baryonic (diquark) condensate, accompanied by a suppression of its magnitude in the chiral limit, suggesting a diquark condensation temperature below the deconfinement temperature. A partially quenched study isolates the gauge-sector response to finite density. We discuss implications and caveats for QCD.

Strong-lensing analyses and cosmological simulations increasingly indicate that galaxy clusters may harbor compact cores that are substantially smaller than the cores inferred from X-ray observations of hot intracluster gas. We present a physically motivated infall model in which two distinct cores can grow simultaneously from the background dark matter: a dense, compact core and a more extended, X-ray–bright core. The formation of an individual cluster in this framework requires a pre-existing localized large fluctuation—plausibly a non-Gaussian density peak in the primordial field—to seed the subsequent growth. Motivated by numerous recent observations that detect no strong evolution in cluster properties up to redshift @xmath0, we compare data with the saturated cluster configuration predicted by our model. In the saturated state, the compact core attains a mass of order few @xmath1 and a characteristic size of ~@xmath2 kpc for a cluster with total mass @xmath3 several @xmath4 within a radius of ~@xmath5 Mpc. The resulting mass and light distributions self-consistently reproduce the dark matter profiles revealed by gravitational lensing, the observed radial distributions of cluster galaxies, the intracluster gas described by the conventional @xmath6 model, and the baryon fraction profiles. When combined with observed X-ray surface brightness profiles, the model predicts an overall radial decline of the intracluster gas temperature, well approximated by a mean polytropic index @xmath7. This temperature stratification, together with the dual-core structure, provides a natural resolution of the so-called @xmath6 discrepancy by reconciling the spectroscopic and X-ray determinations of cluster dynamical support. Our results suggest that compact cores are generic outcomes of early, localized peaks and subsequent dark-matter–driven infall, and that clusters approach a saturated configuration by z ≲ @xmath0 with minimal late-time structural evolution.

This paper investigates parametric resonances in stellar orbits embedded in a galactic potential subject to low-amplitude, strictly periodic perturbations whose pulsation frequency undergoes pseudo-random variations modeled as colored noise. Motivated by evolving density distributions during violent relaxation and by internal substructures, satellite galaxies, and dense environments, we combine perturbative Floquet analyses with ensembles of test-particle integrations with stochastic frequency jitter. We measure resonance growth, energy exchange, action diffusion, and transport as functions of noise amplitude and correlation time. We find that allowing a variable frequency does not suppress parametric resonance; instead, frequency wandering broadens resonance bands and can enhance transport, particularly when noise correlation times are comparable to orbital timescales. Thus, stochastic frequency evolution can increase the impact of systematic pulsations.

We investigate quantum effects on the dielectric and piezoelectric response of barium titanate in its low-temperature rhombohedral phase. Using path-integral molecular dynamics at fixed pressure and temperature, with an efficient Langevin thermostat-barostat and an effective Hamiltonian derived from first-principles, we quantify the impact of quantum fluctuations on ferroelectric observables. Quantum fluctuations markedly increase the static dielectric susceptibility, chi0, by about a factor of two, and enhance piezoelectric constants, revealing strong anharmonicity persisting to very low temperatures. The weak temperature dependence of the dielectric properties below ~100 K is traced to (i) zero-point energy contributions and (ii) effectively harmonic behavior when quantum effects are artificially suppressed. Our results demonstrate that incorporating nuclear quantum motion is essential for accurate modeling of BaTiO3 at cryogenic conditions and provide a framework for assessing quantum-enhanced electromechanical responses in perovskite ferroelectrics and cryogenic device applications.

Magnetic multipolar liquids in the spin-@xmath0 frustrated J@xmath1–J@xmath2 chain under magnetic field extend broadly from saturation into low fields. Building on our recent clarification of the temperature and field dependence of the NMR relaxation rate @xmath3 in the quadrupolar phase, we investigate @xmath3 in the octupolar phase by combining field-theoretical analysis with numerical calculations. We derive asymptotic forms governed by Tomonaga–Luttinger parameters of bound-magnon triplets and identify distinctive temperature and field scalings that discriminate octupolar from quadrupolar and hexadecapolar liquids. The resulting fingerprints of spin-fluctuation suppression and longitudinal dominance are mapped across the phase diagram. Implications for quasi-one-dimensional J@xmath1–J@xmath2 magnets, including @xmath4, @xmath5, and @xmath6, are discussed.

We propose a predictive radiative seesaw model at one-loop having a flavor-dependent gauge symmetry @xmath0 and a Majorana fermion dark matter candidate. Neutrino masses arise from the loop with an @xmath1-type two-zero texture, yielding sharp predictions including normal ordering, correlations among mixing angles, and restricted CP phases. We confront the model with limits from charged-lepton flavor violation, electroweak precision data, relic density and direct detection of dark matter, and collider searches for the new @xmath0 gauge boson. In the viable parameter space, the LHCb anomalies in @xmath2 and @xmath3 with @xmath4 or @xmath5 can be accommodated, and associated @xmath6 signals may be discoverable at the LHC. KIAS-P17007.

Using the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS) aboard Suzaku, we investigated the spatial distribution of elemental abundances in the Fornax cluster. The high spectral sensitivity of XIS resolves the K-shell lines of O and Mg and allows robust measurements of O, Ne, Mg, Si, S, and Fe. In the central region surrounding NGC 1399, we find approximately solar abundances of Fe, Si, and S, while the abundance ratios O/Fe ≈ 0.4–0.5 and Mg/Fe ≈ 0.7 in solar units indicate a relative deficit of α-elements compared to Fe. At larger radii, Fe and Si decline to ~0.4–0.5 of solar with no significant gradient across the studied annulus, and the O/Fe and Mg/Fe ratios remain consistent with those in the core. Around NGC 1404, the Fe abundance is near solar, whereas O, Ne, and Mg are 0.5–0.7 times the Fe level. The pronounced enhancement of Fe in the inner regions of NGC 1399 and NGC 1404 points to dominant enrichment by Type Ia supernovae, in contrast to O, Ne, and Mg, which trace the stellar population and core-collapse yields. We further derive mass-to-light ratios for O and Fe within central 130 kpc of NGC 1399 that are more than an order of magnitude lower than values reported for rich clusters, underscoring the metal production and retention history of this cluster. These results refine the chemical evolution in group-scale environments.

Electroencephalographic (EEG) burst activity in preterm infants provides clinically relevant information on brain maturation and can aid prognostication after perinatal asphyxia. However, many automated burst detectors have been developed for cohorts under 35 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA), and their performance may degrade as neural dynamics evolve toward term-equivalent ages. We evaluated multi-feature, single-channel EEG burst detection in very preterm infants reaching term ages (PMA ≥ 36 weeks) using five machine learning approaches: logistic regression (LR), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machines (SVM), and simple thresholding (TH). Classifiers were trained on visually annotated single-channel EEG from 14 very preterm infants (born after 28 weeks gestation) recorded at 36–41 weeks PMA. Performance was assessed against expert labels using accuracy and human–automatic agreement (Cohen’s kappa), alongside computational efficiency and feature parsimony. The top-performing classifiers (KNN, SVM, and LR) achieved approximately 95% accuracy, while TH reached 84%. LR yielded the highest agreement with human annotations (Cohen’s kappa = 0.71) and the most favorable computational profile, requiring only three EEG features. Applying the LR model to an independent test dataset of 21 infants with PMA ≥ 36 weeks, we observed that longer burst durations and shorter inter-burst intervals characterized infants with higher PMA and greater body weight, consistent with maturational progression of cortical activity. These findings indicate that LR-based single-channel burst detection is accurate, efficient, and scalable for near-term preterm infants, offering a practical tool for continuous maturation assessment in bedside monitoring and portable settings. Such an approach may facilitate longitudinal tracking of neurodevelopment and support research and clinical decision-making where streamlined EEG acquisition is desirable.

Super-spreader (SS) epidemics, exemplified by SARS and potentially MERS, exhibit extreme heterogeneity in individual infectiousness that distinguishes them from more uniform epidemics such as influenza. We combine agent-based simulations with multi-type branching process analysis to quantify how this heterogeneity reshapes emergence, growth, and control. We show that SS epidemics cannot be characterized by a single parameter: at minimum both the mean reproduction number R (expected secondary cases per primary case) and the variance of the offspring distribution must be specified. Strikingly, even when R exceeds 1, the extinction probability of a transmission chain initiated by one case can remain close to one (e.g., 0.97) if variance is large. This yields a prolonged kindling period marked by sporadic introductions that spawn clusters which self-extinguish, potentially fostering a false sense of security before a rare super-spreading event ignites sustained transmission. Interventions targeting early cases—rapid isolation of index patients and contact tracing with quarantine of secondary cases—substantially reduce the risk of emergence and the effective growth rate without necessarily driving R below 1. At fixed R, the efficacy of these measures diminishes only gradually as variance increases, underscoring their robustness in high-heterogeneity settings. We further outline operational thresholds for escalating response based on estimated extinction probabilities and demonstrate that, under resource constraints, concentrating efforts on case-based interventions yields higher marginal returns than broad population-wide measures in SS contexts. These findings are consistent across simulation and analytic approaches and imply that surveillance and control of SS pathogens should routinely estimate and report both mean and variance (or dispersion) of transmission, prioritize rapid case isolation and contact tracing, and focus on identifying high-transmission settings. The distinct dynamics of SS epidemics create actionable opportunities for containment even in the absence of vaccines or therapeutics.

Laser–plasma interactions produce energetic ion beams that drive fusion reactions in secondary targets. We establish universal scaling laws showing that fusion yield scales systematically with laser power across disparate target and pulse parameters. Using hydrodynamic similarity, we derive the origin of this scaling and attribute it to the power dependence of three coupled quantities: the reaction rate, the plasma density, and the projected range of accelerated ions in the target medium. Their combined scaling determines Y ∝ P^α, with α predictable from measurable beam and target properties. The relations reproduce published yields and enable extrapolation to untested nuclear reactions, providing a practical framework for estimating laser-driven fusion performance and guiding experimental design and optimization.

We simulate the implementation of a @xmath0-gate, or @xmath1-gate, on a [7,1,3] Steane-encoded logical qubit subject to a non‐equiprobable error environment. Using circuit-level noise with biased Pauli rates, we assess reliability via gate fidelities for the resulting single‐qubit logical operations. We compare fully fault‐tolerant constructions with resource‐efficient, non‐fault‐tolerant elements, specifically the use of a non‐fault‐tolerant logical zero ancilla for @xmath0‐gate execution. Numerical results show that, after perfect error correction, the logical gate fidelity exhibits no first‐order error terms, indicating that all leading errors are correctable by the code. Thus, certain non‐fault‐tolerant implementations can still achieve fault tolerance while reducing basic resource consumption. Our findings quantify tradeoffs between reliability and overhead and suggest practical pathways for efficient encoded gate synthesis in scalable architectures.

We present preliminary results of a study in progress combining contemporaneous high-resolution spectroscopy and multiband photometry of young weak-line T Tauri and post-T Tauri stars approaching the zero-age main sequence. The program exploits FOCES at the Calar Alto Observatory (CAHA) and SARG at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo (TNG), complemented by synoptic photometry from the Catania and TUBITAK observatories. Our primary goal is to investigate the topology and temporal evolution of magnetic active regions at photospheric and chromospheric levels in young, single, predominantly slow rotators (rotation periods longer than about 2 days), and to relate surface inhomogeneities to fundamental stellar parameters and kinematic group membership. For slow rotators we apply the spectroscopic line-depth ratio method to track rotationally modulated effective-temperature variations, providing a sensitive diagnostic of photospheric spot distributions. Chromospheric activity is assessed through core emission in Ca II H&K and the infrared triplet, and by quantifying the filling-in of H-alpha via spectral subtraction. We also derive lithium abundances, projected rotational velocities, and radial velocities to constrain evolutionary status and potential membership in nearby stellar kinematic groups. Several targets exhibit clear rotational modulation in brightness and temperature, coherent with spectroscopic activity indicators, indicating sizeable cool spots and associated chromospheric plages. As a case study, we briefly report on SAO 51891, for which simultaneous photometry and spectroscopy reveal phase-dependent variations in LDR-derived temperature, Ca II and H-alpha emission, and broadband flux, consistent with a spotted photosphere and spatially correlated plages. To interpret these datasets we have developed a coupled spot/plage modeling framework that simultaneously fits light curves, temperature curves, and chromospheric excess emission, recovering spot filling factors and temperature contrasts, as well as chromospheric flux contrasts and filling factors. The ongoing survey will enable an exploration of trends between global stellar properties (effective temperature, rotation, lithium content, kinematics) and spot/plage characteristics across activity levels and evolutionary stages, thereby providing new constraints on dynamo processes and surface magnetic topology in stars nearing the main sequence. These results will inform models of angular momentum evolution and lifetimes in stars.

We investigate whether asphericities seeded by multi-dimensional convective burning in the Si/O shell influence core-collapse supernova dynamics. Using three-dimensional simulations of a nonrotating massive-star progenitor with energy-dependent neutrino heating and cooling, we compare models initialized with and without realistic, large-scale velocity perturbations representative of late-stage convection. Perturbations amplify postshock turbulence, enhance neutrino-heating efficiency, and increase the residency time of matter in the gain region, facilitating shock expansion. In contrast, the unperturbed counterpart fails to revive the shock. The perturbed model robustly achieves shock revival and explosion. These results demonstrate that presupernova asphericity can qualitatively change postbounce evolution, motivating multi-dimensional progenitor models for reliable supernova predictions and nucleosynthesis outcomes.

We revisit the simplest @xmath0 grand unified frameworks in which the GUT symmetry is broken by an adjoint Higgs, and we recapitulate and extend recent progress on their viability and testability. Going beyond the traditional minimal survival approximation, we perform a refined assessment of gauge coupling unification that incorporates complete one- and two-loop renormalization group evolution with realistic intermediate thresholds stemming from consistent symmetry-breaking chains and scalar spectra. We demonstrate that the minimal survival hypothesis can obscure sizable and phenomenologically rich regions of parameter space in which selected intermediate multiplets required for successful non-supersymmetric unification naturally remain light, with masses possibly descending into the TeV domain and thus amenable to collider and precision probes. In these regions, the stringent minimal-survival-based lower bounds on the @xmath1 (seesaw/B−L) scale are relaxed by up to four orders of magnitude, enabling a fully consistent implementation of the standard seesaw mechanism without the excessive fine-tuning implied in earlier analyses. We present representative spectra that realize unification while respecting perturbativity, vacuum stability, and current proton decay limits, and we delineate the correlations among the unification scale, proton lifetime, and the placement of intermediate thresholds. Finally, we discuss the prospects of the minimal renormalizable @xmath0 GUT as a predictive and calculable framework for proton decay, highlighting discovery opportunities at current and upcoming experiments and outlining the key observables that can discriminate among viable symmetry-breaking patterns.

We investigate multifractal moments of the current distribution in randomly diluted resistor networks near the percolation threshold. When an external current is applied between terminals @xmath0 and @xmath1, the @xmath2th moment scales as @xmath3, with @xmath4 the correlation-length exponent of the isotropic percolation universality class. Using the framework of master operators [Europhys. Lett. 51, 539 (2000)], we derive the family of multifractal exponents @xmath5 for @xmath6 to two-loop order. The resulting exponents show corrections to mean-field behavior and agree with numerical data in three dimensions. Our results clarify transport heterogeneity and universality in disordered networks and provide predictions for multifractal scaling.

We theoretically investigate nonequilibrium quantum transport in a quantum dot attached to a Majorana bound state using the Keldysh Green’s function formalism. This approach provides a unified description of the steady-state electric current over the entire bias range, from the zero-bias limit to the large-bias regime, without resorting to separate approximations. In the low-bias limit, our results reproduce linear-response transport, and in the high-bias limit they agree with master-equation predictions, thereby bridging two standard methodologies with a single nonequilibrium framework. The calculated @xmath0 curves exhibit a characteristic linear-response slope given by @xmath1, where @xmath2 is the ballistic conductance @xmath3, in agreement with Phys. Rev. B 84, 201308(R) (2011). We analyze deviations from this behavior arising when the dot couples asymmetrically to the left and right leads. In this case, the differential conductance extracted from the left or right currents can be either larger or smaller than @xmath4 depending on the degree of coupling asymmetry. Notably, the standard Landauer–Büttiker conductance in the linear-response regime does not coincide with the full nonequilibrium calculation under asymmetric coupling, underscoring limitations of conventional two-terminal formulas when distributions and spectral functions are modified by bias and contact asymmetry. We further contrast transport through a quantum dot coupled to a regular fermionic (RF) zero mode with that coupled to a Majorana bound state (MBS). Distinct signatures emerge across the entire bias range, including the formation of a plateau in the @xmath0 curve at intermediate biases for the MBS case, absent for RF coupling. Thermal effects are also examined: at sufficiently high reservoir temperatures the RF and MBS responses converge for all biases. Our results delineate experimentally relevant markers of Majorana-induced correlations and provide a continuous, internally consistent description of quantum-dot transport from linear to strongly nonequilibrium regimes.

We propose a classically scale-invariant extension of the Standard Model in which electroweak symmetry breaking emerges dynamically from a strongly coupled, vector-like sector (“hypercolor”). The hypercolor condensate forms at the TeV scale, breaking scale symmetry and transmitting a negative mass-squared to the Standard Model Higgs via a bosonic seesaw mechanism, thereby triggering electroweak symmetry breaking without introducing explicit mass scales. An elementary pseudoscalar singlet is introduced to endow the composite Nambu–Goldstone bosons of the hypercolor sector (hypercolor pions) with masses. We show that one such hypercolor pion can be a promising collider target through diphoton production at the LHC. As a consequence of the bosonic seesaw, the fluctuating mode of the pseudoscalar singlet acquires extremely small couplings to Standard Model fields and is predicted to be very light, with its leading interaction in the diphoton channel. This mode can serve as an axion-like, effectively invisible dark matter candidate, with its mass constrained by cosmological and astrophysical observations to lie within a viable light window. We demonstrate that the observed relic abundance can be generated via coherent (misalignment) oscillations. The associated photon coupling motivates dedicated searches in microwave cavity experiments, and we outline the corresponding detection prospects. Our framework links collider diphoton signatures and axion-like dark matter phenomenology within a unified, scale-invariant paradigm.

Motivated by recent studies of one-bubble open inflation, we test simple open cold dark matter (CDM) cosmologies for consistency with observations. We derive the primordial curvature perturbation spectrum by solving the evolution of fluctuations during an open inflationary stage and propagate these initial conditions to the late-time cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies. A likelihood analysis of the COBE DMR maps is performed, considering models based on both the Bunch–Davies and conformal vacuum prescriptions for the initial state. After normalizing the perturbation amplitude to the COBE data, we reassess the viability of open CDM from the standpoint of large-scale structure formation. We find that the COBE likelihood severely constrains the degree of spatial curvature. In particular, models with very low matter density are ruled out in the Bunch–Davies case, yielding a 95% confidence lower bound on the density parameter. The conformal vacuum choice relaxes this bound somewhat, but still disfavors extremely open universes. Once normalized to COBE, the predicted matter power spectra of highly open models fail to reproduce observed clustering and cluster abundances, strengthening the CMB constraints. Our results indicate that one-bubble open inflation can be consistent only for moderate curvature, and highlight the sensitivity of CMB anisotropies to the initial vacuum choice.

Hydrogen burning reaction networks in diverse phases of stellar evolution require accurately determined thermonuclear rates to support reliable astrophysical modeling. The 17O(p,γ)18F reaction is a key process in these environments, but its cross section at low energies is governed by a complex pattern of narrow resonances and direct capture contributions that must be reproduced by theory for robust extrapolation to stellar energies. The scarcity and inconsistency of available experimental data across a broad energy range have compounded uncertainties in the extrapolated astrophysical S factor. To address this, we have measured the total cross section of 17O(p,γ)18F using the activation method, which integrates all capture branches and bypasses several systematic effects typical of in-beam γ-ray spectroscopy, such as cascade summing and absolute efficiency normalization. Measurements were performed for proton energies between 500 keV and 1.8 MeV, achieving typical total uncertainties of about 10%. The resulting excitation function captures the gross resonance structure and agrees well with the overall behavior reported in earlier studies. Quantitatively, a deviation of approximately a factor of 1.5 is observed when our total cross sections are compared with the only available high-energy dataset, indicating a likely overestimation of the direct capture contribution in that work. At the lowest energy measured, our data agree within one standard deviation with two recent datasets and differ by roughly two standard deviations from a third, highlighting the importance of consistent methodologies. A comprehensive R-matrix analysis combining the present measurements with selected previous data yields an astrophysical S factor at zero energy with improved reliability and reduced model dependence. In conclusion, our independent activation measurements confirm the literature cross sections in the resonance-dominated energy region, while supporting a lower direct capture cross section at higher energies. The new dataset provides stringent constraints for theoretical models and enhances confidence in extrapolated reaction rates, thereby improving the input needed for stellar evolution calculations involving hydrogen burning.

The Chelyabinsk superbolide, the largest natural object to enter Earth’s atmosphere since the 1908 Tunguska event, has become a benchmark for understanding, managing, and mitigating future impacts. Despite extensive documentation of the 2013 event, the pre-impact orbit of its parent body remains debated. We revisit this problem with an improved Monte Carlo framework that explicitly incorporates the geodetic coordinates of the impact point, thereby tightening orbital geometry constraints. Our analysis yields a most probable pre-impact orbit characterized by a = 1.62 au, e = 0.53, I = 3.97 deg, Ω = 326.45 deg, and ω = 109.71 deg at the impact epoch. We further subject all published orbital solutions to a simple but robust impact-consistency test that quantifies their ability to produce an Earth encounter at the correct time and location. A significant fraction of the proposed solutions fail this test, indicating that temporal consistency is a stringent and necessary filter for credible reconstructions. Using the improved orbit, we perform six-body N-body integrations that include the dominant planetary perturbations to reassess the dynamical context of a possible Chelyabinsk-related asteroid cluster. The simulations support a linkage to resonant near-Earth asteroids 2007 BD7 and 2011 EO8, suggesting a shared dynamical pathway mediated by mean-motion and secular resonances that enhance Earth-crossing probabilities on 10^4–10^5 year timescales. Finally, leveraging the well-established classification of Chelyabinsk meteorites, we examine meteorite fall records and identify suggestive evidence for an associated LL5 chondrite cluster, consistent with a fragmented source population. Our results refine the pre-impact orbit, provide a reproducible validation test for proposed solutions, and strengthen the case for a resonant dynamical origin of the Chelyabinsk impactor.

Low‐frequency variability in the North Pacific, spanning intraannual to decadal timescales, is evident in observations and models and remains difficult to predict. We evaluate a nonparametric ensemble analog forecasting framework that leverages historical trajectories most similar to a given initial state to predict future evolution. Low‐frequency modes of sea surface temperature and sea ice concentration are extracted with nonlinear Laplacian spectral analysis, yielding noise‐robust, temporally coherent predictors. Forecasts are constructed by selecting analogs in a delay‐embedded state space and forming weighted ensembles without assuming linearity, stationarity, or prescribed stochastic structure. Using hindcasts from reanalyses and coupled model control integrations, we compare skill against persistence and parametric benchmarks, including autoregressive models with and without exogenous inputs. The analog approach delivers higher correlation skill and lower error at seasonal to multiyear leads, particularly for leading basin‐scale modes and coupled SST–ice patterns. Skill gains persist under cross‐validation and sensitivity tests to analog pool size, embedding, and distance metric, indicating that analog, NLSA‐based forecasts offer a promising pathway for prediction of North Pacific low‐frequency variability.

We present results from a Hubble Space Telescope photometric survey of young and intermediate-age (approximately 1-2 Gyr) star clusters in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. Many targets display bimodal or extended main-sequence turn-offs, dual red clumps, and broadened or split main sequences (e.g., NGC 1844, NGC 1856), features not reproduced by single-isochrone models. Using high-precision, multi-band imaging, differential-reddening corrections, artificial-star tests, and field-star decontamination, we quantify the intrinsic CMD widths and morphologies. Synthetic CMDs incorporating rotation and interacting binaries are contrasted with age-spread scenarios. We find that binaries contribute to blue stragglers and MS scatter but cannot by themselves explain eMSTOs or dual RCs. Rotational distributions with a fraction of rapid rotators reproduce much of the MS broadening and RC bifurcation, while residual MSTO widths imply modest age spreads (about 200-500 Myr) in some clusters. These constraints favor a hybrid interpretation in which rotation dominates the CMD complexity, with prolonged star formation in Magellanic Cloud clusters.

Generalized linear models (GLMs) are a popular framework for modeling neural spike trains and are often assessed using goodness-of-fit tools grounded in stochastic point-process theory, such as the time-rescaling theorem. However, when firing rates are high or observations are discretized coarsely, the assumptions enabling this connection are violated, undermining standard diagnostics. We show how point-process goodness-of-fit tests can still be applied to GLMs by constructing equivalent surrogate point processes from time-series observations. In addition, we introduce two complementary tests based on thinning and complementing point processes, which enhance sensitivity to misspecification under challenging regimes. Through theoretical analysis and evaluation, we demonstrate that these procedures yield reliable diagnostics for both continuous-time point-process models and discretized GLMs. Our approach expands the methodological toolkit for assessing neural encoding models and supports more rigorous model validation.

We propose a traveling-wave protocol to generate optical Schrödinger-cat states using weak self-Kerr nonlinearities. Two identically prepared coherent states acquire Kerr-induced phase evolution, are mixed, and one output mode is subjected to homodyne detection. Conditional on the measured quadrature, the remaining mode collapses into a superposition of coherent states drawn from a set of cat states. The quadrature outcome labels which state is produced, enabling heralded, high-probability preparation despite small Kerr strengths. We analyze fidelity, success probabilities, and parameter regimes, showing robustness to losses and detector inefficiencies, and discuss experimental feasibility with photonic platforms.

We present a systematic search for diffuse radio halos and relics in Abell clusters covered by the Westerbork Northern Sky Survey (WENSS). From uniform inspection and filtering of WENSS images, we identify 18 candidates: 11 previously reported and 7 newly recognized with first evidence of cluster-scale diffuse emission. Multiwavelength context indicates that all clusters in this sample bear independent signs of recent or ongoing mergers. We quantify the correlation between cluster X-ray luminosity and halo radio power, finding a positive trend consistent with merger-driven particle acceleration. A simple merger-shock model reproduces the sense of the observed correlation but yields a slope shallower than the data. We discuss observational biases, selection effects, and the predictive use of X-ray–radio scaling for future surveys, emphasizing strategies to optimize detections of faint, extended emission in upcoming facilities.

We address consistent interactions for off-shell fermion fields of arbitrary spin, essential in quantum hadrodynamical descriptions of high-spin baryon resonances in hadronic reactions. The standard Rarita–Schwinger representation embeds lower-spin components that contaminate interactions unless explicitly removed. Imposing invariance under the unconstrained Rarita–Schwinger gauge eliminates the spurious lower-spin content from propagators and vertices, yielding a consistent, causal interaction framework. We construct the most general gauge-invariant interaction Lagrangians for high-spin fermions, detailing their tensorial structure and momentum dependence. A key outcome is that the momentum-power of consistent couplings grows with the fermion spin, which, combined with conventional hadronic form factors, induces unphysical energy behavior in tree-level amplitudes and cross sections. To remedy this, we introduce a novel spin-dependent hadronic form factor tailored to the high-momentum scaling of consistent interactions, suppressing short-distance artifacts while preserving low-energy phenomenology. Illustrative applications to spin-3/2 and spin-5/2 resonances demonstrate improved stability, regulator independence, and agreement with analytic constraints. Our results provide a unified, model-independent prescription for consistently coupling high-spin fermions in hadronic processes and for controlling unphysical off-shell effects in phenomenological analyses and experimental observables relevant.

Under a regularity assumption (no collision and no vanishing of eigenvalues) we develop a rigorous asymptotic theory for formal and actual solutions of q-difference equations with regular singularities. We build fundamental solutions, prove summability of formal solutions, and derive uniform bounds, yielding precise exponential growth for evaluations of regular solutions along arithmetic progressions. The exponential rate is explicitly computable, by an algorithm, from the q-difference operator, using the characteristic roots of its companion matrix, and is stable under small perturbations. As motivation, we revisit the hyperbolic volume conjecture in quantum topology. Since the colored Jones function of a knot satisfies a nontrivial q-difference equation (Le and the author), our results give a direct mechanism predicting exponential growth of its specialized values and express the growth rate from the governing operator. We compare this rate with the hyperbolic volume constant, obtain sharp bounds, and provide new evidence and a framework toward the conjecture.

Motivated by the growing census of giant Jupiter-like planets discovered by Doppler surveys around solar-type stars, we investigate the long-term dynamics of three compact multiplanet systems: GJ 876, HD 82943, and 55 Cnc. The former two host pairs near a 2:1 mean-motion resonance (MMR), while the inner two planets of 55 Cnc lie close to a 3:1 MMR. We perform direct N-body integrations for millions of years on hundreds of orbital realizations per system, sampling observational uncertainties from published Doppler solutions. For GJ 876 and HD 82943, we find that the principal 2:1 resonant angles exhibit sustained libration about 0° or 180°, demonstrating robust resonant locking that suppresses close encounters and enhances long-term stability. In 55 Cnc, all three independent 3:1 resonant arguments for the inner pair librate over Myr timescales, providing strong dynamical evidence that this system is maintained by a 3:1 resonance. We further identify apsidal phase relationships as a second stabilizing mechanism: the relative apsidal longitudes exhibit libration about 0° (alignment) in GJ 876 and about 180° (anti-alignment) in HD 82943, whereas 55 Cnc shows an asymmetric apsidal libration between its inner two planets. These results highlight the complementary roles of mean-motion resonances and apsidal coupling in structuring and stabilizing compact giant-planet systems, with implications for their migration histories. Finally, we briefly assess dynamical habitability, noting that strong resonant perturbations likely restrict stable terrestrial orbits in the classical habitable zones of GJ 876 and HD 82943, while 55 Cnc may permit stable niches exterior to the inner resonant pair depending on orbital architecture.

Understanding synchronous behavior in coupled dynamical systems beyond the identical-case paradigm requires explicit construction of the generalized synchronization manifold. However, the lack of generally workable methods for non-identical systems has limited progress. We address this gap by deriving time-dependent partial differential equations whose stationary solutions coincide exactly with the generalized synchronization manifold and encode its stability properties. We introduce a robust numerical framework that resolves subtle boundary condition challenges inherent to manifold computation, enabling accurate and stable solution of the governing PDE. In addition, we develop first-order perturbative expansions around the identical-case limit, providing analytic insight and computational acceleration when systems are close but not equal. The methodology is demonstrated across examples of increasing complexity, including coupled non-identical Van der Pol oscillators, where the computed manifolds are validated against direct simulations and stability diagnostics. Using the manifold equation, we further show how to design coupling to achieve target synchronization relationships, thereby turning synchronization from a passive observation into an active control objective. Our approach establishes a practical route to computing generalized synchronization manifolds in heterogeneous networks, broadens stability analysis beyond the identity manifold, and offers principled guidelines for the synthesis of coupling in complex, coupled dynamical systems.

Using three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations in the anelastic approximation, we investigate buoyant magnetic flux tubes rising through a stratified model convection zone under solar rotation. We examine the dynamic evolution of an Omega-loop over a range of initial axial field strengths and rotation rates, isolating the role of the Coriolis force in the absence of imposed convective motions. The simulations show that solar rotation suppresses fragmentation at the loop apex during ascent, promoting coherent emergence. Lowering the initial axial field similarly reduces apex fragmentation when convective forcing is absent, indicating a nonlinear coupling between buoyancy, magnetic tension, and rotational deflection. Rotation also slows the rise speed of the tube and drives a retrograde flow that permeates both magnetized core plasma and surrounding unmagnetized material within the emerging active region. We predict that this flow will appear to originate at the leading polarity and terminate at the trailing polarity, providing a diagnostic signature of rotational modulation during flux emergence.

We investigate the hadronic production of the @xmath0 state in the reactions @xmath1, @xmath2, and @xmath3, with the aim of providing inputs for transport and statistical analyses of the @xmath0 meson abundance in heavy ion collisions. Our framework treats @xmath4 as a loosely bound hadronic molecule composed of @xmath5, @xmath6, and @xmath7, and employs effective field Lagrangians consistent with the symmetries and couplings expected for open-charm mesons. For processes that involve @xmath8 meson(s), we demonstrate that an anomalous vertex, @xmath9, plays a crucial role. This vertex is derived from triangular loop mechanisms that naturally arise from the molecular structure of @xmath0 and encapsulate short-distance effects in an effective coupling. We compute the amplitudes and cross sections for the above reactions at tree level supplemented by the loop-induced @xmath9 contribution. For the reaction @xmath2, we find that diagrams containing the @xmath9 vertex provide a dominant or at least a substantial enhancement over nonanomalous contributions across a broad kinematic range. Using these results, we extract an effective coupling for @xmath9, obtaining @xmath10, and employ it to predict the cross section for @xmath3, where the @xmath9 vertex is again found to be phenomenologically significant. We further analyze the impact of the charged components of @xmath4 on the couplings and cross sections, showing that their inclusion modifies both normalization and energy dependence, with implications for @xmath0 yields in the hadronic phase of heavy ion collisions.

I investigate whether non-isothermal MOND models, represented by high-order polytropic spheres, can reproduce the observed radial profile of line-of-sight velocity dispersion in the globular cluster NGC 2419. By constructing models and comparing their kinematic predictions with data, I show that MOND solutions exist and fit the dispersion profile without fine tuning. This finding undermines claims that NGC 2419 poses a challenge to MOND. More broadly, existence and properties of globular clusters appear more problematic for LCDM than for MOND.

Understanding how thermal undulations renormalize the bending moduli of fluid membranes remains contentious. We revisit this problem with a transfer-matrix framework developed in our preceding study and use it to scrutinize how different statistical measures used to define the partition sum affect large-scale elastic properties. We propose a direct and efficient protocol to determine effective moduli: a membrane is constrained to a weakly curved reference plane, and the excess free energy associated with prescribed reference-plane deformations is used to extract the effective bending rigidity and the effective Gaussian-curvature modulus. Implemented with high-precision transfer-matrix calculations and finite-size scaling, this approach accesses the nonperturbative regime of very flexible membranes. Adopting the local mean-curvature measure, we find that the effective bending rigidity increases with scale, demonstrating thermal stiffening that persists even for small bare rigidity. This result supports the scenario proposed by Pinnow and Helfrich and extends it beyond perturbative limits. By contrast, under the commonly used normal-displacement measure, the bending rigidity softens upon coarse-graining. Incorporating the Gaussian-curvature channel, we further show that the effective Gaussian-curvature modulus remains nearly scale invariant across the explored parameter range, exhibiting only weak renormalization, with its behavior likewise dependent on the chosen statistical measure. Our method provides a direct operational route to effective elastic constants without recourse to correlation-function inversion, clarifies the pivotal role of statistical measure, and offers benchmarks for simulations and guidance for interpreting experiments on highly flexible membranes.

We present a current-noise characterization of circular-pad Schottky barrier diodes incorporating guard rings, fabricated on undoped semi-insulating GaAs (SIU-GaAs) at the University of Glasgow. Noise spectra were recorded under reverse bias for devices with two pad diameters, and supplementary measurements were obtained under forward bias for one device. The spectra exhibit a pronounced excess-noise component with a low-frequency corner below 1 kHz, followed by a frequency-independent (white) region at higher frequencies. The magnitude of the white noise is approximately one-half of that predicted by shot-noise theory based on the measured leakage currents, indicating departures from simple Poissonian transport. A distinct reduction in the noise level near 20 kHz is observed and is attributed to the dielectric relaxation time of the semi-insulating GaAs substrate. The dependence on pad size and bias condition is discussed in terms of leakage pathways and charge trapping/detrapping dynamics moderated by the guard ring geometry. These findings constrain models of noise generation in SI GaAs Schottky detectors and provide guidance for optimizing diode architecture and operating bias to minimize noise in high-resolution radiation detection applications.

We present preliminary measurements of inclusive isolated direct-photon production in proton–antiproton collisions at sqrt(s)=1.96 TeV, using 451 pb^-1 of Run II data collected with the upgraded CDF detector at Fermilab. Differential cross sections are measured versus photon transverse momentum for photons with ET>30 GeV and |eta|<1.0, requiring calorimeter isolation. The results are corrected to the hadron level and compared with next-to-leading-order perturbative QCD predictions, exhibiting overall consistency within experimental and theoretical uncertainties and constraining global parton distributions.

We compute stellar evolutionary models over the mass range characteristic of Cepheid variables for several metallicities representative of the Milky Way, Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), and Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). By coupling these tracks to a linear, non-adiabatic pulsation stability analysis, we derive self-consistent mass–period–luminosity relations and instability strip boundaries. We analyze the period–luminosity (PL) relation as a function of metallicity and compare with EROS observations in the Magellanic Clouds. The models reproduce the observed width of the instability strips in both the SMC and LMC. Incorporating evolutionary lifetimes and a Salpeter initial mass function, we construct a statistical PL relation that shows excellent agreement with the SMC PL relation determined by Sasselov et al. (1997). Our models also reproduce the change of slope in the PL relation near a period of about ten days, as reported by the EROS collaboration (Bauer 1997; Bauer et al. 1998), and explain it in evolutionary terms. Some discrepancies persist for LMC Cepheids, possibly linked to metallicity, reddening, depth effects, or convection. The models are consistent with beat Cepheids observed by the MACHO and EROS surveys; most 1O/2O (1H/2H) beat Cepheids have not yet ignited central helium, evolving off the main sequence toward the red giant branch. These results quantify the metallicity dependence of Cepheid PL relations and refine their use as distance indicators. We discuss implications for extragalactic distance scales.

We present a uniform near-infrared spectroscopic study of 41 cataclysmic variables (CVs) to measure donor-star metallicities and key elemental abundances, and to reassess spectral classifications in the presence of accretion-related veiling. Using synthetic spectra spanning 0.8–2.5 μm, we fit temperature-, gravity-, and metallicity-sensitive atomic features (e.g., Na I, Ca I, Fe lines) and molecular bands (notably CO) while accounting for rotational broadening and continuum dilution from accretion light. For systems with K-type donors we determine [Fe/H] directly from the global fits, and for the shortest-period CVs with M-type donors we apply empirical K-band calibrations developed for field M dwarfs to obtain more precise [Fe/H] and effective temperatures. Carbon abundances are inferred from the strengths of the 12CO bandheads, with attention to contamination or masking by CO emission. We find that CV donor stars are, in general, sub-solar in metallicity, with a broad distribution skewed to [Fe/H] < 0. Carbon deficits are common across the sample, corroborating prior indications of C depletion in CV donors and supporting a link to CNO-processed material in the donors’ outer layers. Systems with orbital periods ≲5 hr are the most likely to exhibit unusual abundance patterns, including depressed CO absorption and enhanced Na features. Four CVs show CO in emission, which we identify explicitly; in these objects, emission partially fills in the CO bandheads and complicates direct abundance measurement, implying contributions from the accretion disc or circumbinary gas. Phase-resolved spectra of U Gem allow us to constrain the donor mass and radius and to probe the surface gravity via line profiles. The secondary in U Gem exhibits a lower apparent gravity than a main-sequence star of the same spectral type, consistent with Roche geometry, tidal distortion, and irradiation effects. Extending this insight to the broader sample, we argue that the frequently reported “later-than-expected” spectral types of many CV donors arise primarily from inclination-dependent and gravity/irradiation-driven changes in line depths rather than from extreme intrinsic cooling or anomalous evolution. Among magnetic CVs, all donors except that in the low-accretion-rate polar MQ Dra have subsolar metallicities, implying that subsolar [Fe/H] is not limited to nonmagnetic systems. Two CVs with particularly unusual spectra, EI Psc and QZ Ser, show large sodium excesses together with extreme carbon deficits; synthetic spectra with reduced hydrogen abundance best reproduce their line ratios and continuum shapes, suggesting significant envelope processing or stripping. Our results demonstrate the power of near-infrared spectroscopy and synthetic spectral modeling to disentangle composition, structure, and geometric effects in CV donor stars.

We investigate the impact of supersymmetric (SUSY) threshold corrections on the running quark and charged lepton masses evaluated at the grand unification (GUT) scale in the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) for large tan beta. Beyond the usually dominant SUSY QCD effects for quarks, we include one-loop electroweak thresholds for both quarks and leptons and show that, in the large tan beta regime, they can induce shifts comparable to the gluino–squark contributions. Using two-loop renormalization group evolution with decoupling at the SUSY scale, we present GUT-scale ranges for all quark and charged lepton Yukawa couplings and for ratios such as y_tau/y_b, y_mu/y_s, y_e/y_d, and y_t/y_b, for three regions of SUSY parameters consistent with current constraints. The enlarged and shifted ranges relative to naïve extrapolations have important implications for GUT flavor model building, relaxing or reshaping traditional relations (e.g. third-family Yukawa unification and Georgi–Jarlskog factors) and opening new viable textures for fermion masses and mixings. We provide numerical ranges and assess dependence on the SUSY spectrum, threshold scales, and low-energy inputs.

Newton-Okounkov convex bodies assign convex geometry to projective varieties via valuations on their homogeneous coordinate rings, bridging algebraic geometry and representation theory. Classical examples include Littelmann string polytopes and Feigin-Fourier-Littelmann-Vinberg polytopes. In this paper we identify, for each Schubert variety and a specific valuation arising from a choice of reduced word, the associated Newton-Okounkov convex body with the Nakashima-Zelevinsky polyhedral realization of the corresponding Demazure crystal. The proof combines valuation-theoretic constructions on rational function fields with crystal and PBW-type parametrizations. As an application, we show that Kashiwara's involution (the star-operation) is realized as a change of valuation, yielding a geometric interpretation of crystal duality and links between toric degenerations, Demazure characters, and convex bodies.

We propose a probabilistic framework for the mutual dynamics of tectonic plates, modeling stick–slip interactions as a Markov random process at the micro level. A scaling limit yields a macroscopic description by a system of integro-differential equations that defines a mean-field regime for stress transfer and rupture statistics. Within this mean-field formulation, we derive explicit conditions under which the Gutenberg–Richter empirical law emerges, specifying parameter ranges and invariants that control event-size distributions. These conditions are shown to be robust and largely independent of the detailed form of resistant forces, highlighting universal mechanisms behind seismic scaling behaviors.

We report the identification of a previously unknown radial migration mechanism arising from the overlap of spiral and bar resonances in galactic discs. Using high-resolution N-body simulations and analytical arguments, we show that this process drives angular-momentum exchange far more efficiently than transient spiral scattering. Because resonance overlap is unavoidable in barred galaxies, including the Milky Way, it induces rapid, large-scale redistribution of stars and gas. The predicted consequences are a strong flattening of the disc metallicity gradient, an extended surface density profile, and the swift emergence of a thick-disc component, all developing within only a few gigayears. Such short timescales challenge conventional expectations and impose stringent constraints on the longevity, strength, and pattern speeds of bars and spiral structure in disc galaxies.

We present a multi-epoch, multi-frequency study of the parsec-scale structural variability of the broad-line radio galaxy 3C 111 in connection with its major 2007 radio flux-density outburst. We combine Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) 15 GHz imaging from MOJAVE with contemporaneous single-dish monitoring from UMRAO (4.8–14.5 GHz) and the F-GAMMA program (cm–mm bands with the Effelsberg 100 m and IRAM 30 m). VLBA visibilities are modeled with circular Gaussian components to trace the kinematics of distinct features. The outburst is accompanied by a pronounced brightening of the VLBI core and the emergence of a new superluminal disturbance whose epoch of ejection is consistent, within uncertainties, with the onset of the high-frequency flux rise. Downstream, the disturbance evolves into a leading, high-brightness component followed by a chain of trailing features with progressively lower apparent speeds and flux densities. The separation of these components increases quasi-linearly with time, indicative of ballistic motion of the leading feature, while the trajectories and flux evolution of the trailing features suggest interactions with standing recollimation structures and/or the growth of Kelvin–Helmholtz instabilities. The radio spectra and time lags across cm–mm bands display the frequency-stratified behavior expected from the shock-in-jet scenario, with higher-frequency peaks preceding those at longer wavelengths and a gradual spectral softening as the disturbance propagates. Polarization monitoring reveals rotations and increases in fractional polarization temporally associated with the ejection, consistent with magnetic-field compression and ordering at the shock front. Taken together, the kinematic, spectral, and polarimetric signatures link the 2007 flux-density outburst in 3C 111 to the launch of a strong disturbance from the VLBI core and the subsequent formation of a leading component with multiple trailing components, providing a coherent picture of energy release, shock evolution, and jet–flow coupling on parsec scales.

We present a comprehensive, volume-limited census of dwarf galaxies in and around the Local Group, collating positional, structural, and dynamical parameters for systems with secure distance estimates placing them within 3 Mpc of the Sun. The sample comprises over one hundred nearby galaxies spanning diverse environments: satellites of the Milky Way (MW) and M31, quasi-isolated dwarfs in the outer Local Group regions, and numerous isolated galaxies in its immediate surroundings. The survey extends to, but does not include, members of the next-nearest groupings such as Maffei, Sculptor, and IC 342. We assemble distances (primarily from TRGB, Cepheids, RR Lyrae), systemic velocities (optical spectroscopy and H I 21 cm), magnitudes in standard photometric bands, mean stellar metallicities (spectroscopic and photometric), and structural and dynamical quantities including half-light radius, ellipticity, central surface brightness, dispersion/rotation profiles, gas content, and dynamical-to-stellar mass ratios. Parameters are homogenized onto common distance and photometric scales, with consistent extinction corrections and velocity frame transformations, and are presented in tables intended as a continually updated online resource. We discuss the provenance of each measurement and assess key uncertainties arising from distance zero-points, reddening and crowding, low-surface-brightness selection effects, membership contamination, and kinematic biases. The membership and spatial extent of the MW and M31 sub-groups and of the Local Group are explored using three-dimensional positions and velocities relative to the Local Group barycenter, including assessments of binding and the location of the zero-velocity surface. The morphological diversity of the sample—encompassing dSph, dE, dIrr, transition types, and ultra-faint dwarfs—is characterized, and environmental trends in gas content and star formation are identified. We derive characteristic timescales for Local Group members in the context of their orbital and interaction histories (infall, pericenter passages, quenching delays, and tidal heating). Scaling relations and metallicity trends (luminosity–metallicity, size–luminosity, surface brightness–magnitude, gas fraction vs environment) are presented, and the origin of a possible “floor” in central surface brightness—and, more speculatively, mean stellar metallicity—at faint magnitudes is considered in light of reionization feedback, stochastic enrichment, and detection biases. Existing and forthcoming facilities will markedly refine this picture, enabling increasingly precise constraints on dwarf galaxy formation and evolution.

The equation of state (EoS) of dark energy, @xmath0, remains poorly constrained despite extensive observational campaigns, yet it is central to understanding cosmic acceleration. We propose a new, independent method to measure the dark energy EoS by exploiting gravitational waves from binaries of supermassive black holes (SBHs). Although individual black holes accrete dark energy at an exceedingly slow rate, in a compact binary the gravitational-wave luminosity depends sensitively on the component masses and orbital separation, so even minute, coherent mass drifts imprint detectable signatures on the orbital evolution and waveform. We show that the dark-energy–induced correction to the inspiral is directly proportional to @xmath1 and becomes dominant for SBH binaries with separations of order @xmath2 parsec, where it competes with or exceeds the standard radiation-reaction term. For quintessence-like dark energy (@xmath3), accretion increases the chirp mass and accelerates coalescence; for phantom dark energy (@xmath4), effective mass loss can drive outward migration and even disrupt the binary before merger. These effects produce characteristic, cumulative modifications to the phase evolution, chirp-mass drift, and potentially eccentricity, offering multiple, cross-checkable observables. The resulting signatures are accessible to LISA during the long inspiral of massive binaries and to ground-based detectors such as LIGO near merger, and can be further constrained through electromagnetic timing of periodic X-ray and radio variability with Chandra and VLBA. This approach provides a standard-siren–like probe that is insensitive to inhomogeneous large-scale structures and complements galaxy surveys and supernovae. Joint GW–EM analyses can mitigate astrophysical environmental systematics, opening a path to competitive, model-independent constraints on @xmath0 and its time variation.

We present a new framework for modeling gravitational microlensing events that uses Monte Carlo simulations to sample Galactic phase-space and lens-source populations while enforcing the empirical constraints of each observed light curve. By marginalizing over physically motivated priors and survey selection effects, the method provides an unbiased inference of event parameters even when the light curve leaves them poorly constrained. We apply the technique to OGLE-2003-BLG-423, a single-lens event with the highest recorded maximum magnification, and derive posterior distributions for the lens mass, distance, and relative proper motion. Crucially, we translate sensitivity to companions into the planet mass versus projected physical separation plane, rather than the traditional mass-ratio versus Einstein-radius plane. This yields detection-efficiency maps: for main-sequence hosts, Jupiter-mass companions at 2.5 AU are excluded with 80% efficiency. Our approach enables robust, interpretable constraints on planetary companions and provides a template for analyzing future extreme-magnification events.

We examined whether Co ions crystallographically substitute for Ti sites in rutile and anatase Ti1−xCoxO2 thin films that exhibit room-temperature ferromagnetism. Synchrotron X-ray diffraction was performed while scanning the incident energy across the Co absorption edge, and the intensities of selected Bragg reflections were monitored to detect anomalous dispersion of the Co atomic scattering factor. If Co randomly occupied Ti sites, the Bragg intensities would show characteristic edge anomalies. However, neither the anatase nor rutile films displayed such anomalies, demonstrating that Co ions in Ti1−xCoxO2 are not located exactly at Ti lattice sites of TiO2. The absence of anomalies is consistent with significant local structural deformation around Co, likely induced by oxygen vacancies, which displace Co from ideal cation positions. As a control, identical measurements on paramagnetic Zn1−xCoxO thin films revealed clear edge anomalies, providing direct evidence that Co substitutes for Zn sites. These findings constrain models of ferromagnetism in Co-doped TiO2.

We investigate the stability of strange quark matter at finite temperature within a quark-mass density- and temperature-dependent framework. We find that negative electric charge and larger strangeness fraction enhance stability. A critical baryon number density, n_c, is identified; strange quark matter becomes unstable for n_B < n_c. We quantify the charge and strangeness-fraction dependence of stability windows and discuss relevant implications for compact-star matter and heavy-ion experimental environments.

We present analysis of HST @xmath0-band imaging for a statistically complete sample of 41 radio galaxies spanning three orders of magnitude in 151-MHz radio luminosity at redshift @xmath1. This study forms the first stage of a coordinated programme designed to probe how radio luminosity relates to host-galaxy structure, stellar content, central black-hole mass, and cluster environment over a wide dynamic range in radio power but a restricted range in redshift. The full sample is drawn from four complete, low-frequency selected surveys with progressively fainter flux-density limits (3CRR, 6CE, 7CRS, and the new TEXOX-1000 sample), enabling robust comparisons across radio-luminosity bins. Two-dimensional modelling of the HST images demonstrates that the host galaxies possess surface-brightness profiles consistent with classic ellipticals, well described by a Sérsic parameter @xmath2, with @xmath3 distributed over @xmath4 and a mean of @xmath5. After corrections for passive evolution, host-galaxy absolute magnitudes are comparable to those of galaxies at the bright end of the local cluster luminosity function, spanning @xmath6 with a mean of @xmath7. The sample follows a Kormendy (@xmath8) relation indistinguishable from that of powerful low-redshift radio galaxies and local Abell brightest cluster galaxies, reaffirming the structural similarity between radio-galaxy hosts and massive ellipticals. Combining our measurements with published datasets shows that the effective scalelengths and Kormendy relations of 3C-class radio galaxies exhibit no significant variation over @xmath9, offering no evidence for dynamical evolution of this host population within this interval. Converting host luminosities into central black-hole masses via the local @xmath10 correlation yields masses in the range @xmath11, with a geometric mean of @xmath12. Finally, for objects classified as high-excitation galaxies (HEG) or exhibiting classical double (CD) radio morphologies, we detect a significant (@xmath13) correlation between black-hole mass and 151-MHz radio luminosity, implying a physical link between the mass of the central engine and the time-averaged radio power. These results establish a coherent baseline for the second stage of the programme, which will connect host-galaxy properties and environments to the accretion and feedback processes that regulate radio-loud AGN activity. Future work will integrate spectroscopy, environmental metrics, and dynamical modelling to refine black-hole mass estimates and to test whether the observed scalings persist across wider ranges in redshift and radio luminosity. These insights provide boundary conditions for models of jet launching.

We used the VLA at 43 GHz to image radio continuum emission from three evolved stars and to register their SiO maser emission relative to the stellar photosphere. The continuum regions for all three targets have diameters close to 5.6 AU, matching infrared sizes measured in bands with strong molecular opacity and exceeding by about a factor of two the diameters in line-free infrared windows. These results indicate that the radio photosphere and the infrared molecular layer are coextensive. The 43 GHz continua imply brightness temperatures near 1600 K and opacities dominated by H- free–free interactions in partially ionized gas. While one object appears nearly circular, the other two show significant elongations. The SiO masers form partial rings with diameters near 8 AU, just outside the radio photosphere, constraining maser pumping and mass-loss initiation.

We develop a microscopic theory of electron spin dephasing in (110)-grown zinc-blende quantum wells when the momentum-scattering time is comparable to, or exceeds, the period of spin precession in the spin-orbit-induced effective magnetic field. We treat both homogeneous and spatially fluctuating Rashba fields that dephase spins oriented along the growth axis, and incorporate the Dresselhaus field. Analytical solutions of kinetic spin Bloch equations reveal that the Dresselhaus field aligns the precession axis and strongly suppresses dephasing, enabling long conduction-electron spin lifetimes. The spin lifetime shows a nonmonotonic dependence on electron mobility, with a pronounced minimum near the crossover omega_SO tau ~ 1 separating diffusive and ballistic regimes. Our theory unifies these limits, quantifies disorder-induced Rashba fluctuations, and provides scaling with temperature, well width, and doping.

In bulk ferroelectric liquid crystals, the molecular director forms a helical twist; in confined geometries the helix can be unwound by an applied electric field or by boundary anchoring. We develop a mesoscale simulation framework based on a continuum free-energy functional discretized on a two-dimensional lattice to quantify helix unwinding as a function of field and confinement. The model resolves the director profile across the cell and computes the net electrostatic polarization. By varying cell thickness and anchoring strength, we identify how boundary effects shift the critical unwinding field and reduce the saturation polarization. The predicted polarization-field curves agree with experimental measurements, informing device design and improved operational performance.

Giant molecular clouds (GMCs), the primary sites of star formation, may arise from self-gravitating instabilities within the turbulent, magnetized interstellar medium. We use local, three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations to explore how galactic turbulence driven by the magnetorotational instability (MRI) influences the emergence and properties of massive, self-gravitating clouds. Our vertically stratified disk models incorporate both gaseous and stellar gravity and are subject to uniform shear consistent with a flat rotation curve. We initialize the magnetic field as weak and purely vertical, and adopt an isothermal equation of state. MRI-driven turbulence develops rapidly in all models, reaching a saturated state in which the Shakura–Sunyaev parameter is dominated by Maxwell stresses. Dimensionless characteristics of the turbulence, including the ratio of Maxwell to Reynolds stresses and the relative amplitudes of magnetic and kinetic fluctuations, agree closely with previous MRI studies of accretion disks and are largely insensitive to vertical compression, shear rate, and the inclusion of self-gravity, although self-gravity modestly enhances fluctuation amplitudes. The density-weighted velocity dispersions in non- or weakly self-gravitating disks are substantial, indicating that MRI can contribute meaningfully to the observed level of galactic interstellar turbulence.
