The saturated magnetic field strengths achieved are comparable to typical galactic values, supporting the relevance of MRI-driven amplification in disk environments. When self-gravity is sufficiently strong, high-amplitude density perturbations generated by MRI are swing-amplified, forming bound clouds with masses near the Jeans scale. Relative to unmagnetized or strongly magnetized disk models, the threshold for nonlinear instability and cloud formation occurs at significantly lower surface densities—by at least 50%—corresponding to a reduced Toomre parameter, thereby making gravitational collapse easier in the presence of MRI turbulence and weak vertical fields. We present evidence that self-gravitating clouds formed under these conditions can shed a large fraction of their original spin angular momentum via magnetic braking, with the most efficient angular momentum loss occurring when the threading magnetic fields are oriented nearly perpendicular to the clouds’ spin axes. We discuss the broader implications for GMC formation pathways, angular momentum regulation, and star-forming efficiencies in galactic disks, and outline directions for future work including non-isothermal physics, feedback, and global disk coupling.

The cutoff phenomenon describes a sharp transition in the convergence of a family of ergodic finite Markov chains to equilibrium. Many natural families of chains are believed to exhibit cutoff, yet establishing it rigorously is often challenging. A central example is the random walk on G(n, d), a random d-regular graph on n vertices. It is well known that almost every such graph for fixed d ≥ 3 is an expander, and even essentially Ramanujan, implying a mixing time of order log n. According to a conjecture of Peres, the simple random walk on G(n, d) should then exhibit cutoff. As a special case, Durrett conjectured that the mixing time of the lazy random walk on a random d-regular graph is asymptotically (d/(d−2)) log_{d−1} n. In this work we confirm these conjectures and establish total-variation cutoff, its precise location, and its optimal window, for both simple and non-backtracking random walks on G(n, d). Specifically, for any fixed d ≥ 3, the simple random walk exhibits cutoff at time (d/(d−2)) log_{d−1} n with window of order √log n, while the non-backtracking random walk exhibits cutoff already at time log_{d−1} n with a constant-order window. We further extend these results to G(n, d) for any d = d(n) growing with n, a regime in which the mixing time becomes O(log n / log d), and, once d grows sufficiently rapidly, becomes O(1). In this growing-degree regime we prove sharp concentration of the mixing time on one of two consecutive integers. Our approach combines precise geometric and spectral analysis of random regular graphs with tree-like local structure, comparison of simple and non-backtracking dynamics, and refined coupling and concentration techniques.

We study continuous opinion dynamics under bounded confidence and show that both the Hegselmann–Krause and Deffuant–Weisbuch models admit representations as nonnegative discrete dynamical systems. For the agent-based variants, we provide a complete characterization of the fixed points and prove that the sets of equilibria coincide across the two models. Moving to a mesoscopic description, we reformulate both dynamics in terms of densities over opinion space via interactive Markov chains governed by a discrete master equation. Within this density-based framework we again characterize all stationary distributions and establish their equivalence for HK and DW. Our results unify two prominent modeling approaches, clarify the structure of consensus and clustering outcomes under bounded confidence, and facilitate rigorous comparison of agent-based and density-based descriptions.

We perform a comprehensive fit of two-Higgs-doublet models with a softly broken Z2 symmetry that suppresses tree-level flavor-changing neutral currents. Confronting four Yukawa realizations with LHC Higgs signal strengths, direct searches, electroweak precision tests, flavor observables, and theoretical consistency conditions, we find that the Type-II interaction pattern yields the best agreement with current data. In the allowed region, the light CP-even Higgs couplings to W and Z bosons are Standard Model-like, with small deviations permitted near the alignment limit. We highlight a tightly constrained parameter space previously overlooked, delineating tan beta and alignment ranges and mass spectra for the additional scalars. Extra Higgs bosons are typically in the few-hundred-GeV regime, with phenomenology dominated by A/H -> tau tau, A -> Zh, H -> hh, and H+/- -> tb or tau nu. We present projections indicating sensitivities at Run 3 and High-Luminosity LHC.

Compact astrophysical objects such as black holes and neutron stars demand Einstein’s theory of general relativity to model their dynamics, yet its governing, coupled, nonlinear, mixed hyperbolic–elliptic partial differential equations pose formidable numerical challenges. Recent advances in parallel supercomputing are reaching the speed and memory needed to solve the full Einstein system, enabling the first comprehensive three-dimensional simulations of phenomena including binary black hole and neutron star collisions. This paper surveys the computational progress toward robust numerical relativity, assessing discretization strategies, constraint enforcement, gauge choices, and parallel scalability. We introduce Cactus, a new 3D, multi-purpose, modular parallel code for general relativistic astrophysics, describe its architecture and validation, and demonstrate initial applications to gravitational-wave source modeling. We conclude with directions for further work in algorithmic accuracy, matter coupling, adaptive refinement, performance, and community-driven software development.

Quantum discord (QD) has emerged as an optimal resource for characterizing both classical and non-classical correlations beyond entanglement, while geometric quantum discord (GQD) offers a complementary, distance-based quantifier. Building on the recent formulation of multipartite GQD by Jianwei Xu [arXiv:quant-ph/1205.0330] and motivated by insights reported for bipartite systems [Ann. Phys. 327 (2012) 851], we investigate the dynamics of global QD and GQD for multipartite Werner-@xmath0 states in the presence of external environments. Specifically, we analyze three-qubit and six-qubit families in both inertial and non-inertial settings under amplitude damping, phase damping, depolarizing, and flipping (bit- and phase-flip) channels. Global discord is evaluated via optimized local measurements on all parties, and GQD via the Hilbert–Schmidt distance to the closest classical–quantum state, allowing us to track their evolution with channel strength and acceleration. Our results reveal distinct robustness regimes and channel-dependent decay laws. For three-qubit Werner-@xmath0 states, QD vanishes at @xmath1, whereas for six-qubit Werner-@xmath0 states it vanishes at @xmath2, indicating that larger multipartite registers are more fragile to decoherence for higher values of @xmath3. A rapid sudden death of discord is observed for the phase-flip channel, while no sudden death occurs for six-qubit states under bit flip. Among the studied noise models, the depolarizing channel exerts the most destructive influence on both QD and GQD, substantially exceeding the impact of amplitude damping. From the perspective of accelerated observers, we find that environmental noise affects QD and GQD much more strongly than the acceleration associated with non-inertial frames. Nevertheless, degradation due to the Unruh effect is discernible and compounds the loss of quantum correlations. Across all scenarios, QD exhibits greater robustness than GQD, underscoring the sensitivity of geometric, norm-based measures to isotropic noise. These findings quantify the interplay between multipartite structure, channel type, and relativistic motion, and inform the design of correlation-preserving strategies and error-mitigation protocols for quantum networks and distributed quantum information processing under realistic noise and acceleration. Keywords: multipartite correlations; GQD; Werner-@xmath0 states; decoherence.

We investigate steady, axisymmetric hydrodynamic accretion onto Kerr black holes as a mechanism for efficiently separating a small population of nonthermal particles from the bulk flow via standing dissipative shocks. In this framework, shocks are permitted to be radiatively and mechanically lossy: a finite fraction of the upstream mass, energy, and angular momentum fluxes does not participate in the downstream accretion but is diverted into outflows, either collimated (jets) or uncollimated (winds). Using general relativistic conservation laws in Kerr spacetime and shock jump conditions augmented by sink terms, we map the parameter space for shock formation as a function of the upstream specific energy and angular momentum and the black hole spin, and we quantify the associated mass- and energy-loss fractions at the shock. We find that the fraction of mass lost at the shock can vary over a wide range, controlled primarily by the angular momentum and energy of the incoming flow and by frame-dragging in the Kerr metric. In contrast, the energy-loss fraction is typically modest for accretion onto a non-rotating (Schwarzschild) black hole but can increase by roughly an order of magnitude for accretion onto a rapidly rotating Kerr black hole. By estimating the escape condition for the outflowing material and adopting mass accretion rates relevant to active galactic nuclei, we infer that on the order of 10% of the accreting mass can be redirected into outflows in disks around non-rotating black holes, whereas as much as about 50% may contribute to outflows in disks around rapidly rotating black holes. These results support a disk–jet paradigm in which shock-driven outflows are launched at radii not far from the central engine. The shock front provides a plausible site where nonthermal seed particles are efficiently decoupled from the bulk accretion stream, supplying the initial particle population for jets and winds and linking black hole spin and accretion dynamics to outflow efficiency.

We present an analytical framework for the quasistatic evolution of starless cores subject to a constant external pressure, assuming isothermal conditions and spherical symmetry. Core structure is represented with Plummer-like and Gaussian density profiles, and evolution is explored in both isothermal and adiabatic limits. Turbulent support is treated with Larson-like dissipation, adopting a size–linewidth relation whose index we vary to assess its impact on core trajectories. We derive the radius dependence of the terms in the scalar virial equation—thermal, turbulent, magnetic, external pressure, and self-gravity—and use these to diagnose whether cores evolve toward virial equilibrium or proceed to gravitational collapse. Accretion onto cores is neglected to isolate the internal energy balance and external confinement. We propose a practical parameterization for the magnetic energy contribution based on dimensionless measures of magnetization, facilitating incorporation into analytic virial budgets across core sizes. The resulting evolutionary tracks are mapped into the virial plane to distinguish regimes of pressure confinement, virial binding, and gravitational dominance. Applying the model to the set of L1688 Ophiuchus cores observed by @xcite, we find that not all virially bound, pressure-confined cores inevitably become gravitationally bound. Instead, many contract while asymptotically approaching virial equilibrium with their surroundings. We identify an absence of gravitationally dominated yet virially unbound cores, motivating a hypothesized “starless core desert” in this quadrant of the virial plane, potentially reflecting initial formation under dominant external pressure. Comparing isothermal and adiabatic cases reveals distinct evolutionary behaviors and sensitivity to the adopted size–linewidth index, with stronger turbulence dissipation pushing cores toward pressure–thermal balance rather than collapse. We conclude that a virially bound, pressure-confined core cannot be deemed prestellar by virial criteria alone; only cores that are gravitationally unstable are definitively prestellar and destined for collapse into individual stellar systems. Implications for core lifetimes and star formation efficiency are discussed.

We derive a spacetime formulation of quantum general relativity directly from the Hamiltonian framework of loop quantum gravity. We study the proper-time quantum propagator that evolves 3-geometry, and establish a perturbative expansion that is finite and computable order by order. By introducing a Feynman-like graphical calculus, we express the full amplitude as a sum over topologically inequivalent, branched, colored two-dimensional surfaces embedded in four dimensions. Each surface contributes a weight given by the product of local factors associated with its branching points, which thereby play the role of elementary interaction vertices. These vertex factors are determined by known matrix elements of the Hamiltonian constraint, providing a nonperturbative definition of the dynamics. The resulting continuum framework can be regarded as the continuum limit of Reisenberger’s simplicial quantum gravity, and it shares the algebraic structure of the Ooguri–Crane–Yetter four-dimensional topological field theory, while exhibiting key departures that clarify how quantum gravity extends beyond topological models. In particular, we identify modifications to the Hamiltonian constraint required to implement a crossing symmetry closely tied to four-dimensional diffeomorphism invariance. Our construction offers a concrete bridge between canonical loop quantum gravity and spacetime covariant formulations, furnishes calculable transition amplitudes, and suggests new avenues for relating quantum gravity to topological quantum field theory.

We examine in detail one member of a previously proposed family of central engines for cosmic gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), in which a steadily accreting, strongly magnetized white dwarf collapses to a rapidly and differentially rotating neutron star. For an accreting white dwarf with an evolved O–Ne–Mg composition, collapse to a millisecond-period neutron star occurs across a wide range of steady accretion rates and initial masses. A similar outcome is possible for an initial C–O white dwarf, but only within more constrained accretion regimes. Because the collapsing progenitor begins as a polytrope, the nascent neutron star inherits a pronounced increase of spin frequency with cylindrical radius, establishing strong differential rotation. This shear stably winds the star’s poloidal magnetic field into intense toroidal configurations. The resulting magnetic toroids become buoyant, grow, detach, and rise to partially penetrate the neutron star surface, transiently forming a millisecond pulsar with an extremely strong surface field and a powerful pulsar wind. As the emergent magnetic structures are sheared by the star’s differential rotation, the wind is rapidly suppressed. The wind-up, breakout, and quenching processes can recur on different cylindrical surfaces and may repeat on the same one, with characteristic wind-up and penetration times much longer than the neutron star’s millisecond spin period. In this way, differential rotation intermittently “opens” and “closes” channels through which spin energy is released, naturally producing episodic bursts of magnetized outflow. The predicted properties of this engine—total energy budget, burst durations, sub-burst variability on multiple time scales, event-to-event diversity tied to accretion history and composition, and minimal baryon loading owing to magnetically dominated winds—compare favorably with observational requirements for GRB sources. This model thus provides a physically motivated, temporally structured mechanism for converting neutron star rotational energy into the powerful, intermittent outflows that characterize GRBs.

We present a new technique to analyze the stopping time of gossip protocols based on random linear network coding (RLNC). Our method yields a unified, simple analysis that drastically simplifies, extends, and strengthens prior results across a broad spectrum of network and communication models. Within a framework that subsumes the models previously studied, we show that RLNC gossip converges with high probability in the information-theoretically optimal time in most settings. In particular, we prove that typical stopping times take the form @xmath0, where @xmath1 is the number of messages to be disseminated and @xmath2 is the time required to disseminate one message, establishing that RLNC gossip attains perfect pipelining. The analysis applies verbatim to highly dynamic networks whose topology may change arbitrarily at any time step, even under a fully adaptive adversary with complete knowledge of the system state. Prior work offered virtually no guarantees beyond simple @xmath3 sequential flooding in such adversarially dynamic environments. In contrast, our approach yields high-probability bounds with minimal assumptions and a proof that remains identical across models, avoiding the intricate, case-specific arguments used to obtain weaker conclusions in special cases. These results clarify the efficiency of RLNC gossip and provide a toolset for reasoning about coded dissemination in static, stochastic, and adversarially evolving networks.

We present infrared He I 10830 Å observations from Keck/NIRSPEC and IRTF/CSHELL, combined with far-ultraviolet C III 977 Å and O VI 1032 Å spectra from FUSE, for the classical T Tauri stars TW Hydrae and T Tauri N. The He I and FUV lines exhibit P Cygni profiles, asymmetries, and blueshifted absorption that diagnose a continuous, accelerating outflow reaching ~400 km s^-1 at chromospheric to transition-region temperatures. Line opacity and profile modeling imply a mass-loss rate of at least ~10^-10 solar masses per year. Constraints indicate that the emission and outflow originate in the stellar atmosphere rather than the circumstellar disk. Despite a lower accretion rate in TW Hydrae than in T Tau, its wind attains higher velocities. These results suggest that winds from young stars are substantially hotter and faster than previously assumed.

We investigate production of @xmath0 (and @xmath1) pairs in proton–proton collisions at @xmath2 = 7 TeV, motivated by LHCb measurements. We consider double-parton scattering (DPS) mechanisms of double @xmath3 production with subsequent @xmath4 hadronization, as well as DPS topologies involving double @xmath5 and mixed @xmath6 channels with @xmath7 and @xmath8 hadronization, evaluated using the scale-dependent hadronization functions of Kniehl et al. The single-parton scattering (SPS) digluon mechanism is also included. Predictions are confronted with LHCb correlation observables in the azimuthal angle @xmath9 between @xmath10 mesons and in the dimeson invariant mass @xmath11. The addition of the new mechanisms with @xmath12 fragmentation increases the total and differential cross sections relative to calculations limited to DPS @xmath4 with scale-independent fragmentation functions, and modifies the shapes of the @xmath9 and @xmath11 distributions. We discuss phenomenological consequences, including implications for the extraction of DPS parameters. In particular, a larger @xmath13 is required to reproduce the LHCb data, and indications are found that @xmath13 may depend on the transverse momentum of @xmath14 quarks and/or @xmath15 antiquarks. Prospects for disentangling the competing mechanisms and for future measurements are outlined.

We study affine isometries of three–dimensional Minkowski space with hyperbolic linear part and their Margulis invariant, which records signed Lorentzian displacement along an invariant spacelike line. A constant sign of the invariant across a group is a necessary condition for a proper action. We prove that, when the linear part is the fundamental group of a punctured torus, positivity of the Margulis invariant on any finite generating set does not guarantee properness. We construct explicit families of affine deformations with positive invariants on generators but negative values on longer words, yielding nonproper actions. This contrasts with the pair-of-pants case, where checking a specific triple of generators suffices to ensure properness thereby.

We develop a recent theory for the ordered phase of helical and chiral magnets, exemplified by MnSi, to derive observable consequences of the helical Goldstone modes (“helimagnons”). In clean systems without quenched disorder, helimagnons produce a linear-in-temperature contribution to the specific-heat coefficient, while the quasiparticle inelastic scattering rate is strongly anisotropic in momentum space and depends sensitively on the electronic dispersion. For cubic lattices, the resulting thermodynamics and transport display generic non-Fermi-liquid power laws. Within a Boltzmann treatment, the helimagnon contribution to the resistivity follows a characteristic subquadratic temperature dependence. These modes therefore generate nonanalytic corrections to conventional Fermi-liquid behavior. We discuss implications for experiments on MnSi and related compounds, identify key signatures across thermodynamic and spectroscopic probes, and outline consequences for transport theories beyond Boltzmann, including constraints on more microscopic approaches.

We present numerical simulations exploring the dynamical evolution of cuspy triaxial elliptical galaxies hosting growing central black holes. Unlike earlier work based on cored density profiles, our initial models possess steep central cusps consistent with observations. As the black hole mass increases, we track orbital families and quantify the onset of chaos and shape changes via axis ratios. We find that black hole growth drives substantial roundening of the inner regions by converting box and boxlet orbits into chaotic trajectories that avoid the center, thereby diluting triaxiality. This transformation extends beyond the nominal sphere of influence but proceeds gradually and saturates at radii where the potential remains dominated by the stellar cusp. At larger radii, the models retain triaxiality; centrophilic orbits there remain regular and resist diffusion over dynamical times. No rapid global reshaping to axisymmetry is observed. These results reconcile the triaxiality of elliptical galaxies with the presence of supermassive black holes, constraining coevolution scenarios and the efficiency of black hole–driven evolution.

We present the in-flight technical and operational performance of the Far-Infrared Surveyor (FIS), one of two focal-plane instruments aboard the AKARI satellite. FIS provides four photometric bands centered at 65, 90, 140, and 160 μm, employing two types of cryogenic array detectors integrated with optics designed for wide-area sky surveys with high spatial resolution and redundancy. The instrument scans with a width exceeding eight arcminutes, and the pixel pitch closely matches the telescope’s diffraction limit, enabling efficient mapping. Point-spread functions (PSFs) derived from asteroid observations agree well with the optical model in core shape and width; however, excess power is observed in the PSF wings and tails, contributing approximately 30% of the total flux. Overall, all FIS subsystems operate nominally in orbit, and performance metrics are consistent with laboratory characterization, with the exception of the two longer-wavelength bands, which underperform relative to pre-flight expectations. In addition to photometry, FIS includes a Fourier Transform Spectrometer (FTS) that leverages the photometer optics and detector arrays to obtain simultaneous spectral maps. We outline calibration strategies, stability, and data products, and discuss implications for survey science and spectroscopy with FIS.

We investigate the thermodynamic and cosmological implications of the Magueijo–Smolin formulation of doubly special relativity (DSR) with an invariant Planck energy scale. By reinterpreting the DSR energy-momentum relation in a thermal background, we derive an explicit temperature dependence of the speed of light, c(T), across the expansion history of the universe. Building on this framework, we assess the evolution of other universal constants as functions of the background temperature, including Planck’s constant h, the elementary charge e, and the fine-structure constant α. We find that both h and e were significantly larger in the early universe, while the combination defining α remains invariant over cosmic time. The resulting constancy of α is consistent with laboratory bounds, astrophysical spectroscopy, and cosmological probes, and places constraints on permissible temperature-driven variations of dimensionful constants.

Cellular traffic offloading onto wireless local area networks (WLANs) is theoretically evaluated using spatial models grounded in recent empirical deployments. We analyze datasets of Internet access point locations and observe pronounced heterogeneity across urban fabrics. Motivated by these observations, we propose an inhomogeneous Poisson process with high-, normal-, and low-density subregions, with exclusion zones where AP placement is prohibited, as a spatial point-process model for WLAN configurations. Leveraging integral geometry (geometric probability), we derive closed-form expressions for performance metrics, including mean available user bandwidth and the expected number of vertical handovers (handoffs) between cellular and WLAN coverage. The formulas account for numerous parameters: the number and spatial distribution of APs, the shape of each WLAN coverage region, AP locations, WLAN bandwidth (bps), and the shape and available bandwidth (bps) of cellular subregions indexed by the channel quality indicator (CQI). A salient outcome is that the distribution of experienced bandwidth is effectively insensitive to user mobility. The bandwidth available to a stationary user and to a moving user are shown to be identical or approximately identical in distribution under broad conditions, explaining why mobility does not materially affect offload capacity in the proposed framework. Numerical examples and sensitivity studies reveal that design parameters—particularly the size of AP-forbidden regions and the mean AP intensity in high-density subregions—exert substantial influence on both bandwidth and handover metrics. Moreover, adopting a homogeneous Poisson process as the AP-location model substantially overestimates performance: the mean available bandwidth and vertical handover counts are inflated, with bandwidth overestimation reaching approximately 50% under representative scenarios. These findings underscore the importance of spatial heterogeneity in offload planning, performance evaluation, and practical network planning. Keywords: offload, performance evaluation, spatial characterization of network, access point configuration, spatial point process, inhomogeneous Poisson process, integral geometry (geometric probability), cellular network (mobile network), wireless LAN, internet access, handover (handoff), coverage.

We present a new calibration of the radio surface brightness–diameter (Sigma–D) relation for Galactic C- and S-type supernova remnants (SNRs). To construct a robust Sigma–D dependence, we assembled a calibrator sample comprising remnants with relatively reliable distance estimates and excluded F-type objects, as well as the S-type remnant Cassiopeia A whose exceptionally high surface brightness would bias the fit. The calibration integrates both intrinsic parameters (e.g., explosion energy) and extrinsic environmental factors (e.g., ambient medium density), informed by a comprehensive assessment of values reported in the literature. The resulting relation is best described by a broken power law with a turning point at D ≈ 36.5 pc. In the small-diameter regime (D ≤ 36.5 pc), the fit yields a steeper slope; in the large-diameter regime (D ≥ 36.5 pc), the slope is significantly shallower, consistent with evolutionary changes in shock dynamics, magnetic field amplification, and particle acceleration efficiency. We discuss the theoretical basis for the Sigma–D dependence and identify physical drivers for the change in slope at the break, including transitions between evolutionary phases and ambient density effects. Complementing this, we derive the radio luminosity–diameter relation and find it to be nearly flat (slope close to zero) up to D ≈ 36.5 pc, implying roughly size-independent radio luminosity for younger, smaller remnants. Finally, we provide adopted distances and diameters for all observed Galactic SNRs, synthesizing literature constraints with values inferred from our calibrated Sigma–D relation, thereby offering a consistent distance scale to support demographic, evolutionary, and energetics studies of the Galactic SNR population.

We investigate the spatial organization and velocity fluctuations of non-Brownian spherical particles settling at low Reynolds number in a vertical Hele–Shaw cell. Experiments span particle volume fractions 0.005–0.05 and plate spacing 5–15 particle radii. High-resolution particle tracking shows that particles do not remain uniformly distributed; instead they assemble into transient, gravitationally driven settling clusters. The cluster population statistics follow an exponential distribution, indicating a memoryless aggregation process and turnover. Measured velocity fluctuations scale with cluster size and agree quantitatively with predictions for spherical clusters obtained by balancing apparent weight against viscous drag. The consistency between theory and experiment implicates clustering, rather than random independent spatial arrangements, as the dominant origin of velocity fluctuations in confined sedimenting suspensions. These findings constrain models of suspension hydrodynamics and sedimentation in porous or slit-like geometries.

This review surveys recent advances in spin-dependent transport in magnetic nanostructures, emphasizing spin accumulation and spin currents generated by spin injection into nonmagnetic metals, semiconductors, and superconductors. We discuss tunneling and interfacial engineering, and propose novel phenomena in nano superconductor/ferromagnet hybrids that probe spin–charge separation in superconductors. Mechanisms of spin polarized transport, relaxation, and conversion are examined, highlighting experimental techniques and theoretical frameworks guiding device design and performance. PACS: 72.25Ba, 72.25Hg, 72.25Mk, 73.40Gk.

If @xmath2 initially exceeds @xmath6, the @xmath5 mode may be excited but will decay once @xmath2 drops below @xmath6, which occurs within @xmath7 for a saturation amplitude @xmath8. These results imply that @xmath0-mode activity strongly influences magnetic field topology, constrains the r-mode instability window, and impacts spin evolution and gravitational-wave emission from young and accreting neutron stars.

We report photoactivation measurements of the @xmath0Au@xmath1 reaction at the ELBE superconducting electron accelerator using bremsstrahlung with endpoint energies between 8.0 and 15.5 MeV. The activation yields were determined and compared to previous experimental data and to predictions from Hauser–Feshbach statistical calculations. A satisfactory reproduction of the energy dependence and magnitude of the yields is achieved when employing a two-Lorentzian parametrization of the dipole strength, explicitly accounting for the axial deformation of @xmath0Au. The ELBE activation yields agree within uncertainties with results obtained via photon scattering and neutron detection techniques, confirming the robustness of the activation standard over the investigated energy range. These findings support the reliability of @xmath0Au@xmath1 as a benchmark for photodisintegration studies of astrophysically relevant nuclei.

We report the discovery, in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the SDSS-III Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey, of a rare population of 17 broad absorption line (BAL) quasars that exhibit high-ionization absorption troughs redshifted with respect to the quasar rest frame. In these objects the redshifted absorption extends to large positive velocities and the trough widths exceed 3000 km s-1 in all but one case. A statistical assessment of the parent BAL quasar population shows that approximately 1 in 1000 quasars with the usual blueshifted C IV absorption also displays redshifted C IV absorption, while systems showing C IV absorption only at redshifted velocities are roughly four times rarer still. More than half of the sample exhibits redshifted absorption in low-ionization species (C II or Al III) in addition to C IV, implying that low-ionization absorption is at least an order of magnitude more prevalent among BAL quasars with redshifted troughs than among standard BAL quasars. Despite this enhanced incidence of low-ionization features, the C IV absorption equivalent widths in our objects are, on average, smaller than those measured in canonical low-ionization BAL quasars. We evaluate several mechanisms capable of producing redshifted absorption. Two scenarios appear most promising and may operate either simultaneously or in different objects. First, rotationally dominated outflows viewed against an extended accretion-disk continuum can generate both redshifted and blueshifted troughs; however, multi-epoch spectroscopy available for four sources reveals variability consistent with this picture in only one case. Second, the infall of relatively dense, low-ionization gas to radii as small as ~400 Schwarzschild radii can reproduce the observed diversity of trough profiles, although current models struggle to account for the origin and long-term survival of such gas near the central engine. Regardless of the detailed mechanism, the large redshifted velocities require that the absorbing material resides at small radii, offering a novel observational probe of the inner regions of quasars and motivating future time-domain and high-resolution spectroscopic studies. Keywords: galaxies: nuclei; quasars: general; quasars: absorption lines.

We search for the lepton-flavor-violating decay of @xmath0 into an electron and a muon using @xmath1 @xmath0 events collected with the BESIII detector at BEPCII. Four candidate events are seen in the signal region, consistent with background. No significant excess is observed. Accounting for systematic uncertainties, we set a 90% C.L. upper limit on the branching fraction @xmath2.

Proteins adopt a limited repertoire (~1000) of structural folds, hypothesized to be selected for intrinsic designability and unusual stability. We examine this designability principle using a two-dimensional hydrophobic–polar lattice model to classify folds by designability, and Langevin dynamics to track their time evolution under thermal fluctuations. Across the full ensemble of possible folds, we find that highly designable structures, despite their thermodynamic preference, unfold more readily due to an abundance of surface–core contacts that serve as rupture-prone interfaces. These results reconcile structural selection with mechanical fragility and suggest designability entails specific topological bond patterns governing folding–unfolding behavior.

For both models we identify all cluster types of sizes @xmath8 formed by random dilution and express their occurrence statistics with perimeter polynomials specific to each cluster topology. All cluster types with sizes @xmath9 are shown to produce MSTs via field-induced level crossings of finite antiferromagnetic clusters. From these ingredients we compute isothermal magnetization curves @xmath10 as functions of @xmath1 for widely differing ratios @xmath11 and examine their sensitivity to dilution and temperature. To convey the step structure more directly, we analyze derivative curves, @xmath12 versus @xmath1, and define the “MST spectrum” as the resulting series of peaks. Each peak can be assigned to a specific cluster type and transition, allowing a detailed spectral decomposition of the total magnetization. The spectrum simplifies markedly when @xmath11 is very small, where the exchange-bond structure effectively reduces to dominant @xmath2-bonded clusters weakly perturbed by @xmath3, leading to grouped or unsplit peaks; this limit and its spectral signatures are elaborated in a companion paper.
