The growing interest in nanoparticles has intensified the demand for rapid, non-destructive characterization methods. While powder diffraction offers simplicity and efficiency, its application to ultrafine particles challenges traditional crystallographic assumptions. This study critically evaluates powder pattern diffraction techniques for spherical nanoparticles with log-normal size distributions, focusing on accurate size parameter extraction. A 20-nm CeO2 sample is analyzed to demonstrate the limitations and improvements of current methodologies. By addressing size distribution artifacts and peak broadening effects, the work provides a framework to enhance precision in nanomaterial characterization, advancing reliable nanostructure analysis.

In this study, we present an extension of the Camassa-Holm equation, motivated by the foundational work of Beals, Sattinger, and Szmigielski (Adv. Math. 154, 2000), which retains the integrability and multipeakon solution structure while introducing novel analytical insights. The Camassa-Holm equation, a celebrated model for shallow water waves, is known for its peakon solutions—non-smooth solitary waves with discontinuous derivatives. Building on classical determinant techniques, our approach reformulates the equation’s dispersion relation and conservation laws, enabling a systematic derivation of its generalized form. A central contribution of this work is the explicit construction of multipeakon solutions using a determinant-based framework, which provides a transparent algebraic structure for analyzing interactions and stability of these solutions. Unlike standard Camassa-Holm-type equations, the proposed model incorporates a **nonisospectral Lax pair**, where the spectral parameter’s dependence on time introduces additional degrees of freedom. This nonisospectral character is shown to preserve integrability while broadening the class of admissible solutions. By rigorously proving the existence of multipeakon solutions and verifying the Lax pair’s compatibility, we demonstrate the equation’s robustness as an integrable system. The determinant technique not only streamlines the derivation of peakon dynamics but also reveals deeper connections to inverse spectral theory. Our results contribute to the growing understanding of nonisospectral integrable systems and their geometric interpretations, offering a new perspective on the Camassa-Holm hierarchy. This work bridges classical determinant methods with modern integrable systems theory, opening avenues for further exploration in nonlinear wave phenomena. **Keywords:** nonisospectral Camassa-Holm equation; multipeakon solutions; determinant technique.

This paper presents a comprehensive study of magnetic Ap/Bp stars within a 100 parsec heliocentric radius, representing the first effectively unbiased analysis of magnetic field distributions in intermediate mass stars. By synthesizing data from published catalogs and literature, we identified 57 confirmed magnetic Ap/Bp stars, constituting 1.7% of all intermediate mass stars in this volume. Stellar masses span 1.5–6 solar masses ($M_\odot$), with a peak mass incidence between 3.3–3.6 $M_\odot$. Observations of 30 targets using the MUSICOS spectropolarimeter at the Telescope Bernard Lyot enabled refinement of rotational periods, as well as characterization of magnetic field strength and geometry via Zeeman spectroscopy. The derived magnetic field distribution reveals a predominantly dipolar topology, with median longitudinal field strengths of ~250 Gauss and a peak in mass-specific field incidence. These results provide critical constraints for understanding the origin and evolution of magnetism in intermediate mass stars, highlighting correlations between magnetic topology, rotation, and stellar structure. The unbiased sample and methodology advance empirical models of magnetic field generation and offer a benchmark for comparative studies of magnetic activity in low- and high-mass stellar populations. This work underscores the role of magnetic fields in shaping stellar evolution and galactic chemical enrichment.

This study investigates the impact of rotation on the thermal evolution of neutron stars by solving two-dimensional thermal evolution equations with full incorporation of general relativistic effects. In the early post-formation phase, when the neutron star’s interior is not yet isothermal, rotation significantly enhances the polar surface temperature relative to the equator, reaching up to 63% higher. This anisotropic temperature distribution, potentially detectable through thermal radiation from young, rapidly rotating neutron stars, diminishes as the interior gradually becomes isothermal. During the intermediate epoch (at ~xmath0 yr), the polar-equatorial temperature difference reduces to 31%, but the surface remains non-uniform. By the later stages (~xmath1 yr), photon surface radiation dominates cooling, leading to surface isothermality on a timescale of ~xmath1 yr. Notably, rotation delays the transition from the early to intermediate cooling phase by several hundred years, altering the thermal timeline compared to non-rotating models. An additional consequence of rotation is the reduction in neutrino luminosity, driven by lower central densities in rotating configurations. These findings underscore the critical role of rotational effects in shaping the thermodynamic behavior and observational signatures of neutron stars, particularly in their early evolutionary stages. The predicted temperature anisotropies and delayed cooling transitions provide testable constraints for future multi-wavelength observations of neutron star populations.

This study investigates the properties of ripplonic polarons in a multielectron bubble within liquid helium using a path-integral variational method. By modeling the interplay between electron-induced surface deformations and Coulomb interactions, we demonstrate that a two-dimensional electron gas can stabilize deep dimples—termed ripplopolarons—on the helium surface. These localized deformations enable the system to transition from a liquid to a Wigner crystal phase, distinct from conventional electron solidification. Our analysis derives critical experimental parameters, including temperature, pressure, and electron count, necessary for the formation of this ripplopolaronic Wigner crystal. Notably, this state exhibits a unique melting mechanism: as pressure decreases below a threshold, the ripplopolarons dissociate, with electrons shedding their stabilizing dimples, unlike the lattice melting observed in standard Wigner crystals. These findings highlight the role of surface deformation–mediated interactions in low-dimensional electron systems and offer a framework for experimental realization of such exotic phases under controlled conditions. The results advance understanding of strongly correlated quantum fluids and suggest pathways to manipulate electron solid-liquid transitions in confined geometries.

This study investigates the application of the Peres-Horodecki criterion and scaling separability conditions to multimode Gaussian states of the electromagnetic field, focusing on three-mode and four-mode systems. By analyzing the sensitivity of principal minors of the photon quadrature dispersion matrix to scaling transformations, we demonstrate a direct relationship between the magnitude of negative minors and the degree of entanglement. Empirical results indicate that larger absolute values of these negative minors correspond to higher entanglement, offering a quantitative measure for separability analysis. The findings highlight the utility of these criteria in characterizing multimode entanglement and underscore the role of scaling parameters in detecting non-classical correlations. This approach provides a framework for assessing entanglement in high-dimensional quantum states, with potential applications in quantum information and optical technologies. Keywords: entanglement, Gaussian states, scaling transform, multimode light, separability criterion.

This study investigates the impact of electron-electron scattering on the equilibrium properties of few-electron quantum dots using nonequilibrium Green’s functions theory. By self-consistently solving the Matsubara (imaginary-time) Green’s function, the ground and equilibrium states of spatially inhomogeneous quantum dots are computed, treating spin-polarized charge carriers. Correlation effects are incorporated via the Dyson equation, initiated from a Hartree-Fock reference state, within a conserving second-order self-energy approximation. This approach treats direct and exchange interactions on equal footing, ensuring accurate energy and spectral resolution. Results are presented for zero- and finite-temperature charge carrier densities, orbital-resolved distribution functions, self-consistent total energies, and spectral functions in both isotropic two-dimensional parabolic confinement and anisotropic quasi-one-dimensional geometries. For systems with **N = 1, 2, and 3** electrons, the analysis reveals a crossover from Fermi gas/liquid behavior at high densities to Wigner molecule-like or crystal-like configurations in the low-density regime. The interplay between spatial confinement, electron correlations, and spin polarization is shown to critically influence equilibrium properties. Spectral functions highlight the emergence of discrete energy levels and correlation-driven broadening, particularly in anisotropic systems. This work provides a unified framework for understanding how electron-electron interactions govern the structural and energetic evolution of few-electron quantum dots, offering insights into the design of correlated

We estimate the Gromov norm of the Cartesian product of two surfaces by leveraging its relationship to the minimal size of triangulations of polygon products. For surfaces of genus 2, we prove the Gromov norm lies between 32 and 52. This bound is derived via combinatorial analysis of triangulation complexity, bridging geometric topology and discrete geometry. The method generalizes to arbitrary genera, with the genus-2 case serving as a foundational framework for broader inferences. This work highlights the interplay between simplicial structures and topological invariants in manifold products.

This paper investigates the feasibility conditions of interference alignment (IA) in reverse TDD systems, where one cell operates in downlink (DL) while another operates in uplink (UL). For general MIMO antenna configurations, we derive a *necessary condition* and a *sufficient condition* for achieving one-shot linear IA—i.e., IA without symbol or time extensions—thereby addressing interference alignment in heterogeneous network scenarios. Through analysis of example networks, we characterize the optimal sum degrees of freedom (DoF) enabled by the derived conditions, demonstrating their effectiveness in maximizing spectral efficiency. For symmetric DoF within each cell, we establish a more compact sufficient condition, which further reduces to a *necessary and sufficient condition* for a class of symmetric configurations. To implement these results, we propose an iterative algorithm for constructing transmit and receive beamforming vectors that satisfy one-shot IA constraints. Simulation results validate that the proposed IA approach not only achieves the theoretical DoF gains but also significantly enhances the sum rate in practical signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes, outperforming conventional methods. These findings advance the design of dynamic TDD systems in heterogeneous networks by enabling efficient interference coordination under asymmetric traffic patterns. Keywords: degrees of freedom, dynamic TDD, feasibility conditions, heterogeneous networks, interference alignment, multiple-input and multiple-output (MIMO), reverse TDD.

Recent advancements in lightweight, head-mounted cameras, exemplified by products like Google Glass, have catalyzed the emergence of egocentric vision as a transformative research domain. This paradigm, centered on first-person perspective video analysis, presents unique challenges and opportunities in computer vision. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the field, focusing on three key research areas: object recognition, activity detection/recognition, and video summarization. We systematically categorize recent contributions, synthesize methodologies, and compare evaluation metrics across studies to highlight progress and persistent challenges. Additionally, we analyze the proliferation of benchmark datasets, emphasizing their role in enabling standardized performance comparisons and driving innovation. By consolidating findings and identifying gaps, this work serves as a foundational reference for understanding the current state of egocentric vision, while underscoring the need for future research in robustness, scalability, and cross-domain applicability.

This paper reviews key findings on the energy loss rate of an accelerating quark in strongly coupled $ \mathcal{N} = 4 $ super-Yang-Mills theory at zero and finite temperature. A central result is that, when a quark-antiquark pair is created in the plasma, the quark initially evolves freely until the $ \text{q}\bar{\text{q}} $ separation exceeds a screening length dependent on the coupling strength $ \lambda $. Beyond this threshold, the quark’s motion is governed by an analytic energy loss formula derived under stationary or late-time approximations, as established by Herzog et al. and Gubser. This transition marks the onset of significant plasma interactions, reconciling early-time dynamics with late-time hydrodynamic behavior. The analysis bridges theoretical predictions with phenomenological relevance, offering insights into heavy-ion collision experiments and jet quenching. The text, presented as an expanded version of talks delivered at the XIII Mexican School of Particles and Fields (October 2008), emphasizes the interplay between gauge/gravity duality and real-time quark dynamics in strongly coupled media.

This study investigates the scattering and extinction properties of nanodiamond grains in the interstellar medium (ISM) using discrete dipole approximation (DDA) calculations for ellipsoidal particles ranging from @xmath0 to @xmath1 in size. Nanodiamonds exhibit minimal extinction from the infrared to near-ultraviolet wavelength regimes but demonstrate a pronounced rise in far-ultraviolet extinction. Comparative analysis with observed extinction curves suggests that nanodiamonds cannot exist independently as dominant dust components in the ISM. However, they may contribute as part of composite structures, such as core-mantle models where nanodiamonds form cores surrounded by graphite mantles. For such configurations, the 2175 Å extinction peak is significantly altered: it is lowered, broadened, blue-shifted, and accompanied by enhanced far-ultraviolet extinction. These spectral features align with observations from certain astrophysical sources, indicating potential modifications due to radiation-induced transformations in carbonaceous grains. A three-component dust model incorporating silicates, graphite, and graphite-coated nanodiamonds was evaluated, showing excellent agreement with average galactic extinction across the wavelength range @xmath2 to @xmath3. The best-fitting model requires nanodiamonds to be both small in size and limited in abundance. These findings highlight the importance of nanodiamonds as a minor yet critical component in ISM dust, influencing observed extinction characteristics through structural complexity. This paper presents an analytical evaluation of the end-to-end bit error rate (BER) for multi-hop point-to-point underwater wireless optical communication (UWOC) systems. As a foundational step, the BER expression for a single-hop UWOC link is derived analytically, forming the basis for end-to-end performance analysis. To account for shot noise effects, the photon-counting method is applied, while the Gauss-Hermite quadrature formula is employed to obtain closed-form BER solutions for log-normal fading channels, a common model in underwater environments. The study comprehensively incorporates key impairments of underwater optical channels, including absorption, scattering, and fading. Numerical results demonstrate that multi-hop transmission mitigates these channel degradations, significantly enhancing system performance and enabling longer viable communication distances. For instance, dual-hop relayed links in coastal waters of lengths *X* m and *Y* m achieve *A* dB and *B* dB performance gains, respectively, at a BER of *Z*, highlighting the efficacy of serial relaying in overcoming depth-related challenges. This work provides critical insights into optimizing UWOC systems through multi-hop architectures, offering a tractable framework for evaluating BER under realistic underwater conditions. The findings underscore the potential of multi-hop transmission to extend the operational range and reliability of underwater optical networks, particularly in scenarios with high turbulence and scattering. Keywords: underwater wireless optical communications, BER performance, photon-counting approach, multi-hop transmission, serial relaying.

This study employs three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics simulations to investigate cosmic-ray (CR) production efficiency in supernova remnants, revealing that traditional estimates based on Hα filament proper motions and shock-jump conditions systematically overpredict CR yields. Upstream density fluctuations generate rippled, oblique shocks, redistributing kinetic energy into downstream turbulence and thermal energy tied to the shock’s normal velocity component. Synthetic observations demonstrate that these rippled shocks fail to instantaneously dissipate all upstream kinetic energy, leading to a 10–40% overestimation of CR acceleration efficiency when inferred from reduced downstream plasma temperatures. This overestimation arises because standard methods implicitly assume planar shocks, neglecting the energy partitioning between turbulence and thermalization. The findings highlight the necessity of incorporating upstream medium inhomogeneities and shock rippling in CR acceleration models to reconcile theoretical predictions with observational data, advancing our understanding of particle acceleration mechanisms in astrophysical shocks.

We present the first detection and mapping of the $^{12}\text{C I}$ fine-structure line at 492 GHz in three molecular clouds (TMC-1, L134N, and IC 5146) embedded in weak interstellar ultraviolet (UV) radiation fields. The $^{12}\text{C I}$ emission peaks at a remarkably uniform brightness temperature of $T_{\text{peak}} = 5.5 \pm 0.5\,\text{K}$ across all three clouds, with minimal spatial dispersion, indicating a homogeneous excitation condition. The spatial distribution of $^{12}\text{C I}$ is extended and smooth, contrasting with the more compact and variable emission observed in CO isotopologues (e.g., $^{13}\text{CO}$ and C$^{18}$O) at the same angular resolution. The $^{12}\text{C I}$ peak intensity is approximately one-third that of $^{13}\text{CO}\, J = 2\rightarrow1$, while its emission extends further than CO lines, suggesting differences in line formation regions or excitation mechanisms. The $^{12}\text{C I}$ line widths align with $^{13}\text{CO}$ but exceed those of C$^{18}$O and $^{12}\text{CO}$, and occasional deviations in line shapes imply a combination of opacity effects and spatial offsets between the emitting regions. The observed uniformity in $^{12}\text{C I}$ peak temperatures—despite its origin in the Wien tail of the Planck function—is best explained by optically thick, thermalized emission. This implies that $^{12}\text{C I}$ at 492 GHz directly probes the kinetic temperature of low-UV-exposed clouds. The inferred temperature ($T_{\text{kin}} \sim 7.4\,\text{K}$) is consistent across clouds and regions, with a small dispersion of $0.5\,\text{K}$, supporting a steady thermal balance mechanism in these environments. This study investigates the branching ratios of the $\mathcal{B} \rightarrow X_s \gamma$ decay within the sequential fourth-generation (4G) model. Theoretical predictions for branching ratios, $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{B} \rightarrow X_s \gamma)$, incorporating new physics contributions from 4G fermions, exhibit deviations from Standard Model (SM) results by one to two orders of magnitude. These enhancements arise from additional loop-level corrections in the 4G framework. However, the negligible values of the 4G CKM matrix element $|V_{t'b}|$ suppress new physics effects in $\mathcal{B} \rightarrow X_s l^+ l^-$ decays, making them indistinguishable from SM expectations. In contrast, the $\mathcal{B} \rightarrow K^* \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay remains sensitive to 4G contributions, offering a potential probe of new physics. This highlights the importance of rare $b$-hadron decays in testing 4G scenarios beyond the SM.

This study reexamines the role of nuclear burning in facilitating neutrino-driven explosions of core-collapse supernovae, focusing on its impact on postbounce dynamics. Utilizing one-dimensional (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) simulations with and without a 13-isotope nuclear network, we investigate four progenitor models: three for @xmath1 stars and one for an @xmath2 star. By systematically varying neutrino luminosity and its decay time to achieve parametric explosions, we quantify how energy deposition from nuclear burning of infalling material influences shock propagation. Our results demonstrate that nuclear burning significantly energizes shock expansion, particularly for models yielding only marginal explosions in its absence. This effect is most pronounced when the shock front interacts with silicon- and oxygen-rich layers, where energy input from nuclear reactions elevates the diagnostic explosion energy to several times @xmath3 erg—compared to lower values without burning. The Limongi-Chieffi progenitor, characterized by a massive oxygen layer with an inner-edge radius smaller than other progenitors, exhibits the most notable enhancement. The shock’s early contact with dense nuclear fuel in this model allows rapid energy deposition, accelerating the onset of explosion. In contrast, 2D models show reduced energy differences (generally @xmath4 erg) compared to 1D cases (up to @xmath5 erg). This discrepancy arises because neutrino-driven convection and standing accretion shock instability (SASI) in 2D models enhance neutrino heating efficiency, diminishing the relative contribution of nuclear burning. Despite this, our findings underscore that nuclear burning remains a critical ingredient in the neutrino-driven explosion mechanism, especially for progenitors with extended nuclear fuel layers. The interplay between nuclear energy deposition and neutrino heating is sensitive to progenitor structure, with uncertainties in stellar evolution models necessitating further studies. Overall, this work highlights the importance of incorporating nuclear burning in multidimensional simulations to improve the predictive accuracy of core-collapse supernova models, particularly for scenarios where neutrino heating alone is insufficient to trigger robust explosions.

This study explores the dynamics of monoenergetic electrons interacting with laser fields, demonstrating their potential as a mechanism for generating coherent electrons in the presence of uniform, perpendicular magnetic and electric fields. Utilizing the Green’s function technique, we derive analytic expressions for the field-induced quantum mechanical drift motion of (i) single electrons and (ii) a dilute Fermi gas. Our analysis reveals that the electric field induces a splitting of the $n$th Landau level into $n+1$ sublevels, thereby broadening the energy spectrum of the oscillator eigenstates. This splitting leads to overlapping adjacent Landau levels when the electric field surpasses a critical threshold, fundamentally altering electronic transport properties. The derived drift current quantifies this effect, while the Landau level broadening provides insights into non-equilibrium quantum Hall systems under electric field perturbations. These results are critical for modeling quantum Hall configurations where electric fields play a dominant role, offering a framework to study coherent electron dynamics in complex electromagnetic environments.

This study presents an analytical theoretical model for Poisson’s spot matter wave interferometry, derived from the Babinet principle. By integrating free propagation and single-slit diffraction formalisms, the model quantifies the interplay of wave and particle behaviors in matter wave dynamics. We incorporate environmental effects—coherence loss and finite detection area—via a propagator for quantum particles interacting with a dephasing environment. A key finding is the critical role of the matter wave Gouy phase in stabilizing the central peak, highlighting the phenomenon’s wavelike dominance. The model achieves robust agreement with experimental data for D2 molecules, validating its predictive power. This work advances understanding of macroscopic quantum coherence and provides a framework for analyzing complex matter wave interference patterns, bridging theoretical and experimental advancements in quantum optics.

This study theoretically examines the dynamic interaction and propagation characteristics of co- and counter-propagating Mach cones generated by two supersonic projectile particles traversing a dusty plasma medium. By solving a fluid model incorporating Poisson’s equation to account for the electrostatic contributions of heavily charged dust particles, we analyze the density perturbations and velocity vector fields associated with the Mach cones. For co-propagating projectiles, overlapping Mach wings form interference-like patterns, while counter-propagating configurations yield more intricate structures, marked by a higher density of maxima and minima in the resulting fringe patterns. The temporal evolution of these interactions reveals a reduction in the time interval required for the formation of consecutive maxima/minima at fixed points due to the enhanced coupling between opposing Mach cones. Furthermore, the spacing between adjacent interference maxima increases with the relative velocity of counter-propagating projectiles, while the fringe angle decreases, indicating a velocity-dependent modulation of wavefront geometry. These findings underscore the role of relative motion and dust charging in shaping nonlinear wave dynamics in plasmas, with implications for understanding collective phenomena in astrophysical and industrial plasma environments. The results also highlight the sensitivity of Mach cone interactions to external parameters, offering insights into the self-organization of wave patterns in complex plasma systems.

This work examines the continuous-variable quantum key distribution protocol introduced by Pirandola et al. (2015), where an untrusted relay mediates secret-key generation via continuous-variable Bell detection of coherent states. Focusing on the symmetric configuration—where the relay is equidistant from two authorized parties—we analyze eavesdropping strategies under fixed transmissivity and thermal noise. By comparing two-mode coherent attacks (exploiting both quantum links simultaneously) with one-mode collective attacks (employing independent entangling cloners), we demonstrate that two-mode attacks are optimal. They surpass one-mode strategies in both security threshold and secret-key rate, highlighting the critical role of joint measurement-based eavesdropping in compromising network security. These findings underscore the necessity of considering coherent, multi-mode adversaries in continuous-variable quantum networks and provide a benchmark for evaluating secure relay-mediated protocols. Our results refine the understanding of vulnerability landscapes in such architectures, offering practical guidance for optimizing security against advanced eavesdropping tactics. **Word count:** 146

This study explores the resonant quantum dynamics of a multi-qubit ensemble coupled to a microcavity, with coherent pumping of both the quantum-dot subsystem and the cavity mode. We demonstrate that the microcavity photon statistics are sensitive to the phase difference of the driving lasers, unlike photon intensity at resonant conditions. By leveraging this phase dependence, we achieve tunable two-photon correlations, enabling enhanced photon correlation strengths and amplified steady-state intensities. Additionally, the photon statistics exhibit oscillatory steady-state behaviors and asymmetries, revealing nontrivial quantum interference effects. These findings highlight the potential for precise control of quantum light-matter interactions, with implications for quantum information processing and cavity quantum electrodynamics.

We present an analysis of near-infrared spectroscopic data from the central few hundred parsecs of 47 active galaxies to explore correlations between the stellar velocity dispersion ($\sigma_*$), derived from fitting $K$-band stellar absorption features, and the gas velocity dispersion ($\sigma_{\text{gas}}$), obtained from the emission-line profiles of [S III] $\lambda$9.07 $\mu$m, [Fe II] $\lambda$1.257 $\mu$m, [Fe II] $\lambda$1.644 $\mu$m, and H$\beta$ $\lambda$1.667 $\mu$m. Our results reveal no significant correlations between $\sigma_*$ and $\sigma_{\text{gas}}$ for H$\beta$ and [S III], suggesting these lines are influenced by non-stellar kinematic components or localized outflows. However, a robust linear relationship was found between $\sigma_*$ and the [Fe II] emission-line dispersions at both 1.257 $\mu$m and 1.644 $\mu$m. Excluding barred galaxies from the sample further improved this correlation, yielding a relation: $\sigma_* = (0.88 \pm 0.05)\,\sigma_{\text{[Fe II]}} + (1.2 \pm 0.3)$ km s$^{-1}$, with a correlation coefficient of $r = 0.91$. This tight correlation enables the estimation of $\sigma_*$ when direct measurements are unfeasible, leveraging [Fe II] line kinematics. This paper introduces an efficient interpolation framework tailored for large-scale scattered data sets, leveraging the partition of unity method (PUM) enhanced by radial basis functions (RBFs) as local approximants. A novel block-based space-partitioning data structure is proposed, which subdivides the domain into blocks to optimize the nearest-neighbor search during interpolation. This approach significantly reduces the computational complexity by restricting local searches to a minimal subset of blocks, thereby accelerating the overall algorithm. Rigorous complexity analysis confirms the method's scalability, while extensive numerical experiments in both two and three dimensions validate its accuracy and efficiency compared to existing techniques. Applications in geometric modeling demonstrate the practical utility of the framework. A MATLAB-based software implementation is provided, offering the scientific community an accessible tool for reproducing results and extending the methodology. The work contributes to meshfree approximation by addressing critical challenges in handling high-dimensional, unstructured data, with particular emphasis on fast algorithms and robust searching procedures. The method bridges theoretical innovation with practical applicability, advancing the state of the art in scattered data interpolation. **Keywords:** meshfree approximation, partition of unity method, fast algorithms, searching procedures, radial basis functions, scattered data interpolation. **MSC:** 65D05, 65D15, 65D17, 65Y20.

This study presents a theoretical model for short-range correlations in two-nucleon removal via elastic breakup (diffraction dissociation) on a light target. Key fingerprints of these correlations are observed in the momentum distributions as back-to-back emission of nucleon pairs. Analytical expressions for these distributions are derived, and calculations are conducted for reactions involving stable and unstable nuclear species. Additionally, the signature of short-range correlations is investigated in alternative reaction processes, highlighting their universal significance in nuclear dynamics.

This study dynamically investigates the @xmath0 systems with @xmath1 and @xmath2 within the frameworks of two constituent quark models: the chiral quark model (CQM) and the quark delocalization color screening model (QDCSM). Model parameters are derived from prior work that successfully described proton-antiproton @xmath3-wave elastic scattering cross-section data. The @xmath0 elastic scattering processes, including coupling to the @xmath4 state, are analyzed. Results indicate no evidence of a @xmath5-wave bound state, consistent with the observed threshold enhancement in @xmath0 within @xmath6 decay. However, a @xmath7 @xmath4 resonance is predicted by the QDCSM, highlighting its potential role in the dynamics of @xmath0 systems. These findings provide insights into the interplay between quark-level interactions and meson-meson scattering phenomena.

The young (≤5 Myr) planet-mass companion 2M1207b has long defied a coherent explanation due to its anomalously low luminosity, red near-infrared (NIR) colors, and L-type NIR spectrum, which suggest an effective temperature (T_eff ≈ 1600 K) inconsistent with its small inferred radius. Early hypotheses proposed obscuration by an edge-on disk or a post-collision remnant to explain its underluminosity. However, the discovery of HR8799b—a similarly underluminous, low-gravity, and low-surface-gravity planet-mass object—strongly implies an atmospheric origin for 2M1207b’s properties. By incorporating clouds, non-equilibrium chemistry, and low-gravity effects into atmospheric models, a T_eff aligned with cooling-track predictions for its age and mass is achieved. This eliminates the need for exotic physics or a novel classification of objects. Instead, 2M1207b and comparable companions represent a natural extension of cloudy, low-gravity substellar atmospheres to the lowest surface gravities (log(g)) and masses. A 64, 012310, 2001). A critical challenge lies in the physical generation of quantum codewords. This work demonstrates that ponderomotive interactions between a system and a meter can achieve this task. Such interactions induce a meter frequency shift proportional to the system's position quadrature, enabling a phase measurement on the meter to project the system into an eigenstate of stabilizer generators, provided initial states are appropriately prepared. We present a feasible implementation using trapped ions, where the interaction is mediated by laser-coupled motional modes and external fields. Hydrodynamic models of RR Lyrae pulsation reveal a rich and complex nonlinear behavior, challenging earlier assumptions. Contrary to predictions, high-order resonances significantly influence the interacting modes, driving intricate dynamical patterns. Chaotic attractors emerge across multiple time scales, manifesting both in the pulsation itself and in amplitude equations governing oscillatory modulation. While no direct correlation has been established between modeled nonlinearities and observed phenomena, the diversity of features—such as mode coupling and temporal irregularities—suggests that resonant interactions must be reconsidered in addressing the enigmatic Blazhko effect. This study underscores the necessity of revising traditional interpretations of resonance-driven dynamics, advocating for a more nuanced framework to decode modulated variability in RR Lyrae stars. By highlighting the role of nonlinearities in shaping pulsational behavior, these findings offer critical insights into the unresolved mechanisms underpinning stellar modulation.

We investigate the gravitational instability of galactic discs by treating stars and cold interstellar gas as distinct components, incorporating the observed Larson-type scaling relations of turbulence in the interstellar medium (ISM). Using a large sample of galaxies from the HI Nearby Galaxy Survey (THINGS), we analyze how ISM turbulence modulates disc instability in star-forming spiral galaxies. Our results reveal that turbulence significantly impacts both inner and outer disc regions. In the inner gas disc, turbulence drives a transition between two instability regimes, while in the outer disc, it enhances the susceptibility to star-dominated instabilities. By deriving general properties of such systems, we demonstrate that turbulent pressure alters the classical stability criteria, necessitating revised frameworks for disc dynamics. This study underscores the critical role of turbulence in shaping galactic structure and evolution, bridging ISM-scale processes with large-scale disc behavior. Our findings highlight the interplay between turbulence, gas dynamics, and gravitational instability, offering new insights into star formation regulation in spiral galaxies. *Keywords:* instabilities; turbulence; ISM: kinematics and dynamics; ISM: structure; galaxies: ISM; galaxies: kinematics and dynamics.

The transient X-ray source SW 1644+57, which erupted suddenly as GRB 110328A, presents a unique case for investigating extreme astrophysical phenomena. Located at the center of a galaxy, its activation is linked to the central engine, prompting exploration of the tidal disruption event (TDE) hypothesis proposed by Bloom et al. However, we argue that the traditional TDE framework, which assumes periastron distances near the tidal disruption radius $ r_t $, fails to explain the observed characteristics of SW 1644+57. Three independent analyses challenge the conventional model: first, the early X-ray light curve deviates significantly from theoretical fallback rate predictions, indicating an alternative accretion mechanism. Second, the timing of the transition to a disk-dominated decay phase suggests a more energetic and prolonged jet production than expected from a standard TDE. Third, the inferred TDE rate in the host galaxy is inconsistent with the observed event’s luminosity and duration. Collectively, these findings imply an orbit with a periastron far below $ r_t $, necessitating a deeply plunging trajectory to generate the powerful, relativistic jet observed. The extreme tidal forces at such proximity likely result in complete stellar destruction, surpassing the minimal disruption required in traditional TDEs. We propose the term *tidal obliteration event (TOE)* to capture this scenario, emphasizing the profound and total disintegration of the star, rather than a partial tidal disruption. This reinterpretation offers a more precise description of the physics at play, aligning with the unique observational features of SW 1644+57 and expanding our understanding of extreme compact object interactions.

This study investigates the hypothesis that the pseudogap (PG) and superconducting (SC) states in underdoped high-temperature superconductors (HTSC) emerge from dynamical dimension reduction, a phenomenon where cooling induces a change in effective dimensionality. We propose that the transition to the PG state at temperature $ T^* $ arises as a dimensional crossover, shifting charge motion from three-dimensional (3D) to two-dimensional (2D) behavior. At $ T^* $, 2D confinement enables Jahn-Teller (JT) distortions to bind holes, forming delocalized JT polarons and localized three-spin polarons within copper-oxygen planes. This process triggers charge ordering, eliminating the competition between carrier pairing and localization on JT distortions. As the temperature drops below $ T_c $, local "hole-JT polaron" pairs—zero-dimensional (0D) SC fluctuations—emerge in the $ CuO_2 $ planes. The SC transition at $ T_c $ is then characterized as a sequence of two crossovers: first, 0D→2D growth of SC fluctuations, followed by 2D→3D percolation. Experimental evidence supports the formation of these local "hole-JT polaron" pairs and provides insights into the dynamical dimension reduction framework in PG and SC states. Key findings include the critical role of JT distortions in mediating charge ordering and the hierarchical dimensional evolution of SC fluctuations. These results reconcile longstanding challenges in HTSC physics, such as the coexistence of PG and SC states and the suppression of antiferromagnetic order. By framing the PG

This study presents an analysis of the angular power spectrum of unresolved 3.6 μm infrared (IR) light in the *Spitzer* GOODS fields. The amplitude of the anisotropy spectrum is observed to decline as the flux threshold for removing resolved sources is lowered, indicating a diminishing contribution from brighter objects. When sources brighter than a Vega magnitude of 24.6 are excluded, an excess power of approximately 0.4 nW m−2 sr−1 is detected at arcminute angular scales, attributed to unresolved IRB (infrared background) sources. However, the spectral shape aligns more closely with predictions for faint, low-redshift galaxies fainter than Vega magnitude 23, suggesting a total 3.6 μm intensity of 1.2–2.4 nW m−2 sr−1. This hypothesis is validated by demonstrating a rapid decline in large-scale power when faint ACS sources without IRAC counterparts are masked in the processed HDF-N IRAC image, effectively removing spurious fluctuations. By integrating resolved source counts and unresolved fluctuations, we estimate that galaxies contribute no more than ~7.0 nW m−2 sr−1 to the IRB at 3.6 μm, leaving residual power unaccounted for by conventional astrophysical models. These findings highlight the complex interplay between resolved and unresolved components in shaping the IRB, with implications for identifying exotic or faint extragalactic sources. The results underscore the necessity of high-resolution imaging and precise source masking to disentangle the contributions of low-redshift and high-redshift populations to the IR background.

Opportunistic routing in multi-hop networks enables relay selection based on immediate availability. In blind opportunistic protocols, where transmitters lack knowledge of surrounding nodes, optimizing transmission probability and spectral efficiency is critical for maximizing end-to-end performance—defined as the product of transmitter density, hop distance, and rate. Due to the problem’s intractability, we propose an analytical approximation function validated for accuracy. Our analysis reveals optimal parameter configurations dependent on system characteristics such as path loss exponent and noise level. Results demonstrate that adjusting transmission probability and spectral efficiency according to these parameters significantly enhances network performance, offering practical guidelines for protocol design in dynamic, information-scarce environments. This work bridges theoretical insights with actionable design strategies for efficient opportunistic routing.

In this paper, we present an updated framework for calculating Stark line profiles in autoionizing atomic states within dense plasmas, including warm dense matter and strongly coupled regimes. Traditional approaches rely on the assumption of Boltzmann-distributed atomic populations, which is challenged here due to the intrinsic non-equilibrium nature of autoionizing states in dense environments. Our analysis highlights the critical role of electric microfields generated by plasma charge constituents in modifying atomic populations and, consequently, Stark broadening effects. These microfields significantly alter the standard statistical model by introducing deviations from equilibrium distributions, thereby undermining the accuracy of conventional Stark profile calculations. By integrating advanced plasma microfield models and revised population statistics, we demonstrate a more robust theoretical framework that accounts for these non-Boltzmann effects. The implications of this work are particularly significant for understanding radiation emission spectra from plasmas generated via X-ray free electron laser (XFEL) interactions

We investigate the ordering dynamics of three distinct spin models within the generalized voter class in two dimensions, contrasting their behavior with the linear voter model under unbalanced initial spin configurations. When the initial mixture of up and down spins is asymmetrical, these nonlinear models exhibit a nontrivial exit probability—the likelihood of reaching an all-up consensus—unlike the linear model, which adheres to a trivial identity. This observation marks the first documented case of nontrivial exit probabilities in two-dimensional systems. The deviation arises from the strong nonconservation of average magnetization during the early dynamical stages, which disrupts the equilibrium-like evolution observed in linear models. Furthermore, the time required to achieve consensus displays an anomalous, nonuniversal dependence on the initial spin fraction, reflecting the interplay between nonlinear interactions and dimensionality. Our results highlight the critical role of conservation laws in consensus dynamics and demonstrate how nonlinearity in spin interactions can fundamentally alter the critical behavior of low-dimensional systems.

In a recent study, we introduced a spin expansion framework to analyze binary black hole (BBH) mergers by leveraging symmetry properties of conserved quantities—such as the final black hole mass $ M $, kick velocity $ \vec{v} $, and spin vector $ \vec{S} $—instead of relying on detailed merger dynamics. This approach provides a parsimonious yet robust interpretation of BBH coalescence outcomes. In this work, we extend this formalism, validate its predictions against state-of-the-art numerical simulations, and outline pathways for further development. The spin expansion generates novel, *exact* analytical results for BBH merger observables, some of which have already been verified by simulations, while others await confirmation. Crucially, we demonstrate that as few as 10 equal-mass and 16 unequal-mass simulations can calibrate all coefficients in the spin expansion up to second order, minimizing computational cost. For broader simulation datasets with known covariance, we derive minimum-variance unbiased estimators for the expansion parameters, ensuring optimal precision in coefficient determination. This calibration strategy offers a cost-effective tool for testing numerical relativity codes and constraining BBH merger dynamics in the context of general relativity and astrophysical populations. Furthermore, we explore extensions of the spin expansion to eccentric BBH orbits, suggesting applicability beyond quasicircular inspirals. By unifying symmetry-driven predictions with efficient calibration, our framework advances both theoretical and observational studies of gravitational wave sources, with potential implications for understanding black hole formation channels and the structure of spacetime in extreme regimes.

Using anti-de Sitter (AdS) quantum field theory, we derive a novel class of hypergeometric identities linked to the Källén-Lehmann representation of products of two AdS two-point functions. These identities reveal a rich mathematical structure, which we exploit to investigate the decay of unstable AdS particles. Our analysis shows the total decay amplitude is finite and AdS-invariant, confirming the consistency of AdS QFT in addressing such phenomena. This work bridges mathematical and physical insights in curved spacetime field theory.

This study demonstrates theoretically that nonrelativistic nearly-free electrons in crystalline solids inherently exhibit a trembling motion (zitterbewegung, ZB) in the absence of external fields, a phenomenon traditionally associated with relativistic electrons in vacuum. The origin of ZB in this context is attributed to the influence of the periodic potential of the crystal lattice on electron dynamics. The characteristic frequency of ZB is proportional to the energy gap, $\Delta$, between adjacent bands, while its amplitude depends on the strength of the periodic potential and the lattice period, reaching nanometer-scale magnitudes. Notably, the amplitude remains largely insensitive to the spatial extent of the electron’s wave packet. To analyze this effect, we introduce an analogue of the Foldy-Wouthuysen transformation from relativistic quantum mechanics, enabling decoupling of electron states across bands and revealing that electrons should be regarded as particles of finite size in this regime. Extending our analysis to a two-band model of tightly bound electrons further confirms the persistence of ZB, underscoring its generality. Our findings challenge the notion that ZB is exclusive to relativistic systems and instead establish it as a universal feature of electrons in crystalline solids, driven by band structure interactions. These results suggest that ZB is not an anomaly but a fundamental consequence of the interplay between quantum coherence and periodic potentials in condensed matter systems.

The magnetization dynamics of nanoscale heterostructures combining ferromagnetic (FM) and nonmagnetic materials exhibit unique phenomena arising from two complementary effects relative to isolated magnetic systems. First, time-dependent FM magnetization generates spin angular momentum (SAM) currents via spin pumping into adjacent layers, while second, applied bias mediates nonlocal SAM transfer between FMs, inducing mutual torques. These processes are inherently nonlocal, governed by spin-coherent regions constrained by spin-flip relaxation lengths, and are central to the GHz-scale dynamics of such heterostructures. This review synthesizes recent theoretical advances in elucidating these effects from first principles, emphasizing spin pumping in layered systems. A semiclassical framework, leveraging mean-field Stoner or spin-density functional theories, provides the core analysis, while extensions to quantum-size effects and electron-electron correlations are explored to address nanoscale deviations. Experimental validation has grown significantly, supporting predictions of coupled spin-transfer torques, spin Seebeck effects, and nonlocal magnetization precession. The formalism bridges microscopic physics and macroscopic device behavior, offering critical insights for engineering next-generation spintronic devices, such as low-power magnetic random-access memory (MRAM) elements. By disentangling the interplay between spin pumping and nonlocal SAM transfer, the study underscores the potential to tailor magnetization dynamics in complex heterostructures, advancing both fundamental understanding and applied technologies in nanoscale magnetism.

Using high-quality YBa2Cu3O6.33 single crystals with a superconducting transition temperature $ T_c = 8.4 \, \text{K} $, we investigate spin dynamics via neutron scattering to explore the interplay between superconductivity and antiferromagnetism at near-critical doping $ p \approx 0.055 $. Contrary to expectations of coexisting long-range antiferromagnetic order and superconductivity, our measurements reveal no evidence of such coexistence at this doping level. Instead, short-range three-dimensional spin correlations emerge above $ T_c $, persisting over temperatures significantly higher than the superconducting transition. These correlations exhibit a smooth intensity increase with cooling but lack anomalies indicative of a Néel transition. The spin correlations remain subcritical, with correlations spanning only 1.5 unit cells perpendicular to the CuO2 planes, suggesting a suppressed magnetic order. At low energies ($ \sim \mu \text{eV} $), the spin response is static, transitioning to an overdamped excitation spectrum with a relaxation rate of 3 meV. Crucially, the onset of superconductivity below $ T_c $ does not disrupt these spin correlations, and the elastic interplanar spin response fails to diverge near the superconducting critical point, indicating the absence of a coincident antiferromagnetic critical point within the superconducting dome. Our findings imply that the suppression of long-range Néel order and its conversion into a spin-glass-like texture precedes the emergence of superconductivity. While $ p = 0.052 $ marks a critical threshold for superconducting pairing, it does not correspond to a critical point for spin order. This decoupling between superconducting and spin-ordered phases highlights the distinct mechanisms governing their respective transitions, shedding light on the complex phase diagram of high-temperature superconductors.

The COBE-DMR 4-year cosmic microwave background (CMB) maps revealed a strong non-Gaussian signal in the inter-scale bispectrum components, as their observed values lacked the expected scatter from Gaussian simulations. Re-examination using the WMAP data shows that these and other proposed non-Gaussian features vanish. Given that COBE-DMR's high noise levels and known systematics could at most dilute, not produce, such anomalies, we conclude that the dataset must have contained significant undocumented systematic errors. Analysis identifies a combination of quadcube pixelization and data from the "eclipse season" as the primary

Using muon spin relaxation (μ+SR) and neutron scattering, we probe the magnetic ground state of the multiferroic relaxor ferroelectric Pb(Fe0.5Nb0.5)O3. Below ∼40 K, a transition to a partially disordered spin-glass-like phase coexists with long-range antiferromagnetic order. μ+SR detects no magnetic-ion clustering, confirming homogeneity of this coexistence. These findings reveal complex interplay between order and frustration in relaxor ferroelectrics, offering insights into multiferroic phase competition.

This study explores the feasibility of producing and detecting novel stable particles with low masses at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), under the assumption of weak coupling to the Standard Model (SM). These particles are hypothesized to exist within an extended gauge sector, governed by either an abelian $U(1)$ or non-abelian $SU(N)$ symmetry. In the abelian scenario, new particles emit dark photons ($\mathcal{X}$), which subsequently decay into SM particles. In the non-abelian case, they hadronize into meson-like bound states ($\mathcal{Y}$) that decay hierarchically. Three distinct interaction frameworks between the new sector and the SM are analyzed: direct couplings, mediator-induced interactions, and hidden valley dynamics. Simulations leverage a hidden valley model implemented in Pythia 8 to evaluate event topologies and signal characteristics. The work demonstrates that, despite suppressed couplings, distinctive decay patterns—such as displaced vertices or multi-track jets—can be used to disentangle model-specific features. Key parameters, including gauge coupling strengths and mass splittings, are shown to be measurable via dedicated analyses. The study underscores the LHC’s potential to probe such weakly coupled sectors through precision observables, even in the absence of traditional collider signatures. These findings provide a roadmap for experimental searches targeting hidden sectors and highlight the importance of tailored simulation tools in addressing their complex dynamics. This research is the first systematic investigation of hidden valley models under LHC conditions, offering insights into the interplay between new physics and SM backgrounds. **Word count**: 178

Weather forecasts derived from numerical models often suffer from biases and underdispersion, necessitating statistical postprocessing. Ensemble Model Output Statistics (EMOS) addresses this by calibrating forecasts using parametric distributions whose parameters depend on ensemble members. This study introduces two semi-local EMOS methods that enhance predictive accuracy by incorporating data from climatically and geographically similar stations. These methods augment local training data for a specific observation site with forecasts from neighboring stations, leveraging similarities identified through either distance-based metrics or clustering algorithms. Features such as climatology, forecast errors, ensemble spread, and geographic proximity are integrated to define station similarity. A case study on European wind speed forecasts using the Grand Limited Area Model Ensemble Prediction System (GLAMEPS) demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed semi-local models. Compared to traditional regional and local EMOS approaches, the semi-local methods achieve significant improvements in predictive performance, as measured by the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). These methods also offer greater numerical stability and computational efficiency, particularly when fitting complex truncated normal distributions to capture wind speed characteristics. By combining localized and regional information, the semi-local framework balances model complexity with practicality, addressing challenges in high-resolution probabilistic forecasting. The results underscore the value of similarity-based approaches in postprocessing for operational meteorology, providing a scalable solution for improving ensemble forecasts across diverse geographical and climatic conditions. **Keywords**: Clustering, Continuous Ranked Probability Score, Ensemble Model Output Statistics, Ensemble postprocessing, Probabilistic forecasting, Truncated normal distribution, Weather forecasting, Wind speed.

We investigate the superconducting gap function of (TMTSF)2ClO4 by calculating angle-dependent heat capacity in low magnetic fields using the Kramer-Pesch approximation, combined with first-principles electronic structure calculations. Comparisons with experimental data reveal that a nodal d-wave gap function consistently explains the observed thermodynamic properties. The unique axis-asymmetry in the angular dependence of heat capacity excludes s-wave and nodeless d-wave scenarios. Notably, the directional ordering of ClO4 anions does not significantly alter the Fermi surface topology, contradicting prior models. High-precision first-principles calculations show that the two Fermi surfaces intersect within the system’s accuracy, diminishing the anion ordering’s impact. These findings resolve long-standing debates about the pairing symmetry in this organic superconductor, highlighting the critical role of angular dependencies and the robustness of nodal d-wave pairing. Our study provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding unconventional superconductivity in quasi-one-dimensional systems.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of galaxy interactions using a sample of 1,716 galaxy pairs selected from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 4 (DR4). The pairs are identified within a projected separation of 500 kpc and a relative line-of-sight velocity difference (Δv) < 800 km s−1, with stellar mass ratios (m1/m2) ≥ 0.3 to ensure a focus on both major (mass ratios ≈ 1:1) and minor (mass ratios 1:10) interactions. The sample is drawn from the SDSS Main Galaxy Sample using rigorous criteria for redshift accuracy, spectral quality, and the availability of derived stellar masses and metallicities, ensuring robustness and minimizing selection biases. Our analysis confirms previous findings of an enhanced star formation rate (SFR) in galaxy pairs at projected separations between 30–40 kpc, with the most pronounced enhancement observed in major pairs. This suggests that mass ratio plays a critical role in driving interaction-induced starburst activity, as the SFR boost diminish

Recent advances in the study of strongly interacting field theories at non-zero quark chemical potential ($\mu$) are reviewed, focusing on three key areas: the determination of the QCD critical endpoint in the $T$-$\mu$ plane; superfluid condensates in two-color QCD; and Fermi surface effects in the Nambu–Jona-Lasinio (NJL) model. The QCD phase diagram, summarized in the $T$-$\mu$ plane, highlights ongoing efforts to map regions inaccessible to conventional lattice simulations due to the sign problem. Recent progress includes insights into the upper-left quadrant (non-zero $T$ and $\mu$), relevant to heavy-ion collisions, and the lower-right quadrant (cold dense matter), where diquark condensation may lead to color superconductivity. In the $T$-$\mu$ plane, the critical endpoint—marking the termination of the first-order QCD phase transition—remains a central focus. While lattice studies at $\mu=0$ (e.g., Ejiri’s work) provide foundational insights, the interior of the phase diagram is increasingly accessible via reweighting and complex Langevin techniques. In two-color QCD, where the sign problem is mitigated, evidence for superfluid condensates at high $\mu$ supports the hypothesis of color superconductivity, with BCS gaps ($\Delta$) reaching up to 100 MeV. This challenges traditional quark matter

Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are pivotal cosmological tools due to their utility as standardizable distance indicators, yet the nature of their progenitor systems remains contentious. A central unresolved question is whether a non-degenerate companion star exists at the time of a white dwarf’s thermonuclear explosion. This study investigates whether interactions between the supernova ejecta and such a companion could produce observable signatures around the light-curve peak and in subsequent phases. Using multi-dimensional radiation transfer simulations grounded in hydrodynamic models of the ejecta-companion interaction, we explore how viewing angles influence observational characteristics. Our results reveal that asymmetries in the system generate directional variations in observables, with predictions—redder and fainter light curves when viewed toward the companion—contrary to earlier theoretical expectations. These variations, though modest and often within observational uncertainties, may serve as indirect probes of companion existence, particularly when analyzing large samples of SNe Ia with minimal calibration errors. However, optical color changes in the companion direction could mimic the effects of interstellar extinction, potentially contributing to observed scatter in peak luminosity and inferred distances. Post-peak, hydrogen-rich material stripped from the companion is expected to manifest in hydrogen absorption features. While these signatures are difficult to detect in optical spectra, we find that near-infrared P Cygni profiles in hydrogen lines during the post-maximum phase offer a robust diagnostic. These findings highlight the need for careful, wavelength-dependent analyses to disentangle companion-induced asymmetries from intrinsic or environmental effects, advancing the quest to

This study investigates a string-inspired model based on the $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric framework, where gauge and Yukawa couplings, along with particle masses, are evolved from the string scale $M_{\text{str}}$ using renormalization group equations (RGEs). A key feature of the model is its flavor symmetry structure, which incorporates the binary dihedral group $\mathbb{D}_2$, providing a natural framework for understanding fermion mass hierarchies and mixing patterns. By minimizing the effective potential, we demonstrate that the scalar mass squared of non-singlet matter fields under the gauge symmetry can develop a negative value slightly below $M_{\text{str}}$. This triggers *precocious radiative breaking* of the unified gauge symmetry down to the Standard Model (SM) gauge group at energies significantly lower than the traditional GUT scale. The mechanism relies on the interplay between the large Yukawa coupling—responsible for spontaneous symmetry breaking—and the colored Higgs coupling, which is critical for suppressing proton decay. The identity of these couplings introduces a unique correlation between the dynamics of symmetry breaking and baryon number violation, offering a novel approach to reconciling gauge hierarchy and proton stability in unified theories. Numerical analysis of the RGE flow reveals that the scalar mass squared negativity occurs within a window of parameters compatible with the observed Higgs mass and SM gauge coupling unification. Additionally, the binary dihedral flavor symmetry restricts the structure of Yukawa matrices, yielding testable predictions for neutrino mixing angles and charged lepton flavor violation. This work highlights a viable pathway for addressing the gauge hierarchy and flavor problems in string-derived models, where the interplay of non-trivial

The magnetic properties of the geometrically frustrated diamond-lattice antiferromagnet spinels FeAl2O4 and MnAl2O4 are re-examined through magnetization measurements and diffuse scattering of polarized neutrons. In FeAl2O4, macroscopic measurements reveal a cusp-like anomaly in the zero-field-cooled magnetic susceptibility near 13 K, accompanied by dynamic magnetic susceptibility and memory effect behaviors inconsistent with a canonical spin-glass scenario. Polarized neutron scattering confirms the absence of long-range magnetic order down to 4 K, underscoring the dominance of short-range spin correlations. Modeling of the powder-averaged differential magnetic neutron scattering cross-section suggests spin-spin correlations extending up to the third nearest-neighbor shell. The estimated Land factor (L) further indicates significant orbital contributions from Fe3+, corroborated by Curie-Weiss analysis of susceptibility data, which highlights the role of orbital moments in modulating magnetic frustration. In contrast, MnAl2O4 undergoes a well-defined magnetic phase transition into a long-range antiferromagnetic state below ∼40 K, confirmed by both bulk and single-crystal neutron diffraction. However, polarized neutron studies reveal persistent spin fluctuations coexisting with long-range order, as evidenced by strong diffuse magnetic intensity. The spatial distribution of this diffuse scattering mirrors the short-range correlations observed in FeAl2O4, suggesting similar underlying mechanisms of magnetic frustration. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical role of spin-spin correlations in determining the magnetic response of diamond-lattice spinels. While FeAl2O4 exhibits properties akin to a spin liquid state with extended short-range order, MnAl2O4 demonstrates a delicate balance between ordered antiferromagnetism and residual frustration. The results emphasize that geometric frustration and orbital effects are key to understanding the complex magnetic behaviors in B-site spinel compounds, where short-range correlations can dominate even in the presence of long-range order. This study theoretically investigates the linear and nonlinear characteristics of quantum electron-acoustic (QEA) waves in a degenerate quantum plasma composed of non-relativistically degenerate electrons, superthermal (Kappa-distributed) electrons, and stationary ions. Employing the reductive perturbation method, the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation governing the modulational dynamics of QEA waves is derived. Analytical and numerical analyses of the stationary solitonic solutions of the NLS equation reveal critical insights into QEA envelope solitons. Key findings indicate that the degeneracy pressure and exchange/Bohm potentials of cold electrons, along with the superthermality of hot electrons (quantified by the spectral index $\kappa$), significantly alter the dispersive and nonlinear properties of QEA waves. The study identifies a threshold wave number $k_c$, such that for $k < k_c$, QEA waves exhibit modulational instability. For $k > k_c$, the NLS equation admits bright envelope solitons, which are spatially ($x$) and temporally ($t$) localized. Notably, increasing $\kappa$ (reducing superthermality) decreases the critical wave number $k_c$ while amplifying the soliton amplitude, highlighting the dual role of superthermal electrons in modulating soliton dynamics. These results underscore the interplay between quantum degeneracy effects and superthermal distributions in shaping nonlinear wave behavior in dense plasmas. The implications of this work are relevant to understanding electrostatic perturbations in high-density environments such as solid-state plasmas generated by intense laser irradiation, semiconductor devices, and microelectronic systems

Accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars (AMXPs), such as IGR J00291+5934, provide critical insights into pulsar formation, evolution, and the physics of ultra-dense matter. These systems enable empirical tests of theoretical models governing neutron star spin evolution and gravitational wave

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of equilibrium states for a class of non-positive potentials defined on a full shift with $\@xmath0$ symbols. Specifically, when the potential is locally proportional to the distance from one of $\@xmath1$ disjoint full shifts with $\@xmath2$ symbols, we prove that the equilibrium state converges as the temperature parameter tends to zero. The limiting measure is shown to be a convex combination of two ergodic measures: those with maximal entropy among all maximizing measures and whose supports correspond to the shifts where the potential is flattest. This result provides critical insight into the long-standing selection problem, suggesting that flatness of the potential is the decisive criterion for selection, as conjectured by A.O. Lopes. Additionally, we establish that the eigenfunction of the associated Ruelle operator converges at the logarithmic scale to a unique calibrated subaction, extending the applicability of the thermodynamic formalism in this context. The findings bridge ergodic optimization and statistical mechanics, offering a novel pathway to analyze zero-temperature limits in symbolic dynamics.

We present an analysis of the truncated disc model in the context of the 2005 hard state outburst of the black hole binary Swift J1753.5–0127, utilizing multiwavelength (optical/UV/X-ray) observations. This system, characterized by high brightness and low interstellar absorption, provides an exceptional dataset for investigating the weak, cool disc emission typically obscured in similar sources. Our study employs X-ray-illuminated disc models to constrain the inner disc radius across the outburst evolution, revealing dynamic spectral components and their dependence on accretion state. During the outburst peak, the observed soft X-ray emission aligns with the thermal emission from the inner disc, with its spectral characteristics (enhanced temperature and luminosity) attributed to reprocessing of hard X-rays in the overlap region between the disc and corona. This inner disc emission serves as the seed photon population for Comptonization processes that generate the hard X-ray spectrum. Simultaneously, the outer disc reprocesses hard X-rays into optical emission, consistent with the truncated disc paradigm. However, during the outburst decline phase, the spectral behavior diverges significantly. Optical emission is likely cyclo-synchrotron radiation generated directly by the jet or corona, rather than reprocessed outer disc emission. Additionally, the soft X-ray component during this phase is inconsistent with inner disc emission due to constraints on reprocessing efficiency and emitting area. A complementary analysis of the low/hard state spectrum of XTE J1118+480, a system with even lower interstellar absorption, corroborates these findings. In XTE J1118+480, the UV/EUV emission is well-fit by a truncated disc model, but the soft X-ray component exhibits a small emitting area and high temperature, incompatible with the disc. This suggests the presence of a distinct spectral component, unrelated to the inner disc radius. While the origin of this component remains speculative, its clear separation from the truncated disc in both systems indicates it cannot be used to constrain disc geometry. These results challenge the applicability of truncated disc models

This study compares the Bruzual & Charlot (1993) galaxy evolution models with observational data on faint galaxy counts, sizes, and colours from the Hubble and Herschel Deep Fields (Metcalfe et al. 1996). For $\Lambda$CDM cosmologies, models with exponentially increasing star formation rates (SFRs) out to $z \sim 2$ are consistent with all datasets. However, for non-$\Lambda$CDM models ($\Omega_0 = 1$), these SFR assumptions require an additional high-redshift galaxy population that rapidly fades or disappears, unresolved in current data. The redshifts of faint blue galaxies—indicating the epoch of galaxy formation—are constrained to $z \sim 3–4$ regardless of cosmology, with no evidence for an SFR peak at $z \sim 6$ as previously reported by Madau et al. (1996). Discrepancies with earlier findings are attributed to differences in faint galaxy photometry, treatment of spiral dust attenuation, and normalization of local galaxy counts. These results highlight the importance of model assumptions and observational uncertainties in interpreting galaxy evolution and highlight the need for improved constraints on high-redshift populations. The findings suggest that galaxy formation was more extended and less sharply peaked than previously inferred.

This paper investigates a variant of the successive refinement problem where receivers possess side information and are required to produce identical reconstructions. We derive general inner and outer bounds for the admissible rate region of this problem and provide a single-letter characterization for several classes of joint source and side information distributions. Our results reveal that side information can be optimally leveraged to reduce communication rates via binning strategies, though reconstruction functions depend solely on the Gács–Körner common randomness shared between the two receivers. A key distinction from prior work on successive refinement is that the derived characterization for the admissible rate region in these settings employs only one auxiliary random variable, contrasting with the multiple auxiliary variables typically required in general bounds. Using this characterization, we establish that the rate region is discontinuous in the underlying source distribution, a surprising result given the absence of zero-error or functional reconstruction constraints in the problem formulation. This discontinuity highlights the intricate dependence of communication efficiency on the statistical dependencies between the source and side information. The findings contribute to understanding the fundamental limits of distributed compression with shared and private information and offer practical insights for designing efficient coding schemes in networks with heterogeneous side information.

This study presents a formulation of @xmath0-nucleus quasielastic scattering that mirrors the standard approach for @xmath1-nucleus quasielastic scattering. Unlike the latter, @xmath0 scattering introduces new responses stemming from scalar contributions, alongside the conventional Coulomb (longitudinal) and transverse @xmath2 responses of vector character. Using the relativistic Hartree approximation to quantum hadrodynamics—both for nuclear matter and finite nuclei—and incorporating RPA (random phase approximation) correlations, we compute these responses. Our calculations achieve good agreement with measured @xmath2 responses and new @xmath0 quasielastic scattering data for @xmath3Ca at @xmath4 MeV/c. A critical factor is the strong RPA quenching required to reproduce the Coulomb response, which is significantly less pronounced in the @xmath0 cross section. Despite scalar contributions being more strongly quenched than vector ones, the "differential quenching" disrupts sensitive cancellations in the @xmath0 cross section expression, reducing its suppression relative to individual responses. This behavior underscores the relativistic distinction between vector and scalar contributions as pivotal to accurately modeling both @xmath2 and @xmath0 data within our nuclear structure framework. By contrasting these scattering mechanisms, the study highlights the necessity of incorporating RPA correlations and relativistic effects to resolve discrepancies in experimental data and refine theoretical predictions. The results emphasize the interplay of nuclear correlations and relativistic structure in quasielastic processes, offering insights into the dynamics of scalar and vector channels in medium-mass nuclei. This work advances the understanding of nuclear response functions and reinforces the role of supercomputer-based methodologies in validating and extending quantum hadrodynamics models for nuclear physics.

This study investigates the electronic structure of a partially disordered quaternary pseudo-Heusler alloy in the L21 phase, both in bulk and (100) thin-film configurations, employing the augmented space recursion (ASR) method within a scalar-relativistic tight-binding linear muffin-tin orbitals (TB-LMTO) framework. Orbital-resolved magnetic moment contributions of constituent elements are analyzed, revealing theoretical predictions that align well with experimental data for Fe and Co magnetic moments but overestimate Cr’s contribution. For the (100) thin film, layer- and orbital-resolved properties are systematically explored, highlighting the impact of structural disorder and reduced dimensionality on electronic and magnetic behavior. The findings underscore the utility of ASR-TB-LMTO in capturing complex electronic phenomena in Heusler alloys, while emphasizing challenges in modeling transition metal interactions under partial disorder. Keywords: partial disorder, augmented space recursion, Heusler alloys.

We investigate the role of electron-electron interactions in quantum point contacts (QPCs) on the first conductance quantization plateau, focusing on all scattering processes. Employing both perturbative and self-consistent nonperturbative methods, we compute low-temperature linear and nonlinear conductance, shot noise, and thermopower. On the plateau, low-temperature corrections arise exclusively from momentum-nonconserving processes that alter the imbalance of left- and right-moving electrons. These interactions suppress conductance with increasing temperature or bias voltage, an effect quantified using a realistic saddle-point potential. The suppression is most pronounced at the onset of the plateau, diminishing under higher magnetic fields due to Pauli exclusion principle suppression of interactions. For the first spin-split plateau, interaction corrections are significantly weaker, consistent with experimental trends. Nonperturbative results, derived via a self-consistent nonequilibrium Green’s function approach, reveal conductance saturation at elevated temperatures. These findings align with experimental observations of the 0.7 anomaly, including the interplay of interaction-driven suppression and spin-related effects.
