The galactic center, within a few hundred parsecs of the Milky Way’s nucleus, serves as a critical laboratory for investigating energetic particle production and propagation. Very-high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray observations, particularly from the H.E.S.S. instrument, offer unparalleled insights into these processes. Recent H.E.S.S. data reveal three discrete VHE gamma-ray sources and diffuse emission spatially correlated with molecular gas in this region. These findings highlight the interplay between cosmic ray acceleration, magnetic fields, and interstellar material. By combining multi-wavelength data, this work advances understanding of particle acceleration mechanisms and the role of the galactic center in shaping cosmic ray dynamics. These results underscore the value of the galactic center as a template for studying non-thermal astrophysical processes.

This study presents the first robust near-infrared period-luminosity (PL) relations for contact binaries (CBs), utilizing the largest catalogs to date: 6,090 CBs and 2,167 open clusters. By achieving unprecedentedly low intrinsic scatter, these relations are established as viable distance calibrators, rivaling the precision of classical Cepheid PL relations. To ensure calibration reliability, we impose stringent criteria on open cluster CBs: (i) membership within the host cluster’s core radius, (ii) proper motion alignment with the cluster’s distribution, and (iii) age consistency between the CB and its cluster. A curated sample of 66 CBs, supported by open cluster distances or high-precision parallaxes, forms the calibration basis. Resulting PL relations for both late-type (W Ursae Majoris-type) and early-type CBs exhibit single-band statistical uncertainties of ~0.1 mag, comparable to Cepheid PL relations. For 90% of the full CB sample, distances are constrained to <5% uncertainty. Leveraging photometric data, CBs enable distance tracing with an overall accuracy of ~0.15 mag. Applying this method to the Large Magellanic Cloud’s 102 CBs yields a distance modulus of $18.47 \pm 0.13$ mag, underscoring their utility in extragalactic distance measurements. These findings demonstrate that CBs, previously underutilized as distance indicators, can now serve as competitive tools for precise galactic and extragalactic distance scales, particularly in regions where Cepheids or other standards are scarce. The methodology’s rigor, combining astrometric and photometric constraints, ensures robustness and scalability, opening new avenues for large-scale cosmic distance mapping.

A high-statistics measurement of neutrinos from a galactic core-collapse supernova is critical for elucidating supernova explosion mechanisms and probing intrinsic neutrino properties, including their absolute mass scale. In this study, we investigate the potential of the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) with its 20 kiloton liquid-scintillator detector to constrain the absolute neutrino mass scale via detection of galactic supernova neutrinos. Assuming a nearly-degenerate neutrino mass spectrum and normal mass ordering, we determine an upper bound on the absolute neutrino mass of @xmath1 at the 95% confidence level for a typical galactic supernova located at 10 kiloparsecs. This bound incorporates statistical fluctuations, represented by the mean and standard deviation of the inferred mass distribution. In comparison, the Super-Kamiokande experiment yields an upper limit of @xmath2 under identical assumptions and confidence level, highlighting JUNO’s enhanced sensitivity due to its larger exposure and detector capabilities. However, the derived constraints weaken when uncertainties in the time structure of supernova neutrino fluxes and an inverted mass ordering are considered. These findings underscore the interplay between experimental design, astrophysical modeling, and neutrino mass parameters in extracting precise limits from supernova neutrino signals. The results demonstrate JUNO’s potential as a pivotal tool for future precision measurements of neutrino properties in galactic core-collapse events.

This study extends the "dimple" model introduced by McMeeking et al. (Adv. Eng. Mater., 2010) to investigate bistable adhesion mechanisms by incorporating the effect of surface roughness in the form of a single-scale axisymmetric waviness. The original model demonstrated that a surface with a shallow depression enables switching between "strong adhesion" (full contact) and "weak adhesion" (partial or complete pull-off) regimes under external pressure, akin to systems with periodic waviness. By introducing a simple roughness structure, we show that such features modify the adhesion behavior: roughness resists the transition to full contact, thereby restricting the "strong adhesion" regime, while simultaneously enhancing pull-off resistance and hysteresis from partial contact states, strengthening the "weak adhesion" regime. The system's behavior is governed by two dimensionless parameters, representing the ratio of the work of adhesion to the energy required to flatten the dimple and the waviness, respectively. These parameters determine the pressure-dependent adhesion stability, particularly in intermediate regimes where real-world adhesive systems exhibit sensitivity to applied load. The model mirrors the Guduru analysis of rough spheres (Guduru, J. Mech. Phys. Solids, 2007), sharing its assumption of a connected contact area, but complements it by focusing on depressions rather than protrusions. This approach highlights the role of hierarchical surface features in multiscale adhesion, offering insights into how depressions interact with periodic roughness to modulate adhesion dynamics. The findings align with observations in pressure-sensitive adhesives, where complex interplay between roughness and adhesion energy dictates performance. By dissecting the influence of waviness on bistable adhesion, this work advances the understanding of adhesive systems with multiple scales of roughness and provides a framework for designing surfaces with tunable adhesion properties. Key terms: *roughness, adhesion, dimple model, JKR adhesion*.

We prove rigidity inequalities for discrete, torsion-free subgroups $\Gamma$ of $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})$ (resp. $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{C})$) without parabolic elements, establishing bounds on the $\Gamma$-module cohomology growth. The key innovation is a novel upper bound for the Jacobian of the barycenter map introduced by Besson–Courtois–Gallot. This estimate yields a sharp inequality relating the critical exponent and homological dimension of $\Gamma$, refining Kapovich’s work and resolving open questions in geometric group theory and rigidity.

This work derives the leading-order anapole form factor of the deuteron within the framework of effective field theory (EFT), explicitly highlighting its distinct momentum dependence compared to the matrix element of strange currents in the deuteron. This distinction offers a critical pathway to disentangle these competing contributions in parity-violating electron-deuteron scattering experiments, where their effects are otherwise entangled. Closed-form analytical expressions for the anapole form factor and commonly encountered integrals in the nucleon-nucleon EFT are presented, providing a calculable foundation for precision studies. These results enhance the interpretability of parity-violating observables and underscore the utility of EFT in isolating weak interaction effects in few-nucleon systems.

This study presents spatially resolved optical spectra of three massive Wolf-Rayet (WR)+OB binary systems—WR86, WR146, and WR147—obtained using the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) aboard the *Hubble Space Telescope* (HST). The systems are classified as follows: WR86 (WC7 + B0 III), WR146 (WC6 + O8 I–IIf), and WR147 (WN8 + O5–7 I–II(f)). WR146 and WR147 are known to exhibit strong non-thermal radio emission, attributed to wind–wind collision (WWC) shocks in their binary systems. In contrast, WR86, despite being a long-period WR+OB binary, lacks detectable non-thermal radio emission. Analysis of the spectra reveals that the O-type companions in WR146 and WR147 display P Cygni profiles in emission lines, indicative of high mass-loss rates (̃10−5–10−4 M☉ yr−1), consistent with expectations for WWC-driven emission. These results support the colliding-wind model as a mechanism for non-thermal radio emission in WR+OB binaries. Conversely, the B0 III companion in WR86 exhibits a low mass-loss rate (̃10−7–10−6 M☉ yr−1), which likely localizes the WWC region closer to the B star, reducing its effective collision area and suppressing non-thermal radio output. To contextualize the systems’ luminosities, absolute magnitudes were estimated for each component using spectral-type-based calibrations (Schmidt-Kaler for OB stars, van der Hucht for WR stars). This study presents a theoretical investigation into the Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) of magnetoexcitonic polaritons in a two-dimensional (2D) electron-hole system embedded in a semiconductor microcavity under high magnetic fields. The system is realized in two distinct physical platforms: a graphene layer and a quantum well (QW). The 2D magnetoexcitonic polariton gas is confined within a planar harmonic potential trap, achievable via inhomogeneous local stress, an external electric field, or a parabolically shaped microcavity that traps photons. By deriving an effective Hamiltonian for the ideal polariton gas in graphene and QW systems, we determine the BEC temperature as a function of magnetic field and trapping potential parameters. Key findings include the dependence of the effective polariton mass ($@xmath1$) on the magnetic field, which increases as $@xmath2$. Consequently, the BEC critical temperature ($@xmath3$) decreases with the magnetic field following $@xmath4$ but exhibits a linear increase with the spring constant of the parabolic trap. Additionally, we analyze the Rabi splitting—a critical parameter for optically coupled exciton-photon systems—showing that in graphene, it is tunable by the external magnetic field, as it scales with $@xmath4$, whereas in QWs, Rabi splitting remains independent of the magnetic field under strong confinement. These results highlight the interplay between magnetic fields, material-specific band structures, and trapping geometries in controlling polariton condensation. The proposed framework provides a pathway to engineer coherent quantum states in semiconductor-based systems, with implications for quantum information and ultra-low-energy optoelectronics. This work bridges condensed matter physics and cavity quantum electrodynamics, offering insights into the design of novel 2D polariton platforms for both fundamental research and technological applications.

This paper presents a theorem in $d$-dimensional static, spherically symmetric spacetimes within generic Lovelock gravity coupled to a non-linear electrodynamic (NLM) source. The theorem establishes that, in the case of a pure electric field, the NLM equations are inherently satisfied by the Einstein-Lovelock equations, independent of the orders of the Lovelock Lagrangian or the non-linear Maxwell theory. This universality simplifies the derivation of exact solutions in higher-order gravitational theories. Applications to Chern-Simons (CS) gravity are explored, demonstrating how the theorem constrains black hole solutions in this framework. Additionally, the theorem is extended to radiating spacetimes, generalizing the Bonnor-Vaidya (BV) metric to Lovelock gravity with an NLM field as a radiating source. A specific example is provided for the power-Maxwell case, where finely-tuned constants ensure consistency with the field equations. These results unify and extend known solutions, offering insights into black hole thermodynamics and gravitational dynamics in higher-curvature theories. By bridging Lovelock gravity and non-linear electrodynamics, the work advances the study of exact solutions in modified gravity models and their astrophysical implications.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the major pair fraction and derived major merger fraction and rate for 82 massive ($M_{\ast} \geq 10^{11} M_{\odot}$) galaxies at $z \sim 1.5$, utilizing deep Hubble Space Telescope (HST) NICMOS imaging from the GOODS North and South fields. For the first time, our NICMOS data provides the angular resolution and depth necessary to compile a statistically robust sample of massive galaxies at $z \gtrsim 1.5$, enabling a reliable characterization of their pair fraction history. We find robust evidence that the pair fraction of massive galaxies evolves significantly with redshift. Specifically, we measure a pair fraction of $f_{\text{pair}} = 0.29 \pm 0.06$ for the combined sample at $z \sim 1.5$. By fitting a power-law function of the form $f_{\text{pair}}(z) = A(1+z)^n$ to a merged dataset spanning low-redshift ($z \sim 0.1$) observations from Conselice et al. (2007) and our high-redshift ($z \sim 1.5–3.0$) NICMOS results, we derive best-fit parameters $A = 0.008 \pm 0.003$ and $n = 3.0 \pm 0.4$. This steep redshift evolution suggests a rapid rise in pair fractions at $z \gtrsim 1.5$. Further, fitting a theoretically motivated Press-Schechter model to the data reveals no turnover in the pair fraction curve, indicating that the merger fraction of massive galaxies continues to increase at least up to $z \sim 3$. This contrasts with lower-mass galaxies, whose merger fractions peak at $z \sim 1.5–2.0$, offering compelling evidence for *galaxy assembly downsizing*—where higher-mass systems undergo more mergers at earlier cosmic times. We calculate a major merger rate of $1.2 \pm 0.5 \times 10^{-3}$ Gpc$^{-3}$ Gyr$^{-1}$ at $z = 2.6$, with a marginal decrease to $1.0

This study identifies 93 binary star systems in the field of the *Kepler* spacecraft using proper motion catalogs to test the gyrochronology hypothesis, which posits a relationship between stellar rotation period, age, and mass. Rotation periods were derived via the autocorrelation function (ACF) of *Kepler* photometry, enabling a comparative analysis of binary components. For systems with reliable period measurements, the cooler star in each binary typically exhibits a longer rotation period than its hotter counterpart, aligning with theoretical predictions of angular momentum evolution. However, significant scatter exists in the period-color gradient between binary pairs, suggesting variability in rotational evolution even among coeval stars. Notably, near the solar color range, few stars display periods exceeding the Sun’s, implying that these systems—and their cooler companions—are likely not significantly older than the Sun. A striking feature is an apparent gap in rotation periods among late K- and early M-dwarfs, which may reflect heterogeneous star formation histories, non-uniform evolutionary rates, or mass-dependent differences in angular momentum loss. Additionally, the ACF-derived activity levels reveal a clear anti-correlation between rotation period and activity for F-, G-, and early K-type stars, consistent with magnetic braking. However, mid K- to early M-dwarfs show no such correlation, challenging assumptions of universal gyrochronology relations for low-mass stars. These findings underscore the complexity of rotational evolution and suggest that while gyrochronology holds promise, its application requires careful consideration of binary dynamics, stellar type, and potential evolutionary outliers. The results advocate for revised models incorporating these observed trends to improve age estimation in stellar populations.

**Résumé:** La structure des valeurs propres d’un système quantique, c’est-à-dire son spectre, est cruciale pour en comprendre les propriétés. Dans un article de 1971, Baxter a démontré que les valeurs propres du modèle de la glace s’expriment via des polynômes remarquables. Cette observation a conduit, dès les années 1980-1990, à la conjecture que ces polynômes, désormais appelés *polynômes de Baxter*, régissent le spectre de systèmes quantiques plus généraux. En adoptant le cadre mathématique de la théorie des représentations, nous montrons ici comment ces polynômes émergent naturellement. Cette approche, basée sur la symétrie et la structure algébrique des systèmes, a permis de prouver rigoureusement en 2013 la conjecture générale. Ce travail établit un lien fondamental entre les méthodes combinatoires et la théorie des représentations dans l’étude des systèmes intégrables. (111 mots)

This study investigates the contribution of source cosmic rays (SCRs), accelerated and confined in supernova remnants (SNRs), to the diffuse high-energy γ-ray emission above 1 GeV from the Galactic disk. SCRs produce γ-rays via hadronic interactions and inverse Compton (IC) scattering, with spectra significantly harder than those from Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs). Extending prior work, we employ a simplified SNR population synthesis model to compute the IC emission from SCR electrons and derive the combined γ-ray spectrum from the SNR population. Comparing these predictions with low-latitude diffuse γ-ray data from EGRET and ground-based instruments, we find that SCRs contribute comparably to GCRs at GeV energies, driven primarily by core-collapse SNRs (Types II and Ib) exploding into wind bubbles of massive progenitor stars. At energies above 10 GeV, SCR-dominated emission becomes dominant, while at TeV energies, the contribution arises mainly from SNRs expanding into a uniform interstellar medium. However, the combined hadronic and IC γ-ray flux exceeds observational limits unless the confinement time τ_c, the duration SCRs remain trapped in SNRs, is as short as 10^4 years, and the magnetic field strength in SNRs is as high as 30 μG. These constraints align with theoretical expectations for magnetic field amplification via cosmic ray (CR) backreaction during particle acceleration. Our results suggest that precise measurements of the diffuse Galactic γ-ray spectrum at TeV energies could serve as a critical consistency test for the SNR origin of CRs. Such observations would constrain the efficiency of CR confinement and acceleration mechanisms, while addressing longstanding questions about the role of SNRs in shaping the Galactic CR budget. The findings underscore the necessity of integrating multi-wavelength and multi-messenger data to disentangle the relative contributions of SCR- and GCR-driven emission processes in the high-energy universe.

This article examines the formation of metastable solids through rapid quenching across freezing or structural transitions. Focusing on martensites—a prototypical nonequilibrium solid–solid transformation—we present a perspective on how their morphology critically depends on processing history. By analyzing kinetic and thermodynamic constraints, we emphasize the role of transformation paths in dictating microstructural evolution. Our viewpoint underscores the interplay between intrinsic material properties and external processing parameters, offering insights into controlling metastable states for functional material design.

A survey of radio recombination lines (RRLs) in the Galactic plane (332°–33°) near 327 MHz, conducted using the Ooty Radio Telescope (ORT), has detected carbon RRLs from all observed positions within the longitude range 0°–20°, and sporadically elsewhere. These carbon RRLs originate from "diffuse" interstellar regions, distinct from the "intense" emission sites typically associated with hydrogen RRLs at 3 cm. Comparing the velocity structure and radial distribution of carbon RRLs with hydrogen RRLs reveals a spatial alignment of diffuse carbon-emitting regions with spiral arm components in the inner Galaxy. Central velocities of carbon RRLs at several longitudes coincide with self-absorption features, suggesting a link to cooler, neutral gas phases. However, observed line widths differ between carbon and hydrogen RRLs, potentially due to thermal and non-thermal broadening mechanisms, ionized/neutral medium interactions, or variations in turbulent motions. These findings highlight the distinct kinematic and structural properties of diffuse carbon-emitting regions, offering insights into the interplay between low-density ionized gas and the spiral arm morphology. The study underscores the utility of low-frequency RRL observations in probing the diffuse interstellar medium and its role in Galactic dynamics.

We present the first time-series observations of a short outburst of HT Cam (RX J0757.0+6306), a proposed intermediate polar (IP). On 2001 December 29, the object was detected at a bright magnitude of ~0.5, prompting international joint monitoring via the VSNET collaboration. We present a continuum model for a system of self-propelled particles interacting through alignment and repulsion, derived from a mean-field kinetic description. The particles’ velocities are governed by self-propulsion and repulsion from neighbors, while their direction of motion aligns with neighboring particles, subject to stochastic noise. Starting from a Fokker-Planck-type kinetic equation, we derive a set of non-conservative hydrodynamic equations in the macroscopic limit. This derivation employs a moment closure technique based on the Von Mises-Fisher distribution and generalized collision invariants, which account for the anisotropic alignment and repulsion forces. The resulting model captures collective dynamics such as flocking and swarming, while incorporating noise-induced fluctuations and spatial inhomogeneities. To validate the continuum model, we perform numerical simulations and compare its predictions with those of the underlying particle system. We demonstrate excellent agreement in both equilibrium and non-equilibrium regimes, confirming the model’s fidelity to the microscopic dynamics. Additionally, we benchmark our model against existing self-propelled particle systems, such as the Vicsek model and variants with non-local alignment rules. This study investigates the dynamics of a single chain polymer confined to a two-dimensional cell using a kinetically constrained lattice gas model designed to preserve chain connectivity. Through Monte Carlo simulations, we examine polymer dynamics across a range of densities, including those approaching full packing. Remarkably, even at high densities, monomers exhibit long-range diffusion, achieving root mean square displacements comparable to the system size over timescales where the polymer’s global geometry remains largely preserved. To quantify this shape persistence, we define a local tangent field and analyze the two-time tangent-tangent correlation function, revealing glass-like behavior indicative of slowed structural relaxation. Both closed and open chains display reptational motion and reshaping via localized fingering events, which drive global monomer displacements. These findings highlight the interplay between kinetic constraints and geometric preservation in confined polymers, offering insights into the emergence of collective motion and the role of connectivity in glassy dynamics. This work provides a framework for understanding polymer behavior in confined environments and the balance between mobility and structural coherence in kinetically constrained systems.

This study examines the statistical distribution of isolated recycled pulsars (IRPs) and double neutron star (DNS) binaries in the Galactic disk, addressing their shared origins in binary systems disrupted during stellar evolution. Recycled pulsars, spun up via mass transfer in close binaries, are theorized to become isolated after the ejection of their progenitor companions, while surviving DNS systems remain bound. Observations reveal comparable numbers of IRPs and DNS binaries, contrasting sharply with standard evolutionary models, which predict significantly more IRPs than DNS systems. To resolve this discrepancy, we perform population synthesis calculations incorporating kinematic differences between these populations. We demonstrate that the velocity dispersion of IRPs is broader than that of DNS binaries, influencing their detectability in radio surveys. Accounting for Doppler smearing—a selection effect that biases the detection of DNS binaries due to orbital motion—we identify a modest (~1.5×) detection preference for DNS systems. However, this effect alone cannot reconcile the observed IRP-DNS ratio when using standard neutron star natal kick velocities (σ ≈ 265 km s−1). Our results show that population models assuming a 1D Maxwellian natal kick velocity dispersion of σ ≈ 130 km s−1 align with observational data. This finding reinforces prior evidence that neutron stars formed in close binaries receive smaller natal kicks compared to those inferred from isolated pulsars, suggesting environmental or formation-specific mechanisms modulate kick magnitudes. By integrating kinematic and observational selection effects, this work highlights the critical role of reduced natal kicks in binaries for explaining the Galactic population of compact stellar remnants. These conclusions deepen our understanding of binary evolution and neutron star formation pathways. *Methods: Statistical analysis; stellar kinematics; pulsar population synthesis.*

The role of random disorder in altering the melting behavior of two-dimensional (2D) systems is critically examined through molecular dynamics simulations. By introducing quenched disorder via the random pinning of a minor fraction of particles, we investigate systems governed by core-softened potentials with two repulsive steps. In the absence of disorder, systems with a small repulsive shoulder exhibit a melting sequence consistent with the theoretical framework of a first-order liquid-hexatic transition followed by a continuous hexatic-solid transition, akin to soft-disk models. However, the incorporation of quenched disorder is observed to broaden the hexatic phase without altering the overall transition hierarchy. Notably, for systems with a larger repulsive step at high densities, the absence of disorder yields a conventional first-order solid-liquid transition. Strikingly, the introduction of disorder transforms this single transition into two distinct events: a continuous Kosterlitz-Thouless-Halperin-Nelson-Young (KTHNY)-like solid-hexatic transition, followed by a first-order hexatic-isotropic liquid transition. These findings underscore the profound impact of quenched disorder on 2D melting scenarios, highlighting the necessity to account for such effects when interpreting experimental data. Our results reveal that the interplay between disorder and interaction potential geometry can qualitatively reshape phase transition dynamics, offering insights into the nonequilibrium behavior of disordered 2D materials. This work provides a foundational framework for understanding how structural imperfections influence collective order in confined systems, with implications for both theoretical modeling and experimental analysis.

This paper presents an efficient algorithm for simulating quantum many-body systems in two spatial dimensions using projected entangled pair states (PEPS). The method approximates the environment tensor network, essential for updating tensors during time evolution, with a single-layered structure. This simplification reduces computational costs by an order of magnitude, enabling access to a larger submanifold of the Hilbert space bounded by the tensor network’s bond dimension. Numerical validation on the antiferromagnetic isotropic Heisenberg model demonstrates the algorithm’s stability and accuracy, showing strong agreement with established results. The approach advances practical PEPS simulations by balancing computational efficiency with physical fidelity, offering a scalable framework for studying strongly correlated systems in two dimensions.

This article reviews recent advancements in understanding wave scattering in systems exhibiting intrinsic chaos, disorder, and internal losses, where the non-unitarity of the scattering matrix introduces significant complexity. By mapping the problem onto a nonlinear supersymmetric model, we derive closed-form analytic expressions for the distribution of reflection probabilities in generic disordered systems. A central outcome is the discovery of statistical independence between the phase and modulus of the reflection amplitude in each perfectly open channel, a feature absent in lossless systems. This independence has profound implications for quantities such as local Green functions and time delays, revealing novel connections between loss mechanisms and wave dynamics. Importantly, absorption emerges as a sensitive probe of the Anderson localization transition, offering insights into the interplay between disorder and dissipation. The study further extends random matrix theory to analyze scattering matrix and impedance correlations across symmetry classes, alongside the distribution of transmitted power in systems with broken time-reversal invariance, building on prior theoretical frameworks. These results provide a comprehensive characterization of wave transport in non-Hermitian systems and enable practical applications in measuring impedance and reflection in experimental setups, such as microwave or ultrasonic cavities coupled to antenna arrays. The findings bridge fundamental wave physics and experimental accessibility, advancing the study of disordered and chaotic systems in the presence of loss.

This study derives exact analytical results for the rate of change of thermodynamic quantities along configurational adiabats (isomorphs) in so-called Roskilde liquids, where structural and dynamical properties remain invariant under density and temperature variations. Focusing on the configurational specific heat at constant volume, $ C_{V}^{c} $, we examine its behavior along isomorphs in the density-temperature phase diagram. The slope $ \Gamma $, defined in a double logarithmic plot of the phase diagram, is interpreted as one-third of an effective inverse power-law potential exponent. For liquids where $ \Gamma $ increases (decreases) with density, the contours of $ C_{V}^{c} $ exhibit smaller (larger) slopes compared to isomorphs, revealing a non-trivial interplay between thermodynamic and configurational properties. A fluctuation formula for the slope of $ C_{V}^{c} $-contours is derived, connecting it to the virial-potential energy correlation coefficient and $ \Gamma $. Theoretical predictions are validated using molecular dynamics simulations of the Lennard-Jones and Girifalco fluids. The sign of $ \gamma $, the effective inverse power-law exponent, emerges as a critical parameter characterizing Roskilde liquids, alongside $ \Gamma $ and the virial-potential energy correlation coefficient $ \rho $. Extending beyond isomorph theory, we compare the invariance of the self-diffusion coefficient along isomorphs and $ C_{V}^{c} $-contours. The results demonstrate stronger invariance of self-diffusion along isomorphs, underscoring their role as fundamental thermodynamic curves. These findings advance the understanding of liquid-state universality and provide a framework for linking microscopic interactions to macroscopic behavior in supercooled and glass-forming liquids.

This paper addresses the filtering problem for discrete-time stochastic volatility models with disturbances characterized by rational probability density functions, including Cauchy and Student *t*-distributions with odd degrees of freedom. By leveraging state space realizations to represent these rational densities, an exact solution to the filtering problem is achieved. However, the computational complexity grows exponentially with time due to the increasing dimensionality of the state space matrices. To mitigate this, the paper introduces stochastically balanced truncation techniques to approximate high-order rational functions, ensuring tractability while preserving accuracy. A simulation study validates the effectiveness of the proposed approach in capturing volatility dynamics under these heavy-tailed distributions. Furthermore, a method of moments estimator is derived to facilitate parameter inference. The combination of exact filtering and approximation methods provides a scalable framework for handling stochastic volatility in non-Gaussian settings. Keywords: stochastic volatility, filtering, rational probability density function, state space realization, stochastically balanced truncation.

This study presents high-resolution and spectral imaging X-ray observations of the IC 4329a/IC 4329 galaxy system using *ROSAT* High Resolution Imager (HRI) and Position Sensitive Proportional Counter (PSPC), alongside optical follow-up data from the European Southern Observatory (ESO). Located at a distance of 44 Mpc, the nearby Type 1 Seyfert galaxy IC 4329a and its giant lenticular companion, IC 4329, are surrounded by a rich X-ray source population. The brightest detected point source is IC 4329a itself, exhibiting an ultraluminous X-ray (X-ray luminosity, *L*<sub>X</sub> ≈ 2 × 10<sup>43</sup> erg s<sup>−1</sup>) with spectral properties consistent with a single power-law model (Γ ≈ 1.7) and a distinct spectral break at 0.7 keV. Two additional bright X-ray sources are associated with IC 4329, while a likely quasar is identified 14 arcminutes southwest of the system. Optical observations confirm three other X-ray point sources near IC

This study investigates the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of magnesium dihydride (MgH2) for hydrogen storage, focusing on the effects of alloying with lightweight transition metals (TM = Sc, Ti, V, Cr) to overcome its high stability and sluggish (de)hydrogenation kinetics. Using first-principles density functional theory calculations, we analyze the structural and energetic characteristics of Mg1−xTmxH2 compounds for compositions 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Our results reveal that the experimentally observed decline in hydrogenation rates for x > 0.2 correlates with a structural phase transition of Mg1−xTmxH2 from fluorite to rutile, which impedes hydrogen diffusion. The thermodynamic stability of these compounds decreases systematically along the Sc > Ti > V > Cr series. By tuning TM choice and composition x, the formation enthalpy of Mg1−xTmxH2 is shown to be adjustable across a wide range (ΔH_f = 2.5 eV/f.u.), enabling tailored properties for hydrogen storage applications. Notably, for compositions with high Mg content (x < 0.3), the enthalpy of reversible hydrogenation remains comparable to pure MgH2, provided the alloy Mg1−xTmx remains intact during dehydrogenation. These findings highlight the potential of TM-alloyed Mg hydrides to balance gravimetric capacity with favorable thermodynamics and kinetics, advancing practical hydrogen storage systems.

We investigate the local extrema of two models that introduce anisotropic structures into the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature field, as observed by the five-year *Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe* (*WMAP*): the dipole modulation model and the ACW (axisymmetric correlation) model. This study is motivated by persistent anomalies in *WMAP* data, particularly the hemispherical asymmetry in statistical properties of temperature anisotropies. Using a frequentist framework, we compare the one- and two-point statistics of these models against observational data to assess their viability in explaining large-scale CMB irregularities. For the dipole modulation model, analysis of one-point statistics reveals that the hemispherical variance discrepancy—where one hemisphere exhibits higher power on large scales—appears alleviated. However, new inconsistencies emerge when examining the mean and angular dependence of the statistics. Two-point correlation functions of local extrema, quantified via the temperature pair product ($\xi_1$) and spatial pair-count ($\xi_2$), further demonstrate that the dipole modulation over-asymmetrizes the temperature field on sub-dipole/quadrupole scales, a feature disfavored by the *WMAP* data. In contrast, the ACW model, which introduces a rotationally invariant anisotropic correlation structure, produces predictions consistent with the standard isotropic $\Lambda$CDM hypothesis. The two-point analysis confirms that the ACW model’s impact on extrema statistics is minimal, suggesting that such anisotropic models weakly perturb the CMB’s statistical isotropy. Our results indicate that while the dipole modulation addresses certain aspects of the hemispherical anomaly, its over-prediction of asymmetry on smaller scales undermines its plausibility. The ACW model, though compatible with isotropy, fails to fully resolve the observed anomalies. We conclude that neither model captures the necessary spatial complexity to explain the *WMAP* large-scale asymmetries. Future work should explore models with richer spatial structures, potentially incorporating non-Gaussian or higher-order anisotropic components, to reconcile the observed CMB anomalies with theoretical frameworks. This study underscores the need for refined methodologies to disentangle primordial anisotropies from late-time systematics in CMB analyses. **Methods**: Data analysis focuses on CMB temperature extrema statistics, utilizing *WMAP* 5-year maps. One-point variance and mean are compared across hemispheres, while two-point correlations ($\xi_1$, $\xi_2$) assess spatial dependence under anisotropic models.

This study investigates the equilibrium vortex structures in thin films of anisotropic superconductors subjected to tilted magnetic fields, focusing on the moderate and strong anisotropy limits. By employing two distinct theoretical frameworks—London theory with an anisotropic mass tensor and a Josephson-decoupled layered London-type model—we determine the energetically favorable configurations of isolated vortex lines. Key findings reveal that tilting the magnetic field induces a reconfiguration of vortex interactions. Specifically, the interplay between long-range attractive and repulsive forces in the vortex-vortex interaction potential leads to the emergence of a minimum at specific inter-vortex distances. This minimum, however, exists only within a constrained range of tilting angles, which diminishes as the anisotropy of the system decreases. Such unique interaction profiles drive the formation of vortex clusters, whose sizes depend on the tilting angle, film thickness, or layering effects. Additionally, the vortices self-organize into multi-quantum flux lattices, characterized by unit cells enclosing integer multiples (denoted as $ n\Phi_0 $) of the elementary flux quantum $ \Phi_0 $. The study predicts a series of phase transitions between lattices with distinct $ n $ as the magnetic field tilting increases, signaling structural reconfigurations in the flux arrangement. These results highlight the critical role of anisotropy and field orientation in shaping non-trivial vortex states, offering insights into the design of superconducting materials with tailored vortex dynamics for applications in quantum technologies or high-performance superconducting devices. The interplay of geometric constraints and anisotropic properties emerges as a key mechanism for controlling vortex matter in layered superconductors.

This study investigates the dynamics of Solar Active Region NOAA 11158, a prolific source of strong flares, including an X2.2 event. Current density and helicity complexity are analyzed using a sign-singular measure cancellation approach, revealing power-law scaling in the distribution of magnetic field cancellations. Spectral analysis identifies two distinct scaling ranges with differing spectral indices, indicating heterogeneous energy dissipation processes. Time-resolved examination shows abrupt shifts in cancellation exponents coinciding with major flares, alongside correlations with EUV and X-ray flux variations. These findings suggest that large flares are intrinsically tied to small-scale current structure evolution, highlighting the critical role of localized magnetic reconnection in eruptive events. The results underscore the importance of microphysical processes in driving solar energetic phenomena.

This study investigates the central exclusive production of the Standard Model Higgs boson in the WW decay channel at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We compute the experimental acceptance, incorporating proposed proton tagging detectors positioned at 220 m and 420 m near ATLAS and/or CMS experiments, alongside Level 1 trigger acceptances. By simulating proton detection efficiency and trigger performance, we evaluate the feasibility of isolating the Higgs signal. Additionally, we present the first estimates of photon-photon and gluon-gluon-induced background processes in both semi-leptonic and fully-leptonic WW decay channels. Our results demonstrate that the Higgs signal remains detectable for masses between 140 GeV and 200 GeV, with background contamination shown to be manageable via optimized analysis strategies. The inclusion of forward proton tagging significantly enhances sensitivity, offering a complementary probe of the Higgs sector in this mass range. These findings underscore the potential of exclusive production mechanisms and proton tagging at the LHC for addressing critical questions in the Standard Model and beyond.

This study investigates the dynamical evolution of globular clusters with mass spectra under the influence of a steady galactic tidal field, incorporating the effects of velocity anisotropy. Using Fokker-Planck models, we track the development of anisotropy as clusters evolve. While velocity anisotropy emerges similarly to single-mass systems, its degree is notably suppressed compared to isolated clusters, primarily due to tidal truncation. For most evolutionary phases, mass components—except those in the earliest stages—exhibit tangential anisotropy in outer regions, consistent with observations of real clusters. Comparisons with multi-mass King-Michie models reveal that isotropic King models better reproduce Fokker-Planck results for density profiles, as tangential anisotropy complicates fits for multi-mass anisotropic models. Crucially, density profiles for individual mass components cannot be reconciled with multi-mass King models across all radial ranges, suggesting that attempts to derive global mass functions from observed mass functions in limited radial ranges may yield unreliable results, particularly for low-mass stars. We further analyze the time-dependent evolution of the mass function, finding that its power-law index declines monotonically with the total cluster mass. This aligns qualitatively with observed slopes in selected clusters, though quantitative comparisons remain premature due to additional evaporation mechanisms. Projected velocity profiles in anisotropic models, incorporating the apocenter criterion for stellar evaporation, show significant flattening near the tidal radius compared to isotropic models or anisotropic models using the energy criterion. This behavior mirrors observations of the collapsed core cluster M15, indicating that tidal evolution with anisotropy plays a critical role in shaping kinematic properties. Our results underscore the limitations of multi-mass King models in capturing the interplay between tidal fields and velocity anisotropy, emphasizing the need for self-consistent models that account for these factors. The findings have implications for interpreting observational data, as neglecting anisotropy or using truncated radial samples could mischaracterize mass functions and evolutionary states. These insights contribute to understanding the long-term survival and structural evolution of globular clusters in galactic environments. **Keywords**: celestial mechanics; stellar dynamics; globular clusters: general.

Base station (BS) sleeping has emerged as a promising strategy to improve network energy efficiency by deactivating underutilized BSs. However, this practice introduces trade-offs in user performance, influenced by user association criteria, channel conditions to active BSs, and scheduling policies in loaded networks. This paper addresses these challenges by developing a systematic analytical framework to evaluate the spectral efficiency and outage probability of downlink transmissions for users in sleeping cells. The framework incorporates the interplay between user association strategies, traffic-aware BS selection, and scheduling algorithms, while accounting for spatial and channel-dependent interference effects. A novel user association scheme, termed *Maximum Mean Channel Access Probability* (MMAP), is proposed, wherein a typical user selects the active BS with the highest calculated mean channel access probability, derived from the current traffic loads of active BSs. This approach is contrasted with the conventional *Maximum Received Signal Power* (MRSP)-based association, which prioritizes signal strength regardless of BS load. Both greedy and round-robin scheduling schemes are analyzed for user allocation at active BSs. The study derives exact expressions for access probabilities, received signal and interference power statistics, and corresponding metrics for spectral and energy efficiency. Active Region NOAA 11035, observed in December 2009 during the nascent phase of Solar Cycle 24, exhibited a complex delta sunspot configuration driven by the emergence of parasitic magnetic flux near the rotationally leading polarity. This flux traversed the penumbra of the region’s largest sunspot, creating a magnetically intricate structure. High-resolution visible and infrared imaging spectropolarimetry of the Fe I line pairs at 6302 Å and 15,650 Å revealed pronounced Zeeman splitting in the penumbral region between the parasitic and main umbrae. Polarized Stokes spectra from this area displayed anomalous line profiles, accompanied by localized blueshifts exceeding 3.8 km s−1. To investigate these features, a Milne-Eddington inversion code was employed, capable of fitting either a single magnetic component with stray light or two independent magnetic components. The analysis demonstrated that the anomalous profiles cannot be explained by superposition of moderate-field structures, necessitating the presence of ultra-strong magnetic fields (3500–3800 G). These extreme fields, observed in close proximity to vigorous upflows, challenge the conventional understanding of sunspot magnetohydrostatic equilibrium. The nearly horizontal magnetic configuration near the polarity inversion line further defies standard flux-rope models, suggesting dynamic processes such as flux emergence and shear flows play a critical role in shaping sunspot magnetic topologies. These findings highlight the need for revised models incorporating non-equilibrium dynamics to accurately describe complex active regions and their potential to generate eruptive solar activity. The study underscores the importance of high-cadence, multiwavelength spectropolarimetry in probing the magnetic intricacies of solar active regions.

We present a morphologically stratified redshift distribution of faint field galaxies derived from a statistically unbiased sample of 196 galaxies brighter than *B_J* = 23 mag. Utilizing detailed morphological classifications from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based spectroscopic redshifts, galaxies are categorized into three broad types: early-type (E/S0s), spirals, and a combined class of small disk/spheroidal, dwarf elliptical, irregular, and peculiar (Sdm/De/Irr/Pec) galaxies. The redshift distributions for each class reveal distinct evolutionary behaviors. Notably, Sdm/De/Irr/Pec galaxies exhibit a prominent excess at low to moderate redshifts (*z* ≲ 0.3), confirming a steep faint-end slope (α ≈ –1.4) in their luminosity function (LF). While strong luminosity evolution accounts for their moderate-redshift abundance, their overall number density remains comparable to local observations. At fainter magnitudes, however, the population of irregular/peculiar (Irr/Pec) galaxies at higher redshifts (*z* ≳ 0.5) increases significantly, exceeding predictions from luminosity evolution alone. This suggests that these systems are likely progenitors of present-day ellipticals and spirals undergoing intense star formation or undergoing mergers. In contrast, E/S0s and spirals display redshift distributions consistent with passive luminosity evolution, showing only marginal deviation from a non-evolving model. These results highlight divergent evolutionary pathways among galaxy types, with Sdm/De/Irr/Pec galaxies playing a critical role in shaping the high-redshift galaxy population and contributing to the formation of more massive structures via violent processes. The findings underscore the importance of morphological classification in understanding cosmic evolution and emphasize the interplay between luminosity evolution and structural transformation in galaxy assembly. *Submitted to ApJ, August 4th, 1997, accepted July 27th, 1998*

This article presents practical consequences of a novel numerical algorithm for molecular dynamics simulations, distinct from traditional finite-difference methods. The proposed approach, which complements existing integration techniques for motion equations, operates in two stages: first, it analytically derives polynomials in a formal parameter $\lambda$, approximating solutions to differential equations; second, numerical solutions are obtained by evaluating these polynomials within intervals where the difference between the full polynomial and its truncated form remains below a prescribed accuracy $\epsilon$. This method was applied to benchmark systems, including forced linear and nonlinear oscillators and a 2D Lennard-Jones fluid, with the latter restricted to first-degree polynomials in $\lambda$. The algorithm's flexibility and precision make it particularly suited for modeling unconventional materials, such as auxetics, whose counterintuitive properties demand high numerical accuracy to avoid artifacts. For instance, inaccuracies in simulations could erroneously alter mechanical responses, such as negative Poisson’s ratios. By minimizing such numerical side effects, the algorithm enhances reliability in predicting material behavior. The study highlights the algorithm’s robustness across diverse systems, demonstrating its potential for addressing challenges in molecular dynamics where traditional methods may struggle with stability or accuracy. These findings underscore the importance of tailored numerical techniques in capturing the physical reality of complex materials. The relevance of this work spans computational physics and materials science, offering a pathway to refine simulations of systems with anomalous properties. PACS: 31.15.qg, 02.60.cb, 02.60.-x.

We present the detection of gamma-ray emission from multiple globular clusters (GCs), including Terzan 5, the second confirmed gamma-ray-emitting GC. To date, over a dozen GCs exhibit gamma-ray luminosities above 100 MeV, enabling the first systematic investigation of correlations between their emission and cluster properties. Our analysis reveals robust relationships between gamma-ray luminosity and four key parameters: stellar encounter rate, metallicity [Fe/H], and the energy densities of ambient soft photons (e.g., from stellar fields). These "fundamental planes" of gamma-ray GCs suggest a tight link between emission processes and the population of millisecond pulsars (MSPs) within clusters. The observed correlations imply that gamma-ray emission is primarily driven by MSPs, with their activity modulated by environmental factors such as stellar interactions and photon fields. This study provides critical insights into the mechanisms underlying GC gamma-ray emission, supporting the hypothesis that MSPs are the dominant source while highlighting the interplay between cluster dynamics and high-energy astrophysical phenomena.

This study theoretically investigates electronic transport through a parallel-coupled double quantum dot (DQD) using the Green function technique and the equation of motion approach. The inter-dot coupling in the system generates bonding and antibonding molecular states, which serve as a natural basis to analyze transport properties. Leveraging this framework, the Fano interference observed in the conductance spectra is systematically elucidated, arising from the destructive quantum interference between discrete molecular states and continuum channels. By tuning external parameters—such as dot-lead coupling strength, inter-dot coupling, magnetic flux through the ring linking the dots and leads, and flux differences between sub-rings—this work demonstrates the controllability of the Fano lineshape. Notably, the asymmetric tail of the Fano resonance can be reversibly flipped by magnetic fields, enabling magnetic manipulation of conductance spectra without altering the lineshape symmetry. More significantly, the study identifies a "swap effect," where magnetic flux modulation exchanges the roles of the bonding and antibonding states. This effect, which allows for state reconfiguration, is proposed as a potential mechanism for implementing qubits in quantum computation. The findings highlight the versatility of DQD systems in engineering quantum transport phenomena and underscore their promise for future spintronic and quantum information devices. This work provides a theoretical foundation for harnessing molecular-like states in nanoscale systems for advanced quantum control.

Zeta regularization, a mathematical framework for assigning finite values to divergent series or integrals, has emerged as a robust tool for regularizing vacuum energy density in quantum field theory. Complemented by the Hadamard regularization method, it successfully yields finite, physically meaningful results even in complex scenarios, such as when imposing boundary conditions (BCs) on spatially extended or compactified geometries. These techniques are particularly valuable in addressing the cosmological constant (CC) problem, a longstanding discrepancy between theoretical predictions of vacuum energy and observational data. The naive summation of vacuum contributions from known fields predicts a CC exceeding observed values by up to 120 orders of magnitude, a challenge this work does not resolve directly. Instead, we focus on secondary contributions to the CC arising from non-trivial spatial topologies or BCs in braneworld models—referred to as "cosmological Casimir effects." By assuming that the fundamental CC (ground state) might ultimately be proven zero, as some theories suggest, we isolate these incremental contributions. Our analysis demonstrates that such contributions, when computed using zeta-Hadamard regularization, can match the observed acceleration of the universe’s expansion in several plausible models. These include scenarios with compactified extra dimensions (both small and large scales), brane-induced BCs, and configurations involving supergravitons. The derived values align with the required order of magnitude to explain dark energy, bridging theoretical and observational domains without fine-tuning. This work underscores the versatility of zeta regularization in extracting physically relevant results from intricate boundary- or topology-driven effects, offering a promising pathway to reconcile theoretical predictions with cosmological observations. Future research may explore extensions to dynamic geometries or interactions with non-perturbative field configurations.

This paper introduces a parallel-in-time method for solving the Euler-Lagrange system arising in the optimal control of parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs). The proposed approach reformulates the problem by iteratively updating a sequence of intermediate control targets, decomposing the system into independent sub-problems amenable to parallel computation. By leveraging time-parallelism, the method avoids the sequential dependency of traditional time-stepping schemes, enabling efficient resolution of the coupled state and adjoint equations. Numerical experiments on parabolic control problems demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the algorithm, with significant reductions in computational time compared to sequential methods. The approach is particularly effective for large-scale applications, where parallelization is critical for handling complex dynamics and high-dimensional state spaces. This work establishes a robust framework for time-parallel optimal control, offering a novel contribution to the numerical treatment of parabolic PDE-constrained optimization.

We present an analysis of spectroscopically peculiar subluminous Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) and their host galaxy environments, revealing a significant association with old stellar populations. Of the 16 known subluminous SNe Ia, 10 are located in elliptical (E)/lenticular (S0) galaxies, with the remaining in early-type spiral galaxies. The probability that this distribution occurs by chance is just 0.2%, strongly indicating a preference for old stellar populations as progenitor hosts. This finding implies that subluminous SNe Ia are unlikely to be observed in high-redshift surveys due to the scarcity of such populations at earlier cosmic epochs. Furthermore, progenitor models involving hydrogen- and helium-rich main-sequence stars or helium red giants via Roche lobe overflow are disfavored, given their inconsistency with the observed old host populations. In contrast, previous studies confirming that overluminous SNe Ia originate from young populations are reinforced. The distinct host environments and progenitor origins of subluminous and overluminous SNe Ia align with predictions of the core white dwarf (WD) merger scenario, which posits diverse progenitor systems as the root of SN Ia diversity. These results highlight the importance of host galaxy demographics in constraining progenitor models and refining our understanding of thermonuclear explosion mechanisms in SNe Ia.

This study investigates the distinct features of searches for hypothetical Kaluza–Klein (KK) excitations of Standard Model (SM) gauge bosons—denoted as $Z$, $W$, and $\gamma$ (labeled @xmath0, @xmath1, @xmath2 in the title)—in hadron collider processes, including single top quark production, Drell–Yan, and $Z$ boson ($@xmath3$) generation. Assuming these particles arise from extra dimensions, we analyze their contributions to SM processes where their KK towers play a critical role. For processes mediated by the SM $Z$ boson (@xmath4), interactions are extended to include its entire KK tower. Conversely, processes involving $W$ (@xmath5) and $\gamma$ (@xmath6) receive contributions from both their respective KK towers and the graviton’s KK tower, reflecting the interplay of gauge and gravitational interactions in extra-dimensional scenarios. To account for higher KK modes, effective four-fermion Lagrangians are employed, enabling a systematic inclusion of towers beyond the first excitation. Cross-sections for relevant processes are calculated, incorporating interference effects between SM gauge bosons, their first KK modes, and the corresponding towers. The deployment of millimeter-wave (mmWave) bands in next-generation wireless networks offers unprecedented bandwidth for high-speed communication, yet their susceptibility to blockage by obstacles such as foliage, humans, and vehicles remains a critical challenge. While prior work has highlighted the sensitivity of mmWave signals to such interference, robust analytical models to quantify blockage effects—particularly in urban environments with dynamic human mobility—remain limited. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a novel, tractable model to characterize human-induced blockage in mmWave propagation. The model incorporates key system parameters, including transmitter-receiver (Tx-Rx) locations, device dimensions, human body size and spatial density, and environmental geometry. By treating humans as randomly distributed blockers, the model analytically derives the probability of line-of-sight (LoS) degradation and computes signal reliability metrics. Validation via a ray-launcher tool confirms the model’s accuracy, demonstrating that blockage probability increases with both human density and Tx-Rx separation. Notably, the analysis reveals a non-trivial relationship between transmitter antenna height and received signal strength: an optimal height exists that maximizes signal reliability, dependent on Tx-Rx distance and device dimensions. These findings underscore the importance of spatial parameter tuning for mmWave network design in human-dense urban scenarios. The proposed framework provides a generalizable tool for evaluating blockage-induced performance trade-offs, aiding the deployment of reliable 5G/6G cellular systems operating in mmWave bands. Keywords: 5th-generation networks; cellular mmWave communications; urban environment; human-body blockage.

This study introduces an algebraic phase field matching theory (Pfmt) to model quantum transport of electrons across finite atomic wire nanojunctions at zero bias, within the Landauer-Büttiker formalism. The approach derives transmission and reflection spectra for systems where leads and nanojunctions are composed of the same or distinct materials. As illustrative applications, we investigate two systems: freely suspended monatomic linear sodium wires (mlnaw) bridging sodium leads and diatomic copper-cobalt wires (dlcucow) coupled to copper leads on a Cu(111) substrate. Gaseous and stellar metallicities are critical observables for constraining the evolutionary processes in galaxies. A key parameter in these studies is the average metal yield per stellar generation, denoted $ \langle Y \rangle $, which quantifies the amount of metals released into the interstellar medium (ISM) by a stellar population. Traditionally, $ \langle Y \rangle $ is assumed to be a fixed fiducial value, with deviations from this value interpreted as evidence for gas outflows/inflows, calibration biases, or diagnostic inaccuracies. However, recent studies have revealed that $ \langle Y \rangle $ is strongly influenced by the initial mass function (IMF). Here, we demonstrate that variations in the IMF can alter $ \langle Y \rangle $ by a factor exceeding three across the range of IMFs commonly used in galaxy evolution models. Furthermore, changes to the upper mass cutoff of the IMF can amplify this variation by an additional factor of two.
