This study demonstrates the application of the Gillespie algorithm to simulate collisions between a granular intruder particle and thermalized bath particles. Originally developed for chemical reactions, the algorithm generates a sequence of collision events with variable time intervals, utilizing position-dependent flux of bath particles as input. We validate this method by comparing it to the exact solution of the homogeneous Boltzmann equation in a one-dimensional system. Additionally, we investigate the case of algebraic tails in the bath particle velocity distribution. The algorithm is also applied to a granular needle in a bath of point particles, revealing correlations between the translational and rotational degrees of freedom of the intruder particle. Our work establishes a connection between the Gillespie algorithm and the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method, providing a novel approach for simulating granular systems. The results showcase the algorithm's potential for modeling complex granular dynamics.

This article explores the analogies between gravitation and electromagnetism, a topic of interest since the 1950s, by examining the Plebański-Demiański (PD) solution, a seven-parameter solution of type D. We evaluate the quadratic curvature invariants, R and R*, analytically for the PD solution, providing insight into the spacetime's physical properties. In the asymptotically flat case, we identify the leading terms of the invariants as the gravitoelectric mass and current, drawing parallels with electromagnetism. The square of the Bel-Robinson tensor is also calculated, showing a resemblance to the energy density in electrodynamics. Furthermore, we derive the Bel-Robinson 3-form, analogous to the energy-momentum 3-form in electromagnetism, and determine the Kummer tensor, a curvature-cubic tensor, for a general type D solution. Our calculations are performed in both the original PD coordinates and a modified Boyer-Lindquist-like version, facilitating a more straightforward interpretation of the solution's parameters. This study demonstrates the profound connections between gravity and electromagnetism, shedding light on the underlying structure of spacetime. By establishing these analogies, we gain a deeper understanding of the physical significance of the PD solution and its relevance to our understanding of the universe.

This article presents the results of the Naini Tal - Cape survey, a comprehensive search for rapidly oscillating Ap (roAp) stars in the Northern Hemisphere. The survey has yielded the discovery of HD 12098, a mono-periodic roAp star, with a frequency separation indicating a rotation period of 5.5 days. A multi-site observation campaign was conducted to confirm the rotation period of HD 12098, and the findings are discussed. Additionally, the survey has identified several non-oscillating Ap stars and two promising roAp candidates, HD 17431 and HD 207561. Notably, if confirmed, HD 207561 would become the first Am star exhibiting roAp-type rapid variability, expanding our understanding of this phenomenon. The discovery of these stars contributes significantly to the growing catalog of roAp stars, providing valuable insights into the properties and behavior of these unique celestial objects. Further analysis and confirmation of these findings are underway.

Over the last decade, numerous young star groups, primarily comprising low-mass stars, have been identified in the solar neighbourhood, within a proximity of 0 pc. These discoveries were facilitated by cross-correlation of X-ray, optical spectroscopy, and kinematic data. The young local associations, including a significant fraction of Hipparcos stars, provide valuable insights into star formation processes in low-density environments, shed light on the substellar domain, and may have played a crucial role in shaping the recent history of the local interstellar medium. Previous studies have estimated the ages of these associations using various methods, including HR diagrams, spectral analysis, lithium and Hα widths, and expansion motion. This work investigates the kinematic evolution of young local associations and their relationship with other young stellar groups and structures in the local interstellar medium, offering new perspectives on recent star formation processes in the solar neighbourhood. By compiling published data, including astrometric information from the new Hipparcos reduction, and integrating the orbits of these associations and the Sco-Cen complex using a realistic galactic potential, we propose a recent history of star formation in the solar neighbourhood. Our findings suggest that both the Sco-Cen complex and young local associations originated from the impact of the inner spiral arm shock wave against a giant molecular cloud, with the cloud's core forming the Sco-Cen complex and smaller cloudlets giving rise to young local associations several million years later. Furthermore, we propose that a supernova explosion in young local associations a few million years ago may have reheated the local bubble to its current temperature, providing a comprehensive understanding of the star formation processes in the solar neighbourhood.

This article presents a phenomenological approach to the theory of spin-valve type ferromagnetic junctions, focusing on the description of exchange switching by current flowing perpendicular to interfaces. By considering mobile electron spins as free in all contacting ferromagnetic layers, we investigate the joint action of two key current effects: the nonequilibrium longitudinal spin-injection effective field and the transverse spin-transfer surface torque. New vector boundary conditions are derived, representing the continuity condition for different spin fluxes. We analyze a junction model with spatially localized spin transfer torque and derive a dispersion relation for fluctuations, which is solved to determine the instability threshold. Our results establish a critical value of the Gilbert damping constant, below which spin transfer torque dominates and above which spin-injection effective field dominates. Notably, both mechanisms can contribute to the observable threshold in ferromagnetic metal free layers at room temperature. The interplay between spin transfer torque and spin injection is crucial for producing a hysteretic behavior of the resistance versus current dependence. Our calculations reveal the possibility of non-stationary nonlinear states and yield instability increment values containing contributions from both mechanisms. Furthermore, we observe a softening of the spin wave resonance frequency spectrum as the current approaches the instability threshold, accompanied by oscillatory or aperiodic magnetization fluctuations depending on the damping constant. These findings provide new insights into the complex dynamics of spin-valve type ferromagnetic junctions and have significant implications for the development of spintronics devices.

This article provides an in-depth analysis of the zero-temperature magnetic field-dependent conductance of electrons through a one-dimensional non-interacting tight-binding chain with an interacting side dot. When the dot contains an odd number of electrons, the Kondo effect emerges, resulting in a wide minimum in conductance as a function of gate voltage, reaching zero at the unitary limit. The application of a magnetic field disrupts the Kondo effect, causing the conductance to develop pairs of dips separated by the on-site repulsion energy. Each dip corresponds to perfect spin-polarized transmission, suggesting potential for an optimal spin filter. The results are interpreted through Fano resonances between interfering transmission channels and are applied to recent experimental findings. A comparison is also made with the standard substitutional configuration, where the dot is positioned at the chain's central site, providing valuable insights into the underlying physics of this complex system.

This study explores the universal phenomenon of cosmic object rotation, presenting a novel model for its origin. Investigating phase transitions of a scalar field in de Sitter and Gödel backgrounds, we analyze test particle motion. Computer simulations of particle congruences reveal non-zero local induced rotation, yet global rotation remains below observational limits, shedding new light on this open question in cosmology.

This study presents novel observations from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) onboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), revealing widespread episodic outflows, or jets, in the quiet solar atmosphere. These outflows, with average speeds of approximately 120 km/s, are characterized by temperatures often exceeding one million degrees and are rooted in magnetized regions. Notably, these phenomena are not limited to polar coronal holes, but are also present in equatorial coronal holes and quiet-sun regions, as well as inter-plume regions throughout the atmosphere. The structures traced by these flows exhibit transverse, Alfvénic motion, suggesting a magnetic origin. Our findings indicate that high-speed outflows primarily originate from the magnetic network of the quiet sun and coronal holes, with plume flows highlighted by denser plasma. These outflows may play a crucial role in heating and supplying mass to the corona and solar wind. Furthermore, we demonstrate that quiet-sun plume flows can contaminate spectroscopic observations of adjacent coronal holes, significantly impacting Doppler shift measurements and potentially affecting investigations of these regions. These results have significant implications for our understanding of the solar atmosphere and the mechanisms driving solar wind formation.

This article explores the value function of an optimal stopping game driven by a one-dimensional diffusion, establishing a characterisation via a modified Legendre transformation if and only if a Nash equilibrium exists. Building upon previous probabilistic results, our analytical approach leverages convex analysis to demonstrate that the value function exhibits a semi-harmonic characterisation. Notably, this outcome is achieved without relying on probabilistic arguments, instead utilising solely convex analysis principles. The findings provide a novel perspective on the interplay between optimal stopping games and convex analysis, contributing to a deeper understanding of the underlying mathematical structures. By establishing this equivalence, the study sheds new light on the conditions under which a Nash equilibrium emerges in optimal stopping games, offering insights into the broader applications of convex analysis in mathematical finance and game theory. Key concepts include optimal stopping and convex analysis.

This study investigates the elastic properties of rutile transition metal dioxides using density functional theory. Calculated properties include elastic constants, bulk modulus, and Young's modulus. Results show strong incompressibility in OsO2 and IrO2, but not superhard solidity. Debye temperatures are comparable to those of transition metal dinitrides or diborides, providing insight into their mechanical properties.

This paper explores normal forms for triangles and plane quadrilaterals under similarity, presenting multiple triangle forms and a special quadrilateral case, facilitating mathematics teaching with simple plane objects.

This article proposes a novel 4-factor model for predicting overnight returns, constructed from intraday price and volume data. The model excludes traditional long-horizon fundamental factors such as value and growth, which lack predictive power for short-term returns. Instead, the four factors are analogous to size, volatility, momentum, and liquidity, and are designed to capture the unique characteristics of overnight returns. Historical regressions, following the methodology of Fama and MacBeth (1973), demonstrate that these factors have significant serial t-statistics and are relevant predictors of overnight returns. The efficacy of the 4-factor model is further tested through its application in an intraday mean-reversion alpha strategy. The results suggest that the proposed model can effectively capture the dynamics of overnight returns, providing a valuable tool for investors and researchers seeking to understand and exploit short-term market movements. The model's performance has implications for portfolio management and risk assessment.

This article explores the dependence of computer calculations on the underlying material composition, leveraging quantum properties to enhance algorithmic efficiency. Building on the successes of Shor's factorization and Grover's search algorithms, we propose utilizing quantum incoherent tunneling to tackle NP-hard problems. Specifically, we aim to develop novel algorithms capable of solving complex challenges, such as the Traveling Salesman Problem, which are currently intractable with classical computing methods, thereby pushing the boundaries of computational theory and unlocking new possibilities for quantum computing applications. Quantum incoherent tunneling offers a promising avenue.

This study investigates the stochastic deflection of high-energy negatively charged particles in a bent crystal. Through analytical calculations and numerical simulations, we demonstrate the existence of a maximum angle at which most of the beam is deflected, corresponding to an optimal radius of curvature. Unlike positively charged particles, which can be deflected at increasingly larger angles with longer crystal lengths, negatively charged particles exhibit a maximum deflection angle due to the stronger contribution of incoherent scattering. This phenomenon arises from the closer proximity of negative particles to atomic nuclei and electrons. Our findings provide ideal parameters for exploiting axial confinement in the manipulation of negatively charged particle beams, with potential applications in future high-energy accelerators, such as the International Linear Collider or muon colliders, enabling more efficient and precise beam control.

This study examines the accuracy of the noninteracting electron approximation in a model of vibrationally coupled electron transport in single molecule junctions. Using the multilayer multiconfiguration time-dependent Hartree theory, we analyze the correlation effects in different physical regimes. Our results show that while the noninteracting electron approximation is reasonable for short-time dynamics, it fails to capture the correct long-time limit for certain initial conditions. The interplay between electronic-vibrational and vibrationally induced electron-electron correlation effects is crucial in determining the accuracy of the approximation. This work highlights the importance of considering correlation effects in the description of electron transport in single molecule junctions, particularly in the presence of vibrational coupling. The findings have implications for the development of theoretical models in molecular electronics.

This study extends a previous qualitative investigation of a chaotical nucleonic system's intermittent behavior by incorporating quantitative analyses. A classical "nuclear billiard" with a 2D Woods-Saxon potential well and oscillating surface is examined. Quantitative methods, including configuration and kinetic energy space analysis, power spectra, Shannon entropies, and Lyapunov exponents, are applied. The results support the notion that chaoticity increases as the oscillation frequency shifts from adiabatic to resonance stages for monopole and dipole vibrational modes. The order-chaos-order-chaos sequence is also explored, revealing an intermittency pattern for monopole deformation. Furthermore, the findings highlight the crucial role of coupling between one-nucleon and collective degrees of freedom in generating chaotic states, providing new insights into the complex dynamics of nucleonic systems. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of chaos in nuclear systems.

Here is a 225-word abstract for the given academic article title: We present high-resolution adaptive optics (AO) corrected images of the silhouette disk Orion 218-354, obtained using the Magellan AO (MagAO) system and its visible light camera, VisAO, in simultaneous differential imaging (SDI) mode. This achievement marks the first instance of a circumstellar disk being imaged in silhouette with AO, and is among the pioneering visible light AO results in the literature. Through our analysis, we determine the disk's extent, geometry, intensity, and extinction profiles, revealing that the disk is likely optically thin at Hα. Our findings contradict previous studies, and provide a unique estimate of the column density of primitive, ISM-like grains as a function of radius within the disk. Notably, we estimate that only ~10% of the total sub-mm derived disk mass resides in primitive, unprocessed grains. By combining our data with Monte Carlo radiative transfer modeling and existing literature results, we construct the first self-consistent multiwavelength model of Orion 218-354. Our model successfully reproduces the 1-1000 μm SED with a 12-540 au disk, characterized by the size, geometry, small vs. large grain proportion, and radial mass profile indicated by our data. The inferred inner radius is substantially larger than the disk's sublimation radius, suggesting that the innermost region is likely cleared.

This study examines the pair production of charged Higgs bosons at the CERN Large Hadron Collider within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model framework. A comparative analysis is conducted between contributions from quark annihilation at tree level and gluon fusion at one loop. The results indicate that at extreme values of tan(beta), quark annihilation dominates due to Feynman diagrams involving neutral CP-even Higgs bosons and top quarks. Conversely, gluon fusion is enhanced by squark loop contributions, which can significantly surpass the conventional quark loop contributions. These findings provide new insights into the production mechanisms of charged Higgs bosons, offering a more comprehensive understanding of the MSSM phenomenology.

This study presents a self-consistent quasiparticle random phase approximation (QRPA) calculation of vibrational states in deformed, axially symmetric even-even nuclei. Utilizing the same Skyrme energy density and density-dependent pairing functionals for both mean field and residual interactions, our approach ensures consistency across particle-hole and particle-particle channels. Validation against published spherical nuclei calculations yields excellent agreement. We examine the effects of neglecting spin-orbit and Coulomb residual interactions in QRPA and discuss the improvement achieved by removing spurious modes. Our results for isoscalar and isovector responses in deformed Mg isotopes are compared to experimental data, providing insight into the vibrational properties of these nuclei and the efficacy of our self-consistent QRPA framework. The calculated responses demonstrate good agreement with experimental findings.

This study investigates the origin of weak antilocalization (WAL) in topological insulators, focusing on the role of bulk states. Despite strong spin-orbit coupling in the bulk, the observed WAL appears to have an ambiguous origin. Using an effective model for three-dimensional topological insulators, we derive a magnetoconductivity formula for both two-dimensional bulk subbands and surface bands. Our results show that the bulk subbands can exhibit unitary behavior or weak localization (WL) due to a relatively large gap, leading to small or even compensatory magnetoconductivity. This challenges the conventional assumption that WAL solely arises from surface states. Notably, an inflection in magnetoconductivity curves can occur when bulk WL channels dominate surface WAL channels, providing a distinct signature of bulk weak localization. Our findings offer new insights into the interplay between bulk and surface states in topological insulators, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of WAL in these systems. By elucidating the contributions of bulk states, this research sheds light on the complex mechanisms governing WAL in topological insulators.

This article presents a novel expression for the total age of the universe, formulated in terms of the average deceleration parameter. Notably, this kinematic result is universally applicable, irrespective of the universe's curvature or the underlying gravity theory, including brane-world motivated cosmologies. By leveraging the accurately determined present age parameter of the universe, we demonstrate that the time-averaged value of the deceleration parameter is zero. This finding implies that the cosmic age today aligns with the predictions of a relativistic flat cosmological model comprising k-matter, a fluid characterized by a specific equation of state. Assuming the long-term validity of this relation, we argue that decelerating expansion phases must be precisely counterbalanced by accelerated phases, suggesting a perpetual "coasting" of the observed universe. Furthermore, this implies that the current accelerating stage will be followed by a subsequent decelerating phase, as forecasted by certain scalar field and brane-world motivated cosmologies, providing a fascinating insight into the universe's dynamic evolution.

This study examines the microscopic processes driving chirality flips in the thermal bath of quantum chromodynamics at finite temperature and zero baryon chemical potential. Focusing on the temperature range of approximately 150-200 MeV, where the crossover from a chirally broken phase to quark-gluon plasma occurs, we investigate quark-quark scatterings mediated by collective excitations with pion and σ-meson quantum numbers. Utilizing a Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, we compute equilibrium properties and the scattering kernel to estimate the chiral relaxation time. Our results yield a relaxation time of around 3 fm/c near the chiral crossover, providing insight into the dynamics of chirality flips in the quark-gluon plasma.

We present follow-up observations of the low-velocity H I source HIZSS 3, a nearby galaxy candidate discovered by Henning et al. (2000) and Rivers (2000) in a survey of the Milky Way disk. Our Very Large Array (VLA) and optical observations reveal a low-mass dwarf irregular galaxy with a radio profile consistent with a distance of approximately 10 Mpc. While optical imaging did not resolve a stellar population, an extended Hα emission region was detected, coincident with a partially-resolved H I cloud. Spectroscopic analysis confirms that the Hα source shares a similar radial velocity to the H I emission, establishing an optical counterpart. The Hα emission, spanning 100 pc in diameter with a luminosity of 10^38 ergs s^-1, is characteristic of a single H II region harboring a modest population of O/B stars. The galaxy's radial velocity and distance from the solar apex suggest it may not be a Local Group member, although a more accurate distance measurement is required to confirm this. With properties comparable to those of GR 8, a nearby dwarf irregular galaxy with ongoing star formation, further observations are necessary to characterize HIZSS 3's stellar population, determine chemical abundances, and obtain a reliable distance estimate.

This study introduces a novel Dengue model, combining an Individual-Based Model (IBM) for human populations with a compartmental model (SEI) for mosquito populations. The spread of epidemics is examined under the sole influence of mosquito vectors, considering various distributions (exponential, deterministic, and experimental) for the human exposed period. Two weather scenarios, representing temperate and tropical climates, are analyzed. The results indicate that virus circulation, final epidemic size, and outbreak duration exhibit low sensitivity to the exposed period's statistical distribution, provided the median values coincide. However, the time between an introduced case and the emergence of the first symptomatic secondary case is sensitive to this distribution. Notably, our IBM model is shown to be a realization of a compartmental model, suggesting that the choice between these modeling approaches is largely a matter of convenience. This research contributes to the understanding of Dengue epidemiology, highlighting the importance of considering mosquito-borne transmission and the flexibility of modeling frameworks.

This study applies a renormalization scheme based on energy-momentum and angular momentum balance equations to derive an effective equation of motion for a massless point-like charge. In contrast to the massive case, accelerated massless charges exhibit infinite rates of radiated energy-momentum and angular momentum. The presence of external electromagnetic fields that do not alter the particle's velocity is only possible within the interaction area. The effective equation of motion is equivalent to the equation for eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the electromagnetic tensor. Uniform solutions to this equation reveal that massless charges move along trajectories determined by the eigenvectors. Notably, this solution parallels the magnetosphere model of a rapidly rotating neutron star, as described by Rylov. This research contributes to our understanding of massless charged particles in electromagnetic fields, with implications for astrophysical phenomena. PACS numbers: 03.50.de, 11.10.gh, 97.60.gb.

The physical properties of galactic winds play a crucial role in our understanding of galaxy formation, and their characteristics can be effectively constrained by observing background quasars passing near star-forming galaxies (SFGs). This study utilizes a sample of 14 quasar-galaxy pairs from the VLT/SINFONI Program for Line Emitters (SIMPLE) to investigate the properties of galactic winds. By reobserving the 10 brightest galaxies and their corresponding quasars with high-resolution spectrographs, we applied geometrical arguments to classify the pairs into those probing galactic outflows, extended gaseous disks, or face-on galaxies. Our analysis focuses on the pairs suitable for wind studies, comparing the line-of-sight kinematics with the host galaxy emission kinematics. The results show that a purely geometrical wind model with constant wind speed can reproduce the kinematic profile shapes for most pairs, except for one pair requiring an accelerated wind flow. We find that the outflow speeds are approximately 100-200 km/s, and the mass ejection rates are comparable to the star formation rate, indicating a mass loading factor of around 1.0. Notably, the outflow speeds are lower than the local escape velocity, suggesting that the outflows do not escape the galaxy halo and will likely fall back into the interstellar medium, providing valuable insights into the role of galactic winds in regulating galaxy evolution.

This study presents the results of Chandra observations of off-nuclear X-ray sources in the spiral galaxy M51 (NGC 5194). A total of 113 X-ray sources were detected, with 84 of these sources located within the disk of NGC 5194. Notably, six sources exhibit luminosities exceeding 10^39 ergs s^-1 and 28 sources have luminosities exceeding 10^38 ergs s^-1 in the 0.5-8 keV band. The high number of luminous sources is comparable to galaxies undergoing starburst activity, surpassing that of normal spiral and elliptical galaxies. Spectral analysis reveals that most sources are characterized by a power-law spectrum with a photon index between 1 and 2. However, exceptions include one source with an extremely hard spectrum and two sources with soft spectra. Furthermore, the spectra of ultraluminous sources are consistent with both power-law and multicolor disk blackbody models, while a luminous object with a remarkable spectrum featuring emission lines is also identified and discussed. These findings provide valuable insights into the X-ray source population in M51.

This article presents an in-depth analysis of spectral absorption features in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs), revealing multiple distinct outflow components. The outflowing gas is photoionized by the nuclear continuum source and originates from the accretion flow towards the central black hole. Radiation pressure and magnetic stresses are identified as potential driving mechanisms. Theoretical modeling of these outflows raises key questions regarding the dominant mechanism, gas uplift, radiation shielding, and outflow morphology. This review synthesizes recent theoretical and observational findings, addressing these questions and outlining future research directions. By exploring the complex interplay between outflow components, driving mechanisms, and accretion processes, this study aims to advance our understanding of AGN outflows and their role in galaxy evolution. Recent advances and prospects for further progress are discussed.

This study exactly solves a strongly correlated spin-electron system on a diamond chain using the transfer-matrix method. The system consists of localized Ising spins on nodal sites and mobile electrons on interstitial sites, subjected to a magnetic field. A detailed investigation of ground states, magnetization processes, and correlation functions reveals a complex interplay between fermionic entanglement and kinetically-induced spin frustration. Notably, quantum entanglement emerges only within a frustrated unsaturated paramagnetic phase in the ground state. However, thermal fluctuations can induce entanglement above non-frustrated ground states with saturated paramagnetic or classical ferrimagnetic arrangements, highlighting the intricate relationship between entanglement, frustration, and thermal effects in this correlated system.

The cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus employs a dual mechanism to generate robust circadian rhythms, utilizing both a protein phosphorylation cycle and a transcription-translation cycle. Through stochastic simulations, we investigated the interaction between these cycles in growing, dividing cells. Our results show that a protein phosphorylation cycle alone can maintain robustness when protein turnover is low. However, at high decay or dilution rates, the phosphorylation-based oscillator loses stability, rendering it incapable of generating circadian rhythms. This limitation becomes apparent when the cell doubling time falls below the 24-hour clock period. In contrast, a transcription-translation cycle is essential for sustaining robust circadian rhythms at higher growth rates. Notably, our analysis reveals that while a transcription-translation cycle is necessary to support a phosphorylation cycle at high growth rates, the phosphorylation cycle can significantly enhance the robustness of the transcription-translation cycle at lower protein decay or dilution rates. These findings suggest that both cycles are necessary to generate robust circadian rhythms across a wide range of growth conditions, highlighting the importance of this dual mechanism in maintaining temporal organization in Synechococcus elongatus. This understanding has significant implications for our comprehension of circadian rhythm regulation in cyanobacteria.

We report the spectroscopic detection of silicate emission at 10 and 18 μm in five PG quasars, marking the first detection of these features in galaxies outside the Local Group. This finding supports the unification model for active galactic nuclei, predicting silicate emission in mid-infrared spectra of pole-on AGN tori. The detected silicate emission features exhibit strengths of 0.12-1.25 and 0.20-0.79 times the continuum at 10 and 18 μm, respectively. Silicate grain temperatures, inferred from the 18-to-10 μm feature ratio, range from 140 to 220 K, assuming optically thin emission.

Here is a 133-word abstract for the given article title: Small single crystals of Ga-Se-Te semiconductors with varying compositions (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3) were synthesized using modified Bridgman growth techniques. High-resolution powder X-ray diffractometry revealed a zincblende cubic structure with additional satellite peaks near the (111) Bragg line, indicating ordered vacancy planes along the [111] direction. Positron annihilation spectroscopy showed an average positron lifetime of 5400 ps, suggesting dominant defect-related annihilation sites. Coincidence Doppler broadening measurements indicated a strong presence of large open-volume defects, likely vacancy clusters or voids. These findings provide insight into the structural and defect properties of Ga-Se-Te semiconductors, which is crucial for understanding their potential applications. The presence of vacancy planes and large defects may significantly impact the material's electronic and optical properties, warranting further investigation.

This paper presents a novel method for determining polynomial invariants under stochastic local operations and classical communication (SLOCC) for systems of delocalized fermions with global particle number conservation. These invariants enable the construction of entanglement measures that distinguish between different types of entanglement in such systems. Notably, the invariants and corresponding measures are non-zero only if the system's state exhibits Bell-nonlocal correlations. The approach is demonstrated for systems of two and three spin-1/2 fermions, with examples of maximally entangled states illustrating the distinct types of entanglement captured by the invariants. A general condition for the existence of SLOCC invariants is derived, relating the number of fermions, their spin, and the number of spatial modes. The impact of additional constraints, such as fermion localization, is also explored. Furthermore, a hybrid Ising-Hubbard Hamiltonian is introduced, whose ground state exhibits significant entanglement at the transition between regimes dominated by on-site and Ising interactions. This entanglement is effectively characterized by a measure constructed using the proposed method, highlighting the utility of this approach in understanding complex quantum systems. The results have implications for the study of entanglement and non-locality in fermionic systems.

We report the detection of an infrared nebula surrounding the Cepheid prototype δ Cephei and its hot companion HD 213307. Observations at 5.8, 8.0, 24, and 70 μm reveal large-scale (≥10 au) nebulosity. The 5.8 and 8.0 μm emission is attributed to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission swept from the ISM by a wind from δ Cephei and/or its companion. Stochastically heated small dust grains are the likely source of the 24 and 70 μm extended emission. The 70 μm emission resembles a bow shock aligned with δ Cephei's proper motion, suggesting mass loss at a rate of 10^-7 to 10^-6 M⊙ yr^-1, supporting the hypothesis that δ Cephei is currently losing mass.

This study presents a minimally-parametric reconstruction of the primordial power spectrum using recent cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure data. Our approach aims to constrain the power spectrum's shape while avoiding strong theoretical priors and over-fitting. The results show no deviation from a power law spectral index, and an exact scale-invariant power spectrum is disfavored, although this conclusion is weaker when assuming a theoretically-motivated prior. The reconstruction highlights the need for better data to justify strong theoretical priors. These findings have implications for the robustness of current knowledge and will be crucial in comparing with forthcoming precision data from Planck, ultimately refining our understanding of the primordial power spectrum and its role in cosmology. The results provide a foundation for future investigations into the origins of the universe.

Title: The Long-Standing Problem of Shannon Entropy Estimation in Data Streams is Now an Easy Task Abstract: Shannon entropy estimation in data streams has long been a challenging problem, particularly in the strict turnstile model. Previous studies have shown that achieving a guaranteed additive accuracy requires estimating the frequency moment with a high degree of multiplicative accuracy, resulting in a sample complexity that is often impractically large. In this paper, we propose a novel technique that simplifies this task by reducing the required multiplicative accuracy, thereby achieving a significant reduction in sample complexity. Our algorithm estimates the frequency moment with a guaranteed multiplicative accuracy, which in turn enables the estimation of Shannon entropy with a guaranteed additive accuracy. We demonstrate that our approach is not only theoretically sound but also practically efficient, with a sample complexity that is significantly lower than that of prior algorithms. We compare our approach to existing methods, including those based on symmetric stable random projections and compressed counting (CC) using maximally skewed stable random projections. Our results show that our algorithm outperforms these methods, achieving a sample complexity that is roughly a factor of 1/√n lower than that of symmetric stable random projections and a factor of 1/n lower than that of CC-based algorithms. Furthermore, our extensive experiments verify that our algorithm provides accurate estimates of Shannon entropy using a relatively small number of samples, even when the desired additive accuracy is extremely small. The proposed algorithm is based on a simple and clean estimator for compressed counting, which we prove has a variance that achieves the desired multiplicative accuracy. Our analytical and numerical results provide a comprehensive understanding of the algorithm's performance, including the complexity bound constants. Overall, our work provides a significant breakthrough in Shannon entropy estimation in data streams, making it a practical task with a manageable sample complexity. Our findings have important implications for a wide range of applications, including data mining, machine learning, and network analysis, where accurate entropy estimation is crucial.

Recent observations of surface magnetic field maps for a subset of active M dwarfs have revealed intense, predominantly axi-symmetric poloidal fields in fully convective stars. The rapidly rotating M dwarf V374 Peg (M4) exhibits a stable magnetic topology over a timescale of approximately 1 year, suggesting a strong interplay between its rapid rotation and intense magnetic field. This interaction is expected to drive a magneto-centrifugally accelerated coronal wind. To investigate the structure of the coronal magnetic field in V374 Peg, we employ three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) numerical simulations of the coronal wind, incorporating an observationally derived surface magnetic field map for the first time in MHD models of stellar winds for a low-mass star. Our self-consistent simulations account for the interaction between the outflowing wind and the magnetic field, enabling us to determine the configuration of the magnetic field and the structure of the coronal wind. The results of this study allow us to evaluate the angular momentum loss of V374 Peg, providing valuable insights into the rotational evolution of rapidly rotating M dwarfs. By exploring the complex interplay between magnetic forces and wind forces, this research sheds light on the underlying mechanisms governing the coronal dynamics of low-mass stars.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the short-duration gamma-ray burst (GRB) 130603B, focusing on its peculiar early optical and X-ray afterglow emission. We demonstrate that the observed features can be attributed to continuous energy injection into the blastwave from a supra-massive magnetar central engine. Furthermore, the late infrared bump, known as the kilonova, is found to be consistent with emission from ejecta launched during a neutron star-neutron star (NS-NS) merger, powered by a magnetar central engine. Our results indicate that both the GRB blastwave and the kilonova have isotropic-equivalent kinetic energies of approximately 10^51 erg, suggesting a near-isotropic magnetar wind. However, this relatively small energy output implies that a significant portion of the magnetar's initial rotational energy is carried away by gravitational wave radiation. Our findings support the notion that GRB 130603B originated from an NS-NS binary system, which merged to form a supra-massive neutron star with a lifetime of around 2 seconds. The equation of state of nuclear matter is inferred to be sufficiently stiff to allow for the survival of a long-lived supra-massive neutron star, making it promising to detect bright electromagnetic counterparts of gravitational wave triggers without short GRB associations in the upcoming Advanced LIGO/Virgo era.

This article explores relationships between sequence pairs generated by Lambert series expansions. We derive novel recurrence relations and matrix equations defining these sequences, leveraging Euler's Pentagonal Number Theorem. By expanding the infinite Pochhammer product and partial products, we establish key results. Applications include the Euler phi function, Möbius function, sum of divisors functions, and Liouville's lambda function. Our findings provide new insights into these sequences, enabling a deeper understanding of their properties and interconnections. The results have far-reaching implications, shedding light on the intricate relationships between these fundamental mathematical constructs.

This study presents a quark-diquark approach to describing the nucleon and Roper resonance. We demonstrate that two nucleon-like states can emerge in the ground state of the spatial configuration, facilitated by the presence of scalar-isoscalar and axial-vector-isovector diquarks. The mass difference between these states arises from the distinct masses of the diquarks, which is attributed to spin-spin interactions between quarks within the diquarks. By identifying these states with the nucleon and Roper resonance, our model provides insight into the underlying structure of these particles, offering a novel perspective on their properties and behavior.

Here is an abstract of approximately 200 words based on the given title: This study examines the Axelrod cultural adaptation model through the lens of cluster size entropy, a concept that provides insight into the variability of cultural cluster sizes within the system. By analyzing networks with diverse topologies, ranging from regular to random, we identify the critical point of the nonequilibrium monocultural-multicultural transition as the maximum of the cluster entropy distributions. Notably, the width of these distributions can be used to determine the order of the transition. Furthermore, scaling the cluster entropy distributions reveals a relationship between the critical cultural trait and the number of cultural features in regular networks. We also investigate the impact of mass media on social systems within the Axelrod model, discovering a novel partially ordered phase in square networks where the largest cultural cluster is not aligned with the external field. This finding contradicts recent suggestions that such a phase cannot form in regular networks. Our results yield a new phase diagram for the Axelrod model in regular networks, offering a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying cultural adaptation and social influence.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the Type II Linear (IIL) supernova (SN) 2013by, leveraging multi-band ultraviolet and optical light curves, as well as visual-wavelength and near-infrared spectroscopy. Our findings reveal that SN 2013by, along with other SNe IIL in the literature, exhibit a distinctive sharp decline in their light curves following the linear decline phase post-maximum, akin to that observed in Type II Plateau (IIP) supernovae. This phenomenon, rarely detected in SNe IIL due to their scarcity and intrinsic faintness, may serve as a crucial parameter to differentiate between subclasses of SNe II. Spectroscopic examination of SN 2013by discloses asymmetric line profiles, high-velocity hydrogen signatures, and late-time near-infrared spectra featuring oxygen lines, suggesting substantial mixing within the ejecta. Estimations from the late-time light curve indicate the synthesis of 0.029 M⊙ of 56Ni during the explosion. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the slope of the V-band light curve contributes to the scatter in the luminosity (V magnitude 50 days after explosion) versus 56Ni relation. Our observations of SN 2013by and other SNe IIL through the onset of the nebular phase imply that their progenitors share similarities with those of SNe IIP, providing new insights into the physics of these explosive events.

This study presents thermal expansion, magnetostriction, and specific heat measurements of TlCuCl3, revealing a quantum phase transition from a spin-gap phase to a Néel-ordered ground state with magnetic field variation around 4.5 T. Using Ehrenfest's relation, significant pressure dependencies of the spin gap are found. A diverging Grüneisen parameter is observed, consistent with theoretical predictions. However, experimental data deviate from predicted temperature dependencies, indicating complex magnetoelastic coupling in this low-dimensional magnet, which exhibits Bose-Einstein condensation near the quantum critical point, warranting further investigation of its unique properties.

This article provides a comprehensive review of recent attempts to determine the accretion geometry in radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGN). Radio-loud AGN, comprising a significant portion of the AGN population, are characterized by powerful collimated radio jets extending thousands of parsecs from the host galaxy's center. Multiwavelength surveys have revealed that radio-loudness is more prevalent in low-luminosity AGN, which are likely accreting via a geometrically thick and radiatively inefficient accretion flow. In contrast, X-ray spectroscopic observations of higher luminosity broad-line radio galaxies have found evidence for an untruncated thin disk near the black hole, suggesting similarities with radio-quiet counterparts. Our analysis indicates that jet formation requires three conditions: a rapidly spinning black hole, an accretion flow with a large scale height ratio, and a favorable magnetic field geometry. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of AGN physics and the relationship between accretion and jet formation. By exploring the accretion geometry in radio-loud AGN, this review aims to shed light on the underlying mechanisms driving these complex and powerful objects. Further research is needed to fully elucidate the interplay between accretion and jet formation.

This study numerically implements the reactive flux formalism using a C-number Langevin equation to calculate the transmission coefficient. The method, based on canonical quantization and the Wigner quasiclassical phase space function, incorporates quantum effects order by order. We examine the Kramers turnover, rate enhancement at low temperatures, and temporal behavior of the transmission coefficient over a range of temperatures, noise correlation, and friction for a double-well potential. Our results are compared to existing findings, demonstrating the efficacy of this simple approach in capturing key features, including quantum effects, down to absolute zero. The methodology's accuracy and efficiency are highlighted.

This article introduces the concept of irreducible correspondences, facilitating the efficient calculation of Gromov-Hausdorff distances. Utilizing these correspondences, we demonstrate that the set of all metric spaces with no more than $n$ points is isometric to a polyhedral cone in the space $\mathcal{M}_n$ endowed with the maximum norm. We prove that for any $n$-point metric space with strict triangle inequalities, a neighborhood exists where Steiner minimal trees with boundaries from this neighborhood are minimal fillings. However, we construct a counterexample of an $n$-point boundary in the Gromov-Hausdorff space, showing that its Steiner minimal tree is not a minimal filling, which implies the Steiner subratio of the Gromov-Hausdorff space is less than 1. Leveraging irreducible correspondences, we develop a quick algorithm for calculating Gromov-Hausdorff distances between finite metric spaces. Numerical experiments yield a more precise upper estimate of the Steiner subratio, demonstrating it is less than $\frac{1}{2}$. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the geometric properties of the Gromov-Hausdorff space and its applications in metric geometry.

We investigate Yang-Mills theories with general gauge groups and twists on the four-torus, focusing on the construction of consistent boundary conditions for gauge fields in all instanton sectors. An extended Abelian projection is presented, utilizing the Polyakov loop operator with a time-independent component in the Cartan subalgebra. For arbitrary gauge groups, we construct fundamental domains for the gauge-fixed fields, revealing that gauge fixings in sectors with non-vanishing instanton number necessarily introduce singularities. These singularities can be confined to Dirac strings connecting magnetically charged defects, whose charges are valued in the co-root lattice of the gauge group. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the magnetic charges of these defects, the windings of suitable Higgs fields, and the instanton number. Our analysis provides new insights into the interplay between gauge field theory, magnetic monopoles, and topological invariants, shedding light on the complex structure of Yang-Mills theories at finite temperature. The results have implications for our understanding of gauge fixing, Abelian projection, and the role of instantons in non-Abelian gauge theories.

This study examines the differences in lead neutron skin thickness, binding energy, surface energy, and density profiles using two density-dependent hadron models within the Thomas-Fermi approximation. Results are compared to those from a non-linear Walecka model. A direct correlation is found between neutron skin thickness and symmetry energy slope, reflecting equation of state properties. Notably, the asymmetry parameter for low-momentum transfer polarized electron scattering shows insensitivity to model differences. These findings provide insight into the equation of state and its relation to neutron skin thickness, with implications for nuclear physics and astrophysical applications, highlighting the importance of model choice and approximation methods.

This study investigates the properties of pure disk galaxies (PDS) devoid of bulge components, which appear to have evaded the effects of merger activity and strong internal secular evolution inherent to hierarchical galaxy formation models. Analyzing the Hubble Deep Field and local universe, we find that a significant fraction (≈30%) of disk galaxies are PDS, characterized by a single exponential spatial distribution of light from center to outskirts. The mean central surface brightness and scale length of these galaxies have remained remarkably constant over the last 8 billion years, with values that are brighter and shorter, respectively, than those of disks with bulges. The lack of change in the fraction of PDS and their profile parameters suggests that these galaxies have not undergone major or multiple minor mergers since z≈1. However, they have experienced substantial increases in total stellar mass and size, implying evolution via smooth accretion of cold gas through cosmic filaments. We propose that PDS are dynamically hot and embedded in massive dark matter halos, which may shield them from strong secular evolution, allowing them to maintain their pristine disk structure over billions of years. Our findings provide new insights into the formation and evolution of disk galaxies, highlighting the importance of smooth gas accretion in shaping their properties.

This article delves into the intricate relationship between quantum lithography, Heisenberg-limited parameter estimation, and the dynamical evolution of quantum states. By leveraging entanglement, we demonstrate how enhanced measurement accuracy and increased resolution in quantum lithography can be achieved. The mathematical derivation of Heisenberg-limited parameter estimation naturally yields the hyperresolution characteristic of quantum lithography. Recent experimental proofs of principle for quantum lithography are reviewed, with a focus on state preparation and the fabrication of suitable photoresists. Parameter estimation, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, is limited by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, highlighting the importance of understanding these limitations. We explore the connection between phase estimation and the rate of dynamical evolution of quantum states, leading to the concept of quantum lithography and the role of entanglement. The generation of necessary optical quantum states is also briefly considered, providing a comprehensive examination of the viability of quantum lithography. Our work contributes to the understanding of the interplay between quantum mechanics principles and their applications in quantum lithography, shedding light on the potential of entanglement-based techniques for enhanced resolution and accuracy. The implications of this research have far-reaching potential for advancements in quantum technology and precision measurement.

This study investigates the inverse problem of identifying inhomogeneities or cracks in nonlinear magnetic materials. A piecewise constant level set algorithm is proposed to recover shapes from local measurements. Utilizing the Lagrangian multiplier method, the first variation is derived, and the descent direction is obtained via the adjoint variable method. Numerical results demonstrate the algorithm's robustness and effectiveness in reconstructing complex shapes, showcasing its potential in nonlinear electromagnetism applications.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the galaxy cluster MS 1054-0321 at z=0.83, the most distant and X-ray luminous cluster in the Extended Medium-Sensitivity Survey (EMSS). Utilizing high-resolution imaging from the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and X-ray data, we conduct a weak-lensing and X-ray analysis to investigate the cluster's mass distribution and dark matter substructure. The ACS weak-lensing reconstruction reveals a complex mass distribution, comprising three dominant mass clumps and multiple minor satellite groups. A direct comparison with the X-ray image shows that the eastern weak-lensing substructure is not visible in X-rays, while the two X-ray peaks are displaced from the corresponding mass clumps, potentially due to ram pressure. Notably, the dark matter clumps appear to be offset from the galaxy counterparts, similar to our previous findings in the cluster CL 0152-1357. We examine the significance of these offsets and propose a scenario where the dark matter clumps are moving ahead of the cluster galaxies. Our non-parametric weak-lensing mass modeling yields a projected mass of $M_{\text{WL}}$, with an uncertainty accounting for statistical error and cosmic shear effects. Furthermore, our X-ray temperature measurement of $T_X$ keV, combined with an isothermal beta model, results in a projected mass of $M_{\text{X}}$, consistent with the weak-lensing estimate. This study provides unprecedented insights into the dark matter distribution and dynamics of MS 1054-0321, shedding light on the complex interplay between dark matter, galaxies, and the intracluster medium in high-redshift clusters.

We present the results of a comprehensive search for dropout galaxies behind 11 massive lensing clusters, utilizing 21 arcmin^2 of deep HST NICMOS, ACS, and WFPC2 image data. Our analysis reveals a single robust z∼7 dropout candidate, previously reported around Abell 1689, and four less robust z∼7 and z∼8 dropout candidates. However, simulations suggest that the latter may be low-redshift interlopers due to the limited depth of the available optical data. Comparing our findings to the expected numbers based on the z∼7 UV luminosity function (LF) determined from field searches, we predict 2.7 z∼7 dropouts and 0.3 z∼8 dropouts over our cluster search area, which is in reasonable agreement with our observations. Notably, our results are significantly lower than those reported in previous studies of dropout galaxies behind lensing clusters. Upon examining the candidates from these studies, we conclude that only a small fraction are likely to be genuine z∼7 galaxies. Our findings support models that highlight the value of gravitational lensing from clusters in detecting galaxies at brighter magnitudes (L∼L*), where the LF is expected to be steep. However, the use of these clusters to constrain the faint-end slope or determine the full LF is likely limited due to the shallower effective slope measured at fainter magnitudes and significant uncertainties introduced by modeling both gravitational lensing and incompleteness.

This article presents a comprehensive analytical investigation of the critical behavior of stationary flow configurations in low angular momentum axisymmetric black hole accretion using mathematical formalism from dynamical systems theory. By examining the phase trajectories corresponding to transonic accretion in steady state, we gain valuable insights into the nature of multi-transonic black hole accretion discs without relying on explicit numerical solutions. Our analysis reveals that the general profile of parameter space divisions describing multi-critical accretion remains roughly equivalent across various flow geometries, including those influenced by pseudo-Schwarzschild potentials. However, we find that varying the polytropic index of the flow does not permit a continuous mapping of critical solutions between different flow geometries due to the non-continuous transformation of the numerical domain in multi-dimensional parameter space. We demonstrate the stability of the stationary configuration under linear perturbation for all flow geometries, black hole potentials, and equations of state used to obtain critical transonic solutions. Furthermore, we discuss the structure of the acoustic metric corresponding to the propagation of linear perturbations for various flow geometries. Our results provide a deeper understanding of the complex phenomena involved in black hole accretion and have implications for the study of astrophysical phenomena related to accretion discs and black hole physics.

This article presents a novel method for examining the dynamical interaction between the extended halo and spheroid components of a galaxy and an environmental disturbance. By investigating the resonant interaction between a galaxy and passing interlopers or satellite companions, we demonstrate that such disturbances can be carried deep into the halo, where they can perturb the disk. Applying this methodology to the Milky Way, we find that the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) are sufficient to cause the observed galactic warp, and may also seed other asymmetries. This multi-scale interaction is characterized by a feature in the halo wake at roughly half the satellite orbital radius, resulting from a 2:1 orbital resonance. The rotating disturbance excites a vertical disk mode, producing a classic integral-sign morphology. Notably, a polar satellite orbit yields the largest warp, suggesting that the inferred LMC orbit is nearly optimal for maximum warp production. The magnitude and morphology of the response are sensitive to the details of the disk and halo models, with a change in the halo profile shifting the resonant frequencies and response location. Furthermore, increasing the halo support relative to the disk, as in a sub-maximal disk model, decreases the warp amplitude. The implications of these findings for N-body simulations are discussed, including the potential for discreteness noise in the halo to produce observable warping. These results have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy structure and evolution, and highlight the importance of considering the complex interplay between a galaxy's various components and its environment.

This study presents numerical results on the magnetic dynamo effect in cylindrical von Kármán plasma flow, with parameters relevant to the Madison Plasma Couette Experiment (MPCX). The MPCX is designed to investigate various phenomena in flowing plasmas, where the magnetic Prandtl number can be of order unity, differing from liquid metal experiments. Using the extended magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) Nimrod code, simulations were conducted for an isothermal and compressible plasma model, incorporating the Hall term in Ohm's law to study two-fluid effects. The counter-rotating von Kármán flow was found to result in sustained dynamo action, self-generating a magnetic field when the magnetic Reynolds number exceeds a critical value. For the experiment's plasma parameters, the field saturates at an amplitude corresponding to a new stable equilibrium, characterized as a laminar dynamo. Notably, compressibility in the plasma increases the critical magnetic Reynolds number, while the inclusion of the Hall term in Ohm's law affects the saturated dynamo field's amplitude but not the onset of dynamo action. These findings provide valuable insights into the dynamics of flowing plasmas and the conditions necessary for magnetic dynamo action, contributing to the understanding of complex plasma phenomena. The results have significant implications for the MPCX and similar experiments, shedding light on the intricate relationships between plasma flow, magnetic fields, and dynamo action.

We present a detailed analysis of high-resolution, high-signal-to-noise spectra of SEG 17, an extremely metal-poor, carbon-rich red giant located in the Segue 1 system. This system has been alternatively classified as an unusually extended globular cluster or an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy. Our findings reveal that the radial velocity of SEG 17 aligns precisely with the systemic velocity of Segue 1, providing strong evidence for its membership in this system. The chemical abundance pattern of SEG 17, characterized by [Fe/H] = -3.52, [C/Fe] = +2.3, [N/Fe] = +0.8, [Na/Fe] = +0.53, [Mg/Fe] = +0.94, [Al/Fe] = +0.23, and [Ba/Fe] < +1.0, is remarkably similar to that of the rare and enigmatic class of Galactic halo objects known as CEMP-no stars. Notably, SEG 17 is the first star in a Milky Way satellite to unambiguously occupy the metal-poor, carbon-rich branch of the bimodal distribution defined by field halo stars in the ([C/Fe], [Fe/H]) plane. While the available data do not allow us to conclusively determine whether SEG 17 is a member of an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy or debris from the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy, our results demonstrate that star formation and chemical evolution proceeded similarly in the progenitors of both field halo and satellite systems at extremely low metallicities ([Fe/H] < -3). This finding supports recent suggestions that the most metal-poor dwarf spheroidal and ultra-faint dwarf satellites were the building blocks of the Milky Way's outer halo. Our study provides new insights into the early chemical evolution of the Milky Way and its satellites, highlighting the importance of these systems in understanding the formation and assembly of our Galaxy.

We present radiation-driven wind models for Luminous Blue Variables (LBVs), predicting mass-loss rates. Comparison with AG Car observations reveals variable mass loss is due to Fe IV/III and Fe III/II recombination/ionization. Our model yields a present-day mass of 35 for AG Car, providing insight into LBV evolution and mass loss mechanisms.

This study re-examines the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNO) and Super-Kamiokande (SK) data on charged current, neutral current, and neutrino-electron elastic scattering reactions. The primary goal is to constrain the leading weak axial two-body current, a dominant uncertainty in low-energy weak interaction deuteron breakup processes. By self-calibrating theoretical inputs or using SK and reactor data for calibration, we demonstrate that SNO's determination of charged and neutral current fluxes can be accurately assessed. Assuming a standard spectral shape for the total active neutrino flux, our analysis confirms that SNO's conclusion about the inconsistency of the no-flavor-conversion hypothesis is theoretically robust. Furthermore, we determine the magnitude of the active solar neutrino flux, providing valuable insights into the properties of solar neutrinos and the underlying physics of weak interactions. Our findings have significant implications for the interpretation of solar neutrino data.

This study examines phase flows over @xmath0 and @xmath1 generated by vector fields @xmath2 with finite degree polynomial coefficients. Using a diagrammatic technique, we derive evolution operator expressions as series in powers of @xmath5 and @xmath6, represented as sums over specific tree types. Convergence estimates and fixed point behavior are analyzed, with separate consideration of resonance cases, providing insights into phase flow dynamics.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the kinematic properties of 30 nearby relaxed galaxy clusters, utilizing a phenomenological, fully anisotropic model of the distribution function to investigate the projected phase-space density. By employing the Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach, we constrain the total mass distribution, approximated by the universal Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) profile, and the profile of the anisotropy of galaxy orbits. Our results indicate that the normalization of the mean mass-concentration relation is 5.48 at the virial mass of 10^14.5 M⊙, which is consistent with the calibration from cosmological N-body simulations and agrees at the 1σ level with the results from the WMAP5 data release. Assuming a one-to-one correspondence between the normalization of the mass-concentration relation and the linear power spectrum in the framework of the concordance model, we estimate the normalization of the linear power spectrum to be σ8 = 0.83. Our constraints on the parameters of the mass profile are compared with estimates from X-ray observations and other methods based on galaxy kinematics, demonstrating overall consistency. We also investigate correlations between the virial mass and different mass proxies, including the velocity dispersion, X-ray temperature, and X-ray luminosity. The mass scaling relations with the velocity dispersion and X-ray temperature are found to be consistent with the predictions of the virial theorem. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that galaxy orbits are isotropic at the cluster centers, with a mean ratio of radial-to-tangential velocity dispersions of 1.03, and radially anisotropic at the virial sphere, with a mean ratio of 1.43. Although the central anisotropy appears to be universal, the anisotropy at the virial radius differs between clusters within the range of 0.8-1.8. We also examine the evolutionary states of galaxy clusters using the Bautz-Morgan morphological classification and information on the prominence of a cool core. Our results suggest that less evolved clusters have shallower mass profiles and more radially biased galaxy orbits at the virial sphere, consistent with the expected evolution of mass profiles and the observed orbital segregation of late and early-type galaxies. These findings provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters, highlighting the importance of considering the anisotropy of galaxy orbits and the role of dark matter in shaping the kinematic properties of these systems. Overall, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between galaxy evolution, dark matter, and the large-scale structure of the universe.

This article presents the South Galactic Cap U-band Sky Survey (SCUSS), a deep U-band imaging project covering approximately 5000 square degrees in the South Galactic Cap. With a depth of about 1.5 magnitudes deeper than the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) U-band, SCUSS provides a unique opportunity for quasar selection and study. By combining SCUSS U-band data with SDSS multi-band data and exploiting two-epoch U-band variability, we demonstrate an improved quasar selection methodology. Our results show that the combination of SCUSS U-band and SDSS data enables the selection of fainter quasars and those at redshift around 2.2, beyond the capabilities of SDSS data alone. The variability selection technique is particularly effective for identifying low-redshift quasars with ultraviolet excess and mid-redshift quasars, complementing traditional color-based selection methods and maximizing the utility of SCUSS U-band advantages.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the metallicity distribution function (MDF) of the Sagittarius (Sgr) dwarf spheroidal galaxy, utilizing high-resolution echelle spectroscopy of candidate M giant members. Our findings reveal a significant evolution of the Sgr MDF, with a median [Fe/H] shifting from approximately 0.0 in the core to -1.0 dex over a 22.5-30.0 Gyr dynamical age range along the leading arm. This substantial chemical variation provides direct evidence of differences between current dwarf spheroidal satellites and the stellar population they have contributed to the halo. The observed MDF evolution suggests that Sgr underwent a significant change in binding energy over the past few billion years, resulting in a decreased tidal boundary and exposing a metallicity gradient in the progenitor galaxy. By accounting for MDF variations along the debris arms, we approximate the Sgr MDF several billion years ago. Additionally, our analysis of a moving group of M giants towards the north galactic cap, with radial velocities opposing those of the infalling Sgr leading arm stars, proposes that these stars are part of the Sgr trailing arm, further demonstrating the strong MDF evolution within the Sgr stream. These results provide new insights into the chemical evolution and tidal stripping history of the Sgr galaxy, shedding light on the complex interactions between dwarf spheroidal galaxies and the Milky Way halo.

This study reports detailed measurements of magnetic relaxation phenomena in newly synthesized Cu@xFe@xO nanoparticles and known CuFe@xO@x nanoparticles, with particle sizes ranging from 6.5 to 41.5 nm. Both samples exhibit superparamagnetic behavior, characterized by the blocking of magnetic moments, as evidenced by the splitting of zero-field-cooled and field-cooled magnetic moment curves. The data also reveal dynamical hysteresis and slow quasi-logarithmic relaxation of magnetic moments below the blocking temperature. The scaling of magnetic moment relaxation data at different temperatures confirms the applicability of the simple thermal relaxation model. Notably, the two copper-ferrites with similar structures exhibit significantly different magnetic anisotropy densities and other magnetic properties. The results demonstrate consistency across all measured properties, providing valuable insights into the magnetic behavior of single-domain nanoparticles.

This study investigates the magnetic properties of la@xmath0cu@xmath1moo@xmath2, a cluster antiferromagnet comprising a network of strongly coupled copper spin-1/2 trimers. Using magnetic neutron scattering, we observed low-temperature excitations at 7.5(3) meV and 13.2(5) meV, with an additional peak emerging at 12.5(5) meV upon heating, attributed to a transition between excited states. The wave-vector and temperature dependence of the inelastic magnetic scattering cross-section is consistent with intra-trimer transitions. Magnetic neutron diffraction revealed antiferromagnetic order below T@xmath3 = 2.6 K, characterized by a doubling of the unit cell along the a-direction. The ordered magnetic structure is described as inter-trimer order, with spin correlations within trimers controlled by strong intra-trimer interactions. By combining elastic and inelastic magnetic neutron scattering data with group theoretical analysis, we derived a consistent set of intra-trimer interactions and ordered magnetic structures. This work provides a unique example of magnetism associated with inter-atomic composite degrees of freedom in the extreme quantum limit, offering insights into the complex magnetic behavior of cluster antiferromagnets.

This study presents an investigation of the polar angle distribution of charged hadrons using data collected by the JADE experiment at the PETRA collider at centre-of-mass energies of 35 and 44 GeV. By fitting the polar angle distribution, the longitudinal and transverse cross-sections relative to the total hadronic cross-section are determined at an average energy scale of 38.6 GeV. The results obtained are 0.276 ± 0.034 and 0.724 ± 0.034, respectively, with total errors given, and the results are exactly anti-correlated. Utilizing the next-to-leading order QCD prediction for the longitudinal cross-section, a value of 0.118 ± 0.006 is obtained for the strong coupling constant, which is in agreement with the world average value of 0.117 evolved to an energy scale of 38.6 GeV. These findings contribute to our understanding of hadronic production in e+e- annihilation and provide valuable insights into the strong coupling constant. The results of this study are consistent with previous measurements and support the validity of QCD predictions at high energy scales. The JADE collaboration's precise measurement of the longitudinal and transverse cross-sections demonstrates the importance of continued experimentation in the field of particle physics.

This article delves into the concept of contextuality, a quintessential quantum phenomenon that lacks a classical probability theory analogue. The combination of two independent systems into a single test space raises questions about the representation of such scenarios. Foulis and Randall's premise, based on the no-signalling principle, provides a unique method for composing two contextuality scenarios. However, when composing more than two test spaces, various methods emerge, all of which seem to yield observationally equivalent scenarios in terms of classical and quantum probabilistic models. The invariance of these models under different composition methods prompts an investigation into whether this property is unique to classical and quantum models or applicable to other probabilistic models, including @xmath0 models. Notably, @xmath0 models are significant in physical contexts, as they coincide with almost quantum correlations under specific composition rules. Our research reveals that distinct composition rules can lead to scenarios with non-equivalent sets of @xmath0 models, attributed to the failure of certain composition rules to satisfy local orthogonality. By incorporating the principle of local orthogonality into composition rules, we demonstrate that @xmath0 models exhibit invariance under different composition methods, providing new insights into the fundamental principles governing contextuality and probabilistic models. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the relationships between contextuality, composition methods, and probabilistic models, shedding light on the underlying structures of quantum phenomena.

This study examines the impact of non-perturbative, bubble-like inhomogeneities on the decay rate of false-vacuum states in two and three-dimensional scalar field theories. By inducing large-amplitude oscillations of the field, we demonstrate that these inhomogeneities significantly accelerate the decay rate, transitioning from exponential suppression to power-law suppression. This phenomenon, termed resonant nucleation, is facilitated by long-lived oscillons among non-perturbative fluctuations. A comprehensive phase diagram is constructed, identifying three distinct mechanisms for vacuum decay: homogeneous nucleation, resonant nucleation, and cross-over. Our findings have implications for understanding vacuum stability and decay in various theoretical frameworks, including cosmological inflation. The results of this research contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between non-perturbative effects and vacuum decay, with potential applications in theoretical physics and cosmology. Theoretical models and experimental scenarios are discussed in the context of these findings.

This article presents a systematic analysis of replica field theory calculations using two one-dimensional "toy" random models with Gaussian disorder. The simplicity of these models allows for a step-by-step examination of the replica trick calculations, revealing a crucial limitation: the standard replica program becomes formally impossible to implement at a certain stage. Nevertheless, by adopting a "doublethink" approach, where contradictory assumptions are overlooked, the calculations can be completed to yield a physically sensible result for the free energy distribution function. This work highlights the inconsistencies and challenges inherent to replica field theory, while also demonstrating its potential to produce meaningful outcomes despite these limitations.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the integrated galaxy light (IGL) by combining wide and deep galaxy number-count data from various surveys, including GAMA, COSMOS/G10, HST/ERS, HST/UVUDF, and infrared datasets from ESO, Spitzer, and Herschel. The combined data span a broad wavelength range, from the far-ultraviolet (0.15 μm) to the far-infrared (1000 μm), and demonstrate convergence in the contribution of successively fainter galaxies to the IGL. Utilizing a simple spline fit, we derive the IGL and extrapolated IGL in all bands, accounting for the modest contribution of undetected low surface brightness galaxies and intra-cluster/group light. Our results agree with most previous IGL estimates and direct measurements in the far-infrared, but exhibit significant discrepancies with direct estimates in the optical. Notably, our findings are consistent with recent very high-energy experiments (H.E.S.S. and MAGIC), suggesting that an additional foreground, potentially related to the adopted zodiacal light model, may be affecting direct estimates. We apply a modified two-component model to integrate the extragalactic background light (EBL) and obtain measurements of the cosmic optical background (COB) and cosmic infrared background (CIB). The results yield COB and CIB values of 22.4 nW m^-2 sr^-1 and 29.1 nW m^-2 sr^-1, respectively, with a COB-to-CIB ratio of 48:52%. Future space missions, such as Euclid and WFIRST, are expected to reduce the COB error, enabling comparisons with very high-energy data that could potentially provide a direct detection and measurement of the reionization field.

This study presents new time-resolved data on quasiparticle relaxation and Cooper pair recombination dynamics in YBa2Cu3O7, obtained using femtosecond optical spectroscopy as a function of temperature and doping level.
