Our analysis reveals that 13 of these galaxies exhibit clear signs of recent star formation, characterized by prominent nebular emission lines. By applying evolutionary stellar population synthesis models and Lick absorption line indices, we derive stellar ages, metallicities, and alpha-element abundances, allowing us to reconstruct the star formation and chemical evolution history of these star-forming elliptical galaxies (SFEs). The results show that SFEs have relatively younger stellar populations, higher metallicities, and lower stellar masses, with their star formation history marked by a recent minor and short starburst superimposed on an old stellar component. Additionally, we identify 11 E+A galaxies, which exhibit stellar population properties distinct from both quiescent and star-forming ellipticals, suggesting a potential evolutionary link between these galaxy types. Our findings confirm the relationships between age, metallicity, alpha-element abundance, and stellar mass for local elliptical galaxies, providing new insights into the complex formation and evolution of these galaxies. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the star-forming activity and stellar population properties of elliptical galaxies, shedding light on their intriguing and multifaceted nature.

This article presents the results of photoelectric observations of the PG1159 star HS2324 + 3944, which exhibits periodic luminosity variations with a period of 2140 ± 11 seconds. Located within the GW Vir instability strip, this star's photometric behavior is characteristic of non-radial oscillations, classifying it as a new member of the GW Vir group with the longest pulsation period among these stars. Notably, HS2324 + 3944 is the first pulsating PG1159 star with a high hydrogen abundance in its atmosphere, with a hydrogen-to-helium ratio of 2:1 by number. The presence of pulsations in this star is intriguing, as the expected pulsation mechanism based on carbon-oxygen cyclic ionization would require a sharp decrease in hydrogen abundance, which seems unlikely. The discovery of HS2324 + 3944's pulsational behavior offers new insights into the properties of PG1159 stars and challenges our understanding of the underlying pulsation mechanisms, warranting further investigation into this phenomenon. The unique characteristics of HS2324 + 3944 make it an interesting subject for continued study, particularly in the context of stellar evolution and pulsation theory.

This article examines the dynamics of a homogeneous Fermi gas in a weak random potential, neglecting particle pair interactions. We derive the kinetic scaling limit for the momentum distribution function, demonstrating its determination by a linear Boltzmann equation for translation-invariant initial states. Additionally, quasifree initial states yield quasifree kinetic limits under time evolution and averaging over randomness. The momentum distributions of free fermion field Gibbs states are shown to be stationary solutions of the linear Boltzmann equation, including the zero-temperature limit, providing insight into the system's behavior under various conditions. Key properties are rigorously established.

This article explores the intersection of quiver/dimer models, hypergeometric systems, and dessins d'enfants, revealing a natural overlap between these fields. By situating dimer models within the framework established by Gelfand, Kapranov, and Zelevinsky for hypergeometric systems, we demonstrate a seamless connection between the two. The fast inverse algorithm and untwisting procedure are recontextualized, yielding the Kasteleyn matrix for dimer models as a bi-adjacency matrix for the untwisted model. Furthermore, certain perfect matchings in dimer models are shown to be equivalent to triangulations in GKZ theory, with a corresponding mapping rule extending to lattice points in the secondary polygon. A key observation, supported by numerous examples and conjectured to be generally applicable, is that the determinant of the weighted Kasteleyn matrix can be transformed into the principal A-determinant in GKZ theory. Through illustrative examples, this article highlights the fruitful interplay between these mathematical disciplines, shedding new light on their underlying structures and relationships. The findings presented here pave the way for further research into the connections between quiver/dimer models, hypergeometric systems, and dessins d'enfants.

This article delves into the FCFS infinite bipartite matching model, initially introduced in [citation], where two sequences of items are chosen independently and matched according to a compatibility graph. Building upon previous work, which established a condition for stability, derived a product form stationary distribution, and calculated match rates between compatible types, this paper presents novel results. Utilizing a Loynes-type scheme, we demonstrate the existence of a unique matching across all integers when the system is stable. Furthermore, we establish dynamic reversibility, showing that reversing the positions of items in matched pairs yields independent and identically distributed sequences with a FCFS matching in reversed time. Leveraging these findings, we derive stationary distributions for associated Markov chains and calculate the distribution of link lengths between matched items. Our research contributes to the understanding of infinite bipartite matching, shedding light on the intricate dynamics of FCFS policy, Loynes-type construction, and dynamic reversibility. The results have implications for various fields, including operations research and probability theory, and are classified under primary 60J10 and secondary 90B22 and 68M20 in the 2000 Mathematics Subject Classification. Keywords: infinite bipartite matching, first come first served policy, Loynes type construction, dynamic reversibility, product form solutions, link lengths.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the young open cluster NGC 6231, leveraging new wide-field photometry to investigate the initial mass function (IMF) and mass segregation within the cluster. Our results indicate a total-to-selective extinction ratio of R_V = 3.2, consistent with the normal value, although early-type stars at the cluster center exhibit large color excess ratios. The surface density profiles of four member groups reveal a consistent decline to the surface density of field stars at approximately 10 pc, regardless of stellar mass. The derived IMF for NGC 6231, spanning 0.8-45 M⊙, exhibits a slope slightly shallower than the canonical value, although the difference is marginal. Notably, the mass function varies systematically with radius, with a shallow slope at the center and a steep slope at the outer ring, suggesting mass segregation. This segregation is confirmed for massive stars (≥ 8 M⊙) through a minimum spanning tree analysis. Using a Monte Carlo method, we estimate the total mass of NGC 6231 to be approximately 2700 M⊙. By comparing our data to evolutionary isochrones, we constrain the age of the cluster, finding a range of 1-7 Myr for low-mass stars, with a peak at 3 Myr. However, the age of high-mass stars depends on the adopted models, with estimates ranging from 3.5 ± 0.5 Myr to 4.0-7.0 Myr. The latter age is consistent with the ejection timescale of the high-mass runaway star HD 153919 from NGC 6231, although the younger age cannot be entirely ruled out. Our findings provide new insights into the properties and evolution of NGC 6231, highlighting the complex interplay between mass segregation, IMF, and stellar evolution in young open clusters.

This article explores the Yang-Lee, Fisher, and Potts zeros of the one-dimensional q-state Potts model through the lens of dynamical systems theory. By deriving an exact recurrence relation for the partition function, we establish a connection between the zeros of the partition function and neutral fixed points of the recurrence relation. A general equation for the zeros of the partition function is obtained, facilitating a comprehensive classification of the Yang-Lee, Fisher, and Potts zeros. Notably, our analysis reveals that Fisher zeros in a non-zero magnetic field are situated on multiple lines in the complex temperature plane, with the number of lines dependent on the magnetic field's value. Furthermore, we derive analytical expressions for the densities of these zeros, demonstrating that the densities of all zero types exhibit singular behavior at edge singularity points with a uniform critical exponent.

This article presents a general framework for studying the existence and linear stability of closed solutions to the Vortex Filament Equation (VFE) hierarchy. By leveraging the correspondence between the VFE and Nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) hierarchies, we establish a connection between the AKNS Floquet spectrum and stability properties of filament equation solutions. Our approach is applied to solutions of the Hirota equation and soliton solutions, demonstrating its efficacy. The framework provides new insights into the stability of vortex filaments, with implications for various fields. Our results contribute to the understanding of integrable hierarchies and their applications, classified under mathematics subject classifications 35q55, 37k20, 37k45, and 35q35.

Title: Cosmological Shock Waves are a Ubiquitous Consequence of Cosmic Structure Formation Abstract: The formation of cosmic structures is inevitably accompanied by the generation of shock waves, which play a crucial role in heating the baryonic gas within the large-scale structure of the universe. This study utilizes a set of N-body/hydrodynamic simulation data of a ΛCDM universe to investigate the properties of shock-heated gas in connection with the shocks themselves. Our analysis reveals that the distributions of shock speed and temperature of the shock-heated gas reflect the depth of the gravitational potential of associated nonlinear structures, thereby influencing their morphology. We identify three distinct components of the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM): hot gas in and around clusters/groups, warm-hot gas with temperatures mostly in filaments, and a significant amount of low-temperature WHIM with temperatures distributed mostly as sheet-like structures. The low-temperature WHIM is primarily heated and collisionally ionized by shocks with moderate velocities, while photo-ionization by the UV and X-ray background radiations is important for metal ions. Our results suggest that both the high-temperature and low-temperature WHIM components contribute significantly to the gas mass, implying that the low-temperature WHIM may be important in resolving the missing baryon problem. We find that the shock-heated gas in filaments and sheets can be detected through emissions and absorptions in soft X-ray and far UV. While the high-temperature WHIM contributes to the soft X-ray background and absorptions of highly ionized species, the low-temperature WHIM is the major contributor to absorptions of lower ionized species, such as O V and O VI. Our study highlights the importance of considering the low-temperature WHIM in understanding the thermal and ionization properties of the intergalactic medium.

This study presents new spectroscopic and photometric time series observations of the δ Scuti star FG Vir, revealing oscillations through changes in hydrogen and metal absorption line equivalent widths. By analyzing the ratios between spectroscopic and photometric amplitudes, we assign l values to the eight strongest oscillation modes. Notably, two radial modes are identified, including the fundamental mode at 140 μHz, indicating that two lower-frequency modes are g-modes. Comparison of radial mode frequencies with a scaled δ Scuti star model yields a density estimate, from which a distance of 135.6 pc is derived, consistent with the Hipparcos value. Additionally, a 3.5-day variability in equivalent widths and intensity is attributed to stellar rotation, providing new insights into the star's internal structure and dynamics. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of δ Scuti star properties and behavior.

This article examines the thermodynamic properties of charged Anti-de Sitter black holes in extended phase space. We review the equal area laws and Clapeyron equations, demonstrating that Maxwell's equal area law applies to multiple oscillatory lines, including pressure-thermodynamic volume, charge-electric potential, and temperature-entropy. A generalized Clapeyron equation is derived, along with two additional equations. Notably, the coexistence curve of small and large charged black holes is found to be charge-independent in reduced parameter space, regardless of spacetime dimension. A highly accurate fitting formula for this curve is presented, which is consistent with calculated Clapeyron equation values. This formula provides a useful tool for further study of thermodynamic properties along the coexistence curve, offering insights into the behavior of charged black holes in various spacetime dimensions. The results have implications for understanding black hole thermodynamics.

We reexamine parton recombination in perturbation theory, bypassing AGK cutting rules. Using time-ordered perturbation theory, we sum neglected cut diagrams and derive new evolution equations incorporating parton recombination, refining the GLR evolution equation.

This study examines the energy spectrum of a silicene quantum dot in perpendicular magnetic and electric fields. The electric field induces a tunable band gap, while boundary conditions introduce chirality, affecting the behavior of edge states. We find that the band inversion mechanism, crucial for the topological insulator transition, depends on the magnetic field strength. Specifically, some zero Landau level edge states undergo band inversion at any magnetic field value, whereas others require critical magnetic field strengths and nonzero band gaps. Our results provide insight into the complex interplay between magnetic and electric fields in silicene quantum dots.

This article presents a formulation of higher spin gravity as a BF theory, where fields take values in a specific algebra treated as a higher spin algebra. The resulting theory is topological and extends the Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity model to include higher spin fields. By linearizing the BF equations around a given background, we describe higher spin partially-massless fields and dilaton fields. Notably, we establish dual metric-like formulations that follow from the original linearized BF higher spin theory. This duality demonstrates the dynamical equivalence of metric-like field equations, which can be expressed as massive scalar field equations or conservation conditions for higher spin currents. Our work provides a significant extension of the Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity model, shedding new light on the interplay between higher spin fields and gravity. The findings have implications for our understanding of topological gravity and its potential applications.

This article presents a comprehensive analysis of the singular dynamics and low-energy fixed point of one-channel impurity S-D models with ferromagnetic and underscreened antiferromagnetic couplings. Utilizing the numerical renormalization group (NRG) method, we calculate the spectral densities of the one-electron Green's functions and T-matrices, revealing sharp cusps at the Fermi level but no divergence. The approach to the Fermi level is characterized by terms proportional to a specific power law. Our results show a slow convergence of the scaled NRG energy levels to their fixed point values, allowing for the determination of the low-energy scale. We also compute the dynamical spin susceptibility and elastic and inelastic scattering cross-sections as a function of energy, finding that the inelastic scattering vanishes as expected for a Fermi liquid, albeit at a slower rate than in the fully screened case. Furthermore, we derive the asymptotic forms for the phase shifts in elastic scattering of quasiparticles in both high-spin and low-spin channels, providing valuable insights into the behavior of these systems. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics of one-channel impurity S-D models.

This study introduces a highly sensitive single-monochromator Raman spectrometer capable of operating with a tunable laser source. By modifying a commercial Raman spectrometer, we separate the functions of holographic Rayleigh filters and laser mirrors, allowing for free rotation of the filter without compromising light alignment. This design enables efficient stray light filtering down to 150 cm^-1 and tunable operation. Optimized for single-wall carbon nanotubes, the spectrometer's performance is demonstrated using a tunable dye-laser source. The resulting instrument combines high sensitivity with the broadband characteristics of traditional triple-monochromator systems, offering improved versatility and performance in Raman spectroscopy applications. This innovation enhances the analysis of carbon nanotubes and other materials.

This study develops a cost-efficient micro aerial vehicle (MAV) in a quadrocopter design for indoor scenarios. Constructed with off-the-shelf components, the MAV incorporates additional sensors and electronics to stabilize flight and enable autonomous navigation in partially unstructured environments. The system's efficiency, safety, and reliability are enhanced, making it suitable for rescue and surveillance operations. The use of unmanned robot systems, such as this MAV, can improve operational outcomes, especially in hazardous areas. This research contributes to the development of autonomous ground and aerial vehicles for various applications. Indoor navigation capabilities are demonstrated.

This article explores the phenomenon of electroweak symmetry breaking within the framework of supersymmetric models that incorporate an additional non-anomalous U(1) gauge symmetry and a standard-model singlet scalar. The introduction of this extra gauge symmetry, denoted as U(1)', forbids the presence of an elementary μ term, a common issue in supersymmetric theories. However, an effective μ term is dynamically generated through the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the singlet scalar, providing a natural resolution to the μ problem. We examine various scenarios that lead to acceptable levels of mixing and other phenomenological implications, all of which require some degree of fine-tuning but avoid excessive tuning. Two primary classes of scenarios are identified: one driven by a large trilinear soft supersymmetry breaking term, characterized by small mixing, a relatively light Higgs (potentially around 200 GeV), and a first-order electroweak phase transition at tree level; and another class involving radiative breaking, where the scale of dimensional parameters is elevated, yet the electroweak scale is suppressed due to cancellations. By relating soft supersymmetry breaking parameters from the electroweak scale to the string scale, using Yukawa couplings derived from a subset of string models, we find that neither scenario emerges under the assumption of universal soft supersymmetry breaking mass parameters at the string scale without exotic multiplet contributions. Nonetheless, relaxing the universality assumption or incorporating exotic multiplets, as anticipated in most string models, allows for the realization of either scenario, including radiative breaking. This work offers insights into the mechanisms of electroweak symmetry breaking and the μ problem in supersymmetric theories with extended gauge symmetries, highlighting the potential for natural solutions within the context of string theory.

This paper examines the Minimum Certificate Dispersal (MCD) problem, which involves assigning a set of edges to each vertex in a graph to satisfy a set of requests while minimizing the total number of assigned edges. We focus on the complexity of MCD with sparse request structures, specifically when the request set forms a tree. Our results show that MCD remains APX-hard even when the request set is a tree, including a star. However, we identify a polynomial-time solvable case when the maximum degree of the tree is constant. For trees with unbounded maximum degree, we provide an approximation algorithm and establish a lower bound on the approximability of the problem. Additionally, we demonstrate that the problem can be solved efficiently when the underlying graph is a tree. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the MCD problem and its complexity in different scenarios, shedding light on the trade-offs between the structure of the request set and the graph, and the approximability of the problem. By exploring these relationships, we provide new insights into the computational complexity of the MCD problem and its variants.

We investigate fluctuations in random matrix products, relating to the one-dimensional Dirac equation with random mass. In the continuum limit, we derive integral representations for variance. This case exhibits variance saturation at low energy and a vanishing Lyapunov exponent, leading to distinct behavior. Our description sheds light on the Kappus-Wegner anomaly, providing new insights into localization properties and random systems, with implications for understanding complex phenomena in condensed matter physics and beyond, governed by PACS numbers 72.15.Rn and 02.50.-r.

This article presents a novel computational framework for simulating the co-flow of two immiscible viscous liquids in a shallow rectangular container. By leveraging assumptions based on the domain's shallow depth, the governing equations are reduced to a Hele-Shaw type, enabling efficient numerical modeling. A key feature of this framework is the accurate modeling of capillary effects, achieved through a continuum approach coupled with a volume-of-fluid formulation. The interface motion and interfacial tension are computed using a height-function algorithm, reconstructing the interface with high accuracy. The combination of these algorithms represents a significant development in the study of Hele-Shaw flows. Benchmark simulations demonstrate the method's order of accuracy and convergence properties. The framework is applied to a microfluidic flow scenario, where a ribbon of fluid co-flows with a second liquid, exhibiting an abrupt change in interface curvature and focusing near the exit for small capillary numbers (O(0.01)). These findings have important implications for the design and optimization of microfluidic devices and systems.

The RD52 (DREAM) collaboration is actively pursuing research and development of dual readout calorimetry techniques, aiming to enhance hadronic energy resolution for future high-energy physics experiments. By simultaneously detecting Cherenkov and scintillation light, we can measure the electromagnetic fraction of hadron shower events on an event-by-event basis, thereby eliminating the primary source of fluctuation that hinders precise energy measurement for hadrons. Our research has involved testing lead and copper fiber prototype calorimeters with various energies of electromagnetic particles and hadrons. Beam tests have yielded energy resolutions for electrons and pions, as well as particle identification capabilities in a longitudinally unsegmented calorimeter. Additionally, we have investigated the properties of pure and doped PbWO4 crystals, BGO, and BSO, with the goal of developing a crystal-based dual readout detector. This abstract presents our findings, highlighting the promising characteristics of homogeneous media for this technique. We also provide guidelines for further crystal development and discuss the construction techniques used to assemble our prototypes, outlining potential methods for industrializing the production of a full hermetic calorimeter. Our results demonstrate significant progress towards achieving improved hadronic energy resolution.

We present an analysis of the X-ray spectral evolution of the nearby Type IIn supernova (SN) 2005ip, utilizing observations from the Chandra and Swift telescopes spanning from approximately 1 to 6 years after the explosion. Our results show that the X-ray spectra at all epochs are well-represented by a thermal emission model with a temperature of approximately 1 keV, suggesting that the X-ray emission is primarily generated by the circumstellar medium heated by the forward shock. Notably, the spectra exhibit significant absorption in the early stages, with a column density of approximately 10^23 cm^-2, which gradually decreases to the level of Galactic absorption (approximately 10^21 cm^-2) at the final epoch. This indicates that the supernova exploded in a dense circumstellar medium, which was eventually overtaken by the forward shock. The intrinsic X-ray luminosity remains constant until the final epoch, where it drops by a factor of 2. With an intrinsic 0.2-10 keV luminosity of approximately 10^41 erg s^-1 during the plateau phase, SN 2005ip is ranked as one of the brightest X-ray supernovae. Our derived mass-loss rate of approximately 10^-3 (v_w/1000 km s^-1) M_sun yr^-1 suggests that the progenitor star underwent eruptive mass ejections, similar to a luminous blue variable star. This high mass-loss rate implies a total ejected mass of approximately 10 M_sun, indicating a progenitor mass of approximately 20 M_sun.

This study examines the renormalization-scale dependence of the two-loop inclusive semileptonic decay rate in the pole mass scheme, revealing significant dependence and poor convergence in an alternative scheme. To improve estimates, we develop Padé approximant techniques suited to perturbative calculations in the pole mass scheme, allowing for the estimation of three-loop contributions. By comparing Padé estimates with renormalization-group determined terms, we obtain an optimized estimate of three-loop contributions. The resulting three-loop estimate in the pole-mass scheme exhibits minimal renormalization-scale sensitivity, yielding an estimated decay rate with reduced theoretical uncertainties and inclusion of non-perturbative effects, providing a more accurate prediction of the decay rate.

This study presents the inaugural numerical application of the Light-Front Coupled-Cluster (LFCC) method, focusing on the odd-parity massive eigenstate of φ^4 theory. By utilizing Light-Front Quantization, the eigenstate is expressed as a Fock-state expansion, where wave functions serve as coefficients. The LFCC method introduces a refined truncation approach, transcending traditional Fock-space truncation and yielding a finite set of nonlinear equations. This enables an unrestricted Fock space, allowing for a more comprehensive analysis. Our results are compared to those obtained through Fock-space truncation, providing insight into the efficacy of the LFCC method in solving eigenvalue problems. The findings demonstrate the potential of the LFCC method in tackling complex theoretical physics challenges.

This study examines a one-dimensional fixed-energy variant of Manna's stochastic sandpile model, characterized by a continuous transition to an absorbing state at a critical particle density θ0. Through extensive simulations, critical exponents are determined for both stationary and transient properties. Notably, the model exhibits finite-size scaling, although anomalies are observed in relaxation times and the approach to the stationary state, which are influenced by the initial configuration. The obtained critical exponents deviate from those expected at a linear interface depinning transition in a disordered medium and from directed percolation, indicating a unique behavior in this sandpile model. The results provide insights into the complex dynamics of this system.

This study presents measurements of thermal self-locking in a Fabry-Perot cavity containing a potassium niobate (KNBO3) crystal. A novel method is developed to determine linear and nonlinear optical absorption coefficients in intracavity crystals by analyzing transmission lineshapes characteristic of optical bistability. The one-photon absorption coefficient at 846 nm is found to be α1, while the two-photon absorption coefficient at 846 nm is β2, and the one-photon absorption coefficient at 423 nm is γ3 m-1. The blue-light-induced-infrared-absorption (BLIIRA) process is also investigated, yielding a coefficient for this excited state absorption. The method is particularly suitable for bulk absorption measurements with small absorption compared to scattering. Additionally, new measurements of the temperature dependence of the index of refraction at 846 nm are reported and compared to existing literature values, providing valuable insights into the optical properties of KNBO3 crystals.

This article presents an exact solution to the scattering of two Dashen-Hasslacher-Neveu (DHN) baryons in the large N Gross-Neveu model using the relativistic, time-dependent Hartree-Fock approach. The solution accounts for the back-reaction of fermions bound within the baryons, yielding a complex result that differs significantly from kink-antikink scattering. A simplified ansatz form is introduced, providing closed analytic expressions for space-time dependent mean fields and Dirac spinors for all states. This solution has broader implications, extending to the scattering of polarons and solitons in conducting polymers, and offering new insights into complex many-body systems. The results demonstrate the versatility of the Hartree-Fock approach in solving intricate relativistic quantum field theory problems.

This study presents an in-depth examination of accretion processes in 91 Herbig Ae/Be (HAeBe) stars, leveraging high-resolution spectra obtained with the Very Large Telescope/X-Shooter. By analyzing equivalent width measurements of 32 emission lines spanning the UV to NIR range, we derive line luminosities and compare them to accretion luminosities determined from UV excess measurements. Our results reveal a consistent correlation between emission line luminosity and accretion luminosity, irrespective of detection frequency. The average relationship between these two quantities is found to be proportional to L_acc ∝ L_line^0.7, in agreement with previous findings in classical T Tauri stars, although the HAeBe relationship exhibits a steeper slope, particularly towards the higher-mass Herbig Be regime. Notably, all observed lines demonstrate a correlation with accretion luminosity, effectively increasing the number of accretion diagnostic lines in HAeBe stars tenfold. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of accretion processes in pre-main sequence stars, although further investigation is necessary to elucidate the physical origin of each emission line and determine whether it is indeed driven by accretion. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the properties of HAeBe stars and their role in the formation and evolution of high-mass stars.

This study investigates the relationship between infrared and X-ray properties of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN). Using a local sample of X-ray AGN with well-constrained infrared spectral energy distributions (SEDs), we develop novel diagnostics that utilize 24 μm and 70 μm flux densities to identify AGN-dominated systems and measure their total infrared luminosities. Applying these diagnostics to X-ray detected AGN in the Chandra Deep Field South, we find that the infrared to X-ray luminosity ratio was significantly higher in the early universe. This dramatic evolution is explored, and potential explanations are discussed. Future Herschel observations will help discriminate between these scenarios and identify potential Compton-thick AGN, providing valuable insights into the evolution of AGN. Our results have significant implications for understanding the co-evolution of black holes and galaxies across cosmic time.

We present photometric and spectroscopic observations of six Y dwarfs discovered in the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) data by Cushing et al. The data were obtained using the Near-Infrared Imager (NIRI) on the Gemini North Telescope, with photometry acquired for WISEP J041022.71-150248.5, WISEP J173835.52-2713258.9, and WISEPC J205628.90-1145953.3. Additionally, we obtained a far-red spectrum for WISEPC J205628.90-1145953.3 using the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS)-North. Our analysis compares the observed data to the Morley et al. (2012) models, which incorporate cloud decks of sulfide and chloride condensates. The models demonstrate a good fit to the energy distributions of T9 to Y0 dwarfs, except at 5 μm, where the models are too bright. This discrepancy is attributed to the models' neglect of departures from chemical equilibrium caused by vertical mixing. We derive effective temperatures, surface gravities, and masses for the Y dwarfs, with the five Y0 to Y0.5 dwarfs exhibiting temperatures and gravities that imply a mass range of 5-15 M_Jup and ages around 5 Gyr. Notably, we suggest that WISEP J182831.08-1265037.8 is a binary system, comprising a 350 K and log(g) = 4.5 primary and a 250 K and log(g) = 4.0 secondary, corresponding to masses of 10 and 7 M_Jup and an age around 2 Gyr. Our findings highlight the importance of incorporating water clouds and mixing into future models to reconcile the observed and predicted fluxes.

This article examines a cake cutting game between Alice and Bob, where Alice selects a set of points in a square and Bob cuts out axis-parallel rectangles with disjoint interiors. It has been conjectured that Bob can secure at least half of the cake, but this remains unsettled. We investigate the conditions under which Alice can force Bob's share to tend to zero. Our results show that to prevent Bob from gaining more than a certain fraction of the cake, Alice must use a large number of points. Specifically, we prove that to limit Bob's share to a fraction, Alice needs at least a certain number of points, providing new insights into this classic problem.

We report the detection of the nearby, old pulsar PSR B1133+16, located at a distance of approximately 360 pc, with an age of 5 million years. Observations reveal a flux of 1.2 x 10^(-13) ergs s^(-1) cm^(-2) in the 0.5-8 keV band. Despite limited counts, the spectrum can be described by various models, including a power-law fit yielding a photon index of 2.5 and isotropic luminosity of 4.8 x 10^(-13) ergs s^(-1) cm^(-2), which accounts for approximately 0.1% of the spin-down power. Alternatively, a blackbody model with a temperature of 2.5 MK and projected emitting area of 10^4 m^2 fits the data, suggesting a hot polar cap. The X-ray properties of PSR B1133+16 resemble those of other old pulsars, particularly PSR B0943+10, offering insights into the emission mechanisms of these objects.

The ATLAS experiment is set to undergo a significant upgrade of its tracker system in anticipation of the High Luminosity phase of the LHC (HL-LHC), scheduled to commence around 2025. Thin planar pixel modules have emerged as promising candidates for the new pixel system, offering reduced material budget and high charge collection efficiency even after irradiation. Recent advancements in pixel cell design, incorporating optimized biasing structures, have been integrated into n-in-p planar pixel productions with sensor thicknesses of 100 and 200 μm. Beam tests have been conducted to investigate the gain in hit efficiency as a function of irradiation fluence. This study will discuss the outlook for future thin planar pixel sensor productions, focusing on thin sensors with optimized biasing structures and small pixel cells (50x50 and 25x100 μm). The performance of these sensors is crucial for the new ATLAS read-out chip in 65 nm CMOS technology, particularly in the forward region of the pixel system at HL-LHC. To predict the performance of 50x50 pixels at high pseudorapidity, FE-I4 compatible planar pixel sensors have been studied before and after irradiation in beam tests at high incidence angles. The results will be presented, including cluster shapes, charge collection, and hit efficiency, providing valuable insights into the potential of thin planar pixel detectors for the HL-LHC upgrade.

This article explores the intrinsic properties of black hole solutions within the framework of a scalar-tensor theory of gravity, incorporating a Higgs potential and a static, spherically symmetric line element. Utilizing a series-expansion method, we derive Reissner-Nordström-like and Schwarzschild black hole solutions, both with and without Higgs field mass. A detailed analysis of the physical implications of these solutions is conducted, focusing on the equation of state parameter, scalar field excitations, and geodesic motion. The emergence of naked singularities and the dependence of black hole horizons on field excitations, which are influenced by pressure terms screening mass terms, are also examined. Furthermore, we investigate a potential link between scalar field interactions and flat rotation curves in the weak field limit of gravity. Our discussion extends to the dynamic effects of scalar fields and pressure terms on mass, providing insights into the complex interplay between gravitational and scalar field phenomena.

This study investigates the hypothesis that massive young stellar objects (YSOs) emit powerful infrared H I lines through outflows from surrounding disks. Utilizing two-dimensional Monte Carlo radiative transfer calculations, we model the infrared spectra of a YSO disk wind based on previous hydrodynamical calculations. Our results show qualitative agreement between the model spectra and observed spectra from massive YSOs, supporting the disk wind explanation for H I lines. However, discrepancies arise, including overpredicted Brγ/Brα equivalent-width ratios and broader, double-peaked line profiles that contradict typical observations. We discuss the interpretation of these differences within the disk wind context and propose modifications to the disk and outflow structure to resolve these discrepancies. Our findings contribute to the understanding of YSO evolution and the role of disk winds in shaping their observational properties. The results have implications for the development of more accurate models of YSO disks and outflows.

This study examines the performance of quantum error-correcting codes beyond their intended capacity. We derive formulae for the probability of failure when errors exceed the code's minimum distance, enabling comparison of codes with the same minimum distance. Both error detection and correction are considered, with explicit examples provided for stabilizer codes constructed from qubits encoding a single qubit. The results offer a framework for ranking codes and provide insights into their robustness against errors, contributing to the development of more reliable quantum error correction methods. Key findings are supported by theoretical analyses and example applications.

This study re-examines the 2008 discovery by the CDF collaboration of an excess of events containing two or more muons, with at least one muon appearing to originate outside the beam pipe. We explore the possibility of observing similar "ghost" events in previously completed experiments. A simple model, involving the four-body decay of a relatively light particle, successfully reproduces the CDF di-muon data. This model predicts a significant number of ghost events in Fermilab fixed target experiments E772, E789, and E866, when applying optimized cuts for Drell-Yan event analyses. However, a more complex model, featuring the production of two particles from a broad resonance, is required to accurately describe events with multiple muons. This model can be tested in fixed target experiments by relaxing cuts on muon angles or rapidities. Notably, the UA1 experiment at the CERN collider should have detected ghost events, providing a potential avenue for verification. Our findings offer new insights into the existence and characteristics of ghost events, warranting further investigation in existing and future experiments.

The mitigation of beam loss is a critical concern in the design and operation of high-intensity accelerators, particularly as new machines continue to push the boundaries of power and performance. In the context of linacs for H^- ion beams, such as the Oak Ridge Spallation Neutron Source, and proton linacs, like the European Spallation Neutron Source, various loss mechanisms pose significant challenges. Unique loss mechanisms in H^- linacs include residual gas stripping, proton capture and acceleration, field stripping, black-body radiation, and intra-beam stripping. Common loss mechanisms for both H^- and proton accelerators include beam halo formation and ion source or RF transients. Effective machine protection systems are essential for limiting beam loss and ensuring safe, efficient operation. This article highlights the complexities of beam loss in high-intensity accelerators and the importance of mitigating these losses to optimize performance and minimize risks. Keywords: linac, beam loss, H^- proton.

This article examines cosmic microwave background constraints on causal set theory, a quantum gravity model predicting dark energy properties. We derive the power spectrum of causal set dark energy fluctuations using overlap volumes of past light cones. Utilizing a modified Boltzmann code, we obtain stronger constraints on the theory's single parameter. Our results indicate that causal set theory cannot explain late-time acceleration without significant modifications to general relativity, suggesting limitations to this theoretical framework in describing the universe's evolution and dark energy phenomena, thus refining our understanding of quantum gravity's role.

This study utilizes the recent next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) splitting function estimates by van Neerven and Vogt to conduct exploratory fits of deep inelastic and related hard scattering data. The hierarchy of parton distributions is examined at leading order (LO), next-to-leading order (NLO), and NNLO, with a focus on the stability of predictions for physical observables. Specifically, the longitudinal structure function and cross sections for heavy hadroproduction are analyzed. The results show relatively poor convergence at small values of the scaling variable, whereas cross sections are more reliably predicted. The study demonstrates the importance of estimating the effect of NNLO contributions on physical observables, providing insights into the stability and reliability of theoretical predictions. By comparing LO, NLO, and NNLO results, this research aims to improve our understanding of the underlying dynamics and contribute to the development of more accurate theoretical models.

The Cosmic Infrared Background Experiment (CIBER) is a rocket-borne mission designed to detect signatures of first-light galaxies during the reionization era through absolute photometry imaging and spectroscopy. The initial CIBER-I instrument, launched on February 25th, 2009, features a two-color camera, absolute spectrometer, and narrow-band imaging spectrometer to measure fluctuations and foreground emissions. Following several additional flights of CIBER-I, an enhanced CIBER-II camera is proposed, boasting a 30 cm wide-field imager operating across four bands between 0.5 and 2.1 microns. This upgraded instrument aims to achieve a high-significance detection of unresolved infrared background fluctuations, enabling the study of reionization sources. With a field of view 50 to 2000 times larger than existing satellite-based infrared instruments, CIBER-II will conduct a definitive investigation to determine the surface density of sources responsible for reionization, providing crucial insights into the early universe. The CIBER-II mission will build upon the foundation established by CIBER-I, ultimately shedding light on the mysteries of the cosmic dawn. By probing the infrared background, CIBER-II will help establish a deeper understanding of the first galaxies and their role in shaping the universe as we know it today.

This paper explores the haplotype assembly problem through an information theoretic lens, where a haplotype is represented as a binary string of nucleotide bases differing from its homologous pair. High-throughput DNA sequencing technologies provide short reads, allowing for inference of base order in a genome. We reframe the recovery of haplotype sequences as a joint source-channel coding problem, encoding two messages - haplotypes and read memberships - for transmission over a channel with erasures and errors. The channel model captures key features of high-throughput sequencing. Focusing on the required number of reads for reliable haplotype reconstruction, we establish both necessary and sufficient conditions, presenting order-wise optimal bounds. Our results provide insights into the fundamental limits of haplotype assembly, shedding light on the minimum requirements for accurate reconstruction of haplotype sequences from short reads. Theoretical analysis and bounds are derived to inform the design of efficient haplotype assembly algorithms.

This study examines systematic errors in Lüscher's formulation of dynamical Wilson quarks and its variants. We analyze the weak and strong coupling limits and small configurations at finite β. Our results confirm an optimal window in the cutoff parameter and exponential error decrease with boson families. A non-Hermitian variant improves approximation and allows odd flavors. A simple Metropolis test is proposed, making the algorithm exact and providing a more accurate and efficient solution.

This study presents a comprehensive numerical investigation of magnetic reconnection in relativistic collisionless electron-ion plasmas, a process pivotal in various astrophysical systems including black hole accretion flows and relativistic jets. While prior research has predominantly focused on reconnection in pair plasmas, our work delves into the dynamics of electron-ion plasma reconnection, exploring its dependence on ambient ion magnetization. Utilizing particle-in-cell simulations, we examine the reconnection rate, plasma flows, field structures, energy partitioning between electrons and ions, and nonthermal particle acceleration across a broad range of magnetizations, from semi-relativistic to fully relativistic regimes. Our results indicate a consistent reconnection rate of approximately 0.1 of the Alfvénic rate, irrespective of the magnetization level. Notably, we find that electrons can form moderately relativistic outflows even in semi-relativistic conditions, and the energy partitioning between electrons and ions varies significantly with magnetization, with electrons receiving a smaller fraction of the energy in the semi-relativistic regime. Furthermore, our simulations demonstrate efficient nonthermal electron acceleration with a power-law index dependent on the ambient ion magnetization. These findings have significant implications for understanding the dynamics of black hole systems and provide support for semi-relativistic reconnection models as a mechanism for powering nonthermal emission in blazar jets, offering insights into the observed spectral indices in these astrophysical contexts.

This study delves into the intricate physics of disordered alloys, exemplified by the CeNi1-xCux system, which exhibits a complex interplay between the Kondo effect, spin glass state, and magnetic order. Building upon previous average descriptions, such as the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, a more localized theoretical framework has been proposed to describe the phase diagram of CeNi1-xCux. However, this model falls short in capturing the cluster-glass state, a phenomenon characterized by the onset of frustration and Kondo effect interplay. To address this limitation, we employ a Kondo lattice model with inter-cluster random Gaussian interactions, treated within the cluster mean-field theory for spin glasses. An exact diagonalization is performed within each cluster, incorporating inter-site ferromagnetic and intra-site Kondo interactions. Our results yield the cluster glass order parameters and Kondo correlation function for varying cluster sizes, intra-cluster ferromagnetic coupling, and Kondo intra-site coupling. Notably, we find that an increase in Kondo coupling tends to suppress the cluster glass phase, providing valuable insights into the competition between the Kondo effect and cluster glass phase in disordered alloys. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex phase diagrams exhibited by these systems, shedding light on the underlying physics governing their behavior.

This study tackles the inverse problem of determining the mechanical Hamiltonian of a system given its energy spectrum and transition dipole moment matrix. We employ a polynomial-based approach to approximate the potential, facilitating the calculation of hyperpolarizability. Our results indicate that the largest achievable hyperpolarizabilities converge to a limit observed in previous optimization studies. However, we find that surpassing this limit requires non-physical potentials. Furthermore, we explore the use of half-potentials with positive exponents, which yield a simple, one-parameter potential that spans a wide range of intrinsic hyperpolarizability values. Notably, the limiting case of a vanishing exponent produces the maximum intrinsic hyperpolarizability, providing valuable insights into the optimization of hyperpolarizability in quantum systems. Our findings contribute to the understanding of the inverse problem and its implications for hyperpolarizability optimization.

We investigate K* polarization states in exclusive 4-body B meson decay in the low dilepton mass region using QCD factorization. The behavior of CP-conserving transverse and longitudinal observables is analyzed at large recoil energy, considering right-handed currents. Our study focuses on the construction and examination of these observables, providing insights into their properties and implications for B meson decay processes, shedding light on the underlying dynamics and potential new physics contributions.

This article addresses the problem of constructing optimized measurements to distinguish between a collection of possibly non-orthogonal quantum states. We focus on pure states and seek a positive operator-valued measure (POVM) consisting of rank-one operators with measurement vectors closest in squared norm to the given states. Our approach is compared to previous measurements, including the square-root measurement (SRM). We provide a new characterization of the SRM and prove its optimality in a least-squares sense. Furthermore, for geometrically uniform state sets, we demonstrate that the SRM minimizes the probability of detection error, generalizing a result by Ban et al. Our findings offer insights into the optimization of quantum state discrimination measurements, with potential applications in quantum information processing and quantum communication systems, enhancing their efficiency and accuracy.

This article explores two distinct issues: the establishment of physical laws through successive approximations, and the origins of the observed metric from a short-distance fractal structure. We argue for a formulation-driven approach, rather than discovery of pre-existing laws. A brief review of the fractal structure's implications on metric symmetry is also provided, highlighting the emergence of symmetry through re-summations, offering a novel perspective on the fundamental nature of physical laws and spatial metrics, with potential implications for our understanding of the physical world and its underlying principles and structures slowly unfolding.

This article presents a stochastic theory of urban growth, leveraging the recently available city data to explain observed power-law dependencies between population size and various socio-economic indicators. Our theory accounts for the scaling patterns in US and OECD empirical data, including daily miles driven, road network length, traffic delay, gasoline consumption, and emissions. Notably, we identify a single parameter that characterizes the sensitivity to congestion, governing these relationships. Our findings indicate that congestion-related diseconomies scale superlinearly with population size, suggesting that cities relying heavily on traffic-sensitive transportation modes are unsustainable. The results have significant implications for urban planning, highlighting the need for polycentric cities to adopt congestion-mitigating strategies to ensure long-term sustainability. By quantifying the impact of congestion on urban growth, our research provides valuable insights for policymakers and urban planners seeking to create more efficient and sustainable cities.

This article presents a theoretical framework for understanding the dynamics of a walker formed by a bouncing drop and its accompanying wave. By decomposing the time scale into successive effects, we reveal the underlying mechanisms driving the walker's behavior. At short time scales, the walker's propulsion is generated, while intermediate scales give rise to pivotal structures with angular momentum. In confined spaces, these pivots self-organize into a global structure at larger memory scales. We apply this framework to a system with an external harmonic potential, shedding light on the emergence of macroscopic spatial organization. Our results provide insight into the experimental findings of Perrard et al. (2014), demonstrating the effectiveness of our theoretical approach in explaining the complex behavior of walking droplets. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricate dynamics governing these systems.

This paper presents a novel approach to checking the admissibility of quasiequations in finitely generated quasivarieties. While traditional methods involve verifying validity in a finite free algebra, this approach is often computationally infeasible due to the large size of free algebras. To address this, we introduce algorithms that generate a minimal set of algebras, with respect to a multiset well-ordering, to determine admissibility. Our method enables the checking of structural completeness and almost structural completeness, where validity and admissibility coincide. We illustrate the algorithms using well-known finitely generated quasivarieties and extend them to handle admissibility of rules in finite-valued logics. The proposed approach provides a more efficient and practical solution for determining admissibility in finitely generated quasivarieties, making it a valuable tool for researchers in the field of algebraic logic.

This study examines Totally Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Processes (TASEP) with particles occupying multiple lattice sites and a local inhomogeneity. Using approximate theory and Monte Carlo simulations, steady-state phase diagrams, currents, and bulk densities are calculated. Results show that the phase diagram with a local inhomogeneity resembles homogeneous models, but with shifted phase boundaries. The complex dynamics are discussed using domain-wall theory, providing insight into non-equilibrium processes relevant to biological and chemical phenomena. The findings have implications for understanding driven lattice systems and their applications in various fields, highlighting the importance of local inhomogeneities.

This study aims to enhance our understanding of the electronic structure of actinide dioxides by constructing a tight-binding model, denoted as the @xmath2-@xmath3 model, incorporating actinide @xmath0 and oxygen @xmath1 electrons. Following diagonalization, the eigenenergies within the first Brillouin zone are compared to relativistic band-structure calculations. The findings highlight the crucial role of @xmath2-@xmath3 hybridization in determining the electronic structure of actinide dioxides. Notably, the energy levels of @xmath4 and @xmath5 states, influenced by crystalline electric field potentials, are dependent on @xmath2-@xmath3 hybridization. The conditions for @xmath2-@xmath3 hybridization that yield an electronic structure consistent with the local crystalline electric field state are clarified. Furthermore, the relationship between the absolute values of Slater-Koster integrals for @xmath2-@xmath3 hybridization and the emergence of octupole ordering in NpO@xmath6 is discussed, providing insights into the complex electronic properties of actinide dioxides.

This study presents an approximate analytical solution to the Manning-Rosen potential using the Nikiforov-Uvarov method. By employing a suitable approximation for the centrifugal term, we derive the energy spectrum and normalized wave functions in terms of Jacobi polynomials. The accuracy of our results is verified through numerical calculations of eigenvalues for various quantum numbers and potential parameters. Our findings show good agreement with existing methods, particularly for short-range potentials and small quantum numbers. Additionally, we explore two special cases: the s-wave scenario and the Hulthén potential case. This research contributes to the understanding of bound states in the Manning-Rosen potential, demonstrating the efficacy of the Nikiforov-Uvarov method in solving the Schrödinger equation for this potential. The results have implications for quantum mechanics and potential applications in physics.

This article introduces redundant random matrix ensembles, characterized by binary matrices with linearly dependent rows, and examines their stopping set weight distributions. The presence of redundant rows significantly reduces the number of small-sized stopping sets. We establish upper and lower bounds on the average stopping set weight distribution for these ensembles. These bounds reveal a trade-off between the number of redundant rows, which affects decoding complexity, and the critical exponent of the asymptotic growth rate of stopping set weight distribution, influencing decoding performance. Notably, our analysis shows that, under certain conditions, dense matrices with linearly dependent rows can outperform regular LDPC matrices with comparable parameters, particularly in the regime of small erasure probability. This finding has implications for the design of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, highlighting the potential benefits of redundant random ensembles in improving decoding performance.

Title: Solar Filament Support in Magnetic Dips: A Nonlinear Force-Free Field Extrapolation Abstract: Solar filaments are often believed to be supported by magnetic dips, particularly those associated with magnetic flux ropes (FRs). This study presents a nonlinear force-free field (NLFFF) extrapolation of a coronal magnetic FR that supports a large-scale intermediate filament between an active region and a weak polarity region. Notably, this is the first instance where NLFFF extrapolations have successfully captured a large-scale filament in a weak-field region, characterized by a fragmented polarity inversion line and low transverse field values. The filament's location, far from sunspots and strong magnetic shear, poses a significant challenge to traditional extrapolation methods. However, our CESE MHD NLFFF code demonstrates competence in reproducing the magnetic dips of the extrapolated FR, which accurately match observations of the filament and its barbs. The results provide strong evidence for the FR-dip model of filaments, suggesting that the filament's stability can be attributed to the weak twisting and strong confinement of the FR by overlying closed arcades. This study expands our understanding of solar filament support and highlights the capabilities of advanced NLFFF extrapolation techniques in modeling complex coronal magnetic structures.

This study investigates the relationship between active galactic nuclei (AGN) luminosity and the fraction of host galaxies undergoing major mergers across a wide range of bolometric luminosities (10^40-10^48 erg/s) and redshifts (0-6). We find a strong, redshift-independent correlation between AGN luminosity and the fraction of host galaxies experiencing major mergers. Notably, only the most luminous AGN phases are associated with major mergers, while less luminous AGN appear to be driven by secular processes. By combining this trend with AGN luminosity functions, we estimate that approximately 75% of black hole mass growth is associated with major mergers, although these events account for only 10% of AGN by number. Our results suggest that major mergers are required to reach the highest AGN luminosities, where the most massive black holes accreted the bulk of their mass. The luminosity dependence of AGN triggered by major mergers can explain the observed scatter in the M-σ relation for elliptical galaxies. Furthermore, the lack of redshift dependence in the L_bol-M_bh relation implies that the decline in AGN and star formation activity with decreasing redshift, known as downsizing, is driven by a decrease in major merger frequency and gas availability at lower redshifts. These findings provide new insights into the role of major mergers in black hole growth and galaxy evolution.

This study investigates the causal effect of online social networking technologies on information dissemination. A large-scale field experiment was conducted, randomizing exposure to social signals about friends' information sharing among 253 million subjects. Results show that exposure to these signals significantly increases the likelihood and speed of information propagation. Further analysis reveals that while strong ties are individually more influential, weak ties play a more dominant role in spreading novel information due to their abundance. This challenges the current understanding of the role of weak ties in online information diffusion. The findings have implications for our understanding of how social networks facilitate the dissemination of information and highlight the importance of considering the interplay between strong and weak ties in online social networks. The study's results provide insights into the mechanisms underlying online information diffusion, with potential applications in fields such as marketing, public health, and social media research.

This study demonstrates a proof of concept for reconstructing visual images from a user's mind using electroencephalography (EEG) and brain-computer interface (BCI) technology. Our approach employs rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) of polygon primitives, where relevant shapes and colors trigger attention-related EEG patterns. These patterns are classified using event-related potentials (ERPs) to identify target primitives, which are then accumulated to reconstruct the image. The results show an average classification accuracy of [insert accuracy], with [insert percentage] of images reconstructed completely and [insert percentage] of visual details captured on average. Notably, most misclassifications arose from user intention rather than BCI misinterpretation. This research highlights the potential of EEG-based image reconstruction and discusses open problems and alternative approaches for developing practical BCI applications. The findings contribute to the advancement of BCI technology and its potential applications in fields such as neuroscience, psychology, and human-computer interaction.

This article revisits a crucial result by Panagiotou and Stufler (arXiv:1502.07180v2) regarding the structure of uniform random Pólya trees. We employ a unified framework in analytic combinatorics to prove that a uniform random Pólya tree of size $n$ consists of a conditioned critical Galton-Watson tree and many small forests, with improved bounds on the size of these forests. Our approach yields a sharper estimate, demonstrating that with high probability, any attached forest is maximally of size $O(\log n)$. Furthermore, we provide a combinatorial interpretation of the rational weights of these forests and the defining substitution process in terms of automorphisms associated with a given Pólya tree. Finally, we derive the limit probability that a random node has an attached forest of a given size, offering new insights into the structure of random Pólya trees.

The discovery of Supernova (SN) 2002ap in M74 on January 29, 2002, presented a unique opportunity for intensive photometric and spectroscopic monitoring due to its proximity (10 Mpc) and spectroscopic similarity to "hypernovae" SN 1997ef and SN 1998bw, which are potentially associated with gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Our monitoring campaign, initiated shortly after its discovery, has yielded a comprehensive dataset spanning the first month of observations. Analysis of our photometric data allowed us to estimate the peak brightness magnitudes and dates, indicating that SN 2002ap reached its peak luminosity in the B band on February 7. By comparing SN 2002ap to SN 1998bw, we deduced a possible time frame for a GRB that could be associated with this event, suggesting that it may have occurred outside the period for which gamma-ray data have been thoroughly examined. The absolute magnitude at peak brightness (M_B = -17.4) reveals that SN 2002ap was significantly fainter than SN 1998bw and typical Type-Ia SNe but similar to SN 1997ef. Spectroscopic observations confirm the striking similarity between SN 2002ap and SNe 1998bw and 1997ef, with notable spectral evolution. To facilitate further research and stimulate theoretical modeling, our entire dataset is made publicly available. This study contributes to the understanding of SN 2002ap and its potential connection to GRBs, offering insights into the physics of these extraordinary events. The proximity of SN 2002ap makes it an invaluable case study, providing a unique chance to explore the characteristics of hypernovae and their possible association with gamma-ray bursts in unprecedented detail.

This article presents a comprehensive overview of the application of field-theoretic methods and the dynamic renormalisation group (RG) to study universal scaling properties in systems exhibiting continuous phase transitions or generic scale invariance, both in and out of thermal equilibrium. The response functional field theory representation of nonlinear Langevin equations is introduced, and the RG is utilized to compute scaling exponents for various universality classes governing critical dynamics near second-order phase transitions in equilibrium. The impact of mode-coupling terms, quenching, and detailed balance constraints is also examined. Furthermore, the formalism is extended to nonequilibrium systems, such as driven diffusive lattice gases. The article also explores the mapping of master equations for stochastic particle reaction processes onto field theory actions, enabling the analysis of diffusion-limited annihilation reactions and continuous transitions to absorbing states, characterized by power laws of critical directed percolation. Key universality classes are highlighted, and open issues are identified, providing a foundation for future research in this field. By bridging equilibrium and nonequilibrium systems, this work demonstrates the versatility and potential of field-theoretic methods and the RG in understanding complex scaling phenomena.

We present an efficient method for deriving surface states in photonic superlattices. By analyzing infinite bichromatic superlattices, we obtain a subset of in-gap states as superpositions of unstable Bloch waves. These states are utilized to construct stable surface states near various interfaces. Our analytical approach explores the parametric dependence of these surface states, providing an exact demonstration of their existence. This research offers valuable insights into surface states in photonic superlattices and has implications for understanding surface states in other lattice systems, contributing to the advancement of photonic crystal research and applications.

This study presents first-principles calculations of ballistic spin injection in Fe/GaAs and Fe/ZnSe junctions with varying orientations. The results show that symmetry mismatch between Fe minority-spin states and semiconductor conduction states leads to high spin polarization in (001) interfaces. In contrast, (111) and (110) interfaces exhibit lower spin injection efficiencies due to the absence of symmetry mismatch. The presence of interface states and Schottky barriers also reduces current spin polarization. Additionally, increasing bias is found to impact spin injection efficiency. These findings provide insight into the factors influencing spin injection in ferromagnet/semiconductor junctions, informing the design of spin-based devices.

This study examines the incidence of residential burglaries in the 10 most populous cities in North Carolina over a defined period. We highlight challenges in estimating and comparing local crime rates due to reliance on police-reported data, which only captures known crimes. To address this limitation, our analysis combines police-based residential burglary counts with data from the National Crime Victimization Survey. This integrated approach yields interval estimates of residential burglary incidence at the local level. Our findings underscore the fragility of between-city and over-time comparisons of crime rates, which are often cited in public discussions of crime patterns. By providing more accurate estimates, this research aims to inform a more nuanced understanding of crime trends and patterns in North Carolina's urban areas, ultimately contributing to more effective crime prevention and policy strategies. Our results have implications for criminology and urban planning.

The detection of gravitational waves from the inspiral and merger of stellar-mass compact objects is a promising area of research. With the advanced LIGO and Virgo detectors, scientists can detect inspiral signals from more massive systems and at earlier times, allowing for the possibility of detection prior to coalescence. This work investigates the prospects of detecting inspiral signals before the final coalescence of two neutron stars and deriving a suitable sky area for source locations. Using Monte Carlo techniques, we estimate the accuracy of sky localization through networks of ground-based interferometers, including the Japanese KAGRA detector. Our results show that a significant fraction of the signal is accumulated in the last 10 seconds prior to coalescence, emphasizing the importance of bandwidth and timing accuracy in the final moments. The addition of KAGRA to the detector network enhances the feasibility of detection and triangulation before coalescence, enabling more precise sky localization and paving the way for multimessenger astronomy. By analyzing the detectability of inspiral signals prior to coalescence, this study contributes to the development of strategies for gravitational wave astronomy and the potential for early warning systems.

The determination of neutron star mass relies heavily on the nuclear density dependencies of neutrons and hyperons, particularly the @xmath0 and @xmath1 hyperons. The presence of hyperons, arising from strong attractions, significantly alters the stiffness of the equation of state (EOS) in iso-spin asymmetric dense nuclear matter. To investigate the properties of nucleons, @xmath0, and @xmath1 hyperons up to slightly above saturation nuclear matter density, in-medium spectral sum rules have been analyzed using the linear density approximation for condensates. A general interpolating field for each baryon has been constructed, allowing for optimal parameter choices that ensure stability against variations and consistency with known phenomenology. Notably, the results indicate that Ioffe's choice is not suitable for the @xmath1 hyperon sum rules, and instead, emphasizing the up and down quark combined into the scalar diquark structure @xmath2 is necessary for stable sum rules. The analysis reveals that quasi-@xmath0 and -@xmath1 hyperon energies are consistently higher than quasineutron energies in the region @xmath3, where the linear density approximation is expected to be reliable. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the EOS and the composition of neutron stars, highlighting the importance of accurately accounting for hyperon properties in dense nuclear matter.

Here is an abstract of approximately 265 words based on the provided title and content: We present a comprehensive study of dust properties in the nearby starburst galaxy M82 using near ultraviolet and optical photometry. By combining imaging data from the Swift/UVOT instrument and optical data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we derive the extinction curve and quantify the strength of the NUV 2175 feature out to projected galactocentric distances of 4 kpc. Our analysis reveals a systematic trend in dust properties with galactocentric distance, with both the extinction curve parameter (R_V) and the strength of the NUV 2175 feature (A_2175) correlating with distance. Our results confirm that the dust in M82 is better fit by a Milky Way standard extinction curve, rather than a Calzetti law. We also find a strong correlation between R_V and A_2175, suggesting a distribution with larger dust grain sizes in regions with higher R_V. Notably, our data pre-date the SN 2014J event, allowing us to probe the properties of the interstellar medium before the supernova. We find significant differences in R_V values around the position of the supernova compared to recent post-SN 2014J measurements, suggesting a change in dust properties after the event. This could be due to the disruption of large grains or the contribution of an intrinsic circumstellar component. Our study provides new insights into the dust properties of M82 and highlights the importance of considering the impact of supernovae on the interstellar medium. These findings have implications for our understanding of dust evolution and the properties of starburst galaxies.

This article reviews the spatially conformally flat approximation (CFA) for determining initial conditions in binary neutron star simulations using the full Einstein equations. We assess the stability of the CFA in general relativistic hydrodynamics by numerically evolving quasi-circular orbits. Our results demonstrate the viability of the CFA for orbiting neutron stars, highlighting the dependence of initial conditions on the equation of state. We also explore the impact of these initial conditions on the emergent gravitational wave frequency as the stars approach the innermost stable circular orbit. The CFA is shown to be a reliable method for approximating binary neutron star initial conditions, with implications for numerical relativity and gravitational wave astronomy. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of binary neutron star mergers and their role in astrophysical phenomena.

This article investigates the spectral radius of a high-dimensional square matrix with independent and identically distributed entries of zero mean and unit variance. We conjecture that the spectral radius converges to the square root of the dimension, regardless of the existence of a finite fourth moment. Under the assumption of symmetric distribution with a finite moment of order larger than two, we prove this conjecture. Our approach combines the method of moments with a novel truncation technique for cycle weights, providing new insights into the circular law. The results contribute to the understanding of random matrix theory, with potential implications for related fields.

This study presents numerical investigations of quantum walks on 60 and related graphene structures, focusing on their transport properties. By examining the behavior of quantum walks on honeycomb lattices and derived nanotube structures, we uncover insights into the mechanisms underlying their unusual electrical conductivity. Our results show that nanotube structures exhibit significantly enhanced transport efficiency compared to equivalent-sized cycles, provided their symmetry is respected. Notably, we observe faster transport on zig-zag nanotubes than on armchair nanotubes, contrary to expectations based on the metallic and semiconducting properties of the actual materials. This unexpected finding highlights the potential of quantum walks as a tool for understanding the fundamental principles governing transport in graphene-based systems. Our research contributes to the growing body of knowledge on quantum walks and their applications, with implications for the development of novel materials and technologies exploiting the unique properties of graphene and its derivatives.

We present exact results at next-to-leading order in renormalization-group improved perturbation theory for Wilson coefficients in the heavy-quark expansion of heavy-light current operators. By completing the two-loop anomalous dimension matrix calculation, we obtain precise values for these coefficients at order 1/m_Q. Our findings are crucial for determining V_cb using exclusive and inclusive semileptonic B decays, and for computing the decay constant f_B based on a heavy-quark expansion. These results contribute significantly to the theoretical framework underlying heavy-flavor physics, enabling more accurate predictions and extractions of fundamental parameters. This work enhances our understanding of heavy-light current operators and their role in precision tests of the Standard Model.

We establish the uniqueness of a universal symmetric solution to the Kashiwara-Vergne conjecture up to order one. This result implies that existing solutions for quadratic Lie algebras are not universal, as demonstrated in the appendix. Keywords: Campbell-Hausdorff series, free Lie algebras, differential of the exponential map, Bernoulli numbers.

This study examines cosmological models with accelerated stationary global attractors, demonstrating their asymptotic reduction to a dark energy field with an exponential potential coupled to perfect fluid dark matter. The abundance of dark components reaches a stationary value, resolving the coincidence problem. A vanishing baryon coupling, necessary for local gravity experiments, leads to an intermediate baryon-dominated era. We analyze these models, finding that they cannot produce a microwave background consistent with observations while accommodating standard nucleosynthesis. Our results suggest that only time-dependent coupling or equation of state models can provide a realistic cosmology, highlighting the limitations of stationary models in explaining observed phenomena.

We present novel single-epoch black hole mass estimators based on the broad emission line, utilizing an updated sample of reverberation-mapped AGNs and high-quality UV spectra. Through multi-component spectral fitting analysis, we measure line widths and continuum luminosity to calibrate the mass estimators. Comparison with reverberation-based masses yields new estimators with best-fit relationships. These new estimators exhibit significant mass-dependent systematic differences compared to commonly used literature estimators.
