Applying our recipe to the Sloan Digital Sky Survey QSO catalog, we find that the black hole mass of high-redshift QSOS decreases by an average of 0.3 dex. Our results provide a refined understanding of black hole mass estimation, with implications for the study of high-redshift quasars and the evolution of supermassive black holes. This work contributes to the ongoing effort to improve black hole mass estimation methods.

This study generalizes Fromm and Hill's method for evaluating four-particle integrals to include complex exponential parameters. A novel numerical branch tracking procedure is developed, enabling high-precision variational solutions to the Coulomb four-body problem using exponential-trigonometric functions, with numerical results showcasing the method's efficiency and versatility.

This study presents X-ray observations of the Shapley Supercluster's core, utilizing data from the ROSAT PSPC detector and All-Sky Survey. The observed region encompasses clusters A3562, A3558, and A3556, revealing clear evidence of X-ray emission connecting these clusters. This confirms the existence of a filamentary structure embedding the three clusters. Additional faint emission is detected west of A3556. The filamentary X-ray emission extends up to at least 10 Mpc, with a total luminosity of 1.5 x 10^43 erg/s in the 0.1-2.4 keV energy band. These findings provide insight into the large-scale structure of the Shapley Supercluster, highlighting the complex interconnections between its central clusters. The observed X-ray emission underscores the supercluster's dynamic and evolving nature.

This study examines the scalar and quark number susceptibilities near potential critical end points in the hadronic phase diagram using the two-flavor quark-meson model and proper-time renormalization group approach. The quark-mass dependence of critical end points is discussed, and the critical behavior of in-medium meson masses and quark number density is calculated. Critical exponents are determined to identify universality classes. A comparison with mean-field approximation results highlights the impact of fluctuations. Notably, the inclusion of fluctuations compresses the region of enhanced susceptibilities around the critical end point, providing a more nuanced understanding of the phase diagram's structure and the role of fluctuations in shaping its properties.

This paper examines morphisms from a smooth algebraic curve to the projective line that do not factor through a given triple covering. We generalize classical results on base-point-free pencils to triple covers of arbitrary smooth irrational curves, investigating the existence of such morphisms and providing new insights into algebraic curve theory.

This study explores the renormalization-group evolution of the lepton flavor mixing matrix from the seesaw scale to the electroweak scale. We demonstrate that the Dirac phase can be radiatively generated in the minimal supersymmetric standard model when neutrino masses are nearly degenerate. Similarly, Majorana phases can also be generated through radiative corrections. The one-loop renormalization-group equations for the Jarlskog invariant and off-diagonal asymmetries are derived and numerically illustrated, showcasing their running behaviors. Our findings highlight the entanglement of CP-violating phases in the lepton flavor mixing matrix, providing insights into the evolution of neutrino masses and mixing parameters from high to low energy scales.

This study examines the equilibrium properties of a flexible homopolymer model, where consecutive monomers are represented as tangent hard spheres and non-consecutive monomers interact via a square-well potential. Using replica exchange canonical simulations and micro-canonical Wang-Landau techniques, we analyze relatively short chains and compare the results. Our investigations reproduce the phase diagram of longer chains at a reduced scale and computational effort. This approach enables the refinement of the model and incorporation of specificities, such as those found in protein folding, allowing for more accurate representations of complex biological systems and phenomena.

This article proposes a novel phase-locking configuration for the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) that simplifies its mode of operation while maintaining compatibility with the baseline approach. The proposed scheme generates a single Sagnac signal that is inherently insensitive to laser frequency noise, optical bench motion, and clock noise, without requiring time shifting of data or absolute arm length knowledge. Notably, this configuration eliminates the need for clock synchronization and phase information exchange between spacecraft, as all measurements are made at one spacecraft. However, the orbital motion of the LISA constellation introduces a 14 km path length difference between counter-propagating beams, which would consume the entire optical path noise budget if the current laser frequency stability of 30 Hz/√Hz is used. To achieve full-sensitivity LISA operation in Sagnac mode, significant improvement in laser frequency stability or an additional level of time-delay processing is necessary. The article presents new time-delayed combinations of phase measurements that can mitigate laser frequency noise, providing a potential solution for future LISA operations. The proposed configuration offers a simpler and more robust mode of operation, with potential implications for the development of future gravitational wave detectors.

This study examines the production of φ and ω mesons in nuclear collisions at beam energies between 0.8 and 2.0 GeV within a model assuming equilibrium at hadrochemical and thermal freeze-out. The relative particle yields indicate temperatures of 56-90 MeV and baryon chemical potentials of 780-675 MeV at chemical freeze-out. The midrapidity spectra of φ and ω mesons are consistent with the obtained temperatures when considering transverse expansion. Notably, the deduced freeze-out parameters fall below the phase boundary between a hadron gas and a quark-gluon plasma, contrasting with results from similar analyses of AGS and SPS data, providing new insights into the properties of nuclear matter at these energies.

This study presents an in-depth analysis of the nearby Abell 576 cluster of galaxies, extending beyond the virial radius and into the infall region. By utilizing 1057 redshifts, we employ the infall pattern in redshift space to determine the mass profile of Abell 576, reaching a radius of approximately 6 megaparsecs. Notably, this mass estimation technique does not rely on assumptions regarding the cluster's equilibrium state. Our results reveal that within 2 megaparsecs, the derived mass profile exceeds that obtained from X-ray observations by a factor of 2.5. However, at 4 megaparsecs, the mass profile aligns with virial mass estimates. The observed mass profile is consistent with Navarro, Frenk, & White (1997) or Hernquist (1990) profiles, but inconsistent with an isothermal sphere. Furthermore, R-band images of a 2-degree region centered on the cluster enable an independent determination of the cluster light profile. We calculate the integrated mass-to-light ratio as a function of cluster radius, finding a smooth decrease from the core to 150 kiloparsecs at 6 megaparsecs. The differential mass-to-light profile decreases more steeply, yielding a value of 50 at 6 megaparsecs, in good agreement with individual galaxy mass-to-light ratios. Our findings have significant implications for the understanding of cluster mass profiles and the distribution of galaxies within them, suggesting that the behavior of mass-to-light ratios in Abell 576 may be representative of clusters in general.

This study examines the relationship between geometric entropy and the entropy of black holes. By tracing over degrees of freedom in a subset of space, the vacuum state transforms into a mixed density matrix with non-zero entropy. We demonstrate that the area law for geometric entropy follows from fundamental principles of quantum mechanics and relativity, leveraging the strong subadditive property of quantum entropy. Our approach generalizes previous results, which were limited to specific subsets and plagued by ultraviolet divergences. The findings provide new insights into the connection between geometric entropy and black hole entropy, with implications for our understanding of quantum gravity.

This study examines the domination polynomial of a simple graph, specifically the barbell graph. We demonstrate that for every order, the barbell graph is not domination polynomial unique, meaning there exists a non-isomorphic graph with the same domination polynomial. Our results show that the equivalence class of the barbell graph contains numerous graphs, including the complement of a book graph. Additionally, we identify multiple families of graphs within the equivalence class of the generalized barbell graph. These findings contribute to the understanding of domination polynomials and graph equivalence, shedding light on the complexity of graph structures. Our research provides new insights into the properties of domination polynomials and their applications in graph theory, with implications for further study in this area. The results have significant implications for graph theory and combinatorics.

This article introduces a novel algorithm for computing the complexity of a number, defined as the smallest number of ones required to express it using addition and multiplication. We also investigate the concept of stability, where a number is considered stable if it satisfies a specific condition for all inputs. Building upon previous work, we develop a method to calculate the complexity and demonstrate that the set of stable numbers is computable. Our approach involves analyzing the defect of a number, which enables efficient evaluation of complexities for powers of a given base. As a consequence, we verify a conjecture for specific cases, providing further evidence for its validity. The algorithm is implemented in Haskell, making it accessible for practical applications. This research contributes to the understanding of complexity and stability in numbers, with potential implications for various mathematical and computational fields. The findings and implementation presented in this article offer a foundation for future investigations into these concepts.

This review article explores the microscopic origin of heavy-fermion-like behavior in transition-metal compounds, including LiV2O4, Y(Sc)Mn2, and YMn2Zn20. Through our recent study utilizing muon spin rotation/relaxation, we reveal a common trend in the temperature dependence of the longitudinal spin relaxation rate in these compounds. Notably, the relaxation rate levels off to a constant value below a characteristic temperature, deviating from the Korringa relation predicted for normal metals. This deviation implies a linear dependence of the spin fluctuation rate on temperature, suggesting the development of heavy quasiparticles at lower temperatures. Our findings are consistent with the theory of spin correlation for intersecting Hubbard chains, which models the pyrochlore lattice. The results highlight the crucial role of specific bands that preserve their one-dimensional character at low energies due to geometrical frustration in the undistorted pyrochlore lattice. This insight provides a deeper understanding of the heavy-fermion-like behavior in these compounds, underscoring the significance of spin fluctuations and lattice geometry in determining their unique properties. Our study contributes to the ongoing efforts to elucidate the microscopic mechanisms governing the behavior of these complex materials.

This study employs a wavelet-based approach to investigate the chaotic dynamics of a one-dimensional model exhibiting a direct transition to spatiotemporal chaos. By projecting the model onto a Daubechies basis, we achieve a satisfactory separation of scales, as evidenced by the power spectrum analysis. Our results indicate that the dynamics in the spatiotemporally chaotic regime can be understood through localized dynamics in space and scale. Notably, we find predominantly Gaussian dynamics at most scales, including the most energetic ones. Furthermore, the removal of specific wavelet modes does not alter the system's dynamics, as characterized by the Lyapunov spectrum, demonstrating the robustness of our findings.

This article analyzes border collision bifurcations in 2-dimensional discontinuous maps using piecewise linear approximation near the discontinuity plane. Building on Feigin's work on piecewise smooth continuous maps, we derive conditions for period-1 and period-2 fixed points before and after bifurcations. A specific 2-dimensional discontinuous map example illustrates the method's application, providing insights into the dynamics of these systems and the border collision bifurcation phenomenon, shedding light on their complex behavior and stability.

This study examines the impact of a negative charge on the scattering of light by a dielectric particle with a strong transverse optical phonon resonance. The presence of surplus electrons in the particle alters its scattering behavior due to phonon-limited conductivity. Our results show a charge-dependent increase in extinction efficiency at low frequencies and a shift in the extinction resonance above the transverse optical phonon frequency. Additionally, a rapid variation in polarization angles is observed near this resonance. These charge-induced effects can be leveraged for non-invasive optical measurements of the particle's charge, offering a novel approach for characterizing charged particles in ionized gases.

We propose a theoretical model to describe the suppression of large @xmath0-pions in heavy ion collisions, which is based on the interaction of these pions with the dense medium created during the collision. This model is an extension of a previously introduced framework used to describe @xmath1 suppression, with the key assumption being that the interaction with the dense medium is the primary mechanism responsible for the suppression. Our model successfully reproduces both the @xmath0 and centrality dependence of the experimental data. Furthermore, we apply this model to deuteron-gold collisions and find that the effect of final state interactions with the dense medium is negligible. Encouragingly, the main features of the data are also well-reproduced at both mid and forward rapidities. The implications of our model are significant, as they suggest that the suppression of large @xmath0-pions can be understood within the context of interactions with the dense medium created in heavy ion collisions. Our results provide new insights into the dynamics of heavy ion collisions and highlight the importance of considering the role of the dense medium in modifying particle production. Overall, our model provides a coherent and comprehensive description of the suppression of large @xmath0-pions in heavy ion collisions.

This study examines the angular power spectra of polarized Galactic synchrotron emission across various frequencies (0.4-2.7 GHz) and Galactic latitudes, extending towards the North Galactic Pole. The analysis reveals that electric- and magnetic-parity polarization spectra exhibit slopes of approximately 1 in the Parkes and Effelsberg Galactic-plane surveys. However, significant local fluctuations are observed, particularly at 1.4 GHz in the Effelsberg survey. The polarization-insensitive spectrum is found to be steeper, with a slope of around 1.5. Multifrequency surveys indicate a flattening of spectra below 1 GHz, more pronounced for certain polarization modes. Notably, no evidence of extremely steep spectra is detected. The findings have implications for the detection of E-mode harmonics in the cosmic background radiation, suggesting that synchrotron emission will not significantly interfere with observations at 90 GHz, even at low Galactic latitudes, for a reionization optical depth of 0.08. These results contribute to our understanding of Galactic synchrotron emission and its potential impact on cosmological observations.

We present explicit BPS field configurations for a nonabelian monopole with a minimal't Hooft operator insertion, exploring SU(2) and SU(3) gauge groups. For SU(3), the't Hooft operator is completely screened by the monopole, whereas for SU(2), screening is impossible, yielding a distinct gauge symmetry enhancement near the operator.

This article proposes a non-subtractive method for Casimir energy renormalization, effective in the presence of logarithmically divergent terms. The approach is applicable even when energy levels are only numerically obtainable, without asymptotic behavior or analytical spectral equations. Numerical calculations using this method are compared to results from explicit divergence subtraction. The technique's efficacy is demonstrated, providing a reliable means of calculating Casimir energy in complex scenarios. The method's advantages and accuracy are highlighted through comparative analysis, offering a valuable tool for theoretical physics applications, particularly in Casimir energy calculations.

We examine a superfluid ultracold Fermi gas under spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field. Our calculations show the Fulde-Ferrell superfluid dominates at zero and finite temperatures. This novel phase is systematically analyzed, revealing its origin and properties in the presence of finite-momentum pairing, shedding light on Fermi gas behavior under spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field influences.

This study expands the application of classical acoustoelasticity to determine fourth-order elasticity constants by coupling small-amplitude elastic waves with small-but-finite pre-deformations. We present theoretical results for compressible weakly nonlinear elasticity, drawing connections to Bridgman's historical work on high-pressure physics. Our approach enables the non-destructive evaluation of fourth-order constants, including the determination of the elasticity constant of soft, incompressible, isotropic solids using infinitesimal waves. This advancement offers new insights into material behavior under large pre-tensions and high pressures, with implications for understanding the mechanical properties of complex materials. The methodology has potential applications in materials science and engineering.

This study introduces an observable-based notion of equilibration, applying it to realistic systems such as spin qubits in quantum dots. Utilizing distinguishability, general equilibration bounds are analytically derived and related to the standard deviation of observable fluctuations. The central spin model is employed to describe spin physics in quantum dots, with exact diagonalization used to analyze spin dynamics induced by hyperfine interaction. Notably, even a small number of nuclear spins in carbon or silicon-based quantum dots can significantly equilibrate the electron spin, providing insights into the equilibration process and its implications for quantum systems.

This article examines the robust Nash equilibrium (RNE) in a class of games pertinent to communication systems and networks, where user interactions are characterized by additive strategy functions. The impact of user strategies on one another is measured, but this measurement is susceptible to uncertainties stemming from feedback delays, estimation errors, and user mobility. To analyze the game's outcome under such uncertainties, we employ worst-case robust optimization theory. By leveraging finite-dimensional variational inequalities, we derive conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the RNE. We assess the effect of uncertainty on system performance using two key criteria: the difference in social utility at the RNE and the equilibrium without uncertainty, and the difference in user strategies at these equilibria. These criteria are evaluated for both unique and multiple Nash equilibria. A distributed algorithm based on the proximal response map is proposed to reach the RNE, with convergence conditions duly established. Our theoretical framework is validated through simulations of power control games in interference channels and Jackson networks, underscoring the importance of robust game theory in resource allocation and communication networks.

This article explores the concept of causal sets and their natural extensions, bringing together two distinct classes of random processes. The first class involves generating random natural extensions of a fixed causal set, while the second class entails creating a random causal set by iteratively adding new maximal elements. A key property of interest is order-invariance, where the likelihood of each possible order of generation is equal, conditioned on the causal set's structure. We develop a comprehensive framework for studying order-invariance, casting it as a property of probability measures on a specific space. Our primary contribution is a characterization of the extremal order-invariant measures, providing insight into the underlying structure of these processes. By examining the interplay between causal sets, natural extensions, and random processes, this research sheds light on the intricate relationships between these concepts and their potential applications. Theoretical results, including theorems, propositions, and corollaries, are presented to support our framework and main findings, offering a foundation for further exploration of order-invariance in causal sets and related domains.

This article reviews the recent null results from gravitational-wave detector searches, highlighting the valuable insights gained about celestial objects in our universe. Despite the absence of detected signals, these findings have marked the beginning of gravitational-wave astronomy. We discuss the key results and their implications, demonstrating that the era of gravitational-wave astronomy is already underway. Looking ahead, we predict the transformative impact of future signal detections on our understanding of astrophysics, and explore the potential discoveries that will reshape the field. By examining current results and future prospects, this article provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of gravitational-wave astronomy.

The unique properties of 2D materials, stemming from quantum confinement, have garnered significant attention in recent years. This study reveals that the interplay between quantum confinement and structural anisotropy in 2D black phosphorus gives rise to an electric-field-tunable Dirac cone. Through density functional theory calculations, we demonstrate that applying an electric field normal to a 2D black phosphorus thin film can induce an insulator-to-metal transition at a critical field strength. Further increasing the electric field can lead to the emergence of a Dirac cone, provided the film is sufficiently thin. The position of the Dirac cone and the Dirac-Fermi velocities can be tuned by adjusting the electric field strength, with the latter exhibiting similarities in magnitude to those found in graphene. Our results show that the Dirac cone arises from an anisotropic interaction term between spatially separated frontier orbitals, which becomes negligible in thicker films. Additionally, we investigate the effects of spin-orbit coupling, which can gap out the Dirac cone at certain electric fields, but ultimately leads to a topological-insulator-to-Dirac-semi-metal transition at higher field strengths. These findings have significant implications for the development of tunable 2D electronic devices.

This article explores the relationship between discrete eigenvalues of the Schrödinger Hamiltonian and the coupling parameter using envelope theory. A functional sequence is generated to reconstruct a potential from its spectral data, starting with a seed potential. The method is demonstrated analytically for power-law and log cases, where inversion is complete in two steps. For other cases, numerical convergence is observed. The inversion method is applied to the Hulthén potential and singular potentials with specific shapes. Furthermore, for a class of attractive central potentials, it is proven that the ground-state energy curve uniquely determines the potential. This study provides a novel approach to inverting spectral data and reconstructing potentials, with implications for quantum mechanics and potential applications in physics and engineering. The results are supported by numerical examples and theoretical proofs, showcasing the efficacy of the proposed method.

This article explores the possibility of achieving gauge coupling constant unification at the low TeV scale in four dimensions, without relying on the power-like renormalization group evolution in extra dimensions. The presence of extra particle states at intermediate scales, ranging from 100 GeV to 1 TeV, is shown to facilitate this unification. Explicit examples of such states are provided, which can be observed at future colliders and have significant implications for particle phenomenology. The challenges associated with low-scale grand unification and proton stability are also addressed. Our analysis demonstrates that TeV scale unification can be realized in four dimensions, offering an alternative to extra-dimensional scenarios. The potential discovery of these extra states at upcoming colliders could have a profound impact on our understanding of the universe, and this work highlights the importance of continued exploration in this area of particle physics research.

This paper explores energy-efficient power allocation for the uplink of a multi-cell massive MIMO system. A constrained Markov decision process framework is used to formulate the power allocation problem, considering varying QoS requirements for each user terminal. An offline solution leveraging value iteration and Q-learning algorithms is proposed to obtain the global optimum power allocation policy. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed policy closely approximates the ergodic optimal policy, ensuring efficient power allocation while meeting diverse QoS demands in multi-cell massive MIMO systems, thereby enhancing overall system performance and energy efficiency.

This article examines the Helmholtz equation in a half-space, presenting two methods to determine boundary impedance from the far-field pattern of a time-harmonic incident wave. A potential is introduced, allowing calculation of impedance via explicit formula or WKB approximation. Numerical examples demonstrate the approaches' efficiency, and the validity of the WKB approximation for obstacle impedance determination is discussed, providing insights into wave propagation and scattering in half-spaces with impedance boundaries, enhancing understanding of acoustic and electromagnetic phenomena.

This study investigates the magnetic properties of Navo@XMath0 using the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method. Calculations are performed for three distinct structures, revealing unique magnetic behaviors. At 100 K, the rhombohedral structure exhibits orbital splitting due to trigonal distortion. In contrast, the monoclinic structure at 91.5 K behaves as a frustrated spin lattice with anisotropic exchange interactions. However, at 20 K, lattice distortion driven by orbital ordering relieves magnetic frustration, leading to long-range magnetic ordering. Notably, the small magnetic moment arises from the compensation of orbital and spin moments, providing insight into the complex magnetic properties of Navo@XMath0. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the material's magnetic behavior.

This article presents recent findings on the electrocouplings of excited nucleon states, obtained through the analysis of exclusive meson electroproduction data off protons, measured using the CLAS detector at Jefferson Lab. These results provide valuable insights into the structure of excited nucleons and the non-perturbative strong interaction dynamics governing their formation. The upcoming experiments with the CLAS12 detector in the upgraded Hall-B at JLab will enable the extraction of electrocouplings for all prominent resonances at unprecedented distance scales and photon virtualities. This will shed light on fundamental open problems in the Standard Model, including the origin of hadron mass, quark-gluon confinement, and the emergence of excited nucleon state structure from the QCD Lagrangian. Furthermore, these studies will facilitate a search for hybrid baryons, novel states of hadron matter predicted by QCD. The expected outcomes will significantly advance our understanding of the strong interaction and the complex structure of hadrons, ultimately deepening our knowledge of the underlying dynamics of the Standard Model.

We report the detection of pulsations in the hot DQ white dwarf star SDSS J142625.71+0575218.3, a predicted variable based on theoretical calculations. Observations reveal significant power at 417.7s and its first harmonic at 208.8s, establishing it as a strong candidate for the first pulsating hot DQ white dwarf, or DQV. The folded pulse shape exhibits a unique profile, differing from other white dwarf variables but resembling the cataclysmic variable AM CVn. This similarity suggests the possibility of a carbon-transferring analog, raising intriguing questions about the star's nature. Our findings mark the discovery of a new class of object, offering insights into the properties and behavior of hot DQ white dwarfs and their potential relationships to other variable stars. Further study is warranted to elucidate the characteristics of this exciting new class of pulsating stars.

This study analyzes high-quality data from 149 galaxies within 10 megaparsecs, revealing no correlation between luminosity and peculiar velocity. The expected gravitational effects of bright galaxies and infall toward groups or the supergalactic plane are absent. These findings suggest that dark matter may not mirror luminous matter distribution or that peculiar velocities are not driven by mass fluctuations, highlighting the sensitivity of peculiar velocity studies to background models and challenging our understanding of galaxy dynamics and dark matter distribution.

This study explores wormhole solutions in Brans-Dicke theory, focusing on minimizing the usage of exotic matter. We obtain exact wormhole solutions where normal matter satisfies the null energy condition throughout the geometry. Instead, the effective stress-energy tensor, containing the scalar field, acts as exotic matter, sustaining the wormhole. By assuming a zero redshift function and a specific scalar field, we determine the stress-energy tensor components and shape function. The resulting solution is non-asymptotically flat, requiring a match to an exterior vacuum solution. Our findings demonstrate that the scalar field's role is crucial in supporting the wormhole geometry, highlighting the significance of alternative gravity theories in understanding exotic matter. This research contributes to the ongoing search for viable wormhole models, providing new insights into the interplay between gravity, matter, and exotic energy sources in these enigmatic spacetime structures. Further analysis is warranted to fully explore the implications.

This study numerically investigates the evolution of extended states in a two-dimensional electron gas with white noise randomness and a magnetic field using the Anderson model on square lattices. Focusing on the lowest Landau band, an "anti-levitation" scenario is established, where extended states shift below clean system Landau energies as disorder strength increases or magnetic field strength decreases. A critical magnetic field is identified, below which extended states cease to exist for strong enough disorder. A phase diagram is proposed, separating localized and delocalized states in the disorder-magnetic field plane, providing insight into the complex interplay between disorder and magnetic fields in two-dimensional systems.

This study presents a multi-wavelength analysis of the young cluster L988E, utilizing Spitzer images, near-infrared, and submillimeter data. The cluster's asymmetric structure is revealed, with the western region embedded in a molecular cloud and the eastern region situated on the cloud's edge. By combining these data with existing Hα emission data and a molecular gas emission map, we examine the distribution of young stars in relation to the cloud material. Our investigation focuses on the differences and similarities between the exposed and embedded regions of the cluster. Additionally, we compare star formation in L988E to that in more dense and luminous clusters within 1 kpc of the Sun, as part of a comprehensive study of young clusters. This research aims to provide insights into the star formation processes in low-luminosity clusters and their relationship to the surrounding molecular cloud.

Title: Investigating the Assembly of Galaxy Groups and Clusters using the Millennium Simulations Abstract: This study examines the formation and evolution of galaxy groups and clusters using the Millennium dark matter simulation and associated gas simulations, combined with semi-analytic galaxy catalogs. We focus on identifying observable signatures of early-formed groups, with a particular emphasis on the utility of magnitude gaps as indicators. Our analysis selects galaxy groups and clusters at redshift 0 with dark matter halo masses exceeding 10^13.5 M⊙ and traces their properties to the present day (z=0). Additional constraints are applied to ensure that the selected systems have X-ray luminosities above 10^42 erg s^-1 at z=0. We find that while a large magnitude gap between the two brightest galaxies in a group often suggests early mass assembly, it is not a definitive criterion. In fact, over 90% of fossil groups, defined by their magnitude gaps, lose this characteristic within 4 Gyr due to the accretion of other massive galaxies into their cores. Our results show that an alternative definition of fossil groups, based on a revised magnitude gap criterion, identifies 50% more early-formed systems that retain their fossil phase longer. However, the conventional definition performs slightly better at identifying early-formed groups at the high-mass end. Notably, both criteria fail to identify a majority of early-formed systems, highlighting the complexity of galaxy group evolution. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution, and demonstrate the need for continued refinement of observational and theoretical methods to study the assembly of galaxy groups and clusters.

This article explores the role of Fast Electron Beams (FEBs) in solar active phenomena, with a focus on their interaction with the ambient plasma and magnetic fields. Solar radio bursts, a key diagnostic tool, are influenced by the evolution of FEB energy spectra and velocity distributions as they propagate through the solar plasma. We investigate the effects of energy loss processes and pitch-angle scattering caused by magnetic field inhomogeneities on Electron Cyclotron Maser (ECM) emission, a primary mechanism for producing solar radio bursts. Our results show that the growth rates of ECM emission decrease with energy loss, but increase with magnetic mirror ratio and spectral steepness. Moreover, the evolution of FEBs significantly impacts the fastest growing mode, phase angle, and polarization sense of ECM emission. We find that different evolutionary processes of FEBs can generate distinct types of ECM emission, shedding light on the dynamic spectra of solar radio bursts. Our study provides new insights into the complex relationships between FEBs, solar plasma, and magnetic fields, and has important implications for understanding the mechanisms underlying solar radio bursts. The findings of this research contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of solar radio burst dynamics and the underlying physical processes.

We analyze multi-colour imaging and photometry of the field of Anomalous X-ray Pulsar AXP 1E 1841-045 using accurate Chandra coordinates. Multiple sources are detected within the error circle, but none can be confirmed as the infrared counterpart. The study reaches limiting magnitudes of J, H, and K bands with 95% confidence.

This article presents the results of a comprehensive photometric study of the central cluster of the W5 E region, focusing on the triggered star formation within and around bright-rimmed clouds (BRCs). Utilizing wide-field and deep photometric observations, we determined a distance of 2.1 kpc and a mean age of 2.3 Myr for the central cluster. The identification of young stellar objects (YSOs) was facilitated through near-infrared and mid-infrared observations, revealing an aligned distribution from the ionizing source to the BRCs. Notably, our findings confirm that YSOs located on or inside the rim are younger than those outside, suggesting a series of radiation-driven implosion processes occurred from the central ionizing source towards the periphery of the W5 E HII region. Contrary to previous studies, our results indicate that the age distributions of Class II and Class III sources are similar, challenging the conventional understanding of the evolution of classical T Tauri stars to weak-line T Tauri stars. Furthermore, the initial mass function of the central cluster region is characterized by a power-law distribution, with the cumulative mass functions revealing a higher proportion of low-mass YSOs in the cluster region and BRC NW compared to BRCs 13 and 14. These findings provide valuable insights into the star formation processes within the W5 E region, highlighting the importance of radiation-driven implosion in shaping the distribution of YSOs and the initial mass function of the central cluster. Overall, this study contributes to our understanding of the complex interplay between star formation, HII regions, and the surrounding interstellar medium.

This study examines the viability of exponential gravity in the metric formalism, utilizing the latest 23 Hubble parameter measurements to constrain the model. A joint analysis incorporating luminosity distances of type Ia supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, and cosmic microwave background shift parameters yields tight bounds on the model parameters. The evolution of the deceleration parameter and effective equations of state are investigated, revealing a transition redshift of approximately 0.77. Our results indicate that current observations cannot distinguish between the background dynamics of exponential gravity and ΛCDM models, suggesting that further data are needed to discriminate between these theories. The best-fit parameters are used to constrain the model, providing insights into the cosmological implications of exponential gravity. These findings contribute to the ongoing effort to understand the nature of gravity and the evolution of the universe.

The Kepler satellite has facilitated unprecedented asteroseismic measurements of interior rotation in red giant branch (RGB) stars and those on the helium burning clump. Notably, rotation rates of approximately 100 days for helium degenerate cores on the RGB and 30 days for helium burning cores in clump stars have been inferred. To investigate these findings, we utilized the MESA code to generate state-of-the-art stellar evolution models of low-mass rotating stars, incorporating transport of angular momentum due to rotationally induced instabilities and magnetic fields. Our models, however, consistently overpredict core rotation rates, suggesting an unmodeled angular momentum transport process operates on the early RGB. In contrast, later evolution from the helium burning clump to the cooling white dwarf phase appears to occur at nearly constant core angular momentum. To further elucidate this discrepancy, we applied the ADIPLS adiabatic pulsation code to the Kepler asteroseismic target KIC8366239, explicitly highlighting the shortfall in our current understanding of angular momentum transport in low-mass stars. These findings underscore the need for further refinement of stellar evolution models to accurately capture the complex dynamics governing interior rotation in red giants.

This study examines the efficacy of utilizing photometric redshifts to investigate the evolution of both the global galaxy luminosity function (LF) and the LFs of distinct galaxy types. A comparative analysis is conducted between the LFs derived from photometric redshifts of the CFHT Legacy Survey (CFHTLS) D1 field and those obtained from the spectroscopic survey VIMOS VLT Deep Survey (VVDS), which comprises approximately 4800 galaxies. The results indicate a remarkable agreement between the LFs obtained using photometric and spectroscopic redshifts for galaxies with z ≤ 1, within the considered magnitude interval. This concordance enabled the utilization of all four deep fields of the CFHTLS, encompassing approximately 386,000 galaxies, to compute the combined LF and estimate parameter errors based on field-to-field variations. The Schechter function fits reveal a fading of the characteristic absolute magnitude (M*) by approximately 0.7 mag from z = 0.5 to z = 1, accompanied by an increase in the characteristic density (φ*) by a factor of approximately 2.5 over the same redshift interval. Furthermore, the sample is divided into galaxy types based on template fitting program classifications, yielding distinct evolutionary patterns for each type. These findings suggest that galaxy evolution is a complex interplay of merging, star formation quenching, and mass assembly. The results are consistent with those obtained from spectroscopic surveys, such as VVDS, DEEP2, and zCOSMOS, validating the use of photometric redshifts for studying galaxy evolution. The implications of this study are significant, as future large-scale imaging surveys will enable precise measurements of LF evolution and its dependence on morphology and color, ultimately constraining the mechanisms driving galaxy evolution.

This article examines the complex phenomenon of dynamical mass loss from old globular star clusters in the galaxy, considering both observational and theoretical perspectives. Observationally, evidence of mass loss is manifest in tidal tails, extratidal extensions, kinematic effects, alterations to the mass function, and changes in statistical properties of surviving clusters. Theoretically, even isolated clusters pose unresolved issues. A steady tide imposes a tidal boundary and lowers the escape energy, while induced mass loss introduces complexities, including the ambiguous definition of an "escaper." Relaxation-driven mass loss, as modeled in N-body simulations, exhibits a non-linear relationship with relaxation time due to prolonged escape timescales for stars with energies exceeding the escape threshold. The interplay between relaxation and tidal heating in unsteady tides remains poorly understood, with unclear dominance patterns under varying circumstances. This study aims to elucidate the intricacies of dynamical mass loss, bridging the gap between observational signatures and theoretical frameworks to advance our understanding of globular cluster evolution and survival.

This article presents a novel approach to constructing embedded Weighted Essentially Non-Oscillatory (WENO) methods, which leverage all adjacent smooth substencils to achieve desirable interpolation. Unlike conventional WENO schemes, which underutilize this potential near large gradients or discontinuities, our embedded methods maximize this possibility. We develop embedded versions of existing WENO schemes, including those of Jiang and Shu, and the WENO-Z scheme of Borges et al. Our approach yields improved spectral properties and higher convergence orders, without incurring additional computational costs. Numerical examples demonstrate the superiority of our embedded methods over their standard counterparts, making them a valuable tool for solving hyperbolic conservation laws and other nonlinear interpolation problems.

This study re-examines the structural phase transition in GeTe using high-resolution neutron powder diffraction. The rhombohedral-to-cubic ferroelectric phase transition was investigated over a wide temperature range (309-973 K). Notably, an anomalous volume contraction of 0.6% was observed at the phase transition. To elucidate this phenomenon, phonon calculations based on density functional theory were performed. The results provide insight into the phase transition and associated volume decrease in GeTe. A comparison with experimental data from single crystals of GeTe is also presented, offering a comprehensive understanding of the material's behavior. This research contributes to the growing interest in phase change materials, particularly GeTe and related compounds, and sheds light on their unique properties and potential applications. The findings have significant implications for the development of advanced materials and technologies.

This article examines the behavior of a saturated porous medium in the solid-fluid segregation regime under the influence of external pressure applied to the solid constituent. Our analysis reveals that the dynamics of the system are governed by either a Cahn-Hilliard or an Allen-Cahn-like equation, depending on the dissipation mechanism. Specifically, when dissipation is modeled via Darcy's law, the evolution equation resembles the Cahn-Hilliard equation, provided solid deformation and fluid density variations are small. In contrast, when only Stokes dissipation is considered, the system is described by an Allen-Cahn-like equation. We apply this theoretical framework to investigate interface formation within porous media, utilizing a recently developed model for solid-liquid segregation in consolidation. Our results provide a comprehensive description of interface development between fluid-rich and fluid-poor phases, shedding light on the complex interactions governing phase transformation in porous materials.

This study presents a novel detector system capable of discriminating between lower and higher energy neutrons, enabling the comparison of dd and dt reaction rates to determine plasma temperatures in the 10-200 eV range. The system exploits the production of a 4.44 MeV gamma-ray through inelastic scattering of energetic neutrons by carbon and the preferential attenuation of lower energy neutrons by hydrogenous materials. A figure of merit is defined to evaluate the system's performance, which is calculated over a broad range of parameters. The detector system can operate effectively even at low fluences (≈0 neutrons/sterad) and when time-of-flight methods fail, providing a reliable means for plasma temperature inference from dt/dd neutron discrimination. Keywords: neutron energy discrimination, plasma temperature.

This study presents a revised numerical simulation of the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM), incorporating significant improvements to previous models. We explicitly account for galactic superwind feedback processes and non-equilibrium metal species, while increasing the mass and spatial dynamic ranges by factors of 8 and 2, respectively. Our results indicate that galactic superwinds substantially impact the WHIM, increasing its mass fraction by approximately 20% by heating warm gas near galaxies. The baryon fraction in the WHIM is found to be around 40%, slightly higher than previous estimates. The gas density of the WHIM peaks at approximately 10 times the mean density, spanning a range from underdense to overdense regions. Furthermore, our simulations yield a median metallicity of 0.2 for oxygen, with 50% and 90% intervals of (0.04, 0.38) and (0.002, 0.83), respectively. These findings provide new insights into the evolution and properties of the WHIM, supporting recent observational evidence and refining our understanding of the intergalactic medium's role in the cosmic landscape. Our improved simulations offer a more accurate representation of the WHIM's dynamics and composition, shedding light on the complex interactions between galaxies and their surroundings.

This study investigates the dynamic susceptibility of the diluted Ising antiferromagnet Fe$_{0.3}$Zn$_{0.7}$F$_2$ in zero and finite applied DC fields. The results reveal a para- to antiferromagnetic phase transition at $T_N = 18.5$ K, followed by a significant slowing down of dynamics at low temperatures, described by an Arrhenius law. The application of a DC field influences the phase transition and low-temperature dynamics, leading to a comprehensive static and dynamic phase diagram in the $H$-$T$ plane. The system exhibits a crossover from random-exchange Ising to random-field Ising model behavior for fields $H \leq 1.5$ T. At higher fields, a random-field induced glassy dynamics emerges, destroying the antiferromagnetic phase transition. The low-temperature dynamics shows striking similarities with reentrant antiferromagnets, providing insight into the complex behavior of disordered magnetic systems.

This study examines the collective motion of self-propelled particles with voter-like interactions, where each particle moves at a constant speed in a two-dimensional space and aligns its direction with a randomly chosen neighboring particle. The introduction of external noise significantly impacts the system's behavior, with the absence of noise leading to full nematic order. However, even a small amount of noise can maintain total disorder in the thermodynamic limit. The dynamics of ordering at zero noise are characterized by a slow increase in the order parameter, which transitions from a power-law growth to exponential convergence over time. Notably, the mean convergence time to complete order exhibits non-monotonic behavior with particle density, with faster convergence at high densities compared to all-to-all interactions. Our findings suggest that the rapid achievement of nematic consensus is facilitated by the formation of clusters of equally-oriented particles, disrupting the balance of directional state transitions. These results provide new insights into the behavior of self-propelled particles with voter-like interactions and highlight the importance of considering the interplay between noise, density, and clustering in the emergence of collective motion. The study's findings have implications for understanding the behavior of active matter systems and the development of novel collective motion models.

This article presents a mathematical model of biological neuronal networks comprising a finite number of non-identical cells, governed by finite-dimensional impulsive differential equations. The network's structural framework is represented by a directed and weighted graph, where nodes denote subsets of neurons and edges signify synaptic connections between them. We demonstrate the existence of a dynamical optimum among isomorphic network graphs, which exhibits the most diverse range of responses to external stimuli. Notably, we prove that all neurons in this optimal network must adhere to Dale's principle, being either exclusively excitatory or inhibitory. This principle emerges as a mathematical necessity for achieving dynamical optimization. However, we also show that Dale's principle is insufficient for ensuring optimal network dynamics. Our findings provide new insights into the theoretical underpinnings of neuronal network optimization, highlighting the interplay between network structure and dynamical behavior. The results have significant implications for the study of biological neural networks and the development of mathematical models in biomathematics. By exploring the intricate relationships between network topology, neuron properties, and dynamical responses, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex mechanisms governing biological neuronal networks.

This article presents a novel multiple instance (MI) deep hashing technique for learning discriminative hash codes under weak bag-level supervision, suitable for large-scale retrieval tasks. A dedicated MI pool layer aggregates hierarchical representations across bag members, enabling effective learning. To enhance trainability and retrieval quality, a two-pronged approach is proposed, combining robust optimization with auxiliary single instance hashing. The technique is applied to tumor assessment in mammography and histology datasets, where tumors often coexist with benign masses. Experimental results demonstrate improved retrieval performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, showcasing the potential of MI deep hashing in medical image retrieval and tumor diagnosis. The approach offers a promising solution for large-scale medical image analysis and retrieval applications.

We investigate a two-species Fermi gas with a large mass ratio, where the interspecies interaction is short-ranged. Utilizing the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, we calculate the interaction energy between two heavy fermions immersed in a sea of light fermions as a function of the s-wave scattering length. Our results show that in the BCS limit, the effective interaction between heavy fermions is consistent with perturbative calculations. However, the p-wave projection of the effective interaction exhibits attractive behavior in the BCS limit, transitioning to repulsive behavior near the unitarity limit. Notably, the p-wave attraction reaches its maximum between the BCS and unitarity limits, suggesting optimal pairing of heavy minority fermions. Furthermore, we find that confining heavy fermions to two dimensions enhances the p-wave attraction, exceeding that observed in three dimensions. Our findings provide insight into the behavior of Fermi gases with large mass ratios.

We investigate the pseudogap state in underdoped high-Tc superconductors, considering non-superconducting correlation origins. Two phenomenological models are examined: a simple density of states suppression and an antiferromagnetic correlation-induced pseudogap. Using BTK theory, we calculate tunneling spectroscopy results for both cases and compare them to experimental findings, providing insight into the pseudogap state's nature.

This article derives optimal pointwise estimates for the biharmonic Green function under Dirichlet boundary conditions in arbitrary C^∞-smooth domains. Despite the absence of maximum principles for fourth-order elliptic equations, an asymptotic analysis yields an estimate showing the Green function's positivity near singularities. A potential negative part is bounded by the product of squared distances to the boundary, providing insight into the function's behavior and overcoming complications arising from the lack of a Harnack inequality, a common tool in second-order problems. The estimate sheds new light on the biharmonic Green function's properties.

This study examines the impact of energy-momentum conservation on jet observables in proton-lead (@xmath0pb) collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. We develop a simplistic model that accounts for the hard process and underlying event, utilizing PYTHIA for jet production in proton-proton (@xmath1) collisions and HIJING for the underlying event in @xmath0pb collisions. By extracting the energy of the parton from the proton participating in the hard scattering and reducing the proton's energy accordingly, we simulate the underlying event and superimpose it with the hard process. Our model successfully captures the centrality effect for central to semicentral collisions, reproducing the bulk of the observed effects in dijet data from the CMS collaboration and single jet data from the ATLAS collaboration. However, the model's limitations are evident in peripheral collisions, where the participation of few nucleons from lead renders it ineffective. These findings suggest that energy-momentum conservation plays a significant role in shaping jet observables in @xmath0pb collisions, particularly in central and semicentral events.

Recent collider data sheds light on QCD at low Bjorken-x. Hard diffractive interactions and Regge factorisation are examined using HERA and Tevatron data. Anomalous behaviour in the total cross section is assessed with LEP measurements. Data from HERA, Tevatron, and LEP are presented, exploring potential BFKL effects and discussing various interpretations.

This study presents a comprehensive calculation of one-loop corrections to the Higgs boson coupling constants and electroweak parameters within the Standard Model (SM) framework. The decay rate of the SM-like Higgs boson into diphoton is computed, and renormalized Higgs couplings with weak gauge bosons (W and Z) and the trilinear coupling are evaluated at the one-loop level using the on-shell scheme. The analysis focuses on parameter regions where unitarity and vacuum stability bounds are satisfied, and the predicted W boson mass is consistent with experimental data. The results reveal strong correlations among deviations in Higgs boson couplings, indicating that precise measurements of these coupling constants can discriminate between models. For instance, deviations in the WW and ZZ vertices are predicted to be around 5-10% if the diphoton channel deviates by 10-20% from SM predictions. These findings underscore the importance of accurate measurements of Higgs boson coupling constants in future collider experiments to discern between competing models and refine our understanding of the SM.

This study investigates the electronic properties of periodic corrugated graphene nanoribbons using the tight-binding π-orbital model. We analyze the band structure and conductance of corrugated ribbons with armchair and zigzag edges, considering three types of corrugations. Our results show that armchair host ribbons exhibit band gaps or low-velocity minibands near the charge neutrality point, depending on the corrugation type, while higher energies reveal separated Bloch state bands with mini-stopbands. In contrast, zigzag host ribbons remain unaffected by corrugations, except for rectangular corrugations. The conductance of finite corrugated ribbons is found to follow the number of propagating Bloch states, displaying pronounced oscillations due to Fabry-Pérot interference. Notably, edge disorder significantly impacts the conductance of corrugated ribbons. Our findings suggest that observing miniband formation in corrugated ribbons requires clean, edge-disorder-free samples, particularly for armchair host lattices. These results provide valuable insights into the electronic properties of corrugated graphene nanoribbons and highlight the importance of sample quality in experimental observations. Overall, this study contributes to the understanding of the complex interplay between corrugation, edge type, and electronic properties in graphene nanoribbons.

This article explores the geometric properties of a critical system undergoing a second-order thermal phase transition. By utilizing a local description of the dynamics at the critical point, we demonstrate the emergence of clusters exhibiting fractal geometry, characterized by non-vanishing order parameter values. Treating these clusters as open subsystems, we find that instanton-like configurations play a dominant role in their statistical mechanics. Our analysis reveals a dependence of the fractal dimension on the embedding dimension and the system's isothermal critical exponent. Accounting for finite size effects, we derive an expression for the critical cluster size in terms of the system's total size, critical temperature, and effective long-wavelength interaction coupling. Furthermore, we establish that the cluster size is equivalent to the correlation length at criticality. Within the mean field approximation framework, our local approach is extended to provide a global description of the system, offering a comprehensive understanding of the geometric and thermodynamic properties of critical systems undergoing phase transitions. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex behavior of critical systems and have implications for the study of phase transitions in various physical contexts.

This article presents an overview of the Gaia space astrometry mission, a groundbreaking endeavor by the European Space Agency (ESA) aimed at creating a highly accurate astrometric and spectro-photometric map of over 1000 million celestial objects in our galaxy. The Gaia Data Processing and Analysis Consortium (DPAC) has been established to tackle the complexities of processing the vast amounts of data generated by the mission. With the satellite expected to downlink approximately 100 TB of raw telemetry data over its 5-year mission duration, a sophisticated processing system is required to achieve the mission's objective of few tens of microarcseconds accuracy in astrometry. The Gaia instrument suite, comprising a radial-velocity spectrometer, two low-resolution dispersers, and a common focal plane featuring a 1-gigapixel CCD mosaic, demands intricate processing and interdependence between modules. This article describes the composition and structure of DPAC, as well as the overall architecture of the Gaia processing system, with a focus on the core processing unit, one of nine coordination units that will work in tandem to produce the mission's unprecedentedly accurate celestial maps. The challenges and opportunities presented by this ambitious mission are discussed, highlighting the innovative approaches being developed to analyze and interpret the vast amounts of data generated by Gaia.

This study presents an in-depth analysis of the host galaxies of six BL Lac objects, observed with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 (WFPC2) as part of a complete 1 Jy radio-selected sample. The observations, conducted in Cycle 5, achieved an equivalent limiting flux of 0 mag arcsec^-2, allowing for unprecedented morphological detail between 0.1-10 arcseconds from the nucleus. The sample, combined with three X-ray-selected BL Lacs, spans a redshift range of 0.2-1.0, with host galaxies detected in seven out of nine cases. The host galaxies are found to be luminous ellipticals, with an average absolute magnitude of -23.5 mag and a dispersion of 0.7 mag, comparable to brightest cluster galaxies. The morphologies of these galaxies are generally smooth, with small ellipticities, and show no obvious alignment with the linear radio structures. Color profiles, derived from WFPC2 images in two filters, exhibit no strong spatial gradients, consistent with passively evolving elliptical galaxies. Notably, the host galaxies of radio-selected and X-ray-selected BL Lacs are comparable in both morphology and luminosity, suggesting a common underlying population. These findings provide new insights into the nature of BL Lac objects and their host galaxies, highlighting the importance of high-resolution imaging in understanding the properties of these enigmatic sources. The results of this study have implications for our understanding of the relationship between active galactic nuclei and their host galaxies, and demonstrate the value of combining radio, optical, and X-ray observations to investigate the properties of BL Lac objects.

This study applies extreme-order statistics to branches of an observer in a many-worlds framework. A unitary evolution operator is constructed, generating pseudostochastic behaviour with a power-law distribution. The operator models record generation, dating, and wavefunction splitting. Repeated application yields an ensemble where the branch with the most recalled records dominates, containing nearly all "conscious dimension" due to its immense size near the observer's endpoint, shedding insight into the interplay between observation and quantum mechanics.

This study introduces an imaginary-time Nambu-Bethe-Salpeter (NBS) wave function to investigate hadron-hadron interactions on the lattice. By utilizing scattering states with varying energies, a non-local hadron-hadron potential is extracted without requiring "ground state saturation". The method is applied to nucleon-nucleon interactions in the 1S0 channel, yielding the potential and phase shift. This approach efficiently overcomes challenges associated with multi-baryon systems, providing a valuable tool for lattice QCD studies of nuclear forces and hadron interactions, enabling accurate calculations of scattering phase shifts and potentials.

This paper proposes a nonparametric test for detecting monotone changes in the relationship between two processes using panel data. A CUSUM-type test statistic is developed, based on empirical distribution functions. Asymptotic distribution and finite sample properties are examined through Monte Carlo simulations, providing a robust method for comparing process distributions.

This article introduces a novel quantum effect related to the late-time behavior of decaying states, with significant implications for observational consequences. We demonstrate that charged unstable particles, as well as neutral unstable particles with non-zero magnetic moments, can emit electromagnetic radiation if they survive for a sufficient duration. This phenomenon arises from the non-classical behavior of unstable particles at late times, specifically in the post-exponential time region. Our analysis of the transition period between exponential and non-exponential survival amplitude reveals that the instantaneous energy of the unstable particle can reach exceedingly large values, surpassing those observed in the exponential time region. Based on our model, we propose that this purely quantum mechanical effect may be responsible for the emission of electromagnetic radiation, including X-rays or gamma rays, by unstable particles produced by astrophysical sources and traveling at relativistic velocities, particularly during specific time intervals within the transition region.

This study examines the scattering of a two-particle composite system interacting with a delta-function potential. Utilizing time-independent scattering theory, we analyze the transmission and reflection coefficients' dependence on external potential height, incident momentum, and internal potential strength. Notably, the internal degree of freedom significantly alters these coefficients, even without internal excitation. We investigate two scenarios, where the incident wave's internal state has even or odd parity. Our results show that a symmetric Hamiltonian has a greater influence on odd-parity internal states than on even-parity ones, highlighting the importance of internal degrees of freedom in scattering processes.

Title: A Global Evolution Picture of Protoplanetary Disks (PPDs) is Key to Understanding Almost Every Aspect of Planet Formation, Where Standard Alpha - Disk Models Have Been Constantly Employed for Its Simplicity. Abstract: The study of protoplanetary disks (PPDs) is crucial for understanding planet formation, with standard alpha-disk models being widely used due to their simplicity. However, recent advances in non-ideal magneto-hydrodynamic effects have led to a paradigm shift, suggesting that accretion driven by magnetized disk winds plays a significant role in disk evolution. This article presents a framework for global PPD evolution, incorporating wind-driven accretion and wind mass loss. The results show that disk evolution is dominated by wind-driven processes, with viscous spreading being suppressed. The timescale of disk evolution is controlled by the amount of external magnetic flux threading the disks and how rapidly it is lost. Rapid disk dispersal can occur if the disk retains most of its magnetic flux during evolution. Furthermore, wind kinematics are affected by far-UV penetration depth and disk geometry, with wind launching requiring sufficient ionization at the disk surface. For typical disk lifetimes, the mass lost through the wind is comparable to that accreted onto the protostar, with most wind mass loss occurring from the outer disk via a slow wind. The fractional wind mass loss increases with disk lifetime, potentially enhancing the dust-to-gas mass ratio and promoting planet formation. This new understanding of PPD evolution highlights the importance of considering wind-driven processes in the formation of planetary systems. By incorporating these advances, we can gain a deeper understanding of the complex mechanisms driving planet formation and the role of PPDs in shaping the architecture of planetary systems.

This article proposes a novel camera-based method for robot identification, tracking, and orientation estimation. By mounting coloured lights in a circular pattern around each robot, unique colour sequences are created and observed by a camera. The number of identifiable robots is limited by the number of available colours, lights per robot, and the camera's field of view. To maximize the number of robots, we model this problem as a combinatorial optimization issue, equivalent to finding the maximum disjoint cycles in a de Bruijn graph. We provide existence results for optimal solutions in various cases, including when the number of colours is limited. Additionally, we present a construction method that leverages cycles from smaller de Bruijn graphs to create larger graphs with many cycles. Our approach combines finite field algebra and combinatorics of words to achieve efficient graph decomposition and pose estimation. The proposed method has significant implications for robot network applications, enabling accurate tracking and orientation estimation of multiple robots using a single camera. Our results contribute to the development of efficient and scalable robot identification systems, with potential applications in areas such as robotics, computer vision, and autonomous systems.

This article introduces a novel method, termed "variational sampling," for approximating integrals with respect to a given probability distribution when exact computation is impractical. Variational sampling involves fitting a simplified distribution with a closed-form integral expression, optimized using a set of randomly sampled control points. The approach utilizes a Monte Carlo approximation to the generalized Kullback-Leibler divergence as its objective function, distinguishing it from similar methods like Bayesian Monte Carlo and importance sampling. We establish the well-posedness of variational sampling under a simple condition on sample size and derive a central limit theorem analogous to importance sampling. Numerical simulations demonstrate that variational sampling can outperform existing methods in estimating moments of order up to 2 within comparable computation time. The results highlight the potential of variational sampling as a efficient and accurate method for approximate integration, with potential for further enhancements and applications.

This article presents the VLA-COSMOS large project, outlining its scientific objectives and a catalog of radio sources in the COSMOS field at 1.4GHz. Observations yielded a resolution of 1.5" and a mean rms noise of 12μJy. The catalog features 80 extended radio sources, mostly double-lobed galaxies. Astrometric testing ensured relative and absolute uncertainties of 130mas and 655mas, respectively. The project's results provide valuable insights into radio source morphology and astrometry, contributing to our understanding of the universe's structure and evolution, with implications for cosmological studies and galaxy formation theories.

This study investigates the effects of cold nuclear matter (CNM) on production in pPb and PbPb collisions at the LHC energy of 5.02 TeV. By incorporating gluon shadowing and nuclear absorption, we evaluate the impact of CNM on production yields. Utilizing the LO CSM model, which has demonstrated good agreement with ALICE data at 7 TeV, we provide a comprehensive description of the underlying partonic process. Our results show significant suppression of production in pPb and PbPb collisions due to strong gluon shadowing in the lead ion. The suppression exhibits a pronounced rapidity dependence, potentially compensating for the predicted charm recombination effects in PbPb collisions. These findings offer valuable insights into the interplay between CNM effects and heavy-ion collision dynamics, shedding light on the complex mechanisms governing production in these environments.

This article examines the viability of various inflationary potentials within the frameworks of cold and warm quintessential and tachyonic inflationary scenarios, in light of the Planck 2015 results. Our analysis reveals that, in the context of cold quintessential inflation, exponential and inverse power-law potentials, which yield power-law and intermediate inflations, respectively, are disfavored by the Planck 2015 data. However, the power-law potential can be consistent with the Planck 2015 results at the 95% confidence level (CL). Furthermore, the predictions of the Higgs-like and Coleman-Weinberg potentials, as well as α-attractors inflation, can lie within the 68% CL region of the Planck 2015 data. In the warm quintessential inflationary scenario, we find that the power-law potential with a varying dissipative parameter, the Higgs-like and Coleman-Weinberg potentials, and α-attractors inflation with a constant dissipative parameter can be consistent with the Planck 2015 data at the 68% CL. Additionally, our results show that, in the cold tachyonic inflationary model, the inverse power-law and exponential potentials can be accommodated within the 95% CL region of the Planck 2015 data. In the warm tachyonic inflationary scenario, we find that, for specific varying dissipative parameters, the results of both potentials can be compatible with the Planck 2015 data. Our study provides insights into the viability of different inflationary potentials and scenarios, shedding light on the underlying dynamics of the early universe.

This study examines the steady-state entropy production in non-equilibrium systems, focusing on transport and reaction-diffusion systems. We analyze entropy production at both short and long times, utilizing the mean entropy production rate and large deviation function to characterize interacting many-body systems. Our results reveal a kink-like feature at zero entropy production in the large deviation function, analogous to that observed in a single particle driven along a periodic potential. This phenomenon is a direct consequence of the detailed fluctuation theorem, which governs the probability distribution of entropy production. The presence of this kink is a generic feature of the large deviation function, highlighting its importance in understanding non-equilibrium steady states. Our findings provide insight into the fundamental characteristics of non-equilibrium systems, shedding light on the role of entropy production in shaping their behavior. Theoretical implications and potential applications are discussed.

Title: Central Peaks in the Iron Abundance of Intracluster Plasma: A Common Feature of Cooling-Core Galaxy Clusters Abstract: Observations of cooling-core galaxy clusters have consistently shown central peaks in the iron abundance of intracluster plasma, which are broader than the stellar distribution of the central brightest cluster galaxy (BCG). This suggests that metal-enriched plasma is transported out of the BCG through processes such as turbulent diffusion. Simultaneously, these clusters are heated by central active galactic nuclei (AGN) through jets, cosmic-ray bubbles, and/or convection. We utilize the AGN-driven convection model of Chandran & Rasera to predict the turbulent velocity profile in a steady-state cluster, which is then incorporated into an advection/diffusion model for metal transport in the intracluster medium. By comparing our model results to XMM and Chandra observations of eight clusters, we find that assuming a constant turbulence level over a cluster's lifetime, the model can explain the observed abundance profiles in only five of the eight clusters. However, by developing an analytic fit of the turbulent velocity profile as a function of AGN power, we are able to deduce the average AGN power required to match the abundance profiles for each cluster. Our results indicate that AGN-driven convection can account for the observed abundance profiles if the AGN power varies over a cluster's lifetime, with average values ranging from 10^43 to 10^45 erg/s. This suggests that AGN activity plays a crucial role in shaping the metal distribution in cooling-core clusters, and that variations in AGN power over a cluster's lifetime can have a significant impact on the observed abundance profiles.

This study presents the development and implementation of a two-bunch acceleration scheme at the LINAC, aimed at doubling the positron injection rate into the KEKB ring. The scheme involves accelerating bunches separated by 96 ns at a frequency of 50 Hz, necessitating precise stabilization of energy and orbit for each bunch. To achieve this, the beam energy and orbit feedback systems were upgraded, and the beam-position monitor (BPM) read-out system was improved to accommodate two-bunch requirements. The combined waveforms from BPMs were adjusted using delay cables to enable simultaneous measurement of beam positions for both bunches. The beam energies were balanced by tuning RF pulse timings, and the average energy was stabilized by adjusting accelerating RF phases. Additionally, the average beam orbits were stabilized, and slow feedback systems for charge and bunching stabilities are being planned. The upgraded systems were successfully tested and will be utilized in routine operation, paving the way for enhanced positron injection rates into the KEKB ring.

This article explores conjectures that link computational complexity to the provability of sentences in weak theories. Motivated by the pursuit of finite versions of classical incompleteness theorems, we propose and systematize conjectures that formally connect the computational difficulty of a problem to the length of its proof or its unprovability. Building on previous work, we introduce new conjectures, review existing ones, and establish novel connections between them and other statements in proof complexity. Our aim is to formalize and fully understand these general statements, which seem to encompass special cases of previous results in proof complexity. By doing so, we shed new light on the intricate relationship between computational complexity and proof theory.

This article examines the structure of neutron stars within the framework of the Starobinsky model, a variant of @xmath0 theory of gravity. By adopting an exact and non-perturbative approach, we investigate the implications of the model's additional junction conditions, which require the continuity of the curvature scalar and its first derivative. For an exterior Schwarzschild solution, these conditions must be satisfied at the stellar surface, resulting in a curvature scalar and its derivative of zero. Our analysis reveals that certain equations of state (EOS) of matter are incompatible with these conditions, leading to two significant fine-tuning problems.
