Specifically, only specific classes of EOS are consistent with the Schwarzschild solution at the surface, and for a given EOS, only a narrow set of boundary conditions at the star's center will satisfy the surface conditions. These findings suggest that the Starobinsky model, and potentially other @xmath1 models, are highly unnatural for the existence of compact astrophysical objects, as the EOS of such objects should be determined by nuclear matter physics rather than the theory of gravity. Our results have important implications for the study of neutron stars and the development of modified gravity theories.

This study investigates the dynamical ejection scenario of runaway stars, which are characterized by their large peculiar velocities. We utilize extensive N-body simulations of massive clusters, in conjunction with analytical arguments, to examine the ejection velocity distribution of runaway stars. Our results indicate that the ejection velocity distribution of the fastest runaway stars is dependent on the binary distribution within the cluster, aligning with our analytical toy model. In contrast, the distribution of lower-velocity runaway stars appears to be independent of binary properties. Assuming a realistic log-normal distribution of binary separations, we find that the velocity distribution follows a power law, with distinct exponents for high-velocity and low-velocity runaways. We calculate the total expected ejection rates of runaway stars from our simulated clusters and analyze their mass function and binarity. The mass function of runaway stars is biased towards high masses and exhibits a strong velocity dependence. Furthermore, the binarity of runaway stars decreases with increasing ejection velocity, with no binaries expected to be ejected at very high velocities. Our simulations also suggest that hyper-runaways, characterized by velocities of hundreds of km/s, can be dynamically ejected from stellar clusters, albeit at very low rates, which are insufficient to account for the observed population of hyper-velocity stars in the galactic halo. These findings provide new insights into the formation and properties of runaway stars, shedding light on the dynamical processes that govern their ejection from dense stellar clusters.

This article explores opportunistic amplify-and-forward and decode-and-forward relaying systems, leveraging the "best-relay" selection technique to achieve full diversity order. We derive closed-form expressions for the outage probability of these systems over independent but non-identical imperfect log-normal fading channels, considering channel estimation errors as Gaussian random variables. The resulting estimated channel distributions deviate from log-normal, unlike Rayleigh fading channels. While simulation results do not perfectly align with analytical findings due to this discrepancy, the difference is negligible in most scenarios. Our work provides valuable insights into the performance of relaying systems under imperfect channel conditions, with implications for the design and optimization of wireless communication networks. Theoretical and simulation results are presented to validate our analysis.

We develop a bond-operator mean-field theory in the SU(3) bosons representation to describe the antiferro-nematic phase of the spin-1 bilinear-biquadratic model. Calculated static structure factors reveal the antiferro-nematic state exhibits both ferro- and antiferro-quadrupole long-range orders. This unconventional state, reminiscent of ferrimagnets or canted antiferromagnets, may impact spin wave theory and has possible relevance to quasi-two-dimensional triangular materials, such as NiGa2S4, with unique magnetic properties.

This article presents a modified version of the Gaussian Self-Consistent (GSC) method, which eliminates the need for the Edwards virial expansion. Instead, the mean energy is calculated directly through a convolution of the attractive part of the pairwise non-bonded potential with the Gaussian trial radial distribution function, while the hard sphere repulsion is accounted for using a generalized Carnahan-Starling term. The method is applied to isolated ring, open, and star homopolymers of varying lengths and flexibility, and the results are compared to those obtained from Monte Carlo (MC) simulations in continuous space. The comparison reveals a surprisingly good agreement between the GSC and MC results for mean squared inter-monomer distances, radius of gyration, and mean energy across the coil-to-globule transition. The limitations of the Gaussian technique are discussed, and potential avenues for improvement are explored, highlighting the method's potential for studying polymer behavior.

This article examines the accretion process onto a black hole within a string cloud background, where the horizon's radius is enlarged due to the string cloud parameter. We analyze stationary, spherically symmetric accretion of a polytropic fluid, obtaining an analytic solution for the perturbation. Generalized expressions for accretion rate, critical radius, and other flow parameters are derived. The accretion rate is found to be a function of black hole mass, gas boundary conditions, and string cloud parameter. We also determine gas compression ratios and temperature profiles below the accretion radius and at the event horizon. Notably, the mass accretion rate increases with the string cloud parameter for both relativistic and non-relativistic fluids. Our results provide insight into the effects of string clouds on black hole accretion, highlighting the significance of this parameter in modifying accretion processes. The findings have implications for understanding black hole behavior.

This article re-examines the enigmatic Stephan's Quintet (SQ), a compact group of galaxies that has been extensively studied since its discovery in 1877. Despite its well-documented history, SQ remains shrouded in mystery within the context of Cold Dark Matter Hierarchical Clustering Cosmology (CDMHCC). The observed anomalous redshifts among SQ galaxies pose a significant challenge to CDMHCC, either reducing the group to a trio with two improbable intruders or supporting the Arp (1973) hypothesis of intrinsic redshifts. In contrast, the Hydro-Gravitational-Theory (HGT) proposed by Gibson (1996-2000) offers an alternative explanation. According to HGT, the universe's superclusters, clusters, and galaxies originate from expansion and gravitational fragmentation in the super-viscous plasma epoch. This fluid mechanical cosmology suggests that SQ galaxies gently separated recently and remain aligned due to perspective and small transverse velocities. The observed star and gas bridges, as well as young globular star cluster trails, are triggered by the separation of SQ galaxies through each other's frozen baryonic-dark matter halos. Furthermore, HGT provides a plausible explanation for the discordant redshifts between angularly clustered quasars and bright galaxies, offering a new perspective on the nature of galaxy evolution and the large-scale structure of the universe.

This article explores the implications of the supersymmetric Higgs-lepton inflation model in light of the recent B-mode observation by the BICEP2 experiment. The tensor-to-scalar ratio of primordial fluctuations, as indicated by CMB B-mode polarization, aligns with the predictions of this inflationary model for natural parameter values. A notable aspect of the model is its prediction of the seesaw mass scale from the amplitude of tensor mode fluctuations. Analyzing the 68% and 95% confidence level constraints from the BICEP2 experiment, we derive specific mass ranges for the seesaw scale, which vary depending on the number of e-foldings. For 50 e-foldings, the ranges are 927 GeV to 1.62 TeV (68% CL) and 751 GeV to 2.37 TeV (95% CL), while for 60 e-foldings, the ranges are 391 GeV to 795 GeV (68% CL) and 355 GeV to 1.10 TeV (95% CL). These findings have significant implications for future collider experiments, particularly in the context of type III seesaw mechanisms, where heavy leptons may be detectable. Furthermore, a substantial portion of the parameter space corresponding to the 68% CL of the BICEP2 experiment will be accessible to the Large Hadron Collider at 14 TeV, offering potential avenues for experimental verification.

This study explores laser-induced nonsequential multiple ionization using a simplified statistical model. The model posits that an electron recollides inelastically with its parent ion, thermalizing with remaining bound electrons within a specified time interval. Subsequently, all electrons are ejected. We examine how time delays impact individual contributions from electron orbits, where the returning electron is either accelerated or decelerated by the field, to the resulting ion momentum distributions. Our findings indicate that time delays modify the drift momenta of electrons reaching the continuum by shifting the times towards or away from an electric field crossing. Both types of collisions are influenced distinctly, and their interplay determines the distribution widths and peak momenta. Notably, in the few-cycle pulse case, time delays do not drastically alter the momentum distribution shapes. This suggests that nonsequential multiple ionization could potentially be utilized for absolute-phase diagnosis, even with a thermalization time interval. Our research provides new insights into the complex dynamics of laser-induced ionization, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms and their implications for diagnostic applications.

This article extends a previously proposed context model for assessing database instance quality by introducing multidimensional contexts. By incorporating dimensions, we enable a more comprehensive evaluation of data quality. Multidimensional contexts are represented as ontologies using Datalog, facilitating the expression of dimensional constraints and rules. This framework also supports query answering via dimensional navigation, a crucial auxiliary activity in data quality assessment. The use of Datalog enables the representation of complex relationships and rules, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of data quality. Through examples, we illustrate the application of this approach, demonstrating its potential to enhance data quality evaluation. By providing a more detailed and multifaceted assessment, this multidimensional context model can inform data cleaning and quality improvement efforts, ultimately leading to more reliable and accurate data.

This study presents Very Large Array (VLA) maps of ammonia emission in the Galactic Center region, focusing on the NH3(1,1) and NH3(2,2) transitions. Observations were conducted in three fields covering Sgr A* and the surrounding region. The results reveal emission associated with the Circumnuclear Disk (CND) in the central 3 parsecs, both morphologically and kinematically. A narrow, 2 pc x 10 pc streamer of clumpy molecular gas is detected, extending from a nearby giant molecular cloud (GMC) towards the CND. A velocity gradient is observed along the streamer, with increasing velocities as the gas approaches Sgr A*. The streamer's termination at the CND is marked by a significant increase in line width, potentially indicating accretion onto the CND. The NH3(2,2)/NH3(1,1) emission ratio suggests gas heating at the streamer's northern tip, within the CND's eastern edge. The combined morphology, kinematics, and temperature gradients indicate that the southern streamer is interacting with the CND at the Galactic Center, providing insights into the dynamics of gas accretion and star formation in this region. These findings have implications for our understanding of the Galactic Center's complex gas dynamics and its role in regulating star formation and black hole growth.

This study theoretically examines slow and fast light propagation in semiconductor optical amplifiers via coherent population oscillations. By modulating the injection current, population oscillations are induced, allowing for modification of light signal delay or advancement. The relative phase between the optical signal and bias current modulations is identified as a key factor in switching between delayed and advanced light propagation. Additionally, the impact of modulation current on slow light in vertical cavity surface emission lasers is analyzed, considering cavity effects. The results demonstrate that adjusting the modulation depth enables tuning of the structural resonance, leading to enhanced delay capabilities.

This article presents a novel implementation of a smooth memristor oscillator, derived from Chua's circuit, utilizing a flux-controlled memristor with negative conductance. By replacing the conventional Chua's diode, a practical memristor-based circuit is designed, circumventing realization challenges. The circuit's amplitude and frequency are predetermined, yielding a robust and flexible design without inductors. The proposed analogue circuit exhibits a diverse range of dynamical behaviors, verified through experimental time series, phase portraits, and power spectra, which are corroborated by numerical simulations. The 0-1 test is also applied to confirm the presence of regular and chaotic dynamics. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed circuit, offering a valuable tool for exploring complex dynamics and memristor-based systems. The findings have significant implications for the design and analysis of nonlinear circuits and systems.

This study proposes an innovative all-optical anti-waveguide mechanism for manipulating optical beams beyond the diffraction limit. By utilizing a spatially inhomogeneous pump beam in a Doppler broadened four-level Raman gain medium, we create an anti-waveguide structure that enables steering, splitting, and cloning of a co-propagating weak probe beam. The transverse modulated index of refraction and gain, induced by the pump beam, facilitate precise control over the optical beam. Furthermore, an additional control field allows for diffraction-free and stable propagation. The detuning of this control field can be adjusted to enhance the finesse of the cloned images, demonstrating the potential for high-resolution optical beam manipulation and propagation. This mechanism has significant implications for advanced optical technologies.

This article explores the concept of pattern avoidance in the symmetric group, specifically focusing on involutions that avoid certain permutations. We define two permutations as exchangeable if their avoidance patterns are equivalent under specific conditions. Our main results demonstrate that certain pairs of permutations, namely @xmath9 and @xmath10, and @xmath11 and @xmath12, are exchangeable. The exchangeability of @xmath11 and @xmath12 confirms a conjecture by Guibert, thereby completing the classification of involutions with respect to pattern avoidance. Furthermore, our findings have implications for longer patterns and can be generalized to rook placements on Ferrers boards with symmetry conditions. By providing sufficient conditions for the exchangeability of prefixes in this generalized setting, we show that these conditions are satisfied by the aforementioned permutation pairs. Our approach parallels previous work on pattern avoidance by general permutations, with necessary adaptations to account for the symmetry inherent in involutions.

This article addresses the recovery of an ensemble of Diracs on a sphere from its projection onto spherical harmonics spaces. Under a suitable separation condition, we demonstrate that the ensemble can be accurately recovered through total variation norm minimization. The uniqueness of the solution is proven using dual interpolating polynomials, extending the theory developed for trigonometric polynomials. Furthermore, for non-negative ensembles, a sparsity condition is shown to be sufficient for exact recovery. This work contributes to the fields of super resolution, signal recovery, and sparse spike trains, with applications in signal processing and interpolation theory.

This study examines Hawking radiation in a Schwarzschild black hole from the perspective of various observers, utilizing a novel method introduced by Barcel et al. (Phys. Rev. D 83, 041501). By introducing an "effective temperature" function that varies with time, we analyze the perception of Hawking radiation by different observers in the system. A non-stationary vacuum state for a quantum scalar field is constructed, interpolating between the Boulware and Unruh vacuum states at early and late times, respectively. This mimics the process of switching on Hawking radiation in realistic collapse scenarios. Our analysis reveals a rich physical image, with static observers, freely-falling observers, and observers undergoing a transition from rest to free-fall all perceiving distinct features of Hawking radiation. Notably, we find that freely-falling observers do not perceive vacuum when crossing the horizon, but rather an effective temperature significantly larger than that perceived at the start of their free-fall. This phenomenon is attributed to a diverging Doppler effect at horizon crossing, providing new insights into the behavior of Hawking radiation in the context of quantum field theory in curved spacetime.

This study presents high-spatial-resolution mid-infrared images of the luminous blue variable IRAS 18576+0341, obtained using the VISIR instrument at the Very Large Telescope and the Very Large Array interferometer. The resulting mid-infrared continuum maps reveal a clumpy, approximately circular symmetric nebula, contrasting with the asymmetry observed in the ionized component of the envelope. Radio and line images, obtained with comparable spatial resolution, demonstrate excellent agreement with the 12.8 μm map, suggesting free-free emission from circumstellar ionized material. Color temperature and optical depth maps show uniform dust characteristics over the dust shell. The differing morphologies of the dusty and gaseous components are explored, with various possibilities considered to explain the observed characteristics. Our findings provide new insights into the complex structure of the circumstellar envelope surrounding IRAS 18576+0341, shedding light on the dynamics and evolution of this luminous blue variable star.

This study combines near-infrared and optical data to investigate the star formation histories of five low surface brightness disc galaxies (LSBGs). Both red and blue LSBGs were imaged to compare their stellar populations. The results reveal strong colour gradients, indicative of mean stellar age gradients, in both types of galaxies. The analysis rules out very low stellar metallicities based on metallicity-sensitive optical-near-infrared colours. The findings suggest distinct star formation histories for red and blue LSBGs, representing two separate pathways to low surface brightness. Blue LSBGs are characterized by low, constant star formation rates, while red LSBGs are better described by a'faded disc' scenario, shedding light on the evolution of these enigmatic galaxies and their place in the broader context of galaxy formation and evolution.

This study examines heat transport in a chain of harmonic oscillators subject to random elastic collisions between nearest neighbors. By numerically solving the equations of motion for the covariance matrix under free and fixed boundary conditions, we find that the temperature profile and stationary heat flux in the thermodynamic limit are influenced by boundary conditions and, for free boundaries, coupling strength with heat baths. Notably, a significant deviation from local equilibrium is observed at the chain edges, resulting in two boundary layers with distinct scaling behavior. The relaxation to the stationary state is characterized by two time scales: one associated with hydrodynamic mode relaxation and another reflecting the system's finiteness. Our findings provide insights into the complex interplay between boundary conditions, system size, and heat transport in harmonic oscillator chains. The results have implications for understanding thermal transport in nano-scale systems.

This study examines the rest-frame UV emission from the MareNostrum high-z universe, a smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation utilizing over 2 billion particles. Cosmological simulations of galaxy formation often overestimate the UV rest-frame luminosity function at high redshift, affecting both the bright and faint ends. To address this, we implement a dust attenuation model that applies greater extinction to younger star populations, mimicking the effects of a clumpy interstellar medium. Our results demonstrate that this model provides a reasonable fit to observed UV luminosity functions and UV-continuum slopes. By assuming significant obscuration for stars younger than 10 Myr, embedded in gas clouds at formation, we find that the optical depth in these clouds must be 2-3 times larger than the mean optical depth for the homogeneous interstellar medium. Notably, these values exceed local galaxy estimates by an order of magnitude. Our findings suggest that ΛCDM predictions for high-z UV emission can align with current observations when considering a dust extinction model based on a clumpy high-redshift environment, providing new insights into the role of dust attenuation in galaxy formation at early cosmic times.

Title: A Significant Fraction of Main-Sequence Stars are Encircled by Dusty Debris Discs: Unveiling the Role of Planetary Stirring Abstract: Debris discs, composed of short-lived dust particles replenished through collisions between planetesimals, encircle a significant fraction of main-sequence stars. The relative importance of self-stirring, driven by locally formed Pluto-sized planetesimals, and planetary stirring, caused by secular perturbation from an inner giant planet, in debris systems remains unknown. This study presents new Herschel Space Observatory imagery of 11 massive and extended debris discs, with all discs exhibiting extension at far-infrared wavelengths and five resolved for the first time. By comparing measured disc sizes with model predictions, we find that self-stirring can explain the properties of seven discs. However, for four systems (HD9672, HD16743, HD21997, and HD95086), the predicted pace of outward propagation of the stirring front is insufficient to account for the radial extent of the cold dust, suggesting an alternative explanation is necessary. We propose that planetary stirring is a promising possibility, with known outer giant planets in HR8799 and HD95086 potentially responsible for the stirring process. Notably, the discs around HD9672, HD21997, and HR8799 also harbor detectable amounts of molecular CO gas. Our study demonstrates that self-stirring may not be the sole active scenario in the largest and most massive debris discs, with planetary stirring potentially driving destructive collisions and debris dust production in a subset of systems. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of debris disc evolution and the role of giant planets in shaping the architecture of planetary systems.

This study utilizes Unitary Chiral Perturbation Theory to analyze WA3 data on π^- γ interactions at 63 GeV. Recent findings suggest low-lying axial vector mesons are dynamically generated from pseudoscalar and vector interactions. Our analysis supports the existence of two a_1 resonances, associated with poles in the second Riemann sheet. The results are consistent with previous research, providing further evidence for the dynamic generation of axial vector mesons and shedding light on the properties of the a_1 resonance, with implications for hadronic physics and resonance spectroscopy, confirming predictions from Phys. Rev. D 75, 014017 (2007).

This study examines the statistical properties of gravitational lenses in flat, low-density cosmological models with varying cosmic equations of state. We calculate lensing probabilities as a function of image separation using a lens population described by the Jenkins et al. mass function, modeled as singular isothermal spheres on galactic scales and Navarro, Frenk & White halos on cluster scales. Our results show that COBE-normalized models with certain equations of state underpredict the number of arcsecond-scale lenses observed in the JVAS/CLASS radio survey. The wide-separation lensing rate is found to be a sensitive probe of both the equation of state and halo mass concentration. The absence of wide-separation lenses in current data excludes highly concentrated halos in certain models. Ongoing and future lensing surveys of high-redshift sources will provide improved constraints on these cosmological parameters, offering valuable insights into the nature of the universe.

This study explores the application of a novel X-ray-based method for estimating black hole mass in active galactic nuclei (AGNs). The technique, previously successful in stellar-mass black holes, is tested on a sample of AGNs with known black hole masses determined through reverberation mapping. Utilizing high-quality XMM-Newton archival data, we perform a systematic analysis to validate the method's efficacy in supermassive black holes. Our results demonstrate a good agreement between the black hole masses derived from the X-ray-based method and those obtained through reverberation mapping. This finding suggests that the technique is robust and scale-independent, applicable to both stellar and supermassive black holes. The success of this method has significant implications for understanding the physics of accretion and the cosmological evolution of galaxies, providing a valuable tool for estimating black hole masses in various astrophysical contexts. The scalability of this technique offers new opportunities for black hole research.

This article reviews the potential of neutrino astrophysics in probing new physics beyond the electroweak scale. High-energy neutrinos offer a unique means of accessing exotic phenomena, leveraging their flavor degree of freedom to reveal novel properties. We discuss how neutrino astrophysics can constrain dark matter properties, deriving a robust bound on the total annihilation cross-section. Presented at Neutrino 2008, this work highlights the advantages of neutrino-based astronomy in exploring fundamental physics, particularly in the context of dark matter and new physics searches, providing a promising avenue for future research and discovery.

This study investigates a mixed system of bosons and fermions, comprising up to six particles with equal mass, confined by a harmonic oscillator potential. The two-body interactions are repulsive and equally strong in both the Bose-Bose and Fermi-Boson channels. Focusing on the strongly interacting regime, we analyze the system using both analytical approaches and density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations. Our results reveal significant variations in density profiles for bosons and fermions across different states in strongly interacting mixtures. Notably, the ground state of balanced mixtures of four to six particles exhibits a tendency towards phase separation between bosons and fermions for strong repulsive interactions. In contrast, imbalanced Bose-Fermi mixtures of five particles display pronounced odd-even effects. These few-body results highlight the sensitivity of phase separation in one-dimensional confined mixtures to system composition, affecting both the ground state and excited states. Our findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of mixed boson-fermion systems, shedding light on the complex interplay between interaction strength, system size, and composition. The study's results have implications for understanding the behavior of ultracold atomic gases in confined environments and contribute to the broader understanding of few-body physics in mixed systems.

This study examines the Blume-Capel model with infinite-range interactions and quenched disorder in the crystal field, represented by a superposition of two Gaussian distributions. The model's multicritical behavior is analyzed, yielding a diverse range of phase diagrams with distinct topologies for varying distribution widths and probabilities. The tricritical behavior is investigated through fourth-order critical points, revealing the impact of disorder strength on phase diagram complexity. The mean-field approach is employed to uncover the intricate relationships between model parameters and phase transitions, shedding light on the random-field Blume-Capel model's rich and complex behavior.

This study investigates the role of carbon monoxide (CO) in metal-poor dwarf galaxies, specifically targeting Sextans A, a nearby galaxy with 7% solar metallicity. Using deep observations with the IRAM 30m telescope, we detected weak CO J=1-0 emission from the brightest far-infrared peak. The faint emission allows us to constrain the conversion factor from CO luminosity to molecular gas mass, derived from a spatially resolved dust mass map. Our results indicate that this conversion factor is at least 700 times higher than the Milky Way value, suggesting that CO emission is exceedingly weak in extremely metal-poor galaxies. This challenges the traditional view of CO as a primary coolant and tracer of molecular gas in these galaxies, highlighting the need for alternative tracers and a reevaluation of the role of CO in metal-poor environments.

This study presents an in-depth analysis of RXTE/PCA observations of Cyg X-1, a prominent black hole candidate, from 1996 to 1998. A significant correlation was discovered between the characteristic noise frequencies, such as the break frequency, and spectral parameters during the low spectral state. Notably, as the noise frequency increases, the amplitude of reflection also increases, while the primary radiation spectrum becomes steeper. This phenomenon can be attributed to the inward shift of the optically thick accretion disk's inner boundary towards the compact object, resulting in an increased solid angle and influx of soft photons to the Comptonization region. This, in turn, enhances the amount of reflection and steepens the Comptonized spectrum. Furthermore, the correlation between the primary radiation slope and reflection amplitude extends to the soft spectral state. Additionally, a similar correlation was observed in frequency-resolved spectra across the 0.01-15 Hz range, suggesting that longer timescale variations may originate from regions closer to the optically thick disk, yielding steeper Comptonized spectra with larger reflection. These findings provide new insights into the complex relationships between accretion disk dynamics, radiation processes, and variability in black hole systems.

The progenitors of Super Luminous Supernovae (SLSNe) remain an enigma, with hydrogen-poor SLSN hosts often found in highly star-forming dwarf galaxies characterized by extreme emission lines. This study presents a resolved long-slit examination of the host galaxy of the hydrogen-poor SLSN PTF12dam, focusing on the kiloparsec environment of the supernova site to infer the age of the progenitor. The host galaxy exhibits a "tadpole" morphology with uniform properties, and the supernova occurred within a star-forming region. Our analysis reveals a recent starburst superimposed on an older stellar population, with a very young stellar population at the supernova site, estimated to be approximately 3 Myr old, and a metallicity of 12+log(O/H) ≈ 8.0. Notably, no Wolf-Rayet features are observed. These findings suggest that the progenitor of PTF12dam was a massive star, likely exceeding 60 M, and one of the first stars to explode as a supernova in this extremely young starburst, providing insights into the nature of SLSNe progenitors and their host galaxies.

We examine neutrino mixing with bulk fermions in supernova physics, revealing a feedback mechanism that relaxes energy loss constraints by four orders of magnitude. This mechanism impacts protoneutron star evolution through neutrino diffusion interplay. We discuss consistency with SN 1987A and implications for deleptonization, cooling, neutrino flux composition, and the delayed explosion scenario, shedding new light on supernova physics and neutrino behavior in extreme astrophysical environments, with significant consequences for our understanding of these complex phenomena.

The rapid adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) across various sectors, from industrial to home applications, is revolutionizing the way we perceive and interact with the world. The exponential growth of deployed sensors and connected devices is generating vast amounts of data, presenting both tremendous economic opportunities and challenges. Despite the potential of IoT, its benefits remain underexploited due to the disconnect between the physical and cyber worlds, requiring significant manual effort to integrate and utilize information effectively. To bridge this gap, a knowledge framework is necessary to facilitate bilateral understanding between devices, information systems, and applications. This framework would enable the transformation of data into meaningful knowledge, leveraging semantic web technologies to design smart systems. Building on the foundation established in the previous issue, which explored the growth and potential of IoT through the lens of artificial intelligence, this article delves into the benefits of utilizing semantic web technologies to extract valuable insights from sensor data. By harnessing the power of semantic computing, cognitive computing, and perceptual computing, we can create a more intelligent and interconnected world, where IoT devices and applications work in harmony to enhance our physical and virtual lives. This article aims to demonstrate the potential of semantic web technologies in unlocking the full potential of IoT, enabling the development of innovative, smart, and meaningful applications that transform the way we live and interact with our environment.

We present the first comprehensive catalogue of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) from the INTEGRAL mission, comprising 42 objects. The sample includes 10 Seyfert 1, 17 Seyfert 2, and 9 intermediate Seyfert 1.5 galaxies, with a small fraction of blazars (5 objects) and a single galaxy cluster. Notably, no starburst galaxies are detected. Our analysis reveals a ratio of obscured to unobscured AGN consistent with luminosity-dependent unified models. However, only four Compton-thick AGN are identified, suggesting that the remaining Compton-thick AGN required to explain the cosmic hard X-ray background must have lower fluxes than those detected by INTEGRAL to date. This study provides new insights into the properties of local, low-luminosity AGN and has implications for our understanding of the AGN population and the cosmic X-ray background. Further investigation is warranted to reconcile these findings.

Exponential Backoff (EB) is a widely adopted collision resolution mechanism in random-access networks, including Ethernet and Wireless LAN (WLAN), due to its asymptotic throughput stability. However, recent studies have revealed that EB is unsuitable for delay-sensitive applications, as it induces divergent second- and higher-order moments of medium access delay, resulting in a power law distribution. This paper provides a systematic analysis of the tail delay distribution of general backoff functions, including EB, to understand and alleviate this issue. Our results establish a tradeoff between the tail decaying rate of medium access delay distribution and throughput stability, indicating that convergent delay moments can only be achieved when backoff functions grow slower than exponential functions, while non-zero asymptotic throughput requires backoff functions to grow at least as fast as exponential functions. This implies that bounded delay moments and stable throughput are mutually exclusive. We propose Polynomial Backoff (PB) as a viable alternative to EB, which achieves finite delay moments and good throughput performance within a practical range of user population, making it suitable for multimedia applications with stringent delay requirements. Our findings contribute to the design of efficient medium access control protocols for delay-sensitive applications in WLAN and other random-access networks.

This study explores the time-reversal-invariant Hofstadter-Hubbard model, motivated by recent advancements in engineering artificial non-Abelian gauge fields for ultracold fermions in optical lattices. By incorporating a staggered lattice potential and an artificial Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling term, we investigate the model's behavior with and without interactions. In the non-interacting regime, the system exhibits a rich phase diagram, featuring (semi)-metal, normal insulator, and topological insulator phases, as well as a non-Abelian generalization of the Hofstadter butterfly. Using a combination of real-space dynamical mean-field theory, analytical arguments, and Monte Carlo simulations, we examine the effects of strong on-site interactions and determine the interacting phase diagram. Our results reveal a scenario where interactions induce a transition from a normal to a topological insulator. Furthermore, at half-filling and large interactions, the system is described by a quantum spin Hamiltonian, which exhibits exotic magnetic order due to the interplay between Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling and the artificial time-reversal-invariant magnetic field term. We also determine the magnetic phase diagram using real-space dynamical mean-field theory and Monte Carlo simulations, shedding light on the complex behavior of this model.

This study explores a novel class of actions for Lattice QCD with staggered quarks, designed to mitigate flavour symmetry violations inherent to staggered fermions. By replacing gauge field link fields with covariantly smeared fields, these actions extend upon those developed by the MILC collaboration. Our results demonstrate a systematic reduction in flavour symmetry violations in the weak coupling limit. Utilizing the mass splitting between Goldstone and non-Goldstone pions as a metric, we find that these actions exhibit significantly diminished flavour symmetry violations compared to the standard staggered action, surpassing the improvements achieved with the MILC action on quenched configurations.

We investigate the propagation of Alfvén waves in one-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics. In homogeneous media, circularly polarized waves maintain their form, while high-amplitude linearly polarized waves steepen and form current sheets, leading to Poynting flux loss. However, in stratified media, even high-amplitude circularly polarized waves can experience significant Poynting flux loss. Our numerical solutions of the time-dependent MHD equations reveal the complex behavior of Alfvén waves, highlighting the importance of medium properties on wave propagation and energy dissipation. These findings have implications for understanding astrophysical phenomena.

This article examines the asymptotic behavior of a time-varying collection of points on the positive real axis, modeled as exponentials of Brownian motions with drift vectors determined by relative ranks. Under suitable assumptions, the rescaled point process converges to a stationary distribution as time goes to infinity. We investigate the behavior of this point process under the stationary measure as the number of points tends to infinity. Assuming a'continuity at the edge' condition on the drifts, we prove that the points must converge to one of three possible scenarios: (i) all points converge to a single value, (ii) the maximum value diverges while the rest converge to a single value, or (iii) the processes converge in law to a non-trivial Poisson-Dirichlet distribution. Our proof draws inspiration from Talagrand's analysis of the low-temperature phase of Derrida's random energy model of spin glasses. The main result establishes a universality property for the Banner-Fernholz-Karatzas models, facilitating explicit asymptotic computations using known results about the Poisson-Dirichlet law. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of the behavior of equity markets and provides a foundation for further research in this area. The findings have implications for the study of stochastic processes and their applications in finance and other fields.

This article presents a methodology for synthesizing safety-preserving controllers for a class of feedback linearisable nonlinear systems. A high-gain observer is utilized to estimate the system state, and a bound on the distance between state and output feedback trajectories is derived. As the observer gain increases, this bound converges to zero, enabling the recovery of safety properties under output feedback and control saturation constraints. By designing feedback linearising controllers that ensure stability, we construct the maximal safety-invariant set, which guarantees safe trajectories for all initial states within a given time horizon, thereby ensuring reliable system operation under output feedback control.

This paper improves upon existing upper bounds for the @xmath1-distance domination numbers of grid graphs. Building on Chang's 1992 construction and subsequent work by Goncalves et al. and Fata et al., we refine the approach to @xmath1-distance dominating sets. Our results enhance the understanding of grid graph domination, providing tighter bounds for the @xmath1-distance domination numbers. The improved upper bounds have significant implications for graph theory and its applications, offering a more accurate characterization of grid graph structures and their domination properties, and advancing the field of graph theory research.

This study proposes two novel tests of the cosmic distance duality relation using galaxy cluster observations and X-ray measurements. By employing Gaussian processes, a non-parametric method, we derive constraints on potential departures from the relation. Our results show no evidence of deviation, reinforcing the adopted cosmological and astrophysical hypotheses. These findings are crucial for building a consistent cosmological framework, as any departure from the relation could indicate new physics or systematic errors. Our tests demonstrate the reliability of the cosmic distance duality relation, supporting its role as a fundamental milestone in cosmology, with implications for future research.

This article explores the development of MacWilliams identities for linear codes over poset metrics, a generalized metric that encompasses various well-known metrics, including the Rosenbloom-Tsfasman and Hamming metrics. Recently, research has focused on codes over poset metrics, particularly in the context of channels with localized error occurrences. However, it has been shown that MacWilliams identities are not universally applicable to codes over poset metrics. To address this limitation, this paper introduces novel poset level weight enumerators for linear codes over Frobenius commutative rings. We derive MacWilliams-type identities for these enumerators, which significantly generalize previous results in the literature. Notably, our identities yield several well-known weight enumerators, including Hamming, Rosenbloom-Tsfasman, and complete weight enumerators, as corollaries. This work contributes to the advancement of coding theory, particularly in the realm of poset metrics and MacWilliams identities, with implications for error-correcting codes and data transmission.

We introduce Archeops, a balloon-borne bolometer experiment mapping the sky at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths. Its primary goal is to study cosmic microwave background anisotropies, deriving cosmological parameters. The first scientific flight's sky coverage map is presented, paving the way for understanding the universe's cosmology and interstellar medium properties.

This article presents the results of optical spectroscopy of two flux-density limited samples of radio sources, the 8C-N EC and 7C-III samples, selected at frequencies of 38 and 151 MHz, respectively, in the same region around the North Ecliptic Cap. These samples are among the first low-frequency selected samples with no spectral or angular size selection, and have nearly complete redshift information, making them valuable resources for understanding the cosmic evolution of radio sources and their hosts and environments. The 151-MHz 7C-III sample, with a flux limit of 0.5 Jy, is the more spectroscopically complete, with reliable redshifts obtained for 44 out of 54 radio sources. The 8C sample, with a flux limit of 1.0 Jy, contains 58 sources, with 46 having fairly reliable redshifts. We discuss potential biases in the observed redshift distribution and highlight interesting individual objects, including cases of probable gravitational lensing. By combining the 8C-N EC and 7C-III samples, we create the first sample selected on low-frequency flux in the rest-frame of the source, allowing us to remove the bias associated with an increasing rest-frame selection frequency with redshift. Our analysis reveals that traditional flux-density based selection leads to an overestimate of the steepness of the correlation of radio source size with redshift. This study provides new insights into the properties of low-luminosity radio galaxies and the effects of selection biases on our understanding of the cosmic evolution of radio sources. The results have significant implications for our understanding of the evolution of active galaxies and the role of gravitational lensing in shaping our observations of the universe.

This study applies the Light-Front Quark Model (LFQM) to calculate transition matrix elements for heavy hadron decays. However, traditional LFQM wave functions yield decay constants that contradict experimental data, indicating a need for modification. To address this, we derive a new set of wave functions for the relevant states, ensuring orthogonality and fitting decay constants to experimental values. Inspired by the hydrogen atom, we propose an analytical form for these modified wave functions. Using these refined wave functions, our calculated decay constants align closely with empirical data. Furthermore, we compute radiative decay rates, finding that our predictions are consistent with experimental results within theoretical and experimental uncertainties, thus validating the modified LFQM approach for heavy hadron decay studies. This advancement enhances the model's accuracy and reliability in describing hadronic phenomena.

This study investigates the real-time dynamics of spin chains driven out of thermal equilibrium by an initial temperature gradient using density matrix renormalization group methods. The results show that the nonequilibrium energy current rapidly saturates to a finite value when the linear-response thermal conductivity is infinite, characterized by a nonzero Drude weight. Notably, a nonintegrable dimerized chain may support dissipationless transport. The steady-state current is found to be a function of the linear conductance, following a Stefan-Boltzmann law. This functional form is verified for the XXX ferromagnet using thermodynamic Bethe ansatz, which agrees with numerical results. Additionally, the study briefly explores inhomogeneous systems with varying bulk parameters and Luttinger liquid boundary physics induced by single impurities, providing new insights into nonequilibrium transport phenomena in spin chains. The findings have implications for understanding energy transport in quantum systems.

This study experimentally investigates the diffusion and reaction of gaseous HCl and NH3 in silica aerogel rods with 92% porosity and 50nm average pore size. The reaction forms solid NH4Cl, depositing in thin sheet-like structures. Numerical analysis reveals significant differences from previous studies due to distinct boundary conditions. The impact of random nucleation centers and aerogel inhomogeneities on structure formation is also numerically examined, providing insights into the complex reaction dynamics within the aerogel's unique porous structure. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of reactive transport in porous media.

This study presents the findings of a comprehensive multiplicity survey of T Tauri stars in the Chamaeleon I and Taurus-Auriga star-forming regions. Utilizing high-resolution spectra from the Magellan Clay 6.5m telescope, we achieved a typical radial velocity precision of 20-50 ms^-1, with slower rotators exhibiting better precision. Multi-epoch data were obtained for a significant subset of stars, enabling the identification of binaries based on radial velocity variations. Our results reveal eight close binaries and four close triples, with three and two being new discoveries, respectively. The spectroscopic multiplicity fractions derived for Chamaeleon I and Taurus-Auriga are comparable, mirroring the results of field star surveys in similar mass and period regimes. Notably, our findings suggest that the frequency of close companions does not depend on primary mass, contrasting with results from imaging surveys. Furthermore, no strong correlation was found between accretion and close multiplicity, implying that close companions are unlikely to be the primary cause of accretion shutdown in weak-lined T Tauri stars. These results have significant implications for our understanding of star formation and planetary evolution, highlighting the potential for radial velocity surveys to detect hot Jupiter planets in slowly rotating young stars.

This study explores the transport properties of helimagnets with arbitrary helical structures, considering both magnetic helix and electric polarization. A general scattering matrix treatment is proposed to investigate the spin-dependent diffracted transmission induced by sinusoidal spatial modulation. By modeling a monolayer magnetic helix as a diffraction barrier, we examine the conductance and shot noise properties of a normal metal/helimagnet/normal metal system. Our findings reveal that shot noise is suppressed and exhibits rise-and-fall variations due to interference between diffracted channels. Notably, sharp changes in shot noise occur when diffracted beams transition into evanescent modes at specific helimagnet spiral wave vectors. Furthermore, we apply our approach to a real multiferroic helimagnet, where ferroelectricity and helimagnetism coexist. The results show distinct separation of clockwise and counterclockwise spin helices in the conductance and shot noise spectrum, with variation patterns influenced by both helimagnetism and electric polarization. Our work provides new insights into the transport properties of helimagnets and their potential applications in spintronics and multiferroic devices.

This study explores the density dependence of symmetry energy in asymmetric nuclear matter using the extended relativistic mean field (ERMF) model. The model incorporates self and mixed interaction terms for scalar-isoscalar, vector-isoscalar, and vector-isovector mesons up to the quartic order. Twenty-six parameterizations of the ERMF model are employed, all of which are compatible with the bulk properties of finite nuclei. The symmetry energy behavior for several parameter sets is consistent with empirical constraints derived from isospin diffusion data analysis. The neutron-skin thickness in the 208Pb nucleus is predicted to be within the range of 0.18-0.22 fm, in agreement with Skyrme Hartree-Fock model predictions. The role of mixed interaction terms in shaping the density dependence of symmetry energy is also investigated, highlighting their significance in understanding the behavior of asymmetric nuclear matter. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the nuclear matter equation of state.

The Virgo detector, a French-Italian interferometric gravitational wave observatory, is nearing completion of its commissioning phase. At its core lies a Michelson interferometer, equipped with 3 km long optical cavities in its arms and a power-recycling mirror. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the current status of the system, highlighting its attained sensitivity and performance during recent commissioning runs. The interferometer has progressed through several intermediate stages and is now operational in the recombined configuration. Key features include a 144 m long input mode-cleaner for spatial filtering of the input laser beam and superattenuators that suspend the main optics, providing exceptional seismic isolation. The 3 km long Fabry-Perot arm cavities are maintained in resonance with the laser light, while the Michelson interferometer is stabilized on the dark fringe. An automatic mirror alignment system, utilizing the Anderson technique, has been successfully implemented for the arm cavities. The gravitational wave signal is extracted from the light exiting the dark port, filtered by an output mode-cleaner, and detected by a photo detector. This setup marks the final precursor to the detector's ultimate configuration, which will incorporate power recycling, paving the way for enhanced sensitivity and the detection of gravitational waves.

This study generalizes the 3D spring-pendulum system, examining its integrability based on parameters influencing spring elasticity and nonlinearity. We demonstrate non-integrability for certain parameter values and apply Morales-Ramis theory and higher-order variational equations to investigate a specific case, providing insights into the system's behavior and proving non-integrability under particular conditions, advancing understanding of complex dynamical systems.

This article investigates the problem of parameter estimation for stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with small noise and fast oscillating parameters. We consider three distinct regimes, depending on the relative rates at which the noise intensity and homogenization parameter converge to zero. For each regime, we construct the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) and examine its consistency and asymptotic normality properties. Our theoretical results provide insights into the behavior of the MLE under different scaling limits. To illustrate the practical applicability of our methods, we conduct a simulation study using the first-order Langevin equation with a two-scale potential. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the MLE in estimating the model parameters. This research contributes to the understanding of parameter estimation for multiscale diffusions, which is crucial in modeling complex systems with rough energy landscapes. The findings have implications for various fields, including dynamical systems and statistical inference. Our work also highlights the importance of careful analysis of the scaling limits in SDEs with small noise and fast oscillating parameters.

We prove the generalized second law for semiclassical Rindler horizons with arbitrary interacting quantum fields, requiring boost and null translation symmetry, and discuss potential extensions to more general scenarios.

This article presents the data acquisition system developed for the MuLAN muon lifetime experiment at the Paul Scherrer Institute. The system is designed to record muon decays at high rates of up to 1 MHz and acquire data at speeds of 60 MB/sec. A parallel network of dual-processor machines and a novel acquisition cycle approach enable the system to achieve its design goals. The system also features a flexible control and diagnostics scheme, as well as a custom web interface for real-time monitoring of experimental conditions, ensuring efficient and reliable data collection for the MuLAN experiment.

This study examines the multiphoton dynamics of a qutrit-photon system in ultrastrong and deep strong coupling regimes. A polar-configured qutrit with two lower levels having mean dipole moments is considered. The research investigates direct multiphoton resonant transitions, revealing generalized Rabi oscillations and collapses in atomic excitation probabilities. In the deep strong coupling regime, the ground state exhibits nonclassical properties. The findings provide insight into the system's behavior, highlighting the significance of ultrastrong couplings in inducing unique quantum phenomena, such as revivals in atomic excitation probabilities and strictly nonclassical ground state properties. Quantum coherence is preserved.

Title: Radiative Corrections to Gaugino and Higgsino Masses in the Minimal Supersymmetric Model Abstract: We present a comprehensive one-loop calculation of the radiative corrections to the masses of gauginos and higgsinos in the Minimal Supersymmetric Model (MSSM), incorporating all sectors of the theory within the on-mass-shell renormalization scheme. Our results indicate that a tree-level massless gluino acquires a radiative mass ranging from 0 to 3 GeV, primarily due to the top/stop contribution, which directly depends on the off-diagonal element of the squark mass matrix. For a massive gluino, we find significant corrections to its mass, reaching up to 40% for a 125 GeV gluino. The corrections to neutralino and chargino masses from the gauge/Higgs/gaugino/higgsino sector are generally negligible. However, the lightest neutralino can receive corrections exceeding 25%, with notable variations across the parameter space. By combining our findings with the constraints from LEP and CDF searches, we establish lower bounds on the neutralino and chargino masses at the one-loop level. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these radiative corrections impact the currently excluded regions of the parameter space, providing a refined understanding of the MSSM's phenomenology. Our work offers a precise calculation of the radiative corrections to gaugino and higgsino masses, essential for ongoing and future supersymmetry searches at high-energy colliders.

This study presents a meta-analysis of Keck spectra of extragalactic globular clusters (GCs) in eight galaxies, spanning dwarfs to massive ellipticals. By comparing metal-poor and metal-rich GCs to their Galactic counterparts, we infer ages of ≥10 Gyr. This spectroscopic analysis is the largest to date, constraining GC ages in a diverse galaxy sample. Our findings support the high-redshift formation of most GCs in massive galaxies. We propose a formation scenario that integrates accretion and in situ approaches, contextualized within hierarchical merging galaxy formation. This framework provides new insights into the origins of GC subpopulations, shedding light on galaxy evolution and assembly.

This study presents the first mid-infrared spectral energy distribution of a quiescent molecular cloud in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), obtained using the Infrared Space Observatory's (ISO) camera (ISOCAM). The observed spectrum, which peaks at 6.2, 7.7, and 11.3 μm, exhibits broad emission bands similar to those found in the interstellar medium (ISM) of the Milky Way. The presence of these bands, attributed to large aromatic hydrocarbon molecules, suggests that the same carriers are responsible for the mid-infrared emission in both galaxies. The estimated absorption by these molecules is approximately 10% of the total dust absorption, comparable to the Galactic case. Notably, the SMC's dust extinction curve lacks the prominent 2175 Å feature characteristic of Milky Way dust, which might imply that aromatic hydrocarbons are not the carriers of this feature. However, considering the biased sampling of SMC extinction curves towards hot, luminous stars where aromatic hydrocarbons may be destroyed, the absence of the 2175 bump may not be representative of SMC dust as a whole. The detection of aromatic hydrocarbons in the SMC, a galaxy with an order-of-magnitude lower metallicity than the Milky Way, highlights the ubiquity of these molecules in various interstellar environments. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the composition and properties of dust in different galaxies, and the role of aromatic hydrocarbons in shaping their spectral energy distributions.

This study explores the existence of Z(3) metastable states within the Polyakov Quark Meson (PQM) model, incorporating dynamical quarks. Our results indicate that for temperatures above the chiral transition temperature, Z(3) metastable states emerge, with an energy density of approximately 2 MeV at zero chemical potential. Notably, the introduction of finite chemical potential amplifies this effect. A phase shift of π/3 is observed in the metastable vacua at zero chemical potential. The substantial energy density difference between true and Z(3) metastable vacua suggests a pronounced explicit symmetry breaking effect due to quarks in the PQM model. Comparisons with a modified Polyakov loop potential reveal distinct differences in symmetry breaking. Furthermore, we investigate the potential for domain growth in a quenched transition to the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, shedding light on the quark-hadron transition and Z(3) metastable states.

This study examines the development of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI) in the context of coronal mass ejections (CMEs) expanding through the ambient corona, utilizing high-resolution images from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). Observations suggest a large-scale magnetic field, primarily tangential to the interface, on both the CME and background sides, yet insufficient to suppress the instability. Furthermore, the ambient corona exhibits turbulent characteristics, implying that the criteria for KHI development diverge from the laminar case. To investigate the evolution of KHI in a turbulent environment, we conducted three-dimensional simulations of incompressible magnetohydrodynamic equations, incorporating a hyperbolic tangent velocity profile to mimic the CME-corona interface and a stationary stirring force to generate background turbulence. Our results show that turbulence attenuates the growth rate of the instability. The presence of KHI in observations sets an upper limit to the correlation length of coronal background turbulence, providing valuable insights into the complex dynamics of CMEs and their interaction with the ambient corona. These findings contribute to our understanding of the role of turbulence in shaping the evolution of KHI in astrophysical contexts.

This study examines the scattering of massless planar scalar waves by a charged, non-rotating black hole, utilizing partial wave methods to calculate scattering and absorption cross sections across various incident wavelengths. Our numerical results are compared to semi-classical approximations derived from geodesic analysis, demonstrating excellent agreement. The phenomenon of glory in the backward direction is investigated, revealing a correlation with the properties of the photon orbit. The impact of black hole charge on scattering and absorption is scrutinized, yielding a decrease in absorption cross section and an increase in the angular width of interference fringes at large angles as charge increases. Notably, the glory spot in the backward direction broadens. These effects are interpreted through the lens of our geodesic analysis, providing insight into the interplay between black hole charge and wave scattering phenomena. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of black hole physics.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of the spectral norm of real symmetric random matrices. We consider an ensemble of such matrices with independent, identically distributed entries following a symmetric probability distribution. Our results show that if a moment with a positive exponent exists, the probability of the spectral norm exceeding a certain threshold is bounded as the matrix size increases. This bound is independent of the underlying probability distribution. Our approach builds upon the work of Ya. Sinai and A. Soshnikov, with modifications to study high moments of Wigner random matrices. The method is applied to the ensemble of large dilute random matrices, providing new insights into their spectral properties. The findings have implications for understanding the behavior of large random matrices in various fields.

This article tackles the challenge of continuous action recognition, which requires simultaneous classification and segmentation. Building upon the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) framework, we introduce a novel visual alignment technique called Dynamic Frame Warping (DFW). DFW performs isolated recognition by aligning a test sequence with a model sequence based on per-frame video representations. To enable concomitant recognition and segmentation, we propose two extensions: One-Pass DFW and Two-Pass DFW. These methods, inspired by speech recognition, are novel applications to continuous visual action recognition. We evaluate our techniques using the RAVEL dataset and the public-domain Hollywood-1 and Hollywood-2 datasets. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed isolated and continuous recognition algorithms, which are compared to recently published methods. The findings highlight the potential of DFW and its extensions for improving continuous action recognition, a crucial aspect of human-computer interaction and video analysis applications.

We derive an effective interaction potential for spatially indirect excitons in quantum well structures using an adiabatic approximation. Path integral Monte Carlo simulations are employed to study exciton crystallization and the quantum melting phase transition in a 2D system. The superfluid fraction is calculated as a function of density, vanishing upon crystallization. Our results complement previous studies of quantum dipole systems, predicting a second quantum phase transition at high densities due to softening of the inter-exciton interaction's short-range part, leading to crystal melting. This phenomenon is uniquely captured by our theoretical framework.

This study investigates the spatiotemporal evolution of a confined Bose-Einstein condensate using numerical integration of the time-dependent Gross-Pitaevskii equation. The results show a spiral atomic density profile emerging from self-interference between expanding and reflecting nonlinear matter waves. This profile degenerates into an embedding structure, comprising an inner part retaining initial state memory and an outer part forming necklace-like rings. Phase plot analysis reveals discrete concentric belts with large gradients, indicating dark solitons at ring density notches. The dynamics involve spontaneous creation and annihilation of vortex-antivortex pairs, while total vorticity remains invariant, providing insights into complex nonlinear wave behavior.

This article explores the relationship between Lorentzian distance and global hyperbolicity in spacetime geometry. We prove that a non-total imprisoning spacetime is globally hyperbolic if and only if the Lorentzian distance is continuous for every metric choice in the conformal class. Furthermore, we establish that a non-total imprisoning spacetime is causally simple if the Lorentzian distance is continuous wherever it vanishes, for every metric in the conformal class. Additionally, we show that a strongly causal spacetime is causally continuous if there exists at least one metric in the conformal class for which the Lorentzian distance is continuous wherever it vanishes. These results provide new insights into the interplay between causal structure and Lorentzian distance, shedding light on the fundamental properties of spacetime geometry. Our findings have implications for the study of Lorentzian geometry and its applications in physics.

This study examines the unusual Type IC supernova SN 1998BW, potentially associated with the gamma-ray burst GRB 980425. Utilizing a synchrotron self-absorption model for its radio emission, we infer that the synchrotron-emitting gas is expanding into a circumstellar medium with a density profile of approximately ρ ∝ r^(-1) at relativistic speeds. Assuming constant efficiencies of relativistic electron and magnetic field production, the derived circumstellar density is consistent with expectations around the massive star core thought to be the progenitor of SN 1998BW. The explosion energy in material moving at velocity βc is estimated to be ∼ 10^(52) ergs, with a preference for higher values. The observed rise in radio light curves around days 10-20 is attributed to an increase in the blast wave energy by a factor of ∼ 5, likely caused by a shell of matter catching up with the decelerating shock front. This energy input mechanism is difficult to reconcile with shock-accelerated high-velocity ejecta from a supernova, suggesting instead irregular energy input from a central engine, similar to models invoked for typical gamma-ray bursts. Our findings strengthen the link between SN 1998BW and GRB 980425, providing insights into the nature of these extraordinary events. The implications of this study highlight the importance of continued research into the connection between supernovae and gamma-ray bursts.

This article reexamines the large x behavior of Jacobi polynomials with varying parameters α and β for γ and δ. Despite being a well-studied topic, existing literature often presents complicated or incorrect results. Our approach utilizes a novel representation of the parameters in terms of two integrals, whose asymptotic behavior is analyzed using standard tools: Laplace integral and the method of stationary phase. We prove that when α > -1/2, the Jacobi polynomial exhibits exponential decay, and derive corresponding exponential upper bounds. For α < -1/2, the decay rate is shown to be |x|^(-1-2α), while for α = -1/2, the decay rate is |x|^{-1} log|x|. Furthermore, when β = -1/2, the polynomial decays exponentially if and only if γ is an integer, and increases exponentially otherwise. Our results provide a clear and concise understanding of the asymptotic behavior of Jacobi polynomials, correcting flaws in the existing literature and offering new insights into this fundamental area of study.

This study models the impact of low salinity water injection on contact angles in oil-rich porous media using a network model of disordered pores. A dynamic wettability altering mechanism is introduced, where the wetting property of each pore changes over time based on cumulative water flow. Simulations reveal that deviating from oil-wet conditions remobilizes stuck oil clusters, increasing oil fractional flow. However, the rate of increase depends on the alteration in wetting angle. Notably, at a critical angle, the system exhibits critical slowing down, characterized by two dynamic critical exponents. These findings provide insight into the complex dynamics of wettability alteration in porous media, with implications for enhanced oil recovery and fluid transport in disordered systems. The results have significant implications for optimizing oil extraction and fluid flow in various industrial applications.

Here is a 214-word abstract for the given academic article title: The forthcoming revision of the International System of Units (SI) will introduce a new definition of the ampere based on the elementary charge, replacing the traditional definition rooted in Ampere's force law. This change will enable the full exploitation of quantum physics to realize the ampere, offering enhanced precision and accuracy. However, a quantum-based realization of the ampere, accurate to within a relative value and fulfilling traceability requirements, has remained elusive despite significant efforts to develop single-electron tunneling devices. This article presents a breakthrough in the development of a practical and universal programmable quantum current generator, leveraging Ohm's law in a quantum circuit that combines the quantum Hall resistance and Josephson voltage standards with a superconducting cryogenic amplifier. Our device generates quantized currents in the milliampere range, with a measurement uncertainty of, demonstrating the potential for improved current measurement traceability. The calibration of digital ammeters using this new quantum current source has shown promising results, paving the way for further advancements in metrology and fundamental physics, such as the development of a quantum multimeter or accurate comparisons to single electron pumps. This innovative approach has significant implications for the realization of the new SI definition of the ampere.

This study presents a virial equation of state for low-density nuclear matter, comprising neutrons, protons, and alpha particles. The model-independent approach provides a benchmark for nuclear equations of state at low densities. By calculating second virial coefficients from binding energies and scattering phase shifts, we account for contributions from bound nuclei and the resonant continuum. This framework enables the inclusion of strong-interaction corrections to nuclear statistical equilibrium models. Our results yield model-independent predictions for various properties of nuclear matter across densities, temperatures, and compositions. Notably, the predicted alpha particle concentration deviates from existing equations of state used in supernova simulations, offering new insights into the neutrinosphere physics. The virial equation of state significantly enhances our understanding of low-density nuclear matter, providing a foundational tool for refining supernova models and informing future research in nuclear astrophysics. The implications of this work are far-reaching, with potential to reshape our understanding of complex astrophysical phenomena.

This article reviews recent findings on driven dissipative condensates, focusing on coherence and superfluidity in weakly-interacting boson systems. Dimensionality and anisotropy significantly impact the effects of driving and dissipation. In 3D, equilibrium behavior is observed at large scales for static correlations, while dynamics are altered by microscopic driving. In 2D, isotropic systems exhibit destroyed algebraic order, but anisotropic systems can maintain algebraic phase correlations. The implications for phase coherence experiments are discussed, and potential measurements to directly probe superfluidity are outlined, providing insights into the complex behavior of driven dissipative condensates.

Title: Planetary Formation in Close Binary Star Systems: Numerical Simulations of Terrestrial Planet Growth Abstract: The majority of stars reside in binary or multiple star systems, yet traditional models of planet formation have focused on the growth of bodies orbiting a single, isolated star. Recent observations have revealed disk material surrounding both components of young close binary star systems, suggesting that planet formation can occur in these environments. This study investigates the late stages of terrestrial planet growth in circumbinary disks around close binary star systems, with stellar separations ranging from 0.05 to 0.4 astronomical units (AU) and binary eccentricities between 0 and 0.8. We conducted numerical simulations using an initial disk of planetary embryos similar to those used in previous studies of our solar system and the α Centauri AB binary star system. Our results show that planetary systems formed around binaries with apastron distances less than 0.2 AU are comparable to those around single stars, whereas systems with larger maximum separations tend to be sparser, with fewer planets, particularly interior to 1 AU. We also provide scaling formulae to apply our results to various systems with different total stellar masses, disk sizes, and planetesimal properties. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of planetary formation in binary star systems and the potential for terrestrial planet formation in these environments. Our study demonstrates that the orbital architecture of close binary star systems can significantly impact the formation and stability of terrestrial planets, highlighting the need for further research into the complex interactions between binary star systems and their surrounding planetary disks.

This article introduces the concept of ribbon twists, equivalent to crossing changes for knots, to Seifert surfaces. A Seifert surface is considered untwisted if isotopic to a standard n-fold punctured torus. We prove that canonical Seifert surfaces are twist trivial, meaning they can be untwisted via ribbon twists, establishing a foundational result in the study of Seifert surface topology and its relation to knot theory.

Here is a potential abstract for the given article title: We present high angular resolution (sub)millimeter line and continuum observations of the massive star forming region W3(OH) obtained with the Submillimeter Array. Our observations reveal the first detection of two bipolar outflows emanating from the young and massive Turner-Welch (TW) protobinary system, as traced by carbon monoxide emission. These outflows are characterized by masses of approximately 10 M⊙ and high collimation factors (>10), suggesting a strong connection to the radio jets and 22 GHz maser water outflow energized by the TW system. Additionally, our observations of 890 μm continuum emission and thermal CH3OH emission imply the presence of two rotating circumstellar disk-like structures, with sizes of approximately 1500 AU and masses of a few M⊙. These disk-like structures appear to be the driving force behind the molecular outflows and radio jets. Our findings suggest that the young stars powering the outflows and surrounded by these massive disk-like structures may be B-type stars, providing new insights into the early stages of massive star formation.

This paper addresses the limited integration of mathematical modeling in undergraduate biology programs due to differing perceptions between mathematics and biology disciplines. We extend the "rule of five" to develop a modeling framework that distinguishes between models as representations and modeling as a process. This framework facilitates cross-disciplinary communication and enhances student learning by providing a common language and structure for modeling. By applying this framework, we aim to promote the incorporation of quantitative skills in biology education and foster collaboration between mathematicians and biologists. Improved communication and student outcomes are anticipated.

This study explores the potential of nanoporous materials with anisotropic pore lattices to induce strong heat transport directionality in isotropic materials, a desirable property for various applications. Using density functional theory and the phonon Boltzmann transport equation, we investigated the thermal conductivity of nanoporous silicon with different anisotropic pore lattices. Our calculations reveal a significant directionality in thermal conductivity, governed by the variation in pore-pore distances along the Cartesian axes. The anisotropic pore lattice distortion creates a phonon bottleneck, leading to directionality in heat transport.
