In contrast, diffusive heat transport calculations using Fourier's law yield substantially smaller anisotropy, highlighting the crucial role of phonon-size effects in modulating thermal transport directionality. Our findings not only enhance our understanding of nanoscale heat transport but also demonstrate the promise of nanoporous materials in controlling thermal conductivity anisotropy, paving the way for innovative applications in transverse thermoelectrics and thermal management in electronic devices. The results of this study have significant implications for the development of materials with tailored thermal properties.

This article explores the electron transport properties of a device comprising two linear chain leads connected by a time-dependent interleads coupling, which is switched on non-adiabatically. Utilizing time-dependent nonequilibrium Green's functions, we derive a numerically exact expression for the particle current and examine its evolution from the transient to the long-time steady-state regime. Our results show that the current initially overshoots its expected steady-state value, oscillates, and decays as a power law before settling into a steady-state value consistent with the Landauer formula. The power-law parameters are found to depend on the applied bias voltage, coupling strengths, and switch-on speed, with lower bias voltages leading to a longer decay time for the oscillating transient current. Furthermore, the power-law decay suggests an equivalent series resistor-inductor-capacitor circuit with time-dependent properties, which is a generic feature in nano-circuits with dynamical switches. We also investigate the current characteristics in a nano-oscillator model, where the interleads coupling is sinusoidally modulated, and find that the current does not strictly follow the sinusoidal form of the coupling. Instead, the maximum current occurs at times dependent on the bias potential, nearest-neighbor coupling, and interleads coupling, highlighting the complex dynamics of electron transport in nano-devices with time-dependent couplings. Our findings provide new insights into the transient and steady-state behavior of electron transport in nano-scale devices, which is crucial for the design and optimization of future nano-electronic devices.

This article addresses the problem of coloring k-colorable graphs using the minimum number of colors. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm is presented, which colors a 3-colorable graph with Δ + 1 colors, where Δ is the maximum degree of any vertex. This achievement marks the first non-trivial approximation result as a function of the maximum degree, surpassing the best known approximation ratio in terms of the number of vertices. The result is generalized to k-colorable graphs, yielding a coloring using O(Δ) colors. Inspired by recent work on semidefinite optimization, a duality relationship is established between the optimal solution to the semidefinite program and the Lovász θ-function. Additionally, lower bounds are demonstrated on the gap between the optimal solution and the actual chromatic number, revealing new insights into the Lovász θ-function. The findings contribute to the understanding of graph coloring and semidefinite optimization, with implications for approximation algorithms and combinatorial optimization.

This study demonstrates the significant impact of static longitudinal and transverse electric fields on electron acceleration by a long laser beam in a sub-critical plasma, leading to the generation of super-ponderomotive electrons. The plasma fields reduce the axial dephasing rate between the electron and the laser, enhancing axial momentum and total electron energy. This mechanism is relevant to experiments with solid-density targets, where a sub-critical plasma layer forms due to prepulse effects. The findings highlight the crucial role of plasma fields in modifying electron acceleration, with implications for high-energy particle generation and laser-plasma interactions in dense plasma environments.

Title: The Numbers and Types of Evolved Massive Stars Found in Nearby Galaxies Provide an Exacting Test of Stellar Evolution Models Abstract: The Magellanic Clouds, due to their proximity and abundant massive star populations, have long been a crucial testing ground for stellar evolution models. Despite their perceived completeness, ongoing discoveries of Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars in these systems highlight the need for continued exploration. This study presents the second year of our multi-year survey for WR stars in the Magellanic Clouds, building upon the nine new Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) WRs discovered in the first year, including six novel WN3/O3-type stars. These stars exhibit WN3-type emission and O3-type absorption features but are significantly fainter than expected for WN3+O3 V binaries. Our second-year findings include four additional WR stars, two of which are also WN3/O3s, and two slash WRs, increasing the total known LMC WRs to 152, with 13 (8.2%) discovered by our survey, now estimated to be approximately 60% complete. The spatial distribution of WN3/O3s mirrors that of other LMC WRs, suggesting a common progenitor. Notably, five of the 12 known Small Magellanic Cloud WRs may be analogous to these WN3/O3s rather than binaries. Additional discoveries include an ONfp-type star and a peculiar emission-line object. Our study underscores the importance of comprehensive surveys in refining stellar evolution models and highlights the complexities of massive star populations in the Magellanic Clouds, with implications for our understanding of these critical phases of stellar life.

This study presents high-resolution observations of photoevaporating disk-tail systems located near O-type stars, utilizing HST/NICMOS Paschen α (Paα) images and low- and high-resolution IRS spectra. Notably, no Paα emission is detected in any of the systems, yielding upper limits that correspond to approximately 2.3 × 10^4 M⊙ of mass in hydrogen in the tails. This suggests a severe depletion of gas in these systems. Complementary IRAC data and low-resolution IRS spectra (5-12 μm) indicate the presence of an inner disk, while high-resolution, long-wavelength IRS spectra (14-30 μm) confirm the existence of a gas-free "tail" composed of 0.01-1 μm dust grains originating from the outer regions of circumstellar disks. Our findings support theoretical predictions that photoevaporation efficiently removes gas from the outer regions of protoplanetary disks within approximately 10^7 years, leaving behind a more robust, potentially gas-rich inner disk component. The absence of gas in the outer disk enables larger solid bodies to undergo frequent collisions, producing elevated amounts of dust that are subsequently stripped from the system by the O star's photon pressure, forming a gas-free dusty tail. These observations provide valuable insights into the dynamics and evolution of photoevaporating disk-tail systems.

This article addresses a fundamental problem in accelerator physics: the errors introduced by finite beam position monitor (BPM) resolution in the reconstruction of orbit parameters through least squares fitting. Despite the existence of manual calculations for the covariance matrix of reconstruction errors in the case of transversely uncoupled motion, the application of these solutions to the design of optimal measurement systems remains non-trivial. To deepen our understanding of this issue, we introduce a dynamic perspective to what initially appears to be a static problem. By conceptualizing a virtual beam composed of particles generated from all possible BPM reading errors, we can analyze its propagation along the beam line. This virtual beam exhibits characteristics such as emittances, energy spread, dispersions, and betatron functions, which become inherent properties of the BPM measurement system. By examining these parameters, particularly error emittances and root mean square (RMS) error energy spreads, it becomes possible to compare the performance of different BPM systems or to adjust a given system to achieve a desired balance between coordinate and momentum reconstruction errors. This approach enables the matching of error betatron functions at points of interest, thereby enhancing the precision of beam parameter reconstruction. Our method offers a novel framework for optimizing BPM systems and mitigating the impact of finite resolution on orbit parameter determination, contributing to advancements in accelerator physics and performance.

This article presents a theoretical examination of the static structure factor of a Bose gas. Utilizing low-order expansion theory, the two-body density distribution is constructed, and various trial functions for the radial distribution function are employed to introduce atomic correlations. The Bose gas is studied in both homogeneous and inhomogeneous states, with the latter trapped in a harmonic oscillator well. The results show that a suitable parametrization of the trial functions can accurately reproduce experimental values of the static structure factor in both cases. The phonon range behavior of the calculated static structure factor is also investigated and discussed for finite and infinite Bose gases, providing insights into the system's correlations and structure.

This study utilizes 20,000 @xmath0 @xmath1 decays from Fermilab Experiment 789 to investigate @xmath2 and @xmath3 production in 800GeV proton-nucleon collisions. Differential cross sections and nuclear dependences are measured for charmonium, charm, and beauty production. Results show charm and beauty production align with perturbative QCD calculations, while charmonium cross sections exceed color-singlet model predictions. This discrepancy suggests additional mechanisms, such as color-octet production, may be involved. The nuclear dependence of production cross sections offers a new tool for understanding charmonium production, providing valuable insights into its underlying mechanisms.

This article examines the dynamics of an electric charge in the presence of a magnetically charged event within a three-dimensional spacetime framework. By leveraging the conservation of spacetime angular momentum, we derive a first integral of the equations of motion, facilitating a comprehensive analysis. Numerical simulations reveal that upon crossing the event's light cone, an initially stationary electric charge begins to rotate and decelerate. The problem involves two key length scales: the characteristic length, dependent on the electric charge, mass, and magnetic charge, and the spacetime impact parameter. Notably, for specific impact parameters, the particle undergoes a abrupt quarter-turn rotation, coming to rest at the event's past spatial location after a time proportional to the impact parameter. This phenomenon serves as a distinct signature of the magnetic event's presence. An alternative derivation of the angular momentum expression, utilizing Noether's theorem in the magnetic representation, is provided in the appendix, offering additional insight into the underlying physics. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the intricate interactions between electric charges and magnetically charged events in spacetime.

This study examines the generation of two-mode entanglement in a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate trapped in a double-well potential. By utilizing the Holstein-Primakoff transformation, we demonstrate the problem's exact solvability for low excitation numbers due to atom-atom interactions. The condensate's symmetric Gaussian nature allows for direct measurement of entanglement of formation via quadrature fluctuations. Our results reveal significant two-mode squeezing occurs with sufficiently strong interspecies interaction, leading to strong entanglement between the components. This finding has implications for quantum information processing and highlights the importance of interspecies interactions in generating entanglement in Bose-Einstein condensates. Theoretical analysis confirms the potential for strong entanglement in these systems.

Here is an abstract of approximately 171 words based on the given title: We report the detection and analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary IGR J19149+1036, first identified by INTEGRAL in 2011. Using 103 months of Swift/BAT survey data, we detect this source at a significance level of 9.1 standard deviations. A timing analysis of the long-term BAT light curve reveals a strong sinusoidal intensity modulation with a period of 116.6 days, interpreted as the orbital period of the binary system. Combining BAT and XRT spectra from follow-up observations, we perform a broadband (0.3-150 keV) spectral analysis. The spectrum is well-modeled by an absorbed power law with a high-energy cutoff at 12.7 keV and an absorption cyclotron feature at 14.3 keV. Correcting for gravitational redshift, we infer a magnetic field of 1.4 × 10^12 Gauss at the neutron star surface. Our results provide new insights into the properties of this high-mass X-ray binary and demonstrate the importance of long-term monitoring and multi-wavelength observations in understanding these complex systems.

Here is a 110-word abstract: Superperiodic patterns observed in nanographene sheets via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) are analyzed in terms of electronic wave function interference. The oscillation period and amplitude decrease spatially in one direction. A static linear potential model explains these patterns, with the @xmath0 model reproducing the decreasing oscillation period. The spatial potential difference is estimated to be 1.3 eV over 200 nm, a reasonable value. The long-distance oscillations are attributed to the two-dimensional graphene sheet's band structure, providing insight into the material's electronic properties. This study sheds light on the underlying mechanisms governing superperiodic patterns in nanographene.

Title: A Well-Calibrated Method for Describing the Environment of Galaxies at All Redshifts Abstract: Understanding the environment of galaxies is crucial for studying structure formation in the universe. A robust calibration method that correlates with halo mass and distinguishes between central and satellite galaxies is essential. Focusing on redshifts z=0 and z=1, we propose an environmental calibration method applicable to next-generation low-to-medium resolution spectroscopic surveys. Utilizing a state-of-the-art semi-analytic model of galaxy formation, we measure local galaxy densities within fixed apertures at various scales. Our results show a clear correlation between density and halo mass for satellite galaxies, while low-mass central galaxies are found in high-density regions near massive haloes. To identify central and satellite galaxies, we employ a stellar mass rank method, which demonstrates high purity and completeness, particularly in massive haloes. We test our method by examining the passive fraction of galaxies and its dependence on stellar and halo mass for centrals and satellites. Our findings indicate that observationally defined quantities can accurately recover known trends in the model, even with reduced redshift accuracy, provided the sample is deep enough to preserve a wide dynamic range of density. This study contributes to the development of a reliable environmental calibration method, enabling a better understanding of galaxy evolution and the large-scale structure of the universe. Our approach has significant implications for the analysis of upcoming spectroscopic surveys, facilitating a more accurate description of the galaxy environment at all redshifts.

This study investigates neutron backgrounds in the CRESST II dark matter experiment using Monte Carlo simulations. Neutrons from various sources are analyzed to determine their impact on the experiment's sensitivity. The results inform strategies to mitigate neutron-induced backgrounds, crucial for achieving projected sensitivities in future phases of CRESST. By understanding and addressing neutron backgrounds, the experiment can optimize its detection capabilities for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) and advance the search for dark matter.

This study explores the potential for causality violation detection at higher energies using a scalar nonlocal theory with a mass scale. A preliminary investigation is conducted to identify an observable that would indicate causality violation. The formulation of this observable is presented, along with an analysis of the energy ranges and couplings suitable for its detection. The results provide insight into the possible observation of causality violation in a non-local scalar model, contributing to the understanding of fundamental physics principles. Theoretical implications and potential experimental applications are discussed, highlighting the significance of this research in the context of high-energy physics.

We present the results of a lattice computation of the vector and axial-vector current matrix elements relevant for the semileptonic decay $B \to \rho l \nu$. The computations are performed in the quenched approximation of lattice QCD on a $24^3 \times 48$ lattice at $\beta = 6.2$, using an $O(a)$ improved fermionic action. Our principal result is for the differential decay rate, $d\Gamma/dq^2$, for the decay $B \to \rho l \nu$ in a region beyond the charm threshold, allowing a model-independent extraction of $|V_{ub}|$ from experimental measurements. We also discuss heavy quark symmetry relations between radiative and semileptonic decays of $B$ mesons into light vector mesons. The calculation is a significant step towards a first-principles determination of the CKM matrix element $|V_{ub}|$, which is crucial for testing the Standard Model description of CP violation. Our results are reported in the context of a model-independent analysis, providing a framework for the extraction of $|V_{ub}|$ from future experimental data. This work is a collaborative effort of the UKQCD collaboration and demonstrates the potential of lattice QCD to provide precise predictions for hadronic matrix elements, complementary to experimental studies.

We present the results of deep H-band spectroscopy of the H-band dropout galaxy candidate UDFJ-39546284 using MOSFIRE on Keck-I. Our data achieve a sensitivity of 5.2 × 10^(-18) erg/s/cm^2 per 4.4 resolution element between sky lines. Previous studies have suggested that this source could be either a large equivalent width line-emitting galaxy at z=8.5 or a luminous galaxy at z=12. We detect a 4.7σ peak associated with a line candidate in deep Hubble Space Telescope Wide-Field Camera 3 infrared grism observations, but at a lower flux than expected. After considering various possibilities, we conclude that these data cannot conclusively confirm or reject the previous line detection. Deeper spectroscopic observations are required to resolve this ambiguity. Additionally, we searched for low-redshift emission lines in ten other Y, J, and H-dropout candidates, yielding no significant detections.

This article presents the completed observations of the NGC 7448 galaxy group and its background volume, obtained as part of the Blind Neutral Hydrogen Arecibo Galaxy Environment Survey (AGES). The survey covers a 5° × 4° region, spanning a redshift range of approximately -2,000 to 20,000 km/s. A total of 334 objects were detected, primarily within three overdensities. Notably, the galaxy density is exceptionally high, with 15 objects per square degree, and 42% of galaxies exhibit extended HI emission. The observed environment is characterized by its kinematics, galaxy colors, and mass-to-light ratios, as well as substructure. To facilitate data cataloging, a new FITS viewer, FRELLed, is introduced, enabling interactive source cataloging and increasing source extraction speed by a factor of 50. This study provides valuable insights into the evolution of galaxies within dense environments, shedding light on the complex interactions and processes that shape galaxy formation and evolution.

This study examines various representations of a covariant hadronic interaction theory. We introduce parametrized nucleon-meson vertices and apply the mean field approximation to nuclear matter at zero temperature, calculating the equation of state and Landau parameters. QCD sum rules inform the treatment of isospin channels, extending density dependent hadronic field theory and yielding insights into collective modes and nuclear properties.

This article presents a time-dependent density matrix renormalization group method, utilizing a matrix product ansatz, to explicitly compute non-equilibrium steady state density operators in integrable and non-integrable quantum spin chains. These systems are driven out of equilibrium by Markovian couplings to external baths at their ends. Although time-evolution simulation is hindered by rapid entanglement growth, steady states can be accurately approximated, enabling the study of chains with lengths of the order of hundreds of sites. Simulations and calculations of energy, spin densities, and currents in various heat and spin transport problems are demonstrated. The results reaffirm, with high accuracy, the previously conjectured relationship between quantum chaos and normal transport, now confirmed on larger systems. This approach provides a powerful tool for investigating non-equilibrium phenomena in quantum spin chains, shedding light on the intricate dynamics of these systems.

This study presents the first very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) investigation of a radio-loud Narrow-Line Seyfert 1 (NLS1) galaxy, SDSS J094857.3+002225, which exhibits the highest known radio loudness for its class. Utilizing the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) at 1.7-5.4 GHz, we observed a highly compact source with very high brightness temperatures, inferred from both its compactness in VLBA images and significant flux variations. To comply with the intrinsic brightness temperature limit, a Doppler factor exceeding 2.7-5.5 is required, indicating the presence of highly relativistic non-thermal jets in this NLS1. Our findings suggest that the Doppler factor plays a crucial role in determining the radio loudness of NLS1s. Furthermore, by drawing an analogy with X-ray binaries exhibiting strong radio outbursts and superluminal jets, we propose that the accretion disk of SDSS J094857.3+002225 is likely in the very high state, rather than the high/soft state. This research provides new insights into the nature of radio-loud NLS1s and the relationship between their accretion disks and relativistic jets.

This article explores the application of the Green's function (GF) method to investigate boundary effects in Chern-Simons (CS) extended electrodynamics, specifically in the context of θ-electrodynamics (θ-ED). The θ-ED model, which describes topological insulators (TI) at low energy, introduces a piecewise constant θ term that varies across different spatial regions separated by a common interface, known as the θ boundary. We derive the static GF for various geometrical configurations of the θ boundary, including planar, spherical, and cylindrical θ-interfaces. Furthermore, we adapt the standard Green's theorem to account for the θ boundary effects, enabling the calculation of static electric and magnetic fields for arbitrary sources and boundary conditions in these geometries. Our approach provides a robust foundation for analytical or numerical approximations in cases where exact solutions are not feasible. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by solving explicit cases in each geometry, including the interaction of a point-like electric charge with a planar TI, and the calculation of static fields produced by a point-like electric charge near a spherical θ boundary, an infinitely straight current-carrying wire near a cylindrical θ boundary, and an infinitely straight uniformly-charged wire near a cylindrical θ boundary. Our results are in agreement with previously reported findings, which were obtained using image methods, thereby validating the versatility and accuracy of our GF approach. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of the magnetoelectric effects and boundary phenomena in CS extended electrodynamics, with potential implications for the study of topological insulators and related systems.

This study investigates Bianchi Type V bulk viscous fluid cosmological models with a dynamic cosmological term. Using a generation technique, Einstein's field equations are solved for arbitrary cosmic scale functions. Particular solutions are obtained, revealing a decreasing cosmological constant over time, consistent with Type Ia supernovae observations. Physical and geometrical aspects are discussed, providing insight into the models' behavior. The results have implications for our understanding of cosmology, particularly in relation to the Bianchi Type V universe and cosmological constant. Key findings support current cosmological observations.

The Solar Probe Plus (SPP) spacecraft is set to explore the near-Sun environment, reaching unprecedented heliocentric distances. As it approaches the perihelion, the solar-wind speed becomes comparable to the Alfvén speed, rendering Taylor's "frozen turbulence" hypothesis inapplicable in its traditional form. This hypothesis is crucial for translating time-domain measurements of fluctuating velocities and magnetic fields into spatial structure information about the solar wind. In this paper, we revisit Taylor's hypothesis and propose a modified version suitable for the near-Sun region. By focusing on the transverse, non-compressive component of fluctuations at length scales exceeding the proton gyroradius, we employ an approximate theoretical framework to describe these fluctuations. Our analysis reveals that fluctuations propagating away from the Sun in the plasma frame obey a relation analogous to Taylor's hypothesis under certain conditions. Specifically, when the spacecraft velocity perpendicular to the mean magnetic field and the Elsasser variable corresponding to transverse fluctuations satisfy specific inequalities, the modified Taylor's hypothesis holds. Observations and simulations suggest that these conditions are met in the near-Sun solar wind, where the derived fluctuations account for most of the turbulence energy. The modified Taylor's hypothesis presented here may enable the characterization of the spatial structure of the dominant turbulence component encountered by SPP, providing valuable insights into the near-Sun environment. This research has significant implications for our understanding of solar wind turbulence and its role in shaping the near-Sun region.

This study presents a systematic investigation of the cooperative binding of substrate molecules to the active sites of a single oligomeric enzyme under chemiostatic conditions. By formulating a stochastic master equation, we analyzed the spatial and temporal aspects of cooperative binding, enabling the calculation of the average number of bound substrates and the net velocity of the enzyme-catalyzed reaction. Using kinetic Monte Carlo simulations and single-trajectory analysis, we estimated the entropy production for cooperative binding schemes. Our results show that both total and medium entropy production exhibit a generic diagnostic signature for detecting cooperativity, which is typically characterized by the net reaction velocity. Furthermore, we introduced an index of cooperativity, C, defined as the ratio of surprisals or stochastic system entropy associated with fully bound states in cooperative and non-cooperative cases. By comparing this index with the Hill coefficient, we provide a microscopic understanding of cooperative binding on a single oligomeric enzyme, complementing traditional macroscopic reaction rate characterizations. Our findings offer new insights into the complex mechanisms underlying enzyme cooperativity, with implications for the analysis and interpretation of biochemical reaction kinetics.

The proliferation of language data and associated technologies has led to difficulties in locating and reusing existing resources. To address this challenge, we introduce the Open Language Archives Community (OLAC), a digital infrastructure for language resource discovery based on the Open Archives Initiative. OLAC provides a standardized metadata set and controlled vocabularies, enabling consistent description and focused searching of language resources. This paper reports on the development of the OLAC metadata set and controlled vocabularies, highlighting current issues and inviting input from the language resources community. By facilitating resource discovery and reuse, OLAC aims to support the rapid expansion of the language resources community and promote more efficient collaboration and research. We discuss the potential benefits and applications of OLAC, and outline future directions for its development and implementation.

This study presents an exploration of evolutionary synthesis models for massive stellar populations, generated using the Starburst99 code in conjunction with novel stellar evolution models that account for rotational effects. The new models, compiled from the Geneva group's data releases, span heavy-element abundances from twice solar to one-fifth solar and incorporate rotation velocities of 0 and 300 km/s. These models also utilize the latest stellar mass-loss rates. Although the mass coverage is incomplete, particularly for non-solar chemical compositions, our preliminary parameter study reveals notable differences in stellar population properties compared to earlier models. Specifically, the new models yield more luminous and bluer stars on the blue side of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, resulting in increased light-to-mass ratios at ultraviolet to near-infrared wavelengths and enhanced output of hydrogen ionizing photons. These findings suggest that, if confirmed, recalibrations of certain star-formation and initial mass function indicators may be necessary. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating rotational effects and updated stellar evolution models in the analysis of massive stellar populations, with potential implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and star formation processes. Further refinement of the evolution models is needed to solidify these conclusions.

This article explores scalar-tensor cosmologies using the Hojman conservation theorem, enabling the determination of the coupling and potential forms. The existence of a symmetry transformation vector yields a conserved quantity, facilitating exact solutions for the cosmic scale factor and scalar field. By leveraging conformal transformations, minimally coupled Einstein frame solutions are converted into non-minimally coupled Jordan frame solutions. The framework is applied to physically relevant examples, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in deriving exact solutions for cosmological models. This method provides new insights into scalar-tensor cosmologies, offering a powerful tool for analyzing complex cosmic phenomena.

This article delves into the concept of assisted quintessence, where multiple scalar fields with identical potentials interact. We investigate the dynamics of such systems, focusing on potentials that exhibit tracking solutions. In the context of inflation, this leads to assisted inflation, where collective action from multiple fields drives inflationary periods that individual fields cannot sustain alone. Our analysis of exponential potentials confirms existing literature on fixed points and stability, and numerical simulations demonstrate the realization of assisted quintessence. In contrast, inverse power-law potentials do not exhibit assisted behavior, with multiple fields behaving akin to a single field in the same potential. We also present an algorithm for generating equivalent single-field potentials that replicate the dynamics of multi-field assisted quintessence, providing a valuable tool for understanding complex cosmological phenomena. Our findings shed new light on the intricate dynamics of assisted quintessence.

This study examines the absorption probability and Hawking radiation of scalar fields in rotating black holes on codimension-2 branes. We investigate how finite brane tension alters the standard results of Hawking radiation compared to negligible brane tension. The rotation of the black hole introduces richer physics, with nonzero angular momentum triggering super-radiance that strengthens as angular momentum increases. Rotations at different angles influence absorption probability and Hawking radiation. Notably, black holes spinning on the brane exhibit less super-radiance effect compared to those rotating orthogonal to the brane. Additionally, brane tension expands the frequency range for super-radiance. Our findings provide insight into the behavior of rotating codimension-2 black holes, offering a deeper understanding of these complex systems. The results have implications for our knowledge of black hole physics and the effects of brane tension on Hawking radiation.

This study examines the observed velocity structures of Al III and singly ionised species in Damped Lyman-alpha systems (DLAs), suggesting the presence of ionised gas in regions where metal absorption lines are formed. A simplified two-region model is constructed, comprising an ionisation-bounded region with internal radiation and a neutral region with lower metal content. The results indicate that ionisation effects are significant and, when accounted for, yield element abundance ratios consistent with those observed in Milky Way stars and metal-poor H II regions in blue compact dwarf galaxies. The findings imply that DLAs and metal-poor galaxies may share a common primary nitrogen origin. Notably, the models do not require dust depletion of heavy elements, although some depletion is not entirely ruled out. These results have important implications for our understanding of the chemical evolution and properties of DLAs.

This study builds upon our previous research on the surface tension of ionic solutions, focusing on acids and salts with strong ion-surface interactions. These interactions introduce a non-linear boundary condition, resulting in an effective surface charge due to ion adsorption. Utilizing the loop-expansion technique, we calculate the surface tension analytically to one-loop order. The mean-field contribution modifies the Poisson-Boltzmann surface tension, while the one-loop contribution generalizes the Onsager-Samaras result. Our theoretical framework accurately describes the surface tension of a wide range of acids and salts, and is consistent with the reverse Hofmeister series for acids. The findings of this study provide new insights into the behavior of ionic solutions at interfaces, with implications for various fields, including chemistry and materials science. The developed theory offers a robust tool for predicting surface tension in complex systems.

This article reviews the significance of giant lyman alpha nebulae associated with high redshift radio galaxies, believed to be progenitors of giant ellipticals. These nebulae have provided valuable insights into the evolutionary status, chemical enrichment, and star formation histories of their host galaxies. Summarizing key results from the last three decades, this paper explores the implications for our understanding of massive elliptical galaxy evolution. With a focus on observational cosmology and early universe studies, this review builds upon earlier work, such as McCarthy (1993), to shed light on the early phases of galaxy formation and evolution.

This article presents a comprehensive review and in-depth analysis of the spin-orbit density wave (SODW) phenomenon, a proposed explanation for the enigmatic "hidden order" phase in URu2Si2. By examining the interplay between inter-orbital Coulomb interaction and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in this compound, we demonstrate that the SODW emerges from Fermi surface nesting instability between two spin-orbit split bands. Utilizing density-functional theory (DFT) and an effective low-energy Hamiltonian, we calculate the gapped quasiparticle spectrum, entropy loss, and spin-excitation spectrum, which exhibit detailed agreement with experimental findings. Notably, despite governing dynamical spin excitations, the static magnetic moment is found to be zero due to time-reversal invariance imposed by SOC, rendering the SODW susceptible to destruction by finite magnetic fields even at zero temperature. Our estimated location of the quantum critical point aligns closely with experimental values. Furthermore, we extend the SODW concept to other SOC systems, including iridium oxides and two-dimensional electronic systems, where we observe hints of quasiparticle gapping, reduced magnetic moments, and large magneto-resistance, all of which can be consistently explained within the SODW framework. This work provides new insights into the intricate relationships between spin-orbit coupling, density waves, and quantum phase transitions in heavy fermion systems.

This article presents a formal approach to classical descent theory, leveraging the commuting properties of bilimits to derive both established and novel results. By employing pseudomonad theory, we develop a framework for analyzing idempotent pseudomonads and prove a 0-dimensional version of the adjoint triangle theorem. Additionally, we introduce the concept of pointwise pseudo-Kan extension, which provides a structured approach to discussing bilimits, commutativity, and the descent object. Our formal methodology yields proofs of key theorems, including the Bénabou-Roubaud theorems and a Galois theorem, as well as embedding results and techniques for obtaining effective descent morphisms. This work offers an alternative perspective on descent theory, as outlined in Janelidze-Tholen's "Facets of Descent II", and provides a guiding template for the development of higher descent theory, paving the way for further research in this area. The formal approach presented here enhances understanding of classical descent theory.

This study enhances the initial conditions for terrestrial-type planet formation simulations by utilizing a semi-analytical model to mimic protoplanetary disk evolution during the gas phase. The model's results inform the initial conditions for subsequent n-body simulations. Our findings indicate that the planetary systems' outcomes are insensitive to the initial distribution of embryos and planetesimals, yielding globally similar results to previous research. This approach improves upon ad hoc initial conditions, providing a more robust foundation for understanding terrestrial planet formation and the resultant planetary systems' architectures. The results have implications for planetary system formation theories.

The formation of present-day massive galaxies is believed to occur through the accretion of multiple satellite galaxies, resulting in the creation of stellar streams around these massive galaxies in the local universe. Cosmological simulations predict a high frequency of these tidal streams, which are difficult to observe, particularly in dense cluster environments where they are readily destroyed. This study focuses on the edge-on spiral galaxy, NGC 4216, located in the vicinity of the Virgo cluster, where a series of interlaced narrow filamentary stellar structures, loops, and plumes were previously identified. Utilizing deeper, higher-resolution, and precisely calibrated optical images from the Next Generation Virgo Cluster Survey (NGVS), we confirm the previously identified features and discover additional structures. Our analysis reveals that the likely progenitors of these low-surface-brightness features are either already cataloged VCC dwarfs or newly discovered satellites in the process of being destroyed. These structures exhibit similar color indices and stellar populations, suggesting a common origin. The alignment of three dwarfs along a single stream is intriguing, and we cannot rule out the possibility that these are second-generation dwarf galaxies forming from the debris of an original dwarf. The observed complex structures, including a stream emanating from a satellite of a satellite, indicate a high rate of ongoing dwarf destruction and accretion in the region of the Virgo cluster where NGC 4216 is located. We discuss the age of these interactions and the possibility that they occurred in a group that is falling into the cluster, exhibiting "pre-processing" before being affected by the cluster environment. Alternatively, these interactions may have occurred in a group that has already ventured into the central regions of the Virgo cluster. Notably, NGC 4216 appears to be experiencing an unusually high rate of interactions compared to other spiral galaxies in the Virgo cluster and those in lower-density environments. The results of this study have implications for our understanding of galaxy mass assembly and the role of mergers in shaping the structure of massive galaxies. While our survey reaches a surface brightness limit of approximately 29 mag arcsec^-2, further studies are needed to determine whether the observed number of streams around NGC 4216 is consistent with predictions from cosmological simulations or if the lack of similar structures around other galaxies poses a challenge to the merger-based model of galaxy mass assembly. Ultimately, this research contributes to our understanding of the complex processes driving galaxy evolution and the formation of massive galaxies in the local universe.

This study explores the three-family local gauge group @xmath0 with right-handed neutrinos, utilizing a minimal scalar sector to break symmetry and generate fermion masses. The structure is embedded within a simple gauge group, and experimental data from CERN LEP, SLAC, and atomic parity violation are used to constrain parameters for new neutral and charged currents. The mass spectrum for gauge bosons and spin 1/2 particles is examined. By introducing discrete symmetries and extra scalar fields, a consistent mass spectrum is constructed, providing insight into the model's viability and potential implications for particle physics and beyond.

This study employs the network paradigm to investigate the underlying structural causes of resilience in consensus formation within dynamic collective behaviors, as well as the controllability of swarm dynamics. By constructing a dynamic signaling network based on directed interagent connectivity and topological neighborhood interactions, we uncover a significant relationship between group size and the number of interacting neighbors. This finding is consistent with empirical observations of starling flocks. Utilizing a dynamical model, we generate collective behaviors that reveal the swarm signaling network to be a homogeneous, clustered small-world network, facilitating emergent outcomes when connectedness is maintained. We test the resilience of consensus formation by introducing environmental noise, highlighting the intricate interplay between swarm dynamics in physical and network spaces. Notably, our analysis enables the analytical determination of the minimum number of driver agents required to fully control swarm dynamics, providing valuable insights into the controllability of collective behaviors. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex inter relationships between network structure, collective behavior, and resilience, with implications for the control and manipulation of swarm dynamics in various biological and artificial systems.

This study examines the critical behavior at the frozen/active transition in the Domany-Kinzel stochastic cellular automaton (DKCA) via a surface growth process in (1+1) dimensions. At criticality, this process exhibits a kinetic roughening transition, and simulations are used to measure the critical exponents. Two update schemes are considered, with the symmetric scheme yielding growth surfaces that belong to the directed percolation (DP) universality class, except at a terminal point where the transition is discontinuous. The nonsymmetric scheme alters surface growth dramatically. Additionally, the damage spreading technique is used to study the critical behavior of rough surfaces at the nonchaotic/chaotic transition, confirming DP values for the symmetric scheme. The results provide insights into the kinetic roughening transition and the associated critical exponents in the DKCA model.

This article presents counterexamples to a question posed by Bowditch, demonstrating that a non-elementary type-preserving representation of a punctured surface group sending non-peripheral simple closed curves to hyperbolic elements is not necessarily Fuchsian. The counterexamples are derived from relative Euler class representations of the four-punctured sphere group. Furthermore, we establish the ergodicity of the mapping class group action on non-extremal components of the character space, confirming a conjecture by Goldman. Our approach utilizes Kashaev-Penner's lengths coordinates of decorated character spaces, providing new insights into the representation theory of surface groups.

This study examines the propagation of transverse elastic waves in crumpled media. A Lagrangian formalism is used to derive the wave equation for curved, strained surfaces. The analysis reveals that ridges act as barriers, trapping modes within specific frequency ranges on flat facets. Simulation results support this finding, demonstrating unique effects of ridges on wave propagation, and providing insight into the complex dynamics of crumpled media, with implications for understanding wave behavior in disordered systems.

This study utilizes measurements from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) to investigate interstellar gamma-ray emission in the second galactic quadrant. The region of interest, encompassing the Cassiopeia, Cepheus, and Polaris Flare clouds, as well as distant atomic and molecular complexes, offers a unique opportunity to probe gamma-ray emission from the interstellar medium beyond the solar circle. The LAT's exceptional sensitivity and angular resolution provide refined constraints on the cosmic-ray density gradient and the increase of the CO-to-H2 conversion factor in the outer galaxy. By analyzing the kinematically distinct local, Perseus, and outer arms, this research sheds light on the distribution and properties of cosmic rays and interstellar gas in the galaxy's outer regions. The findings have significant implications for our understanding of cosmic-ray propagation and the interstellar medium's structure.

This study examines the behavior of a rotating ferrofluid cylinder under the influence of a homogeneous magnetic field applied perpendicular to its axis. The resulting nonequilibrium state is characterized by constant and homogeneous magnetization and internal magnetic field. We analyze various theoretical models to determine the magnetization as a function of frequency and field strength. Our comparisons of model results reveal significant differences, particularly in the predictions for perpendicular field components. By investigating the relationships between magnetization, internal magnetic field, and applied field, we provide insights into the complex dynamics of ferrofluids in rotating systems. The findings of this research contribute to a deeper understanding of the interactions between magnetic fields and ferrofluids, with potential applications in fields such as materials science and engineering. Theoretical models are evaluated for their accuracy in predicting the behavior of ferrofluids under rotating conditions.

This study investigates the maximum number of similar copies of a finite set of points in a plane. Focusing on an isosceles right triangle, we derive exact solutions for small point sets and establish novel upper and lower bounds for larger sets, addressing a problem posed by Erdős and Purdy. Our results provide new insights into geometric combinatorics, shedding light on the complex relationships between point sets and their similar copies.

The existence of an ultra-compact concentration of dark mass associated with the radio source Sgr A* in the galactic center has garnered significant evidence in recent years. However, definitive proof that this object is a black hole remains elusive. A key characteristic of a black hole is the event horizon, which casts a "shadow" due to light bending, with an apparent diameter of approximately 10 gravitational radii. The predicted size of this shadow for Sgr A* is approximately 10 arcseconds, approaching the resolution of current radio-interferometers. If the black hole is maximally spinning and viewed edge-on, the shadow will be offset and slightly flattened. Considering scatter-broadening and finite telescope resolution, we demonstrate that the shadow of Sgr A* may be observable using very long-baseline interferometry at sub-millimeter wavelengths, assuming an optically thin accretion flow. This offers a realistic expectation of imaging a black hole's event horizon within the next few years, providing conclusive evidence for its existence. The potential to directly observe the event horizon of Sgr A* would not only confirm its status as a black hole but also enable unprecedented insights into the properties and behavior of these enigmatic objects, revolutionizing our understanding of the universe.

This study aims to address the solar abundance problem by experimentally evaluating the accuracy of modeled iron opacity at solar interior conditions. To achieve reliable opacity measurements, we focus on three crucial requirements: control of sample conditions, independent diagnostics, and verification of sample uniformity. Our experiments utilize iron/magnesium layered samples tamped by plastic, allowing us to control the iron plasma conditions by varying the plastic thickness. We successfully achieved three distinct conditions, characterized by electron temperatures and densities of 167 eV and 2.7 x 10^24 cm^-3, 170 eV and 3.4 x 10^23 cm^-3, and 196 eV and 4.4 x 10^22 cm^-3, as measured by magnesium tracer K-shell spectroscopy. Additionally, we conducted a separate experiment to assess sample uniformity, incorporating aluminum and magnesium into opposite sides of the sample. The results confirm uniform iron conditions within measurement uncertainties, as verified by aluminum and magnesium K-shell spectroscopy. These controlled conditions are suitable for testing opacity calculations essential for modeling the solar interior, other stars, and high-energy density plasmas, ultimately contributing to a better understanding of the solar abundance problem.

This paper introduces a novel Lattice Boltzmann model for simulating combustion and detonation phenomena. The fluid behavior is captured using a finite-difference Lattice Boltzmann model, while the chemical reaction is described by the Lee-Tarver model. The reaction heat is naturally coupled with the flow behavior, allowing for a seamless integration of thermodynamic and chemical processes. To address the disparate time scales involved, an operator-splitting scheme is employed, enabling efficient and accurate simulations. The model is rigorously verified and validated against well-established benchmark tests, demonstrating its reliability and accuracy. As a specific application, the model is used to study simple steady detonation, with a focus on the reaction zone to elucidate non-equilibrium effects. Notably, the results show that at the von Neumann peak, the system approaches thermodynamic equilibrium, whereas on either side, the system deviates from equilibrium in opposite directions. The compression and thermal expansion in the reaction zone drive these deviations, providing valuable insights into the macroscopic effects of non-equilibrium behavior. The model's capability to capture these effects is highlighted through the introduction of a novel metric, @xmath0, which quantifies the deviation from thermodynamic equilibrium. This work contributes to the understanding of complex combustion and detonation phenomena, offering a powerful tool for simulating and analyzing these processes. The Lattice Boltzmann model's advantages over traditional methods are underscored, particularly in its ability to capture non-equilibrium effects in the reaction zone.

This article presents a concise introduction to calculating leading chiral logarithms and showcases recent evaluations of the LLog series for nucleon mass within heavy baryon theory. Notably, these results mark the first LLog calculation in nucleon CHPT. Observations of regularities in the leading logarithmic series for nucleon mass are also discussed. Initially presented at Quark Confinement and Hadron Spectrum XI, this work contributes to ongoing research in the field, providing new insights into nucleon mass calculations and the behavior of chiral logarithms. The findings have implications for our understanding of hadron spectrum properties.

This study examines the propagation of Hermite-Gauss, Bessel-Gauss, and finite-energy Airy beams in a linear medium with parabolic potential. The results show that these beams undergo oscillation and unexpectedly perform an automatic Fourier transform, periodically transitioning between the beam and its Fourier transform. Notably, parity-asymmetric beams exhibit twice the oscillation period of parity-symmetric beams. Additionally, finite-energy Airy beams display periodic inversion during propagation. These findings lead to the introduction of self-Fourier beams, whose Fourier transforms are identical to the original beams, offering new opportunities for optical applications and research.

We report the detection of 11 Rydberg bands of CO in FUSE spectra towards HD203374A, with eight bands observed in the interstellar medium for the first time. A simultaneous fit of five non-Rydberg and the strongest Rydberg band yields a 4-component cloud structure. This model is used to synthesize other Rydberg bands, allowing derivation of their oscillator strengths. Our results indicate that some band strengths were previously underestimated in laboratory measurements. This has significant implications for theoretical calculations of interstellar CO abundance, as dissociation and self-shielding depend on these oscillator strengths, highlighting the importance of accurate laboratory measurements for astrophysical applications.

This study examines the relative phases of diffracted X-ray waves in crystals, highlighting the dual mathematical descriptions of forward propagating waves. We demonstrate that physically measurable quantities remain invariant regardless of the chosen definition, a fact often overlooked in established equations. Generalizing key equations, we discuss the consequences of conflicting definitions and their implications for X-ray diffraction techniques, providing a foundation for further exploration and refinement of these methods.

We examine a rotating black string falling into a rotating horizon in 5D spacetime, considering axisymmetric configurations with a smooth intersection. Our analysis extends to rotating and charged flows, exploring the dynamics of Kerr black holes and black string flows in this regime, shedding light on the intricate relationships between these objects in higher-dimensional spacetimes.

This study examines the statistical properties of the sum of time spent in positive or negative states by a spin in a d-dimensional Ising model under Glauber dynamics. The distribution and first-passage statistics of this quantity are investigated across three temperature regimes: high, critical, and low. Particular attention is given to the temperature dependence of the persistence exponent and the spectrum of exponents in the low-temperature phase. The probability of the temporal mean exceeding the equilibrium magnetization is found to decay according to a specific power law. This discovery enables the numerical determination of the persistence exponent in the low-temperature phase of the two-dimensional Ising model and above the roughening transition in the three-dimensional model. The results provide new insights into the dynamics of the Ising model, shedding light on the behavior of spins in different temperature regimes and dimensions.

This article explores the development of highly accurate optical clocks, driven by demands from various scientific and technological fields. The current cesium atomic clocks, limited by microwave frequency regime, are being surpassed by next-generation optical clocks aiming for 1 part in 10^18 uncertainty. Focusing on the promising candidate, Yb, we investigate the electric quadrupole and hyperfine shifts in its clock transition. Utilizing relativistic coupled cluster theory, we determine the electric quadrupole moment and magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole hyperfine constants for the relevant states. The crucial role of electron correlation in accurately determining these quantities is discussed. Our research contributes to the understanding of frequency standards in Yb, paving the way for the development of ultra-precise optical clocks. The calculated values are essential for mitigating systematic errors and achieving the desired level of accuracy in optical clock operations.

This study investigates the physical scales of star-forming regions in high-redshift luminous and ultraluminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs and ULIRGs) and submillimeter galaxies (SMGs), comparing them to those in local normal star-forming galaxies. Our findings indicate that the star-forming regions in these high-redshift galaxies have similar physical scales to their local counterparts, with their higher infrared (IR) luminosities resulting from higher luminosity surface density. A strong correlation is observed between IR luminosity and IR luminosity surface density in starburst galaxies, spanning over five orders of magnitude of IR luminosity. However, local ULIRGs exhibit smaller star-forming regions, diverging from this correlation and suggesting they belong to a distinct population. We propose that luminosity surface density is a more accurate indicator of the IR emitting environment and observable properties of star-forming galaxies than IR luminosity. This approach is demonstrated by the aromatic features of high-redshift ULIRGs and a lensed galaxy, which agree with those of local LIRGs having similar IR luminosity surface density but lower IR luminosity. The implications of this relationship suggest that the aromatic emission strength in star-forming galaxies will appear to increase at high redshifts for a given IR luminosity compared to local galaxies, highlighting the importance of considering luminosity surface density in the study of star-forming galaxies.

This study evaluates the mean value and cross-covariance function of chaotic binary sequences generated by chaotic maps with specific properties. The impact of fixed- and floating-point representations on statistical properties is assessed. Statistical tests are applied to identify suitable candidates for pseudo-random binary sequences. The results demonstrate potential for security enhancement in IEEE 802.11 standard, leveraging chaotic binary sequences for improved cryptography and random number generation, with implications for chaos-based security applications.

This article explores the performance limits of ambient backscatter systems in broadband fading environments, where small devices harness power from radio-frequency (RF) signals to compute and communicate. By reflecting existing RF signals from legacy systems, such as digital TV broadcasting, cellular, or Wi-Fi, ambient backscattering devices can convert interference into a usable signal. We develop a detailed signal model to analyze the capacity of both legacy and backscatter systems, considering various amounts of network state information at the receivers. Our results show that, under reasonable conditions, a legacy system using multicarrier modulation can exploit RF interference from backscattering as a form of multipath diversity, significantly enhancing its performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that simple single-carrier modulation techniques can achieve substantial data rates over short distances, particularly when the backscatter receiver is co-located with the legacy transmitter. This study provides insights into the ultimate performance bounds of ambient backscatter systems, including ergodic and outage capacity, symbol variance, and amplitude constraints, shedding light on the potential of this innovative wireless communication paradigm. Our findings have implications for the design and optimization of ambient backscatter systems, enabling efficient and reliable communication in various applications.

This study presents an in-depth analysis of the spectrum of an unusually low-mass white dwarf, SDSSJ123410.37-022802.9, identified in our recent catalog of white dwarfs from the SDSS DR1 data release. Utilizing two independent model atmosphere fits, we accurately determine the atmospheric and stellar parameters of this object, yielding a effective temperature of 17,470 ± 1750 K and a surface gravity of 6.38 ± 0.10. Our analysis suggests that this object cannot be classified as a main sequence A star, horizontal branch, or subdwarf B star. Instead, we interpret it as a very low-mass white dwarf with a helium core, possessing a mass of 0.18-0.19 M⊙, similar to the companion of the millisecond pulsar J1012+5307. We propose that this star may be in a binary system, potentially with an undiscovered or dead pulsar companion, or a more ordinary star that underwent Roche lobe mass transfer. A second low-mass white dwarf candidate from the SDSS is also examined, although the poorer quality spectrum hinders definitive classification. Further investigation of this sample is warranted to confirm the presence of additional extremely low-mass white dwarfs, emphasizing the need for precise observation and interpretation.

This study presents a novel method for recovering and investigating spiral structures in the nuclear regions of galaxies through a harmonic expansion of the observed line-of-sight velocity field. We apply this technique to the emission-line velocity field within the circumnuclear star-forming ring of NGC 1097, obtained using the GMOS-IFU spectrograph. The results reveal a three-arm spiral pattern in the non-circular motions, which is consistent with a two-arm dust spiral observed in the surface brightness. The nuclear spiral is found to be a weak perturbation in the gravitational potential, characterized by a two-arm logarithmic spiral with a pitch angle of approximately 10 degrees. Using a simple spiral perturbation model, we estimate the fraction of non-circular motions due to radial inflow and combine it with the gas density in the spiral arms to determine the mass inflow rate as a function of radius. Our calculations yield a mass inflow rate of approximately 0.02 solar masses per year at a distance of 100 parsecs from the center, which corresponds to about 0.6% of the Eddington mass accretion rate onto the central black hole in NGC 1097. These findings are consistent with previous mass accretion models and suggest that the presented method provides a valuable tool for quantitatively studying nuclear spirals and their role in fueling the centers of galaxies. The technique offers a cleaner view of nuclear spirals than traditional methods and allows for the estimation of mass inflow rates as a function of radius, making it a promising approach for future studies of galaxy evolution and black hole growth.

This study examines the stability of fundamental defects in an unstretchable flat sheet by expanding the bending energy to second order in deformations about the defect. The deformations are found to occur as eigenstates of a fourth-order linear differential operator, with unstretchability imposing a global linear constraint. Conical defects with a surplus angle exhibit an infinite number of states, which possess an n-fold symmetry labeled by an integer, n, if the angle is below a critical value. A nonlinear stability analysis reveals that the 2-fold ground state is stable, while excited states have two unstable modes that come in even and odd pairs. These findings have significant implications for understanding the behavior of defects in unstretchable materials, such as paper, and shed light on the complex interplay between geometry, elasticity, and stability in these systems. The results provide new insights into the mechanical properties of thin sheets.

This article presents the Silicon Track Trigger (STT), commissioned in 2004 at the D experiment. The STT enriches the data sample with b-meson events at the second trigger level, providing tracks with impact parameter resolution. Preliminary results and a fast b-identification algorithm for the second trigger level are shown, demonstrating the STT's capability to efficiently select b-meson events.

This article investigates Moser's Shadow Problem, which seeks to estimate the minimal value of vertices in a polyhedron's shadow when illuminated from a specific direction. We derive asymptotic bounds for the shadow functions associated with bounded and unbounded convex polyhedra. For bounded polyhedra, we confirm the existing result of Θ(n^2) vertices, building on the 1989 work of Chazelle, Edelsbrunner, and Guibas. In contrast, the unbounded case exhibits a distinct asymptotic growth rate of Θ(n^3) vertices, providing new insights into the problem's complexity. Our findings establish the correct order of magnitude for these functions, shedding light on the intricacies of Moser's Shadow Problem.

This article presents the Spitzer Deep, Wide-Field Survey (SDWFS), a four-epoch infrared survey of ten square degrees in the Bootes field of the NOAO Deep Wide-Field Survey, conducted using the IRAC instrument on the Spitzer Space Telescope. As a Spitzer Cycle 4 Legacy project, SDWFS occupies a unique position in the area-depth survey space, enabling the selection of infrared-variable and high proper motion objects over a wide field on timescales of years. The survey's large volume makes it sensitive to galaxies out to high redshifts with minimal impact from cosmic variance, making it an ideal dataset for characterizing galaxy evolution beyond z=1. This paper outlines the SDWFS observing strategy and data processing, and presents the resulting mosaics and source catalogs. The publicly released catalogs contain over 6.78, 5.23, 1.20, and 0.45 million distinct sources detected to the average 3", 4" diameter, aperture-corrected limits of 19.77, 18.83, 16.50, and 15.82 Vega mag at 3.6, 4.5, 5.8, and 8.0 microns, respectively. Preliminary scientific findings include consistent number counts and color-color distributions with other Spitzer surveys, as well as the detection of isolated first radio sources and on-axis XBootes sources. Notably, the multi-epoch imaging has allowed for the identification of four high proper motion IRAC-selected sources, two of which are likely field brown dwarfs of mid-T spectral class. The SDWFS datasets are poised to make significant contributions to our understanding of galaxy evolution, variable and moving objects, and the properties of faint infrared sources.

This article explores the critical properties of a self-avoiding loop model with variable bending rigidity, which is equivalent to the strong coupling lattice Schwinger model with Wilson fermions. Two approximate analytical methods are employed to investigate the model's behavior: the independent loop approximation and a method based on the exact solution of the self-avoiding loop model with bending rigidity. The results confirm that the strong coupling lattice Schwinger model undergoes a second-order phase transition, belonging to the Ising model universality class, when the monomer weight reaches a critical value. The critical behavior of the model is analyzed, and the central charge of the strong coupling Schwinger model at criticality is predicted. The findings are compared to known Monte Carlo results, validating the approximate methods used. The study provides insight into the critical properties of the self-avoiding loop model and sheds light on the behavior of the strong coupling lattice Schwinger model, contributing to our understanding of phase transitions in statistical mechanics and field theory. The results have implications for the study of polymers, liquid helium, and cosmic strings, and demonstrate the effectiveness of approximate analytical methods in investigating complex systems.

This article approaches the portfolio selection problem from a signal processing perspective, investigating how and when to diversify capital across assets to achieve optimal expected growth. We first consider two-asset markets with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) discrete-time returns and proportional transaction costs. By constructing threshold portfolios with recursive updates for expected wealth calculation, we demonstrate that the set of achievable portfolios forms an irreducible Markov chain under mild conditions. We evaluate the stationary distribution of this chain, providing an efficient method for calculating cumulative expected wealth. The parameters are then optimized to yield the growth-optimal portfolio in two-asset markets. We extend our analysis to markets with more than two assets and to discrete-time markets sampled from continuous-time Brownian markets. Furthermore, we address the case of unknown discrete distributions of price relative vectors by incorporating a maximum likelihood estimator into the optimization framework. Our simulations demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in solving the optimal portfolio selection problem in various scenarios, offering a novel and efficient solution to a longstanding problem in finance. The results have significant implications for investment strategies and portfolio management, highlighting the potential of signal processing techniques in optimizing financial performance.

This article presents an analytical investigation of the quasicontinuum method, a multiscale approach used to model the behavior of materials at the atomic scale. We compare the discrete-to-continuum analysis of a one-dimensional atomistic model with a corresponding quasicontinuum model, considering Lennard-Jones type interactions between nearest and next-to-nearest neighbors. Our analysis, utilizing Γ-convergence techniques, reveals that in an elastic setting, the minimizers and minimal energies of the atomistic and quasicontinuum models exhibit the same limiting behavior as the number of atoms increases. However, in the presence of fracture, this equivalence does not hold in general. The choice of representative atoms in the quasicontinuum approximation is shown to influence the fracture energy and crack location. We establish sufficient conditions for selecting representative atoms that ensure the minimal energies of the atomistic and quasicontinuum models coincide in the limit, with the crack forming in the atomistic region as desired. Our findings provide valuable insights into the quasicontinuum method's performance and its application to modeling material behavior at the atomic scale.

We propose a novel method for solving Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov equations in weakly bound nuclei. This approach improves continuum treatment with finite-range interactions by utilizing a mixed eigenfunction expansion and resonance expansion, overcoming continuous spectrum discretization issues and enhancing accuracy in unstable nuclei calculations with finite-range interactions.

This paper presents surface links with link groups that are free abelian groups of rank three or four, contradicting classical link group restrictions. Infinitely many examples of rank three are provided, including one with four triple points, expanding the understanding of link group structures and their potential ranks.

This study presents age measurements for 195 star clusters in the Small Magellanic Cloud, derived from a comparison of integrated colors from the Magellanic Clouds Photometric Survey with simple stellar population models. Our analysis reveals that non-uniform color changes with age can introduce artificial peaks in the cluster age distribution. The observed cluster numbers decrease smoothly with age, and we find that cluster disruption time scales with mass according to a power-law relation. Despite the abundance of young clusters, our results suggest that the dominant epoch of cluster formation occurred initially. Significant spatial variations are also observed in the distribution of clusters of different ages. While limitations in age measurement precision preclude a detailed comparison with field star formation history, this sample provides a foundation for future studies targeting specific age intervals, enabling a more nuanced understanding of star cluster evolution and formation in the Small Magellanic Cloud.

This study examines quintessence models comprising multiple scalar fields coupled to dark matter components. For exponential potentials, scaling solutions are reduced to a single field, yielding simple expressions for effective logarithmic slope and coupling. We also explore solutions with negligible scalar potential, including transient matter-dominated phases. Furthermore, evolution equations for linear perturbations are derived, enabling these models to be tested against observational data. Our findings provide a framework for understanding complex quintessence scenarios and their potential implications for cosmological observations, facilitating future model testing and refinement. Key predictions are thus generated.

This study presents a detailed analysis of high-resolution spectra of six core-helium burning'clump' stars in the open cluster NGC 6134. Building on our previous work, which determined the atmospheric parameters of these stars, we have derived abundances of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and up to 24 other chemical elements. Our analysis reveals significant deviations from solar abundances, including a depletion of carbon by approximately 0.2 dex, an overabundance of nitrogen by around 0.3 dex, and an underabundance of oxygen by about 0.1 dex. These abundance patterns result in a lowered mean C/N ratio and altered 12C/13C ratios. In contrast, the abundance ratios of other elements, including sodium, magnesium, and iron-group elements, are found to be close to solar values. Our findings provide new insights into the chemical evolution of clump stars in open clusters and have implications for our understanding of stellar nucleosynthesis and the enrichment of the interstellar medium. The results of this study contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the complex processes governing the abundances of chemical elements in stellar populations, and highlight the importance of high-resolution spectroscopy in probing the properties of stars in open clusters.

This study examines the Gaussianity of the 4-year COBE-DMR data utilizing spherical Haar wavelets in the HEALPix pixelization. We analyze pixels outside the galactic cut, computing skewness, kurtosis, and scale-scale correlation spectra for wavelet coefficients at each scale. The method's sensitivity to input signal orientation is also considered. Our results indicate a non-Gaussianity detection at a 0% level in one statistic, but after accounting for the total number of statistics computed, the probability of this detection occurring by chance in an underlying Gaussian field is estimated to be 0.69. Consequently, the spherical wavelet technique reveals no strong evidence of non-Gaussianity in the COBE-DMR data, supporting the notion of Gaussianity in the cosmic microwave background. This research contributes to the ongoing analysis of cosmic microwave background data using advanced statistical methods.

This article examines the emerging threats to user privacy resulting from the subversion of privacy infrastructures. Despite their intended purpose of safeguarding user privacy, these infrastructures are being exploited by attackers for illicit activities. Focusing on the prominent Tor network, we outline the critical privacy infrastructures developed to protect user anonymity. An assessment of the rising threats to Tor's integrity is presented, highlighting the severity of these risks. Our analysis underscores the need for further research to mitigate the dangers posed by the exploitation of privacy infrastructures. We conclude by recommending avenues for future studies to strengthen the security and integrity of these vital systems, ultimately protecting user privacy in the face of widespread surveillance.

This article revisits the concept of strange stars, composed of absolutely stable strange quark matter, first proposed by E. Witten nearly a quarter of a century ago. A notable feature of these objects is the potential presence of ultra-strong electric fields on their surfaces, with ordinary strange matter exhibiting fields of approximately 0 V/cm. However, if strange matter forms a color superconductor, the electric field strength may increase to over 1 V/cm. The associated energy density of such fields is comparable to that of the strange matter itself. Our research demonstrates that this phenomenon alters the masses and radii of strange quark stars by 15% and 5%, respectively. Consequently, this mass increase facilitates the interpretation of massive compact stars, with masses around 2, as strange quark stars, providing new insights into the properties and behavior of these exotic celestial objects. Theoretical implications are discussed.

This study presents low-resolution, ultraviolet-to-visual spectra of two candidate globular clusters in the merger remnant galaxy NGC 3921. Located at projected distances of approximately 5 kpc from the galaxy center, these clusters exhibit halo-type radial velocities and strong Balmer absorption lines, indicating main-sequence turnoffs dominated by A-type stars. Spectral comparisons with model clusters yield age estimates ranging from 200-530 Myr and metallicities near solar levels. The clusters' small half-light radii and ages corresponding to multiple core-crossing times suggest they are gravitationally bound, confirming their status as young globular clusters. Assuming a Chabrier-type initial mass function, their estimated current masses are substantial, roughly half that of omega Centauri. The presence of these young, metal-rich globular clusters in NGC 3921, a galaxy exhibiting characteristics of a 1 Gyr old proto-elliptical, provides evidence that major mergers of gas-rich disks can lead to an increase in the number of metal-rich globular clusters, supporting the notion that such mergers play a key role in the formation of elliptical-like galaxies. These findings contribute to our understanding of globular cluster formation and the evolution of galaxy morphology in the context of major mergers.

This study proposes a novel many-variable variational Monte Carlo (MVMC) method integrated with tensor networks to investigate fermionic models. By combining the strengths of both approaches, the variational wave function is constructed from a pair product wave function modified by real-space correlation factors and tensor networks.
