The method is further enhanced by applying quantum number projections, including spin, momentum, and lattice symmetry projections, to restore the symmetry of the wave function and improve accuracy. Benchmark tests on one- and two-dimensional Hubbard models demonstrate significant improvements over individual MVMC or tensor network results. The method is then applied to the hole-doped Hubbard model on a square lattice, revealing a stripe charge/spin order coexisting with a weak d-wave superconducting order in the ground state for doping concentrations below 0.3. Notably, a charge-homogeneous and highly superconducting state is also found as a metastable excited state for doping concentrations below 0.25, providing new insights into the complex phase diagram of the Hubbard model.

This study proposes a generalized Skyrme model to describe nuclei as near-Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield (BPS) skyrmions, motivated by the relatively small binding energy in nuclei. By incorporating terms up to sixth order in derivatives of the pion fields and treating nonlinear and Skyrme terms as perturbations, we derive well-behaved analytical BPS-type solutions. Our model yields non-shell configurations for baryon density, contrasting with the complex shell-like configurations found in other Skyrme model extensions. We calculate static and rotational energies, and include Coulomb energy and isospin breaking terms to obtain the total mass of nuclei. Fitting the model parameters, we find excellent agreement between the predicted binding energy per nucleon and experimental data. These results support the notion that nuclei can be effectively represented as near-BPS skyrmions, providing a promising approach to understanding nuclear structure and properties. The model's simplicity and accuracy make it an attractive framework for further nuclear physics research.

In this paper, we examine the reaction recently investigated by the BESIII collaboration, which reported the existence of a resonance, dubbed X, in the invariant mass spectrum with a mass of approximately 4026 MeV and a width of about 26 MeV. Our analysis of the invariant mass distribution reveals that while the BESIII collaboration's explanation is plausible, alternative interpretations, such as a tetraquark resonance or a bound state, are equally possible. Furthermore, we find that the data can be explained without invoking the existence of a resonance or bound state, highlighting the ambiguity of the current results. To resolve this ambiguity, we propose a strategy to distinguish between the possible origins of the observed signal by studying the dependence of the invariant mass spectrum on the total center-of-mass energy. Our findings suggest that increasing the center-of-mass energy from 4.26 GeV to 4.6 GeV could provide valuable insights into the nature of the signal, allowing for a more definitive identification of its origin. These results have important implications for future experiments aiming to clarify the properties of this enigmatic state. Our study underscores the need for further investigation to determine the true nature of the X state.

This article examines the scattering of a time-harmonic acoustic incident wave by a bounded, penetrable, and isotropic elastic solid immersed in a homogeneous compressible air or fluid. A numerical solution is developed for this acoustic-elastic interaction problem in three dimensions. An exact transparent boundary condition is established to reduce the problem to a bounded domain, and the perfectly matched layer technique is used to truncate the unbounded physical domain. The well-posedness and exponential convergence of the solution are proven, and an adaptive finite element method is developed to solve the scattering problem. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, showcasing its competitive behavior in solving acoustic-elastic interaction problems. The approach provides a reliable and efficient tool for simulating wave propagation in complex media.

This study presents measurements of the Raman mode in graphene and carbon nanotubes at varying laser excitation energies. The mode, observed between 1050-1150 cm^-1, is attributed to a double-resonant scattering process involving longitudinal acoustic phonons and defects. We examine its dependence on excitation energy, graphene layer thickness, and carbon nanotube diameter. Our findings assign this mode to inner processes with resonant phonons primarily from the high-symmetry direction. The mode's asymmetry is attributed to additional phonon contributions. These results highlight the significance of inner contributions in double-resonance scattering and provide a rapid method for investigating acoustic phonons in graphene and carbon nanotubes using optical spectroscopy, offering new insights into their properties.

This study examines the viability of a CPT-violating neutrino mass spectrum proposed to reconcile discrepancies between various neutrino experiments. A three-generation analysis of global data is performed to assess the compatibility of the LSND results with other experiments. Our findings indicate a significant incompatibility between LSND and other datasets, with no overlap below 3σ CL. Furthermore, the global data, excluding LSND, show no evidence of CPT violation, with the best-fit point occurring near a CPT-conserving scenario. These results suggest that the CPT-violating solution is not supported by the current experimental data, prompting a reevaluation of alternative explanations for the observed neutrino oscillation phenomena.

This paper explores the properties of integral circulant graphs, specifically the clique number, and its relationship to the number of vertices. We investigate a conjecture proposing that the clique number divides the number of vertices, previously proposed in existing literature. Our research provides a complete solution for integral circulant graphs with one and two divisors. However, for graphs with more divisors, we construct counterexamples that disprove the conjecture, shedding new light on the properties of these graphs and contributing to the understanding of their structure. Our findings have implications for graph theory and related fields.

This article proposes a novel formalism for classical nonrelativistic mechanics of a mass point, grounded in thermodynamic theory. By treating particle trajectories as geometric dynamical variables on a smooth manifold, a classical statistical mechanics framework is constructed. Thermodynamic variables are introduced via a partition function based on a canonical ensemble of trajectories. This approach reveals classical mechanics as an equilibrium state of statistical mechanics. The relationship between classical and quantum mechanics is examined, with the maximum-entropy principle providing a unified perspective on both. This framework offers new insights into the underlying connections between these fundamental theories.

We re-examine the holographic superconductor in hyperscaling violation geometry, incorporating the coupling between the Maxwell field and background dilaton. Our results show that superconductivity persists, but with altered properties. The critical temperature decreases with increasing hyperscaling violation exponent, while the dynamical exponent's influence is complex, depending on the scalar field's mass and hyperscaling violation. Notably, the frequency gap deviates significantly from the expected universal relation, highlighting the impact of this coupling on superconducting behavior.

We propose an all-dielectric photonic crystal structure supporting 2D confined helical topological edge states. Crystal parameters control topological properties, and an interface between differing band topologies yields edge states in a dielectric slab. These states propagate around sharp corners without backscattering, confined by total internal reflection. 3D finite-difference time-domain calculations confirm out-of-plane confinement. This architecture enables strong interactions between photonic edge states and quantum emitters, paving the way for innovative nanoscale photonic devices with potential applications in quantum optics and information processing, offering new avenues for exploring topological photonics.

This study examines the exclusive production of vector meson pairs in electron-positron collisions, facilitated by annihilation into two virtual photons. At high energies, the cross section is dominated by independent fragmentation of virtual photons into vector mesons. Utilizing the fragmentation approximation, we calculate cross sections and angular distributions for vector meson pairs producible at B factories. Our predicted cross sections for certain meson productions align with Babar collaboration measurements. Additionally, non-fragmentation corrections for charmonium vector meson production are calculated using the NRQCD factorization formalism, yielding predicted cross sections compatible with Belle collaboration upper limits, providing insight into the production mechanisms of vector meson pairs.

This article presents the results of a one-year observational campaign of the Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) 1996X, conducted at the European Southern Observatory (ESO). The campaign included UBVR photometry and optical spectra, supplemented by late-time Hubble Space Telescope (HST) photometry. Spectroscopic analysis reveals that SN 1996X is a'normal' SN Ia, with an apparent magnitude at maximum and color consistent with this classification. The luminosity decline rate is close to average for a SN Ia, and estimates suggest negligible reddening within the parent galaxy, NGC 5061. A detailed comparison of the light and color curves with other'normal' SNe Ia highlights the limitations of describing multicolor light curves as a one-parameter family. This, combined with calibration issues, may explain discrepancies in distance modulus estimates derived from different calibrations of absolute magnitude vs. light curve shape relations. Our analysis yields a range of distance modulus values, from 32.02 to 32.48, depending on the method employed. Furthermore, model light curve and synthetic spectra computations confirm that SN 1996X is a normal Type Ia SN, and that a satisfactory fit can be obtained using a W7 progenitor structure only if a short distance is adopted. A larger distance would imply an excessively large nickel mass for this fainter-than-average SN Ia. These findings contribute to our understanding of SNe Ia and the complexities involved in determining their distances and properties.

The increasing ability of telescopes like ALMA to resolve Giant Molecular Clouds (GMCs) in external galaxies necessitates a thorough understanding of the observational biases that affect measured GMC properties. This study utilizes a hydrodynamical simulation of a barred spiral galaxy to compare the physical properties of GMCs in 3D position-position-position space (PPP) to those observed in 3D position-position-velocity space (PPV). The effects of disc inclination (face-on and edge-on) and resolution (1.5 pc vs 24 pc) on GMC properties are assessed, including the implications for Larson's scaling relations. Low-resolution PPV data are simulated using ALMA Cycle 3 observations with the CASA package. Results indicate that median properties differ minimally between PPP and face-on PPV at both resolutions, but edge-on PPV clouds exhibit significant deviations. These discrepancies are amplified at lower resolutions, leading to opposing conclusions about the virial parameter and dynamical state of the clouds. The power-law indices of Larson's scaling relations decrease from PPP to edge-on PPV to face-on PPV, and from high to low resolutions, suggesting that these relations are not solely driven by physical origins. Therefore, caution is advised when applying these relations to understand environmental dependencies, dynamical states, and the extragalactic CO-to-H2 conversion factor of GMCs. This study highlights the importance of considering observational biases when interpreting GMC properties in external galaxies.

We report on a search for solar axions using a helioscope equipped with a 2.3-m long, 4-t superconducting magnet and pin-photodiode X-ray detectors. A new mass region was explored, and no evidence for axions was found. This null result sets a limit on the axion-photon coupling constant, with a 95% confidence level limit of g_aγ < @xmath1 for an axion mass of @xmath2. This study is the first to investigate the @xmath3-@xmath4 parameter region of preferred axion models using a magnetic helioscope, providing new constraints on axion properties and contributing to the ongoing effort to detect these hypothetical particles.

This article presents a systematic approach to developing convergent finite element schemes for the Darcy-Stokes flow problem. By combining mixed finite elements that are separately convergent for Darcy and Stokes problems, we establish a methodology that ensures global mass conservation. Unlike existing methods that impose the transmission condition weakly, our approach enforces this condition exactly in the global velocity field space. Theoretical analysis of the Galerkin discretization reveals that stable mixed finite element spaces in the Darcy domain can be paired with stable Stokes mixed finite elements of the same order to achieve a stable global method with quasi-optimal convergence rates. A crucial requirement is that the mixed finite element space in the Darcy domain admits an H(div)-stable discrete lifting of the normal trace. Numerical tests are provided to validate our theoretical convergence estimates, demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed method in solving the Darcy-Stokes flow problem.

This study delves into the thermodynamic properties of conformal holography in four dimensions, focusing on the computation of the area (or entropy) functional relation for a black hole in both de Sitter (dS) and anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetimes. The thermodynamic stability is examined through the calculation of the specific heat, revealing a phase transition under specific conditions. The phase structure is analyzed for various values of key parameters, yielding distinct patterns. Notably, in the limiting cases, the results converge to those of Schwarzschild-dS and Schwarzschild-AdS spacetimes, as well as Grumiller spacetime. Furthermore, the thermodynamic volume functional relation is derived in the extended phase space, and a mass-independent entropy functional relation is obtained, which may prove to be a universal quantity. This research contributes to the understanding of conformal gravity and its implications for black hole thermodynamics, highlighting the potential for universal principles underlying these complex systems. The findings have significant implications for the study of gravity and spacetime, particularly in the context of conformal holography.

We synthesized Na@C60OxH2O powder samples by varying water volume in the hydration process and investigated their superconducting properties. The results showed that water volume is crucial for obtaining a single-phase sample with good superconductivity. The transition temperature changed over time in a humid atmosphere, affecting superconducting behavior under high magnetic fields, with high-quality samples exhibiting high sensitivity to temperature.

This article revisits the longstanding pursuit of a definitive signal for the manifestation of scale-chiral symmetry in nuclear interactions, inspired by Gerry Brown's unpublished note on the pivotal role of pions and vector mesons. As a tribute to Brown, this work presents a clear example of an unambiguous signal in axial-charge transitions in nuclei. By integrating Brown's ideas with recent developments on hidden symmetries in nuclear physics, a surprising conclusion emerges: the Landau-Migdal fixed point interaction, nuclear tensor forces, and Brown-Rho scaling are all encoded in scale-invariant hidden local symmetry. This symmetry underlies the equivalence of all forces, providing a simple and elegant description of strongly correlated nuclear interactions. The article honors Brown's legacy while shedding new light on the intricate dynamics of nuclear physics, highlighting the significance of hidden symmetries in understanding nuclear interactions.

This study examines the development of econophysics through scientific communication networks. A weighted, directed network is constructed from 1992-2003 publications, incorporating collaboration, citation, and discussion. Analysis of static properties, including degree distribution and betweenness centrality, provides insight into research dynamics. The introduced method for measuring connection weights offers a general approach to constructing weighted networks, shedding light on the evolution of econophysics research and its complex network structure.

This article provides an overview of recent advancements in the statistical mechanics of isolated quantum systems, with a focus on quantum thermalization and the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH). We introduce the concept of single-eigenstate statistical mechanics, which arises from the ETH, and then delve into a class of systems that defy quantum thermalization: many-body Anderson localized systems. These systems exhibit eigenstates that violate the ETH, leading to long-time properties that cannot be captured by conventional quantum statistical mechanics ensembles. Notably, many-body localized systems can retain information about their initial conditions indefinitely, making them promising candidates for quantum information storage. We explore the key characteristics of many-body localization (MBL) and review the phenomenology of the MBL phase, highlighting the emergence of dynamically stable ordered phases and phase transitions that are invisible to equilibrium statistical mechanics, even at high energies and low spatial dimensionalities where equilibrium ordering is typically forbidden.

This article presents a robust a posteriori error estimator for the Hybridizable Discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) method applied to convection-diffusion equations with dominant convection. The estimator's reliability and efficiency are established in an energy norm, which remains bounded even as the diffusion coefficient approaches zero. Utilizing a weighted test function technique and Oswald interpolation, the analysis demonstrates uniform bounds on error estimates with respect to the diffusion coefficient. Numerical results confirm the estimator's robustness, providing a reliable tool for error estimation in convection-dominated problems. Theoretical and numerical findings validate the proposed estimator's effectiveness.

This article proposes a novel telescope design incorporating Baker-Nunn optics for the observation of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) and high-energy neutrinos. The optical system achieves an image resolution of <0.02° within a 50° angular diameter field of view. When paired with a high-quality imaging device, the design enables precise determination of UHECR and neutrino directions with an accuracy of better than 1 arcmin. The telescope's exceptional resolution allows for the separation of charge-separated cosmic rays, facilitating accurate source identification. This significant improvement in angular resolution will facilitate multi-wavelength and multi-particle observations of astronomical objects, enhancing collaborative research with established astronomical observations. The proposed design has the potential to revolutionize the field of UHECR research, offering unparalleled insights into these extreme cosmic phenomena. The Baker-Nunn optics-based telescope is poised to make groundbreaking contributions.

This study investigates charge exchange spin-dipole excitations in @xmath0Zr and @xmath1Pb using a Skyrme Hartree-Fock + Random Phase Approximation. Calculated spin-dipole strength distributions are compared to experimental data from @xmath0Zr(p, n)@xmath0Nb and @xmath0Zr(n, p)@xmath0Nb reactions. The model-independent sum rule values are analyzed to determine @xmath0Zr's neutron skin thickness. The neutron matter equation of state and nuclear matter symmetry energy are discussed in relation to neutron skin thickness and peak energies of spin-dipole strength distributions, providing insights into nuclear structure and astrophysical applications. Theoretical and experimental results are compared to constrain the neutron skin thickness and its implications.

This study explores the thermodynamics of complexation between functionalized charged nano-spheres and viral proteins. The interaction is governed by electrostatic forces, screened by salt ions, and configurational degrees of freedom of charged protein tails. A complexation free energy functional is constructed to approach this problem. Through numerical and analytical studies, a phase diagram is developed, revealing assembled structures in thermodynamic equilibrium. The diagram depends on the nano-sphere core's size and surface charge density. Results show that both core charge and radius determine the capsid size forming around the core. This research provides insight into the assembly of viral proteins and nano-spheres, shedding light on the role of electrostatic interactions and configurational entropy in shaping the resulting structures. The findings have implications for understanding viral assembly and designing nano-scale systems.

This article highlights the crucial role of planetary ephemerides in interplanetary spacecraft navigation, solar system dynamics, occultation prediction, and tests of general relativity. To enhance the accuracy of the Saturn ephemeris, we conducted a series of astrometric Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations of the Cassini spacecraft in orbit around Saturn using the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA). Between 2006 and 2009, eight observing epochs yielded positions for the center of mass of Saturn in the International Celestial Reference Frame (ICRF) with accuracies of 0.3 milli-arcseconds (1.5 nrad), equivalent to approximately 2 km at Saturn's average distance. Combining these data with previous VLBA observations and a gravitational deflection measurement, we constrained a new ephemeris (DE 422) with post-fit residuals of 0.2 mas for Saturn. While additional observations are necessary to refine the positions of phase reference sources, our results demonstrate the potential for significant improvements in the Saturn ephemeris, ultimately enhancing the link between inner and outer solar system ephemerides and the inertial ICRF. By continuing these observations, we anticipate improving the accuracy of Saturn's ephemeris by a factor of at least three, contributing substantially to our understanding of solar system dynamics and the refinement of fundamental astronomical reference frames.

We introduce three right-handed Majorana neutrinos, combining type-I seesaw and inert doublet mechanisms. The resultant neutrino mass matrix splits into two parts with distinct energy scales, yielding a hierarchical mass spectrum. Applying this scheme to inverted and normal hierarchy cases reveals a correlation between the smallest mixing angle and lightest neutrino mass, providing insight into neutrino properties.

We studied @xmath0sn+@xmath1ni and @xmath2sn+@xmath3ni reactions at 35 AMeV using the CHIMERA detector. Central collisions were selected via multidimensional analysis. Source characteristics, such as size and temperature, were examined. Isotope yield ratios of light fragments provided insight into neutron-to-proton density ratios, offering a glimpse into the reaction dynamics.

This article examines energy functionals focused on discontinuity lines of divergence-free 2D vector fields valued in the circle. Introduced by Aviles and Giga, these energies are lower semicontinuous with cubic cost functions. However, we present a counter-example demonstrating that line energies with cost functions of a specific form are not lower semicontinuous. Furthermore, we show that the viscosity solution for a convex domain does not minimize the energy, highlighting the limitations of this energy functional for certain cost functions, and contributing to the understanding of its properties and applications.

This study explores the relationship between contact matrices (xmath0-matrices) and contact energy matrices (xmath1-matrices) in native proteins, with a focus on understanding the properties that enable native conformations to achieve the lowest energy states. Assuming that the total conformational energy of a protein can be approximated by the sum of pairwise interaction energies, we investigate the connections between xmath0-matrices and xmath1-matrices. Our analysis reveals that native xmath0-matrices exhibit a relationship with xmath1-matrices akin to a Go-like potential, where the lowest bound of the total energy function corresponds to the total energy of the native conformation interacting in a Go-like pairwise potential. This relationship is characterized by parallel relationships between the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of xmath0-matrices and xmath1-matrices, as well as between contact number vectors and the principal eigenvectors of these matrices. Furthermore, the spectral expansion of xmath1-matrices includes an additional constant term, which is indicative of a threshold of contact energy that separates native from non-native contacts. Our examination of 182 proteins from the SCOP database reveals parallel tendencies between the principal eigenvectors of xmath0-matrices, xmath1-matrices, and contact number vectors. Using a statistical contact potential estimated from protein crystal structures, we evaluate pairwise residue-residue interactions and find that they are insufficient to uniquely determine native structures as the lowest energy conformations. Instead, our results suggest that other interactions, including residue connectivities and steric hindrance, are necessary to achieve this unique energy minimum. The findings of this study provide new insights into the complex interplay between contact matrices, energy matrices, and the conformational energies of native proteins.

We report the groundbreaking detection of the first extrasolar planet, ET-1 (HD 102195b), utilizing the Exoplanet Tracker (ET), a state-of-the-art Doppler instrument. This pioneering discovery was made possible by the ET's innovative interferometer-based approach, which enables high-precision radial velocity measurements. The planet orbits HD 102195, a young star with solar metallicity, potentially part of the local association. Our observations reveal that the planet induces radial velocity variability with a semiamplitude of 0 m/s and a period of 4.11 days, resulting in a planetary minimum mass of 0.45 M_Jup. The detection was initially made using the Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO) 0.9 m Coudé feed telescope in the spring of 2005 and subsequently confirmed by radial velocity observations with the ET at the KPNO 2.1 m telescope and the 9 m Hobby-Eberly Telescope (HET) with its high-resolution spectrograph. Notably, this discovery was facilitated by the ET's high throughput of 49%, demonstrating the instrument's capability for detecting planets around relatively faint stars. Furthermore, our photometric observations using the Automated Photometric Telescopes (APTs) at Fairborn Observatory reveal that HD 102195 is a spotted variable star, with an amplitude of 0.02 mag and a 4.08 day period. These findings are consistent with spectroscopically observed Ca II H and K emission levels and line broadening measurements, ruling out rotational modulation of surface activity as the cause of the radial velocity variability. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the ET concept and its potential for future multiple-object Doppler observations or high-precision observations with a cross-dispersed echelle spectrograph.

This article presents the results of a long-term spectral monitoring of the unique double pulsar binary PSR J0737-3039, conducted through two large programs using XMM-Newton in 2006 and 2011. Over a five-year period, despite significant relativistic spin precession, no evident spectral variability was observed in the soft X-ray emission of the pulsars. Notably, our analysis reveals, for the first time, evidence of hard X-ray emission from the system in the 5-10 keV energy band. By combining standard spectral analysis with energy-dependent spatial analysis, we confirm an excess that is likely attributed to iron line emission. The detection of the Fe Kα emission line at 6.4 keV is unprecedented in non-accreting binary systems and suggests the presence of a relic disk that survived the supernova explosions of the double pulsar's stellar progenitors. This finding supports speculation about the existence of similar structures around other isolated neutron stars, offering new insights into the evolution and properties of these enigmatic systems.

This paper investigates cross-layer resource optimization in OFDM systems without explicit channel state information at the base station (CSIT), instead relying on ACK/NACK feedback flows. Conventional cross-layer designs require CSIT, which is challenging to obtain in practice. We model the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and derive a simple, closed-form solution that is asymptotically optimal for sufficiently small target packet error rates (PER). The proposed solution has low complexity, making it suitable for real-time implementation. Our approach achieves significant performance gains compared to systems that do not utilize ACK/NACK feedback for cross-layer designs or those that rely on unreliable CSIT with mismatched error statistics. Asymptotic analysis provides valuable design insights, highlighting the benefits of our method. By adapting power, rate, and user allocation based on feedback, our solution enhances system capacity without requiring explicit CSIT. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of leveraging ACK/NACK feedback for cross-layer optimization in OFDM systems, offering a promising alternative to traditional CSIT-based approaches. Overall, this work contributes to the development of efficient and practical cross-layer scheduling techniques for modern wireless communication systems.

This study examines the representation of a simply connected exponential solvable Lie group induced from a unitary character of a closed connected subgroup. We investigate the spectrum's correspondence to coadjoint orbits and prove that the spectral measure's absolute continuity is equivalent to the subgroup acting freely on a point. A corollary establishes a condition for admissible vectors in nonunimodular groups, providing new insights into the orbital condition's role in representation theory, with implications for the Plancherel measure and spectral variety, shedding light on the intricate relationships between these concepts in Lie group representations.

This study utilizes the Advanced Camera for Surveys aboard the Hubble Space Telescope to investigate the debris disk surrounding the F2V star HD 15745. The circumstellar disk is observed between 2.0 and 7.5 arcseconds radius, corresponding to 128-1480 AU. Notably, the disk exhibits an asymmetric morphology, resembling a fan, which is consistent with forward scattering grains in an optically thin disk inclined at 26-73 degrees to our line of sight. Modeling the spectral energy distribution and scattered light morphology suggests a disk composed of silicate grains between 60 and 450 AU, with a total dust mass of 4 × 10^-3 M⊕. The star's galactic space motions are similar to those of the Castor moving group, implying an age of approximately 210 ± 70 million years, although further research is necessary to confirm the age of HD 15745 using alternative indicators.

This study examines a remarkable class of high-redshift objects, specifically extended Lyα emission-line blobs, discovered in an over-dense region at redshift 3.1. Observations at submillimeter wavelengths reveal a spectral energy distribution similar to that of Arp 220, a local ultraluminous starburst galaxy. This similarity suggests that the superwind model is applicable to these Lyα blobs, implying a dust-enshrouded, extreme starburst galaxy with a large-scale galactic outflow. Notably, the blob's infrared luminosity exceeds that of Arp 220 by a factor of 30, indicating a new population of hyperwind galaxies at high redshift. Our findings support the superwind scenario proposed by Taniguchi & Shioya, providing insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies in the early universe. The discovery of these hyperwind galaxies sheds new light on the extreme star-forming processes occurring at high redshifts.

This article presents the electronics and data acquisition system of the DS-50 experiment, a direct search for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS). The experiment utilizes a 50 kg dual-phase liquid argon Time Projection Chamber (TPC) embedded in water and liquid scintillator veto detectors. The TPC is equipped with 38 photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) to detect the light emitted from nuclear excitation due to WIMP-nuclear collisions. The veto detectors, instrumented with PMTs, shield the TPC and identify background events caused by cosmogenic and local radioactivity. The system triggers, data flow synchronization, and event building for both the TPC and veto detectors are described in detail. All PMT signals are digitized and transferred to event building computers running the artdaq software, allowing for efficient data acquisition and analysis. The described system enables the DS-50 experiment to effectively search for evidence of WIMP-nuclear collisions, providing valuable insights into the nature of dark matter. The implementation of this system demonstrates the capabilities of modern detection technologies in the pursuit of rare and elusive physics events.

This article examines the wave propagation in a two-layered medium comprising a homogeneous compressible air or fluid overlying a homogeneous isotropic elastic solid, with an unbounded rough surface at the interface. We conduct a time-domain analysis of the acoustic-elastic interaction problem in three dimensions, utilizing an exact transparent boundary condition and suitable interface conditions. By coupling the Helmholtz equation and the Navier equation, we establish the well-posedness and stability of the reduced initial-boundary value problem. Our proof employs the method of energy, the Lax-Milgram lemma, and the inversion theorem of the Laplace transform. Furthermore, we derive a priori estimates with explicit time dependence for the acoustic pressure and elastic displacement by selecting special test functions for the time-domain variational problem. These estimates provide valuable insights into the behavior of the acoustic and elastic waves in this complex medium, shedding light on the stability and dynamics of the system.

Title: Enhanced Sensitivity for Pulsar Detection in Supernova Remnants with the GLAST Large Area Telescope Abstract: The detection of at least three pulsars in supernova remnants by the Energetic Gamma Ray Experiment Telescope (EGRET) on the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory at energies above 100 MeV has sparked significant interest in the gamma-ray emission from these objects. However, efforts to identify additional pulsars in the EGRET data have been hindered by limited statistics. The upcoming GLAST Large Area Telescope (LAT) promises to revolutionize the field with its enhanced effective area, narrower point-spread function, and larger field of view. These improvements will increase the photon detection rate and enable better discrimination of diffuse interstellar emission, leading to more sensitive pulsation searches. The LAT's capabilities will also facilitate the resolution of point sources from extended emission in supernova remnants, allowing for a more precise understanding of the associations between gamma-ray sources and supernova remnants. Furthermore, ongoing multiwavelength studies will provide targeted candidate sources for gamma-ray investigation, maximizing the discovery potential of the GLAST LAT. With its unprecedented sensitivity and observational capabilities, the GLAST LAT is poised to make significant contributions to our understanding of pulsars and supernova remnants in the gamma-ray regime.

This study presents an analysis of 55 distant luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) selected from the ISOCAM deep survey fields. Utilizing high-quality optical spectra from VLT/FORS2, we derive oxygen abundances and extinction coefficients with sufficient accuracy. The extinction coefficient is estimated through two independent methods: the Balmer-line ratio and the energy balance between infrared and Hα luminosities. The results show a median extinction coefficient of 2.36 and oxygen abundances ranging from 8.36 to 8.93, with a median value of 8.67. This is 0.5 lower than that of local bright disks at the given magnitude. Our findings suggest that a significant fraction of distant large disks are LIRGs, which could have formed a substantial portion of their metals and stellar masses recently. The results provide insights into the chemical evolution and star formation history of these galaxies, highlighting the importance of accurate extinction corrections and moderate-resolution spectroscopy in deriving reliable metal abundances. The study contributes to our understanding of the properties and evolution of LIRGs, shedding light on the role of these galaxies in the cosmic context.

We present a detailed analysis of observations of the low-mass X-ray binary 2S0921-63, obtained using the gratings and CCDs on Chandra and XMM. This high-inclination system exhibits evidence of an accretion disk corona (ADC), which offers valuable insights into the properties of the heated accretion disk. Our study reveals line emission consistent with previous findings, with the detection of additional lines. Notably, we identify multiple components of the iron K line, a first for this source. By fitting the spectra to photoionization models, we derive constraints on line widths, velocity offsets, and the flux in the medium-ionization region of the ADC. Utilizing density constraints from the O VII line ratio, we estimate the location of the emitting region. Our results suggest that the intrinsic luminosity of the source is comparable to the observed luminosity, under various assumptions about the source's luminosity. These findings, combined with estimates of the emission measure, favor a scenario where the ADC is a significant contributor to the system's overall emission. This study provides new insights into the properties of ADCs in low-mass X-ray binaries, with implications for our understanding of accretion processes in these systems.

This article presents a comprehensive study of exclusive semileptonic decays of heavy mesons to light mesons within the framework of heavy quark effective field theory. Transition matrix elements are characterized by a set of wave functions, independent of heavy quark mass, and form factors are calculated using the light cone sum rule method. Branching ratios are evaluated, and symmetry breaking effects are investigated. Comparisons are made with predictions from other approaches, including large energy effective theory. Our results provide insight into the dynamics of heavy-to-light transitions, shedding light on the interplay between heavy quark and light flavor symmetries. The calculations are performed at leading order of the heavy quark expansion, offering a systematic and consistent treatment of these decays.

We present the discovery of an edge-on debris disk surrounding the 17 Myr old A-type member HD 110058 of the Scorpius-Centaurus OB association, using VLT/Sphere near-infrared dual-band imaging and integral field spectroscopy. The disk is traced to a projected separation of approximately 65 AU, with two prominent, bright, and symmetrically placed knots at 32 AU from the star in its northern and southern wings. These knots are interpreted as a ring of planetesimals, whose collisions may produce the observed dust. Notably, the disk exhibits symmetric, hook-like features in both wings, but lacks a bow-shaped structure. We propose that this wing-tilt asymmetry is indicative of an outer planetesimal belt inclined with respect to the disk midplane or radiation-pressure-driven dust blown out from an unseen, inner belt. The misalignment of the inner or outer disk may be a result of interaction with an unseen planet. The disk's geometry bears resemblance to the nearby Beta Pictoris disk, albeit at smaller radial scales. This discovery provides insights into the complex architecture and dynamics of debris disks, highlighting the potential for planet-disk interactions and the importance of high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy in understanding these systems.

This article explores the concept of utilizing a time-dependent dissipative environment to manipulate the quantum state of a two-level atom. By modulating the frequency and coupling strength of microscopic reservoir modes, while maintaining a fixed reservoir structure, we demonstrate the possibility of dynamically decoupling the atom from its environment. Notably, this decoupling can occur even when the atom and environment remain resonant, resulting in Markovian dynamics. The environmental modulation leads to a sideband structure in the reservoir occupation spectrum, with peaks separated by the modulation frequency. A key outcome of this approach is the significant reduction in spontaneous emission rates, surpassing that achievable through oscillatory atom-bath detuning with identical parameters. Our findings highlight the potential of time-dependent dissipative environments as a tool for quantum control, enabling the manipulation of atomic states in a controlled and efficient manner. This has implications for quantum information processing and related applications.

This study examines boson stars and black holes within the framework of scalar electrodynamics, incorporating a V-shaped scalar potential. Two distinct types of boson stars emerge, characterized by either ball-like or shell-like charge density distributions. An in-depth analysis of these solutions reveals their properties and existence domains. Notably, when mass and charge are equal, a throat-like structure forms in the spacetime. Shell-like solutions may not always be globally regular, potentially possessing a horizon, thereby giving rise to a composite spacetime comprising a Schwarzschild-type black hole surrounded by a shell of charged matter, enclosed within a Reissner-Nordström-type exterior. These findings challenge black hole uniqueness, and a mass formula is derived, relating the mass of black hole solutions to that of regular shell-like solutions, analogous to the isolated horizon framework. The implications of these results on our understanding of black hole physics are discussed.

This study extends our previous research on the Parker-Shearing instability by conducting numerical simulations of magnetic flux tube dynamics in the thin flux-tube approximation. Our results indicate that the evolution of flux tubes in numerical simulations closely resembles linear solutions when vertical displacements are less than the vertical scale height of the galactic disc. However, when vertical displacements approach the scale height, nonlinear effects dominate, leading to rapid inflation of the flux tube and eventual singularity in simulations that only account for cosmic rays. We also investigate the impact of a nonuniform external medium, finding that the dominant wavelength of the Parker instability aligns with the wavelength of external medium modulations. This has significant implications for the dynamo α-effect, which is substantially more efficient for short-wavelength modulations than for long-wavelength modes. Furthermore, our simulations demonstrate that differential forces arising from differential rotation and density waves amplify the α-effect in spiral arms while diminishing it in interarm regions, corroborating our previous linear approximation findings. These results provide new insights into the complex interplay between magnetic flux tubes, cosmic rays, and galactic dynamics, shedding light on the nonlinear behavior of the Parker-Shearing instability and its role in shaping the magnetic structure of galaxies.

This study presents a novel bi-objective minimization model (BOMM) for inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from experimental data. The BOMM simultaneously minimizes the fitting error of derivatives and the number of connections in the network. To efficiently solve the BOMM, a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) is proposed, combined with the separable parameter estimation method (SPEM) to decouple the ordinary differential equation (ODE) system. The Akaike information criterion (AIC) is then used to select the optimal inference result from the obtained Pareto set. Applying this method to the S-system GRN model, our approach accurately identifies network topologies and parameter values without requiring pre-set problem-dependent parameters. This versatility makes our method applicable to inferring various GRN models, addressing a significant challenge in bioinformatics and providing a valuable tool for understanding complex biological systems. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

This study investigates the reionization history of the universe, exploring the impact of various astrophysical and cosmological factors on this pivotal process. We calculate the reionization history for different stellar population models, incorporating the effects of primordial magnetic fields, dark matter decay, and dark matter annihilation. Our results indicate that stellar populations based on a Scalo-type initial mass function for Population II stars are insufficient to drive reionization, unless high star formation efficiencies or photon escape fractions are assumed. The presence of primordial magnetic fields significantly influences the thermal evolution and ionization history of the post-recombination universe, with the magnetic Jeans mass altering the characteristic mass scale of star-forming halos. We derive upper limits to the magnetic field strength and constrain the thermally averaged cross section for dark matter annihilation and the lifetime of dark matter particles. Our findings provide independent confirmation of existing constraints from the recombination era, offering valuable insights into the complex interplay of processes shaping the universe's reionization history. By exploring these factors, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the universe's evolution, highlighting the importance of considering multiple astrophysical and cosmological components in models of reionization.

We present a novel modeling approach to understand the complex structure and chemistry of molecular clouds, treating them as ensembles of transient cores. Each core undergoes a lifecycle of growth, densification, and decay, influencing the surrounding gas and dust. The chemical composition within each core responds to its dynamic state and interactions with dust grains, leading to the formation of ices that are subsequently returned to the gas phase as the core expands. Our models, comprising approximately 1000 cores with random positions and evolutionary phases, are used to simulate molecular line emission maps of a dark cloud. The resulting maps exhibit striking similarities to observations of the dark cloud L673, replicating key features such as morphology, emitting region sizes, molecular column densities, and peak emission separations. By comparing our models to observational data, we gain valuable insights into the dynamics and chemical processes governing molecular clouds, providing significant constraints on the interstellar medium. This work offers a powerful tool for understanding the intricate relationships between gas, dust, and chemistry in these complex systems, shedding light on the nature of molecular clouds and their role in the universe.

This article explores the parametric estimation of the driving Lévy process in a multivariate continuous-time autoregressive moving average (MCARMA) process observed at discrete time intervals. A novel state space representation is developed to exactly recover the driving Lévy process from continuous observations of the MCARMA process. By leveraging numerical analysis and infinitely divisible distributions, this approach is extended to approximate the recovery of unit increments from discrete-time observations. Theoretical results demonstrate that when the sampling interval is chosen appropriately, a generalized method of moments estimator based on reconstructed unit increments achieves the same asymptotic distribution as one using true increments, yielding asymptotic normality. This finding has significant implications for statistical inference in MCARMA models, enabling accurate estimation and inference from discrete-time data. The methodology developed in this article provides a foundation for further research in this area.

This study examines the impact of two-body nucleon-nucleon correlations on heavy-ion collision signatures. We investigate the effects of these correlations on various quantities, including particle production fluctuations, @xmath0 fluctuations, and size fluctuations. Our results indicate that while particle production fluctuations are influenced, other quantities remain unaffected by the presence of nucleon-nucleon correlations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fluctuations in the transverse size of the initial source lead to fluctuations in the transverse flow velocity at hadronic freeze-out, resulting in event-by-event fluctuations of the transverse momentum of produced particles, @xmath1. Notably, our findings suggest that nearly all observed event-by-event @xmath1 fluctuations can be attributed to this mechanism, providing a comprehensive understanding of the underlying dynamics. These results have significant implications for our understanding of heavy-ion collisions and the role of nucleon-nucleon correlations.

This study delves into the realm of mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) and entropic uncertainty relations, crucial components of quantum cryptographic protocols. Despite their importance, these concepts remain poorly understood. Here, we construct special sets of up to $n$ MUBs in dimension $d$ with notable symmetry properties derived from the Clifford algebra. A unitary transformation is identified, which cyclically permutes these bases, generalizing the Fourier transform to multiple complementary aspects. We establish a lower bound for min-entropic uncertainty relations for any set of MUBs, highlighting the central role of symmetry in achieving tight bounds. Notably, a tight bound is obtained for four MUBs in dimension $d=4$, achieved by an eigenstate of our complementarity transform. The relationship between these symmetries and those obtained through discrete phase space transformations is explored, revealing a connection between the extrema of discrete Wigner functions and min-entropic uncertainty relations for MUBs, shedding new light on the underlying principles.

Here is an abstract of approximately 200 words based on the provided title: We report the results of an extensive photometric study of V4743 Sgr (Nova Sgr 2002 #3) conducted over 11 nights in 2003 and 2005 using CCD unfiltered photometry. Our analysis reveals two distinct periodicities in the 2005 data: 0.2799 days (approximately 6.7 hours) and 0.01642 days (approximately 24 minutes). While the longer period is also evident in the 2003 data, the shorter period is only weakly detected in that year. Notably, the 24-minute period is slightly longer than the 22-minute period previously identified in X-ray observations. We interpret the 6.7-hour periodicity as the orbital period of the underlying binary system and propose that the 24-minute period represents the beat frequency between the orbital period and the X-ray period, which is likely the spin period of the white dwarf. This classification suggests that V4743 Sgr is an intermediate polar (DQ Her star). Furthermore, our findings support the hypothesis that the transition phase in novae may be related to intermediate polars, as evidenced by the presence of quasi-periodic oscillations in the optical light curve approximately six months after the nova outburst.

We present a phenomenological model for the 0.7 conductance feature in quantum point contacts. Our model, focusing on finite source-drain bias transconductance, deviates from single-particle expectations. Comparison with experimental data from ultra-low-disorder GaAs systems shows good agreement. This simple phenomenology establishes key boundary conditions for a microscopic theory, shedding light on quantum wire behavior near zero bias.

This article proposes an extension of Gauss-Bonnet gravity to an energy-dependent theory, dubbed Gauss-Bonnet gravity's rainbow, and couples it with Maxwell's theory. We investigate black hole solutions within this framework and calculate the resulting modifications to their thermodynamics. Our analysis reveals that although the thermodynamics are altered, the first law of thermodynamics remains valid. Furthermore, we examine the thermal stability of black hole solutions in this theory, providing insights into the behavior of these gravitational systems. The energy-dependent Gauss-Bonnet gravity's rainbow offers a novel perspective on black hole physics, with potential implications for our understanding of gravitational phenomena and the interplay between gravity, electromagnetism, and thermodynamics.

This article introduces Galamost, a novel GPU-accelerated molecular simulation toolkit designed to harness the computational power of graphics processing units. Galamost is specifically tailored for the study of polymeric systems at the mesoscopic scale, focusing on self-assembly, phase transition, and other properties. The toolkit employs a hybrid particle-field molecular dynamics technique, replacing particle-particle interactions with interactions between particles and density fields, enabling accelerated simulations. Additionally, Galamost incorporates numerical potentials obtained through bottom-up coarse-graining methods, allowing for the simulation of large system sizes over extended periods. The toolkit also features two specialized models: a soft anisotropic particle model and a chain-growth polymerization model, facilitating the investigation of hierarchical self-assembly and polymerization-related phenomena. This article provides a detailed overview of Galamost's optimized algorithms, package characteristics, and benchmarking results, highlighting its potential for efficient and accurate simulations of complex polymeric systems. By leveraging GPU acceleration, Galamost offers a powerful tool for researchers to explore the behavior of polymers at the mesoscopic scale, advancing our understanding of these complex systems. The toolkit's capabilities and applications are discussed, demonstrating its value for the scientific community.

This article presents a theoretical description of central exclusive @xmath0 production in proton-proton collisions. The feasibility of measuring this process using the ATLAS detector and ALFA stations during low-luminosity LHC runs is explored. An estimated visible cross section of 21 @xmath1b at @xmath2 TeV is reported, yielding over 2000 events for 100 @xmath1b@xmath3 of integrated luminosity. Differential distributions of kinematic variables are also examined, providing insight into the production mechanism.

This article explores energy level crossings in the one-dimensional Hubbard model using the Bethe ansatz, building upon the work of Heilmann and Lieb. By constructing degenerate eigenstates at crossing points, we verify level crossings observed through numerical diagonalization with one down-spin. Our numerical solutions to the Lieb-Wu equations enable the construction of Bethe ansatz eigenstates, allowing us to track energy spectral flows along the interaction parameter. Notably, some level crossings cannot be explained by symmetries independent of the interaction parameter, highlighting the importance of dynamical symmetries in identifying spectral lines. We demonstrate that degenerate Bethe ansatz eigenstates at crossing points have distinct eigenvalues of higher conserved operators. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a twofold permanent degeneracy in terms of the Bethe ansatz wavefunction, providing new insights into the Hubbard model's spectral properties and the role of dynamical symmetries in shaping its energy landscape.

This study investigates chromospheric swirls, rotational features in the solar atmosphere associated with magnetic tornadoes. These swirls appear as dark, rotating structures in the Ca II 854.2 nm spectral line, often subtle and challenging to detect amidst dynamic chromospheric changes. To develop a systematic detection method, we compiled and characterized a statistically significant sample of observed and simulated swirls. Our research provides a refined definition of chromospheric swirls and introduces a morphological classification system comprising three types: ring, split, and spiral. We also examine the underlying magnetic field structures and the impact of limited spatial resolution on their photospheric footpoints. This work aims to enhance our understanding of magnetic tornadoes and their role in the solar atmosphere, ultimately contributing to a more comprehensive model of solar dynamics and magnetic field evolution. Our findings have significant implications for solar physics research.

This article presents the startup of the PSI UCN source, a new user facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute. The source provides ultracold neutrons for fundamental physics research, enabling detailed studies of neutron properties. Completed in December 2010, the facility produced its first ultracold neutrons and received operational approval in June 2011. We provide an overview of the source and its initial status, highlighting its potential for groundbreaking research in neutron physics, with capabilities to store and observe ultracold neutrons for hundreds of seconds, advancing our understanding of the neutron's fundamental properties.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to describing the evolution of the universe by utilizing the group analysis of symmetries of dynamical systems. This methodology is employed to search for the unknown equation of state, particularly in the context of noninteracting scaling multifluids. Our results demonstrate that the group of symmetries constrains the form of the equation of state, yielding a commonly used expression in cosmology. We apply this framework to the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) model filled with a scaling fluid, known as a homological fluid, and confront it with observations of distant Type Ia supernovae. Statistical analysis of the supernovae data reveals a class of admissible model parameters, and we find that the model with scaling fluid provides a good fit to the data. The estimated parameters suggest a universe with high density, potentially corresponding to (hyper) phantom fluid. However, assuming a prior on the equation of state parameter, our results indicate a preference for a model close to the concordance ΛCDM model. Notably, our predictions imply that distant Type Ia supernovae should appear brighter, while intermediate distant supernovae should appear fainter, compared to the ΛCDM model. Furthermore, using the Akaike model selection criterion, we find that the model with noninteracting scaling fluid is preferred over the ΛCDM model, offering a promising alternative for understanding the evolution of the universe.

This study examines the mechanism of pattern formation in systems described by a reaction-diffusion equation coupled with ordinary differential equations, which model interactions between cellular processes and diffusing growth factors. Focusing on the Marciniak-Czochra and Kimmel model of early carcinogenesis, we investigate the emergence of periodic and irregular spike patterns due to diffusion-driven instability. Utilizing a numerical code based on the finite element method and adaptive mesh, our simulations demonstrate the formation of nonstationary structures that asymptotically tend towards the sum of Dirac deltas. This novel pattern formation phenomenon is characterized by the concentration of mass at specific points, indicating a potential mechanism for the development of heterogeneous patterns in biological systems. Our findings contribute to the understanding of pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems, with implications for the study of early carcinogenesis and other biological processes.

This study examines the X-ray emission line profiles observed in the XMM-Newton RGS spectrum of the OI star ζ Puppis using radiative transfer in a clumped wind. The results indicate that the X-ray spectrum can be attributed to a multi-temperature collisional plasma situated in the wind acceleration zone. The X-rays are attenuated in the clumped stellar wind, yielding distinctive profiles for the emergent lines. A detailed analysis of the NVII emission line reveals a structured profile, which is attributed to self-absorption in the hot plasma. The presence of NVII in the cool wind component is ruled out based on the atmosphere model. Furthermore, the impact of wind clumping on the transfer of ionizing radiation in high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) is investigated, and analytical formulae for the ionization parameter are derived in relation to wind clumping parameters. These findings provide insights into the complex radiative processes in stellar winds.

This article presents the results of a BeppoSAX observation of the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 253. The X-ray emission from this galaxy is found to be largely concentrated in the nuclear region. Analysis of the 0.2-60 keV data from the central region reveals a continuum that can be well-fitted by two thermal models: a soft component with a temperature of approximately 0.5 keV and a hard component with a temperature of around 3 keV, absorbed by a column density of 1.2 x 10^22 cm^-2. Notably, the Fe K line at 6.7 keV is detected for the first time in this object, with an equivalent width of 300 eV. This detection, along with the shape of the 2-60 keV continuum, suggests that the hard X-ray emission is primarily thermal in origin. The iron abundance of this component is constrained to be approximately 0.25 of solar. Other detected lines include Si, S, and Fe L/Ne, consistent with previous ASCA results. These findings are discussed within the framework of the starburst-driven galactic superwind model, providing new insights into the X-ray properties of this galaxy.

This article challenges the traditional worst-case approach to evaluating covertness in covert communication with noise uncertainty. Instead, we consider the distribution of noise uncertainty to statistically assess covertness. New metrics are defined to measure covertness, enabling analysis of maximum achievable rates under bounded and unbounded noise uncertainty models. Our approach provides a more realistic evaluation of physical layer security, offering insights into covert communication systems' performance under various noise conditions, ultimately enhancing the design of secure communication systems with stringent covertness requirements and noise uncertainty considerations. Novel metrics and models are introduced.

We investigate deep inelastic scattering in the saturation region, governed by non-linear Wilson-line operator evolution. The BK equation describes color dipole evolution in the leading logarithmic approximation. At next-to-leading order, quark and gluon loops contribute, along with tree gluon diagrams. This study calculates the gluon contribution to small-x Wilson line evolution, complementing earlier quark part results, to refine understanding of high-energy QCD dynamics and saturation phenomena.

This paper presents a novel approach to evaluating the suitability of alternative formulations of Einstein's evolution equations. Rather than searching for well-behaved formulations, we develop analytical tools to identify those that are particularly ill-behaved, exhibiting rapid growth of constraint-violating errors. By examining the amplification of transients in the future domain of dependence of the initial data slice, we can eliminate formulations with unacceptable numerical behavior. This technique has the potential to impose stringent constraints on the set of applicable formulations. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply our method to the 2-parameter family of evolution equations proposed by Kidder, Scheel, and Teukolsky, considering both flat space in Rindler coordinates and Schwarzschild space in Painleve-Gullstrand coordinates. Our results provide valuable insights into the stability and reliability of these formulations, highlighting the potential of this approach to guide the development of robust numerical relativity simulations.

This study investigates the structural, electronic, and energetic properties of corundum grain boundaries (GBs) and their role in ion diffusion, a crucial phenomenon in stainless steel corrosion. Using density functional theory (DFT+U) calculations, we constructed four GB planes (rhombohedral, basal, prismatic, and pyramidal) with various interface symmetries. Our results show that the prismatic screw GB with a Cr-O plane interface is the most energetically preferred, followed by the rhombohedral GB with screw symmetry and Cr vacancy termination. The stability of the prismatic GB is enhanced by an increase in in-plane Cr atoms at the interface, as evident in the electronic density of states. These findings provide valuable insights into the preferred interfaces within corundum and their implications for oxide layer growth on stainless steel, ultimately informing strategies to mitigate corrosion. Theoretical understanding of GB properties can guide the development of corrosion-resistant materials.

This result enhances understanding of @xmath8 production and @xmath1 decay dynamics to four-body processes, providing insight into near-threshold coupling to @xmath9.

The primordial lithium abundance inferred from spectroscopic observations of metal-poor stars is significantly lower than the theoretical prediction in the standard Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) model. This discrepancy, known as the lithium problem, has been a long-standing issue in cosmology. In an effort to resolve this problem, we investigate the effects of a sterile neutrino decay on the primordial lithium abundance. We assume a simple model consisting of standard model particles and a sterile neutrino with a mass of a few MeV, which decays long after BBN. The decay of the sterile neutrino produces energetic active neutrinos and electrons, which can induce non-thermal nucleosynthesis and affect the primordial abundance of light elements. We derive the injection spectrum of non-thermal photons induced by the sterile neutrino decay, taking into account the generation of electrons and positrons, muons, and active neutrinos, as well as the primary photon production via inverse Compton scattering of cosmic background radiation (CBR) by energetic electrons. The steady-state injection spectrum is then derived as a function of the sterile neutrino mass and the photon temperature. We find that the sterile neutrino decay can produce energetic active neutrinos that are not thermalized, as well as electrons that are thermalized. To determine the effects of the sterile neutrino decay on the primordial lithium abundance, we consistently solve the cosmic thermal history, non-thermal nucleosynthesis, and the baryon-to-photon ratio and effective neutrino number. We find that an effective destruction of 7Be can occur only if the sterile neutrino decays at a photon temperature of around 0.3 keV. The amounts of energy injection at the sterile neutrino decay are constrained by limits on primordial D and 6Li abundances, the effective neutrino number, and the CBR energy spectrum. Our results indicate that 7Be can be photodisintegrated, and the lithium problem can be partially solved for a sterile neutrino lifetime of around 1000 s and a mass of around 5 MeV. However, 7Be destruction by more than a factor of three is not possible due to an associated over-destruction of D. In the parameter region, the baryon-to-photon ratio is decreased slightly, while the effective neutrino number is increased by a factor of around 0.1. We also correct errors in photodisintegration cross sections of 7Be and 6Li that have propagated through the literature and derive new functions based on recent nuclear experiments. The correct cross sections indicate significantly smaller efficiencies of 7Be and 6Li photodisintegration, which implies that the abundances of sterile neutrino necessary for the 6Li reduction are much smaller than thermal freeze-out abundances. Therefore, the relic sterile neutrino must be diluted between the freeze-out and BBN epochs by some mechanism. Our study provides a new perspective on the lithium problem and highlights the importance of considering non-standard cosmological scenarios in resolving this long-standing issue.

This study presents a novel measurement of the iron-to-hydrogen abundance ratio in the solar corona, utilizing a distinct approach that deviates from traditional spectroscopic and solar wind measurements. By combining EUV line data from the CDS spectrometer on SOHO with thermal bremsstrahlung radio data from the VLA, we derive the coronal iron abundance. Our method involves equating calculated and observed thermal bremsstrahlung radio emission, treating the iron-to-hydrogen abundance as the sole unknown. Applying this technique to a compact cool active region yields an iron-to-hydrogen abundance ratio of 1.56 ± 0.10, approximately four times its photospheric value. Uncertainties in calibration, intensity measurements, atomic parameters, and spectral analysis assumptions result in a net uncertainty of ±20%. These findings suggest that low first ionization potential elements, such as iron, are enhanced in the solar corona relative to photospheric values, providing new insights into coronal composition and dynamics.

This article presents an optimization of rateless codes for unequal error protection (UEP) in multimedia multicasting applications. The proposed design aims to provide either guaranteed or best-effort quality of service (QoS) to a set of heterogeneous users. A novel randomly interleaved rateless encoder is introduced, allowing users to decode symbols up to their own QoS level. The encoder is optimized based on the transmission properties of standardized Raptor codes over wireless channels. By formulating the guaranteed QoS problem as a convex optimization problem, a globally optimal solution is obtained. Numerical results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed optimized UEP rateless coder, outperforming other recently proposed UEP rateless codes. The findings of this study have significant implications for efficient and flexible multimedia transmission, particularly in wireless environments where error control and QoS are crucial. The proposed approach enables enhanced video transmission and reception.

We present predictions of Lyman-alpha (Lyα) forest-galaxy correlations at z=3 from Eulerian simulations that incorporate the effects of galactic winds driven by supernova explosions. These simulations reveal that galactic winds produce expanding bubbles of shock-heated gas within 1-2 comoving megaparsecs of luminous galaxies, akin to observed Lyman break galaxies (LBGs). However, the majority of low-density intergalactic gas, which dictates the observed properties of the Lyα forest, remains unaffected by winds. Our analysis shows that the impact of winds on Lyα optical depth near galaxies is relatively subdued, as winds only heat a small fraction of the gas in the surrounding regions. Consequently, Lyα absorption from gas outside the wind bubbles is dispersed over the same velocity range as the wind-heated gas. Notably, Lyα absorption is expected to be stronger near galaxies due to high gas density, with winds resulting in a modest reduction of this increase. These predictions can be compared to future observations to detect wind effects and infer their strength, albeit with the caveat that the results depend on the correspondence between simulated galaxies and observed LBGs. Our simulations suggest that wind effects are insufficient to reproduce the high Lyα transmission observed within 0.5 comoving megaparsecs of galaxies, implying that more powerful galactic explosions or ejecta with hyper-escape velocities may be necessary, which are unlikely to be produced by ordinary star formation and supernovae alone.

This article presents a systematic approach to constructing graphs associated with binary stabilizer codes. Our scheme involves three key steps: realizing the stabilizer code as a codeword-stabilized quantum code, determining its canonical form, and attaching input vertices to the graph. We demonstrate the scheme's effectiveness by constructing graphs for various stabilizer codes with single and multi-qubit encoding operators. The error-correcting capabilities of these codes are verified using graph-theoretic methods. Our results align with the work of Schlingemann and Werner, and we discuss potential extensions of our scheme to nonbinary, nonadditive, and continuous-variable quantum codes, highlighting its versatility and potential for broader applications in quantum coding theory.

This article explores the production of the composite Higgs boson in topcolor models through the gluon fusion process, incorporating the effects of color-octet massive gauge bosons, known as colorons, and nonstandard contributions from the top-Yukawa coupling and heavy colored fermions. By deriving a low-energy effective theory, we examine the contribution of colorons to the effective gluon-gluon-Higgs operator and find its coefficient to be proportional to the ratio of the coloron mass to the dynamically generated mass. Our analysis reveals that the coloron contribution can be comparable to the top-loop effect for specific parameter values, particularly in top-seesaw models where a large dynamical mass can be achieved consistently with the experimental top quark mass. In contrast, topcolor assisted technicolor models exhibit enhancement of the top-Yukawa coupling. We demonstrate that the coloron contribution can dominate the real part of the Higgs boson amplitude for a Higgs mass of approximately 1 TeV, while the top-loop contribution dominates the imaginary part. Furthermore, we show that signatures of the Higgs boson can be observed in topcolor assisted technicolor models at the Tevatron Run II and the LHC, with estimated cross sections for an integrated luminosity of 2 fb^-1 and a center-of-mass energy of 1.96 TeV. Our results highlight the potential for discovering the composite Higgs boson in topcolor models and emphasize the importance of considering nonstandard contributions in the gluon fusion process.

This study systematically investigates the temperature-dependent thermal conductivities of one-dimensional nonlinear Klein-Gordon lattices with soft on-site potential (soft-KG). The existence of renormalized phonons in soft-KG lattices is confirmed, and their temperature-dependent frequency is verified through numerical simulations and classical field theory. Notably, the thermal conductivities of soft-KG lattices exhibit an opposite temperature dependence trend compared to hard-KG lattices. However, both types of lattices can be interpreted within the framework of effective phonon theory, which predicts that the exponents of the power-law dependence of thermal conductivities on temperature are determined by the exponents of the on-site potentials. Extensive numerical simulations consistently verify these theoretical predictions, providing a unified understanding of thermal transport in soft- and hard-KG lattices. The findings of this study contribute to the understanding of thermal conductivity in nonlinear lattice systems and highlight the importance of effective phonon theory in interpreting thermal transport phenomena.

We report on a search for near-infrared emission from baryonic dark matter in the form of low-mass stars and/or brown dwarfs in the halo of the nearby edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 5907. Utilizing a 256x256 InSb array with a pixel scale of 1.7" on a liquid-helium-cooled telescope carried by a sounding rocket, we conducted observations in the 3.5-5 μm wavelength range. Contrary to previous studies that detected a halo around NGC 5907 in various bands at galactic radii 6 kpc ≤ r ≤ 10 kpc, our search yielded no evidence for emission from a halo at 10 kpc ≤ r ≤ 30 kpc. Assuming a halo mass density that scales as r^(-3), consistent with the observed flat rotation curves out to 32 kpc, we derived a lower limit for the mass-to-light ratio at 3.5-5 μm for the halo of NGC 5907 to be 250 (2σ) in solar units. This limit is comparable to our previous finding for NGC 4565. Based on recent models, our non-detection suggests that hydrogen-burning stars contribute less than 15% of the mass of the dark halo of NGC 5907. Our results support the possibility that the previously detected extended emission at r ≥ 10 kpc is caused by a stellar population ejected from the disk due to tidal interactions. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the dark halo of NGC 5907, evident from extended rotation curves, is not composed of hydrogen-burning stars, providing new insights into the nature of dark matter in galaxies.

This article explores the conjugacy problem for finitely generated groups, specifically the decidability of whether an arbitrary pair of elements are conjugate. We construct examples of computably presented groups where the conjugacy problem for individual elements is decidable in quadratic time, yet the global conjugacy problem exhibits arbitrary worst-case complexity. This complexity can range from any computably enumerable Turing degree to mirroring the time hierarchy theorem or being complete for a given class. Notably, these groups possess a generically linear time conjugacy problem, meaning that hard instances are rare and a linear time partial algorithm exists for a dense subset of instances. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the conjugacy problem and the "half-conjugacy" problem, and discuss groups with algorithmically finite conjugation, highlighting the extremes of conjugacy problem complexity in finitely generated groups.

This study utilizes archival Chandra observations of 19 Low Ionization Nuclear Emission-line Regions (LINERs) to investigate the X-ray properties of their inner kiloparsec. The sample's composition reflects the relative numbers of LINER types found in optical spectroscopic surveys. Our analysis reveals that diffuse, thermal emission is prevalent and concentrated within the central few hundred parsec.
