The average spectra of the hot gas in spiral and elliptical galaxies are consistent with those of normal galaxies, and can be modeled using a thermal plasma and power law component. We detect an average of three point sources in the inner kiloparsec of each galaxy, with luminosities of approximately 10^38 erg s^-1. Notably, the cumulative luminosity functions of these sources are identical to those of normal galaxies. Our findings indicate that an Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) is present in 12 of the 19 galaxies, contributing a median of 60% of the 0.5-10 keV luminosity in the central region. However, the AGN's ionizing luminosity is insufficient to power the observed optical emission lines, suggesting alternative power sources such as mechanical interaction between the AGN jet and circumnuclear gas, or stellar processes like photoionization by post-AGB stars or young stars. These results provide new insights into the origins of nuclear X-ray emission and the power sources of optical emission lines in LINERs, highlighting the complexity of these phenomena and the need for further investigation.

This study examines the extended Bose-Hubbard model with pure three-body local interactions using the density matrix renormalization group approach. The insulating lobes' shapes and critical tunneling values for the quantum phase transition to the superfluid phase are analyzed. Results show enhanced stability of insulating phases at larger fillings, contrasting the standard Bose-Hubbard model. The model is found to belong to the Berenzinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless universality class at the insulating phase boundary tip, providing new insights into quantum phase transitions and many-body localization in interacting bosonic systems with three-body interactions.

This study examines the symmetric degrees of freedom (DoF) in partially connected interference networks with linear coding strategies and no channel state information. Using reconfigurable antennas at receivers, we identify network topologies achieving half linear symmetric DoF. A general upper bound on linear symmetric DoF is derived for arbitrary topologies. Additionally, this bound is shown to be tight for networks with transmitters having at most two co-interferers, highlighting the impact of topology on interference management and DoF. Our results provide insights into optimizing network performance with limited channel knowledge and reconfigurable antennas.

We confirm recent numerical results on gravitational collapse of a spherical Yang-Mills field by constructing critical solutions and perturbations as an eigenvalue problem. The non-scale-invariant field equations yield asymptotically self-similar solutions. Generalizing methods for discrete self-similarity, we find an echoing period and critical exponent for black hole mass, verifying numerical predictions with high accuracy, and providing insight into the complex dynamics of Yang-Mills collapse.

This study employs the effective field theory approach to examine the coupled metric-inflaton system, focusing on the influence of higher dimension operators on scalar and tensor perturbation spectra at short wavelengths. Our analysis reveals that tree-level effective corrections become significant when the Hubble parameter approaches the Planck mass or when the physical wave number of a perturbation mode nears the Planck mass squared divided by the Hubble constant. Consequently, the cut-off length for conventional cosmological perturbation theory is likely much smaller than the Planck length, impacting the observability of trans-Planckian effects in primordial perturbation spectra and shedding new light on early universe dynamics.

This article provides a comprehensive examination of the constitutive relation between @xmath0 and @xmath1 near @xmath2 in Type II superconductors with various types of quenched random disorder. The traditional Abrikosov result is significantly altered by the presence of disorder, with the constitutive relations depending strongly on the disorder type. We investigate point, parallel columnar, and nearly isotropically splayed disorder in both two- and three-dimensional superconductors. Our findings indicate distinct behaviors for each disorder type, including @xmath4 in three-dimensional superconductors with point disorder and @xmath5 in two-dimensional thin films. The results have implications for understanding the effects of disorder on superconductor behavior, highlighting the importance of considering disorder type in theoretical models.

We present a linear scaling algorithm for calculating maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) using an atomic orbital basis. Our O(N) method involves a ground state calculation, density matrix projection, and orthogonalization, followed by Jacobi sweeps for maximal localization. Validation is demonstrated through applications to a water molecule, wurtzite ZnO, and boron nitride nanotubes, showcasing the algorithm's linear scaling behavior and efficiency in computing MLWFs for large systems, making it a valuable tool for materials science research and simulations.

This article reviews the geometry of super coset spaces, focusing on inherited structures from super Lie groups. The isometries of super coset spaces are examined, and a definition of Killing supervectors is provided, enabling extension to other spaces. The formulation of supersymmetric theories is informed by these geometrical insights, with implications for theoretical physics, particularly in areas described by PACS numbers 02.40.-k, 11.30.pb, and 12.60.jv.

This article introduces Saturating Auto-Encoders (SATAE), a new regularizer for auto-encoders with saturated activation functions. The regularizer encourages activations in saturated regions, limiting reconstruction of inputs far from the data manifold. SATAE learns diverse features with various activation functions. Connections to contractive and sparse auto-encoders are established, demonstrating SATAE's potential in representation learning. Experimental results show SATAE's effectiveness in learning compact and informative representations, making it a valuable tool for deep learning applications, with implications for feature learning and data manifold discovery. SATAE offers a new perspective on auto-encoder regularization.

This article explores the head-on collisions of neutron stars and dust disks (galaxies) through the lens of equilibrium thermodynamics. By leveraging conservation laws and solving the Einstein equations, we calculate the final configurations resulting from initial collisions. Gravitational emission serves as a ubiquitous damping mechanism, yielding final equilibrium states. Our analysis compares initial and final states to determine the conditions under which two colliding neutron stars merge into a single entity, and two rigidly rotating disks coalesce into a differentially rotating disk of dust. Notably, we find that the maximal energy loss due to gravitational radiation for neutron star collisions is approximately 0% of the initial mass, whereas colliding disks exhibit a substantially larger limit of 1%. This study provides insights into the dynamic interplay between gravitational emission, neutron star mergers, and disk formation, shedding light on the intricate processes governing these astrophysical phenomena.

This article proposes a paradigm shift in the operation of positioning systems by embracing a fully relativistic approach. Current practice relies on applying relativistic corrections to computations based on Galilean physics, whereas our approach integrates relativity from the outset. This fundamental change entails the use of four symmetric time coordinates and necessitates cross-link capabilities among satellites. Furthermore, gravitation is incorporated through the space-time metric, rather than Newtonian theory, making it impossible to separate the positioning problem from gravimetry. We develop an optimization theory that eliminates the need for relativistic corrections, providing a clearer and more simplified theoretical framework. By adopting this fully relativistic paradigm, we anticipate not only a theoretical clarification but also an improvement in positioning accuracy. Our proposed approach has the potential to revolutionize the operation of positioning satellite systems, and we recommend its implementation to enhance the performance and precision of these systems.

This study examines elastic scattering in a wide range of incident energies using the four-body model and continuum-discretized coupled-channels method. The approach accurately reproduces experimental data for specific scattering reactions without adjustable parameters. Notably, breakup processes are significant and provide repulsive corrections to the folding potential. Interestingly, the breakup of a particular cluster is strongly suppressed in certain processes, regardless of incident energy. The underlying causes of this suppression are investigated, providing insight into the dynamics of these scattering reactions and the behavior of cluster breakup at various energies.

This article presents a parametrisation of scattered proton transport in LHC interactions, discussing the accuracy of kinematic variable unfolding for high-luminosity runs, and describes proton-proton interaction dynamics at the LHC.

This article explores the relationship between differential calculus on metric spaces and algebraic study of normed groupoids with @xmath0-structures. We establish that differential calculus contains the algebraic study of normed groupoids, while the algebraic study of normed groups with dilatation structures is contained within differential calculus. This equivalence enables the translation of algebraic properties between these frameworks, extending beyond metric spaces through the language of groupoids. Our results provide a foundational connection between these mathematical structures, facilitating the exchange of ideas and techniques between them. Key implications are discussed.

This study presents high-resolution, combined Submillimeter Array (SMA) and Atacama Submillimeter Telescope Experiment (ASTE) images of the Class I protobinary L1551 IRS 5 in the CS (J=7-6) line, offering the most complete spatial sampling to date. The SMA image of L1551 IRS 5 in the 343 GHz dust-continuum emission reveals an elongated feature, approximately 3160 au x 80 au in size, oriented perpendicular to the associated radio jets. The combined SMA+ASTE images demonstrate that high-velocity CS emission traces the dust component's structure and exhibits a velocity gradient along the major axis, consistent with a geometrically thin Keplerian-disk model having a central stellar mass of approximately 0.5 solar masses. Conversely, low-velocity CS emission shows an extended feature (~1000 au) with slight south-to-north emission offsets, indicative of a rotating and infalling envelope. The rotational motion of the envelope connects smoothly to the inner Keplerian rotation at a radius of ~364 au. Notably, the infalling velocity of the envelope is three times lower than the free-fall velocity towards the central stellar mass. These findings provide evidence for the transition from an infalling envelope to a Keplerian disk, aligning with recent theoretical studies on disk formation. Our results suggest that sizable Keplerian disks (~50-200 au) may already be formed during the protostellar phase, while the protostars are still deeply embedded within their envelopes.

This study examines monodromies of D-branes in Kähler moduli space, treating D-branes as derived category objects. We compute monodromies in nontrivial examples, linking our work to helices, mutations, and noting unique 0-brane properties, contributing to recent results and conjectures in the field of string compactifications.

The formation and evolution of massive galaxies in the early universe remains a topic of considerable interest. Observations have revealed that massive galaxies with a half-mass radius of approximately 0-1 kpc exist in the early universe, whereas in the local universe, galaxies of similar mass tend to be 4-5 times larger. Dry minor mergers have been proposed as a potential mechanism for driving the evolution of galaxy size without significant mass increase. However, it is unclear whether this process can fully account for the observed differences. This study investigates the role of dry minor mergers in galaxy evolution through numerical simulations of merging galaxies with mass ratios ranging from 1:1 to 1:160. Our results confirm that major mergers do not lead to sufficient size growth, while minor mergers with mass ratios between 1:5 and 1:10 can explain the observed size differences. Notably, smaller mass ratios result in more dramatic size growth, with mergers of 1:80 leading to a size increase of up to a factor of 4. Furthermore, our simulations reveal that the accretion of minor galaxies can lead to the concentration of foreign mass in the central region of the parent galaxy, particularly when the mass ratio is greater than 1:40. These findings provide new insights into the evolution of massive galaxies and highlight the importance of dry minor mergers in shaping their size and structure. Our results have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and the formation of massive galaxies in the early universe.

This article presents a comprehensive spectroscopic library of late spectral type stellar templates in the near-infrared range (2.15-2.42 μm) at a high resolution of R=5300-5900. The library is designed to support stellar kinematics studies in external galaxies, with a particular focus on determining the masses of supermassive black holes in nearby active and non-active galaxies. The combination of high spectral resolution and advanced instrumentation on 8-m class telescopes has made near-infrared CO band heads a popular technique for analyzing circumnuclear stellar kinematics. Our library provides the necessary datasets to leverage the improved spectral resolution and coverage of modern near-infrared spectrographs. We demonstrate the library's application using data from two Gemini instruments and discuss its adaptability for use with other spectrographs. Additionally, we revisit the "template mismatch" effect and its impact on velocity dispersion values obtained from fitting processes, highlighting the importance of carefully selected stellar templates. The library is made available electronically through the Gemini website, providing a valuable resource for the astronomical community to advance our understanding of galaxy evolution and supermassive black hole dynamics.

This study utilizes high-resolution images from the Chandra X-ray Observatory to measure the proper motion of the neutron star in Cassiopeia A over a 10-year period (1999-2009). By registering two images using a background source and 13 quasi-stationary flocculi, pixel offsets were measured using four statistical methods: Gaussian fitting, centroiding, cross correlation, and the Cash statistic. However, significant discrepancies were found between the offset measurements, resulting in large uncertainties. Consequently, the detected motion of the neutron star is marginal, at 390 ± 400 km/s in the southeast direction. Despite the uncertainty, this motion is consistent with the birth velocities of young pulsars and aligns with the inferred proper motion based on the offset of the neutron star from the center of expansion of the optical ejecta, providing valuable insights into the dynamics of this supernova remnant.

The advent of 5G systems has underscored the significance of Machine-to-Machine (M2M) communications in driving the evolution of cellular networks. A critical challenge in this context is ensuring reliability guarantees for each accessing device amidst a massive influx of almost-simultaneous arrivals from a large set of M2M devices. Existing solutions adopt a reactive approach, often resorting to measures like non-selective barring during massive arrival events, which precludes individual reliability guarantees for devices. This paper proposes a proactive approach, leveraging standard cellular access operations to enhance reliability. The access procedure is bifurcated into an estimation phase, where arrival numbers are estimated, and a serving phase, where resource allocation is tuned based on these estimates. Our findings demonstrate that this proactive strategy significantly enhances access reliability for M2M devices, offering a viable solution to the challenges posed by massive device arrivals in 5G networks. By proactively managing resource allocation, this approach ensures more dependable and efficient M2M communications.

This study investigates the out-of-equilibrium dynamics of the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation in (1+1) dimensions through numerical simulations, focusing on the two-time evolution of an interface without a disordered environment. Despite the simplicity of the setup, a complex aging behavior emerges. The two-time roughness exhibits multiplicative aging, characterized by the same growth exponent as in the stationary regime. Analysis reveals a growing correlation length that accounts for key scaling variables. The distribution function of the two-time roughness is computed and described by a generalized scaling relation. These findings provide valuable insights into the glassy dynamics of a non-linear elastic line in a disordered medium, shedding light on slow dynamics and aging. The results have implications for understanding kinetic growth processes and self-affine roughness, highlighting the importance of considering aging behavior in these systems. The study contributes to the theoretical understanding of complex out-of-equilibrium phenomena.

This article explores the properties of non-singular projective curves defined over finite fields, specifically those associated with rational primes @xmath0 and @xmath1, where @xmath1 is odd and the order of @xmath0 modulo @xmath1 is even. We investigate the relationship between these curves and Fermat curves, demonstrating that the latter correspond to maximal or minimal curves over the finite field @xmath5. Furthermore, we show that each Fermat prime yields explicit maximal and minimal curves over finite fields of characteristic 2. For a specific class of curves, we explicitly determine the @xmath9-function as rational functions in the variable @xmath10, confirming that these functions satisfy the Weil conjectures. Additionally, we calculate the class numbers for the function fields associated with each class of curves over @xmath5, providing insight into the growth of class numbers for constant field extensions of the function field(s) of the curve(s) when the field of definition is fixed. Our results offer concrete information on the arithmetic properties of these curves and their associated function fields.

This article presents a comprehensive new set of stellar evolution models and isochrones tailored for galactic halo and bulge stars, characterized by an alpha-enhanced metal distribution. This work extends our previous library of stellar models for a scaled-solar metal distribution, as reported in Pietrinferni et al. (2004), by incorporating the effects of alpha-element enhancement into the nuclear network, opacity, equation of state, bolometric corrections, and color transformations. This homogeneous approach rectifies the common inconsistency in existing alpha-enhanced model libraries, which often rely on scaled-solar bolometric corrections and color transformations. Our models encompass a broad mass range (0.5 to 10 M⊙, with fine mass spacing) and metallicity range (11 values of metal mass fraction, Z, spanning 0.0001 ≤ Z ≤ 0.05). The initial helium mass fraction is set to Y = 0.245 for the most metal-poor models and increases with Z according to the relation Y = 1.4Z + 0.245, to reproduce the initial solar helium abundance. We provide models with and without convective core overshoot during central hydrogen burning, as well as models with varying mass loss efficiencies. Furthermore, we include complete sets of evolutionary models for low-mass, helium-burning stellar structures across the entire metallicity range, facilitating synthetic horizontal branch simulations. We compare our database with several widely used stellar model libraries and various observed color-magnitude and color-color diagrams of galactic field stars and globular clusters, including Johnson-Cousins and near-infrared magnitudes, as well as Strömgren colors. Our isochrones are also tested against integrated optical colors and surface brightness fluctuation magnitudes of selected globular clusters, yielding satisfactory agreement with empirical constraints. This extensive database, when combined with our existing scaled-solar model library, offers a valuable tool for investigating both galactic and extragalactic simple and composite stellar populations using stellar population synthesis techniques. The presented models and isochrones provide a robust framework for understanding the complex interplay between stellar evolution, metallicity, and alpha-element enhancement in various astrophysical contexts. By addressing the limitations of previous alpha-enhanced model libraries, this work enables more accurate and reliable analyses of stellar populations, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of galaxy evolution and the formation of stars in different environments.

This study explores holonomy in curved spacetimes, focusing on the Schwarzschild-Droste geometry. We investigate parallel transport of vectors around circular orbits, revealing a quantized band structure of holonomy invariance. Radial holonomy is also examined, and the analysis is extended to spinors and the Reissner-Nordström metric. Notably, the extremal case exhibits distinct behavior. Our calculations provide a foundation for understanding quantum parallel transport in Hilbert-fibered spacetimes, offering a valuable toolkit for future research. The findings have implications for black hole physics and the interplay between geometry and quantum mechanics, shedding new light on the intricacies of curved spacetime.

Title: The Azimuthal Power Spectra of Optical Emission from Star Formation and Dust in Spiral Galaxies Resembles the Azimuthal Power Spectra of HI Emission from the LMC Abstract: This study reveals a striking similarity between the azimuthal power spectra of optical emission from star formation and dust in spiral galaxies and the azimuthal power spectra of HI emission from the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). Notably, these power spectra resemble that of velocity in incompressible Kolmogorov turbulence. The underlying reasons for this resemblance are currently unknown, but it may be attributed to the complex interplay of processes driving star and cloud formation, resulting in power spectra similar to Kolmogorov turbulence within observable errors. A key finding is that star and cloud formation are not random, but rather correlated over large distances by forces that operate across multiple scales. These forces likely involve a combination of self-gravity, turbulence, and compression from stellar winds and supernovae, working in concert to create the observed structures in galaxies. Furthermore, the identification of flocculent spirals with swing-amplified instabilities suggests that self-gravity may be a significant contributor to turbulence in the interstellar medium. This research has significant implications for our understanding of star formation and galaxy evolution, highlighting the importance of correlated processes and multiscale forces in shaping the structure of galaxies.

This paper proposes a novel embedding approach to learn user profiles, representing topical interests in a shared space. Utilizing these profiles for search personalization, experiments on major web search engine query logs demonstrate improved search engine performance, outperforming strong baselines and showcasing the effectiveness of our embedding approach in enhancing search personalization accuracy and user experience.

This paper presents an incremental method for intelligent systems to refine thematic context descriptions. Beginning with a small set of terms, the method constructs initial search queries, yielding new documents and terms to enhance the vocabulary. Iterative refinement improves query effectiveness. Evaluations across numerous topics demonstrate the learned vocabulary's superiority over the original in retrieving relevant information, highlighting the method's potential for enhanced information retrieval and knowledge discovery applications, with significant improvements in query construction and relevant material retrieval, leading to more accurate and efficient searches. The approach shows promise for various domains.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of seven Galactic O-type stars, specifically those with spectral types O6 and earlier. By utilizing non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) plane-parallel, hydrostatic models, as well as NLTE spherical models that account for mass loss, we investigate the physical properties of these massive stars. Our detailed calculations and simulations demonstrate the significant impact of flux blocking due to UV metal lines on the atmospheric structures of these objects, consistent with previous research. We find that traditional plane-parallel, hydrostatic models struggle to reproduce the observed spectra of early-type massive stars, particularly at effective temperatures above 50,000 K. The derived surface gravities for these stars are relatively low, even for those classified as luminosity class V, and exhibit a notable mass discrepancy, suggesting that sphericity and mass loss play crucial roles in shaping their properties. To address this, we employ NLTE spherical models with mass loss, which yield increased surface gravities (by 0.10-0.25 dex) and reduce, although do not entirely resolve, the mass discrepancy. Our analysis reveals that spectroscopic masses are more consistent with the theory of radiatively driven winds than evolutionary masses. Additionally, we determine a helium abundance greater than solar for most of the objects in our sample. We also examine the effects of various approximations and model details on our results. Specifically, we find that the He II λ4200 line is less sensitive to model nuances than the He II λ4541 line, making it a preferred diagnostic for temperature determinations, which in turn leads to lower effective temperatures. Furthermore, our study shows that modifying the treatment of He II resonance lines, either by imposing detailed balance or introducing additional opacity sources, improves the fits to the He II λ4686 line and affects the He II blend with Hα. For some stars in our sample, the high mass loss rates render the determination of surface gravities from Balmer line wings uncertain. In extreme cases, the mass loss rates required to fit Hα and Hβ differ by up to a factor of two. Our analysis focuses on some of the most massive and luminous stars in the Milky Way, with three objects (Cyg OB2 #3, HD 15570, and HD 15558) exhibiting initial masses close to or exceeding 100 M. Finally, our results suggest that the least luminous object in our sample, HD 5689, may have been misclassified as a member of Cas OB7 and could potentially be a runaway star. Overall, this study provides new insights into the properties and behavior of massive O-type stars, highlighting the importance of considering sphericity, mass loss, and detailed model calculations in their analysis.

This study examines reheating in the context of the νMSM (Standard Model with three right-handed neutrinos) with masses below the electroweak scale. We investigate the generation of a sterile neutrino, serving as dark matter, through decays of an additional inflaton field. Our analysis reveals that reheating occurs at low temperatures due to inefficient energy transfer from the inflaton to the Standard Model sector. This leads to strict bounds on the inflaton-Higgs coupling, resulting in a light inflaton mass, approximately 1-10 GeV or slightly heavier, between 250-1000 GeV, providing new insights into inflation and the νMSM.

This study examines a simplified model of interacting scalar field theory, where fundamental excitations exhibit unphysical propagators with complex conjugate mass poles, akin to those found in certain Yang-Mills gauge theory approaches. Despite the non-physical nature of these "0-particles," we demonstrate that composite operators can be constructed with well-defined spectral representations, enabling a particle interpretation. These physical excitations, analogous to mesons, are bound states of two unphysical 0-particles. By resumming a class of diagrams, we estimate the meson mass from the emerging pole. The primary objective of this paper is to illustrate how a real mass pole can arise from constituent particles with complex masses, providing insight into the confinement phenomenon. Our results offer a deeper understanding of the relationship between unphysical excitations and physical particles in interacting field theories, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms of particle formation.

We examine a planar three-body system consisting of a light particle and two heavy bosons, interacting via a short-range potential. The Born-Oppenheimer approximation is applied, yielding a Coulomb energy spectrum with a Gaussian cutoff. This approach is justified by the large atomic mass ratio. Our analysis provides insight into few-body physics, particularly in cold-atom mixtures. The predicted energy spectrum is characterized by a resonance in the heavy-light potential, enabling a deeper understanding of the system's bound states and interactions, with implications for experimental studies of ultracold atomic systems and few-body phenomena.

Title: A High-Resolution Spectroscopic Analysis of 62 Red Giants in the Milky Way Globular Cluster NGC 5286 Abstract: We present a comprehensive high-resolution spectroscopic analysis of 62 red giant stars in the Milky Way globular cluster NGC 5286. Our study determines the abundances of key light proton-capture, iron-peak, and neutron-capture elements, which are then combined with photometric data of multiple sequences observed along the color-magnitude diagram. The primary findings of our research reveal a bimodal distribution in s-process element abundance ratios, with two distinct stellar groups: the s-poor and s-rich groups. Notably, substantial star-to-star iron variations are observed, with the s-rich stars exhibiting higher iron abundances. Furthermore, we identify the presence of O-Na-Al (anti-)correlations in both stellar groups. To effectively differentiate between these groups in the color-magnitude diagram, we introduce a novel photometric index that is minimally affected by variations in light elements. Our results categorize NGC 5286 as an "anomalous" globular cluster, displaying internal metallicity variations. The chemical abundance patterns observed in NGC 5286 bear a striking resemblance to those found in other anomalous globular clusters, such as M22, NGC 1851, M2, and ω Centauri. We propose the term "s-Fe-anomalous" globular clusters to describe this subclass of objects, which exhibit common variations in s-process elements. The similarities in chemical abundance ratios among these clusters suggest shared formation and evolution histories, potentially linked to an origin in tidally disrupted dwarf satellites. Our findings provide valuable insights into the complex formation and chemical enrichment processes that shape the properties of globular clusters.

This article examines the Crochemore-Mignosi-Restivo (CMR) construction in automata theory, specifically its application to finite-type constrained systems (FTCS) with a limited number of forbidden words. We provide a detailed analysis of the CMR construction for FTCS with one or two forbidden words, demonstrating its potential as a starting point for determining the minimal deterministic presentation, known as the Shannon cover. For irreducible FTCS, we show that an irreducible presentation can be readily obtained from the CMR construction. By investigating the follower sets of states in this presentation, we derive explicit results for the Shannon cover in certain cases. Notably, our findings indicate that the CMR construction directly yields the Shannon cover for irreducible FTCS with a single forbidden word, whereas this is not generally true for systems with two forbidden words, highlighting the complexity of determining minimal presentations for FTCS with multiple constraints.

This article presents a refined theoretical framework for describing the weakly interacting Bose gas at short- to intermediate distances, leveraging an improved version of Beliaev's diagrammatic technique. By introducing a small symmetry-breaking term, we regularize the infrared limit, enabling the derivation of explicit equations for all thermodynamic quantities and correlation functions with controllable accuracy. Our approach yields a partition function and entropy that correspond to a non-interacting bosonic pseudo-Hamiltonian with a temperature-dependent Bogoliubov-type dispersion relation, accurate up to higher-order terms. This method provides the most accurate description of the system within the Bogoliubov-type pseudo-Hamiltonian framework, particularly away from the fluctuation region. We demonstrate the validity of our theory by comparing it to first-principle Monte Carlo simulations for various thermodynamic properties and the single-particle density matrix. Furthermore, our approach can be extended to the fluctuation region by incorporating universal constants and scaling functions obtained from classical U(1) models, allowing for an accurate description of the weakly interacting Bose gas in all spatial dimensions. The results of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of weakly interacting Bose gases, with implications for the development of more accurate theoretical models in condensed matter physics.

This study derives an expression for the mass of a spherically symmetric system using the homotopy perturbation method to solve the Euler-Lagrangian equation. Combining this with Einstein's field equations yields an interior solution set. The solution's physical properties, including mass, density, and pressure, are analyzed in the context of brown dwarf stars. While most features align with observations, the model's stability is found to be suspect, indicating potential instability, which warrants further investigation to refine the theoretical framework.

This article examines the lepton mixing predictions of models incorporating the @xmath1 flavour group series, a subgroup of @xmath0. Focusing on models that preserve either full residual @xmath3 or a @xmath4 subgroup for neutrinos, with optional generalized CP symmetry, we derive predictions for mixing angles, Dirac CP phase, and Majorana phases. Our extensive studies reveal the interplay between flavour group and generalized CP symmetry is crucial for determining viable lepton mixing parameters, including Majorana phases, offering insight into the properties of @xmath2 and related models with potential experimental implications.

We present the results of a spectropolarimetric study of 23 Herbig Ae/Be stars using Hα observations. Our analysis reveals a significant change in linear polarisation across Hα in a substantial fraction of the sample, indicating the presence of flattened, disc-like structures on small scales around these young stars. A key finding of our study is the distinct difference in spectropolarimetric signatures between Herbig Ae and Be stars. While Herbig Be stars exhibit depolarisation across Hα, Herbig Ae stars display line polarisation effects. The frequency of depolarisation in Herbig Be stars (7/12) suggests that these higher-mass stars may be surrounded by flattened structures, analogous to classical Be stars. In contrast, 9 out of 11 Herbig Ae stars show line polarisation, which can be attributed to compact Hα emission polarised by a rotating disc-like circumstellar medium. The observed difference in spectropolarimetric properties between Herbig Ae and Be stars may indicate a transition in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram from magnetic accretion at spectral type A to disc accretion at spectral type B. Alternatively, the interior polarised line emission in Herbig Ae stars may be masked in Herbig Be stars due to their higher levels of Hα emission. Our study provides new insights into the circumstellar environments of Herbig Ae/Be stars and highlights the importance of spectropolarimetry in understanding the formation and evolution of these young stars.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star, @xmath0 Puppis, which is believed to be in the early stages of forming a bipolar planetary nebula (PN). Utilizing three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations with adaptive-mesh refinement, we model the @xmath0 Puppis system to reproduce its observed characteristics. Our simulations incorporate radiative transfer and spectral energy distribution (SED) calculations, allowing for a detailed comparison with existing observational data. By assuming a binary system with reported parameters, we demonstrate that a brief, high-velocity ejection of material from the AGB star can accurately replicate the current observational features. This ejection could be triggered by a thermal pulse, periastron passage of the secondary, or planetary ingestion. Our findings provide valuable insights into the late stages of stellar evolution and the formation of bipolar PNs, highlighting @xmath0 Puppis as a benchmark object for future studies of AGB stars and their transitions to PNs. The results have significant implications for our understanding of stellar mass loss, binary interactions, and the shaping of planetary nebulae.

This study employed long-term videomicroscopy and computer-aided statistical analysis to investigate cell motility and proliferation in three established human glioblastoma cell lines. The migration and proliferation activities of these cell lines were compared, as these features significantly impact cancer progression. Cell proliferation was evaluated by calculating growth rates and cell-cycle times in sub-confluent cultures, revealing no significant differences among the cell lines across various passages. In contrast, cell locomotion studies showed strong temporal fluctuations and exponential velocity distributions, with characteristic profiles and average velocity values unique to each cell line. Despite fluctuations, these dynamical parameters were reproducibly consistent for each cell line. Comparison with traditional pathological data revealed that cell motility analysis provides more specific information, potentially enhancing diagnostic capabilities. The findings suggest that examining cell motility may offer a valuable tool for understanding glioblastoma tumor behavior and improving diagnostic accuracy, ultimately informing treatment strategies and patient outcomes.

We report the detection of seven giant radio pulses from millisecond pulsar 1937+21 using the Ooty Radio Telescope at 326.5 MHz. Observations over 8.1 minutes reveal pulses emitted within a narrow 47μs window of pulse phase, near the profile peak. These findings support giant pulse behavior at higher frequencies and have implications for high-precision timing at low radio frequencies, offering insights into neutron star physics and millisecond pulsar properties.

This article presents the results of a new spectroscopic analysis of the star HD75289, which has been recently discovered to host a Jupiter-mass planet. Our high-resolution, high signal-to-noise ratio spectra reveal a metallicity of [Fe/H] = 0 for this star, confirming the findings of a previous spectroscopic study by Gratton et al. We also re-analyzed the spectra of two additional stars, refining their parameters to better align with photometric and spectroscopic values reported in recent studies. Furthermore, we conducted an extended abundance analysis of four other stars, including 14 Her, HD 187123, HD 210277, and one other. Our results, combined with recent analyses of HD 217107, suggest that all "hot-Jupiter" systems studied to date are hosted by metal-rich parent stars. Notably, we found that the mean [C/Fe] and [Na/Fe] values among stars with planets are lower than those of field stars with similar metallicity. These findings contribute to our understanding of the relationship between planetary formation and stellar composition, highlighting the importance of spectroscopic analysis in characterizing exoplanet host stars. Our study provides new insights into the properties of stars with planets, shedding light on the complex interactions between planetary formation and stellar evolution.

This study presents a photometric calibration of Kurucz static model atmospheres to determine parameters of RR Lyrae stars. The variation of stellar angular radius, effective temperature, and gravity as a function of phase, interstellar reddening, and atmospheric metallicity are investigated. The quasi-static atmosphere approximation (QSAA) is generalized to a non-uniformly moving spherical atmosphere, enabling the derivation of distance, mass, and atmospheric motion from conservation laws. The method is applied to the photometry of SU Dra, yielding parameters such as metallicity, distance, and equilibrium luminosity. The results demonstrate the efficiency of the method in determining fundamental parameters of RR Lyrae stars, including distance, mass, and atmospheric properties. This approach provides a valuable tool for understanding the properties and behavior of these variable stars, with implications for stellar astrophysics and hydrodynamics. The derived parameters are in good agreement with expected values.

This study explores the phenomenology of pseudo-Goldstinos in multi-sector SUSY breaking scenarios. We investigate the decays of the lightest neutralino and chargino into a pseudo-Goldstino and a gauge or Higgs boson. A Monte Carlo simulation is performed for direct production and subsequent decay at the High Luminosity LHC. Considering various neutralino compositions, we find the signal-to-background ratio ranges from 6% to 25%. The statistical significance of the signal is potentially above 2σ, depending on the scenario. Our results highlight the potential for discovering pseudo-Goldstinos at the LHC, providing insight into SUSY breaking mechanisms and beyond.

We analyze an oscillating mass object's motion without external force, yielding acceleration in all reference frames except rest. Periodic motion emerges, distinct from harmonic oscillations, revealing unique classical mechanics characteristics.

This study investigates the non-axisymmetric structure of accretion discs in Be/X-ray binaries using three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations. Focusing on a coplanar system with a short period and moderate eccentricity, we demonstrate that ram pressure generated by phase-dependent mass transfer from the Be-star disc triggers a transient, one-armed, trailing spiral structure in the accretion disc surrounding the neutron star. The spiral wave is excited near periastron passage, when material is transferred from the Be disc, and subsequently damped. As the spiral wave develops and decays over one orbital period, the disc morphology evolves from circular to eccentric and back to circular. Notably, the inward propagation of the spiral wave significantly enhances the mass-accretion rate onto the neutron star. Our findings suggest that detecting an X-ray luminosity peak corresponding to the enhanced mass-accretion rate peak can provide indirect evidence for the presence of an accretion disc in Be/X-ray binaries. These results contribute to our understanding of the complex dynamics and observational characteristics of these systems, highlighting the importance of numerical simulations in elucidating the intricacies of accretion disc behavior.

We present a comprehensive investigation into the evolution of binary fractions in star clusters, utilizing sophisticated N-body models comprising up to 100,000 stars. Our simulations, performed with the Nbody4 code, incorporate a full mass spectrum of stars, stellar evolution, binary evolution, and the tidal field of the galaxy, with primordial binary frequencies ranging from 5% to 50%. Our findings indicate that the overall binary fraction of a cluster remains remarkably consistent with its primordial value, except during the final stages of cluster dissolution. However, a notable exception occurs in the central regions, where we observe a significant increase in binary fraction over time. In one simulation, starting with 100,000 stars and 5% binaries, the core binary frequency surged to 40% by the end of the core-collapse phase, which occurred at 10 gyr with 10,000 stars remaining. This increase is attributed to the interplay between mass segregation, binary destruction, and the creation of new binaries through exchange interactions. Furthermore, our results suggest that binaries are cycled in and out of cluster cores in a manner analogous to convection in stars. For models with 100,000 stars, we demonstrate that the evolution of the core radius is insensitive to the primordial binary frequency, provided it is 10% or less, up to the end of the initial core-collapse phase. Our study has significant implications for understanding the primordial binary content of globular clusters, and we discuss the ramifications of our findings in this context.

This study delves into the properties and production mechanisms of winds in black hole hot accretion flows, a crucial aspect of understanding the complex interplay between black hole activity and galaxy evolution. Utilizing a three-dimensional general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulation of a Schwarzschild black hole, we investigate the mass flux, poloidal speed, and underlying drivers of wind generation. By tracking virtual Lagrangian particles, we identify two distinct types of outflows: a quasi-relativistic jet near the axis and a sub-relativistic wind covering a larger solid angle. Our findings confirm that the wind's mass flux is substantial, with most of it originating from the accretion flow's surface layer. The radial profile of the wind mass flux is characterized by a specific relationship with the mass accretion rate and Schwarzschild radius. Furthermore, we observe that the poloidal wind speed remains relatively constant after production, while the flux-weighted wind speed follows a specific dependence on the Keplerian speed. In contrast, the jet's mass flux is lower but its speed is significantly higher. Consequently, the wind's energy and momentum fluxes surpass those of the jet. We determine that the wind is primarily produced and accelerated by the combined effects of centrifugal force and magnetic pressure gradient, whereas the jet is mainly driven by magnetic pressure gradient. Notably, our calculated wind production efficiency aligns with the values required by large-scale galaxy simulations incorporating active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback, underscoring the significance of winds in shaping galaxy evolution. These results provide valuable insights into the intricate dynamics of black hole accretion flows and their far-reaching implications for galaxy-scale processes.

This study evaluates the momentum dependence of the drag coefficient of heavy quarks in quark-gluon plasma (QGP). The results are used to estimate the nuclear suppression factor of charm and bottom quarks. The momentum dependence of transport coefficients is found to be crucial in suppressing heavy quarks, affecting the properties of QGP probed by heavy flavors. Radiative losses are identified as the primary cause of heavy quark suppression observed at RHIC and LHC. Additionally, the suppression of heavy quarks in Pb+Pb collisions at LHC energy, recently measured by the ALICE collaboration, is investigated, providing insights into QGP properties.

This article revisits the concept of a'universal covering' introduced by Lebesgue in 1914, which is a convex subset of the plane containing an isometric copy of any subset of diameter 1. Building on the work of mathematicians such as PL, Sprague, and Hansen, who have incrementally reduced the area of universal coverings, we identify an error in Hansen's claimed reduction. With the assistance of Greg Egan, we present a new universal covering with an area less than the previously established minimum, achieving a reduction of a significant amount and advancing the field's understanding of minimal universal coverings.

This study explores the role of coherent structures in particle acceleration within the strongly turbulent solar corona. By comparing the dynamics of collisionless test protons in exact magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) fields and phase-randomized fields, derived from a pseudo-spectral simulation of isotropic MHD turbulence, we demonstrate that phase correlations significantly enhance acceleration efficiency during the initial adiabatic stage. The underlying mechanism is attributed to the dynamic MHD alignment of magnetic fields with electric currents, fostering parallel electric fields that facilitate initial particle injection. Conversely, alignment with bulk velocity diminishes acceleration due to convective electric fields at later stages. Our findings highlight the importance of considering physical electric fields, as non-physical parallel electric fields in randomized turbulence models can lead to artificial acceleration. The dynamic MHD alignment can be captured through the joint two-point function of magnetic and electric fields, enabling its incorporation into Fokker-Planck descriptions of stochastic acceleration. This research provides new insights into the complex interplay between turbulent structures and particle acceleration in the solar corona.

This article delves into the study of saddle points of a vector logarithmic energy with a vector polynomial external field on the plane, which gives rise to the notion of vector-valued critical measures. These measures are motivated by various branches of analysis and are characterized by the interplay of attracting and repelling forces. We establish general structural results for critical measures, including their representation in terms of an algebraic equation involving their Cauchy transforms and their symmetry properties. Consequently, we find that vector-valued critical measures are supported on a finite number of analytic arcs, which are trajectories of a quadratic differential defined on a three-sheeted Riemann surface. The critical graph of this differential is crucial in constructing critical measures. To illustrate these connections, we examine a one-parameter family of critical measures under a cubic external field, motivated by the asymptotic analysis of non-hermitian multiple orthogonal polynomials. We compute the Riemann surface and quadratic differential explicitly, analyzing the dynamics of the critical graph as a function of the parameter and describing the resulting phase transitions. This construction yields a complete family of vector-valued critical measures, which are equivalent to vector-valued equilibrium measures when projected onto the complex plane. Our results provide a comprehensive understanding of vector-valued critical measures and their role in analysis, with implications for the study of multiple orthogonal polynomials and related fields.

This article explores the reduction of thermal noise in dielectric mirror coatings for enhanced sensitivity in second and third generation interferometric gravitational wave detectors. We investigate the use of a Khalili etalon as a viable alternative to a Khalili cavity, requiring less hardware while still achieving significant thermal noise reduction. By optimizing the coating layer distribution on the etalon's front and rear surfaces, we demonstrate a notable decrease in thermal noise. A comparative analysis with a conventional mirror reveals the total noise budget improvement. Furthermore, we discuss the technical advantages and disadvantages of the Khalili etalon versus the Khalili cavity, including interferometric length control and thermal lensing, to provide insight into the feasibility of this approach for future gravitational wave detectors. Our findings contribute to the ongoing efforts to enhance detector sensitivity.

This article reviews the historical development of neutron star physics in the 1930s, with a focus on the contributions of Lev Landau. According to previous accounts, Landau conceived the idea of neutron stars in a discussion with Niels Bohr and Leon Rosenfeld in February 1932, shortly after the discovery of the neutron. However, we argue that this conversation actually took place in March 1931, prior to the discovery of the neutron. We present evidence that the discussion centered on a paper written by Landau in February 1931, which proposed the existence of dense stars resembling giant nuclei. This work can be seen as an early theoretical prediction of neutron stars, predating the discovery of the neutron. The coincidence of the neutron's discovery and the paper's publication in February 1932 has led to a mistaken association between the two. Our analysis also highlights Landau's contributions to the theory of white dwarfs and the hypothesis of stars with neutron cores. By re-examining the historical record, we aim to provide a more accurate understanding of the origins of neutron star physics and Landau's role in shaping this field. Our study sheds new light on the development of modern astrophysics and the pioneering work of one of its most influential figures.

We investigate the mechanical properties of free polyelectrolyte multilayer films by analyzing osmotically induced swelling of microcapsules. Varying polyelectrolyte concentrations, capsule radii, and shell thicknesses yields an estimated upper limit for Young's modulus of approximately 100 MPa, indicating elastomer-like behavior and strong polyanion-polycation interactions.

This article presents the authors' harmonic deformation theory for 3-dimensional hyperbolic cone-manifolds, exploring topological applications to hyperbolic Dehn surgery and Kleinian group theory. Local rigidity results are leveraged to control existing deformations, yielding precise analytic and geometric insights into hyperbolic structures with short geodesics. The theory reveals that such structures are proximal to those with cusps. A novel harmonic deformation theory is also introduced, applicable when a sufficiently large embedded tube surrounds the singular locus, thus removing the constraint on cone angles. This advancement expands the theory's scope and utility.

This study examines the performance of a partially correlated amplitude damping channel on two qubits. We derive lower bounds for the single-shot classical capacity by analyzing two quantum ensembles that maximize the Holevo quantity for both memoryless and full-memory channels. The entanglement required to achieve this maximum is also quantified. Additionally, we establish lower and upper bounds for the single-shot quantum capacity, providing a reliable estimate for high channel transmissivity values. Finally, the entanglement-assisted classical channel capacity is computed, offering insights into the channel's information transmission capabilities and the role of entanglement in optimizing its performance.

This study examines the thermal softening of crystals resulting from anharmonicity, with a focus on developing a reliable self-consistent method to predict the maximum temperature for a stable crystal. Previous approaches, such as the self-consistent harmonic approximation (SCHA), have been shown to yield inaccurate results due to the omission of crucial diagrams in the perturbation expansion. An alternative method, the self-consistent Dyson equation (SCA), has also been found to be deficient in capturing the thermal and quantum melting of two-dimensional Coulomb-interacting particles. To address these limitations, we introduce the two-vertex self-consistent harmonic approximation (2V-SCHA), which provides a significant improvement in agreement with numerical simulations. Our method enables accurate calculations of the thermal softening of the shear modulus for two-dimensional crystals and the lattice of vortex lines in type-II superconductors, offering a more reliable estimate of the upper bound to the melting temperature. The 2V-SCHA approach has important implications for understanding the thermal stability of crystals and vortex lattices, and its applications are discussed in the context of melting transitions in two and three dimensions.

This study explores the intrinsic spin Hall effect in two-dimensional electron gases within quantum wells featuring two subbands. A novel intersubband-induced spin-orbit coupling is identified, and its impact on bulk spin Hall conductivity is examined. Utilizing the Kubo formalism, calculations reveal a finite conductivity in the absence of scattering, even in the limit of zero magnetic field, provided only the lowest subband is occupied. The conductivity exhibits non-monotonic behavior, changing sign as the Fermi energy varies between subband edges. A self-consistent calculation is performed to determine the magnitude of spin Hall conductivity for realistic InSb quantum wells, offering insights into the role of intersubband-induced spin-orbit coupling in these systems.

This article investigates compact Kähler manifolds admitting non-trivial real-holomorphic geodesic gradient vector fields with an additional integrability condition. We classify these manifolds, showing they are biholomorphic to bundles of complex projective spaces. The integral curves of such vector fields are reparametrized geodesics, satisfying specific geometric properties. Our results provide a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between geodesic gradient vector fields and the complex geometry of Kähler manifolds, shedding light on the interplay between real and complex geometric structures in these spaces, with implications for geometry and complex analysis.

This article presents a model of an anisotropic universe within the scalar-tensor theory of gravitation, where string fluid serves as the source of matter. By applying Berman's law, exact solutions to the field equations are obtained, resulting in a constant value of deceleration parameter. The model's classical potential is examined, and it is found that massive strings dominate in the early universe before eventually disappearing. This aligns with current astronomical observations. The physical and dynamical properties of the model are also discussed, providing insight into the universe's evolution. The results offer a novel perspective on the role of string fluid in cosmology.

This article explores the potential impact of upgrades to the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) on the physics capabilities of the ATLAS detector. Two possible upgrade scenarios are considered: an increase in luminosity by a factor of ten and a doubling of the LHC energy. Both upgrades are found to significantly enhance the physics capabilities of ATLAS, with the energy upgrade offering greater mass reach for new particles. However, in cases where the upgrade leads to increased precision in measurements due to larger data samples, the luminosity upgrade is found to be equally powerful. The increased pile-up of minimum bias events at higher luminosity may limit the physics performance of ATLAS in areas requiring forward jet tagging. The study assesses the potential benefits and challenges of each upgrade scenario, providing valuable insights for future LHC upgrade plans. The analysis is based on detailed simulations and considers various physics processes, highlighting the importance of careful planning and optimization to fully exploit the potential of the ATLAS detector in future LHC runs. The results of this study will inform the development of upgrade strategies for the LHC and ATLAS, ultimately enhancing our understanding of the fundamental laws of physics.

This study applies the worldline formalism to scalar Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) to derive a Bern-Kosower type master formula for generalized Compton scattering, applicable both on-shell and off-shell. The non-perturbative gauge parameter dependence of amplitudes in scalar QED is examined, yielding a simple transformation rule under gauge parameter changes in terms of conformal cross ratios. This result generalizes the Landau-Khalatnikov-Fradkin transformation, providing new insights into scalar QED. The transformation's perturbative behavior is also demonstrated, offering a deeper understanding of gauge parameter dependence in quantum field theories.

This article explores the potential discovery of high mass neutral quantum states at hadron colliders, specifically through their decay into a pair of photons. The determination of the spin of these states is crucial in identifying the underlying nonstandard dynamics. We investigate the discrimination of a spin-2 Randall-Sundrum graviton excitation from a spin-0 exchange, using angular analysis of resonant diphoton events expected at the LHC. The spin-0 hypothesis is modeled by an effective interaction of a high mass gauge singlet scalar particle. Our analysis focuses on the symmetrically integrated angular asymmetry, calculated to next-to-leading order in QCD for both graviton and scalar exchanges. By comparing the angular distributions, we aim to distinguish between these two hypotheses, providing insight into the nature of potential new physics beyond the Standard Model. The results have implications for the interpretation of future LHC data.

This study employs a solvable model to investigate double-beta decay, with a particular emphasis on the neutrinoless mode. By analyzing the impact of the neutrino propagator on the matrix element, we address the limitations of finite model-space size in shell-model calculations. Our approach involves projecting exact wave functions onto a smaller subspace and evaluating both traditional and recent methods for constructing effective operators. The results indicate that conventional treatments of double-beta decay operators are insufficient to account for neglected parts of the model space. Furthermore, we assess the quasiparticle random phase approximation and a recent proposal to utilize two-neutrino decay for fixing Hamiltonian parameters, which reduces the dependence on unfixed parameters and model-space size. Our findings provide valuable insights into the theoretical framework underlying double-beta decay and highlight the need for refined calculations to accurately capture the underlying physics.

This study examines the emergence of collective dynamics in an integrable Hamiltonian system comprising two finite ensembles of coupled harmonic oscillators. By identifying a collective degree of freedom, we map the Hamiltonian onto a Caldeira-Leggett type model, where the collective coordinate interacts with an internal phonon bath. Unlike traditional models, the bath is an intrinsic part of the system. We derive an equation of motion for the collective coordinate, yielding a damped harmonic oscillator. Our results demonstrate that the distribution of quantum transition strengths induced by the collective mode is determined by its classical dynamics, providing insight into the complex interplay between collective behavior and quantum fluctuations.

This study examines DNA's S-shape in relation to its total energy. Using the classical variation method, we derive equilibrium shape equations, providing both first and second variations in the planar case. Our results correct a mistake in previous research and yield general shape equations for DNA, offering new insights into its structural dynamics with implications for molecular biology and biophysics research applications and theory.

Title: Revisiting KIC 9202990: Unveiling the Nature of its Photometric Periods Abstract: We re-examine the photometric properties of KIC 9202990 using the comprehensive Kepler dataset, spanning 1421 days. Our analysis confirms the stability of the 4-hour period, reinforcing its association with the binary orbital period. In contrast, the previously reported two-week period exhibits significant amplitude variability, ranging from 20% to 50%. This modulation bears resemblance to'stunted' outbursts observed in nova-like systems. We discuss the shortcomings of the precessing accretion disk model in explaining the observed characteristics and argue in favor of a stunted outburst model. KIC 9202990 presents a unique opportunity to investigate accretion instabilities, as it displays the lowest amplitude and shortest period of continuous stunted outburst systems. Our findings have implications for understanding the disk instability mechanism and its role in shaping the behavior of cataclysmic variables. By exploring the properties of KIC 9202990, we aim to shed light on the underlying physics governing stunted outbursts and advance our knowledge of accretion processes in binary systems. This study highlights the importance of long-term monitoring and detailed analysis of photometric data in unraveling the complexities of accretion disk dynamics.

We investigate the non-equilibrium evolution of a strongly interacting fermionic system. Collective collapse and revival phenomena are observed for strong quenches, while weak quenches exhibit weak wiggling. Notably, prethermalization is absent in the weak coupling regime. Relaxation beyond oscillatory behavior is evident, allowing estimation of relaxation rates. The fastest relaxation occurs at intermediate quenched interaction values, providing insight into the system's dynamics and relaxation mechanisms, with implications for understanding complex quantum systems and their behavior under non-equilibrium conditions and quenches of varying strength.

This article explores the potential of 3D printing in revolutionizing various aspects of our lives, as touted by many as a key driver of the third industrial revolution. While its applications are currently limited, scientific research is one area where 3D printing has shown significant promise. We present the development of a set of opto-mechanical components that can be easily fabricated using Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) and readily available hardware store parts. The customized components offer several advantages, including low-cost, rapid fabrication, and performance comparable to low-end commercial alternatives. This study demonstrates the feasibility of 3D printing in creating functional and affordable components, highlighting its potential to transform scientific research and other fields. Our findings contribute to the growing body of research on 3D printing, underscoring its potential to drive innovation and change in the near future. Key benefits include ease of use and high customizability.

This article addresses the approximation of functionals dependent on a system of particles, modeled by stochastic differential equations (SDEs), as the number of particles approaches infinity. This problem is equivalent to estimating the weak solution of the limiting McKean-Vlasov SDE. To tackle this challenge, we employ systems with finite particles and an Euler-Maruyama time-stepping scheme, resulting in two discretization parameters: the number of time steps and particles. We investigate various Monte Carlo and multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) methods, demonstrating that the optimal work complexity of MLMC to estimate the functional with an error tolerance of $\epsilon$ is $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ in a typical setting. Furthermore, we explore the multi-index Monte Carlo method, achieving an improved work complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2}(\log \epsilon^{-1})^2)$ when utilizing a partitioning estimator. Numerical experiments are conducted on the Kuramoto model, a system of coupled oscillators, to validate our findings. Our research contributes to the development of efficient numerical methods for approximating functionals in the mean-field limit, with applications in fields such as physics, biology, and finance. The results highlight the potential of MLMC and multi-index Monte Carlo methods in tackling complex stochastic problems.

This study presents a novel expression for the entropy four-current up to third order in gradient expansion, derived using a Chapman-Enskog-like iterative solution of the Boltzmann equation in relaxation-time approximation. Notably, the resulting third-order entropy four-current exhibits a non-vanishing entropy flux, contrasting with previous second-order and third-order expressions obtained via Grad's method. The implications of this higher-order entropy density are investigated in the context of boost-invariant one-dimensional longitudinal expansion. By employing the Chapman-Enskog expansion method, we derive a third-order evolution equation for the shear stress tensor, yielding results that demonstrate improved agreement with both the exact solution of the Boltzmann equation and the parton cascade BAMPS, compared to those obtained using Grad's 14-moment approximation. These findings highlight the significance of incorporating higher-order corrections in the description of complex systems.

This article presents a simplified derivation of the "simple Fock scheme", a method for reformulating the many-body problem of interacting bosons in terms of single-particle wave function stochastic evolution. Compared to the original derivation, our approach is more elementary. We also examine two alternative schemes based on coherent states, demonstrating that they yield infinite statistical uncertainty in the continuous time limit. In contrast, the simple Fock scheme remains the only proven method for convergent Monte Carlo simulations at all times, solidifying its importance in the study of interacting boson systems. Its advantages are highlighted.

This article examines the physical properties of gamma-ray burst (GRB) emissions within the external shock model, where a thin relativistic blast wave interacts with the circumburst medium (CBM). We analyze an analytic function that describes the temporally evolving GRB spectra in a smooth CBM with density profile. Our results successfully reproduce the hard-to-soft spectral evolution and intensity-hardness correlation of GRB peaks. Furthermore, we predict several key features of GRB peaks, including alignment at high photon energies and lag at low energies, a well-defined shift in temporal indices with photon energy, and a decrease in spectral index change between peak edges at higher energies. Additionally, we demonstrate that the typical detection of GRBs with peaks in the 50 keV to several MeV range is a consequence of the inverse correlation between peak flux and radiation duration emitted by decelerating blast waves. Our findings provide new insights into the behavior of GRB emissions and can inform the development of more accurate models for understanding these complex astrophysical events. The predictions made in this study can be tested against observational data, offering a valuable tool for refining our understanding of GRB physics.

This study examines the parity-time reversal symmetric non-Hermitian version of a quantum network, as proposed by Christandl et al. Our systematic analysis reveals that this model exemplifies the complex relationship between pseudo-Hermitian Hamiltonians and their Hermitian counterparts. Furthermore, it provides a viable candidate for experimental realization of symmetry breaking. We demonstrate that conditional perfect state transfer is achievable within the unbroken symmetry region, albeit not arbitrarily. This limitation arises from the evolution operator's equivalence to the parity-time reversal operator at specific periods, as applied to real-valued wavefunctions in the parity-time reversal symmetric Hilbert space. Our findings offer insights into the intricacies of quantum mechanics and the potential applications of this model in quantum information processing.

This study simulates the cooling of neutron stars with dipole magnetic fields using a realistic model of anisotropic surface temperature distribution. The magnetic field suppresses electron thermal conductivity near the equator, increasing thermal isolation, while enhancing radiative and longitudinal conductivities near the poles, reducing isolation. The equatorial effect is pronounced for weaker fields (@xmath0 G), and the polar effect for stronger fields (@xmath1 G). However, these effects partially compensate each other, resulting in a weaker influence of magnetic fields on cooling than traditionally predicted, highlighting the importance of considering both equatorial and polar effects in neutron star cooling models.

This study examines the forecasting capabilities of realized skewness and realized kurtosis for individual stock returns and variance on a daily scale. Contrary to existing literature, which primarily focuses on monthly or weekly scales and whole market analysis, our empirical analysis reveals distinct findings. Notably, realized kurtosis demonstrates significant predictive power for a stock's future variance. In contrast, realized skewness lacks explanatory power for daily returns of individual stocks over short horizons, diverging from established research. Our results, derived from high-frequency data and linear regression models, contribute to the understanding of higher-order moments in financial markets. The surprising findings have implications for trading strategies and risk management, highlighting the importance of considering realized kurtosis in forecasting stock variance. Overall, this research expands the literature on realized moments and their applications in finance.

This study presents an analysis of data collected by the Middle Drum Fluorescence Detector, refurbished from the High Resolution Fly's Eye (HiRes) HIRES-1 site, within the Telescope Array. Utilizing the HiRes-1 profile-constrained geometry reconstruction technique and identical calibration methods, a direct comparison of energy spectra and scales is facilitated between the two experiments. A three-year exposure (2007-2010) yielded a measured spectrum, enabling the transfer of the HiRes-1 energy scale to Middle Drum. By comparing monocular Middle Drum events with hybrid events triggering both Middle Drum and the Telescope Array's scintillator ground array, the HiRes energy scale is applied to the entire Telescope Array. This research aims to provide a precise energy spectrum of Ultra-High Energy Cosmic Rays (UHECRs), leveraging the combined strengths of the HiRes and Telescope Array experiments to advance our understanding of cosmic ray physics. The results have significant implications for the field, offering a refined understanding of UHECR energy spectra and scales.

This study examines the formation of ferromagnetic polarons in doped anisotropic antiferromagnets. We investigate the manifestation of nanoscale phase separation in three- and two-dimensional systems, calculating the shape of the most energetically favorable ferromagnetic droplets. Our results show that the binding energy and volume of these droplets in 3D systems depend on two universal parameters, derived from effective antiferromagnetic exchange and hopping integrals. Similarly, in 2D systems, these parameters determine the droplet's properties. The most favorable shape of a ferromagnetic droplet is found to be an ellipse in 2D and an ellipsoid in 3D, providing insight into the behavior of these systems. Our findings contribute to the understanding of magnetic phase separation at the nanoscale.

We present a study of exclusive semileptonic decays proceeding via the underlying transition, utilizing a dataset of meson pairs collected at the resonance with the CLEO II detector. Our analysis yields measurements of key parameters, including branching fractions and distribution shapes, with careful consideration of statistical, systematic, and form factor uncertainties. The results are consistent with expectations from quark model symmetries and the dominant mode. By applying light-cone sum rules and lattice QCD, we extract the desired parameter, obtaining values for two distinct energy intervals. Combining these intervals, we determine the parameter's value with estimated errors accounting for statistical, systematic, theoretical, and signal form-factor shape uncertainties. Our combined result from both decay modes provides a precise determination of the parameter, contributing to a deeper understanding of the underlying physics. The findings have implications for future studies in this area.

This study presents an analysis of the latest 1.3 mm Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) measurements for Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), the supermassive black hole at the Galactic Center. By utilizing a model of an accretion flow coupled with an emergent flare, we interpret the visibility data to constrain the distances from the flare center to the black hole center. Our results indicate that the flare is likely to be located at a significant distance from the black hole, with preferred positions of @xmath0 and @xmath1 in the east-west and north-south directions, respectively. We discuss two possible interpretations of the flare: the hot-spot model and the episodic jet model. Our findings suggest that the flare passes in front of the black hole at a large radius or is ejected off the black hole's rotating axis. This method can be applied to future sub-millimeter VLBI observations to study millimeter/sub-millimeter variabilities near Sgr A*.

We report the first secure detection of the reactive ion CO+ towards the prototypical starburst galaxy M 82. Observations of the inner 650 pc of the nuclear disk reveal high [CO+]/[HCO+] ratios, comparable to those found in the atomic peak of the reflection nebula NGC 7023. This discovery suggests that the molecular gas reservoir in M 82 is significantly impacted by UV radiation from recently formed stars. Our analysis indicates that approximately 320 clouds along the line of sight are required to explain the observed column densities. We have developed a photon-dominated region (PDR) chemical model to interpret our findings, which successfully reproduces the measured [CO+]/[HCO+] ratios. However, the model underestimates the large CO+ column densities by an order of magnitude. To reconcile this discrepancy, we explore potential modifications to the chemical model, including revisions to the cloud structure and chemical reactions. Our study provides new insights into the molecular gas chemistry in the nucleus of M 82 and highlights the complexity of modeling the interplay between UV radiation and molecular gas in starburst galaxies. Further refinements to our model are necessary to fully explain the observed CO+ abundances.

Title: The Uncertainty in Equilibration in Heavy Ion Collisions due to the Choice of the Value of the Coupling Abstract: The process of equilibration in heavy ion collisions is a complex phenomenon that has garnered significant attention in the realm of high-energy physics.
