The numerical results for the spectral function of the double-occupied Green function are also presented. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the Hubbard model and strongly correlated systems, with implications for the development of more accurate theoretical models. The findings are relevant to various fields, including condensed matter physics and materials science.

We prove a version of Kontsevich's formality theorem for two subspaces. This result implies the Kontsevich deformation quantizations of associated quadratic Poisson structures are Koszul dual, answering an open question in Shoikhet's recent paper on Koszul duality in deformation quantization, with implications for mathematical physics and algebra.

We report the detection of propylene (C3H6) in a dark cloud using the IRAM 30-m radio telescope. Notably, propylene is the most saturated hydrocarbon detected in space via radio astronomy, despite its weak dipole moment. Six doublets and an additional line were observed with main beam temperatures above 20 mK. The derived column density of propylene is 4 × 1014 cm−2, corresponding to an abundance relative to H2 of 4 × 10−9, comparable to other abundant hydrocarbons in this cloud. The discovery of propylene, an isomer of C3H6, highlights the need for a thorough re-examination of gas-phase chemistry in dark clouds, as its formation pathway is not well understood. This finding has significant implications for interstellar chemistry, suggesting that current models may be incomplete. Further analysis is necessary to understand the role of propylene in dark cloud chemistry.

This study examines the pathology underlying the dependence of tropical eigenspaces of distinct supertropical eigenvalues in a nonsingular matrix. We demonstrate that in lower dimensions, eigenvectors of distinct eigenvalues are independent. The index set distinguishing between essential monomials of the characteristic polynomial yields an eigenvalue and corresponds to columns of the eigenmatrix from which eigenvectors are derived. However, in higher dimensions, independence fails, unless a "difference criterion" is met, defined by disjoint differences between index sets of subsequent coefficients. Our findings have implications for the eigenvectors of related matrices and the connection to generalized eigenvectors, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms governing eigenvector independence.

This study presents a comprehensive multiannual climatology of airborne dust on Mars, spanning Martian years 24 to 31 (April 1999 to July 2013). By combining observations from multiple orbiting instruments, including the Thermal Emission Spectrometer (TES), Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS), and Mars Climate Sounder (MCS), we have developed a robust dataset of column dust optical depth (CDOD) retrievals and estimates. Our methodology involves gridding the available data onto a regularly spaced, yet potentially incomplete, spatio-temporal grid, utilizing an iterative procedure that accounts for spatial, temporal, and retrieval uncertainty. The resulting gridded maps are accompanied by weighted standard deviation values, allowing for evaluation of their strengths and weaknesses. Validation of our dataset is achieved through comparison with independent observations from Pancam cameras, Mini-TES spectrometers, and the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars. Statistical analysis of the gridded maps reveals the interseasonal and interannual variability of Martian dust, providing a detailed understanding of the planet's dust climatology over an eight-year period. Furthermore, we have generated multiannual, daily maps of CDOD through spatial interpolation using a kriging method, which are incorporated into the Mars Climate Database version 5 and are freely available for use in various modeling applications and instrument intercomparisons. The derived dust maps (version 1.5) offer a valuable resource for the scientific community, enhancing our understanding of Martian dust storms and their impact on the planet's atmosphere.

This study presents novel findings from a series of high-resolution @xmath0cdm simulations of cluster mass halos, leveraging exceptional force and mass resolution. A comparative analysis is conducted with recently published simulations utilizing various codes, including pkdgrav, art, tpm, grape, and gadget. Through rigorous resolution tests, it is demonstrated that 25 million particles within the high-resolution region enable resolution to approximately 0.3% of the virial radius. The density profiles of 26 high-resolution clusters, obtained using different codes and initial conditions, exhibit excellent agreement. The average logarithmic slope at one percent of the virial radius is determined to be @xmath1, with a scatter of @xmath2. Furthermore, the density profiles are well-represented by a smooth function that asymptotes to a central cusp @xmath3, yielding @xmath4 from the mean of the fits to the six highest-resolution clusters. These results provide valuable insights into the formation and structure of cluster mass halos.

This study combines computer simulations and analytical theory to examine glassy dynamics in dense assemblies of athermal, self-propelled particles. As persistence time of self-propulsion increases, simulations show enhanced local structure and a non-monotonic effect on long-time dynamics. A novel nonequilibrium microscopic theory is developed to explain these findings, yielding predictions that agree with simulation results. The theory highlights the crucial role of steady-state correlations of local velocities in governing nonequilibrium dynamics of dense self-propelled particles, providing new insights into the complex behavior of these systems and their glassy dynamics under self-propulsion.

This study utilizes the Nearby Optical Galaxy (NOG) sample to map the galaxy density field in the local universe. Comprising 7076 optical galaxies, the NOG sample is volume-limited (6000 km/s) and magnitude-limited (m=14 mag), covering 2/3 of the sky (8.29 sr) with 98% redshift completeness. To trace the galaxy density field on small scales, we employ hierarchical and percolation "friends of friends" methods to identify NOG galaxy systems. The NOG sample offers high spatial resolution and detailed morphological galaxy classification, providing a foundation for constructing a statistically robust galaxy sample with homogenized photometric data spanning most of the celestial sphere. This research aims to lay the groundwork for a comprehensive understanding of the local universe's galaxy distribution and evolution.

This study presents the first application of mid-infrared period-luminosity relations to determine the distance to a Cepheid beyond the Magellanic Clouds. Using archival IRAC imaging data from the Spitzer Space Telescope, we measured single-epoch magnitudes for Cepheids in NGC 6822 at 3.6, 4.5, 5.8, and 8.0 μm. The observed slopes and scatter conform to previously established relations for Large Magellanic Cloud Cepheids. Fitting these relations yields apparent distance moduli, which, when combined with previously published optical and near-infrared moduli, allow for a correction of interstellar reddening. The resulting true distance modulus of 23.49 ± 0.03 mag corresponds to a metric distance of 500 ± 28 kpc. This distance determination demonstrates the effectiveness of mid-infrared period-luminosity relations in measuring extragalactic distances, paving the way for future applications in astronomy. The results have significant implications for our understanding of the universe's structure and evolution.

This study investigates the long-term evolution of the Hilda collisional family, a group of asteroids located in the 3/2 mean-motion resonance with Jupiter. By modeling the effects of the Yarkovsky/Yorp effect on the family's eccentricity distribution, we estimate the age of the Hilda family to be approximately 0. Our analysis assumes isotropic impact disruption and a uniform albedo distribution among small and large asteroids. The results indicate that current collisional rates are extremely low, with a negligible probability of collisional disruption over gigayear timescales. Given the family's advanced age and low collisional activity, we propose that the Hilda family may have formed during the Late Heavy Bombardment, a period of intense asteroid collisions. This hypothesis suggests that the Hilda family could serve as a probe of planetary orbital behavior during this era. Our simulations of giant planet migration scenarios reveal that fast migration timescales are necessary to reproduce the observed characteristics of the Hilda family. Furthermore, our findings imply that Jupiter and Saturn were not in a compact configuration at the time of the family's formation. These results provide new insights into the orbital evolution of the Hilda family and the early solar system, highlighting the importance of considering the complex interplay between asteroid collisions, planetary migration, and orbital resonances.

This study explores the strongly-coupled phase of the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) using a matrix formulation, where the medium is treated as a non-ideal gas of interacting quasiparticles. Focusing on the temperature range of 1-5 Tc, where Tc is the deconfinement temperature, we investigate the formation of bound states due to strong interactions. The dissociation temperature of these binary bound states is calculated, revealing that heavier quasiparticles form more resilient bound states. We then compute the QGP equations of state at zero and small baryonic potential using the Dashen, Ma, and Bernstein statistical mechanics formulation. Our results are compared to current lattice QCD data, providing insight into the behavior of the QGP in the strongly-coupled phase. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the QGP's properties and behavior in high-energy environments.

This article presents an updated estimate for the Astrodynamical Space Test of Relativity using Optical Devices (ASTROD) in detecting solar g-modes through their gravitational signature. With recent estimates of g-mode surface amplitude, we compare the detection capabilities of ASTROD and the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). Our analysis suggests that LISA's detection capability is uncertain, whereas ASTROD's sensitivity curve, shifted towards lower frequencies, may be better suited for detection, particularly in the 1 Hz range. This study provides new insights into the prospects of ASTROD for unambiguous detection of solar g-modes, offering a promising alternative to LISA.

This study examines the effect of surface imperfections on the Casimir force in the lens-plate geometry, a critical consideration for spherical lenses with centimeter-size curvature radii. The commonly employed proximity force approximation is found to be inadequate for lenses with surface defects, such as bubbles and pits. To address this limitation, we derive more comprehensive expressions for the Casimir force that account for surface imperfections. Our results indicate that these imperfections can significantly modify the magnitude of the Casimir force, leading to increases or decreases of up to several tens of percent compared to the ideal case of a perfectly spherical lens. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Casimir force between a spherical lens and a plate can be made equivalent by introducing appropriate surface imperfections, regardless of the material models employed. This finding has significant implications for the interpretation of measurement data, highlighting a fundamental challenge in comparing experimental results with theoretical predictions for the Casimir force in systems utilizing spherical lenses with centimeter-size radii. Our research underscores the need for careful consideration of surface imperfections in the design and analysis of Casimir force experiments.

This study investigates the frequency evolution of pulsar pulse profiles using the inverse Compton scattering (ICS) model. We present theoretical simulations of integrated pulse profiles and their frequency dependence, providing a framework for understanding emission mechanisms. By applying the ICS model's "beam-frequency figure," we perform Gaussian fits to multi-frequency pulse profiles for several pulsars. Our results demonstrate that the model successfully reproduces various observed frequency evolution behaviors, offering new insights into pulsar phenomenology. This work addresses a previously unexplored aspect of pulsar research, shedding light on the complex relationships between pulse profiles and observing frequencies.

We approximately solve the QCD gluon equation of motion using the Green function, reformulating the QCD Lagrangian to explicitly feature the gluon propagator in interaction terms, and analyze the nature and coordinate-space form of these interactions in the static, non-relativistic limit.

This study presents a novel approach to identifying emergent clusters within price evolutions using a master-slave parallel Genetic Algorithm (PGA) with a bespoke log-likelihood fitness function. Leveraging the computational power of Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), our PGA implementation enables rapid cluster recovery in sub-second speed, utilizing a subset of stocks from the South African market. Compared to a serial implementation in an optimized C-based language, our GPU-based approach demonstrates significant speed enhancements, offering a pragmatic solution for low-cost, scalable parallel computing. By integrating our method with fast online intraday correlation matrix estimation from high-frequency data, we provide a cost-effective framework for near real-time risk assessment in financial markets. The proposed implementation has substantial implications for financial practitioners, enabling unsupervised clustering and maximum likelihood clustering for informed decision-making. Our findings highlight the potential of parallel computing in financial data processing, facilitating efficient and accurate cluster identification.

We present a novel, time-dependent, multi-group, multidimensional relativistic radiative transfer code designed to simulate radiation from relativistic fluids, such as those found in gamma-ray bursts and active galactic nuclei. Our code, based on the spherical harmonic discrete ordinate method (SHDOM), incorporates anisotropic scattering and solves the radiative transfer equation using ray tracing in discrete ordinates. Key features include time dependence, multi-frequency bins, Lorentz transformation, and both elastic Thomson and inelastic Compton scattering. A mixed frame approach is adopted, evaluating the source function in the comoving frame and solving the radiative transfer equation in the laboratory frame. The code's validity is confirmed through various test problems and comparisons with a relativistic Monte Carlo code, demonstrating accurate calculation of intensity evolution. The code also enables computation of the Eddington tensor, relating energy density and radiation pressure, a crucial closure relation in radiation hydrodynamics calculations. This new tool facilitates detailed investigations of relativistic radiative processes, enhancing our understanding of high-energy astrophysical phenomena. The code's capabilities and applications are poised to significantly impact the field of relativistic astrophysics.

This study investigates the spectral properties of the brightest γ-ray blazar 3C 454.3 using 138 weeks of observations from the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope. We analyze the source's behavior over time at varying brightness levels, finding that the Fermi spectra in the GeV range can be described by a lognormal distribution with photon-photon absorption breaks. Notably, we discover a power-law dependence of the peak energy on flux and an anti-correlation between the Lyman recombination continuum column density and flux. These findings suggest that the γ-ray emission zone is located near the boundary of the broad-line region's high-ionization part and recedes from the black hole as flux increases. Our results imply that the relativistic jet is accelerated at sub-parsec distances from the central black hole, supporting the Blandford-Znajek process as the jet launching mechanism. This research provides valuable insights into the physics of black hole jets and the emission mechanisms of active galaxies, shedding light on the complex interplay between the accretion disk, broad-line region, and relativistic jet.

This study utilizes Red Clump Giant (RCG) stars as distance indicators to investigate the mass distribution of the Galactic bar. Analyzing 44 bulge fields from the OGLE-II microlensing collaboration database, we constrain analytic tri-axial models for the Galactic bar. Our results indicate that the bar's major axis is oriented at an angle of approximately 20-30 degrees to the Sun-Galactic centre line-of-sight. The semi-major and semi-minor axis scale lengths ratio is found to be around 1.5, with a vertical scale length ratio of 0.4, suggesting a slightly more prolate bar structure than previously proposed models. These findings contribute to our understanding of the Galaxy's central structure and evolution.

This study highlights the significance of incorporating time-odd components into the wave function for an accurate description of rotational motion using the angular-momentum-projection method. Specifically, we investigate the effects of infinitesimal cranking about three independent axes on the energy spectrum of triaxially deformed nuclei. Our results show that cranking about each axis has distinct effects, and including all three axes substantially modifies the energy spectrum compared to calculations without cranking. Using the Gogny D1S force as an effective interaction, we apply this method to calculate the multiple gamma vibrational bands in 168Er, a typical example of a triaxially deformed nucleus. The angular-momentum-projected configuration-mixing approach yields both the one- and two-phonon gamma vibrational bands with considerable anharmonicity. Our calculations demonstrate reasonable agreement with experimental data for both the energy spectrum and transition probabilities, assuming a small average triaxial deformation for the ground state rotational band. Additionally, we discuss the relation of our findings to the wobbling motion observed at high-spin states, providing new insights into the rotational dynamics of triaxially deformed nuclei.

This paper explores the identification of insurance models with multidimensional screening, where insurees possess private information about their risk and risk aversion. The proposed model incorporates a random damage component and allows for multiple claims, with screening based on the certainty equivalence of insurees. We examine the impact of data availability on the number of offered coverages and reported claims on the identification of model primitives across four distinct scenarios. Our results demonstrate that the model structure can be identified despite the presence of bunching due to multidimensional screening and/or a limited number of offered coverages. The observed number of claims plays a crucial role in identifying the joint distribution of risk and risk aversion. Furthermore, we derive the restrictions imposed by the model on observable variables, providing a constructive framework with explicit equations for estimation and model testing. The identification of insurance models with multidimensional screening has significant implications for understanding adverse selection in insurance markets. Our findings contribute to the development of more accurate and efficient insurance models, enabling policymakers and insurers to better design and implement insurance contracts that account for the complex interactions between risk, risk aversion, and screening. By providing a rigorous framework for analyzing insurance models with multidimensional screening, this paper sheds new light on the intricacies of insurance markets and informs the development of more effective insurance policies.

This article presents the Bolocam Galactic Plane Survey (BGPS), a comprehensive 1.1 mm continuum survey of the Galactic plane visible from the Northern Hemisphere. The survey encompasses an effective resolution of 33 and covers approximately 170 square degrees of the Galactic plane. Notably, the BGPS is one of the first large-area, systematic surveys of the Galactic plane in the millimeter continuum without pre-selected targets, providing an unbiased view of the region. The survey area includes a contiguous region spanning 0° to 90° in Galactic longitude, with additional coverage towards the Cygnus X spiral arm and cross-cuts at specific Galactic longitudes. The total surveyed area is approximately 133 square degrees, with four targeted regions in the outer Galaxy also observed. The BGPS has detected approximately 8,400 clumps across the entire survey area, with a limiting non-uniform 1-σ noise level ranging from 11 to 53 mJy beam-1. The survey's data reduction methods and observations are detailed in this paper, including the determination of astrometric and flux density calibration uncertainties. Comparison with existing literature reveals a possible systematic offset in flux calibration, although the cause remains unknown. The data processing algorithms employed to separate astronomical signals from time-variable atmospheric fluctuations are also presented, along with their limitations and potential artifacts. The BGPS provides a valuable complementary dataset to ongoing surveys, such as ATLASGAL and Herschel-SPIRE, and will serve as an important context for future observations with SCUBA-2 and ALMA. The survey's public data release is available through NASA's Infrared Processing and Analysis Center (IPAC) Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), with future improvements to the reduction pipeline to be released accordingly. The BGPS offers a unique opportunity to study the Galactic plane in unprecedented detail, enabling new insights into the structure and evolution of our Galaxy. By leveraging the BGPS dataset, researchers can investigate a range of topics, from star formation and molecular cloud properties to the Galactic magnetic field and cosmic ray distribution. As such, the BGPS is poised to make significant contributions to our understanding of the Milky Way and its constituent components.

This study explores the hydrodynamic predictions of long-lived sound and shear waves, where thermal fluctuations induce momentum density diffusion, contributing to shear viscosity and transport coefficients. Within 3+1 dimensional viscous hydrodynamics, a positive, finite contribution to shear viscosity is observed, inversely proportional to microscopic shear viscosity, resulting in a bounded effective infrared viscosity. However, the contribution to the second-order transport coefficient is divergent, rendering second-order relativistic viscous hydrodynamics inconsistent below a certain frequency scale. The implications for the quark-gluon plasma are assessed, revealing minor effects for certain parameters, but significant effects for others, highlighting the importance of these hydrodynamic considerations.

This article presents a comprehensive spectral-timing analysis of the bare Seyfert 1 galaxy Ark 120, utilizing a long (140 ks) XMM-Newton observation consisting of four individual observations, each lasting 35 ks, conducted in March 2014. During this period, the galaxy exhibited alternating episodes of decreased and increased 0.3-10 keV X-ray flux. Our analysis employs broadband X-ray spectroscopy, fractional root mean square (rms) spectral modeling, hardness-intensity diagrams, and flux-flux analysis to investigate the energy-dependent variability of Ark 120. The X-ray spectra (0.3-10 keV) are well-described by a power-law continuum, two reflection components, and an additional Comptonization model to account for the soft X-ray excess emission below 3 keV. Notably, the X-ray fractional rms variability exhibits distinct energy-dependent behavior across the four observations. We find that the rms variability spectra can be modeled by a soft excess component with variable luminosity and a variable intrinsic power-law continuum, with correlated normalization and spectral slope. The source hardness is observed to decrease with increasing luminosity, consistent with expectations for a radio-quiet active galaxy. Furthermore, the flux from the more ionized reflection component is found to be correlated with the continuum flux on the observed 4-day timescale. Our results suggest that the observed energy-dependent variability of Ark 120 is likely driven by variations in the spectral shape and intrinsic luminosity of the primary X-ray emitting hot corona, as well as the luminosity of the soft excess emitting warm corona. These findings provide new insights into the complex X-ray emission mechanisms at play in this active galaxy.

Here is a 282-word abstract based on the provided title: We present a comprehensive analysis of the X-ray variability and spectral timing properties of the ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX) NGC 5408 X-1, a highly variable source with a complex accretion history. By examining the variability properties, we aim to diagnose the accretion state of the source and constrain the mass of the black hole (BH). Our results show that NGC 5408 X-1 exhibits a high level of fast X-ray variability, characterized by a fractional root-mean-square (RMS) amplitude of ~10% in the hard energy band. The fractional RMS spectrum hardens with increasing energy, and the properties of the quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) are consistent with a source in a hard-intermediate accretion state. We confirm the presence of a soft lag in the X-ray light curves, which persists over a range of frequencies, including the QPO frequencies. The soft lag displays energy dependence, with the amplitude increasing as a function of energy separation. Our findings draw close analogies with soft lags associated with type-C QPOs in BH binary systems, as well as with reverberation lags observed in active galactic nuclei (AGN). These similarities suggest that NGC 5408 X-1 is likely powered by an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH). Our study provides new insights into the accretion dynamics and BH mass of this enigmatic ULX, highlighting the importance of continued monitoring and multi-wavelength observations to unravel the mysteries of these extreme objects. The implications of our results are discussed in the context of BH physics, accretion disk theory, and the emerging understanding of ULXs as a class of objects.

This study presents the initial findings of a search for rapid optical variability in five narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. Notably, IRAS 13224-3809 exhibits clear evidence of variability on hourly timescales. In contrast, the results for Markarian 766, PG 1244+026, PG 1404+226, and Arakelian 564 are less conclusive, with only hints of potential variability. IRAS 13224-3809 provides the sole definitive evidence of rapid optical variability detected among the sample. These findings contribute to our understanding of active galaxies, quasars, and Seyfert galaxy variability, highlighting the complexities of optical variability in these astronomical objects. Further research is warranted to elucidate these phenomena.

This article introduces novel properties of the fractional Poisson process and field on a plane, providing a martingale characterization. Extensions to fractional Poisson fields yield additional characterizations. Fractional differential equations are examined, and a mixed-fractional Poisson process is shown to solve a system of fractional differential-difference equations. Simulations of the fractional Poisson field on a plane are also presented, enhancing understanding of these stochastic processes.

This study explores the DBI-Essence dark energy model within the framework of a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) universe. We derive exact solutions for the potential, warped brane tension, and DBI scalar field. Statefinder parameters are calculated to differentiate our model from other dark energy models. A correspondence is established between the DBI-Essence model and the Modified Chaplygin Gas (MCG) model, allowing for the reconstruction of potential and warped brane tension. Our results show an increase in DBI scalar field and potential, and a decrease in warped brane tension, over the universe's evolution. Furthermore, we examine the validity of the Generalized Second Law (GSL) of thermodynamics for both models, finding that the GSL is violated for the DBI-Essence model but consistently satisfied for the MCG model.

This study examines the average formation lengths of hadrons produced during deep inelastic scattering of leptons on protons using the symmetric Lund model. The results indicate that formation lengths are significantly influenced by the electric charges of the hadrons. For electroproduction and charged current neutrino production, positively charged particles exhibit longer formation lengths than negatively charged antiparticles. Conversely, charged current antineutrino production yields shorter formation lengths for positively charged particles. Direct hadron production is the primary mechanism in these processes. However, resonance decay contributes substantially to pion production, leading to decreased average formation lengths. These findings provide insight into the dynamics of hadron production in lepton-proton interactions, highlighting the importance of charge-dependent effects and secondary production mechanisms. The research has implications for our understanding of particle formation and interaction in high-energy collisions.

This article presents the findings of a spatially-resolved spectroscopic analysis of the galaxy cluster Abell 496, conducted using the S3 chip on board the Chandra satellite. The results confirm the presence of a central positive temperature gradient, indicative of a cooling flow, with a minimum gas temperature of 0.50-0.9 keV. The cluster exhibits distinct features, including sharp edges in gas density and temperature, characteristic of "cold front" substructures. Notably, the iron abundance profile is not radially symmetric, with a flat distribution towards the northern cold front and an off-center peak in the southern direction. Abundance ratios suggest that the central regions are dominated by SN Ia ejecta, while at larger radii (>100 kpc), the abundance ratios vary, leading to differing estimates of the SN Ia/II ejecta proportion. However, the continuity of abundances across the cold fronts implies that they are unlikely to be the result of a subcluster merger. Instead, we propose that the cold fronts in Abell 496 are caused by the sloshing of the central cooling flow gas, induced by the motion of the cluster's central dominant galaxy about the cluster center. These findings provide new insights into the dynamics and evolution of galaxy clusters, highlighting the complex interplay between gas flows, metal enrichment, and gravitational interactions.

This study presents an analysis of the star formation history (SFH) of the galactic disk using an infall model. By examining the observed SFH, we determine the timescales of gas infall into the disk and gas consumption to form stars. Due to the interdependence of these timescales, we fix one parameter and minimize the other, resulting in three potential parameter sets: (6.0, 23), (11, 12), and (15, 9.0), assuming a galactic age of 15 Gyr. Notably, all three cases yield nearly identical SFH predictions. Furthermore, we investigate the intermittency of the star formation rate (SFR) and find that the observed SFH exhibits significant time-variation, suggesting a violent and variable SFH. Our analysis reveals that the amplitude of the variable component is comparable to the smooth component, strongly indicating an intermittent SFH for the galactic disk. Additionally, we examine the metallicity distribution of G-dwarfs and find that the true parameter set likely falls between (6, 23) and (11, 12), although a more sophisticated model incorporating metal enrichment processes within the galactic halo is necessary for further refinement. Our results provide new insights into the complex SFH of the galactic disk, highlighting the importance of considering both smooth and variable components.

This study utilizes simulations to investigate the microscopic origins of strain hardening in polymer glasses, challenging the conventional understanding based on entropic network models. While stress-strain curves can be fit to the predicted functional form, the underlying physical picture is inconsistent with the observed results. The stresses exhibited are too large to be entropic and display an incorrect temperature trend. Notably, significant hardening at large strains is attributed to increases in energy as chains are stretched between entanglements, rather than entropic changes. Entropic stress is only observed during shape recovery of deformed samples heated above the glass transition. Furthermore, simulations reveal that short chains exhibit partial shape recovery, orientation, and strain hardening, despite lacking an entangled network. By plotting stresses against a microscopic measure of chain stretching, a universal behavior is observed across chain lengths. The thermal contribution to stress is found to be proportional to the rate of plasticity, as measured by interchain bond breaking and reforming. These findings suggest that a glassy state physics approach, rather than rubber elasticity, is necessary to accurately describe the microscopic theory of strain hardening in polymer glasses.

This article addresses the critical challenge of spectrally efficient multi-antenna wireless communications, which is exacerbated by increasing service demands and the environmental impact of powering radio access networks. To mitigate these issues, we propose a novel directional modulation precoder designed for M-QAM modulation with a focus on energy efficiency. Our approach involves defining extended detection regions in the constellation using analytical geometry, followed by the optimal placement of constellation points to maintain the minimum Euclidean distance to neighboring points and the detection region boundary. Furthermore, we introduce relaxed detection regions for inner constellation points to enhance energy efficiency. By leveraging these detection regions and modulation characteristics, we formulate convex symbol-level precoder design problems aimed at minimizing transmission power while ensuring the required signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at the destination. Our results demonstrate that the proposed methods outperform benchmark schemes in terms of power reduction, peak power reduction, and symbol error rate reduction across a wide range of SNRs, making them a promising solution for future wireless communication systems.

This article presents a novel approach to constructing a consistent physical theory of quantum mechanics based on a non-Hermitian complex Hamiltonian that satisfies space-time reflection symmetry. Contrary to expectations, this framework does not violate unitarity, as a previously overlooked physical symmetry of the Hamiltonian enables the construction of a positive definite inner product. This formulation governs unitary time evolution and is compatible with conventional quantum mechanics. The introduction of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that satisfy space-time reflection symmetry opens up new avenues for explaining experimental data, with infinitely many possible constructions. The implications of this extension of quantum mechanics into the complex domain are far-reaching, with potential observable and experimental consequences in both particle physics and solid state physics, offering a new paradigm for understanding complex quantum systems. This theory provides a foundation for further research and exploration.

This study examines the directed flow in Au+Au collisions at √s = 200 and 39 GeV using a multiphase transport model. The partonic phase's evolution over time leads to a change in the slope of the parton directed flow at mid-rapidity, transitioning from negative to positive at 200 GeV, while remaining negative at 39 GeV due to the shorter partonic phase lifetime. Directed flow splitting is observed among quark species at 39 GeV, whereas it is minimal at 200 GeV. The effects of hadronization and hadronic rescatterings on directed flow are also investigated. This research provides a foundational understanding of directed flow in the absence of mean-field potentials and exotic mechanisms, offering a baseline for further study. The findings shed light on the complex dynamics of particle collisions at varying energies.

This study investigates the non-equilibrium nature of the spin glass phase in Ag(11 at%Mn) at temperatures below the zero-field spin glass temperature. Through experiments on the time dependence of the response function, we find that the response is primarily governed by the thermal history near the measurement temperature. The thermal history outside this narrow range has little impact on the measured response. Our results suggest that the cooling process imprints the spin structure, retaining this information even when higher temperatures are reached. We interpret these findings using a real-space droplet/domain phenomenology. The importance of controlled cooling procedures for obtaining reproducible and interpretable results on non-equilibrium dynamics in spin glasses is highlighted, emphasizing the need for careful experimental design to uncover the complex behavior of these systems. Our work provides new insights into the thermal history dependence of spin glasses.

This study examines topological interactions in theories with compact extra dimensions, where fermionic chiral zero modes exhibit distinct localizations. Utilizing deconstruction techniques, we investigate these interactions in warped extra dimension models, particularly focusing on the localization of right- and left-handed top quarks. Our analysis reveals that topological interactions manifest as trilinear and quadrilinear gauge boson couplings in low-energy effective theories. We derive the form of these interactions for various gauge groups, including abelian, non-abelian, and product groups. The results provide insight into the fundamental aspects of these theories and may yield unique signatures at the Large Hadron Collider, offering a potential window into the underlying structure of these models and their phenomenological implications.

This study examines the impact of non-standard interactions on neutrino oscillation parameters in the MINOS experiment. By incorporating non-standard interactions, we find an expansion of the allowed parameter space for θ23 and θ13, but a loss of predictability for θ12. Our analysis also investigates the sensitivity of the MINOS experiment to non-standard interaction parameters, revealing a degeneracy between θ12 and the non-standard interaction parameter ε. This degeneracy accounts for the reduced predictability of θ12. Furthermore, we determine that a competitive bound on ε can be achieved only if a stringent external bound on θ12 is applied, highlighting the need for additional constraints to resolve this degeneracy and improve the accuracy of neutrino oscillation parameter determinations.

This article establishes functional central and non-central limit theorems for generalized variations of the anisotropic $d$-parameter fractional Brownian sheet (FBS) for any natural number $d$. The applicability of either limit theorem depends on the Hermite rank of the variation functional and the smallest component of the Hurst parameter vector. For central limit theorems, the limit is an independent FBS, while non-central limit theorems yield an Hermite sheet driven by the same white noise as the original FBS. As an application, we derive functional limit theorems for power variations of the FBS and discuss proper interpolation methods to ensure functional convergence, providing insights into the asymptotic behavior of FBS variations.

This study implements an optical quantum eraser to examine state discrimination phenomena. A single photon is entangled with a which-path marker, affecting interference visibility and which-path information based on the overlap between non-orthogonal marker states. To analyze these states and perform measurements, a probabilistic method is utilized, enabling the unambiguous modification of the inner product between the which-path marker states. This approach facilitates the investigation of the interplay between quantum erasure and state discrimination, providing insights into the fundamental principles governing quantum mechanics. The results have implications for quantum information processing and the understanding of quantum phenomena.

This study examines the structural properties of weighted networks through an empirical analysis of a linguistic network. By comparing a real network to a shuffled counterpart, we reveal that scale-free degree and weight distributions are driven by a scale-free strength distribution, conforming to Zipf's Law. We validate these findings on a scientific collaboration network and introduce the concept of vertex selectivity, a measure capable of distinguishing real networks from shuffled ones. Using a stochastic growing network model with second-order correlations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of vertex selectivity in capturing topological correlations. Our results provide insights into the underlying mechanisms governing complex network structures.

We present high-resolution imaging of the nucleus of NGC 4258, utilizing observations from 1.1 to 18 μm. Our findings indicate that the previously identified compact emission source remains unresolved at near-infrared resolutions of 0.2 arcsec FWHM, corresponding to approximately 7 pc at the galaxy's distance. This suggests that the emission source is likely located near the purported 3.5 × 10^6 M⊙ black hole. After correcting for approximately 18 magnitudes of visual extinction, the infrared data exhibit a flat spectrum from 1.1 to 18 μm, implying a non-thermal origin. The total extinction-corrected infrared luminosity of the central source is calculated to be 2 × 10^7 L⊙. Our analysis reveals that the infrared spectrum and luminosity of the central source can be explained without a substantial contribution from a standard, thin accretion disk. Instead, we estimate an accretion rate of approximately 10^-4 M⊙/yr through an advection-dominated accretion flow. The consistency between our observations and theoretical spectral energy distributions for advection-dominated flows provides strong evidence for the existence of such a flow in this low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN).

This study presents a groundbreaking observation of the thermal dominant state in an ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX), a phenomenon rarely detected in these extreme objects. Utilizing simultaneous Chandra and XMM-Newton observations of M82, we identify the thermal dominant state in a ULX for the first time, characterized by the disappearance of X-ray oscillations, low timing noise, and a spectrum dominated by multicolor disk emission. The luminosity of the source varies with the fourth power of the disk temperature, suggesting a strong similarity to galactic black hole binaries (BHBs). By fitting the brightest X-ray spectrum with a relativistic disk model, we propose two possible interpretations: a highly super-Eddington non-rotating black hole or a rapidly rotating black hole near the Eddington limit. The latter scenario is preferred, implying the presence of a 200-800 solar mass black hole with nearly maximal spin. Our findings provide new insights into the nature of ULXs, suggesting they may be similar to galactic BHBs, and shed light on the properties of these enigmatic objects. The source exhibits a regular 62-day orbital modulation and irregular flaring activity, with thermal dominant states occurring during outbursts.

This article reexamines the formulation of the general form of the @xmath0-@xmath1-@xmath2 vertex within the framework of hidden local symmetry (HLS), focusing on the intrinsic parity-odd part of the effective action. The gauge-invariant terms in this context are derived from the homogeneous part of the general solution to the Wess-Zumino (WZ) anomaly equation, which, contrary to previous claims, are not uniquely determined by the anomaly. Instead, these terms contain free parameters, similar to the HLS formulation. We demonstrate that even within the framework underlying the Harvey-Hill-Hill (HHH) action, the @xmath0-@xmath1-@xmath2 vertex is not anomaly-determined but rather depends on the homogeneous, anomaly-free part of the general solution, with the HHH action representing a specific choice of these free parameters. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the @xmath0-@xmath1-@xmath2 vertex relevant to the neutrino (@xmath3) - nucleon (@xmath4) scattering cross section @xmath5 is also determined by the anomaly-free part, not the anomaly itself. However, through the Ward-Takahashi identity, we find that the cross section @xmath5 is related to @xmath6, which shares the same parameter dependence, allowing the ratio @xmath7 to be fixed independently of these parameters. By adjusting another set of free parameters to fit the @xmath8 process, which deviates significantly from the HHH action, we obtain a prediction for the cross section @xmath9. This prediction can be tested in future @xmath3-@xmath4 collision experiments, offering a new avenue for verifying our formulation and understanding the underlying dynamics. Our work provides a nuanced view of how the @xmath0-@xmath1-@xmath2 vertex and related cross sections are determined, highlighting the role of anomaly-free contributions and the potential for experimental validation.

This study reexamines the ultraviolet luminosity density and star-formation rate density of the universe, utilizing photometric redshifts of galaxies in the Hubble Deep Field. By accounting for errors, including sampling error, our analysis suggests that a flat distribution of comoving ultraviolet luminosity density is statistically indistinguishable from a peaked distribution at redshifts around 1. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of cosmological surface brightness dimming on these measurements by applying a uniform surface brightness cut. Our results indicate a significant increase in ultraviolet luminosity density contributed by high intrinsic surface brightness regions from redshift 3 to 4. This implies the existence of a population of objects with exceptionally high star formation rates at high redshifts, which are absent at low redshifts. Our findings suggest that the peak of star formation likely occurs at redshifts beyond 5, challenging current understanding of the universe's star formation history and highlighting the need for further investigation into the early universe's evolution.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the time- and position-dependent point spread function (PSF) variation of the Wide Field Channel (WFC) of the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) using the Principal Component Analysis (PCA) technique. The temporal variation of the focus and changes in aberrations and charge diffusion across the detector are identified as the primary causes of PSF variation. A PSF library is constructed using archival images of star cluster fields, covering a diverse range of observational environments. The results show that interpolation of a small number of principal components, or "eigen-PSFs", can accurately reproduce the observed variation in PSF ellipticity and size. The primary application of this PSF library is in precision weak-lensing analyses, where accurate knowledge of the instrument's PSF is crucial. However, the high fidelity of the model also makes it potentially useful in other applications, such as crowded field stellar photometry, galaxy profile fitting, and AGN studies, which require accurate knowledge of the PSFs at object locations. The publicly available PSF models, applicable to any WFC image rectified with the Lanczos3 kernel, provide a valuable resource for the astronomical community. The agreement between the model and observed PSFs demonstrates the robustness and accuracy of the PCA technique in characterizing the complex PSF variation of the ACS/WFC, enabling precise and reliable astronomical measurements.

This article presents analytical stationary solutions for the Gross-Pitaevskii equation of a Bose-Einstein condensate trapped in a double-well potential. Our results are compared to existing solutions, providing further evidence that symmetry-preserving solutions correspond to linear Schrödinger equation eigenstates. Notably, symmetry-breaking solutions can emerge from both bifurcations and isolated points in the chemical potential-nonlinear interaction diagram. Additionally, moving nodes are observed in symmetry-breaking solutions, offering new insights into the behavior of Bose-Einstein condensates in double-well potentials. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics of BECs in such systems.

In this article, we explore the potential of SO(10) grand unified theories to provide a straightforward path towards gauge coupling unification, which can be achieved through the modification of the renormalization group evolution of gauge couplings above an intermediate scale. This intermediate scale may also be related to the seesaw mechanism for neutrino masses. We investigate the possibility that SO(10) unification can provide a natural dark matter candidate, with stability guaranteed by a leftover symmetry. Our analysis, performed at the two-loop level, systematically examines possible intermediate gauge groups that allow for a non-degenerate, fermionic, standard model singlet dark matter candidate while respecting gauge coupling unification. We consider various phenomenological constraints, including suitable neutrino masses, proton decay, and reheating. Surprisingly, despite the richness of SO(10), we find that only two models survive our analysis. These models demonstrate the potential for SO(10) unification to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding gauge coupling unification, neutrino masses, and dark matter. Our results highlight the importance of considering the interplay between these phenomena in the context of grand unified theories. By exploring the constraints on SO(10) models, we shed light on the possible connections between gauge coupling unification, neutrino masses, and dark matter, and provide a framework for further investigation into the nature of these phenomena. Overall, our analysis demonstrates the potential for SO(10) unification to provide a natural and comprehensive explanation for several open questions in particle physics.

This study examines the simulation of phase-transition sequences in ferroelectric perovskites, such as BaTiO3, using a first-principles derived effective Hamiltonian. The impact of external pressure on these materials is investigated by considering the enthalpy rather than the Hamiltonian itself. However, this approach relies on two crucial assumptions: that relevant degrees of freedom remain unchanged at finite pressures, and that the truncation of the Taylor expansion of the energy remains a valid approximation. We scrutinize these assumptions and present illustrative first-principles results for BaTiO3, highlighting the legitimacy of this method. Furthermore, we discuss the construction of effective Hamiltonians in scenarios where these assumptions are invalid, providing a comprehensive understanding of the simulation of phase transitions in ferroelectric perovskites under external pressure. Our findings have significant implications for the study of ferroelectric materials and their behavior under various external fields.

This note explores the construction of exact soliton solutions to the KP equation from complex web-like patterns formed by nonlinear waves on shallow water surfaces. By analyzing metric data of solitary waves within these patterns, an inverse problem approach is employed to derive a KP soliton solution. This solution describes the non-stationary dynamics of the web-pattern, providing insight into the nonlinear interactions governing its formation. The method enables the reconstruction of exact solutions from observed wave patterns, offering a novel perspective on the study of nonlinear waves in shallow water environments. Key metrics are utilized.

This study presents the detection of a strong magnetic field in HD 142184, a B2V star, using ESPaDons spectropolarimeter. A rotational period of 0.50833 days is found, making it the fastest-rotating non-degenerate magnetic star. Emission line variability is observed, indicating a structured magnetosphere. These findings are consistent with previous records, such as HR 7355, and contribute to the Magnetism in Massive Stars survey, providing insights into the properties of magnetic massive stars and their magnetospheres, shedding light on stellar evolution and rotation.

This article confirms the converse direction of Rivin's conjecture, demonstrating that the conjugacy growth series of a non-elementary hyperbolic group is transcendental, hence not rational. This result, combined with previous work by Ciobanu et al., establishes that a hyperbolic group has a rational conjugacy growth series if and only if it is virtually cyclic. We also explore variations of Rivin's conjecture, including those related to commensurability classes and primitive conjugacy classes. Furthermore, we investigate the conjecture for finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic groups, proving a formal language analogue that no set of minimal length conjugacy representatives can be unambiguous context-free. Our work contributes to the understanding of conjugacy growth and its connections to geometric and language-theoretic properties of groups. The results have implications for the study of hyperbolic and acylindrically hyperbolic groups.

This article presents an approximate analytical solution to a two-dimensional problem involving the Navier-Stokes, continuity, and Fourier-Kirchhoff equations. The solution describes free convective heat transfer from an isothermal surface of a half-infinite vertical plate, assuming fluid noncompressibility and the Boussinesq approximation. With boundary conditions of constant temperature and zero velocity on the plate, the solution is represented as a Taylor series in the horizontal variable. The coefficients depend on the vertical variable, allowing for a detailed analysis of the flow and heat transfer characteristics. The proposed solution provides a valuable tool for understanding natural convection phenomena, offering insights into the complex interactions between fluid flow and heat transfer near a vertical plate.

We quantize the electromagnetic field near a rotating body using a Lagrangian approach. Response functions and fluctuation-dissipation relations are derived, yielding a general formula for rotational friction and radiated power in terms of the dyadic Green's tensor. The Hamiltonian is determined, and potential generalizations are discussed. As an example, we calculate the rotational friction and radiated power for a spherical dielectric near a semi-infinite dielectric plane, examining limiting cases to illustrate the theory's applicability.

This study explores the enhanced particle identification (PID) capabilities achieved by combining the Time Projection Chamber (TPC) and Time-of-Flight (TOF) detector at the STAR experiment. By leveraging the complementary strengths of these detectors, the identification capability of charged hadrons is significantly extended beyond what is possible with either detector alone. Utilizing particle spectra from p+p, d+Au collisions at 200 GeV and Au+Au collisions at 62.4 GeV, the methods developed demonstrate improved PID capabilities for transverse momentum ranges of 0.2-6.0 GeV/c for pions, kaons, and protons. Notably, a novel approach is introduced for electron identification, combining dE/dx measurements from the TPC with velocity information from the TOF detectors, which will be crucial for future low-mass dilepton programs at STAR. These advancements have significant implications for enhancing the precision of particle identification in high-energy physics experiments.

This study investigates superconducting cobaltite via Raman scattering, examining effects of Na content and hydration. Phonon scattering and continua are analyzed in terms of lattice strain and disorder. Hydration releases strain, and Raman data reveal a connection between disorder on Na sites, the split of a specific energy level, and superconductivity, providing insights into the material's properties and behavior. The findings shed light on the complex relationships between structure, disorder, and superconductivity in cobaltite.

This study examines the interaction between a quantized electromagnetic field within a cavity resonator and a Coulomb-interacting electronic system in a nanostructure under an external magnetic field. The effects of the electronic system's geometry and the electromagnetic field's polarization are considered. Numerical results show that the two-level system approximation and Jaynes-Cummings model are valid in the weak electron-photon coupling regime. However, in the strong coupling regime, the quadratic vector potential significantly corrects the energy spectrum. Moreover, coupling to a strong cavity photon mode polarizes the charge distribution, necessitating a large basis of single-electron eigenstates in the model. These findings have implications for understanding electron-photon interactions in nanostructures and cavity quantum electrodynamics, highlighting the importance of considering geometric and polarization effects.

This study examines the formation of hot spheroidal systems within the context of galaxy evolution, considering the gentle mass aggregation history and primordial angular momentum of protogalaxies. Two scenarios are explored: the formation of spheroidal systems from stellar disk instabilities and their formation during dissipative gas collapse. Our findings indicate that the former scenario yields results consistent with observations of late-type galaxies. In contrast, the latter scenario suggests that achieving tidal stability is challenging, requiring the collapsed gas to be highly clumpy and dense to prevent tidal destruction of star-forming units. These results provide insights into the complex interplay between galaxy formation and evolution, highlighting the importance of initial cosmological conditions in shaping the properties of hot spheroidal systems. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of galaxy evolution and the role of dark matter halos.

This study presents an analysis of the angular and spatial clustering of 671 extremely red objects (EROs) within a 2 square degree sub-region of the NOAO Deep Wide-Field Survey (NDWFS). With a sample size twice that of previous studies and covering nearly five times the area, our research provides improved constraints on ERO clustering. The angular clustering of EROs is found to be slightly weaker than previously measured, with a notable decrease in clustering strength for fainter EROs. The spatial clustering of EROs is well-represented by a power-law model, with a correlation length of approximately 10 Mpc in comoving coordinates, similar to that of early-type galaxies at z~1. This suggests that the brightest EROs may be the progenitors of the most massive elliptical galaxies. Additionally, our analysis reveals a potential decrease in angular clustering with increasing apparent magnitude, and a possible decline in spatial clustering from bright to faint EROs, unless the redshift distribution of faint EROs is exceptionally broad. These findings contribute to our understanding of the distribution and evolution of EROs, providing insights into the formation and assembly of massive galaxies in the early universe.

We introduce the writhe of a permutation, a circular variant of the inversion number. This statistic has multiple interpretations, yielding interesting properties. For a uniformly random permutation, we study the writhe's asymptotics, obtaining a non-Gaussian limit distribution. Motivated by random knot theory, we describe a model for random framed knots, refining the Petaluma model. The framing distribution in this model equals the writhe of random permutations, providing new insights into knot theory and permutation statistics, with potential applications in topology and combinatorics, shedding light on complex structural properties.

This study investigates the pion structure function using a simple model with pseudoscalar coupling between pion and constituent quark fields. The imaginary part of the forward scattering amplitude is evaluated and linked to structure functions. Non-perturbative effects, preserving gauge invariance, are introduced to connect with quark distribution. Results predict higher-twist terms become negligible for scales larger than 2 GeV and quarks in pions carry smaller momentum fractions than in protons. This research provides insights into pion structure and quark distribution, shedding light on non-perturbative effects and gauge invariance in hadronic physics.

This study examines the implications of enhanced Higgs boson couplings with weak gauge bosons, as suggested by current Large Hadron Collider data. Using the Georgi-Machacek model, we find that these couplings can exceed Standard Model values by a factor of approximately 2.5, within allowed parameter regions. The modified couplings lead to significant enhancements in weak boson scattering processes, resulting in notable excesses in transverse mass distributions around 126 GeV. Additionally, the mass of heavy Higgs bosons can be observed, providing a clear signal of beyond-Standard Model physics. Our results highlight the potential for discovering new physics at the LHC, and demonstrate the importance of continued exploration of Higgs boson properties. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the Higgs sector and weak gauge boson interactions.

This study examines the behavior of maximum entangled coherent states as they traverse an amplitude damping channel. The results indicate that for low transmissivity rates, the traveling state is highly susceptible to noise, leading to a high probability of phase flip errors. In contrast, entanglement decay occurs smoothly for larger transmissivity rates and rapidly for smaller rates. Furthermore, increasing the number of modes accelerates entanglement loss over the noise channel. Notably, both odd and even states disappear at the same field intensity value. The findings have significant implications for quantum communication, highlighting the fragility of entangled coherent states in the presence of decoherence. By exploring the dynamics of entanglement decay, this research contributes to the development of more robust quantum communication systems, ultimately enhancing our understanding of the complex interplay between entanglement, noise, and quantum information transmission. Theoretical models and simulations support these conclusions.

This article presents a statistical-mechanical theory of semiflexible polymers, drawing a connection between the Kratky-Porod model and the quantum rigid rotator in an external homogeneous field. By utilizing the quantum mechanical propagator method, we establish a framework for generalizing expressions and relations from flexible polymers to semiflexible ones. This is achieved by replacing the Fourier-Laplace transform of the end-to-end polymer distance with a matrix formulation, incorporating the spectrum of the quantum rigid rotator. Our approach enables the study of semiflexible polymers in external fields, including the behavior of tangents and the structure factor of the polymer. We investigate the transversal fluctuations of a free end with a fixed tangent at the other end and the localization of a semiflexible polymer onto an interface. Furthermore, we derive the partition function of a semiflexible polymer in half-space with Dirichlet boundary conditions, expressed in terms of the end-to-end distribution function of a free semiflexible polymer. Our theory provides insights into the behavior of semiflexible polymers near a surface and their adsorption properties, offering a comprehensive understanding of these complex systems. The results have significant implications for the study of semiflexible polymers in various contexts.

This study investigates the properties of interacting polarons in parabolic quantum dots in two and three dimensions, utilizing a path integral formalism to account for fermion statistics. The approach is applied to both closed-shell and open-shell systems, enabling the derivation of the ground-state energy, addition energies, and optical absorption spectra. By employing a generalized Jensen-Feynman variational principle, the ground-state energy of a confined polaron system is analyzed as a function of the electron-phonon coupling constant and the number of polarons. The results reveal three possible types of spin polarization for the ground state of few-polaron systems, including a spin-polarized state, a state governed by Hund's rule, and a state with minimal spin. A transition from a Hund's rule state to a spin-polarized state is predicted as the electron density decreases, while the strong-coupling limit yields a state with minimal spin. These transitions are expected to be observable in the optical absorption spectra of quantum dots, providing a means to experimentally verify the theoretical predictions. The findings of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of interacting polarons in quantum dots and their potential applications in optoelectronic devices.

We present the results of a comprehensive study of the star HD 81032, combining photometric and spectroscopic observations obtained between 2000 and 2004. Our analysis reveals a photometric period of approximately 0 days, indicating a likely rotational modulation due to the presence of starspots. The data also suggest the existence of a large group of spots with a migration period of around 1 year, as inferred from the first three years of observations. Furthermore, the detection of Hα and Ca II H and K emissions from the star points to high chromospheric activity, a characteristic commonly associated with RS CVn binaries. The available photometry in the BVRIJHK bands is consistent with the previously determined spectral type of K0 IV for this star. We also investigated the spectral energy distribution of HD 81032 for signs of infrared excess using 2MASS JHK and IRAS photometry, but found no significant excess in any band, indicating that the star does not have a substantial circumstellar disk. In addition, we analyzed the X-ray emission properties of HD 81032 using data from the ROSAT X-ray observatory, which revealed an X-ray flare lasting approximately 12 hours. The X-ray spectrum, although limited by the small number of counts, is inconsistent with a single-temperature component solar-abundance coronal plasma model, suggesting the presence of multiple plasma components, non-solar abundances, or a combination of both. Taken together, these findings strongly suggest that HD 81032 is a newly identified, evolved RS CVn binary, characterized by high chromospheric activity, X-ray emission, and spot activity, making it an interesting target for further study. Our results contribute to the growing understanding of the properties and behavior of RS CVn binaries, which are important for understanding the evolution of binary star systems and the effects of magnetic activity on stellar properties.

The discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe, driven by a mysterious form of dark energy, has reinvigorated interest in testing Einstein's theory of general relativity. At the core of this theory lies the concept of geodesic motion, which describes the trajectory of a small, structureless test particle in curved spacetime. This fundamental concept has far-reaching implications, as it is used to calculate the orbital dynamics of celestial bodies, such as the advance of a planet's perihelion and the motion of binary pulsar systems. Verifying geodesic motion is essential to validating general relativity and other theories of fundamental physics. Recent observations of the LARES satellite have provided unprecedented evidence for geodesic motion, with its orbit exhibiting the smallest deviations from test-particle motion predicted by general relativity. After accounting for non-gravitational perturbations, the residual mean acceleration of LARES away from geodesic motion is less than 0.01 picometers per second squared. This remarkable agreement demonstrates the potential of LARES-type satellites for precise measurements and tests of gravitational and fundamental physics. Moreover, with only a few months of observation, LARES has already provided more accurate determinations of low-degree geopotential coefficients, which describe the Earth's gravitational deviations from sphericity, than any other satellite or combination of satellites. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the universe and the underlying laws of physics.

This article presents a novel parametrisation of the real photon structure function in the low-x and low-Q^2 region, incorporating both the Vector Meson Dominance (VMD) and Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) components. The QCD component is extrapolated to the low-x region using arbitrary parton distributions in the photon. When combined with the GRV and GRS parton densities, this parametrisation provides a reasonable description of existing high-energy data on F_2^γ, F_L^γ, and low-x data on σ_γ^*p. Predictions are also made for F_L^γ and σ_γ^*p at energies accessible in future linear colliders. The parametrisation is further applied to predict the photon structure function at low-x and the photon-photon and photon-proton cross sections at high energies. The results demonstrate the versatility of this parametrisation in describing various aspects of photon physics, making it a valuable tool for future experimental analyses and theoretical investigations in the field of particle physics. The presented framework provides a comprehensive understanding of the photon structure and its interactions, shedding light on the complex dynamics of QCD and VMD processes.

This article explores the geometric structures that can be constructed from vierbein (frame/coframe) variables and their relation to field models, particularly those alternative to General Relativity (GR). Focusing on coframe field models, which are viable models for gravity due to their inclusion of the Schwarzschild solution, we investigate the implications of violated local Lorentz invariance. This violation necessitates a physical interpretation of the additional six degrees of freedom present in these models. Typically, the geometry of such models is described by two distinct connections: the Levi-Civita symmetric and metric-compatible connection, and the Weitzenböck flat connection. Our research constructs a general family of linear connections that encompass these two as special cases. A crucial finding is that for the dynamical propagation of the six additional degrees of freedom, the gauge field of infinitesimal transformations must satisfy a system of two first-order differential equations, analogous to the vacuum Maxwell system. This leads to the derivation of "Maxwell-compatible connections." Alternatively, we obtain the same Maxwell-type system by imposing symmetry conditions on the viable models' Lagrangian. This results in a non-trivial decomposition of the coframe field into a pure metric field and a dynamical field of infinitesimal Lorentz rotations. Notably, we derive an exact spherical symmetric solution for our dynamical field, which remains bounded near the Schwarzschild radius and approximates a Coulomb field at greater distances. This work provides new insights into the geometric and dynamic properties of coframe field models, offering a deeper understanding of their potential as alternative theories of gravity.

This study analyzes Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) data from multiple observations of GRS 1915+105 using a thermal Comptonization model. The results show a strong positive correlation between the inner disk temperature and luminosity. In contrast, the hard Comptonized luminosity remains relatively constant with respect to total luminosity. Notably, the spectral hardness, fraction of scattered seed photons, Thomson optical depth, and fraction of power dissipated in the hot plasma all exhibit strong anti-correlations with luminosity. Furthermore, the inner disk radius is found to be nearly constant, while the hot Comptonizing corona contracts at high luminosities. A comparison with the XSPEC diskbb + power law model reveals significant discrepancies, including underestimation of the blackbody component and overestimation of absorption column density and total luminosity. These findings provide new insights into the complex relationships between disk and corona properties in GRS 1915+105.

This study explores the relationship between word length and geometric length of directed closed curves on a hyperbolic pair of pants surface. Using computational methods, we investigate the distribution of geometric lengths among classes with a fixed word length. Our experiments reveal a surprising trend, suggesting that the distribution of geometric lengths converges to a normal distribution. This finding has significant implications for understanding the interplay between algebraic and geometric invariants of curves on surfaces, and prompts further research into the underlying mechanisms driving this phenomenon in hyperbolic geometry. Results are presented and discussed.

This article presents a theoretical framework for the Su(2) classical colored Coulomb plasma, focusing on the construction of the Liouville operator for arbitrary Coulomb coupling values. By analyzing the resolvent in the classical colored phase space, we derive a hierarchy of equations, which are then closed using a free streaming approximation. This leads to an integral equation for the time-dependent structure factor, and its reduction yields hydrodynamical equations in the long-wavelength limit. Our results show that the shear viscosity exhibits a minimum near the liquid point, resulting from the crossover between single-particle and hydrodynamical collisional regimes. Furthermore, the self-diffusion constant is found to decrease with increasing coupling, irrespective of the regime. Theoretical predictions are compared to molecular dynamics simulations of the Su(2) colored Coulomb plasma, and implications for the quantum and strongly coupled quark-gluon plasma are discussed. This study provides insight into the transport properties of the colored Coulomb plasma, shedding light on the complex dynamics of strongly coupled systems. The findings have significant implications for understanding the behavior of quark-gluon plasmas in various physical contexts.

This study investigates the effects of orbital inclination and exozodiacal dust on the direct imaging and characterization of extrasolar Earth-like planets. Through simulations, we quantify the impact of prior knowledge of inclination on the efficiency of coronagraphic or occulter-based missions. Our results show that inclination has a significant impact on mission efficiency, surpassing that of exozodiacal brightness. However, the two factors exhibit excellent complementarity, highlighting the importance of considering both when planning a mission. We examine various methods for determining inclination and discuss their applicability to precursor science for an imaging mission. Our findings suggest that a combined effort to determine inclinations and exozodiacal brightnesses using ground-based facilities could substantially enhance the efficiency of a space-based mission. By prioritizing the determination of these key parameters, we can optimize the success of future missions aimed at imaging and characterizing Earth-like planets orbiting solar-type stars.

This article presents a derivation of the equations of motion for two point masses in harmonic coordinates using dimensional regularization at the third post-Newtonian (3PN) approximation. The dimensionally regularized equations of motion are found to contain a pole part that diverges as the space dimension approaches 4. However, it is demonstrated that this pole part can be renormalized away by introducing suitable shifts of the world-lines representing the point masses. The same shifts also renormalize the pole part of the bulk metric tensor. The resulting finite renormalized equations of motion are shown to be consistent with the general parametric equations of motion derived using an extended Hadamard regularization method. Furthermore, the 3PN ambiguity parameter is uniquely determined to be a specific value, which is consistent with recent determinations using alternative methods. This work provides a new consistency check for the dimensional regularization method in the context of classical gravitational interactions, confirming its validity and reliability. The results have implications for our understanding of gravitational physics and the behavior of point masses in harmonic coordinates.

The coexistence of diverse individuals in nature, despite competition, has significant implications for ecological biodiversity and societal altruism. Various mechanisms, including spatial structure and heterogeneity, facilitate coexistence. We investigate how network heterogeneity influences coexistence in cyclically competing species models, demonstrating that heterogeneous degree distributions promote stable coexistence through analytical and numerical methods, shedding light on the complex interactions driving biodiversity in networked systems, with potential applications for understanding and preserving ecological balance.

This study reexamines the dynamics of diffusive proximity systems comprising superconductors and normal metals or ferromagnets with magnetic disorder. Focusing on length scales exceeding the correlation length, we incorporate the effect of weak magnetic disorder as a local spin-flip term in the Usadel equations. A comprehensive derivation of this spin-flip term is presented for a three-dimensional disordered Zeeman-type field with an arbitrary correlation length. Our analysis identifies three distinct regimes: pointlike impurities, medium-range disorder, and long-range disorder, characterized by their correlation lengths relative to the Fermi wavelength and mean free path. By employing the Usadel equations, non-linear sigma model, and diagrammatic expansion, we establish a consistent framework that reconciles these regimes. The derived expressions for the spin-flip rate align with existing results obtained in more specialized contexts, providing a unified understanding of diffusive proximity systems with magnetic disorder.
