This article examines quartic spectrahedra in a specific mathematical space, forming a semialgebraic set of dimension 9. The set is stratified based on the location of ten nodes of the corresponding real quartic surface, with twenty maximal strata identified. We provide a new, self-contained, and algorithmic proof, extending Cayley's characterization of quartic symmetroids. This involves analyzing the branch locus of projections from nodes, which consist of two cubic curves. Our work represents a foundational step towards classifying spectrahedra of given degrees and dimensions, offering a novel approach to this complex mathematical problem.
We develop theory for time-inhomogeneous Markov chains using Nash and logarithmic-Sobolev inequalities, exploring @xmath0-stability and providing illustrative examples.

This article describes the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) project, a multi-institution collaboration aiming to create high-resolution maps of the microwave background temperature. The project seeks to survey 200 square degrees of the sky in three frequency bands with arcminute resolution and micro-kelvin sensitivity. We outline the scientific motivations, telescope design, and detector technology. Additionally, we discuss site considerations, scan strategy, and associated optical and X-ray galaxy cluster surveys. The ACT project will provide valuable insights into cosmology, enabled by its custom six-meter telescope and advanced bolometer array detector technology, from the Atacama site.

This study presents a novel approach to measuring the Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) and cosmic growth rate by leveraging the multipole components of the galaxy power spectrum. We demonstrate that nonlinear redshift-space distortions, specifically the "fingers-of-god" effect, induce high-multipole anisotropies in galaxy clustering, such as the hexadecapole and tetra-hexadecapole. Using simulated samples of luminous red galaxies (LRGs), we show that the input HOD parameters can be accurately recovered from the multipole measurements. Furthermore, incorporating high-multipole information helps break the degeneracy among HOD parameters, leading to improved estimates of the cosmic growth rate, satellite fraction, and velocity dispersions. Our results highlight the potential of using small-scale information from high-multipole moments to refine our understanding of galaxy evolution and cosmology. This new method offers a promising avenue for upcoming galaxy surveys to constrain models of structure formation and evolution.

This study investigates the evolution of galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) by measuring the angular auto-correlation functions of galaxies selected based on photometric redshifts and absolute magnitudes. The galaxies are divided into five overlapping redshift shells, and the auto-correlation function is measured in each subsample to examine the evolution of galaxy clustering. The results show a substantial increase in bias with redshift, exceeding expectations for a passively evolving sample. To interpret this finding, a halo-model analysis is employed to determine the best-fit halo occupation distribution (HOD) for each subsample. By converting halo masses to their corresponding passively evolved biases, a direct comparison of the HODs at different redshifts is enabled. The analysis reveals that the minimum halo mass required to host a galaxy decreases with decreasing redshift, indicating that galaxies are forming in lower-mass halos over the observed redshift range. Furthermore, the occupation number of halos with constant bias is found to peak at a specific average halo mass, suggesting that the bias of galaxies decreases as the universe evolves due to the formation of galaxies in halos of this characteristic mass. These findings provide new insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies, shedding light on the complex interplay between galaxy properties and their large-scale environment.

This study examines the dynamic behavior of adhesion clusters, which play a crucial role in cell adhesion, under constant loading and rebinding conditions. A theoretical analysis is presented, focusing on the stochastic dynamics of parallel bonds within a cluster. Analytical solutions are derived for special cases, while exact stochastic simulations are employed for the general case. The mean cluster lifetime is calculated, and fluctuation effects are analyzed in detail. The results demonstrate that the completely dissociated state can be modeled as an absorbing boundary, yielding a finite mean cluster lifetime. Various approximations to the full stochastic description are also discussed, providing insights into the complex behavior of adhesion clusters and their ability to respond to environmental changes. The findings have implications for understanding biological systems' dynamic responses to their environment.

This article explores the F-theory duals of singular heterotic K3 models, specifically those corresponding to Abelian toroidal orbifolds. Our primary focus is on the standard embedding, although we also examine models incorporating Wilson lines and more general gauge embeddings. To construct these duals, we develop a Weierstrass description of the heterotic toroidal orbifold models, which exhibit Kodaira-type singularities. This approach reveals key properties, including the instanton number per fixed point and a correlation between the orbifold order and the multiplicities in the Dynkin diagram. By utilizing the Weierstrass description, we constrain the complex structure of the F-theory Calabi-Yau threefold to replicate the gauge group and matter spectrum of the heterotic theories. Our results provide an explicit connection between the various orbifold models and their F-theory descriptions, offering a distinct perspective on the duality. This work builds upon previous approaches, highlighting the differences and nuances of our construction, and contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between heterotic and F-theory models.

This article presents a novel proof of Lin and Wang's discovery on torus Green functions, utilizing anti-holomorphic dynamics. The proof confirms three or five critical points, dependent on the torus modulus. As a byproduct, a one-parametric family of anti-holomorphic systems is identified, featuring hyperbolic components and separating analytic curves, shedding new light on dynamical systems.

This study presents a simplified dielectric breakage model for simulating the kinetics of cellular material breakage under pulsed electric field (PEF) treatment. The model, based on an effective media approximation, incorporates morphology parameters from percolation theory and estimates the probability of whole cell breakage using electroporation theory. The bridging effect, resulting from local conductivity deviations near the selected cell, is also accounted for. Notably, the model exhibits "jamming" behavior, characterized by distinct transitions, which is consistent with experimental observations of biological tissue breakage. Experimental results from PEF-treated thin apple slices are presented, with parameters including field strengths of 1-2 kV, pulse durations of 10-100 μs, and pulse repetition times of 100 ms. The model's predictions are found to be generally consistent with the experimental data. The correlation between cellular material destruction, field strength, treatment time, and power consumption is discussed, providing insights into the optimization of PEF treatment for various applications. Overall, the proposed model offers a valuable tool for understanding and predicting the effects of PEF on cellular materials.

This article explores the analysis of dynamical systems with slow mixing rates, particularly those exhibiting intermittent behavior between regular and chaotic dynamics. Despite recent advancements in mathematical methods, applying these techniques to realistic models remains challenging. We present a practical scheme that simplifies existing methods, enabling the derivation of nearly optimal bounds on mixing rates. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through its application to various classes of chaotic billiards with slow mixing. Additionally, we discuss limitations of the method, highlighting examples where it falls short, and outline potential avenues for further refinement and improvement of the technique.

The formation of planets is a complex process that is believed to originate from the collision of planetesimals, solids larger than a kilometer in size. However, the formation of these planetesimals themselves is still not well understood. This article reviews the possibility that planetesimals form through the self-gravity of vast ensembles of small particles, rather than through two-body collisions. We discuss how aerodynamic processes can accumulate solids relative to gas, leading to gravitational collapse. Numerical simulations have shown that particles as small as 10 cm in size can undergo gravitational collapse in turbulent disks. The feedback of solids on gas can trigger both vertical shear instabilities that obstruct self-gravity and streaming instabilities that concentrate particles. We outline areas for future research, including the possibility that even smaller objects can self-gravitate, and highlight the importance of understanding the interplay between solids and gas in the formation of planetesimals and ultimately, planets.

The proliferation of small-cells in macro-cell networks has led to a significant increase in aggregate power consumption, despite the relatively low individual power consumption of small-cells. In contrast to macro-cell base stations, whose power consumption increases substantially with traffic load, small-cell base stations exhibit a relatively flat power consumption curve, independent of their load. To mitigate the total power consumption of heterogeneous networks (HetNets), we propose a dynamic operation scheme that toggles the operating states of small-cell base stations (SBSs) between on and off, while maintaining the macro-cell base station (MBS) in an active state to ensure uninterrupted service. Our approach involves two phases: firstly, we develop an optimal location-based operation scheme for uniformly distributed users, where SBSs closer to the MBS are gradually switched off. Secondly, we extend this scheme to accommodate non-uniform user distributions, yielding a joint location and user density-based operation scheme that achieves near-optimal performance in polynomial time, with less than 1% performance loss observed in simulations. This research contributes to the development of green communication strategies for HetNets, enabling efficient traffic offloading and reduced power consumption. By optimizing SBS operation, our scheme offers a promising solution for mitigating the environmental impact of wireless networks while maintaining high-quality service.

This study examines the observed distribution of initial mass function (IMF) shapes, suggesting they arise from statistical sampling and stellar-dynamical processes. Young star clusters exhibit a low-mass biased IMF, differing from the galactic disk IMF. We discuss challenges in determining the IMF and present evidence for its structure. Our findings indicate that an invariant IMF is unlikely, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of star formation episodes and their impact on the IMF over gigayears. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the IMF's complexity and variability.

This study investigates the microphysics of collisionless shocks in plasma outflows from gamma-ray bursts, supernovae, and relativistic jets, with a focus on the effects of an ambient magnetic field on the evolution of the electron Weibel instability. Using three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations, we examine the interaction between a jet and an unmagnetized plasma, as well as plasmas with ambient magnetic fields parallel and perpendicular to the jet flow. Our results show that a threshold magnetic field strength exists, below which the Weibel two-stream instability dominates, and that the interstellar medium magnetic field strength is typically below this threshold. For strong magnetic fields parallel to the jet, the Weibel instability is suppressed, whereas perpendicular fields lead to significant electron acceleration and complex electromagnetic topologies, including anti-parallel field configurations. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the microphysics of collisionless shocks and the interpretation of observations in astrophysical contexts. By exploring the parameter space of collisionless shocks, this research aims to improve our knowledge of the underlying physics and reduce uncertainties in the analysis of high-energy astrophysical phenomena. The results of this study provide new insights into the role of magnetic fields in shaping the behavior of collisionless shocks and highlight the need for further investigation into the complex interactions between jets, plasmas, and magnetic fields.

This study proposes utilizing magnetic resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to reveal orbital occupancies in strongly correlated transition metal compounds. Unlike neutron scattering, RIXS intensity depends on orbital symmetry, allowing access to orbital degrees of freedom. By exploiting this property, we can determine ground state orbital occupancies. This approach offers a promising experimental method to investigate orbital physics in complex systems, providing new insights into the behavior of transition metal compounds. Theoretical framework and potential applications are discussed, paving the way for future experimental investigations at the Institute for Theoretical Solid State Physics.

This article presents a one-dimensional toy model of globular clusters, extending the gravitational sheets system to account for mass and energy loss due to star evaporation at boundaries. Utilizing exact event-driven dynamics, numerical integration is performed with initial uniform density and Gaussian random velocities. The results yield two distinct quasi-stationary asymptotic regimes, dependent on the system's initial energy. The density and velocity profiles are approximated, enabling the calculation of the self-consistent gravitational potential. The asymptotic number of stars and collision times are found to follow power-laws. This model provides insight into the complex dynamics of globular clusters, offering a simplified yet informative framework for understanding their behavior and evolution. The findings have implications for astrophysical systems and gravitational dynamics.

Cytoplasmic streaming, a large-scale motion of cytoplasm, is a vital process in certain large eukaryotic cells, including Drosophila oocytes, where it facilitates the mixing of cellular constituents. Recent observations have revealed that microtubules in these cells exhibit undulating motion, forming travelling waves during cytoplasmic streaming. This study provides a physical explanation for this wave-like motion, attributing it to the hydrodynamic drag of streaming impellers attached to kinesin motors moving along microtubules. The tangential forces applied by kinesin motors cause microtubules to bend, leading to chiral symmetry breaking and the propagation of long travelling waves. Notably, these waves share similarities with those observed in flagellar motion, but operate on a distinct physical mechanism and longer timescale. Our analysis demonstrates that kinesin movement can generate bulk flow of cytoplasm surrounding microtubules, with hydrodynamic coupling between impellers significantly enhancing the range of flow. This phenomenon enables a small number of motors to move a substantial amount of fluid, resulting in efficient mixing. Furthermore, the chaotic nature of fluid motion caused by kinesin movement along dynamic microtubule trajectories amplifies mixing efficiency. Our findings are supported by existing data from in vitro microtubule gliding assays, which exhibit chiral instability in two dimensions, providing quantitative estimates for motor forces and drag coefficients. This research sheds light on the physical mechanisms underlying cytoplasmic streaming, with implications for our understanding of cellular transport and mixing processes.

Title: Reassessing Quantum Measurement Theory: Beyond the Conventional Framework Abstract: The study of quantum measurement has been hindered by attempts to explain the fundamental axioms of quantum theory within the theory itself, leading to confusion and a narrow focus on a limited class of measurements. This paper seeks to expand our understanding of quantum measurement by exploring novel types of measurements that fall outside the traditional textbook descriptions. By recognizing the conflation of distinct concepts under a single term, we can disentangle valid questions and broaden our perspective on the types of measurements considered within the theory. Rather than proposing new interpretations of quantum mechanics, this work advocates for the use of distinct terms for distinct concepts, thereby clarifying the discussion. Recent insights, particularly those from the group around Aharonov, are reviewed, highlighting novel types of measurement that have been overlooked. By acknowledging and addressing these limitations, we can gain a deeper understanding of quantum measurement theory and its applications. This paper aims to stimulate a reevaluation of the field, encouraging researchers to explore new avenues of investigation and consider the implications of these novel measurement types on our understanding of quantum mechanics. Ultimately, this work seeks to contribute to a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of quantum measurement theory.

This study presents a systematic approach to identifying statistically significant words in DNA and protein sequences using the maximal entropy principle. Applying this method to Saccharomyces cerevisiae genomes, we found that regulatory binding sites tend to occur significantly in promoter regions. Analyzing two correlated gene families, our approach successfully extracted known binding sites and proposed novel putative regulatory sites in upstream regions. Notably, some regulatory sites exhibited directional preference, while others were active in both directions. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in uncovering nonrandom patterns in genetic sequences, providing valuable insights for future genetic studies and experimental validations.

This study extends the concept of coherent shift to the extended Bose-Hubbard and Fermi-Hubbard models. We identify two local bound pair types for Bose systems and one for Fermi systems, demonstrating that perfect coherent shift is achievable. For Bose on-site bound pairs, the shift condition depends on nearest-neighbor interaction and incident wavepacket momentum. In contrast, the other bound pair types exhibit shift conditions independent of the initial state, revealing unique properties of the proposed systems. Our findings provide new insights into the behavior of these models, shedding light on their potential applications in quantum physics.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of chemical freeze-out in various collision systems, including p-p, C-C, Si-Si, and Pb-Pb collisions at multiple beam momenta. Utilizing the statistical hadronization model, we examined the hadronic multiplicities to determine the source parameters as a function of participating nucleons and beam energy. The results exhibit a smooth behavior of temperature, baryon chemical potential, and strangeness under-saturation parameter with respect to energy and nucleus size. We provide interpolating formulas to predict chemical freeze-out parameters in central collisions at various centre-of-mass energies and for different colliding ions. However, discrepancies between data and model are observed in Pb-Pb collisions at SPS energies between 20 and 40 GeV, indicating limitations in the considered model schemes. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the chemical freeze-out process in high-energy collisions, highlighting the need for further refinement of theoretical models to accurately describe the underlying physics.

This study investigates the water radiolysis induced by low-energy carbon projectiles using first-principles molecular dynamics simulations. Carbon projectiles with kinetic energies ranging from 175 eV to 2.8 keV are simulated to interact with liquid water, resulting in translational, rotational, and vibrational excitation, as well as water dissociation. The most abundant products of radiolysis are H and OH fragments. Notably, the maximum spatial production of radiolysis products occurs at low velocities, below the maximum energy deposition, with a significant yield of one H fragment every 5 events at the lowest velocity studied. The energy required for water dissociation is found to be constant and substantially smaller than the projectile's energy. The simulations also reveal that high-velocity projectiles lead to well-defined binary collisions, whereas lower velocities result in multiple collision events. Furthermore, the generation of new species, including hydrogen peroxide and formic acid, is observed through distinct mechanisms involving O radicals and C projectiles reacting with water molecules. These findings provide valuable insights into the mechanisms of water radiolysis by low-energy carbon projectiles, highlighting the importance of velocity-dependent effects and the formation of secondary projectiles and new species. The results of this study have implications for understanding radiation-induced damage in aqueous environments.

This study presents low-temperature measurements on micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS) driven into the non-linear regime while maintaining elastic domain integrity. The observed non-linearity is geometric in origin. Two measurement techniques, harmonic drive and free decay, are employed, each with a corresponding analytic theory that accurately fits the data. The harmonic drive response is characterized by a Lorentz-like lineshape, derived from an extended version of Landau and Lifshitz's non-linear theory. The free decay evolution is modeled using an amplitude-dependent frequency decaying function, based on the Lindstedt-Poincaré theory of non-linear differential equations. The methodology is universally applicable to any single-degree-of-freedom mechanical device composed of ideally elastic materials, enabling an experimental definition of its non-linear dynamics equation. These findings provide a robust framework for understanding and predicting the non-linear behavior of MEMS and similar systems. The results have significant implications for the design and optimization of micro-scale devices.

This study investigates the response of bilayer lipid membranes (BLMs) to transverse static electric fields, a crucial aspect of understanding electroporation and membrane stability. A phenomenological free energy model is developed, incorporating a continuum description of membrane dipoles and the coupling between headgroup dipoles and membrane tilt. The results show that the membrane becomes unstable through buckling modes, which are weakly coupled to thickness fluctuations. These fluctuations, combined with the increased interfacial area produced by membrane buckling, enhance the likelihood of localized membrane breakdown and potential pore formation. The instability is found to be strongly dependent on the coupling strength between dipolar headgroups and membrane tilt, as well as the degree of dipolar ordering in the membrane. This research provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying electroporation and membrane stability, shedding light on the complex interplay between electric fields, membrane structure, and functional integrity.

We present a constructive proof of the Ambrosetti-Rabinowitz Mountain Pass Theorem, yielding an efficient algorithm via bisection method. This approach requires fewer flow line computations, enhancing convergence, particularly in high-dimensional problems, and outperforms existing methods, such as Choi and McKenna's.

This study explores the concept of dark matter as a mixture of two non-interacting perfect fluids with distinct four-velocities and thermodynamic parameters. The two-fluid model is reduced to an effective single anisotropic fluid, characterized by different radial and tangential pressures. We derive the fundamental equations governing the equilibrium structure of this model and the tangential velocity of test particles in stable circular orbits, assuming a spherically symmetric static geometry. Numerical integration of the gravitational field equations yields the density profile and tangential velocity of the dark matter mixture, using a non-relativistic kinetic model. Our results have implications for cosmology, demonstrating that the anisotropic two-fluid model evolves towards isotropy over large time scales, providing new insights into the nature of dark matter and its role in the universe. The model's potential to explain observed phenomena is also discussed.

This study delves into the vibrational properties of a non-convective solid star with an axisymmetric, purely toroidal intrinsic magnetic field, exploring its implications in white dwarf asteroseismology. Focusing on node-free global Lorentz-force-driven vibrations, we analyze material displacements akin to those in nodeless spheroidal and torsional vibrations. Particular emphasis is placed on even-parity poloidal Alfvén modes, for which we derive analytic frequency spectra. Our findings demonstrate how purely toroidal magnetic fields, submerged beneath the star's surface, can influence seismic vibrations in non-magnetic white dwarfs. The obtained spectral formulae are compared to those for Alfvén modes in a solid star model with a poloidal, homogeneous internal, and dipolar external magnetic field, providing insights into Alfvén vibrations in magnetic white dwarfs. This research contributes to the understanding of the complex interplay between magnetic fields and seismic activity in white dwarf stars.

This study presents a novel model to explain the significant shear-dependent fluid slip observed at partially wetting fluid-solid surfaces. Motivated by recent discoveries of nanobubbles on hydrophobic surfaces, our model investigates the dynamic response of these bubbles to changes in hydrodynamic pressure. The compression and diffusion of gas within the bubbles reduce the force on the oscillating surface, creating an apparent slip. Our results, based on bubbles similar to those observed via atomic force microscopy, demonstrate force decreases consistent with experimental measurements by Zhu and Granick. This "leaking mattress" effect offers a plausible explanation for the large shear-dependent slip phenomenon, providing new insights into fluid-solid interactions at the nanoscale.

This study extracts the electric dipole strength distribution in @xmath0sn from proton inelastic scattering experiments at @xmath1 MeV and forward angles, including @xmath2. Below neutron threshold, results differ from @xmath0sn@xmath3 experiments, peaking at 8.3 MeV. The total strength corresponds to 2.3(2)% of the energy-weighted sum rule, exceeding @xmath3 reaction observations. This implies strong E1 strength fragmentation and/or small ground-state branching ratios of excited @xmath4 states, shedding light on @xmath0sn's nuclear structure through relativistic Coulomb excitation and @xmath6 MeV proton scattering.

Observations of the diffuse intergalactic medium (IGM) and the hot gas in large clusters of galaxies (ICM) have revealed significant metal enrichment, with the IGM reaching approximately 0.1 solar metallicity and the ICM reaching up to 0.3 solar metallicity. The origin of these metals is thought to be galaxies, where they are formed through stellar processes. However, the mechanisms by which metals are removed from galaxies and distributed throughout the IGM and ICM are not well understood. This study presents a novel approach to investigating the chemical enrichment of the IGM and galaxies using cosmological simulations. We incorporate dust and metals into the simulations, assuming instantaneous recycling, and distribute them according to three parameterized prescriptions representing different enrichment mechanisms: dynamical removal, supernova-driven winds, and radiation-pressure driven dust efflux. Our method allows for the exploration of a large number of models, each yielding a specific realization of the cosmic metal distribution that can be directly compared to observations. Our results suggest that dynamical removal of metals from small galaxies cannot account for the observed metallicity of low-column density Lyα absorbers, and that removal from larger galaxies cannot explain the high metallicities observed in the ICM. Furthermore, dynamical removal fails to produce a strong mass-metallicity relation in galaxies. In contrast, wind or radiation-pressure ejection of metals from larger galaxies can plausibly explain the observed metallicities in both the IGM and ICM. However, we note that uniform distribution of metals in low-density regions and the enrichment of clusters remain challenges for these models. Our study provides a framework for understanding the chemical enrichment of the IGM and galaxies, and highlights the need for further investigation into the mechanisms governing metal distribution and the properties of galaxies and galaxy clusters.

This study examines the behavior of low angular momentum accretion flows, focusing on the presence of standing and oscillating shock waves. We investigate the parameter space where multiple sonic points occur in viscous flows with various cooling effects, such as bremsstrahlung and Comptonization. Our analysis reveals that cooling has opposing effects to viscosity, altering the solution topology. However, a balance between the two is unattainable due to their distinct dependencies on dynamic and thermodynamic parameters. Notably, beyond a critical cooling threshold, the flow no longer sustains a shock wave, providing new insights into accretion flow dynamics.

This study presents the findings of a high-resolution survey of 11 starless cores in the Perseus molecular cloud, utilizing the CARMA and SZA telescopes to observe 3 mm continuum emission. Of the 11 cores, two were detected, each comprising a single structure, with a median upper limit of 0.2 Jy/beam for non-detections. These results align with previous studies, which reported a low detection rate of compact 3 mm continuum emission in dense cores. The absence of multiple components in all observed cores suggests that starless core mass functions derived from bolometer maps are unlikely to be significantly biased by blending of lower-mass cores. Our observations support the notion that most starless cores in Perseus have inner density profiles shallower than ρ ∝ r^(-2), providing valuable insights into the properties of starless cores and their role in star formation.

We present optical and near-infrared observations of the field of GRB980329, commencing 20 hours post-event, utilizing the ESO NTT, NOT, and TIRGO telescopes. Our initial observations revealed a faint object (R = 23.6 ± 0.2) within the BeppoSAX NFI error box, coincident with a transient VLA source proposed as the radio afterglow. The source exhibited a decay of 1.6 ± 0.5 magnitudes over 2.1 days, consistent with previous GRB optical afterglows. Near-infrared observations yielded a 2σ detection, marginally consistent with the VLA source position. The transient's spectrum shows significant absorption within the GRB host galaxy. We interpret the afterglow energetics as synchrotron radiation from an expanding blast wave, supporting the notion that this transient is the optical counterpart of GRB980329. These findings contribute to our understanding of GRB afterglow properties and the role of host galaxy absorption.

This study utilizes the biomembrane force probe to investigate the dynamic strength of multiple biotin-streptavidin adhesion bonds under linear loading. By comparing measured rupture force histograms to a master equation model, we determine the distribution of initially closed bonds and extract molecular parameters, which align with single bond experiment results. Notably, the rupture force histograms exhibit peak positions that deviate from simple multiples of single bond values, instead resulting from a superposition process that generates distinct peak positions, providing new insights into the complex behavior of multiple adhesion bonds under load.

This study examines the dynamics of a two-level system driven by large-amplitude external fields, with a focus on resonance properties near avoided level crossings. We address three key questions: the resonance condition, the frequency of oscillations on resonance, and the resonance width. By dividing the evolution into discrete time steps, we develop a geometric picture that provides a simple understanding of the dynamics and yields quantitative results. This approach is compared to the rotating-wave approximation, and we identify the regions of validity for different approximations. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the geometric picture in a large region of the parameter space. The study also touches on the potential of strong driving as a tool for manipulating two-level systems, highlighting its prospects for applications. Overall, this work enhances our understanding of resonance dynamics in driven two-level systems and explores the possibilities of exploiting strong driving for system control.

This article presents a novel system designed to continuously maintain a cryocooler on a rotating table for extended periods. The system comprises a cryostat housing the cryocooler, positioned on the rotating table, and a ground-based compressor supplying high-purity (99.999%) and high-pressure (1.7 MPa) helium gas and electricity. To facilitate operation, custom interface components were developed to bridge the gap between the ground and rotating table, utilizing access holes and rotary joints to enable simultaneous transmission of electricity and helium gas. The system demonstrates two key functions under rotating conditions: cooling from room temperature and prolonged maintenance of a cold state. Experimental validation confirmed temperature stability during continuous rotation at 20 revolutions per minute. The developed system has far-reaching applications in fields such as Lorentz invariance testing, axion searches, radio astronomy, and cosmology, with a planned implementation in a radio telescope for observing cosmic microwave background radiation, highlighting its potential for advancing various scientific endeavors.

This article reviews the properties and dynamics of giant molecular clouds (GMCs), the primary birthplaces of stars in galaxies. Observations indicate that GMCs are gravitationally bound, with high mass surface densities and inefficient star formation. Star formation is highly clustered within GMCs, with similarities between star-forming clumps and young stellar clusters (YSCs). Theoretical models of GMC evolution highlight the role of turbulence and collisions in shaping cloud dynamics. Feedback from newly formed stars limits the overall star formation efficiency, but a turbulent and clumpy medium can facilitate the formation of bound clusters. The article discusses the importance of GMC properties, including mass and density, in regulating star formation activity. By exploring the complex interplay between cloud dynamics, star formation, and feedback, this review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms governing star formation in galaxies, with implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution.

We examine the spectral weight near the Fermi level in NDNiO@x thin films using ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy across the metal-insulator transition. Thermal hysteresis is observed, similar to DC conductivity. Analysis reveals two distinct spectral loss regimes, with one regime's temperature evolution independent of the metal-insulator transition, providing insight into the underlying physics of this phenomenon.

This study investigates the electron-phonon coupling in self-assembled InGaAs quantum dots, revealing a relatively weak interaction at low light intensities. However, intense optical pulses tuned within the phonon sideband can dynamically enhance coupling to acoustic phonons. Recent experiments have demonstrated the potential for population inversion and rapid de-excitation using blue-shifted and red-shifted lasers, respectively. Our research confirms the incoherent nature of phonon-assisted pumping and explores the temperature dependence of this mechanism. Furthermore, we show that combining blue- and red-shifted pulses can create and destroy an exciton within a timescale of approximately 0 ps, determined by the pulse duration and limited by phonon thermalisation time. These findings have significant implications for the development of quantum dot-based devices and highlight the importance of considering dynamic vibronic coupling in the design of optoelectronic systems. The temperature dependence is a key factor.

This study investigates a class of one-dimensional, nonequilibrium, conserved growth equations, examining both nonconserved and conserved noise statistics through numerical integration and stochastic simulation of an atomistic model. The models with nonconserved noise exhibit mound formation and power-law coarsening with slope selection across a range of parameter values, distinct from previous models which often rely on the Ehrlich-Schwoebel step-edge barrier for instability. Instead, mound formation in these models arises from a nonlinear instability where the height of spontaneously generated pillars increases rapidly if the initial height is sufficiently large. The introduction of higher-order gradient nonlinearities to control this instability leads to a first-order dynamical phase transition from a rough self-affine phase to a mounded phase, characterized by a newly defined order parameter. The mounded phase displays power-law coarsening with a selected slope retained over time, though the coarsening exponents differ between the continuum equation and the discrete model, a discrepancy explained and verified through simulation. Furthermore, the growth equation with conserved noise reveals a region of parameter space where both kinetically rough and mounded phases are locally stable, with the system's steady-state behavior determined by its initial configuration. These findings provide new insights into the complex behavior of nonequilibrium growth systems and highlight the importance of considering both nonconserved and conserved noise statistics in understanding mound formation and coarsening dynamics.

Thermally driven colloidal transport is largely attributed to the thermoelectric effect in charged solutions. Contrary to the single-particle picture, our findings indicate that transport coefficients depend on colloidal concentration. Collective effects significantly impact thermophoretic mobility, even in hydrodynamically dilute solutions. This explains recent observations on polyelectrolytes and charged particles, suggesting collective behavior is prevalent in charged colloids, rather than an exception.

The development of the Zeeman-Doppler Imaging (ZDI) technique has enabled comprehensive observations of surface magnetic fields on low-mass stars, prompting the adoption of modeling techniques from solar physics. However, many of these techniques, though widely used in stellar astrophysics, have been largely abandoned by the solar community due to their inability to accurately reproduce solar observations. Despite this, some models continue to be employed in simulating the coronae and winds of solar analogs. This study presents a comparative analysis of two magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) models for the solar corona and solar wind: a polytropic wind model and the physics-based Alfvén Wave Solar Model (AWSoM). Our results show that while the AWSoM model consistently replicates numerous solar observations, the polytropic model fails to do so, often yielding unphysical solutions. We recommend that polytropic models, commonly used to estimate mass-loss rates and other parameters in solar analogs, be calibrated against solar observations or more advanced models like AWSoM, which capture the intricate physics of the solar corona. Without such calibration, the results from polytropic models cannot be validated, potentially leading to misguided applications. This study highlights the need for rigorous validation of modeling techniques to ensure accurate and reliable predictions in stellar astrophysics.

This study integrates the electrostatic continuum solvent model by Fattebert and Gygi with a first-principles cavitation energy formulation, utilizing a quantum-mechanical definition for the solute surface. The resulting cavitation contribution shows remarkable agreement with complex algorithms. This model enables efficient Car-Parrinello simulations of finite or extended systems in solution, demonstrating accuracy comparable to established quantum-chemistry continuum solvent methods. Applying this approach to tetracyanoethylene dimers in dichloromethane yields valuable insights into the dimerization phenomenon, providing structural and dynamical information. The simplicity and accuracy of this method make it a promising tool for simulating complex systems in solution.

This study explores the relationships between galaxy morphology, local density, and radius within nearby clusters, utilizing the extensive Wings database. By analyzing a comprehensive sample of 5,504 galaxies brighter than m_r = 19.5 across 76 clusters, we investigate the morphology-density (@xmath0-@xmath1) and morphology-radius (@xmath0-@xmath2) relations. Our findings indicate that the @xmath0-@xmath1 relation is predominantly observed in the inner regions of clusters, whereas the @xmath0-@xmath2 relation remains relatively consistent across various local densities. We validate the robustness of these results through numerical simulations and tests, confirming their independence from cluster mass and galaxy stellar mass. Notably, the strength of the @xmath0-@xmath1 relation correlates with galaxy stellar mass, but this trend is absent in the @xmath0-@xmath2 relation. The presence or absence of subclustering significantly influences the @xmath0-@xmath1 relation, suggesting that morphological transformations are more pronounced in dynamically evolved regions. Our results imply that mechanisms of morphological broadening or redistribution operate in the intermediate and outer regions of substructured clusters, leading to a weakening of the @xmath0-@xmath1 relation. This research provides new insights into the complex interplay between galaxy morphology, environment, and cluster dynamics, shedding light on the evolutionary processes that shape galaxy populations in nearby clusters.

This article presents a comprehensive review of plasma waves and instabilities in homogeneous collisionless magnetized plasmas, utilizing kinetic theory to examine the anisotropic response of the generalized relativistic dielectric tensor and Onsager symmetry properties for arbitrary distribution functions. Our analysis reveals that the anisotropy affects only those electromagnetic modes with magnetic-field perturbations perpendicular to the ambient magnetic field, whereas oblique propagation exhibits anisotropic effects in all modes. Focusing on non-relativistic bi-Maxwellian distributions, we derive dispersion relations for various modes and instabilities, demonstrating that thermal anisotropies impact electromagnetic R- and L-waves, whistler modes, pure Alfvén modes, firehose instability, and whistler instability. In contrast, perpendicularly propagating X-modes and their derivatives remain unaffected. We observe that thermal anisotropy modifies parallel propagating modes through the parallel acoustic effect and perpendicular propagating modes via the Larmor-radius effect. Furthermore, our study shows that thermal anisotropy has a more significant impact on the kinetic regime of oblique propagating kinetic Alfvén waves than on the inertial regime. The generalized fast mode exhibits distinct acoustic effects in parallel and perpendicular directions to the ambient magnetic field, and the magneto-sonic wave suppresses the firehose instability in the fast-mode instability. Our findings are supported by graphic illustrations, and threshold conditions for various instabilities are obtained, providing a deeper understanding of the complex behavior of homogeneous collisionless magnetized plasmas. This work contributes to the advancement of plasma physics, with implications for the study of space and astrophysical plasmas.

This article examines the implications of current precision electroweak data, Z' searches, and dark matter constraints on an extended Standard Model featuring an additional massive gauge boson and a "hidden valley" sector with a confining gauge group. We derive a lower mass limit of 3 GeV for the Z' boson from direct searches and precision tests. The model includes a pseudoscalar dark matter candidate, and we find that dark matter constraints impose an upper bound on the Z' mass of approximately 5 TeV. A TeV-scale mass is required for the hidden valley states, and the Sommerfeld factor significantly suppresses the allowed parameter space for p-wave dark matter annihilation. Our analysis provides new insights into the interplay between electroweak precision data, Z' searches, and dark matter constraints, shedding light on the viable parameter space of this extended Standard Model. The results have important implications for model-building and experimental searches.

This study examines the spectral and temporal properties of X-ray flares emitted by several Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs). A sample of GRBs with large amplitude variations and multiple rebrightenings in their X-ray light curves is analyzed. The origin of these fluctuations is investigated to distinguish between refreshed shocks and late internal shocks. Time-resolved spectral analysis of select bursts supports the presence of a long-lived central engine, where rebrightenings are consistent with energy injection in refreshed shocks. This occurs when slower shells, generated during the prompt phase, catch up with the afterglow shock at later times, providing diagnostic insights into the underlying mechanisms driving these complex phenomena.

This study examines the applicability of a novel X-ray scaling method for estimating the mass of supermassive black holes in low-accreting active galactic nuclei (AGN). Our previous work demonstrated the reliability of this method for moderately to highly accreting black holes. However, for low-accreting AGN, the underlying assumption that the photon index correlates with accretion rate breaks down. Using a control sample with high-quality X-ray data and dynamically measured masses, we find that the X-ray scaling method is not applicable in these cases. Nevertheless, an inverse correlation observed in low-accreting black holes can be utilized to constrain masses within a factor of 3 of dynamically determined values. We propose a simple recipe using X-ray spectral data to estimate black hole masses, providing a sanity check for indirect optical methods. This work contributes to the understanding of black hole mass estimation in low-accreting AGN, with implications for active galaxy research.

This study proposes a novel approach to observe ultra-high energy astrophysical neutrinos and identify their flavors in future neutrino telescopes. The flavor ratio of astrophysical neutrinos detected on Earth is influenced by both the initial flavor ratio at the source and flavor transitions during propagation. A model-independent parametrization is used to classify flavor transition mechanisms. A new parameter, @xmath0, is introduced to directly probe flavor transitions without assuming @xmath1 symmetry. Several flavor transition models are tested using this parametrization, and observational constraints on flavor transition mechanisms are discussed. This research aims to advance our understanding of astrophysical neutrino flavor transitions, with implications for neutrino telescopes and cosmology, categorized under PACS numbers 95.85.ry, 14.60.pq, and 95.55.vj.

This article presents a general variational framework for modeling finite temperature effects in superfluid systems, with a focus on complex scenarios such as the mixed neutron superfluid/proton superconductor expected in neutron star cores. By treating excitations as a massless "entropy" fluid, we demonstrate the formal equivalence of our approach to the traditional two-fluid model for superfluid helium, highlighting the role of entropy entrainment in encoding the normal fluid density. The superfluid constraint of irrotationality is shown to reduce the number of dissipation coefficients, providing insight into the more general problem of vortex presence and the incorporation of mutual friction forces. Our hydrodynamic formalism, applicable to single superfluid condensates, can be readily extended to more complex situations, including colour-flavour locked quark superconductors potentially present in deep neutron star cores. The developed framework offers a foundation for understanding finite temperature effects in superfluid systems, with implications for the study of neutron star physics and other extreme environments. By exploring dissipative mechanisms and finite temperature effects, this work aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics governing superfluid systems, ultimately informing the development of more accurate models for these phenomena.

The internal structure of neutrons remains poorly understood compared to protons, primarily due to the lack of free neutron targets. Typically, neutron information is extracted from data on nuclear targets like deuterium, which requires corrections for nuclear binding and nucleon off-shell effects. These corrections are model-dependent and plagued by significant uncertainties, particularly for large values of the Bjorken scaling variable x. As a result, the same data can yield different conclusions, such as the behavior of the d-quark distribution in the proton at large x. The Barely Off-shell Nucleon Structure (BONUS) experiment at Jefferson Lab aimed to address this limitation by measuring the inelastic electron-deuteron scattering cross section, tagging spectator protons in coincidence with scattered electrons. This novel approach substantially reduces nuclear binding uncertainties, enabling the first nearly model-independent extraction of the neutron structure function F2n in the resonance and deep-inelastic regions. The experiment employed a custom-built compact radial time projection chamber to detect protons with momenta between 70 and 150 MeV/c and over a nearly 4π angular range. To extract the free-neutron structure function F2n, spectator protons at backward angles and with momenta below 100 MeV/c were selected, ensuring that the scattering occurred on a nearly free neutron. Scattered electrons were detected using Jefferson Lab's CLAS spectrometer, with data collected at beam energies near 2, 4, and 5 GeV. The extracted neutron structure function F2n and its ratio to the inclusive deuteron structure function F2d are presented in both the resonance and deep-inelastic regions, covering a range of kinematic variables. The dependence of the semi-inclusive cross section on spectator proton momentum and angle is investigated, and tests of the spectator mechanism are performed for different kinematics. The results provide new insights into neutron resonance excitations, quark-hadron duality in the neutron, and binding effects, including the nuclear EMC effect. This study offers a unique opportunity to develop more precise parametrizations of structure functions and investigate the asymptotic behavior of the d-quark distribution at large x, ultimately enhancing our understanding of neutron structure and its role in nuclear physics.

This article explores the nonlinear theory of dust-acoustic waves (DAWs) in an unmagnetized dusty negative-ion plasma, considering the extreme scenario where free electrons are absent. The dynamics of cold, massive charged dusts are modeled using fluid equations, while the two species of ions (positive and negative) are described by kinetic Vlasov equations. A Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation with Landau damping is derived to govern the behavior of weakly nonlinear and weakly dispersive DAWs. The results indicate that, for typical laboratory and space plasmas, Landau damping and nonlinear effects dominate over finite Debye length effects, rendering the KdV soliton theory inapplicable to DAWs in dusty pair-ion plasmas. The study examines the properties of linear phase velocity, solitary wave amplitudes, and Landau damping rate, taking into account the effects of the positive ion to dust density ratio, as well as the ratios of positive to negative ion temperatures and masses. The findings provide insight into the behavior of DAWs in extreme plasma conditions, highlighting the significance of Landau damping and nonlinear effects in shaping the dynamics of these waves.

Title: Evaluating the Preservation of Information in Dimensionality Reduction Techniques for Complex Networks Abstract: The increasing complexity of large networks has led to the development of various dimensionality reduction techniques, including network motif analysis, graph spectra, and spectral sparsification methods. However, the extent to which these techniques preserve or lose information remains unclear. This study introduces a framework based on algorithmic information theory to quantify the preservation of information in over 20 biological and artificial networks. Our results show that spectral sparsification is highly sensitive to edge deletion, leading to significant inconsistencies, while graph spectral methods capture algebraic information but lose most of the original network's information content. In contrast, network motif analysis excels at preserving the relative algorithmic information content of a network, enabling the recovery of essential properties across different networks. This methodology provides a rigorous framework for assessing and comparing dimensionality reduction methods, facilitating the evaluation of their capabilities. By applying algorithmic information theory, we validate the effectiveness of network motif analysis in preserving information and demonstrate the potential of this approach in identifying and characterizing complex networks. Our findings have implications for the development and application of dimensionality reduction techniques in various fields, including biology, social science, and computer science. Keywords: dimensionality reduction techniques, Kolmogorov complexity, network, graph spectra, graph motifs, graph sparsification.

This article examines the problem of quickest detection in a distributed sensor system, where multiple sensors receive sequential observations from the environment and employ cumulative sum (CUSUM) strategies. The sensors communicate with a central fusion center using one-shot schemes, where each sensor transmits a single message after which a detection decision is made. We consider an asynchronous communication scenario, where the fusion center declares an alarm upon receiving the first communication. Assuming independent observations at each sensor and random signal appearance times, we analyze the performance of one-shot schemes in comparison to centralized detection. Our results show that one-shot schemes do not incur a performance loss in an extended Lorden min-max sense, as the minimum of multiple CUSUMs is asymptotically optimal when the mean time between false alarms increases without bound. This finding has significant implications for distributed inference and decision-making in multisensor systems, highlighting the effectiveness of one-shot schemes in quickest detection applications.

This study proposes a time-dependent phenomenological model to investigate @xmath0-CDM cosmology. A time-dependent equation of state parameter is derived, enabling a sign flip in the deceleration parameter. Calculated universe age matches observational data for specific parameter values, validating the model's effectiveness in describing cosmic evolution accurately.

This study demonstrates the feasibility of realizing a Photonic Floquet Topological Insulator (PFTI) in an atomic ensemble. By interfering three coupling fields, a periodic refractive index structure with a honeycomb profile is formed, which can be modulated by adjusting the frequency detunings and intensities of the coupling fields. This structure gives rise to Dirac cones in momentum space, whose appearance is influenced by the honeycomb lattice's helical ordering. When the lattice sites are ordered, gaps open at the Dirac points, yielding a PFTI in the atomic vapor. The edge states of the PFTI can confine an obliquely incident beam, allowing it to propagate along the lattice's zigzag edge without scattering. Notably, the third-order nonlinear susceptibility can shut down the Dirac cones and PFTI formation, while the fifth-order nonlinear susceptibility can reopen them, offering a unique means of controlling topological phenomena in photonic systems.

This article addresses estimating the effective dimension-reduction subspace in multi-index regression models. A new procedure for recovering subspace directions is proposed, proven to be consistent under mild assumptions. Numerical simulations demonstrate the algorithm's empirical behavior, offering insights into its effectiveness in dimension reduction with additive noise and deterministic design, particularly when structural dimension is limited.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of entropy in flexible chains comprising multiple monomers placed on stripes, utilizing the transfer matrix approach. Focusing on high-density regimes, we analyze the entropy's dependence on monomer density and stripe width, building upon recent analytical work on dimers. Our calculations yield the asymptotic entropy for chains with numerous monomers, as well as the special case of polymers with a large number of monomers. The results exhibit regular behavior, consistent with analytical findings for dimers. Furthermore, our transfer matrix calculations validate the mean-field expression for entropy in the low-density limit, demonstrating the accuracy of our approach. These findings provide valuable insights into the thermodynamic properties of flexible chains in confined geometries, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms governing their behavior.

This article examines the nonstationary circuit QED setup, where multiple qubits interact with a single electromagnetic field mode in a resonator. We apply harmonic time modulation to the atomic transition frequency or atom-field coupling strength and derive unitary dynamics up to the second order. Our analysis reveals that resonant phenomena occurring at modulation frequencies equal to the cavity frequency also occur at halved frequencies, albeit with significantly reduced transition rates. The effectiveness of modulating the coupling strength is also diminished at these lower frequencies. We explicitly calculate transition rates and discuss the potential applications of second-order resonances in dynamical Casimir effect-related phenomena, providing new insights into the behavior of nonstationary circuit QED systems. The results have implications for quantum information processing and quantum optics.

This study presents pioneering worldline analytical and numerical results on the intricate relationship between geometric and thermal dependencies of the Casimir effect. Notably, our findings indicate that the temperature dependence of the Casimir force is substantially more pronounced in open geometries, such as perpendicular plates, compared to closed geometries like parallel plates. For surface separations relevant to experimental settings, thermal corrections in the perpendicular plates configuration exhibit a stronger parameter dependence, surpassing those in parallel plates by an order of magnitude at room temperature. This disparity stems from the gapless spectrum of open geometries, facilitating thermal excitation of low-lying modes at low temperatures, whereas closed geometries have a gapped spectrum, inhibiting such excitations.

This study examines the impact of longitudinal structuring on fast kink modes in coronal loops. By deriving analytical dispersion relations and mode profiles for the magnetic field perturbation, we investigate deviations from homogeneous loop frequencies and mode profiles as a function of density scale height. The effects of fixed and variable column masses, negative scale heights, and density contrasts are analyzed. Our results provide tools to estimate solar photospheric parameters, including frequency ratios, mode profiles, and antinode shifts from homogeneous loop sine profiles. We expand relevant factors up to the second order in the stratification parameter, verifying that first overtone antinode shifts are within the millimeter range, accessible to current observational resolutions. This research offers new insights into coronal loop dynamics and the potential to infer solar photospheric properties through the analysis of fast kink modes. The findings have implications for our understanding of the solar corona and its underlying structures.

This article explores the possibility that dark matter halos can be described by the Fermi-Dirac distribution at finite temperature, a scenario that arises if dark matter is composed of massive neutrinos in statistical equilibrium or if it can be treated as a collisionless gas undergoing violent relaxation. To rigorously analyze the stability of such systems, we employ the fermionic King model, focusing on the non-degenerate limit that yields the classical King model. Originally developed to describe globular clusters, we propose extending this model to large dark matter halos where quantum effects are negligible. Our analysis reveals that equilibrium states exist only above specific critical energy and temperature thresholds in the microcanonical and canonical ensembles, respectively. Below these thresholds, the system undergoes either a gravothermal catastrophe or an isothermal collapse. We compute density, circular velocity, and velocity dispersion profiles, comparing the classical King model's predictions with observations of large dark matter halos. The model accurately describes these halos near the point of marginal microcanonical stability, where it generates a density profile akin to the modified Hubble profile, featuring a flat core and a large-distance decay similar to the observed Burkert profile. Our findings suggest that statistical mechanics provides a viable framework for understanding dark matter halos, with discrepancies attributable to incomplete relaxation, analogous to stellar systems. This work supports the notion that dark matter halos can be described by the Fermi-Dirac distribution at finite temperature, offering new insights into the nature and behavior of dark matter. By applying the principles of statistical mechanics to dark matter, we may uncover a more comprehensive understanding of the universe's large-scale structure and the role of dark matter within it.

This article explores the properties of @xmath0-optimal fields, a subclass of @xmath0-minimal fields that encompasses all known examples. By utilizing methods rooted in Denef's work, we establish a cell decomposition theorem, which in turn yields the existence of definable Skolem functions and strong @xmath0-minimality. We then focus on strongly @xmath0-minimal fields that satisfy the extreme value property, a characteristic present in fields elementarily equivalent to a @xmath0-adic one. For such fields, we demonstrate that definable subsets with fibers over the field that are inverse images of subsets of the value group are semi-algebraic. Combining these results, we derive a preparation theorem for definable functions, leading to the conclusion that infinite definable sets over these fields are in definable bijection if and only if they have the same dimension, shedding light on the structural properties of these fields.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of simultaneous radio and X-ray observations of the atoll-type X-ray binary 4U 1728-34, conducted in 2000 and 2001. Our findings reveal a significant correlation between radio emission and X-ray states, with the strongest and most variable radio emission occurring during transitions between hard and softer X-ray states. A positive correlation is observed between the radio flux density at 8.46 GHz and the 2-10 keV X-ray flux, as well as between radio flux density and X-ray timing features. These correlations provide evidence for a disc-jet coupling in atoll-type X-ray binaries, a phenomenon previously observed in black hole binaries. Furthermore, our results confirm that accreting neutron stars are less radio-loud than black holes, with a significant difference in radio emission factors. This research contributes to our understanding of the complex relationships between accretion, jet formation, and radiation mechanisms in neutron star X-ray binaries, and has implications for the study of compact objects and their environs. The observations and analysis presented here offer new insights into the physics of atoll-type X-ray binaries and their role in the broader context of astrophysical research.

This article presents a comprehensive study of double parton distributions (DPDFs), including both conventional and parton splitting contributions, for various two-parton combinations. Our calculations reveal that the conventional and splitting DPDFs exhibit similar shapes in the momentum fractions $x_0$ and $x_1$. We provide the first quantitative evaluation of the single-ladder-splitting contribution to double parton scattering (DPS) production of two S- or P-wave quarkonia, two Higgs bosons, and $W^+W^-$. The ratio of single-ladder-splitting to conventional contributions is investigated as a function of center-of-mass energy, mass of the produced system, and other kinematical variables. Using a simple model for the conventional two-parton distribution, we find that the single-ladder-splitting contribution is comparable to the conventional contribution. This implies that phenomenological analyses of DPS processes must be revised to include the single-ladder-splitting contributions. While the differential distributions in rapidity and transverse momenta are similar for conventional and single-ladder-splitting DPS processes, making experimental separation challenging, the existence of both components leads to an energy and process dependence of the empirical parameter $\sigma_{\text{eff}}$. Our results have significant implications for the understanding of DPS processes and highlight the need for a more comprehensive treatment of DPDFs in phenomenological analyses.

We present sensitive dual-frequency (1.7 and 5 GHz) European VLBI Network (EVN) observations of the central regions of nine Seyfert galaxies, which are among the faintest and least luminous members of a complete sample of nearby (≈ 20 Mpc) low-luminosity Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN). Our high-resolution observations reveal radio emission on milliarcsecond scales in the nuclei of four galaxies, while upper limits of ≈ 1 mJy are set for the remaining five sources. Notably, three sources (NGC 3227, NGC 3982, and NGC 4138) exhibit radio emission at both frequencies, resolved into two or more components. We characterize the structural and spectral properties of these features, finding high brightness temperatures (≈ 10^4-10^5 K) and flat/intermediate spectral indices (α ≈ -0.5 to 0.5) in the primary components, accompanied by secondary steep-spectrum extended components. These findings suggest non-thermal emission from jets or outflows as the most plausible explanation. Additionally, a faint feature detected in NGC 4477 at 5 GHz may originate from the hot corona, given the unrealistic magnetic field values required by synchrotron self-absorption. Our results provide new insights into the nature of these low-luminosity AGN, while the non-detections highlight the need for further observations on intermediate scales to elucidate their properties.
